units.la: IV[?]E merita in patriam ac meipsum æqualia (viri præstantissimi) siue animorum, studiorumq; inter vos coniunctionem,siue mutuam vobiscū cognationem confidero:hoc[?] operis maioris exemplum, æquo iure,vobis offerre non abs re mihi visum est:cu-ius etiam suscipiendi corã,ac literis,nec absimili quoq; exemplo,fuistis hortatores.Idq; vnius vestrum Tacitus Gallicus,& Gallici Annales perpetuo testabuntur,non ad triuialia puerorum exempla, aut ea quæ Rhetores discipulis in schola solent proponere, sed ad eorum vsum,qui iam in ipsis rebus gerendis occupati sunt,ad-commodati. Alter, amplissimę totius Europæ vrbis, & Augustissimi Senatus Parisiensium suffragio, è multis vnus electus est ad vrbis consuetudines repetita præelectione reformandas. quod opus paucis ab hinc annis ita perfectum, vt non minus, ab eo, inter suos, quàm inter Romanos Decemvir,meritus fit. His permotus exemplis, in publicum prodire ausus sum. Parine forte,aut euentu, dicere non ausim. Periculum tamen subire animus est , nec me (sat scio) poenituerit vnquam, amicis hominibus, dum meos in vniuersum Iuris corpus Commentarios absoluo , praecida-neum hoc opus,maioris operis, meíque in rempublicam, posterósque animi si-gnum[?] obtulisse. Datum ex Musæo x i. Kalend. Mart. Anno 1583.
units.tr: Considering the equal merits of our country and of myself, most distinguished men, and the bond of union between you in mind and study, or else our mutual kinship, I thought it not out of place to offer you, with equal right, this example of a greater work. You also urged me to take it up, both in person and by letter, and that example is no unlike this one. The Gallic Tacitus and the Gallic Annals of one of you will bear constant witness to this: they are adapted not to the trivial examples set for boys, or those which rhetoricians usually propose to pupils in school, but to the use of men already engaged in conducting affairs themselves. The other was chosen from many by the vote of the most magnificent city of all Europe and the most august Senate of the Parisians, to reform the customs of the city by a repeated election. That work was completed within a few years, so that he has earned no less credit among his own people than the Decemvir among the Romans. Moved by these examples, I have ventured to come forward in public. Whether this is by chance or by design I dare not say. Yet I am willing to run the risk, and I am (I know well) never going to regret, while I finish my commentaries on the whole body of the law, having offered to my friends this preliminary work of a greater undertaking, and a sign of my spirit toward the commonwealth and posterity. Given at the Musaeum, 19 February 1583.
Dionysius Gothofredus to the Reader.

units.la: CUM ad Institutiones notas haec componerem (amice Lector) propositum illud initio fuit, a reliquis iuris partibus eas non disiungi. Paucis-simis enim legibus ad oram Institutionum no-tatis, fontes earum indicabam, ut iis inventis numerosiores illico leges adparerent. Fecit tua postmodum utilitas, ut id propositum mutaretur in melius, breviorèque forma Institutiones tibi offerrentur. Quare, quod Institutio-nibus reliquis Iuris corporis partibus coniunctis fieri antea oportebat, hoc disiunctis facias a te postulo, facturo mei erga te animi, partiumque reliquarum (quas paucissimos intra menses exhibiturus sum) iudicium, ex titulis aliquot ff. quos Institutionibus hisce adiunxi. Titulis, inquam, De origine iu-ris, De verborum significatione, & De regulis iuris. Quibus si notas ad Historiam Iuris à Iustiniano compositi, & ad leges XII. Tabularum, ad Ulpianum, ad Caium, & titulum De regulis iuris in Sexto adiungas, meo voto, mihique feceris satis: gratitudinis istius vice, faustam ac perpetuò fœlicem vitam ti-bi precaturo.
units.tr: When I was putting together these notes on the Institutes (friendly reader), my original plan was not to separate them from the other parts of the law. For I noted only a very few laws in the margins of the Institutes, indicating their sources, so that once these had been found, many more laws would appear at once. Your usefulness afterwards brought it about that this plan was changed for the better, and the Institutes were offered to you in a shorter form. Therefore, I ask you to do with the Institutes separately what previously ought to have been done with them joined to the other parts of the body of law. In return you will show your goodwill towards me, and your judgment of the remaining parts (which I intend to publish within a very few months), by the titles of the Digest which I have added to these Institutes. I mean, I say, the titles On the Origin of Law, On the Meaning of Words, and On the Rules of Law. If you add notes to these, on the History of Law compiled by Justinian, on the Laws of the Twelve Tables, on Ulpian, on Gaius, and on the title On the Rules of Law in the Sixth Book, you will have satisfied my wish and my claim; in return for this kindness I shall pray for your life to be happy and always prosperous.

PREFACE ON THE CONFIRMATION OF THE INSTITUTES.

units.la: IN NOMINE DOMINI nostri Iesu Christi. ||
units.tr: IN THE NAME OF OUR LORD Jesus Christ.

units.la: IMPERATOR Caesar Flauius Iustinianus, Alamanicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, Pius, Felix, inclytus, victor, ac triumphator, semper Augustus, cupida legum iuuentuti. [S.D.]
units.tr: Caesar Flavius Justinian, Emperor, Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, Pius, Felix, Illustrious, Victor and Triumphator, ever Augustus, to the youth eager for the laws, sends greeting.

units.la: IMPERATORIAM maiestatem nō solum armis decorata, sed {b}etiā legibus oportet esse armatam, vt vtrumque tempus, & bellorum, & pacis, rectè posset gubernari: & princeps Romanus non solum in hostilibus praeliis victor existat, sed etiā per legitimos tramites, calumniantium iniquitates expellat: {d}& haec tam iuris religiosissimus, {c}quàm victis hostibus triumphator magnificus.
units.tr: The imperial majesty ought to be armed not only with weapons but also with laws, so that both kinds of time, that of war and that of peace, may be rightly governed. The Roman prince should not only be victor in hostile battles but should also, by lawful means, drive out the injustices of those who make false accusations. He should be as scrupulous in law as he is a magnificent triumphator over conquered enemies.

units.la: Quorum vtramque viam cum summis vigiliis, summáque prouidentia, annuente Deo, perfecimus. Et bellicos quidem sudores nostros Barbaricae gentes sub iuga nostra redactae cognoscunt, & tam Africa, quàm aliae innumerae prouinciae, post {f}tanta temporum spatia, nostris victoriis à coelesti numine praestitis, iterum ditioni Romanae, nostroque additae imperio, protegatur. Omnes vero populi legibus tam à nobis promulgatis, quàm compositis, reguntur. 2 ¶ Et cùm {g}constitutiones, antea confusas, in lucidulentam ereximus consonantiam: tunc nostram extendimus curam ad immensa {h}veteris prudentiae volumina: & opus desperatum, quasi per medium profundum euntes, coelesti fauore iam adimpleuimus.
units.tr: We have carried out both of these tasks with the greatest vigilance and the highest foresight, with God's assent. The barbarian nations brought under our yoke know the sweat of our wars, and Africa, as well as countless other provinces, after so long an interval of time, is protected by our victories, granted by the heavenly power, as they are once again brought under Roman rule and added to our empire. All peoples are governed by laws, both those promulgated by us and those compiled by us. 2 And when we had brought the constitutions, previously confused, into a clear harmony, we then turned our care to the immense volumes of ancient wisdom; and, going through this despaired-of work as if across a deep sea, we have now completed it by the favour of heaven.

units.la: 3 ¶ Cumque hoc, Deo propitio, peractum est: Triboniano viro magnifico, magistro, & exquaestore sacri palatij nostri, ||& excolule|| necnō Theophilo, & Dorotheo, viris illustribus, antecessoribus, (quorum omnium solertiam, & legum scientiam, & circa nostras iusiones fidem, iam ex multis rerum argumen-tis accepimus) conuocatis, mandauimus speciali-ter: ut ipsi nostra auctoritate, nostrisque suasionibus, Institutiones componerent. ut liceat vobis prima legum cunabula {*}nō ab antiquis fabulis discere, sed ab imperiali splendore appetere: & tam aures, quàm animi vestri, nihil inutile, nihilque perperam positum: sed quod in ipsis rerum obtinet argumentis, accipiant. & quod priore tepore {b}vix post quadriennium ‖prioribus‖ cōtingebat, ‖ut tunc cōstitutiones imperatorias legerēt: ‖hoc vos à primordio ingrediamini. di-[?]gni tanto honore, tantaque reperti felicitate, ut & initium vobis & finis legū eruditionis a vore principali procedat. 4 ¶Igitur post libros quinquaginta Digestorum seu Pandectarum, (in quibus omne ius antiquum collectum est. quod per eundem virum excelsum, Tribonianum: necnon cæteros viros illustres, & facundissimos confecimus) in quatuor libros eisdem Institutiones partiri iussimus: ut sint totius legitimæ scientiæ prima elementa.
units.tr: 3 When this had been accomplished, by the favour of God, we specially commissioned Tribonian, a magnificent man, master and ex-quaestor of our sacred palace, together with Theophilus and Dorotheus, illustrious men and teachers of law (whose skill, knowledge of the law, and loyalty to our commands we have already learned from many proofs), to compose the Institutes by our authority and at our suggestion. We wished that you might learn the first cradle of the laws not from old fables but seek it from imperial splendour; and that your ears and minds might receive nothing useless and nothing badly arranged, but what holds good in the very substance of the matter. And whereas in former times it scarcely happened until four years had passed before students read the imperial constitutions, you should enter upon them from the very beginning. You are deemed worthy of so great an honour and found so fortunate that both the beginning and the end of your legal education may proceed from the imperial source. 4 Therefore, after the fifty books of the Digest or Pandects (in which all the ancient law has been collected, which we have completed through the same distinguished man Tribonian, and the other illustrious and most eloquent men), we have ordered these Institutes to be divided into four books, so that they may be the first elements of the whole science of law.

units.la: 5 ¶In quibus breuiter expositum est: & quod antea obtinebat: & quod {c}postea desuetudine inumbratū, imperiali remedio illuminatum est.
units.tr: 5 In them, what formerly held force has been briefly set out, and what afterwards was obscured by disuse has been brought to light by imperial remedy.

units.la: 6 ¶Quas ex omnibus antiquorum Institutionibus, & præcipuè ex Commentariis Caij nostri, tam institutionum, quàm rerū quotidianarum, aliisque multis commentariis compositas, cùm tres viri prudentes prædicti nobis obtulerunt: & legimus, & recognouimus, & plenissimum nostrarum constitutionum robur eis accommodauimus.
units.tr: 6 These have been composed from all the ancient Institutes, and especially from the Commentaries of our Gaius, both the Institutes and the Everyday Matters, and from many other commentaries; when the three prudent men mentioned above offered them to us, we read them, revised them, and gave them the full force of our constitutions.

units.la: 7 ¶Summa itaque ope, & alacri studio has leges nostras accipite, & vosmetipsos sic eruditos ostendite: ut spes vos pulcherrima foueat, toto legitimo opere perfecto, posse etiam nostram rempubl. in partibus eius vobis credendis gubernari.
units.tr: 7 Accept therefore these our laws with the greatest diligence and eager zeal, and show yourselves so learned that the most glorious hope may cherish you: that, once the whole legal work is complete, you may also be entrusted with the governance of our commonwealth in its parts.
Given at Constantinople.

units.la: 3.[?] Kalend. Decemb. D. IVSTI-NIANO PP. A. III.
units.tr: Given on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the third year of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus.
Consulship of 533.

units.la: INSTITVTIO-NVM, SEV ELEMENTORVM D.Iustiniani sacratissimi Principis, LIBER PRIMVS. DE IVSTITIA ET IVRE, TITVLVS I.
units.tr: INSTITUTES, OR ELEMENTS, of the most sacred Prince D. Justinian, BOOK ONE. ON JUSTICE AND LAW, TITLE I.

units.la: IVSTITIA est {a}constàs & perpetua {b}volūtas ius suum cuiq. tribuendi.
units.tr: Justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to each person his own right.

units.la: 1 ¶Iurisprudētia est divinarum atque humanarū rerum notitia, iusti atq. iniusti scientia. {c}
units.tr: 1 ¶Jurisprudence is the knowledge of divine and human things, the science of the just and the unjust.

units.la: 2 ¶His igitur generali ter cognitis, & incipientibus nobis exponere iura populi Romani: ita videntur posse tradi commodissimè, si primo leui ac simplici via, post deinde diligentissima atque exactissima interpretatione, singula tradantur. alioqui si statim ab initio rudem adhuc & infirmum animum studiosi, multitudine ac varietate rerū onerauerimus: duorum alterum, aut desertorem studiorum efficiemus, aut cum magno labore sæpe etiam cum diffidētia, (quæ plerumque iuuenes auertit) seriùs ad id perducemus: ad quod, leuiore via ductus, sine magno labore, & sine vlla diffidentia, maturius perduci potuisset.
units.tr: 2 ¶Having therefore grasped these general matters, and beginning now to set out the laws of the Roman people, they seem most conveniently taught if first by a light and simple path, and afterwards by a most diligent and exact interpretation, each point is delivered. Otherwise, if from the very beginning we burden the still raw and weak minds of students with the multitude and variety of matters, one of two things will follow: we shall make them deserters of their studies, or we shall bring them to it late, with great labour and often with discouragement (which commonly drives young people away). Whereas, led by an easier path, without great labour and without any discouragement, they could have been brought to it sooner.

units.la: 3 ¶Iuris præcepta sunt hæc: honestè viuere, alterum non lædere, suum cuique tribuere. {d}{e}
units.tr: 3 ¶The precepts of law are these: to live honourably, not to harm another, to render to each his own.

units.la: 4 ¶Huius studij {f}duæ sunt {g}positiones, publicū. & priuatum. Publicum ius est, quod ad statum rei Romanæ spectat. Priuatum, quod ad singulorum vtilitatem. Dicēdum est igitur de iure priuato: quod {h}tripertitū est: collectum est enim ex naturalibus præceptis, aut gentium, aut ciuilibus.
units.tr: 4 ¶Of this study there are two divisions: public and private. Public law is that which concerns the state of the Roman commonwealth; private law, that which concerns the advantage of individuals. It must therefore be said concerning private law, which is threefold: for it is gathered from the precepts of nature, or of the nations, or of the civil law.

units.la: DE IVRE NATVRALI, gentium, & ciuili, TIT. II.
units.tr: ON NATURAL LAW, THE LAW OF NATIONS, AND CIVIL LAW, TIT. II.

units.la: IUS naturale est, quod natura omnia animalia docuit. nam ius istud non humani generis proprium est: sed omnium animaliū, quæ in cœlo, quæ in terra, quæ in mari nascuntur. Hinc descendit maris atque fœminæ coniunctio, quam nos matrimonium appellamus: hinc liberorum procreatio, hinc educatio. videmus etenim cætera quoque animalia iuris peritia cesseri.
units.tr: Natural law is that which nature has taught all animals. For this law is not peculiar to the human race, but belongs to all animals born in the heavens, on the earth, and in the sea. From it comes the union of male and female, which we call marriage; from it comes the procreation of children, and from it their upbringing. Indeed, we see that other animals too yield to a kind of legal skill.

units.la: ¶Ius autem ciuile a iure gentium distinguitur: quod omnes populi, qui legibus, & moribus reguntur, partim suo proprio, partim communi omnium hominum iure utuntur. nam quod quisque populus ipse sibi ius constituit, id ipsius proprium ciuitatis est: vocaturque ius ciuile, quasi ius proprium ipsius ciuitatis. quod vero naturalis ratio inter omnes homines constituit, id apud omnes peræque custoditur: vocaturque ius gentium, quasi quo iure omnes gentes utuntur. Et populus Romanus partim suo proprio, partim communi omnium hominum iure utitur. Quæ singula qualia sint, suis locis proponemus.
units.tr: Civil law is distinguished from the law of nations, because all peoples who are governed by laws and customs use partly their own particular law and partly the law common to all men. For whatever law each people has established for itself is proper to that state, and it is called civil law, as the particular law of that state. But what natural reason has established among all men is observed equally by all, and it is called the law of nations, as the law which all nations use. The Roman people also uses partly its own law and partly the law common to all men. We shall set out each of these in its proper place, showing what kind it is.

units.la: 2 ¶Sed ius quidem ciuile ex vnaquaq. ciuitate appellatur, veluti Atheniensium. nam si quis velit Solonis, vel Draconis leges appellare ius ciuile Atheniensium: non errauerit. sic enim & ius, quo Romanus populus utitur, ius ciuile Romanorum appellamus: vel ius Quiritium, quo Quirites utuntur. Romani enim a Romulo, Quirites a Quirino appellantur. Sed quoties non addimus nomen, cuius sit ciuitatis: nostrum ius significamus, sicuti cum Poetam dicimus, nec addimus nomen: subauditur apud Græcos egregius Homerus, apud nos Vergilius. Ius autem gentium omni humano generi commune est. nam usu exigente, & humanis necessitatibus, gentes humanæ iura quædam sibi constituerunt. Bella etenim orta sunt, & captiuitates sequutæ, & seruitutes, quæ sunt naturali iuri contrariæ. Iure enim naturali omnes homines ab initio liberi nascebantur. Et ex hoc iure gentium omnes pene contractus introducti sunt, vt emptio & venditio, locatio & conductio, societas, depositum, mutuum, & alij innumerabiles.
units.tr: 2 Civil law is named after each individual state, as the law of the Athenians, for example. If someone were to call the laws of Solon or Draco the civil law of the Athenians, he would not be wrong. So too we call the law which the Roman people uses the civil law of the Romans, or the law of the Quirites, which the Quirites use. For the Romans are named after Romulus, and the Quirites after Quirinus. But whenever we do not add the name of the state to which a law belongs, we mean our own law, just as when we say "the Poet" without adding a name: among the Greeks "the excellent Homer" is understood, among us Virgil. The law of nations, however, is common to the whole human race. For, as custom and human need demanded, the peoples of men established certain laws for themselves. Wars arose, and captivities followed, and slaveries, which are contrary to natural law; for by natural law all men were born free at the beginning. And from this law of nations almost all contracts were introduced, such as buying and selling, letting and hiring, partnership, deposit, loan, and countless others.

units.la: 3 ¶Constat autem ius nostrum, quo utimur, aut scripto, aut sine scripto: vt apud Græcos τῶν νόμων οἱ μὲν ἔγγραφοι, οἱ δὲ ἄγραφοι, alii [sunt] scripte, alii non scripte. Scriptū autem ius est lex, plebiscitū, Senatusconsultū, principum placita, magistratuum edicta, responsa prudentum.
units.tr: 3 Our law, which we use, consists either of written or unwritten law, as among the Greeks, of the laws, some are written [ἔγγραφοι], others unwritten [ἄγραφοι]. Written law comprises statute, plebiscite, senatorial decree, the decisions of the princes, the edicts of magistrates, and the responses of the learned.

units.la: 4 ¶Lex est, quod populus Romanus senatorio magistratu interrogate (veluti Consule) constituebat: Plebiscitum est, quod plebs plebeio magistratu interroga nte (veluti Tribuno) constituebat. Plebs autem à populo eo differt, quo species à genere: nam appellatione populi, vniuersi ciues significantur, connumeratis etiam patriciis & senatoribus. Plebis autem appellatione, sine patriciis & senatoribus ceteri ciues significatur. sed & plebiscita lege {*}Hortensia lata non minus valere, quàm leges coeperút.
units.tr: 4 A statute is what the Roman people established when questioned by a senatorial magistrate (such as a consul). A plebiscite is what the plebs established when questioned by a plebeian magistrate (such as a tribune). The plebs differs from the people as a species differs from its genus: for by the name "people" all citizens are meant, including the patricians and senators; by the name "plebs," the rest of the citizens are meant, without the patricians and senators. Moreover, plebiscites, once the Hortensian law had been passed, began to have no less force than statutes.

units.la: 5 ¶Senatusconsultum est, quod senatus iubet, atque constituit. Nam cùm auctus esset populus Romanus in eum modum, vt difficile esset in vnum eum conuocari legis sanciendæ causa: æquum visum est, senatum vice populi consuli.
units.tr: 5 A senatorial decree is what the Senate orders and establishes. For when the Roman people had grown so large that it was difficult to gather it together in one place to enact a law, it seemed fair that the Senate should act in place of the people.

units.la: 6 ¶Sed & quod principi placuit, legis habet vigorem, quum lege {b}Regia, quæ de eius imperio lata est, populus {c}ei, & {d}in eũ omne imperium suum & potestatem concedat. Quodcunque ergo Imperator per epistolam constituit: vel cognoscens decreuit, vel edicto præcepit, legem esse constat. hæc sunt, quæ Constitutiones appellantur. Plane ex his quædam sunt personales, quæ nec ad exemplum trahuntur, quoniā non hoc princeps vult. nam quod alicui ob meritum indulsit, vel si quam poenam irrogauit, vel si cui sine exemplo subuenit: personam nō {e}transgreditur. Aliæ autem quum generales sint, omnes proculdubio tenent.
units.tr: 6 Moreover, what pleased the prince also has the force of law, since by the Royal Law, which was passed concerning his authority, the people grants to him all its power and authority. Therefore, whatever the Emperor establishes by letter, or decides upon hearing a case, or commands by edict, is agreed to be law. These are what are called Constitutions. Plainly some of these are personal, and are not drawn into precedent, since the prince does not wish this; for what he has granted to someone on account of merit, or what penalty he has imposed, or what help he has given to someone without precedent, extends no further than that person. Others, however, since they are general, undoubtedly bind everyone.

units.la: 7 ¶Prætorū quoque edicta non modicam obtinent iuris auctoritatem. Hoc etiam ius honorarium solemus appellare, quòd qui honores gerunt, id est, magistratus auctoritatem huic iuri dederunt. Proponebant & AEdiles Curules edicta de quibusdã causis, quod & ipsum iuris honorarij portio est.
units.tr: 7 The edicts of the praetors also hold no small authority in law. We are accustomed to call this the honorary law as well, because those who hold offices, that is, the magistrates, gave authority to this law. The curule aediles also published edicts concerning certain matters, and this too is a part of the honorary law.

units.la: 8 ¶{f}Responsa prudentiũ sunt sententiæ & opiniones eorũ, quibus permissum erat de iure respondere. nam antiquitus constitutum erat, vt essent, qui iura publicè interpretarentur, quibus à Cæsare ius respondendi datum est, qui Iuriconsulti appellabantur, quorum omnium sententiæ & opiniones eam auctoritatem tenebant, vt iudici recedere à responso eorũ non liceret, vt est constitutum.
units.tr: 8 The responses of the learned are the judgments and opinions of those who were permitted to give legal answers. For in ancient times it was established that there should be men who would interpret the laws publicly; those to whom Caesar gave the right to respond were called jurists, and the judgments and opinions of all of them held such authority that it was not permitted for a judge to depart from their response, as has been established.

units.la: 9 ¶Sine scripto ius venit, quod vlus approbauit. nam diuturni mores consensu vtentium comprobati, legem {g}imitatur.
units.tr: 9 Unwritten law comes from custom, which usage has approved. For long-standing customs, approved by the consent of those who observe them, imitate a law.

units.la: 10 ¶Et nos ineleganter in duas species ius ciuile. distributum esse videtur. nam origo eius ab institutis duarum civitatum, Athenarum scilicet, & Lacc-dæmoniorum[?] fluxisse videtur. In his enim civitatibus ita agi solitum erat, ut Lacedæmonii quidem magis ea, quæ pro legibus observabant, memoriæ mandarent. Athenienses vero ea, quæ in legibus scripta comprehendissent, custodirent.
units.tr: 10 And we are thought to have divided civil law into two kinds, rather inelegantly. For its origin seems to have flowed from the institutions of two states, namely Athens and Lacedaemon. For in those states it was customary to act so that the Lacedaemonians committed to memory those things which they observed as laws, while the Athenians guarded those things which they had set down in written laws.

units.la: ii {*}Sed naturalia quidem iura, quæ apud omnes gentes perequè observantur: divina quædam providentia constituta, semper firma atque immutabilia permanent. ea verò, quæ ipsa sibi quæque civitas constituit, sæpe mutari solent vel tacito cõsensu populi, vel alia postea lege lata. iii Omne autem ius, quo utimur, vel ad personas pertinet, vel ad res, vel ad actiones. Et prius de personis videamus. nam parum est ius nosse, si personae, quarum causa constitutum est, ignorentur.
units.tr: ii But natural laws, which are observed equally among all nations, being established by a certain divine providence, remain always firm and unchanging. Those, however, which each state establishes for itself, are often wont to be changed, either by the tacit consent of the people or by another law passed afterwards. iii Now all the law which we use pertains either to persons, or to things, or to actions. And let us first consider persons, for it is of little use to know the law if the persons for whose sake it was established are unknown.
On the Law of Persons, Title III.

units.la: SUMMA itaque divisio de iure personarum hæc est, quod omnes homines, aut liberi sunt, aut servi.
units.tr: The chief division of the law of persons is therefore this: all men are either free or slaves.

units.la: 1 Et libertas quidem (ex qua etiá liberi vocátur) est naturalis facultas eius, quod cuique facere libet, nisi si quid {c}vi aut iure prohibetur. 2 Servitus autem est constitutio iuris gentium, qua quis dominio alieno contra naturam subiicitur.
units.tr: 1 Liberty (from which the free are also so called) is the natural power of doing whatever one likes, unless force or law forbids it. 2 Slavery, on the other hand, is an institution of the law of nations, by which someone is made subject to another's dominion, contrary to nature.

units.la: 3 Servi autem ex eo appellati sunt, quod Imperatores captivos vendere, ac per hoc servare, nec occidere solent. qui etiam macipia dicti sunt, ideo[?] ab hostibus manucapiuntur. 4 Servi autem aut nascuntur, aut fiunt. nascuntur ex ancillis nostris. fiunt autem iure gentium, id est, ex captivitate: aut iure {d}civili, cum liber homo maior viginti annis ad pretium participandu {†}se venundari passus est. 5 In servorum conditione nulla est differentia: in liberis autem multæ. aut enim sunt ingenui, aut libertini.
units.tr: 3 Slaves were so called because the commanders were accustomed to sell captives rather than kill them, and thus to preserve them. They were also called macipia, because they are taken by the hand (manucapiuntur) by their enemies. 4 Slaves are either born or made. They are born of our female slaves. They are made by the law of nations, that is, through captivity; or by civil law, when a free man over twenty years of age has allowed himself to be sold in order to share in the price. 5 Among slaves there is no difference of status; among free persons, however, there are many. For they are either freeborn (ingenui) or freedmen (libertini).
ON FREE-BORN PERSONS, TITLE IV.

units.la: INGENUUS est is, qui statim, ut natus est, liber est. sive ex duobus ingenuis matrimonio editus est, sive ex libertinis duobus, sive ex altero libertino, & altero ingenuo. Sed & si quis ex matre nascitur libera, patre vero servo, ingenuus nihilominus nascitur: quèadmodum[?] qui ex matre libera & incerto patre to patre natus est, quoniam vulgò conceptus est. Suf-ficit autem liberam fuisse matrem eo tempore, quo nascitur, licet ancilla conceperit. Et è contrario si li-bera {*}conceperit, deinde ancilla facta pariat: placuit eum, qui nascitur, liberum nasci: quia non debet cala-mitas matris ei nocere qui in ventre est. Ex his illud quaesitum est, si ancilla praegnans manumissa sit, dein-de ancilla postea facta pepererit: liberum, an seruum pariat? Et Martianus probat liberum nasci. sufficit e-nim ei, qui in vtero est, liberam matrem vel medio tempore habuisse, ǁvt liber nascatur.ǁ quod & verum est. ¹ ¶ Cùm autem ingenuus aliquis natus sit, nō of-ficit ei in seruitute fuisse, & postea manumissum es-se. saepissimè enim constitutum est, {b}natalibus non of-ficere manumisionem.
units.tr: A free-born person (ingenuus) is one who is free from the moment of birth. He is so whether he was born in lawful marriage of two free-born parents, or of two freed parents, or of one freed parent and one free-born parent. Likewise, if someone is born of a free mother and a slave father, he is nonetheless born free, just as one who is born of a free mother and an unknown father, because he was conceived outside marriage. It is enough that the mother was free at the time of birth, even if she conceived while a slave. Conversely, if a free mother conceives and afterwards, having become a slave, gives birth, it has been decided that the child is born free, because the misfortune of the mother ought not to harm the child who is in her womb. On this point the question has been raised: if a pregnant slave is manumitted and afterwards, having become a slave again, gives birth, is the child born free or a slave? Martianus holds that the child is born free, for it is enough for the one who is in the womb that the mother was free at some point in the meantime, so that he is born free; and this is also true. ¶ Although a person has been born free, it does not prejudice him that he was in servitude and was afterwards manumitted. For it has very often been determined that manumission does not harm free birth (natalibus).
DE LIBERTINIS, TIT. V.

units.la: LIBERTINI sunt, qui ex {e}iusta seruitute manumisi sunt. manumisio autem est de manu {d}datio. nam quandiu aliquis in seruitute est, manni & potestati suppo-situs est: & manumissus liberatur potesta-te. Quae res à iure gentium originem sumpsit: vtpote cùm iure naturali omnes liberi nascerentur, nec ef-set nota manumisionis, cum seruitus esset incognita. Sed postquàm iure gentium seruitus inuasit: sequu-tum est beneficium manumisionis, & cùm vno com-muni nomine omnes hominēs appellarentur, iure gentium tria ǁ hominum ǁ genera esse coeperunt: li-beri, & his contrarium serui, & tertium genus liber-tini, qui desicerant esse serui.
units.tr: Freedmen (libertini) are those who have been manumitted from lawful slavery. Manumission, however, is the giving of release from the hand. For as long as a person is in slavery, he is placed under the hand and power of another; and the one who is manumitted is freed from that power. This institution took its origin from the law of nations: since by the law of nature all men were born free, and manumission was not known, slavery being unknown as well. But after slavery crept in by the law of nations, the benefit of manumission followed; and although all men were called by one common name, three classes of men began to exist under the law of nations: free men, their opposite the slaves, and a third class, the freedmen, who had ceased to be slaves.

units.la: ¹ ¶Multis autem modis manumisio procedit, aut enim ex sacris constitutionibus in sacrosanctis {c}eccle-siis, aut vindicta, aut inter amicos, aut per epistolam, aut per testamentum, aut per aliā quamlibet {f}vlti-mam voluntatem. Sed & aliis {g}multis modis libertas seruo competere potest, qui tam ex veteribus, quàm ex nostris constitutionibus introducti sunt. ² ¶Serui ǁverò ǁ à dominis {h}semper manumitti solent: adeò, vt vel in {i}transitu manumittantur, veluti cùm praetor, aut praeses, aut proconsul in balneum, vel in theatrum eant. ³ ¶ Libertinorum autem status tripertitus an-tea fuerat. Nam qui manumittebantur, modo maio-rem & iustam libertatem consequebantur, & fiebant ciues Romani, modo minorem, & Latini ex lege Iu-nial. Th. aia Norbana fiebant: modò inferiorem, & fiebat ex lege AElia Sentia deditiij. Sed quoniam deditiorum quidè pessima cōditio iam ex multis temporibus in desuetudinem abierat, Latinorum vero nomē non frequentabatur: idóque nostra pietas omnia augere, & in meliorem statum reducere desiderans, duabus constitutionibus hoc emendauit, & in pristinū statum reduxit: quia & à primis urbis Romæ cunabulis una atque simplex libertas cōperebat: id est, eadem, quam habebat manumissor: nisi quod scilicet libertinus sit, qui manumittitur, licèt manumissor ingenuus sit. Et deditīos quidem per constitutionem no stram expulimus, quā promulgauimus inter nostras decisiones: per quas suggerente nobis Triboniano viro excelso quæstore {ꝯ}nostro, {ꝯ}antiqui iuris altercationes placauimus. Latinos autē Iunianos, & omnem quę circa eos fuerat obseruantiā, alia constitutione per eiusdē quæstoris suggestionē correximus, quæ inter imperiales radiat sanctiones. Et omnes libertos, nullo nec ætatis manumissi, nec domini manumittentis, nec in manumissionis modo discrimine habito(sicut iam antea obseruabatur) ciuitate Romana decorauimus: multis modis additis, per quos possit libertas seruis cum ciuitate Romana, quæ sola est in præsenti, præstari.
units.tr: Manumission takes place in many ways: either by the sacred constitutions in the holy churches, or by the rod (vindicta), or among friends, or by letter, or by will, or by any other final expression of intention. But freedom may also come to a slave by many other means, which have been introduced both by the older laws and by our own constitutions. Slaves are indeed usually set free by their masters even in passing: so that they may be manumitted in transit, as when the praetor, the governor, or the proconsul goes to the baths or to the theatre. The status of freedmen was formerly threefold. For those who were manumitted sometimes obtained full and lawful liberty and became Roman citizens; sometimes a lesser liberty, and became Latins under the Junian and Norban laws; sometimes a lower condition, and became "dediticii" under the Aelian Sentian law. But since the worst condition of the dediticii had for many ages fallen into disuse, and the name of Latins was no longer commonly used, our piety, wishing to enlarge all things and restore them to a better state, corrected this by two constitutions and returned it to its former state: for from the earliest cradle of the city of Rome there was one and the same simple liberty, namely the very same that the manumitter had, except that the one manumitted is a freedman, even though the manumitter be freeborn. We have expelled the dediticii by our constitution, which we published among our decisions, through which, at the suggestion of Tribonian, our most excellent quaestor, we settled the disputes of the ancient law. The Latins called Junian, and all the observance that had pertained to them, we corrected by another constitution, at the suggestion of the same quaestor, which shines among the imperial sanctions. And all freedmen, whether of any age, or of any manumitter, or without distinction in the mode of manumission (as was formerly observed), we have adorned with Roman citizenship, with many additional modes by which liberty may be conferred on slaves together with Roman citizenship, which at present is the only one.

units.la: QUIBUS EX CAUSIS MANUMITTERE NON LICET. TIT. VI.
units.tr: WHO MAY NOT BE MANUMITTED, FOR WHAT CAUSES. TIT. VI.

units.la: NON tamen cuicunque volenti manumittere licet. nam is, qui in fraudem creditorum manumittit, nihil agit: quia lex AElia Sentia impedit libertatē. 1 ¶ Licet autem domino, qui soluendo non est, in testamento seruū suum cum libertate heredem instituere, vt liber fiat, hæresq. ei solus & necessarius: si modo ei nemo alius ex eo testamento heres extiterit: aut quia nemo heres scriptus sit, aut quia is, qui scriptus est, qualibet ex causa heres ei non extiterit. Idque eadem lege AElia Sentia prouisum est. & recte. Valde enim prospiciendum erat, vt egentes homines, quibus alius heres extiturus non esset, vel seruum suum necessarium heredem haberent, qui satisfacturus esset creditoribus: aut hoc eo non faciēt, creditores res hereditarias seruī nomine vendāt, ne iniuria defuncti afficiatur. 2 ¶ Idémque iuris est, & si siue libertate seruus heres institutus est. Quod nostra constitutio non solùm in domino, qui soluendo non est, sed generaliter constituit, noua humanitatis ratione vt ex ipsa scriptura institutionis etiam libertas ei competere videatur: quum non fit verisimile, eum, quem heredem sibi elegit, fi praetermiserit libertatis datione, seruum remanere voluisse & neminem sibi heredem fore. 3 In fraudem autem creditorum manumittere videtur, qui vel iam tempore quo manumittit, soluendo non est: vel qui datis libertatibus, desiturus est soluendo esse. Praesumuisse tamen videtur (nisi animum quoque fraudandi manumissor habuerit) non impediri libertatem, quamuis bona eius creditoribus non sufficiant. Saepe enim de facultatibus suis amplius, quam in his est, sperant homines. Itaque tunc intelligimus impediri libertatem, cum utroque modo fraudantur creditores, id est, & consilio manumittentis, & ipsa re, eo ipsius bona nō sunt suffectura creditoribus. 4 Eadem lege AElia Sentia domino minori viginti annis nō aliter manumittere permittitur, quàm si vindicta apud consilium, iusta causa manumissionis adprobata, fuerint manumissi. 5 Iuste autem manumissionis causae hae sunt: veluti si quis patrem aut matrem, filium filiamve, aut fratres sororesve naturales, aut paedagogum, aut nutricem, aut educatorem, aut alumnum alumnamve, aut collactaneum manumittat: aut seruum procuratoris habendi gratia: aut ancillam matrimonij habendi causa: dum tamen intra sex menses in uxorem ducatur, nisi iusta causa impediat: & seruus, qui manumittitur procuratoris habendi gratia, nō minor decem & septem annis manumittatur. 6 Sentiel[?] aut causa adprobata, siue vera sit, siue falsa, non retractetur. 7 Cum ergo certus modus manumittendi minoribus viginti annis dominis per legem AElian Sentiam constitutus esset: eueniebat, vt qui quatuordecim annos expleuerat, licet testamentum facere, & in eo sibi heredem instituere, legatarium què relinquere possetiamen si adhuc minor esset viginti annis, libertatem seruo dare non posset. Quod non erat ferendum. nam cui totorum suorum bonorum in testamento dispositio data erat: quare non similiter et, quemadmodum alias res, ita de seruis suis in vltima voluntate disponere, quaedmodum volucerit, permittimus, vt & libertatem eis post sit praestare? Sed quum libertas inaestimabilis res sit, & propter hoc ante xx. aetatis annum antiquitas libertatem seruo dare prohibebat: ideo nos mediam quodammodo viam eligentes, non aliter minori vi-ginti annis libertatem in testamento dare seruo suo concedimus{†},nisi decimum septimum annum implevit, & decimum octauum atri[?] gerit. Quum enim an-tiquitas huiusmodi ætati, & pro aliis postulare con-cesserit: cur non etiam sui iudicij stabilitas ita eos ad iuuare credatur, vt ad libertatem dandam seruis suis possint peruenire?
units.tr: Yet it is not lawful for everyone who wishes to manumit. For he who manumits in fraud of creditors accomplishes nothing, because the Aelian Sentian law prevents the liberty. It is lawful, however, for a master who is not solvent to institute his slave in his will as heir with liberty, so that he may become free, provided that he is the sole and necessary heir: if indeed no other heir arises from that will, either because no one has been named heir, or because the one who has been named does not become heir for whatever reason. This too was provided by the same Aelian Sentian law, and rightly so. For it was very necessary to provide that needy men, for whom no other heir would arise, should have their own slave as a necessary heir, who would satisfy the creditors; otherwise the creditors would sell the hereditary goods in the slave's name, and the injury would fall upon the deceased. The same rule of law holds also if the slave is instituted heir without liberty. Our constitution has established this not only for a master who is not solvent but generally, by a new principle of humanity, so that from the very writing of the institution liberty seems to belong to him: since it is not likely that a man who chose someone as his heir, if he has passed him over without granting liberty, wished him to remain a slave and to have no heir. A man seems to manumit in fraud of creditors if he is already insolvent at the time he manumits, or if by granting liberties he is about to become insolvent. Yet it is presumed (unless the manumitter also had the intent of defrauding) that liberty is not impeded, although his goods are not sufficient for the creditors; for men often hope for more from their resources than they actually have. Thus we understand liberty to be impeded only when the creditors are defrauded in both ways, that is, both by the design of the manumitter and in fact, since his goods will not suffice for the creditors. By the same Aelian Sentian law, a master under twenty years of age is not permitted to manumit except by the rod, before a council, with a just cause of manumission approved, and the freed persons being thus manumitted. The just causes of manumission are these: for example, if someone manumits his father or mother, son or daughter, or natural brothers or sisters, or a pedagogue, or a nurse, or a tutor, or a foster child, or a milk-brother; or a slave for the purpose of having a procurator; or a female slave for the purpose of having a marriage, provided that she is taken as wife within six months, unless a just cause prevents it; and a slave who is manumitted for the purpose of having a procurator should not be manumitted under seventeen years of age. Once a cause has been approved, whether it is true or false, it is not to be revoked. Since, therefore, a fixed mode of manumitting had been established for masters under twenty years of age by the Aelian Sentian law, it happened that one who had completed fourteen years could make a will, institute an heir for himself and leave a legatee, yet if he was still under twenty years of age he could not give liberty to his slave. This could not be tolerated. For to one to whom the disposition of all his goods in his will had been granted, why should we not likewise permit him to dispose of his slaves in his last will as he pleases, as with other things, so that he may also grant them liberty afterwards? But since liberty is a thing beyond price, and for this reason antiquity forbade granting liberty to a slave before the twentieth year of age, we, choosing in some sort a middle way, therefore grant that a minor under twenty may give liberty to his slave in a will only if he has completed his seventeenth year and is in his eighteenth. For since antiquity has allowed persons of this age both to make demands for others, why should it not be believed that the stability of their judgment is likewise to be relied upon, so that they may be able to attain the giving of liberty to their slaves?
ON REPEALING THE LEX FUSIA CANINIA,
TITLE VII.

units.la: E[?] E Fufia Caninia certus {b}modus constitutus erat in seruis testamento manumittendis: quam, quasi libertates impe-dientem, & quodammodo inuidam, tollendam esse cẽsuimus: quum satis fuerat inhumanum, vinos quidem licentiam habere totam suam familiam libertate donare, nisi alia causa impe-diat libertatem: morientibus autem huiusmodi licen-tiam adimere.
units.tr: A fixed limit had been established by the Lex Fufia Caninia for manumitting slaves by will. We have decided that this law, as though it hindered liberty and was in some way ill-disposed toward it, should be abolished. For it was quite inhuman that living masters should have the full liberty to free their whole household, unless some other cause prevented the freedom, while the dying were deprived of this same power.

units.la: DE HIS, QVI SVI, VEL alieni iuris sunt,
units.tr: CONCERNING THOSE WHO ARE UNDER THEIR OWN OR ANOTHER'S POWER
TITLE VIII.

units.la: SEQVITVR de iure personarum alia diuisio. Nam quædam personæ sui iuris sunt, quædam alieno iuri {c}subiectæ sunt. Rursus earum, quæ alieno iuri subiectæ sunt, aliæ sunt in potestate parentum, aliæ in potestate dominorum. Videamus itaque de his, quæ alieno iuri subiectæ sunt. nam si cognouerimus, quæ istæ personæ sunt, simul intelligemus quæ sui iu-ris sunt. ac prius inspiciamus de his, quæ in {d}potesta-te dominorum sunt.
units.tr: Next comes another division of persons according to their legal status. Some persons are sui iuris, and some are subject to another's right. Again, of those subject to another's right, some are in the power of parents and others in the power of masters. Let us therefore look at those who are subject to another's right, for if we understand who these persons are, we will at the same time understand who is sui iuris. First, let us examine those who are in the power of masters.

units.la: 1 ¶In potestate itaque dominorum sunt serui. quæ quidem potestas, iuris gentium est. nam apud {e}omnes peræque gentes animaduertere possumus, dominis in seruos {f}vitæ, necisque potestatem fuisse: & quodcumque per seruum adquiritur, id {g}domino adquiri.
units.tr: 1 ¶Those in the power of masters, then, are slaves. This power belongs to the law of nations. For among all nations alike we can observe that masters had the power of life and death over slaves, and whatever is acquired through a slave is acquired for the master.

units.la: 2 ¶Sed {h}hoc tempore nullis hominibus, qui sub imperio nostro sunt, licet sine {i}causa legibus cognita, in seruos suos ‖supra modū‖ sæuire. Nam ex con-stitutione diui Antonini, qui sine causa seruum suum occiderit, non minus puniri iubetur, quam si alienū seruum occiderit. Sed & maior asperitas dominorū eiusdē principis constitutione coercetur: nam Antoninus consultus à quibusdam præsidibus prouinciarum de his seruis, qui ad ædem sacram, vel ad statuam principum confugiunt, præcepit, vt si intolerabilis videatur sæuitia dominorum, cogantur seruos suos bonis conditionibus vendere, vt pretium domi suæ daretur. & rectè, expedit enim reipublicæ, ne sua re quis male vtatur. Cuius rescripti ad Aelium Marcianum emissa verba sunt hæc: Dominorum quidem potestate in seruos suos illibatam esse oportet, nec cuiquam hominum ius suum detrahi. Sed dominorū c interest, nc auxilium cōtra sæuitiam, vel famem, vel intolerabilem iniuriam denegetur iis, qui iuste deprecātur. Ideoque d cognoscē de querelis eorum, qui ex familia Iulij Sabini ad statuā confugerunt, & si vel durius habitos, quàm æquum est, vel infami e iniuria adfectos esse cognoueris: venire iube, ita vt in potestatem domini non reuertatur. Quod si meæ constitutioni fraudem fecerit, sciat me noc admissum seuerius executurum.
units.tr: 2 ¶But at this time, no one among the men who are under our rule may, without a cause recognized by the laws, rage against his slaves beyond measure. For by the constitution of the divine Antoninus, one who kills his slave without cause is ordered to be punished no less than if he had killed another man's slave. But the greater harshness of masters is also restrained by a constitution of the same emperor. For Antoninus, consulted by certain governors of the provinces about those slaves who take refuge at a sacred temple or at the statue of the emperors, ordered that if the cruelty of the masters seems intolerable, they should be compelled to sell their slaves on fair terms, so that the price be paid to them at home. And rightly so, for it is in the interest of the commonwealth that no one misuse his own property. The words of the rescript sent to Aelius Marcianus are these: "The power of masters over their slaves ought indeed to remain unimpaired, and no one's right is to be taken from him. But it is in the interest of masters that aid not be denied to those who justly appeal against cruelty, or hunger, or intolerable injury. Therefore take cognizance of the complaints of those of the household of Julius Sabinus who have fled to the statue, and if you find that they have been treated more harshly than is fair, or subjected to shameful injury, order them to be sold, so that they do not return to the power of the master. But if he commits fraud against my constitution, let him know that I will proceed against the offense more severely."
CONCERNING PATERNAL POWER. TITLE IX.

units.la: IN potestate nostra sunt liberi f nostri, quos ex g iustis nuptiis procreauimus.
units.tr: THE children whom we have begotten in lawful marriage (f) are in our power (g).

units.la: 1 ¶Nuptiæ autem, siue matrimonium, est viri & mulieris h coniunctio, indiuiduam vitæ consuetudinem continens.
units.tr: 1 ¶ Marriage, or matrimony, is the union of a man and a woman, involving a lifelong fellowship of life.

units.la: 2 ¶Ius autem potestatis, quod in liberos habemus, proprium est ciuium Romanorum. nulli enim alij sunt homines, qui talem in liberos habeant potestatem, qualem nos habemus.
units.tr: 2 ¶ The power that we hold over our children is peculiar to Roman citizens. For no other men have such power over their children as we have.

units.la: 3 ¶Qui igitur ex te & vxore tua nascitur, in tua potestate est. Item qui ex filio tuo & vxore eius nascitur, id est, nepos tuus & neptis, æquè in tua sunt potestate, & pronepos, & proneptis, & deinceps exteri. Qui autem ex filia tua nascuntur, in potestate tua non sunt, sed in patris eorum, [?]inde à Romuli temporib. Halic. 2. quo ἀπολιτ[?]εἰς & peregrini priuantur. §. cum autem. Imperio Iudxi. Genes.38.24. & 42.37. Iob.1, Numer.31.12.15. & omnes ex iure diuino. l.10.§.1. Cod. de adopt.
units.tr: 3 ¶ Whoever is born of you and your wife is in your power. Likewise, whoever is born of your son and his wife, that is, your grandson and granddaughter, are equally in your power, and your great-grandson and great-granddaughter, and the descendants after them. But those who are born of your daughter are not in your power but in the power of their father. This has been the case since the time of Romulus (Halic. 2.), when the [ἀπολιτ[?]εἰς] and foreigners are deprived of it (§. cum autem). Imperium of the Jews (Gen. 38.24; 42.37; Job 1; Num. 31.12, 15), and all of this by divine right (l. 10 §. 1, Cod. de adopt.).

units.la: {f} quibus βα[?] σιλιχῶς καὶ ἀπολιτικῶς. non [?] impe-ramus.
units.tr: (f) over whom [βασιλικῶς καὶ ἀπολιτικῶς], that is, royally and civically, we do not rule.

units.la: {g} secus in iniustis. §.pe-nul. ƒ.t.prox. h v.l.1.ff.de uit.
units.tr: (g) Otherwise in unlawful marriages (§. penult.; ƒ. t. prox.; h v. l. 1 ff. de uit.).
On Marriage, Title X.

units.la: USTAS autem nuptias inter se ciues Romani contrahunt, qui secundum præcepta legum coeunt: masculi quidem puberes, fœminæ autem {b}viripotentes, siue patresfamiliarum sint, siue filiifamilia-rum: dum tamen si filiifamiliarum sint, {c}consensum {d}habeat parentum, quorum in potestate sunt. Nam hoc fieri debere, & {e}ciuilis & {f}naturalis ratio suadet: in tantum, vt iussus parentis præcedere debeat. Vnde quæsitum est, an furiosi filia nubere, aut furiosi filius uxorē ducere possit. cumque super silio[?] variabatur, nostra processit {g}decisio, qua permissū est ad exem-plum filiæ furiosi, filiū quoque sfuriosi[?] ꝑ[?] posse & sine patris interuentu matrimonium sibi copulare, secundum datū ex nostra constitutione modum.
units.tr: Lawful marriages are contracted between Roman citizens who come together according to the precepts of the laws: males who have reached puberty, and females who are capable of marriage, whether they are heads of families or still under power, provided that if they are under power they have the consent of the parents in whose power they are. For both civil and natural reason suggest that this ought to happen, to such an extent that the parent's command must come first. Hence it was asked whether the daughter of a madman could marry, or the son of a madman take a wife. While opinion varied on the son's case, our decision was issued, by which it was permitted, after the example of the madman's daughter, for the madman's son also to contract marriage without the father's intervention, according to the procedure given by our constitution.

units.la: 1 ¶ Ergo non omnes nobis uxores ducere licet. nam à quarumdam nuptiis abstinendum est. * inter eas enim personas, quæ parentum liberorumve locum inter se obtinent, contrahi nuptiæ non possunt: veluti inter patrem & filiam, vel auum & neptem, vel matrem & filium, vel auiam & nepotē, & usque in {h}infinitum. Et si tales personas inter se coierint: nefarias atq; incestas nuptias contraxisse dicuntur. Et hæc adeo vera sunt, vt quàmis per {i}adoptionem parentum liberorum vice loco sibi esse coeperint, nō possint inter se matrimonio iungi: in tātum, vt etiam dissoluta adoptio-ne, idem iuris maneat. Itaque eam, quæ tibi per ado-ptione filia vel neptis esse coeperit, nō {k}poteris uxorem ducere, quàuis eam {l}emancipaueris.
units.tr: 1 ¶ So we may not all take wives. For we must abstain from the marriages of certain persons. Marriage cannot be contracted between those who stand in the place of parent and child to one another: for example, between father and daughter, grandfather and granddaughter, mother and son, grandmother and grandson, and so on without limit. If such persons have come together, they are said to have entered into an impious and incestuous marriage. And this is so true that even when persons have begun to stand in the place of parent and child through adoption, they cannot be joined in marriage; and this rule so holds that even when the adoption has been dissolved, the same law remains. Therefore you cannot take as your wife her who has begun to be your daughter or granddaughter by adoption, even though you have emancipated her.

units.la: 2 ¶ Inter eas quoque personas, quæ ex trā-suerso gradu cognatio-nis iunguntur, est quædam similis obseruatio, sed nō[?] tanta. Sanè enim inter {m}fratrem sororemq; nuptiæ prohibitæ sunt, siue ab eodem patre eademq; matre nati fuerint, siue ex altero eorum. Sed si qua *per adoptionem soror tibi esse coeperit: quandiu quidem costat adoptio, sanè inter te & eam nuptiæ consistere non possunt. cum vero per emancipationem adoptio sit dissoluta, poteris eam uxorem ducere. Sed & si tu emancipatus fueris, nihil est impedimento nuptiis. Et ideo constat, si quis generum adoptare velit, debere eum antea filiam suam emancipare: & si quis velit nurum adoptare, debere eum antea filium suum emancipare.
units.tr: 2 ¶ Among persons joined by collateral degree of kinship there is a similar rule, though not as strict. Indeed, marriage between brother and sister is forbidden, whether they were born of the same father and mother or of only one of them. But if a woman has begun to be your sister through adoption, then, as long as the adoption stands, marriage cannot exist between you and her. When the adoption has been dissolved by emancipation, you may take her as your wife. And if you yourself have been emancipated, this is no impediment to marriage. Hence it is agreed that if anyone wishes to adopt a son-in-law, he must first emancipate his own daughter; and if anyone wishes to adopt a daughter-in-law, he must first emancipate his own son.

units.la: 3 ¶ Fratris vero, vel {o}sororis filiā, uxo-rem ducere non licet. Sed nec neptem fratris vel so-roris [?]roris quis ducere potest, quamuis quarto gradu sint. cuius enim filiam vxorem ducere non licet, neque eius neptem permittitur. Eius vero mulieris, quam pater tuus adoptauit, filiam non videris impediri vxorem ducere: quia neque naturali, neque ciuili iure tibi coniungitur. 4 ¶ Duorum autē fratrum vel sororum liberi, vel fratris & sororis, coiungi pos-sunt. 5 ¶Item amitam, si licet adoptiuā, ducere vxorem non licet, item nec materteram: quia parentum loco habentur. Qua ratione verum est, magnam quoque amitam, & materteram magnam prohiberi vxore ducere. 6 ¶ Adfinitatis quoque veneratione, à quarundam nuptiis abstinere necesse est, vt ecce priuignam aut nurum vxorem ducere non licet: quia vtrāque filiæ loco sunt. Quod ita scilicet accipi debet, si fuit nurus aut priuigna tua. Nam si adhuc nurus tua est, id est, si adhuc nupta est filio tuo, alia ratione vxorem eam ducere non poteris: quia eadem duobus nupta esse non potest. Item si adhuc priuigna tua est, id est, si mater eius tibi nupta est, ideo eam vxorem ducere non poteris, quia duas vxores eodem tempore habere non licet.
units.tr: 3 ¶ But it is not lawful to take a wife who is the daughter of a brother or sister. Nor can anyone marry the granddaughter of a brother or sister, although they are of the fourth degree. For the granddaughter of a woman whose daughter you may not marry is not permitted to you either. Indeed, you do not appear to be prevented from marrying the daughter of a woman whom your father adopted, since she is not joined to you by either natural or civil law. 4 ¶ The children of two brothers or two sisters, or of a brother and a sister, may be joined in marriage. 5 ¶ Likewise it is not lawful to take as wife your aunt, even an adoptive one, nor your mother's sister, because they are held in the place of parents. For the same reason it is true that a great-aunt and a great-aunt on the mother's side are also forbidden as wives. 6 ¶ Out of reverence for affinity too, we must abstain from the marriages of certain persons: thus you may not take your stepdaughter or your daughter-in-law as wife, because both stand in the place of a daughter. This must of course be understood to apply if she was your daughter-in-law or stepdaughter. For if she is still your daughter-in-law, that is, if she is still married to your son, you cannot take her as wife on another ground, since the same woman cannot be married to two men. Likewise, if she is still your stepdaughter, that is, if her mother is still married to you, you cannot take her as wife for this reason, since a man may not have two wives at the same time.

units.la: 7 ¶ Socrum quoque & nouercam s prohibitū est vxorē ducere: quia matris ᵇ loco sunt. Quod & ipsum dissoluta demum adfinitate procedit. alioquin si adhuc nonerca est, id est, si adhuc patri tuo nupta est: communi iure impeditur tibi nubere, quia eadem duobus nupta esse non potest. Item si adhuc socrus est, id est, si adhuc filia eius tibi nupta est: ideo impediuntur tibi nuptiæ quia duas vxores habere non potes.
units.tr: 7 ¶ It is also forbidden to take as wife your mother-in-law or stepmother, because they stand in the place of mother. This too holds only once the affinity has been dissolved. Otherwise, if she is still your stepmother, that is, if she is still married to your father, you are barred from marrying her by the common law, since the same woman cannot be married to two men. Likewise, if she is still your mother-in-law, that is, if her daughter is still married to you, marriage is barred for you because you cannot have two wives.

units.la: 8 ¶Marim tamē filius ex alia vxore, & vxoris filia ex alio marito, vel contrà, matrimonium rite contrahunt: licet habeant fratrē sororemve ex matrimonio postea contracto natos. 9 ¶Si vxor tua post diuortium ex alio filiam procreauerit: hæc non est quidem priuigna tua: sed Iulianus ab humusmodi nuptiis abstinere debere ait. nam constat nec sponsam filij nurum esse, nec patris sponsam nouercam esse: re-ctius tamen & iure fauturos eos, qui ab huiusmodi nuptiis abstinuerint. 10 ¶Illud certū est, si forte pater & filia, aut frater & soror manumisi fuerint. 11 ¶ Sunt & alix personæ quæ propter diuersas rationes nuptias contrahere prohibentur, quas in libris {a}Digestorum,seu Pandestarum,ex vetere iure collectarū,enumerari permisimus. 12 ¶Si {b}aduersus ea,qnæ diximus,aliqui coicrint[?]:nec vir, nec vxor, nec nuptiæ, nec matrimonium,nec dos intelligitur.
units.tr: 8 ¶ Yet a son by another wife, and a wife's daughter by another husband, or the reverse, contract marriage validly, even though they have a brother or sister born of a marriage contracted afterwards. 9 ¶ If your wife, after divorce, has borne a daughter to another man, she is not indeed your stepdaughter; but Julian says that one ought to abstain from marriages of this kind. For it is agreed that a son's betrothed is not a daughter-in-law, nor a father's betrothed a stepmother; yet those who have abstained from such marriages will be more rightly and more lawfully favoured. 10 ¶ This is certain: if a father and daughter, or a brother and sister, have been manumitted... 11 ¶ There are also other persons whom various reasons forbid to contract marriage; these we have permitted to be listed in the books of the Digest, or Pandects, collected from ancient law. 12 ¶ If anyone has come together in defiance of what we have said, neither husband, nor wife, nor marriage, nor matrimony, nor dowry is recognised.

units.la: Itaque ij,qui ex eo coitu nascuntur,in potestate patris non sunt:sed tales sunt(quantum ad patriam potestatem pertinet)quales sunt ij, quos mater vulgò concepit. Nam nec hi patrem habere intelligūtur, cùm & his pater incertus fit.vnde solent spurij appellari {c}ἀ[?]πὸ τὴν σπορὰν ἰ.ἀ[?] ... quasi fine patre filij. Sequitur ergo,vt dissoluto tali coitu nec dotis, nec donationis exactioni locus fit. Qui autem prohibitas nuptias contrahunt, & alias pœnas patiuntur,quæ sacris constitutionibus continen tur.
units.tr: Therefore those who are born of such a union are not in the power of the father; rather, so far as paternal power is concerned, they are in the position of those whom a mother has conceived promiscuously. For they are not understood to have a father either, since the father too is uncertain. Hence they are commonly called spurii, [ἀπὸ τὴν σπορὰν] from the sowing, as if they were sons without a father. It follows that when such a union is dissolved, there is no room for a claim to the dowry or to a gift. Those who contract forbidden marriages also suffer other penalties, which are contained in the sacred constitutions.

units.la: 13 ¶Aliquādo autē euenit,vt liberi, q statim, vt nati sunt,in potestate parentum non sunt, postea redigātur in potestatem patris:qualis est is,qui dum naturalis fuerat,postea {d}curiæ datus,potestati patris subiicitur:necnon is qui à muliere libera procreatus, cuius matrimonium minimè legibus interdictum fuerat, sed ad quam pater consuetudinem habucrat,postea ex nostra constitutione dotalibus {e}in-strumentis compositis, in potestate patris efficitur. Quod & aliis liberis qui ex eodē matrimonio postea fuerint ,pcreati, similiter nostra constitutio præbuit.
units.tr: 13 ¶ It sometimes happens that children who, as soon as they are born, are not in the power of their parents, are afterwards brought under the power of the father: such is one who, while he was a natural child, was afterwards given to the curia, and who becomes subject to his father's power; and likewise one born of a free woman whose marriage was not forbidden by law, but with whom the father had been living in concubinage, and who, afterwards, by our constitution, with dotal instruments drawn up, comes under the father's power. Our constitution has likewise provided the same for other children born afterwards of the same marriage.
ON ADOPTIONS, TIT. XI.

units.la: NON[?] solùm autē naturales liberi, secundum ea,quæ diximus, in potestate nostra sunt,veruetiam ij,quos adoptamus. 1 ¶Adoptio autem duobus {g}modis fit,aut principali rescripto, aut imperio magistratus. Imperatoris auctoritate adoptare quis potest eos easve,qui quæve[?] sui iuris sunt, quæ spe-cies adoptionis dicitur {h}adrogatio. Imperio magistra-tus adoptamus eos easve,qui quæve in potestate parentum sunt:siue primum gradum liberorum obtinent:qualis est filius,filia:siue inferiorem,qualis est nepos,neptis,pronepos,proneptis. 2 ¶Sed hodie ex nostra {i}constitutione,cum filiusfamiliâs à patre naturali extraneæ personæ in adoptionem datur:iura patris naturalis minimè dissoluuntur, nec quicquam ad patrem adoptiuum transit: nec in potestate eius est,licet ab interestato iura successionis ei à nobis tributa sint. Si vero pater naturalis non extraneo, sed suo filij sui materno,vel [?]si ipse pater naturalis fuerit emancipatus, etiam auo vel proauo simili modo paterno vel materno filium suum dederit in adoptionem: in hoc casu, quia concurrunt in unam persona & naturalia, & adoptionis iura: manet stabile ius patris adoptiui, & naturali vinculo copulatum, & legitimo adoptionis modo constitutu: ut & in familia, & in potestate huiusmodi patris adoptiui sit.
units.tr: Not only natural children, as we have said, are in our power, but also those whom we adopt. 1 ¶Adoption takes place in one of two ways: either by an imperial rescript or by the authority of a magistrate. By the authority of the Emperor one may adopt those persons, male or female, who are their own masters (sui iuris); this kind of adoption is called adrogation. By the authority of a magistrate we adopt those persons, male or female, who are in the power of their parents, whether they hold the first degree of children, such as a son or daughter, or a lower one, such as a grandson, granddaughter, great-grandson, or great-granddaughter. 2 ¶But today, by our constitution, when a son under his father's authority is given in adoption to a stranger, the rights of the natural father are by no means dissolved, nor does anything pass to the adoptive father; nor is the son in his power, although rights of succession by intestacy are granted to him by us. But if the natural father gives his son in adoption not to a stranger but to his own son's son (his grandson) through the maternal line, or if the natural father himself has been emancipated, and likewise gives his son in adoption to his grandfather or great-grandfather, on the paternal or maternal side, then in this case, because the rights of nature and of adoption meet in one person, the adoptive father's right remains firm, joined to the natural bond and constituted in the lawful manner of adoption, so that the son is in the family and in the power of such an adoptive father.

units.la: 3 ¶Cum autem impubes per principale{a} rescriptum adrogatur, causa cognita adrogatio fieri permittitur, & exquiritur causa adrogationis an honesta sit, expediatque pupillo. Et cum quibusdam conditionibus adrogatio fit, id est, ut caveat adrogator{b} p̄sonæ publicæ, si intra pubertatem pupillus decesserit, restituturum se bona illis, qui, si adoptio facta non esset, ad successionem eius venturi essent. Item non aliter emancipare eum potest adrogator, nisi causa cognita dignus emancipatione fuerit, & tunc sua bona ei reddat. Sed & si decedens pater eum exheredauerit, vel vinus sine iusta causa emancipauerit, imbetur quartam partem ei bonorum suorum relinquere, videlicet praeter bona, quae ad patrem adoptivum transtulit, & quorum commodum ei postea acquisitur.
units.tr: 3 ¶When a minor (impubes) is adrogated by an imperial rescript, adrogation is permitted only after the cause has been examined, and it is inquired whether the cause of the adrogation is honourable and advantageous to the ward. And adrogation takes place under certain conditions: namely, that the adrogator give security to the public persons that, if the ward dies before puberty, he will restore the goods to those who would have come to his inheritance had the adoption not been made. Likewise the adrogator may not emancipate him otherwise than when, the cause having been examined, he is found worthy of emancipation, and then he must return his goods to him. But also, if the father dies and disinherits him, or emancipates him without just cause, he is bound to leave him a fourth part of his goods, namely apart from the goods which he transferred to the adoptive father, and whose benefit is afterwards acquired for him.

units.la: 4 ¶Minorem natu, maiore{d} non posse adoptare placet. adoptio enim naturam imitatur: & pro monstro est, ut maior sit filius, quam pater. Debet itaque is, qui sibi filium per adoptionem vel adrogationem facit, plena pubertate, id est, decem & octo annis praecedere.
units.tr: 4 ¶It is agreed that a younger man cannot adopt an older one. For adoption imitates nature, and it is monstrous for the son to be older than the father. Therefore he who makes a son for himself by adoption or adrogation must be ahead of him by full puberty, that is, by eighteen years.

units.la: 5 ¶Licet{e} autem & in locum nepotis vel neptis, pronepotis vel proneptis, vel deinceps adoptare, quamuis{f} filium quis non habeat.
units.tr: 5 ¶Moreover, one may adopt in the place of a grandson or granddaughter, great-grandson or great-granddaughter, or further descendants, even though one has no son.

units.la: 6 ¶Et tam filium alienum quis in locum nepotis adoptare potest, quàm nepotem in locum filij.
units.tr: 6 ¶And one may adopt another's son in the place of a grandson, just as one may adopt a grandson in the place of a son.

units.la: 7 ¶Sed si quis nepotis loco adoptet, vel quasi ex filio, quem habet iam adoptatum: vel quasi ex illo, quem naturalem in sua potestate habet: eo{g} casu & filius consentire debet, ne ei invito suus heres adgnascatur. Sed ex contrario, si avus ex filio nepotem det in adoptionem, non est necesse filium consentire.
units.tr: 7 ¶But if someone adopts in the place of a grandson, either as if born of a son whom he has already adopted, or as if born of one whom he holds as a natural son in his power, then in that case the son too ought to consent, lest a heir of his own be born to him against his will. On the contrary, if a grandfather gives a grandson born of a son in adoption, it is not necessary for the son to consent.

units.la: 8 ¶In plurimis autem causis adsimilatur is, qui adoptatus vel adrogatus est, ei, qui ex legitimo matrimonio natus est. & ideo si quis per Imperatorem, vel apud praetorem, vel praesidem provinciae non extraneum adoptaverit,{h} potest eundem in adoptione alii dare.
units.tr: 8 ¶In most matters, however, one who has been adopted or adrogated is regarded as equal to one who was born of a lawful marriage. And therefore, if someone has adopted a non-stranger before the Emperor, or before the praetor or the governor of a province, he may give the same person in adoption to another.

units.la: 9 ¶Sed & illud utriusque adoptionis commune est, quod & ij{i}, qui generare non possunt (quales sunt spadones) adoptare pos-sint[?], castrati aut non possuat[?].
units.tr: 9 ¶This too is common to both kinds of adoption: those who cannot beget children (such as eunuchs) may adopt, whether they are castrated or not.

units.la: 10 ¶Fœmine{k} quoque adoptare non possunt: quia nec naturales liberos in sua potestate habent: sed ex indulgentia principis ad solatium liberorum amissorum adoptare possunt.
units.tr: 10 ¶Women also cannot adopt, because they do not have natural children in their power; but by the indulgence of the prince they may adopt, as a solace for children they have lost.

units.la: II. ¶Illud proprium est adoptionis illius, quę per tierum[?] oraculum fit, quod is, qui liberos in potestate habet, si se adrogandum dederit, non solum ipse potestati adrogatoris subiicitur, sed etiam liberi eius in eiusdem fiunt potestate tanquam nepotes.sic etenim diuus Augustus non ante Tiberium adoptauit, quam is Germanicus adoptasset: vt protinus adoptionis facta, inciperet Germanicus Augusti nepos esse.
units.tr: II. ¶It is peculiar to that adoption which is made by the oracle of the people (per tierum oraculum) that one who has children in his power, if he gives himself to be adrogated, is not only himself made subject to the power of the adrogator, but his children also come into the same power as grandchildren. For thus the deified Augustus did not adopt Tiberius before Germanicus had been adopted by him, so that, as soon as the adoption was made, Germanicus would begin to be the grandson of Augustus.

units.la: 12. ¶Apud Catonē bene scriptū refert antiquitas, seruos, si a domino adoptati sint, ex hoc ipso posse liberari. Vnde & nos eruditi, in nostra constitutione etiam eum seruum, quē dominus actis interuenientibus filium suum nominauerat, liberum esse constituimus: licet hoc ad ius filij accipiēdū nō sufficiat.
units.tr: 12. ¶The ancients, as Cato reports, wrote well that slaves, if they were adopted by their master, could for that very reason be freed. Hence we too, learned men, in our constitution have declared free also that slave whom his master, with the acts intervening, had named as his son, although this is not sufficient for receiving the right of a son.

units.la: QUIBUS MODIS IUS PA-TRIÆ POTESTATIS SOLUITUR.
units.tr: BY WHAT MODES THE RIGHT OF PATERNAL POWER IS DISSOLVED.
TITLE XII.

units.la: VIDEAMUS nunc, quibus modis ij, qui alieno iuri sunt subiecti, eo iure liberentur. Et quidem quemadmodum liberentur serui a potestate dominorum, ex iis intelligere possumus, quę de seruis manumittendis superius exposuimus. Hi vero, qui in potestate parentis sunt, mortuo eo, e sui iuris fiunt. Sed hoc distinctionem recipit. nam mortuo patre, sane omni modo filij filiæve sui iuris efficiuntur. Mortuo vero auo, non omnino nepotes neptesque sui iuris fiunt: sed f ita, si post mortem auui in potestatem patris sui recasuri non sunt. Itaque si moriente auo pater eorum viuit, & in potestate patris sui est, tunc post obitum aui in potestate patris sui fiunt. Si vero is, quo tempore auus moritur, aut iam mortuus est, aut {g}per g emancipatione exiit de potestate patris: tunc ij, qui in potestatem eius cadere non possunt, sui iuris fiunt. 1. ¶Cùm autē is,qui ob aliquod maleficium in insulam deportatur, h ciuitatem amittit: sequitur, vt i qui eo modo ex numero ciuium Romanorum tollitur, perinde k quasi eo mox tuo, desinant liberi in potestate eius esse. Pari ratione & si is, qui in potestate parentis sit, in insulam deportatus fuerit, desinit l esse in potestate paretis. sed ex indulgentia principis m restituti fuerint: per omnia pristinum statu recipiunt.
units.tr: Let us now see by what means those who are subject to another's authority are freed from it. How slaves are freed from the power of their masters we can understand from what we set out above concerning the manumission of slaves. Those who are in a parent's power become independent when the parent dies. But this admits of a distinction. When the father dies, sons and daughters certainly become independent in every case. But when the grandfather dies, grandsons and granddaughters do not all become independent; only those who will not fall back under their father's power after the grandfather's death do. So if their father is alive when the grandfather dies, and is himself under his own father's power, then after the grandfather's death the grandchildren come under their father's power. But if, at the time the grandfather dies, the father is already dead, or has been released from his father's power by emancipation, then those who cannot fall under the grandfather's power become independent. 1. Since a man who is deported to an island for some crime loses his citizenship, it follows that the person removed in this way from the number of Roman citizens ceases to have his children in his power, just as if he had died at that moment. By the same reasoning, if a person who is in his parent's power is deported to an island, he ceases to be in his parent's power. But if they are restored by the emperor's indulgence, they recover their former position in every respect.

units.la: 2. ¶Relegati n autem tem patres in insulâ, in potestate liberos retinent. Et ex contrario liberi relegati, in potestate paretum manent. ꝯ Poenæ seruus effectus, filios in potestate habere Serui autem poenæ ꝯ efficiuntur, qui in metallum damnatur, & qui bestiis subiiciuntur.
units.tr: 2. ¶Fathers who are relegated to an island keep their children in their power, and conversely, children who are relegated remain in their parents' power. A slave is made a slave by punishment; but slaves become so as a punishment when they are condemned to the mines or handed over to the beasts.

units.la: 4 ¶Filiusfamilias si militauerit, vel si senator, vel consul factus fuerit: remanet in potestate patris, militia enim, vel consularis dignitas de patre potestate filium non liberat. Sed ex constitutione nostra summa Patriciatus dignitas illico, imperialibus codicillis praestitis, filiũ à patria potestate liberat. quis enim patiatur patrem quidem posse per emancipationis modum potestatis suæ nexibus filium liberare: impe- ratoriam autem celsitudinem non valere eum, quem sibi patre elegit, ab aliena eximere potestate? ¶Si ab hostibus captus fuerit parens, quamuis seruus hostium fiat, tamen ꝯ pendet ius liberorum propter ius postliminij: quia hi, qui ab hostibus capti sunt, si reuersi fuerint, omnia pristina iura recipiunt. idcirco re uersus etiā liberos habebit in potestate: quia postliminium fingit eum, qui captus est, in ciuitate semper fuisse. Si vero ibi decesserit: exinde, ex quo captus est pater, filius sui iuris fuisse videtur. Ipse quoque filius, nepos ve, si ab hostibus captus fuerit similiter dicimus propter ius postliminij, ius quoque potestatis parentis in suspenso esse. Dictum est autem postliminium a limine, & post. Vnde cum, qui ab hostibus captus est, & in fines nostros postea peruenit, postliminio reuersum recte dicimus. Nam limina, sicut in domo finem quendam faciunt: sic & imperij finem esse limen veteres voluerunt. Hinc & limen dictum est, quasi finis quidam & terminus. ab eo postliminium dictum est, quia ad idem limen reuertebatur, quod amiserat. Sed & qui captus vinctis hostibus recupera- tur, postliminio redijsse existimatur.
units.tr: 4. ¶If a son in a family has served in the army, or has been made a senator or consul, he remains in his father's power, since military service or the consular dignity does not free a son from his father's power. But by our constitution the highest dignity of patrician, once the imperial codicils are granted, immediately frees the son from paternal power. For who would allow a father to free his son from the bonds of his power by the mode of emancipation, while the imperial majesty would have no power to take from another's power the one whom it has chosen for itself? ¶If a parent is captured by enemies, then although he becomes a slave of the enemy, the rights of his children are nonetheless suspended by the right of postliminy, because those who have been captured by enemies, if they return, recover all their former rights.
