Accordingly, when he returns he will also have his children in his power, since postliminy treats the one who was captured as having always been in the state. But if he dies there, then from the time the father was captured, the son is regarded as having been sui iuris. The son himself, or a grandson, if captured by enemies, we likewise say that, by the right of postliminy, the right of parental power is also in suspense. Now postliminium is so called from limen and post. Hence, when someone captured by the enemy later comes into our borders, we rightly say he has returned by postliminy. For just as thresholds mark a certain boundary in a house, so the ancients wished the limen to be the boundary of the empire. Hence limen is also called, as it were, a certain end and boundary. From this the term postliminium derives, because a person returned to the same limen which he had lost. And one who is recovered from the enemy when the enemy is bound is considered to have returned by postliminy.

units.la: 6 ¶Præterea emancipatione quoque desinunt liberi in potestate parentum esse. Sed emancipatio antea quidem vel per antiquam legis obseruationem procedebat, quæ per imaginarias venditiones, & intercedentes manumissiones celebrabatur, vel ex imperiali rescripto. Nostra autem prouidentia etiam hoc in melius per constitutionem reformauit: vt fictione pristina explosa, legis Corneliæ.
units.tr: 6. ¶Moreover, children also cease to be in their parents' power by emancipation. Formerly emancipation took place either by the old observance of the law, which was carried out through imaginary sales and intervening manumissions, or by imperial rescript. Our providence, however, has reformed this for the better by a constitution, so that the old fiction is done away with.

units.la: s quę extabat in quarta 12.Tab. Halic. 2: Vlp. tit. 10. de adop.
units.tr: [Which stood in the fourth of the Twelve Tables.] Halic. 2; Vlp. tit. 10, de adoptionibus.
Anastasius, l. 5 C. de emancipationibus.

units.la: ᵐ l.vlt.C.de emanc.vt Iustinianea emancipatio à legitima & Anastasij differat. recta via ad competentes iudices vel magistratus, parentes intrent: & filios suos, vel filias, vel nepotes, vel neptes, ac deinceps, a sua manu dimittant. Et tunc ex edictoprætoris in bonis huiusmodi filij, vel filiæ, vel nepotis, vel nepris, qui quæve a parente manumissus, vel manumissa fuerit, eadem iura præstantur paren-ti,ꝗ[?] tribuitur patrono in bonis liberti. {a}Et præterea si impubes sit filius, vel filia, vel cæteri: ipse parens ex manumissione{b} tutela eius nancisci-tur.
units.tr: l. vlt. C. de emancipationibus. That Justinian's emancipation differs from the legitimate one and from that of Anastasius: parents go by the direct route before the competent judges or magistrates, and dismiss from their hand their sons, daughters, grandsons, granddaughters and so on. Then, by the praetor's edict, the same rights are granted to the parent over the goods of such a son, daughter, grandson or granddaughter who has been manumitted by the parent, as are granted to a patron over the goods of a freedman. Moreover, if the son or daughter or the others are under puberty, the parent himself acquires guardianship over them through the manumission.
ON GUARDIANSHIPS, TITLE XIII.

units.la: ¶ 7 Admonendi{c} autem sumus, liberum arbitrium esse ei, qui filium, & ex eo nepotem vel neptem in potestate habebit: filium quidem de potestate dimittere, nepotem vero vel neptem retinere. & e conuerso filium quidem in potestate retinere, nepotem vero vel neptem manumittere, vel omnes sui iuris efficere. Eadem & de pronepote, & pronepte dicta esse intelligantur.
units.tr: ¶ 7 We must also point out that it is a matter of free choice for the person who has a son in his power, and through him a grandson or granddaughter: he may release the son from his power while keeping the grandson or granddaughter in it, or conversely keep the son in his power while manumitting the grandson or granddaughter, or make them all sui iuris. The same is to be understood as said of a great-grandson and a great-granddaughter.

units.la: ¶ 8 Sed & si pater filium, quem in potestate habet, auo vel proauo naturali secundum nostras constitutiones super his habitas, in adoptionem dederit: id est, si hoc ipsum actis interuenientibus apud competentem iudicem manifestauerit, præsente eo, qui adoptatur, & non contradicente, necnon eo ‖præsente,‖[?] qui adoptat: soluitur quidem ius potestatis patris naturalis: trâsit[?] autem in huiusmodi paretem[?] adopti-onem, in cuius personam & adoptionem esse plenissi-mam antea diximus.
units.tr: ¶ 8 But also, if a father gives a son in his power in adoption to a natural grandfather or great-grandfather, according to our constitutions issued on these matters, that is, if he declares this itself before a competent judge by means of the acts, the son being adopted being present and not objecting, and the adopter being present too, then indeed the power of the natural father is dissolved, and the adopted son passes into the power of the adoptive parent, in whose person, as we said earlier, the adoption is also most complete.

units.la: ¶ 9 Illud autem scire oportet, quod si nurus tua ex filio tuo conceperit, & filium postea emancipaueris, vel in adoptionem dederis, prægnate nuru tua: nihilominus quod ex ea nascitur, in potestate tua nascitur. Quod si post emancipationem vel adoptionem conceptus fuerit: patris sui emancipati, vel aui adoptiui potestati subiicitur.
units.tr: ¶ 9 But you must know this: if your son has made your daughter-in-law pregnant, and you afterwards emancipate or give the son in adoption while your daughter-in-law is pregnant, nevertheless the child who is born from her is born in your power. But if she is conceived after the emancipation or adoption, the child is subject to the power of the emancipated father or of the adoptive grandfather.

units.la: ¶ 10 Et qui-dem neque naturales liberi, neque adoptiui vllo pe-ne modo possunt cogere parentes, de potestate sua eos dimittere.
units.tr: ¶ 10 Natural children and adopted children can by no means, or almost by no means, compel their parents to release them from their power.

units.la: TRANSEAMVS nunc ad aliam dinisionem personarum. Nam ex his personis, quæ in potestate non sunt, quædam vel in tutela sunt vel in curatione, quædam neutro iure tenentur. Videamus cr-go de his, quæ in tutela vel in curatione sunt. Ita enim intelligemus cæteras personas, quæ neutro iu-re tenentur. Ac prius dispiciamus de his, qui in tute-la sunt. Ia[?] sunt.
units.tr: Let us now pass to another division of persons. Among those persons who are not in power, some are either under guardianship or under curatorship, and some are held under neither. Let us therefore look at those who are under guardianship or curatorship; for in this way we shall understand the other persons, who are held under neither. And first let us examine those who are under guardianship. So they are.

units.la: 1 ¶Est autè tutela (ut Servius definiuit) vis a potestas in capite b libero ad tuedum c eum, qui propter ætatem se defendere nequit, iure ciuili data ac permissa.
units.tr: 1 ¶ Guardianship (as Servius defined it) is the power and authority over a free person to protect one who cannot defend himself because of his age, given and permitted by civil law.

units.la: 2 ¶Tutores autè sunt,qui eam vim ac potestatem habent,exque ipsa re nomen acceperunt. Itaque appellantur tutores quasi tuitores atque defensores: sicut ædituì dicuntur,qui ædes tuentur.
units.tr: 2 ¶ Guardians are those who hold that power and authority, and they have taken their name from the thing itself. Thus they are called guardians, as it were protectors and defenders, just as those are called custodians of a temple (aedituus) who guard the temple buildings.

units.la: 3 ¶Permissum est itaque parentibus, liberis impu-beribus,quos in d potestate habent,testamento tutorese dare. Et hoc in filios filiasq. ꝑcedit omnimodo. nepotibus vero neptibusque ita demum parentes pos-sunt testamento tutores dare , si post mortem eorum in potestatem patris sui non sunt recasuri. Itaque si filius tuus mortis tuæ tempore in potestate tua sit: nepotes ||ex||eo non poterunt ex testamèto tuo tutores habere,quamuis in potestate tua fuerint:scilicet quia mortuo te,in potestate patris sui recasuri sunt.
units.tr: 3 ¶ It is therefore permitted to parents to appoint guardians by will for their children under puberty whom they have in their power. This applies in every way to sons and daughters. But parents may appoint guardians by will for grandsons and granddaughters only if they will not return to the power of their own father after the parent's death. Thus if your son is in your power at the time of your death, your grandchildren by him cannot have guardians appointed by your will, although they were in your power, namely because on your death they will return to the power of their father.

units.la: 4 ¶Cùm autem in cõpluribus aliis causis posthu-mif pro iam natis habeātur & in hac causa placuit non minus posthumis, quàm iam natis testamento tutores dari posse: si modo in ea causa sint,ut si vivis parētibus nascerētur,sui||heredes,||& in potestate eo-rum fierent.
units.tr: 4 ¶ Although in many other cases posthumous children are regarded as already born, in this case it has been decided that guardians can be appointed by will for posthumous children no less than for those already born, provided they are in the position that, if they had been born while the parents were alive, they would become heirs in their own right (sui heredes) and in the power of those parents.

units.la: 5 ¶Sed & si emācipato filio tutorg à patre datus fuerit testamēto:confirmandus est ex sen-tētia præsidis omni modo, id est, sineh inquisitione.
units.tr: 5 ¶ But also, if a guardian has been appointed by will by the father for an emancipated son, it must be confirmed by the sentence of the governor in every way, that is, without inquiry.

units.la: QVI TESTAMENTO TU-tores dari possunt, TITULUS XIIII.
units.tr: Who may be given tutors by will, TITLE XIV.

units.la: DARI autem tutor potest testamento non solùm paterfamilias, sed etiam fi-liusfamilias.
units.tr: A tutor may be given by will not only to a head of household (paterfamilias) but also to a son who is under his father's authority (filiusfamilias).

units.la: 1 ¶Sed & servus proprius testamento cum libertate rectè tutor dari potest. Sed sciendum est,cum & sine li-bertate turorem datum, tacitèi libertatem diredam† accepisse videri,& per hoc rectè tutorem esse. Plane si perk errore,quasi liber,tutor datus sit alind dicendum est. Servus autem alienus pure inutiliter testamento datur tutor : sedl ita,cùm liber erit, utiliter datur , proprius autem servus inutiliterm eo modo tutor datur.
units.tr: 1. A slave belonging to the testator may validly be given as tutor by will together with his freedom. But it must be noted that when a tutor is given without freedom, he is seen to have received freedom tacitly, and so is validly tutor. Plainly, if he was appointed as though he were free, through error, a different rule applies. A slave belonging to another person is given as tutor by will in an invalid way, but if he becomes free he may then be validly given. A slave of the testator himself, however, is not validly given as tutor in that manner.

units.la: 2 ¶Furiosus, vel minor vigintiquinque annis tutor testamèto datus,tutor tunc erit, cùmn compos mēris aut maioro viginti quinque annis fuerit factus.
units.tr: 2. A madman, or a person under twenty-five years of age, given as tutor by will, will become tutor only when he has become of sound mind or has passed twenty-five years.

units.la: 3 ¶Ad certum tempus,p vel ex certo tempore,vel sub conditione, vel ante heredis institutio-neq posse dari tutorem,non dubitatur.
units.tr: 3. It is not doubted that a tutor cannot be appointed for a fixed time, or from a fixed time, or under a condition, or before the institution of the heir.

units.la: 4 ¶Certæ autè{a} rei vel causæ tutor dari non potest: quia personæ, nō causæ, vel rei ‖tutor‖ datur. § 5 ¶Si quis filiâbus suis vel filiis tutores dederit: etiam{b} posthumæ vel ‖posthumo‖ dedisse videtur: quia filij vel filiæ appellatione & posthumus & posthuma continentur. Quòd si nepotes sint, an appellatione filiorum & ipsis tutores dati sint? Dicendum est, vt & ipsis quoque dati videantur: si modò liberos dixerit. Cæterùm si filios: non continebuntur, aliter enim filij, aliter nepotes appellantur. Planè si posteris dederit, tam filij posthumi, quàm ceteri liberi continebuntur{c}
units.tr: 4. A tutor cannot be given for a particular affair or cause, because a tutor is given to a person, not to a cause or a thing. 5. If someone has appointed tutors for his daughters or his sons, he is held to have appointed them also for a posthumous son or daughter, since both posthumous son and posthumous daughter are included under the name of son or daughter. But if there are grandchildren, is it held that tutors have also been given to them under the name of sons? It must be said that they are seen to be given to them too, provided he said "children." Otherwise, if he said "sons," they are not included, since sons and grandsons are called by different names. But if he appointed tutors for "descendants," both posthumous sons and all other children are included.

units.la: DE LEGITIMA ADGNA-TORUM tutela, TIT. XV.
units.tr: On the legitimate tutelage of agnates, TIT. XV.

units.la: VIBUS autem testamento tutor datus non est: his ex lege duodecim tabularum adgnati sunt tutores, qui{d} vocantur legitimi. † 1 ¶Sunt{e} autè adgnati ‖cognati‖ per virilis sexus cognationem comuncti, quasi à patre cognati: veluti frater ‖ex‖ eodem patre natus, fratris filius nepósve ex eo: item patruus, & patrui filius nepósve ex eo. At qui per fœmininini sexus personas cognatione iunguntur, adgnati non sunt: sed alias naturali iure cognati. Itaque amitæ tuæ filius non est tibi adgnatus, sed cognatus: & inuicem tu illi eodem iure coniungeris: quia qui ‖ex ea‖ nascuntur, patris, fnō{f} matris familiâ sequuntur. 2 ¶Quòd autè ‖lex duodecim tabularū‖ ab intestato vocat ad tutelâ adgnatos: non{g} hâc habet significatione, si omnino nō fecerit testamenti is, qui poterat tutores dare: sed si quantum ad tutelam pertinet, intestatus decesserit. quod tunc quoque accidere intelligitur, cùm is, qui datus est tutor, viuo testatore decesserit{h}. 3 ¶Sed agnationis quidè ius omnibus capitis deminutione plerumque perimitur: nā adgnatio iuris ‖ciuilis‖ nomen est: cognationis verò ius non omnibus modis commutatur: quia *ciuilis ratio ciuilia quidè iura corrumpere potest, naturalia verò non ² vtique.
units.tr: Those to whom no tutor has been given by will have as their legitimate tutors, by the law of the Twelve Tables, their agnates, who are called legitimate. 1. Agnates, however, are kinsmen joined through kinship of the male sex, as relatives from the father's side: for example, a brother born of the same father, the son or grandson of a brother through him; likewise a paternal uncle, and the son or grandson of a paternal uncle through him. Those, however, who are joined by kinship through female persons are not agnates, but are kinsmen by natural law. Thus the son of your paternal aunt is not your agnate but your cognate, and conversely you are joined to him by the same right, because those born of her follow the family of their father, or of their mother. 2. The law of the Twelve Tables calls agnates to tutelage from intestacy; but it does not have this meaning, that the man who could have appointed tutors made no will at all, but rather that he died intestate so far as the tutelage is concerned. This is understood to happen also when the man who was given as tutor dies while the testator is still alive. 3. The right of agnation is for the most part destroyed by loss of status for all persons, for agnation is a name of civil law, whereas the right of kinship is not changed in every way, because civil reason can corrupt civil rights, but certainly not natural ones.
On loss of status (capitis deminutio), TIT. XVI.

units.la: ST{i} autè capitis deminutio, status mutatio. Eáque tribus modis accidit{l}. Nam aut maxima est capitis deminutio, aut minor, (quam quidam mediam vocant) aut minima. 1 ¶Maxima capitis deminutio est,cùm aliquis simul & ciuitatem & libertatem amittit.quod accidit in his,qui seruit pœnæ efficiuntur atrocitate sententiæ:vel libertis vt ingratis erga patronos côdemnatis:‖vel his,‖ qui se ad pretiu participandū{†}venundari passi sunt. 2 ¶Minor, siue media capitis deminutio est, cùm ciuitas quidem amittitur,libertas verò retinetur. quod accidit ei,cui aqua & igni interdictum fuerit: vel ei, qui in iusulā deportatus est. 3 ¶Minima capitis deminutio est,cùm ciuitas retinetur & libertas,sed status homi nis commutatur. quod accidit in his,qui cùm sui suris fuerint,coeperunt alieno iuri subiecti esse , vel contrà. ‖veluti si filiusfamilias à patre emancipatus fuerit, est capite deminutus.‖ 4 ¶Seruus autē manumissus , capite non minuitur : quia nullum caput {b}habuit. 5 ¶Quibus aut dignitas magis,quàm status permutatur:capite nō minuūtur.& ideo à senatu motos capite non minui {c}constat. 6 ¶Quod autem dictum est, manere cognationis ius etiam post capitis deminutionem:hoc ita est,si minima capitis demi nutio interueniat.manet enim cognatio.nam si maxima capitis deminutio interueniat: ius quoque cognationis perit , vtputa seruitute alicuius cognati: & {d}ne quidè si manumissus fuerit,recipit cognationem.Sed & si in insulam quis deportatus sit, cognatio soluitur. 7 ¶Quum autem ad agnatos tutela pertineat: non simul ad omnes pertinet , sed ad eos tantum,qui {e}pr‹ximiore gradu sunt:vel si plures eiusdē gradus sunt,ad {f}omnes ‖pertinet:veluti si plures fratres sunt, qui vnum gradum obtinent, pariter ad tutelam vocantur.‖
units.tr: Loss of status (capitis deminutio) is a change of condition. It happens in three ways: for loss of status is either greatest, or lesser (which some call middle), or least. 1. The greatest loss of status is when someone loses at once both citizenship and liberty. This happens to those who are made slaves of punishment by the severity of the sentence, or to freedmen condemned for ingratitude towards their patrons, or to those who have allowed themselves to be sold to share the price. 2. The lesser or middle loss of status is when citizenship is lost but liberty is retained. This happens to one who has been forbidden fire and water, or to one who has been deported to an island. 3. The least loss of status is when citizenship and liberty are retained but the person's status is changed. This happens to those who, having been in their own power, have begun to be subject to another's power, or the reverse. For example, if a son under his father's authority has been emancipated by his father, he has suffered loss of status. 4. A slave who has been manumitted does not suffer loss of status, because he never had a status to lose. 5. Those whose dignity rather than their standing is changed do not suffer loss of status; and so it is agreed that those removed by the Senate do not suffer loss of status. 6. As for what was said, that the right of kinship remains even after loss of status: this holds true only if the least loss of status intervenes, for kinship remains. But if the greatest loss of status intervenes, the right of kinship also perishes, for example through the enslavement of some kinsman; and even if he is manumitted, he does not recover kinship. But also if someone has been deported to an island, kinship is dissolved. 7. Since tutelage pertains to agnates, it does not pertain to all of them at once, but only to those who are nearest in degree; or, if there are several of the same degree, it pertains to all of them: for example, if there are several brothers who hold one degree, they are called equally to the tutelage.

units.la: DE LEGITIMA PATRONORUM TUTELA. TIT. XVII.
units.tr: On the legitimate guardianship of patrons. Title 17.

units.la: Xeadem[?] lege duodecim tabularum libertorum & libertarum tutela ad patronos liberosque eorum pertinet, quæ & ipsa legitima tutela vocatur: non quia nominatim ‖in‖ ea lege de hac tutela caueatur: sed quia perinde accepta est per interpretationem {g},ac si verbis legis introducta esset. Eo enim ipso,quod hereditates libertorum libertarumque, si intestati decessissent, iusserat lex ad patronos liberosve eorum pertinere: crediderunt veteres voluisse legem etiam tutelas ad eos pertinere: cùm & ad-
units.tr: By the same law of the Twelve Tables, the guardianship of freedmen and freedwomen belongs to their patrons and the patrons' children. It is also called legitimate guardianship, not because that law names this guardianship, but because it was received by interpretation as though it had been introduced in the words of the law. For since the law had ordered that the inheritances of freedmen and freedwomen, if they died intestate, belong to the patrons or their children, the ancients believed the law also meant the guardianships to belong to them, since where there is the advantage of succession, there the burden of guardianship ought also to be.
{†} Today this has been abrogated.

units.la: {b} Iuris,nō est poris.Uvif.l.3.in fi.ff.co. {c} l.3.ff.de senator.
units.tr: {b} Iuris, non est poris. Uvif. l.3 in fin. ff. co. {c} l.3 ff. de senator.

units.la: {d} l.7.ff.de cognati. {e} nouell. ns. c.5. {f} l.9. ff. de legit.hæ. {g} l.6.in sin. ff.de verb.sig. gnatos. quos ad hereditatem ‖ lex ‖ vocat, eosdem & tutores esse iusserit: quia plerúque ubi {a}successionis est emolumentum, ibi & tutelæ onus esse debet. Ideo autem diximus plerunque: quia si a fœmina impubes manumittatur, ipsa ad hereditatem vocatur, quum alius sit {b}tutor.
units.tr: {d} l.7 ff. de cognati. {e} Novell. ns. c.5. {f} l.9 ff. de legit. hæ. {g} l.6 in sin. ff. de verb. sig. The law calls to the inheritance those same persons, and has ordered them to be guardians too, because for the most part where there is the advantage of succession, there the burden of guardianship ought also to be. I said "for the most part" because if a child is manumitted by a woman, she herself is called to the inheritance, although someone else is the guardian.
On the legitimate guardianship of parents.
TITLE XVIII.

units.la: EXEMPLO {c}patronorum recepta esse & alia tutela, quæ & ipsa legitima vocatur.nam si quis filium aut filiam ,nepotem,aut neptem ex filio,& deinceps impuberes emācipauerit: legitimus eorum tutor erit.
units.tr: By the example of patrons, another guardianship was also adopted, which is itself called legitimate. For if anyone has emancipated a son or daughter, a grandson or granddaughter through a son, and so on down the line, while they are still under puberty, he will be their legitimate guardian.
CONCERNING FIDUCIARY GUARDIANSHIP.
TIT. XIX.

units.la: EST & alia tutela,quæ fiduciaria appel-latur.nam si pater filium, vel filiam,nepotem,vel neptem,vel deinceps impuberes manumiserit:legitimam nancisci-tur eorum tutelam.Quo defuncto,si liberi ‖eius‖ virilis sexus existant: fiduciarij {d}tutores vel fratris, vel sororis efficiuntur. Atqui patrono legitimo tutore mortuo,liberi quoque eius legitimi sunt tutores:quoniam filius quidem defuncti,si non effet a vivo patre emancipatus,post obitum, eius sui iuris efficeretur,nec in fratrum potestatem recideret,ideo que nec in tutelam.Libertus autem si servus manisset,utique eodem iure apud liberos domini post mortem eius futurus esset. Ita tamen hi ad tutelam vocantur,si perfectæ sint ætatis, quod nostra constitutio in omnibus tutelis & curationibus obseruari generaliter præcepit.
units.tr: There is also another kind of guardianship, which is called fiduciary. For if a father has manumitted his son or daughter, grandson or granddaughter, or any further descendants who are under puberty, the guardianship of these persons falls by law to the manumitter. When he dies, if his children of the male sex survive, they become fiduciary guardians of their brother or sister. Indeed, when the legitimate guardian, the patron, has died, his children also are legitimate guardians; for the son of the deceased, if he had not been emancipated by his living father, would after the death become his own master (sui iuris), and would not fall back under the power of his brothers, and therefore not under their guardianship either. But if the freedman had remained a slave, he would certainly, by the same law, have passed after his death to the children of his master. Yet these persons are called to guardianship only if they have reached full age, which our constitution has generally commanded to be observed in all guardianships and curatorships.

units.la: DE ATILIANO TUTORE, ET EO qui ex lege Iulia & Titia dabatur,
units.tr: CONCERNING THE GUARDIAN ATILIANUS, AND THE ONE WHO WAS APPOINTED UNDER THE LAW OF JULIA AND TITIA.
TIT. XX.

units.la: Si[?]{f} cui nullus omnino tutor fuerat: ei dabatur in urbe quidem a prætore urbano, & maiore{g} parte tribunorum plebis tutor ex lege{h} Atilia : in provinciis vero a præsidibus provinciarum ex lege
units.tr: If anyone had no guardian at all, a guardian was given to him in the city by the urban praetor, and by most of the tribunes of the plebs, under the Atilian law; in the provinces, a guardian was given by the governors of the provinces under the law

units.la: Iulia & Titia. 1 ¶Sed & si in testamento tutor sub conditione, aut ex die certo datus fuerat: quamdiu {a}conditio aut dies pendebat, ex eisdem legibus tutor dari poterat. Item si pure datus fuerat: quamdiu ex testamento nemo heres existebat, tamdiu ex eisdem legibus tutor petendus erat: qui desinebat esse tutor, si conditio extiterat, aut dies venerat, aut heres extiterat. 2 ¶Ab {b}hostibus quoq. tutore capto, ex his legibus tutor petebatur: qui desinebat esse tutor, si is, qui captus erat, in civitatem reversus fuerat. nam reversus recipiebat tutela iure {c}postliminij. 3 ¶Sed ex his legibus tutores pupillis desierunt dari, postea quàm primò consules pupillis utriusque sexus tutores ex inquisitione dare coeperunt, deinde prætores ex constitutionibus. Nam supradictis legibus neque de cautione à tutoribus exigenda, rem salvam pupillis fore: neque de compellendis tutoribus ad tutelæ administrationem, quidquam cavebatur. 4 ¶Sed hæc iure utimur, ut {d}Romæ quidem præfectus urbi, vel prætor secundum suam iurisdictionem: in provinciis autem præsides ex inquisitione tutores crearent, vel magistratus iussu præsidum, si non sint magnæ pupilli facultates. 5 ¶Nos autem per constitutionem nostram huiusmodi difficultates hominum resecantes: nec expectata iussione præsidum, dispositimus, si facultates pupilli vel adulti usque ad quingentos solidos valeant, defensores civitatum una cum eiusdem civitatis religiosissimo antistite, vel alias publicas personas, id est, magistratus vel iuridicum Alexandrinæ civitatis, tutores vel curatores creare: legitima cautela secundum eamdem constitutionis normam præstanda, videlicet eorum periculo, qui ea accipiunt. 6 ¶Impuberes autem in tutela esse naturali {§}iuri conveniens est: ut is, qui perfectæ ætatis non sit, alterius tutela regatur.
units.tr: Julian and Titian. 1. And if a guardian had been appointed in a will under a condition, or from a certain day, a guardian could be given under the same laws while the condition or day was still pending. Likewise, if he had been appointed unconditionally, then, as long as no one had become heir under the will, a guardian was to be sought under the same laws. That guardian ceased to be guardian if the condition was fulfilled, or the day arrived, or an heir came into being. 2. Also, if the guardian was taken captive by the enemy, a guardian was sought under these laws. That guardian ceased to be guardian if the man who had been captured returned to the state, for on his return he regained the guardianship by right of return (postliminium). 3. But guardians ceased to be given to wards under these laws after the consuls first began to appoint guardians for wards of either sex after an inquiry, and then the praetors did so by imperial edicts. For the aforementioned laws provided nothing about requiring security from guardians that the ward's property would be kept safe, nor about compelling guardians to administer the guardianship. 4. But by present law the practice is this: at Rome the city prefect or the praetor, according to his jurisdiction, appoints guardians after an inquiry; in the provinces the governors do so, or a magistrate by order of the governor, if the ward's resources are not large. 5. We, however, cutting away these difficulties for men by our constitution, have ordained, without waiting for the governor's order, that if the property of a ward or minor is worth up to five hundred solidi, the defenders of the cities, together with the most reverend bishop of that same city, or other public persons, namely the magistrates or the judicial officer of the city of Alexandria, may appoint guardians or curators, provided that legal security is given according to the rule of the same constitution, at the risk, namely, of those who accept the office. 6. Moreover, it accords with natural law that those below puberty be under guardianship, so that one who is not of full age be governed by another's guardianship.

units.la: 7 ¶Quum ergo pupillorum pupillarumque tutores negotia gerant: post pubertatem tutelæ iudicio {h}rationem reddunt.
units.tr: 7. Since, therefore, guardians conduct the affairs of wards, both boys and girls, after puberty they render account in a suit of guardianship.
On the Authority of Guardians. Title 21.

units.la: AUCTORITAS ante tutoris in quibusdam causis necessaria pupillis est, in quibusdam non est necessaria. ut ecce si quid dari sibi stipulentur lx: non est necessaria tutoris auctoritas, quòd si aliis promittant pupilli, necessaria est tutoris auctoritas. Namque placuit meliorem quidem conditionem licere eis facere etiam sine tutoris auctoritate: deteriorem vero no aliter, quàm cum tutoris auctoritate{a}. Vnde in his causis, ex quibus obligationes mutuae nascuntur, vt in emptionibus, venditionibus, locationibus, conductionibus, mandatis, depositis: si tutoris auctoritas non intereuenit: ipsi quidem, qui cum his contrahunt, obligantur: at inuicem pupilli non obligantur.
units.tr: The authority of a guardian is necessary for pupils in some matters and not necessary in others. For example, if they stipulate to be given something, the guardian's authority is not necessary; but if the pupils promise something to others, the guardian's authority is necessary. For it has been decided that they may make a better condition for themselves even without the guardian's authority, but a worse one only with the guardian's authority. Hence in those matters from which mutual obligations arise, as in purchases, sales, lettings, hirings, mandates, and deposits: if the guardian's authority does not intervene, those who contract with the pupils are indeed bound, but the pupils are not bound in turn.

units.la: 1 ¶ Neque tamen {b}hereditatem adire, neque bonorum possessionem petere, neque hereditatem ex fideicommisso suscipere aliter possunt, nisi tutoris auctoritate (quamuis illis lucrosa sit) nec vllum damnum habeant.
units.tr: 1 ¶ Nor can pupils enter upon an inheritance, seek possession of goods, or take up an inheritance under a trust in any other way than with the guardian's authority (even though it is profitable to them), and they suffer no loss thereby.

units.la: 2 ¶ Tutor autem statim in ipso negotio {c}praesens debet auctor fieri, si hoc pupillo prodesse exitimauerit, post tempus vero, vel per epistolam interposita auctoritas, nihil agit.
units.tr: 2 ¶ A guardian, moreover, ought to become the authorising party immediately in the transaction itself, if he judges it to be of benefit to the pupil; but authority given after the time has passed, or interposed by letter, accomplishes nothing.

units.la: 3 ¶ Si inter tutorem pupillumque iudicium agendum sit: quia * ipse tutor in {d}rem suam auctor esse non potest: non praetorius tutor (vt olim) constituitur, sed {e}curator in locum eius datur: quo curatore interueniente, iudicium peragitur, & eo peracto curator esse desinit.
units.tr: 3 ¶ If a lawsuit has to be conducted between the guardian and the pupil, then, because the guardian himself cannot be the authorising party in his own affair, a guardian is not appointed by the praetor (as formerly), but a curator is given in his place; with this curator intervening, the suit is carried on, and when it is concluded the curator ceases to hold office.
TIT. XXII.
By what means guardianship is ended.

units.la: PVPILLI pupillaeque, cum pubertas esse coeperint, tutela liberantur. Pubertatem autem veteres quidem non solùm ex annis, sed etiam {g}ex habitu corporis in masculis aestimari volebant. Nostra autem maiestas dignum esse castitate nostrorum temporum existimans, bene putauit: quod in foeminis etiam antiquis impudicum esse visum est, id est, inspectionem habitudinis corporis, hoc etiam in masculos extendere. Et ideo {h}nostra sancta constitutione promulgata, pubertatem in masculis post decimum quartum annum completum illico initium accipere disposuimus: antiquitatis normam in foeminis bene positam, suo ordine relinquentes, vt post duodecim annos completos viri potentes esse credantur.
units.tr: Boys and girls, when they have begun to reach puberty, are released from guardianship. The ancients wanted puberty in males to be judged not only by age but also by the physical condition of the body. Our majesty, however, thinking it fitting for the chastity of our times, has rightly judged that what even the ancients considered indecent in females, namely the inspection of the physical condition of the body, should also be extended to males. And so, by our sacred constitution promulgated, we have decreed that puberty in males begins at once upon the completion of the fourteenth year, while leaving the ancient rule, well established for females, in its own place, so that after twelve full years they are believed to be capable.

units.la: 1 ¶ Item finitur tutela, si adrogati sint ad-huc impuberes, vel {i}deportati: item si in seruitutem pupillus redigatur, vel si ab hostibus captus fuerit.
units.tr: 1 ¶ Guardianship also ends if those not yet of age have been adrogated, or deported. Likewise, if the pupil is reduced to slavery, or if he has been captured by enemies.

units.la: 2 ¶Sed & si usque ad certâ conditionem datus sit tutor testamento: æque euenit,ut desinat esse tutor existente conditione. 3 ¶Simili modo finitur tutela morte {a}vel pupillorum, vel tutorum. 4 ¶Sed & capitis deminutione tutoris, per quam libertas vel ciuitas amittitur, omnis tutela perit.Minima autem capitis deminutione {b} tutoris, veluti si se in adoptionem dederit,legitima tantum tutela perit, cetera non percunt. Sed pupilli & pupillæ capitis deminutio, licet minima sit, omnes tutelas tollit.
units.tr: 2 ¶ But also, if a tutor has been given by will until a certain condition, it equally happens that he ceases to be tutor when the condition occurs. 3 ¶ In a similar way, guardianship ends by the death either of the pupils or of the tutors. 4 ¶ But also by the capitis deminutio of the tutor, through which liberty or citizenship is lost, all guardianship perishes. But by the smallest capitis deminutio of the tutor, for example if he has given himself into adoption, only legitimate guardianship perishes; the others do not perish. But the capitis deminutio of the pupil or ward, however minor it may be, abolishes all guardianships.

units.la: 5 ¶Præterea qui ad certum tempus testamento dantur tutores,{c} finito eo,deponunt tutelam. 6 ¶Desinunt etiam tutores esse, qui vel remouentur à tutela ob id quòd suspecti visi sunt: vel qui ex iusta causa sese excusant, & onus administrandæ tutelæ deponunt, secundum ea quæ inferius proponemus.
units.tr: 5 ¶ Moreover, tutors who are given by will for a certain time lay down the guardianship when that time has ended. 6 ¶ Tutors also cease to be tutors who are either removed from guardianship because they have been seen as suspect, or who excuse themselves for a just cause and lay down the burden of administering the guardianship, according to what we shall set out below.
ON CURATORS, TITLE 23.

units.la: MASCVLI quidē puberes, & fœminæ viri potentes,usque ad vicesimumquintum annum {e}cōpletum curatores accipiunt: quia licet puberes sint, adhuc tamen eius ætatis sunt,ut sua negotia tueri non possint. ¶Dantur autem curatores ab {f}eisdem magistratibus à quibus & tutores, Sed curator testamento non datur: datus tamen confirmatur decreto prætoris vel præsidis. 2 ¶Item inuiti {g}adolescentes,curatores non accipiunt, præterquàm in litem. curator enim & ad certam causam dari potest. 3 ¶Furiosi quoq. & prodigi,licet maiores viginti-quinque annis sint: tamen in curatione sunt adgnatorum ex lege duodecim tabularum. Sed solent Romæ præfecti urbi vel prætores,& in prouinciis præsides ex inquisitione {h}eis curatores dare. 4 ¶Sed & mente captis, & surdis,& mutis, & qui perpetuo morbo laborant (quia rebus suis superesse non possunt) curatores dandi sunt. 5 ¶Interdum autem & pupilli curatores accipiunt, utputa si legitimus tutor {i}non sit idoneus: *quoniam habeti turorem tutor dari non potest. Item si testamento datus tutor, vel à prætore, aut præside, idoneus non sit ad administrationem,nec tamen fraudulenter negotia administret: solet ei curator adiungi. Item loco tutorum, qui non in perpetuum,sed {k}ad tempus à tutela excusanrum,solent curatores dari.
units.tr: Males who have reached puberty, and females who are of full age, receive curators until they complete their twenty-fifth year, because although they are of puberty, they are still of an age at which they cannot look after their own affairs. Curators are given by the same magistrates who give tutors. But a curator is not given by will; a curator so given is nevertheless confirmed by a decree of the praetor or the governor. 2. Likewise, minors who are unwilling do not receive curators, except for a lawsuit, since a curator may also be given for a particular matter. 3. Madmen and spendthrifts, even if they are over twenty-five, are nonetheless under curatorship of their agnates by the law of the Twelve Tables. But at Rome the prefects of the city or the praetors, and in the provinces the governors, usually appoint curators for them after inquiry. 4. Also, those who are mentally incapacitated, as well as the deaf, the mute, and those who suffer from a permanent illness (because they cannot manage their own affairs), must be given curators. 5. Sometimes wards also receive curators, for instance if the legitimate tutor is not fit; since a tutor cannot be given to someone who already has a tutor. Likewise, if a tutor appointed by will, or by the praetor or governor, is not fit for administration, yet does not manage the affairs fraudulently, a curator is usually added to him. Likewise, curators are usually given in place of tutors who are excused from guardianship not permanently but for a time.

units.la: 6 ¶Quod si tutor aduersa valetudine, vel alia necessitate impediatur, quo minus negotia pupilli administrare possit. & pupillus vel abiit, vel infans sit: quem velit actorem {a}pe-riculo ipsius tutoris, praetor, vel qui prouinciæ praeerit, decreto constituet.
units.tr: 6. But if a tutor is prevented by ill health or some other necessity from being able to administer the ward's affairs, and the ward is either absent or an infant, the praetor, or the one who presides over the province, will by decree appoint whomever he wishes as agent, at the risk of the tutor himself.

units.la: DE SATISDATIONE TUTORUM vel curatorum, TIT. XXIIII.
units.tr: ON THE SECURITY TO BE GIVEN BY TUTORS OR CURATORS, TIT. XXIIII.

units.la: NEtamen pupillorum pupillarumve, & eorum qui quæve in curatione sunt, negotia à curatoribus, tutoribusve consumantur, vel deminuantur: curet prætor, ut & tutores, & curatores eo nomine {c}satisdent. Sed hoc non est perpetuum. nam tutores testamento dati {d}satisdare non coguntur: quia fides eorum & diligentia ab ipso testatore approbata est. item ex inquisitione tutores vel curatores dati, satisdatione non {e}onerantur: quia idonei electi sunt.
units.tr: Yet when the business of wards (pupils, male or female, and of those who are under curatorship) is consumed or diminished by their curators or tutors, the praetor takes care that the tutors and curators give security (satisdatio) on that account. But this is not absolute. For tutors appointed by will are not compelled to give security, because their good faith and diligence have been approved by the testator himself. Likewise, tutors or curators appointed after inquiry are not burdened with giving security, because they were chosen as fit persons.

units.la: 1 ¶Sed si ex testamento vel inquisitione duo pluresve dati fuerint: potest {f}unus offerre satisdationem de indemnitate pupilli vel adolescentis, & contutori suo vel concurratori præferri, ut solus administret: vel ut cotutor aut concurator satis offerens præponatur ei, ut & ipse solus administret. Itaque per se non potest petere satisdationem a contutore suo vel concuratore: sed offerre debet, ut electionem det {g}cocuratori vel contutori suo, utrum velit satis accipere, an {b}satisdare. Quod si nemo eorum satis offerat: si quidem adscriptum fuerit a testatore, quis gerat: {h}ille gerere debet. Quod si non fuerit adscriptum: {i}quem maior pars elegerit, ipse gerere debet, ut edicto prætoris cauetur. Sin autem ipsi tutores dissenserint circa eligendum eum, vel eos, qui gerere debet: prætor partes {k}suas interponere debet. Idem & in pluribus ex inquisitione datis comprobandum est: id est, ut maior pars eligere possit, per quem administratio fiat.
units.tr: 1 ¶But if two or more have been appointed, either by will or after inquiry, one of them may offer security for the indemnity of the ward or the young man, and be preferred to his co-tutor or co-curator, so that he alone administers; or else a co-tutor or co-curator who offers security is put before him, so that he himself alone administers. Accordingly, one cannot himself demand security from his co-tutor or co-curator; he must offer it, so that he gives the choice to his fellow co-curator or co-tutor, whether he wishes to receive security or to give it. But if none of them offers security: if indeed the testator has named who is to manage, that person ought to manage; but if no one has been named, the one whom the greater part has chosen ought himself to manage, as is provided by the praetor's edict. But if the tutors themselves disagree about choosing him, or those who ought to manage, the praetor must interpose his own authority. The same is to be observed also where several have been appointed after inquiry: namely, that the greater part may choose through whom the administration is carried out.

units.la: 2 ¶Sciedum autem est,non solum tutores vel curatores pupillis, vel adultis, cæterisque personis ex administratione rerum teneri: sed etiam {l}in eos, qui satisdationem accipiunt, subsidiariam actionem esse, quæ ultimum eis præsidium possit afferre. Subsidiaria autem actio in eos datur, qui aut omnino à tutoribus vel curatoribus satisdari non cu-rauerunt. raverunt, aut non idonee passi sunt caveri. Quæ quidem tam ex prudentium responsis, quàm ex constitutionibus imperialibus etiam{a} in heredes eorum extenduntur.
units.tr: 2 ¶It should be known that tutors or curators are bound not only to pupils, or to adults, and other persons, for the management of their property; but there is also a subsidiary action against those who accept the security, which can afford them a last resort. A subsidiary action is given against those who either have not at all taken care that security was given by the tutors or curators, or have allowed security to be given in an unsatisfactory manner. And these actions, both from the responses of the jurists and from imperial constitutions, extend even against their heirs.

units.la: 3 ¶Quibus constitutionibus & illud exprimitur, ut nisi caveant tutores & curatores, "pi-gnoribus captis coerceantur."
units.tr: 3 ¶By these constitutions it is also expressed that, unless tutors and curators give security, they are to be constrained by seizure of pledges.

units.la: 4 ¶Neque autem præ-sectus urbi, neque prætor, neque præses provinciæ, neque quisquam alius, cui tutores dandi ius est, hac actione tenebitur: sed hi tantummodo, qui satisfactionem exigere solent.
units.tr: 4 ¶Moreover, neither the prefect of the city, nor the praetor, nor the governor of a province, nor anyone else who has the right of appointing tutors, will be liable in this action; but only those who are accustomed to exact the security.

units.la: DE EXCUSATIONIBUS TUTORUM{b} vel curatorum. TIT. XXV.
units.tr: ON THE EXCUSES OF GUARDIANS OR CURATORS. TITLE XXV.

units.la: EXCUSANTUR autem tutores & curatores variis ex causis: {c}propter liberos, sive in potestate sint, sive emancipati. Si enim tres liberos suos perstites Romæ quis habeat, vel in Italia quatuor, vel in provinciis quinque: a tutela vel cura potest excusari, exemplo ceterorum munerum. nam & tutelam & curam placuit publicum{d} munus esse. Sed adoptivi liberi non prosunt. in adoptionem autem dati, naturali patri prosunt. Item nepotes ex filio prosunt ut in locum patris sui succedant: ex filia non prosunt. Filii autem superstites tantum ad tutelæ vel curæ muneris excusationem prosunt: defuncti autem non prosunt. Sed si in bello amissi sunt: quæsitum est, an prosint? Et constat eos{e} solos prodesse, qui in acie amittuntur. * hi enim, qui pro republica ceciderunt, in perpetuum per gloriam vivere intelliguntur.
units.tr: Guardians and curators may be excused for various reasons: on account of children, whether they are under power or emancipated. For if someone has three surviving children at Rome, or four in Italy, or five in the provinces, he may be excused from guardianship or curatorship, following the example of the other public duties, for guardianship and curatorship have been held to be public burdens. But adopted children do not count for this purpose; children given in adoption do count in favour of their natural father. Likewise, grandchildren through a son count, so that they may take their father's place; grandchildren through a daughter do not. Moreover, only surviving sons give grounds for excusing one from the burden of guardianship or curatorship; dead sons do not. But if they were lost in war, the question has been raised whether they count. And it is agreed that only those who fall in battle count, for those who died for the commonwealth are understood to live forever in glory.

units.la: 1 ¶Item divus Marcus in Semestribus rescripsit, cum,{f} qui res fisci administrat, a tutela vel cura, quandiu administrat, excusari posse.
units.tr: 1 Likewise, the divine Marcus wrote in the Semestria that a man who administers the public treasury may be excused from guardianship or curatorship for as long as he administers it.

units.la: 2 ¶Item qui{g} reipublicæ causa absunt, a tutela vel cura excusantur.
units.tr: 2 Likewise, those who are absent on public business are excused from guardianship or curatorship.

units.la: Sed & si fuerint tutores vel curatores ||dati||, deinde reipublicæ causa abesse coeperint: a tutela vel{h} cura excusantur, quatenus reipublicæ causa absunt: & interea curator loco eorum datur: qui si reversi fuerint, recipiunt onus tutelæ. nam nec{i} anni habent vacationem, ut Papianus libro quinto Responsorum scripsit. nam hoc spatium habent ad novas tutelas vocati.
units.tr: But also, if men have been appointed guardians or curators and then begin to be absent on public business, they are excused from guardianship or curatorship to the extent that they are absent on public business, and in the meantime a curator is given in their place; if they return, they take up the burden of guardianship again. For they do not have a year's exemption, as Papinian wrote in the fifth book of his Responsa; for men called to new guardianships have that period of time.

units.la: 3 ¶Et qui{j} potestatem aliquam habent, se excusare possunt, ut divus Marcus rescripsit: sed suscepta tutelam deserere non possunt.
units.tr: 3 Those who hold some office may excuse themselves, as the divine Marcus wrote, but once they have undertaken a guardianship they may not abandon it.

units.la: 4 ¶Item propter litem, quam cum pupillo vel adulto tutor vel curator habet, excusari non potest: nisi forte de omnibus bonis, vel hereditate controuersia fit.
units.tr: 4 Likewise, a guardian or curator who is in a lawsuit with a ward or an adult cannot be excused on that account, unless perhaps the dispute concerns all the goods or an inheritance.

units.la: 5 ¶Itē tria onera tutelæ non adfectatæ, vel curæ, præstant vacationem, quandiu administrantur: vt tamen plurium pupillorum tutela vel cura eorundem bonorum, veluti fratrum, pro vna computetur.
units.tr: 5 Likewise, three burdens of guardianship or curatorship that were not sought after confer exemption for as long as they are being administered; yet the guardianship or curatorship of several wards with the same property, such as brothers, is counted as one.

units.la: 6 ¶Sed & propter paupertatē excusatione tribui, tam diu fratres, quàm per se diuus Marcus rescripsit, si quis imparem se oneri iniuncto possit docere.
units.tr: 6 But also, on account of poverty, an excuse is granted, for as long as the brothers, as the divine Marcus himself wrote, can show that they are unequal to the burden imposed on them.

units.la: 7 ¶Item propter aduersam valetudinē, propter quam ne suis quidem negotiis interesse potest, excusatio locū habet.
units.tr: 7 Likewise, an excuse holds on account of serious ill health, on account of which a man cannot even attend to his own affairs.

units.la: 8 ¶Similiter eos, qui literas ne-sciunt, esse excusandos, diuus Pius rescripsit: quanuis & imperiti literarum possint ad administrationem negotiorum sufficere.
units.tr: 8 Similarly, the divine Pius wrote that those who do not know letters are to be excused, although men unskilled in letters may also be sufficient for the administration of affairs.

units.la: 9 ¶Item si propter inimicitias aliquem testamento tutorem pater dederit: hoc ipsum præstat ei excusationem: sicut per contrarium non excusantur, qui se tutelam administraturos patri pupillorū promiserant.
units.tr: 9 Likewise, if a father has appointed someone as guardian in his will on account of enmities, this itself gives him an excuse; just as, on the contrary, those are not excused who had promised the fathers of the wards that they would administer the guardianship.

units.la: 10 ¶Non esse autē admittendam excusationem eius, qui hoc solo vtitur, quòd ignotus patri pupillorum fit, diu fratres rescripserunt.
units.tr: 10 The divine brothers wrote that the excuse of one who relies on this alone, that he is unknown to the father of the wards, is not to be admitted.

units.la: 11 ¶Inimicitiæ, quas quis cū patre pupillorū vel adultorum exercuit: si capitales fuerunt, nec reconciliatio interuenit: à tutela vel cura solent excusare.
units.tr: 11 Enmities that someone has had with the father of the wards or of the adults, if they were capital and no reconciliation has taken place, usually excuse from guardianship or curatorship.

units.la: 12 ¶Itē is, qui status controuersiā lx à pupil-lorum patre passus est, excusatur à tutela.
units.tr: 12 Likewise, one who has suffered a lawsuit over his status at the hands of the father of the wards is excused from guardianship.

units.la: 13 ¶Item maior septuaginta annis à tutela & cura se potest excusare. minores autem viginti quinque annis, olim quidem excusabantur: nostra autem constitutione prohibentur ad tutelam vel curam adspirare: adeò, vt nec excusatione opus sit. Qua constitutione cauetur, vt nec pupillus ad legitimam tutelam vocetur, nec adultus: quum {*}sit inciuile, eos, qui alieno auxilio in rebus suis administrandis egere noscuntur, & ab aliis reguntur, aliorum tutelam vel curam subire.
units.tr: 13 Likewise, a man over seventy years of age may excuse himself from guardianship and curatorship. Those under twenty-five used formerly to be excused, but by our constitution they are forbidden to aspire to guardianship or curatorship, so that no excuse is even needed. By this constitution it is provided that neither a ward nor an adult shall be called to legitimate guardianship, since it is unseemly that persons who are known to need the help of others in managing their own affairs, and who are governed by others, should take on the guardianship or curatorship of others.

units.la: 14 ¶Idem & in milite obseruādum est, vt nec volens ad tutelæ onus admirtatur.
units.tr: 14 The same must be observed in the case of a soldier, so that he is not admitted to the burden of guardianship even if he is willing.

units.la: 15 ¶Item Romæ grammatici, rhetores, & medici, & qui in patria sua has artes exercent, & intra numerum sunt: à tutela & cura habet vacationem.
units.tr: 15 Likewise, at Rome, grammarians, rhetoricians and physicians, and those who practise these arts in their own homeland and are on the official list, have exemption from guardianship and curatorship.

units.la: 16 ¶Qui autē vult se excusare, si plures habeat excusationes, & de quibusdam non probauerit: aliis vti intra tempora ¶ constituta non prohibetur, Qui autem excusare se voluat, non appellant: sed intra quinquaginta dies continuos, ex quo cognouerint se esse tutores vel curatores datos, se excusare debent, cuiuscunque generis sint, id est, qualitercunque dati fuerint tutores: si {a}intra centesimum lapidem sunt ab eo loco, vbi tutores dati sunt. Si vero vltra centesimum lapidem habitant: dinumeratione facta viginti milium diurnorum, & amplius triginta dierum. qui tamen (vt Scaevola dicebat) sic debent computari, ne minus sint, quam quinqua-ginta dies. 17 ¶Datus autem tutor, ad {b}vniuersum patrimonium datus esse creditur. 18 ¶Qui tutelam alicuius gesiit, {c}innitus curator eiusdem fieri non compellitur: intantum, vt licet paterfamilias, qui testamento tutorem dedit, adiecerit se eundem curatorem dare: tamen inuitum eum curam suscipere non cogendum, diui Seuerus {d}& Antoninus rescripserunt. 19 ¶Idem rescripserunt maritum vxori suae curatorem datum, excusare se posse, licet se immisceat. 20 ¶Si quis aut falsis {e}allegationibus excusa-tione tutelae meruerit: non est liberatus onere tutelae.
units.tr: 16 Anyone who wishes to excuse himself, if he has several excuses and has not proved some of them, is not forbidden to use the others within the fixed time limits. But those who wish to excuse themselves need not appeal; they must excuse themselves within fifty continuous days from the day on which they learned that they had been appointed guardians or curators, of whatever kind they are, that is, however they were appointed, if they live within a hundred miles of the place where the guardians were appointed. If indeed they live beyond a hundred miles, then, after a reckoning of twenty thousand days, and thirty days more. Yet, as Scaevola used to say, these periods are to be counted so that they are not less than fifty days. 17 A guardian who has been appointed is understood to have been appointed over the whole estate. 18 A man who has administered someone's guardianship is not compelled to become that person's curator against his will, to such an extent that, although the father of the family who appointed him guardian in his will added that he should also be curator, the divine Severus and Antoninus wrote that he is not to be compelled to take up the curatorship against his will. 19 The same emperors wrote that a husband appointed curator of his wife may excuse himself, even though he has interfered in her affairs. 20 If anyone has obtained an excuse from guardianship by false pleas, he is not freed from the burden of guardianship.

units.la: DE SVSPECTIS TVTORI-bus, vel curatoribus, TIT. XXVI.
units.tr: On Suspect Guardians, or Curators, Title 26.

units.la: S[?]CIENDVM est, suspecti crimen ex lege duodecim tabularum descendere. 1 ¶Datum est autem ius remouendi tutores suspectos Romae praetori, & in prouinciis praesidibus earum, & legato proconsulis. 2 ¶Ostendimus,qui possint de suspecto cognoscere: nunc videamus, qui suspecti fieri possint. Et possunt quidem omnes tutores fieri suspecti, siue sint {b}testamentarij, siue non sint: sed alterius generis tutores. Quare & si legitimus fuerit tutor, accusari poterit. Quid si patronus? Adhuc idem erit dicendum: dummodo meminerimus, {i}famae patro-ni parcendum esse, licet vt suspectus remotus fuerit. 3 ¶Consequens est,vt videamus,qui possint suspectos postulare. Et iciendum est,quasi publicam esse hanc accusationem, hoc est, omnibus patere. Quinimmo & mulieres {d}admittuntur ex rescripto diuorum Seueri & Antonini: sed ex solx,quae pietatis necessitudine ductae,ad hoc procedunt: vt puta mater, sutrix quoque, & auia, potest & soror. sed & si qua alia mulier fuerit, quam praetor propensa pietate intellexerit, sexus verecundiam non egredientem, sed pietate productam, non sustinere iniuriam pupillorum: admittet ea ad accusationem. 4 ¶Impuberes {a}non possunt tutores suos suspectos postulare. pube-res autem curatores suos ex consilio necessariorum suspectos possunt arguere. & ita diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt. 5 ¶ *Suspectus autem est, qui non ex fide tutelam gerit, licet {b}soluendo sit, vt Iulianus quoque scripsit. Sed & ante, quam incipiat tutelam gerere tutor, posse eum quasi suspectum removeri idem Iulianus scripsit, & secundum eum constitutum est. 6 ¶Suspectus autem remotus[?], si quidem {c}ob dolum: famosus est. si ob culpam: non at-que. 7 ¶Si quis autem suspectus postulatur: quoad cognitio finiatur: {d}interdicitur ei administratio, vt Papiniano visum est. 8 ¶Sed si suspecti cognitio suscepta fuerit: posteaquam tutor vel curator {e}decesse-rit, extinguitur suspecti cognitio. 9 ¶Si quis tutor copiam sui non faciat, vt alimenta pupillo decer-nantur: cautetur epistola diuorum Seueri & Antonini, vt in {f}possessionem bonorum eius pupillus mit-tatur: & quae mora deteriora futura sunt, dato cura-tore distrahi iubentur. Ergo vt suspectus removeri potest, qui {g}non praestat alimenta. 10 ¶Sed si quis presens negat propter inopiam alimenta posse decerni: si hoc per mendacium dicat: remittendum eum esse ad praefectum urbi puniendum placuit: sicut ille remittitur, qui data {h}pecunia ministerium tutelae adquisierit, vel redemerit. 11 ¶Libertus quoque, si fraudulenter tutelam filiorum vel neporum patroni gesisse probetur, ad praefectum urbi remittitur puniendus. 12 ¶Nonisime[?] autem sciendum est eos, qui fraudulenter tutelam administrant, etiam si satis oferant, remouendos esse a tutela: quia {i}satisfactio tutoris propositum maleuolum non mutat, sed diutius grassandi in re familiari facultatem praestat. Suspectum eriam eum putamus, qui moribus talis est, vt suspectus sit. Enimuero tutor vel curator, quamuis pauper est, fidelis tamen & diligens, remouendus non est quasi suspe-ctus,
units.tr: It must be understood that the crime of suspicion arises from the Law of the Twelve Tables. 1 ¶The right to remove suspect guardians was given at Rome to the praetor, in the provinces to their governors, and to the proconsul's legate. 2 ¶We have shown who may take cognizance of a suspect guardian; now let us see who may become suspect. Indeed, all guardians may become suspect, whether they were appointed by will or not, though guardians of different kinds are treated differently. Hence, even if a guardian was appointed by law, he may be accused. What if he is a patron? The same must still be said, provided we remember that the reputation of a patron must be spared, even if he is removed as suspect. 3 ¶It follows that we should see who may bring a charge of suspicion against guardians. It should be understood that this accusation is, as it were, public, that is, open to all. Indeed, women too are admitted by a rescript of the deified Severus and Antoninus, but only those who come forward moved by the bond of duty, such as a mother, a sister, or a grandmother, may do so. And if any other woman, whom the praetor perceives, with a well-inclined sense of duty, to be acting from devotion, not overstepping the modesty of her sex, but impelled by affection, and unwilling to let the orphans suffer wrong, he will admit her to the accusation. 4 ¶Those below puberty cannot bring charges of suspicion against their guardians. Those who have reached puberty, however, may accuse their curators as suspect on the advice of their close relatives. Severus and Antoninus, the deified emperors, so rescripted. 5 ¶A guardian is suspect if he does not administer the guardianship in good faith, even though he is solvent, as Julian also wrote. Moreover, Julian wrote, and it was settled according to his view, that a guardian may be removed as suspect even before he begins to administer the guardianship. 6 ¶A suspect guardian who is removed is infamous if he was removed for fraud; he is not infamous if removed for fault. 7 ¶If anyone is charged as suspect, then, until the inquiry is concluded, the administration is forbidden to him, as Papinian thought. 8 ¶But if the inquiry into suspicion has been undertaken, and afterwards the guardian or curator dies, the inquiry into suspicion lapses. 9 ¶If a guardian does not make his property available so that maintenance may be assigned to the ward, it is provided by the letter of the deified Severus and Antoninus that the ward be sent into possession of the guardian's goods, and that, a curator being appointed, those goods which would deteriorate through delay are ordered to be sold. Therefore a guardian who does not provide maintenance can be removed as suspect. 10 ¶But if a guardian, present in court, denies that maintenance can be assigned on account of poverty, and says this falsely, it has been decided that he is to be sent back to the prefect of the city to be punished, just as one is sent back who has obtained or bought the office of guardianship with money. 11 ¶A freedman too, if he is proved to have administered the guardianship of the children or grandchildren of his patron fraudulently, is sent back to the prefect of the city to be punished. 12 ¶Lastly, it must be understood that those who administer a guardianship fraudulently must be removed from the guardianship even if they offer adequate security, because the giving of security does not change a malicious purpose, but merely affords the opportunity of plundering the estate for a longer time. We also consider suspect the man whose character is such that he is open to suspicion. Indeed, a guardian or curator who, though poor, is faithful and diligent, is not to be removed as suspect,

units.la: INSTITVTIONVM, SEV ELEMENTORVM D. Iustiniani sacratissimi Principis. LIBER II.
units.tr: THE INSTITUTES, OR ELEMENTS, OF THE MOST SACRED EMPEROR D. JUSTINIAN. BOOK II.

units.la: DE RERVM DIVISIONE, ET {b}adquirendo ipsarum dominio, TITVLVS I.
units.tr: ON THE DIVISION OF THINGS AND THE ACQUISITION OF OWNERSHIP OF THEM. TITLE I.

units.la: SUPERIORE libro de iure per-sonarum expositimus : modo videa-mus de rebus, quae vel in nostro patrimonio,vel extra patrimonium {c}no-strum habentur. Quaedā{d} enim natu-rali iure communia sunt omnium, quaedam publica,quaedam vniuersitatis,quaedam nullius, pleraque singulorum, quae ex variis causis cuique adquiruntur, sicut ex subiectis apparebit.
units.tr: In the previous book we set out the law of persons. Now let us consider things, which are held either within our patrimony or outside it. For some things are common to all by natural law, some are public, some belong to a community, some belong to no one, but most belong to individuals, and these are acquired by various causes, as will appear from what follows.

units.la: 1 ¶Et quidem naturali iure communia sunt omnium hęc: aer, {e}aqua profluēs,& mare,& per hoc littora maris. Nemo {f}igitur ad littus maris accedere prohibetur: dum tamen à villis,& monumentis & ædificiis {g}abstineat: quia non sunt iuris gentium, sicut est mare.
units.tr: 1. By natural law these things are common to all: air, flowing water, the sea, and with the sea its shores. Therefore no one is forbidden to approach the seashore, provided he keeps away from villas, tombs and buildings, because these are not of the law of nations, as the sea is.

units.la: 2 ¶Flumina autem omnia,& portus publica{h} sunt. idcoque ius piscādi{i} omnibus commu-ne est in portu fluminibusque.
units.tr: 2. All rivers and harbours are public. Hence the right of fishing in harbours and rivers is common to all.

units.la: 3 ¶Est autem littus {k}maris, quatenus hybernus fluctus maximus excurrit.
units.tr: 3. The shore of the sea extends as far as the greatest winter wave runs up.

units.la: 4 ¶Riparū quoque vsus {l}publicus est iure gētium, sicut ipsius fluminis. Itaque {m}naues ad eas appellere, funes arboribus ibi natis religare, onus aliquod in his reponere, cuilibet liberū est, sicut per ipsum flumen nauigare. sed proprietas earum illorum est, quorum prędiis hærent. qua de causa arbores quoque in iisdem natę, eorundem sunt.
units.tr: 4. The use of riverbanks too is public by the law of nations, just as the river itself is. So it is open to anyone to moor ships to them, to tie ropes to trees growing there, to set down some load upon them, just as it is to sail along the river itself. But ownership of them belongs to those whose estates they adjoin. For this reason the trees growing on them also belong to the same owners.

units.la: 5 ¶Littorum quoque vsus publicus est, & {n}iuris gentium,sicut & ipsius maris. & ob id cuilibet liberum est casam ibi ponere,in quam se recipiat: sicut retia siccare, & ex mari deducere. proprietas autem eorum potest in telligi nullius esse : sed eiusdem iuris esse, cuius & mare,& quae subiacet mari terra vel arena.
units.tr: 5. The use of the shores too is public and falls under the law of nations, just as the sea itself does. For that reason it is open to anyone to set up a hut there in which to take shelter, or to dry nets and haul them up from the sea. Ownership of the shores can be understood to belong to no one, but to fall under the same law as the sea, and the land or sand that lies beneath the sea.

units.la: 6 ¶ Vniuersitatis sunt,non singulorum, quae in ciui-tatibus sunt theatra,stadia,& si qua alia sunt commūnia ciuitatum. 7 ¶ Nullius aute sunt res sacrae, & religiosae,& sanctae. * quod enim diuini iuris est,id nullius in bonis est. 8 ¶ Sacrae res sunt,q rite per pontifices Deo consecratae sunt: veluti aedes sacrae, & donaria quae rite ad ministerium Dei dedicata sunt: quae etiam per nostra constitutionem alienari & obligari prohibuimus : excepta causa redemptionis captiuorum. Si quis autem auctoritate sua quasi sa-cru sibi constituerit: sacrum non est,sed profanum. Locus autem,in quo aedes sacrae sunt aedificatae:etiā diruto aedificio, sacer adhuc manet,vt & Papinianus scribit. 9 ¶ Religiosum locum vnusquisque sua vo-luntate facit,dum mortuum infert in locum suum. ¶ In communem autem locum purū inuito socio inferre nō licet. ¶ in commune vero sepulchrum etiam inuitis cęteris licet inferre. ¶Itē si alienus vsufructus est: proprietarius placet, nisi consentiente vsufructuario, locum religiosum non facere.¶ In alienum locum cōsentiente domino licet inferre:& licet postea ratū non [?] habuerit, quam illatus est mortuus, tamen locus religiosus fit. 10 ¶Sacrae quoque res veluti muri & portae ciuitatis,¶ quodammodo diuini iuris sunt: & ideo nullius in bonis sunt. Ideo autem muros sanctos dicimus, quia poena capitis constituta est in eos, qui aliquid in muros deliquerint.Ideo & legum eas partes, quibus poenas constituimus aduersus eos, qui contra leges fecerint,sanctiones vocamus. 11 ¶Singulorum autem hominum multis modis res fiunt. quarundam enim rerum dominium nancisci-mur iure naturali, quod (sicut diximus) appellatur ius gentium: quarundam iure ciuili [?]. Com-modius est itaque a vetustiore iure incipere. palam est autem vetustius esse ius naturale, quod cum ipso genere humano rerum natura prodidit. ciuilia autem iura tunc esse coeperunt, cum & ciuitates condi, & magistratus creari,& leges scribi coeperunt. 12 ¶ Fere
units.tr: 6. Things belonging to a community, not to individuals, are the theatres and stadiums in cities, and whatever else is common to cities. 7. Things belonging to no one are sacred, religious and holy things, for what is of divine law is in no one's possession. 8. Sacred things are those which have been duly consecrated to God by the pontiffs, such as sacred buildings and gifts that have been rightly dedicated to the service of God. By our constitution we have also forbidden these to be alienated or pledged, except for the redemption of captives. If anyone, however, on his own authority sets something up for himself as sacred, it is not sacred but profane. The place in which sacred buildings have been erected remains sacred even when the building has been pulled down, as Papinian also writes. 9. Each person makes a place religious by his own will when he carries a dead body into a place of his own. But it is not lawful to carry a corpse into a common place against the will of a partner; into a common tomb, however, it is lawful to carry one even against the will of the others. Likewise, if the usufruct belongs to another, it is held that the owner does not make a place religious without the consent of the usufructuary. Into another's place it is lawful to carry a body with the owner's consent, and even if he afterwards does not ratify it, the place becomes religious once the body has been carried in. 10. Sacred things too, such as the walls and gates of a city, are in a sense of divine law, and therefore are in no one's possession. We call the walls holy because a capital penalty is established against those who offend against the walls. For the same reason we call those parts of the laws in which penalties are set against those who act contrary to the laws sanctions. 11. Things are made the property of individuals in many ways. For we acquire ownership of some things by natural law, which (as we have said) is called the law of nations, and of others by civil law. It is convenient, therefore, to begin with the older law. It is plain that natural law is the older, since the nature of things revealed it together with the human race itself. Civil laws, however, began to exist when cities began to be founded, magistrates to be created, and laws to be written. 12. Almost all wild beasts, birds, fish, and all animals that are born in the sea, the sky and the land, as soon as they have been captured by someone, at once begin by the law of nations to be his. For what belongs to no one before is granted by natural reason to the one who takes possession of it. It makes no difference whether someone captures wild beasts and birds on his own land or on another's. Certainly, one who enters another's land to hunt or fowl can be forbidden by the owner, if the owner prohibits his entry. Whatever of these you have caught is understood to be yours only as long as it is held in your custody. But when it has escaped your custody and has recovered its natural liberty, it ceases to be yours and again becomes the property of whoever seizes it. It is understood to have recovered its natural liberty when it has either escaped your sight, or is in your sight in such a way that pursuing it has become difficult.

units.la: {o} l.41.s. de poenis. {p} octodecim. Vvif. {q} i. causis & titulis cēn formis iustificandi dominij. Mynsing. {r} [illegible, ~24 letters] Th. igitur bestię,& volucres,& pisces,& ||omnia|| animalia,quæ mari,cœlo ,& terra nafcûtur:simulatque ab aliquo capta fuerint,iure gentiū statim illius esse incipiunt. quod enim ante nullius est, id naturali ratione occupanti conceditur.nec interest,feras bestias & volucres vtrum in suo fundo quis capiat,an in alieno. Plane qui alienum fundum ingreditur venandi aut aucupandi gratia: potest à domino,si is prohiberi, ne ingrediatur. Quicquid autem eorum ceperis: eousque tuum esse intelligitur, donec tua custodia coercetur.Cum vero tuam cuaserit custodiam,& in libertatem naturalem sese receperit: tuum esse desinit,& rursus occupantis fit. Naturalem autem libertatem recipere intelligitur,cum vel occupuis tuos effugerit,vel ita fit in cõspectu tuo, vt diffi-cilis fit eius f persequutio. 13 ¶Illud quæsitū est,an si fera bestia ita vulnerata sit, vt capi possit, statim tua esse intelligatur? ||Et|| quibusdam placuit,statim esse tuam: & eousque tuam videri,donec eam perse-quaris. quòd si desieris persequi: desinere esse tuam, & rursus fieri occupantis. Alij verò putauerunt, non aliter tuam esse, quàm si eam ceperis.Sed posteriorē sententiam nos confirmamus, quòd multa accidere soleat, vt eam nõ capias. 14 ¶Apium quoque fera natura est.Itaque,||apes,||q in arbore tua cõsederint, antequam à te alueo includatur, non magis tuæ intelligantur esse, quàm volucres, quæ in arbore tua nidũ fecerint. ideóque si alius eas inclùserit: is earũ dominus erit. Fauos quoque, si quos effecerint, exi-mere quilibet potest. Plane integra re, si præuideris ingredientem fundum tuum, poteris eum iure pro-hibere, ne ingrediatur. Examen quoque, quod ex alueo tuo euolauerit,eousque intelligitur esse tuum, donec in conspectu tuo est,nec difficilis persequutio eius est,alioquin occupatis fit. 15 ¶Pauonũ s quo-que & columbarũ fera natura est. nec ad rè pertinet, quod ex consuetudine euolare & reuolare solent, nã & apes idem faciunt,quarum constat feram esse natu-ram.Cernos quoque quidam ita mansuetos habet, vt in syluam ire, & redire soleant: quorum & ipsorũ feram esse naturam,nemo negat.In iis autem animalibus, quæ ex consuetudine abire & redire ᵃ solet,talis regula comprobaꝑa est:vt eousque tua esse intelli-gantur, donec animum ᵇ reuertendi habeant. nam si reuertendi animum habere desierint:etiam tua esse desinunt, & fiunt occupantium.Reuertendi autem ani-
units.tr: {o} l.41.s. de poenis. {p} eighteen. Vvif. {q} i.e., causes and titles, with the forms of justifying ownership. Mynsing. {r} [illegible, ~24 letters] Th. 13. It has been asked whether, if a wild beast has been wounded so that it can be captured, it is at once understood to be yours. Some have held that it is at once yours, and is understood to be yours for as long as you pursue it; but if you stop pursuing it, it ceases to be yours and becomes again the property of whoever seizes it. Others have thought that it is not yours unless you have actually caught it. But we confirm this latter opinion, because it often happens that you do not catch it. 14. Bees too are of wild nature. Therefore bees that have settled in your tree, before you have enclosed them in a hive, are understood to be no more yours than birds that have built a nest in your tree. So if another encloses them, he will be their owner. Anyone may also take away honeycombs, if the bees have made any. Indeed, while the thing is still whole, if you foresee someone entering your land, you may lawfully forbid him to enter. A swarm that has flown out of your hive is understood to be yours as long as it is in your sight, and pursuit of it is not difficult; otherwise it becomes the property of whoever seizes it. 15. Peacocks s and pigeons are also of wild nature. Nor does it matter that they are accustomed to fly away and return, for bees do the same, and it is agreed that their nature is wild. Some deer are so tame that they are accustomed to go ᵃ away into the woods and return; that their nature too is wild, no one denies. In those animals which are accustomed to go away and return, this rule has been approved: that they are understood to be yours only for as long as they keep the ᵇ intention of returning. For if they cease to have the intention of returning, they also cease to be yours and become the property of those who seize them.

units.la: ᵃ Οὐκ ἐμπορεύονται [?] mum videntur desinere habere tunc,cum reuertendi consuetudine {a} deseruerint.
units.tr: ᵃ [Οὐκ ἐμπορεύονται] they seem to cease having the intention of returning when they have abandoned the habit of returning.

units.la: ¶ 16 Gallinarū autem & anserū non est fera natura. idque ex eo possumus intelligere, quod aliæ sunt gallinæ, quas feras vocamus: item alij sunt anseres, quos feros appellamus. Ideoque si anseres tui, aut gallinæ tuæ, aliquo modo turbati turbatæve euolauerint: licet conspectum tuū effugerint, quocunque tamen loco sint, tui tuæve esse intelligūtur: & qui lucrandi animo ea animalia detinet, furtū {b} comittere {c} intelligitur.
units.tr: 16. Hens and geese, however, are not of wild nature. We can understand this from the fact that there are some hens which we call wild, and likewise there are some geese which we call wild. So if your geese or your hens, having been somehow disturbed, have flown off, then although they have escaped your sight, wherever they are they are understood to be yours; and whoever keeps those animals with intent to gain commits theft.

units.la: ¶ 17 Item ea, quæ ex hostibus capimus, iure gentium statim nostra fiunt: adeo quidem, ut & liberi homines in seruitutem nostram {d} deducātur, qui tamen, si euaserint nostram potestatem, & ad suos reuersi fuerint: pristinum statum recipiunt.
units.tr: 17. Likewise, what we take from enemies becomes ours at once by the law of nations; indeed, even free men are brought into our slavery, who nevertheless, if they escape our power and return to their own people, recover their former status.

units.la: ¶ 18 Item lapilli, & gemmæ, & cætera, quæ in littore maris inueniuntur, iure naturali statim inuentoris siunt.
units.tr: 18. Likewise, pebbles, gems and other things found on the seashore become at once the property of the finder by natural law.

units.la: ¶ 19 Item ea, quæ ex animalibus dominio tuo subiectis nata sunt, eodem iure tibi adquiri rūtur[?].
units.tr: 19 Likewise, those things born from animals subject to your dominion are acquired by you under the same law.

units.la: ¶ 20 Præterea quod per {e}alluuionē agro tuo slumē adiecit, iure gentium tibi adquritur. {*}Est aūt alluuio incrementū latēs. Per alluuionem aūt id videtur adiici, quod ita paulatim adiicitur, ut intelligi nō possit, quantum quoquo tēporis momēto adiiciatur.
units.tr: 20 Moreover, what a river adds to your field by alluvion is acquired for you by the law of nations. Alluvion is a gradual increase of land. What is added by alluvion is that which is added so slowly that one cannot tell how much is added at any given moment of time.

units.la: ¶ 21 Quōd si vis slsúminis de tuo prædio partē aliquī detraxerit, & vicini prēdio attulerit: palam est eā tuā p̄manere. Plane si slogiore tēpore fundo vicini tui heserit, arborésque,quas secū traxit,in eū fundū radices egerint: ex eo tēpore videntur vicini fundo adquisitæ esse.
units.tr: 21 But if a river has torn some part away from your property and carried it onto a neighbour's estate, it is clear that it remains yours. But if after a long time it has attached itself to your neighbour's land, and the trees it carried with it have put down roots in that land, then from that time they are considered to have been acquired by the neighbour's land.

units.la: ¶ 22 Infula,q̈ in mari nata est, (quod raro accidit) occupantis fit. nullius enim esse creditur. At infula in slumine nata (quod frequenter accidit) siquidē mediam partem slu minis tenet: communis {g}est eorum, qui ab vtraque parte prope ripam prædia possidēt:pro modo [?]scilicet[?] latitudinis cuiusque fundi, quæ prope ripam sit.
