Quōd si alteri parti proximior sit: eorum est tantū, qui ab ea parte prope ripam prædia possident. Quōd si aliqua parte diuisum sit slumen, deinde infra vnitum, agrum alicuius in formā infulæ redegerit: eiusdē permanet is ager, cuius & fuerat.
units.tr: 22 An island that arises in the sea (which happens rarely) becomes the property of whoever occupies it, for it is believed to belong to no one. But an island that arises in a river (which happens often): if it occupies the middle of the river, it is common to those who possess estates on either bank near the shore, in proportion to the width of each estate that lies near the bank. But if it lies nearer to one side, it belongs only to those who possess estates near the bank on that side. But if the river, divided at some point and reunited further down, has turned someone's field into the form of an island, that field remains the property of the one to whom it belonged.

units.la: ¶ 23 Quōd si naturali aluco in vniuersum derelicto, ad aliam partem sluere cœperit: prior quidem alueus eorum est, qui prope ripam eius prædia possident: pro modo scilicet latitudinis cuiusque agri, quæ prope ripam sit. nouus autem alueus eius iuris esse incipit, cuius & ipsum slumen est,id est, {h}publicus.Quōd si post aliquod tēpus ad priorē alueum reuersum fuerit flumen : rursus nouus alueus eorū esse incipit, qui prope ripā eius prędia possident.
units.tr: 23 But if a river, having wholly abandoned its natural bed, begins to flow in another direction, the former bed belongs to those who possess estates near its bank, in proportion to the width of each field lying near the bank. The new bed begins to belong to the one to whom the river itself belongs, that is, to the public. But if after some time the river returns to the former bed, the new bed again begins to belong to those who possess estates near its bank.

units.la: 24 ¶Alia sane causa est,si cuius totus ager inundatus fuerit,neque enim *inundatio fundi specie cōmutat. & ob id, si recesserit aqua : palàm est eum fundū eius manere,cuius & fuit.
units.tr: 24 Another case, certainly, is when someone's whole field has been flooded, for inundation does not change the form of the land. Therefore, if the water recedes, it is plain that the field remains the property of the one to whom it belonged.

units.la: 25 ¶Quum ex aliena materia species aliqua fa&a sit ab aliquo: quæri solet, quis eorum naturali ratione dominus sit: verum is,qui fecerit,an potius ,ille , qui materiæ dominus fuerit? vt ecce,si quis ex alienis vuis,aut oliuis,aut spicis vinum,aut oleum,aut frumentum fecerit: aut ex alieno auro,vel argento,vel æere vas aliquod fecerit: vel ex alieno vino & melle mulsum miscuerit: vel ex medicamētis alienis emplastrum aut collyrium composuerit: vel ex aliena lana vestimentum fecerit: vel ex alienis tabulis nauem, vel armarium,vel subsellia fabricauerit. Et post multam Sabinianorum & Proculianorū ambiguitatem, *plaecuit media sententia existimantium , si ea species ad priorem & rudem materiam reduci possit : eum videri dominum esse,qui materiæ dominus fuerit,si nō possit reduci : eum potius intelligi dominum, qui fecerit. vnum autem,vel oleum,aut frumentum ad vuas , vel oliuas, vel spicis reuerti non potest. at ne mulsum quidem ad vinum & mel resolui potest. Quòd si partim ex sua materia, partim ex aliena speciem aliquam fecerit quis: veluti ex suo vino & alieno melle mulsum miscuerit, aut ex suis & alienis medicamentis emplastrum aut collyrium,aut ex sua lana & aliena vestimentum fecerit: dubitandum nō est,hoc casu eum esse dominum qui fecerit: cùm non solùm operam suā dederit, sed & partē eiusdem materiæ præstiterit.
units.tr: 25 When some form has been made by someone out of another's material, the question is usually asked which of them is the owner by natural reason: the one who made it, or rather the one who owned the material? For example, if someone has made wine, oil or grain from another's grapes, olives or ears of corn; or made some vessel from another's gold, silver or bronze; or mixed mulsum from another's wine and honey; or compounded a plaster or eye-salve from another's medicines; or made a garment from another's wool; or built a ship, a cupboard or benches from another's planks. After much disagreement between the Sabinians and the Proculians, the middle opinion of those who judged was approved: if the form can be reduced to its earlier, raw material, the owner of the material is deemed the owner; if it cannot be reduced, the one who made it is rather understood to be the owner. But wine, oil or grain cannot be turned back into grapes, olives or ears of corn, and mulsum cannot even be resolved into wine and honey. But if someone has made a form partly from his own material and partly from another's (for example, mixed mulsum from his own wine and another's honey, or made a plaster or salve from his own and others' medicines, or a garment from his own wool and another's), there is no doubt that in this case the one who made it is the owner, since he has not only given his labour but has also supplied part of the same material.

units.la: 26 ¶Si si tamē alienam purpuram vestimēto suo quis intexuerit: licet pretiosior sit purpura , tamen accessionis vice cedit vestimento : & qui dominus fuit purpurę,aduersus eum,qui vestimen- tū fecit,siue alius. nam ex*instæ[?] res, licet vindicari non possint, codici [?]tamē furibus,& quibusque aliis possessoribus possunt.
units.tr: 26 If someone has woven another's purple into his own garment, then although the purple is more valuable, it nevertheless yields to the garment as an accession, and the former owner of the purple has an action against the one who made the garment, or against any other holder. For things so made, although they cannot be vindicated, can nevertheless be claimed from thieves and from any other possessors.

units.la: 27 ¶Si duorū materiē ex gvo[?]-luntate dominorum confusæ sint: totum id commu- ni fit, quod ex confusione fit. vtriusque commune est: veluti si qui vina sua confuderint, aut massas argenti vel auri conflauerint. Sed & si diuersæ materiæ sint, & ob id propria species facta sit: forte ex vino & mellmulsum, aut ex auro & argento electrū. idem iuris est. nam & hoc casu communem esse speciem non dubitatur. Quod si fortuitu, & non voluntate dominorum confusiae fuerint, vel eiusdem generis materiae, vel diuersae: idem iuris esse placuit.
units.tr: 27 If the materials of two owners have been mixed together by the will of the owners, the whole thing that results from the mixing becomes common: it belongs to both. For example, if they have mixed their wines, or fused masses of silver or gold. But also if the materials are different, and so a distinct form is produced (for instance mulsum from wine and honey, or electrum from gold and silver), the same law applies, for in this case too it is not doubted that the resulting form is common. But if the materials have been mixed by chance and not by the will of the owners, whether of the same kind or of different kinds, it has been held that the same law applies.

units.la: 28 ¶Quod si frumentum Titij frumento tuo mistum fuerit: si quidem ex voluntate vestra, commune est: quia singula corpora, id est, singula grana, quae cuiusque propria fuerunt, ex consensu vestro communicata sunt. Quod si casu id mistum fuerit, vel Titius id miscuerit sine tua voluntate, non videtur commune esse: quia singula corpora in sua substantia durant. Sed nec magis iustis casibus commune fit frumentum, quam grex intelligitur esse communis, si pecora Titij tuis pecoribus mista fuerint. Sed si ab alterutro vestrum totum id frumentum retineatur: in rem quidem actio pro modo frumenti cuiusque competit: arbitrio autem iudicis continetur, vt ipse estimet, quale cuiusque frumentū fuerit.
units.tr: 28 But if Titius's grain has been mixed with your grain: if indeed this happened by your mutual consent, it is common, because the individual bodies, that is the individual grains, which were each one's own, have been shared by your agreement. But if it was mixed by chance, or Titius mixed it without your consent, it does not seem to be common, because the individual bodies remain in their own substance. Yet grain does not become common in such accidental cases any more than a herd is understood to be common when Titius's cattle have been mixed with yours. But if the whole of that grain is kept by one of you, an action in rem lies for each one's share in proportion to his grain, but it rests with the judge's discretion to estimate what quality each grain was.

units.la: 29 ¶Cum in suo solo aliquis ex aliena materia aedificauerit, ipse intelligitur dominus aedificij: quia omne, quod solo inaedificatur, solo cedit. Nec tamen ideo is, qui materiae dominus fuerat, desinit dominus eius esse: sed tantisper neque vindicare eam potest, neque ad exhibendum de ea re agere, propter legem duodecim tabularum, qua caue-tur, ne quis tignum alienum aedibus suis iunctum eximere cogatur, sed duplum pro eo praestet per actionem, quae vocatur de tigno iuncto. Appellatione autem tigni omnis materia significatur, ex qua aedificia fiunt. Quod ideo prouisum est, ne aedificia rescindi necesse sit. Quod sit aliqua ex causa dirutum sit aedificium, poterit materiae dominus, si non fuerit duplum iam consequutus, tunc eam vindicare, & ad exhibendum de ea re agere.
units.tr: 29 When someone has built on his own soil with another's material, he is understood to be the owner of the building, because whatever is built into the soil yields to the soil. Nor, however, does the owner of the material cease to be its owner on that account; but for the time being he can neither vindicate it nor bring an action for exhibition concerning it, on account of the Law of the Twelve Tables, which provides that no one may be compelled to remove a beam joined to his building that belongs to another; instead he pays double its value by the action called "concerning a joined beam." By the word "beam" is meant all material from which buildings are made. This was provided so that buildings need not be torn down. If, for some reason, the building has been demolished, the owner of the material, if he has not already recovered double, may then vindicate it and bring an action for exhibition concerning it.

units.la: 30 ¶Ex diuerso, si quis in alieno solo ex sua materia domū aedificauerit, illius fit domus, cuius & solum est. Sed hoc casu materiae dominus proprietatem eius amittit: quia voluntate eius intelligitur esse alienata, vtique si non ignorabat se in alieno solo aedificare. & ideo licet dirutā sit domus, materiam tamen vindicare non potest. Certe illud constat, si in possessione constituto aedificatore, soli dominus petat domum suam esse, nec soluat pretium materiae, & mercedes fabrorum: posse eum per exceptionem doli mali repelli: vtique si bonae fidei possessor fuerit, qui aedificauit. Nam scienti alienum solum esse, potest obiici culpa,quòd ædificaue-rit temere in eo solo, quod intelligebat alienū esse {4}.
units.tr: 30 Conversely, if someone has built a house on another's land from his own material, the house belongs to the owner of the soil. But in this case the owner of the material loses his ownership of it, because it is understood to have been alienated by his will, especially if he did not know that he was building on another's land. And so, even if the house has been demolished, he cannot vindicate the material. It is certainly established that if the builder is in possession and the owner of the soil claims the house as his own, without paying the price of the material and the workmen's wages, the builder can be repelled by the exception of fraud, especially if the builder was a possessor in good faith. For against one who knew the soil was another's, fault can be objected: that he built rashly on land he knew belonged to someone else.

units.la: 31 ¶Si Titius alienam platam in solo suo posuerit, ipsius erit. Et ex diuerso si Titius suam plantam in Mæuij solo posuerit,Mæuij planta erit: si modo v-troque casu radices egerit. ante enim, quàm radices egerit,eius permanet,cuius fuerat.Adeo autem ex eo tempore,quo radices egerit planta, proprietas eius commutatur: vt si vicini arbor ita terram Titij præ-servit, vt in eius fundum radices egerit: Titij effici ar-borem dicamus,ratio enim{b} non permittit,vt alterius arbor esse intelligatur, quàm cuius in fundum radi-ces egerit. Et ideo prope confinium arbor posita, si etiam in vicini fundum radices egerit,{c} comunis fit.
units.tr: 31 If Titius has planted another's plant in his own soil, it will be his. And conversely, if Titius has planted his own plant in Maevius's soil, it will be Maevius's plant, provided that in either case it has put down roots. For before it has put down roots, it remains the property of the one to whom it belonged. Indeed, from the time the plant has put down roots, its ownership is changed: so that if a neighbour's tree has leaned over Titius's land so that its roots have gone into his field, we say the tree becomes Titius's, for reason does not allow a tree to be understood as belonging to anyone other than the one into whose field its roots have gone. And so a tree planted near the boundary, if it also puts roots into the neighbour's field, becomes common.

units.la: 32 ¶Qua ratione aute plante, quæ terræ coalescunt, solo cedunt,eadem ratione frumenta quoque, quæ sata sunt,solo cedere intelligutur.Ceterùm sicut is, qui in alieno solo ædificauit: si ab eo dominus petat ædificium, defendi potest per exceptionem doli mali secundum ea,quæ diximus:ita eiusdem{n} exceptionis auxilio tutus esse potest is, qui alienū fundū sua im-pensa, ‖bona fide‖cóseuit[?]. 33 ¶Litere quoque,licet aurex sint, perinde chartis membranisve{d} cedūt, ac solo cedere solent ea, quæ inædificantur, aut infe-runtur,ideoque si in chartis membranisve tuis car-men,vel historiam, vel orationem Titius scripserit: huius corporis non Titius, sed tu dominus esse vide-ris. Sed si à Titio petas{e} tuos libros tuasve{f} membranas,nec impensas scripturæ soluere paratus fis:potest rit se Titius defendere per exceptionem doli mali, vtique si earum chartarum membranarumve possessi-bionem bona fide nactus est. 34 ¶Si quis in aliena tabula pinxerit, quida{g} putat tabulâ pictura cedere: aliis{h} videtur, pictura, qualiscunque sit, tabulæ ce-dere: sed nobis videtur melius {+} esse, tabulam pictu-ræ cedere. Ridiculum est enim picturam Apellis vel Parrhasij in accessionem vilissimæ tabulæ cedere. Vnde si a domino tabulæ imaginem possidente, is, qui pinxit,eam petat, nec soluat pretium tabulæ,po-terit per exceptionem doli mali submoueri. At si is qui pinxit, ‖ eam ‖ possideat:consequens est, vt vti-lis actio domino tabulæ aduersus eum detur: quo ca-su si non soluat impensam picturæ, poterit per exce-ptionem doli mali repelli,vtique{i} si bona fide possef-sor fuerit ille, qui picturam imposuit. Illud enim pa-tàm est,quod siue is,qui pinxit, subripuit tabulas, &ue alius : comperit domino tabularum furti actio.
units.tr: 32 By the same reasoning by which plants that take root in the ground pass to the owner of the soil, the sown grain too is understood to pass to the soil. Moreover, just as a man who built on another's land can be defended, if the owner sues him for the building, by the plea of fraud (exceptio doli mali), according to what we have said, so too the man who cultivated another's field at his own expense, in good faith, can be safe by the help of the same plea. 33 Letters too, even though they are golden, pass to the paper or parchment just as the things that are built upon or brought onto land usually pass to the land. So if Titius has written a poem, a history or a speech on your paper or parchment, you are seen to be the owner of that writing, not Titius. But if you sue Titius for your books or your parchment, and you are not prepared to pay for the writing, Titius can defend himself by the plea of fraud, especially if he obtained possession of those papers or parchment in good faith. 34 If someone paints on another's panel, some think the picture passes to the panel, but others hold that whatever the picture is, it passes to the panel. For our part, we think it better that the panel passes to the picture. It would be absurd for a painting by Apelles or Parrhasius to become an accessory of a very cheap board. Hence, if the owner of the panel, who possesses the image, is sued by the painter for it, and does not pay the price of the panel, the painter can be repelled by the plea of fraud. But if the painter himself possesses it, it follows that an actio utilis is granted to the owner of the panel against him. In that case, if he does not pay the cost of the painting, he can be repelled by the plea of fraud, especially if he who applied the picture was a possessor in good faith. For it is plain that whether the painter or someone else stole the panels, the action for theft lies to the owner of the panels.

units.la: 35 ¶Si quis à non domino, quem dominum esse crediderit, bona fide fundum emerit, vel ex donatione, aliáve qualibet iusta causa æque bona fide acceperit: naturali ratione placuit fructus,quos percepit,eius esse cultura & cura. Et ideo si postea dominus fundum vindicet, de fructibus ab eo consumptis agere non poterit. Et vero qui alienum fundum scicus [?] possederit, non idem concessum est:itaque cum fundo etiam fructus,licet consumpti sint, cogitur restituere.
units.tr: 35 If someone in good faith buys a field from a non-owner whom he believed to be the owner, or in good faith receives it by gift or by any other just cause, the fruits he has gathered are his, as the cultivation and care of them are, by natural reason. Therefore, if the owner later claims the field, he cannot sue for the fruits already consumed. But one who knowingly possesses another's field is not granted the same indulgence, so that he is compelled to restore the fruits along with the field, even if they have been consumed.

units.la: 36 ¶Is vero ad quem vsufructus fundi pertinet, nō aliter fructuum dominus efficitur, quàm si ipse eos perceperit. Et ideo licet maturis fructibus, nondum tamen perceptis, decesserit: ad heredes eius non pertinent, sed domino proprietatis adquiruntur. Eadem fere & de colono dicuntur.
units.tr: 36 But one to whom the usufruct of a farm belongs does not become owner of the fruits unless he himself has gathered them. So if he dies with ripe fruits not yet gathered, they do not pass to his heirs but are acquired by the owner of the property. Much the same is said of a tenant farmer.

units.la: 37 ¶In pecudum fructu etiam foetus est, sicuti lac, pilus, & lana. itaque agni, hordi, & vituli, & equuli, & suculi statim naturali iure domini fructuarij sunt. Partus vero ancillæ in fructu non est, itaque ad dominum proprietatis pertinet. absurdum enim videbatur, hominem in fructu esse: quum omnes fructus rerum natura gratia hominis comparauerit.
units.tr: 37 In the fruit of animals the offspring is included, as are milk, hair and wool. So lambs, kids, calves, foals and piglets belong at once, by natural right, to the usufructuary. But the offspring of a female slave is not part of the fruit, so it belongs to the owner of the property. For it seemed absurd that a human being should be part of the fruit, since nature has produced all the fruits of things for the sake of man.

units.la: 38 ¶Sed si gregis vsufructum quis habeat, in locum demortuorum capitum ex foetu fructuarius submittere debet,(vt & Iuliano visum est) & in vinearum demortuarum vel arborum locum, alias debet substituere. recte enim colere, & quasi bonus paterfamilias vti debet.
units.tr: 38 But if someone has the usufruct of a flock, the usufructuary must replace dead animals from the offspring (as Julian also held), and must substitute other vines or trees for dead ones. For he must cultivate properly and use the property as a good householder would.

units.la: 39 ¶Thesauros, quos quis in loco suo inuenerit, dimus Hadrianus naturalem æquitatem sequutus, ci concesserit,qui eos inuenerit. Idemque statuit,si quis in sacro, aut religioso loco fortuito casu inuenerit. At si quis in alieno loco,non data ad hoc opera,sed fortuitu inuenerit: dimidium domino soli concessit,& dimidium inuentori.Et conuenienter, siquis in Cesaris loco inuenerit, dimidiu inuentoris,& dimidium esse Cæsaris statuit. Cui conueniens est vt si quis in fiscali loco,vel publico vel ciuitatis inuenerit,dimidium ipsius esse debeat, & dimidium fisci,vel ciuitatis.
units.tr: 39 Treasure which someone finds in his own place, the deified Hadrian, following natural equity, granted to the finder. He decided the same if someone found it by chance in a sacred or religious place. But if someone found it by chance in another's place, not by working for that purpose, he granted half to the owner of the soil and half to the finder. Accordingly, if someone found it on Caesar's land, he ruled that half went to the finder and half to Caesar. In keeping with this, if someone finds it on fiscal land, or on public land or on the land of a city, half should be his and half should go to the treasury or the city.

units.la: 40 ¶Per traditionem quoque iure naturali res nobis adquiruntur: nihil enim tam conueniens est naturali æquitati, quàm voluntatem domini volentis rem suam in alium transferre,ratam haberi.& ideo cuiuscunque generis sit corporalis res,tradi potest, & à domino tradita aliena-
units.tr: 40 Things are also acquired by us through delivery, by natural right. For nothing is so consonant with natural equity as that the will of an owner who wishes to transfer his thing to another should be held valid. Therefore, whatever kind of corporeal thing it is, it can be delivered, and once delivered by the owner it is alienated.

units.la: ᵃ nota duas: Bonæ fidei causa, errore & iustum titulum. Vnif. alienatur.Itaque stipédiaria quoq.& tributaria prædia eodé modo alienantur.Vocátur autè stipendiaria & tributaria prædia, quæ in prouinciis fiunt, inter quæ,necnon & Italica prędia,ex nostra constitutione {a}nulla est differentia. sed si quideni ex causa donationis aut dotis,aut qualibet alia ex causa tradantur, sine dubio transferuntur.
units.tr: a Note two: a cause of good faith, error, and a just title. Uniform... It is alienated. Thus stipendiary and tributary lands are alienated in the same way. Lands are called stipendiary and tributary when they are situated in the provinces; by our constitution there is no difference between these and Italian lands. But if they are delivered from a cause of gift, or of dowry, or for any other cause, they undoubtedly pass.

units.la: 41 ¶Venditæ verò res & traditæ,non aliter emptori adquirùtur,quàm,si is venditori pretium soluerit, vel alio {b}modo ei satis-fecerit: veluti expromissore aut pignore dato. quod quanquam cauetur ex lege duodecim tabularum,tamen recte dicitur & iure gentium, id est iure naturali,id effici. sed si is,qui vendidit, fidè emptoris sequutus fuerit,dicendū est, statim rem emptoris fieri.
units.tr: 41 Things sold and delivered, however, are not acquired by the buyer unless he has paid the seller the price or otherwise satisfied him, for instance by giving a surety or a pledge. Although this is provided for by the law of the Twelve Tables, it is rightly said to take effect also by the law of nations, that is by natural law. But if the seller has relied on the good faith of the buyer, it must be said that the thing becomes the buyer's at once.

units.la: 42 ¶Nihil autem interest, vtrùm ipse dominus tradat alicui rem suam, an voluntate eius alius, ||cui eius rei possessio permissa sit.||
units.tr: 42 It makes no difference whether the owner himself delivers his thing to someone, or someone else does so by the owner's will, the person to whom possession of that thing has been permitted.

units.la: 43 ¶Qua ratione, si cui "libera vniuersorū negotiorum administratio pmissa fuerit àdomino,isque ex his negotiis rè vedi-derit & tradiderit: faciet eā accipientis.
units.tr: 43 By the same reasoning, if the owner has granted someone free administration of all his affairs, and that person has sold and delivered things from those affairs, he makes them the property of the recipient.

units.la: 44 ¶In-terdum etiā sine traditione {c}nuda voluntas domini sufficit ad rem transferendam:veluti si rem,quam tibi aliquis commodauerit, aut locauerit, aut apud te deposuerit: ||postea aut vendiderit {d}tibi,|| aut donauerit, ||aut dotis nomine dederit||. Quamuis enim ex ea causa tibi eam non tradiderit:eo tamè ipso, quod patitur tuam esse statim tibi adquiritur proprietas, perinde ac si eo nomine tibi tradita fuisset.
units.tr: 44 Sometimes even without delivery the bare will of the owner suffices to transfer a thing: for example, if someone has lent you a thing, or let it out to you, or deposited it with you, and afterwards sells it to you, or gives it to you, or gives it as a dowry. For although he has not delivered it to you on that account, yet by the very fact that he allows it to be yours, ownership is at once acquired by you, just as if it had been delivered to you under that title.

units.la: 45 ¶Item si quis merces in horreo depositas vendiderit, simul atque {e}clauës horrei tradiderit emptori, trăsfert proprietatem mercium ad emptorem.
units.tr: 45 Likewise, if someone sells goods stored in a warehouse, he transfers ownership of the goods to the buyer as soon as he hands over the keys of the warehouse to him.

units.la: 46 ¶Hoc amplius, interdum & in incertam personam collata voluntas domini trăsfert rei proprietatem: vt ecce,prætores & consules,cum missilia ia-ctant in {f}vulgus,ignorant {g}quod eorum quisque sit excepturus: & tamen quia volunt quod quisque ac-ceperit, eius esse: statim eum dominum efficiunt.
units.tr: 46 Moreover, the owner's will, directed at an uncertain person, sometimes also transfers ownership of a thing. For instance, when praetors and consuls throw largesse among the crowd, they do not know which person will catch which item; yet because they want whatever each one receives to be his, they make him the owner at once.

units.la: 47 ¶Qua ratione verius esse videtur, si rem pro {h}derelicto à domino habitá occupauerit quis,statim eum dominum effici. Pro derelicto autem habetur, quòd dominus ea mente abiecerit,vt id ||in numero|| rerum suarum esse nolit: ideòque statim dominus e-ius esse desinit.
units.tr: 47 By the same reasoning it seems more correct that if someone takes possession of a thing that the owner has held as abandoned, he at once becomes its owner. A thing is held as abandoned when the owner has cast it off with the intention of not wishing it to remain among his possessions; therefore it at once ceases to be his.

units.la: 48 ¶Alia sanè causa est earum rerum, quæ in tempestate {i}leuandæ nauis causa ei-ciuntur. hæ enim dominorum permanent: quia pa-[illegible, ~6 letters] iam est eas non eo animo eüci, quòd quis eas habere. nolit, sed quo magis cum ipsa navi maris periculum effugiat. Qua de causa, si quis eas fluctibus expulsas, vel etiam in ipso mari nactus, lucrandi animo abstulerit, furtum committit. Nec longe videntur discedere ab his quae de rheda currente non intelligentibus dominis{a} cadunt.
units.tr: 48 The case is different for things thrown out to lighten a ship in a storm. These remain the property of their owners, because it is clear that they were not thrown out by someone who was unwilling to keep them, but so that he might escape the danger of the sea along with the ship. For this reason, if someone takes them, having found them cast up by the waves or even in the sea itself, with a view to gain, he commits theft. Nor do these seem to differ much from those things that fall from a moving cart without the knowledge of their owners.

units.la: DE REBUS CORPORALIBUS, & incorporalibus. TIT. II.
units.tr: On corporeal and incorporeal things. TIT. II.

units.la: QUAEDAM praeterea res corporales sunt, quaedam incorporales. 1 ¶ Corporales hae sunt, quae tangi possunt: veluti fundus, homo, vestis, aurum, argentum, & denique aliae res innumerabiles.
units.tr: Some things, moreover, are corporeal and others incorporeal. 1 ¶ Corporeal things are those that can be touched: for example a farm, a man, a garment, gold, silver, and, in short, countless other things.

units.la: 2 ¶ Incorporales autē sunt, quae tangi non possunt: qualia sunt ea, quae in iure{b} cōsistunt: sicut hereditas, usfructus, usus || & || obligationes quoquo modo contractae. Nec ad rem pertinet, quod in hereditate res corporales continentur: nam & fructus qui ex fundo percipiuntur, corporales sunt: & id, quod ex aliqua obligatione nobis debetur, plerumque corporale est: veluti fundus, homo, pecunia. nam ipsum ius hereditatis, & ipsum ius utendi fruendi, & ipsum ius obligationis incorporale est.
units.tr: 2 ¶ Incorporeal things, however, are those that cannot be touched, such as those that consist in law: an inheritance, usufruct, use, and obligations contracted in any way. Nor is it relevant that corporeal things are contained in an inheritance. For the fruits gathered from a farm are corporeal, and what is owed to us under some obligation is usually corporeal too: a farm, a man, money. But the right of inheritance itself, the right of using and enjoying, and the right of obligation itself are incorporeal.

units.la: 3 ¶ Eodem numero sunt intra praediorum urbanorum, || & rusticorum, quae etiam seruitutes vocantur.
units.tr: 3 ¶ In the same class are the easements of urban and rural estates, which are also called servitudes.
On Servitudes of Estates, Title III.

units.la: RUSTICORUM{c} praediorum iura sunt haec: iter, actus, via, aquae ductus. Iter est ius eundi ambulandi hominis{d}, non etiam iumentum agendi, || vel vehiculum ||. Actus est ius agendi vel iumentum ||, vel vehiculum. Ita qui habet iter, actu non habet: qui actum habet, & iter habet, || eoque uti potest || etiam sine iumento. Via est ius eundi & agendi & ambulandi: nam & iter & actum via in se continet. Aquaeductus est ius aquae ducendae per fundum alienum.
units.tr: The rights of rustic estates are these: iter, actus, via, and aquaeductus. Iter is the right of a person to go and walk, not also the right to drive a beast of burden or a vehicle. Actus is the right to drive a beast of burden or a vehicle. So whoever has iter does not thereby have actus, but whoever has actus also has iter, and can use it even without a beast. Via is the right to go, to drive, and to walk, for via contains both iter and actus within itself. Aquaeductus is the right to lead water through another's land.

units.la: 1 ¶ Praediorum urbanorum seruitutes sunt haec, quae aedificiis inhaerent{e}, ideo urbanorum praediorum dicuntur, quoniam{f} aedificia omnia, urbana praedia appel-
units.tr: 1 ¶ The servitudes of urban estates are these, which adhere to buildings. They are so called urban estates because all buildings are called urban estates

units.la: {a} & iacent. l. 43.§. qui alie-num ff.de fur-tis.
units.tr: {a} and lie. l. 43 §. qui alienum, ff. de furtis.

units.la: {b} huius distin-ctionis beneficio una & eadem res corpore tenus, uni: iuris vero interuentu, alteri utilis esse potest. de quo vide Oldendorp Classe. 2. actione 6. in pr.
units.tr: {b} By the benefit of this distinction, one and the same thing can be useful to one person in respect of the body itself, and to another in respect of right by intervention. On this see Oldendorp, Classe 2, actione 6, in principio.

units.la: {c} quomodo ab urbano rustico differat. v.l.16 Cod. de praedijs & dijs
units.tr: {c} How it differs from the rustic. See l. 16 Cod. de praedijs & dijs.
{d} l. 1, l. 7, l. 8 ff. de servitutibus rusticorum praediorum.
{e} l. 1 ff. communia praediorum.

units.la: {f} l.198.ff.de verb.sig. lamus, etsi in villa ædificata sint . Item vrbanorum prædiorum seruitutes sunt,vt vicinus onera vicini sustineat: vt in parietē eius liceat vicino tignum immittere:vt stillicidium vel flumen recipiat quis in ædes suas,vel in aream,vel in cloacam :ne altius quis tollat ædes suas , ne luminibus vicini officiat.
units.tr: {f} l. 198 ff. de verborum significatione: even if they are built in the country. Likewise the servitudes of urban estates are these: that a neighbour bears the burdens of his neighbour, so that it is lawful for a neighbour to insert a beam into his wall; that one receives into one's house, or into the courtyard, or into the drain, the rainwater dripping from the eaves or the flow of water; and that one does not raise one's house higher, lest it obstruct the light of the neighbour.

units.la: 2 ¶ Inter rusticorum prædiorum seruitutes quidā cōputari recte putant aquæ haustū, pecoris ad aquā adpulsum, ius pascendi, calcis coquendæ, arenæ fodiendæ. 3 ¶ Ideo autem hæ seruitutes prædiorum appellantur, quoniam sine prædiis cōstitui nō possunt. Neminem enim potest seruitutem adquirere vrbani vel rustici prædij, nisi qui habet prædiū. 4 ¶ Si quis velit vicino aliquod ius constituere: pactionibus atque stipulationibus id efficere debet. Potest etiā testamento quis heredē suum damnare ne altius tollat ædes suas,ne luminibus ædiū vicini officiat:vel vt pariatur eum tignum in parietem suum immittere, stillicidiumve aduersus eum habere: vel vt patiatur eum per fundum ire,agere,aquamve ex eo ducere.
units.tr: 2 ¶ Some rightly reckon among the servitudes of rustic estates the drawing of water, the driving of cattle to water, the right of pasture, the right to burn lime, and the right to dig sand. 3 ¶ These are called servitudes of estates because they cannot be established without estates. For no one can acquire a servitude over an urban or rustic estate unless he himself has an estate. 4 ¶ If someone wishes to grant a neighbour some right, he must do so by pacts and stipulations. A person may also, by his will, charge his heir not to raise his house higher, not to obstruct the light of his neighbour's building, or to allow the neighbour to insert a beam into his wall or to have a rainwater drip against him; or to allow him to go or drive across the estate, or to lead water from it.
OF USUFRUCT, TITLE IV.

units.la: SVSFRVCTVS est ius alienis rebus vtendi fruendi salua rerū substantia. Est autem ius in corpore: quo sublato,& ipsum tolli necesse est. 1 ¶ Vsufructus à proprietate separatione recipit: idque pluribus modis accidit,vt ecce si quis vsumfructum alicui legauerit.nam heres nudam habet proprietatem,legatarius vero vsumfructum. Et contra,si fundum legauerit deducto vsufructu:legatarius nudam habet proprietatem:heres vero vsumfructu. Item alij vsumfructum,alij deducto eo fundum legare potest.Sine testamento vero si quis velit vsumfructum alij constituere: pactionibus & stipulationibus id efficere debet. Ne tamen in vniuersum inutiles essent proprietates, semper abscedente vsufructu: placuit certis modis extingui vsumfructum,& ad proprietatem reuerti. 2 ¶ Constituitur autem vsufructus non tantum in fundo & ædibus,verumetiam in seruis,& iumentis , & cæteris rebus: exceptis iis,quæ ipso vsu consumuntur. Nam hæc res neque naturali ratione, neque ciuili recipiunt vsumfructu. quo ‖ ia ‖ numero sunt vinum,oleum, frumentum, vestimenta, quibus proxima est pecunia numerata: namque ipso viu aisidua permutatione quodammodo extinguitur. Sed vtilitatis causa senatus censuit posse etiam earum rerum viumfructum constitui: vt tamen eo nomine heredi vtiliter caueatur {a}Itaque si pecuniae vsusfructus legatus sit: ita datur legatario, vt eius fiat, & legatarius satisdet heredi de tanta pecunia restituenda, si morietur, aut capite minuetur. Caeterae quoque res ita tradun-ur legatario, vt eius fiant: sed aestimatis his, satisdatur{b} vt si moriatur, aut capite minuatur, tanta pecunia restituatur, quanti hae fuerint aestimatae. Ergo senatus non fecit quidem ea rerum rerum usumfructu m,(nec enim poterat) sed per cautionem{c} quasi usufructu constituit.
units.tr: Usufruct is the right of using and enjoying the things of another, with the substance of the things preserved. It is a right in the body of the thing, and when this is removed, the usufruct itself must necessarily be removed too. (1) Usufruct admits of separation from ownership, and this happens in several ways: for example, if someone bequeaths the usufruct to another, for the heir then holds the bare ownership, and the legatee holds the usufruct. And conversely, if someone bequeaths the land with the usufruct deducted, the legatee holds the bare ownership and the heir holds the usufruct. Likewise one person may bequeath the usufruct and another the land with it deducted. Without a will, if someone wishes to constitute a usufruct for another, he must do so by agreements and stipulations. Yet so that ownerships should not become wholly useless, with the usufruct always falling away, it has been settled that the usufruct is extinguished by certain means and reverts to the ownership. (2) A usufruct may be constituted not only over land and buildings, but also over slaves, beasts of burden and other things, except those which are consumed by the very use. For these things admit of usufruct neither by natural reason nor by civil law. Among them are wine, oil, grain, clothing, and, closest to these, coined money; for these are in a sense extinguished by their very use through constant exchange. But for the sake of usefulness the Senate decreed that a usufruct of these things also may be constituted, provided that the heir is properly secured on this account. Thus, if a usufruct of money has been bequeathed, it is given to the legatee so that it becomes his, and the legatee gives security to the heir for restoring that sum of money if he dies or suffers loss of status. Other things too are handed over to the legatee so that they become his; but after they have been appraised, security is given that, if he dies or suffers loss of status, a sum equal to their appraised value will be restored. Therefore the Senate did not indeed create a usufruct of these things (for it could not), but by means of security it constituted something like a usufruct.

units.la: 3 Hinc autem ususfructus morte usufructuarii, & duabus capitis deminutionibus maxima & media, & non utendo per modum & tempus: quae omnia nostra{d} statuit constitutio. Item finitur ususfructus, si domino proprietatis ab usufructuario cedatur: (nam cedendo extraneo: nihil agitur) vel ex contrario, si usufructuarius proprietatem rei adquisierit: quae res{e} consolidatio appellatur. Eo amplius constat, si aedes incendio consumptae fuerint, vel etiam terraemotu, vel vitio suo corruerint: extinguitur usumfructum, & ne aree{f} f quidem usufructum deberi.
units.tr: (3) A usufruct is ended by the death of the usufructuary, by the two capitis deminutiones, maximal and medial, and by not using it according to the manner and time; all these things our constitution has established. Likewise a usufruct ends if it is ceded to the owner of the ownership by the usufructuary (for ceding it to a stranger accomplishes nothing), or conversely, if the usufructuary acquires the ownership of the thing; this is called consolidation. Moreover, it is settled that if a building has been consumed by fire, or even by an earthquake, or has collapsed through its own defect, the usufruct is extinguished, and not even the site is owed as usufruct.

units.la: 4 Cum autem finitus fuerit totus ususfructus: reuertitur scilicet ad proprietatem, & ex eo tempore nudae proprietatis dominus incipit plenam in re habere potestatem.
units.tr: (4) When the whole usufruct has ended, it of course reverts to the ownership, and from that time the owner of the bare ownership begins to have full power over the thing.
Of Use and Habitation.
TITLE V.

units.la: ISDEM illis modis,quibus usufructus constituitur,etiam nudus usus constitui solet: isdemque illis modis finitur, quibus & ususfructus desinit.
units.tr: By the same modes by which usufruct is created, bare use is usually also created; and it is ended by the same modes by which usufruct also ceases.

units.la: 1 Minus autem iuris est in usu,quam in usufructu nam is, qui fundi nudum habet usum, nihil ulterius habere intelligitur, quam ut oleribus, pomis,floribus, foeno, stramentis, & lignis ad usum cotidianum utatur{h}in eoque fundo hactenus ei morari licet, ut neque domino fundi molestus sit{i} , neque iis, per quos opera rustica fiunt, impedimento: nec vlli alii ius,quod habet, aut vendere, aut gratis{k} concedere potest: quum is, qui usumfructum habet, possit hæc omnia facere. ‖
units.tr: 1. There is, however, less right in use than in usufruct. For he who has the bare use of an estate is understood to have nothing further than to use vegetables, fruit, flowers, hay, straw and wood for daily needs; and he may stay on that estate only so far as he is not troublesome to the owner of the estate, nor an obstacle to those by whom the farm work is done. Nor can he sell or freely grant to anyone else the right he has; whereas the one who holds the usufruct can do all these things.

units.la: 2 ¶Item is, qui ædium vsum habet, hactenus ius habere intelligitur, vt ipse tantum inhabitet, nec hoc iu- ad alium trans-ferre possit. & vix receptum esse videtur, vt hospitē ei recipere liceat: & cum vxore, liberisque suis, item libertis: necnon personis aliis liberis, quibus nō minus, quàm serui vtitur, habitandi ius habeat. Et conuenienter, si ad mulierem vsus ædium pertineat, cum marito ei habitare{4} liceat.
units.tr: 2. Likewise, he who has the use of a house is understood to have a right only so far that he himself alone may live in it, and he cannot transfer this right to another. And it seems scarcely accepted that he may receive a guest, along with his wife and children, and likewise freedmen, and also other free persons, whom he has a right to house no less than he uses slaves. And accordingly, if the use of a house pertains to a woman, she may be allowed to live there with her husband.

units.la: 3 ¶Item is, ad quem serui vsus pertinet, ipse tantum opera atque ministerio eius vti potest: ad alium vero nullo modo ius suum transferre ei concessum est. Idem scilicet iuris est & in iumento.
units.tr: 3. Likewise, he to whom the use of a slave pertains may use only the slave's own labour and service; but it is by no means permitted for him to transfer his right to another. The same law applies also to a beast of burden.

units.la: 4 ¶Sed & si pecorum, vel ouium vsus legatus sit: neque lacte, neque agnis, neque lana vtetur vsuarius: quia ea in fructu sunt. Plane ad stercorandum agru.suum pecoribus vti potest.
units.tr: 4. But even if the use of flocks or sheep has been bequeathed, the user will not use the milk, the lambs or the wool, because these belong to the fruits. Clearly, however, he may use the flocks to manure his field.

units.la: 5 ¶Sed si cui habitatio legata, sine aliquo modo constituta sit, neque vsus videtur, neque vsufructus, sed quasi{b} proprium aliquod ius: quanquam habitationem ha-benribus, propter rerum vtilitatem, secundum Marcelli sententiam nostra{c} decisione promulgata permisimus non solum in ea degere, sed etiam aliis{d} lo-care.
units.tr: 5. But if habitation has been bequeathed to someone without any further specification, it seems to be neither use nor usufruct, but rather some peculiar right; although, by our decision published for the sake of the usefulness of the thing, following the opinion of Marcellus, we have permitted those having habitation not only to dwell in it but also to let it to others.

units.la: 6 ¶Hæc de seruitutibus, & vsufructu, & vsu, & habitatione dixisse sufficiat. De hereditatibus autem & obligationibus, suis locis proponemus. Expositis summatim quibus modis iure gentium res adquiruntur: modo videamus, quibus modis legitimo & ciuili iure adquiruntur.
units.tr: 6. Let it suffice to have said these things about servitudes, usufruct, use and habitation. Concerning inheritances and obligations, we will set them out in their proper places. Having summarily explained by what modes things are acquired by the law of nations, let us now see by what modes they are acquired by the civil and statutory law.

units.la: DE VSUCAPIONIBVS, {e}ET LONG-gi temporis PRÆSCRIPTIONIBVS, TIT. VI.
units.tr: ON USUCAPIONS AND PRESCRIPTIONS OF LONG TIME, TIT. VI.

units.la: I[?]VRE ciuili constitutum fuerat, vt qui bona fide ab eo, qui dominus non erat, cum crederet eum dominum esse, rem emerit, vel ex donatione, aliaue quauis iusta causa acceperit, is eam rem, si mobilis erat, anno vbique vno: si immobilis, biennio tantùm in Italico solo vsucaperet, ne rerum dominia in incerto essent. Et quum hoc placitum erat, putantibus antiquioribus, dominis sufficere ad inquirendas res suas præfata tempora: nobis melior sententia re-sedit [?], ne domini maturius suis rebus defraudentur, neque certo loco beneficium hoc concludatur. & ideo constitutionem super hoc promulgauimus, qua cautum est, vt res ꝗidem mobiles, per triennium: immobiles vero per longi temporis possessionem (id est, inter præsentes decennio, inter absentes viginti annis) vsucapiantur, & his modis nō solum in Italia, sed etiam in omni terra, quæ nostro imperio gubernatur, dominia rerum iusta causa possessionis præcedente adquirantur.
units.tr: By the civil law it was laid down that whoever bought a thing in good faith from one who was not its owner, believing him to be the owner, or received it by gift or by any other just cause, should acquire it by usucapion: a movable thing in one year wherever it was, an immovable thing in two years only on Italian soil, so that ownership of things should not remain uncertain. While this rule stood, the older jurists thought these periods enough for owners to recover their property. But a better opinion has prevailed with us: owners should not be deprived of their property too hastily, nor should this benefit be confined to one place. So we have promulgated a constitution on the matter, by which it is provided that movables are acquired by usucapion over three years, and immovables by long possession (that is, ten years between parties present and twenty years between parties absent). By these means, with a just cause of possession preceding, ownership of things is acquired not only in Italy but in every land governed by our empire.

units.la: 1 ¶Sed aliquando etiam si maxime quis bona fide rem possederit: non tamen illi vsucapio vllo tempore procedit: veluti si quis liberum hominem, vel rem sacram, vel religiosam, vel seruum fugitiuum possideat.
units.tr: 1 Sometimes, however, even if someone has possessed a thing in the fullest good faith, usucapion never avails him. For example, this is so if he possesses a free man, a sacred or religious thing, or a fugitive slave.

units.la: 2 ¶Furtiuæ quoque res, & quæ vi possessæ sunt, nec si prædicto longo tempore bona fide possessæ fuerint, vsucapi possunt. nam furtiuarum rerum lex duodecim tabularum, & lex Atilia, inhibent vsucapionem: vi possessarum, lex Iulia & Plautia.
units.tr: 2 Stolen things, and things taken by force, cannot be usucapted even if they have been possessed in good faith for the said long time. For the law of the Twelve Tables and the Atilian law forbid usucapion of stolen things, and the Julian and Plautian laws forbid it of things possessed by force.

units.la: 3 ¶Quod autem dictum est, furtiuarum & vi possessarum rerum vsucapione per leges prohibitam esse: non eo pertinet, vt ne ipse fur, vel qui vi possidet, vsucapere possit (nam his alia ratione vsucapio non competit, quia scilicet mala fide possident) sed ne vllus alius, quamuis ab eis bona fide emerit, vel ex alia causa acceperit, vsucapiendi habeat. Vnde in rebus mobilibus non facile procedit, vt bonæ fidei possessoribus vsucapio competat. Nam qui sciens alienam rem vendiderit, vel ex alia causa tradiderit, furtum eius committit.
units.tr: 3 But what has been said, that usucapion of stolen and forcibly possessed things is prohibited by the laws, does not mean that the thief himself, or one who possesses by force, cannot usucapt. On other grounds usucapion is not open to them, since they possess in bad faith. It means that no other person may have the right to usucapt, even one who bought from them in good faith or received the thing from some other cause. Hence, with movables, usucapion does not easily avail possessors in good faith. For one who knowingly sells or hands over another's thing on some other ground commits theft.

units.la: 4 ¶Sed tamen id aliquando aliter se habet. nam si heres rem defuncto commodatam, aut locatam, vel apud eum depositam, existimans hereditariam esse, bona fide accipienti vendiderit, aut donauerit, aut dotis nomine dederit: quin is, qui acceperit, vsucapere non potest, dubium non est: quippe cum eares in furti vitium non ceciderit: quum vtique heres [?]qui bona fide tanquam suam alienauerit, furtum non committit.
units.tr: 4 Sometimes, however, the matter stands otherwise. If an heir sells, gives or gives as a dowry a thing that was lent, let or deposited with the deceased, believing it to be part of the estate, to a recipient in good faith, there is no doubt that the recipient cannot usucapt. The thing has not fallen into the taint of theft, since an heir who alienates in good faith, as his own, does not commit theft.

units.la: 5 ¶Item si is, ad quem ancillæ vsusfructus pertinet, partum suum esse credens vendiderit, aut donauerit, furtum non committit. furtum enim sine affectu furandi non committitur.
units.tr: 5 Likewise, if one to whom the usufruct of a female slave belongs sells or gives her offspring, believing it to be his own, he does not commit theft, for theft is not committed without intent to steal.

units.la: 6 ¶Aliis quoque modis accidere potest, vt quis sine vitio furti, rem alienam ad aliquem transferat, & efficiat, vt a possessore vsucapiatur.
units.tr: 6 It can also happen in other ways that someone transfers another's thing to a third party without the fault of theft, and brings it about that it is usucapted by the possessor.

units.la: 7 ¶Quod autem ad eas res, quæ solo continentur, expedit: iuris ita procedit, vt si quis loci vicinitis possessionem propter absentiam aut negligentiam domini, aut quia sine successore decesserit, sine vi nanciscatur: quamuis ipse mala fide possideat (quia intelligit se alienum fundum occupasse). passe) tamen si alij bona fide accipienti tradiderit, poterit ei longa possessione res adquiri: quia neque furtiuum, neque vi possessum acceperit. Abolita est enim quorundam {a}veterum sententia, existimantiū etiam fundi locive furtum fieri. & eorum utilitati, qui res soli possident, principalibus constitutionibus prospicitur, ne cui longa & indubitata possessio debeat auferri. 8 Aliquando etiam furtiua, vel vi possessa res vsucapi poterit: veluti si {c}in domini potestate reuersa fuerit, tunc enim vitio rei purgato, procedit eius vsucapio.
units.tr: 7 As for things that are attached to the soil, the law proceeds thus. If someone takes possession, without force, of a neighbouring plot because the owner is absent or negligent, or because he has died without a successor, then even though he himself possesses in bad faith (since he knows he has occupied another's land), yet if he hands it over to another who receives it in good faith, that person can acquire it by long possession, since he has received it neither stolen nor by force. For the opinion of certain older jurists, who held that land and places could also be stolen, has been abolished. Imperial constitutions also provide for the benefit of those who possess land, so that no one should be deprived of a long and undisputed possession. 8 Sometimes even a stolen or forcibly possessed thing can be usucapted: for example, if it has returned into the power of the owner. For then, the taint of the thing having been purged, its usucapion proceeds.

units.la: 9 Res fisci nostri vsucapi non potest {d}. Sed Papinianus scripsit {e}, bonis vacantibus fisco nondum nunciatis bonae fidei emptorem traditam sibi rem ex his bonis vsucapere posse: & ita diui Pius, & diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt.
units.tr: 9 The property of our fisc cannot be usucapted. But Papinian wrote that when goods have fallen vacant and the fisc has not yet been notified, a buyer in good faith may usucapt a thing delivered to him from those goods. The deified Pius, and the deified Severus and Antoninus, rescripted to the same effect.

units.la: 10 Nouissime sciendum est, rem talem esse debere, vt in se non habeat vitium {f}, vt a bonae fidei emptore vsucapi possit, vel qui ex alia iusta causa possidet.
units.tr: 10 Lastly, it must be understood that the thing must have no defect in itself, so that it can be usucapted by a buyer in good faith, or by one who possesses from another just cause.

units.la: 11 Error autem falsae causae vsucapione {g} non parit: veluti si quis cum non emerit, emisse se existimans, possideat: vel cum ei donatu non fuerit, quasi ex donatione possideat.
units.tr: 11 An error about a false cause, however, does not produce usucapion. For example, this is so if someone possesses believing that he has bought, when he has not bought, or as if by gift when no gift was made.

units.la: 12 Diutina possessio, quae prodesse coeperat defuncto, & heredi {h}, & bonorum possessori continuatur, licet ipse sciat praedium alienum esse. quòd si ille initium iustum non habuit: heredi & bonorum possessori licet {i} ignoranti, possessio non prodest. Quod nostra constitutio {k}similiter & in vsucapionibus obseruari constituit, vt tempora continuentur. Inter venditorem quoque & emptorem coniungi tempora, diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt.
units.tr: 12 Long possession which had begun to avail the deceased continues to avail the heir and the possessor of goods, even if he himself knows that the estate belongs to another. But if the deceased had no just beginning, the possession does not avail the heir or the possessor of goods, even if they are ignorant of the defect. Our constitution has likewise established that the periods be joined in usucapions. The deified Severus and Antoninus also rescripted that periods are joined between seller and buyer.

units.la: 13 Edicto diui Marci cauetur, eum, qui a fisco rem alienam emit, si post venditionem quinquennium praeterierit, posse dominum {l}rei exceptione repellere. Constitutio autem diuae memoriae Zenonis {m}bene proisperit iis, qui a fisco per venditionem, aut donationem, vel alium titulum acciperunt aliquid: vt ipsi quidem securi statim fiant, & victores existant, siue experiantur, siue conueniantur. Aduersus autem sacratissimum aerarium vsque ad quadriennium liceat iis intendere, qui pro domino vel hypotheca earum rerum, quae alienatae sunt, putauerint sibi quasdam competere actiones. Nostra {n}aute diuina constitutio, quam nuper promulgauimus etiam de iis, qui a nostra, vel venerabilis Augustae domo aliquid acceperint, haec statuit, quae in fiscalibus alienationibus praefatae Zenonianae constitutionis continentur.
units.tr: 13 By an edict of the deified Marcus it is provided that one who buys another's thing from the fisc may repel the owner by an exception if five years have passed since the sale. The constitution of the deified Zeno, of blessed memory, has favoured those who receive anything from the fisc by sale, gift or other title: they become secure at once and are victors, whether they sue or are sued. Against the most sacred treasury, however, claims may be brought until four years have passed, by those who thought that certain actions were available to them on behalf of the owner or of the mortgage of those things which were alienated. Our divine constitution, lately promulgated, concerning those who have received anything from our house or from that of the venerable Augusta, lays down the provisions contained in the aforesaid Zenonian constitution on fiscal alienations.
CONCERNING GIFTS, TITLE VII.

units.la: EST & alind genus adquisitionis, do-natio. Donationum autem duo sunt genera: mortis causa, & non mortis causa.
units.tr: There is also another kind of acquisition, gift. Gifts are of two kinds: those made in contemplation of death, and those not made in contemplation of death.

units.la: 1 ¶Mortis causa donatio est, quę pro-pter mortis fit suspicione: cum quis ita donat, ut si quid humanitus ei contigisset, haberet is, qui accepit. sin aut superuixisset: is, qui donauit, reciperet: vel si eū donationis poenituisset: aut prior decesserit is, cui donatū sit. Hae mortis causa donationes ad exemplū legatorū redactę sunt per omnia; nam cum prudentibus ambiguū fuerat, utrum donationis, an legati instar eā obtinere oporteret, & utrisque causę quaedā habebat insignia, & alij ad aliud genus eam retrahebant: a nobis constitutū est ut per omnia fere legatis conumeretur, & sic procedat, quemadmodum nostra constitutio eam formauit. Et in summa mortis causa donatio est, cum magis se quis velit habere, quam eum, cui donat: magisque eum, cui donat, quam heredem suū. sic & apud Homerum Telemachus donat Pirae.
units.tr: 1 ¶ A gift in contemplation of death is one made from fear of death, when someone gives on the understanding that, if anything should happen to him from the human lot, the recipient shall have it; but if the giver survives, he takes it back; or if he repents of the gift; or if the recipient dies first. These gifts in contemplation of death have been brought into line with legacies in every respect. For although the jurists were uncertain whether such a gift ought to be treated as a gift or after the manner of a legacy, and each view had certain distinguishing marks while others drew it toward another kind, we have determined that it be counted almost entirely among legacies and proceed as our constitution has shaped it. In short, a gift in contemplation of death is one where a man wishes to keep himself in possession rather than the one to whom he gives, and that person rather than his own heir. So too in Homer, Telemachus gives to Pira.

That is:

units.la: Pirae, incertus quoniam rerum exitus harum est, Si tacita incautum stolidi me forte necare Morte proci poterunt, & opes vexare paternas: Hac ego te nolo, quam illorum quempiam habere. Sin ego eos iusta meritos affecero clade, Tum ibi tu laeto reddes illa omnia laetus.
units.tr: Pira, since the outcome of these affairs is uncertain, if the foolish suitors, off their guard, should by some chance kill me by a secret death and be able to waste my paternal wealth, I do not want you to hold it any more than one of them. But if I should punish them with a just ruin, then you, rejoicing there, will gladly give back all those things.

units.la: 2 ¶Aliae vero donationes sunt, quae sine vlla mortis cogitatione fiunt, quas inter vivos appellamus, quae non omnino comparantur legatis.quae fuerint perfectae, temere reuocari non possunt. Perficiuntur autem cum donator suam voluntatem scriptis,aut sine scriptis manifestauerit. Et ad exemplum venditionis, nostra constitutio eas etiā in se habere necessitatem traditionis voluit: ut etiam si non tradantur, habeant plenissimum & perfectum robur, & traditionis necessitas incumbat donatori. Et cum Et cùm retrò principum dispositiones insinuari eas actis interuenientibus volebant, si maiores fuerant ducentorum solidorum: constitutio nostra eam quantitatem usque ad quingentos solidos amplia-uit, quam stare etiam sine insinuatione statuit: sed & quasdam donationes inuenit, quæ penitus insinuatione fieri minimè desiderát, sed in se plenissimam habent firmitatē. Alia insuper multa ad uberiorem exiruum donationum inuenimus: quæ omnia ex nostris constitutionibus, quas super his exposuimus, colligenda sunt. Sciendum est tamen, quòd etsi plenissimæ sint donationes: si tamē ingrati existant homines, in quos beneficium collatum est: donatoribus per nostram constitutionem licentiam præstitimus certis ex causis eas reuocare: ne illi, qui suas res in alios contulerint, ab his quandam patiantur iniuriā vel iacturam secundum enumeratos in côstitutione nostra modos. 3 ¶ Est & aliud genus inter viuos donationis, quod veteribus quidē prudentibus penitus erat incognitum, postea autem à iunioribus diuis principibus introductū est, quod ante nuptias vocabatur: & tacitam in se conditionē habebat, vt tunc ratum esset, cum matrimonium esset insequuntur. Ideòque ante nuptias appellabatur, quod ante matrimonium efficiebatur, & nunquam post nuptias celebratas talis donatio procedebat. Sed primus quidem diuus Iustinus pater nost[?]er, cùm augeri dotes & post nuptias fuerat permissum: si quid tale euenirèt & ante nuptias augeri donationem & constante matrimonio, sua constitutione permisit. sed tamen nomen inconueniens remanebat, cùm ante nuptias quidem vocabatur, post nuptias autem tale accipiebat incrementum. Sed nos plenissimo fini tradere sanctione cupientes, & consequentia nomina rebus esse studentes: constituimus, vt tales donationes non augeantur tantùm, sed etiam constante matrimonio initium accipiant: & non ante nuptias, sed propter nuptias vocentur: & dotibus in hoc exaequentur, vt quemadmodum dum dotes constante matrimonio non solum augentur, sed etiam fiunt: ita & istæ donationes, quæ propter nuptias introductæ sunt, non solum antecedant matrimonium, sed eo etiam contracto augeantur, & constituantur.
units.tr: 2 ¶ Other gifts, however, are made without any thought of death; these we call inter vivos, and they are not at all comparable to legacies. Once they have been perfected, they cannot be lightly revoked. They are perfected when the donor declares his will, either in writing or without writing. Following the model of sale, our constitution wished these also to carry in themselves a necessity of delivery, so that even if they are not delivered they have full and perfect force, and the obligation of delivery falls upon the donor. The emperors of old wanted such gifts to be recorded in documents with the intervention of officials if they exceeded two hundred solidi; our constitution extended that sum to five hundred solidi and decided that it should stand even without registration. But it has also found some gifts which by no means need registration and have full firmness in themselves. We have found many other additions for a fuller development of gifts, all of which are to be gathered from our constitutions that we have published on these matters. It should be known, however, that although gifts are fully binding, if those on whom the benefit was conferred prove ungrateful, we have granted donors, by our constitution, the license to revoke them for certain causes, so that those who have transferred their goods to others do not suffer some wrong or loss from them, in the ways enumerated in our constitution. 3 ¶ There is also another kind of gift inter vivos, which was entirely unknown to the prudent of old but was later introduced by the more recent deified emperors, and was called "before marriage." It had a tacit condition, that it would be ratified when the marriage followed. It was called ante nuptias because it took effect before the marriage, and such a gift never went forward once the wedding had been celebrated. But first our father, the deified Justin, when it had been permitted that dowries could be increased even after the wedding, allowed by his constitution that, if such a case arose, the gift made before the wedding could be increased during the marriage. Yet the name remained unsuitable, since it was called "before the wedding" but received such an increase after the wedding. We, wishing to bring this to a most complete end by our sanction, and wanting names to agree with things, have decreed that such gifts not only be increased but also begin during the marriage, and that they be called not "before the wedding" but "on account of the wedding." They are made equal to dowries in this respect: just as dowries during the marriage are not only increased but also come into being, so these gifts, introduced on account of the wedding, not only precede the marriage but, once it has been contracted, are also increased and established.

units.la: 4 ¶ Erat olim & alius modus ciuilis adquisitiōis per ius adcrescendi, quod est tale: Si communem seruum habens aliquis cum Titio, solus libertate ei im-posuerit vel vindicta, vel testamento: eo casu pars eius amittebatur, & socio adcrescebat. Sed cum pessimum fuerat exemplo, & libertate serui defraudari, & ex ea humanioribus quidem dominis damnum inferri, sequioribus autem dominis lucrum accedere: hoc quasi inuidia plenum, pio remedio per nostram constitutionem mederi necessarium duximus. Et inuenimus viam, per quam & manumissor, & socius eius, & qui libertate accepit, nostro beneficio fruantur, libertate cum effectu procedente (cuius fauore antiquos legum latores multa etiam contra {e}communes regulas statuisse manifestum est) & eo, qui eam libertatem imposuit, suae liberalitatis stabilitate gaudente: & socio indemni conseruato, pretiumque serui secundum partem dominij, quod nos definiuimus, accipiente.
units.tr: 4 ¶ There was formerly also another civil mode of acquisition, by the right of accrual, which was as follows: if one of several owners of a common slave, together with Titius, freed him alone, either by vindicta or by will, then in that case his share was lost and accrued to the partner. But since it was a very bad precedent to defraud a slave of his liberty, and from this a loss was inflicted on the more humane masters while a gain accrued to the harsher ones, we judged it necessary to remedy this abuse, which is full of ill will, by a pious remedy through our constitution. We have found a way by which the manumitter, his partner, and the one who received liberty all enjoy our benefit: liberty takes effect (for the sake of which favour it is clear that the ancient lawgivers decreed many things even against common rules), the one who granted the liberty rejoices in the stability of his generosity, the partner is kept unharmed, and the price of the slave is received according to the share of ownership which we have defined.

units.la: QVIBVS ALIENARE LICET, vel non. TITVLVS VIII.
units.tr: Which persons may alienate, or not. Title 8.

units.la: ACCIDIT aliquando, vt qui dominus sit, alienare non posset: & contra, qui dominus non sit, alienandae rei potestatem habeat. Nam dotale praedium maritus inuita muliere per legem Iuliam {g}prohibetur alienare: quamuis ipsius sit, dotis causa ei datum. quod nos, legem Iuliam corrigentes, in melius statum deduximus. Cum enim lex in solis tantummodo rebus locum habebat, quae Italicae fuerant: & alienationes inhibebat, quae inuita muliere fiebant, hypothecas autem earum rerum, etiam vel nte ea: utrique remedium imposuimus, vt etiam in eas res, quae in prouinciali solo positae sunt, interdicta sit alienatio vel obligatio: vt neutrum eorum neque consentientibus mulieribus procedat, ne sexus mulieb-ris fragilitas in perniciem substantiae earum convertatur.
units.tr: It sometimes happens that the owner of a thing cannot alienate it, and conversely that one who is not the owner has the power to alienate it. Thus under the Julian law a husband is forbidden to alienate a dotal estate without his wife's consent, although it is his own, given to him for the sake of the dowry. We, correcting the Julian law, have brought this into a better state. For the law had application only to things that were in Italy, and it forbade alienations made against the wife's will, and mortgages of those things even with her consent. We have applied a remedy to both: the alienation or mortgage of things situated on provincial soil is also forbidden, so that neither of these proceeds even with the wives' consent, lest the frailty of the female sex be turned to the ruin of their property.

units.la: {1}¶Contra autem creditor pignus ex pactione, quamuis eius ea res non sit, alienare potest. Sed hoc forsitan ideo videtur fieri, quod voluntate dominus intelligitur pignus alienari, quia ab initio contractus pactus est, vt liceret creditori pignus vendere, si pecunia non soluatur. Sed ne creditores ius suum persequi impedirentur, neque debitores teme-
units.tr: On the other hand, a creditor may alienate a pledge given under an agreement, although the thing is not his. But this seems to be done perhaps because the owner is understood by his will to have allowed the pledge to be alienated, since it was agreed at the outset of the contract that the creditor might sell the pledge if the money were not paid. But so that creditors should not be hindered from pursuing their right, and debtors should not seem rashly

units.la: 62. l v.l. 46. ff. de adq.rer. re suarum rerum dominiū amittere viderentur: no-stra{A} constitutione consultū est, & certus modus im-positus est, per quem pignorum distractio possit pro- cederer: cuius tenore utrique parti, creditorum & de-bitorum, satis abundè prouisum est.
units.tr: 62. l v.l. 46. ff. de adq.rer. to lose ownership of their own things, provision has been made by our constitution and a fixed procedure imposed by which the sale of pledges may proceed. By its terms both parties, creditors and debtors, have been amply provided for.

units.la: 2 ¶Nunc admonendi sumus, neque pupillum, neque pupillam ullam rem sine tutoris auctoritate alienare posse{b}, Ideoque si mutuā pecuniam sine tutoris auctoritate alicui dederit, non contrahit obligationē: quia pecu-niam non facit "accipientis, ideoque vindicari num-mi possunt, sicubi extant. Sed si nummi, quos mutuò minor dederit; ab co, qui accepit, bona fide consumpti sunt: condici possunt. si mala fide, ad exhibendum de his agi potest. At ex contrario, omnes res pupillo & pupillae sine tutoris auctoritate recte dari{c} possunt.
units.tr: 2 ¶ Next we must be reminded that neither a male ward nor a female ward can alienate any thing without the authority of the guardian. Therefore, if a ward has lent money to someone without the guardian's authority, he does not contract an obligation, because he does not make the money the property of the recipient; so the coins can be vindicated wherever they still exist. But if coins that the minor lent were consumed in good faith by the one who received them, they can be claimed by condictio; if he consumed them in bad faith, an action for production may be brought concerning them. On the contrary, all things can validly be given to a ward, male or female, without the guardian's authority.

units.la: {d} Ideoque si debitor pupillo soluat: necessaria est de-bitori tutoris auctoritas, alioqui non liberabitur. Sed hoc etiam euidentissima ratione statutum est in constitutione, quam ad Cæsarienses aduocatos{e} ex sug-gestione Triboniani viri eminentissimi, quastoris sacri palatij nostri, promulgauimus: qua dispositum est, ita licere tutori vel curatori debitorem pupillarem soluere, ut prius iudicialis sententia sine omni damno celebrata, hoc permittat.{f} quo subsequuto, si & iudex pronunciauerit, & debitor soluerit: sequatur huiusmodi solutionem plenissima securitas. Sin autem aliter, quàm disposuimus, solutio facta fuerit, pecu-niam autem saluam habeat pupillus, aut ex ea locupletior sit, & adhuc eandem pecuniæ summam petat: per exceptionē{§} doli mali poterit submoueri. Quod si male consumpserit, aut furto, aut vi amiserit: nihil proderit debitori doli mali exceptio, sed nihilo-minus condemnabitur: quia temere sine tutoris auctoritate, & non secundum nostram dispositionem sol-uerit. Sed ex diverso, pupilli vel pupillę soluere sine tutoris auctoritate non possunt: quia id, quod soluunt, non fit{k} accipientis: quum sciscet nullius rei alienatio eis sine tutoris auctoritate concessa sit.
units.tr: Therefore, if a debtor pays a ward, the guardian's authority is necessary for the debtor, otherwise he will not be discharged. This has been established also on the most evident reasoning in the constitution which we issued to the Caesarian advocates on the suggestion of Tribonian, the most eminent man, quaestor of our sacred palace. By it it is laid down that a guardian or curator may pay a ward's debtor only in such a way that a judicial sentence, conducted without any loss, first permits this. If the judge then pronounces, and the debtor pays, the payment is followed by the fullest security. But if payment is made otherwise than we have ordained, yet the ward keeps the money safe, or is richer by it, and still demands the same sum, the debtor can be protected by the exception of fraud. But if the ward has spent it badly, or lost it by theft or by force, the exception of fraud will avail the debtor nothing, and he will nonetheless be condemned, because he paid rashly, without the guardian's authority and not according to our arrangement. But conversely, wards cannot pay without the guardian's authority, because what they pay does not become the property of the recipient, since no alienation of any thing is granted to them without the guardian's authority.

units.la: PER QVAS PERSONAS cuique adquiritur. lx TIT. IX.
units.tr: By what persons one acquires for another. Title 9.

units.la: DQVIRITVR{l} vobis nō solū per vosmetipsos, sed etiā per eos, quos in po-testatę habetis: || item per seruos, in qui-bus usumfructum habetis:|| item per ho-mines liberos, & per seruos alienos quos bona fide possidetis, de quibus singulis diligentius dispiciamus.
units.tr: Acquisition is made for you not only through yourselves but also through those whom you have in your power; likewise through slaves in whom you have the usufruct; likewise through free men and through other men's slaves whom you possess in good faith. We shall examine each of these more carefully.

units.la: 1 ¶Igitur liberi vestri utriusque sexus, quos in potestate habetis, olim {*}quidem, quicquid ad eos pernenerat[?] (exceptis videlicet ca-strensibus[?] peculiis) hoc parentibus suis adquirebant, sine vlla distinctione: & hoc ita parentum fiebat, vt etiam esset eis licentia, quod per vnum vel vnam eo-rum adquisitum esset, alij filio, vel extraneo donare, vel vendere, vel quocumque modo voluerant, adpli-care. Quod nobis inhumanum visum est: & generali constitutione {b}emissa,& liberis pepercimus,& patri-bus honorem debitum reseruauimus. Sancitum ete-nim à nobis est, vt si quid ex re patris ei obueniat, hoc secundum antiquam obseruationem totum pareti[?] adquiratur. Quae enim innidia[?] est, quod ex patris oc-cafione[?] profectum est, hoc ad eum reuerti? Quod au-tem ex alia causa sibi filiusfamilias adquisiuit: huius usumfructum patri quidè adquirat, dominium autem apud eum remaneat: ne quod ei suis laboribus, vel prospera fortuna accesserit, hoc in alium peruneniens[?], luctuosum ei procedat.
units.tr: 1 ¶ Therefore your children of either sex, whom you have in your power, formerly acquired for their parents whatever came to them (excepting, of course, camp property), without any distinction. This was so much the parents' right that they had licence to give to another son or to a stranger, to sell, or to apply in whatever way they wished, whatever had been acquired through one of them. This seemed inhuman to us. By a general constitution we have both spared the children and preserved the honour due to fathers. For it has been sanctioned by us that if anything comes to a son from his father's property, it is all acquired for the father, according to the ancient observance. For what injustice is there in what has proceeded from the father's occasion returning to him? But what the son under power has acquired from some other cause, the father acquires the usufruct, while ownership remains with the son. This ensures that whatever has come to him by his own labours or by good fortune does not turn to his sorrow by passing to another.

units.la: 2 ¶Hoc quoque à nobis dispositum est & in ea specie, vbi parens emancipado liberos suos ex rebus, quæ adquisitione effugiebant, sibi tertiam partem retinere ( si voluerat ) licentiam ex antecioribus[?]{c}constitutionibus habebat, quasi pro {d}pretio quodāmodo emācipationis: & inhumanum quiddam accideb at, vt filius rerum suarum ex hac e-mancipatione dominio pro parte ⅓[?] tertia] defrauda-retur: & quod honoris ei ex emancipatione additum erat, quod sui iuris effectus esset, hoc per rerum de-minutionem decresceret[?]. Ideoque statuimus,{e}vt pa-rens pro tertia parte domini) quam retinere poterat dimidiā non dominij rerum, sed usufructus retineat. Ita etenim res intactæ[?] apud filiu[?] remanebunt, & pater ampliore summa fruetur, pro tertia dimidia poti-turus.
units.tr: 2 ¶ This too has been provided by us in the case where a parent, emancipating his children, had by earlier constitutions the licence to retain for himself a third part (if he wished) of the things that were acquired by them, as if in some way as the price of emancipation. Something inhuman followed: the son was defrauded of the ownership of a third part of his own things by this emancipation, and the honour added to him by emancipation, namely that he became sui iuris, was diminished by the reduction of his property. Therefore we have decreed that the parent, instead of the third part of ownership that he could retain, keep half of it, not as ownership of the things but as usufruct. For in this way the things will remain intact with the son, and the father will enjoy a larger sum, obtaining half of the third part.

units.la: 3 ¶Item vobis adquiritur, quod serui vestri ex traditione nanciscuntur: siue quid stipulentur, siue ex donatione,{f} vel ex legato, vel ex qualibet alia causa adquiran⁊[?]. Hoc enim vobis ignorantibus & inuitis {g}obuenit. Ipse enim seruus, qui in potestate alterius est, nihil suum habere {h}potest. Sed si heres institutus sit, non alias nisi vestro iussu, hereditatem adire potest. Et si vobis iubentibus adierit: vobis hę-reditas adquiritur, perinde ac si vos ipsi heredes insti-tuti essetis. Et conuenienter scilicet vobis legatū peu[?] eos adquiritur. Non solum autem proprietas per eos quos in potestate habetis,vobis adquiritur:sed etiam possessio. Cuiuscumque enim rei possessionem adepti fuerint,id vos possidere videmini. Unde etiā per eos usucapio, vel longi temporis possessio vobis accidit.
units.tr: 3 ¶ Also acquired for you is what your slaves obtain by delivery, whether they stipulate something, or through gift, legacy, or any other cause. For this comes to you without your knowledge and against your will. A slave who is in another's power can have nothing of his own. But if a slave has been instituted heir, he can enter upon the inheritance only by your command. And if he enters at your command, the inheritance is acquired for you, just as if you yourselves had been instituted heirs. Similarly, legacies are acquired for you through them. Not only ownership but also possession is acquired for you through those whom you have in your power. For whatever thing they have obtained possession of, you are seen to possess it. Hence also usucaption, or long possession, accrues to you through them.

units.la: 4 ¶De iis autem seruis in quibus tantummodo usumfructu habeatis,ita placuit.ut quicquid ex re vestra,vel ex operis suis adquirat,{a}id vobis adiiciatur. quod vero extra eas causas consequuti sunt: id ad dominum proprietatis pertinebat.Itaque si is seruus heres institutus sit,legatumve quid ei,aut donatum fuerit:non usufructuario, sed {b}domino proprietatis adquiritur. Idem placet & de eo, qui a vobis bona fide possidetur: siue is liber sit,siue alienus seruus. Quod enim placuit de usufructuario, idè placet & de bonā fidei possessore. Itaque ꝯ extra istas duas causas adquiritur:id vel ad ipsum pertinet, si liber est: vel ad dominum,si seruus est.Sed bonae fidei possessor cum usuceperit seruū,(quia eo modo dominꝰ fit) ex omnibus causis per eum sibi adquirere potest. Fructuarius vero usucapere {c}non potest: primum,quia non possidet,sed habet ius utendi fruendi: deinde quia scit seruum alienum esse.
