Non solùm autem proprietas per eos seruos,in quibus usumfructum habetis, vel quos bona fide possidetis, aut per liberam personam, quae bona fide vestri,vobis adquiritur:sed etiā{d} possessio. Loquimur autem in utriusque persona secun-dum distinctionē,quàm proximè exposuimus: id est, si quam possessionem ex re vestra, vel ex suis operis adepti fuerint.
units.tr: 4 ¶ As for those slaves in whom you have only the usufruct, it has been decided that whatever such a slave acquires from your property or by his own labours is added to you. But whatever they obtain outside those causes belongs to the owner of the property. Thus if that slave is instituted heir, or something is left or given to him, it is acquired not for the usufructuary but for the owner of the property. The same rule applies to one whom you possess in good faith, whether he is free or another's slave. For what has been decided for the usufructuary is likewise decided for the possessor in good faith. Thus whatever is acquired outside these two causes belongs to the person himself if he is free, or to the owner if he is a slave. But a possessor in good faith, when he has usucapted the slave (since by that means he becomes owner), can acquire to himself through him from all causes. A usufructuary, however, cannot usucapt: first, because he does not possess but only has the right of using and enjoying; second, because he knows the slave belongs to another. Not only ownership but also possession is acquired for you through those slaves in whom you have the usufruct, or whom you possess in good faith, or through a free person who is in good faith yours. We speak of each person according to the distinction we have just set out: that is, if they have obtained any possession from your property or from their labours.

units.la: 5 ¶Ex his itaque apparet,per liberos homines, quos neque vestro iuri subiectos habetis, neque bona fide possidetis:item per alienos seruos,in quibus neque usumfructum habetis,neque possessionem instam: nulla ex causa vobis adquiri posse. Et hoc est,quod dicitur,per extraneā personā {e}nihil adquiri posse: excepto eo, quod per liberā personam (veluti per procuratorem)placet non solùm scienti-bus,sed & {f}ignoratibus vobis adquiri possessionem, secundū diui Seueri {g}constitutionem: & per hāc possessionē etiā dominium, si dominus fuerit,qui tradi-dit:vel usucapione aut longi tèporis prœscriptionem, si dominus non sit.
units.tr: 5 Hence it is evident that nothing can be acquired for you through free persons whom you neither have under your power nor hold in good faith, nor through the slaves of others in whom you have neither the usufruct nor a legitimate possession. This is what is meant by the saying that nothing can be acquired through a stranger, except that, according to the constitution of the divine Severus, possession may be acquired for you through a free person (for instance, through a procurator), not only when you know of it but even when you are ignorant of it; and through this possession ownership also passes to you, if the one who delivered the thing was its owner, or, if he was not the owner, by usucapion or by prescription of long time.

units.la: 6 ¶ Hactenus tantisper admonuisse sufficiat,quemadmodum singulae res vobis adquirātur. nam legatorum ius , quo & ipso singulae rei vobis adquiruntur : item fideicommissorum, ubi singulae res vobis relinquuntur : opportunius inferiore loco {h}referemus. Videamus itaque nunc,quibus modis per vniuersitatē res vobis adquirantur. Si cui ergo heredes facti sitis, siue cuius bonorum possessione petieritis,vel si quem adrogaueritis,vel si cuius bona libertatum conseruandarum causa vobis addicta fuerint: eius res omnes ad vos transfeūt. Ac prius de hereditatibus despiciamus, quarū duplex conditio est. nam vel ex testamento,vel ab intestato ad vos pertinent.Et prius est,vt de his dispiciamus,quae ex Testamento vobis obuenīunt.qua in re necessarium est,initium de ordinandis Testamentis exponere.
units.tr: 6 It will be enough to have explained thus far in general how single things are acquired for you. The right of legacies, by which single things are also acquired for you, and likewise of fideicommissa, by which single things are left to you, we shall treat more conveniently in a later place. Let us now see in what ways things are acquired for you by universal succession. Therefore, if you have become heirs to anyone, or have sought possession of anyone's goods, or have adrogated anyone, or if anyone's goods have been assigned to you for the sake of preserving their liberties, all his property passes over to you. And first let us look at inheritances, of which there are two kinds: for they come to you either by testament or by intestacy. And it is right to look first at those things which come to you by testament, and in this matter it is necessary to set out first the rules for making wills.
ON ORDERING WILLS, TITLE X.

units.la: T[?]ESTAMENTVM ex eo appellatur, quod testatio mentis fit{b}. 1 ¶Sed vt nihil antiquitatis penitus ignoretur: sciendum est,olim quidem duo genera Testamentorum in vsu fuisse : quorum altero in pace & otio vtebantur, quod calatis{c} comitiis appellabant:altero,cum in proelium exituri essent,quod procinctu{d} dicebatur. Accesit deinde tertium genus Testamentorum,quod dicebatur per aes & libram: scilicet quod per emancipationem, id est{e}, imaginariam quandam venditione agebatur, quinque testibus, & libripende , ciuibus Romanis puberibus praesentibus, & eo , qui familiae emptor dicebatur.Sed illa quidem priora duo genera testamentorum ex veteribus temporibus in desuetudinem abierunt. quod vero per aes & libram fiebat, licet diutius permanserit,attamen partim{f} & hoc in vsu esse desiit.
units.tr: A will (testamentum) is so called because it is a testimony of the mind (testatio mentis) made. 1 ¶But so that nothing of antiquity is wholly unknown, it should be understood that formerly two kinds of wills were in use: one, used in peace and leisure, which they called the calata comitia; the other, used when men were about to go out to battle, which was called procinctus. Then a third kind of will was added, which was called per aes et libram, namely that which was effected through emancipation, that is, by a certain imaginary sale, with five witnesses, the scale-holder (libripens), and Roman citizens of full age present, and the one called the purchaser of the family. But those earlier two kinds of wills went out of use in ancient times. As for the will made per aes et libram, although it lasted longer, nevertheless this too partly ceased to be in use.

units.la: 2 ¶Sed praedicta quidem nomina testamentorum ad ius ciuile referrebantur . postea vero ex edicto praetoris forma alia faciendorum testamentorum introducta est.Iure enim honorario nulla emancipatio desiderabatur: sed septem testium & signa sufficiebant,cum iure ciuili signa testium non essent necessaria.
units.tr: 2 ¶But the aforementioned names of wills belonged to the civil law. Later, however, by the praetor's edict another form of making wills was introduced. For under the praetorian law no emancipation was required, but seven witnesses and their seals sufficed, whereas under the civil law the seals of witnesses were not necessary.

units.la: 3 ¶Sed cum paulatim tam ex vsu hominum,quàm ex constitutionum emendationibus coepit in vnam consonantiam ius ciuile & praetorium iungi: *constitutum est{b}, vt vno eodemque tempore (quod ius ciuile quodammodo exigebat) septem testibus adhibitis,& subscriptione testium (quod ex constitutionibus inuentum est,& ex edicto praetoris) signacula
units.tr: 3 ¶But when gradually, both from the custom of men and from the amendments of the constitutions, the civil and praetorian law began to be joined into one harmony, it was established that at one and the same time (which the civil law in a way required), with seven witnesses present, and with the subscription of the witnesses (which was devised from the imperial constitutions and from the praetor's edict), seals should be placed on

units.la: {a} Forma scripti Testamenti. signacula testamentis imponerentur: ita, ut hoc ius tripertitum esse videatur: & testes {a}quidem & eorum praesentia uno {b}contextu testamenti celebrandi {c}gratia, à iure ciuili descendant: subscriptiones autem testatoris & testium, ex sacrarum constitutionum observatione adhibeantur: signacula autem, & testium numerus, ex edicto praetoris.
units.tr: {a} Form of a written will. the will: so that this law appears to be threefold. The witnesses and their presence, for the sake of executing one continuous text of the will, derive from the civil law; the subscriptions of the testator and witnesses are required by observance of the sacred constitutions; the seals and the number of witnesses come from the praetor's edict.

units.la: 4 ¶Sed his omnibus à nostra constitutione {d}propter testamentorum sinceritatem, ut nulla fraus adhibeatur, hoc additum est: ut per manus testatoris uel testium nomen heredis exprimatur, & omnia secundum illius constitutionis tenorem procedant.
units.tr: 4 ¶But to all these, by our constitution, for the sake of the sincerity of wills, so that no fraud be practised, this has been added: that through the hand of the testator or of the witnesses the name of the heir be expressed, and everything proceed according to the tenor of that constitution.

units.la: 5 ¶Possunt autem omnes testes & uno annulo {e}signare testamentum. quid enim si septem anuli una sculptura fuerint, secundum quod Papiniano visum est? Sed & alieno quoque anulo licet signare testamentum {f}.
units.tr: 5 ¶All witnesses may seal a will with one ring. For what if the seven rings bore one design, as seemed right to Papinian? But it is also permitted to seal a will with another's ring.

units.la: 6 ¶Testes autem adhiberi possunt ij, cum quibus testamenti factio {g}est. Sed neque mulier, neque impubes, neque seruus {h}, neque furiosus, neque mutus, neque surdus, neque is, cui bonis interdictum est, neque ij, quos leges iubent improbos intestabiles esse: possunt in numerum testium adhiberi.
units.tr: 6 ¶Those may be admitted as witnesses who have testamentary capacity. But neither a woman, nor a minor below puberty, nor a slave, nor a madman, nor a mute, nor a deaf person, nor one under interdiction of his goods, nor those whom the laws order to be infamous and incapable of giving testimony, can be admitted into the number of witnesses.

units.la: 7 ¶Sed cum aliquis ex testibus testamenti quidem faciendi tempore liber exstitit, postea autem seruus apparuit: tam diu Hadrianus Catoni {i}, quam postea diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt, subuenire ex sua liberalitate testamento: ut sic habeatur firmum, ac si ut oportebat, factum esset: cum eo tempore quo testamentum signaretur, omnium consensu hic testis liberi loco fuerit: neque quisquam esset, qui status ei quaestionem moueret.
units.tr: 7 ¶But when one of the witnesses was free at the time the will was made, yet afterwards appeared to be a slave, Hadrian, in a rescript to Cato, and afterwards the deified Severus and Antoninus, rescribed that by their own generosity the will should be aided, so that it is held firm as if it had been done as it ought to have been: since at the time the will was sealed, by the common consent of all, this witness was regarded as free, and no one would raise a question about his status.

units.la: 8 ¶Pater, nec non is, qui in potestate eius est, item duo fratres, qui in eiusdem patris potestate sunt, utique testes in uno testamento fieri possunt. quia nihil nocet, ex una domo plures testes alieno {k}negotio adhiberi.
units.tr: 8 ¶A father, and likewise the one who is in his power, and two brothers who are in the power of the same father, can indeed all be witnesses to one will. For it does no harm that several witnesses from one household are admitted in another's business.

units.la: 9 ¶In testibus autem non debet esse is, qui in potestate testatoris est. Sed si filius familias de castrensi peculio post missionem faciat testamentum, nec pater eius recte adhibetur testis, nec is, qui in potestate eiusdem patris est: reprobatum est enim in {m}ea re domestica testimonii.
units.tr: 9 ¶But the one who is in the power of the testator must not be a witness. But if a son under power makes a will concerning his camp-peculium after his discharge, neither his father is rightly admitted as a witness, nor the one who is in the power of the same father: for in this domestic matter testimony has been rejected.
10 ¶But neither the instituted heir

units.la: {k} l.22.§.2.ff.eo. eo exemplo dici potest morte testis testamenti non decidere. v.l.4.ff.quemad.testamenta aper. suo.l.10.ff.de testib.
units.tr: {k} l.22 §2 ff. eo. By this example it may be said that the death of a witness does not undo a will. See l.4 ff. quemad. testamenta aper. and l.10 ff. de testib.
Nov. 107; on gift in view of death, and codicils. Vigl.

units.la: {m} & aliis, l.2.Cod.de testib. res scriptus,neque is,qui in potestate eius est,neque pater eius,qui eum habet in potestate, neq. fratres, qui in eiusdem patris potestate sunt, testes adhiberi possunt: quia hoc totū negotium,quod agitur testamenti ordinandi gratia,creditur hodie inter testatorem & heredem agi.Licet autē totum ius tale co-turbatū fuerat,& veteres quidem familiæ emptorē, & eos qui per potestatem ei coniuncti fuerant, à testamentariis testimoniis repellebātur: heredi‖autē,‖[?] & iis, qui per potestatem ei coniuncti fuerat, concedebāt testimonia in testamentis præstare: licet ii, qui id permittebant, hoc iure minimē abuti eos debere suadebant: tamen nos eandem obseruationem corrigentes,& quod ab illis suasum[?] est, in legis nescitatem transferentes, ad imitationem pristini familiæ emptoris, merito{*}nec heredi, (qui imagine vetustissimi familiæ emptoris obtinet) neque al iis personis, quæ ei (ut dictum est) coniunctæ sunt, licentiā concedimus, sibi quodammodo testimonia præstare. ideoq. nec eiusmodi veteres constitutiones nostro Codici inseri permisimus. 11
units.tr: {m} and others, l.2 Cod. de testib. ...nor the one who is in his power, nor his father who has him in power, nor brothers who are under the power of the same father, can be admitted as witnesses: because this whole transaction, which is carried out for the sake of ordering a will, is believed today to take place between testator and heir. Although indeed the whole law on this was once confused, and the ancients rejected the purchaser of the family and those joined to him by power from testamentary testimony, but allowed the heir, and those joined to him by power, to give testimony in wills; although those who permitted it advised that they ought not abuse this right at all, yet we, correcting the same observance, and transferring what they advised into ignorance of the law, in imitation of the former purchaser of the family, rightly grant license neither to the heir (who holds the likeness of the most ancient purchaser of the family) nor to the persons joined to him as said, to give testimony for themselves in a way. Therefore we have not permitted such ancient constitutions to be inserted into our Code. 11 ¶But to legatees and fideicommissaries, because they are not successors by law, and to other persons joined to them, we do not deny testimony: indeed, in a certain constitution of ours we have granted this to them specially. And much more do we give this license to those who are in their power, or who have them in power. 12

units.la: ¶Legata-riis autem & fideicommissariis,quia non iuris{b} successores sunt, & aliis personis eis coniunctis testimonium non denegamus{c}:immo in quadam nostra constitutione{d} & hoc specialiter eis concessimus. Et multo magis iis,qui in eorum potestate sunt,vel qui eos habent in potestate, huiusmodi licentiā damus. 12
units.tr: ¶But to legatees and fideicommissaries, because they are not successors by law, and to other persons joined to them, we do not deny testimony: indeed, in a certain constitution of ours we have granted this to them specially. And much more do we give this license to those who are in their power, or who have them in power. 12

units.la: ¶Nihil autem interest,testamentum in tabulis{f},an in chartis,membranisue, vel in alia materia fiat. 13
units.tr: ¶It makes no difference whether a will is made on tablets, on paper or parchment, or in some other material. 13

units.la: ¶Sed § & unum testamentum plurimis codicibus conficere quis potest,secundum obtinentem tamen obseruatione omnibus factis. quod interdū etiā necessarium est: veluti si quis nauigaturus & secum ferre,&‖domi[?]‖relinquere iudiciorum suorum contestatione velit,vel propter alias innumerabiles causas,quę humanis necessitatibus imminēt. 14
units.tr: ¶One person may also make a single will in several codices, provided that all are executed according to the prevailing observance. This is sometimes even necessary: for example, if someone about to sail wishes to take one with him and leave one at home, as an attestation of his decisions, or for other countless reasons that press upon human needs. 14

units.la: ¶Sed hæc quidem de testamentis,quę scriptis conficiuntur,‖sufficiunt[?]‖,si quis autem sine scriptis voluerit ordinare iure ciuili testamentum: septē testibus adhibitis,& sua voluntate coram eis nuncupata,sciat hoc perfectissimum testamentum iure ciuili,firmúmque constitutum.
units.tr: ¶But these things are enough concerning wills that are made in writing. If anyone wishes to make a will under civil law without writing, with seven witnesses admitted and his wishes declared orally before them, let him know that this is established under civil law as the most perfect and firm will.

units.la: interpretum calumnias idem sæpius inculcari oportuit Vigl.
units.tr: It was often necessary to inculcate the same point, against the calumnies of the interpreters. Vigl.

units.la: {f} v.l.15, in sin. Cod, cod[?], an & notis? v. nouell. 107. c.1. § l.24. ff.eodem.
units.tr: {f} See l.15, at the end, Cod.; or notes? See Nov. 107 c.1 §; l.24 ff. eodem.
On the Military Will, Title XI.

units.la: SVPRA-dicta diligens obseruatio {a}in ordinandis testamentis, militibus propter nimiā imperitiā {b}eorū, cōstitutionibus principalibus {c}remissa est. Nā quamuis ij neque legitimum numerū testium adhibuerint, neque aliā testamentorū solemnitatem obseruauerint: rectè {d}nihilominus testantur, videlicet cùm in expeditionibus occupati sunt: quod merito [?]nostra {e}constitutio introduxit. Quoquo {f}enim modo voluntas eius supremā inueniatur, siue scripta, siue sine scriptura: valet testamentum ex voluntate eius. Illis autem tempo-ribus, per quæ citra expeditionum necessitatem in aliis locis vel suis ædibus {g}degunt: minimè ad vendicandum tale priuilegium adiuuantur. Sed testari quidem, etsi filiifamiliarum sint, propter militiā concedūtur: iure tamen communi eadē obseruatione & in eorum testamentis adhibenda, quā in testamentis paganorum pximè [?]exposuimus.
units.tr: The careful observance prescribed above in drawing up wills has been relaxed for soldiers, because of their great inexperience, by imperial constitutions. For although they neither observe the lawful number of witnesses nor any other formality of wills, they nevertheless make valid wills, namely when they are engaged in campaigns. Our constitution rightly introduced this. For whatever way their last wishes are found, whether written or unwritten, the will is valid according to their intention. But during those times when they live in other places or in their own homes, away from the necessity of campaigns, they are not at all helped in claiming such a privilege. Yet soldiers who are sons under paternal power are also allowed to make wills because of their military service. Under the common law, however, the same formality must be observed in their wills as we have just set out for the wills of civilians.

units.la: ¶ Plane de testamentis militū diuus Traianus Catilio {h}Seuero rescripsit: Id priuilegiū, quod militantibus datū est, vt quoquo modo facta ab his testamenta rata sint: sic intelligi debet, vt vtique prius cōstare debeat, testamentū factū esse, quod & sine scriptura & à militantibus fieri potest. Si ergo miles, de cuius bonis apud te quæritur, couocatis ad hoc {i}hominibus, vt voluntatē suā testaretur, ita loquutus est, vt declararet, quem vellet sibi heredem esse, & cui libertatē tribueret: potest videri sine scripto hoc modo {k}esse testatus, & voluntas eius rata habenda est.
units.tr: Indeed, the deified Trajan wrote a rescript to Catilius Severus concerning the wills of soldiers. The privilege granted to soldiers, that wills made by them in any manner are valid, must be understood in this way: it must first be established that a will was made, which can be done even without writing and by soldiers. So if a soldier, about whose goods you are inquiring, having summoned men for this purpose, spoke in such a way as to declare whom he wished to be his heir and whom he wished to grant freedom, it may be held that he made his will in this way without writing, and his intention is to be regarded as valid.

units.la: Cæterum si (vt plerumque sermonibus fieri solet) dixit alicui, ego te heredem facio, aut, bona mea tibi relinquo: non oportet hoc pro testamento obseruari. Nec vllorum magis interest, quàm ipsorum, quibus id priuilegium datum est, ciusmodi exemplum non admitti. Alioqui non difficulter post mortē alicuius militis testes existerent, qui adfirmarent se audisse dicentē aliquē, relinquere se bona, cui visum sit, & per hoc vera iudicia subuerterentur.
units.tr: But if (as is commonly the case in conversation) he said to someone, "I make you my heir," or "I leave my goods to you," this ought not to be observed as a will. Nor is anyone more concerned than those themselves to whom this privilege has been granted that such an example not be admitted. Otherwise, after the death of any soldier, witnesses would easily appear who would affirm that they had heard someone say that he left his goods to whomever he pleased, and in this way true judgments would be overturned.

units.la: ¶ Quinimo & mutus & surdus {k}miles testamentum facere po-[illegible, ~6 letters] classici, audiendi, atque petendæ factionis testamenti à principe incapax.) sed ex accidenti, & quidem scribendi ignarus. teft4. 3 ¶Sed hactenus hoc illis à principalibus constitutionibus coceditur, quatenus militant, & in castris degunt. Post missione vero veterani, vel extra castra alij, si faciant adhuc militantes testamentu, communi omniū ciuiū Romanorum iure id facere debent. Et quod in castris fecerint testamentu, non communi iure, sed quomodo voluerint: post misiones intra annū tantum valebit. Quid ergo si intra annū quis decesserit, conditio autē heredi adscripta post annū extiterit? an quasi militis testamentū valeat? Et placet valere quasi militis. 4 ¶Sed & si quis ante militiā nō iure fecit testamentū, & miles factus, & in expeditione degens resignauit illud, & quaedam adiecit, sine detraxit, vel alias manifesta est nullitis voluntas hoc valere volentis: dicendum est valere hoc testamentū, quasi ex noua militis volun-tate. 5 ¶Denique & si in adrogatione datus fuerit miles, vel filius familias emancipatus est, testamentū eius quasi ex noua militis voluntate valet, nec videtur capitis deminutione irritum fieri.
units.tr: Indeed, even a soldier who is mute and deaf can make a will [illegible, ~6 letters] ... of the fleet, unable to hear, and unable to seek the making of a will from the emperor; but by accident, and indeed one ignorant of writing. But so far this is granted to them by the imperial constitutions, insofar as they are serving and living in camp. After discharge, however, veterans, or others outside the camp, if they still make a will while serving, must make it under the common law of all Roman citizens. And a will that they made in camp is valid not under the common law but in whatever way they chose, but only for a year after discharge. What then if someone dies within the year, but a condition attached to the heir arises after the year? Is the will valid as that of a soldier? And it is held that it is valid as a soldier's. (4) But also, if someone made a will before entering military service, not validly, and having become a soldier and staying on campaign, he cancelled it and added or removed certain things, or otherwise his clear intention that it should stand is evident, it must be said that this will is valid, as from the soldier's new intention. (5) Finally, if a soldier has been given in adrogation, or a son under paternal power has been emancipated, his will is valid as from the soldier's new intention, and it is not thought to be made void by a loss of status.

units.la: 6 ¶Sciendum tamen est, quod cum ad exemplū castrensis peculij, tam anteriores leges, quàm principales constitutiones quibusdam quasi castrensia dederant peculia, & horū quibusdā permissum fuerat etiā in potestate degentibus testari nostra idꝯ constitutio latiūs extendens, permiserit omnibus in huiusmodi peculiis testari quidē, sed iure cōmuni. Cuius constitutionis tenore perspecto, licētia est, nihil eorū, quae ad praefatū ius pertinent, ignorare.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that since the earlier laws, as well as the imperial constitutions, had granted certain peculia as if they were camp peculia, and since it had been permitted to some of these even for those under paternal power to make a will, our own constitution, extending this more widely, has permitted everyone to make a will in such peculia, but under the common law. Once the tenor of this constitution has been carefully considered, it is permissible to be ignorant of nothing that pertains to the aforesaid law.

units.la: QVIBVS NON EST PERMISSVM facere Testamentum. TIT. XII.
units.tr: Persons who are not permitted to make a will. Title XII.

units.la: NON tamen omnibus licet facere testamentū. Statim enim ij, qui falieno iuri subiecti sunt, testamenti faciendi iis nō habent: adeo quidem, vt quamuis parentes eis permiserint, nihilo magis iure testari possunt g: exceptis iis, quos antea enumerauimus, & praecipue militibus, qui in potestate parentū sunt, quibus de eo, quod in castris adquisierunt, permissum est ex constitutionibus principum testamentū facere. Quod quidē ius ab initio tantum sit inciuile, donare patris iussu non æque. militantibus datū est,tàm ex auctoritate diui Augusti,quàm Neruæ, necnon optimi Imperatoris Traiani: postea'verò subscriptione diui Hadriani, etiā dimissis à militia, id est,veteranis concessum est. Itaq; si quidē fecerint de castrensi peculio testamentum: pertinebit hoc ad eū,quē heredē reliquerūt.si verò intestati decesserint, nullis liberis vel fratribus superstitibus: ad parentes eorū iure communi a per-tinebit.Ex hoc intelligere possumus : {*}quod in castris adquiescerit miles, qui in potestate patris est, neque ipsum patrē adimere posse, neque patris creditores id vendere, vel aliter inquietare, neq. patre mortuo cum fratribus cōmune esse:sed scilicet propriū eius esse,qui id in castris adquisierit:quanquam iure ciuili omniū, qui in potestate parentum sunt, peculia perinde in bonis parentū cōputentur, ac seruorū peculia in bonis dominorū numerātur: exceptis videlicet iis,quæ ex sacris constitutionibus & præcipuè nostris propter diuersas causas non adquiruntur.Præter hos igitur, qui castrense peculiū vel quasi castrense habet,si quis alius filius familiās testamentū fecerit inutile est, licet suæ potestatis factus decesserit.
units.tr: Not everyone, however, is permitted to make a will. Those who are subject to another's authority are not allowed to make a will at all. Indeed, even if their parents have given them permission, they cannot make a will by right, with the exception of those whom we listed earlier, and especially soldiers who are under their parents' power. By imperial constitutions, soldiers have been permitted to make a will concerning what they acquired in the camp. At first this right was purely civil, and it was granted to soldiers by the authority of the deified Augustus, as well as Nerva and the excellent emperor Trajan. Later, by a rescript of the deified Hadrian, it was extended even to those discharged from military service, that is, to veterans. Therefore, if they have made a will of their castrense peculium, it will pass to the person they named as heir. If, however, they die intestate, with no children or brothers surviving, it will pass by common law to their parents. From this we can understand that what a soldier under his father's power has acquired in the camp cannot be taken away by the father himself, nor sold or otherwise harassed by the father's creditors, nor, after the father's death, is it held in common with the brothers. It is rather the sole property of the one who acquired it in the camp. Although by civil law the peculia of all who are under parental power are counted among the parents' goods, just as slaves' peculia are counted among their masters' goods, the exceptions are those things which, by sacred constitutions and especially by our own, are not acquired for various reasons. Therefore, apart from those who hold a castrense or quasi-castrense peculium, if any other son under power makes a will, it is invalid, even if he dies having become his own master.

units.la: 1 ¶Præterea testamentum facere nō possunt impuberes: quia nullū eorum animi iudiciū est.Ité furiosi: quia mentē carent. Nec ad rē pertinet,si impubes,postea pubes: aut furiosus, postea cōpos mentis factus fuerit,& decesserit. Furiosi ante,si per id tempus fecerint testamentū,quo furor eorū intermissus est: iure testati esse videtur,cer te eo,quod ante furorem fecerint,testamento valente. Nam neque testamentū rectè factū,neque vllū aliud negotiū rectè gestū, postea furor interueniens perimit.
units.tr: 1 ¶Furthermore, those under puberty cannot make a will, because none of them has the judgment of mind. Likewise the insane, because they lack a sound mind. It does not matter whether one who was under puberty later reaches it, or a madman later recovers his wits and dies. If the insane made a will during the time when their madness was suspended, they are considered to have made it validly, since the will made before the madness is valid. For a will rightly made, and any other transaction rightly done, is destroyed by madness that supervenes afterward.

units.la: 2 ¶Item prodigus,cui bonorū suorū admi-nistratio interdicta est, testamentum facere nō potest. sed id,quod ante fecerit,quàm interdictio bonorum suorū ei fiat,ratum est.
units.tr: 2 ¶Likewise a prodigal, whose administration of his goods has been interdicted, cannot make a will. But what he made before the interdiction of his goods was imposed on him is valid.

units.la: 3 ¶Item surdus & mutus non semper testamentum facere possunt. Vtique ante de eo surdo loquimur,qui omnino nō exaudit, non qui rarde[?] exaudit.nam & mutus is intelligitur, qui eloqui nihil potest,nō qui tarde loquitur. sæpe enim etiam literati & eruditi homines variis casibus & audiendi & loquendi facultatem amittunt. Vnde nostra constitutio etiā hiis subuenit,vt certis casibus & modis secundū normā eius possint testari, aliáque facere, quæ eis permissa sunt. Sed si quis post testamentū factū,aduersa valetudine, aut quo-
units.tr: 3 ¶Likewise the deaf and the mute cannot always make a will. We speak here of a deaf man who does not hear at all, not of one who hears with difficulty; for a person is understood to be mute if he can say nothing, not if he speaks slowly. Indeed, even learned and educated men often lose the ability to hear and to speak through various accidents. Hence our constitution also provides for them, so that in certain cases and in certain ways, according to its rule, they may make a will and do the other things that are permitted to them. But if someone, after making a will, begins to be mute or deaf through poor health or by some other accident,

units.la: a Olim quasi peculium l.2. ff.de castrensi. hodie iure successionis. nouel.118.c.2. libet alio casu mutus aut surdus esse coeperit, ratu nihilominus manet eius testamentu.
units.tr: a Formerly a quasi-castrense peculium: l. 2 ff. de castrensi. Today by the law of succession: Novel 118, c. 2. his will nevertheless remains valid.

units.la: 4 ¶Cæcus aute nō {a}potest facere tastamentū,nisi per obseruatione,quā lex {b}diui iustini patris nostri introduxit.
units.tr: 4 ¶A blind man cannot make a will, except by the observance which the law of the deified Justinian, our father, introduced.

units.la: 5 ¶Eius, qui apuchostes[?] est {c}testamentū, quod ibi fecit,non valet,quamuis redierit.sed quod,dum in ciuitate fuerat,feceritsiue redierit,valet iure postliminij: siue illic decesserit,valet ex lege Cornelia.
units.tr: 5 ¶A will which someone made while among the enemy is not valid, even if he returns. But what he made while he was in the city, whether he later returns or dies there, is valid: if he returns, by right of postliminium; if he dies there, by the Cornelian law.
On Disinheritance of Children, TIT. XIII.

units.la: ON[?] tamen vt omnino valeat testamentum, sufficit hæc obseruatio,quam supra exposuimus: sed qui filium in potestate habet,curare debet, vt eū heredē instituat {e}vel exheredē eū nominatim sciat {f}alioqui si eum silentio præterierit , inutiliter testabitur {g}: adeò quidē,vt si viuo patre, filius mortuus sit,nemo heres ex eo testamento existere possit, quia scilicet ab initio non constiterit testamentum. Sed non ita de filiabus,& aliis per virilem sexū descendentibus liberis vtriusque sexus antiquitati suē obseruatū: sed si nō fuerāt scripti heredes scripte,vel exheredati exheredatæue: testamentū quidem non infirmabatur,iuris tamen adcrescendi eis ad certā portione præstabatur. sed nec nominatim eas personas exheredare parentibus necesse erat, sed licebat inter cæteros hoc facere*. Nominatim autem quis exheredari videtur,siue ita exheredetur,Titiꝰ filius meus exheres esto: siue ita, filius meus exheres esto, non adiecto proprio nomine,scilicet si alius filius non exstet {h}.
units.tr: Yet for a will to be fully valid, the observance we explained above is enough. But a man who has a son under his power must take care either to institute him heir or to name him expressly as disinherited. Otherwise, if he passes him over in silence, he makes an ineffective will. Indeed, if the son dies while the father is still alive, no heir can come into the inheritance under that will, because the will never took effect from the beginning. It was not so with daughters and other children descended through the male line, of either sex, under ancient practice. If they had not been written in as heirs, or had not been disinherited, the will was not invalidated, but they were granted a right of accrual to a certain portion. Nor was it necessary to disinherit those persons by name; it was allowed to do so among the others. A person is considered to be disinherited by name either if he is disinherited thus: "Titius, my son, let him be disinherited," or thus: "my son let him be disinherited," without adding his proper name, provided, of course, that no other son exists.

units.la: ¶ Posthumi quoque liberi,vel heredes institui debent, vel {†}exheredari. Et in eo par omniū conditio est, quod & filio posthumo, & quolibet ex cæteris liberis,siue fœminini sexus,siue masculini,præterito: valet quidē testamentum, sed postea adgnatione posthumi siue posthumæ rupitur, & ea ratione totū infirmatur.Idcoque si mulier, ex qua posthumus aut posthuma sperabatur,abortu se-ceritnihil impedimento est scriptis heredibus ad hereditate adeundâ.Sed fœminini quidē sexus per exheredari sine caussa : quç in posthumo nulla esse potest.
units.tr: Posthumous children too must either be instituted as heirs or disinherited. In this all are alike: whether a posthumous son or any other child, of either sex, is passed over, the will is indeed valid, but afterwards it is broken by the agnation of the posthumous son or daughter, and for that reason the whole is invalidated. Therefore, if the woman from whom a posthumous son or daughter was expected miscarries, this is no obstacle to the written heirs taking up the inheritance. But daughters may be disinherited without cause, which in the case of a posthumous child cannot be.

units.la: {h} Ioan. 3. sonæ vel nominatim,vel inter ᵃ cæteros exheredari solebant: dū tamé,si inter cæteros exheredarentur, aliquid eis legaretur, ne viderentur præteritæ esse p obliuione.Masculos verò posthumos,id est, Filios & deinceps placuit non aliter recte exheredari, nisi nominatim exheredarentur:hoc scilicet modo, quicunque mihi filius genitus fuerit, exheres esto.
units.tr: Ioan. 3. Persons were customarily disinherited either by name or among the rest, provided that, if they were disinherited among the rest, something was left to them, so that they would not seem to have been passed over through forgetfulness. But it was held that male posthumous children, that is, sons and their descendants, could be disinherited validly only by name, in this form: "Whatever son shall be born to me, let him be disinherited."

units.la: ¶ Posthumorūᵇ autē loco sunt & hi,qui in suì heredis locū succedendo,quasi agnascendo fiunt parentibus suì heredes,vt ecce,si quis filium, & ex eo nepotem neptemue in potestate habeat: quia filius gradu præcedit,is solus iura suì heredis habet,quanuis nepos quoque & neptis ex eo in eadē potestate sunt.Sed si filius eius viuo eo moriatur,aut qualibet alia ratione exeat de potestate eius: incipit nepos neptisue in eius locū succedere,& eo modo iura suo rum heredū quasi adgnatione nancisccuntur. Ne ergo eo modo rumpatur eius testamentū: sicut ipsum filiū vel heredē instituere,vel nominatim exheredare debet testator,ne nō iure faciat testamentum: ita & nepotē neptemue ex filio necesse est ei vel heredē instituere,vel exheredare: ne forte eoviuo filio mortuo succedendo in locum eius nepos neptisue, quasi adgnatione rumpat testamentū.ldq.lege Iulia Velleaᶜ prouisum est, in qua similis exheredationis modus ad similitudinē posthumorū demonstratur.
units.tr: Those also are in the position of posthumous children who, by succeeding into the place of a heir of their own, become heirs of their own to their parents, as it were by agnation. For example, if someone has in his power a son and, through that son, a grandson or granddaughter, the son, as he comes first in degree, alone holds the rights of an heir of his own, although the grandson and granddaughter born of him are also under the same power. But if that son dies while his father is alive, or leaves his power in some other way, the grandson or granddaughter begins to succeed into his place and so acquires the rights of heirs of their own, as if by agnation. Therefore, so that the will is not broken in this way, the testator must either institute as heir or expressly disinherit the grandson or granddaughter born of the son, just as he must do with the son himself, lest he make the will invalidly. For otherwise, if the son should die while the father is still alive, the grandson or granddaughter, succeeding into his place, might break the will as if by agnation. This was provided for by the Julian-Velleian law, in which a similar mode of disinheriting is prescribed on the model of posthumous children.

units.la: 3 ¶ Emancipatos liberos iure ciuili neq. heredes instituere neque exheredare necesse est: quia non sunt sui heredes. Sed prætor omnes, tam fœminini sexus,quàm masculini, si heredes non instituantur, exheredari iubet:virilis sexus nominatim:fœminini verò inter cæteros: quia si neque heredes instituti fuerint neque ita (vt diximus) exheredati permittit eis prætor contra tabulas testamenti bonorū possessionē.
units.tr: Emancipated children need not be instituted as heirs or disinherited under the civil law, because they are not heirs of their own. But the praetor orders that all of them, daughters as well as sons, if they are not instituted as heirs, be disinherited: sons by name, but daughters among the rest. For if they have neither been instituted as heirs nor disinherited in the manner we have described, the praetor allows them possession of goods against the tablets of the will.

units.la: 4 ¶ Adoptini liberi quamdiu sunt in potestate patris adoptiui,ciusdē iuris habētur,cuius sunt iustis nuptiis quæsiti. itaq. heredes instituendi, vel exheredandi sunt secundum ea,quæ de naturalibus exposuimus. Emancipati vero a patre adoptiuo, neq. iure ciuili,neque eo iure,quod ad edictū prætoris attinet,inter liberos connumerantur. Qua ratione aui ex filio præmortuo nasciturum, instituendum. Velleius vt idem esset, si viuo auo nasceretur, constituit, eamque legem Scævola posteā interpretatus est. l.29.ff.de leg. & posth. accidit, ut ex diverso (quod ad naturale parente at-tinet) quamdiu quidē siunt in adoptiua familia, ex-traneorū numero habeantur: ut eos neque heredes instituere, neque exheredare necesse sit. cūm verò emācipati fuerint ab adoptiuo patre: tūc incipiāt in ea causa esse, in qua futuri essent, si à naturali patre emancipati fuissent. §[?] ¶Sed hæc quidē vetustas introducebat. {*}nostra{a} vero constitutio inter mas-cu-los & fœminas in hoc jure nihil interesse existimās: quia utraq. persona in hominū procreatione simili naturæ officio fungitur, & lege antiqua}duodecim tabularū|omnes similiter ad successionē ab intesta-to vocabantur, quod & prætores postea sequnuti esse videntur: ideo simplex ac simile jus, & in filiis, & in filiabus, & in cæteris descendentibus per virilem se-xum personis, non solum iam natis, sed etiam posthumi-s,introduxit: ut omnes siue sui, siue emācipati sint, vel heredes instituantur, vel nominatim exheredēn-tur: & eundem habeant effectum circa testamenta parentū suorum infirmanda, & hereditatem auferendā, quem filii sui vel emancipati habent, siue iam nati sint, siue adhuc in utero constituti, postea nati sint.
units.tr: Adoptive children, for as long as they are in the power of the adoptive father, are regarded as having the same status as those born in lawful marriage. Therefore they must be instituted as heirs or disinherited in the same way as we have set out for natural children. But once emancipated by the adoptive father, they are counted among the children neither under the civil law nor under the law that relates to the praetor's edict. For this reason, Velleius provided that a grandson born after the death of his son should be instituted as heir, and that the same rule should hold if he were born while his grandfather was alive; and Scaevola later interpreted that law (Dig. 29, de legatis et posthumis). The reverse holds with respect to the natural parent: as long as children remain in the adoptive family, they are counted among strangers, so that there is no need to institute or disinherit them; but when they have been emancipated by the adoptive father, they begin to stand in the position they would have occupied had they been emancipated by their natural father. But this was the old rule. Our constitution, however, judging that in this matter there is no difference between males and females, since each person performs a similar natural office in the procreation of human beings, and since under the old law of the Twelve Tables all were called alike to succession on intestacy (which the praetors also seem later to have followed), has introduced a single and uniform law, for sons, daughters and other descendants through male lines, not only those already born but also posthumous ones. Thus all of them, whether in the power of their father or emancipated, must either be instituted as heirs or expressly disinherited, and they have the same effect in invalidating their parents' wills and in taking away the inheritance that sons or emancipated sons have, whether they were already born or were in the womb and were born afterwards.

units.la: Circa adoptiuos autem | filios | certam induximus divisionē, quæ in nostra constitutione{b}, quam super adoptiuis tulimus, continetur. ¶ 6 ¶Sed si in ex-peditione occupatus miles testamentum faciat, & liberos suos iam natos, vel posthumos nominatim nō exheredauerit, sed | silentio | præterierit, non igno-rans, an habeat liberos: silentium eius pro exhere-datione nominatim sacta valere, constitutionibus{c} principum cautum est. 7 ¶Mater, vel avus ma-ternus, necesse non habent liberos suos, aut heredes instituere, aut exheredare{d}: sed possunt eos silētio o-mittere{e}. nam silentium matris, aut aui materni, & cæterorum per matrem ascendentium tantum facit, quantum exheredatio patris. Neque enim matri fi-lium filiamve, neque auo materno nepotem neptemve ex filia, si eum eamve heredem non instituat, ex-heredare necesse est: siue de iure ciuili quæramus, siue de edicto prætoris, quo | prætor | præteritis li-beris contra tabulas bonorum possessionem permit-tit: sed aliud eis adminiculum seruatur, quod paulò postea vobis manifestum fiet.
units.tr: Concerning adoptive sons, however, we have introduced a certain distinction, which is contained in our constitution that we issued about adoptions. A soldier who, occupied on an expedition, makes a will, and does not disinherit by name his children already born or posthumous, whom he has passed over in silence although he was not ignorant whether he had children, is by imperial constitutions secured so that his silence is valid as a disinheritance made by name. A mother, or a maternal grandfather, need not institute their children as heirs or disinherit them, but they may pass them over in silence. For the silence of a mother, or of a maternal grandfather, and of other ascendants through the mother, has only the same effect as the disinheritance of a father. Indeed, a mother is not required to disinherit her son or daughter, nor a maternal grandfather his grandson or granddaughter born of a daughter, if she or he does not institute them as heir, whether we inquire under the civil law or under the praetor's edict, by which the praetor allows possession of goods against the tablets to children who have been passed over. But another safeguard is preserved for them, which will shortly become clear to you.
On Instituting Heirs, Title 14

units.la: HEREDES instituere permissum est tam liberos homines, quàm servos : & tam proprios, quàm alienos. Proprios autem olim quidem secundùm plurium sententias non aliter, quàm cum libertate, rectè instituere licebat. Hodie vero etiam sine libertate, ex nostra constitutione heredes eos instituere permissum est. Quod non per innovationē induximus, sed quoniam æquius erat, & Atilicino placuisse Paulus suis libris, quos tam ad Masurium Sabinum, quàm ad Plautium scripsit, refert. Proprius autem servus etiam is intelligitur, in quo nudam proprietatem testator habet, alio usumfructum habente. Est tamen casus, in quo nec cum libertate utiliter servus à domina heres instituitur, ut constitutione divorum Severi & Antonini cauetur, cuius verba hæc sunt: Servum a-dulterio maculatum , non iure testamento manumissum ante sententiam ab ea muliere videri, quæ rea fuerat eiusdem criminis postulata, rationis est . Quare sequitur, ut in eundem à domina collata heredis institutio, nullius momenti habeatur . Alienus servus etiam is intelligitur, in quo usumfructum te-stator habet.
units.tr: It is permitted to institute heirs both free men and slaves, and both one's own and another's. Formerly, according to the opinion of most jurists, one could validly institute one's own slaves only if they were also freed. Today, by our constitution, it is permitted to institute them as heirs even without freedom. We did not introduce this by innovation, but because it was more equitable, and Paulus, in his books written both to Masurius Sabinus and to Plautius, reports that Atilicinus had held this view. A slave is also understood to be one's own if the testator holds only the bare ownership of him while another has the usufruct. There is, however, a case in which a slave cannot validly be instituted heir by his mistress even with freedom, as is provided by the constitution of the deified Severus and Antoninus, whose words are these: "It is reasonable that a slave stained by adultery, not freed by will before sentence, is regarded as belonging to that woman who had been accused of the same crime as a defendant. Hence it follows that the institution of heir made in his favour by his mistress is considered of no effect." A slave of another is also understood to be one in whom the testator holds the usufruct.

units.la: Servus autem à domino suo he-res institutus, si quidem in eadem causa manserit: fit ex testamento liber hæresque ei necessarius. Si vero à vivo testatore manumissus fuerit, suo arbitrio adire hereditatem potest: quia non fit heres necessarius, cum utrumque ex domini testamento non consequatur. Quod si alienatus fuerit: iussu noui domini adire hereditatem debet, & ea ratione per eum dominus fit heres. Nam ipse alienatus, neque liber neque heres esse potest, etiam si cum libertate heres institutus fuerit, destitisse enim à libertatis datione videtur dominus, qui eum alienauit. Alienus quoque servus heres institutus, si in eadem causa duraverit, iussu eius domini adire hereditatem debet. Si vero alienatus fuerit ab eo, aut vivo testatore, aut post mortem eius, antequam adeat, debet iussu noui domini adire. At si manumissus est vivo testatore, vel mortuo antequam adeat, suo arbitrio adire potest hereditatem.
units.tr: A slave instituted heir by his master, if he remains in the same condition, becomes free by the will and is a necessary heir. But if he is freed by the testator while the testator is alive, he may enter upon the inheritance at his own discretion, because he does not become a necessary heir, since he does not obtain both things under the master's will. But if he has been alienated, he must enter upon the inheritance on the order of the new master, and by that means the master becomes heir through him. For the slave himself, having been alienated, can be neither free nor heir, even if he was instituted heir with freedom; for the master who alienated him is held to have abandoned the grant of liberty. A slave of another, instituted heir, if he remains in the same condition, must enter upon the inheritance on the order of that master. But if he has been alienated by that master, either while the testator is alive or after his death and before he enters, he must enter on the order of the new master. But if he has been freed while the testator is alive, or after the testator's death and before he enters, he may enter upon the inheritance at his own discretion.

units.la: ² ¶Servus etiam alienus post domini morte recte heres instituitur: quia & cum hereditariis servis est testamenti factio. Nondum enim adita hereditas persone vicem sustinet,non heredis futuri,sed defun-cti[?] {4}: qum etiam eius, qui in utero est, seruus recte heres instituatur. 3 ¶Seruus autem {b} pluriū, cum quibus testamenti factio est,ab extraneo institutus heres vnicuique dominorum, cuius iussu adierit, pro portione domini adquirit hereditatē. 4 ¶Et vnum hominem,& plures vsque in {c} infinitum,quot quis heredes velit facere licet. 5 ¶Hereditas {d} plerumque diuiditur in duodecim vncias, quae assis appellatione continentur. Habent autem & haec partes propria nomina ab vncia vsque ad asse haec {e} sex tans,quadrans,triens,quincunx, semis, septunx,bes, dodrans,dextans,deunx. Non autem vtique semper duodecim vncias esse oportet.nam tot vnicae asses efficiunt,quot testator {f} voluerit.& si vnum tantum quis ex semisse (verbi gratia) heredem scripserit, totus as in semisse erit. ¶Neque enim idem {g} ex parte testatus, & ex parte intestatus decedere potest:nam si sit {h} miles, cuius sola voluntas in testando spectatur.Et contrario potest quis in quotcunque voluerit plurimas vncias suam hereditatem dividere. 6 ¶Si plures instituantur heredes:ita demum in hoc casu partium distributio necessaria est,si nolit testator eos ex aequis partibus heredes esse. Satis enim constat, nullis partibus nominatis,ex aequis partibus eos heredes esse. Partibus autem in quorundam personis expressis,si quidam alius sine parte nominatus erit: si quidem aliqua pars assi deerit:ex {k} ea parte heres fit.Et si plures sine parte scripti sunt,omnes in eandem partem concurrunt{l}. Si vero totus as copletus sit:ijqui nominatim expressas partes habet,in dimidiam partem vocantur:& ille vel illi omnes in alteram dimidiam {m}. Nec interest {n},primus, an medius,an nouissimus,sine parte heres scriptus sit. ea enim pars data intelligitur, quae vacat. 7 ¶Videamus,si pars aliqua vacet,nec tamen quisquam sine parte sit heres, institutus, quid iuris sit.veluti si tres ex quartis partibus heredes scripti sint.Et constat vacante parte singulis tacite pro hereditaria parte accedere, & perinde haberi,ac si ex tertiis partibus heredes scripti essent. & ex diuerso, si plures heredes scripti in portionibus sint:tacite singulis decrescere:vt si(verbi gratia)quatuor ex tertiis partibus heredes scripti sint,perinde habeatur,ac si vnusquisque ex quarta parte heres scriptus fuisset. * v.l.20.ff.eo. * l.78 §.2.ff.e. ¶ l.13.§.2.ff.eo. ¶ d.l. 13.§.3. ¶Et si plures vnciae, quàm duodecim distributae sint: is, qui sine parte institutus est, q dupondio deest, habebit. Idemque erit si dupodius expletus fit, quę omnes partes ad alterum postea renocantur, quaouis sint pluriū vnciarū. 9 ¶Heres & pure & sub tione institui potest: ex certo tempore, aut ad certū tempus non potest veluti, post quinquennium quam moriar, vel ex calendis illis, vel vsque ad kalendas illas heres esto. Denique die adiecto haberi pro superuacuo pla cet: & perinde esse, ac si pure heres institutus esset. 10 ¶Impossibilis codicilio in institutionibus & legatis, necnō in fideicommissis & libertatibus, pro nō scripta haberur. 11 ¶Si plures codiciliones in institutionibus adscriptę sunt: siquidē coniunctim, vtputa si illud & illud factum fuerit: omnibus parendū est. si separatim, veluti si illud aut illud factū erit: cuilibet f conditioni obtēperare satis est. 12 ¶Ij, quos nunquam testator, vidit: heredes institui posiunt, ve-luti & si fratris filios peregrinātes, ignorans qui esset, heredes instituerit. ignorantia enim testantis inuti-lem institutionem non facit.
units.tr: A slave of another is also validly instituted heir after the master's death, because there is testamentary capacity also with slaves belonging to an estate. For an inheritance not yet entered upon takes the place of a person, not of the future heir, but of the deceased [?] {4}; so too the slave of one who is still in the womb is validly instituted heir. 3 ¶ A slave of several persons, with whom there is testamentary capacity, instituted heir by a stranger, acquires the inheritance for each master in proportion to his share, on whose order he enters. 4 ¶ One man or several, indeed as many as one wishes, up to infinity, may be made heirs. 5 ¶ An inheritance is generally divided into twelve ounces, which are comprised under the name of the as. These parts also have their own names, from the ounce up to the as: sextans, quadrans, triens, quincunx, semis, septunx, bes, dodrans, dextans, deunx. It is not always necessary that there be twelve ounces; for as many ounces make up the as as the testator wishes. And if someone names only one heir to a half (for example), the whole as will lie in the half. For one cannot die partly testate and partly intestate, since in making a will only the testator's will is regarded. Conversely, one may divide one's inheritance into as many ounces as one wishes. 6 ¶ If several heirs are instituted, a distribution of shares is necessary in this case only if the testator does not wish them to be heirs in equal shares. For it is well established that, with no shares named, they are heirs in equal shares. When shares are expressed for some persons, and another is named without a share: if some part of the as is lacking, he becomes heir to that part. And if several are named without a share, all come together into that same part. But if the whole as is filled, those who have expressly named shares are called to one half, and he or they all to the other half. Nor does it matter whether he who is named without a share is first, middle, or last; for that share is understood to be given which is vacant. 7 ¶ Let us consider, if some part is vacant and yet no one instituted is without a share, what the law is: for example, if three are named heirs to quarters. It is established that, with a part vacant, each accrues tacitly to his hereditary share, and they are treated as if they had been named heirs to thirds. Conversely, if several heirs are named in shares that exceed the whole, they tacitly diminish each other; so that if four are named heirs to thirds, it is treated as if each had been named heir to a quarter. 8 ¶ And if more than twelve ounces are distributed, the one instituted without a share will have what is lacking to the dupondius. The same will be the case if the dupondius is filled, since all the parts are afterwards recalled to the other, however many ounces there are. 9 ¶ An heir may be instituted both purely and under a condition; but he cannot be instituted from a certain time or up to a certain time, as for example "after five years from the day I die," or "from those calends," or "be heir until those calends." Finally, it is held that a day added is superfluous, and it is held to be as if he had been instituted heir purely. 10 ¶ An impossible condition in institutions and legacies, and likewise in fideicommissa and manumissions, is held as not written. 11 ¶ If several conditions are attached to institutions: if conjunctively, for example "if this and that is done," all must be obeyed; if separately, for example "if this or that happens," it is enough to obey any one condition. 12 ¶ Those whom the testator never saw can be instituted heirs, just as if he instituted the sons of his brother, living abroad, not knowing who they were; for the testator's ignorance does not make the institution useless.
ON ORDINARY SUBSTITUTION. TIT. XV.

units.la: P[?]OTEST autem quis in testamento suo plures gradus heredum facere: vtputa, Si ille heres non erit, ille heres esto: & deinceps, in quantum velit testator: vt nouissimo loco in subsidium vel seruum necessarium heredem instituere possit. 1 ¶Et plures in vnius locum possunt substitui, vel vnus in plurium, vel singuli in singulorum, vel inuicem ipsi, qui heredes instituti sunt. 2 ¶Et si ex disparibus partibus heredes scriptos inuicem substituerit, & nulla mentione in substitutione partium habuerit: eas videtur in substitutione partes dedisse, quas in institutione expressit. & ita diu Pius rescripsit. 3 ¶Sed si instituto heredi, coheredé substituto dato, alius ei substitutus fuerit: diui Seuerus & Antoninus sine distinctione rescripserunt, ad utramque partem substitutum admitti. 4 ¶Si seruus alienum quis parˈtur, ... Greek sentence ...
units.tr: A person may make several degrees of heirs in his will, for example: "If that heir does not take up the inheritance, let that one be heir," and so on as far as the testator wishes, so that in the last place he may appoint a necessary slave as heir in support. (1) Several heirs may be substituted in the place of one, or one in the place of several, or each in the place of each, or the instituted heirs may be substituted for one another. (2) If he has substituted instituted heirs for one another in unequal shares, and has said nothing about the shares in the substitution, it is held that in the substitution he has given those shares which he expressed in the institution. And so the divine Pius rescribed. (3) But if, when an heir was instituted, a co-heir was given as substitute, and another was also substituted to him, the divine Severus and Antoninus rescribed without distinction that the substitute is admitted to either part. (4) If someone acquires a slave belonging to another, [...]

units.la: tur, ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἀρμόζει, τοῦτο μὲν ἐξαιτικῶς, τοῦτο δὲ καὶ πᾶσιν [?]. Theophil. §. tit. proxim. vel φ a quocunque, de quocunque, in quecunque casum concipi possit, nihil speciale habens.
units.tr: ...applies to all cases; this indeed especially [ἐξαιτικῶς], and this also to all [...]. Theophilus, at the title cited above, or "whoever" [φ a quocunque], "concerning whomever," may be conceived in whatever case, having nothing special about it.

units.la: § l.36. in prin. ff. cod. tremfamilias arbitratus, heredem scripserit: & si heres nō esset, Mæuiū ꝗ ei substituerit: isque seruus insu domini adierit hereditatem: ∥ Mæuius ∥ substitutus, in partem admittitur, illa enim verba, si heres nō erit, in eo quidem, quem alieno iuri subiectum esse testator scit, sic accipiuntur: si neque ipse heres erit, neque alium heredem efficerit. in eo vero, quem patremfamilias esse arbitratur, illud significant: si hereditatem sibi, vel ei, cuius iuri postea subiectus esse coeperit, non adquisierit {b}. Idque Tiberius Cæsar in persona Parthenij serui sui constituit.
units.tr: Digest, same title, at the beginning, law 36: if a man, thinking a slave to be a head of household, named him heir, and if he should not be heir, substituted Maevius; and that slave, by his master's order, entered upon the inheritance, Maevius the substitute is admitted to a share. For the words "if he should not be heir" are understood in the case of a person whom the testator knows to be under another's power thus: if neither he himself shall be heir nor shall make another heir. But in the case of one whom he thinks to be a head of household, they mean: if he shall not acquire the inheritance for himself, or for him to whose power he afterwards began to be subject. And Tiberius Caesar laid this down in the person of his slave Parthenius.
TIT. XVI. CONCERNING PUPILLARY AND SUBSTITUTION.

units.la: IBERIS suis impuberibus {d}, quos in potestate quis habet {e}, non solum ita, vt supra diximus, substituere potest: id est, vt si heredes ei non exstiterint, alius sit eis heres: sed eo amplius vt si heredes ei exstiterint, & adhuc impuberes mortui fuerint, sit eis aliquis heres: veluti si quis dicat hoc modo, Titius filius meus heres mihi esto. Et si filius meus heres mihi non erit: sive heres erit, & prius moriatur, quam in suam & tutelam venerit: tunc Seius heres esto. quo casu, siquidem non extiterit heres filius: tunc substitutus patri fit heres. si vero exstiterit heres filius, & ante pubertatem decesserit: ipsi filio fit heres substitutus. nam moribus {h} institutum est, vt quum eius ætatis filij sint, in qua ipsi sibi testamentum facere nō possunt: parentes eis faciant. 1 ¶ Qua ratione excitati, etiam constitutione {i} posuimus in nostro Codice, qua prospectum est, vt si qui mente captos habeant filios, vel nepotes, vel pronepotes cuiuscunque sexus vel gradus: liceat eis, & si puberes sint, ad exemplum pupillaris substitutionis, certas personas substituere. In autem resipuerint, eandem substitutionem infirmari. & hoc ad exemplum pupillaris substitutionis, quæ postquam pupillus adoleuerit, infirmatur. 2 ¶ Igitur in pupillari substitutione secundum præfatum modum ordinata, duo {l} quodammodo sunt testamenta: alterum patris, alterum filij, tanquam si ipse filius sibi heredem instituisset: aut certe vnum testamentum est duarum causarum, id est, duarum hereditatum. 3 ¶ Sin autem quis ita formidolosus
units.tr: A man may substitute heirs for his children who are below the age of puberty and under his power, not only in the way we have described above, namely that if they do not become his heirs, someone else shall be their heir, but further, that if they have become his heirs and then die while still below puberty, someone else shall be heir to them. For example, one may say in this form: Let Titius, my son, be my heir. And if my son shall not be my heir, or if he shall be heir and die before he comes into his own control and guardianship, then let Seius be heir. In this case, if the son does not become heir, the person substituted becomes heir to the father. But if the son becomes heir and dies before puberty, the substitute becomes heir to the son himself. For custom has established that when children are of an age at which they cannot make a will for themselves, their parents make one for them. 1 ¶ Prompted by this reasoning, we have also laid down, in a constitution in our Code, a provision that if anyone has children, grandchildren or great-grandchildren of either sex and of any degree who are mentally incapacitated, they may substitute certain persons for them, even if these are adults, after the model of pupillary substitution. If they recover their wits, this substitution is invalidated, just as pupillary substitution is invalidated once the pupil has grown up. 2 ¶ Therefore, in a pupillary substitution ordered in the aforesaid manner, there are in a sense two wills: one of the father and one of the son, as if the son himself had instituted an heir for himself. Or, certainly, there is one will with two causes, that is, two inheritances. 3 ¶ But if anyone is so anxious
{b} The principal and the pupillary, namely the last law of the Digest, title on wills.

units.la: {k} & tamen vnum. l.20.ff.eo. st, ut timeat, ne filius suus pupillus adhuc, ex eo, quod palam substitutum acceperit, post obitum eius periculo insidiarum subiaceat: vulgarem quidem substitutionem palam facere, & in primis testamenti partibus || ordinare || debet: illam autem substitutionem, per quam heres exstiterit pupillus, & intra pubertatem decesserit, substitutus vocatur: separatim in inferioribus partibus {a}scribere, eamque partem ꝓprio lino, propriaqué cera consignare: & in priore parte testamenti cauere, ne inferiores tabulae viuo filio & adhuc impubere aperiantur {b}. Illud palam est, non indeo minus valere substitutionem impuberis filij, quod in eisdem tabulis scripta sit, quibus sibi quisque heredem instituerit, quamuis pupillo hoc periculosum sit.
units.tr: {k} [And yet it is one: Dig. 20, same title.] lest his son, still a pupil, be exposed to the danger of plots after his death because of the substitution openly made for him, he ought to declare the ordinary substitution openly and set it out in the first parts of the will; but that substitution by which the pupil becomes heir and dies below puberty, and which is called the substitution of the substitute, he should write separately in the lower parts, seal that part with its own thread and its own wax, and in the front part of the will provide that the lower tablets are not to be opened while the son is alive and still below puberty. It is clear that the substitution of an impubescent son is not less valid because it is written on the same tablets on which each man has instituted his own heir, although this is risky for the pupil.

units.la: 4 ¶Non solum autem heredibus institutis impuberibus liberis ita substituere parentes possunt, vt si heredes eis exstiterint, & ante pubertatem mortui fuerint, sit eis heres is, quem ipsi voluerint: sed etiam exheredatis, itaque eo casu si quid ‖exheredato ‖pupillo ex hereditatibus, legatis ve, aut donationibus propinquorum atque amicorum adquisitum fuerit: id {c}omne ad substitutum pertinebit. Quaecunque dixi- mus de substitutione impuberum liberorum vel heredi institutorum, vel exheredatorum: eadem etiam de posthumis intelligimus.
units.tr: 4 ¶ Parents may substitute for their children below puberty not only when they have instituted them as heirs, so that if they become heirs and die before puberty, the heir of their choice takes their place; but also when they have disinherited them. So in that case, if anything is acquired by the disinherited pupil from inheritances, legacies or gifts from relatives and friends, all of it shall pass to the substitute. Whatever we have said about the substitution of children below puberty, whether instituted as heirs or disinherited, we understand to apply equally to posthumous children.

units.la: 5 ¶Liberis autem suis testamentum nemo facere poterit, nisi & {d}sibi faciat. nam pupillare testamentu, pars & sequela est paterni testamenti: adeo, vt si patris testamentu non valeat, nec filij quidem valebit.
units.tr: 5 ¶ No one can make a will for his children unless he also makes one for himself. For the pupillary will is a part and a consequence of the father's will; so much so that if the father's will is not valid, neither will the son's be valid.

units.la: 6 ¶Vel {e}singulis liberis, vel ei, qui eorum nouissimus impubes moriẽtur, substitui potest. singulis quidem, si neminē eorū intestatum decedere voluerit: nouissimo, si ius legitimarum hereditatum integrum inter eos custodiri relict.
units.tr: 6 ¶ A substitution may be made either for each child individually, or for the one of them who dies last while still below puberty. It is made for each individually if the testator does not wish any of them to die intestate; for the last to die, if he wishes the right of the lawful inheritances to be kept whole among them.

units.la: 7 ¶Substituitur autem impuberi aut nominatim, veluti Titius: aut generaliter, vt {f}quisquis mihi heres erit. Quibus verbis vocantur ex substitutione, impubere mortuo filio, illi, qui & scripti sunt heredes, & exstiterunt, & pro qua parte heredes facti sunt.
units.tr: 7 ¶ A substitution for a child below puberty is made either by name, for example Titius, or in general terms, such as "whoever shall be my heir." By these words, when the son dies below puberty, those who were both named as heirs and have become heirs are called to the substitution, and in the proportion in which they became heirs.

units.la: 8 ¶Masculo igitur vsque ad quatuordecim {g}annos substitui potest: fœminae vsque ad duodecim annos. & si hoc tempus excesserint, substitutio evanescit.
units.tr: 8 ¶ Thus a boy may be substituted up to the age of fourteen, and a girl up to the age of twelve. If they exceed this time, the substitution lapses.

units.la: 9 ¶Extraneo vero, vel filio puberi heredi instituto, ita {h}substituere nemo {i}potest, vt si heres exstiterit, & intra aliquod tempus decesserit, alius ei sit heres: sed hoc solum permissum est, vt eum per fideicommissum testator obligetalij hereditatem eius
units.tr: 9 ¶ But no one can substitute for a stranger, or for a son of full age instituted as heir, in such a way that if he becomes heir and dies within some period, another shall be his heir. Only this is permitted: the testator may bind the heir by fideicommissum to restore his inheritance to another, wholly or in part.

units.la: E vel totam, vel pro parte restituere. quod ius quale sit, suo loco trademus.
units.tr: This right, and what kind of right it is, we shall set out in its proper place.

units.la: QUIBUS MODIS TESTA-menta infirmentur. TIT. XVII.
units.tr: How wills are invalidated. Title 17.

units.la: TESTAMENTUM iure {b}factū usque eo valet, donec rumpatur, irritumve fiat.
units.tr: A will validly made remains in force until it is broken or made void.

units.la: 1 ¶Rumpitur autē testamentū, cū in eodē statu manente testatore, ipsius testa-meti[?] ius vitiatur. Si quis enim post {c}factū testamentum adoptauerit sibi filiū per Imperatorē, eū, qui est sui iuris: aut per prætorē secundū nostram constitutionē, eū, qui in potestate parentis fuerit: testamenti eius rumpitur, quasi adgnatione sui heredis.
units.tr: A will is broken when, while the testator remains in the same status, the validity of the will itself is impaired. If someone, after making a will, adopts a son by imperial rescript, one who is sui iuris, or, under our constitution, by the praetor's process, one who was in the power of a parent, his will is broken, as if by the agnation of a suus heres.

units.la: 2 ¶Posteriore quoque testamento, q{4}iure perfectum est, superius {e}rumpitur f. nec interest, exstiterit aliquis heres ex eo, an nō. hoc enim fo-lum spectatur, an aliquo casu existere potuerit. Idēo-que si quis aut noluerit heres esse, aut vivo testatore, aut post mortem eius ante, quam hereditate adi-ret, decesserit, aut conditione, sub qua heres institu-tus est, defectus sit: in his casibus paterfamilias in-testatus moritur. Nam & prius testamentū nō valet, rumptū à posteriore:& posterius æquè nullas habe vires, cum ex eo nemo heres exstiterit.
units.tr: A later will, validly made, also breaks an earlier one, and it does not matter whether anyone became heir under the later will. The only question is whether it could take effect in some case. So if the heir named either refuses to be heir, or dies during the testator's lifetime or after his death but before accepting the inheritance, or the condition under which he was instituted heir fails, in these cases the head of the household dies intestate. The earlier will is not valid, having been broken by the later one; and the later will likewise has no force, since no one became heir under it.

units.la: 3 ¶Sed & si {f}quis priore testamento iure perfecto, posterius e-que iure fecerit: etiam si ex certis {h}rebus in eo heredē instituerit: superius tamē testamentū sublatū esse, diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt. cuius constitutionis verba ||& hic|| inseri iussimus, quum aliud quoque pretereā in ea constitutione expressum sit. Imperatores Seuerus & Antoninus Cocceio Cam-pano Testamentū secundo loco factū, licet in eo cer-tarū rerum heres scriptus sit, perinde iure valere {i}, ac si rerum mentio facta non esset: sed & retineri heredē scriptum, vt contentus rebus sibi datis, aut suppleta quarta ex lege Falcidia {l}, hereditatē restituat his, qui in priore testamento scripti fuerant, propter inserta fideicomissi verba, quibus vt valeret priu[?] testamentum, expressum est: dubitari non oportet. Er[?] ruptum quidē testamentū hoc modo efficitur.
units.tr: Likewise, if someone, having validly made an earlier will, afterwards validly makes another, even if in it he names an heir only to certain things, the earlier will is nonetheless set aside. The divine Severus and Antoninus rescripted this. We have ordered the words of that constitution to be inserted here, although something else also stated in that constitution is set out elsewhere. The emperors Severus and Antoninus to Cocceius Campanus: "A second will, although in it an heir is named only to certain things, is valid in law just as if no mention of particular things had been made. But the heir named is also to be kept, so that, content with the things given to him, or with the fourth made up under the Falcidian law, he restores the inheritance to those who were named in the earlier will, because of the inserted words of trust by which it was expressed that the earlier will should stand. There ought to be no doubt." In this way a will is indeed broken.

units.la: 4 ¶Alio autē modo testamenta iure facta infirmantur: veluti cum is, qui fecit testamentū, capite {k}deminutus sit, quod quibus modis accidat, primo libro retulimus.
units.tr: Wills validly made are invalidated in another way, for example when the testator has suffered a loss of status (capitis deminutio). We set out in the first book how this may happen.

units.la: 5 ¶Hoc autem casu irrita fieri testamenta dicutur quû alioqui & quæ rumpuntur,irrita fiant:& ea,quæ statim ab initio non iure fiunt, irrita sint.sed & ea, quæ iure facta sint,& postea per capitis deminutio- nē irrita fiunt , possumus nihilominus rupta dicere. Sed quia sanè cómodius erat singulas causas singulis appellationibus distinguí:ideo quædã non iure facta dicuntur,quædam iure facta rumpi, vel irrita fieri.
units.tr: In this case wills are said to become void, although in other respects those that are broken also become void, and those that were not validly made from the beginning are void. Yet we may nonetheless call wills that were validly made but later became void through loss of status "broken." But since it was more convenient to distinguish each cause by its own name, some wills are said not to have been validly made, and others to be broken or made void by law.

units.la: 6 ¶Non tamè per omnia inutilia sunt ea testamenta,quæ ab initio iure facta, per capitis deminutionē irrita facta sunt.nam si septem testium signis signata sunt: potest scriptus heres {*}secundū tabulas testa-menti bonorū possessionem agnoscere. si modo defunctus, & ciuis Romanus, & suæ potestatis mortis tempore fuerit,Nam si ideo irritum factum sit testamentum,quia ciuitatem,vel etiam libertate testator amisit,aut quia in adoptione se dedit,& mortis tempore in adoptiui patris potestate sit:nō potest scriptus heres secundū tabulas bonorū possessionem petere{b}.
units.tr: Yet those wills are not entirely useless which, validly made from the beginning, have become void through loss of status. For if they were sealed with the seals of seven witnesses, the heir named may claim possession of the goods according to the terms of the will, provided the deceased was a Roman citizen and sui iuris at the time of death. But if the will became void because the testator lost his citizenship or his freedom, or because he gave himself in adoption and at his death was in the power of his adoptive father, the heir named cannot seek possession of the goods according to the tablets.

units.la: 7 ¶Ex eo autē solo non potest infirmari testamentū,quòd postea testator id noluerit valere: visque adeo,vt & si quis post factum prius testamentū posterius facere coeperit.& aut mortalitate præuētus, aut quia eū eius rei pœnituit, id nō perfecerit:diui Pertinacis oratione {c}cautum[?] fit,ne aliàs tabulæ priores iure factæ,irritæ fiant,nisi sequentes iure ordinatę & perfectæ fuerint. nam imperfectum testamentū sine dubio nullum est.
units.tr: A will cannot be invalidated merely because the testator afterwards no longer wished it to stand. This holds even if someone, after making an earlier will, begins a later one, and, prevented by death or repenting of the matter, does not complete it. By the pronouncement of the divine Pertinax it was provided that earlier tablets validly made are not made void, unless the later ones were validly drawn up and completed. For an incomplete will is undoubtedly no will at all.

units.la: 8 ¶Eadem oratione expressit,non admissurum se hereditate eius,qui litis {d}causa principem reliquerit heredem:neque tabulas non legitimè factas, in quibus ipse ob eam causam heres instituturus erat probaturum: neque ex nuda voce heredis nomen admissurum: neque ex vlla scriptura, cui iuris auctoritas deest, aliquid adepturum. Secundum hoc diui Seuerus & Antoninus sæpissimè rescripserunt. Licèt enim (inquiunt) legibus soluti sumus,attamen {e}legibus viuimus.
units.tr: In the same pronouncement he declared that he would not admit the heir of one who had named the prince as heir for the sake of a lawsuit; nor would he approve tablets not legally made, in which he himself was about to name an heir for that reason; nor would he admit an heir's name on a bare word, nor obtain anything from any writing lacking legal authority. Accordingly the divine Severus and Antoninus very often rescripted to this effect. "For," they say, "although we are released from the laws, nevertheless we live by the laws."
On the inofficious will.
TITLE XVIII,

units.la: VIA plerúque parentes sine causa {f}li beros suos exheredant, vel omittût: inductum est,vt de inofficioso testamento agere possint liberi,qui querentur, aut inique se exheredatos,aut inique preteritos: hoc colore, quasi nō sanx mentis fuerint, cū testamentū ordinarent. Sed hoc dicitur, nō quasi vere furiosus fit, sed rectē quidē fecerit testamentū, non autē ex officio pietatis. Nam si vere furiosus sit, nihil lū testamentum est.
units.tr: Very often parents disinherit their children, or pass them over, without cause.
