It was therefore introduced that children who complain that they have been disinherited unjustly, or passed over unjustly, may bring an action concerning an unduly made will (de inofficioso testamento). They allege as a pretext that the parent was not of sound mind when he drew up the will. But this is said not as if the parent were truly insane, but as if he had made the will correctly, though not from a sense of duty of affection. For if he were truly insane, the will is nothing.

units.la: 1 ¶ Non autē liberis tantum permissum est testamentū parentum inofficiosum ac cusare, verūm etiam liberorū parentibus c. Soror au tem & frater d, turpibus personis scriptis heredibus, ex sacris constitutionibus prelati sunt. Non ergo cōtra omnes heredes agere possunt. Vltra e fratres igitur & sorores cognati nullo modo aut agere possunt, aut agētes vincere.
units.tr: 1. Not only children are permitted to accuse a parent's will as unduly made, but parents also may accuse children's wills. Brothers and sisters, however, have been set aside by the sacred constitutions when disreputable persons have been written as heirs. Therefore they cannot bring action against all heirs. Beyond this, brothers, sisters and cognates can in no way either bring the action or win it.

units.la: 2 ¶ Tā autē naturales liberi, quā secundū nostrę constitutionis f diuisione adoptati, ita demū de inofficioso testamento agere possūt, si nul lo alio iure ad defunctī bona venire possint. Nā qui ad hereditatē tota vel partē ciᵒalio iure veniūr, de in officioso agere nō possūt. Posthumi quoque, quinullo alio iure venire possūt, de inofficioso agere † possūt.
units.tr: 2. Both natural children and those adopted under the division of our constitution may bring an action on an unduly made will only if they cannot come to the deceased's goods by any other right. For those who come to the inheritance, wholly or in part, by another right cannot sue on the unduly made will. Posthumous children also, if they cannot come by any other right, may sue on the unduly made will.

units.la: 3 ¶ Sed hęc ita accipiēda sūt, si nihil eis penitᵃ à testa toribus testamento relictum est. quod nostra ʰconsti tutio ad verecundiam naturę introduxit. Sin verò quantacunque pars hereditatis vel res eis fuerit relicta: de inofficioso querela quiescente, id, quod eis deest, vsque ad quartam legitimę partis ⁱ re pleatur ᵏ: licet non fuerit adeċtum, boni viri ˡ ar bitratu debere eam compleri ᵐ.
units.tr: 3. But these things are to be understood as applying if nothing at all was left to them by the testators in the will, which our constitution introduced out of regard for natural affection. But if any part of the inheritance, or any thing whatever, was left to them, the complaint on the unduly made will ceases, and what is lacking to them is made up to the fourth of the lawful portion. Even if it was not adjudged, it ought to be completed at the discretion of a good man.

units.la: 4 ¶ Si tutor no mine pupilli, cuius tutelam gerebat, ex testamento patris sui legatum acceperit, cūm nihil erat ipsi tu tori relictum à patre suo: nihilominus poterit nomi ne suo de inofficioso patris testamento agere ⁿ.
units.tr: 4. If a tutor, in the name of a ward whose guardianship he held, received a legacy under the father's will, when nothing had been left to him personally by the father, he may nevertheless bring an action in his own name on the father's unduly made will.

units.la: 5 ¶ Sed si è contrario pupilli nomine, cui nihil relictum fuerat, de inofficioso egerit, & superatus est ipse [tutor], quod sibi in testamento eodem legatum relictum est, non amittit.
units.tr: 5. But if, conversely, in the name of a ward to whom nothing had been left, he brought an action on the unduly made will, and he himself was defeated, he does not lose the legacy left to him personally in the same will.

units.la: 6 ¶ Igitur quartam † quis debet habere, vt de inofficioso agere non pos sit: siue iure hereditario, siue † iure legati, vel fidei commissi: vel si mortis causa ei quarta donata fuerit, vel inter viuos: in iis tantummodo casibus, quorum quarta relinquenda est. novell.115.cap.2.in pr.& §.5. mentionem facit nostra constitutio: vel aliis modis, qui ||in nostris|| constitutionibus continentur. Quod autem de quarta diximus, ita intelligendum est: vt siue vnus fuerit, siue plures, quibus agere de inoffi-cioso testamento permittitur: vna quarta eis dari possit, vt ea pro rata eis distribuatur.{*}
units.tr: 6. Therefore, whoever has the fourth, so that he cannot bring an action on an unduly made will, whether by hereditary right, or by right of legacy or trust, or if a fourth was given to him in case of death or between living persons, is covered only in those cases for which a fourth must be left. Our constitution makes mention of this in Novell. 115, cap. 2, in pr. & §. 5., or by other modes contained in our constitutions. What we have said about the fourth is to be understood thus: whether there is one or several to whom it is permitted to sue on the unduly made will, one fourth may be given to them, so that it is distributed among them pro rata.

units.la: DE HEREDVM QVALITATE, & differentia. TIT. XIX.
units.tr: On the Quality of Heirs, and Their Difference. Title 19.

units.la: HEREDES autem aut necessarij dicuntur, aut sui & necessarij, aut extranei.
units.tr: Heirs are called either necessary, or self-and-necessary, or extraneous (outside heirs).

units.la: 1. ¶Necessarius heres est seruus heres institutus. Ideoque sic appellatur, quia siue velit, siue nolit,{b} omnino post mortem testatoris protinus liber & necessarius heres fit. Vnde qui facultates suas suspectas habent: solent seruum suum primo aut secundo aut etiam vlteriore gradu heredem instituere: vt si creditoribus satis nō fiat, potius eius heredis bona quam ipsius testatoris à creditoribus possideantur, vel distrahantur, vel inter eos diuidantur. Pro hoc tamen incommodo, illud ei commodum præstatur: vt ea, quæ post mortem patroni sui sibi adquisierit, ipsi reseruentur. Et quàuis bona defuncti non sufficiant creditoribus: ||iterū|| tamen ex ea causa res eius, quas sibi adquisierit, non veneunt.
units.tr: 1. A necessary heir is a slave instituted as heir. He is so called because, whether he wishes it or not, he becomes free and a necessary heir immediately upon the testator's death. Hence those whose property is doubtful usually institute their slave as heir in the first, second, or even a later degree, so that if the creditors are not satisfied, the goods of that heir, rather than those of the testator himself, may be taken into possession, sold, or divided among the creditors by them. In return for this disadvantage, however, a benefit is granted to him: whatever he acquires after the death of his master is reserved to him. And even if the goods of the deceased are not enough for the creditors, nevertheless, for that reason, the things he has acquired for himself are not sold.

units.la: 2. ¶Sui{c} autem & necessarij heredes sunt, veluti filius, filia, nepos neptisve ex filio.& deinceps cæteri liberi, qui in potestate{d} morientis modo fuerint. Sed vt nepos, neptisve sui heredes sint, non sufficit eum eamve in potestate [?]ani mortis tempore fuisse: sed opus est, vt pater eius viuo patre suo desierit suus heres esse, aut morte interceptus, aut qualibet alia ratione liberatus à patris potestate: tunc enim nepos neptisve in locum patris sui succe-dit. Sed sui quidem heredes ideo appellantur, quia domestici heredes sunt, & viuo quoque patre quo-dammodo{e} domini existimatur. Vnde etiam si quis intestatus moriatur: prima causa est in successione liberorum{f}. Necessarij vero ideo dicuntur, quia omnino, siue velint, siue nolint, tam ab intestato, quàm ex testamento ||ex lege duodecim tabularum|| heredes fiunt. Sed his prætor permittit{g} volenti-
units.tr: 2. Self-and-necessary heirs are, for example, a son, a daughter, and a grandson or granddaughter through a son, and the other children who were under the power of the deceased at the time of death. But for a grandson or granddaughter to be self-heirs, it is not enough that he or she was in the power of the [grandfather] at the time of death; it is necessary that his or her father has ceased to be a self-heir while his own father was still alive, either by dying or by being released from the father's power in some other way. For then the grandson or granddaughter succeeds in the place of their father. Those are called self-heirs because they are domestic heirs, and even while the father is living they are considered in some way masters. Hence, even if someone dies intestate, the first claim to succession belongs to the children. They are called necessary because, whether they wish it or not, they become heirs in every case, both on intestacy and by testament under the law of the Twelve Tables. However, the praetor permits these heirs, if they wish,

units.la: tfl.1. in pr.ff.fi tabulæ test. § l. 57. in princip.ff.de adquir.haered. bus abstinere hereditate: vt potius parentis, quàm ipsorum bona similiter à creditoribus posideantur.
units.tr: to abstain from the inheritance, so that the goods of the parent, rather than their own, are likewise taken into possession by the creditors. (Cited: ff. fi tabulae test., pr.; l. 57, princip., ff. de adquir. haered.)

units.la: 3 ¶Cæteri,qui testatoris iuri subiecti non sunt,extranei heredes appellantur. Itaque liberi quoque nostri qui in potestate nostra non sunt,heredes à nobis instituti,extranei heredes nobis videntur. Qua de causa,& qui heredes à matre instituuntur, eodem numero sunt: quia fœminæ in potestate liberos non habent {*}. Seruus quoque heres à domino institutus, & post testamentum factum ab eo manumissus, eodem numero habetur.
units.tr: 3. All the others, who are not subject to the testator's power, are called extraneous heirs. Thus our children also, who are not in our power, when instituted heirs by us, are regarded by us as extraneous heirs. For this reason, those instituted heirs by a mother are in the same class, since women do not have children in their power. A slave instituted heir by his master, and manumitted by him after the will was made, is likewise counted in the same class.

units.la: 4. ¶In extraneis heredibus illud obseruatur, vt sit cum eis testamenti factio: siue heredes ipsi instituantur, siue hi, qui in potestate eorum sunt.& id duobus temporibus inspicitur: testamenti quidem facti tempore, vt constituit institutio: mortis vero testatoris, vt effectum habeat: hoc amplius, & cùm adit hereditatem, esse debet cum eo testamenti factio, siue pure, siue sub conditione heres institutus sit. nam ius heredis eo maximè tempore inspiciendum est, quo adquirit hereditatem. Medio autem tempore inter factum testamentum,& mortem testatoris, vel conditionem institutionis existentem, mutatio iuris non nocet heredi: quia (vt diximus) tria tempora inspici debent. Testamenti autem factionem non solùm ishabere videtur, qui testamentum facere potest: sed etiam qui ex alieno testamento vel ipse capere potest, vel alij adquirere, licèt non posit facere testamentum. Et ideo furiosus, & mutus, & posthumus, & infans, & filiusfamilias,& seruus alienus testamenti factionem habere dicuntur. Licèt enim testamentū facere non possint, attamen ex testamento vel sibi, vel alij adquirere possunt.
units.tr: 4. With extraneous heirs this is observed: that they must have testamentary capacity, whether they are instituted heirs themselves or those who are in their power. This is judged at two times: at the time the will is made, so that the institution may take effect, and at the death of the testator, so that it may have effect. Moreover, when he enters upon the inheritance, the heir must also have testamentary capacity with him, whether he has been instituted heir outright or under a condition. For the heir's right is to be examined especially at the time when he acquires the inheritance. In the interval between the making of the will and the death of the testator, or the fulfilment of the condition of institution, a change in the law does no harm to the heir, because (as we have said) three times must be examined. Moreover, testamentary capacity is seen to belong not only to one who can make a will, but also to one who can either take under another's will himself or acquire for another, although he cannot make a will. And therefore a madman, a mute, a posthumous child, an infant, a son under power, and another's slave are said to have testamentary capacity. For although they cannot make a will, yet by a will they can acquire either for themselves or for another.

units.la: 5. ¶Extraneis autem heredibus deliberandi potestas est de adeunda hereditate, vel non adeunda. Sed siue is, cui abstinendi potestas est, immiscuerit se bonis hereditatis: siue extraneus, cui de adeunda hereditate deliberare licet, adierit: postea relinquendæ hereditatis facultatem non habet, nisi minor sit vigintiquinque annis. Nam huius ætatis hominibus, licut in cæteris omnibus casibus deceptis: ita & si temerè damnosam hereditatem susceperint, prætor succurrit. Sciendum est tamen diuum Hadrianum etiam maiori vigintiquinque annis veniam dedisse, cùm post aditam hereditatem grandes alienum, quod aditæ hereditatis tempore latebat, emersisset. Sed hoc quidem diuus Hadrianus cuidam speciali beneficio praestitit{a}: dinus autem Gor-dianus postea militibus tantummodo hoc concessit.
units.tr: 5. Extraneous heirs have the power to deliberate whether to enter upon the inheritance or not. But if one who has the power to abstain has meddled with the goods of the inheritance, or an extraneous heir who may deliberate about entering has entered, he no longer has the opportunity to relinquish the inheritance, unless he is under twenty-five years of age. For the praetor comes to the aid of people of this age, as in all other cases of being deceived, so also if they have rashly undertaken a ruinous inheritance. It should be noted, however, that the deified Hadrian granted pardon even to those over twenty-five, when after entering upon the inheritance a great debt, which had been hidden at the time of entry, came to light. But Hadrian granted this as a special favour to a certain person; the deified Gordian later granted it only to soldiers.

units.la: {b}¶ Sed nostra benevolētia cōmune omnibus subie-ctis Imperio nostro hoc beneficium praestitit: & constitutionem tam æquissimam, quam nobilissimam scripsit: cuius tenorem si observauerint homines, licet eis adire hereditatem, & in tantum teneri, quantum valere bona hereditatis contingit: ut ex hac cau-sa neque deliberationis auxilium sit eis necessarium, nisi omissa observatione nostræ constitutionis, & deliberandum exististimauerint, & sese veteri grauamini additionis supponere maluerint.
units.tr: But our goodwill has granted this benefit in common to all subjects of our Empire, and has written a constitution as just as it is noble. If people observe its terms, they are permitted to enter the inheritance and be bound only so far as the goods of the inheritance happen to be worth. Thus for this reason they do not need the aid of deliberation at all, unless, having neglected the observance of our constitution, they judge that they must deliberate, and prefer to subject themselves to the old burden of full liability.

units.la: 7 ¶Item extraneus heres testamento institutus, aut ab intestato ad legitimam hereditatem vocatus, potest aut pro herede gerendo, aut etiam nuda voluntate suscipiendæ hereditatis heres fieri. Pro herede autem gerere quis videtur{c}, si rebus hereditariis tanquam heres vtatur, vel vendendo res hereditarias, vel prædia colendo locandove, & quoquo modo voluntatem suam declaret vel re, vel verbo de adeunda hereditate: dummodo sciat eum, in cuius bonis pro herede gerit, testatum intestatumve obiisse, & se ei heredē esse. Pro herede enim gerere, est pro domino gerere. veteres enim heredes pro dominis appellabant. Sicut autem nuda voluntate extraneus heres fit: ita contraria{d} destinatione statim ab hereditate repellitur{d}. Eum, qui surdus vel mutus natus, vel postea factus est, nihil prohibet pro herede gerere, & adquirere sibi hereditatem: si tamen intelligit, quod agit.
units.tr: 7. Likewise an extraneous heir instituted by will, or called to the lawful inheritance on intestacy, may become heir either by acting as heir or even by the mere intention of taking up the inheritance. A person is seen to act as heir if he uses the hereditary goods as heir, either by selling hereditary goods or by cultivating or letting out estates, and in any way declares his intention to enter the inheritance, by deed or by word, provided he knows that the one in whose goods he acts as heir has died testate or intestate and that he is his heir. For "to act as heir" means "to act as owner," since the ancients called heirs "owners." But just as an extraneous heir becomes heir by mere intention, so by a contrary declaration he is at once repelled from the inheritance. Nothing prevents a man who is deaf or mute, whether born so or made so later, from acting as heir and acquiring the inheritance for himself, provided he understands what he is doing.
ON LEGACIES, TITLE XX.

units.la: POST hæc videamus de legatis: quæ pars iuris extra propositam quidem materiā videtur. (nam loquimur de iis iuris fi-guris{f}, quibus per vniuersitatem{g} res nobis adquiruntur) sed cum omnino de testamentis, & de heredibus, qui in testamento institu-untur, loquuti simus: non fine causa sequenti loco poterit haec iuris materia tractari. 1. ¶Legatum itaque est{h} donatio quædam a defuncto relicta, ab herede præstanda. 2 ¶Sed olim quidem erant legatorum genera quatuor: per vindicationem, per damnationem, sinendi modo, per præceptionem: certa quædam verba cuique generi legatorum ad-
units.tr: Having dealt with these matters, let us now consider legacies. This part of the law seems to lie outside the subject proposed (for we are speaking of those legal forms by which things are acquired for us through universal succession). But since we have spoken at length about testaments and about heirs instituted in them, this subject can be treated in the next place, and not without reason. 1. A legacy, then, is a certain gift left by the deceased, to be paid by the heir. 2. Formerly there were four kinds of legacy: by vindication, by condemnation, by permission, and by preception. Each kind of legacy was signified by certain fixed words.

units.la: {f} Causis is printed as "causis" in the text. significabantur. Sed ex constitutionibus diuorum Prin-cipum {*} solenitas huiusmodi verborum penitus sublata est. Nostra autem constitutio, quam cū magna cura fecimus lucubratione, defunctorum voluntates validiores esse cupientes, & non verbis, sed voluntatibus eorum fauentes, disposuit, vt omnibus legatis vna sit natura, & quibuscunque {b} verbis aliquid statui sit, liceat legatariis id persequi non solum per actiones personales {c}, sed etiam per in rem, & per hypo-thecariam {d}. Cuius constitutionis perpensum modum ex ipsius tenore perfectissime accipere possibile est.
units.tr: {f} Causis is printed as "causis" in the text. But by the constitutions of the deified emperors, the solemnity of such words was entirely abolished. Our own constitution, which we drew up with great care and labour, desiring the wills of the dead to be more valid and favouring their intentions rather than their words, ordained that all legacies should have one nature, and that whatever words are used to establish a gift, legatees may pursue it not only by personal actions but also by real and hypothecary actions. The exact scope of this constitution can be understood most perfectly from its own wording.

units.la: 3 Sed non usque ad eam constitutionem standum esse existimauimus. Cum enim antiquitatem inne-nimus legata quidem stricte concludentem, fideicommisis autem, quæ ex voluntate magis desiderabant defunctorum, pinguiorem naturam indulgentemne-cessarium esse duximus, omnia legata fideicommissis exæquare {e}, vt nulla sit inter ea differentia: sed quod deest legatis, hoc replcatur ex natura fideicommissorum: & si quid amplius est in legatis, per hoc crescat fideicommissorum natura. Sed ne in primis legum cunabulis permissim de his exponendo, studiosis adolescentibus quandam introducamus difficultatem: operæpretium esse duximus, interim separatim prius de legatis: & postea de fideicommissis tractare, vt natura utriusque iuris cognita, facile possint permissionem eorum eruditi subtilioribus auribus accipere.
units.tr: 3. But we did not think that we must stop at that constitution. For when we found that the ancients construed legacies strictly, while they allowed fideicommissa, which depended more on the wishes of the dead, a looser and more generous nature, we judged it necessary to equate all legacies with fideicommissa, so that there is no difference between them: whatever is lacking in legacies is supplied from the nature of fideicommissa, and whatever more there is in legacies increases the nature of fideicommissa. But lest, in the very cradle of the laws, by setting out these matters we introduce some difficulty for young students, we thought it best meanwhile to treat legacies separately first and fideicommissa afterwards, so that, with the nature of each branch of law known, learned readers may more easily take in their treatment with subtler ears.

units.la: 4 Non solum autem {f} testatoris vel heredis {g} res, sed etiam aliena {h} legari poteST: ita, vt heres cogatur reddimere eam, & praestare: vel si eam {i} non poteSt redimere, aestimationem eius dare. Sed si talis sit res, cuius commercium non est, vel adiSci non poteSt{k}: nec aestimatio eius debetur, veluti si campum in Martium, vel basilicas, vel templa, vel quæ publico {l} vsui destinata sunt, legauerit. nam nullius momenti tale legatum est. Quod autem diximus alienam rem posse legari: ita intelligendum est, si defunctus sciebat alienam rem esse, non si ignorabat. Forsitan enim si sciuisset alienam rem esse, non legasset & ita dixit Pius rescripsit. Et verius est ipsum {n} qui agit, id est, legatarium probare oportere, sciuisse alienam rem legare defunctum: non heredem probare oportere, ignorasse alienam: quia sem-per necessitas probandi incumbit illi {o}, qui agit.
units.tr: 4. Not only the property of the testator or of the heir, but also another's property, may be bequeathed, so that the heir is compelled to buy it back and deliver it, or, if he cannot buy it back, to give its value. But if the thing is such that it cannot be traded or acquired, neither is its value owed: for example, if someone bequeathed a field in the Campus Martius, or basilicas, or temples, or things destined for public use. Such a legacy is of no effect. But when we say that another's thing can be bequeathed, this must be understood to hold if the deceased knew that the thing belonged to another, not if he was ignorant of it. For perhaps, had he known it was another's, he would not have bequeathed it; and so Pius rescripted. And it is truer that the one who sues, that is the legatee, must prove that the deceased knew he was bequeathing another's thing; the heir need not prove that he was ignorant of it, since the burden of proof always lies on the one who sues.

units.la: 5 Sed & si rem obligatam creditori aliquis lega[?]erit,necesse habet heres, [?]eā{a} [?]luere. Et [?]in [?]hoc quoque casu idem placet,quod in re aliena: vt ita demum luere necesse habeat heres, si sciebat defunctus rem obligatam esse. & ita diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt. Si tamen defunctus voluerit legatarii luere,& hoc expresserit: non debet heres eam luere.
units.tr: 5. But if someone bequeathed a thing pledged to a creditor, the heir is bound to redeem it. And in this case too the same rule holds as for another's property: the heir is bound to redeem it only if the deceased knew the thing was encumbered. So the deified Severus and Antoninus rescripted. If, however, the deceased wished the legatee to redeem it and expressed this, the heir is not bound to redeem it.

units.la: 6 ¶Si res aliena legata fuerit: & eius rei viuo testatore legatarius dominus factus fuerit: si quidem ex causa emptionis{b}: ex testamento actione pretiu consequi potest. Si vero ex causa lucratiua{c}, veluti ex donatione, vel ex alia simili causa agere non potest. nam *traditum est duas lucratiuas causas in eundem {d}hominem,& eandem rem concurrere non posse. Hae ratione,si ex duobus testamentis eadem res eide debeatur: interest, vtrum rem, an aestimationem ex testamento consequutus sit. nam si rem habet agere non potest, quia habet eam ex causa lucratiua{e}, si aestimationem, agere potest.
units.tr: 6. If another's thing was bequeathed, and while the testator was living the legatee became its owner: if he did so by a cause of purchase, he can recover the price by action under the will. But if he did so by a gratuitous cause, such as a gift or some similar cause, he cannot sue. For it is established that two gratuitous causes cannot concur for the same person and the same thing. Therefore, if the same thing is owed to the same person under two wills, it matters whether he obtained the thing itself or its value under the will. For if he has the thing, he cannot sue, because he has it from a gratuitous cause; if he has the value, he can sue.

units.la: 7 ¶Ea quoque res, quae in rerum natura non est, si{f} modo futura est, recte legatur: veluti fructus, qui in illo fundo nati erunt, aut quod ex illa ancilla natu erit.
units.tr: 7. A thing which does not yet exist in nature may also be validly bequeathed, provided that it is going to exist, for example the fruits which will be born on that farm, or the offspring which will be born of that maidservant.

units.la: 8 ¶Si eadem res duobus legata sit, siue coniunctim, siue disiunctim: si ambo perueniant ad legatum, scinditur{g} inter eos legatum: si alter deficiat (quia aut spreuerit legatum, aut vino testatore decesserit, vel alio quoquo modo defecerit) {h}totum ad collegatarium pertinet. Coniunctim autem legatur, veluti si quis dicat, Titio & Seio hominem Stichū do lego: disiunctim ita, Titio hominem Stichum do lego. Seio hominem Stichum do lego. Sed & si expresserit eundem hominem Stichum, atque disiunctim legatum intelligitur.
units.tr: 8. If the same thing is bequeathed to two persons, either jointly or separately: if both come to the legacy, it is divided between them; if one fails (because he rejects the legacy, or dies before the testator, or fails in some other way), the whole goes to the co-legatee. A legacy is made jointly, for example, if someone says: "I give and bequeath the slave Stichus to Titius and Seius"; separately, thus: "I give and bequeath the slave Stichus to Titius. I give and bequeath the slave Stichus to Seius." But even if he names the same slave Stichus, it is understood as a separate legacy.

units.la: 9 ¶Si cui fundus alienus legatus sit, & emerit proprietatem dedu&to vsufructu, & vsufructus ad eum peruenerit,{k} & postea ex testamento agat: recte eum agere, & fundum petere, Iulianus ait: quia vsusfructus, in petitione, seruitutis locum obtinet{l}. sed officio iudicis continetur, vt deducto vsufructu, iubeat aestimationem praestari.
units.tr: 9. If another's farm was bequeathed to someone, and he bought the ownership with the usufruct deducted, and the usufruct came to him, and afterwards he sues under the will, Julian says he may rightly sue and claim the farm, because in a claim the usufruct takes the place of a servitude. But it lies within the judge's office to order that the value be paid with the usufruct deducted.

units.la: 10 ¶Sed si rem legatarij quis ei legauerit, inutile est legatum:{m} quia quod proprium est ipsius, amplius eius fieri non potest. & licet alienauerit eam, non debetur{n} nec ipsa res, nec aestimatio eius.
units.tr: 10. But if someone bequeathed to a legatee the legatee's own property, the legacy is ineffective, because what already belongs to him cannot become more his. And even if he has alienated it, neither the thing itself nor its value is owed.

units.la: 11 ¶Si quis re suam quasi alienam legauerit: valet legatum. nam plus valet quod in veritate est, quam quod in opinione{o}.
units.tr: 11. If someone bequeathed his own property as if it were another's, the legacy is valid. For what is true counts for more than what is merely believed.

units.la: {o} [?]hætur. l.1, in fine de reg. Caton. ♦ Immo aliud. l.15, Sed & si legatarij esse putauit, valere constat: quia exitum voluntas defuncti habere poterit. 12 Si rem suam legauerit testator, posteaque eam alienauerit: Celsus putat, si non adimendi animo vendidit, nihilominus deberi. Idemque diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt. Idem rescripserunt eum, qui post testamentum factum praedia, quae legata erant, pignori dedit, ademisse legatum non videri: & ideo legatarium cum herede eius agere posse, vt praedia a creditore luantur. Si vero quis partem rei legatę alienauerit: pars, quae non est alienata, omnino debetur. pars autem alienata ita debetur, si non adimendi animo alienata sit.
units.tr: {o} Obscura. l.1, in fine de reg. Caton. ♦ Immo aliud. l.15, But also if he thought the thing belonged to the legatee, it is agreed that the legacy is valid, because the will of the deceased can have its effect. 12. If a testator bequeathed his own thing and afterwards alienated it, Celsus thinks that if he sold it without intending to revoke the legacy, it is nonetheless owed. The deified Severus and Antoninus rescripted the same. They also rescripted that one who, after making the will, pledged the estates that had been bequeathed has not been seen to revoke the legacy; and so the legatee can sue the heir for the estates to be redeemed from the creditor. But if someone alienated part of a bequeathed thing, the part not alienated is owed in full; the part alienated is owed only if it was alienated without intent to revoke.

units.la: 13 Si quis debitori suo liberationem legauerit, legatum vtile est: & neque ab ipso debitore, neque ab herede eius poterit heres petere: neque ab alio, qui heredis loco fit. Sed & poterit a debitore conueniri, vt liberet eum. Potest etiam quis vel ad tempus iubere, ne heres petat.
units.tr: 13. If someone bequeathed liberation to his debtor, the legacy is valid, and the heir can claim nothing from the debtor himself, nor from his heir, nor from anyone who stands in the heir's place. But the debtor may also be sued so that he is released. One may also order, even for a time, that the heir shall not demand payment.

units.la: 14 Ex contrario, si debitor creditori suo quod debet, legauerit: inutile est legatum, si nihil plus est in legato, quam in debito: quia nihil amplius per legatum habet. Quod si in diem vel sub conditione debitum ei pure legauerit: vtile est legatum propter repraesentationem. Quod si vivo testatore dies venerit vel conditio extiterit: Papinianus scripsit, vtile esse nihilominus legatum: quia semel constitit quod & verum est. Non cum placuit sententia exstiterit, quum extinctum esse legatum, quia in eam causam peruenerit, a qua incipere non poterit.
units.tr: 14. Conversely, if a debtor bequeathed to his creditor what he owes, the legacy is ineffective if there is nothing more in the legacy than in the debt, since he gains nothing more through the legacy. But if he bequeathed to him, outright, a debt due on a day or under a condition, the legacy is valid on account of its present effect. But if, while the testator was alive, the day came or the condition was fulfilled, Papinian wrote that the legacy is nonetheless valid, because what was once validly established remains, and is true. It is not as when the opinion prevailed that the legacy was extinguished, because it had come to a state from which it could never have begun.

units.la: 15 Sed si vxori maritus dotem legauerit, valet legatum: quia plenius est legatum, quam de dote actio. Sed si quam non accepit dotem legauerit: diu Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt, si quidem simpliciter legauerit, inutile esse legatum: si vero certa pecunia, vel certum corpus, aut instrumenta dotis in relegando demonstrata sunt, valere legatum.
units.tr: 15 But if a husband has bequeathed a dowry to his wife, the legacy is valid, because a legacy is broader than an action on the dowry. But if he has bequeathed a dowry she did not receive, the emperors Severus and Antoninus long ago rescribed that, if he bequeathed it simply, the legacy is void; but if a certain sum of money, a certain thing, or the instruments of the dowry were specified in the bequest, the legacy is valid.

units.la: 16 Si res legata sine facto heredis perierit: legatario decedit. Et si seruus alienus legatus sine facto heredis manumissus fuerit: non tenetur heres. Si vero heredis seruus legatus sit, & ipse eum manumiserit: teneri ipsum Iulianus scripsit, nec interest, sciuerit, an ignorauerit a se legatum esse. Sed & si alij donauerit seruum, & is, cui donatus est, eum manumiserit: tenetur heres quamuis ignorauerit ei eum legatum esse.
units.tr: 16 If a bequeathed thing perishes without the heir's act, it is lost to the legatee. And if another's slave was bequeathed and is manumitted without the heir's act, the heir is not liable. But if the heir's own slave was bequeathed and he himself manumitted him, Julian wrote that the heir is liable, and it makes no difference whether he knew the slave had been bequeathed to the legatee. But also if he gave a slave to another, and the person to whom he was given manumitted him, the heir is liable even though he did not know the slave had been bequeathed to the legatee.

units.la: 17 Si quis ancillas cum suis natis legauerit, etiam si ancillae mortuae fuerint, partus legato cedunt. Idem est, & si ordinarij serui p cū vicariis legati fuerint: quia licet mortui sint ordinarij, tamen vicarij legato cedunt. Sed si seruus fuerit cum peculio legatus: mortuo seruo, vel manumisso, vel alienato, peculij legatum extinguitur. Idem est, si fundus instructus, vel cum instrumento legatus fuerit. Nam fundo alienato, & instrumenti legatum extinguitur. 18 ¶Si gyex legatus fuerit: & postea ad vnam ouem peruenerit: quod superfuerit, vindicari potest. Grege autem legato, etiam eas oues, quae post testamentum factum gregi adiiciuntur, legato cedere, Iulianus ait. Est autem gregis vnum corpus est distantibus capitibus, sicut aedium vnum corpus est ex cohaerentibus lapidibus. 19 ¶AEdibus denique legatis, columnas & marmora, quae post testamentum factum adiecta sunt, legato [?]dicimus[?] cedere. 20 ¶Si peculium legatum fuerit: sine dubio quicquid peculio accedit, vel decedit vno testatore, legatarij lucro vel damno est. Quod si post mortem testatoris ante aditam hereditatem [?]ali-quid[?] [?]seruus[?] adquisierit: Iulianus ait, si quidem ipsi manumisso peculium legatum fuerit: omne, quod ante aditam hereditatem adquisitum est, legatario cedere, quia huiusmodi legati dies ab adita hereditate cedit. Sed si extraneo peculium legatum fuerit: non cedere ea legato, nisi ex rebus peculiaribus auctu fuerit peculium. Peculium autem, nisi legatum fuerit, manumisso non debetur: quamuis si viuus manumiserit, sufficit, si non admittatur. & ita diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt. Idem rescripserunt, peculio legato, non videri id relictum, vt petitionem habeat peculiam, quam in rationes dominicas impenderit. ¶ Item rescripserunt, peculium videri legatum, cum rationibus redditis liber esse iussus est, & ex eo reliqua inferre. 21 ¶Tam autem corporales res legari possunt, quam incorporales. & ideo quod defuncto debetur, potest alicui legari, vt actiones suas heres legatario praestet: nisi exegerit viuus testator pecuniam. nam hoc casu legatum extinguitur. Sed & tale legatum valet, damnas esto heres meus dominum illius reficere, vel, illum ære alieno liberare. 22 ¶Si generaliter seruus vel res alia legetur: cliio legatarij est, nisi aliud testator dixerit. 23 ¶Optionis legatum, || id est, || vbi testator ex seruis suis, vel aliis rebus optare legatarium iusserat, habebat olim in se condicionem. & ideo nisi ipse legatarius viuus optasset: ad heredem legatum non vt.
units.tr: 17 If someone bequeathed female slaves together with their children, the offspring pass to the legacy even if the mothers have died. The same holds if ordinary slaves were bequeathed together with their vicars: although the ordinary slaves have died, the vicars pass to the legacy. But if a slave was bequeathed with his peculium, and the slave dies, is manumitted, or is alienated, the legacy of the peculium is extinguished. The same is so if a farm was bequeathed equipped or with its instruments: when the farm is alienated, the legacy of the instruments is extinguished too. 18 If a flock was bequeathed and has been reduced to a single sheep, what remains can be claimed. But when a flock is bequeathed, Julian says the sheep added to it after the will was made also pass to the legacy. A flock is one body with separate heads, just as a building is one body of cohering stones. 19 Likewise, when a building is bequeathed, we say the columns and marble added after the will was made pass to the legacy. 20 If a peculium was bequeathed, then without doubt whatever is added to or subtracted from the peculium while the testator lives is the legatee's gain or loss. But if after the testator's death and before the inheritance is entered upon the slave acquires something, Julian says: if the peculium was bequeathed to the slave himself upon manumission, everything acquired before entry on the inheritance passes to the legatee, because the day of such a legacy falls due from the entry on the inheritance. But if the peculium was bequeathed to a stranger, the acquisitions do not pass to the legacy, unless the peculium was increased from its own assets. The peculium, unless it is bequeathed, is not owed to one manumitted; although if the master manumitted him while alive, it suffices that he is not excluded. And so the emperors Severus and Antoninus rescribed. They likewise rescribed that where a peculium was bequeathed, it is not regarded as left so that the slave may have a claim for the peculium he spent on his master's accounts. They also rescribed that the peculium is regarded as bequeathed when the slave is ordered to be free after accounts are rendered, and to pay any balance out of it. 21 Corporeal things can be bequeathed, and incorporeal ones as well. So what is owed to the dead man can be bequeathed to someone, so that the heir hands over his actions to the legatee, unless the testator while alive collected the money; for in that case the legacy is extinguished. Such a legacy is valid too: "let my heir be bound to indemnify the owner of that thing," or "to free him from debt." 22 If a slave or other thing is bequeathed generally, the choice belongs to the legatee, unless the testator said otherwise. 23 A legacy of option, that is, where the testator ordered the legatee to choose a slave or other thing from his property, once carried a condition in itself; so unless the legatee himself had made the choice while alive, the legacy did not pass to the heir.

units.la: [?] transmittebant {a}.sed ex constitutione {b}nostra & hoc in meliorem statum reformatum est: & data est {c}libera-centia heredi legatarii optare || seruum , || licet vi-ctam negato- uus legararius hoc non fecerit. Et diligentiore tra-ctatu habito, & hoc in nostra constitutione additum est: siue plures legatarii extiterint, quibus oprio re-licta est, & dissentiant in corpore eligendo: siue v-nius legatarii plures heredes || sint ||, & inter se cir-ca optandum dissentiant, alio aliud corpus eligere cupiente: ne pereat legatum (quod plerique prudentium contra beneuolentiam introducebant) fortunam esse huius optionis iudicem,& sorte {d}hoc esse dirimendum, vt ad quem fors venerit,illius sententia in optione præcellat.
units.tr: [They did not pass to heirs.] But by our constitution this was reformed for the better, and the legatee's heir was given the freedom to choose the slave, even though the legatee himself had not done so while alive. After a more careful consideration, this was also added in our constitution: whether there are several legatees to whom the option is left and they disagree about choosing the object, or whether there are several heirs of one legatee who disagree among themselves about the choice, one wishing to take one thing and another a different one, the legacy should not perish (which most jurists, contrary to goodwill, had introduced). Instead, chance shall decide this option, and the matter shall be settled by lot, so that the judgment of whoever the lot falls to prevails in the choice.

units.la: 24 ¶ Legari autem illis solum potest, cum quibus {e}testamenti factio est.
units.tr: 24 A legacy can be left only to those with whom there is testamentary capacity.

units.la: 25 ¶ Incertis vero personis neque legata, neque fideicommissa olim frelinqui concessum erat. Nam ne miles quidem incertæ personæ poterat relinquere,vt divus Hadrianus rescripsit.Incerta autem persona vi-debatur,quâ incerta opinione animo suo testator subiiciebat:veluti si quis ita dicat. quicunque §filio mea filiâ suâ in matrimonii dederit,ci heres meus illâ fundâ dato. Illud quoque,quod iis relinquebatur, qui post testamentum scriptû primi cosules designati essent: æquè incertæ personæ legari videbatur. & denique multæ aliæ huiusmodi species sunt {h}Libertas quoq; incertæ personæ non videbatur posse dari:quia placebat nominatum seruos liberari. Sub certa vero demonstratione,id est, ex certis personis incertæ personæ rectè legabatur: veluti, ex cognatis meis,qui nunc sunt, si quis filiam meam uxorem duxerit, et heres meus illam rem dato. Incertis autem personis legata vel fideicommissa relicta, & per errorem soluta {k}repeti non posse sacris constitutionibus cautum erat.
units.tr: 25 Formerly, legacies and fideicommissa could not be left to uncertain persons. For not even a soldier could leave something to an uncertain person, as the divine Hadrian rescribed. A person was regarded as uncertain when the testator placed him under a vague notion in his mind, as when someone says: whoever shall give my daughter in marriage to his son, let my heir give him that farm. Also a legacy to those who were designated consuls after the will was written was likewise regarded as a legacy to an uncertain person; and finally there are many other kinds of this sort. Freedom also could not be given to an uncertain person, because it was held that only named slaves may be freed. But under a certain description, that is, from certain persons, a legacy to an uncertain person was validly made, for example: to whichever of my relatives who now exist shall marry my daughter, let my heir give that thing. But that legacies or fideicommissa left to uncertain persons, and paid by mistake, cannot be recovered was provided by the sacred constitutions.

units.la: 26 ¶ Posthumo quoque alieno inutiliter ||antea||legabatur.Est autem alienus posthumus, qui natus inter suos,heres testatori futurus non est, Ideóque ex emancipato filio conceptus nepos, extraneus erat posthumus auo.
units.tr: 26 A legacy to another's posthumous child was also ineffective before. A posthumous child of another is one who, born among his own, will not be heir to the testator. Hence a grandson conceived from an emancipated son was a stranger posthumous to the grandfather.

units.la: 27 ¶ Sed nec huiusmodi species penitus est sine iusta emendatione relicta: quum in nostro Codice {l}constitutio posita sit, per quam & huic parti medemur non solum in hereditatibus,sed etiam in legatis & fideicommissis: quod euidenter ex ipsius constitutionis lectione claret.Tutor autem nec per nostram constitutionem incertus {m}dari debet:quia certo iudicio debet quis pro tutela suæ posteritati cauere.
units.tr: 27 But this kind has not been left entirely without proper correction, for a constitution is placed in our Code by which we remedy this part not only in inheritances but also in legacies and fideicommissa, as is clear from reading the constitution itself. A tutor, however, must not be given in an uncertain way even under our constitution, because one must provide for one's posterity by a certain judgment in the matter of guardianship.

units.la: 28 ¶Posthumus autē {a}alienus heres instituì & ante poterat {b}, & nunc potest: nisi in vtero eius sit,quæ iure nostro vxor esse non potest.
units.tr: 28 A posthumous stranger could be instituted heir even before, and now can be, unless he is in the womb of one who by our law cannot be a wife.

units.la: 29 ¶Si quidem {c}in nomine, cognomine, prænomine,‖ agnomine ‖ legatarij testator errauerit: cum de persona constat, nihilominus valet legatum.Idemque in heredibus seruatur,& rectè. Nomina enim, significandorum hominum gratia reperta sunt: qui si alio quolibet modo intelligantur,nihil interest.
units.tr: 29 If the testator erred in the name, cognomen, praenomen, or agnomen of the legatee, but there is no doubt about the person, the legacy is nonetheless valid. The same is observed for heirs, and rightly. For names were devised for the sake of signifying men; if they are understood in any other way, it makes no difference.

units.la: 30 ¶Huic proxima est illa iuris regula *, falsa {d}demonstratione legatum non permi[?]mi.veluti si quis ita legauerit, Stichū seruum meum vernam do lego. licet enim non verna, sed emptus sit: si tamen de seruo constat, vtile est legatum. Et conuenienter, si ita demonstrauerit. Stichum seruum,quem à Seio emi, siue[?] ab alio emptus: vtile est legatū si de seruo constat.
units.tr: 30 Closely related to this is that rule of law: a legacy is not lost by a false description. For example, if someone bequeathed thus: I give and bequeath my slave Stichus, my home-born slave. For although he was not home-born but bought, if there is no doubt about the slave, the legacy is valid. And similarly if he described him thus: Stichus the slave whom I bought from Seius, or bought from someone else: the legacy is valid if there is no doubt about the slave.

units.la: 31 ¶Longe magis *legato falsa {e}causa ‖ adiecta ‖ non nocet: veluti cum quis ita dixerit, Titio, quia me absente negotia mea curauit, Stichum do lego: vel ita, Titio, quia patrocinio eius capitali crimine liberatus fuit, Stichum do lego. Licet enim neq. negotia testatoris vnquam gesserit Titius,neque patrocinio eius liberatus sit,legatum tamen valet. Sed si conditionaliter enunciata fuerit causa: aliud iuris est,veluti hoc modo: Titio,si negotia mea curauerit, fundum ‖ eum do lego.
units.tr: 31 Much more, a legacy is not harmed by a false cause added to it. For example, when someone says: To Titius, because he looked after my affairs while I was away, I give Stichus; or thus: To Titius, because by his advocacy he was freed from a capital charge, I give Stichus. For although Titius never managed the testator's affairs, nor was freed by his advocacy, the legacy is nonetheless valid. But if the cause is stated conditionally, the law is different, as in this form: To Titius, if he has looked after my affairs, I give that farm.

units.la: 32 ¶An seruo heredis rectè legemus, quæritur. & constat pure inutiliter legari,nec quicquam proficere,si viuo testatore de potestate heredis exierit: quia * quod {g}inutile foret legatum, si statim post factum testamentum decessisset testator, hoc non debet ideo valere,quia diutius testator vixerit. Sub {h}conditione vero rectè legatur ‖ seruo ‖, vt requiramus,an quo tempore dies legati cedit, in potestate heredis non sit.
units.tr: 32 Whether we may validly bequeath to the slave of an heir is a question. It is agreed that a pure legacy is invalid and achieves nothing if the slave passes out of the heir's power while the testator is still alive, because a legacy that would have been void had the testator died immediately after making the will should not become valid merely because the testator lived longer. A legacy made under a condition, however, may validly be left to the slave, so we must ask whether he is still in the heir's power at the time the legacy falls due.

units.la: 33 ¶Ex diuerso,heredè instituto seruo,quin domino rectè etiam sine conditione legetur, non dubitatur {i}. Nam etsi statim post factum testamentum decesserit testator: non tamen apud eum,qui heres sit,dies legati cedere intelligitur: cum hereditas à legato separata sit: & posset per eum seruum alius heres effici, si prius, quam iussu domini adeat,in alterius potestate transLatus sit: vel manumissus ipse heres efficitur, quibus casibus vtile est legatum. Quod si in eadem causa permanserit,& iussu legatarij adierit: euanescet legatum.
units.tr: 33 Conversely, where the slave has been instituted heir, it is not doubted that a legacy to the master may validly be left even without a condition. For even if the testator dies immediately after making the will, the legacy is not understood to fall due while the slave is the heir, since the inheritance is separate from the legacy. Another heir could be made through that slave if he is transferred into another's power before he enters on the inheritance by his master's order, or the slave himself becomes heir if he is manumitted. In these cases the legacy is valid. But if the situation remains unchanged and he enters on the inheritance by the legatee's order, the legacy lapses.

units.la: 34 ¶Ante heredis institutionem inutilitas antea legabatur: scilicet quia testamenta vim ex institutione heredis accipiunt,& ob id veluti caput atque fundamentum intelligitur totius testamenti heredis institutio. Pari ratione nec libertas ante heredis institutionem dari poterat. Sed quia inciuile esse putauimus, scripturæ ordinem quidem sequi (quod & ipsi antiquitati vituperandū fuerat visum) sperni autem testatoris voluntatem: per nostra constitutionem & hoc vitium emendauimus: vt liceat & ante heredis institutionem,& inter medias heredum institutiones legatum relinquere,& multo magis libertatem. cuius visus fauorabilior est.
units.tr: 34 Formerly a legacy made before the institution of an heir was invalid, because wills derive their force from the institution of the heir, and so the institution of the heir is understood as the head and foundation of the whole will. For the same reason, freedom could not be given before the institution of an heir either. But since we thought it unreasonable to follow the form of the writing (which even the ancients had judged deserving of censure) while disregarding the testator's will, we have corrected this defect by our constitution. It is now permitted to leave a legacy before the institution of an heir, or between the institutions of several heirs, and much more so a grant of freedom, whose favour is greater.

units.la: 35 ¶ Post mortem quoque heredis aut legatarij similí modo inutiliter legabatur: veluti si quis ita dicat, cum heres meus mortuus fuerit, do lego. Item: pridie quam heres aut legatarius moriatur. Sed simili modo & hoc correximus, firmitatem huiusmodi legatis ad fideicommissorum similitudinem præstan tes: ne in hoc casu deterior causa legatorum, quàm fideicommissorum inueniatur.
units.tr: 35 Likewise, a legacy made after the death of the heir or the legatee was formerly invalid. For example, if someone said: "When my heir has died, I give and bequeath." Or: "The day before the heir or legatee dies." We have also corrected this, giving such legacies the same firmness as trust bequests, so that in this case the position of legacies should not be found worse than that of trust bequests.

units.la: 36 ¶ Pœnæ quoque nomine inutiliter antea legabatur &,adimebatur, vel transferebatur. Pœnæ autem nomine legari videtur, quod coercendi heredis causa relinquitur, quo magis aliquid faciat, aut non faciat: veluti si quis ita scripserit: heres meus si filiam suam in matrimonium Titio collocauerit: vel ex diuerso, si non collocauerit, dato decem aureos Seio: aut si ita scripserit, heres meus si fernū[?] fichum[?] alienauerit: vel ex diuerso, si non alienauerit, Titio decem aureos dato. Et in tantum hæc regula obseruabatur, vt quàm plurimis principalibus constitutionibus significaretur, nec principem agnoscere, quod ei pœnæ nomine legatu[?] fit. nec ex militis quidem testamento talia legata valebant, quamuis aliæ militum voluntates in ordinandis testamentis valde obseruabantur. quin etiã nec libertates pœnæ nomine dari posse placebat. eo amplius nec heredem pœnæ nomine adici posse, Sabinus existimabat: veluti si quis ita dicat, Titius heres esto, si Titius filiam suam in matrimonium Seio collocauerit, Seius quoque heres esto. Nihil enim interebat, qua ratione Titius coerceretur, vtrum legati datione, an coheredis adiectione. Sed huiusmodi scrupulositas nobis non placuit: & generaliter ea, quæ relinquuntur, licet pœnæ nomine fuerint relicta, vel adempta, vel in alium translata: nihil distare à cæteris legatis constituimus, vel in dando, vel in adimendo, vel in transferendo: exceptis videlicet iis, quæ impossibilia sunt, vel legibus interdicta, aut aliàs probrosa{a}. Huiusmodi enim testamentorum dispositiones valere, secta meorum temporum non patitur.
units.tr: 36 Formerly a penalty-legacy was also invalid, and could be revoked or transferred. A legacy is understood as a penalty when it is left to coerce the heir, so that he does or does not do something; for example, if someone wrote: "If my heir marries his daughter to Titius, let him give ten gold pieces to Seius"; or conversely, "If he does not marry her, let him give ten gold pieces to Titius"; or if he wrote: "If my heir alienates the slave Stichum," or conversely, "If he does not alienate him, let him give ten gold pieces to Titius." This rule was observed so strictly that many imperial constitutions declared that the prince does not recognise a legacy made to him under the name of a penalty. Such legacies were not valid even in a soldier's will, although the other wishes of soldiers were greatly respected in making their wills. Indeed, it was also held that freedom could not be given under the name of a penalty. Sabinus further thought that an heir could not be added under the name of a penalty; for example, if someone said: "Let Titius be heir, if Titius marries his daughter to Seius; let Seius also be heir." For it made no difference by what means Titius was coerced, whether by the giving of a legacy or by the addition of a co-heir. But we have not approved this excessive scruple, and in general we have decided that things left, whether they were left, revoked, or transferred under the name of a penalty, differ in no way from other legacies, whether in giving, revoking, or transferring them. The exceptions, of course, are those things that are impossible, forbidden by law, or otherwise disgraceful. For the school of our own time does not allow such dispositions in wills to be valid.
On the Revocation of Legacies, Title 21.

units.la: ADEMPTIO legatorum (siue eodem testamento adimantur, siue codicillis) firma est, sed & siue contrariis verbis{b} fiat ademptio: veluti si quis ita quid legauerit, do lego: ita adimatur, non do, non lego: siue non contrariis, sed aliis quibuscumque verbis.
units.tr: The revocation of legacies is firm, whether they are revoked in the same will or in codicils, and whether the revocation is made by contrary words, as when someone has bequeathed something in this way, I give and bequeath, and revokes it thus: I do not give, I do not bequeath; or by words that are not contrary, but any other words whatever.

units.la: 1 ¶Transferri{d} quoque legatum ab alio ad alium potest: veluti si quis ita dixerit, hominem stichum, quem Titio legaui, Seio do lego: siue in eodem testamento, siue in codicillis hoc fecerit, quo casu simul Titio adimi videtur, & Seio dari.
units.tr: 1 A legacy may also be transferred from one person to another. For example, if someone says: The slave Stichus, whom I bequeathed to Titius, I give and bequeath to Seius; whether he does this in the same will or in codicils, the legacy to Titius is understood to be revoked at the same time and given to Seius.
On the Falcidian Law, Title 22.

units.la: SVPEREST, ut de lege Falcidia. dispi-ciamus, qua modus nouissimè legatis impositus est. Cùm enim olim lege duodecim tabularum libera erat legandi potestas, vt liceret vel totum patrimonium legatis erogare (quippe cùm ea lege ita cautum esset: vti quisquè legasset suæ rei, ita ius esto) visum est hanc legandi licentiam coarctare: idque ipsorum testatorum gratia prouisum est, ob id, quod plerumque intestati moriebantur, recusantibus scriptis heredibus pro nullo aut minimo lucro hereditates adire. Et cùm super hoc tam lex Furia{i}, quàm lex Voconia{k} latæ sunt, quarum neutra sufficiens ad rei consummationem videbatur: nouissimè{l} lata est lex Falcida, qua cauctur, ne plus legare liceat, quàm dodrantem totorum bonorum: id est, vt siue vnus heres institutus fit, siue plures, apud eū cosue pars{m} quarta remaneat.
units.tr: It remains to consider the Falcidian law, by which the last limit was placed on legacies. For although under the law of the Twelve Tables the power of bequeathing was unrestricted, so that one could even give away the whole estate in legacies (since that law provided: as a man has bequeathed concerning his property, so let it be law), it was thought right to restrain this freedom of bequeathing. This was provided for the sake of the testators themselves, because they often died intestate, since the written heirs refused to enter on inheritances for no profit or a very small one. Although both the Furian law and the Voconian law were passed on this matter, neither seemed sufficient to bring the matter to completion. Finally the Falcidian law was passed, which provides that one may not bequeath more than three-quarters of the whole estate; that is, whether one heir or several is instituted, a quarter part must remain with him.

units.la: 2 ¶Et cùm quæsitum esset, duobus heredibus institutis (veluti Titio & Seio) si Titij pars, aut tota exhausta sit legatis, quæ nominatim ab eo data sunt, aut supra modum onerata: à Seio vero aut nulla relicta sint legata, aut quę partem eius dumtaxat in partem dimidiam minuant: an quia is quartam partem totius hereditatis aut amplius habet, Titio nihil ex legatis, quæ ab eo relicta sunt, retinere licear, vt quartam partem suæ partis saluam habeat: placuit posse retinere, etenim in singulis heredibus ratio legis Falcidiæ ponenda est. 3 ¶ Quantitas autem patrimonij, ad quam ratio legis Falcidiæ redigitur, mortis tempore spectatur. Itaque (verbi gratia) si is,qui centum aureorum patrimonium in bonis habeat, centum aureos legauerit: nihil legatariis prodest, si ante aditam hereditatem per seruos hereditarios, aut ex partu ancillarum hereditariarum, aut ex fœtu pecorum tantum accesserit hereditati, vt centū|aureis||legatorum nomine erogatis heres quartam partem hereditatis habuiturus sit: sed necesse est, vt nihilominus quarta pars legatis detrahatur. Ex diuerso, si septuagintaquinque legauerit, & ante aditam hereditatem in tantum decreuerint bona (incendijs forte, vt non amplius, quàm septuaginta quinque aureorum substantia, vel etiam minus relinquatur: solida legata debentur: Nec ea res damnosa est heredi, cui liberum est non adire hereditatem, quæ res efficit, vt sit necesse legatarijs, ne destituto testamento to nihil consequantur, cum herede in portione paciscI. 4 ¶ Cùm autem ratio legis Falcidiæ ponitur, ante deducitur æs alienum: item funeris impensa, & pretia seruorum manumissorum: tunc demum in reliquo ita ratio habetur, vt ex eo quarta pars apud heredem remaneat, ⅔ tres vero partes inter legatarios distribuantur, pro rata scilicet portione eius, quod cuique eorum legatum fuerit. Itaque si fingamus quadringentos aureos legatos esse, & patrimonij quantitatem, ex qua legata erogari oportet, quadringentorum esse: quarta pars legatariis singulis debet detrahi. Quod si trecentos quinquaginta legatos fingamus: octaua debet detrahi. Quod si quingentos legauerit: initio quinta, deinde quarta detrahi debet. Ante enim detrahendum est, quod extra pias caussas.
units.tr: 2 Again, when it was asked whether, where two heirs were instituted (for example Titius and Seius), Titius's share is exhausted or wholly consumed by legacies that were given by name from it, or overburdened beyond the limit, while from Seius's share either no legacies were left or only a half of that share is diminished, whether Titius may retain nothing of the legacies left by him, so that he keeps a quarter of his own share intact, it was decided that he may retain them, for the reckoning under the Falcidian law must be made for each heir separately. 3 The amount of the estate to which the reckoning under the Falcidian law is applied is determined at the time of death. Thus, for example, if a man who has an estate of a hundred gold pieces bequeaths a hundred gold pieces, it does not help the legatees if, before the inheritance is entered upon, the estate gains only through the heritable slaves, or from the offspring of the heritable female slaves, or from the increase of the flocks, so that the heir will have a quarter of the inheritance even after the hundred gold pieces have been paid out as legacies; rather, a quarter must nevertheless be deducted from the legacies. Conversely, if he bequeathed seventy-five, and before the inheritance is entered upon the goods diminish so far (perhaps by fire) that only seventy-five gold pieces, or even less, are left, the legacies are owed in full. Nor is this a loss to the heir, who is free not to enter upon the inheritance; this circumstance makes it necessary for the legatees, lest the will fall through and they receive nothing, to come to terms with the heir over a share. 4 When the reckoning under the Falcidian law is made, debts are first deducted, likewise the expense of the funeral, and the prices of slaves manumitted; only then is the reckoning made on the remainder, so that a quarter remains with the heir, while the other three quarters are distributed among the legatees, in proportion to what each of them has been bequeathed. Thus, if we suppose that four hundred gold pieces have been bequeathed, and the amount of the estate from which the legacies must be paid is four hundred, a quarter must be deducted from each legatee. But if we suppose that three hundred and fifty have been bequeathed, an eighth must be deducted. If he has bequeathed five hundred, a fifth must first be deducted, and then a quarter. For what is outside the pious causes must be deducted first.

units.la: 1 non remanebit ex legato ad pias caussas & dotis prælegatę: & verito alienari à legatario ac eius successoribus. si miles testatus: si testator procurabit detrahi, si id eidem pollicitus, si sciens integra legata soluit: si inuentario non confecto hereditatem adiit: Schnid. bonorum quantitatem est, deinde quod ex bonis apud heredem remanere oportet {a}.
units.tr: nothing shall remain from the legacy for pious causes and from the legacy of a dowry: and it is to be feared it may be alienated by the legatee and his successors. If the soldier made the will; if the testator shall arrange for the deduction; if he promised this to the same person; if, knowing it, he pays the legacies in full; if, the inventory not having been completed, he entered upon the inheritance: Schnid. the quantity of the goods, and then what ought to remain from the goods with the heir {a}.

units.la: DE FIDEICOMMISSARIIS HEREDITATIBUS, & ad senatus consultum Trebellianum, {b}. TIT. XXIII.
units.tr: On Fideicommissary Inheritances, and the Senatus Consultum Trebellianum, {b}. TITLE XXIII.

units.la: NVNC transfeamus ad fideicommissa.sed prius est,vt de hereditatibus fideicommissariis videamus. 1 ¶Sciendum itaque est, omnia fideicommissa primis {c}temporibus infirma fuisse : quia nemo inuitus cogebatur praestare id,de quo rogatus erat. Quibus enim non poterant hereditatem, vel legata relinquere{d},si relinquebant,fideicommittebant eorum,qui capere ex testamento poterant ‖hereditatem‖.Et ideo fideicommissa appellata sunt,quia nullo vinculo iuris, sed tantum pudore eorum, qui rogabantur,continebantur.Postea diuus Augustus primus,semel iterumque gratia personarum motus,vel quia per ipsius salutem rogatus quis diceretur, aut ob insignem quorundam perfidiam, iusit consulibus auctoritatem suam interponere. Quod quia iustum videbatur,& populare erat : paulatim conuersum est in aliam iurisdictionem : tantumque eorum suor factus est, vt paulatim etiā {e}praetor proprius crearetur,qui de fideicommissis ius diceret, quem fideicommissarium appellabant. 2 ¶In primis igitur sciendum est,opus esse,vt aliquis recto iure testamento heres instituatur: eiusque fidei committatur, vt eam hereditatem alij restituat{f}. alioqui * inutile est testamentum,in quo nemo heres instituitur{g}. Cum igitur aliquis scripserit,Lucius Titius heres esto: potest adiicere ,rogo te Luci Titi, vt cum primum poteris hereditatem meam adire, eam Caio Seio reddas restituas. Potest autem quisque & de {h}parte restituenda heredem rogare. Et liberū est, vel pure, vel sub conditione relinquere fideicommissum, vel ex certo die. 3 ¶Restituta autem hereditate, is quidem,qui restituit, nihilominus heres permanet{i}: is vero qui recipit hereditatem, aliquando heredis,aliquando legatarij loco habetur. 4 ¶Et Neronis quidem temporibus Trebellio Maximo & Annaeo Seneca consulibus{k} senatusconsultum factum est; quo cautum est, vt si hereditas ex fideicommisi causa restituta fit:omnes actiones,quæ itre ciuili heredi,& in heredem competerent,ei,& in eum darentur,cui ex fideicommisso restituta esset hereditas.{a} Post quod senatusconsulti prætor utiles actiones ei,& in eum, qui recepit hereditatem, quasi heredi,& in heredem dare coepit.
units.tr: Now let us pass on to fideicommissa. But first we should look at fideicommissary inheritances. 1 ¶ It must be understood, then, that in the earliest times all fideicommissa were ineffective, because no one was compelled against his will to perform what he had been asked to do. Those who could not leave an inheritance or legacies to certain persons, if they did leave them, entrusted them to those who could take under a will. They were called fideicommissa because they were held by no bond of law, but only by the conscience of those who were asked. Later the deified Augustus, moved once or twice by favour toward particular persons, or because someone was said to have been asked in the name of his own safety, or on account of the notorious faithlessness of certain persons, ordered the consuls to interpose their authority. Since this seemed just and was popular, it was gradually turned into another jurisdiction, and it grew so much that a special praetor was gradually appointed to declare the law concerning fideicommissa. He was called the fideicommissary praetor. 2 ¶ In the first place, then, it must be understood that someone must be validly instituted heir by will, and that his good faith is entrusted with handing the inheritance over to another. Otherwise a will in which no one is instituted heir is useless. So when someone has written, "Let Lucius Titius be my heir," he may add, "I ask you, Lucius Titius, that as soon as you can enter upon my inheritance, you hand it over and restore it to Gaius Seius." One may also ask the heir to restore a part. It is free to leave a fideicommissum purely, or under a condition, or from a certain day. 3 ¶ When the inheritance has been restored, he who restores it nonetheless remains heir. But he who receives the inheritance is sometimes regarded in the place of an heir, and sometimes in the place of a legatee. 4 ¶ Under Nero, in the consulship of Trebellius Maximus and Annaeus Seneca, a senatus consultum was passed by which it was provided that if an inheritance is restored by reason of a fideicommissum, all actions which by civil law would lie for and against the heir should be given for and against him to whom the inheritance was restored under the fideicommissum. After this senatus consultum, the praetor began to give useful actions for and against him who received the inheritance, as if he were heir and as against an heir.

units.la: 5 ¶Sed quia heredes scripti, cùm aut totam hereditatem, aut pene totam plerumque restituere rogabantur, adire hereditatem ob nullum vel minimum lucrum recusabant,atque ob id extinguebantur fideicommissa: postea Vespasiani Augusti temporibus Pegaso & Pusione consulibus{b} senatus censuit: ut ei, qui rogatus esset hereditatem restituere, perinde liceret quartam partem retinere, atque ex lege Falcidia ex legatis retinere concedebatur[?]. Ex singulis quoque rebus, quæ per fideicommissum relinquuntur, eadem retentio permissa est. Post quod senatusconsultum ipse heres onera hereditaria sustinebat. Ille autem, qui ex fideicommisso recipiebat partem hereditatis, legatarij partiarij loco erat, id est, eius legatarij,cui pars bonorum legatur. quæ species legati, partitio{c} vocabatur; quia cum herede legatarius partiebatur hereditatem. Unde quæ solebant stipulationes inter heredem & partiarium legatarium interponi{d}: eadem interponebantur inter eum qui ex fideicommisso recepit hereditatem, & heredem, id est, ut lucrum & damnum hereditarium pro{e} rata parte inter eos commune esset.
units.tr: 5 ¶ But because the appointed heirs, when they were commonly asked to restore the whole inheritance, or nearly the whole, refused to enter upon it for little or no gain, and so fideicommissa lapsed, later, in the time of the emperor Vespasian, in the consulship of Pegasus and Pusio, the senate decreed that he who had been asked to restore the inheritance should be allowed to keep a fourth part, just as he was permitted to keep a fourth of legacies under the Falcidian law. The same retention was allowed from individual things left by fideicommissum. After this senatus consultum the heir himself bore the burdens of the inheritance. He who received a part of the inheritance under the fideicommissum stood in the place of a partiary legatee, that is, of a legatee to whom a share of the goods is left. This kind of legacy was called a partition, because the legatee shared the inheritance with the heir. Hence the stipulations which were customarily entered into between the heir and a partiary legatee were also entered into between him who received the inheritance by fideicommissum and the heir; namely, that the gain and loss of the inheritance should be shared between them in proportion.

units.la: 6 ¶Ergo siquidem non plus, quàm do-drantem hereditatis scriptus heres rogatus sit restitu-ere: tunc ex Trebelliano senatusconsulto restitu-batur[?] hereditas,& in utrumque actiones hereditariæ pro rata parte dabantur:in heredem quidem iure ciuili: in eum vero, qui recipiebat hereditatem, ex senatusconsulto Trebelliano tanquam in heredem. At si plus, quàm dodrantem, vel etiam totam hereditatem restituere rogatus esset: locus erat Pegasiano senatusconsulto: & heres, qui semel adierat hereditatem (si modo{f} sua voluntate adierat) siue retinuerat quartam partem, siue retinere noluerat: ipse u-niversa onera hereditaria sustinebat. Sed quarta qui-dem retenta, quasi partis &{g} pro parte stipulationes interponebantur, tanquam inter partiarium legatarium & heredem. Si vero totam hereditatem restituere ret:emptoræ[?] & venditæ hereditatis stipulationes interponebantur. Sed si recusabat scriptus heres adire he-reditatem reditatem ob id,quòd diceret eam sibi suspestam esse quasi damnosam: cauebatur Pegasiano senatusconsulto, vt desiderante eo, cui restituere rogatus esset, iussu praetoris adiret , & restitueret hereditatem: perindeque ei & in eum, qui reciperet hereditatem, actiones darentur, ac iuris est ex Trebelliano senatusconsulto. quo casu nulli stipulationibus est opus: qui semel & huic, qui restituit, securitas datur & actiones hereditariae ei & {b}in eum transferuntur. qui recipit hereditatem, utroque senatusconsulto in hac specie concurrente.
units.tr: 6 ¶ Therefore, if the appointed heir was asked to restore no more than three quarters of the inheritance, then the inheritance was restored under the Trebellian senatus consultum, and the hereditary actions were given for and against each of them in proportion to their share: against the heir by civil law, and against him who received the inheritance under the Trebellian senatus consultum, as against an heir. But if he was asked to restore more than three quarters, or even the whole inheritance, the Pegasian senatus consultum applied. The heir, who had once entered upon the inheritance (provided he had entered by his own will), whether he had kept a fourth part or had not wished to keep it, bore all the burdens of the inheritance himself. But when the fourth was kept, stipulations were entered into as if for a part and in proportion to the part, just as between a partiary legatee and the heir. If, however, he was asked to restore the whole inheritance, stipulations of sale and purchase of an inheritance were entered into. But if the appointed heir refused to enter upon the inheritance on the ground that he thought it burdensome, as if it would cause loss, it was provided by the Pegasian senatus consultum that, at the request of him to whom he was asked to restore it, he should enter by order of the praetor and restore the inheritance. Then actions were given for and against him who received the inheritance just as they are by law under the Trebellian senatus consultum. In this case no stipulations are needed, since security is at once given to him who restores, and the hereditary actions are transferred to him and against him who receives the inheritance, when both senatus consulta apply in this type of case.

units.la: 7 Sed quia stipulationes ex senatusconsulto Pegasiano descendentes, & ipsi antiquitati displicuerunt, & quibusdam casibus captiosas {c}eas homo excelsi ingenij Papinianus appellat, & nobis in legibus magis simplicitas, quàm difficultas placet: ideo omnibus nobis suggestis tam similitudinibus, quàm differentiis utriusque senatusconsulti: placuit, explosa senatusconsulto Pegasiano, quod postea superuenit, omnem auctoritatem Trebelliano senatusconsulto praestare, ut ex eo fideicommissariae hereditates restituantur: sive habeat heres ex voluntate testatoris quartam {d}, sive plus, sive minus, sive nihil penitus: ut tunc quando vel nihil, vel minus quarta apud eum remanet, liceat ei vel quartam, vel quod deest, ex nostra auctoritate retinere, vel repetere solutum {e}quasi ex Trebelliano senatusconsulto: pro rata portione actionibus, tam in heredem, quàm in fideicommissarium competentibus. si vero totam hereditatem sponte restituerit: omnes hereditariae actiones fideicommissario, & adversus eum competant. Sed etiam id, quod praecipuum Pegasiani senatusconsulti fuerat, ut quando re cusarer heres scriptus sibi datam hereditatem adire, necessitas ei imponeretur totam hereditatem volenti fideicommissario restituere, & omnes ad eum & contra eum transferre actiones: & hoc transposuimus ad senatusconsultum Trebellianum, ut ex hoc solo necessitas heredi imponatur, si ipso nolente adire, fideicommissarius desideret restitui sibi hereditatem, nullo nec damno nec commodo apud heredem remanente.
units.tr: 7 But because the stipulations arising from the Pegasian senatus consultum displeased even the ancients, and a man of lofty genius, Papinian, calls them captious in certain cases, and because we prefer simplicity rather than difficulty in the laws, therefore, after we had considered both the similarities and the differences of the two senatus consulta, we resolved to discard the Pegasian senatus consultum, which came later, and to give all authority to the Trebellian senatus consultum, so that fideicommissary inheritances may be restored under it. Whether the heir has a fourth by the will of the testator, or more, or less, or nothing at all, then, when he has nothing, or less than a fourth, remaining with him, he may keep either a fourth or what is lacking, by our authority, or recover what he has paid, as under the Trebellian senatus consultum, with actions lying for and against both the heir and the fideicommissary in proportion to their shares. But if he has voluntarily restored the whole inheritance, all the hereditary actions shall lie for and against the fideicommissary. Moreover, what was the chief feature of the Pegasian senatus consultum, namely that when the appointed heir refused to enter upon the inheritance given to him, he was obliged, if the fideicommissary wished, to restore the whole inheritance and to transfer all actions to him and against him, this we have also carried over to the Trebellian senatus consultum, so that from this alone the heir is obliged, if against his will he refuses to enter, and the fideicommissary asks that the inheritance be restored to him, with nothing remaining with the heir either as loss or gain.

units.la: 8 Nihil autem interest, utrum aliquis ex asse heres institutus, aut totam hereditatem, aut pro parte restituere rogatur: an ex parte heres institutus, aut totam eam partem, aut partem partis
units.tr: 8 It makes no difference whether someone is instituted heir to the whole estate and is asked to restore the whole inheritance or a part of it, or whether he is instituted heir to a part and is asked to restore that whole part or part of a part.

units.la: {c}Creditoribus & haeredi praesertim, cui ut fidei-commissarius ita eidem accepta restituere semper tenebatur.
units.tr: Creditors, and especially the heir, to whom as fideicommissary he was always bound to restore what had been received.

units.la: cui ut fidei-commissarius ita eidem accepta restituere semper tenebatur
units.tr: to whom as fideicommissary he was always bound to restore what had been received.

units.la: ita haeredi de resarciendo damno aditae hereditatis. restituere rogatur. Nam & hoc casu eadem obseruari praecipimus, quae in totius hereditatis restitutione diximus. {a}9 ¶Si quis vna aliqua re deducta, siue praecepta, quae quartam continet (veluti fundo, vel alia re) rogatus sit restituere hereditatem: similiter modo ex Trebelliano senatusconsulto restitutio fiet, perinde ac si quarta parte retenta rogatus esset reliquam hereditatem restituere. Sed {b}illud interest, quod altero casu, id est, cum deducta, siue praecepta aliqua re, restituitur hereditas: in solidum ex eo senatusconsulto actiones transferuntur: & res, quae remanet apud heredem, sine vllo onere hereditario apud eum remanet, quasi ex legato ei adquisita. Altero vero casu, id est, cum quarta parte retenta rogatus est heres restituere hereditatem, & restituit: scindun-tur actiones, & pro dodrante quidem transferuntur ad fideicommissarium, pro quadrante remanent apud heredem. Quinetiam licet vna re aliqua deducta, aut praecepta, restituere aliquis hereditatem rogatus sit, in qua maxima pars hereditatis continetur: aeque in solidum transferuntur actiones: & secum deliberare debet is, cui restituitur hereditas, an expediat sibi restitui. Eadem scilicet interueniunt, & si duabus pluribusve deductis praeceptisve rebus, restituere hereditatem rogatus sit. Sed & si certa summa deducta praeceptave, quae quartam vel etiam maximam partem hereditatis continet: rogatus sit aliquis hereditatem restituere: idem iuris est. Quae autem diximus de eo, qui ex alie institutus est: eadem transferimus & ad eum, qui ex parte heres scriptus est.
units.tr: to the heir for the making good of the damage of the entered inheritance, is asked to restore.
