For in this case also we direct that the same rules be observed which we stated for the restoration of the whole inheritance. 9 ¶ If someone, with a single thing deducted or taken in advance, which contains a fourth (for example, an estate or some other thing), is asked to restore the inheritance, then the restoration is made in the same way under the Trebellian senatus consultum, just as if he had been asked to restore the rest of the inheritance with a fourth part retained. But there is this difference: in the one case, namely when the inheritance is restored with some thing deducted or taken in advance, the actions are transferred in full under that senatus consultum, and the thing that remains with the heir remains with him free of any hereditary burden, as if acquired from a legacy. In the other case, namely when the heir is asked to restore the inheritance with a fourth part retained, and he does restore it, the actions are divided: three quarters are transferred to the fideicommissary, and one quarter remains with the heir. Moreover, even if someone is asked to restore an inheritance with a single thing deducted or taken in advance, in which the greater part of the inheritance is contained, the actions are likewise transferred in full, and he to whom the inheritance is restored must consider with himself whether it is advantageous for him to have it restored. The same things happen if he is asked to restore the inheritance with two or more things deducted or taken in advance. But if someone is asked to restore an inheritance with a certain sum deducted or taken in advance, which contains a fourth or even the greater part of the inheritance, the law is the same. What we have said of one who is instituted heir to the whole, we likewise transfer to one who is instituted heir to a part.

units.la: 10 ¶Praeterea intestatus quoque moriturus, potest rogare eum, ad quem bona sua, vel legitimo iure, vel honorario pertinere intelligit: vt hereditatem suam totam, partemve eius, aut rem aliquam (veluti fundum, hominem, pecuniam) alicui restituat: cum alioqui legata, nisi ex testamento, non valeant.
units.tr: 10 Moreover, a person who is about to die intestate may also request that whoever he understands his goods to belong to, by legitimate or by praetorian right, restore his whole inheritance, or a part of it, or some particular thing (such as an estate, a slave, or money) to someone. Otherwise legacies are not valid unless they are made in a will.

units.la: 11 ¶Eum quoque, cui aliquid restituitur, potest rogare, vt id rursum alij aut totum, aut partem, vel etiam aliquid aliud restituat. 12 ¶Et quia prima fideicommissorum cunabula a fide heredum pendet, & tam nomen, quam substantiam acceperunt: ideo diuus Augustus ad necessitatem iuris ea retraxit. Nuper & nos eundem principem superare contendentes, ex facto, quod Tribonianus vir excellentissimus exquaestore sacri palatij suggesit, constitutione {e}fecimus: per quam disposuimus, si testator fidei heredis
units.tr: 11 He may also request that the person to whom something has been restored should in turn restore it, wholly or in part, or some other thing, to another. 12 And since the first beginnings of fideicommissa depended on the good faith of heirs, and took both their name and their substance from it, the deified Augustus therefore drew them back under the necessity of law. Recently we too, striving to surpass that same emperor, made a constitution based on a matter which Tribonian, a most excellent man and former quaestor of the sacred palace, brought to our attention, by which we provided that if a testator has entrusted to the good faith of his heir either to restore the inheritance or a thing in specie as a fideicommissum, and the matter cannot be shown either by writing or by the number of five witnesses (which is recognised as legitimate in fideicommissa), but there were fewer than five witnesses, or no witness at all, took part;
{a} v.l. 13, l. 14 ff. si quis omiserit.
{b} v.l. 30, §. multa interest ff. eo.

units.la: {c} interdum tamen in solum fideicommissarium data actio l.13.§.idem erit. De petit. hær.
units.tr: {c} Yet sometimes the action is given to the fideicommissary alone: l. 13, §. idem erit. De petit. hær.

units.la: {d} etiā ab intestato fideicommissa relinqui potuit. l.1.§.hoc ante l.78 in pr. ff.eo. l.3.Cod.eo. vlp.25.§.4. l.13. ff.de inoffic.testo. l.114 §.2.de leg.1. l.89 §.Lucius. de leg.2. l.4.Cod.de codicill.§.1. in pr. §.de codicillis.
units.tr: {d} A fideicommissum could also be left even by one who died intestate: l. 1, §. hoc ante l. 78 in pr. ff. eo. l. 3 Cod. eo. Ulp. 25, §. 4. l. 13 ff. de inoffic. testo. l. 114, §. 2, de leg. 1. l. 89, §. Lucius, de leg. 2. l. 4 Cod. de codicill. §. 1. in pr. §. de codicillis.

units.la: {e} l.vlt.Cod.de fideicommiss. [?] dis sui commisit, vt vel hereditatem, vel specie fi-deicommissum restituat,& neque ex scriptura,neque ex quinque testium numero (qui in fideicommisis legitimus esse nosciturposfit res manifestari,sed vel pauciores quàm quinque,vel nemo penitus testis in-teruenerit. {†}tunc siue pater heredis, siue alius quicunque fit,qui fidem heredis elegerit, & ab eo restituti aliquid voluerit:si heres perfidia tentus adimple-re fidem recusat, negando rem ita esse subsequutam, si fideicommissarius iusiurandum ei detulerit{a} cum prius ipse de calumnia iurauerit. necesse eum habe-re vel iusiurandum subire,quòd nihil tale à testatore audiuerit,vel recusantem ad fideicommissi vel vniuersalis,vel specialis solutionē coarctari,ne depereat vltima voluntas testatoris fidei heredis commissa.Ea dem obseruari censuimus, & si à legatario vel fideicommissario aliquid similiter relictum sit. Quòd si is,à quo relictum dicitur, ¶ postquam negauerit ¶, confiteatur quidē aliquid à se relictū esse,sed ad legis subtilitatem recurrat: omnino soluere cogendus est.
units.tr: {e} l. ult. Cod. de fideicommiss. then, whether the father of the heir or any other person whatever it may be, who chose the good faith of the heir and wished something to be restored by him: if the heir, caught in perfidy, refuses to fulfil the trust, denying that the matter followed in this way, and the fideicommissary has deferred the oath to him after first swearing himself about calumny, he must either undergo the oath, that he heard nothing of such a thing from the testator, or, if he refuses, be compelled to pay the fideicommissum, whether universal or particular, lest the last will of the testator, committed to the good faith of the heir, perish. We have decided that the same should be observed if something has similarly been left by a legatee or a fideicommissary. But if he by whom it is said to have been left, after he has denied it, confesses indeed that something was left by him, but has recourse to the subtlety of the law, he must be compelled to pay in full.

units.la: DE SINGVLIS REBVS PER fideicommissum relictis, TITVLVS XXIIII.
units.tr: CONCERNING INDIVIDUAL THINGS LEFT BY FIDEICOMMISSUM, TITLE 24.

units.la: P[?]OTEST tamè quis etiam singulas res per fideicommissum relinquere : veluti fundum argentum,hominè,vestem, ¶&¶ pecuniam numeratam: & vel ipsum heredem rogare,vt alicui restituat, vel legatarium a, quamuis à legatario legari non possit{†}. ¶Potest autem nō solum proprias res testator per fideicommissum relinquere: sed & heredis,aut legatarij,aut fideicommissarij, aut cuiuslibet alterius. Itaque & legatarius & fideicommissarius non solum de ea re rogari potest,vt eam alicui restituat, quæ ei relicta sit: sed etiam de alia, siue ipsius, siue aliena sit. Hoc solum obseruandum est, ne plus quisquam rogetur alicui restituere{c}, quàm ipse ex testamento ceperit. nā quod amplius est, inutiliter relinquitur. Cum autè aliena res per fideicommissum relinquitur: necesse est ei,qui rogatus est, aut ipsam redimere & præstare, aut æstimationem eius soluere. 2 ¶Libertas quoque seruo per fideicommissum dari potest, vt heres eum rogetur manumittere{d},vel legatarius, vel fideicommissarius. nec {a}interest, vtrum de suo proprio seruo testator roget, an de eo, qui ipsius heredis, aut legatarij, vel etiam extranei sit. Itaque & alienus seruus redimi & manumitti debet. Quod si dominus cū non vendat: si modo {b}nihil ex iudicio eius, qui reliquit libertatem, recepit nō statim extinguitur fideicommissaria libertas, sed differtur: quia possit tempore procedente, vbicunque occasio serui redimendi fuerit, praestari libertas. Qui autē ex fideicommisso causa manumittitur: non testatoris fit libertus, etiam si testatoris seruus sit, sed eius, qui manumisit. At is, qui directo ex testamento liber esse iubetur, ipsius testatoris libertus fit, qui etiam orcinus {c}appellatur. Nec alius vllus directo ex testamento libertate habere potest, quam qui {d}vtroque tempore testatoris fuerit, & quo faceret testamētū, & quo moreretur. Directa autē libertas tunc dari videtur, cum non ab alio seruū manumitti rogat, sed {e}velut ex suo testamento libertate ei competere vult. 3 ¶Verba autē fideicommissorum hęc maxime in vsu habentur, peto, rogo, volo, mando, fidei tuæ committo. quæ perinde singula firma sunt, atque si omnia in vnū cogesta essent.
units.tr: Yet someone may also leave individual things by fideicommissum: for example a field, silver, a man, a garment, or counted money; and may ask either the heir himself to hand them over to someone, or the legatee, although a legacy cannot be left by a legatee. Moreover, the testator may leave by fideicommissum not only his own things but also those of the heir, or of the legatee, or of the fideicommissary, or of anyone else. So both the legatee and the fideicommissary may be asked to hand over to someone not only the thing that was left to him, but also another thing, whether it is his own or another's. The only thing to observe is that no one should be asked to hand over more than he himself has received under the will, for whatever is beyond that is left ineffectually. When someone else's thing is left by fideicommissum, the one who was asked must either buy it back and deliver it, or pay its value. 2 Freedom too can be given to a slave by fideicommissum, so that the heir, or the legatee, or the fideicommissary is asked to manumit him. It makes no difference whether the testator asks about his own slave or about one belonging to the heir, the legatee, or even a stranger. So a slave belonging to another must also be bought back and manumitted. But if the owner does not sell, and provided he has received nothing from the estimate of the one who left the freedom, the fideicommissary freedom is not extinguished at once but is deferred, because as time goes on freedom can be granted whenever the opportunity to buy the slave arises. However, a person manumitted by reason of a fideicommissum does not become freedman of the testator, even if he was the testator's slave, but of the one who manumitted him. But one who is ordered to be free directly by the will becomes freedman of the testator himself, and is also called orcinus. No one else can have freedom directly by the will except one who belonged to the testator at both times, both when he made the will and when he died. Freedom seems to be given directly when the testator does not ask that the slave be manumitted by another, but wishes freedom to come to him as if from his own will. 3 The words of fideicommissa most commonly in use are these: I ask, I request, I wish, I command, I commit to your good faith. Each of these alone is as binding as if all were gathered into one.
ON CODICILS, TITLE XXV.

units.la: ANTE Augusti tempora constat codicillorum {g}ius in vsu non fuisse, sed primus Lucius Lentulus (ex cuius persona eriā[?] fideicommissa || esse || coeperunt) codicillos introduxit. Nam cum decederet in Africa, scripsit codicillos testamento cōfirmatos, quibus ab Augusto petiit per fideicommissum, vt faceret aliquid. Et cum diuus Augustus voluntatem eius implesset: deinceps reliqui eius auctoritatem sequuti, fideicommissa praestabant: & filia Lentuli legata, quae iure non debebat, soluit. Dicitur autem Augustus conuocasse sapientes viros, interque eos Trebatium quoque, cuius tunc auctoritas maxima erat, & quaesisse, an posset recipi hoc, nec absonans a iuris ratione codicillorum vsus esset: & Trebatium suasisse Augusto, quod diceret vtilissimum & necessarium {h}hoc ciuibus esse propter magnas & longas peregrinationes, quae apud veteres fuissent: vbi si quis testamentu facere non posset, tamen codicillos posset. Post quae tepora cum & Labeo codicillos fecisset: iam nemini dubium erat, quin codicilli iure optimo admitteré-tur. 1 ¶ Non tantum autem testamento facto po-test quis codicillos facere{4}, sed ‖& ‖ intestatus quis decedens fideicommittere codicillis potest. Sed cum ante testamentum factum codicilli facti erant: Papinianus ait, non aliter vires habere, quàm si speciali postea voluntate confirmentur. Sed diui Seuerus & Antoninus rescripserunt: ex iis codicillis{b}, qui testa-mentū præcedunt, posse fideicommissum peti:si appareat eum, qui testamentum fecit, à voluntate, quam in codicillis expresserat, nō recesisse{c}. 2 ¶Codicillis autē hereditas neque dari, neque adimi potest: ne confundatur ius testamentorum & codicillorum. & ideò nec exheredatio scribi. Directò{d} autē hereditas codicillis neque dari, neque adimi potest. nam per fideicommissum hereditas codicillis iure relinquitur. Nec conditionem heredi institutô codicillis adiicere, neque substituere directò ‖ quis ‖ potest. 3 ¶Codicillos autem etiam plures quis facere potest, & nullam solennitatem ordinationis desiderant.
units.tr: It is agreed that before the time of Augustus the use of codicils was unknown, but Lucius Lentulus (from whose case fideicommissa also began to be used) was the first to introduce codicils. For when he was dying in Africa, he wrote codicils, confirmed by his will, in which he asked Augustus by way of fideicommissum to do something. When the divine Augustus had carried out his wish, his successors followed his authority and paid fideicommissa, and Lentulus's daughter, who had been left a legacy that she could not claim by law, was paid. It is said, moreover, that Augustus summoned wise men, among them Trebatius also, whose authority was then very great, and asked whether this could be accepted, and whether the use of codicils was not at odds with the principle of law. Trebatius advised Augustus that it would be most useful and necessary for citizens, because of the great and long journeys that were made in earlier times, where someone who could not make a will could nevertheless make codicils. After this time, when Labeo also had made codicils, no one any longer doubted that codicils were admitted by the best law. 1 ¶ Now, a person may make codicils not only after making a will, but also a person who dies intestate may leave a fideicommissum by codicils. But since codicils made before a will was drawn up, Papinian says, have no force unless they are afterwards confirmed by a specific later intention. The divine Severus and Antoninus, however, rescripted that a fideicommissum may be claimed from codicils that precede the will, provided it appears that the one who made the will did not depart from the intention he had expressed in the codicils. 2 ¶ Now an inheritance can be neither given nor taken away by codicils, lest the law of wills and of codicils be confused; and for this reason neither can a disinheritance be written. An inheritance, however, cannot be directly given or taken away by codicils; for an inheritance is left by codicils lawfully only through a fideicommissum. Nor can anyone add a condition to an heir instituted in a will by codicils, nor directly substitute one. 3 ¶ Moreover, a person may make several codicils, and they require no formality of execution.

units.la: INSTITUTIONUM, SEU ELEMENTORUM D. Justiniani sacratissimi Principis, LIBER III.
units.tr: INSTITUTIONUM, SEU ELEMENTORUM D. Justiniani sacratissimi Principis, LIBER III.

units.la: DE HEREDITATIBUS, quae ab intestato deferuntur, TITULUS I.
units.tr: DE HEREDITATIBUS, quae ab intestato deferuntur, TITULUS I.

units.la: INTESTATUS decedit qui aut omnino testamentum non fecit: aut non iure fecit: aut id, quod fecerat, ruptum irritumve factum est, aut si ex eo nemo heres extiterit.
units.tr: A man dies intestate who either has made no will at all, or has not made one validly, or whose will has been broken or made void, or if no one has become heir under it.

units.la: 1 ¶Intestatorum autem hereditates ex lege duodecim tabularum, primum ad suos heredes pertinent.
units.tr: 1 ¶The inheritances of those who die intestate pass first, by the law of the Twelve Tables, to their own heirs.

units.la: 2 ¶Sui autem heredes existimantur (ut supra diximus) qui in potestate morientis fuerint, veluti filius filiave, nepos neptisve ex filio, pronepos proneptisve ex nepote ex filio nato prognatus prognatave. Nec interest, utrum naturales sint liberi, an adoptivi. Quibus connumerari necesse est etiam eos, qui ex legitimis quidem ‖ nuptiis vel ‖ matrimonii nō sūt progeniti, curiis tamē civi tatu dati secundū divalium constitutionum, quae super his positae sunt, tenorem, ‖heredū ‖suorum iura nancisciuntur. Necnon eos, quos noxtrae amplexae sunt constitutiones, per quas iuisimus, ‖ut ‖si quis mulierem in suo contubernio copulauerit, non ab initio affectione maritali, eam tamen, cum qua poterat habere coniugium, & ex ea liberos sustulerit: postea vero affectione procedente, etiam nuptialia instrumenta cum ea fecerit, & filios vel filias habuerit: non solum eos liberos, qui post dotem editi sunt, iustos & in potestate patris esse: sed etiam anteriores, qui & iis, qui postea nati sunt, occasionem legitimi nominis præstiterunt. Quod obtinere censuimus, & si non progeniti fuerint post dotale instrumentum confectum liberi,vel etiam nati ab hac luce fuerint subtracti. Ita demum tamen nepos neptisve, pronepos proneptisve, suorum heredum numero sunt, si a præcedens persona desierit in potestate parentis esse: siue morte id acciderit, siue alia ratione, velut emancipationeb. Nam si per id tempus , quoc quis moritur, filius in potestate eius sit:nepos ex eo, suus heres esse non potestd. Idque & in cæteris deinceps liberorum personis dictum || esse || intelligimus. Posthumie quoque , qui si viuo parente nati essent, in potestate || eius || futuri forent, sui heredes sunt. 3 ¶Sui autem heredes siunt etiam ignorantes & licet furiosi sint, heredes possunt existere: quia * quibusf ex causis ignorantibus nobis acquiritur: ex his causis & furiosis acquiri potest.Et statim morte parentis quasig cætinuatur dominium. & ideo nec tutoris auctoritate opus est pupillis , cum etiam ignorantibus acquiratur suis heredibus hereditas. nec curatoris assensu acquiritur furioso, sed ipso in-reg. 4 ¶Interdū autem, licet in potestate || parentis || mortis tempore suus heres nō fuerit,tamé suus heres pareti efficitur: veluti || si || ab hostib.quis reuersus fuerit post morte patris || sui. || ius enim post-liminij hoc facit. 5 ¶Per contrarium || autem hoc || euenit, vt licet quis in familia defuncti sit mortis tempore, tamen suus heres non fiat: veluti si post mortem suam pater iudicatus fuerit perduellionis reus, ac per hoc memoria eius damnata fuerit. suum enim heredem habere nō potest, cum fiscus ei succe-dath. sed potest dici ipso || quidem || iure suum heredem esse, sed desinere. 6 ¶Cū filius filiáve, & ex altero filio nepos neptisve existunt, pariter ad hereditatem || aui || vocantur:nec qui gradu proximior est,vlteriorem excludit. AEquum enim esse videtur, nepotes neptésque in patris sui locū succederei. Patri ratione & si nepos neptisve sit ex filio,& ex nepote pronepos proneptisve:simul vocantur.Et quia pla cuit nepotes neptésve, item pronepotes proneptésve in parentis sui locum succedere : conueniens esse visum est,non in capitalx, sed in stirpes hereditatem diuidi,vt filius partem dimidiam hereditatis habeat, & ex altero filio duo plurésve nepotes alteram dimidiam.Item si ex duobus filiis nepotes neptésve exi-stant,ex altero vnus forte aut duo, ex altero tres aut quatuor:ad vnum aut duos dimidia pars pertineat, ad tres vel ad quatuor altera dimidia. 7 ¶Cùm autem quærìtur, an quis suus heres existere possit: eo tempore quærendum est, quo certum est aliquē sine testamento decesisse, quod accidit & ᵃ destituto testamento. Hac ratione ᵇ, si filius exheredatus fuerit, & extraneus heres institutus, & filio mortuo, postea certum fuerit heredem institutum ex testamento non fieri heredem, aut quia noluit esse heres, aut quia non potuit, nepos avo suus heres existet: quia quo tempore certum est intestatum decesisse patremfamilias, solus inuenitur nepos. & hoc certum est.
units.tr: 2 ¶Those are deemed to be own heirs (as we said above) who were in the power of the deceased, such as a son or daughter, a grandson or granddaughter through a son, a great-grandson or great-granddaughter born of a grandson through a son. It makes no difference whether the children are natural or adopted. To these must also be added those who were not born of lawful marriage or matrimony, but who were given a place in the curiae of the city according to the tenor of the imperial constitutions issued on these matters; they acquire the rights of own heirs. Likewise those whom our constitutions have embraced, by which we have decreed that if a man has lived with a woman in his household, not at first with marital intent, yet with one with whom he could have a lawful marriage, and has begotten children by her, and afterwards, the intent of marriage developing, has also drawn up marriage documents with her and has had sons or daughters, then not only those children born after the dowry instrument are lawful and in the father's power, but also the earlier ones, who have given the later-born the occasion of a legitimate name. We have decided this should hold even if children were not born after the dowry instrument was executed, or even if they were taken from this light after birth. Yet a grandson or granddaughter, great-grandson or great-granddaughter, count among the own heirs only if the preceding person has ceased to be in the power of the parent, whether by death or by some other means, such as emancipation. For if at the time of the man's death the son is in his power, a grandson by him is not an own heir. We understand the same to be said of the later generations of children. Posthumous children also, who, if they had been born while the parent lived, would have been in his power, are own heirs. 3 ¶Own heirs also become heirs even when they are ignorant or insane: for by the same causes by which an inheritance is acquired for us even when we are ignorant, by these causes it may be acquired for the insane too. And at once upon the parent's death ownership is, as it were, continued. Therefore neither the authority of a guardian is needed for pupils, since an inheritance is acquired for own heirs even when they are unaware; nor is the consent of a curator required for the insane, but it is acquired by the very law itself. 4 ¶Sometimes, however, although a person was not in the power of the parent at the time of death, he nevertheless becomes an own heir to the parent: for example, if someone returns from the enemy after his father's death, for the right of postliminy produces this effect. 5 ¶Conversely, it may happen that although someone was in the family of the deceased at the time of death, he does not become an own heir: for example, if after his death the father is condemned as guilty of treason, and by this his memory is damned. For he cannot have an own heir, since the treasury succeeds to him. But it may be said that by law he is indeed an own heir, but ceases to be one. 6 ¶When a son or daughter and a grandson or granddaughter through another son both exist, they are called equally to the inheritance of the grandfather; nor does the nearer in degree exclude the more remote. For it seems fair that grandchildren should succeed in the place of their father. If there is a grandson or granddaughter through a son, and a great-grandson or great-granddaughter through a grandson, they are called together. And since it has been agreed that grandchildren, and likewise great-grandchildren, succeed in the place of their parent, it has seemed fitting that the inheritance be divided not by heads but by stocks, so that the son has half of the inheritance and the two or more grandchildren through the other son have the other half. Likewise, if grandchildren exist through two sons, one or two through one and three or four through the other, half the inheritance goes to the one or two, and the other half to the three or four. 7 ¶When it is asked whether someone can become an own heir, the time must be considered at which it is certain that a person has died without a will, which also happens when a will has been set aside. Thus, if a son has been disinherited and a stranger instituted heir, and after the son's death it becomes certain that the instituted heir does not become heir under the will, either because he was unwilling or because he could not, then the grandson becomes an own heir to his grandfather, because at the time when it is certain that the head of the family died intestate, only the grandson is found. And this is certain.

units.la: 8 ¶Et licèt post mortem aui natus sit: tamē ᶜ auo viuo conceptus, mortuo patre eius, posteaque deserto aui testamento, suus heres efficitur. Plane si & conceptus & natus fuerit post mortem aui: mortuo patre suo, desertóque postea aui testamento, suus heres auo non existet: quia nullo iure cognationis patrem sui patris attigit. Sed nec ᵈ ille est inter liberos aui, quem filius emancipatus adoptauit. Hi autem, cùm non sint sui (quantum ad hereditatem) liberi: neque bonorum possessionem petere possunt quasi proximi cognati. Hæc de suis heredibus.
units.tr: 8 ¶Although a child is born after the grandfather's death, yet if conceived while the grandfather was alive, and his father has died and afterwards the grandfather's will has been set aside, he becomes an own heir. But if both conception and birth occurred after the grandfather's death, then, when his father has died and the grandfather's will has afterwards been set aside, the child does not become an own heir to the grandfather, because by no right of kinship did he touch his father's father. Nor is that person among the grandfather's children whom an emancipated son adopted. Such persons, since they are not own children (as far as inheritance is concerned), can seek possession of goods neither as nearest kin. So much on own heirs.

units.la: 9 ¶Emancipati autem liberi, iure ciuili nihil iuris habēr. neq.enim sui heredes sunt, qui in potestate parentis esse desierunt: neque vllo alio iure per legem duodecim tabularum vocantur. sed ᵉ prætor naturali æquitate motus, dat eis bonorum possessionem Unde liberi, perinde ac si in potestate parentis tempore mortis fuissent: siue soli sint, siue cum suis heredibus concurrāt. Itaque duobus liberis existentibus, emancipato vno, & eo qui tempore mortis in potestate fuerit: sanè qui dem is, qui in potestate fuit, solus iure ciuili heres est, & solus suus heres. sed cùm emancipatus beneficio ᶠ prætoris in partem admittitur: euenit, vt suus heres pro parte heres fiat.
units.tr: 9 ¶Emancipated children, however, have no right under the civil law. For those who have ceased to be in the parent's power are not own heirs, nor are they called by any other right under the law of the Twelve Tables. But the praetor, moved by natural equity, grants them possession of goods, as if they had been in the parent's power at the time of death, whether they are alone or concur with own heirs. Thus, where there are two children, one emancipated and the other who was in the power of the parent at death, the latter alone is heir under the civil law and alone is own heir. But when the emancipated child is admitted to a share by the benefit of the praetor, it results that the own heir becomes heir in part.

units.la: 10 At hi ᵍ, qui emancipati à parente in adoptionem se dederunt, nō admittuntur ad bona naturalis patris quasi liberi: si modò,cùm is moreretur, in adoptiua familia fuerint: Nam viuo eo emancipati ab adoptiuo patre,per inde admittuntur ad bona naturalis patris, ac si emancipati ab ipso essent, nec vnquam in adoptiua familia fuissent. Et conuenienter, quod ad adoptiuū patrem pertinet, extraneorum loco esse incipiunt. Post mortem verò naturalis patris emancipati ʰ ab adoptiuo patre : & quantum ad hunc adoptiuum patrem pertinet, æquè extraneorum loco fiunt : & quantum ad naturalis patris bona pertinet, nihilo magis liberorum gradum nancisscuntur. Quod ideo sic placuit, quia iniquum erat, esse in potestate patris adoptiui {a} ad quos bona naturalis patris pertineant, vtrum ad liberos eius, an ad agnatos.
units.tr: 10 But those who, having been emancipated by a parent, gave themselves in adoption are not admitted to the goods of their natural father as children, provided that when he died they were in the adoptive family. For if, while he was alive, they were emancipated by the adoptive father, they are admitted to the goods of the natural father just as if they had been emancipated by him, and had never been in the adoptive family. And accordingly, so far as the adoptive father is concerned, they begin to stand in the place of strangers. But after the death of the natural father, those emancipated by the adoptive father are likewise made into strangers so far as this adoptive father is concerned, and so far as the goods of the natural father are concerned they gain no more the degree of children. This has been decided thus because it would be unjust that those in the power of an adoptive father should have goods of a natural father pass to them, whether to his children or to his agnates.

units.la: II ¶Minus ergo iuris habent adoptiui filij, quàm naturales, namque naturales emancipati, beneficio {b}prætoris gradum liberorum retinent {c}, licèt iure ciuili perdant: adoptiui verò emancipati & iure ciuili perdunt gradum liberorum, & à prætore non admittuntur. & reté. naturalia {d}enim iura ciuilis ratio perimere non potest, nec quia desinunt sui heredes esse, possunt desinere filij filiæve, aut nepotes neptésve esse. adoptiui verò emancipati, extraneorum loco incipiunt esse: quia ius nomenque filij filiæve, quod per adoptionem confequuti sunt, alia ciuili ratione {e}, id est, emancipatione perdunt.
units.tr: II ¶Adopted sons therefore have less right than natural ones. For natural sons, when emancipated, retain the degree of children by the benefit of the praetor, although they lose it under the civil law; but adopted sons, when emancipated, lose the degree of children both under the civil law, and are not admitted by the praetor. For the civil reason cannot destroy natural rights, nor because they cease to be own heirs can sons or daughters, or grandsons or granddaughters, cease to be such. But adopted sons, when emancipated, begin to stand in the place of strangers, because they lose the right and name of son or daughter, which they obtained through adoption, by another civil reason, namely emancipation.

units.la: 12 ¶Eadem hæc obseruantur, & in ea bonorum possessione, quàm {f}contra tabulas testamenti parentis liberis præteritis, id est, neque heredibus institutis, neque vt oportet exheredatis, prætor pollicetur. Nam eos quidem qui in potestate mortis tempore fuerint, & emancipatos, vocat prætor ad eandem bonorum possessionem:eos verò, qui in adoptiua familia fuerint per hoc tempus {g}quo naturalis parens moreretur,repellit.
units.tr: 12 The same rules apply also to the possession of goods which the praetor grants against the testament of a parent, to children who have been passed over, that is, who have been neither instituted as heirs nor properly disinherited. For the praetor summons to this same possession of goods those who were under power at the time of death, and those emancipated, but he excludes those who were in the adoptive family during the time in which the natural parent died.

units.la: Item adoptiuos liberos emancipatos ab adoptiuo patre, sicut ab intestato, ita longè minus contra tabulas testamenti ad bona eius ‖ non ‖ admittit. quia desinunt ‖ in ‖ nu-mero liberorum ‖ eius ‖ esse {h}. 13 ¶Admonendi tamen sumus, eos, qui in adoptiua familia sunt, quiue post mortem naturalis parentis ab adoptiuo patre emancipati fuerint: intestato parente naturalis mortuo, licèt ea parte edicti, qua liberi ad bonorum possessionem vocantur, non admittantur {i}, alia tamen parte vocari, scilicet qua cognati defuncti vocatur {k}. Ex qua parte ita admittuntur, si neque sui heredes liberi, neque emancipati obstent, neque adgnatus quidem vllus interueniat {l}. Ante enim prætor liberos vocat tam suos heredes, quàm emancipatos, deinde legitimos heredes, deinde proximos cognatos. 14 ¶Sed ea omnia antiquitati quidem ‖ placuerunt ‖ aliquam autem emendationem à nostra constitutione {m} acceperunt,
units.tr: Likewise, adoptive children who have been emancipated by the adoptive father are admitted to his goods against the testament far less than in intestacy, because they cease to be counted among his children. 13 We must nevertheless note that those who are in the adoptive family, or who after the death of the natural parent have been emancipated by the adoptive father, are not admitted under that part of the edict by which children are called to possession of goods when the natural parent dies intestate; but they are called under another part, namely that by which the cognates of the deceased are called. They are admitted under this part only if no children who are heirs under the father's power and no emancipated children stand in the way, and no agnate at all intervenes. For the praetor calls first the children who are his heirs under power, and the emancipated children alike, then the legitimate heirs, and then the nearest cognates. 14 All these rules, indeed, have pleased antiquity, but they have received some amendment from our constitution,

units.la: {h} l.1.ff. quæ ordo. in bon. poss.
units.tr: {h} l. 1 ff. quae ordo in bon. poss.

units.la: {m} l.pen.Cod. de adopt. quam super iis personis composuimus, quæ à patribus suis naturalibus in adoptionem aliis dantur. Inuenimus etenim nonnullos casus, in quibus filij & naturalium parentum successionem propter adoptionem amittebant: & adoptione facile per emancipationem soluta, ad neutrius patris successionem vocabantur. Hoc solito more corrigentes {*}, constitutionem scripsimus, per quam definimus, quando parens naturalis filium suum adoptandum alij dederit, integra omnia iura ita seruari, atque si in patris naturalis potestate permansisset, nec penitus adoptio fuisset subsequuta: nisi in hoc tantum modo casu, vt {4}posit ab intestato ad patris adoptiui venire successionem. Testamento autem ab eo facto: neque iure ciuili, neque prætorio, ex hereditate eius aliquid persequi poterit, neque contra tabulas bonorum possessione agnita, neque inofficiosi querela instituta: cùm nec necessitas patri adoptiuo imponatur, vel heredem eum instituere, vel exheredatum eum facere, vtpote nullo vinculo naturali copulatum, neque si ex Sabiniano senatusconsulto ex {b}tribus maribus fuerit adoptatus. Nā & in eiusmodi casu, neque quarta ei seruatur, neque vlla actio ad eius persequutionem ei competit. Nostra autem constitutione exceptus est is, quem parens naturalis adoptandum suscepit. Vtroque enim iure tam naturali, quàm legitimo in hanc personam concurrente: pristina iura tali adoptioni seruamus, quemadmodum si paterfamilias sese dederit adrogandum, quæ specialiter & singulatim ex præfatæ constitutionis tenore possunt colligi.
units.tr: {m} l. pen. Cod. de adopt. which we have drawn up concerning those persons who are given in adoption to others by their natural fathers. For we have found several cases in which children lost the succession of their natural parents because of the adoption, and, the adoption being easily dissolved by emancipation, they were called to the succession of neither father. Correcting this by our usual method, we have written a constitution by which we determine that, when a natural parent has given his son to be adopted by another, all rights remain intact just as if he had remained under the power of his natural father and no adoption had followed at all; except only in this case, that he may come to the intestate succession of his adoptive father. But if the adoptive father has made a testament, the son can pursue nothing from his inheritance, neither by civil nor by praetorian law, neither by possession of goods obtained against the tabulae, nor by instituting a complaint of undutiful testament, since the adoptive father is under no necessity either to institute him heir or to disinherit him, being joined to him by no natural bond; nor if he was adopted under the Sabinian senatusconsult from three males. For in such a case neither is a fourth reserved for him, nor does any action for pursuing it belong to him. But by our constitution the one whom the natural parent gave for adoption is excepted. For when both the natural and the legal right concur in this person, we preserve the former rights in such an adoption, just as if a head of a family had given himself for adrogation; these matters can be gathered specifically and individually from the tenor of the aforesaid constitution.

units.la: 15 ¶Itè vetustas{c} ex masculis progenitos plus diligens, solos nepotes vel neptes, qui ‖ quæ ve ‖ ex virili sexu descendunt, ad suorum vocabant successionem, & iure adgnatorum eos anteponebat: nepotes autem, qui ex filiabus {d}nati sunt, & proponepotes ex neptibus, cognatorum loco connumerans, post adgnatorum lineam eos vocabat tam in aui vel proaui materni, quàm in aui-x vel proauix, siue paternæ, siue maternæ successionem. Diui autem principes {e}non passi sunt talem contra naturam iniuriam sine competenti emendatione relinquere: sed cum nepotis & pronepotis nomen commune sit utrisque, tam qui ex masculis, quàm qui ex fœminis descendunt: ideo eundem gradum & ordinem successionis eis donauerunt. Sed vt amplius aliquid sit eis, qui non solum naturæ, sed etiam veteris iuris suffragiis muniuntur: portionem nepotum, vel neptum, vel deinceps (de quibus supra diximus) paulo minuendam esse existimauerunt: vt minus tertia parte acciperent, quàm mater eorum, vel auia fuerat acceptura, vel pater eorum,vel auus paternus, siue maternus, quando fœmina mortua fit, cuius de hereditate agitur:iisque (licet soli sint) adeuntibus, adgnatos minimè vocabant. Et quemadmodum lex duodecim tabularum filio mortuo nepotes, vel neptes, pronepotes vel proneptes in locum patris sui {a} ad successionem aui sui vocat: ita & principalis dispositio in locum matris suæ vel aui, eos cum iam designata partis tertiæ deminutione vocat.
units.tr: 15 Likewise antiquity, loving more those descended from males, called to the succession of their own only grandchildren or granddaughters who descend from the male sex, and preferred them by the right of agnates; but grandchildren born of daughters, and great-grandchildren through granddaughters, counting them as in the place of cognates, called them after the line of agnates, both to the maternal succession of grandfather or great-grandfather, and to that of grandmother or great-grandmother, whether paternal or maternal. But the divine emperors did not allow such a wrong, contrary to nature, to remain without a due correction; and since the name of grandchild and great-grandchild is common to both, those descended from males and those descended from females, they gave them the same degree and order of succession. But, so that something more may belong to those who are protected not only by the support of nature but also by that of ancient law, they judged that the portion of grandsons or granddaughters, or of those further down (of whom we have spoken above), should be somewhat diminished, so that they should receive less than a third part, which their mother or grandmother, or their father or paternal or maternal grandfather, would have received, when the woman whose inheritance is in question has died; and when these (even though they are alone) come to it, they did not call the agnates at all. And just as the law of the Twelve Tables calls grandchildren or granddaughters, great-grandchildren or great-granddaughters, in the place of their dead father, to the succession of their grandfather, so also the imperial disposition calls them in the place of their mother or grandmother, with the portion of a third already fixed by diminution.

units.la: 16 ¶Sed nos, cum adhuc dubitatio maneret inter adgnatos & memoratos nepotes, quartam partem substantiæ defuncti adgnatis sibi vindicantibus ex cuiusdam constitutionis auctoritate: memoratam quidem constitutionem à nostro Codice segregauimus, neque inseri eam ex Theodosiano Codice in eo concessimus. Nostra {b} autem constitutione promulgata, toti iuri eius derogatum est: & sanximus, talibus nepotibus ex filia, vel pronepotibus ex nepte, & deinceps, superstitibus, adgnatos nullam partem mortui successionis sibi vindicare: ne hi, qui ex transuersa linea veniunt, potiores iis habeantur, qui recto iure descendunt. Quam constitutionem nostram obtinere sancimus: ita tamen, vt quemadmodum inter filios & nepotes ex filio antiquitas statuit {c}, non in capita, sed in stirpes diuidi hereditatem: similiter nos inter filios & nepotes ex filia, distributionem fieri iubeamus, vel inter omnes nepotes & neptes, & inter pronepotes & proneptes, & alias deinceps personas: vt vtraque progeniei, matris vel patris, auiæ vel aui {d} portionem sine vlla deminutione consequatur: vt si forte vnus vel duo ex vna parte, ex altera tres aut quatuor extent: vnus aut duo dimidiam, alteri tres aut quatuor alteram dimidiam hereditatis habeant.
units.tr: 16 But we, since doubt still remained between the agnates and the aforesaid grandchildren, the agnates claiming for themselves a fourth part of the substance of the deceased by the authority of a certain constitution, have indeed separated that constitution from our Code, and have not allowed it to be inserted from the Theodosian Code. But by our constitution, once promulgated, the whole right of that constitution has been abrogated; and we have sanctioned that, when such grandchildren through a daughter, or great-grandchildren through a granddaughter, and so on, survive, the agnates claim for themselves no part of the succession of the deceased, lest those who come through the transverse line be held superior to those who descend in the direct line. We command that this our constitution be observed, provided however that, just as antiquity established between sons and grandsons through a son that the inheritance is divided not per capita but per stirpes, so we likewise order that the distribution be made between sons and grandchildren through a daughter, or among all grandchildren and granddaughters, and among great-grandchildren and great-granddaughters and other persons further down, so that each line, of mother or father, grandmother or grandfather, obtains its portion without any diminution; so that if perchance one or two stand on one side and three or four on the other, one or two receive half of the inheritance and the others three or four receive the other half.

units.la: DE LEGITIMA ADGNATORUM † successione. TIT. II.
units.tr: On the Legitimate Succession of Agnates. TIT. II.

units.la: Inemo[?] suus heres, quos in-ter suos heredes praetor, vel constitutio-nes vocant, existat, qui successionem quoquo modo amplectatur: tunc ex le-ge {e} duodecim tabularum ad {f} agnatum proximum pertinet hereditas.
units.tr: If there is no sui heres, whom the praetor or the imperial constitutions call among the heirs of the household, and who takes up the succession in any way, then by the law of the Twelve Tables the inheritance passes to the nearest agnate.

units.la: 1 ¶ Sunt autem adgnati (vt primo quoque libro tradidimus)cogna-ti per virilis sexus personas cognatione coniunc̄ti, quasi a patre connati. Itaque ‖ ex ‖, eodem patre nati fratres, adgnati sibi sunt, qui & consanguinei vocantur ♭: nec requiritur, an etiam eandem matrem habuerint. Item patruus fratris filio,& inuicem is illi adgnatus est. Eodem numero sunt fratres pa-trueles, id est, qui ex duobus fratribus procreati. Sunt ♮ qui etiam consobrini vocantur. Qua ratione etiam ad plures gradus adgnationis peruenire potest: rimus. Ij etiam, qui post mortem patris nascuntur, iura consanguinitatis nancisciuntur. Non tamen omnibus simul adgnatis dat lex hereditatem: sed iis, qui tunc proximiores ♮ gradu sunt, cum certum esse coeperit aliquem intestatum decessisse. 2 ¶ Per adoptionem ♮ quoque adgnationis ius consistit: veluti inter filios naturales, & eos, quos pater eorum adoptauit. Nec dubium est, quin improprie consanguinei appellentur. Item si quis ex cæteris adgnatis ‖ tuis ‖: veluti frater, aut patruus, aut denique is, qui longiore gradu est, adoptauerit aliquem: adgnatus inter suos heredes esse non dubitatur.
units.tr: 1. Agnates, as we explained in the first book, are cognates related through persons of the male sex, who are joined by kinship as if born of the same father. Thus brothers born of the same father are agnates to one another, and they are also called consanguinei; it does not matter whether they also had the same mother. Likewise a paternal uncle is an agnate of his brother's son, and conversely the nephew is an agnate of the uncle. Of the same kind are the paternal cousins, that is, those born of two brothers; these are also called consobrini. In this way agnation can extend to several degrees. Those also who are born after their father's death acquire the rights of consanguinity. Yet the law does not give the inheritance to all agnates at once, but to those who are nearest in degree at the time when it has become certain that someone has died intestate. 2. The right of agnation also arises through adoption, for example between natural sons and those whom their father has adopted. There is no doubt that such persons are improperly called consanguinei. Likewise, if any of your other agnates adopts someone, for example a brother, a paternal uncle, or in short a man of more remote degree, the adopted person is not doubted to be an agnate among the heirs of the household.

units.la: 3 ¶ Cæterum inter masculos quidē adgnationis iu-re hereditas, etiam si longissimo gradu ƒ sint, vtrōque citróque capitur. Quod ad fœminas vero attinet: ita placebat, vt ipsæ consanguinitatis iure tantum capiant hereditatem, si sorores sint: vlterius non capiunt. Masculi autem ad earum hereditates (etiā si longissimo gradu sint) admittantur. Qua de causa fratris tui, aut patrui tui filiæ, vel amitæ tuæ hereditas ad te pertinebat: tua vero ad illas non pertinebat. Quod ideo ita constitutum erat, quia commodius videbatur ita iura constitui, vt plerumque hereditates ad masculos confluerent. Sed quia sanè iniquum erat, in vniuersum eas quasi extraneas repelli: prætor eas ad bonorum possessionem admittit ea parte, qua ƒ proximitatis nomine bonorum possessionem pollicetur, ex qua parte ita scilicet admittuntur, si neque adgnatus vllus, neque proximior cognatus interueniat. Et hæc quidem lex duodecim tabularum nullo modo introduxit: sed simplicitate legibus amicam amplexa, simili ƀ modo omnes adgnatos, siue masculos, siue fœminas, cuiuscumque gradus, ad similitudinem suorum inuicem ad successionem vocabat. Media autem iuris-prudentia ꝛ[?], quæ erat quidem lege duodecim tabularum iunior, imperiali autem dispositione anterior: subtilitate quadam excogitata, praefatam differentiam inducebat, & penitus eas à successione adgnatorum repellebat: omni alia successione incognita, donec praetores paulatim asperitatem iuris ciuilis corrigentes: siue quod deerat, implentes humano proposito, alium ordinem suis edictis addiderunt: & cognationis lineam proximitatis nomine introducta, per bonorum possessionem eas adiuuabant, & pollicebantur his bonorum possessionem, quae unde cognati appellatur.
units.tr: 3. Among males, indeed, inheritance by right of agnation is taken both ways, even when they stand in the most remote degree. As for females, the rule was that they take an inheritance by the right of consanguinity only if they are sisters; beyond this they do not take. Males, however, are admitted to their inheritances, even in the most remote degree. For this reason the inheritance of your brother, or of your paternal uncle's daughter, or of your aunt, belonged to you, but yours did not belong to them. This was established because it seemed more convenient to arrange the law so that inheritances would for the most part flow to males. But since it was plainly unfair to repel them altogether as strangers, the praetor admits them to possession of goods on the part where he promises possession of goods on the ground of nearness of kin; they are admitted on that part only if no agnate and no nearer cognate intervenes. The Twelve Tables certainly introduced none of this. Rather, embracing simplicity, the law called all agnates, male or female, of whatever degree, equally to succession among themselves, as among their own kin. But the middle jurisprudence, which was indeed younger than the Twelve Tables yet older than the imperial enactment, devised a certain subtlety, introduced the aforementioned difference, and entirely excluded women from the succession of agnates, no other succession being recognised. Later the praetors, gradually softening the harshness of the civil law and supplying what was lacking with a human purpose, added another order in their edicts. Introducing the line of cognation under the name of nearness of kin, they helped these women through possession of goods, and promised them the possession of goods which is called unde cognati.

units.la: Nos vero legem duodecim tabularum sequentes, & eius vestigia in hac parte conseruantes, laudamus quidem praetores suae humanitatis, non tamen eos in plenum ‖ huic ‖ causae mederi inuenimus. Quare etenim vno eodemque gradu naturali {a}concurrente, & adgnationis titulis, tam in masculis, quam in feminis aequa lance constitutis, masculis quidem da-batur ad successionem venire omnium adgnatorum, ex adgnatis autem mulieribus nulli penitus, nisi soli sorori, ad adgnatorum successionem patebat aditus? Ideo ‖ nos ‖ in plenum omnia reducetes, & ad ius duo-decim tabularum eandem dispositionem exaequates, nostra constitutione sancimus, omnes legitimas personas, id est, per virilem sexum descendentes (siue {b}masculini generis, siue foeminini sint) similiter modo ad iura successionis legitimae ab intestato vocari secundum sui gradus praerogatiuam: nec ideo excluden-das, quia consanguinitatis iura, sicut germanae, non habent.
units.tr: We, indeed, following the Twelve Tables and preserving their traces in this matter, praise the praetors for their humanity, yet we find that they did not fully remedy this cause. For why, when the same natural degree concurs, and the titles of agnation are established on an equal footing for males and females alike, should it be granted to males to come to the succession of all agnates, while for agnate women access to the succession of agnates lies open to no one at all, except to a sister alone? Therefore we, restoring everything fully, and making the same arrangement equal to the law of the Twelve Tables, sanction by our constitution that all legitimate persons, that is, those descending through the male sex (whether they are of the masculine or the feminine sex), are called in the same way to the rights of legitimate succession on intestacy according to the precedence of their degree, and are not to be excluded merely because they do not have the rights of consanguinity, as full sisters have.

units.la: 4 ¶Hoc etiam addendum nostrae constitutioni existimauimus, vt transferatur vnus tantummodo gradus à iure cognationis in legitimam successionem: vt non solùm fratris filius & filia (secundum quod iam definiuimus) ad successionem patris {c}sui vocentur: sed etiam germanae consanguineae, vel ororis vterinae filius & filia soli, & non deinceps personae vnà cum his ad iura auunculi sui peruenient{d}: & mortuo eo, qui patruus quidem est sui fratris fi-liis, auunculus autem ororis suae soboli: simili modo ab vtroque latere succeadant, tanquam si omnes ex masculis descendentes, legitimo iure veniant, scilicet vbi frater & soror superstites non sunt. His etenim personis praecedentibus & successionem admittentibus, caeteri gradus remanent penitus semoti {†}, videlicet hereditate non in stirpes, sed in capita diuidenda.
units.tr: 4. We have also thought that this should be added to our constitution: that only one degree be transferred from the right of cognation to legitimate succession, so that not only the son and daughter of a brother (as we have already defined) are called to the succession of their paternal father, but also the son and daughter of a full-blooded sister or of a uterine sister alone, and not further persons together with these, come to the rights of their maternal uncle; and, when he has died, who is a paternal uncle to the sons of his brother and a maternal uncle to the offspring of his sister, they likewise succeed from either side, as if all the descendants through males came by legitimate right, namely where no brother or sister survives. For when these persons precede and admit to the succession, the other degrees remain wholly removed, the inheritance being divided not by stocks but by heads.

units.la: 5 ¶Si plures sint gradus adgnatorum: aperte lex duodecim tabularum {e}proximum vocat, Itaque fi(verbi gratia)sint defuncti frater,& alterius fratris filius, aut patruus: frater potior habetur. Et quamuis singulari numero vsa lex ‖duodecim tabularum‖ proximum vocet, tamen dubium non est, quin si plures sint eiusdem gradus, omnes {a}admit-tatur {b}. Nam & proprie proximus ex pluribus gradi-bus intelligitur: & tamen non dubium est, quin li-cet vnus sit gradus adgnatorum, pertineat ad eos hereditas.
units.tr: 5. If there are several degrees of agnates, the law of the Twelve Tables clearly calls the nearest. Thus, for example, if a brother and the son of another brother, or a paternal uncle, of the deceased survive, the brother is considered preferable. And although the law of the Twelve Tables uses the singular and calls the nearest, there is no doubt that if several persons are of the same degree, all are admitted. For the nearest is properly understood even among several in the same degree, and yet there is no doubt that the inheritance belongs to them, although there is only one degree of agnates.

units.la: 6 ¶Proximus autem,si quidem nullo testamento facto quisquam decesserit, per hoc tempus requiritur, quo mortuus est is, cuius de hæreditate quæritur{c}. Quod si facto testamento quisquam decesserit: per hoc tempus requiritur, quo certum esse coeperit, nullum ex testamento heredem exstiturum: tunc enim proprie quisque intestatus decesisse intelligitur. Quod quidem aliquando longo tempore declaratur. In quo spatio temporis sæpe accidit, vt proximiore mortuo, proximus esse incipiat, qui moriente testatore non erat proximus.
units.tr: 6. If someone dies with no testament made, the nearest is sought at the time of the death of the man whose inheritance is in question. But if someone dies after a testament has been made, the nearest is sought at the time when it has become certain that no heir will arise under the testament; for then one is properly understood to have died intestate. This indeed is sometimes made clear only after a long time. In that interval it often happens that, when a nearer person has died, someone becomes the nearest who was not nearest when the testator died.

units.la: 7 ¶Placebat autem in eo genere percipiendarum hereditatum successionem non esse: id est, vt quamuis proximus, qui secundum ea, quæ diximus, vocatur ad hereditatem, aut spreverit hereditatem, aut antequam adeat, decesserit: nihilo magis legitimo iure sequentes admittantur. Quod iterum prætores imperfecto iure corrigentes, non in totum sine adminiculo relinquebant: sed ex cognatorum ordine eos vocabant, vtpote adgnationis iure eis reclusō[?]. Sed nos nihil perfectissimo iuri deesse cupientes, nostra constitutione{d}, quam de iure patronatus, humanitate suggerente protulimus, ‖sancimus‖ successionem in adgnatorum hereditatibus non esse eis {†}denegan-dam: cum satis absurdum erat, quod cognatis a prætore apertum est, hoc adgnatis esse reclusum: maxime cum in onere quidem tutelarum & primo gradu deficiente, sequens succedit: & quod in onere obtinebat, non erat in lucro permissum.
units.tr: 7. It was held, however, that in this kind of acquisition of inheritances there is no succession; that is, although the nearest, who is called to the inheritance according to what we have said, either rejects the inheritance or dies before he enters upon it, those who follow him are not admitted by legal right at all. The praetors, correcting this imperfect law, did not leave them altogether without help, but called them from the order of cognates, as by right of agnation had been closed to them. But we, wishing nothing to be lacking to the most perfect law, sanction by our constitution, which we published concerning the right of patronage, prompted by humanity, that succession in the inheritances of agnates is not to be denied to them. For it was quite absurd that what the praetor had opened to cognates should be closed to agnates, especially since, when the first degree fails in the burden of guardianships, the next succeeds, and what was imposed as a burden was not permitted as a gain.

units.la: 8 ¶Ad legitimam successionem nihilominus vocatur {e}etiam parens, qui contracta fiducia filium vel filiam, nepotem vel neptem, ac deinceps emancipat. quod ex nostra constitutione{f} omnino inducitur, vt emancipationes liberorum semper videantur quasi contracta fiducia fieri: cum apud veteres non aliter hoc obtinebat, nisi specialiter contracta fiducia parens manumisisset.
units.tr: 8. Nevertheless, a parent also is called to legitimate succession who, having contracted a fiducia, emancipates a son or daughter, grandson or granddaughter, and so on. This is entirely introduced by our constitution, so that the emancipations of children always seem to be made as if under a contracted fiducia; whereas among the ancients this held only when the parent had manumitted by a specially contracted fiducia.
On the Tertullian Senatusconsult, TITLE III.

units.la: EX duodecim tabularum ita strictò iure utebatur, & præponebat masculorum progeniē.& eos, qui per fœminini sexus necessitudinem sibi iunguntur, adeo expellebat, ut ne quidem inter matrem & filium filiamve ultro citroque hereditatis capie-dæ ius daret: nisi quod prætores ex proximitate cognatorum eas personas ad successionem, bonorum possessione, unde cognati, adcommodata, vocabant.
units.tr: The strict law of the Twelve Tables was used in this way: it gave preference to the line of males, and it so completely excluded those who are joined by a female relationship that it did not even give a right of mutual inheritance between mother and son or daughter. The praetors, however, on the basis of the closeness of kinsfolk, called those persons to the succession through possession of goods, which is called the unde cognati, as an aid.

units.la: 1 ¶Sed hæ iuris angustiæ postea emendatæ sunt. Et primus quidem divus Claudius matri ad solatium liberorum amissorum, legitimam eorum detulit hereditatem.
units.tr: 1 ¶But these narrow limits of the law were later relaxed. And first the deified Claudius granted the mother the legitimate inheritance of her children, as a consolation for their loss.

units.la: 2 ¶Postea autem senatusconsulto Tertulliano, quod divi Hadriani temporibus sanctum est, plenissime de tristi[?] successione matri † non etiam aviæ deferenda cautum est: ut ingenua trium liberorum ius habens, libertina quatuor ad bona filiorum filiarumve intestato mortuorum, licet in potestate parentis sit: ut scilicet cum alieno iuri subiecta est, iussu eius adeat||heredi-tatem||, cuius iuri subiecta est.
units.tr: 2 ¶Afterwards, however, by the Tertullian senatusconsult, which was enacted in the time of the deified Hadrian, it was fully provided that the succession of a mother, but not also of a grandmother, is to be deferred in the case of sad inheritances: so that a freeborn woman with the right of three children, or a freedwoman with four, may succeed to the goods of sons or daughters who die intestate, even though the children are under the power of a parent. For, since a child subject to another's right, if ordered by that parent, takes up the inheritance of the one under whose right he is.

units.la: 3 ¶Præferuntur autem matri liberi defuncti, qui sui sunt, quive suorum loco sunt, sive primi gradus, sive ulterioris. Sed & filiæ suæ mortuæ filius vel filia præponitur ex constitutionibus matri defunctæ, id est, aviæ suæ. Pater vero utriusque, non etiam avus & proavus matri anteponitur †, scilicet cum inter eos solos de hereditate agitur. Frater autem consanguineus tam filij, quam filiæ excludebat matrem †: soror autem consanguinea pariter cum matre admittebatur. Sed si fuerant frater & soror consanguinei, & mater liberis onerata: frater quidem matrem excludebat, communis autem erat hereditas ex æquis partibus fratribus & sororibus.
units.tr: 3 ¶Living children who are the children of the deceased, or who stand in their place, are preferred to the mother, whether they are of the first degree or of a later one. But the son or daughter of a deceased daughter is also preferred to the mother of the deceased, that is, to their grandmother, under the constitutions. The father of both, however, and the grandfather and great-grandfather are not put before the mother, namely when the dispute over the inheritance is between those persons alone. A full brother, moreover, excluded the mother both from a son's and from a daughter's inheritance; a full sister, however, was admitted equally with the mother. But if there were a brother and a sister of the full blood, and the mother was burdened with children, the brother indeed excluded the mother, and the inheritance was common to the brothers and sisters in equal shares.

units.la: 4 ¶Sed nos constitutione, quam in Codice nostro nomine decorato posuimus, matri subveniendum esse existimavimus: respicientes ad naturam, & puerperiū, & periculum, & sepe mortem ex hoc casu matribus illatam. Ideoque impium esse credidimus, casum fortuitum in eius ad-
units.tr: 4 ¶But by the constitution which we have placed in our Code under its honoured name, we judged that the mother should be assisted, having regard to nature, to childbirth, to the danger, and often to the death that such a case brings upon mothers. Therefore we believed it impious that a chance accident should work to the mother's loss.

units.la: Cod.cod. i .4.cod.eo. + hodie frater defuncti, eius matrem non excludit.l.vlt. in prin.Cod.cod.
units.tr: Cod. cod. i. 4, cod. eo. Today the brother of the deceased does not exclude his mother. l. vlt. in prin. Cod. cod.

units.la: k v.l.vlt.C.qui potiores. mitti detrimentum. si enim ingenua ter,vel libertina quater non peperit, immerito detraudabatur{a} successione suorum liberorum.quid enim peccauit, si non plures sed paucos peperit? Et dedimus ius legitimum plenum matribus (siue ingenuis siue libertinis) & si non ter enixae fuerint vel quater, sed eum tantum vel eam,qui quaeve morte intercepti sunt,vt sic vocentur in liberorum suorum legitima successionem.
units.tr: k v. l. vlt. C. qui potiores. For if a freeborn woman has not borne three children, or a freedwoman four, she would undeservedly be deprived of the succession to her children. What fault has she committed if she has borne not many but few? We have therefore given full legitimate right to mothers, whether freeborn or freedwomen, even if they have not borne three or four times, but only the one or the one whom death has snatched away, so that they may thus be called to the legitimate succession of their children.

units.la: 5 ¶Sed cum antea constitutiones iura legitimae successionis perscrutantes, partim matrem adiuuabant, partim eam praegrauabant, nec in solidum eam vocabant, sed in quibusdam casibus tertiam ei partem abstrahentes, certis legitimis dabant personis, in aliis autem contrarium faciebant: nobis visum{b} est recta & simplici via matre omnibus personis legitimis anteponi, & sine vlla deminutione filiorum suorum successione accipere : excepta fratris & sororis persona, siue consanguinei sint, siue sola cognationis iura habentes: vt quemadmodum eā toti alij ordini legitimo praeposuimus, ita omnes fratres & sorores, siue legitimi sint, siue non, ad capiendas hereditates simul vocemus: ita tamen, vt si quidem solae sorores adgnatae vel cognatae, & mater defuncti vel defunctae supersint{e}: dimidiam quidem mater,{†} alteram vero dimidiam partem omnes sorores habeant. Si vero matre superstite & fratre, vel fratribus solis, vel etiam cum sororibus siue legitima, siue sola cognationis iura habentibus, intestatus quis vel intestata moriatur: in capita distribuatur eius hereditas.
units.tr: 5 ¶But since the earlier constitutions, while examining the rights of legitimate succession, partly aided the mother and partly burdened her, and did not call her to the whole, but in certain cases took away a third part from her and gave it to certain legitimate persons, while in other cases they did the contrary, it has seemed best to us, by a straight and simple way, to place the mother before all legitimate persons and to let her receive the succession of her children without any diminution. Excepted is the person of a brother or sister, whether they are of the full blood or have only the rights of kinship. Just as we have placed her before all the other legitimate order, so we call all brothers and sisters, whether they are legitimate or not, to take the inheritances together with her. Yet this is so: if only sisters, agnate or cognate, survive together with the mother or father of the deceased, the mother takes one half, and all the sisters have the other half. But if a person dies intestate, whether a man or a woman, with the mother surviving and with a brother, or with brothers alone, or also with sisters having either legitimate or merely cognate rights, the inheritance is to be distributed per capita.

units.la: 6 ¶Sed quemadmodum nos matribus prospeximus, ita eas oportet suae soboli consulere: scituris eis, quod si tuores{d} liberis non petierint, vel in locum remoti vel excusati, intra annum petere neglexerint: ab eorum impuberum morientium successione merito repellentur.
units.tr: 6 ¶But just as we have provided for mothers, so they ought to look after their offspring: they should know that if they have not sought guardianship for their children, or have neglected to seek it within a year when they were removed or excused, they will rightly be shut out from the succession of those impubescent children who die.

units.la: 7 ¶Licet autem vulgo quaesitus sit filius filiaue: potest tamen ad bona eius mater ex Tertylliano senatusconsulto admitti.
units.tr: 7 ¶Although a son or daughter born out of wedlock is sought in common, the mother can nevertheless be admitted to that child's goods under the Tertullian senatusconsult.
On the Orphitian Senatusconsult,
TITLE IV.

units.la: PER contrarium autem liberi{g} ad bona matrum intestatarum admittuntur ex senatusconsulto Orphitiano{h}, quod Orphitio & Rufo consulibus effectum est, divi Marci temporibus, & data est tam filio, quàm filiæ legitima hereditas etiam {a} si alieno iuri subiecti sint: & præferuntur consanguineis & adgnatis defunctæ matris. 1 ¶Sed cùm ex hoc senatusconsulto nepotes‖& neptes‖ ad auiæ successionem legitimo iure non vocarentur: postea hoc constitutionibus principalibus emendatum est,vt ad similitudinem filiorum filiarúmque & nepotes & neptes vocentur. 2 ¶Sciendum autem est huiusmodi successiones, quæ ex Tertylliano & Orphitiano senatusconsultis deferuntur,capitis deminutione non perimi,propter illam regulam qua{*} nouæ hereditates legitimæ capitis deminutione {b} non perennt,sed illæ solæ,quæ ex lege duodecim tabularum deferuntur. 3 ¶Nouissime sciendum est etiam il[?]los liberos,qui vulgò quæsiti sunt {c}, ad matris hereditatem ex hoc senatusconsulto admitti. 4 ¶Si {d} ex pluribus legitimis heredibus quidam omiserint hereditatem,vel morte,vel alia causa impediti fuerint,quominus adeant:reliquis,qui adierint, adcresceit illorum portio: & licet ante decesserint, ad heredes tamen eorum pertinet.
units.tr: On the other hand, children are admitted to the goods of their mothers who died intestate under the senatusconsultum Orphitianum, which was enacted in the consulship of Orphitius and Rufus, in the times of the divine Marcus; and the lawful inheritance is given to a son as much as to a daughter, even if they are subject to another's power; and they are preferred to the consanguineous and agnate relatives of the deceased mother. 1 ¶But since under this senatusconsultum grandchildren, male and female, were not called by lawful right to the succession of their grandmother, this was later corrected by imperial constitutions, so that grandchildren, male and female, are called in the same way as sons and daughters. 2 ¶It should be known, moreover, that successions of this kind, which are conferred under the senatusconsulta Tertullianum and Orphitianum, are not destroyed by loss of civil status, on account of that rule by which new lawful inheritances do not perish through capitis deminutio, but only those which are conferred by the law of the Twelve Tables. 3 ¶Lastly, it should be known that those children who were born outside marriage are also admitted to their mother's inheritance under this senatusconsultum. 4 ¶If some of several lawful heirs have declined the inheritance, or have been prevented by death or some other cause from entering upon it, their share accrues to the others who have entered; and even if they have died before, it nevertheless passes to their heirs.
ON THE SUCCESSION OF COGNATES,
TITLE V.

units.la: POST suos heredes,eósque, quos inter suos heredes prætor & constitutiones vocant,& post legitimos (quo numero sunt adgnati,& hi,quos in locū adgna-torum tam supradicta senatusconsulta, quàm nostra erexit {e} constitutio) proximos cognatos prætor vocat. 1 ¶Qua parte naturalis cognatio spectatur. nam adgnati capite deminuti, quique ex his progeniti sunt,ex lege duodecim tabularum inter legitimos non habentur, sed à prætore tertiq ordine vocantur: exceptis solis tantummodo fratre & sorore emancipatis, non etiam liberis eorū, quos lex Anastasiana {f} cum fratribus integri {g} iuris con-stitutis,vocat quidem ad legitimam fratris heredi-tatem,sine sororis: non æquis tamen partibus,sed cum aliqua deminutione, quam facile est ex ipsius constitutionis verbis colligere. Aliis vero adgnatis inferioris gradus,licet capitis deminutionem passi non sunt, tamen anteponit eos, & procul dubio cogna-tis. 2 ¶Eos etiá,qui per fœminini sexus personas ex transuerso cognatione iunguntur, tertio gradu proximitatis nomine praetor ad successionem vocat.
units.tr: After their own heirs, whom the praetor and the constitutions call "heirs among the family," and after the legitimate heirs (among whom are the agnates, and those whom both the aforementioned senatusconsults and our constitution have raised to the place of agnates), the praetor calls the nearest cognates. 1 ¶In this part, natural kinship is what is looked at. For agnates who have suffered loss of status, and those born of them, are not counted among the legitimate heirs under the Law of the Twelve Tables, but are called by the praetor in the third order; the only exceptions are brothers and sisters who have been emancipated. Not even their children are excepted, whom the Anastasian law calls, along with brothers who remained in full rights, to the legitimate inheritance of a brother, but without a sister. Yet they are not called in equal shares, but with some reduction, which is easy to gather from the wording of that constitution itself. But agnates of a lower degree, even if they have not suffered loss of status, are nevertheless preferred to them, and undoubtedly to cognates. 2 ¶The praetor also calls to succession, in the third degree of nearness, those who are joined in collateral cognation through persons of the female sex.

units.la: 3 ¶Liberi quoque, {a}qui in adoptiua familia sunt,ad naturalium parentum hereditate hoc eodem gradu vocantur.
units.tr: 3 ¶Children who are in an adoptive family are also called to the inheritance of their natural parents in this same degree.

units.la: 4 ¶Vulgo quaesitos, {b}nullos habere adgnatos,manifestum est: quum adgnatio à patre sit, cognatio à matre, hi autem nullum patrem habere intelligantur.Eadem ratione ne inter se quidem possunt videri consanguinei esse: quia consanguinitatis ius speciem est adgnationis. Tantum ergo cognati sunt sibi,sicut & matri cognati sunt. Itaque omnibus istis§ex§ea[?] parte competit bonorum possessio, qua proximitatis nomine cognati vocantur.
units.tr: 4 ¶It is clear that those born out of wedlock have no agnates, since agnation comes from the father and cognation from the mother, and these are understood to have no father. For the same reason they cannot even be seen as blood relatives of one another, since the right of blood relationship is a kind of agnation. Therefore they are cognates only to themselves, just as they are cognates to their mother. Thus for all of these, on this side, the possession of goods belongs by that rule by which cognates are called on the ground of nearness.

units.la: 5 ¶Hoc loco & illud necessario admonendi sumus: adgnationis quidem iure admitti aliquem ad hereditatem, etsi decimo {c}gradu fit: siue de lege duodecim tabularum quaeramus, siue de edicto, quo praetor legitimis heredibus datur bonorum possessionem pollicetur. Proximitatis vero nomine iis solis praetor promittit bonorum possessionem, qui vsque ad †sextum gradum cognationis sunt, & ex septimo sobrino sobrinaque nato natæve.
units.tr: 5 ¶At this point we must also necessarily note this: by the right of agnation, someone is admitted to an inheritance even if he stands in the tenth degree, whether we inquire under the Law of the Twelve Tables or under the edict by which the praetor promises possession of goods to legitimate heirs. But on the ground of nearness of kinship, the praetor promises possession of goods only to those who are within the sixth degree of cognation, and to the son or daughter of a first cousin born in the seventh degree.
On the Degrees of Cognation, Title VI.

units.la: HOC loco {e}necessarium est exponere, quemadmodum gradus cognationis numerentur. Quare in primis admonendi sumus,cognationem {f}aliam supra numerari,aliam infra, aliam ex transuerso,quae etiam à latere dicitur. superior cognatio est parentum, inferior liberorum, ex transuerso fratrum sororumque, & eorum,qui quaeve ex his generantur: & conuenienter patrui,amitæ, auunculi, materterae.
units.tr: Here it is necessary to explain how the degrees of cognation are counted. First, we must note that cognation is reckoned in three ways: one upward, another downward, and another across, which is also called lateral. Upward cognation is that of parents, downward that of children, and across that of brothers and sisters and of those who are born of them. Correspondingly, it includes the paternal uncle (patruus), the paternal aunt (amita), the maternal uncle (avunculus) and the maternal aunt (matertera).

units.la: Et superior quidem & inferior cognatio à primo gradu incipit, at ea,quæ ex transuerso numeratur, à secundo.
units.tr: Upward and downward cognation begin from the first degree, but lateral cognation is counted from the second.

units.la: 1 ¶Primo gradu est supra pater, mater: infra filius,filia {g}.
units.tr: 1 In the first degree, upward, are the father and mother; downward, the son and daughter.

units.la: 2 ¶Secundo gradu supra auus, auia: infra nepos, neptis: ex transuerso frater,soror {h}.
units.tr: 2 In the second degree, upward, are the grandfather and grandmother; downward, the grandson and granddaughter; across, the brother and sister.

units.la: 3 ¶Tertio gradu supra proauus, proauia: infra pronepos,proneptis: ex transuerso fratris sororisque filius,filia,& conuenienter patruus, amita, auunculus,matertera {i}. Patruus est frater patris, qui Graecè πατράδελφος [?] appellatur. Auunculus est frater matris, qui Graecè μητράδελφος [?] dicitur, & vterque promiscuè θεῖος appellatur amita est patris soror,{a} quæ Græcè πατραδέλφη [?] appellatur. Matertera vero matris soror, quæ Græcè μητραδέλφη [?] dicitur, & utraque promiscuè θεία appellatur.
units.tr: 3 In the third degree, upward, are the great-grandfather and great-grandmother; downward, the great-grandson and great-granddaughter; across, the son and daughter of a brother or sister. Correspondingly, there are the paternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal uncle and maternal aunt. The patruus is the brother of the father, called in Greek πατράδελφος. The avunculus is the brother of the mother, called in Greek μητράδελφος, and both are indiscriminately called θεῖος. The amita is the sister of the father, called in Greek πατραδέλφη. The matertera is the sister of the mother, called in Greek μητραδέλφη, and both are indiscriminately called θεία.

units.la: 4 ¶ Quarto{c} gradu supra abavus, abavia: infrà abnepos, abneptis: ex transverso fratris sororisque nepos, neptisve: & convenienter patruus magnus, amita magna, id est, avi frater & soror; item avunculus magnus, & matertera magna, id est, aviæ frater & soror. Consobrinus, consobrina, id est, qui quæve ex sororibus aut fratribus procreantur. Sed quidâ rectè consobrinos eos proprie dici putat, qui ex duabus sororibus progenerantur, quasi consororinos. Eos vero, qui ex duobus fratribus progenerantur, proprie fratres patrueles vocari. Si autem ex duobus fratribus filiæ nascuntur, sorores patrueles appellari. At eos, qui ex fratre & sorore progenerantur, amitinos proprie dici putant. Amitæ tuæ filij, consobrinum te appellant, tu illos amitinos.
units.tr: 4 In the fourth degree, upward, are the abavus and abavia; downward, the abnepos and abneptis; across, the grandson and granddaughter of a brother or sister. Correspondingly, there are the great paternal uncle (patruus magnus) and great paternal aunt (amita magna), that is, the brother and sister of the grandfather; likewise the great maternal uncle (avunculus magnus) and great maternal aunt (matertera magna), that is, the brother and sister of the grandmother. Then there are the consobrinus and consobrina, that is, those who are born of sisters or of brothers. But some rightly think that consobrini are properly those born of two sisters, as if they were consororini. Those born of two brothers are properly called paternal cousins (fratres patrueles). If daughters are born of two brothers, they are called paternal female cousins (sorores patrueles). But those born of a brother and a sister are properly said by some to be amitini. The sons of your paternal aunt call you consobrinus, and you call them amitini.

units.la: 5 ¶ Quinto{b} gradu supra avus, avia: infrà adnepos, adneptis: ex transverso fratris sororisque pronepos, proneptis: & convenienter propatruus, proamita, id est, proavi frater & soror. & proavunculus & promatertera, id est, proaviæ frater & soror. Item fratris patruelis, vel sororis patruelis, consobrini & consobrinæ, amitini & amitinæ filius filia, propius consobrino, propius consobrina. Hi sunt patrui magni, amitæ magnæ, avunculi magni, matertera magnæ filius filia.
