units.tr: 5 In the fifth degree, upward, are the avus and avia; downward, the adnepos and adneptis; across, the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of a brother or sister. Correspondingly, there are the propatruus and proamita, that is, the brother and sister of the great-grandfather; and the proavunculus and promatertera, that is, the brother and sister of the great-grandmother. Likewise, the son or daughter of a paternal cousin of a brother or sister, of a consobrinus or consobrina, or of an amitinus or amitina, is called propius consobrino or propius consobrina. These are the great paternal uncles, great paternal aunts, great maternal uncles, and the sons and daughters of great maternal aunts.

units.la: 6 ¶ Sexto{f} gradu supra tritavus, tritavia: infrà trinepos, trineptis: ex transverso fratris sororisque abnepos, abneptis: & convenienter abpatruus, abamita, id est, abavi frater & soror: abavunculus, abmatertera, id est, abaviæ frater & soror. Item propatrui, proamitæ, proavunculi, promatertera filius filia. Item propius consobrino consobrinave filius, filia: item consobrini, consobrinæ, id est, qui quæve ex fratribus vel sororibus patruelibus vel consobrinis vel amitinis progenerantur{d}.
units.tr: 6 In the sixth degree, upward, are the tritavus and tritavia; downward, the trinepos and trineptis; across, the abnepos and abneptis of a brother or sister. Correspondingly, there are the abpatruus and abamita, that is, the brother and sister of the abavus; the abavunculus and abmatertera, that is, the brother and sister of the abavia. Likewise, the sons and daughters of the propatrui, proamitae, proavunculi and promatertera. Likewise, the son or daughter of a propius consobrinus or consobrina; and the consobrini and consobrinae, that is, those who are born of paternal cousins, consobrini or amitini, whether brothers or sisters.

units.la: 7 ¶ Hactenus ostendisse sufficiat, quemadmodum gradus cognationis numerentur. Namque ex his palam est intelligere, quemadmodum ulteriores quoque gradus numerare debeamus: quippe{e} semper generata persona gradum adiicit, ut longè facilius
units.tr: 7 It is enough to have shown so far how the degrees of cognation are counted. For from these examples it is clear how we ought to count the further degrees too, since the person who is generated always adds a degree, so that it is much easier

units.la: {e} Siquidè gradus nihil aliud est quàm generatio: ut quaevis quæstione propositâ, quot inter utramq. personam generationes exiterint, totidem gradus sint constituendi. Hotomi. sit respondere, quoto quisque gradu sit, quàm propria cognationis appellatione quemquâ denotare.
units.tr: Hotomanus. For a degree is nothing other than a generation: so that, whatever question is raised, as many degrees must be assigned as there have been generations between the two persons. It is better to say what degree each person is in than to designate anyone by a particular term of kinship.

units.la: 8 ¶Adgnationis quoque gradus eodem modo numerantur. 9 ¶Sed cum magis veritas oculata fide, quàm per aures animis hominum infigatur ideo necessarium duximus post narratione graduū, eos etiam praesenti libro inscribi, quatenus posint & auribus, & oculorum inspectione adolescentes perfectissimam graduum doctrinam adipisci.
units.tr: 8 Degrees of agnation are counted in the same way. 9 But since truth is fixed in men's minds more by what the eyes see in faith than by what the ears hear, we have thought it necessary, after the account of the degrees, to set them down also in this book, so that young people may be able to grasp the most complete teaching on the degrees both by hearing and by looking at them.
On Servile Kinship,
TITLE VII.

units.la: ILLUD cerum est, ad seruiles cognationes illam partem edicti, qua proximitatis nomine bonorum possessio prmittitur, non pertinere: nam nec ulla antiqua lege talis cognatio computatur. Sed nostra constitutione, qua pro iure patronatus fecimus (quod iis vsque ad nostra tempora satis obscurū, atque nube plenū, & undique confusum fuerat) & hoc humanitate suggerente censuimus, vt si quis in seruili condicione constitutus consortio liberum vel liberos habuerit, siue ex libera, siue ex seruilis conditionis muliere: vel contra serua mulier ex libero vel seruo habuerit liberos cuiuscumque sexus: & ad libertatem his peruenientibus, ij, qui ex seruili ventre nati sunt, libertatem meruerint, vel dum mulieres liberae erant, ipsi in seruitute eos habuerint, & postea ad libertatem peruenerint vt hi omnes ad successionem patris vel matris veniant Hos enim liberos non solum in suorum parentum successione, sed etiā alterum in alterius successione, mutuam vocauimus, sive illa lege specialiter eos vocantes: siue soli inueniantur, qui in seruitute nati, & postea manumisi sunt: siue vnà cum aliis, qui post libertatem parentum concepti sunt: siue ex eodem patre, siue ex eadem matre, siue ex aliis nuptiis, ad similitudinem eorum, qui ex iustis nuptiis procreati sunt. 1 ¶Repetitis itaque omnibus, quae iam tradidimus, apparet non semper eos, qui parem gradum cognationis obtinent, pariter vocari, eóq. am-matrimonium sed contubernium. l.3. Cod. de incestis
units.tr: This much is certain: the part of the edict by which possession of goods is granted on the ground of proximity of blood does not extend to kinship through slaves, for no ancient law reckoned such kinship at all. But by our constitution, which we enacted concerning the right of patronage (a matter that until our own time was rather obscure, clouded in darkness, and confused on every side), and which we have also decreed out of humanity, we ordain as follows. If a man in servile condition has children by a union, whether with a free woman or with a woman of servile condition, or if a female slave has children by a free man or by a slave, of either sex, and these children attain liberty, then those who were born of a servile womb and gained their liberty, or those whom their parents kept in slavery while the mothers were free and who later attained liberty, all of them shall come to the succession of their father or mother. For we call these children mutual heirs, not only in the succession of their own parents but also in the succession of one another, whether the law calls them specifically, or whether only those are found who were born in slavery and afterwards manumitted, or together with others who were conceived after the parents obtained liberty, or whether they are of the same father or the same mother, or of different marriages, in the likeness of those who were born of lawful marriage. 1 Therefore, having recalled all that we have already set out, it is clear that those who hold an equal degree of kinship are not always called alike, and so it is not a marriage but a cohabitation. l.3. Cod. de incestis

units.la: de iure Pontificio secus. c.1. de coniug. seruor. plius,ne eum quidè,qui proximior sit cognatus,sem per potiorè esse. Cùm enim prima causa sit suorum heredum,& eorum,quos inter suos heredes enume-rauimus: apparet pronepotem vel abnepotè defun-cti potiorem esse,quàm fratrem aut patre matremq; defuncti: cùm alioqui patet quidè & mater (vt su-prà quoque tradidimus) primum gradum cognatio-nis obtineant,frater vero secundum , pronepos autè tertio gradu sit cognationis,& abnepos quarto. Nec interest,in potestate morientis fuerit, an non, quod vel emancipatus,vel ex emancipato, aut ex fœmi-neo sexu propagatus est. Amotis quoque suis here-dibus,& quos inter suos heredes vocari diximus:ad-gnatus,qui intregum ius habet adgnationis,etiá si longissimo gradu sit,plerumque potior habetur,quá proximior cognatus.Nam patrui nepos vel pronepos auunculo vel materterae præferitur.Totiens igitur dicimus aut potiorem haberi eum, qui proximiore gradu cognationis obtinet, aut pariter vocari eos, qui cognati sunt : quotiens neque suorum heredum, quique inter suos heredes sunt , neque adgnationis iure ][?],aliquis præferri debeat secundum ea, quæ tra-didimus: exceptis fratre & sorore emancipatis, qui ad successionem fratrum vel sororum vocantur: qui etsi capite deminuti sunt, tamen præferuntur cæte-ris vlterioris gradus adgnatis.
units.tr: By the law of the Papists it is otherwise. c.1. de coniug. seruor. Nor is even the nearer kinsman always the preferred one. For since the first cause is that of one's own heirs, and of those whom we have counted among one's own heirs, it is evident that a great-grandson or great-great-grandson of the deceased is preferred to a brother or to the father or mother of the deceased; since otherwise it is plain that the mother (as we have also said above) holds the first degree of kinship, the brother the second, the great-grandson the third, and the great-great-grandson the fourth. Nor does it matter whether the deceased had the person in his power or not, whether the heir was emancipated, or descended from an emancipated person, or was born of the female sex. Likewise, when one's own heirs have been set aside, and those whom we said are called among one's own heirs, the agnate who has the full right of agnation is generally regarded as preferred, even if he stands at a very remote degree, over a nearer cognate. For the grandson or great-grandson of a paternal uncle is preferred to a maternal uncle or a maternal aunt. Therefore, as often as we say that the one who holds the nearer degree of kinship is regarded as preferred, or that those who are kin are called equally, so often is it so, as long as, according to what we have set out, no one ought to be preferred on the ground of one's own heirs, of those among one's own heirs, or by the right of agnation; except that emancipated brothers and sisters, who are called to the succession of brothers or sisters, are preferred to the other agnates of more remote degree, even though they have undergone a diminution of status.
On the succession of freedmen {4}, Title VIII,

units.la: NVNC de libertorum bonis videamus. Olim itaque licebat libero patronum suû impunè testamento praeterire. nam ita demum lex duodecim tabularum ad hereditatē liberti vocabat patronū {b},si intestatus mortuus esset libertus, heredē suo nullo relicto. Itaque intestato mortuo liberto, si is suum heredem reliquisset, patrono nihil in bonis eius iu-ris erat. Et si quidem ex naturalibus liberis aliquem suum heredem reliquisset, nulla videbatur querela: si vero adoptiuus filius fuisset, aperte iniquum erat, nihil iuris patrono superesse.
units.tr: Now let us look at the goods of freedmen. Formerly a freed person could pass over his patron in his will with impunity. For the law of the Twelve Tables called the patron to the inheritance of the freedman only if the freedman died intestate and left no heir. So when a freedman died intestate and had left a suus heres, the patron had no right to his goods. If the heir was one of his natural children, no complaint seemed to arise; but if the heir was an adoptive son, it was plainly unjust that the patron should have no right at all.

units.la: 1[?] ¶Quâ de causa postea praetoris edicto hæc iuris iniquitas emenda-ta est,siue enim faciebat testamentum libertus, iu-bebatur ita testari, ut patrono partem {c} dimidiam bonorum suorum relinqueret, & si aut nihil, aut minus parte dimidia reliquerat : dabatur patrono contra tabulas testamenti partis dimidiæ bonorû possessio. Siue intestatus moriebatur, suo herede relicto filio adoptivo: dabatur æque patrono contra hunc suum heredem, patris dimidiæ bonorum possessio. Prodesse autem liberto solebant ad excludendum patronum naturales liberi, non solum quos in potestate mortis tempore habebat, sed etiam emancipati, & in adoptionem dati: si modo ex aliqua parte scripti heredes erant, aut præteriti contra tabulas bonorum possessionem ex edicto prætorio petierant. nā exheredati nullo modo repellebant patronum.
units.tr: 1[?] ¶For this reason the praetor's edict later corrected this injustice of the law. For if the freedman made a will, he was ordered to make it so as to leave the patron half of his goods; and if he had left nothing, or less than half, the patron was given possession of half the goods against the tablets of the will. If he died intestate, leaving an adoptive son as suus heres, the patron was likewise given possession of half the father's goods against this suus heres. Natural children, however, used to benefit the freedman by excluding the patron, not only those he had in his power at the time of death, but also those who had been emancipated and given in adoption, provided they were instituted heirs in some part, or had been passed over and had sought possession of the goods against the tablets under the praetor's edict. For the disinherited in no way kept out the patron.

units.la: 2 ¶Postea {b}vero lege Papia adaucta sunt iura patronorum, qui locupletiores libertos habebant. Cautum est enim, ut ex bonis eius qui sestertiū centū milium patrimonii reliquerat, & pauciores, quàm tres liberos habebat: sive is testamento facto, sive intestatus mortuus erat: virilis pars patrono deberetur. Itaq. cum unū quidé filiū filiámve heredem reliquerat libertus: perinde pars dimidia debebatur patrono ac si is sine ullo filio filiáve intestatus decessisset. cū vero duos duásve heredes reliquerat, tertia pars debebatur patrono.
units.tr: 2 ¶Later, however, by the Papian law the rights of patrons were increased where the freedmen were wealthier. For it was provided that from the goods of one who had left an estate of 100,000 sesterces, and had fewer than three children, a share per head should be owed to the patron, whether he died having made a will or intestate. Thus when the freedman had left one son or daughter as heir, half a share was owed to the patron, just as if he had died intestate with no son or daughter. But when he had left two sons or daughters as heirs, a third part was owed to the patron.

units.la: 3 ¶Sed nostra constitutio, quam pro omni natione, Græca lingua compendioso tractatu habito composuimus: ita huiusmodi causam definiuit, ut si quidem libertus vel liberta minores centenariis sint, id est, minus centū aureis habeant substantiam (sic enim legis Papiæ summa interpretati sumus, ut pro {f}mille sestertiis unus aureus computetur) nullum locum habeat patronus in eorum successione: si tamen testamentum fecerint. Sin autem intestati decesserint, nullo liberorum relicto: tunc patronatus ius (quod erat ex lege duodecim tabularum) integrum reservauit. Cum vero maiores centenariis sint, si heredes vel bonorum possessores liberos habeant, sive unum, sive plures, cuiuscunque sexus vel gradus: ad eos successiones parentum deduximus, patrono[?]
units.tr: 3 ¶But our constitution, which we drew up in Greek for all nations after a concise treatise, settled this matter as follows. If the freedman or freedwoman are under the centenaria, that is, have an estate of less than 100 gold pieces (for we have interpreted the sum of the Papian law so that one gold piece is reckoned as a thousand sesterces), the patron has no place in their succession, provided they made a will. But if they die intestate, leaving no children, we have kept the patronage right (which came from the Twelve Tables law) entire. But when they are above the centenaria, if they have children as heirs or as possessors of goods, whether one or several, of whatever sex or degree, we have transferred the successions of the parents to them, excluding the patron...

units.la: solidum aestimari mille sestertiis quia in l. 49. soluto matrimonio decem solidi paulo post vocantur decemmillia. De aurei aestimatione. ne.v.Cuiac.19.obser.31. ut ut sit, pauperes vocantur qui minus quam 50. habeant. l.10. de accusa.non igitur male locupletiores liberti hic dicentur qui centū millium sestertium. i. centum aureos patrimonium reliquerint. eaque summa poena erat popularis actionis. l.25.
units.tr: ...a solidus is valued at a thousand sesterces, because in l. 49 (soluto matrimonio) ten solidi are soon called ten thousand. On the valuation of the gold piece, see Cuiacius, Observations 19.31. However that may be, those are called poor who have fewer than 50. See l. 10, de accusationibus. Therefore it is not wrong that those are called wealthier freedmen here who left an estate of 100,000 sesterces, that is, 100 gold pieces; and that sum was the penalty for a popular action. See l. 25.

units.la: in f. de Sillan. & ambitus. l. unic. §. 1. & ult. ff. ad l. Iul. de ambitu. nis omnibus modis vnà cum sua progenie semotis. Sin autem sine liberis decesserint: si quidem intestati, ad omnem hereditatem patronos patronasque vocamus. Si vero testamentum quidem fecerint, patronos autem aut patronas praeterierint, cum nullos liberos habuerint, vel habentes eos exheredauerint, vel mater siue auus maternus eos praeterierint, ita quod non possint argui inofficiosa eorum testamenta: tunc ex nostra constitutione per bonorum possessionem contra tabulas, non dimidiam (ut antea) sed tertiam partem bonorum liberti consequuntur: vel quod deest, eis ex constitutione nostra repleatur, si quando minus tertia parte bonorum suorum libertus vel liberta eis reliquerit: ita sine onere, ut nec liberis liberti libertaeve ex ea parte legata vel fideicommissa praestentur, sed ad coheredes eorum hoc onus redundet: multis aliis casibus a nobis in praefata constitutione congregatis, quos necessarios esse ad huiusmodi dispositionem iuris perspeximus, ut tam patroni patronaeque, quam liberi eorum, necnon qui ex transuerso latere veniunt, usque ad quintum gradum ad successionem libertorum libertarumue vocentur, sicut ex ea constitutione intelligendum est: & si eius dem patroni vel patronae, vel duorum duarumque plurimumue liberi sint: qui proximior est, ad liberti vel libertae vocetur successionem, & in capita{a} non in stirpes diuidatur successio: eodem modo & in iis, qui ex transuerso latere veniunt, seruando. Penè enim consonantia iura ingenuitatis & libertinitatis in successionibus{b} fecimus.
units.tr: in f. de Sillan. & ambitus. l. unic. §. 1. & ult. ff. ad l. Iul. de ambitu. ...in every way, together with their offspring. But if they die without children: if indeed intestate, we call patrons and patronesses to the whole inheritance. If they have made a will but have passed over their patrons, when they had no children, or having children have disinherited them, or the mother or maternal grandfather has passed them over, so that their wills cannot be challenged as inofficious: then by our constitution, through possession of goods against the tablets, they obtain not half (as before) but a third part of the freedman's goods; or whatever is lacking is made up to them by our constitution, if the freedman or freedwoman left them less than a third of their goods. This is without burden, so that legacies or fideicommissa from that part are not paid by the children of the freedman, but the burden falls back on their coheirs. We have gathered many other cases in the aforementioned constitution, which we saw were necessary for this arrangement of law, so that patrons and patronesses, as well as their children, and also those who come by the side line up to the fifth degree, are called to the succession of freedmen, as is to be understood from that constitution. If there are children of the same patron or patroness, or of two or more, the nearer one is called to the succession of the freedman or freedwoman, and the succession is divided per heads, not per stocks; the same applies, observing this, to those who come by the side line. For we have made the rights of freeborn and freed persons in successions almost consonant.

units.la: 4 ¶Sed haec de iis libertinis hodie dicenda sunt, qui in ciuitatem Romanam peruenerunt: cum nec sint alij liberti, simul & Dediticiis{c} & Latinis sublatis, cum Latinorum legitimae successiones nullae penitus erant, quia licet ut liberi vitam suam peragebant, attamen ipso vltimo spiritu simul animam atque libertatem amittebant, & quasi seruorum bona eorum iure quodammodo peculij ex lege Iunia || Norbana || manu-missores detinebant. Postea vero senatusconsulto Largiano cautum fuerat, ut liberi manumissoris non nominatim exheredati facti, extraneis heredibus eorum in bonis Latinorum praeponerentur. Quibus e-tiam superuenit diui Traiani edictum, quod eundem hominem, si inuito vel ignorante patrono ad ciuitatem Romanam venire ex beneficio principis festi-narat, faciebat quidem viuum ciuem Romanum, Latinum vero morientem. Sed nostra constitutione propter huiusmodi conditionum vices,& alias difficultates, cum ipsis Latinis etiam lege Iuniam, & senatusconsultum Largianum, & edictum diui Traiani,in perpetuum deleri censuimus: vt omnes liberti ciuitate Romana fruantur. & mirabili modo quibusda adiectionibus ipsas vias, quæ in Latiniratem ducebāt,ad ciuitatē Romanā capiendā trásposuimus.
units.tr: 4 ¶But these things about freedmen are to be said today of those who have come into Roman citizenship, since there are no other kinds of freedmen: the Dediticii and the Latins have been abolished together. The legitimate successions of the Latins were altogether null, because although they lived their lives as free persons, at their last breath they lost their soul and their liberty together, and the manumitters, by the Lex Iunia Norbana, held their goods in some way by right of peculium, as if they were slaves' goods. Later, however, by the Largian senatus consultum it had been provided that children of the manumitter, not expressly disinherited, were preferred to outside heirs in the goods of Latins. To these also came the edict of the divine Trajan, which made the same man a living Roman citizen, but a Latin when he died, if he had hastened to Roman citizenship by the emperor's favour against the will or without the knowledge of the patron. But by our constitution, on account of such changes of condition and other difficulties, we have resolved to abolish for ever the Latins themselves, together with the Lex Iunia, the Largian senatus consultum, and the edict of the divine Trajan, so that all freedmen enjoy Roman citizenship. And in a wonderful manner, by certain additions, we have transferred the very paths which led to Latinity to the acquisition of Roman citizenship.
On the Assignment of Freedmen, Title 9.

units.la: [?]umma (quod ad bona libertorum attinet[?]) admonendi sumus, censuisse senatum,vt quamuis ad omnes patroni liberos , qui eiusdem gradus sunt, æqualiter bona libertorū pertineāt: tamen liceret parenti , vni ex liberis adsignare libertum,vt post mortem eius solus sis patronus habeatur,cui adsignatus est: & cæteri liberi , qui ipsi quoque ad eadem bona,nulla adsignatione interne-niente pariter admitterentur,nihil iuris in his bonis habeant: sed ita demum pristinū ius recipiant, si is, cui adsignatus est, decesserit nullis liberis reliĉtis.
units.tr: Finally (as far as the goods of freedmen are concerned) we must be reminded that the senate decreed that, although the goods of freedmen pass equally to all the children of the patron who are of the same degree, nevertheless it is lawful for a parent to assign a freedman to one of his children, so that after his death that child alone is regarded as the patron to whom the freedman has been assigned. The other children, who would likewise be admitted equally to the same goods when no assignment intervened, have no right in those goods; but they recover their former right only if the child to whom the freedman was assigned dies leaving no children.

units.la: 1 ¶ Nec tantum libertum,sed etiam libertam, & non tantum filio,nepotive,sed etiam filiæ neptive adsignare permittitur.
units.tr: 1 ¶ Nor is it permitted to assign only a freedman; a freedwoman may be assigned too, and not only to a son or grandson, but also to a daughter or granddaughter.

units.la: 2 ¶ Datur autē hæc adsignandi facultas ei,qui duos plurésve liberos in potestate habebit,vt eis,quos in potestate habet, adsignare libertum libertámve liceat. Vnde quærebatur, si eum,cui adsignauit,postea emancipauerit: num euanescat adsignatio? Sed placuit euanesceré, quod & Iuliano & aliis plerisque visum est.
units.tr: 2 ¶ This power of assignment is given to one who has two or more children in his power, so that he may assign a freedman or freedwoman to those whom he has in his power. Hence the question was raised: if he later emancipates the child to whom he assigned them, does the assignment vanish? But it was decided that it does vanish, as Julian and most others also thought.

units.la: 3 ¶ Nec interest, an[?] testamento quis adsignet, an sine testamento, sed etiam quibuscumque verbis patronis hoc permittitur facere ex ipso senatusconsulto,quod Claudianis temporibus factum est,Sabellio Rufo & Asterio Scapula consulibus.
units.tr: 3 ¶ It makes no difference whether someone makes the assignment by will or without a will; and the senatusconsult, which was passed in the time of Claudius, in the consulship of Sabellius Rufus and Asterius Scapula, permits patrons to do this in any words whatever.
On Possessions of Goods, Title X.

units.la: VS[?] bonorum possessionis introductum est à prætore emendandi veteris iuris gratia. Nec solum in intestatorum hereditatibus vetus ius eo modo prætor emendauit,sicut supra diĉtum est : sed in quod successione Prætoria p vniuersitatē adiicitur [?]visem. hinc oritur bonorū possessoria hereditatis petitio quæ datur ei cui de iure Prætoriodefertur patrimonium defuncti. eorum quoque qui testamēto facto decesserint. Nam si alienus posthumus heres fuerit institutus: quam-uis hereditatem jure civili adire non poterat, cum institutio non valebat: honorario tamen jure bonorum possessor efficiebatur, videlicet cum a praetore adjuvabatur. sed & is a nostra constitutione hodie recte heres instituitur, quasi & jure civili non incognitus. Aliquando tamen neque emendandi, neque impugnandi veteris juris, sed magis confirmandi gratia ||praetor|| pollicetur bonorum possessionem. Nam illis quoque, qui recte testamento facto heredes instituti sunt, dat secundum tabulas bonorum possessionem. Item ab intestato suos heredes, & adgnatos ad bonorum possessionem vocat. Sed & remota quoque bonorum possessione, ad eos pertinet hereditas jure civili.
units.tr: The possession of goods (bonorum possessio) was introduced by the praetor to amend the old law. He did not amend the old law only in intestate inheritances, as was said above, but also where a succession is added to the whole estate by praetorian right. From this arises the praetorian action for inheritance of goods (bonorum possessoria hereditatis petitio), which is given to the person to whom the estate of the deceased is granted by praetorian law, including those who died after making a will. For if a posthumous stranger was instituted heir, although he could not take up the inheritance by civil law, since the institution was void, he was nevertheless made possessor of the goods by honorary law, namely when the praetor gave him assistance. Under our constitution, such a person is now rightly instituted heir, as one not unknown to civil law as well. Sometimes, however, the praetor grants possession of goods not to amend or overturn the old law but rather to confirm it. For he gives possession according to the tablets (secundum tabulas) to those also who have been rightly instituted heirs in a valid will. Likewise, he calls the children under power (sui heredes) and the agnates to possession of goods in intestacy. And even when possession of goods is set aside, the inheritance still belongs to them by civil law.

units.la: 2 ¶Quos autem solus vocat praetor ad hereditatem, heredes quidem ipso jure non fiunt. nam praetor heredem facere non potest. per legem enim tantùm, vel similem juris constitutionem heredes fiunt, veluti per senatusconsulta, & constitutiones principales, sed cum eis praetor dat bonorum possessionem, loco heredum cōstituuntur, & vocantur bonorum possessores. Adhuc autem & alios complures gradus praetor fecit in bonorum possessionibus dandis, dum id agebat, ne quis sine successore moreretur. Nam angustissimis finibus constitutum per legem duodecim tabularum jus perci-piendarum hereditatum, praetor ex bono & aequo dilatavit.
units.tr: 2. Those whom the praetor alone calls to an inheritance do not become heirs by the law itself, for the praetor cannot make an heir. Heirs are made only by statute or a similar legal enactment, such as senatorial decrees and imperial constitutions. But when the praetor grants them possession of goods, they are placed in the position of heirs and are called possessors of goods. Moreover, in granting possessions of goods, the praetor also established several other degrees, out of his concern that no one should die without a successor. For the right of taking inheritances, which the law of the Twelve Tables had confined within very narrow limits, the praetor extended on the basis of what is good and fair.

units.la: 3 ¶Sunt autem bonorum possessiones ex testamento quidem hae. Prima, quae praeteritis liberis datur, vocaturque contra tabulas. Secunda, quam omnibus jure scriptis heredibus praetor pollicetur, idcoque vocatur secundum tabulas. Et cùm de testamentis prius loquutus est, ad intestatos transitum fecit. Et primo loco suis heredibus, & iis, qui ex edicto praetoris inter suos heredes connumerantur, dat bonorum possessionem quae vocatur unde li-beri. Secundo, legitimis heredibus. Tertio, decem per-sonis, quas extraneo manumissori praeferebat. sunt autem decem personae hae: pater, mater, avus, avia, tam paterni, quàm materni: item filius, filia, nepos, neptis, tam ex filio, quàm ex filia: frater, sororve, consanguinei, vel uterini. Quarto, cognatis proximis. Quinto, tanquam ex familia. Sexto, patrono patronaeque, liberisque eorum, & parentibus. Septimo, viro & uxori. Octavo, cognatis manumissoris.
units.tr: 3. There are the following possessions of goods arising from a will. First, the one given to children who have been passed over, called "against the tablets" (contra tabulas). Second, the one the praetor promises to all heirs written in the tablets, and so called "according to the tablets" (secundum tabulas). After he had spoken of wills, he passed on to those who die intestate. First, to the children under power and to those counted among the children under the praetor's edict, he gives the possession called "from the children" (unde liberi). Second, to the lawful heirs. Third, to the ten persons whom he preferred to an outside manumitter. The ten persons are these: father, mother, grandfather, grandmother, on the paternal and maternal side alike; likewise son, daughter, grandson, granddaughter, whether through a son or through a daughter; brother or sister, whether of the whole or half blood. Fourth, to the nearest kindred. Fifth, as if from the family. Sixth, to the patron and patroness, their children, and their parents. Seventh, to husband and wife. Eighth, to the kindred of the manumitter.

units.la: 4 ¶Sed eas quidem prætoria introduxit iuris-dictio. à nobis tamen 4[?] nihil incuriosum prætermis-sum est, sed nostris constitutionibus omnia corrigen-tes, contra tabulas quidem & secundum tabulas bo-norum possessiones admisimus, utpote necessarias constitutas: necnon ab intestato unde liberi & unde legitimi bonorum possessiones. Quæ autem in præ-toris edicto quinto loco posita fuerat, id est unde de eam persona: eam pio proposito, & compendioso sermone superuacuam ostendimus. Cùm enim præfata bonorum possessio decem personas præponebat ex-traneo manumissoris: nostra constitutio, quàm de e-mancipatione liberorum fecimus, omnibus parenti-bus, eiusdemque manumissoribus contracta fiducia manumissionem facere dedit: ut ipsa manumissio eorum hoc in se habeat privilegium, & superuacua fiat supradicta bonorum possessio. Sublata igitur præ-dicta quinta bonorum possessione, in gradu eius sextā antea bonorum possessionē induximus: & quintā feci-mus, quam prætor proximis cognatis pollicetur. Cumque antea fuerat septimo loco bonorum possessio tanquam ex familia, & octauo. unde patroni patronaque & parentes eorum: utramque per constitutionem no-stram, quam de iure patronatus fecimus, penitus eua-cuauimus. Cum enim ad similitudinem successionis ingenuorum, libertinorum successiones posuimus, quas usque ad quintum gradum tantummodo coar-tauimus, ut sit aliqua inter ingenuos & libertinos differentia: sufficit eis tam contra tabulas bonorum possessio, quàm unde legitimi, & unde cognati, ex qui-bus possunt sua iura vindicare, omni scrupulositate & inextricabili errore istarum duarum bonorum possessionum resoluta. Aliam verò bonorum possessionem, quæ unde viri & uxor appellatur, & nono loco inter veteres bonorum possessiones posita fuerat, & in suo vigore seruavimus, & altiore loco, id est, sexto cum posuimus: decima quoque bonorum possessione, quæ erat unde cognati manumissoris, propter causas enu-meratas merito sublata, ut sex tantummodo bono-rum possessiones ordinariæ permaneant, suo vigore pollentes. Septima eas secuta, quam optima ratione prætores introduxerunt. Nouissimè enim promitti-tur edicto iis etiam bonorum possessio, quibus ut de-tur c, lege, vel senatusconsulto, vel constitutione co-prehensum est: quam neque bonorum possessionibus, quæ ab intestato veniunt, neque iis, quæ ex testamē-toto sunt,prætor stabili iure connumerauit : sed quasi vltimum & extraordinarium auxilium (prout res exegit) accommodauit, scilicet iis, qui ex legibus, senatusconsultis, constitutionibusue principum, ex nouo iure,vel ex testamento,vel ab intestato veniunt. Cum igitur plures species successionum prætor introduxisset, easque per ordinem disposuisset: & in vnaquaque specie successionis sæpe plures exstét dispari gradu personæ: ne{a} actiones creditorum differrentur, sed haberent,quos conuenirent,& ne facile in possessionem bonorum defuncti mitterentur, & eo modo sibi consulerent: ideo petendæ bonorum possessioni{b} certum tempus præsiniuit. Libertis itaque & parentibus,tam naturalibus, quàm adoptiuis in petenda bonorum possessione anni{e} spatium , cæteris sautē adgnatis,vel cognatis,centum dierum dedit.
units.tr: 4. The praetorian jurisdiction introduced these possessions. We, however, have overlooked nothing carelessly, but in correcting everything by our constitutions, we have admitted the possessions against the tablets and according to the tablets as necessary, and likewise the possessions in intestacy from children and from lawful heirs. The possession that stood fifth in the praetor's edict, namely from the same person, we have shown to be superfluous, on a pious plan and with a brief statement. For when that possession placed the ten persons before an outside manumitter, our constitution concerning the emancipation of children, which we made, gave all parents, and likewise the manumitters, the power to effect manumission by a trust agreed upon, so that manumission itself carries this privilege and the aforementioned possession becomes superfluous. Therefore, with the aforesaid fifth possession removed, we introduced in its place the sixth possession, which had been before, and made the fifth the one the praetor promises to the nearest kindred. Whereas before the possession as if from the family stood seventh and the one from patrons, patronesses and their parents eighth, we entirely abolished both by our constitution concerning the right of patronage. For since we have established the succession of freedmen on the model of the succession of freeborn persons, and have restricted it to the fifth degree only, so that some difference remains between the freeborn and freedmen, the possession against the tablets is enough for them, as is the possession from lawful heirs and from kindred, by which they can claim their rights, the complicated scruples and inextricable errors of those two possessions having been removed. The other possession, called from husband and wife, which had stood ninth among the old possessions, we have kept in its force, and when we placed it higher, namely sixth, the tenth possession, which was from the manumitter's kindred, was rightly removed for the reasons listed, so that only six ordinary possessions of goods remain, having their force. The seventh is that which followed them, which the praetors introduced on the best reasoning. For last, by the edict, the possession of goods is promised to those also who are covered by a statute, a senatorial decree, or a constitution. The praetor did not count this among the possessions of goods by fixed law, whether arising in intestacy or from a will, but provided it as a last and extraordinary aid, as circumstances required, namely for those who come to the succession by statutes, senatorial decrees, or imperial constitutions, under new law, or by will, or in intestacy. Therefore, since the praetor had introduced several kinds of succession and arranged them in order, and within each kind there were often several persons in unequal degree, the creditors' actions would be delayed; so that they might have whom to sue, and so that heirs would not easily be put into possession of the deceased's goods and thereby look after their own interests, he set a fixed time for claiming possession of goods. Thus to freedmen and to parents, both natural and adoptive, he gave a year's time for claiming possession of goods, but to the other agnates or kindred a hundred days.

units.la: 5 ¶Et si intra hoc tempus aliquis bonorum possessionem non petierit: eiusdem gradus personis adcrescit: vel si nullus sit, deinceps cæteris bonorum possessionem perinde ex successorio edicto pollicetur,ac si is,qui præcedebat,ex eo numero non esset. Si quis itaque delatam sibi bonorum possessionem repudiauerit,non quousque tempus bonorum possessioni præsinitū excesserit,expeƈtatur{d}: sed statim cæteri ex eodem edicto admittuntur. In petenda autem bonorum possessione dies vtiles singulí considerantur. 6 ¶Sed bene anteriores principes & huic causæ prouiderunt,ne quis pro petenda bonorum possessione curet{e}: sed quocumq. modo admittentis eam{f} iudicium (intra statuta tamen tempora) ostenderit, plenum habeat earum beneficium.
units.tr: 5. If anyone does not claim possession of goods within this time, it accrues to persons of the same degree; or if there is none, the praetor grants possession to the others in the same way under the successory edict, as if the one who preceded had not been among that number. Thus if anyone has rejected possession of goods offered to him, the others are admitted at once under the same edict, and they need not wait until the time fixed for possession of goods has expired. In claiming possession of goods, the useful days are counted individually. 6. Moreover, earlier emperors well provided for this matter too, so that no one would take care to claim possession of goods; but whoever shows by any means that he is admitted to it by judgment (within the fixed times, nevertheless) shall have the full benefit of them.

units.la: DE ADQVISITIONE PER ADROGATIONEM, TIT. XI.
units.tr: ON ACQUISITION BY ADROGATION, TIT. XI.

units.la: ET & alterius generis per vniuersitatem successio, quæ neque lege duodecim tabularum, neque prætoris edicto, sed eo iure, quod consensu receptum est, introducta est. 1 ¶Ecce enim cum pater familias sese in adrogationem dat,omnes res eius corporales & incorporales,quaeque ei debitæ sunt, adrogatori antea quidem pleno iure adquirebantur: exceptis iis,quæ per capitis deminutionem pereunt, vxor hic à Iustiniano probatur.ʒ.§.4.mum sine scripto, dein longius per visum productum: postremo à prudentibus confirmatum. Theoph. quales sunt operarum obligationes, & ius adgnationis, vsus etenim & vsufructus, licet his antea connumerabantur, attamen capitis deminutione minima cos tolli prohibuit nostra constitutio 4. 2 ¶Nunc autem nos eandem adquisitionem, quae per adrogationem fiebat, coarctauimus ad similitudinem naturalium parentum. Nihil enim aliud, nisi tantummodo vsufructus tam naturalibus parentibus, quàm adoptiuis per filiosfamiliarum adquiritur in iis rebus, quae extrinsecus filiis obueniunt, dominio eis, integro seruato. Mortuo autem filio adrogato in adoptiua familia, etiam dominium rerum eius ad adrogatorem pertransit: nisi supersint aliae personae, quae ex constitutione nostra patrem in iis, quae adquiri non possunt, antecedant.
units.tr: There is also another kind of succession by universal title, which was introduced neither by the Law of the Twelve Tables nor by the praetor's edict, but by a right received through consent. 1 ¶ For when a head of household gave himself up into adrogation, all his property, corporeal and incorporeal, and whatever was owed to him, was formerly acquired by the adrogator by full right, with the exception of those things that perish through loss of status. Justinian approves this, Theoph. This right first existed without writing, then was extended further by usage, and finally was confirmed by the jurists. Such are the obligations of services and the right of agnation; for usufruct and use, although formerly counted among these, our constitution, in Inst. 3 §4, forbade them to be lost by even the smallest loss of status. 2 ¶ Now, however, we have restricted that acquisition which took place through adrogation to the likeness of natural parents. For nothing else is acquired, except only the usufruct, both by natural parents and by adoptive parents, through sons under power, in those things which come to the sons from outside, the ownership remaining whole to them. But when the adrogated son dies in the adoptive family, the ownership of his property also passes to the adrogator, unless other persons survive who, under our constitution, take precedence over the father in those things which cannot be acquired.

units.la: 3 ¶Sed ex diuerso, pro eo, quod is debuit, qui se in adoptionem dedit ipso quidem iure adrogator non tenetur, sed nomine filij conuenitur: & si noluerit eum defendere, permittitur creditoribus per competentes nostros magistratus bona, quae eius cum vsufructu futura fuissent, si se alieno iuri non subiecisset, possidere, & legitimo modo ea disponere.
units.tr: 3 ¶ On the other hand, for what he owed, the man who gave himself into adoption is not himself liable by law to the adrogator, but is sued in the name of the son. And if the adrogator is unwilling to defend him, creditors are permitted, through our competent magistrates, to take possession of the goods which would have been his, with usufruct, had he not placed himself under another's power, and to dispose of them in a lawful manner.

units.la: DE EO, CVI LIBERTATIS causa bona addicuntur, TIT. XII.
units.tr: ON HIM TO WHOM GOODS ARE ADJUDGED FOR THE SAKE OF LIBERTY, TIT. XII.

units.la: ACCESSIT nonus casus successionis ex constitutione diui Marci. Nam si ij, qui libertatem acceperunt a domino in testamento, ex quo non aditur hereditas, velint bona sibi addici libertatum conseruandarum causa: audiuntur.
units.tr: A ninth case of succession was added by a constitution of the divine Marcus. For if those who have received freedom from their master in a will, where the inheritance is not entered upon, wish the goods to be adjudged to them for the sake of preserving the freedoms, they are heard.

units.la: 1 ¶Et ita diui Marci rescripto ad Pompilii Rufum continetur. verba rescripti ita se habent: Si Verginio Valenti, qui testamento suo libertate quibusdam adscripsit, nemine successore ab intestato exstante, in ea causa bona ipsius esse coeperunt, vt venire debeant: is, cuius de ea re notio est, aditus rationem desiderij tui habebit, vt libertatum tam earum, quae directo, quamque earum, quae per speciem fideicommisi, relictae sunt, tuendarum gratia addicantur tibi: si idoneè f crediteribus caueris de solido, quod cuique debetur, solvendo. Et ij quidem, quibus directa libertas data est, perinde liberi erunt, ac si hereditas adita esset. Ij autem, quos heres manumittere rogatus est, à te libertatem consequuntur: ita, vt si non alia conditione velis tibi bona addici, quàm vt [?]iij[?] etiam, qui directo li{a}Ato[?] libertate acceperunt, tui liberti fiant. Nam huic etiam voluntati tuae, si ij, quorum de statu agitur, consentiant, auctoritatem nostram accommodamus. Et ne huius rescriptionis nostrae emolumentum alia ratione irritum fiat: si {a}fiscus bona agnoscere vo-luerit, & ij, qui rebus nostris attendunt, sciant {b}com-modo pecuniario praeferendam esse libertatis causam: & ita bona cogenda, ut libertas iis salua sit, qui eam adipisci potuerunt, ac si hereditas ex testamento a dita esset.
units.tr: 1 ¶ And so it is contained in the rescript of the divine Marcus to Pompilius Rufus. The words of the rescript are as follows: "If, when Verginius Valens, who by his will granted freedom to certain persons, died without any successor on intestacy, goods of his began to be in such a state that they ought to be sold, the magistrate who has cognizance of the matter, having been approached, shall take account of your request, so that for the sake of protecting the freedoms, both of those which were given directly and of those which were given by way of a trust, the goods may be adjudged to you, provided you give sufficient security to the creditors for the whole sum owed to each of them. Those to whom freedom was given directly shall be free just as if the inheritance had been entered upon. Those whom the heir was asked to manumit shall obtain their freedom from you; so that, if you do not wish the goods to be adjudged to you on any other condition than that those also who received freedom directly become your freedmen, we extend our authority to this your wish, provided those whose status is in question agree. And lest the benefit of this our rescript be made void in some other way: if the fisc wishes to take notice of the goods, and those who attend to our affairs know that the cause of freedom is to be preferred to pecuniary advantage, then the goods are to be gathered in such a way that freedom remains safe for those who were able to obtain it, just as if the inheritance had been entered upon under the will."

units.la: 2 ¶Hoc rescripto subventum est & libertatibus, & defunctis, ne bona eorum a creditoribus possideantur & veneant {c}. Certe si fuerint hac de causa bona addicta: cessat bonorum venditio, exi-stit enim defuncti defensor, & quidem idoneus, qui de solido {d}creditoribus cauet.
units.tr: 2 ¶ This rescript has given relief both to freedoms and to the dead, so that their goods are not taken into possession by creditors and sold. Certainly, if goods have been adjudged for this cause, the sale of the goods ceases, for a defender of the deceased comes into existence, and indeed a suitable one, who gives security to the creditors for the whole sum.

units.la: 3 ¶In primis hoc rescriptum totiens locum habet, quotiens testamento libertates datae sunt. Quid ergo si quis intestatus decedens, codicillis libertates dederit, ne-que adita sit ab intestato hereditas: ‖an‖ fauor constitutionis debebit locum habere? Certe si intestatus decesserit, & codicillis dederit libertate: competere eam, nemini dubium est.
units.tr: 3 ¶ First, this rescript applies whenever freedoms have been given by will. What then if someone dying intestate has given freedoms by codicils, and the inheritance on intestacy has not been entered upon? Shall the favour of the constitution have a place here? Certainly, if he died intestate and gave freedom by codicil, no one doubts that it is due.

units.la: 4 ¶Tunc‖enim‖ constitutioni locum esse verba ostendunt, cum nemo successor ab intestato existat. Ergo quandiu {e}in-certum erit, utrum existat, an non: cessabit constitutio. Si vero certum esse coeperit, neminem existere: tunc erit constitutioni locus.
units.tr: 4 ¶ For the words show that the constitution has its place only when no successor on intestacy exists. Therefore, as long as it is uncertain whether one exists or not, the constitution will cease to apply. But if it has begun to be certain that no one exists, then the constitution will have its place.

units.la: 5 ¶si is, qui in integrum restitui potest, abstinuerit hereditate: an quamuis potest in integrum restitui, possit admitti constitutio, & bonorum addictio fieri? Quid ergo si post addictionem libertatum conservandarum causa factam, in integrum sit restitutus? Utique non erit dicendum revocari libertates: quia {f}semel compe-tierunt.
units.tr: 5 ¶ If one who can be restored to the former position has abstained from the inheritance, can the constitution be admitted, and an adjudication of goods take place, even though he can be restored? What then if, after an adjudication has been made for the sake of preserving freedoms, he is restored to the former position? Surely it is not to be said that the freedoms are revoked, because they have already come into being.

units.la: 6 ¶Haec constitutio libertarum tuen-darum causa introducta est. Ergo si libertates nullae sunt datae: cessat ‖haec‖ constitutio{g}. Quid ergo si vinus[?] decederit libertates, vel mortis causa: & ne de hoc quaeratur, utrum in fraudem creditorum, an non factum sit, idcirco velint sibi addici bona: an audiendi sint? Et magis est, ut audiri debeant, etsi deficiant verba constitutionis.
units.tr: 6 ¶ This constitution was introduced for the sake of protecting freedoms. Therefore, if no freedoms have been given, this constitution ceases. What then if a certain person has died having granted freedoms, or in contemplation of death, and they wish the goods to be adjudged to them so that it is not inquired whether this was done in fraud of creditors or not: are they to be heard? And it is rather the case that they ought to be heard, even if the words of the constitution fail.

units.la: 7 ¶Sed cum multas divisiones eiusmodi constitutioni{h} deesse perspexi-mus: lata est a nobis plenissima constitutio, in qua multae species collatae sunt, quibus ius huiusmodi successionis plenissimum est effectum, quas ex ipsius dedione[?] constitutionis potest quis cognoscere.
units.tr: 7 ¶ But since we have seen that many such divisions are lacking in the constitution, a most full constitution has been issued by us, in which many kinds are gathered, by which the right of this kind of succession has been made most full; which one may learn from the giving of the constitution itself.

units.la: DE SVCCESSIONIBVS SVB-sublatis, quæ fiebant per bonorum venditiones, & ex senatusconsulto Claudiano{a},
units.tr: ON SUCCESSIONS ABOLISHED, WHICH TOOK PLACE THROUGH SALES OF GOODS, AND BY THE CLAUDIAN SENATUS CONSULTUM,
TITLE XIII.

units.la: ERANT ante præ-dictam{b} successionem olim & aliæ per vniuersitatem successiones, quales fuerat bonorum emptio{c}, quæ de bonis debitoris vendendis per multas ambages fuerat introducta, & tunc locum habebat, quando iudicia ordinaria{d} in vsu fuerant, sed cum extraordinariis iudiciis po-fteritas vsa est: ideo cum ipsis ordinariis iudiciis etiam bonorum venditiones expirauerunt, & tam-modo creditoribus datur officio iudicis{e} bona possidere, & prout vtile eis visum est, ea disponere, quod ex latioribus Digestorum libris{f} perfectius apparebit.
units.tr: Before the aforementioned succession there were formerly also other successions by universal title, such as the purchase of goods (bonorum emptio), which had been introduced by many circuitous procedures for selling a debtor's goods, and which applied at the time when the ordinary legal actions were in use. But when the later age adopted the extraordinary legal actions, the ordinary actions also lapsed along with the sales of goods; and now creditors are simply granted, by the office of the judge, to take possession of the goods and to dispose of them as they see fit. This will appear more fully from the longer books of the Digest.

units.la: 1 ¶Erat & ex senatusconsulto Claudiano miserabilis per vniuersitatem adquisitio{g}: cum libera mulier seruili amore bacchata, ipsam libertatem per senatusconsultum amittebat, & cum libertate substantiam. quod indignum nostris temporibus esse existimantes, & a nostra ciuitate deleri, & non inseri nostris Digestis concesimus.
units.tr: 1 ¶There was also a wretched acquisition by universal title under the Claudian senatus consultum: when a free woman, mad with love for a slave, lost her very liberty by the senatus consultum, and her property along with her liberty. Considering this unworthy of our own times and to be erased from our city, we have permitted it not to be inserted into our Digest.
On Obligations, Title 14.

units.la: VNC transeamus ad obligationes{i}. Obligatio{k} est iuris vinculu, quo necessitate adstringimur alicuius rei soluendæ secundum nostræ ciuitatis iura. 1 ¶Omnium autem obligationum summa di-
units.tr: Now let us pass on to obligations. An obligation is a bond of law, by which we are bound by necessity to pay something according to the laws of our state. 1. The sum of all obligations is divided...

units.la: {f} libro 42.tit.5.quib.ex causis in possess.& de rebus iudicis authorit.& 7. Cod.72. & de qua v.l.vnic.Cod.de Sc.Claud.vlp.tit.11.§.11.Tacit. 12.annal. {h} 44.ff.7:4. Cod.10.
units.tr: Book 42, title 5, Quibus ex causis in possessionem, and De rebus iudicis authoritate; and 7 Cod. 72; and on it the single law of the Code De Senatusconsulto Claudiano; Ulpian, title 11, §11; Tacitus, Annals 12; 44 Dig. 7:4; Cod. 10.

units.la: {i} ex quibus,personalis : vt ex dominio realis actio nascitur.
units.tr: {i} From which, personal: as a real action arises from ownership.

units.la: {k} Naturalis et Ciuilis simul ceu mixta. ex qua actio & vis exigendi promanat.
units.tr: Natural and civil at once, as if mixed. From it comes the action and the power of exacting.

units.la: Quippe Naturalis tantum obligatio (cuius causa est vel contractus vel delictum) destituta ciuili approbatione, exceptionem quidem habet, sed actionem (veluti inter patrem & filium in potestate, dominum & seruum, creditorem & pupillum mutuum sine tutoris authoritate accipietem) nonparit. Ciuilis tantum, actionem quidem parit, sed non habet effectum exigendi: quia ciuiliter tantum obligatus, tutus est exceptione, puta vel nudi pacti, vel merus illati, vel pecuniæ sibi non numeratæ. Neutra vero obligatio nascitur quado lex nominatim factu improbat veluti contractu inter tutorem & pupillum, donationem inter coiuges, & similia. nisio in duo genera diducitur. namq. aut ciuiles sūt, aut prætoriæ.Ciuiles sunt,quæ aut legibus cōstitutę, aut certo iure ciuili comprobatæ sunt.Prętoriæ sunt, quas prætor ex sua iurisdictione constituit, quæ etiā honorariæ vocantur.
units.tr: For a purely natural obligation (whose cause is either a contract or a delict), lacking civil approval, does indeed carry an exception, but does not produce an action (as between a father and a son under his power, a master and a slave, or a creditor and a ward receiving a loan without the guardian's authority). A purely civil obligation does produce an action, but has no force of exacting, because one bound only civilly is protected by an exception, for instance of a bare pact, of fear inflicted, or of money not counted out to him. Neither kind of obligation arises when the law expressly forbids the act, as in a contract between guardian and ward, a gift between spouses, and similar cases. Obligations are divided into two kinds, for they are either civil or praetorian. Civil obligations are those established by laws or approved by some fixed rule of civil law. Praetorian obligations are those which the praetor set up by his jurisdiction; these are also called honorary.

units.la: 2 ¶Sequēs diuisio in quatuor species diuiditur. Aut enim ex contractu sunt, aut quasi ex maleficio, aut quasi ex contractu, aut ex maleficio. Prius est, vt de iis, quæ ex cōtractu sunt, disputiamus. Harum æquè quatuor sunt species. Aut enim re contrahuntur, aut verbis, aut literis, aut con-sensu{a}. de quibus singulis disputiamus.
units.tr: 2. The following division falls into four species. For they arise either from contract, or as if from a delict, or as if from contract, or from a delict. We shall first discuss those which arise from contract. Of these there are likewise four species: they are contracted either by the thing, by words, by writing, or by consent, and we discuss each of these in turn.

units.la: QVIBVS MODIS RE CON-trahitur obligatio, TIT. XV.
units.tr: HOW AN OBLIGATION IS CONTRACTED BY THE THING ITSELF (RE), TIT. XV.

units.la: Re contrahitur obligatio{b}, veluti mu-tui datione. Mutui autem datio in iis rebus cōsistit, quæ pondere, numero, me-sura constant: veluti vino, oleo frumēto, pecunia numerata, ære, argento, auro: quas res aut numerando, aut metiendo, aut adpendendo in hoc damus, vt accipiētium fiant{c}. Et quoniam nobis non eædem res, sed aliæ eiusdē naturæ & qualitatis redduntur{d}: inde etiam mutuū appellatū est, quia ita à me tibi datur, vt ex meo tuū fiat: & ex eo contractu nascitur actio, quæ vocatur condictio.
units.tr: An obligation is contracted by the thing itself (re), as by the giving of a loan (mutuum). The giving of a loan consists in those things which consist of weight, number or measure: for example wine, oil, grain, money counted out, bronze, silver, gold. These things we give, by counting, measuring or weighing them out, in such a way that they become the property of the recipients. And since the same things are not returned to us, but others of the same kind and quality, the transaction is also named mutuum (loan), because it is given by me to you in such a way that from being mine it becomes yours. From this contract arises an action which is called condictio.

units.la: 1 ¶Is quoque,qui non debitū accepit ab eo,qui p[?] minimè necessaria (veluti vt mihi venditori fundū ad certū tempus loces) considerari. v.Hotom. quæst.35.
units.tr: 1 Also he who receives what was not owed, from him who... (the least necessary) should be considered; for example, if you let me, as seller, a farm for a fixed time. See Hotomannus, quaest. 35.

units.la: {b} Reducitur contrahi obligatio, quoties præter consensum rem interuenire necesse est actu ipso.l.3.§.2.ff.eo. vt vtrumque inter nos conueniat de mutuo dando, obligatio tamen ex mutuo non nascitur: cum aliud sit contractus,aliud de contrahendo facta promissio.
units.tr: {b} An obligation is contracted by the thing itself whenever, apart from consent, the thing must actually be handed over. See Dig. 3.2 (l. 3 §2), ff. eo. Even if we agree between ourselves that a loan will be given, no obligation arises from the loan, since the contract is one thing and a promise to contract is another.

units.la: {c} in eodem ac nō diuerso genere: eodem inquam,& similitudine & vtilitate:vel alter, non eædem res in indiuiduo, sed in specie, redduntur.
units.tr: {c} Of the same kind and not of a different one: of the same kind, I say, both in likeness and in usefulness; or the other things are returned not as the same individual things but as the same in kind.

units.la: {d} Qui solvit id quod ciuiliter tantum vel naturaliter & ciuiliter debuit (quod petitum tamen poterat elidere dubij euentus,vel perpetua exceptione puta Velleiani) is solutum repetet. At qui debitum vel naturaliter tantum,vel naturaliter & ciuiliter (quod tamen elidere potuisset exceptione perpetua fauorabili vt Macedoniani) Item qui indebitum vel ratione diei vel confidentiforum[?] (veluti cum potuisset vti Epistola D.Hadriani) soluit, is solutum non repetet. Cessabit quoque hæc actio quoties quis vel sciens,vel secutus rei iudicatę,aut causæ pietatis, aut transactionis aut iurisiurandi authoritatem soluit. idem, si alienum debitum,si ex ea causa vnde lis inficiando crescit soluerit. Mynsf. errore soluit,re obligatur datúrque agenti cótra est propter repetitione condictitia actio. Nam perinde et condici potest,si apparet eū dare oportere,ac si mutuū accepisset. Vnde pupillus,si ei sine tutoris auctoritate indebitum per errorem datū est, non tenebi-tur indebiti condictione: non magis,quàm mutui datione. Sed hæc species obligationis non videtur ex cōtractu consistere: cùm is, qui soluendi animo dat, magis voluerit negotium distrahere, quàm cōtrahere.
units.tr: {d} He who pays what was owed only civilly, or naturally and civilly (which the claimant could nevertheless have defeated by an uncertain outcome of a dispute, or by a perpetual exception, as in the case of the Velleian senatusconsult), may reclaim what he paid. But he who pays a debt that was owed only naturally, or naturally and civilly (which he could have defeated by a perpetual and favourable exception, as in the case of the Macedonian senatusconsult), and likewise he who pays what was not owed, on account of the day or of confidence (as when he could have used the letter of the divine Hadrian), shall not reclaim it. This action also ceases whenever someone pays knowingly, or following the authority of a judgment already given, or of a pious cause, or of a settlement, or of an oath. The same holds if he pays another's debt, when it is for the cause from which a lawsuit grows by denial. Mynsinger: he pays through error, and is bound by the thing, and the one who sues is given the condictio action against him for recovery. For it can be claimed in the same way if it appears that he ought to give, just as if he had received a loan. Hence a ward, if something not owed was given to him by mistake without his guardian's authority, is not bound by the condictio of what was not owed, no more than by the giving of a loan. But this kind of obligation does not seem to consist of a contract, since he who gives with the intention of paying wants to dissolve a transaction rather than to contract one.

units.la: 2 ¶Item is,cui res aliqua vtenda datur, id est,cōmodatur,re obligatur, & tenetur commodati actione{a}. Sed is ab eo,qui mutuū accepit,lōge distat. namque nō{b} ita res datur, vt eius sit: & ob id dea re ipsa restituenda tenetur. Et is quidem, qui mutuū accepit, si quolibet{c} fortuito casu amiserit, {p}accepit: velut incendio,ruina,naufragio, aut latrocinio hostiūmve incursu: nihilominus obligatus remaneat. At is qui vtendum accepit,sane quidem exactam diligentiam custodiendæ rei præstare iubetur: nec sufficit ei tantam diligentiam adhibuisse, quantam suis rebus adhibere solitus est,si modo alius diligentior poterat eam rē custodire: sed propter maiorem vim maioresve casus non tenetur,si modo non ipsius culpa is casus intervenit. alioqui si id,q tibi cōmodatum est domi, peregrē tecum ferre malueris,& vel incursu hostiū prædonūmve, vel naufragio amiseris: dubium nō est,quin de restituenda ea re tenearis. Cō-modata autem res tunc proprie intelligitur, si nulla mercede accepta vel cōstituta,|| res || tibi vtēda data est. alioqui mercede interveniente, locatus tibi vsus rei videtur. Gratuitum enim debet esse commodatū.
units.tr: 2 Likewise, he to whom a thing is given for use, that is, lent, is bound by the thing and is held by the action of loan for use (commodatum). But he differs greatly from him who received a loan. For the thing is not given so as to become his, and for that reason he is bound to return the very thing itself. He who received a loan, if he has lost it by any chance accident, such as fire, collapse, shipwreck, robbery, or an attack of enemies, remains bound nonetheless. But he who received a thing for use is bound to show exact diligence in keeping it; nor is it enough for him to have applied the same care he is accustomed to apply to his own things, if another more diligent person could have kept the thing. Yet he is not held responsible for greater force or greater accidents, provided that such an accident did not happen through his own fault. Otherwise, if you prefer to carry with you abroad what was lent to you at home, and you lose it through an attack of enemies or pirates, or through shipwreck, there is no doubt that you are bound to restore it. A thing is properly understood to be lent only when it is given to you for use without any fee being received or agreed; otherwise, if a fee intervenes, the use of the thing seems to have been let to you. For a loan for use must be gratuitous.

units.la: 3 ¶Præterea & is, apud quem res aliqua{d} depo-nitur,re obligatur,tenetur{f}. actione{e} depositi: quia & ipse de ea re,quam accepit, restituenda tenetur{f}. Sed is ex eo solo tenetur{g}, si quid dolo commiserit. culpæ autem nomine, id est,desidiæ ac negligentiæ, non tenetur. Itaque securus est, qui parum diligenter custoditam rem furto amiserit: quia qui negligenti amico rem custodiendam tradit, || non ei || sed suæ facilitati id imputare debet.
units.tr: 3 Moreover, he with whom a thing is deposited is also bound by the thing and held by the action of deposit, because he too is bound to return the thing he received. But he is liable for it only if he has committed fraud. He is not liable on account of fault, that is, of laziness and negligence. So he is secure who loses through theft a thing kept with too little care, because he who hands a thing to be kept by a careless friend ought to impute it not to him but to his own credulity.

units.la: 3 ¶Creditor quoque,qui pignus accepit, re obligatur:quia & ipse de ea re quam accepit, restituenda tenetur actione pignoratitia{h}. Sed quia pignus vtriusq.{i} gratia datur,& debitoris,quo magis pecunia ei creditur,& creditoris,quo magis ei in tuto sit creditū: placuit sufficere, si ad eam rem custodiendā exactam diligentiā adhi[illegible, ~2 letters]hibeat: quā si praestiterit, & aliquo fortuito casu re amiserit: securum esse, nec impediri creditum petere.
units.tr: 3 A creditor who has taken a pledge is also bound by the thing, because he too is bound to restore the thing he received, by the action on pledge. But since a pledge is given for the benefit of both the debtor, so that money may be lent to him more readily, and of the creditor, so that the loan may be safer for him, it has been decided that it is enough if he applies exact diligence to keeping the thing; and if he has done so, and loses the thing by some chance accident, he is safe, and is not prevented from demanding repayment of the loan.
DE VERBORVM OBLIGATIONIBVS.
TIT. XVI.

units.la: VERBIS obligatio contrahitur ex interrogatione & responsione, cum quid dari fierive nobis stipulamur. ex qua duae proficiscuntur actiones, tam condictio certi, si certa sit stipulatio: quā ex stipulatu, si incerta sit. quae hoc nomine inde vtitur, quod stipulū apud veteres firmum appellabatur, forte à stipite descendens. 1 ¶In hac re olim talia verba tradita fuerunt, Spondes? Spondeo. Promittis? Promitto. ‖ Fidepromittis? Fidepromitto. ‖ Fideiubes? Fideiubeo. Dabis? Dabo. Faciesne? Faciam. Vtrum autem Latina, an Graeca, vel qualibet alia lingua stipulatio coci-piatur, nihil interest: scilicet si vterque stipulantium intellectum eius linguae habeat, nec necesse est eadem lingua vtrunque vti, sed sufficit congruenter ad interrogata respondere. Quinetiam duo Graeci Latina lingua obligationem contrahere possunt. Sed haec solenia verba olim quidem in vsu fuerunt: postea autem Leonina constitutio lata est, quae solennitate verborum sublata, sensum & consonantem intellectu ab vtraq. parte solum desiderat, quibuscunque tandem verbis expressum est.
units.tr: An obligation is contracted by words through question and answer, when we stipulate that something be given or done to us. From this two actions arise: the condictio of a certain thing, if the stipulation is certain, and the action ex stipulatu, if it is uncertain. The latter takes its name from the fact that a stipulation was called among the ancients "firm" (stipulum), perhaps descending from stipes (a stake). (1) In this matter, these words were handed down in former times: "Do you promise? I promise. Do you pledge your faith? I pledge my faith. Do you become surety? I become surety. Will you give? I will give. Will you do it? I will do it." It makes no difference whether the stipulation is conducted in Latin, in Greek, or in any other language, provided that both parties of the stipulation understand that language; nor is it necessary for both to use the same language, but it is enough to answer the questions appropriately. Indeed, two Greeks can even contract an obligation in the Latin language. But these solemn words were indeed in use in former times; afterwards, however, the constitution of Leo was enacted, which, abolishing the solemnity of words, requires only meaning and agreement understood by each party, in whatever words it is expressed.

units.la: 2 ¶Omnis stipulatio aut pure, aut in diem, aut sub conditione fit. Pure, veluti, quinque aureos dare spondes? Idque confestim peti potest. In diem: cum adiecto die, quo pecunia soluatur, stipulatio fit: veluti, decem aureos primis calendis martiis dare spondes? Id autem quod in diem stipulamur, statim quidem debetur: sed peti prius, quam dies venerit, non poterit. at ne eo quidem ipso die, in quem stipulatio facta est, peti potest: quia totus is dies arbitrio soluentis tribui debet. Neque enim certum est eo die, in quem promissum est, datum non esse, prius quam is praeterierit.
units.tr: (2) Every stipulation is made either purely, or for a day, or under a condition. Purely, for example: "Do you promise to give five gold pieces?" and this can be demanded at once. For a day: when a stipulation is made with a day added on which the money is to be paid, for example: "Do you promise to give ten gold pieces on the first day of March?" What we stipulate for a day is indeed owed immediately, but it cannot be demanded before the day has come. But it cannot be demanded even on that very day on which the stipulation was made, because the whole of that day ought to be granted to the discretion of the one paying; for it is not certain that on the day promised the thing has not been given until that day has passed.

units.la: 3 ¶At si ita stipuleris, decem aureos annuos, quoad viuam, dare spondes? & pure facta obligatio intelligitur, & perpetuatur: quia ad tempus non poterit deberi: sed heres petendo, pacti exceptione submouebitur.
units.tr: (3) But if you stipulate thus: "Do you promise to give ten gold pieces yearly, as long as I live?" the obligation is understood to be made purely and is perpetuated, because it cannot be owed for a time; but when the heir demands it, he will be repelled by the exception of the pact.
(4) A stipulation is made under a condition
{l} Indeed on that very day. See l. 118 §pen. ff. eodem.

units.la: {m} {n} l.52.inf. ff.de pactis. pulatio fit,cùm in aliquem casum differtur {a}obliga-tio:ut si aliquid factum fuerit, vel non fuerit,cómit-tatur stipulatio: veluti, si Titius consul fuerit {b}factus, quinque aureos dare spondes? Si quis ita stipulétur, si {c}in capitolium non ascendero, dare spondes? perinde erit ac si stipulatus esset cum morerentur,sibi dari.Ex con-ditionali stipulatione tantùm spes {d}est debitum iri: eámque ipsam spem in heredem transmittimus {e}, si prius quàm conditio exstet, mors nobis contigerit.
units.tr: {m} {n} See l. 52 inf. ff. de pactis. when the obligation is deferred until some event, so that, if something has been done or has not been done, the stipulation is put in suspense: for example, "If Titius has been made consul, do you promise to give five gold pieces?" If someone stipulates thus: "If I do not ascend the Capitol, do you promise to give?" it will be just as if he had stipulated that it be given to him when they died. From a conditional stipulation there is only the hope that a debt will arise, and we transmit that very hope to the heir, if death has overtaken us before the condition comes to pass.

units.la: 5 ¶ Loca etiā inseri stipulationi solet:veluti,Cartha-gini dare spondes? Quæ stipulatio licèt pure fieri videtur:tamè re ipsa habet tēpus {f}adiectū, quo promissor utatur ad pecuniā Carthagini dadā. Et ideo siquis Romæ[?] ita stipulētur, hodie Carthagini dare spondes? inutilis erit stipulatio, cùm impossibilis sit repromissio.
units.tr: (5) It is also customary to insert a place into a stipulation: for example, "Do you promise to give at Carthage?" Although this stipulation seems to be made purely, yet in fact it has a time added, in which the promisor may use the time for paying the money at Carthage. And therefore if someone stipulates at Rome thus: "Do you promise to give at Carthage today?" the stipulation will be useless, since the repromission is impossible.

units.la: 6 ¶ Conditiones,quæ {g}ad præsens vel præteritum tempus referuntur:aut statim infirmant obligationē, aut omnino nō differunt. veluti,Si Titius Consul fuit, vel si Mænius[?] vinit, dare spondes? Nam si ea ita nō sunt, nihil valet stipulatio:sin autē ita se habent,statim va-let.Quæ enim per rerum naturam sunt certa:nō mo-rantur obligationem, licet apud nos incerta sint.
units.tr: (6) Conditions which refer to the present or past time either immediately invalidate the obligation, or do not defer it at all. For example: "If Titius was consul, or if Maevius is alive, do you promise to give?" For if these are not so, the stipulation is worth nothing; but if they are so, it is valid at once. For things that are certain by the nature of things do not delay the obligation, although with us they are uncertain.

units.la: 7 ¶ Nō solum res in stipulatum deduci possunt, sed etiam {i}factum:ut si stipulemur aliquid fieri,vel nō fieri,& in huiusmodi stipulationib {l}optimū erit pœ-nam subiicere, ne quantitas stipulationis in incerto sit,ac necesse sit actori probare,quod eius interfit.Itaque si quis ut fiat aliquid,stipulétur: {h}ita adiici pœnā debet, Si ita factum non erit,tunc pœnæ nomine decem aureos dare spondes? Sed si quædam fieri,quædam non fieri, una eademq. conceptione stipulatur quis: clausula huiusmodi erit adiicieda, Si {k}aduersus ea factum erit,sive quid ita factum non fuerit: tunc pœnæ no-mine decem aureos dare spondes?
units.tr: (7) Not only things but also an act can be brought into a stipulation: as if we stipulate that something be done or not be done; and in stipulations of this kind it will be best to add a penalty, so that the amount of the stipulation is not uncertain, and it is not necessary for the plaintiff to prove what his interest is. Thus, if someone stipulates that something be done, a penalty ought to be added in this way: "If it is not done so, do you promise to give ten gold pieces by way of penalty?" But if someone stipulates that certain things be done and certain things not be done, by one and the same formulation, a clause of this kind is to be added: "If anything is done contrary to these, or if anything is not done so, do you promise to give ten gold pieces by way of penalty?"
DE DUOBUS REIS STIPULANDI & PROMITTENDI.
TITLE XVII.

units.la: Stipulandi ita,si post omnium interrogatione promissor respondeat, Spondeo: utputa cum duobus separatim stipulantibus ita promissor respondeat, Utrique vestrum dare spondeo. Nā si prius Titio spoponderit, deinde alio interroganti spondeat, alia atque alia erit obligatio, nec creduntur duo rei stipulandi esse. Duo plures ve rei promittendi ita fiunt, Mævi decem aureos dare spondes? & Seii eosdem decem aureos dare spondes? || si || respondeant singuli separatim, spondeo. 1 ¶Ex huiusmodi obligationibus, & stipulationibus solidū singulis debetur, & pro mittentes{a} singuli in solidū † tenentur. In utraque tamen obligatione una res vertitur: & vel alter debitum accipiendo, vel alter soluendo, omnium perimit obligationem, & omnes liberat. 2 ¶Ex{b} duobus reis promittendi, alius pure, alius in die, vel sub codi-tione obligari poterit. nec impedimento erit dies aut codicitio, quo minᵃ ab eo, qui pure obligatᵃ est, petatur.
units.tr: A stipulation is made thus, if after the question has been put to all, the promisor answers, "I promise." For example, when two parties stipulate separately and the promisor answers, "I promise to give to each of you." For if he first promised to Titius and then, when another asks, promises again, there are separate and distinct obligations, and they are not regarded as two stipulators of one thing. Two or more promisors are created thus: "Do you, Maevius, promise to give ten gold pieces? And do you, Seius, promise to give the same ten gold pieces?" If each answers separately, "I promise." 1 From obligations and stipulations of this kind, the whole is owed to each creditor, and each promisor is bound for the whole. In both kinds of obligation, however, there is one thing at issue: whether one party receives the debt or the other pays it, the obligation of all is destroyed and all are released. 2 Of two promisors, one may be bound purely, and the other at a day or under a condition. The day or the condition will be no hindrance to demanding the debt from the one who is bound purely.
ON THE STIPULATION OF SLAVES, TITLE XVIII.

units.la: SERVVS ex persona domini ius stipulandi habet. Sed & hereditas in plerisque personæ defuncti{d} vicē sustinet. ideoque quod servus hereditarius ante aditam hereditatem stipulatur, adquirit{e} hereditati: per hoc etiam heredi postea facto adquiritur. 1 ¶Sive autem domino, sive sibi, sive{f} coservo suo, sive{g} impersonaliter servus stipuletur: domino adquirit. Idē iuris est & in liberis, qui in potestate patris sunt, ex quibus causis adquirere possūt. 2 ¶Sed cum factum in stipulatione continebitur: omnimodo persona stipulantis continetur: veluti si servus stipuletur, ut{h} sibi ire agere liceat. ipse enim tantum prohiberi non debet, non etiā dominus eius. 3 Servus communis stipulando, vnicuique domino rum pro{i} portione dominij adquirit: nisi{k} iussu v-nius eorum, aut nominatim alicui eorum stipulatus est. tunc enim soli ei adquiritur. Quod servus communis stipulatur{l}, si alteri ex dominis adquiri non potest: solidum alteri adquiritur, veluti si res, quam dari stipulatus est, unius domini sit.
units.tr: A slave acquires the right to stipulate from the person of his master. But an inheritance, in many respects, takes the place of the person of the deceased; hence what a hereditary slave stipulates before the inheritance is entered upon is acquired for the inheritance, and through this it is also acquired for the heir afterwards appointed. 1 Whether the slave stipulates for his master, for himself, for his fellow slave, or impersonally, it is acquired for the master. The same law holds for children who are in the power of their father, from whatever causes they are able to acquire. 2 But when the stipulation contains a deed, the person of the one stipulating is always included: for example, if a slave stipulates that he may go and act freely for himself; for he himself ought not to be prevented, and not his master either. 3 A common slave, stipulating, acquires for each of his masters in proportion to his share of ownership, unless he has stipulated by the order of one of them, or expressly for one of them; for then it is acquired for that one alone. What a common slave stipulates, if it cannot be acquired for one of the masters, is acquired in full for another, for example if the thing which he stipulated to be given belongs to one master.
ON THE DIVISION OF STIPULATIONS, TITLE XIX.

units.la: STIPVLATIONVM{m} aliæ || sunt || iudiciales, aliæ prætoriæ, aliæ conuētionales, aliæ cómunes, tam prætorię, quàm iudiciales. 1 ¶Iudiciales sunt duntaxat, quæ à mero iudicis officio proficiscūtur{n}: veluti de dolo cautio, || vel de{o} persequendo servo, qui in fuga est; restituendóve pretio. ||
units.tr: Some stipulations are judicial, some praetorian, some conventional, and some common, both praetorian and judicial. 1 Judicial stipulations are only those which proceed from the mere office of the judge: for example, a security concerning fraud, or concerning the pursuit of a slave who is in flight, or the restoration of the price.
{a} Var. lect. 2, ff. eo.
{b} L. 7, ff. eo.

units.la: {d} v.l.31. in f. ff.de hær. inst. 2 ¶Prætoriæ ‖ sunt ‖,quæ à mero prætoris officio proficiscuntur{a}, veluti damni infecti, ‖ vel legato-rum ‖.
