Prætorias autem stipulationes sic exaudiri oportet, vt in his etiam contineantur ædilitiæ,nam & hæ à iurisdictione ‖ prætoris ‖ veniunt. 3 ¶Con-tentionales sunt,quæ ex conuentione vtriusque par-tis concipiuntur: ‖hoc est,neque iussu iudicis neque iussu prætoris, sed ex conuentione contrahentium,‖ quarum totidem genera sunt,quot(pene dixerim) re-rum contrahendarum. 4 ¶Communes sunt{b}, veluti rem saluam fore pupillo. Nam & Prætor iubet rem saluam fore pupillo, caueri:& interdum iudex, si aliter hæc res expediri non potest : vel de rato stipulatio.
units.tr: {d} Var. lect. 31, in fine, ff. de hær. inst. 2 Praetorian stipulations are those which proceed from the mere office of the praetor, for example concerning damage not yet done, or concerning legacies. But praetorian stipulations ought to be understood so as to include also those of the aediles, for these too come from the jurisdiction of the praetor. 3 Conventional stipulations are those framed by the agreement of both parties, that is, neither by order of the judge nor by order of the praetor, but by agreement of the contracting parties; and there are as many kinds of these as (I would almost say) of the matters to be contracted. 4 Common stipulations are, for example, that the thing will be safe for the pupil. For the praetor also orders security that the thing be safe for the pupil; and sometimes the judge does so, if the matter cannot otherwise be settled; or a stipulation concerning ratification.
On Useless Stipulations. Title 20.

units.la: MNIS res,quæ dominio nostro subiici-citur, in stipulationem deduci potest : siue mobilis sit,siue soli. 1 ¶At si quis rem,quæ in rerum natura non est, aut{d} esse non potest,dari stipulatus,fuerit:ve-luti Stichum{e}, qui mortuus sit,quem viuere crede-bat:aut hippocentaurum,qui esse non possit{f} : inutilis erit stipulatio. 2 ¶Idem iuris est, {g}si re sacram aut religiosam, quam humani iuris esse credebat:vel rem publicam,quæ vsibus populi perpetuò exposita sit, vt forum,vel theatrum:vel{h} liberum hominem,quem seruum esse credebat, vel cuius comercium non ha-buerit:vel rem{i} suam dari quis stipuletur.Nec in pe-denti erit stipulatio ob id,quod publica res in priua-tum deduci,& ex libero seruus fieri potest{k},& comer-cium adipisci stipulator potest,& res ‖ sua ‖ stipulato-ris esse desinere potest:sed protinus inutilis est{l}.Item contrà,licet initio vtiliter res in stipulatum deducta sit: si ‖ tamè ‖ postea{m} in aliquâ eorum causam,de qui-bus supra dictum est, sine facto ꝓ[?]missoris deuenerit: extinguitur stipulatio . At nec statim ab initio talis stipulatio valebit,Lucium Titium{n},cū seruus erit,d.ve spondes? & similia.quæ enim natura sui dominio no-stro exempta sunt,in obligatione deduci nullo modo naturale est. d.l.83.§.sacram.in f. quia de his recte stipulamur
units.tr: Anything that is subject to our ownership can be brought into a stipulation, whether it is movable or immovable. §1 But if someone stipulates for a thing that does not exist in nature, or cannot exist, such as Stichus, who was dead though he believed him alive, or a hippocentaur, which cannot exist, the stipulation will be useless. §2 The same law applies if someone stipulates for a sacred or religious thing which he believed to be of human right; or for a public thing that is perpetually open to the use of the people, such as the forum or a theatre; or for a free man whom he believed to be a slave, or one who has no commercium; or if someone stipulates for his own thing. Nor is a stipulation left pending merely because a public thing can pass into private ownership, a free man can become a slave, the stipulator can acquire commercium, or his own thing can cease to be his; in such cases it is at once useless. Likewise, conversely, although a stipulation was at first validly made concerning a thing, if afterwards, without any act of the promisor, the thing falls into one of the cases mentioned above, the stipulation is extinguished. Nor will such a stipulation be valid from the start, as in "Do you promise to give Lucius Titius, when he is a slave?" and similar cases. For it is never natural to bind by obligation things that nature has removed from our ownership. See d. l. 83, § sacram, in fin., because we stipulate validly about those things that can at once be subject to our ownership.
because we rightly stipulate concerning these things

units.la: quæ dominio nostro subiici statim possunt d. §. sacram. {m} v.l.98. l.140. §.vlt.de verb.oblig. {n} d.§. sacram. vers. sed hæc. possunt{a} 3 ¶ Si quis{b} alium datúrū faciturum-ve quid promiserit: non obligabitur{c}, veluti si sponderet Titiū quinque aureos daturū. Quòd si effectūrū sit, vt Titius daret, sponderit, obligatur. 4 ¶ Si quis alij, quā{d} ei, cuius iuri subiectus sit, stipuletur: nihil agit{e}. Plane solutio etiā in extraneā personam conferri potest: veluti si quis ita stipuletur, Mihi aut Scio dare spondes? vt obligatio quidā stipulatori adquiratur, solui tamē Scio, etiā{f} inuito eo, recte possit, vt liberatio ipso iure contingat: sed ille aduersus Scium habeat{g} mandati actione. Quòd si quis sibi, & alij, cuius iuri subiectus nō sit, dari decē aureos stipulatur{h}, est: valet quidem stipulatio. sed vtrum totū debeatur stipulatori ||, quod in stipulationem deductum est, an vero pars dimidia dubitatum est: sed placuit, non plus, quā dimidiam partē ei adquiri. Ei ||vero||, qui iuri tuo subiectus est, si stipulatus fis, tibi adquiris: quia vox tua, tanquā fili sit, sicuti & filij vox, tanquā tua intelligitur in{i} iis rebus, quæ tibi adquiri possunt. 5 Præterea inutilis{k} est stipulatio, si quis ||ad ea, quæ interrogatus fuerit, non respondeat: veluti si quis decē aureos à te dari stipuletur, tu quinque promittas, vel contra: aut si ille pure stipuletur, tu sub conditione promittas: vel contra: si modo scilicet id exprimas, id est, si cui sub conditione vel in die stipulanti, tu respondeas, præsenti die spondeo. Nā si hoc solùm respondeas promitto: breuiter videris in eandem diem vel conditionem spopondisse. Neque enim necesse est in respondendo eadē omnia repeti, quæ stipulator expresserit. 6 ¶ Ite inutilis est stipulatio, si vel ab eo stipuleris, qui tuo iure subiectus est, vel si is à te stipuletur. Sed seruus quidem non solùm domino suo obligari non potest, sed{m} ne quidē vlli alij: filij vero familiarum: aliis{n} obligari possunt. 7 ¶ Mutū neque stipulari, neq. promitte-re posse palàm est{o}. quod & in surdo receptum est: quia & is, qui stipulatur, verba promittētis, & is, qui promittit, verba stipulantis audire debet. vnde appa-ret non de eo nos loqui, qui tardius exaudit: sed de eo, qui omnino nō audit. 8 ¶ Furiosus nullum ne-gotium gerere potest: quia nō intelligit, quod agit{p}. 9 ¶ Pupillus omne negotium rectè gerit: ita tamen,
units.tr: which can at once be brought under our ownership: d. §. sacram; see l. 98; l. 140, §. ult., de verb. oblig.; d. §. sacram, vers. sed haec, possunt. 3 ¶ If anyone promises that another will give or do something, he is not bound, as when he promises that Titius will give five gold pieces. But if he promises that he will bring it about that Titius gives, he is bound. 4 ¶ If anyone stipulates for someone other than the person under whose power he is, he accomplishes nothing. But payment can plainly be made to a stranger. For example, if someone stipulates thus: "Do you promise to give to me or to Seius?", so that the obligation is acquired for the stipulator, payment may nonetheless properly be made to Seius, even against his will, so that the release takes effect by law itself; but the stipulator then has an action of mandate against Seius. If anyone stipulates that ten gold pieces be given to himself and to another who is not under his power, the stipulation is indeed valid; but it was doubted whether the whole of what was brought into the stipulation is owed to the stipulator, or only half. It was settled, however, that no more than half is acquired for him. But if you stipulate for one who is under your power, it is acquired for you, because your voice is understood as that of your son, just as the voice of a son is understood as yours, in those matters which can be acquired for you. 5 Moreover, a stipulation is invalid if the one promising does not answer to what he has been asked. For example, if someone stipulates that ten gold pieces be given by you, and you promise five, or the reverse; or if he stipulates unconditionally and you promise under a condition, or the reverse. This holds provided, of course, that you express it, that is, if you answer a man stipulating on a condition or at a day, "I promise on the present day," and not merely "I promise," for in that case you seem to have promised briefly for the same day or condition. For in answering it is not necessary to repeat all the things that the stipulator has expressed. 6 ¶ Likewise a stipulation is invalid if you stipulate from one who is under your power, or if he stipulates from you. But a slave cannot be bound not only to his master but not even to anyone else; sons under power, however, can be bound to others. 7 ¶ It is plain that a mute person can neither stipulate nor promise; and this has been accepted also of a deaf person, because the one who stipulates ought to hear the words of the promiser, and the one who promises ought to hear the words of the stipulator. Hence it is clear that we are not speaking of one who hears more slowly, but of one who does not hear at all. 8 ¶ A madman can conduct no business, because he does not understand what he is doing. 9 ¶ A ward conducts every transaction rightly, yet in such a way that where the authority of a guardian is necessary, the guardian is called in, as when he himself is to be bound; for he can bind another to himself even without his guardian's authority.

units.la: sjofo ff.de fideiuss.l.5. l. 40. de reg.iur. ut ubi tutoris auctoritas necessaria sit, adhibeatur tu-tor: veluti si ipse obligetur. nam alium sibi obligare etiam sine tutoris auctoritate potest. 10 Sed qp[?]
units.tr: ff. de fideiuss. l. 5; l. 40. de reg. iur.: so that where the authority of a tutor is required, a tutor is to be called in, as when he himself is bound; for he can bind himself to another even without the tutor's authority. §10 But what we have said about pupils holds true for both, that is, for those who already have some understanding.

units.la: diximus de pupillis, utrique de iis verum est, qui iam habent aliquē intellectum. nā infans, & qui infantiae proximus est, nō multum à furioso distat: quia huiusmodi aetatis pupilli nullum habet intellectū. Sed in proximis infantiae, propter utilitatem eorū, benignior iuris interpretatio facta est: ut idem iuris habeat, quod pubertati proximi. Sed qui in potestate parentis est pubes, nec auctore quidē patre obligatur. 11 Si impossibilis conditio obligationibus adiiciatur: nihil valet stipulario. Impossibilis autem conditio habetur, cui natura impedimento est, quo min°existat: veluti siquis ita dixerit, Si digito caelum attigero, dare spondes? At si ita stipuletur, Si digito caelum attigero, dare spondes? pure facta obligatio intelligitur, ideoque statim peti poterit. 11 Ite verborum obligatio in praesentes[?] non fui-[?] ter absentes concepta, inutilis est. Sed cum hoc materia litium contentiosis hominibus praestabat, forte post tempus tales allegationes opponentibus, & nō praesentes fuisse vel se vel aduersarios suos contendentibus: ideo nostra constitutio propter celeritatē dirimendarum litium introducta est, quam ad Caesarienses aduocatos scripsimus: per quā dispositum, tales scripturas, quae praesto esse partes indicat, omnino esse credendas, nisi is, qui talibus utitur improbis allegationibus, manifestissimis probationibus vel per scripturā, vel per testes idoneos adprobauerit, toto eo die quo conficiebatur instrumentum, sese vel aduersarium suum in aliis locis fuisse. 12 Post mortem suam dati sibi nemo stipulari poterat: nō magis, quā post eius mortem, à quo stipulabatur. Ac nec is, qui in alicuius potestate est, post mortem eius stipulari poterat: quia patris vel domini voce loqui videretur. Sed & si quis ita stipulatur, Pridie quā moriar, vel pridie quā moriēris, dare spondes? inutilis erat stipulatio. Sed cum (ut iā dictum est) ex consensu contrahentium stipulationes valeant: placuit nobis etiā in hunc iuris articulum necessaria inducere emendatione, ut sive post mortem, sive pridie quā moriatur stipulator, sive promissor, stipulatio concepta sit: stipulatio valeat. 13 Ite si quis ita stipulatur, admittatur probatio absentiae: & negatiua quae directò probari nequit, per obliquum probari possit.
units.tr: For an infant, and one who is closest to infancy, does not differ much from a madman, because pupils of that age have no understanding. But for those nearest to infancy, the interpretation of the law has been made more lenient for their benefit, so that they have the same law as those nearest to puberty. But a pubescent son who is in his father's power is not bound even with his father's authority. §11 If an impossible condition is added to an obligation, the stipulation is worth nothing. A condition is held to be impossible when nature stands in the way of its existence, as when someone says, "If I touch heaven with my finger, do you promise to give?" But if the stipulation is framed thus, "If I do not touch heaven with my finger, do you promise to give?", the obligation is understood to be made outright, and therefore can be demanded at once. §11 Likewise, a verbal obligation framed for persons present, and not for absent ones, is useless. But since this gave occasion for lawsuits to contentious men, who after some time, opposing such allegations, contended that either they or their adversaries had not been present, our constitution was introduced for the speedy settlement of disputes, which we wrote to the Caesarian advocates. By it we ordained that such writings, which show that the parties were present, are wholly to be believed, unless he who uses such dishonest allegations proves by most manifest proofs, either by a document or by suitable witnesses, that on the whole day on which the instrument was drawn up he or his adversary was in other places. §12 No one could stipulate for something given to him after his own death, nor after the death of the person from whom he was stipulating. Nor could one who is in another's power stipulate after that person's death, since he would seem to speak with the voice of his father or master. But also if someone stipulates, "The day before I die, or the day before you die, do you promise to give?", the stipulation was useless. But since, as has been said, stipulations are valid by the consent of the contracting parties, we have resolved to introduce a necessary correction into this article of law as well, so that whether the stipulation is framed after the death of the stipulator or the promisor, or the day before the stipulator dies, the stipulation shall be valid. §13 Likewise, if someone stipulates thus, let proof of absence be admitted, and a negative fact which cannot be proved directly may be proved indirectly.

units.la: {h} l.ur. i.vlt. Cod.de contr.stipul. pulat°erat, si nauis ex Asia venerit{a}, hodie dare spodes? inutilis erat stipulatio, quia prępostere concepta est. Sed quum Leo inclytę recordationis, quę prępostera nuncupatur, non esse reiiciendā existimauerit: nobis placuit, & huic p-sectum robur accomodare, vt nō solum in dotib{b}, sed etiā in omnibus valeat huiusmodi coceptio stipulationis.
units.tr: {h} l. ult. Cod. de contr. stipul.: if someone had stipulated, "If the ship comes from Asia, do you promise to give today?", the stipulation was useless, because it was framed back to front (praeposterously). But since Leo of illustrious memory judged that this so-called praeposterous form should not be rejected, we have decided also to give full force to it, so that this kind of stipulation is valid not only in dowries but in all cases.

units.la: ¶14 Ita aute stipulatio concepta, veluti si Titius dicat, cum{c} morior, dare spodes? vel cū morieris? & apud veteres utilis erat, & nunc valet.
units.tr: §14 A stipulation framed thus, as when Titius says, "When I die, do you promise to give?" or "When you die?", was useful among the older jurists and is valid now.

units.la: ¶15 Ite post{d} mortem alterius rectè stipulamur.
units.tr: We may also validly stipulate after the death of another.

units.la: ¶16 Si scriptum in instrumento fuerit, pmifille aliquē: perin-de habetur{e}, atq. si interrogatione praecedēte respō-sum sit.
units.tr: If it is written in the instrument that someone has promised, it is held to be just as if the promise had been given in answer to a preceding question.

units.la: ¶17 Quotiens plures res una stipulatione comprehenduntur, si quidē promissor simpliciter respondeat, dare spondeo: propter omnes tenetur{f}. Si vero unā ex his, vel quasdā daturum se spoponderit: obli-gatio{g} in iis, pro quibᵛ spoponderit, contrahitur. Ex pluribus enim stipulationibus una, vel quedā videtur esse perfecte, singulas enim res stipulari, & ad singulas respondere debemus.
units.tr: Whenever several things are included in one stipulation: if the promisor simply answers, "I promise to give," he is bound for all of them. But if he has promised to give only one of them, or some of them, the obligation is contracted only for those things for which he has promised. For a stipulation made for several things is in effect several stipulations, one or some of which may be perfected; we must stipulate for each thing separately and answer to each separately.

units.la: ¶18 Alteri{h} stipulari (ut supra dictū est) nemo potest. [illegible, ~8 letters] enim sunt huiusmodi ||stipulationes vel|| obligationes ad hoc, ut unusquisq. adquirat sibi, quod sua interest, ceterū si alij detur, nihil interest stipulatoris. Plane si quis ve-lit hoc facere, poenā stipulari coueniet ut nisi ita fa-ctum sit, ut est comprehensum, committatur poenę stipulatio etiā ei, cuius nihil interest. Poenā enim cum stipulatur quis, non illud inspicitur, q interest eius, sed quę sit quātitas in codicione stipulationis. Ergo quis [ita] stipuletur, Titio dari? nihil agit. sed adiecerit poenā, nisi dederis, tot aureos dare spondes? tunc committitur stipulatio.
units.tr: No one can stipulate for another, as was said above. [illegible] For stipulations or obligations of this kind are made so that each person may acquire for himself what is in his own interest; but if something is given to another, it is of no interest to the stipulator. Clearly, however, if someone wishes to do this, he should stipulate a penalty, so that if the thing is not done as agreed, the stipulation of the penalty falls due, even in favour of the person in whose interest nothing lies. For when someone stipulates a penalty, one looks not at what is in his interest, but at the amount named in the terms of the stipulation. So if someone stipulates, "Do you promise to give to Titius?", he gains nothing. But if he adds a penalty, "If you do not give, do you promise to give ten gold pieces?", then the stipulation falls due.

units.la: ¶19 Sed ||&|| si quis stipuletur sibi, cū eius interesset, placuit stipulationē valere. Nā{i} si is, qui pupilli tutelā administrare coeperat, cesserit administratione cōtutori suo, & stipuletur re pupilli salua fore: quoniā interest stipulatoris fieri, q stipulatus est (cum obligat futurus sit pupillo, si male res gesserit) tenet obligatio. Ergo etsi quis pcuratori suo dari stipulat fit: habebit vires stipulatio. Etsi credito-ri suo ||quis stipulat fit||: quod sua interest, ne forte vel poena committatur, vel prędia distrahatur, quę pignori data erat: valet stipulatio.
units.tr: But if someone stipulates for himself, where it is in his interest, the stipulation has been held to be valid. For if a man who had begun to administer a ward's guardianship has handed over the administration to his co-guardian, and stipulates that the ward's property will be safe, the obligation holds, because it is in the interest of the stipulator that what he stipulated should come about (since he will be liable to the ward if he manages the affairs badly). So too, if someone stipulates that something be given to his agent, the stipulation will have force. And if someone stipulates for his creditor, that is in his own interest, lest a penalty be incurred or the estates given in pledge be sold off, the stipulation is valid.

units.la: 20 ¶Versa vice, q aliū factūrum, pmisit, videtur in ea esse causa, ut non teneatur, nisi poena ipse pmiserit.
units.tr: Conversely, one who has promised that another will do something is held to be in such a position that he is not bound, unless he has himself promised the penalty.

units.la: 21 ¶Ite nemo suam futurā{k}, in eum casum, quo sua sit, utiliter stipulatur. 22 ¶Si de alia re stipulator senserit, de alia ꝓmissor: ꝓinde nulla cōtrahitur obligatio, ac si ad interrogatum respōsum[?] non esset: veluti si hominem Stichum a te quis stipulatus fuerit{a}, tu de Pamphilo senseris, quę Stichum vocari crediderìs. 23 ¶Quod turpi{b} ex causa ꝓmissum est: veluti si quis homicidiū vel sacrilegium se facturum promittat: non valet. 24 ¶Cum quis sub aliqua conditione stipulatus fuerit: licèt ante conditionē decesserit: postea existente conditione heres eius agere potest{c}. Idé est & ex ꝓmisso ris parte. 25 ¶Qui hoc anno, aut hoc mense dari stipulatus est: nisi{d} omnibus partibus anni vel mensis praeteritis, non recte petet. Si fundum dari stipuleris, vel hominem: non poteris continuo agere: nisi{e} tantum spatium praeterierit, quo traditio fieri posit.
units.tr: Likewise, no one validly stipulates for something that will be his own in the event that it becomes his. If the stipulator intends one thing and the promisor another, no obligation is contracted, just as if no answer had been given to the question; for example, if someone has stipulated for the slave Stichus from you, and you understood him to mean Pamphilus, whom you believed to be called Stichus. A promise made on a disgraceful ground is void: for example, if someone promises that he will commit murder or sacrilege, it is not valid. When someone has stipulated under some condition, even if he dies before the condition is fulfilled, his heir can sue once the condition has been fulfilled afterwards. The same applies on the side of the promisor. One who has stipulated for something to be given this year or this month cannot rightly demand it until all parts of the year or month have passed. If you stipulate for a farm or a slave to be given, you cannot sue at once, unless enough time has passed for delivery to be made.
ON SURETIES (DE FIDEIUSSORIBUS), TITLE XXI.

units.la: Reo[?] eo qui promittit, solent alij obligari, qui fideiussores appellantur: quos homines accipere solent, dum curant, vt diligentius sibi cautum sit. 1 ¶In omnibus autem obligationibus adsumi possunt: id est, siue re, siue verbis, siue literis, siue consensu contractę fuerint. At nec illud quidem interest, vtrum ciuilis, an naturalis sit obligatio, cui adijciȣr fideiussor: adeo quidem, vt pro seruo quoq. obligetur, siue extraneus sit, qui fideiussorem à seruo accipiat, siue ipse dominus in id, quod sibi naturaliter debetur. 2 ¶Fideiussor non tantum ipse obligatur, sed etiam heredem relinquit obligatum. 3 ¶Fideiussor & {g}praecedere obligatione, & sequi potest. 4 ¶Si plures sint fideiussores: quotquot erunt numero, singuli in solidum tenentur. Itaque liberum est creditori, à quo velit solidum petere. Sed ex epistola diui Hadriani copellitur creditor à singulis, qui{h} modo soluendo sunt litis contestatę tempore, partes petere. Idēoque si quis ex fideiussoribus eo tempore soluendo non sit: hoc cęteros onerat. Sed si ab vno fideiussore creditor totum consequutus fuerit: huiꝰ sc-[illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: Others are usually bound along with the one who promises; these are called sureties (fideiussores). People are accustomed to take them so that they may be more carefully secured. 1. Sureties may be taken in all obligations, that is, whether the contract was made by a thing (re), by words, by writing, or by consent. It makes no difference whether the obligation to which a surety is added is civil or natural. Indeed, a surety is bound even for a slave, whether the outsider who takes the surety from a slave is the one, or the master himself is the one, for what is naturally owed to him. 2. A surety is not only bound himself, but also leaves his heir bound. 3. A surety can both precede the obligation and follow it. 4. If there are several sureties, each one, however many they are, is held for the whole. Therefore the creditor is free to demand the whole from whichever one he wishes. But by an epistle of the divine Hadrian the creditor is compelled to demand from each only his share, those who are solvent at the time of litis contestation. So if one of the sureties is not solvent at that time, the loss falls on the others. But if the creditor has recovered the whole from one surety: this [illegible]

units.la: copellitur quoque creditor principalem praesentem primo conuenire: aut eo absente, definire fideiussori certum tempus, intra quod principalem sistat, nouel.4.c.1.
units.tr: The creditor is also compelled to sue the principal debtor first, if he is present; or, if he is absent, to fix a certain time for the surety within which he must produce the principal. Nov. 4, c. 1.
{g} v.l. 4, in sin. ff. eo.
{h} v.l. 50, in pr. ff. de pecul.

units.la: {i} v.l.3.C.eo. {k} v.l.28. ff.eo. lius detrimetū erit, si is, pro quo fideiussit, solvendo nō sit{4}: & sibi imputare debet, cum potuerit iuvari ex epistola divi Hadriani, & desiderare, ut pro partein se detur actio.
units.tr: {i} v.l. 3, C. eo. {k} v.l. 28, ff. eo. The loss will be his if the one for whom he stood surety is not solvent; and he must impute it to himself, since he could have been helped by the epistle of the divine Hadrian, and ask that the action be assigned to him for a share.

units.la: 5 ¶Fideiussores ita obligari non possunt{b}, ut plus debeat, quàm debet is, pro quo obligantur. Nā eorum obligatio, accessio est principa-lis obligationis: nec plus in accessione potest esse, quàm in principali re. At ex diversō, ut minus debeat aut obligari possunt. Itaq. si reus decē aureos {c}promi-serit, fideiussor in quinque recte obligatur: cōtrà vero obligari nō poterit. Itē si ille pure promiserit: fideiussor sub conditione promittere poterit: contrà vero non poterit. Non solum autē in quantitate{c}, sed etiam in tempore minus aut plus intelligitur. Plus est enim statim aliquid dare: minus est post tempus dare{d}.
units.tr: 5. Sureties cannot be bound so as to owe more than the one for whom they are bound. For their obligation is an accessory of the principal obligation, and there can be no more in the accessory than in the principal thing. But conversely they may be bound to owe less. So if the debtor has promised ten aurei, the surety is validly bound for five; but conversely he cannot be bound for more. Likewise, if the principal promised purely, the surety can promise under a condition; but conversely he cannot. Moreover, more or less is understood not only in amount but also in time. For to give something at once is more; to give it after a time is less.

units.la: 6 ¶Si quid aut fideiussor pro reo soluerit{e}: eius re cuperandi causa habet cum eo mandati iudicium{f}.
units.tr: 6. If the surety pays anything on behalf of the debtor, he has against him the action of mandate for the purpose of recovering it.

units.la: 7 ¶Græcè etiā fideiussor ita accipitur, τῆς ἐμῆς [?]ἀπ[?]ὸς ἐγὼ. i. mea fide iubeo ego. ¶sed & si dixerit ζεὺς sive ξάλομαι. i. volo, sed & ὀμνύω. i. affirmo: p eo erit, ac si dixerit λέγω. i. dico g. 8 ¶In stipulationibus fideiussorum sciendum est hoc generaliter accipi: ut quodcunq. scriptum sit quasi actū, videatur etiam actum. Ideoq; constat, si quis scripserit se fideiussisse: videri{h} omnia solenniter acta.
units.tr: 7. In Greek too the surety is understood in this way: τῇ ἐμῇ πίστει ἐγγυῶ, that is, "I bind myself by my faith." But even if he says ἐθέλω, that is "I will," or ὀμνύω, that is "I swear," it will be the same as if he had said λέγω, that is "I say." 8. In stipulations of sureties it must be understood generally that whatever is written as if done is also to be taken as done. Therefore it is settled that if someone writes that he has stood surety, all things are considered to have been done with the proper solemnities.
ON OBLIGATIONS BY WRITING (DE LITERARUM OBLIGATIONIBUS), TITLE XXII.

units.la: OLIM scriptura fiebat obligatio, quæ nominibus fieri dicebatur, quæ nomina hodie non sunt in vsu. Plane si quis debere se scripserit, quod sibi numeratū nō est de pecunia minimè numerata, post multum temporis exceptionem opponere non (q arbitrio iudicis finitur) si tempus solutionis infec-tum, si ipse fideiussor ad solutionem condemnatus est{f}: sed quomodo? v.l.20. in sin.ff.mandat. Nisi pro inuito aut pro eo qui mādare non potuit, nisi donandi & nunquam agendi animo fideiusit. adde.l.12.C.cm.l.8.ff.eo.{h} §.16.§.tit.prox.l.30.l.134.§.pen.de verb.obl.j.l.1.C.de con-trab.stip.{i} & earum speciebus & effectu. v. quæ notaui novel.73. {k} priuatim vel publicē, si modo in huiusmodi publica cau-tione numerationis non sit facta mentio, alias auctoritas instru-menti publici, onus probandi transfert in negantem: l.18.Cod. de probat. §.11.inf.5.tit.prox.non.73.c.2.3.4.5. {l} hanc exce-ptionem Theophilus vocat [?]ἀντιγραφὴν [?]. {m} An hæc exceptio locum habeat in solo mutuo. v.l.3. C.de non num.pec.
units.tr: Formerly an obligation was created by writing, which was said to be made "by names" (nominibus); these entries are not in use today. Plainly, if someone writes that he owes what has not in fact been counted out to him, money not really counted out, he may not, after much time has passed, raise the exception (which is decided at the discretion of the judge) if the time for payment has gone by unperformed, or if the surety himself has been condemned to pay. But how? See law 20 at the end of the Digest on mandates, unless he stood surety against the wishes of the debtor, or for one who could not give a mandate, unless he stood surety with the intention of giving and never of suing. Add law 12, C.; law 8, ff. eo. {h} §16; §tit. prox.; law 30; law 134, §pen., de verb. obl.; law 1, C. de contrab. stip. {i} and its species and effect; see what I noted in Nov. 73. {k} Privately or publicly, if only in such a public security no mention of the counting out has been made; otherwise the authority of a public instrument shifts the burden of proof onto the one denying: law 18, Cod. de probat.; §11, inf. 5, tit. prox.; Nov. 73, c. 2, 3, 4, 5. {l} Theophilus calls this exception [ἀντιγραφή]. {m} Whether this exception has a place in a loan of money alone: see law 3, C. de non num. pec.

units.la: {l} Lim. ... potest. hoc enim sæpissime constitutum est. sic fit,ut & hodie,dum quæri non potest, scriptura obligetur: & ex ea nascatur condictio, cessante scilicet verbo-rum obligatione.
units.tr: {l} Lim. ... can be sought. For this has very often been settled. Thus it happens that even today, while it cannot be sought, the writing binds, and from it a condictio arises, the obligation by words having of course ceased.

units.la: Multum autem tempus in hac ex-ceptione antea quidem ex principalibus constitutio-nibus usque ad quinquennium procedebat. sed ne creditores diutius possint suis pecuniis forsitan de-fraudari: per constitutionem nostram tempus coar-ctatum [?] est, ut ultra {a} biennii metas huiusmodi exce-ptio {b} minime {c} extenuatur {d}.
units.tr: Formerly, under the principal constitutions, the time allowed for this exception ran up to five years. But so that creditors may not be defrauded of their money for too long, by our constitution the time has been shortened, so that beyond the limits of two years such an exception is in no way weakened.

units.la: DE OBLIGATIONIBUS ex consensu. TITUL. XXIII.
units.tr: DE OBLIGATIONIBUS ex consensu. TITUL. XXIII.

units.la: CONSENSU fiunt obligationes in emptionibus, venditionibus, locationibus, conductionibus, societatibus, mandatis. Ideo autem istis modis obligatio dicitur consensu contrahi: quia neque scriptu-ra, neque præsentia omnimodo opus est. at nec dari quicquam necesse est, ut substantiam capiat obliga-tio: sed sufficit eos, qui negotia gerunt, consentire. Unde inter absentes quoque talia negotia cotrahun-tur, veluti per epistolam, vel per nuntium. Item in hi, [?] contractibus alter alteri obligatur in id, quod alterum ex bono & æquo præstare oportet {e}, cum alioqui in verborum obligationibus alius stipulatur, alius promittat ||{f}.
units.tr: Obligations arise by consent in sales, purchases, lettings, hirings, partnerships and mandates. The reason these contracts are said to bind by consent is that neither writing nor the presence of the parties is needed in any way. Nor is it necessary that anything be given for the obligation to take effect; it is enough that those who transact the business agree. Hence such dealings are also contracted between absent persons, as for instance by letter or by messenger. Likewise in these contracts each party is bound to the other for whatever ought to be performed between them according to good faith and fairness, whereas in obligations by words one person stipulates and the other promises.

units.la: DE EMPTIONE ET venditione, TITUL. XXIIII.
units.tr: On Buying and Selling, Title 24.

units.la: EMPTIO & VENDITIO contrahitur {b} si-mulatque de pretio conuenerit: quam-uis nondum pretium numeratum sit, ac ne arrha quidem data fuerit. Nam quod arrhæ nomine datur, argumentum{i} est.
units.tr: A contract of buying and selling is made as soon as the parties agree on the price, even though the price has not yet been paid and no earnest money has been given. For what is given as earnest money is evidence of the contract.

units.la: {f} Note: printed "||" sign as in the original. {a}emptionis & venditionis contractæ. Sed hoc quidem de ||emptionibus & venditionibus quę sine scriptura consistunt, obtinere oportet: nam nihil à nobis in huiusmodi emptionibus & venditionib. innovatū est, in {b}iis autem, quę scriptura conficiuntur, non aliter perfectam esse venditionem constituimus, nisi & instrumenta emptionis fuerit conscripta, vel manu propria contrahentium, vel ab alio quidem scripta, à contrahentibus autem subscripta: & si per tabellionem fiunt, nisi & completiones acceperint, & fuerint partibus absoluta. Donec enim aliquid deest ex his{c} & pœnitentiæ locus est, & potest emptor vel venditor sine pœna recedere ab emptione || & venditione||. Ita tamen impune || eis recedere|| concedimus{d}, nisi iam arrharum nomine aliquid fuerit datum. hoc enim subsequuto: sive in scriptis, sive sine scriptis venditio celebrata est: is, qui recusat adimplere contractum, si quidem est emptor: perdit, quod dedit. si vero venditor: duplum restituere compellitur, licet super arrhis nihil expressum est. Pretium autem constitui oportet. nā nulla emptio sine {e}pretio esse potest.
units.tr: This rule must hold for buyings and sellings that exist without writing, since we have introduced nothing new into such purchases and sales. But for those that are made in writing, we decide that the sale is not complete unless the instrument of purchase has been drawn up, either in the hand of the contracting parties or written by another and signed by the parties. If they are made through a notary, they must also have received their completions and been finished for both parties. For as long as something is lacking from these, there is room for repentance, and buyer or seller may withdraw from the purchase and sale without penalty. We allow them to withdraw in this way without consequence, unless something has already been given as earnest money. For once this has happened, whether the sale was concluded in writing or without writing, the one who refuses to fulfil the contract loses what he gave if he is the buyer; if he is the seller, he is compelled to restore double, even though nothing was said about the earnest money. But a price must be fixed, for no purchase can exist without a price.

units.la: 1 ¶ Sed & {f}certum esse pretium debet, alioqui si inter aliquos ita convenerit, ut quanti Titius rem æstimaverit, tanti sit empta: inter veteres satis abundeque hoc dubitabatur, constaretne venditio, an non. Sed nostra {g}decisio ita hoc constituit, ut quotiens sic composita sit venditio, quanti ille æstimaverit, sub hac conditione staret contractus: ut si quidem ille, qui nominatus est, pretium definierit: || tunc || omnimodo secundum eius æstimationem & pretium persolvatur, & res tradatur, & venditio ad effectum perducatur: emptore quidem ex {h}empto actione, venditore ex {i}vendito egente. Sin autem ille, qui nominatus est, vel noluerit, vel non potuerit {k}pretium definire: tunc pro nihilo esse venditionem quasi nullo pretio statuto. Quod ius cum in venditionibus nobis placuit: non est absurdum & {l}in locationibus. & ||in || conductionibus trahere.
units.tr: 1. The price must also be certain. Otherwise, if between certain parties it was agreed that the thing should be bought for as much as Titius valued it, there was among the ancients a great and considerable doubt whether the sale would stand or not. Our decision settles this: whenever a sale is arranged in this way, for as much as he values it, the contract stands under this condition: if he who was named fixes the price, then in every case the price is paid according to his estimate, the thing is delivered, and the sale is carried into effect, the buyer having the action on purchase and the seller the action on sale. But if he who was named either is unwilling or unable to fix the price, then the sale counts for nothing, as though no price had been set. Since we have approved this law for sales, it is not absurd to extend it to lettings and hirings as well.

units.la: 2 ¶ Item pretium in {m}numerata pecunia consistere debet. Nam in exteris rebus, an pretium esse posset, valde quærebatur: veluti an homo, aut fundus, aut toga alterius rei pretium esse posset. || Et || Sabinus & Cassius etiam in alia reputabant {n}pretium posse, consistere, unde illud est, quod vulgo dicebatur, permutatione {o}rerum emptionem & venditionem contrahi, eámque speciem emptionis & venditionis vetustissimam esse: argumentóque vtebantur Græco poëta Homero, quì aliquam partem exercitus Achiuorum vinu sibi cō-parasse ait, permutatis quibusdam rebus, his verbis:
units.tr: 2. Likewise the price must consist of money that is counted out. For in other things it was much disputed whether they could serve as a price: for example, whether a man, or a farm, or a toga could be the price of another thing. Sabinus and Cassius thought that other things too could constitute a price. Hence came the common saying that a purchase and sale is contracted by the exchange of things, and that this kind of purchase and sale is the most ancient. They relied on the Greek poet Homer, who says that a part of the army of the Achaeans got wine for themselves by exchanging certain things, in these words:
Then the long-haired Achaeans went up: some with bronze [Ἔνθ' ἄρ' ἀνίοντο κάρηκομόωντες Ἀχαιοί]

units.la: Ἄλλοι μὲν χαλκῷ[?] ἄλλοι δ' αἰθομένοιο σιδήρου[?]
units.tr: others with bronze of the blazing iron [Ἄλλοι μὲν χαλκῷ, ἄλλοι δ' αἰθομένοιο σιδήρου]
others with hides of oxen [Ἄλλοι δὲ βοέῃσι]
others with slaves [ἄλλοι δ' ἀνδραπόδεσσιν].
That is:

units.la: Hinc sibi certatim gentis de more comati / Vina parant Graij ære dato, fulgentéque ferro, / Tergoribúsque, bubus sed & ipsis, rúancipúsque[?].
units.tr: Hence, as the long-haired Greeks eagerly, each in turn according to custom, get wine for themselves, giving bronze and gleaming iron, hides and oxen too, and slaves.

units.la: Diuersæ scholæ auctores{a} contrà sentiebant: aliúdq. esse existimabát permutationem rerū, aliud emptio-nem & venditionem: alioqui non posse rem expediri, permutatis rebus, quæ videatur res venisse, & quæ pre-tij nomine data esse. nã vtranque videri & venisse, & pretij nomine datam esse, ratione non pati. Sed Pro-culi sententia, dicentis permutationem propriâ esse speciem contractus à venditione separatam, merito præualuit: cùm & ipse aliis Homericis versibus adiu-uabatur, & validioribus rationibus argumentabatur: quod & anteriores diui principes admiserunt, & in nostris Digestis latius significatur.
units.tr: The authors of the opposing school held otherwise. They thought that the exchange of things is one thing and buying and selling another. Otherwise, they said, it could not be explained, when things are exchanged, which thing seems to have been sold and which to have been given as the price, since it is unreasonable to hold that each was both sold and given as price. But the opinion of Proculus prevailed, rightly so, saying that exchange is a kind of contract of its own, separate from sale. He was also supported by other Homeric verses and argued with stronger reasons. The earlier divine emperors admitted this, and it is set out more fully in our Digest.

units.la: 3 ¶ Quum autem emptio & venditio contracta fit (quod effici di-ximus{b}, simulatque de pretio conuenerit, cùm sine scriptura res agitur) periculum rei venditæ statim{c} ad emptorem pertinet, tametsi{d} adhuc ea res emptori tradita non sit. Itaque si homo mortuus fit, vel aliqua parte corporis læsus fuerit, aut ædes totæ vel aliqua ex parte incendio consumptæ fuerint: aut fun-dus vi fluminis totus vel aliqua ex parte ablatus fit, siue etiam inundatione aquæ aut arboribus turbine deiectis longè minor aut deterior esse coeperit: emptoris damnum est, cui necesse est, licèt rem nó fuerit nactus, pretium soluere. Quicquid enim{e} sine dolo & culpa venditoris accidit, in eo venditor se-curus est. Sed & si post emptionem fundo aliquid{f} per alluuionem accesserit: ad emptoris commodum pertinet. Nam & commodum eius esse debet, cuius periculum est. Quòd si fugerit homo, qui venit, aut subrectus[?] fuerit, ita vt neque dolus, neque culpa venditoris interuenerit: animaduertendum{g} erit, an custodiam eius vsque ad traditionem venditor sus-ceperit, Sanè enim si suscêperit: ad ipsius periculum casus pertinet. si non susceperit: securus est. Idem & in cæteris animalibus, cæterisque rebus intelligimus. Vtique tamen vindicationem rei & condictionem exhibere debebit emptori: quia sane qui nondum rem emptori tradidit,adhuc ipse dominus est.Idem etiam est de furti & de damni iniuriæ actione.
units.tr: 3. When a purchase and sale is contracted (which, as we said, takes effect as soon as they agree on the price, when the matter is transacted without writing), the risk of the thing sold passes at once to the buyer, even though the thing has not yet been handed over to him. So if the slave who was sold dies, or is injured in some part of the body, or if a house is wholly or partly destroyed by fire, or a farm is wholly or partly carried off by the force of a river, or if through flooding or trees thrown down by a whirlwind it begins to be much smaller or worse, the loss is the buyer's, who must pay the price even though he has not received the thing. For whatever happens without the fraud or fault of the seller, the seller is safe. But also if, after the purchase, something has been added to the farm by alluvion, it belongs to the buyer's advantage, for the advantage ought to belong to him whose the risk is. But if the slave who was sold has run away, or has been stolen, without any fraud or fault of the seller intervening, it must be considered whether the seller undertook custody of him up to the delivery. For if he undertook it, the chance falls on his own risk; if he did not undertake it, he is safe. We understand the same of other animals and other things. Nevertheless the seller must provide the buyer with the action of vindication and the condiction, since surely he who has not yet handed the thing over to the buyer is still himself the owner. The same holds for the action of theft and the action for wrongful damage.

units.la: 4 ¶Emptio tam sub conditione, quàm pure contrahi potest. Sub conditione,veluti, Si Stichus intra certum diem tibi placuerit, erit tibi emptus aureis tot. ꝯ
units.tr: 4. A purchase can be contracted under a condition as well as purely. Under a condition, for example: "If Stichus pleases you within a certain day, he shall be bought by you for so many gold pieces."

units.la: 5 ¶Loca sacra vel religiosa, item publica (veluti forum, basilicam) frustra quis sciens emit. quæ tamen si pro profanis vel priuatis deceptus à venditore quis emerit: habebit actionem ex empto, quod non habere ei liceat, vt consequatur, quod sua interest eum deceptum non esse. Idem iuris est, si hominem liberum pro seruo emerit.
units.tr: 5. Whoever knowingly buys sacred or religious places, or public ones (such as the forum or a basilica), buys in vain. Yet if someone, deceived by the seller, has bought such places as profane or private, he will have an action on the purchase, by which he may obtain what his interest was in not being deceived. The same law holds if he has bought a free man as a slave.

units.la: DE LOCATIONE ET conductione §, TITVL. XXV.
units.tr: Concerning Letting and Hiring, §, Title XXV.

units.la: LOCATIO & conductio proxima est emptioni & venditioni, iisdemque iuris regulis consistit. Nam vt emptio & venditio ita contrahitur,si de pretio conuenerit: sic & locatio & conductio ita contrahi intelligitur, si merces constituta sit.& compellit locatori quidem locati actio, conductori vero conducti. 1 ¶Et quæ suprà diximus, si alieno arbitrio pretium promissum fuerit: eadem & de locatione & conductione dicta esse intelligimus,si alieno arbitrio merces permissa fuerit.Qua de causa si fulloni polieda curandæve, ac sarcinatori sarcieda ve stimenta quis dederit, nulla statim mercede constituta, sed postea tantum daturus, quantum inter eos conuenerit:non proprie locatio & conductio cōtrahi intelligitur,sed eo nomine actio præscriptis verbis datur. 2 Præterea sicut vulgò quærebatur, an permutatis rebus emptio & venditio contraheretur: ita quæri solebat de locatione & conductione, si forte rem aliquam vtendam sine fruendam tibi aliquis dederit: & inuicem à te vtendam sine fruendam aliam ‖ rem ‖ acceperit. Et placuit non esse locationem & conductionem, sed proprium genus contractus. veluti si cum vnum bouem quis habet, & vicinus eius vnum, placuerit inter eos, vt per denos dies inuicem boues commodarent,vt opus facerent,& apud alterum ‖ alterius ‖ bos perierit:neque locati,neque conducti, neque commodati com-petit actio: quia non fuit comodatum gratuitum.ve-rum prescriptis verbis agendum est.
units.tr: Letting and hiring is closest to buying and selling, and rests on the same rules of law. For just as a sale is made when agreement is reached on the price, so letting and hiring is understood to be made when the rent has been fixed. The action of the lessor (locati) and that of the lessee (conducti) arise in the same way. 1 And what we said above, that if the price was promised at another's discretion, is also to be understood of letting and hiring, if the rent was left to another's discretion. For this reason, if someone gives clothes to a fuller to be cleaned or cared for, or to a tailor to be mended, without any rent being fixed at once but only with the intention of paying afterwards what they agree, letting and hiring is not properly understood to have been made. Instead an action is given on that ground, with prescribed words. 2 Furthermore, just as it was commonly asked whether a sale and purchase were made when goods were exchanged, so it used to be asked about letting and hiring: if someone gives you a thing to be used or enjoyed, and in turn receives from you another thing to be used or enjoyed. It was decided that this is not letting and hiring but a distinct kind of contract. For example, if one man has an ox and his neighbour has one, and they agree that for ten days in turn they will lend each other their oxen so that they may do their work, and the ox of one of them dies with the other: no action of letting (locati), of hiring (conducti), or of loan (commodati) lies, because the loan was not gratuitous. Instead the case must be brought with prescribed words.

units.la: 3 ¶Adeo au-tem aliquam familiaritate{^} inter se videtur,habere emptio & venditio,ite locatio & conductio: vt in qui-busdam causis quaeri soleat, vtru emptio & venditio contrahatur,an locatio & conductio. vt ecce de praediis,quae perpetuo{*} quibusdam fruenda traduntur, id est,vt{b} quamdiu pensio fiue reditus pro his domino praefetur,neque ipsi conductori,neque heredi eius cuiue conductor heresve eius id praedium ven-diderit,aut donauerit,aut dotis nomine dederit, a-lienauerit[?], quocunque modo alienauerit, auferre liceat. Sed talis contractus,quia inter veteres dubitabatur, & a quibusdam locatio,a quibusdam venditio existimabatur:lex Zenoniana{c} lata est,quae emphyteuseos contractus propriam statuit naturae, neque ad locatione, neque ad venditione inclinante, sed suis{d} pactionibus fulciendae: & fi quidem aliquid pactu fuerit, hoc ita obtinere,ac fi naturalis effet contractus. sin autem nihil de periculo rei fuerit pactu: tunc fi quidem totius rei interitus acceferit: ad dominu super hoc redundare periculum . sin autem particularis: ad em-phyteuticarium huiusmodi damnu venire.quo iure vtimur.
units.tr: 3 Indeed, buying and selling and letting and hiring have some such close kinship with each other that in certain cases it is customarily asked whether a sale and purchase or a letting and hiring is made. For example, in the case of estates which are handed over to certain people to be enjoyed in perpetuity, that is, on condition that so long as the rent or revenue is paid to the owner, neither the lessee himself, nor his heir, nor anyone to whom the lessee or his heir has sold, given or conveyed the estate as a dowry, or alienated it by any means, may be deprived of it. But since such a contract was doubted among the ancients, and some thought it a letting and others a sale, the Zenonian law was passed. It established that the contract of emphyteusis has a nature of its own, leaning neither towards letting nor towards sale, but supported by its own agreements. And if any term has been agreed, this holds as if it were a natural element of the contract. But if nothing about the risk of the thing has been agreed, then if the thing has perished entirely, the loss falls on the owner; but if the loss is only partial, it falls on the emphyteuta. This is the law we follow.

units.la: 4 ¶Item queritur,fi{e} cum aurifice Ti-tius conuenerit,vt is ex auro suo certi ponderis certaeque formae annulos ei facerer, & acciperet (verbi gratia) decem aureos: vtrum emptio & venditio, an locatio & conductio contrahi videatur? Cassius ait, materiae quidem emptione & venditione contrahi, operae aute locatione & conductionem. Sed placuit tantum emptionem & venditionem contrahi. Quod fi suum aurum Titius dederit,mercede pro opera con-ftituta: dubium non est,quin locatio & conductio fit.
units.tr: 4 Likewise it is asked: if Titius agreed with a goldsmith that he should make rings of a certain weight and a certain shape from the goldsmith's own gold, and receive (for example) ten gold pieces, is a sale and purchase or a letting and hiring understood to be made? Cassius says that the material is bought and sold, but the labour is let and hired. But it was decided that only a sale and purchase is made. If, however, Titius gives his own gold, with a fee fixed for the work, there is no doubt that a letting and hiring is made.

units.la: 5 ¶Conductor[?] autem omnia fecundum{f} legem conductionis facere debet{g}: & fi quid in lege praeterminiffum fuerit: id ex bono & aequo praestare. Qui pro vsu aut vestimentorum,aut argenti, aut iumenti, mercede aut dedit,aut promisit : ab eo custodia talis desideratur,qualem diligentissimus paterfami-non poterit,nisi is in contrariu protestatus fit: ni-fi Emphiteuta rem deteriore reddidit vel alienauit. Schnid.
units.tr: 5 A lessee must do everything according to the terms of the hiring, and whatever has been omitted from the terms is to be made good according to good faith and fairness. One who has given or promised a rent for the use of clothing, silver or a beast of burden must provide the sort of care that the most diligent householder provides for his own things, unless he has protested to the contrary; and if he has returned the thing in worse condition or alienated it, he must answer for it. Schnid.
{c} l.1. Cod. de iure Emphit.
{e} l.2. §.1. ff. eo. & l.20. 65. de contr. empt.
{f} l.25. §. conductor. ff. cod. l.19. Cod. eod.

units.la: {g} potest autem rem alteri locare. l.6.Cod.eo. [?]iis suis rebus adhibet.quam si praestiterit,& aliquo casu fortuito eam rem amiserit: de restituenda ea non tenebitur. 6 ¶Mortuo conductore intra tempora conductionis,heres eius eodem iure in conductione succedit .
units.tr: {g} The lessee may also let the thing to another. l.6. Cod. eo. He uses it as he uses his own things; and if he has done so, and has lost the thing through some chance event, he will not be bound to restore it. 6 If the lessee dies during the term of the hiring, his heir succeeds to the hiring on the same terms.
ON PARTNERSHIP, TITLE 26

units.la: SOCIETATEM coire solemus aut totorum bonorum, quam Graeci specialiter κοινωνίαν[?] appellant: aut unius alicuius negotiationis,veluti mancipiorum vendendorum emendorumque,aut olei,aut vini,aut frumenti emendi vendendique.
units.tr: We usually enter into partnership either of all goods, which the Greeks specifically call koinōnia [κοινωνία], or of a single line of business, such as buying and selling slaves, or buying and selling oil, wine, or grain.

units.la: 1 ¶Et quidem si nihil de partibus lucri & damni nominatim convenerit: æquales e scilicet partes & in lucro & in damno spectantur. Quòd si expressæ fuerint partes: hæ seruari debent. Nec enim vnquam dubiû fuit,quin valeat conuentio,si duo inter se pacti sint,vt ad vnum quidem duæ partes & lucri & damni pertineant,ad alium tertia. 2 ¶De illa sane conuentione quæsitû est, si Titius & Seius inter se pacti sint,vt ad Titii lucri duæ partes pertineant f, damni tertia: ad Seii duæ partes damni, lucri tertia: an rata debeat haberi conuentio? Quintus Mutius contra naturam societatis Stale pactionem esse exiistimauit, & ob id non esse ratam habendam. Seruius Sulpitius (cuius sententia prævaluit) contra sensit h: quia sæpe quorundam ita pretiosa est opera in societate, vt eos iustum sit conditione meliore in societate admitti. Nam & ita coiri posse societatem non dubitatur, vt alter pecuniam conferat i, alter nō conferat,& tamen lucrum inter eos commune sit, quia sæpe opera alicuius pro k pecunia valet. Et adeo contra Quinti Mutij sententiam obtinuit, vt illud quoq. constituerit posse conuenire, vt quis lucri partem ferat, de damno l non teneatur, quod & ipsum Seruius conuenienter sibi fieri exiistimauit. Quod tamen ita intelligi oportet, vt si in alia re lucrum, in alia damnum illatum sit: compensatione facta, solum, quod superest,
units.tr: 1 Indeed, if nothing has been expressly agreed about the shares of profit and loss, the shares are taken to be equal, both in profit and in loss. But if the shares have been stated, they ought to be kept. It was never doubted that an agreement is valid if two parties agree that two shares of profit and loss go to one partner and a third share to the other. 2 Concerning a different agreement, the question has been raised: if Titius and Seius agree that two shares of Titius's profit go to him and one third of his loss, and that Seius bears two shares of the loss and takes one third of the profit, should the agreement be held valid? Quintus Mucius thought that such an agreement was contrary to the nature of partnership and for that reason should not be held valid. Servius Sulpicius, whose opinion prevailed, thought otherwise, because the work of some people in a partnership is often so valuable that it is fair for them to be admitted on better terms. For it is not doubted that a partnership may be formed in such a way that one partner contributes money and another does not, and yet the profit is shared between them, because one person's labour often counts for as much as another's money. And so Servius's view prevailed over the opinion of Quintus Mucius to such an extent that he also held it could be agreed that one partner takes a share of the profit without being liable for losses, a view Servius himself judged to be consistent with his own position. This, however, must be understood so that if a profit has arisen in one matter and a loss in another, only the balance that remains after set-off is counted as profit.

units.la: tur restituo & ob id nō esse ratā habendā. Ser.Sulpit.sensit,cui sententia contraria prævaluit:quia sæpe,&c. Vvisem.tamen sic interpre- tatur: contra sensit,inquit,nō in genere & quo ad regulam: sed in specie, quo ad exceptionem. i l.1.C.eod. k l.5.§.1.l.52.§.vtrum.ff.eod. l pecuniæ, sc. à socio collatæ,cū satis ei fit operas suas perdere: q: locū nō haberet in eo q pecunias coferret. v.Anton.Gry.2.obs.34. intelligatur lucro esse.
units.tr: ...and for that reason should not be held valid. Servius Sulpicius held the contrary view, but the opposite opinion prevailed, because often, and so on. Wissembach, however, interprets it thus: he thought otherwise, he says, not in general and as to the rule, but in the particular case and as to the exception. (Partner's money contributed by the partner, that is, since it is enough for him to lose his labours; this would not apply to the partner who contributed money.) See Antonius Gryphius, 2 Observations, 34. Let it be understood as belonging to the profit.

units.la: 3 ¶Illud expeditū est 4[?], si in vna causa pars fuerit expressa, veluti in solo lucro vel in solo damno, in altera verò omissa: in eo quoque, quod prætermissum est, eandē parte seruari.
units.tr: 3 It is settled that if a share has been stated in one matter, for example in profit alone or in loss alone, and omitted in another, then in the omitted matter the same share is also kept.

units.la: 4 ¶Manet autē societas eo vsque, donec in eo-dem cōsensu perseuerauerint. At cum aliquis renunciauerit societati: soluitur societas. Sed plane si quis callidè in hoc renunciauerit societati, vt obueniens aliquod lucrū solus habeat, veluti si totorū bonorū socius, cum ab aliquo heres esset relictus, in hoc renunciauerit societati, vt hereditate solus lucrifaceret: cogitur hoc lucrū communicare. Si quid verò aliud lucrifaciat, quod non captauerit: ad ipsum solum pertinet. Ei verò, cui renunciatum est, quicquid omnino post renunciatā societatem adquiritur soli {b}conceditur.
units.tr: 4 A partnership continues for as long as the partners remain in the same agreement. But when one partner renounces the partnership, the partnership is dissolved. However, if someone renounces the partnership cunningly, so that he alone may have some gain that comes his way, for example if a partner of all goods, having been left an inheritance by someone, renounces the partnership in order to profit from the inheritance alone, he is compelled to share that gain. But if he gains something else that he did not seek, it belongs to him alone. Whatever is acquired after the partnership has been renounced belongs solely to the one to whom the renunciation was made.

units.la: 5 ¶Soluitur adhuc societas etiam morte socij {c}:quia qui societatē contrahit, certā personam sibi eligit. Sed & si consensu pluriū societas contracta sit: morte vnius socij soluitur, etsi plures superstint nisi in coeunda societate aliter conuenerit.
units.tr: 5 A partnership is also dissolved by the death of a partner, because the one who enters a partnership chooses a particular person for himself. And if a partnership was formed by the agreement of several, it is dissolved by the death of one partner, even though several remain, unless the partners agreed otherwise when forming it.

units.la: 6 ¶Item si alicuius rei contracta societas sit, & finis negotio impositus est: finitur societas.
units.tr: 6 Likewise, if a partnership was formed for some matter, and the business has been brought to an end, the partnership is finished.

units.la: 7 ¶Publicatione{d} quoque distrahi societatem manifestū est: scilicet si vniuersa bona socij publicentur, nam cūm in eius locum alius succedat, pro mortuo habetur.
units.tr: 7 It is also clear that a partnership is dissolved by confiscation, namely if all the goods of a partner are confiscated; for since another person takes his place, he is regarded as dead.

units.la: 8 ¶Item si quis ex sociis moles debiti prægrauat⁹[?], bonis suis cesserit, & ideo propter publica aut priuata debita substantia eius veneat{e}: soluitur societas: sed hoc casu si adhuc consentiant in societatem, noua videtur incipere societas.
units.tr: 8 Likewise, if one of the partners, weighed down by a heavy burden of debt, makes a surrender of his goods, and so his property is sold to meet public or private debts, the partnership is dissolved. In this case, however, if they still agree to the partnership, a new partnership seems to begin.

units.la: 9 ¶Socius socio vtrūm eo nomine tantum teneatur pro socio actione{f}, si quid dolo commiserit, sicut is, qui deponi apud se passus est: an etiā culpæ, id est, desidiæ atque negligentiæ nomine: quæsitum est. præualuit tamen etiam{g} culpæ{h} nomine teneri eum. Culpa autē non ad exactissimā diligentiam dirigenda est. Sufficit enim tale diligentiā communibus rebus ‖socium‖[?] adhibere, qualem suis rebus adhibere solet. Nam qui parum diligentem socium sibi adsumit: de se queri, sibique hoc imputare debet.
units.tr: 9 It has been asked whether one partner is liable to another under the action on partnership only for what he has committed by fraud, just as one who has allowed something to be deposited with him is liable, or also for fault, that is, on account of idleness and negligence. Nevertheless, it has prevailed that he is liable also for fault. Fault, however, is not to be measured by the most exact diligence. For it is enough for a partner to apply to the common affairs the same diligence that he is accustomed to apply to his own. For one who takes into partnership a partner who is not very diligent must complain of himself and impute this to himself.
Concerning Mandate, Title 27.

units.la: MANDATVM cōtrahitur quinq. modis: siue sua tantum gratia aliquis tibi mandet, siue sua & tua, siue aliena tantum, siue sua & aliena, siue tua & aliena. At si tua tantum gratia mandatū fit:fuperuæcuu est mandatum,& ob {a}id nulla ex eo obligatio, nec mandati inter vos actio nascitur.
units.tr: A mandate is contracted in five ways: either someone commissions you purely for his own sake, or for his sake and yours, or purely for another's sake, or for his own and another's, or for yours and another's. But if a mandate is given purely for your sake, it is superfluous, and for that reason no obligation arises from it, nor does an action of mandate arise between you.

units.la: 1 ¶Mandatis‖tantum‖gratia interuenit mandatū: veluti si quis tibi mādet {b}, vt negotia eius gere-res,vel vt fundū ei emeres,vel vt pro eo sponderes.
units.tr: 1. A mandate is made purely for the mandator's sake, for example, if someone commissions you to manage his affairs, or to buy an estate for him, or to stand surety for him.

units.la: 2 ¶Tua gratia & mandatis: veluti si mādet tibi, vt pecuniā sub vsuris crederes ei,qui in rem ipsius mutuaretur. aut si volente te agere cum eo ex fide-iussoria causa,mandet tibi {c}, vt cum reo agas, periculo mandantis: vel vt ipsius periculo stipuleris, ab eo,quem tibi deleget in id,quod tibi debuerat.
units.tr: 2. A mandate is for your sake as well as his: for example, if he commissions you to lend money at interest to a person who will borrow it for his own purposes; or if, when you wish to proceed against someone on a fideiussory obligation, he commissions you to proceed against the principal debtor at the mandator's risk, or to take a stipulation from the person whom he assigns to you, to secure what was owed to you, at his risk.

units.la: 3 ¶Aliena aut‖tantum‖causa interuenit mandatū,veluti si tibi aliquis mandet, vt Titij negotia gereres,vel vt Titio fundū emeres {d},vel vt pro Titio sponderes.
units.tr: 3. A mandate is made purely for another's sake, for example, if someone commissions you to manage Titius's affairs, or to buy an estate for Titius, or to stand surety for Titius.

units.la: 4 ¶Sua & aliena: veluti si de communibus suis & Titij negotiis gerendis tibi mandet,vel vt sibi & Titio fundū emeres, vel vt pro eo & Titio sponderes.
units.tr: 4. A mandate is for the mandator's own sake and another's: for example, if he commissions you to manage his common affairs with Titius, or to buy an estate for himself and Titius, or to stand surety for himself and Titius.

units.la: 5 ¶Tua & aliena:veluti si tibi mādet, vt Titio sub vsuris crederes: quia si fine vsuris pecuniā crederes,aliena tantum gratia intercedit mandatum.
units.tr: 5. A mandate is for your sake and another's: for example, if he commissions you to lend money to Titius at interest; for if you were to lend money without interest, the mandate would be made purely for another's sake.

units.la: 6 ¶Tua {e} tantum gratia interuenit mandatū: veluti si tibi mandet,vt pecunias tuas in emptiones potius prædiorū colloces,quàm fœneres: vel ex diuerso,vt pecunias tuas fœneres potius,quàm in emptione prædiorū colloces.Cuius generis mandatū,magis consilii,quàm mandatū est {f},& ob id non est obligatorium: quia nemo ex consilio mandati obligatur,etiā si non expediat ei,cui mandabatur: cum liberū cuique sit apud se explorare, an sibi expediat consilium. Itaque si otiosam pecuniā domi te habentē hortatus fuerit aliquis,vt rem aliquā emeres, vel eā crederes: quamuis nō expediat eam tibi emisse, vel credidisse,nō tamen tibi mandati tenetur {g}. Et adeò hæc ita sunt,vt quæsitū sit,an mandati teneatur,qui mandauit tibi,vt pecuniā Titio fœnerares? sed obtinuit Sabini sententia, obligatorium esse in hoc casu mandatū:quia {h} nō aliter Titio credidisses, quàm si tibi mandatum esset.
units.tr: 6. A mandate is made purely for your sake: for example, if he commissions you to invest your own money in buying estates rather than lending it out at interest; or conversely, to lend your money at interest rather than invest it in buying estates. A mandate of this kind is more a piece of advice than a mandate, and therefore it does not bind: no one is bound by advice given to him, even if it is not to the advantage of the person to whom it was given, since it is open to each person to judge for himself whether the advice suits him. Thus, if someone has urged you, when you have idle money at home, to buy some thing or to lend it, then, although it may not be to your advantage to have bought or lent it, he is not bound to you by mandate. And indeed these matters are so settled that it has been asked whether a man who commissioned you to lend money to Titius is bound by mandate; but the opinion of Sabinus prevailed, that in this case the mandate is binding, because you would not have lent to Titius except on the strength of the mandate.

units.la: 7 ¶Illud quoque mandatū non est obligatorium,quod {i} contra bonos mores est: veluti si Titius de furto,aut‖de‖damno faciendo,aut de iniuria facienda mandet tibi. licet enim pœnam istius facti nomine præstiteris,non tamen vllam habes aduersus Titium actionem.
units.tr: 7. A mandate that is contrary to good morals is likewise not binding: for example, if Titius commissions you to commit a theft, or to cause damage, or to do an injury. For although you may have paid the penalty for such an act, you have no action against Titius.

units.la: 8 ¶Is,qui exequitur mandatum,non {k} debet excedere fines mandati.vt ecce,si quis vsque ad centum aureos mandauerit tibi,vt fundū emeres,vel {k} pro Titio sponde-rit tibi,vt fundū emeres,vel {k} pro Titio sponderes. res: neque pluris emere debes, neque in ampliorem pecuniam fideiubere. alioqui non habebis cum eo mandati actionem adeò quidem, vt Sabino & Cassio placuerit, etiam si vsque ad centum aureos cum eo agere volueris: inutiliter te acturum. ||Sed|| diuersæ scholæ auctores recte vsque ad centum aureos te acturum existimant, quæ sententia sanè benignior est. Quòd si minoris emeris, habebis scilicet cū eo mandati actionem: quoniam qui mandat, vt sibi centum aureorum fundus emeretur, is vtique mandasse intelligitur, vt minoris (si posset) emeretur.
units.tr: 8. A person who carries out a mandate must not exceed the limits of the mandate. For instance, if someone has commissioned you to buy an estate for up to a hundred gold pieces, or has stood surety for you to Titius, or has stood surety for Titius, you must neither buy for a higher price nor stand surety for a larger sum. Otherwise you will have no action of mandate against him; indeed, according to Sabinus and Cassius, if you wish to sue him for the full hundred gold pieces, you will act in vain. But the authors of the other school rightly think that you may sue for the full hundred gold pieces, and that opinion is certainly the more lenient. But if you have bought for less, you will of course have an action of mandate against him, since one who commissions the purchase of an estate for a hundred gold pieces is understood to have commissioned that it be bought for less, if that were possible.

units.la: 9 ¶Recte quoque mandatum contractu, si dum adhuc integra res sit, revocatum fuerit, euanescit.
units.tr: 9. A mandate that is revoked while the matter is still unchanged is rightly extinguished, as a contract.

units.la: 10 ¶Item si adhuc integro mandato, mors alterutrius interueniat, id est, vel eius qui mandauerit, vel illius, qui mandatum susceperit: soluitur mandatum. Sed vtilitatis causa receptum est: si eo mortuo, qui tibi mandauerat, tu ignorans eum decessisse, executus fueris mandatum: posse te agere mandati actione, alioqui iusta & probabilis ignorantia tibi damnum adferret. Et huic simile est, quod placuit, si debitores manumisso dispensatore Titij, per ignorantiam liberto soluerint, liberari eos: cum alioqui strictæ iuris ratione non possent liberari, quia alij soluissent, quàm cui soluere debuerint.
units.tr: 10. Likewise, if, while the mandate is still unexecuted, the death of either party intervenes, that is, of the mandator or of the one who has accepted the mandate, the mandate is dissolved. But it has been established for the sake of convenience that if, after the death of the man who commissioned you, you carry out the mandate in ignorance that he has died, you may bring an action of mandate; otherwise, a reasonable and excusable ignorance would cause you loss. Similar to this is the rule that, if debtors of Titius, after the release of his steward, pay the freedman in ignorance, they are discharged; for otherwise, by the strict rule of law, they could not be discharged, since they would have paid someone other than the person to whom they were bound to pay.

units.la: 11 ¶Mandatum non suscipere, cuilibet liberum est: susceptum autem consummandum est, aut quàm primum renunciandum, vt per semetipsum aut per alium eandem rem mandator exequatur. Nam nisi ita renunciet, vt integra causa mandatori reseruetur eandem rem explicandi: nihilominus mandati actio loco habet: nisi iusta causa intercesserit, aut non renunciandi, aut intempestiuè renunciandi.
units.tr: 11. It is open to anyone to decline a mandate; but once accepted, it must be carried out, or else renounced as soon as possible, so that the mandator may execute the same matter himself or through another. For unless he renounces it in such a way that the mandator's opportunity to carry out the matter is kept intact, an action of mandate nevertheless lies, unless a just cause has intervened, either for not renouncing or for renouncing at an unseasonable time.

units.la: 12 ¶Mandatum & in diem differri, & sub conditione fieri potest.
units.tr: 12. A mandate may both be deferred to a day and be made subject to a condition.

units.la: 13 ¶In summa sciendum est, mandatum, nisi gratuitum sit, in aliam formam negotij cadere. Nam mercede constituta, incipit locatio & conductio esse. Et (vt generaliter dicamus) quibus casibus sine mercede suscepto officio, mandati siue depositi contrahitur negotium: iis casibus interueniente mercede locatio & conductio intelligitur contrahi. Et ideo si fulloni polienda curandáve quis dederit vestimenta, aut sarcinatori sarcienda, nulla mercede constituta neque promissa: mandati competit actio.
units.tr: 13. In sum, it must be understood that a mandate, unless it is gratuitous, passes into another kind of transaction. For once a fee has been fixed, the contract begins to be one of letting and hiring. And (to speak generally) in those cases where a duty undertaken without payment gives rise to the contract of mandate or deposit, in those cases, when a fee intervenes, the contract is understood to be letting and hiring. So if someone has given clothes to a fuller to be cleaned and pressed, or to a tailor to be mended, with no fee fixed or promised, the action of mandate lies.

units.la: DE OBLIGATIONIBVS, ||quæ|| quasi ex contractu ||na-scuntur,|| TIT. XXVIII.
units.tr: CONCERNING OBLIGATIONS WHICH ARISE AS IF FROM CONTRACT, TITLE XXVIII.

units.la: POST genera contractuum enumerata dispiciamus etiam de iis obligationibus, quæ quidem non proprie nasci ex contractu intelliguntur: sed tamen quia non ex maleficio subsistantiam capiunt, quasi ex contractu nasci videntur.
units.tr: After enumerating the kinds of contracts, let us also examine those obligations which are not properly understood to arise from contract, but which, because they do not take their origin from a wrong, seem to arise as if from contract.

units.la: 1 ¶Igi-tur cum quis {a}negotia abstentis gesserit: vtrò citroque inter eos nascuntur actiones, quæ appellantur negotiorum gestorum, sed domino quidem rei gestæ aduersus eum, qui gesit, directa {b}competit actio: negotiorum autem gestori, contraria, quas ex nullo contractu proprie nasci, manifestum est: quippe ita nascuntur istæ actiones, si sine mandato quisque alienis negotiis gerendis se obtulerit. Idque vtilitatis {c}causa receptum est: ne absentium, qui subita festinatione coacti, nulli demandata negotiorum suorum administratione, peregrè profecti essent, desererentur negotia: quæ sanè nemo, curaturus esset, si de eo, quod quis impedisset, nullam habiturus esset actionem. Sicut autem is, qui vtiliter gesit negotia, dominum habet obligatum negotiorum gestorum: ita & contrà ille quoque tenetur, vt administrationis reddat rationem. Quo casu ad exactissimam quisque diligentiam compelli-tur reddere rationem: nec sufficit ||alem[?]|| diligentiam adhibere, qualem suis rebus adhibere solet: si modo alius diligentior ||eo|| commodius administraturus esset negotia.
units.tr: 1. When someone has managed the affairs of an absent person, actions arise between the two of them on each side: the action called "of business managed" (negotiorum gestorum). The direct action lies to the owner of the business against the one who managed it, while the contrary action belongs to the manager. It is plain that these actions do not properly arise from any contract: they arise in this way when someone, without a mandate, has offered himself to manage another's affairs. This was adopted for the sake of usefulness, so that the affairs of absent persons, who, compelled by sudden haste, had gone abroad without entrusting the administration of their business to anyone, should not be abandoned; and no one would undertake such care if he were to have no action concerning what he had taken on. Just as the one who has managed the business usefully holds the owner bound by the action of business managed, so conversely he himself is bound to render an account of his administration. In this case each person is compelled to render an account with the most exact diligence: it is not enough to apply such diligence as he is accustomed to apply to his own affairs, if another would manage the business more diligently and more advantageously.

units.la: 2 ¶Tutores quoque qui tutelæ iudicio tenentur, non {d}proprie ex contractu obligati ||esse|| intelliguntur (nullum enim negotium inter tutorem & pupillum contrahitur) sed quia sanè nô ex maleficio tenentur, quasi ex contractu teneri videntur. Hoc autem casu mutuæ sunt actiones. Non tantum enim pupillus cū tutore habet tutelæ actionem: sed & contrà tutor cum pupillo habet contrariam {e}tutelæ, si vel impenderit aliquid in rem pupilli, vel pro eo fuerit obligatus, aut rem suam creditoribus eius obligauerit.
units.tr: 2. Tutors also, who are bound by the action of guardianship, are not understood to be bound properly by contract (for no business is contracted between tutor and ward), but because they are certainly not bound by a wrong, they seem to be bound as if by contract. In this case the actions are reciprocal. For the ward has the action of guardianship against the tutor, but conversely the tutor has the contrary action of guardianship against the ward, if he has spent something on the ward's property, or has become bound on his behalf, or has pledged his own property to the ward's creditors.

units.la: 3 ¶Item si inter aliquos communis res sit {f}sine societate: veluti quod pariter cis legata donatáve esset. & alter eorum alteri ideo teneatur communi diuidundo iudicio, quòd solus fructus ex ea re perceperit, aut quod socius eius solus in eam rem necessarias impensas fecerit: non intelligitur ex contractu proprie obligatus esse: quippe nihil inter se contraxerunt. sed quia ex maleficio non tenetur: quasi ex contractu teneri videtur.
units.tr: 3. Likewise, if a thing is held in common between some persons without partnership, as when a thing has been bequeathed or given to them equally, and one of them is bound to another by the action for dividing the common thing, because he alone has taken the fruits of that thing, or because his co-owner alone has made necessary outlays on it: he is not understood to be properly bound by contract, since they have contracted nothing between themselves; but because he is not bound by a wrong, he seems to be bound as if by contract.

units.la: 4 Idem iuris est de eo, qui coheredi familiæ erciscundæ iudicio ex his causis obligatus est.
units.tr: 4. The same law holds for one who is bound to a coheir in the action for dividing the inheritance (familiae erciscundae) for these reasons.

units.la: 5 Heres quoque legatorum nomine non proprie ex contractu obligatus intelligitur: (neq. enim cum herede, neque cum defuncto ullum negotium legatarius gesisse proprie dici poterit) & tamen quia ex maleficio non est obligatus: quasi ex contractu debere intelligitur.
units.tr: 5. An heir is also understood not to be properly bound by contract on account of legacies (for the legatee cannot properly be said to have transacted any business either with the heir or with the deceased); and yet, because he is not bound by a wrong, he is understood to owe as if by contract.

units.la: 6 Item is, cui quis per errorem non debitum soluit, quasi ex contractu debere videtur. Adeo enim non intelligitur proprie ex contractu obligatus esse, ut si certiorem rationem sequamur: magis (ut supra diximus) ex distractu, quam ex contractu possit dici obligatus esse. nam qui soluendi animo pecuniam dat: in hoc dare videtur, ut distrahat potius negotium, quam contrahat.
