Sed tamen perinde is, qui accipit, obligatur, ac si mutuum ei daretur. & ideo condictione tenetur.
units.tr: 6. Likewise, one to whom someone pays by mistake what is not owed seems to owe as if by contract. Indeed he is not understood to be properly bound by contract, so that, if we follow the more accurate reasoning, he may be said to be bound (as we said above) rather by a dissolving transaction than by a contract. For the one who gives money with the intention of paying seems to give it in order to dissolve a relation rather than to contract one. Yet the recipient is bound just as if a loan had been given to him, and therefore he is liable to the action for condiction.

units.la: 7 Ex quibusdam tamen causis repeti non potest, quod per errorem non debitum solutum fit. sic namque definierunt veteres, ex quibus causis infitiando lis crescit, ex iis causis non debitum solutum repeti non posse: veluti ex lege Aquilia, item ex legato. Quod veteres quidem in iis legatis locum habere voluerunt, quæ certa constituta, per damnationem cuique legata fuerant. nostra autem constitutio, cum unam naturam omnibus legatis & fideicommissis induluit, huiusmodi augmentum in omnibus legatis & fideicommissis extendi voluit: sed non omnibus legatariis hoc præbuit, sed tantummodo in iis legatis & fideicommissis, quæ sacrosanctis ecclesiis, & cæteris venerabilibus locis, quæ religionis vel pietatis intuitu honorantur, relicta sunt: quæ si indebita soluantur, non repetuntur.
units.tr: 7. For some causes, however, what has been paid by mistake when not owed cannot be reclaimed. Thus the ancients defined that from those causes for which the suit grows by denial, what was paid when not owed cannot be reclaimed: for example, under the Lex Aquilia, and likewise under a legacy. The ancients wished this to hold in those legacies which had been bequeathed to someone in fixed amounts by damnation. Our constitution, however, when it granted one single nature to all legacies and fideicommissa, wished this increase to extend to all legacies and fideicommissa; but it did not grant this to all legatees, only in those legacies and fideicommissa which have been left to the most holy churches and other venerable places that are honoured for the sake of religion or piety; these, if paid when not owed, cannot be reclaimed.

units.la: PER QUAS PERSONAS NOBIS obligatio adquiritur
units.tr: BY WHAT PERSONS OBLIGATION IS ACQUIRED FOR US
TITLE XXIX.

units.la: EXPOSITIS generibus obligationum, quæ ex contractu vel quasi ex contractu nascuntur: admonendi sumus adquiri nobis non solum per nosmetipsos, sed per eas quoque personas, quæ in nostra potestate lfunt,veluti per seruos & filios nostros: vt tame,quod per seruos [nostros] nobis adquiritur, totum nostrum fiat:quod autem per liberos,quos in potestate habemus,ex obligatione fuerit. adquisitû, hoc dividatur secundum imaginem rerum proprietatis & vsusfructus, quam nostra decreuit constitutio: vt quod ab actione commodû peruleniat,huius vsumfructum quidem habeat pater, proprietas autem filio seruetur,scilicet patre actionem mouente secundum nostrae constitutionis diuisione.
units.tr: Having set out the kinds of obligations that arise from contract or quasi-contract, we must note that we acquire not only through ourselves but also through those persons who are in our power, such as our slaves and sons. Provided, however, that whatever is acquired for us through a slave becomes wholly ours, while whatever is acquired through the children we have in our power by an obligation is divided according to the model of the rules of ownership and usufruct laid down by our constitution. So what comes to them from the action, the father has the usufruct, but ownership is kept for the son, the father bringing the action, in accordance with the division made by our constitution.

units.la: 1 ¶Item per liberos homines,& alienos seruos, quos bona fide posidemus adquiritur nobis: sed ratum ex duabus causis,id est, fi quid ex operis suis, vel ex re nostra adquirant.
units.tr: 1. Likewise we acquire through free men and through other people's slaves whom we possess in good faith. But this holds only on two grounds, namely if they acquire something by their own work or from our property.

units.la: 2 ¶Per eum quoque seruum,in quo vsumfructum vel vsum habemus, similiter ex duabus istis causis nobis adquiritur.
units.tr: 2. Likewise, through a slave in whom we have usufruct or use, we acquire in the same way, on those two grounds.

units.la: 3 ¶Communem seruum pro dominica parte dominis adquirere certum est: excepto eo,quod nominatim vni stipulando,aut per traditionem accipiendo,illi soli adquirit : veluti cum ita stipulatur, Titio Domino meo dare spondes? Sed si domini vnius iussu seruus fuerit stipulatus, licet antea dubitabatur,tamen post nostram decisionem res expedita est, vt illi tantum adquirat,qui hoc ei facere iussit, vt supra dictum est.
units.tr: 3. It is certain that a slave held in common acquires for the owners in proportion to their shares, except that if he stipulates expressly for one of them, or receives by delivery in that one's name, he acquires for that one alone, as when he stipulates thus: Do you promise to give to Titius, my master? But if a slave has stipulated at the command of one owner, although this was doubted before, the matter has now been settled by our decision, so that he acquires only for the one who ordered him to do so, as was said above.

units.la: QVIBVS MODIS TOLLITVR obligatio, TIT. XXX.
units.tr: BY WHAT MODES OBLIGATION IS DISSOLVED, TIT. XXX.

units.la: OLLITVR autem omnis obligatio solutione eius,quod debetur: vel si quis consentiente creditore, aliud pro alio soluerit. Nec interest,quis soluat: vtrum ipse,qui debet, an alius pro eo. liberatur enim & alio soluente: sine sciente, siue ignorante debitore vel inuito [eo] solutio fiat. Item si reus soluerit: etiam ij, qui pro eo interuenerunt, liberantur. Idem ex contrario contingit si fideiussor soluerit,nō enim ipse solus liberatur,sed etiā reus.
units.tr: Every obligation is dissolved by the payment of what is owed, or if, with the creditor's consent, someone pays one thing in place of another. It makes no difference who pays, whether the debtor himself or another on his behalf, for the debtor is released even by payment from another, whether the debtor knows of it or not, or even against his will. Likewise, if the principal debtor pays, those who intervened on his behalf are also released. The reverse happens if the surety pays: he is not released alone, but the principal debtor is released too.

units.la: 1 ¶Ite per acceptilationē tollitur obligatio. Est autē acceptilatio, imaginaria solutio. Quod enim ex verborum obligatione Titio debetur, id si velit Titius remittere, poterit sic fieri, vt patiatur haec verba
units.tr: 1 ¶Again, an obligation is dissolved by acceptilation. Acceptilation is an imaginary payment. If Titius wishes to remit what is owed to him under a verbal obligation, this can be done by letting the debtor say these words: What I promised you, do you have it as received? {m} l.36. de fideiussor.
{m} l.36. de fideiussor.
{n} l.1. de acceptilat.

units.la: {o} v.l.8. §. acceptum. & §. vlt. ff. de acceptilat. debitorem dicere : Quod ego tibi promisi, habésne acceptum? & Titius respondeat, habeo. Sed & Graecè potest acceptilatio fieri: dummodo sic fiat, vt Latinis verbis solet exigi, ἔχεις λαβὼν δηναρία τόσα; ἔχω λαβών[?] i. tot denarios acceptos habes? acceptos habeo. Quo genere (vt diximus) tantùm ex soluuntur obligationes, quae ex verbis consistunt, non etiá caeterae. Consentaneum enim visum est, verbis factam obligationem, aliis posse verbis dissolui. Sed & id, quod alia ex causa debetur{a}, poterit in stipulationem deduci, & per acceptilationem dissolui. Sicut autem quod debetur, pro parte recte soluitur{b}: ita in parte debiti acceptilatio fieri poterit.
units.tr: {o} v.l.8. §. acceptum. & §. vlt. ff. de acceptilat. and Titius answers, I have it as received. Acceptilation can also be made in Greek, provided it is done in the form that is customarily required in Latin words: [ἔχεις λαβὼν δηναρία τόσα; ἔχω λαβών] Do you have so many denarii as received? I have them as received. By this kind (as we have said) only those obligations that arise from words are dissolved, and not the others. For it seemed fitting that an obligation created by words should be dissolvable by words. But whatever is owed from some other cause may also be brought into a stipulation and dissolved by acceptilation. Just as what is owed may be properly paid in part, so acceptilation may also be made for part of a debt.

units.la: 2 ¶Est autem prodita stipulatio, quae vulgò Aquiliana appella-tur{c}, per quam contingit, vt omnium rerum obligatio in stipulatum deducatur, & ea per acceptilationem tollatur. Stipulatio enim Aquiliana renouat omnes obligationes, & à Gallo Aquilio ita composita est: Quicquid te mihi ex quacunque causa dare facere oportet, oportebit, praesens in diemve, quarumcum-que rerum mihi tecum actio est, quaeque aduersus te persecutio est, eritve{d} quodve tu meum habes, tenes, possides{e}, si dolove malo fecisti, quanti quaeque earum rerum res erit, tantam pecuniam dari stipulatus est Aulus Agerius, spopondit Numerius Negidius. quod Numerius Negidius Aulo Agerio spopondit, id haberetne à se acceptum Numerius Negidius Aulum Agerium rogauit. Aulus Agerius Numerio Negidio acceptum fecit.
units.tr: 2 ¶There is also a well-known stipulation, commonly called the Aquilian, by which all obligations are brought into a stipulation and then removed by acceptilation. For the Aquilian stipulation renews all obligations, and it was framed by Gallus Aquilius as follows: Whatever you owe me on any ground, to give or to do, now or at any future time, whatever actions I have against you, whatever claims I may bring against you, or whatever you hold, have, or possess that is mine, whether by your malicious act or otherwise, for as much money as each of those things is worth, Aulus Agerius has stipulated, and Numerius Negidius has promised. What Numerius Negidius promised to Aulus Agerius, has Numerius Negidius asked Aulus Agerius to hold as received from him? Aulus Agerius has made it received for Numerius Negidius.

units.la: 3 ¶Praeterea nouatione tollitur obligatio: veluti si id quod tibi Scias debebat, à Titio dari stipulatus fis.Nam interuentu nouae{f} personae noua{g} nascitur obligatio, & prima tollitur, translata in posteriorem: adeo, vt interdum, licet posterior stipulatio inutilis sit, tamen prima nouationis iure tollatur: veluti si id, quod tu Titio debes, à pupillo{h} sine tutoris auctoritate stipulatus fuerit, quo casu res amittitur, nam & prior debitor liberatur{i}, & posterior obligatio nulla est. Non{k} idem iuris est, si à seruo quis fuerit stipulatus. nam tunc prior perinde obligatus manet, ac si posteà nullus stipulatus fuisset. Sed si eadem persona fit, à qua postea stipuleris: ita demum nouatio fit, si quid in posteriore stipulatione nouui fit: forte si conditio aut dies, aut fideiussor adiiciatur, aut de-trahatur. Quod autem diximus, si conditio adiicia-tur, nouationem fieri: sic intelligi oportet, vt ita di-camus eamus[?] factam nouationem{a}, si conditio extiterit. alioqui si defecerit, durat prior obligatio. Sed, cùm hoc quidem inter veteres constabat, tunc fieri noua- tionem{b}, cùm nouandi animo in secundam obliga- tionem irum fuerat : per hoc autem dubium erat, quando nouandi animo videretur hoc fieri,& quasi-dam de hoc praesumptiones alij in aliis casibus in- troducebant: ideo nostra{c} processit constitutio,quę apertisime definiuit, tunc solùm nouationem prio- ris obligationis fieri {†}quoties hoc ipsum inter cô- trahentes expressum fuerit, quòd propter nouatio- nem prioris obligationis conuenerunt. alioqui & manere pristinam obligationem, & secundam ei ac- cedere,vt maneat ex vtraque causa obligatio secun- dum nostrę constitutionis definitionem,quam licet ex ipsius lectione apertius cognoscere. 4 ¶Hoc amplius,eę obligationes,quę consensu contrahun- tur{d}, contraria voluntate dissoluuntur. Nam si Ti- tius & Seius inter se consenserint,vt fundum Tuscu- lanum emptum Seius haberet centum aureis : dein- de re nondum secuta{e}, id est, neque pretio soluto, neque fundo tradito, placuerit inter eos,vt discede- retur ab ea emptione & venditione : inuicem libe- rantur.Idem si est in conductione & locatione,& in omnibus contractibus, qui ex consensu descendunt, sicut iam dictum est{g}.
units.tr: 3. Furthermore, obligation is dissolved by novation: for example, if you stipulate that what Scias owed you be given by Titius. For by the intervention of a new person a new obligation arises, and the first is extinguished, transferred to the later one. So much so that sometimes, even though the later stipulation is invalid, the first is nonetheless dissolved by the law of novation: for example, if what you owe to Titius is stipulated from a ward without the authority of his guardian. In that case the thing is lost, for the first debtor is released and the later obligation is void. It is not the same if one has stipulated from a slave; for then the first debtor remains bound just as if no stipulation had afterwards been made. But if the stipulation is made with the same person from whom you stipulated afterwards, novation takes place only if something new is added in the later stipulation, perhaps a condition, a day, or a surety is added or removed. When we said that novation occurs if a condition is added, this must be understood so that we say novation takes place if the condition is fulfilled. Otherwise, if it fails, the earlier obligation endures. But although it was agreed among the ancients that novation takes place when there was an intention to novate in making the second obligation, it was uncertain from this when it was judged that novation was intended, and different authorities introduced various presumptions about this in different cases. Therefore our constitution was issued, which most clearly declared that the first obligation is novated only when this very thing has been expressed between the contracting parties, namely that they agreed to novate the earlier obligation. Otherwise the earlier obligation remains and the second is added to it, so that the obligation remains from both causes. This is according to the definition of our constitution, which can be understood more clearly from reading it. 4. Moreover, obligations which are contracted by consent are dissolved by a contrary will. For if Titius and Seius have agreed between themselves that Seius should have the Tusculan farm bought for a hundred gold pieces, and then, before anything has followed, that is, neither the price paid nor the farm handed over, they agree that the purchase and sale be abandoned, they are mutually released. The same holds in hiring and letting, and in all contracts which arise from consent, as has already been said.

units.la: dos tollendæ obligationis ipso iure, copensatione. cofusione hæreditatis.l.50.de fideiuff. oblatione,depositione & cofignatione pecuniæ l.19.Cod.de solut. transfusionem debiti in a-lium.l.47.de fideiuss. Chirographi redditionem, l.2.ff. depastis.
units.tr: Modes of dissolving an obligation by law itself: compensation; confusion of inheritance, l.50. de fideiussor.; offer, deposit and consignation of money, l.19. Cod. de solut.; transfer of the debt to another, l.47. de fideiussor.; return of the chirograph, l.2. ff. de pactis.

units.la: INSTITVTIO-NVM, SEV ELEMEN-torum D.Iustiniani sacratis-simi Principis,
units.tr: The Institutes, or Elements, of the most sacred Prince Justinian,
BOOK IV.

units.la: DE OBLIGATIONIBVS, quæ ex delicto nascuntur TIT. I.
units.tr: ON OBLIGATIONS ARISING FROM DELICT. TITLE I.

units.la: C[?]VM fit expositum superiore {b}libro de obligationibus ex contractu, & quasi ex contractu: sequitur, ut de obligationibus ex maleficio, & quasi ex maleficio dispiciamus. Sed illæ quidé (ut suo loco tradidimus) in quatuor genera diuiduntur. hæc vero unius generis sunt. nam omnes ex re nascuntur {c}, id est ex ipso maleficio, veluti ex furto, rapina, damno, iniuria.
units.tr: Since we have explained in the previous book the obligations arising from contract and quasi-contract, it follows that we should now consider obligations arising from wrongdoing and quasi-wrongdoing. Those obligations, as we set out in their place, fall into four kinds. These, however, belong to one kind only, for all of them arise from the deed itself, that is, from the wrongful act: for example, from theft, robbery, damage, and injury.

units.la: 1 ¶Furtû est contrectatio {d} fraudulosa {e}, lucri {f} faciendi gratia, vel ipsius rei, vel etiam usus eius possessionisve. quod lege naturali {g} prohibitum est admittere.
units.tr: 1. Theft is the fraudulent handling of a thing, done for the sake of gain, whether of the thing itself or even of its use or possession. Natural law forbids it.

units.la: 2 ¶Furtum autē vel a furvo, id est nigro, dictum est, quòd clàm & obscure fiat, & plerumque nocte: vel a fraude, vel a ferendo, id est, auferendo: vel a Graeco sermone, quod φῶ-ρας appellant fures. Imò & Graeci à ferendo φῶρες dixerunt.
units.tr: 2. Theft (furtum) is said to derive either from furvus, that is, black, because it is done secretly and in the dark, and usually at night; or from fraud; or from ferre, that is, to carry off; or from the Greek word, since the Greeks call thieves [φῶρας]. Indeed the Greeks also derived [φῶρες] from ferre.

units.la: 3 ¶Furtorum autem duo sunt genera: manifestum, & nec manifestum. Nam conceptum & oblatum, species potius actionis sunt furto cohaerentes, quàm genera furtorum, sicut, inferius apparebit. Manifestus fur est, quem Graeci ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ {h}appellant: nec solùm is, qui in ipso furto deprehenditur, sed etiam is, qui in eo loco deprehenditur, quo furtum fit: veluti qui in domo furtum fecit & nondum egressus ianuam deprehensus fuerit: & qui in oliueto oliuarum, aut in vineto uvarum furtum fecit, ecit,quamdiu in eo oliueto aut vineto deprehensus fuerit.Imo vlterius furtum manifestum est exten-dendum,quamdiu eam rem fur tenens visus vel de-prehensus fuerit: fiue in publico,fiue in priuato: vel domino, vel ab alio,antequam {d}eo peruenerit,quo deferre {b}vel deponere deftinaffet. Sed fi pertulit, quo destinauit,tametsi deprehendatur cum re furti- ua,non est manifestus fur.Nec manifestum furtum quid fit,ex iis,quæ diximus, intelligitur. nam quod manifestum non est,id scilicet nec manifestum est.
units.tr: 3. There are two kinds of theft: manifest and non-manifest. For the conceived and the offered theft are rather kinds of action attached to theft than kinds of theft, as will appear below. A manifest thief is one whom the Greeks call [ἐπ' αὐτοφώρῳ], caught in the very act; and this applies not only to one caught in the act of the theft itself, but also to one caught in the place where the theft is done: for example, one who has committed a theft in a house and is caught before he has left the doorway; and one who has committed a theft of olives in an olive grove, or of grapes in a vineyard, as long as he is caught in that grove or vineyard. Moreover, manifest theft extends further, for as long as the thief is seen or caught holding the thing, whether in a public or a private place, whether by the owner or by another, before he has reached the place where he intended to carry or deposit it. But if he has reached the place he intended, even though he is caught with the stolen goods, he is not a manifest thief. What a non-manifest theft is can be understood from what we have said: for what is not manifest is, of course, non-manifest.

units.la: 4 ¶ Conceptum furtum dicitur,cùm apud aliquem testibus præfentibus furtiua res quæsita{c} & inuenta fit. nam in eû propria actio constituta est, quamuis fur non fit,quæ appellatur concepti. Oblatum furtû dici ur,cùm res furtiua ab aliquo tibi oblata fit, fugitiuis. eáque apud te concepta fit: vtique fi ea mente tibi data fuerit,vt apud te potius, quàm apud eû,qui de- dit,concipi eretur{d}. nam tibi,apud quê concepta fit, propria aduersus eum,qui obtulit, quanuis fur non lit,constituta est actio, quæ appellatur oblati.Est et- iam prohibiti furti actio aduersus eum, qui furtum quærere testibus præfentibus volente prohibuerit{e}. Præterea pœna coftituitur edicto prætoris per actio- nem furti non exhibiti aduersus eum, qui furtiuam rem apud fe quæsitam & inuentam non exhibuit. Sed hæ actiones, scilicet concepti & oblati, & furti prohibiti,necnon furti non exhibiti in desuetudine abierunt. Quum enim requifitio rei furtiuæ hodie fecundum veterem Fobferuatione non fiat: merito ex consequentia etiam præfatæ actiones ab vsu co- muni receffer uut: quum manifeftû fit,quod omnes, qui scientes rem furtiuam susceperint{g}, & celaue- rint,furti nec manifesti obnoxij sunt.
units.tr: 4. Conceived theft is said to occur when stolen goods are sought and found in someone's possession in the presence of witnesses. For against the finder an action is established, called the action for conceived theft, even though he is not the thief. Offered theft is said to occur when stolen goods are offered to you by someone and are received by you, provided they were given to you with the intention that they be conceived in your house rather than in the house of the one who gave them. For against you, in whose house they were conceived, an action is established against the one who offered them, called the action for offered theft, even though you are not the thief. There is also an action for forbidden theft against one who, when witnesses are present, forbids another to search for stolen goods. Furthermore, by the praetor's edict, a penalty is imposed through the action for failure to produce stolen goods against one who has not produced stolen goods sought and found in his possession. But these actions, namely for conceived and offered theft, for forbidden theft, and for failure to produce, have fallen into disuse. For since the search for stolen goods is not carried out today according to the old observance, these actions have properly, by consequence, passed out of common use; since it is clear that all who knowingly receive and conceal stolen goods are liable for non-manifest theft.

units.la: 5 ¶ Pœna manifesti furti,quadrupuli est tam ex ferui,quàm ex liberi persona: nec manifesti,dupli.
units.tr: 5. The penalty for manifest theft is fourfold, whether the thief is a slave or a free person; for non-manifest theft it is double.

units.la: 6 ¶ Furtum autem fit,non solum cum quis intercipiendi causa rem alienam amouet: sed generaliter cum quis alienâ rem inuito domino contrectat. Itaque fiue creditor{h} dit, teste Dio- scoride) conditû,in lance ceremoniæ causa deferetes,ei qui furti su-spectus fiebat offerre soliti effent. Alij,quia is ritus effet furti quæ-rendi sicuti in emptionib. æs & libra folenniter adhibebatur. Alij (Mar.Tat. Alpinus & Balduinus) furto per lancé & licium fignifi-cari putant furtû rerum ad sacrificia collectarum, quo fini mini-stri sacrorum licio cin&ti lancem ad eas comportandas gestabant. pignore,siue is,apud quē res deposita est, ea rc vtatur: siue is,qui rē vrendā,accepit, in aliū vsum eā transferat,quàm cuius gratia ei data est: furtū committit. veluti si quis argentum vtendum acceperit, quasi amicos ad cœnam inuitaturus,& id peregrè secum tulerit: aut si quis equum gestandi causa commodatum sibi,longius{a} aliquo duxerit: quod veteres scripserunt de eo,qui in aciem equū perduxisset.
units.tr: 6. Theft is committed not only when someone removes another's property for the purpose of appropriating it, but generally whenever someone handles another's property against the owner's will. Thus, whether a creditor uses the pledge, or the one with whom the thing was deposited makes use of it, or the one who received the thing for use transfers it to a use other than that for which it was given to him, he commits theft. For example, if someone has received silver to use, as though he were going to invite friends to dinner, and has carried it off abroad with him; or if someone has led away for a longer journey a horse lent to him for riding; which the ancients wrote of one who had led a horse into battle. [The commentators explain the term: the lance and the licium. Dioscorides, as witness, says that the vessel was made in the lance (dish) for the sake of ceremony, and those suspected of theft were accustomed to offer it. Others, because that was the rite of seeking theft, just as in purchases the bronze and the scales were solemnly employed. Others (Marcus Tatius Alpinus and Balduinus) think that theft of goods gathered for sacrifices was signified by the lance and licium, since the ministers of the sacred rites, girded with the licium, carried the lance to bring them together.]

units.la: 7 ¶Placuit tamen eos qui rebus commodatis aliter vterentur,quàm vtendas acceperint,ita furtum committere: si{b} se intelligant,id inuito domino facere: eumque,si intellexisset,non permissurum. at si permissurum credant, extra crimen videri, optima sane distinctione: quia furtum sine affectu furandi non committatur.
units.tr: 7. It has nevertheless been decided that those who use goods lent to them in a way other than that for which they received them commit theft only if they understand that they are doing so against the owner's will, and that he would not have permitted it had he known. But if they believe he would have permitted it, they are seen to be outside the crime, a distinction indeed most sound, since theft is not committed without the intention of stealing.

units.la: 8 ¶Sed & si credat aliquis inuito domino se rem commodatam sibi cōtrectare{c}, domino autem volente id fiat: dicitur furtum non fieri. Vnde illud quæsitum est, cum Titius seruum Mæuij solicitauerit, vt quasdam res domino subripere,& ad eum perferret, & seruus id ad Mæuium perrulerit: Mæuius autem dum vult Titium in ipso delicto deprehendere, permiserit seruo quasdam res ad eum perferre: vtrum furti,an serui corrupti indicio teneatur Titius,an neutro? Et cum nobis super hac dubitatione suggestum est, & antiquorum prudentium super hoc altercationes perspeximus, quibusdam neque furti, neque serui corrupti actionem præstantibus, quibusdam furti tantummodo: nos huiusmodi calliditati obviam euntes, per nostram decisionem{d} sancimus, non solum furti actionem, sed & serui corrupti contra eum dari. Licet enim is seruus deterior a solicitatore minimè factus est, & ideo non{e} concurrant regulæ, quæ serui corrupti actionem introducunt: tamen consilium corruptoris ad perniciem probitatis serui introductum est, vt sit ei pœnalis actio impositea, tanquam si re ipsa fuisset seruus corruptus: ne ex huiusmodi impunitate & in alium seruum, qui facile posset corrumpi, tale facinus à quibusdam perpetratur.
units.tr: 8. But if someone believes that he is handling a thing lent to him against the owner's will, while the owner in fact consents, it is said that no theft occurs. Hence the question arose: when Titius solicited Maevius's slave to steal certain things from his master and bring them to him, and the slave reported this to Maevius, and Maevius, wishing to catch Titius in the very act of the crime, allowed the slave to bring certain things to him, is Titius liable for theft, or for the corruption of a slave, or for neither? And since this doubt has been brought to our attention, and we have examined the disputes of the ancient jurists on this matter, some granting neither action for theft nor for corruption of a slave, others only the action for theft, we, meeting such cunning, by our decision sanction that an action is given not only for theft but also for corruption of a slave against him. For although the slave was in no way made worse by the solicitor, and therefore the rules which introduce the action for corruption of a slave do not apply, nevertheless the intention of the corrupter, aimed at destroying the integrity of the slave, has been brought into account, so that a penal action is imposed on him as though the slave had actually been corrupted; lest from such impunity such a crime be committed by some against another slave who could easily be corrupted.

units.la: 9 ¶Interdum{f} etiam liberorum hominū furtum fit. veluti si quis liberorum nostrorum, qui in potestate nostra sunt, subreptus fuerit.
units.tr: 9. Sometimes theft is also committed of free persons. For example, if one of our children who are in our power is kidnapped.

units.la: 10 ¶Aliquando autem etiā suæ rei furtum quis committit: veluti si debitor rem,{g} & quam creditori pignoris causa dedit, subtraxerit.
units.tr: 10. Sometimes, too, someone commits theft of his own property: for example, if a debtor removes a thing which he gave to his creditor as a pledge.

units.la: 11 ¶Interdum quoque furti tenetur, qui ipse furtum non fecit: qualis est is,cuius{h} ope & consilio furtum factum est. In quo numero est qui {a} tibi nummos excusit,ut alius eos raperet:aut tibi obsti- terit,ut alius rem tuam exciperet, aut oues tuas vel boues fugauerit,ut alius eas acciperet. Et hoc veteres scripserunt de eo, qui panno rubro fugauit {b} armentum.Sed si quid eorum per lasciuiam {c}, & non data opera,ut furtum admitteretur , factum est: in factum actio dari debet.At vbi ope Maxuii Titius furtum fecerit: ambo furti tenentur. Ope & consilio eius quoque furtum admitti videtur, qui scalas fortè fenestris supponit: aut ipsas fenestras vel ostiū {d} effringit ut alius furtum faceret : quiue ferramenta ad effringendum,aut scalas, ut fenestris supponeren-tur,commodauerit,sciens cuius rei gratia commodauerit.Certè qui nullam opem ad furtum faciendum adhibuit,sed tantùm consilium dedit, atque hortatus est ad furtum faciendum,nō tenetur furti.
units.tr: 11. Sometimes one is also liable for theft who did not himself commit the theft, such as one by whose aid and counsel the theft was done. In this class is one who shakes out coins for you so that another may snatch them, or who obstructs you so that another may take your property, or who drives off your sheep or oxen so that another may seize them. The ancients wrote this also of one who drove off a herd with a red cloth. But if any of these things happened through wantonness, and not by design so that the theft might be carried out, an action on the case ought to be given. But where Titius committed the theft with the aid of Maevius, both are liable for theft. One is also seen to have admitted the theft by aid and counsel if he sets ladders against windows, or breaks open the windows or doors so that another may commit the theft; or lends tools for breaking in, or ladders to be set against windows, knowing for what purpose he lent them. Certainly one who has given no aid to the commission of the theft, but only counsel, and urged another to commit it, is not liable for theft.

units.la: 12 Hi,qui in parentum vel dominorum potestate sunt,si rem eis subripiunt, furtum quidem faciunt,& res in furtiuam causam cadit (nec ob id ab vllo vsucapi potest {e},antequam in domini potestate reuertatur) sed furti actio {f} non nascitur : quia nec ex {g} alia vlla causa potest inter eos actio nasci. Si vero ope & consilio alterius furtum factum fuerit: quia utrique furtum committitur, conuenienter ille furti tenetur: quia verum est , ope & consilio eius furtum factum esse.
units.tr: 12. Those who are under the power of their parents or masters, if they steal a thing from them, do commit theft, and the thing falls into the category of stolen goods (and on that account it cannot be acquired by anyone by usucaption until it returns to the power of its owner). But no action for theft arises, because no action of any other kind can arise between them. If, however, theft is committed with the help and counsel of another, then that person is rightly liable for theft, since both commit the theft, and it is true that the theft was committed with his help and counsel.

units.la: 13. Furti autem actio ei competit,cuius {h} interest rem saluam esse,licet dominus non sit.Itaque nec domino aliter competit, quàm si eius interfit rem non perire.
units.tr: 13. The action for theft belongs to the person whose interest it is that the thing be safe, even if he is not the owner. Thus it belongs to the owner only if it is his interest that the thing not perish.

units.la: 14 Vnde constat creditorem {i} de pignore subrepto furti ‖actione‖ agere posse,etiā si idoneum debitorem habeat: quia expedit {k} ei pignori potius incubere , quàm in persona agere : adeò quidem, ut quamuis {l} ipse debitor eam rem subripuerit, nihilominus creditori competat actio furti.
units.tr: 14. Hence it is established that a creditor may bring the action for theft concerning a pledge that has been stolen, even if he has a solvent debtor, because it is more advantageous for him to rely on the pledge than to sue the person. Indeed, even if the debtor himself stole the thing, the action for theft nonetheless belongs to the creditor.

units.la: 15 Item si fullo {m} pollienda curandave,aut sarcinator, sarciendă vestimenta mercede certa ‖constituta‖ acceperit,eâmque furto amiserit: ipse furti habet actionem,non dominus, quia domini nihil interest {n} eam rem nō perire, quum iudicio locati à fullone aut sarcinatore rem suam persequi
units.tr: 15. Likewise, if a fuller or a tailor has accepted clothes to clean, or to mend for a fixed wage, and has lost them by theft, he himself has the action for theft, not the owner, because it is of no concern to the owner that the thing should not perish, since he can pursue his property by the action on hire against the fuller or tailor.

units.la: {n} nisi fullo soluendo non fit.l.12.ff.eodem. posit.Sed & bonæ fidei emptori subrepta re, quam[?] emerit, quamuis dominus nō fit, omnino cōpetit furti actio, quemadmodū & creditori. Fulloni verò & sarcinatori non aliter furti actionem competere placuit, quàm si soluendo fuerint: hoc est, si domino rei æstimationem soluere posint. Nam si soluendo non sint: tunc quia ab eis suū dominus consequi nō posit: ipsi domino furti cōpetit actio: quia hoc casu ipsius interest rem salua esse. Idem est, & si in parte soluendo fuerit fullo, aut sarcinator. 16 ¶ Quæ de fullone & sarcinatore diximus, eadem & ad cum, cui commodata res est, transferenda veteres existimabant. Nam ut ille fullo mercedem accipiendo, custodiā præstat: ita is quoque, qui commodatū utendi causa accepit, similiter necesse habet custodiam præstare. Sed nostra puidentia etiā hoc in nostris decisionibus emendauit, ut in domini voluntate sit: siue commodati actione aduersus eum, qui rem commodatam accepit, mouere desiderat: siue furti aduersus eum, qui rem subripuit: & alterutra earum electa, dominum non posse ex pœnitentia ad alteram venire actionem. sed si quidem furem elegerit: illum, qui rem utendam accepit, penitus liberari. sin autē commodator veniat adversus eum, qui rem utendam accepit: ipsi quidem nullo modo competere posse adversus furem furti actionem. eum autem, qui pro re commodata convenitur, posse adversus furē furti habere actionem: ita tamen, si dominus sciens rem esse subreptam. adversus eum, cui res commodata fuerit, peruenit. sin autem nescius & dubitans rem esse subreptam, apud eum commodati actione instituerit, postea autem re comperta voluerit remittere quidem commodari actionem, ad furti autē actione peruenire: tunc licentia ei conceditur & adversum furem venire obstaculo nullo ei opponendo, quoniā incertus constitutus mouit adversus eum, qui rem utendam accepit, commodati actione: nisi domino ab eo satisfactum fuerit, tunc etenim omnino furem à domino quidem furti actione liberari: suppositū autem esse ei, qui pro re sibi commodata domino satisfecit: cum manifestissimum fit, etiam si ab initio dominus actionem commodati instituerit, iguarus rem esse subreptam, postea autem hoc ei cognito, adversus furem transferit: omnino liberari eum, qui rem commodatam acceperit, quemcunq. causæ exi-tum dominus adversus furem habuerit; eadem defiaitione obtinente,siue in parte,siue in solidum sol-uendo sit is, qui rem commodatam acceperit.
units.tr: Unless the fuller is solvent, it does not happen; see l. 12, ff. eodem, posit. But also, where a thing has been stolen from a bona fide buyer, which he has bought, the action for theft belongs to him in full, even though he is not the owner, just as it does to a creditor. It has, however, been settled that the fuller and the tailor have the action for theft only if they are solvent, that is, if they can pay the owner the value of the thing. For if they are not solvent, then, since the owner cannot recover his property from them, the action for theft belongs to the owner himself, because in this case it is his interest that the thing be safe. The same holds if the fuller or tailor is solvent only in part. 16. What we have said about the fuller and the tailor, the ancients thought should equally be applied to the one to whom a thing has been lent. For just as the fuller, by accepting a wage, undertakes to take care of the goods, so too the one who has received a thing on loan for use is likewise bound to take care of it. But our foresight has also corrected this in our decisions, so that it rests with the owner's will: whether he wishes to bring the action of loan against the one who received the thing lent, or the action for theft against the one who stole it; and once he has chosen one of these, he cannot, having changed his mind, turn to the other action. If he has chosen the thief, the one who received the thing for use is wholly released. But if the lender proceeds against the one who received the thing for use, then indeed he cannot in any way have the action for theft against the thief; yet the one who is sued for the lent thing may have the action for theft against the thief, but only if the owner, knowing the thing was stolen, has proceeded against the one to whom the thing was lent. If, however, the owner, ignorant of and doubting that the thing was stolen, has brought the action of loan against him, and afterwards, on discovering the thing, wishes to drop the action of loan and turn to the action for theft, then he is given licence to proceed against the thief, with no obstacle placed in his way, since, being uncertain, he brought the action of loan against the one who received the thing for use; provided the owner has been satisfied by him. For then the thief is indeed wholly freed from the owner's action for theft, and the burden falls on the one who has satisfied the owner for the thing lent to him. It is most clear that, even if at first the owner brought the action of loan while ignorant that the thing had been stolen, and afterwards, having learned this, turns against the thief, the one who received the thing on loan is entirely released, whatever outcome the owner has obtained against the thief; the same rule holds whether the one who received the lent thing is solvent in part or in full.

units.la: 17 ¶Sed is apud quem res deposita est,cufto-diam non præstat : sed tantùm in eo obnoxius est, fi quid ipse dolo {b}malo fecerit, qua de causa fi res ei subrepta fuerit: quia restituendæ eius rei nomine depositi non tenetur,nec ob id eius interest rem sal-uam esse: furti agere non potest,sed furti actio do-mino competit. 18 ¶In summa fciendū est,quæ-situm esse, an impubes {c}rem alienā amouendo, fur-tum faciat? Et placuit, quia furtum ex affectu furādi consistit {d},ita demum obligari eo crimine impu-berem,fi proximus pubertati fit,&ob id intelligat fe delinquere.
units.tr: 17. But the one with whom a thing has been deposited does not undertake to keep it safe; he is liable only if he himself has acted with malice, for which reason, if the thing was stolen from him, he cannot be sued. Since he is not bound to restore the thing on account of the deposit, it is not his interest that the thing be safe, so he cannot bring the action for theft; the action for theft belongs to the owner. 18. In sum, it should be known that the question has been raised whether a minor who removes another's property commits theft. And it has been settled that, since theft consists in the intent to steal, a minor is bound by this crime only if he is nearly of the age of puberty and so understands that he is doing wrong.

units.la: 19 ¶Furti actio,fiue dupli,fiue qua-drupli,tantum ad pœnæ persecutione pertinet. Nam ipsius rei persecutione extrinsecus habet dominus, quâ aut vindicando {e}, aut condicendo potest aufer-re.Sed rei vindicatio quidè aduersus possessore est: fiue fur ipse possidet, fiue alius quilibet. conditio autem aduersus furem ipsum heredemve eius, licet non possidcat,competit.
units.tr: 19. The action for theft, whether for double or for quadruple damages, pertains only to the pursuit of the penalty. For the recovery of the thing itself the owner has a separate remedy, by which he can take it back either by vindication or by condiction. The action of vindication lies against the possessor, whether the thief himself possesses it or any other person. The action of condiction, however, lies against the thief himself or his heir, even if he does not possess the thing.

units.la: DE VI BONORVM raptorum f, TIT. II.
units.tr: Of the Action for Goods Seized by Force, Title II

units.la: VI res alienas rapit, tenetur {g}quidè etiam furti (quis enim magis alienam rem inuito domino contrectat, quàm qui vi rapit? ideoque recte dictum est {h}eum {i}improbum furem esse) sed tamen propriam actionem eius delicti nomine prætor introduxit,quæ appellatur vi bonorum raptorum : & est intra annum quadrupli {k}, post annum simpli: quæ actio vtilis est, etiam si quis vnam rem, licet minimam,rapuerit.Quadruplum autem non totum pœna est {l},sicut in actione furti manifesti diximus, sed in quadruplo inest & rei persecutio: vt pœna tripli sit,siue comprehendatur raptor in ipso delicto,siue non.'Ridiculum enim {m} esset leuioris condi-tionis esse eum, qui vi rapit,quàm qui clàm amo-
units.tr: Whoever seizes another's property by force is also liable for theft. For who handles another's property against the owner's will more than one who takes it by violence? So it is rightly said that such a person is a dishonest thief. Nevertheless, the praetor introduced a special action for this delict, called the action for goods seized by force. It lies for four times the value within a year, and for simple value after a year. This action is available even if someone seized only one thing, however small. The quadruple, however, is not wholly a penalty, as we said of the action for manifest theft. The recovery of the thing is included within the quadruple, so that the penalty is threefold, whether the robber is caught in the act or not. For it would be absurd for one who seizes by force to be in a better position than one who secretly removes something.

units.la: {l} furti vero,pecuniaria pœna est. Ea vox refertur ad illa superiora:fiue comprehendatur raptor in ipso delicto, fiue non. non ad illa: non tota pœna est sicut in actione furti. ac fi diceret cum non distinguatur in hoc delicto sicut in furto fit ne manifestum nec ne,raptorem grauius sure punıri constat. uet.
units.tr: {l} In the case of theft, however, the penalty is pecuniary. This phrase refers to the earlier words, "whether the robber is caught in the act or not," and not to the words, "the whole is not a penalty, as in the action for theft." It is as if he said: since in this delict no distinction is made, as in theft, between manifest and non-manifest, it is agreed that the robber is punished more severely than the thief.

units.la: 1 ¶Ita tamen competit hæc actio, si dolo malo quis rapuerit. Nam qui aliquo errore ductus, rem suam esse existimans, & imprudens iuris, eo animo rapuerit, quasi domino liceat etiam per vim rem suam auferre à possessoribus: absolui debet. Cui scilicet conueniens est, nec furti teneri eum, qui eodem hoc animo rapuit. Sed ne dum talia excogitatur, inueniatur via per quam raptores impune suam exerceant auaritiam: melius diualibus {a}constitutionibus pro hac parte prospectum est, vt nemini liceat vi rapere vel rem mobilem vel se mouentem, licet suam eandem rem existimet: sed si quis contra statuta principum fecerit, rei quidem suæ dominio cadere: sin autem aliena || res || sit, post restitutionem eius, etiam æstimationem eiusdem rei præstare. Quod non solum in mobilibus rebus, quæ rapi possunt, constitutiones obtinere censuerunt: sed etiam || in || inuasionibus, quæ circa res soli fiunt, vt ex hac causa ab omni rapina homines abstineant.
units.tr: 1 ¶This action lies only if someone seized the property with malicious intent (dolus malus). For one who seized with the intention that, as owner, he might lawfully take his own property from its possessors by force, and who acted under some mistake, believing the thing to be his, and ignorant of the law, should be absolved. It is fitting that one who seized with this same intention is not liable for theft either. But lest, while such schemes are devised, a way be found by which robbers may indulge their greed with impunity, the imperial constitutions have made better provision in this matter. No one may seize by force either a movable thing or one that moves of itself, even if he believes it to be his own. If anyone acts contrary to the imperial statutes, he forfeits ownership of the thing if it is his own. But if it belongs to another, he must, after restoring it, also pay its value. The constitutions have held this to apply not only to movable things that can be seized, but also to invasions made upon immovable property, so that men may refrain from every kind of robbery.

units.la: 2 ¶Sane in {b}hac actione non vtique expectatur, rem in bonis actoris esse. nam siue in bonis sit {c}, siue non: si tamen ex bonis sit, locum hæc actio habebit. Quare siue locata, siue commodata, siue etiam pignorata, siue deposita sit || res || apud Titium, sic vt interfit eius eam rem || per vim || non auferri (veluti si in deposita re culpam quoque promisit) siue bona fide possideat, siue vsufructum quis habeat in ea, vel quid aliud iuris, vt interfit eius non rapi: dicendum est ei competere hanc actionem, non vt dominium accipiat: sed illud solum, || quod || ex bonis eius, qui rapinam passus est, || id est, quod || ex substantia eius ablatum esse proponatur. Et {d}generaliter dicendum est, ex quibus causis furti actio competit in re clam facta, ex eisdem causis omnes habere hanc actionem.
units.tr: 2 ¶Indeed, in this action it is by no means required that the thing belong to the plaintiff's goods. For whether it is among his goods or not, if it is taken from his goods, this action will lie. Hence, whether the thing has been let, lent, pledged, or deposited with Titius, so that it is in his interest that it not be seized by force (for example, if he also promised care in the case of the deposited thing), or whether he holds it in good faith, or someone has a usufruct in it or some other right, so that it is in his interest that it not be seized: it must be said that this action belongs to him. It does not give him ownership, but only in respect of what is proposed as having been taken from the goods, that is, from the substance, of the one who suffered the robbery. And in general it must be said that all persons have this action on the same grounds on which the action for theft of a thing secretly taken lies.
On the Aquilian Law, Title III.

units.la: AMNI iniuriæ actio {f}constituitur per legem Aquiliam {g}: cuius primo capite cautum est, vt si quis alienum homine {h}, alienámve quadrupedem, quæ pecudum numero sit, iniuria occiderit: quanti ea res in eo anno plurimi fuerit, tantum domino dare damnetur. 1 ¶Quod autem non præcise de quadrupede, sed de ea tantum, quæ pecudum numero est, cautum est: eo pertinet, vt neque de feris bestiis, neque de canibus cautum esse intelligamus: sed de iis tantum, quae || gregatim || proprie pasci dicuntur: quales sunt equi, muli, asini, oues, boues, caprae. De suibus quoque idem placuit. Nam & sues {a}pecudum appellatione continentur: quia & hi gregatim pascuntur. Sic denique & Homerus in Odyssea {b}ait (sicut AElius Martianus in suis institutionibus refert)
units.tr: The action for ordinary injury (iniuria) is established by the Aquilian Law. Its first chapter provides that if anyone wrongfully kills another's slave, or another's four-footed animal that belongs to the herd, he is to be condemned to give the owner whatever the thing was worth at its highest price in that year. 1. It must be understood that the chapter does not speak of four-footed animals in general, but only of those that belong to the herd. Thus it does not cover wild beasts or dogs, but only those animals that are properly said to graze in herds: horses, mules, asses, sheep, oxen, and goats. The same has been ruled for swine, since swine are also included under the name of herd animals, because they too graze in herds. Homer also speaks thus in the Odyssey (as Aelius Martianus reports in his Institutes):

units.la: Ἀνεὶς τὸν γε σύεσι παρηλιφον[?] οἱ δὲ νέμοντες Παρ Κοέλκας[?] πίτυῃ[?] ἐπί τε κρήνῃ Ἀρεβούσῃ.
units.tr: Ἀνεὶς τὸν γε σύεσι παρηλιφον[?] οἱ δὲ νέμοντες Παρ Κοέλκας[?] πίτυῃ[?] ἐπί τε κρήνῃ Ἀρεβούσῃ.
that is,

units.la: Sectantem videas, qui errant per pascua, porcos Ad Coracis saxum, iuxta fontemque Arethusam.
units.tr: You may see him driving the swine that wander through the pastures, by the rock of Coracus and beside the spring Arethusa.

units.la: 2 ¶Iniuria autem occidere intelligitur {c}, qui nullo iure occidit. Itaque qui {d}latronem || insidiatore|| occiderit: non tenetur, utique si aliter periculum effugere non potest.
units.tr: 2. A person is understood to kill wrongfully when he kills without any right. So one who kills a robber or an ambusher is not liable, provided that he could not otherwise escape the danger.

units.la: 3 ¶Ac ne is quidem hac lege tenetur, qui casu occidit, si modo culpa eius nulla inveniatur. Nam alioqui non minus ex dolo quam ex culpa quisque hac lege tenetur.
units.tr: 3. Nor is a person liable under this law even if he kills by accident, so long as no fault of his can be found. For otherwise a person is liable under this law no less for malice than for negligence.

units.la: 4 ¶Itaque si quis dum {e}iaculis ludit, vel exercitatur, transeuntem seruum tuum traiecerit: distinguitur. Nam si id a milite in eo campo, ubi solitum est exercitari, admissum est: nulla culpa eius intelligitur. Si alius tale quid admiserit: culpae reus est. Idem iuris est de milite, si in alio loco, quam qui ad exercitandum militibus destinatus est, id admiserit.
units.tr: 4. Thus if someone, while playing or practising with javelins, throws one through a slave of yours who is passing by, a distinction is made. For if this happened to a soldier in the field where soldiers are accustomed to exercise, no fault is seen in him. If someone else did such a thing, he is liable for negligence. The same rule holds for a soldier if he did it in a place other than the one assigned for the exercise of soldiers.

units.la: 5 ¶Item si putator ex arbore deiecto {f}ramo seruum tuum transeuntem occiderit: si prope viam publicam aut vicinalem id factum est, neque proclamauit, ut casus evitari posset: culpae reus est. Sed si proclamauit, nec ille curauit praecauere, extra culpam est putator. AEque extra culpam esse intelligitur, si seorsum a via forte, vel in medio fundo caedebat, licet non proclamauit: quia || in || eo loco nulli extraneo ius fuerat versandi.
units.tr: 5. Likewise, if a pruner, by letting a branch fall from a tree, kills your slave who is passing by, then if this happened near a public or local road, and he did not call out so that the accident could be avoided, he is liable for negligence. But if he called out, and the other did not take care to guard himself, the pruner is free of fault. Likewise he is understood to be free of fault if he was cutting at a distance from the road, or in the middle of a field, even though he did not call out, because no outsider had any right to be in that place.

units.la: 6 ¶Praeterea, si medicus, qui seruum suum secuit {g}, dereliquerit curationem || eius ||, & ob id mortuus fuerit seruus, culpae reus erit.
units.tr: 6. Furthermore, if a physician who has cut open your slave abandons the treatment, and the slave dies as a result, he will be liable for negligence.

units.la: 7 ¶Imperitia quoque {h}culpae adnumeratur: velut si medicus || ideo || seruum tuum occiderit, quia male eum secuerit, aut perperam ei medicamentum dederit.
units.tr: 7. Lack of skill also counts as negligence: for example, if a physician kills your slave because he cut him badly, or gave him the wrong medicine.

units.la: 8 ¶Impetu quoque mulariu, quas mulio propter imperitiam retinere non potuit, si seruus tuus oppressus fuerit: culpae reus est mulio. Sed si & propter infirmitatem eas retinere non potuerit, cum alius firmior eas retinere potuisset: aeque culpa tenetur. Eadem placuerunt de eo quoque, qui cum equo ve-heretur, impetum eius aut propter infirmitatem, aut propter imperitiam suam retinere non potuerit.
units.tr: 8. Likewise, if a slave of yours is crushed by the charge of mules which a muleteer could not restrain through lack of skill, the muleteer is liable for negligence. But if he also could not restrain them through weakness, when another stronger man could have restrained them, he is equally bound by fault. The same has been ruled concerning one who is riding a horse and cannot control its charge, whether because of weakness or because of his own lack of skill.

units.la: 9 ¶His autem verbis legis, quanti {a}id eo in anno plurimi fuerit, illa sententia exprimitur: ut si quis hominem tuum, qui hodie claudus, aut mancus, aut luscus erit, occiderit, qui in eo anno integer, aut prae-tiosus fuerit: non tanti teneatur, quanti hodie erit, sed quanti in eo anno plurimi fuerit. Qua ratione creditum est poenalem esse huius legis actionem: quia non solum tanti quisque obligatur, quantum damni dederit, sed aliquando longe pluris. Ideoque constat in heredem eam actionem non transire ": quae transi-tura fuisset, si ultra damnum nunquam lis aestimare-tur.
units.tr: 9. By the words of the law, "for whatever it was worth at its highest price in that year," this meaning is expressed: if someone kills your slave who is today lame, or maimed, or one-eyed, but who in that year was sound and valuable, he is not bound to pay what the slave is worth today, but what he was worth at his highest price in that year. For this reason it has been held that the action under this law is penal, since a person is bound not only to pay the amount of the loss he has caused, but sometimes far more. Hence it is established that this action does not pass to the heir; it would have passed, if the case were never assessed at more than the loss.

units.la: 10 ¶Illud non ex verbis legis, sed ex interpretatione placuit: non solum perempti corporis aestimationem habendam esse, secundum ea quae dixi-mus: sed eo amplius, quicquid praeterea perempto eo corpore, damni vobis illatum fuerit: veluti si {b}ser-vum tuum heredem ab aliquo institutum, ante quis occiderit, quam is iussu tuo hereditatem adierit, nam hereditatis quoque amissae rationem esse habendam constat. Item si ex pari mularum unam, vel ex quadrigis equorum unum quis occiderit, vel {c}ex comcedis[?] unus servus occisus fuerit: non solum occisi fit aestimatio, sed eo amplius, id quoque computatur, quanti depretiati sunt, qui superfuit.
units.tr: 10. This has been ruled not from the words of the law but from its interpretation: that not only the value of the body destroyed is to be reckoned, as I have said, but also whatever further loss was caused to you by the destruction of that body. For example, if someone kills your slave, whom another had appointed heir, before he has entered on the inheritance at your command, then the loss of the inheritance too must be taken into account. Likewise, if someone kills one of a pair of mules, or one horse of a team of four, or one slave of ... is killed, then not only the value of the one killed is assessed, but also what the survivor has lost in value is reckoned in addition.

units.la: 11 ¶Liberum autem est ei, cuius servus occisus fuerit, & ex judicio privato legis Aquiliae damnum persequi, & capitalis criminis {d}|| eū || reum facere.
units.tr: 11. The owner of a slave who has been killed is free both to pursue the loss by a private suit under the Aquilian Law and to make the offender liable to a capital charge.

units.la: 12 ¶Caput secundum legis Aquiliae in usu non est {e}.
units.tr: 12. The second chapter of the Aquilian Law is not in use.

units.la: 13 ¶Capite tertio de omni caetero damno cauetur. Itaque si quis servum vel eam quadrupedem, quae pecudum numero est, vulnerauerit: sive eam quadru-pedem, quae pecudum numero non est, veluti canem aut feram bestiam {f}vulnerauerit, aut occiderit: hoc capite actio constituitur. In caeteris {g}quoque omnibus animalibus, item in omnibus rebus {h}, quae anima carent, damnum per iniuriam datum, hac parte vindicatur. Si quid enim utum[?], aut ruptum, aut fractum fuerit: actio ex hoc capite constituitur, quanquam poterat sola rupti appellatio in omnes istas causas sufficere. Ruptum enim intelligitur {i}, quod
units.tr: 13. The third chapter deals with all other kinds of loss. Thus if someone wounds a slave, or a four-footed animal that belongs to the herd, or wounds or kills a four-footed animal that does not belong to the herd, such as a dog or a wild beast, an action is established under this chapter. Under this part, damage caused wrongfully is claimed also for all other living creatures, and likewise for all things that lack life. If anything is spoiled, or broken, or shattered, an action arises from this chapter; although the word "broken" alone could have sufficed to cover all these cases. For that is understood to be "broken" which has been spoiled in any way whatever.

units.la: {h} fune,retiis,naue, tecto , aqua & similibus d.l.29. & l.2.Cod.eod.
units.tr: (h) By rope, nets, ship, roof, water and similar things: D.L. 29 and L. 2 Cod. eod.

units.la: {i} l. 27. §. inquit lex §. rupisse ff. eo. quoquo modo corruptum est. Unde non solùm fracta, aut usta, sed etiam scissa, & collisa, & effusa, & quo quo modo perempta atque deteriora facta, hoc verbo continentur. Denique responsum est, si {a}quis in alienum vinum aut oleum, id miscuerit, quo naturalis bonitas vini aut olei corrumperetur: ex hac parte legis ‖Aquiliæ‖ eum teneri.
units.tr: (i) L. 27 §. inquit lex and §. rupisse ff. eo.: whatever has been damaged in any way. Hence not only things broken or burned, but also things torn, struck together, poured out, and destroyed or made worse in any way, are included under this word. Finally, it has been answered that if someone mixes his own wine or oil with another's, so that the natural quality of the wine or oil is spoiled, he is liable under this part of the Aquilian Law.

units.la: 14 ¶Illud palam est sicut ex primo capite ita demum quisque tenetur, si dolo aut culpa eius homo aut quadrupes occisus occisave fuerit: ita ex hoc capite {b}de dolo aut culpa, ‖&‖ de cætero damno quemque teneri. ‖Ex‖ hoc tamen capite non quanti in eo anno, sed {c}quā-ti in diebus triginta proximis res fuerit, obligatur is, qui damnum dederit.
units.tr: 14. It is clear that, just as under the first chapter a person is liable only if the slave or four-footed animal was killed through his malice or negligence, so under this chapter a person is liable for malice or negligence and for any other loss. Yet under this chapter the offender is bound not to the amount the thing was worth in that year, but to the amount it was worth in the thirty days before.

units.la: 15 ¶At nec {d}plurimi quidem verbum adiicitur. Sed Sabino rectè placuit, perinde habendam æstimationem, ac si etiam hac parte plurimi verbum adiectum fuisset.nam plebem Romanam, quæ Aquilio tribuno interrogante hanc legem tulit, contentam fuisse{e}, quòd prima parte eo verbo usa esset.
units.tr: 15. Nor is the word plurimi added here. But Sabinus rightly held that the assessment should be made just as if the word plurimi had also been added in this part; for the Roman plebs, which passed this law at the request of the tribune Aquilius, was content that the word plurimi had been used in the first part.

units.la: 16 ¶Cæterum placuit, ita demùm directam ex hac lege actionem esse, si quis præcipuè {f}corpore suo damnum dederit. Ideóque in eum, qui alio modo damnum dederit, vtiles {g}actiones dari solent. veluti si quis hominem alienum, aut pecus ita incluserit, vt {h}fame necaretur: aut iumentum ita vehementer egerit {i}, vt rumperetur: aut pecus in tantū exagitaverit, vt præcipitaretur: aut si quis alieno seruo persuaserit, vt in arborem ascenderet, vel in puteum descenderet, & is ascendendo, vel descendendo, aut mortuus, aut aliqua parte corporis læsus fuerit, vtilis actio in eum datur. Sed si quis alienum seruum aut de {k}ponte aut de ripa in flumen deiecerit, & is suffocatus fuerit: eo, quod proiecit, corpore suo damnum dedisse, non difficulter intelligi potest: ideóque ipsa lege Aquilia tenetur. Sed si non corpore damnum fuerit datum, neque corpus læsum fuerit, sed alio modo alicui damnum contigerit: quum non sufficiat, neque directa, neque vtilis {l}legis Aquiliæ actio: placuit eum, qui obnoxius fuerit, in factum actione teneri: veluti si quis misericordia {m} ductus alienum seruum compeditum soluerit, vt fugeret.
units.tr: 16. Moreover, it has been held that the direct action under this law lies only if someone has caused loss chiefly by his own body. Therefore, against one who has caused loss in another way, the usual practice is to grant analogous actions. For example, if someone shuts up another's man or flock so that it dies of hunger; or drives a beast of burden so violently that it breaks down; or drives an animal so hard that it falls over a cliff; or if someone persuades another's slave to climb a tree or go down a well, and the slave, in climbing or descending, is killed or injured in some part of his body, an analogous action is given against him. But if someone throws another's slave off a bridge or a bank into a river, and the slave is drowned, it is not hard to see that he has caused the loss by his own body, in the act of throwing, and so he is liable under the Aquilian Law itself. But if the loss was not caused by the body, and the body was not hurt, but some loss came to someone in another way, then since neither the direct nor the analogous action under the Aquilian Law suffices, it has been ruled that the one who is at fault is liable by an action on the case: for example, if someone, moved by pity, unbound another's chained slave so that he might escape.
ON INJURIES. TITLE IV.

units.la: ENERALITER iniuria dicitur{b} omne, quod non iure fit. Specialiter, aliàs contumelia, quæ à contemnendo dicta est, quam Græci ὕβριν appellant: aliàs culpa, quam Græci ἔγκλημα dicunt, sicut in lege Aquilia damnum iniuria datum accipitur, aliàs iniquitas & iniustitia, quam Græci ἀδικίαν vocant. Cum enim prætor vel iudex non{c} iure contra quem pronuntiat: iniuriam accepisse dicitur.
units.tr: Generally, injury (iniuria) means anything done not in accordance with law. In a narrower sense it sometimes means contumely, named from contempt, which the Greeks call hybris [ὕβριν]; sometimes it means fault, which the Greeks call enklema [ἔγκλημα], as "damage done by injury" is understood in the Lex Aquilia; and sometimes it means iniquity and injustice, which the Greeks call adikia [ἀδικίαν]. For when a praetor or judge gives a judgment against someone not in accordance with law, the person against whom it is given is said to have suffered an injury.

units.la: 1 Iniuria autem committitur non solùm cùm quis pugno pulsatus, aut fustibus cæsus vel etiam verberatus erit: sed & si cui conuicium factum fuerit, siue cuius bona quasi debitoris, qui nihil deberet, possessa fuerint ab eo, qui intelligebat nihil eum sibi debere: vel si quis ad infamiam alicuius libellum[?] aut carmen, aut historiam scripserit, composuerit, ediderit, dolòve id fecerit, quo quid eorum fieret: siue quis matre-familiàs, aut prætextatus, prætextatàmve adfectatus fuerit: siue cuius pudicitia attentata esse dicetur: & denique aliis plurimis modis admittit iniuriam mani-festum est.
units.tr: 1. An injury is committed not only when someone is struck with a fist, beaten with clubs, or even whipped, but also when abuse is hurled at him, or when the goods of a man are taken into possession as if he were a debtor, though he owed nothing, by someone who knew that he owed nothing; or when someone writes, composes, or publishes a libel, a poem, or a history to another's infamy, or does anything with the intent that any of these should happen; or when a respectable matron or a boy in the toga praetexta, or one who is assailed in the same way, is harassed; or when someone's chastity is said to have been assaulted; and, in short, it is clear that an injury is committed in many other ways.

units.la: 2 Patitur autem quis iniuriam non solùm per semetipsum, sed etiam per liberos suos, quos in potestate habet: itemque per vxorem suam. id enim magis per præualuit. Itaque si filiæ alicuius, quæ Titio nupta est, iniuriam feceris: non solùm filiæ nomine tecum iniuriarum agi potest, sed etiam patris quoque & mariti nomine. Contra autem, si viro iniuria facta sit: vxor ꝗ[?] iniuriarum agere non potest. Defendi enim vxores à viris, non viros ab vxoribus, æquum est. Sed & socer nurus nomine, cuius vir in potestate est, iniuriarum agere potest.
units.tr: 2. A person suffers injury not only in his own person but also through his children in his power, and likewise through his wife. For this injury is the more serious. So if you have injured the daughter of someone who is married to Titius, an action for injury can be brought against you not only in the daughter's name but also in the name of her father and husband. On the other hand, if an injury is done to a husband, the wife cannot bring an action for injury. For it is fair that wives be defended by their husbands, not husbands by their wives. A father-in-law may also bring an action for injury in the name of his daughter-in-law, if her husband is under his power.

units.la: 3 Seruis autem ipsis quidem nulla iniuria fieri intelligitur, sed domino per eos fieri videtur, non tamen iisdem modis, quibus etiam per liberos & vxores: sed ita, cùm quid atrocius comissum fuerit, & quod apertè ad contumeliam domini respicit: veluti si quis alienum seruum atrociter verberauerit, & in hunc
units.tr: 3. Now, no injury is understood to be done to slaves themselves, but it is held to be done to their master through them. Yet it is not done in the same ways as through children and wives; it is done only when something more atrocious has been committed, and which plainly reflects on the master's contumely, as when someone savagely beats another's slave, and against him

units.la: {p} v.l.2.Cod.e. {q} l.1.ff.eo. multo minus vlteriores adgnati, quod tamen in causis tantum ciuilibus non criminalibus intelligendum est. {r} facta tamen puniuntur l.1. Cod.eo: l. 2.ff.de his qui sunt sui.
units.tr: (v. l. 2 Cod. eo.). (l. 1 ff. eo.) Much less so the more distant agnates; but this must be understood only in civil, not criminal, cases. Deeds are nevertheless punished (l. 1 Cod. eo.; l. 2 ff. de his qui sunt sui).

units.la: {s} aduersus bonos mores & iniussu domini l.15. §. Prætor.ff.eo. Casum actio proponitur. At si quis seruo conuicium fecerit, vel pugno eum percusserit: nulla in eam actio domino competit.
units.tr: (Contrary to good morals and without the owner's command, l. 15 §. Praetor ff. eo.) An action for the case is set out. But if someone abuses a slave in words, or strikes him with a fist, no action accrues to the master for that.

units.la: 4 ¶Si communi{4}seruo iniuria facta sit: æquum est, non pro ea parte, qua dominus quisque est, æstimationem iniuriæ fieri, sed ex dominorum persona{b}, quia ipsis fit iniuria.
units.tr: 4. If an injury is done to a slave owned in common, it is fair that the estimate of the injury be made not in proportion to the share each owner holds, but according to the persons of the owners, since the injury is done to them themselves.

units.la: 5 ¶Quod si vsufructus in seruo Titij est, proprietas Mæuij: ita gis Mæuio{c} iniuria fieri intelligitur.
units.tr: 5. But if the usufruct of a slave belongs to Titius and the ownership to Maevius, the injury is understood to be done to Maevius as well.

units.la: 6 ¶Sed si libero ||homini||, qui tibi bona fide seruit, iniuria facta sit: nulla tibi actio dabitur, sed suo nomine is experiri poterit: nisi in contumeliam tuam pulsatus sit, tunc enim competit & tibi iniuriarum actio. Idem ergo est & in seruo alieno bona fide tibi seruiente: vt totiens admittatur iniuriarum actio, quotiens in tua contumeliam iniuria ei{d} facta sit.
units.tr: 6. But if an injury is done to a free man who serves you in good faith, no action is given to you; he himself may sue in his own name. Unless he was struck in your contumely; for then an action for injury belongs to you too. The same holds for another's slave who serves you in good faith: an action for injury is granted whenever the injury is done to him in your contumely.

units.la: 7 ¶Poena autem iniuriarum ex lege duodecim tabularum propter membrum quidem ruptum talio erat: propter os vero fractum nummariæ{e} poenæ erant constitutæ, quasi in magna veterum paupertate. Sed postea prætores permittebant ipsis, qui iniuriam passi sunt, eam æstimare: vt iudex vel tanti reum condemnet, quanti iniuriam passus æstimauerit, vel minoris, prout ei visum fuerit. Sed poena quidem iniuriæ, quæ ex lege duodecim tabularum introducta est{f}, in desuetudinem abiit. Quam autem prætores introduxerunt (quæ etiam honoraria appellatur) in iudiciis{g} frequentatur. Nam secundum gradum dignitatis, vitæque honestatem, crescit aut minuitur æstimatio iniuriæ. Qui gradus condemnationis & in seruili persona non immerito seruatur: vt aliud in seruo actore{h}, aliud in mediocri homine, aliud in vilissimo vel compedito ius ||æstimationis|| constituatur.
units.tr: 7. The penalty for injuries under the Law of the Twelve Tables was, for a broken limb, talion; for a broken bone, fixed monetary fines were set, reflecting the great poverty of the ancients. But later the praetors allowed those who had suffered an injury to estimate it themselves, so that the judge might condemn the defendant to as much as the injured party had estimated, or to less, as seemed fit to him. The penalty for injury introduced by the Law of the Twelve Tables has fallen into disuse. The one introduced by the praetors (which is also called honorary) is in common use in trials. For the estimate of an injury rises or falls according to the degree of dignity and the respectability of life. This gradation is rightly observed even in the case of slaves: a different estimate is set for a slave who is a steward, another for a man of middling condition, and another for the lowest or a fettered slave.

units.la: 8 ¶Sed & lex Cornelia de iniuriis loquitur, & iniuriarum actionem introduxit, quæ competit ob{i} eam rem, quod se pulsarum quis, verberatumve, vel domum suam{k} vi introitam esse dicat. Domum autem accipimus, siue in propria domo quis habitet, siue{l} in conducta: siue gratis, siue hospitio receptus sit{m}.
units.tr: 8. The Cornelian Law also deals with injuries and introduced an action for injury, which is granted when someone says that he has been struck or beaten, or that his house has been entered by force. We understand "house" to mean either one in which a person lives in his own home or one he rents, whether he is received free or as a guest.

units.la: 9 ¶Atrox iniuria æstimatur{n} vel ex facto: veluti si quis ab alio vulneratus sit, vel fustibus cæsus, vel ex loco: veluti si cui in theatro, vel in foro, vel conspectu
units.tr: 9. An atrocious injury is estimated either by the deed, as when someone has been wounded by another or beaten with clubs, or by the place, as when it is done to someone in the theatre, in the forum, or in sight

units.la: ff. depositi. {i} 1. his tribus de causis l. 5. in pr. ff. eo. {k} v. l. 23.
units.tr: ff. depositi. {i} For these three reasons, l. 5 in pr. ff. eo. {k} See l. 23 ff. eo.

units.la: ff. eo. {l} l. 5. §. domum ff. eo. {m} non momentaneo, sed ad longius aliquod tempus, puta domicilio. v. l. 1. §. domum ff. de aleatoribus.
units.tr: {l} l. 5 §. domum ff. eo. {m} Not for a momentary stay, but for some longer time, such as a dwelling. See l. 1 §. domum ff. de aleatoribus.

units.la: {n} l. 7. §. atrocem. l. 8. l. 9. ff. eo: l. 4. Cx. eo: Paul. 5. sent. 4 §. 10. prætoris iniuria facta fit.vel ex persona: veluti si magistratus iniuriam passus fuerit, vel si senatori ab humili persona iniuria facta fit,aut parenti {b}patronóve fiat à liberis vel libertis. Aliter enim senatoris & parentis patronique,aliter extranei & humilis per fonæ iniuria æstimatur.Nonnunquá & locus vulneris atrocé iniuriá facit,veluti si in{c} oculo quis percussus fuerit.Parui autè refert,vtrum patrifamiliâs an filiofamiliâs talis iniuria facta sit.nam & hæc atrox iniuria æstimabitur. 10 ¶ In summa sciendum est,de omni iniuria eum , qui passus est, posse vel criminaliter {d}agere vel ciuiliter {e}. Et si quidem ciuiliter agitur : æstimatione facta secundum quod dictum est,poena reo imponitur. Sin autem criminaliter:officio iudicis extraordinaria poena reo irrogatur : hoc videlicet obseruando, quod Zenoniana {f} constitutio introduxit,vt viri illustres, quique super eos sunt,& per procuratores possint actionem iuiuriarum criminaliter vel persequi vel suscipere, secundum eius tenorem , qui ex ipsa manifestius apparet. 11 ¶ Non solum autem is iniuriarum tenetur , qui fecit iniuriam,id est,qui percusit:verum {g}ille quoque tenetur,qui dolo fecit ‖iniuriam‖ , vel qui procurauit, vt cui mala pugno percuteretur. 12 ¶ Hæc actio dissimulatione {h} aboletur.& ideo si quis iniuriam dereliquerit,hoc est,statim passus ad animum suum non reuocauerit:postea ex poenitentia remissam iniuriam non poterit recolere.
units.tr: {n} l. 7 §. atrocem; l. 8; l. 9 ff. eo; l. 4 Cod. eo; Paul. 5 sent. 4 §. 10. An injury is done to a praetor, or it is estimated by the person: as when a magistrate has suffered an injury, or when an injury is done to a senator by a person of low rank, or when it is done to a parent or patron by his children or freedmen. For the injury to a senator, a parent, or a patron is estimated differently from that to a stranger or a man of low rank. Sometimes the place of the wound also makes the injury atrocious, as when someone is struck in the eye. It matters little whether such an injury is done to a man who is his own master (paterfamilias) or to one under power (filiusfamilias); for this too will be estimated as an atrocious injury. 10. In sum, it should be known that for every injury the one who has suffered it may bring either a criminal or a civil action. If it is brought as a civil action, after the estimate has been made as described, the penalty is imposed on the defendant. But if it is brought criminally, an extraordinary penalty is imposed on the defendant at the judge's discretion, observing especially what the constitution of Zeno introduced: that illustrious men, and those above them, may pursue or take up an action for injury criminally, either in person or through procurators, according to its terms, which are more clearly apparent from the constitution itself. 11. Not only is he liable for injury who committed the injury, that is, who struck; but also he is liable who did the injury by fraud, or who arranged for someone to be struck with a fist. 12. This action is extinguished by dissimulation. Therefore, if someone has let an injury pass, that is, having suffered it at once, has not called it back to mind, he cannot afterwards recall the injury as forgiven through regret.

units.la: DE OBLIGATIONIBVS, quae quasi ex delicto nascuntur {i}. TIT. V.
units.tr: On Obligations That Arise as if from Delict. TITLE V.

units.la: 1 Iudex {k}litem suam fecerit: non proprie ex maleficio obligatus videtur. sed quia neque ex maleficio,neque ex contractu obligatus est , & vtique peccasse aliquid intelligitur,licet per imprudentiam: ideo videtur quasi ex maleficio teneri , & in quantum de ea re æquum religioni iudicantis videbitur, poenam sustinebit.
units.tr: 1 A judge who makes a case his own is not properly regarded as bound by a delict. But since he is bound neither by delict nor by contract, and it is understood that he has done something wrong, though through carelessness, he is therefore regarded as bound as if by delict, and he will bear whatever penalty seems fair to the conscience of the judge in that matter.

units.la: 1 ¶ Item is {l}, ex cuius coenaculo,vel proprio ipsius,vel conducto, vel in quo gratis habitat,deiectum effusumve aliquid,est,ita vt alicui noceret:quasi ex maleficio obligatus intelligitur. Ideo autem non proprie ex maleficio obligatus intelligitur, quia plerunque ob alterius culpam tenetur, aut serui, aut liberi. Cui similis est is, qui ea parte, qua vulgò iter fieri solet, id positum aut suspensum habet, quod potest (si ceciderit) alicui nocere: quo casu poena decem aureorum constituta est. De eo verò, quod deiectum effusumve est, dupli, quantum damni datum sit, constituta est actio.Ob hominem verò liberum occisum, quinquaginta aureorum poena constituitur. Si verò viuat, nocitumque ei esse di catur: quantum ob eam rem æquum iudici videtur, actio datur. Iudex enim computare debet mercedes medicis præstitas, cæteráque impendia, quæ in curatione facta sunt: præterea operas, quibus caruit, aut cariturus est ob id, quod inutilis est factus. 2 ¶ Si filiusfamilias scorsum a patre habitauerit, & quid ex cœnaculo eius deiectum effusumve fuerit, siue quid positum suspensumve habuerit, cuius casus periculosus est: Iuliano placuit in patre nullam [?]actionem, sed cum ipso filio agendum esse, sed cum filiofamiliâs iudice obseruandum est, qui litem suam fecerit. 3 ¶ Item exercitor nauis aut cauponæ aut stabuli de dolo aut furto, quod in naui aut caupona aut stabulo factum erit, quasi ex maleficio teneri videtur, si modo ipsius nullum est maleficium, sed alicuius eorum, quorum opera nauem aut cauponam aut stabulum exercet. Cùm enim neque ex maleficio, neque ex contractu fit adversus eum constituta hïc actio, & aliquatenus culpæ reus est, quod opera malorum hominum vteretur: ideo quasi ex maleficio teneri videtur. In his autem casibus in factum actio competit, quæ heredi quidem datur, adversus heredem autem non competit.
units.tr: 1 Likewise, the person from whose upper room, whether his own, hired, or occupied free of charge, something has been thrown or poured out so as to harm someone, is understood to be bound as if by delict. He is not properly understood to be bound by delict, because he is usually liable for another's fault, whether of a slave or a free person. Similar to this is the person who has placed or hung something in the part of the street where people commonly pass, which could harm someone if it fell; in that case a penalty of ten gold pieces has been fixed. For something thrown or poured out, an action for double the amount of the damage done is established. For a free man killed, a penalty of fifty gold pieces is set. If, however, he survives and is said to have been harmed, an action is given for whatever amount seems fair to the judge in that matter.
