For the judge ought to reckon the fees paid to physicians and the other expenses incurred in the cure, and besides the labour of which he has been deprived, or will be deprived, because he has been made unfit for work. 2 If a son under power has lived apart from his father, and something has been thrown or poured out from his upper room, or he has placed or hung something whose fall is dangerous, Julian held that no action lies against the father, but the action must be brought against the son himself; yet the son under power, as a judge who has made a case his own, must be dealt with accordingly. 3 Likewise, the master of a ship, an inn, or a stable is regarded as bound as if by delict for a fraud or theft committed on board the ship, in the inn, or in the stable, provided that the wrong was not his own but that of one of those whose work he uses to run the ship, inn, or stable. For since this action is established against him neither by delict nor by contract, and he is in some measure at fault for using the services of wicked men, he is therefore regarded as bound as if by delict. In these cases an action in factum lies, which is given against the heir but does not lie against the heir of the wrongdoer.
On Actions, Title 6.

units.la: SVPEREST, vt de actionibus loquamur. Actio autem nihil aliud est, quàm ius persequendi in iudicio, quod sibi debetur. 1 ¶ Omnium autem actionum quibus inter aliquos apud iudices arbitrósve de quacunque re quæritur, summa diuisio in duo genera deducitur, aut enim in rem sunt, aut in personam. Nàque agit vnusquisque aut cum eo, qui ei obligatus est, vel ex contractu, vel ex maleficio: quo casu prodítæ sunt actiones in persosonam[?],per quas intendit adnerfarium ei dare aut facere oportere,& aliis quibusdam modis{4}.Aut cum ea agit,qui nullo iure ei obligatus est,mouet tamen alicui de aliqua re controuersiam. quo casu proditae actiones in rem sunt: veluti si rem corporalem possi-deat quis, quam Titius suam esse affirmet, possessor autem dominum eius se esse dicat{b}.nam si Titius suā esse intendat: in rem actio est.
units.tr: It remains to speak of actions. An action is nothing other than the right to pursue in court what is owed to us. 1. Of all the actions by which a question is raised between parties before judges or arbitrators about any matter, the main division is into two kinds: they are either in rem or in personam. For each person sues either someone who is bound to him, by contract or by wrong, and in that case actions are provided in personam, by which he claims that his opponent ought to give or do something, or in certain other ways. Or he sues someone who is bound to him by no right, but still raises a dispute with him about some matter. In that case the actions provided are in rem: for example, when someone possesses a corporeal thing which Titius affirms to be his, and the possessor says that he himself is its owner. For if Titius claims that it is his, the action is in rem.

units.la: {2} ¶Aeque si agat quis, ius sibi esse fundo forte vel aedibus vtendi fruendi, vel per fundum vicini eundi agendi, vel ex fundo vicini aquam ducendi:in re actio est. Eiusdem generis est actio de iure prediorum vrbanorum: veluti{c} si quis agat ius sibi esse altius aedes suas tollendi prosiciendive, vel proiiciendi aliquid, velimmittendi tignum in vicini aedes. Contra quoque de vsufructu,& de seruitutibus praediorū rusticorum, item praediorum vrbanorum, inuice quoque proditae sunt actiones: vt{d} si quis intendat ius non esse aduersario vtendi fruendi,eundi agendi,aquamve ducendi,item altius tollendi prospiciendive, vel proiiciendi immittendive: iste quoque actiones in rem sunt, sed negatiuae. Quod{e} genus actionis in controuersiis rerum corporalium proditum non est. Nam in his is agit, qui non possidet:ei vero,qui possidet,nō est actio prodita, per quam neget rem actoris esse. Sane vno casu qui possidet, nihilominus is actoris partes obtinet, sicut in latioribus Digestorum libris opportunius apparebit.
units.tr: 2. Likewise, if someone sues that he has a right to use and enjoy a farm or a house, or to pass and drive across his neighbour's farm, or to draw water from his neighbour's farm, that is an action in rem. Of the same kind is the action concerning the rights of town properties: for example, when someone claims that he has a right to raise his buildings higher, or to build so as to look out, or to project something, or to insert a beam into his neighbour's building. Conversely, actions are also provided concerning usufruct and the servitudes of rural properties, and likewise of urban properties, in turn. So, if someone claims that his opponent has no right to use, enjoy, pass, drive, draw water, raise higher, look out, project or insert, those actions too are in rem, but negative. This kind of action has not been provided in disputes over corporeal things. For in these the one who does not possess is the one who sues; but no action is given to the one who possesses, by which he may deny that the thing belongs to the plaintiff. Indeed, in one case the possessor nonetheless takes the part of plaintiff, as will appear more fittingly in the larger books of the Digest.

units.la: {3} ‡ Sed iste quidem actiones,quarum mentionem habuimus,& si quae sunt similes,ex legitimis & ciuilibus causis descendunt. Aliae autem sunt, quas praetor ex sua iurisdictione comparatas habet tam in rem, quam in personam, quas & ipsas necessarium est exemplis ostendere. [vt] ecce, Plerumque ita permittit ||praetor|| in rem agere, vt{h} nudè rem possessoris non esse dixerit,nō iuuabitur: vt cui necesse fit vlterius progredi:edum ac fundū ipsum, quem non possidet, vindicare.
units.tr: 3. But those actions which we have mentioned, and any similar ones, arise from legitimate and civil causes. Others, however, are those which the praetor has by his own jurisdiction, both in rem and in personam, and these too it is necessary to show by examples. For instance, the praetor often allows one to sue in rem in such a way that, if the possessor merely says the thing is not his, he gets no help; since the plaintiff must go further and vindicate the very farm which the other does not possess.

units.la: {f} Rectè Hotomanus hic ait: torquere illud esse, nō docere: interea, dum apertius loquatur Imperator, sibi videri ait, legendum sane illo casu: vt superior significetur. vel {a}actor dicat se quasi vsucepisse, quod non vsuceperit: vel ex diuerso possessor{b} dicat aduersarium suum non vsucepisse, quod vsuceperit.
units.tr: Hotomanus rightly says here that this is "to twist," not "to teach." Meanwhile, since the Emperor speaks more plainly, he thinks that in that case one must read, of course, so that the earlier point is indicated: either the plaintiff says that he has, as it were, acquired what he has not acquired, or, conversely, the possessor says that his opponent has not acquired what he has acquired.

units.la: 4 ¶ Nam-que si cui ex iusta causa res aliqua tradita fuerit (veluti ex causa emptionis, aut donationis, aut dotis, aut legatorum ||&|| necdum eius rei dominus effectus est: si eius rei possessionem casu amiserit, nullam habet in rem directam{c} actionem ad eam persequendam: quippe ita productae sunt iure ciuili actiones{d} vt quis dominium suum vindicet. sed quia sane durum erat, eo casu deficere actionem: inuenta est a praetore actio, in qua dicit is, qui possessionem amisit, eam rem se vsucepisse, quam vsu non cepit, & ita vindicat suam esse. quae actio Publiciana appellatur, quoniam primum a{e} Publicio praetore in edicto proposita est.
units.tr: 4. For if a thing has been handed over to someone from a just cause (for example, from purchase, gift, dowry or legacies), and he has not yet become its owner, then if he has lost possession of it by chance, he has no direct action in rem to pursue it. Indeed, the actions under civil law are framed so that someone vindicates his ownership. But because it was truly hard that the action should fail in that case, the praetor devised an action in which he who has lost possession says that he acquired by usucapion the thing which he did not acquire by use, and so claims it as his own. This is called the Publician action, because it was first put forward in the edict by the praetor Publicius.

units.la: 5 ¶ Rursus ex diuerso, si quis{f} cum reipublicae causa abesset, vel{g} in hostium potestate esset, rem eius, qui in ciuitate esset, vsucepit: permittitur domino, si possessor reipublicae causa abesse desierit, tunc intra annum rescissa vsucapione eam petere: id est, ita petere, vt dicat possessorem vsu non cepisse, & ob id suam rem esse. Quod genus actionis quibusdam & aliis similis aequitate motus praetor adcommodat, sicut ex latiore Digestorum seu Pandectarum volumine intelligere licet.
units.tr: 5. Conversely, if someone acquired by usucapion the property of a man who was absent on public business or in enemy hands, while the owner was in the city, the owner is permitted, if the possessor has ceased to be absent on public business, to seek the thing within a year, the usucapion being rescinded. That is, he may seek it by saying that the possessor did not acquire it by use, and that on that account the thing is his. The praetor, moved by equity, grants this kind of action to certain other similar cases as well, as may be understood from the larger volume of the Digest, or Pandects.

units.la: 6 ¶ Item si quis in fraudem creditorum{h} rem suam alicui tradiderit: bonis eius a creditoribus possessis ex sententia praesidis permittitur ipsis creditoribus, rescissa traditione, eam rem petere, id est, dicere eam rem traditam non esse, & ob id in bonis debitoris manifeste.
units.tr: 6. Likewise, if someone has handed over his thing to another in fraud of creditors, then, when the creditors have taken possession of the debtor's goods by the governor's sentence, the creditors themselves are permitted, the handing over being rescinded, to seek that thing. That is, they may say that the thing was not handed over, and that on that account it is manifestly among the debtor's goods.

units.la: 7 ¶ Item Seruiana & quasi Seruiana (quae etiam hypothecaria vocatur) ex ipsius praetoris iurisdictione substantiam capiunt. Seruiana{i} autem experitur quis de rebus coloni, quae pignoris iure{χ} pro mercedibus fundi ei tenentur. Quasi Seruiana autem est, qua{l} creditores pignora hypothecaefve persequuntur. Inter pignus autem & hypothecam (quantum ad actionem hypothecariam attinet) nihil interest. nam de qua re inter creditorem & debitorem conuenerit, vt sit pro debito obligata: utraque hac appellatione continetur. sed in a-
units.tr: 7. Likewise the Servian action and the quasi-Servian action (which is also called hypothecary) take their substance from the praetor's own jurisdiction. A man brings the Servian action concerning the goods of a tenant, which are held under the right of pledge for the rent of a farm. The quasi-Servian action is that by which creditors pursue pledges or hypothecs. As far as the hypothecary action is concerned, there is no difference between pledge and hypothec. For whatever thing has been agreed between creditor and debtor to be bound for the debt is included under either name. But in

units.la: {χ} hic. {χ} v.l.4. ff. ex quib. caus. pignus. Hic obiter nota, pignus praetorium, ob contumaciam ante sententiam: iudiciale, ad executionem sententiae: legale, vi legis, idque tacite: conuentionale, partium consensu contrahi. {l} v.l.16. §.3. l.17. ff. de pignoribus. dicitur etiam hypothecaria. liis differentia est. Nam pignoris appellatione eam proprie rem contineri dicimus,quæ simul etiam traditur creditori, maximè si mobilis sit. At eam,quæ sine traditione, nuda conuentione tenetur, proprie hypothecæ appellatione contineri dicimus. 8 ¶ In personam quoque actiones ex sua iurisdictione proposita habet prætor: veluti de pecunia constituta, cui similis videbatur receptitia. Sed ex nostra constitutione (cùm & si quid plenius habebat, hoc in actionem pecuniæ constitutæ transfusum est) & ea quasi superuacua iussa est cum sua auctoritate à nostris legibus recedere. Item prætor proposuit actionem de peculio seruorum, filiorumque familiarum: & eam, ex qua quæritur, an actor iurauerit, & alias complures.
units.tr: {χ} here. Note in passing: a pledge may be praetorian, on account of contumacy before sentence; judicial, for the execution of a sentence; legal, by force of law, and this tacitly; or conventional, contracted by agreement of the parties. It is also called hypothecary. There is a difference between these. For we say that under the name of pledge is properly contained the thing which is also delivered to the creditor at the same time, especially if it is movable. But what is held without delivery, by bare agreement, we say is properly contained under the name of hypothec. 8. The praetor also has actions in personam provided by his own jurisdiction: for example, concerning money promised (pecunia constituta), to which the action on a receipt seemed similar. But by our constitution (since whatever fuller provision it had was transferred into the action on money promised), that too, as if superfluous, has been ordered to withdraw from our laws together with its authority. Likewise the praetor provided an action concerning the peculium of slaves and of sons under power, and that by which it is inquired whether the plaintiff has sworn, and many others.

units.la: 9 ¶ De constituta autem pecunia cum omnibus agitur a, quicumque pro se vel pro alio soluturos se constituerint: nulla scilicet stipulatione interposita, nam alioqui si stipulanti promiserint, iure ciuili tenentur.
units.tr: 9. An action on money promised is brought against all who have undertaken a to pay, for themselves or for another, with no stipulation interposed; for otherwise, if they promised in answer to a stipulation, they are bound by civil law.

units.la: 10 ¶ Actiones autem de peculio, ideo aduersus patrem b dominumve c comparauit prætor: quia licet ex contractu filiorum seruorumve ipso iure non teneantur: æquum tamen est peculio tenus (quod veluti patrimonium est filiorum filiarumque, item seruorum) condemnari eos.
units.tr: 10. The praetor provided actions concerning the peculium against the father b or master c, because although by law they are not bound by contract of sons or slaves, yet it is fair that they be condemned up to the amount of the peculium, which is, as it were, the patrimony of sons and daughters, and likewise of slaves.

units.la: 11 ¶ Item si quis postulate aduersario iurauerit, deberi sibi pecuniam, quam peteret, neque ei soluatur: iustissime accommodat ei talem actionem, per quam non illud quæritur, an ei pecunia debeatur d sed an iurauerit.
units.tr: 11. Likewise, if someone, when his opponent has been asked, swears that the money he sues for is owed to him, and it is not paid to him, the praetor most justly grants him such an action, in which the question is not whether the money d is owed to him, but whether he swore.

units.la: 12 ¶ Poenales quoque actiones prætor multas ex sua iurisdictione introduxit: veluti aduersus eum, qui ex albo eius e corrupisset: & in eum, qui patronum vel parentem f in ius vocasset, cum id nô impetrasset: item aduersus eum g, qui vi exemerit eum, qui in ius vocaretur, cuiusve dolo alius exemerit, & alias innumerabiles.
units.tr: 12. The praetor also introduced penal actions by his own jurisdiction: for example, against one who had corrupted his album e, and against one who had summoned his patron or parent f to court without obtaining leave; likewise against one who by force freed g a man who was being summoned to court, or by whose fraud another freed him, and countless others.

units.la: 13 ¶ Præiudiciales actiones in rem esse videntur: quales sunt per quas quæritur, an aliquis liber h, an libertus i sit, vel de partu agnoscendo k. Ex quibus fere vna illa legitimam causam habet, per quam quæritur, an aliquis liber sit. cæterae ex ipsius prætoris iurisdictione substantiam ca-piunt.
units.tr: 13. Prejudicial actions seem to be in rem. Such are those by which it is inquired whether someone is free h, or a freedman i, or concerning the acknowledgment of a child's birth k. Of these, only the one by which it is asked whether someone is free has a legitimate cause; the others derive their substance from the praetor's own jurisdiction.
capiunt.

units.la: 14. ¶Sic itaque discretis actionibus, certum est, non posse actorem suam rem ita ab aliquo petere, si apparet eum dare oportere{a}. Nec enim quod a-ctoris est, id ei dari oportet: scilicet quia dari cuiquam id intelligitur, quod ita datur, vt eius fiat. Nec res quae ‖iam‖ actoris est, magis eius fieri potest. Plane odio furum, quo magis pluribus actionibus te-neantur,effectum est ut extra poenam dupli aut qua-drupli, rei recipiendae nomine fures etiam hac actio-ne{c} teneantur,si appareat eos dare oportere: quamuis sit aduersus eos etiam ‖haec‖ in rem actio per quam rem suam quis esse petit.
units.tr: 14. Thus, with the actions so distinguished, it is certain that a plaintiff cannot claim his own property from someone by the action if it appears that he ought to give. For it is not right that what already belongs to the plaintiff should be given to him, since something is understood to be given to someone only when it is given so that it becomes his. Nor can a thing that already belongs to the plaintiff become more his. Yet out of hatred for thieves, who are bound by more actions the more there are, it has been provided that, besides the penalty of double or quadruple, thieves are also bound for the recovery of the thing by this action, if it appears that they ought to give, although against them there is also the real action by which someone claims his own thing as his.

units.la: 15 ¶Appellamus autem in rem quidem actiones, vindicationes{d}: in personam vero actiones, quibus dare aut facere oportere intenditur, condictiones. Condicere enim est denuntiare prisca lingua. nunc vero abusiue dicimus condictio-nem actionem in personam esse, qua actor intendit dari sibi oportere. Nulla enim hoc tempore eo nomine denuntiatio fit.
units.tr: 15. We call actions against things (in rem) vindications, but personal actions, in which it is claimed that something ought to be given or done, are condictions. For condicere means to denounce in the old language. Nowadays, however, we loosely say that a condiction is a personal action by which the plaintiff claims that something ought to be given to him, since at present no denunciation is made under that name.

units.la: 16 ¶Sequens illa diuisio est, quod quaedam actiones rei persequendae gratia comparatae sunt, quaedam poenae persequendae, quaedam mistae sunt.
units.tr: 16. The following division applies: some actions are designed to pursue a thing, some to pursue a penalty, and some are mixed.

units.la: 17 ¶Rei persequendae causa comparatae sunt omnes in rem actiones. Earum vero actionum, quae in personam sunt, ex contractu nascuntur, fere{e} omnes rei persequendae causa comparatae videntur: veluti quibus mutuam pecu-niam, vel in stipulatum deductam petit actor, item commodati, depositi, mandati, pro socio, ex empto, vendito, locato, conducto. Plane si depositi agatur eo nomine, quod tumultus, incendij, ruinae, naufragij causa depositum sit: in duplum actionem praetor reddit: si modo cum ipso, apud quem depositum sit, aut cum herede eius de dolo ipsius agitur, quo casu mista est actio.
units.tr: 17. All actions in rem are designed to pursue a thing. Of the personal actions, which arise from contract, nearly all appear designed to pursue a thing: for example, those by which the plaintiff claims a loan of money or money promised by stipulation, and likewise those of commodatum, deposit, mandate, partnership, sale, purchase, letting and hiring. But if an action of deposit is brought on the ground that the deposit was made because of tumult, fire, collapse or shipwreck, the praetor grants an action for double, provided it is brought against the depositary himself, or against his heir, for his fraud; in that case the action is mixed.

units.la: 18 ¶Ex maleficiis vero prodita actiones, aliae tantum poenae persequendae causa comparatae sunt: aliae tam poenae, quam rei persequendae, & ob id mistae sunt. Poenam tantum persequitur quis actione furti{f}. siue enim manifesti agatur quadru-pli, siue non manifesti dupli: de sola poena agitur. nam ipsam rem propria actione persequitur quis, id est, suam esse petens: siue fur ipse eam rem possideat, siue alius quihibet. Eo amplius aduersus furem etiam condictio est ‖rei‖.
units.tr: 18. Of the actions arising from wrongdoing, some are designed only to pursue a penalty, while others pursue both penalty and thing, and so are mixed. One pursues only a penalty by the action for theft. For whether it is brought for manifest theft (fourfold) or non-manifest theft (double), only the penalty is at issue. One pursues the thing itself by its own action, that is, by claiming it as one's own, whether the thief himself possesses it or anyone else. Moreover, against the thief there is also a condiction of the thing.

units.la: 19 ¶Vi autem bonorum ra-ptorum actio, mista est: quia in quadruplo rei perse-cutio continetur: poena autem tripli est. Sed & legis Aquiliae actio de damno iniuria ‖dato,‖mista est: non solum si adversus infitiantem in duplum agatur, sed interdum & si in simplum quisque agat: veluti si quis hominem claudum aut luscum occiderit, qui in eo anno integer & magni pretij fuerit: tanti enim damnatur, quanti {a}is homo eo in anno plurimi fuerit secundum jam traditam diuisionem. Item mista est {b}actio contra eos, qui relicta sacrosanctis ecclesiis, vel aliis venerabilibus locis, legati vel fideicommissi nomine, dare distulerint: usque adeo, ut etiam in iudicium vocarentur. tunc enim & ipsam rem vel pecuniam, quae relicta est, dare compelluntur, & aliud tantum pro poena, & idem in duplum eius fit condemnatio.
units.tr: 19. The action for goods taken by violence is mixed, because recovery of the thing is contained in the fourfold, while the penalty is threefold. The action under the Aquilian law for damage wrongfully done is also mixed, not only when one sues the denier for double, but sometimes even when one sues for single. For example, if someone has killed a lame or one-eyed man who was sound in that year and of great value, he is condemned for as much as the man was worth at his highest in that year, according to the division already described. Likewise the action against those who, having been left something by legacy or trust for sacred churches or other venerable places, have delayed giving it, is mixed; so much so that they may even be summoned to court. For then they are compelled to give both the thing or money that was left and, as a penalty, another equal amount, and the condemnation is for double of it.

units.la: 20 Quaedam actiones mistam causam obtinere videntur, tam in rem quam in personam: qualis est familiae erciscundae actio, quae competit coheredibus de dividenda hereditate. Item com-muni dividundo, quae inter eos redditur, inter quos aliquid commune est, ut id dividatur. Item finium regundorum actio, qua inter eos agitur, qui confines agros habent. In quibus tribus iudiciis permitti-tur {f}iudici rem alicui ex litigatoribus ex bono & aequo adiudicare: & si unius pars praegranari [?] videbitur, eum innuicem certa pecunia alteri condemna-re.
units.tr: 20. Some actions seem to have a mixed character, both in rem and in personam. Such is the action for dividing an inheritance, which belongs to coheirs for dividing the estate; likewise the action for common division, brought between those among whom something is held in common, so that it may be divided; and likewise the action for fixing boundaries, brought between those who hold neighbouring fields. In these three judgments the judge is permitted to award a thing to one of the litigants according to good and fair dealing, and, if one party's share appears (text unclear), to condemn him to pay a certain sum of money to the other in turn.

units.la: 21 Omnes autem actiones, vel in simplum conceptae sunt, vel in duplum, vel in triplum, vel in quadruplum, ulterius autem nulla actio extenditur.
units.tr: 21. All actions are framed either for single, double, triple or quadruple, and no action extends beyond quadruple.

units.la: 22 In simplum agitur: veluti ex stipulatione, ex empto, vendito, locato, conducto, mandato, & denique ex aliis quam plurimis {h}causis.
units.tr: 22. We sue for single in actions such as those on stipulation, purchase, sale, letting, hiring, mandate, and, in short, on very many other grounds.

units.la: 23 In duplum agimus: veluti furti nec manifesti, damni iniuriae, ex lege Aquilia, depositi ex quibusdam {i}causis. Item servi corrupti {k}: quae competit in eum, cuius hortatu consiliove servus alienus fugerit, aut continuamax [?] adversus dominum factus est, aut luxurio se vincere coeperit, aut denique quolibet modo deterior factus sit. In qua actione earum etiam rerum, quas fugiendo servus abstulerit, aestimatio deducitur. Item ex legato, quod venerabilibus locis relictum est secundum ea quae supra diximus.
units.tr: 23. We sue for double in actions such as non-manifest theft, damage wrongfully done under the Aquilian law, and deposit on certain grounds. Likewise for corrupting another's slave, which lies against the one at whose urging or counsel another's slave has fled, or has become continually insolent towards his master, or has begun to outdo others in debauchery, or has in any way become worse. In this action, the value of the things which the slave carried off in fleeing is also deducted. Likewise, from a legacy left to venerable places, according to what we said above.

units.la: 24 Tripli vero ||agimus||, cum quidam maiorem vera aestimatione quantitatem in libello conventionis infernat [?], ut ex hac causa viatores {l}, id est, executores litium {m}, ampliorem summam [?] sportularum nomine exigerent, tunc enim id, quod propter eorum causam damnum passus fuerit reus, [in]triplum ab actore consequetur: ut in hoc triplo etiam simplum, in quo damnum passus est, connumeretur. Quod nostra constitutio introduxit, quæ in nostro Codice {a}ful-get, quam {b}proculdubio certum est ex lege condi-ctitia emanare. 25 ¶ Quadrupli autem agitur, ve-luti furti manifesti. item, de eo quod metus causa factum sit, deque ea pecunia quæ in hoc data sit, vt is cui datur calumniæ causa, negotium alicui faceret, vel non faceret. Item,{c}ex lege conditicia nostra constitutio oritur, in quadruplum condemnatione inponens iis executoribus litium, qui contra nostræ constitutionis normam à reis quicquam exegerint.
units.tr: 24. We sue for triple when someone inserts in the libel of summons a sum greater than the true valuation, so that by this means the summoners (viatores), that is, the executors of suits, may exact a larger sum under the name of fees. For then the defendant who suffered loss on their account will obtain the triple from the plaintiff, so that within this triple the single amount by which he was harmed is also counted. Our constitution, which shines in our Code, introduced this; and it is certainly held to proceed from the conditional law. 25. We sue for quadruple in actions such as that for manifest theft, likewise concerning what was done through fear, and concerning money given in this matter, so that the one to whom it is given, out of calumny, should do or not do some business for another. Likewise our constitution arises from the conditional law, imposing condemnation to fourfold on those executors of suits who have exacted anything from defendants contrary to the rule of our constitution.

units.la: 26 ¶ Sed furti quidem nec manifesti actio, & ferui corrupti, à cæteris, de quibus simul locuti sumus, eo differunt, quod hæ actiones omnimodo dupli sunt. at illæ, id est, damni iniuriæ ex lege Aquilia, & interdum depositi, infitiatione duplicantur, in confitentem autem in simplum dantur. Sed illa, quæ de his competit, quæ relicta venerabilibus locis sunt, non solum infitiatione duplicatur {d}, sed etiam si distulerit relicti solutionem vsquequo iuxta magistratuum [nostrorum] conueniatur. In confitentem vero, ante quàm iussu magistratuum conueniatur, soluentem simpli redditur.
units.tr: 26. The action for non-manifest theft and that for corrupting a slave differ from the others we have discussed together in this: these actions are always double. But the others, namely damage wrongfully done under the Aquilian law and, sometimes, deposit, are doubled by denial, while against one who confesses they are granted as single. But the action concerning those things left to venerable places is not only doubled by denial, but also, if payment of the legacy is delayed, until the defendant is summoned before our magistrates. Against one who confesses, before he is summoned by order of the magistrates, the payment is reduced to single.

units.la: 27 ¶ Item, actio de eo quod metus causa factum sit, à cæteris, de quibus simul locuti sumus, eo differt: quod eius natura tacitè continetur, vt qui iudicis iussu ipsam rem actori restituat{e}, absoluatur, quod in cæteris casibus non est ita: sed omnimodo quisque in quadruplum condemnatur, quod est & in furti manifesti actione.
units.tr: 27. Likewise, the action concerning what was done through fear differs from the others we have discussed together in this: its nature tacitly includes that one who restores the thing itself to the plaintiff by the judge's order is acquitted, which is not so in the other cases. But in every case one is condemned to fourfold, as also in the action for manifest theft.

units.la: 28 ¶ Actionum autem quædam bonæ fidei sunt, quædam stricti iuris. Bonæ fidei {f}sunt hæ: ex empto, venditio, locato, conducto, negotiorum gestorum, mandati, depositi, pro socio, tutelæ, commodati, pignoratitia, fiduciæ, familiæ erciscundæ, communi diuidundo, præscriptis verbis, quæ de æstimato proponitur, & ea quæ ex permutatione competit, & hereditatis petitio. Quamuis enim usque adhuc incertum erat, inter bonæ fidei iudicia connumeranda hereditatis petitio esset, an non: nostra tamen constitutio {g}aperte eam esse bonæ fidei disposuit.
units.tr: 28. Some actions are of good faith, others of strict law. Of good faith are these: those on purchase, sale, letting, hiring, management of affairs, mandate, deposit, partnership, guardianship, commodatum, pledge, fiducia, division of an inheritance, common division, praescriptis verbis (which is brought concerning a valued thing), that which arises from exchange, and the petition of inheritance. For although it was uncertain until now whether the petition of inheritance should be counted among the judgments of good faith, our constitution has openly ruled that it is of good faith.

units.la: 29 ¶ Fuerat antea & rei uxoriæ actio una ex bonæ fidei iudiciis: sed cum plenior esset ex stipulatu actionem inuenientes, omne ius quod res uxoria antea habebat, cum multis diuisionibus in actionem ex stipulatu, quæ de dotibus exigendis proponitur, transtulerimus, merito rei uxoriæ actione sublata ex stipulatu [actio,] quæ pro ea introducta est, naturam bonae fidei iudicij tantum in exactione dotis meruit, vt bonae fidei sit. ‖Sed‖ & tacitam ei dedimus hypothecam. Praeferri autem aliis creditoribus{*} in hypothecis tunc censuimus, cùm ipsa mulier de dote sua experiatur, cuius solius prouidentia hoc induximus.
units.tr: 29. The action on the dowry was formerly also one of the judgments of good faith. But since they found a fuller action on stipulation, and we have transferred all the rights that the dowry action previously had, through many divisions, into the action on stipulation which is proposed for exacting dowries, the dowry action has rightly been abolished. The action on stipulation introduced in its place has earned the nature of a judgment of good faith only in exacting the dowry, so that it is of good faith. We have also given it a tacit mortgage, and we have decided that it is preferred to other creditors in mortgages when the woman herself sues for her own dowry. It was for her sake alone that we introduced this.

units.la: 30 ¶In bonae fidei iudiciis libera potestas permitti videtur iudici ex bono & aequo aestimandi, quantum actori restitui debeat. In quo & illud continetur, vt si quid inuicem praestare actorem oporteat: eo compensato, in reliquum is, cum quo actum est, debeat condemnari. Sed & in stricti iuris iudiciis ex rescripto diui Marci opposita doli mali exceptione, compensatio inducebatur. Sed nostra constitutio {b}eadem compensationes, quae iure aperto {c}nituntur, latius introduxit, vt actiones ipso iure minuant, siue in rem, siue in personam, siue alias quascunque: excepta {d}sola depositi actione, cui aliquid compensationis nomine opponi, sane iniquum esse credimus: ne sub praetextu compensationis, depositarum rerum quis exactione defraudetur.
units.tr: 30 In actions of good faith the judge seems to be given free power to assess, according to what is good and fair, how much must be restored to the plaintiff. This includes the rule that if the plaintiff also owes something in return, the judge, after setting off the one against the other, must condemn the defendant for the balance. In actions of strict law, a plea of fraud (exceptio doli mali) granted by a rescript of the divine Marcus used to bring in set-off. Our constitution has extended these set-offs, which rest on open law, so that they reduce actions by law itself, whether in rem, in personam, or of any other kind. The only exception is the action on deposit: we think it wrong to allow any set-off against it, lest anyone be defrauded of deposited goods in the recovery of them under the pretext of set-off.

units.la: 31 ¶Praeterea quasdam actiones arbitrarias, id est, ex arbitrio iudicis pendentes appellamus. In quibus, nisi arbitrio iudicis is, cum quo agitur, actori satisfaciat: veluti rem restituat, vel exhibeat, vel soluat, vel ex noxali causa seruum dedat: condemnari debeat. Sed istae actiones, tam in rem, quàm in personam inueniuntur. In rem veluti Publiciana, Serviana de rebus coloni, quasi Ser-viana, quae etiam hypothecaria vocatur. In personam, veluti quibus de eo agitur, quod {e}‖vi‖ aut metus causa, aut {f}dolo malo factum est. Item cùm id {g}quod certo loco promissum est, petitur. Ad exhibendum quoque actio, ex arbitrio iudicis pendet {h}. In his enim actionibus & caeteris similibus permittitur iudici ex bono & aequo secundum cuiusque rei, de qua actum est, naturam aestimare, quèadmodum actori satisfieri oporteat{i}
units.tr: 31 We also call certain actions arbitrary, that is, dependent on the judge's discretion. In these, unless the defendant satisfies the plaintiff at the judge's discretion, for example by restoring or producing the thing, paying, or surrendering a slave in a noxal case, he must be condemned. Such actions are found both in rem and in personam. In rem, for example the Publician action, the Serviana concerning the goods of a tenant (called the Serviana, which is also called hypothecary), and the action in personam concerning what was done by force, by fear, or by fraud. Likewise when something promised at a certain place is demanded; and the action for production also depends on the judge's discretion. In these actions and similar ones the judge is allowed to assess, according to what is good and fair, the nature of each matter in dispute, and how the plaintiff ought to be satisfied.

units.la: ratione §.30.s.eo[?]VVisemb. tradit, natura sua stricti iuris esse: ex accideti vero (quia incerta quantitas & aestimatio vel iureiurando in litem vel arbitrio iudicis petita postea certo taxatur §.32. s.eodem) arbitrarias.
units.tr: Accordingly, by its nature (as the citation to §30 of this title reports) it belongs to strict law; but by accident (because the uncertain amount and its valuation, sought either by oath in litem or at the judge's discretion, is afterwards fixed with certainty, §32 of the same title) it is arbitrary.

units.la: 32 ¶Curare autem debet iudex, vt omnino quantum possibile ei fit, certae pecuniae vel rei sententiam ferat: etiam si de incerta quantitate apud eum actum est.
units.tr: 32 The judge must take care, so far as is at all possible, to pronounce sentence for a certain sum of money or a definite thing, even if the matter was brought before him as an uncertain amount.

units.la: 33 ¶Si quis ages, ‖in‖intentione sua plus complexus fuerit, quam ad eum pertineat: à causa cadebat, id est, rem amittebat: nec facile integrum restituebatur, à prætore, nisi minor erat viginti quinque annis. Huic enim, sicut in aliis causis causa {a}cognita succurrebatur, si laesus iuuenture fuerat: ita & in hac causa succurri solitum erat. Sane si tam magna causa iusti erroris interueniebat, vt etiam constantissimus quisque labi posset, etiam maiori viginti quinque annis succurrebatur, veluti si quis totum legatum petierit: post deinde prolati fuerint codicilli, quibus aut pars legati adempta sit, aut quibusdam aliis legata data sint, quæ efficiebant, vt plus petiisse videretur petitor, quam dodrantem, atque ideo lege Falcidia legata minuebantur {b}. Plus autem quatuor modis petitur: re, tempore, loco, [?]causa. Re: veluti si quis pro decem aureis qui ei debebantur, viginti petierit: aut si is, cuius ex parte res est, totam eam, vel maiorem partem suam esse intenderit. Tempore: veluti si quis {c}ante diem, vel ante conditionem {d} perierit. Qua enim ratione qui tardius soluit, quam soluere deberet, minus soluere intelligitur: eadem ratione qui præmature petit, plus petere videtur.
units.tr: 33 If a plaintiff in his intentio claimed more than was due to him, he used to lose his case, that is, he lost the thing itself; nor was he readily restored to his former position by the praetor, unless he was under twenty-five years old. For, as in other cases, a minor who had been harmed was helped after the circumstances were examined, so in this case too help was customarily given. Indeed, if so great a cause of honest error intervened that even the most steadfast person could slip, help was given even to one over twenty-five; for example, if someone demanded the whole legacy, and afterwards codicils were produced by which either part of the legacy was revoked or other legacies were given to others, which made the claimant appear to demand more than three-quarters, and so the legacies were reduced under the Falcidian law. A claim is made for more in four ways: in the thing, in time, in place, and in cause. In the thing: for example, if someone who was owed ten gold pieces demands twenty; or if a person who owns only part of a thing claims the whole of it or a greater part as his own. In time: for example, if someone sues before the day or before the condition. For just as one who pays later than he ought is understood to pay less, so one who claims early is understood to claim more.

units.la: Loco plus peritur: veluti cum quis id, quod certo loco sibi [?]dari[?] stipulatus est, alio loco petit, sine commemoratione illius loci, in quo sibi dari stipulatus est: verbi gratia, si is, qui ita stipulatus fuerit, Ephesi dare spondes? Romæ pure intendat sibi dari oportere. Ideo autem plus petere intelligitur: quia vtilitatem quam haberet promissor, si Ephesi soluceret, adimit ei pura intentione. Propter quam causam alio loco petenti arbitraria actio proponitur {e}: in qua scilicet ratio habetur vtilitatis, quæ promissori comperitura fuisset, si illo loco soluceret, quo se soluturum spopondit. Quæ vtilitas plerun-que in mercibus {f} maxima inuenitur: veluti vino, oleo, frumento: quæ per singulas regiones diuersa habent pretia. Sed & pecuniæ numeratæ non {g}in omnibus regionibus sub eisdem vsuris fœnerantur.
units.tr: Claiming more by place occurs, for example, when someone claims at another place what he stipulated should be given him at a certain place, without mentioning the place where he stipulated it should be given. For example, if a man who has stipulated, "Do you promise to give at Ephesus?", claims at Rome, purely, that it ought to be given to him. He is understood to claim more because by a pure claim he takes away from the promisor the advantage he would have had if he paid at Ephesus. For this reason an arbitrary action is provided to one who claims at another place, in which account is taken of the advantage that would have been found for the promisor if he had paid in the place where he promised to pay. This advantage is most often found in goods such as wine, oil and grain, which have different prices in different regions. Likewise, money counted out is not lent at the same interest in every region.

units.la: Si quis tamen Ephesi petat, id est, eo loco petat, quo vt sibi detur, stipulatus est: pura {h}actione recte agit: idque etiam prætor monstrat: scilicet quia vtilitas soluendi salua est promissori. Huic autem, qui loco plus petere intelligitur, proximus est is, qui causa plus petit. Vt ecce, si quis ita à te stipulatur, Homine[?]
units.tr: If, however, someone claims at Ephesus, that is, claims at the place where he stipulated that it should be given to him, he rightly sues by a pure action, and the praetor also shows this, because the promisor's advantage in paying is preserved. Next to the one who is understood to claim more by place is the one who claims more by cause. For example, if someone stipulates from you in this way: "Do you promise to give a man"

units.la: {h} .i. sine arbitrij mentione l.4. in pr. ff. quod certo loco. Stichum, aut decem aureos dare spondes? deinde alte-rum petat, veluti hominem tantum aut decem au-reos tantum. Idco autem plus petere intelligitur, quia in eo genere stipulationis promissoris{a} est ele-ctio, vtrum pecuniam, an hominem soluere malit. Qui igitur pecuniam tantum, vel hominem tantum sibi dari oportere intendit, cripit electionem ad-uersario: & eo modo suam quidem conditionem meliorem facit, aduersarij vero [fui] deteriorem. Qua de causa, talis in ea re prodita est actio, vt quis intendat hominem Stichum, aut aureos decem sibi dari oportere: id est, vt eodem{b} modo peteret, quo stipulatus est. Praeterea,si quis generaliter hominem stipulatus sit, & specialiter Stichum petat: aut generaliter vinum stipulatus sit,& specialiter Campanum petat: aut generaliter purpuram stipulatus sit, deinde specialiter Tyriam petat: plus petere intelligitur: quia electionem aduersario tollit, cui stipulationis{c} iure liberum fuit, aliud soluere, quàm quod petere-tur. Quinetiam licet vtilissimum sit, quod quis petat: nihilominus plus petere intelligitur: quia saepe accidit vt promissori facilius sit illud soluere, quod maioris pretij est{d}. Sed haec quidem antea in vsu fuerant: postea vero lex Zenoniana{e} & nostra{f} rem coarctauit. Et si quidem tempore plus fuerit petitum: quid statui oporteat, Zenonis diu memoriæ loquitur constitutio: sin autem quantitate, vel alio modo plus fuerit petitum: [in] omne si quod forte damnum ex hac causa acciderit ei, contra quem plus petitum fuerit, commissa tripli condemnatione (sicuti supra diximus) puniatur.
units.tr: That is, without mention of arbitration; see l. 4 in pr. ff. quod certo loco. "Do you promise to give Stichus, or ten gold pieces?" Then he claims the other, for example only the man, or only the ten gold pieces. He is understood to claim more for this reason: in that kind of stipulation the promisor has the choice whether he would rather pay money or a man. Whoever claims that only money, or only a man, ought to be given to him takes the choice away from his opponent, and so makes his own position better and his opponent's worse. For this reason, an action has been devised in such a case, so that one claims that the man Stichus or ten gold pieces ought to be given to him; that is, so that he claims in the same way as he stipulated. Moreover, if someone stipulated generally for a man and then specifically claims Stichus; or stipulated generally for wine and then specifically claims Campanian wine; or stipulated generally for purple and then specifically claims Tyrian purple: he is understood to claim more, because he takes away the choice from his opponent, to whom it was free by the right of the stipulation to pay something other than what was claimed. Indeed, although what one claims may be most advantageous, he is nevertheless understood to claim more, because it often happens that it is easier for the promisor to pay what is of greater value. But these things were formerly in use; afterwards, however, the Zenonian law and ours restricted the matter. If more was claimed in time, the constitution of Zeno of blessed memory speaks of what should be decided; but if more was claimed in amount or in some other way, then whatever loss may befall the one against whom more was claimed from this cause shall be punished by a threefold condemnation, as we said above.

units.la: 34 ¶ Si minus in intentione sua complexus fuerit actor, quàm ad eum pertineat: veluti si cum ei decem [aurei] deberentur, quinque sibi dari oportere intenderit: aut [si] cum totus fundus eius esset, partem dimidiam suam esse petierit: sine periculo agit. in reliquum enim nihilominus iudex aduersarium in eodem iudicio{§}[ei] condemnat, ex constitutione diuæ memoriæ Zenonis.
units.tr: 34. If the plaintiff has included less in his claim than belongs to him, for example, if ten gold pieces were owed him and he claimed that five should be given him, or if, when his whole farm was his, he claimed that half of it was his, he sues without risk. For the judge nevertheless condemns the opponent in the same proceeding for the remainder, by the constitution of Zeno of blessed memory.

units.la: 35 ¶ Si quis aliud pro alio intenderit: nihil eum periclitari placet, sed in eodem iudicio, corrigere{h} [ei] permittitur: veluti si is, qui homine Stichum petere debeaet,
units.tr: 35. If someone claims one thing in place of another, it is held that he runs no risk, but he is permitted to correct it in the same proceeding; for example, if he who ought to claim the slave Stichus claims

units.la: {h} vsque ad sententiam v.l.vlt. Cod. de error. ex doctoribus quando emendare & mutare libellum Erotem petierit: aut si quis ex testamento dari sibi oportere intenderit, quod ex stipulatu debetur.
units.tr: Note: up to the sentence; see the last law of the Code, de errore, and the doctors on when one may amend and change the pleading. ...the slave Erotes; or if someone claims under a will that something ought to be given to him which is owed from a stipulation.

units.la: 36 ¶ Sunt praeterea quaedam actiones, quibus non semper solidum, quod nobis debetur, persequimur: sed modo solidum persequimur, modo minus, ut ecce, si in peculio filii seruive agamus. Nam si non minus in peculio sit, quam persequimur: in solidum dominus paterve condemnatur. si vero minus inueniatur: eatenus condemnat iudex, quatenus in peculio sit. Quemadmodum autem peculium intelligi debeat, suo ordine proponemus.
units.tr: 36. There are, moreover, certain actions in which we do not always pursue the whole of what is owed us, but sometimes the whole and sometimes less, as for example when we sue concerning the peculium of a son or slave. For if there is not less in the peculium than we claim, the master or father is condemned for the whole; but if less is found, the judge condemns only so far as there is in the peculium. We will set out in its proper place how the peculium ought to be understood.

units.la: 37 ¶ Ite si de dote in § iudicio mulier agit: placet eatenus maritum c condemnari debere, quatenus facere possit, id est, quatenus facultates eius patiuntur. Itaque § dotis quantitati concurrant facultates eius, in solidum damnatur: si minus, in tantum, quantum facere potest. Propter retentionem d quoque dotis repetitio minuitur. Nam ob impensas in res dotales factas marito quasi retentio concessa est: quia ipso iure necessarius sumptibus dos minuitur, sicut ex latioribus Digestorum libris cognoscere licet.
units.tr: 37 Likewise, if a woman sues for her dowry in a judicial action, it is held that the husband ought to be condemned only so far as he is able to pay, that is, so far as his resources allow. Accordingly, if his means match the amount of the dowry, he is condemned for the whole; if less, he is condemned for as much as he is able to pay. The claim for return of the dowry is also reduced on account of the retention allowed. For the husband is granted, as it were, a right of retention on account of expenses made on the dotal property, because by the law itself the dowry is diminished by necessary outlays, as may be learned from the broader books of the Digest.

units.la: 38 ¶ Sed & si quis cum parente suo f patronove g agat: item si socius h cum socio, iudicio societatis agat: non plus actor consequitur, quam aduersarius eius facere poterit. Idem est si quis ex i donatione sua conueniatur.
units.tr: 38 But also, if someone sues his parent or patron, or if one partner sues another in an action on partnership, the plaintiff recovers no more than the defendant will be able to pay. The same holds if someone is sued on a gift he has made.

units.la: 39 ¶ Compensationes quoque oppositae, plerumque efficiunt ut minus quisque consequatur, quam ei debeatur. Nam ex bono & aequo habita ratione eius, quod inuicem actorem & ex eadem causa praestare oportet, in reliquum eum, cum quo actum est, condemnat, sicut iam dictū est.
units.tr: 39 Set-offs that have been pleaded also often make it so that a person recovers less than is owed to him. For, taking into account on the principle of good faith what each party owes the other from the same cause, the judge condemns the defendant only for the balance, as has already been said.

units.la: 40 ¶ Cum eo quoque qui creditoribus suis bonis cessit l, si postea aliquid acquisierit, quod idoneum emolumentum habeat: ex integro in id, quod facere poterit, creditores experiuntur. inhumanum enim erat spoliatum fortunis suis, in solidum damnari.
units.tr: 40 Likewise, against one who has ceded his goods to his creditors, if he afterwards acquires anything that yields a suitable gain, the creditors may proceed afresh against him for whatever he is able to pay. For it would be inhumane for a man stripped of his fortune to be condemned for the whole.

units.la: QVOD CVM EO m, QVI IN aliena potestate est, negotium gestum esse dicitur,
units.tr: ON THE BUSINESS CONDUCTED WITH ONE WHO IS UNDER ANOTHER'S POWER, THAT IS, SAID TO HAVE BEEN CONDUCTED
TIT. VII.

units.la: VIA tamen superius mentionem habuimus de actione qua in peculium filiorum familiarum seruorumque agitur; opus est, ut de hac actione & de ceteris, quae eorundem nomine in partes dominosve dari solent, diligentius admoneamus. Et quia sine cum seruis negotium gestum sit, siue cum his, qui in potestate parentum sunt, eadem fere iura seruantur: ne verbosa fiat disputatio, dirigamus sermonem in personam serui dominique, idem intelligetur de liberis quoque & parentibus, quorum in potestate sunt. Nam si quid in his proprie seruetur, separatim ostendemus. 1 ¶Si igitur iussu domini cum seruo negotium gestum erit: in solidum praetor aduersus dominum actionem pollicetur: scilicet quia is, qui ita contrahit, fidem domini sequi videtur.
units.tr: Although we mentioned earlier the action by which suit is brought against the peculium of sons under power and of slaves, it is necessary to explain more carefully this action and the others that are customarily granted against masters or heads of households on account of these persons. And since whether a transaction is conducted with a slave or with those under a parent's power, nearly the same rules are observed, so that the discussion does not become verbose, we will direct our account to the person of the slave and the master. The same will be understood of children and parents under whose power they are. If anything is observed specially in these cases, we will show it separately.

units.la: 2 ¶Eadem ratione praetor duas alias in solidum actiones pollicetur: quarum altera exercitoria, altera institoria appellatur. Exercitoria tunc habet locum, cum quis seruum {c}suum magistrum navi praeposuerit, & quid cum eo eius rei gratia, cui praepositus erit, contractum fuerit. Ideo autem exercitoria vocatur, quia exercitor is appellatur, ad quem quotidianus nauis quaestus pertinet{d}. Institoria tunc locum habet{e}, cum quis tabernae forte, aut cuilibet negotiationi seruum suum praeposuerit, & quid cum eo eius rei causa, cui praepositus erit, contractum fuerit. Ideo autem institoria appellatur, quia qui negotiationibus praeponuntur, institores vocantur{f}. Itas tamen duas actiones praetor reddit, & si liberum quis hominem, aut alienum seruum naui aut tabernae aut cuilibet negotiationi praeposuerit: scilicet quia eadem aequitatis ratio etiam eo casu intereueniat.
units.tr: 1. If therefore a transaction is conducted with a slave by the master's command, the praetor promises an action against the master for the whole amount, obviously because the one who contracts in this way is seen to rely on the master's good faith. 2. By the same reasoning the praetor promises two other actions for the whole amount, one called exercitoria and the other institoria. The exercitoria action applies when someone places his slave as master over a ship, and something is contracted with him for the purpose of the business over which he has been placed. It is called exercitoria because the exercitor is the name given to the one to whom the daily profit of the ship belongs. The institoria action applies when someone places his slave over a shop or any other business, and something is contracted with him for the purpose of the business over which he has been placed. It is called institoria because those placed over businesses are called institores. The praetor grants these two actions even if someone has placed a free man or another's slave over a ship, shop or any business, obviously because the same reason of equity applies in that case too.

units.la: 3 ¶ Introduxit & aliam actionem praetor, quae tributoria vocatur. Namque si seruus in peculiari merce sciente{h} domino negotietur, & quid cum eo eius rei causa contractum erit: ita praetor iis dicit, vt{i} quicquid in his mercibus erit, quod inde receptum erit, id inter dominum, si quid ei debebitur, & caeteros creditores, pro rata portione distribuatur, & ideo tributoria vocatur, quia ipsi domino distributionem praetor permittit. Nam si quis ex creditoribus quasi minus ei tributum sit, quam oportuerit, hanc ei actionem adcommodat, quae tributoria appellatur.
units.tr: 3. The praetor also introduced another action, which is called tributoria. For if a slave trades with his peculiar merchandise with the master's knowledge, and something is contracted with him for that purpose, the praetor speaks thus: whatever is in those goods, and whatever has been received from them, is to be distributed in proportion between the master, if anything is owed to him, and the other creditors. It is called tributoria because the praetor allows the distribution to the master himself. For if any creditor has been given less from the tribute than he ought to have, the praetor grants him this action, which is called tributoria.

units.la: 4 ¶ Praeterea introducta est actio de peculio, deque eo, quod in re domini versum erit: vt quauis sine voluntate{l} domini negotium gestum erit, tamen sine quid in re eius versu fuerit, id totum praestare debeat.
units.tr: 4. Moreover, an action concerning the peculium, and concerning what has been turned to the master's advantage, was introduced, so that although a transaction was conducted without the master's will, nevertheless whatever has been turned to his use, he must make good in full.

units.la: {f} {g}quia actione de peculio conuentus dominus vel pater ante omnes creditores suum debitum praecipit. l.9.§.2. ff.de peculio.
units.tr: [f][g] Because when sued by the action concerning the peculium, the master or father takes his own debt first, before all creditors. l.9 §2 ff. de peculio.

units.la: {h} i. non prohibente: vt non sit necesse dominum velle, sufficiat aute nō nolle l.1. §. scientiae ff.de tribut.
units.tr: [h] That is, not forbidding; so that it is not necessary for the master to wish it, it is enough that he not be unwilling. l.1 §scientiae ff. de tribut.

units.la: {i} l.1.in pr.ff. de tributoria, l.5.in f. de tributoria.
units.tr: [i] l.1 in pr. ff. de tributoria; l.5 in f. de tributoria.

units.la: {l} De in rem verso actio non nititur domini voluntate, sed utilitate.
units.tr: [l] The action concerning what was turned to the master's advantage rests not on the master's will but on his benefit.

units.la: {m} l.1.ff. de in rem verso. {a}siue quid non fit in rem eius versum, id catenus praestare debeat, quatenus peculium patitur. In rem autem domini versum intelligitur, quicquid necessario in rem eius impenderit seruus: veluti si mutuatus pecuniam creditoribus eius soluerit, aut aedificia ruentia fulserit, aut familiae frumentum emerit, vel etiam fundum, aut quamlibet aliam rem necessariam mercatus erit. Itaque si ex decem puta aureis, quos seruus tuus à Titio mutuò accepit, creditori tuo quinque aureos soluerit, reliquos vero quinque quolibet modo consumpserit: pro quinque ‖ quidem ‖ in solidum damnari debes: pro caeteris vero quinque catenus, quatenus in peculio fit. Ex quo scilicet apparet, si toti decem aureos Titium consequi posse. Licet enim una est actio, qua de peculio, deque eo, quod in rem domini versum fit, agitur: tamen duas habet condemnationes. Itaque iudex, apud quem de ea actione agitur, ante dispicere solet, an in rem domini versum sit: nec aliter ad peculij aestimationem transit, quam aut nihil in rem domini versum intelligatur, aut non totum. Cum autem quaeritur, quantum in peculio sit: ante {b} deducitur, quicquid seruus domino, eive, qui in potestate eius sit, debet: & quod superest, id solum peculium intelligitur. Aliquando tamen id, quod ei debet seruus, qui in potestate domini sit, non deducitur ex peculio: veluti si is in ipsius peculio sit, quod eo pertinet, ut si {c}quid vicario suo seruus debeat: id ex peculio eius non deducatur.
units.tr: [m] l.1 ff. de in rem verso. Or if something has not been turned to his advantage, he must make it good only so far as the peculium allows. Whatever the slave has necessarily spent for the master's benefit is understood as turned to his advantage: for example, if he borrowed money and paid it to the master's creditors, or propped up collapsing buildings, or bought grain for the household, or bought an estate or any other necessary thing. So if, of ten gold pieces that your slave borrowed from Titius, he paid five to your creditor and spent the other five in some way, you must be condemned in full for the five, but for the other five only so far as there is peculium. From this it clearly appears that Titius can pursue all ten. For although there is one action, by which suit is brought concerning the peculium and concerning what has been turned to the master's advantage, it has two condemnations. So the judge before whom the action is heard usually first examines whether anything was turned to the master's advantage, and he does not proceed to the valuation of the peculium unless either nothing is understood to have been turned to the master's advantage, or not all of it. When it is asked how much is in the peculium, first is deducted whatever the slave owes to the master, or to one who is under the master's power, and what remains alone is understood as peculium. Sometimes, however, what a slave under the master's power owes is not deducted from the peculium: for example, if it belongs to his peculium that, should the slave owe something to his vicarius, this is not deducted from his peculium.

units.la: 5 ¶Caeterum dubium non est, quin is quoque qui iussu domini contraxerit, cuiusque institoria vel exercitoria actio competit: de peculio, deque eo, quod in rem domini versum est, agere potest. Sed erit stultissimus, si omissa actione, qua facillime solidum ex contractu consequi possit, se ad difficultatem perducat probandi in rem domini versum esse, vel habere seruum peculium & tantum habere, ut solidum sibi solvi possit. Is quoque, cui tributoria actio competit, aeque de peculio & de in rem verso agere poterit. Sed sane huic modo tributoria expedit agere, modo de peculio, & de in rem verso. Tributoria ideo expedit agere, quia in ea domini conditio praecipua {d}non est, id est, quod domino
units.tr: 5. Moreover, there is no doubt that he who contracted by the master's command, and to whom the institoria or exercitoria action belongs, can also sue concerning the peculium and what was turned to the master's advantage. But he would be most foolish if, passing over the action by which he could most easily recover the whole from the contract, he led himself into the difficulty of proving that it was turned to the master's advantage, or that the slave has a peculium and has so much of it that the whole can be paid to him. The one to whom the tributoria action belongs can likewise sue concerning the peculium and what was turned to advantage. But it is sometimes expedient to sue by the tributoria action, and sometimes by the action concerning the peculium and what was turned to advantage. The tributoria is expedient because in it the master has no preferred position, that is, what is owed to the master

units.la: {b} uilegio singulari parentum & dominorum. l. 9. §. 2. ff. de peculio.
units.tr: [b] A singular privilege of parents and masters. l.9 §2 ff. de peculio.

units.la: {c} v. l. 17. ff. de peculio. {d} l. 1. ff. de tributoria. debetur, non deducitur, sed eiusdem iuris est domi-nus: cuius & caeteri creditores. At in actione de peculio ante {a}deducitur, quod domino debetur: & in id, quod reliquum est, creditori dominus condemnatur. Rursus de peculio ideo {b}expedit agere, quod in hac actione totius peculij ratio habetur, at in tributoria, eius tantum, quo negotiatur. Et potest quisque tertia forte parte peculij, aut quarta, vel etiam minima negotiari: maiorem autem partem in praediis, vel mancipiis, aut foenebri pecunia habere. Prout ergo expedit, ita quisque vel hanc actionem, vel illam eligere debet. Certe qui poterit probare in rem domini versum esse: de in rem verso agere debet {c}.
units.tr: [c] See l.17 ff. de peculio. [d] l.1 ff. de tributoria. is owed, is not deducted, but the master has the same right as his other creditors. But in the action concerning the peculium, what is owed to the master is deducted first, and the master is condemned to pay the creditor what remains. Conversely, it is expedient to sue concerning the peculium because in this action account is taken of the whole peculium, but in the tributoria only of that part with which he trades. Anyone may trade with perhaps a third part of his peculium, or a quarter, or even a very small part, keeping the greater part in estates, slaves or money lent at interest. Therefore, as is expedient, each should choose either this action or that. Certainly, one who can prove that something was turned to the master's advantage ought to sue by the action concerning what was turned to advantage.

units.la: 6 ¶Quae diximus de seruo & domino, eadem {d}intelligimus & de filio & filia, & nepote & nepte, & patre auove, cuius in potestate sunt.
units.tr: 6. What we have said of slave and master we understand equally of son and daughter, grandson and granddaughter, and of the father or grandfather under whose power they are.

units.la: 7 ¶Illud proprie seruatur in eorum persona, quod senatusconsultum Macedonianum {e}prohibuit mutuas pecunias dare eis, qui in potestate parentis sunt: & ei qui crediderit, denegatur actio tam aduersus ipsum filium filiamve, nepote neptemve(sive adhuc in potestate sint,sive morte parentis,vel emancipatione suae potestatis esse coeperint) quam aduersus patrem avumve:sive eos habeat adhuc in potestate,sive emancipauerit. Quae ideo senatus prospexit,quia saepe one-rati ere alieno creditarum pecuniarum,quas in luxuriam consumebant, vitae parentum insidiabantur {f}.
units.tr: 7. This is strictly observed in their case: the Macedonian senatus consultum forbade lending money to those under a parent's power, and the lender is denied an action both against the son or daughter, grandson or granddaughter (whether they are still under power or have begun to be independent through the parent's death or emancipation), and against the father or grandfather, whether he still has them under his power or has emancipated them. The senate provided this because often, weighed down with debt from borrowed money which they spent on luxury, they plotted against the lives of their parents.

units.la: 8 ¶Illud in summa admonendi sumus, id quod iussu patris dominiue contractum fuerit, quodque in rem eius versum erit: directo & quoque posse a patre dominoue condici,tanquam si principaliter cu ipso negotium gestum esset. Ei quoque, qui exercitoria vel institoria actione tenetur, directo posse condici placet: quia huius quoque iussu contractum intelligitur.
units.tr: 8. In summary, we must be reminded that what is contracted by the father's or master's command, and what has been turned to his advantage, can be sued for directly against the father or master, just as if the transaction had been conducted principally with him. It is also held that one who is bound by the exercitoria or institoria action can be sued directly, since it is understood to have been contracted by his command too.
On Noxal Actions, Title VIII.

units.la: X maleficiis seruorum [?]veluti si furtum fecerint,aut bona rapuerint, aut damnū dederint,aut iniuriam commiserint: noxales actiones proditae sunt, quibus domino damnato permittitur {k}, aut litis aestimationem sufferre, aut ipsum hominem noxae dedere.
units.tr: If slaves have committed wrongs, such as theft, robbery of goods, damage, or injury, noxal actions have been established, by which the owner, once condemned, is allowed either to pay the assessed value of the suit or to surrender the man himself in noxal surrender.

units.la: 1 Noxa autem,est{*} ||ipsum|| corpus quod nocuit,id est seruus: noxia ipsum maleficium,veluti furtum,damnum,rapina,iniuria.
units.tr: 1. Now the noxa is the body itself which did the harm, that is, the slave; the noxious act is the wrongdoing itself, such as theft, damage, robbery, or injury.

units.la: 2 ¶Summa autem ratione permissum est noxæ deditione fungi. Namque erat iniquum,nequitiain eorum ultra ipsorum corpora dominis damnosam esse.
units.tr: 2. It was granted, on the highest principle, that one might discharge the matter by noxal surrender. For it would have been unjust for the wickedness of slaves to be harmful to their owners beyond their own bodies.

units.la: 3 ¶Dominus noxali iudicio serui sui nomine conuentus,seruum actori noxæ dedendo liberatur{b}: nec minus in perpetuum eius serui dominium à domino transfertur.Sin autem damnum et [?] cui deditus est, ||seruus|| refarcierit quæsita pecunia: auxilio prætoris inuito domino manumittetur{c}.
units.tr: 3. An owner sued in a noxal action on account of his slave is released by surrendering the slave to the plaintiff; and the ownership of that slave passes from the owner to the plaintiff in perpetuity. But if the slave, to whom he was surrendered, makes good the damage out of money he has earned, he is manumitted by the aid of the praetor, against the owner's will.

units.la: 4 ¶Sunt autem constitutæ noxales actiones aut legibus,aut edicto prætoris.Legibus: veluti furti ex lege duodecim tabularum,damni iniuriæ ex lege Aquilia.Edicto prætoris: veluti iniuriarum, & vi bonorum raptorum.
units.tr: 4. Noxal actions are established either by statutes or by the praetor's edict. By statute: for example, the action for theft under the Law of the Twelve Tables, and the action for damage under the Lex Aquilia. By the praetor's edict: for example, for injuries, and for goods taken by force.

units.la: 5 ¶Omnis autem noxalis actio caput{d} sequitur.Nam si seruus tuus noxa commiserit:quamdiu in tua potestate sit,tecum est actio. Si autem in alterius potestatem peruenerit: cum illo incipit actio esse. At si manumissus fuerit: directo ipse tenetur, & extinguitur noxæ deditio. Ex diuerso quoque directa actio noxalis esse incipit{e}. Nam si liber homo noxiam commiserit, & is seruus tuus esse coeperit (quod quibusdam casibus effici primo{f} libro tradidimus) incipit tecum esse noxalis actio, quæ ante directa fuisset.
units.tr: 5. Every noxal action follows the person (caput). For if your slave has committed a noxal wrong, the action lies against you for as long as he is in your power; but if he has passed into another's power, the action begins against that person. And if he has been manumitted, he himself is directly liable, and the noxal surrender is extinguished. Conversely, a direct action may also become noxal: for if a free man has committed a wrong and afterwards becomes your slave (which, as we explained in the first book, happens in certain cases), the noxal action, which before was direct, begins to lie against you.

units.la: 6 ¶Si seruus domino noxiam commiserit: actio nulla nascitur. Namque inter{g} dominum & eum qui in potestate eius est, nulla obligatio nasci potest. Ideoque & si{h} in alienam potestatem seruus peruenerit, aut manumissus fuerit: neque cum ipso, neque cum eo, cuius nunc in potestate sit, agi potest. Unde si alienus seruus noxiam tibi commiserit, & is{i} postea in potestate tua esse coeperit, interdicitur actio: quia in cum casum deducta sit, in quo consistere non potuit. Ideoque licet exierit de tua potestate,agere non potes:quem admodum si dominus in seruum suum aliquid commiserit,nec si manumissus aut alienatus fuerit,seruus ullam actionem contra dominum habere potest.
units.tr: 6. If a slave has committed a wrong against his owner, no action arises; for no obligation can arise between the owner and one who is in his power. Therefore, even if the slave has passed into another's power, or has been manumitted, no action can be brought either against him or against the person in whose power he now is. Hence, if another's slave has committed a wrong against you, and afterwards comes into your power, the action is barred, because the case has been brought into a state in which it could not subsist. Thus, although he has left your power, you cannot sue; just as, if an owner has committed some wrong against his own slave, the slave has no action against the owner, even if he has been manumitted or alienated.

units.la: 7 Sed veteres quidem hoc in filiisfamiliarū masculiis & fœminis admiscere: noua autem hominum conuersatio huiusmodi asperitatem{ꝛ} recte respuendam esse existimauit, & ab usu communi hoc penitus recessit. Quis enim patiatur filium suum, & maxime filiam [?], in noxam alij dare: ut pene per ||filij|| corpus pater magis {a}, quàm filius periclitetur: cùm filiabus etiam pudicitiæ fauor hoc bene excludat? Et ideo placuit in seruos tantummodo noxales actiones esse proponendas: cùm apud veteres legum commentatores imenerimus sæpius dictum, ipsos filiosfamiliarum pro {b} suis delictis posse conueniri.
units.tr: 7. The ancients, indeed, used to include in this the sons and daughters of the household; but modern society has rightly judged such harshness to be rejected, and this practice has entirely fallen out of common use. For who would allow his son, and especially his daughter, to be given over in noxal surrender to another, so that through the son's body the father would be endangered more than the son himself, when the favour shown to chastity also well excludes this for daughters? And so it was decided that noxal actions are to be proposed only against slaves, since we have found in the ancient commentators on the laws that it was often said that the sons of a household could themselves be sued for their own offences.

units.la: SI QVADRVPES ꝯ PAVPERIEM FECISSE DICATVR,
units.tr: IF A QUADRUPED IS SAID TO HAVE CAUSED DAMAGE (ON THE POVERTY OF...)
TIT. IX.

units.la: ANIMALIVM nomine, quæ ratione ceperint {d}, si {e}, qua lasciuia, aut pauore, aut feritate pauperiem {f} fecerint: noxalis actio lege duodecim tabularum prodita est. Quæ animalia si noxæ dedantur, prouiciunt ad liberationem: quia ita lex duodecim tabularum scripta est, vtputa, Si equus calcitrosus calce pepcusserit, aut bos cornu petere solitus petierit. Hæc autem actio in iis, quæ contra naturam mouentur, locum habet. Cæterum si genitalis sit feritas: cessat actio. Denique si vrsus fugerit à domino, & sic nocuerit: non poterit quondam dominus conueniri: quia desiit dominus esse, vbi fera euasit. Pauperies autem est damnum sine iniuria facientis datum. Nec enim potest animal iniuriam fecisse dici, quod sensu caret. Hæc quidem ad noxalem pertinent actionem.
units.tr: Concerning the names of animals which have done harm, whether by wantonness, fear or savagery, when they were caught by reason (if they were caught by reason), a noxal action was established by the Law of the Twelve Tables. If such animals are surrendered in noxal fashion, the owner is freed from liability, because the law of the Twelve Tables was written thus, for example: "If a horse kicking has struck with its heel, or an ox accustomed to butt has gored." This action, however, applies to those animals which are moved contrary to their nature. But if the savagery is natural to the species, the action ceases. Finally, if a bear has escaped from its owner and in this way has done harm, the former owner cannot be sued, because the owner ceased to be owner when the wild beast escaped. Now "pauperies" is damage given without wrong on the part of the one causing it. For an animal cannot be said to have done wrong, since it lacks sense. These points, indeed, pertain to the noxal action.

units.la: ¶ Cæterum sciendum est, ædilitio edicto {g} prohiberi nos canem, verrem, aprum, vrsum, leonem ibi habere, quà vulgo iter fit: & si aduersus ea factum erit, & nocitum libero homini esse dicatur: quod bonum & æquum iudici videtur, tanti dominus condemnetur. cæterarum vero rerum, quanti damnum datum fit, dupli. Præter has autem ædilitias actiones, & de pauperie locum habebit. Nunquam enim actiones, præsertim poenales, de eadem re concurrentes, alia {h} aliam consumit.
units.tr: Furthermore, it must be known that by the edict of the aediles we are forbidden to keep a dog, a boar, a wild boar, a bear or a lion there, where the common road runs; and if this has been done contrary to that, and harm is said to have been done to a free man, the owner, as seems good and fair to the judge, is condemned to pay that amount. For other things, double the amount of the damage done. Besides these aedilician actions, the action concerning pauperies will also apply. For actions, especially penal ones, concurring over the same matter, the one does not consume the other.

units.la: DE IIS, PER QVOS agere possumus,
units.tr: CONCERNING THOSE THROUGH WHOM WE CAN ACT,
TIT. X.

units.la: NVNC admonendi sumus agere, posse quemlibet hominem, aut suo nomine, aut alieno. Alieno: veluti procuratorio, tutorio, curatorio: cum olim in visu fuisset, alterius nomine agere non posse, nisi pro populo, pro libertate, pro tutela. Præterea lege HostiliHostilia pmissū {a} erat furti agere eorū nomine, quia apud hostes ellent,aut reipublicæ causa abesset, quive in eorum cuius tutela essent. Sed quia hoc non minimam incommoditatem habebat, quod alieno nomine,neque agere, neque excipere actionem licebat:coeperunt homines per procuratores litigare. Nā & morbus {b},& æras,& necessaria peregrinatio, itemque aliæ multæ causæ sæpe hominibus impedimento sunt, quo minus rem suam ipsi exequi possint.
units.tr: We must now be reminded that any man may act either in his own name or in another's. In another's name: for example, as a procurator, a tutor, or a curator. For formerly it was the rule that no one could act in another's name, except on behalf of the people, for liberty, or for a ward. Moreover, by the Hostilian law, an action for theft could be brought in the name of those who were among the enemy, or who were absent on the business of the republic, or who were under the guardianship of another. But since it caused no small inconvenience that one could neither bring nor receive an action in another's name, men began to litigate through procurators. For sickness, age, necessary travel, and many other causes often prevent people from managing their own affairs in person.

units.la: 1 ¶Procurator neque certis verbis, neque præsente ||semper|| aduersario, imò plerumque eo ignorante {c} constituitur. Cuicunque enim permiseris rem tuam agere,aut defendere: is tuus procurator intelligitur.
units.tr: 1 A procurator is appointed neither by fixed words nor with the opponent always present; indeed, for the most part he is appointed even without the opponent's knowledge. For whomever you have allowed to manage or defend your affair, that person is understood to be your procurator.

units.la: 2 ¶Tutores & curatores quemadmodum constituantur,primo libro expositum est.
units.tr: 2 How tutors and curators are appointed was explained in the first book.
On Satisdations, Title XI.

units.la: SATISDATIONVM modus aliis antiquitati placuit, alium nouitas per vsum amplexa est. Olim enim si in rem agebatur, satisdare possetor[?] {e} compellebatur: vt si victus ||esset||, nec rem ipsam restitueret,nec litis æstimationem: potestas esset petitori, aut cum eo agendi,aut cum fideiussoribus eius. quæ satisdatio appellatur iudicatum solui. Vnde autem sic appelletur, facile est intelligere. Nanque stipulabatur quis,vt soluerentur sibi, quod fuisset iudicatū. Multo magis is,qui in rem actione conueniebatur,satisdare cogebatur,si alieno nomine iudicium accipiebat {f}. Ipse autem,qui in rem agebat,si suo nomine petebat, satisdare non cogebatur. Procurator vero si in rem agebat:satisdare iubebatur,rem ratam dominum habiturum. Periculum enim erat, ne iterum dominus de eadem re experiretur. Tutores ||ve-rò|| & curatores eodem modo, quo & procuratores satisdare debere,verba {g} edicti faciebant: sed aliqua-do his agentibus satisdatio remittebatur. Hæc ita ||ierant||, si in rem agebatur.
units.tr: Antiquity favoured one method of satisdation, and newer practice, through use, has adopted another. Formerly, if an action in rem was brought, the defendant was compelled to give security: if he were defeated and neither restored the thing itself nor the assessed value of the suit, the claimant would have the option of suing either him or his sureties. This security is called "judgment to be paid" (iudicatum solvi). Why it is so called is easy to see. Someone stipulated that what was adjudged should be paid to him. Much more was the one who was sued in an action in rem compelled to give security if he accepted the suit in another's name. The plaintiff who sued in rem in his own name, however, was not compelled to give security. A procurator who sued in rem, however, was ordered to give security that the owner would hold the matter ratified, since there was a danger that the owner might sue again over the same thing. The words of the edict made tutors and curators give security in the same way as procurators, but sometimes security was remitted for these acting. These rules held when the action was in rem.

units.la: 1 ¶Si vero in perso-nam:ab actoris quidem parte eadem obtinebant,quæ diximus in actione, qua in rem agitur. ab eius vero parte,cum quo agitur, si quidem alieno nomine aliquis interueniret: omnimodo satisdaret, quia *nemo defensor in aliena re sine {h} satisdatione idoneus esse creditur.
