Quòd si proprio nomine aliquis iudicium accipiebat in personam: iudicatum solui satisdare non cogebatur. 2 ¶Sed hodie hæc aliter ob-servantur. {*}Siue enim quis in rem actione conveni-tur, siue personali suo nomine: nullam satisdationem pro litis æstimatione dare compellitur: sed pro sua tantum persona, quòd in iudicio permanet {a}usque ad terminum litis, vel committitur suæ promissio-ni cum {b}iureiurando (quam iuratoriam cautionem vocant) vel nudam promissionem {c}, vel satisdatione pro qualitate personæ suæ dare compellitur.
units.tr: 1. But if the action was in personam, the plaintiff's side followed the same rules as we have said for an action in rem. On the side of the defendant, if someone appeared in another's name, he gave security in every case, because no defender of another's affair is considered fit without security. But if someone accepted an action in personam in his own name, he was not compelled to give security for "judgment to be paid." 2. Today, however, these matters are observed differently. For whether someone is sued in an action in rem or in a personal action in his own name, he is compelled to give no security for the assessed value of the suit, but only for his own person, that he remain in the case until the end of the suit. He is either entrusted on his promise with an oath (which they call the oath caution), or given a bare promise, or compelled to give security according to the quality of his person.

units.la: 3 ¶Sin autem per procuratorem lis vel infertur, vel suscipitur: in actoris quidem persona, si non mandatum actis insinuatum est, vel præsens dominus litis in iudicio procuratoris sui personam confirmaverit {d}, ratam rem dominum habiturum satisdationem procurator dare compellitur: eodem observando, & si tutor, vel curator, vel aliæ tales personæ, quæ alienarum rerum gubernationem receperunt, litem quibusdam per alium inferunt.
units.tr: 3. But if the suit is brought or taken up through a procurator: on the plaintiff's side, if the mandate has not been entered in the acts, or the principal, present in court, has confirmed the person of his procurator, the procurator is compelled to give security that the principal will hold the matter ratified. The same is to be observed if a tutor, a curator, or other such persons who have taken on the management of others' affairs bring a suit against certain persons through another.

units.la: 4 ¶Si verò aliquis conuenitur: si quidem præsens procuratorem dare paratus est: potest vel ipse in iudicium venire, & sui procuratoris personam per iudicatum solui satisdationem {e} solenni stipulatione firmare, vel extra iudicium satisdationem exponere, per quam ipse sui procuratoris fideiussor exstat pro omnibus iudicatum solui satisdationis clausulis, ubi & de hypotheca suarum rerum conuenire compellitur: sive in iudicio promiserit, sive extra iudicium cauerit: ut tam ipse, quàm heres {f} eius obligentur. Alia insuper cautela, vel satisdatione propter personam ipsius exponenda, quòd tempore sententiæ recitandæ in iudicium veniet: vel si non venerit, omnia dabit fideiussor, quæ in condemnatione continentur, nisi fuerit provocatum.
units.tr: 4. But if someone is sued: if he is present and ready to give security, he may either come into court himself and confirm his procurator's person by a solemn stipulation of security for "judgment to be paid," or he may set out security outside court, by which he himself stands surety for his procurator for all the clauses of the security for "judgment to be paid." In that case he is also compelled to agree to a pledge of his own goods, whether he promised in court or gave caution outside it, so that both he and his heir are bound. Another caution, or security, is also to be given on account of his person, that he will come to court when the sentence is read out; or if he does not come, the surety will pay everything contained in the condemnation, unless an appeal has been made.

units.la: 5 ¶Si verò reus præsto ex quacumque causa non fuerit, & alius velit defensionem eius subire: nulla differentia inter actiones in rem vel personales introducenda, potest hoc facere: ita tamen, ut satisdationem iudicatum solui pro litis æstimatione præstet. {*}Nemo enim secundum veterem regulam (ut iam dictum est) alienæ rei sine {g}satisdatione defensor idoneus intelligitur.
units.tr: 5. But if the defendant is not present for whatever reason, and another wishes to undertake his defence, there is no difference between actions in rem and personal actions for this purpose: he may do so, provided that he gives security for "judgment to be paid" in proportion to the assessed value of the suit. For, by the old rule (as has been said), no one is considered a fit defender of another's affair without security.

units.la: 6 ¶Quæ omnia apertius & perfectius à quotidiano iudiciorum usu in ipsis rerum documentis apparent.
units.tr: 6. All these points appear more clearly and fully from the daily practice of the courts, in the very records of the cases.

units.la: 7 ¶Quam formam non solum in hac regia urbe, sed etiam[?] in omnibus nostris provinciis (etsi propter imperitiam forte aliter celecelebratur ) obtinere censemus: quum necesse sit, omnes prouincias, caput omnium nostrarum ciuitatum, id est, hanc regiam vrbem, eiusque obseruantiam sequi.
units.tr: 7. We hold that this form prevails not only in this royal city but also in all our provinces (although through inexperience it may be practised otherwise in some places), since it is fitting that all the provinces follow the custom of the capital of all our cities, that is, this royal city, and its observance.

units.la: TIT. XII. DE PERPETVIS ET TEMPORALIBVS ACTIONIBVS, & quae ad haeredes transeunt.
units.tr: TIT. XII. Concerning Perpetual and Temporal Actions, and Which Pass to Heirs.

units.la: HOC loco admonendi sumus, eas quidem actiones, quae ex lege, senatusve consulto, sive ex sacris constitutionibus {b} prohi-ficiscuntur: perpetuo solere antiquitus competere, donec sacrae constitutiones, tam in rem, quam in personam actionibus certos fines dederunt{c}: eas vero, quae ex propria praetoris iurisdictione pendent, plerunque intra annum viuere. nam & ipsius praetoris intra annum erat imperium. Aliquando tamen & in perpetuum extendun-tur,id est, vsque ad finem ex constitutionibus introductum:quales sunt eae,quas bonorum possessori,ceterisque,qui heredis loco sunt, adcommodate{d}. Furti quoque manifesti actio, quamuis ex ipsius praetoris iurisdictione proficiscatur: tamen perpetuo datur: absurdum enim esse existimauit anno eam terminari. 1 ¶Non autem omnes actiones quae in aliquem aut ipso iure{e} competunt,aut a praetore dantur:& in heredem aeque competunt, aut dari solent. Est enim certissima iuris regula *, ex maleficiis{f} poenales actiones in heredem ||rei|| non compe-tere||veluti||furti,vi bonorum raptorum,iniuriarum, damni iniuriae. Sed heredibus huiusmodi actiones competunt, nec denegantur: excepta iniuriarum{g} actione, & si qua alia similis inueniatur. Aliquando tamen etiam ex contractu actio contra heredem non competit: veluti cum testator dolose versatus sit, & ad heredem eius nihil ex eo dolo peruenit.Poenales autem actiones, quas supra diximus, si ab ipsis principalibus personis fuerint contestatae, & heredibus dantur, & contra heredes transeunt{g}. 2 ¶Super-est,vt admoneamus, quod si ante rem iudicatam is, cum quo actum est, satisfaciat actori: officio iudicis conuenit eum absoluere,licet in ea causa fuisset iudicij accipiendi tempore, vt damnari deberet, & [illegible, ~6 letters] hoc est, quod antea vulgo dicebatur, omnia iudicia absolutoria esse.
units.tr: Here we must remind the reader that those actions which arise from a law, from a decree of the Senate, or from the sacred constitutions were anciently wont to last perpetually, until the sacred constitutions set fixed limits to them, both for actions in rem and for actions in personam. Those actions, however, which depend on the praetor's own jurisdiction generally lapse within a year, for the praetor's own authority also lasted only a year. Sometimes, nonetheless, these too are extended in perpetuity, that is, until the limit introduced by the constitutions; of this kind are those which are granted to the possessor of goods and to others who stand in the place of heir. The action for manifest theft also, although it arises from the praetor's own jurisdiction, is nevertheless given in perpetuity, for he thought it absurd that it should be ended by a year. 1 Now not all actions which lie against someone either by the law itself, or are granted by the praetor, equally lie against the heir or are customarily granted against him. For it is a most certain rule of law that penal actions arising from wrongful acts do not lie against the heir of the wrongdoer: for example, for theft, for the seizure of goods by force, for injury, or for damage caused by wrong. But actions of this kind do lie for heirs and are not denied to them, except the action for injury and any other similar action that may be found. Sometimes, however, even an action arising from contract does not lie against the heir: for example, when the testator acted fraudulently and nothing from that fraud came to his heir. Penal actions, however, which we mentioned above, if they have been brought against the principal persons themselves, are granted to heirs and pass against heirs. 2 It remains for us to remind the reader that if, before judgment is given, the defendant satisfies the plaintiff, it is the duty of the judge to acquit him, although at the time the case was accepted for trial he was in a position where he ought to have been condemned; and [illegible]; this is what was formerly said commonly, that all judgments are acquittals.
ON EXCEPTIONS, TITLE XIII.

units.la: EQVITVR[?], vt de exceptionibus dispiciamus. Comparatae autem sunt exceptiones defendendorum {b}eorum gratia, cum quibus agitur. Saepe enim accidit, vt licet ipsa perfecntio, qua actor experitur, iusta sit: tamen iniqua sit aduersus eum, cum quo agitur. 1 ¶Verbi gratia, si metu coactus{c}, aut dolo inductus{d}, aut errore {e}lapsus, stipulanti Titio promisisti, quod non debueras promittere; palam est, iure ciuili te obligatum esse: & actio, qua intenditur dare oportere, efficax est: sed iniquum est te condemnari. Ideoque datur tibi exceptio, quod metus causa, aut doli mali, aut in {f}factum compositā ad impugnandam actionem.
units.tr: Next, let us examine exceptions. Exceptions were devised for the defence of those against whom an action is brought. For it often happens that although the action by which the plaintiff sues is just, it is nonetheless unjust against the defendant. 1. For example, if, compelled by fear, or induced by fraud, or having slipped into error, you promised Titius, who was stipulating for it, something you ought not to have promised; it is plain that you are bound by civil law, and the action by which he claims that you ought to give is valid. But it is unjust that you should be condemned. Therefore an exception is given to you, that the promise was made through fear, or through fraud, or an exception framed on the facts is available to oppose the action.

units.la: 2 ¶Idem iuris est, si quis quasi {g}credendi causa pecuniam a te stipulatus fuerit, neque numeraverit. Nam eam pecuniam a te petere posse eum, certum est. dare enim te oportet: quum ex stipulatione tenearis. Sed quia iniquum est, eo nomine te condemnari: placet exceptione {h}pecuniae non numeratae te defendi debere. cuius tempora {i}nos (secundum quod iam superioribus libris scriptum est) constitutione nostra coarctauimus.
units.tr: 2 The same law applies if someone has stipulated from you a loan of money, on the pretext of lending it, and has not actually paid it over. It is certain that he can demand that money from you, since you are bound by the stipulation and ought to give it. But because it is unjust that you should be condemned on that ground, it is settled that you ought to be protected by the exception of money not paid over. We have restricted the time limits for this exception by our constitution (as has already been written in the earlier books).

units.la: 3 ¶Praeterea debitor si pactus fuerit cum creditore, ne a se pecunia peteretur, nihilominus obligatus manet: quia pacto conuento obligationes non omnino {k}dissoluuntur: qua de causa efficax est aduersus eum actio, quam actor intendit, Si apparet eum dare oportere. Sed quia iniquum est, contra pactionem eum condemnari: defenditur per exceptionem pacti conuenti {l}.
units.tr: 3 Moreover, if a debtor has agreed with his creditor that money should not be demanded from him, he nonetheless remains bound, because obligations are not entirely dissolved by an agreement. For this reason the action which the plaintiff brings, claiming that it appears that the defendant ought to give, is effective against him. But because it is unjust that he be condemned in breach of the agreement, he is defended by the exception of an agreed pact.

units.la: 4 ¶Aeque si debitor creditore deferente iurauerit, nihil se dare oportere: adhuc obligatus permanet {m}. Sed quia iniquum est de periurio quaeri: defenditur {n}per exceptionem iurisiurandi. In iis quoque actionibus, quibus in {o}rem agitur, aeque necessariae sunt exceptiones, veluti si petitore deferente possessor iurauerit eam rem suam esse, & nihilominus petitor eandem rem vindicet. Licet enim verum sit, quod intendit, id est, rem eius esse: iniquum tamen est possessorem condemnari.
units.tr: 4. Likewise, if the debtor, when the creditor offers him the oath, swears that he owes nothing, he nonetheless remains bound. But because it is unjust to inquire into perjury, he is protected by the exception of the oath. In those actions also which are brought in rem, exceptions are equally necessary; for example, if the possessor swears, when the claimant offers him the oath, that the thing is his own, and the claimant nevertheless claims that same thing. For although what the claimant asserts is true, namely that the thing is his, it is nonetheless unjust that the possessor be condemned.

units.la: 5 ¶Item si in iudicio tecum actum fuerit, siue in rem, siue in personam: nihilominus obligatio durat: & ideo ipso iure de eadem re poltea aduersus te agi potest, sed debes per exceptionem {a}rei iudicatae adiu-uari. 6 ¶Haec exempli causa retulisse sufficiat. Alioqui quàm ex multis variisque causis exceptiones necessariae sint: ex latioribus Digestorum seu Pa-dectarum libris intelligi potest. 7 ¶Quarum quaedam ex legibus, vel ex iis, quae legis vicem obtinent, vel ex ipsius praetoris iurisdictione substantiam capiunt. 8 ¶Appellantur autem exceptiones aliae{b} perpetuae & peremptoriae, aliae temporales & dilatoriae. 9 ¶Perpetuae & peremptoriae sunt, quae semper agentibus obstant, & semper rem, de qua agitur, perimunt: qualis est exceptio doli mali, & quod metus causa factum est, & pacti conuenti, cum ita conuenerit, nec[?] omnino pecunia petertur[?]. 10 ¶Temporales atque dilatoriae sunt{c}, quae ad tempus nocent, & temporis dilationem tribuunt: qualis est pacti conuenti, cum ita conuenerit, ne intra certum tempus ageretur, veluti intra quinquennium. nam finito eo tempore non impeditur actor rem exequi. Ergo ij, quibus intra certum tempus agere volentibus obiicitur exceptio aut pacti conuenti, aut alia si-milis: differre debent actionem, & post tempus agere. Ideo enim & dilatoriae istae exceptiones appellantur. Alioqui si intra tempus egerint, obiectaque sit exceptio: neque eo iudicio quicquam consequebantur, propter exceptionem, neque post tempus olim agere poterant: cum temere rem in iudicium deducebant, & consumebant, qua ratione rem amittebant. Hodie autem non ita stricte hoc procedere volumus: sed cum, qui ante tempus paćtionis vel obligationis litem inferre ausus sit, Zenonianae {d}constitutioni subiacere censemus: quam sacratissimus legislator de iis, qui tempore plus petierint, protulit: vt & inducias, quas ipse actor sponte indulserit, vel quas natura actionis continet, si contempserit: in duplum habeant ij, qui talem iniuriam passi sunt: & post eas finitas non aliter litem suscipiant, nisi omnes expensas litis antea acceperint: vt actores tali poena perterriti, tempora litium deceantur obseruare. 11 ¶Praeterea etiam ex persona sunt dilatoriae{e} exceptiones, quales sunt procuratoriae, veluti si per mi-litem aut mulierem agere quis velit. Nam militi-bus,nec pro patre,vel matre, vel vxore, nec ex sacro rescripto procuratorio nomine experiri conceditur. Suis vero negotiis superesse sine offensa militaris disciplinæ possunt. Eas vero exceptiones, quæ olim procuratorib. propter infamiam {a}vel datis vel ipsius procuratoris opponebantur: cum in iudiciis frequentari nullo modo perspeximus, conquiescere sancimus: ne dum de iis altercatur, ipsius negotij disceptatio protelatur[?].
units.tr: 5. Likewise, if an action has been brought against you in court, whether in rem or in personam, the obligation nonetheless endures; and so by the law itself an action may afterwards be brought against you concerning the same matter, but you ought to be aided by the exception of a thing already adjudged. 6. It is enough to have related these by way of example. Otherwise, how many and what varied causes make exceptions necessary may be understood from the fuller books of the Digest or Pandects. 7. Some of these derive their substance from statutes, or from those things which have the force of statute, or from the jurisdiction of the praetor himself. 8. Now some exceptions are called perpetual and peremptory, others temporal and dilatory. 9. Perpetual and peremptory are those which always stand in the way of plaintiffs and always destroy the matter in dispute: such is the exception of fraud, and that of what was done through fear, and of an agreement made, when it was so agreed that no money at all should be demanded. 10. Temporal and dilatory are those which harm only for a time and grant a postponement: such is the exception of an agreement, when it was so agreed that one should not sue within a certain time, for example within five years. For once that time has ended, the plaintiff is not prevented from pursuing the matter. Therefore those to whom the exception of an agreement, or some similar exception, is raised when they wish to sue within the fixed time must defer the action and sue after the time has passed. That is why these exceptions are called dilatory. Otherwise, if they sued within the time and the exception was raised, they gained nothing from that trial because of the exception, and afterwards they could not sue in the past, since by rashly bringing the matter into court they had used it up, and by that reasoning they lost it. Today, however, we do not wish this to proceed so strictly; rather, we judge that one who has dared to bring suit before the time of the agreement or obligation falls under the Zenonian constitution, which the most sacred lawgiver issued concerning those who have sought more than is due at the time. Thus, if they have disregarded the respite which the plaintiff himself granted voluntarily, or which the nature of the action contains, those who have suffered such an injury shall have double that amount; and after those periods have ended, they shall not take up the suit unless they have first received all the expenses of the earlier litigation, so that plaintiffs, frightened by such a penalty, may learn to observe the times of lawsuits. 11. Besides, there are also dilatory exceptions arising from the person, such as those concerning procurators, for example if someone wishes to sue through a soldier or a woman. For soldiers are not permitted to sue on behalf of a father, mother or wife, nor by procuratorial letter from a sacred rescript. They may, however, attend to their own affairs without offence to military discipline. Those exceptions which were formerly raised against procurators on account of infamy, whether against those appointed or against the procurator himself, since we have observed that they are in no way frequent in trials, we decree shall be laid to rest, so that while people dispute about them, the settlement of the matter itself is not delayed.
ON REPLICATIONS, TITLE XIIII.

units.la: INTERDVM evenit, ut exceptio, quæ prima facie iusta videtur, [tamen] iniquè noceat. Quod cum accidit: alia allegatione opus est, adiuuandi actoris gratia, quæ {b}replicatio vocatur, quia {e}per eam replicatur, atque resoluitur ius exceptionis.{c} Ve-luti cum pactus est aliquis cum debitore suo, ne ab eo pecuniam petat {d}, deinde postea in contrarium pacti sunt, id est, ut creditori petere liceat: si creditor agat, & excipiat debitor, ut ita demum condemnetur, si non convenerit, ne eam pecuniam creditor petat: nocet ei exceptio. Convenit enim ita, namque nihilo-minus hoc verum manet, licet postea in contrarium pacti sunt. Sed quia iniquum est creditorem excludi, replicatio ei dabitur ex posteriore pacto convento.
units.tr: Sometimes it happens that an exception which seems just at first sight nonetheless harms the plaintiff unjustly. When this happens, another allegation is needed to help the plaintiff. It is called a replication, because by it the right of the exception is answered and dissolved. For example, suppose someone has agreed with his debtor not to demand money from him, and afterwards they agree to the contrary, namely that the creditor may demand it. If the creditor sues and the debtor pleads an exception, so that he is condemned only if it was not agreed that the creditor should not demand that money, the exception harms the creditor. For it was agreed in that way, and this remains true even though they afterwards agreed to the contrary. But since it is unjust for the creditor to be shut out, a replication will be given to him from the later agreement.

units.la: 1 ¶Rursus interdum evenit, ut replicatio, quæ prima facie iusta est, iniquè noceat. Quod cum accidit, alia allegatione opus est, adiuuandi rei gratia, quæ {e}duplicatio vocatur. 2 ¶Et si rursus ea prima facie iusta videatur, sed propter aliquam causam actori iniquè noceat: rursus alia allegatione opus est, qua actor adiuuetur: quæ dicitur triplicatio.
units.tr: 1 Again, it sometimes happens that a replication which seems just at first sight harms unjustly. When this happens, another allegation is needed to help the defendant, which is called a duplication. 2 And if this again seems just at first sight, but for some reason harms the plaintiff unjustly, then yet another allegation is needed by which the plaintiff is helped. This is called a triplication.

units.la: 3 ¶Quarum omnium exceptionum vsum interdum vlterius, quàm diximus, varietas negotiorum introducit, quas omnes apertius ex Digestorum latiore volumine facile est agnoscere. 4 ¶Exceptiones autem, quibus debitor defenditur, plerunque adcommodari solent etiam {f}fideiussoribus eius & reæ: quia quod ab iis petitur, id ab ipso debitore peti videtur: quia mandati iudicio redditurus est eis, quod ii[?] pro eo soluerint. Quà ratione, & si de non petenda pecunia pactus quis cum reo fuerit, placuit perinde succurrendum esse per exceptionem pacti con-
units.tr: 3 The variety of business sometimes introduces the use of all these exceptions further than we have said, and all of them can easily be recognised more clearly from the larger volume of the Digest. 4 Exceptions by which a debtor is defended are commonly also accommodated to his sureties and to his co-debtor, because what is demanded from them is considered to be demanded from the debtor himself, since he will repay them by the action of mandate whatever they have paid on his behalf. For this reason, too, if someone has agreed with the principal debtor not to demand the money, it has been decided that help should equally be given through the plea of the agreed pact

units.tr: that is, of them, and of cheapness. l.30. Cod. de locato: l.4. C. de decurion.

units.la: {f} l.7. ff. de except. l.16. ff. de fideiuss: l.11. C. de exceptionib. conventi illis quoque, qui pro eo obligati sunt, ac si etiam cum ipsis pactus effet,ne ab eis ea pecunia pe-teretur.Sane quaedam exceptiones non solent his accommodari.Ecce enim {a}debitor si bonis suis cesserit,& cum eo creditor experiatur: defenditur per exceptionem, si bonis cesserit. Sed haec exceptio iussoribus non datur: ideo scilicet,quia qui alios pro debitore obligat, hoc maxime prospicit, ut cum facultatibus lapsus fuerit debitor, possit ab iis, quos pro eo obligauit,suum consequi.
units.tr: f l.7. ff. de except. l.16. ff. de fideiuss: l.11. C. de exceptionib. agreed, also to those who are bound on his behalf, just as if the agreement had been made with them as well, that the money should not be demanded from them. Certainly some exceptions are not usually extended to these persons. For example, if a debtor has ceded his goods and the creditor sues him, he is defended by the exception that he has ceded his goods. But this exception is not given to sureties, namely because one who binds others as surety for a debtor takes especial care that, when the debtor has fallen into insolvency, he may be able to obtain what is his from those whom he bound on the debtor's behalf.
On Interdicts, Title XV

units.la: SEQVITVR, ut dispiciamus de interdictis seu actionibus, quae pro his exercentur. Erant autem interdicta formulae atque conceptiones verborum, quibus praetor aut iubebat aliquid fieri, aut fieri prohibebat. quod tunc maxime fiebat, cum de possessione, aut quasi possessione inter aliquos contendebatur. 1 ¶Summa autem divisio interdictorum haec est{c}: quod aut prohibitoria sunt, aut restitutoria, aut exhibitoria. Prohibitoria sunt, quibus praetor vetat aliquid fieri, velut vim sine vitio possidenti, vel mortuum inferenti{d}, quo ei ius erat inferendi: vel in sacro loco aedificari, vel in flumine publico ripave eius aliquid fieri, quo peius navigetur. Restitutoria sunt, quibus restitui aliquid iubet, veluti bonorum possessori possessionem eorum, quae quis pro herede aut pro possessore possidet, ex[?] ea hereditate: aut cum iubet ei, qui vi de possessione fundi deiectus sit, restitui possessionem. Exhibitoria sunt, per quae iubet exhibere: veluti eum, cuius de libertate agitur: aut libertum, cui patronus operas indicere velit: aut parenti liberos, qui in potestate eius sunt. Sunt tamen, qui putent, proprie interdicta ea vocari, quae prohibitoria sunt, quia interdicere sit denunciare & prohibere: restitutoria autem & exhibitoria, proprie decreta vocari. Sed tamen obtinuit omnia interdicta appellari: quia inter duos dicitur.
units.tr: Next we must consider interdicts, or the actions that are brought under them. Interdicts were formulas and set wordings by which the praetor either ordered something to be done or forbade it. This was done above all when two parties disputed possession, or quasi-possession, of something. 1 ¶The main division of interdicts is this: they are either prohibitory, restitutory, or exhibitory. Prohibitory interdicts are those by which the praetor forbids something to be done, for example, forbidding force against one who holds possession without a defect of title, or the bringing of a corpse onto land where one has a right to bury, or building on a sacred place, or making any alteration in a public river or its bank by which navigation would be made worse. Restitutory interdicts are those by which he orders something to be restored, for example, the possession of the goods that someone holds as heir or as possessor, from that inheritance, to be given back to the holder of the bonorum possession; or when he orders that possession be restored to one who has been driven out of possession of a farm by force. Exhibitory interdicts are those by which he orders something to be produced, for example, a person whose freedom is in question, or a freedman whom his patron wishes to call upon for services, or children who are in their parent's power, to be produced to the parent. Some, however, think that only the prohibitory interdicts are properly called interdicts, since to interdict means to announce and forbid, while the restitutory and exhibitory ones are properly called decrees. Nevertheless the custom prevailed of calling all of them interdicts, because they are issued between two parties.

units.la: 2 ¶Sequens divisio{e} interdictorum haec est: quod quaedam adipiscendae possessionis causa comparata sunt, quaedam retinendae, quaedam recuperandae.
units.tr: 2 ¶The following division of interdicts is this: some have been devised for the sake of obtaining possession, some for retaining it, and some for recovering it.

units.la: {e} quae à fine sumitur l.2.§. hac autem ff. eo. modatur bonorum possessori,quod appellatur , quo-rum bonorum{a}. eiusque vis & potestas haec est: ut quod ex his bonis quisque, quorum possessio alicui data est,pro herede aut pro possessore possideat:id ei, cui bonorum possessio data est, restituere debeat. Pro herede autem possidere videtur,qui{b} putat se here-dem esse. Pro possessore{c} is possidet, qui nullo iure rem hereditariam, vel etiam totam hereditatem, sciens ad se non pertinere, possidet. Ideo autem adi-piscendæ possessionis vocatur interdictum : quia ei tantum vtile est, qui nunc primum conatur adipisci rei possessionem. Itaque si quis adeptus possessionem, amiserit eam : hoc interdictum ei inutile est. Inter-dictum quoque ,quod appellatur Saluianum{d}, adi-piscendæ possessionis causa comparatum est : eoque vtitur dominus fundi de rebus coloni , quas is pro mercedibus pignori futuras pepigisset.
units.tr: {e} taken from its purpose (ab fine), l.2 §. hac autem ff. eo. The interdict is granted to the bonorum possessor, the one called the interdict concerning the goods of which. Yet "to hold as heir" means to hold in the belief that one is heir. A person holds "as possessor" who holds a hereditary thing, or even the whole inheritance, knowing that it does not belong to him by any right. It is called the interdict for obtaining possession because it is useful only to one who is now for the first time trying to acquire possession of the thing. So if someone has obtained possession and then lost it, this interdict is of no use to him. The interdict also called the Salvian interdict was devised for obtaining possession, and the owner of a farm uses it concerning the goods of the tenant, which the tenant had pledged as security for his rent.

units.la: 4 ¶ Re-tinendæ possessionis causa comparata sunt interdi-cta, vti possidetis, & utrubi: cum ab utraque parte de proprietate alicuius rei controuersia fit:&{e} ante quæratur, vter ex litigatoribus possidere, & vter petere debeat. Namque nisi ante exploratum fuerit , vtrius eorum possessio sit:non potest petitoria actio instituì: quia & ciuilis,& naturalis ratio facit, vt alius possideat, & alius à possidente petat. Et quia longè commodius est \\& potius\\ possidere , quam petere: ideo plerumque & fere semper ingens existit contentio de ipsa possessione. Commodum{f} autem possidendi in eo est, quòd etiam si eius res non sit, qui possidet: si modo actor non potuerit suam esse probare,rema-net\\in\\suo loco possessio.propter quam causam cum obscura sunt vtriusque iura : contra petitorem iu-dicari solet. Sed interdicto quidem vti possidetis, de {g}fundi vel ædium possessione contenditur:utrubi vero interdicto,de rerum mobilium possessione. Quorum vis ac potestas plurimam inter se differentiam apud veteres habebat.Nam vti possidetis interdicto is vincebat, qui interdicti tempore possidebat: si modo nec vi,nec clam,nec precario nactus fuerat ab aduersario possessionem:etiam {h}si alium vi expulerat, aut clam abripuerat alienam possessionem ,aut precario rogauerat aliquem , vt sibi possidere liceret. utrubi vero interdicto is vincebat , qui maiore parte eius anni,nec vi,nec clam,nec precario ab aduersario possidebat. Hodie tamen aliter obseruatur.Nam vtriusque interdicti potestas (quantum ad possessionem pertipertinet)exæquata est: uti ille vincat [?] in re so-li,& in re mobili,qui possessionem nec vi,nec clàm, nec precario ab aduersario litis contestatæ tempore detinet. 5 ¶Possidere autem videtur quisque,nō solùm si ipse possideat,sed & si eius nomine aliquis in possessione sit, licet is eius iuri subiectus non sit, qualis est colonus & inquilinus. Per eos quoque, apud quos depositum quis, aut quibus commodauerit, ipse possidere videtur. Et hoc est, quod dicitur, retinere possessionem posse aliquem per quemlibet, qui eius nomine sit in possessione.Quinetiam animo quoque solo retineri possessionem placet: id est,vt quamuis neque ipse sit in possessione, neque eius nomine alius: tamen si non relinquendæ possessionis animo, sed postea reuersurus inde discesserit, retinere possessionem videatur.Adipisci vero possessionem per quos aliquis poterit, secundo libro expositionis.Nec vlla dubitatio est, quin animo solo adipisci possessionem nemo possit. 6 ¶Recuperandæ possessionis causa solet interdici, si quis ex possessione fundi vel ædium vi deiectus fuerit. Nam ei proponitur interdictum unde vi,per quod is,qui deiecit,cogitur ei restituere possessionem: licet is ab eo, qui vi deiecit, vi vel clàm vel precario possideat. Sed ex constitutionibus sacris (vt supra diximus) si quis rem per vim occupauerit, siquidem in bonis eius est dominio eius priuatur.si aliena: post eius restitutionem,etiam æstimationem rei dare vim passo compellitur. Qui autem aliquem de possessione per vim deiecerit:tenetur lege Iulia de vi priuata, aut de vi publica. sed de vi priuata,si fine armis vim fecerit, sin autem cum armis eum de possessione vi expulerit:de vi publica tenetur. Armorum aut ut pellatione non solum scuta, & gladios, & galeas,sed & fustes, & lapides significari intelligimus.
units.tr: 4 ¶Interdicts for retaining possession are devised: uti possidetis and utrubi, when there is a dispute between two parties about the ownership of a thing, and first it must be inquired which of the litigants ought to possess and which ought to sue. For unless it is first established whose possession it is, a petitory action cannot be brought, because both civil and natural reason require that one should possess and another should sue the possessor. And since it is far more advantageous to possess than to sue, a fierce contest over possession itself almost always arises. The advantage of possessing is that even if the thing is not his, the possessor keeps his place if the plaintiff cannot prove that it is his own. For this reason, when the rights of both parties are unclear, the judgment is usually given against the one who sues. Yet by the interdict uti possidetis the contest concerns possession of land or buildings, and by the interdict utrubi it concerns possession of movable things. Among the ancients the force and power of these two differed greatly. For under the interdict uti possidetis he won who was in possession at the time of the interdict, provided he had obtained possession from his opponent neither by force, nor by stealth, nor by request; even if he had driven another out by force, or secretly carried off another's possession, or had asked someone as a favour that he be allowed to possess. Under the interdict utrubi he won who, for the greater part of that year, had possessed without force, stealth or request from his opponent. Today, however, the practice is different. For the power of both interdicts, as far as possession is concerned, has been made equal, so that in land and in movable things he wins who, at the time the suit is joined, holds possession from his opponent neither by force, nor by stealth, nor by request. 5 ¶A person is held to possess not only when he himself possesses, but also when someone is in possession in his name, even if that person is not subject to his authority, as a tenant or lodger is. A person is also held to possess through those with whom he has deposited something or lent something. And this is what is meant when it is said that one can retain possession through anyone who is in possession in his name. Moreover, it is held that possession can be retained by intention alone: that is, although one is not himself in possession, and no one else is in his name, yet if he has left the place not with the intention of giving up possession but intending to return later, he is held to retain possession. How possession may be acquired through others is explained in the second book of the exposition. And there is no doubt that no one can acquire possession by intention alone. 6 ¶An interdict is usually devised for recovering possession when someone has been driven by force out of possession of a farm or a building. For the interdict unde vi is offered to him, by which the one who drove him out is compelled to restore possession to him, even if the one who drove him out holds it by force, by stealth or by request. But under the sacred constitutions (as we said above), if someone has seized a thing by force, if it is among his own goods he is deprived of ownership of it; if it belongs to another, he is compelled, after restoring it, to give the victim of the force also its estimated value. Moreover, one who has driven another from possession by force is liable under the Julian law concerning private force or public force: under private force if he used force without arms, but if he drove him out of possession by force with arms, he is liable under public force. And by "arms" we understand not only shields, swords and helmets, but also clubs and stones.

units.la: 7 ¶Tertia diuisio interdictorum hæc est, quod aut simplicia sunt, aut duplicia. Simplicia sunt, veluti in quibus alter actor, alter reus est: qualia sunt omnia restitutoria aut exhibitoria.Nam actor is est, qui desiderat aut exhiberi,aut restitui: reus autem is est,a quo desideretur,vt restituat, aut exhibeat. Prohibitoriorum autem interdictorum alia simplicia sunt,alia duplicia.Simplicia sunt, veluti cùm prætor prohibet in loco sacro, vel in flumine publico ripa- alloquitur, vt unde tu illam deiecisti ve cius aliquid fieri .Nam actor est,qui desiderat,ne quid fiat:reus est,qui aliquid facere conatur. Duplicia sunt veluti vtri possidetis interdictum, & utrubi. Item autem duplicia vocantur,quia par utrinque litigatoris in his conditio est, nec quisquam præcipue reus vel actor intelligitur: sed vnusquisque tam rei, quàm actoris partes sustinet. 8 ¶ De ordine & vetere exitu interdictorum superuacuum est hodie dicere. Nam quotiens extra ordinem ius dicitur (qualia sunt ) non reddi interdictum: sed perinde iudicatur siue interdictis, ac si vtilis actio ex causa interdictorum data fuisset.
units.tr: 7 ¶The third division of interdicts is this: they are either simple or double. Simple interdicts are those in which one party is plaintiff and the other defendant, such as all restitutory and exhibitory interdicts. For the plaintiff is the one who demands that something be produced or restored, and the defendant is the one from whom it is demanded that he restore or produce it. Of the prohibitory interdicts, some are simple and some double. They are simple when the praetor forbids something to be done in a sacred place, or in a public river or on its bank, or when he says, "Whence you have driven him out," or "Let nothing be done to it." For the plaintiff is the one who asks that nothing be done, and the defendant is the one who tries to do something. They are double, for example, the interdict uti possidetis and utrubi. They are also called double because in these the condition of each litigant is equal, and neither is especially regarded as defendant or plaintiff; each one bears the parts both of defendant and of plaintiff. 8 ¶It would be superfluous today to speak of the order and the old procedure of interdicts. For whenever law is declared outside the ordinary order (as is the case with…), the interdict is not given, but judgment is pronounced just as if a utilitarian action had been granted from the cause of the interdicts.

units.la: VNC admonendi sumus, magnam curam egisse eos,qui iura sustinebant, ne facile homines ad litigandum procederent:quod & nobis studio est. Idque eo maximè fieri poterat, quòd temeritas agentium,quam eorum, cum quibus agitur, modo pecuniaria poena, modo iurisiurandi religione, modo infamiæ metu coercetur. Nam enim iusiurandum omnibus,qui conueniunt, ex constitutione nostra deferrur. Nam reus aliter suis allegationibus vtitur, nisi prius iurauerit, quod putans se bona instantia vti, ad contr. dicendum peruenit. At aduersus inficiantes, ex quibusdam causis dupli [vel triplij actio constituitur: veluti ⁱ si damni iniuriæ, aut ˡ legatorum locis venerabilibus relictorum nomine agitur ᵐ. Statim autem ab initio pluris, quam simpli est actio: veluti furti manifesti, quadrupli: nec manifesti, dupli. Nam ex his & aliis quibusdam causis (siue quis neget, siue fateatur) pluris, quam simpli est actio. Item actoris quoque calumnia coercetur. Nam etiam actor pro calumnia iurare cogitur ex nostra constitutione. Vtriusque etiam partis aduocati iusiurandum subeunt, quod propter calumniam.
units.tr: Here we must be reminded that those who upheld the laws took great care that men should not be too ready to go to law, and this is also our concern. This could be achieved especially well because the rashness of plaintiffs is restrained, and that of those sued is restrained as well: sometimes by a pecuniary penalty, sometimes by the sanction of an oath, sometimes by the fear of infamy. For by our constitution an oath is deferred to everyone who comes into court. The defendant cannot use his pleas unless he has first sworn, and thinking he has a good objection, he comes to make his reply. Against those who deny the claim, in certain cases a double or triple action is established, for example when suit is brought for damage done by injury, or for legacies left to pious places. From the outset the action is for more than the simple amount: for example, fourfold for manifest theft, double for non-manifest theft. For in these and certain other cases, whether the defendant denies or confesses, the action is for more than the simple amount. Likewise the calumny of the plaintiff is restrained, for by our constitution the plaintiff too is compelled to swear against calumny. The advocates of each party also undertake an oath, which is taken on account of calumny.

units.la: ᵏ v.l.4.C.ad L.Aquil. ˡ §.26.5. de aEt. ᵐ altera pecuniaria poena,est caussæ amissio l.1.C.de poena iud. & condemnatio ad expensas l.79.ff.de iudicijs. alia {4}nostra constitutione comprehensum est. Hæc autem omnia pro veteris calumniæ actione introducta sunt, quæ in desuetudinem abiit: quia in {†}partem decimam litis actores multabat, quod nusquam factum esse invenimus, sed pro his introductum est ‖&‖ præfatum jusjurandum, & ut improbus litigator ‖&‖ damnum, & {b}impensas litis inferre adversario suo cogatur.
units.tr: ᵏ See l. 4 C. ad L. Aquil. ˡ See §. 26, 5 de act. ᵐ Another pecuniary penalty is the loss of the case (l. 1 C. de poena iud.) and condemnation to the expenses (l. 79 ff. de iudiciis). What is contained in another of our constitutions {4}. All these were introduced in place of the old action for calumny, which has fallen into disuse, because it fined plaintiffs a tenth part of the suit, which we find was never done anywhere. In its place was introduced the aforesaid oath, and the requirement that a dishonest litigant pay damages and {b} costs to his opponent.

units.la: 2 ¶Ex quibusdam judiciis damnati, ignominiosi fiunt:veluti furti, vi bonorum raptorum, injuriarum, de dolo, {c}item tutelæ , mandati, deposi-ti,directis,non contrariis actionibus {d}. Item pro socio, quæ ab utraque parte directa est: & ob id quilibet ex sociis eo judicio damnatus, ignominia notatur. Sed furti quidem, aut vi bonorum raptorum, aut injuriarum, aut de dolo, non solùm damnati no-tantur ignominia, sed {e}& pacti, & recti. plurimum enim interest, {f}utrum ex delicto aliquis, an ex contractu debitor sit.
units.tr: 2 ¶ Those condemned in certain judgments become infamous: for example, in suits for theft, forcible robbery of goods, injury, fraud, and likewise guardianship, mandate, deposit, which are brought by direct and not by contrary actions. Likewise partnership, which is direct on both sides; and for this reason each partner condemned in that judgment is marked with infamy. But in suits for theft, or forcible robbery, or injury, or fraud, not only the condemned are marked with infamy, but also in actions of pact and of the direct action {c}. For it matters a great deal whether someone is a debtor from a delict or from a contract.

units.la: 3 ¶Omnium autem actionum instituendarum principium, {g}ab ea parte edicti prouisicitur[?] qua prætor edicit de in jus vocando. Utique enim in primis adversarius in jus vocandus est: id est,ad eum vocandus, qui jus dicturus sit {h}. Qua parte prætor parentibus {i}& patronis, {k} item paren-tibus liberisque {l} patronorum & patronarum hunc præstat honorem: ut non aliter liceat liber-isque eos in jus vocare, quàm si id ab ipso prætore postulaverint, & impetraverint. Et si quis aliter vocaverit: in eum pœnam solidorum quinquaginta {m} constituit.
units.tr: 3 ¶ The starting point of all actions to be brought is laid down in that part of the edict where the praetor provides for summoning someone to court. For first of all the opponent must be summoned to court, that is, summoned to the one who is to give judgment. In that part the praetor grants this honour to parents and patrons, and likewise to the parents and children of patrons and patronesses: so that it is not lawful to summon them to court, nor for children to do so, unless they have asked the praetor himself for permission and obtained it. And if anyone summons them otherwise, he sets a penalty of fifty solidi against him.
ON THE OFFICE OF THE JUDGE, TIT. XVII.

units.la: SVPEREST, ut de officio judicis di-spiciamus. Et quidem in primis illud observare debet judex, ne aliter judicet {n}, quàm legibus aut constitutioni-bus, aut moribus proditum est.
units.tr: It remains to consider the office of the judge. First of all, a judge must take care not to decide otherwise than is laid down by the laws, the imperial constitutions, or custom.

units.la: 2 ¶Ideoque si noxali judicio aditus est: observa-re[?] debet, ut si condemnandus videtur dominus, ita debeat condemnare, Publium Mœvium Lucio Titio in decem aureos condemnare, aut noxam dedere.
units.tr: 2 Therefore, if a noxal action has been brought, he must observe this: if the master seems deserving of condemnation, he must condemn him in the form that Publius Maevius is to pay Lucius Titius ten gold pieces, or else surrender him for the noxa.

units.la: 2 ¶Et si in rem actum sit ‖ coram judice ‖: sive contra pe-
units.tr: 2 And if an action in rem has been brought before the judge, whether against the claimant (petitor)

units.la: judicijs. l.1.§.sed & si quis. ff. de falsis. l.2. Cod.de pœna titorem iudicauerit,absoluere debet possessorem: sive contra possessorem, iubere ei debet, ut rem ipsam restituat {a} cum fructibus. Sed si possessor negat in praesenti se restituere posse, & sine frustratione videbitur tempus restituendi causa petere, iudulgendum {b}est ei: ut tamen de litis aestimatione caveat {c} cum fideiussore, si intra tempus quod ei datum est, non restituerit. Et si hereditas petita sit: eadem circa fructus interveniunt, quae diximus intervenire de singularum rerum petitione. Illorum autem fructuum, quos culpa sua possessor non perceperit: ‖sive illorum‖, quos perceperit: in utraque actione eadem ratio pene habetur, si praedo fuerit {d}. Si vero bonae fidei possessor fuerit: non habetur ratio ‖neque‖ consumptorum, neque non perceptorum. Post inchoatam autem petitionem, etiam illorum ‖fructuum‖ ratio habetur, qui culpa possessoris percepti non sunt, vel percepti consumpti sunt {e}. ¶3 Si ad exhibendum actum fuerit: non sufficit, si exhibeat rem is, cum quo actum est: sed opus est, ut etiam rei causam debeat exhibere, id est, ut eam causam habeat actor, quam habituras esset, si cum primum ad exhibendum egisset, exhibita res fuisset {f}. Ideoque si inter moras ‖exhibendi‖ usucapta fit res a possessore: nihilominus condemnabitur. Praeterea fructuum medii temporis, id est, eius quod post acceptum ad exhibendum iudicium, ante rem iudicatam intercesserit: rationem habere debet iudex: Quod si neget reus, cum quo ad exhibendum actum est, in praesenti se exhibere posse, & tempus {g} exhibendi causa petat, idque sine frustratione postulare videatur: dare ei debet, ut tamen caveat se restituturum. quod si neque statim iussu iudicis rem exhibeat, neque postea exhibiturum se caveat: condemnandus sit in id, quod actoris interesset, si ab initio res exhibita esset. ¶4 Si familiae erciscundae ‖iudicio‖ actum sit: singulas res singulis {h} hereditatis iudicare debet. & si in alterius persona praegravare videatur adiudicatio: debet hunc invicem coheredi certa pecunia (sicut iam dictum est) condemnare. Eo quoque nomine coheredi {i} quisque suo condemnandus est, quod solus fructus hereditarij fundi perceperit, aut rem hereditariam corruperit {k}, aut consumpserit. Quae quidem similiter inter plures quoque, quam duos coheredes, subsequuntur. ¶5 Eadem interveniunt, & si communi dividundo de pluribus rebus actum sit. Quod si de una re, vel luti de fundo : si quidem iste fundus commodè regionibus diuisionem recipiat: partes eius singulis adiudicare debet. & si vnius pars praegrauare videbitur : is inuicem certa pecunia alteri condemnandus est. Quod si commodè diuidi non possit: veluti si homo forte,aut mulus erit,de quo actum sit : tunc totus vni adiudicandus est,& is inuicem alteri certa pecunia condemnandus est.
units.tr: judiciis. l. 1 §. sed & si quis. ff. de falsis. l. 2. Cod. de poena. ...has judged against the claimant, he must absolve the possessor; or, if against the possessor, he must order him to restore the thing itself together with its fruits. But if the possessor says that he cannot restore it at once, and seems to ask for time for restoring it without mere delay, that time should be granted to him, provided, however, that he gives security with a surety for the assessment of the suit, in case he does not restore within the time given. And if an inheritance has been sued for, the same matters arise concerning fruits as we said arise in a claim for individual things. Of those fruits, however, which the possessor did not gather through his own fault, and of those which he did gather, the same reckoning is generally made in either action, if he was a robber (praedo). But if the possessor was in good faith, no account is taken either of fruits consumed or of fruits not gathered. After the petition has been begun, however, an account is also taken of those fruits which were not gathered through the possessor's fault, or which were gathered and consumed. 3 If an action for exhibition has been brought, it is not enough that the defendant exhibit the thing; it is also necessary that he exhibit the cause of the thing, that is, that the plaintiff be in the position he would have been in if, when he first brought the action for exhibition, the thing had been exhibited. Therefore, if during the delay in exhibiting the thing is acquired by usucaption by the possessor, he will nonetheless be condemned. Moreover, the judge must take account of the fruits of the intervening time, that is, of those which fell between the acceptance of the action for exhibition and the judgment in the case. But if the defendant against whom the action for exhibition was brought says that he cannot exhibit the thing at once, and asks for time for exhibiting it, and seems to ask this without delay, the judge must grant it to him, provided that he gives security that he will restore it. But if he neither exhibits the thing at once by order of the judge, nor gives security that he will exhibit it later, he is to be condemned to the amount by which it would have been to the plaintiff's advantage had the thing been exhibited from the beginning. 4 If an action for partition of an inheritance (familiae erciscundae) has been brought, the judge must assign the individual things of the inheritance to individual heirs; and if the adjudication seems to bear too heavily on one person, he must in turn condemn that person to pay a certain sum of money to the co-heir (as has already been said). On this same ground, each heir is to be condemned to his co-heir for having alone gathered the fruits of an inherited estate, or for having spoiled or consumed an inherited thing. These matters likewise arise among more than two co-heirs. 5 The same matters arise also when an action for dividing a common thing (communi dividundo) has been brought concerning several things. But if it concerns one thing, or, for example, an estate: if that estate can conveniently be divided by regions, the judge must adjudicate its parts to the individual parties; and if the share of one party seems to bear too heavily, that party is in turn to be condemned to pay a certain sum of money to the other. But if it cannot conveniently be divided, as for example if the thing in question is a man or a mule, then the whole is to be adjudicated to one party, and that party is in turn to be condemned to pay a certain sum of money to the other.

units.la: 6 Si finium regundorum actum fuerit,dispicere debet iudex,an necessaria sit adiudicatio. quae sane vno casu necessaria est,si euidentioribus finibus distingui agros commodius sit, quam olim fuissent distincti. Nam tunc necesse est ex alterius agro partem aliquam alterius agri domino adiudicari. quo casu conueniens est, vt is alteri certa pecunia debeat condemnari. Eo quoque nomine condemnandus est quisque hoc iudicio, quod forte circa fines aliquid malitiosè commisit: verbi gratia, quia lapides finales furatus est,vel arbores finales excidit. Contumaciae quoque nomine quisque eo iudicio condemnatur: veluti si quis iudice metiri agros passus non fuerit.
units.tr: 6 If an action for the fixing of boundaries has been brought, the judge must consider whether an award is necessary. This is indeed necessary in one case: when it is more convenient to mark the fields with clearer boundaries than they were formerly marked. For then it is necessary that some part of one field be awarded to the owner of the other field, and in that case it is fitting that he be condemned to pay the other a certain sum of money. On this ground also, each party is to be condemned in this action for anything he may have maliciously done near the boundaries, for example, for stealing boundary stones or cutting down boundary trees. Likewise, each party is condemned in that action for contumacy, for example, if someone has refused to let the judge measure the fields by paces.

units.la: 7 Quod autem istis iudiciis alicui adiudicatum fuerit: id statim eius sit,cui adiudicatum est.
units.tr: 7 Whatever has been awarded to anyone in these actions belongs at once to the person to whom it was awarded.
ON PUBLIC COURTS, TITLE XVIII.

units.la: PUBLICA iudicia neque per actiones ordinantur, neque omnino quicquam simile habent cum caeteris iudiciis, de quibus locuti sumus: magnaque diuersitas eorum est & in instituendo, & in exercendo. 1 Publica autem dicta sunt, quod cuiuis ex populo executio eorum plerumque datur. 2 Publicorum iudiciorum 3 priuata iudicia apud iudices datos: publica apud quaestorem instituebantur, aut tribus recuperatoribus in comitio fiebant. Publica, in foro,palam, sub dio vel ab ipsis praetoribus (sex lictoribus eius tribunal circunstantibus) siue quaestoribus pro tribunali,in sella curuli sedentibus, quibus adeant iudices in subselliis sedentes 50. vel 60, exercebantur. Vide hic Hot. adde ordinem veterem vsu desiisse l.8. ff. de accusat. formam accusationis, v.l.vlt. Cod. de accusat. quædam capitalia sunt, quædam non capitalia. Capitalia dicimus, quæ vltimo supplicio afficiunt homines, vel etiam aquæ & ignis interdictione, vel deportatione, vel metallo. Cætera, si quam infamiam irrogant cum damno pecuniario: hæc publica quidem sunt, non tamen capitalia.
units.tr: Public courts are not conducted by actions, nor do they have anything at all in common with the other courts we have discussed; and there is great difference between them both in how they are instituted and in how they are conducted. (1) They are called public because their execution is generally open to anyone from the people. (2) Private courts were held before appointed judges; public ones were instituted before the quaestor, or were conducted before three recuperators in the Comitium. Public trials took place in the forum, openly, under the open sky, either before the praetors themselves (with six lictors surrounding the tribunal) or before the quaestors, who sat on the curule chair before the tribunal; the judges, fifty or sixty of them, sat on the benches. See Hotman here. Add that the old order fell out of use: Dig. 48.2.8, the form of accusation: Cod. 9.2 last law, "On accusations." Some public crimes are capital, others are not. We call capital those which punish men with the final penalty, or also with interdiction from water and fire, or with deportation, or with the mines. The rest, if they impose some infamy together with a pecuniary loss, are public but not capital.

units.la: ¶ 3 Publica autem iudicia hæc sunt: lex Iulia {b}maiestatis, quæ in eos, qui contra Imperatorem, vel rempublicam aliquid moliti sunt, suum vigorem extendit. Cuius poena animæ amissionem sustinet, & memoria rei etiam post mortem damnatur.
units.tr: ¶ 3 The public courts are these: the Julian law on treason (maiestas), which extends its force against those who have plotted anything against the Emperor or the commonwealth. Its penalty involves loss of life, and the memory of the offence is condemned even after death.

units.la: ¶ 4 Item lex Iulia de adulteriis coercendis, quæ non solum temerarores alienarum nuptiarum gladio {c}punit, sed & eos {d}, qui cum masculis nefandam libidinem exercere audent. Sed eadem lege Iulia etiam stupri flagitium punitur, cum quis sine vi vel virginem, vel viduam honestè viuentem, stupraverit. Poenam autem eadem lex irrogat stupratoribus {e}, si honesti sunt, publicationem partis dimidiæ bonorum: si humiles, corporis coercitionem cum relegatione.
units.tr: ¶ 4 Likewise the Julian law on the suppression of adultery, which punishes with the sword not only those who rashly violate other men's marriages, but also those who dare to practise unspeakable lust with males. But by the same Julian law the shameful crime of illicit intercourse (stuprum) is also punished, when someone without force has debauched either a virgin or a respectable widow. The same law imposes on debauchers, if they are of good standing, the confiscation of half their goods; if they are of humble rank, bodily punishment together with relegation.

units.la: ¶ 5 Item lex Cornelia de sicariis {f}, quæ homicidas vltore ferro persequitur, vel eos, qui hominis occidendi causa cum {g}telo ambulant. Telum {h}autem (vt Caius noster ex interpretatione legum duodecim tabularum scriptum reliquit) vulgò quidem id appellatur, quod ab arcu mittitur. Sed & omne significat, quod manu cuiusque iacitur. Sequitur ergo, vt lignum & lapis, & ferrum hoc nomine contineatur: dictum ab eo, quod in longinquum mittitur, [?]Græca voce τηλὲ[?] figuratum. Et hanc significationem inuenire possumus & in Græco nomine. nam quod nos telum appellamus, illi βέλος appellant. {i}Admonent nos epigrammata in Xerolopho vrbis fauftissimè scripta, καὶ τὰ βέλη ὀφθῶς ἐφέρετο, λόγχαι[?], τοξεύματα, σφενδόναι, πλίνθοι δὲ καὶ λίθοι. i. Et huiusmodi tela simul ab eis ferebantur, lancea, spicula, funda, plurimi autem & lapides. Sicarij autem appellantur a fi-ca, quod significat ferreum cultrum. Eadem lege & veneficii capite damnantur, qui artibus odiosis, tam venenis, quàm susurris magicis homines occiderint, vel mala medicamenta publicè vendiderint.
units.tr: ¶ 5 Likewise the Cornelian law on assassins, which pursues homicides with avenging steel, or those who walk about with a weapon for the purpose of killing a man. Now a weapon (as our Gaius left it written from his interpretation of the Twelve Tables) is commonly called that which is shot from a bow; but it also signifies everything that is thrown by the hand of anyone. It follows, therefore, that wood and stone and iron are included under this name, named from the fact that it is sent far off, shaped from the Greek word τηλέ. We can also find this meaning in the Greek name: for what we call a weapon (telum) they call βέλος. The epigrams inscribed most auspiciously in Xerolophus remind us: "and the weapons were borne in good order, lances, arrows, slings, bricks and stones," that is, such weapons as these were carried at once by them: lance, dart, sling, and very many stones too. Sicarii are so called from the sica, which means an iron dagger. By the same law those are condemned to the capital penalty for poisoning who have killed men by hateful arts, whether with poisons or with magical whisperings, or have publicly sold harmful drugs.

units.la: ¶ 6 Alia deinde lex asperrimum crimen nova poena persequitur, quæ Pompeia de parricidiis {k}vocatur: qua cauetur, vt si quis parentis aut filij, aut omnino adfinitatis eius, quæ nuncupatione parentum continetur, fata præparauerit (siue clàm, siue palàm id ausus fuerit ) ‖ necnon is, cuius dolo malo id fa-ctum est, vel conscius criminis existit, licet extraneus sit, ‖ poena parricidij puniatur, & neque gladio neque ignibus, neque vlli alij foleinni poenæ subiiciatur , sed insutus culleo cum Cane, & Gallo gallinaceo, & Vipera, & Simia, & inter eas ferales angustias comprehensus (secundùm quod regionis qualitas tulerit) vel in vicinum mare, vel in amnem proiiciatur: vt omnium elementorum vsu viuus carere incipiat, & ei cælum superstiti, ‖ & ‖ terra mortuo ause-ratur.
units.tr: ¶ 6 Next, another law pursues the most harsh crime with a new penalty; it is called the Pompeian law on parricides. It provides that if anyone has prepared the death of a parent or child, or indeed of any relation included under the name of parents (whether he has dared to do it secretly or openly), and likewise he by whose wicked contrivance the deed was done, or who is a party to the crime, although he be a stranger, shall be punished with the penalty for parricide, and shall not be subjected to the sword or fire or any other usual penalty, but, sewn into a sack with a dog, a cock, a viper and an ape, and enclosed among these deadly confines (according to what the nature of the region allows), he shall be thrown either into the nearby sea or into a river, so that, deprived of the use of all the elements while alive, he may be denied the sky while he survives and the earth when he is dead.

units.la: Si quis autem alias cognatione vel adfinitate personas cœniunctas necauerit: poenam legis Corneliæ de sicariis sustinebit.
units.tr: If anyone, however, has killed persons joined by kinship or marriage in other ways, he shall incur the penalty of the Cornelian law on assassins.

units.la: 7 ¶ Item lex Cornelia de falsis, quæ etiam testamentaria vocatur, pœnam irrogat ei, qui testamentum , vel aliud instrumentum falsum scripserit, signauerit, recitauerit, subiecerit: vel signum adulterinum fecerit, sculpserit, expresserit sciens dolo malo. Eiusque legis poena in seruos, vltimum supplicium est (quod etiam in lege de sicariis & veneficis seruatur) in liberos vero deportatio .
units.tr: 7 ¶ Likewise the Cornelian law on forgeries, which is also called the testamentary law, imposes a penalty on him who knowingly and with wicked intent has written, sealed, read out, or inserted a false will or other instrument, or has made, carved, or impressed a counterfeit seal. The penalty of this law is the final punishment for slaves (which is also observed in the law on assassins and poisoners), but for free persons it is deportation.

units.la: 8 ¶ Item lex Iulia de vi publica seu priuata, aduersus eos exoritur, qui vim vel armatam, vel sine armis commiserint. Sed si quidem armata vis arguatur: deportatio ei ex lege Iulia de vi publica irrogatur. Si vero sine armis: in tertiam partem bonorum ‖ suorum ‖ publicatio imponitur. Sin autem per vim raptus virginis, vel viduæ, vel sanctimonialis, vel alterius fuerit perpetratus: tunc & raptores, & ij, qui opem [huic] flagitio dederunt, capite puniuntur, secundum nostræ constitutionis definitionem, ex qua hoc apertius posse fit scire.
units.tr: 8 ¶ Likewise the Julian law on public or private violence arises against those who have committed violence either with arms or without arms. If indeed violence with arms is proved, deportation is imposed on him under the Julian law on public violence. But if it was without arms, confiscation of a third part of his goods is imposed. But if the rape of a virgin, or of a widow, or of a nun, or of another woman has been committed by force, then both the ravishers and those who gave aid to this crime are punished with death, according to the definition of our constitution, from which this can be known more clearly.

units.la: 9 ¶ Item lex Iulia peculatus eos punit, qui pecuniam, vel rem sacram, vel religiosam furati fuerint. Sed si quidem ipsi iudices tempore administrationis publicas pecunias subtraxerint: capitali animadversione puniuntur: & non solum hi, sed etiam , qui ministerium eis ad hoc exhibuerint, vel qui fabricatas ab his scientes suscepserint. Alij vero, qui in hanc legem inciderint: pœnæ deportationis subiugentur.
units.tr: 9 ¶ Likewise the Julian law on peculation punishes those who have stolen money, or a sacred or religious thing. But if judges themselves, during their administration, have embezzled public moneys, they are punished with capital punishment; and not only they, but also those who have furnished them with service for this purpose, or who have knowingly received things fabricated by them. Others, however, who have fallen under this law are subjected to the penalty of deportation.

units.la: 10 ¶ Est & inter publica iudicia lex Flauia de plagiariis * quæ interdum p capitis pœnam ex sacris constitutionibus irrogat, interdum leuiorem.
units.tr: 10 ¶ Among the public courts there is also the Flavian law on kidnappers, which sometimes imposes the penalty of death from the sacred constitutions, and sometimes a lighter one.

units.la: 11 ¶ Sunt præterea publica iudicia, lex plagiarijs. ¶ Est enim extraordinaria l. vlt. ff. ad l. Fauiam
units.tr: 11 ¶ Besides these there are public courts: the law on kidnappers. For it is an extraordinary law: Dig. last law, on the Fabian law.

units.la: * plagiarijs. Iulia de ambitu {a}, lex Iulia repetundarum {b}, & lex Iulia de annona {c}, & lex Iulia de residuis {d}, quae de certis capitulis loquuntur: & animas quidem amis-sionem non irrogant: aliis autem poenis eos subii-ciunt qui praecepta earum neglexerint. Sed de publi-cis iudiciis haec exposuimus, ut vobis possibile fit summo digito, & quasi per indicem ea tetigisse, alioqui diligentior eorum scientia vobis ex latioribus Digestorum seu Pandectarum libris Deo propitio aducentura est.
units.tr: The Julian law on electoral bribery (ambitus), the Julian law on extortion (repetundae), the Julian law on the grain supply (annona), and the Julian law on arrears (residua), which speak of certain specific heads: these do not impose loss of life, but subject to other penalties those who have neglected their precepts. But we have set out these matters concerning public courts so that it may be possible for you to touch on them with the highest finger, and, as it were, through an index; otherwise, with God favouring, a more diligent knowledge of them will be brought to you from the wider books of the Digest or Pandects.
END OF THE INSTITUTES.
EPITOME OF THE INSTITUTES.

units.la: IUSTITIA est constans & perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi. Quæ iustitiam docet scientia, Iurisprudentia est. Ea primò leui ac simplici via, post diligentissima interpretatione tradenda est. Docet autem honestè viuere, alterum non lædere, suum cuique tribuere. Refertur ad publicam vtilitatem vel singulorum seu priuatam. Collecta est vel ex naturali, vel gentium, vel ciuili iure. Ius naturale omnium animalium. Ciuile cuiusque ciuitatis proprium est. gentium, omni humano generi commune est, ex eoque omnes pene contractus introducti. Ciuile, aut scriptum est aut non scriptum. Scripti species, lex quæ ab vniuerso populo: plebiscitum, quod à plebe: senatusconsultum, quod à Senatu: principum placita, quæ à principe, vel per epistolam, vel per decretum, vel edictum, personaliter vel generaliter sunt constituta: edicta, quæ vel à Prætoribus vel ædilibus curulibus: responsa prudentum, sunt opiniones eorum quibus permissum erat de iure respondere. Non scriptum ius, est quod vsus approbauit. hoc Lacedæmonii, illo Athenienses vtebantur. Ciuilia iura tacitè, vel expressè mutari possunt, naturalia non item. Ciuilis iuris obiecta sunt persona, res, actiones.
units.tr: Justice is a constant and perpetual will to render to each his own. The science that teaches justice is jurisprudence. It is to be taught first by a light and simple path, and afterwards by the most careful exposition. It teaches us to live honourably, not to injure another, and to render to each his own. It is directed either to the public good or to that of individuals, which is private. Law is gathered either from natural law, or from the law of nations, or from civil law. Natural law belongs to all animals. Civil law is proper to each state. The law of nations is common to the whole human race, and almost all contracts have been introduced from it. Civil law is either written or unwritten. The kinds of written law are: the lex, which comes from the whole people; the plebiscitum, which comes from the plebs; the senatusconsultum, which comes from the Senate; the decrees of the princes, which are issued by the prince either by letter, by decree or by edict, whether addressed to individuals or in general terms; the edicts, which are issued either by the praetors or by the curule aediles; and the responses of the jurists, which are the opinions of those who were permitted to give answers on law. Unwritten law is what custom has approved. The Lacedaemonians used the one, the Athenians the other. Civil laws can be changed tacitly or expressly; natural laws cannot be changed in that way. The objects of civil law are persons, things and actions.

units.la: Personarum prima diuisio, est in liberas & seruas: Libertas à natura, Seruitus à iure gentium ꝑcedit. Serui dicuntur, captiui seruari, nec occidi solent. Nascuntur ex ancillis, fiunt iure gentium, si capiuntur: ciuili, si liber seipsum vēdit. Liberi, sunt ingenui aut libertini. Ingenuus est, qui statim vt natus est liber. {a}est , cui non officit in seruitute fuisse, & postea manumissum esse {b}. Libertini, qui ex iusta seruitute manumissi {c}. Manumissio fit aut in Ecclesiis, aut vindicta apud Praetorem, aut inter amicos, aut epistola, aut vltima voluntate, aut aliis modis {d}: quocunque tempore & loco {e}. Manumissi hodie cives Romani {f}. In fraudem creditorum non licet manumittere {g}. In fraudem non manumittit, qui, licet soluendo non sit, seruum suum cum libertate in testamento haeredem instituit {h}: vel sine libertate {i}. In fraudem manumittit, qui non tantum cum soluendo non est manumittit, sed qui animo fraudandi {k}. Non licet quoque minori 25. annis, nisi causa cognita {l}: qui tamen 17. annum impleuit, & 18. annum tigit manumittere poterit {m}. Poterit & is, vt & quiuis alius, omnes serui testamento manumittere {n}.
units.tr: The first division of persons is into free and slaves. Liberty comes from nature, servitude from the law of nations. Slaves are so called because captives are kept, and they are not usually killed. They are born of slave women; they become slaves by the law of nations if they are captured, and by civil law if a free person sells himself. Free persons are either freeborn or freedmen. A freeborn person is one who is free from the moment he is born. [Also one] to whom it is no obstacle to have been in servitude and afterwards to have been manumitted. Freedmen are those manumitted from lawful servitude. Manumission is made either in the churches, or by the vindicta before the praetor, or among friends, or by letter, or by last will, or in other ways, at whatever time and place. Those manumitted today are Roman citizens. It is not lawful to manumit in fraud of creditors. A man does not manumit in fraud if, though not solvent, he institutes his slave as heir in his will with freedom, or without freedom. He manumits in fraud who manumits not merely when he is insolvent, but with intent to defraud. Nor is it lawful for one under twenty-five years of age to manumit, unless cause is shown; yet one who has completed seventeen years and reached eighteen may manumit. He may also, as anyone else may, manumit all his slaves by will.

units.la: Secunda personarum diuisio est, qua personarum aliae, alieni iuris sunt, vel sui {o}: alieni vt serui, vt filii, serui dominis acquirunt, quicquid acquirunt {p}. Non tamen in eos ius vitae & necis habent domini, nisi causa cognita: quin eos durius tractare non licet {q}. Liberi vero variis modis patri adquiruntur. Primo, si ex iustis nuptiis procreati sunt in potestate sunt parentum {r}. Nuptiae, sunt viri & mulieris coniunctio, cum individua vitae consuetudine {s}. Talis potestas Romanorum est propria {t}. Liberos hic intelligi, qui ex te & vxore, filio eiusve vxore, non qui ex filia tua nascuntur {u}. Iustae nuptiae dicuntur quas ciues, puberes, filiifam. cum consensu parentum {x}, & omnes intra gradus a lege definitos contraxerunt. Huc pertinet quod dicitur ratione consanguinitatis vel honestatis inter parentes & liberos, etiam seruos {y}, etiam adoptiuos, (quantumuis dissoluta sit adoptio {z},) nuptias non posse contrahi. Item inter fratres & sorores, etiam adoptiuos, (nisi dissoluta sit adoptio {a}.) Non possumus quoque ducere fratris vel sororis filiam vel neptem (neptis non est quae nata est ex sorore tua adoptiua {b}) amita materteram, (licet magnam, licet adoptiuam {c}.) Non idem est in duorum fratrum vel sororum liberis {d}. Affinitatis ratione priuignam, nurum {e}, socrum, nouercam {f} (non idem est in compriuignis {g}.) Priuignae loco habetur, quam vxor tua post diuortium ex alio procreauit. Nurus loco habentur, filij sponsae, socrus, sponsa patris {h}.
units.tr: The second division of persons is that some persons are under the law of another, and others are sui iuris. Those under another's law are, like slaves and sons: slaves acquire for their masters whatever they acquire. Masters, however, do not have the right of life and death over them except when cause is shown; nor is it lawful to treat them more harshly. Children, indeed, are acquired by the father in various ways. First, those born of lawful marriage are in the power of their parents. Marriage is the joining of man and woman in an indivisible custom of life. This power is peculiar to the Romans. Here children are understood to be those born of you and your wife, or of your son and his wife, not those born of your daughter. Lawful marriages are called those which citizens, who have reached puberty, sons-in-family, contract with the consent of the parents, and within the degrees defined by law. To this belongs the rule that, by reason of consanguinity or of propriety, marriage cannot be contracted between parents and children, even slaves, even adoptive ones (however much the adoption may have been dissolved). Likewise between brothers and sisters, even adoptive ones (unless the adoption has been dissolved). We also cannot marry a brother's or sister's daughter or granddaughter (a granddaughter is not one born of your adoptive sister), nor a paternal or maternal aunt (even a great-aunt, even an adoptive one). It is not the same with the children of two brothers or two sisters. By affinity we cannot marry a stepdaughter, a daughter-in-law, a mother-in-law or a stepmother (it is not the same for stepchildren of one another). A stepdaughter is regarded as one whom your wife bore to another man after divorce. Daughters-in-law are regarded as the wives of sons, and a mother-in-law as the betrothed of a father.

units.la: Alia impedimenta nuptiarum vide in Digestis {i}. Si à quoquam aduersus ea præcepta contrastæ sunt nuptiæ, vir, vxor, nuptiæ, matrimonium, dos, potestas patria, dotis, donationis exactio nulla est, & alias etiam pœnas patitur. & hoc quidem primo modo liberi parentibus adquiruntur. Secundo, per oblationem Curiæ. Tertio, legitimatione in parentum suorum liberi potestatem redigunter. Quarto, adoptione. Quoties adoptamus eos qui sui iuris sunt, principis authoritate, Adrogatio: quoties imperio magistratus eos, eaïvc, qui quæve in potestate parentum sunt, Adoptio dicitur. Hic titulus plura capita continet, sed quia hodie parum est in viu, omitto.
units.tr: For other impediments to marriage, see the Digest. If marriage has been contracted by anyone against these precepts, there is no husband, wife, marriage, dowry, paternal power, or exaction of dowry or donation, and they also suffer other penalties. And indeed this is the first way in which children are acquired by parents. Second, through the offering to the curia. Third, by legitimation, children are brought back into the power of their parents. Fourth, by adoption. When we adopt those who are sui iuris, by authority of the prince, it is called adrogation; when, by the command of a magistrate, we adopt those who are in the power of their parents, it is called adoption. This title contains many chapters, but since it is little in use today, I omit it.

units.la: Nunc videndum est, quibus modis iure patriæ potestatis quis soluitur. Soluitur morte patris, depor-tatione einsdem (non relegatione, ) seruitu-te pœnæ (hic tamen casus hodie est abrogatus. patriciatus (non tamen militia, non senatoria vel consulari) dignitate, capitis minutione. tris ius patris suspenditur, emancipatione patria potestas soluitur, fitque ea recta via apud competentem iudicem non inuito patre. Reliqua non sunt ita magni momenti in hoc titulo. & hæc de per-sonis alieni iuris. Quæ sui iuris sunt vel in tutela, vel in curatione sunt. Tutela, est potestas in caput liberum ad tuendum eum qui se defendere nequit, iure ciuili data & permissa. Tutor est, qui eam potestatem habet. Tutelæ variæ sunt species, Prima Testamentaria: est enim permissum paretibus, liberis impuberibus, quos in potestate habet, ac non in alte-rius potestate recasuris testamento tutores dare, vt & posthumis, & emancipatis, sed hoc casu tutor confirmandus est sententia prædidis sine inquisitio-ne. Dari tutor potest paterfam. filiusfam. ferinus proprius, etiam sine libertate: seruus alienus, cum li-ber erit: furiosus, cum compos mentis: minor, cum maior 25. annis factus fuerit, ad certum tempus, ex certo tempore, sub conditione, ante hæredis in-stitutionem, non certæ rei vel causæ. Filiabus vel filiis tutor datus, posthumo vel posthumæ, non ta-men nepotibus: liberis, posteris & posthumis & natis datus intelligitur. Secunda tutelæ species, est legitima ab intestato, eaque multiplex, veluti agna-torum proximorum, id est, cognatorum per virilem sexũ, (agnatio omnibus modis capitis minutione ple-rumque perimitur.) Item patronorum, per quam libertorum & libertarum tutela ad patronos eorumque liberos pertinet{4} Item parentum, per quam parentes filiorum suorum ac deinceps emancipato- rum tutelam habent{h}: Item fratrũ,quæ & fiducia- ria dicitur{c}. Tertia species,datiua : quæ defficiente testamentaria, & legitima locum habet{d}.
