Dantur tutores Romæ à Præfecto vrbi, vel Prætore in pro- uinciis,à Præside: vel si facultates pupilli quingentos solidos non excedunt, vel à defensoribus ciuitatum vna cum Antistite ciuitatis,vel à magistratibus, vel iurrdico Alexandrino exacta cautione{e}. Porro , post pubertatem, tutelæ iudicio tutores rationem reddere coguntur{f}: constante vero tutela, authoritatem pupillis interponent præsentes,statim, non post rem- pus aut per epistolã{g}. Nec enim sine tutore pupilli obligari possunt ( quamuis alios possint obligare) vel mutuo aliquo contractu{h}, vel hæreditatem ad- eundo,vel bonorum possessionem , vel fideicommis- sum petendo{i}. Quod si inter tutorem pupillumque iudicium agendum sit, ipse quidem tutor in rem suam auctor esse non potest:ideoque curator pupillo dabitur,ad iudicium peragendum:eoque peracto,cu- rator esse desinet{k}.
units.tr: Now we must see by what means a person is released by law from paternal power. He is released by the death of the father; by the deportation of the same (not relegation); by servitude as a penalty (though this case has been abrogated today); by the dignity of patrician (not, however, military, senatorial or consular dignity); and by loss of status (capitis minutio). The father's right is suspended [...]; by emancipation paternal power is released, and this is done properly before a competent judge, without the father being unwilling. The rest are not of great importance in this title. And these are the things about persons under the law of another. Those who are sui iuris are either in tutelage or in curatorship. Tutelage is a power over a free person, given and permitted by civil law, to protect one who cannot defend himself. A tutor is one who holds that power. The kinds of tutelage are various. The first is testamentary: for it is permitted to parents to appoint tutors by will for impubescent children whom they have in their power, and who would not fall under another's power, and likewise for posthumous and emancipated children; but in this case the tutor must be confirmed by the sentence of the aforesaid judge, without inquiry. A tutor can be given to a father of a family or a son of a family; to a slave of one's own, even without freedom; to another's slave, when he shall be free; to a madman, when he is of sound mind; to a minor, when he has become older than twenty-five; for a certain time, from a certain time, under a condition, before the institution of an heir; but not for a particular matter or cause. A tutor given to daughters or sons is understood to be given to a posthumous child, but not to grandchildren; a tutor given to children is understood to be given to descendants, posthumous children and those born. The second kind is legitimate tutelage by intestacy, and this is of several sorts: as of the nearest agnates, that is, kinsmen through the male line (agnation is for the most part destroyed by any loss of status); likewise of patrons, by which the tutelage of freedmen and freedwomen belongs to the patrons and their children; likewise of parents, by which parents have the tutelage of their children, and then of those emancipated; likewise of brothers, which is also called fiduciary. The third kind is datival, which takes place when testamentary and legitimate tutelage are lacking. Tutors are given at Rome by the Prefect of the city, and in the provinces by the praetor or by the governor; or, if the pupil's property does not exceed five hundred solidi, by the defenders of the cities together with the bishop of the city, or by the magistrates, or by the Alexandrian juridicus, security having been exacted. Moreover, after puberty, tutors are compelled to render account by the action of tutelage. While the tutelage continues, the tutors who are present shall at once give their authority to the pupils, not after a time or by letter. For pupils cannot be bound without their tutor (though they can bind others) by any mutual contract, or by entering upon an inheritance, or by seeking possession of goods or a fideicommissum. But if an action is to be brought between tutor and pupil, the tutor himself cannot be the authority in his own affair; therefore a curator will be given to the pupil to conduct the lawsuit, and when that has been done, the curator ceases to be in office.

units.la: Tutela ,finitur pubertate in masculis post 14. annum completum, in fœminis post 12,{l} si pupilli ad- rogati,vel deportati, vel in seruitutem redacti, vel ab hostibus capti{m}, conditione sub qua datus e- rit{n}, vel tempore ad quod tutor datus erit,existen- tibus{o}, morte vel pupillorum vel tutorum{p}, maxima & media tutorum capitis minutione, omni ve- rò pupillorum{q}, si tutores remoti vel excusati{r}. Interea sciendum est , vtcunque tutela finiatur pu- bertate,puberes tamen vsque ad 25. annum curatores accipere{s}, ab iisdem magistratibus à quibus & tu- tores accipiunt. testamento non accipiunt,datus ta- men confirmatur decreto Prætoris{t}. Non accipiunt etiã inuiti,præterquã in litem{u}. Nec tantum eis solis curator datur,sed & furiosis & prodigis, licet maio- ribus 25.annis{x}: sed & mete captis, surdis & mutis, & perpetuo morbo laborantibus{y}. Quin etiam ipsi impuberes interdum curatorem non accipiunt si tu- tore idoneo careant{z}. Ad tutores & curatores, vt sæpius, pertinet tutelæ nomine satisfdare de indem- nitate pupilli,adeo vt nisi caueant,pignoribus captis coerceri possint{a}, nisi testamento vel ex inquisitio- ne dati sint{b}. eo tamen casu pluribus datis, potest vnus contutori,vel curatori offerre vel ab eo exigere satisfa-
units.tr: Guardianship ends with puberty: in males after the completed fourteenth year, in females after the twelfth. It also ends if the wards are adrogated, deported, reduced to slavery or taken captive by enemies; when the condition under which the guardian was given has come about, or the time for which he was given has run out; on the death of either the wards or the guardians; on the greatest and middle loss of status of the guardians, but on any loss of status of the wards; and if the guardians are removed or excused. Meanwhile it should be understood that, however guardianship ends with puberty, those who have reached puberty still take curators up to their twenty-fifth year, from the same magistrates from whom they receive guardians. They do not receive them by will, but a curator appointed by will is nevertheless confirmed by decree of the Praetor. Nor do they receive them against their will, except in a lawsuit. A curator is given not only to these, but also to madmen and spendthrifts, even if they are over twenty-five; also to the mentally ill, the deaf and mute, and those suffering from a permanent illness. Indeed, even impuberes sometimes receive no curator if they lack a suitable guardian. As is often the case, it belongs to guardians and curators, in the name of guardianship, to give security for the indemnity of the ward, so that unless they give security they can be coerced by seizure of pledges, unless they were appointed by will or by inquiry. In that case, however, when several have been appointed, one co-guardian or curator may offer security to the other, or demand it from him, so that the guardianship is administered by one alone.

units.la: [?] satisfactionem, vt ab vno tantum tutela adminiftre-tur. quod si nemo eorum fatis offerat, is geret quem testator adscripserit: si nullus adscriptus sit, quem maior pars elegerit: si dissensio circa eligendum sit, Prætor partes suas interponet. Quod si indemnes pupilli vel puberes esse non possunt, puta, quia tutores non sunt soluendo, subsidiaria eis dabitur actio in eos eorumve hæredes, (excipe Prætorem, Præsidem prouinciæ & alios quibus tutores dandi ius est) qui (cum satisfactionem exigere debeant) aut omnino, aut non idonee à tutoribus vel curatoribus satisdari non curauerunt. Antea diximus tutores curatores esse desinere, quoties vel remouentur vel excusantur, de vtroque videndum est. Excusantur ergo Romæ propter tres liberos superstites, (Tales sunt in bello mortui) in Italia propter quattuor, in puinciis propter quinque. Liberos intellige etiam nepotes ex filio & adoptatos à patre naturali. Excusatur pariter quis quandiu res fisci administrat, quandiu reipublicæ causa abest, qui potestatem aliquam habet, qui litem de omnibus bonis, vel hæreditate cum pupillo vel adulto habet, quandiu quis tria onera tutelæ non affectatæ, vel curæ habet, propter paupertatem, aduersam admodum valetudinem, si litteras pingere vel legere nesciat, si propter inimicitias testamento tutor datus sit (inimicitias intellige capitales non reconciliatas) si status contro-uerfiam à pupillorum patre passus est, maior 70. annis, minor 25. miles, adeo vt nec voles ad tutelæ onus admittatur, qui Grámaticam vel Medicinâ vel Rhetoricam Romæ, vel in patria sua exercet. Intra quod tepus tutores dati excusare se debeat vide Non iusta excusatio est in eo qui hoc solo vtitur, quod patri pupilli fuerit ignotus. datus tutor ad vniuersum patrimonium datus intelligitur. inuitus curator esse non compellitur, quemadmodum & maritus vxoris. falsa allegatione excusatus non plene liberatur onere tutelæ. Et hæc de excusationibus. Remouentur autem tutores suspecti, à iudicibus ordinariis, suspecti inquam tutores, siue testamentarii, siue alterius generis, siue patroni, dum tamen eorum famæ parcatur. Postulantur suspecti etiam à quauis muliere, verecunda tamen, & pietate producta, ab ipsis puberibus consilio necessario-rum. Porrò suspectus est, qui non ex fide tutelam gerit, vel gerere potest, licet sit soluendo, qui muribus talis est vt suspectus sit ,qui sui copia non facit, & absens nō praestat alimenta. tunc enim in bonorum possessionē eius,pupillus mittitur : si praesens mendacirer id dicit, punitur à iudice, quemadmodum & is qui data pecunia ministerium tutelae adquisiit vel redemit , vt libertus fraudulenter tutelam filiorum patroni administrans remotus ob dolum famosus est . quoad cognitio suspecti finiatur interdicitur tutori administratio suspecti cognitio extinguitur morte tutoris . fraudulenter tutelam administrans, etiam si fatis offerat, removendus est . De personis dictum est. Sequitur vt de rebus videamus.
units.tr: [?] satisfaction. If none of them offers adequate security, the one whom the testator named shall manage the affair; if no one was named, the one whom the greater part chooses; if there is disagreement about the choice, the Praetor will interpose his authority. But if wards or those who have reached puberty cannot be indemnified, for instance because the guardians are insolvent, a subsidiary action will be given to them against those guardians or curators, or their heirs (except the Praetor, the governor of a province and others who have the right to appoint guardians), who, although they ought to have demanded security, either did not do so at all or did not see to it that security was properly given by the guardians or curators. We said earlier that guardians and curators cease to hold office whenever they are removed or excused; both must be considered. Guardians are excused at Rome on account of three surviving children (such as are dead in war), in Italy on account of four, in the provinces on account of five. By "children" understand also grandchildren through a son, and children adopted by their natural father. Likewise a person is excused for as long as he administers the affairs of the treasury, as long as he is absent on public business, as long as he holds some power, as long as he has a lawsuit concerning the whole estate, or an inheritance, with the ward or the adult, and as long as he holds three guardianships or curatorships not sought by him; on account of poverty, very poor health, if he cannot write or read, if he was appointed guardian by will because of enmity (understand capital enmity not reconciled), if he has suffered a dispute over status with the father of the wards; he who is over seventy, or under twenty-five, or a soldier; so that no one who teaches grammar, medicine or rhetoric at Rome or in his own homeland is admitted to the burden of guardianship, not even a willing one. Within what time appointed guardians ought to make their excuse, see... It is not a just excuse for one who uses only this, that he was unknown to the ward's father. A guardian appointed to the whole estate is understood to have been appointed for the whole. A curator is not compelled against his will, just as a husband is not compelled to act for his wife. One who is excused on a false allegation is not fully freed from the burden of guardianship. And so much for excuses. Suspect guardians, whether testamentary, or of another kind, or patrons, are removed by the ordinary judges, provided that their reputation is spared. Suspect guardians may be challenged by any woman, though modest and moved by affection, and by the wards themselves when they reach puberty, and by necessary advisers. Moreover, a guardian is suspect who does not manage, or cannot manage, the guardianship in good faith, even if he is solvent; who is of such a character as to be suspect; who does not make an inventory of his property; and who, when absent, does not provide maintenance. For then the ward is sent into possession of his goods. If he says this falsely while present, he is punished by the judge, just as one who acquired or bought the office of guardian for money, or a freedman who administers the guardianship of the children of his patron fraudulently and is removed, is infamous on account of the fraud. The inquiry into a suspect guardian ends when the guardian is forbidden to administer; the inquiry is extinguished by the death of the guardian. One who administers a guardianship fraudulently must be removed even if he offers adequate security. Enough has been said about persons. It follows that we should look at things.

units.la: Quarum aliae in nostro patrimonio, aliae extra, sunt . Et hae quidem sunt vel naturali iure communes (vt aer,mare,maris littora ) vel publicae (vt flumina,portus , & ripae,viu tamen: nam proprietas riparum illorum est quorum praediis haerent ) vel nullius, vt littora, quae viu publica sunt,proprietate nullius : vt res sacrae, quae per Pontifices Deo consecratae : religiosae, veluti locus in quem mortuus est illatus : sanctae, vt muri, portae ciuitatis, leges : vel vniuersitatis, vt Theatra,stadia, communia ciuitatum . singulorum vero, res fiunt multis modis. Primum, iure naturali seu gentium , idque multifariam. Siquidem ferae bestiae, vt volucres,& pisces, & alia fera animalia quoties capiuntur,& nostra custodia coercentur,nostra fiunt : capta non sunt quae tantum vulnerata ,quae in arbore nostra tantum nidum fecerunt, quae ex alueo nostro euolarunt apes , quae reuertendi animum ceu consuetudinem non habent . Aliud est in cicuribus animantibus, puta gallinis & anseribus,licet enim ea animalia consuetum nostrum effugerint, nostra tamen manent: & qui ea animo lucrandi detinet, furtum committit . Eodem iure gentium, quaecunque ex hostibus capimus nostra fiunt : vt & ea quae in littore inuenimus , quae ex animalibus nostris nascuntur , quae per alluuionem,seu incrementum latens, agris nostris flumen adiecit . quae vi fluminis praediis nostris adiecta longiore tempore heserunt, & radices egerunt . de insula hoc tenendum: in mari natam, fieri occupantis: in medio flumine, confinium promodo latitudinis agri fui:citimam,eius qui ab ea parte praedia possidet. nasci non dicitur insula, fi ager meus in foramam insulae redactus est . Idem est ius in alueo fluminis derelicto, nisi quod ager meus, alueus factus, fit publicus{a}. Quod si meus ager inundatus fuerit, meus manebit: inundatio fundi speciem non commutat{b}. Ad hæc,eodem iure gentium, quam ex a- liena materia speciem feci, mea est, si ad priorem materiam reduci non poterit: multo magis si ex mea & aliena specie fecero{c}. Eodem modo,quam purpu- ram meo vestimento intexui, mea fit{d}. Res aliena meę confusa,vel fortuito,vel mea voluntate,fit com-munis{e}: mixta fortuito,mea manet: voluntate, fit communis{f}.Quæ,(etiam alterius) in meo fundo(quæ- uis a me ædificata fuerit) mea erit{g}: & e contrà, rem meam amitto quam in alieno fundo ædificaue-ro{h}, vel plantauero{i}, vel seuero{l}, vel in aliena charta scripsero. Non idem est in pictura, cui tabula cedit{l}. Eodem iure gentium, bonę fidei posses- for fructus suos facit, malæ fidei possessori nul- los{m}. Bonę fidei possessori adsimilis est vsufructua- rius & colonus{n}.Fœtus pecudum sunt in fructu: an- cillę, non sunt{o}. Vsufructuarii officio incumbit in locum demortuorum animalium alia submittere:de-mortuarum vinearum vel arborum alias substitue-re{p}. Eodem etiam iure gentium quem in meo, e- tiam sciens,vel sacro, vel religioso(fortuito tamen) thesaurum inueni,sit meus : quem in alieno , etiam Cæsaris,fisci, publico, vel ciuitatis , fortuito tamen, dimidio tenus{q}. Eodem etiam iure res nostrę fiunt quoties nobis traduntur à domino{r}, vel eius pro- curatore , seu alio eius voluntate{s}. Nuda etiam vo- luntate,sine traditione, res nostrę siunt,puta patien-tia{t}, clauum traditione{u}. Nostrę etiam res siunt quę cùm in vulgus missę essent{x}, vel pro derelicto habitę , à nobis occupatę sunt{y}. Derelictę non cen- sentur, quę in tępestate, leuadę nauis causa, eiiciun- tur : vel quę de rheda currente, non intelligentibus dominis,ceciderunt{ꝯ}. Hic dicendum erat de modis rerum acquirendarum iure ciuili,sed quia Tribonia-nus hic interseruit alteram rerum diuisionem,præter eam de qua superius dictum est,ea nobis consideranda est. Sit igitur hęc alia rerum diuisio, Rerum alias esse corporales,alias incorporales{a}. Illę innumerabiles, tangi possunt{b}: hę non possunt,in iure consistunt: si- cut hereditas vsus, vsufructus , obligationes{c}, iura seu seruitutes prędiorum vrbanorū & rusticorum{d}. Harū iura sunt,iter,actus,via,aquę ductus{e}: & secū- dum quosdā,aquę haustus,pecoris ad aquā pulsus,,us pascendi, ad calcis coquendę, arenę fodiendę{s}: illarum iura, ędificiis inhærent, suntque plurima: vt seruitus oneris sustinendi, tigni immittendi, stillicidii vel fluminis recipiendi, altius non tollendi, luminibus non officiendi{4} acquiruntur huiusmodi seruitutes pactionibus, stipulationibus, testamento{5}.
units.tr: Some things are in our patrimony, others outside it. Of these, some are common by natural law (such as air, the sea, and the seashores), some are public (such as rivers, harbours and banks; the use, however, is public, for the ownership of the banks belongs to those whose estates they border), and some belong to no one, such as the shores, which are public for use but belong to no one. Some things are sacred, those consecrated to God by the Pontiffs; religious, such as the place where a dead body has been carried; holy, such as the walls and gates of a city, and the laws; or belonging to a whole community, such as theatres, stadia and the common property of cities. Things become the property of individuals in many ways. First, by natural law or the law of nations, and this in many ways. For wild beasts, such as birds, fish and other wild animals, as often as they are caught and confined by our custody, become ours; those are not caught which are only wounded, which have made a nest only in our tree, which have flown out of our hive, or which do not have the habit of returning, as it were. It is otherwise with tame animals, such as hens and geese; for even if those animals have escaped our usual custody, they nevertheless remain ours; and whoever keeps them with the intention of gain commits theft. By the same law of nations, whatever we take from enemies becomes ours; so too do things we find on the shore, what is born of our animals, and what the river adds to our fields through alluvion or gradual increment, and what the force of the river has added to our estates and has stayed there for a long time and taken root. Concerning an island, this must be held: an island born in the sea becomes the property of the one who occupies it; one born in the middle of a river belongs, in proportion to the breadth of the field, to the neighbour of the field, and the nearest one is the one who possesses the estates on that side. An island is not said to be born if my field has been reduced to the form of an island. The same law applies to a riverbed left dry, except that my field, once it has become a riverbed, becomes public. But if my field has been flooded, it will remain mine; flooding does not change the form of the land. Further, by the same law of nations, whatever form I have made from material belonging to another is mine, if it cannot be reduced to its former material; much more so if I have made it from my own material together with another's. By the same means, purple that I have woven into my garment becomes mine. Another's thing mixed with mine, either by chance or by my will, becomes common; mixed by chance, it remains mine; by my will, it becomes common. Whatever is built on my land, even by another, will be mine, and conversely I lose my own thing if I build, plant or sow it on another's land, or write on another's paper. It is not the same with painting, to which the panel yields. By the same law of nations, a possessor in good faith makes the fruits his own, a possessor in bad faith none. A usufructuary and a tenant are similar to a possessor in good faith. The offspring of livestock are part of the fruit; female slaves are not. It is the duty of the usufructuary to put other animals in the place of those that have died, and to substitute other vines or trees for dead ones. By the same law of nations, a treasure that I find in my own land, knowingly, or in a sacred or religious place (though by chance), is mine; one found in another's land, even Caesar's, the treasury's, a public place or a city's, though by chance, is mine to the extent of one half. By the same law, our things become ours whenever they are handed over to us by the owner, or by his agent, or by another with his will. Even by bare will, without delivery, things become ours, for instance by consent, and by delivery of the key. Things also become ours which, when they had been thrown into the common crowd, or had been held as abandoned, were taken by us. Those things are not considered abandoned which are thrown out in a storm to lighten a ship, or which fell from a moving cart without the owners noticing. Here it was necessary to speak of the modes of acquiring things under civil law; but since Tribonian has interposed here another division of things, apart from the one discussed above, we must consider that also. Let this, then, be the other division of things: some things are corporeal, others incorporeal. The former are countless and can be touched; the latter cannot be touched and exist in law, such as an inheritance, the use, usufruct, obligations, and the rights or servitudes of urban and rural estates. Among these are the rights of way, passage, road and water-conduit; and according to some, the right of drawing water, of driving cattle to water, of pasturage, and of digging lime or sand. The rights of the others attach to buildings, and there are very many of them: such as the servitude of bearing a burden, of inserting a beam, of receiving the drip or the flow of water, of not raising a building higher, of not obstructing light. Servitudes of this kind are acquired by pacts, stipulations, and by will.

units.la: Sic vsusfructus adquiritur{c}: eo possumus alienis rebus vti salua earum substantia{d}: non tamen in aeternum. Siquidem, certis modis extinguitur, & ad proprietarium reuertitur{e}: constituitur vero in omnibus rebus, etiam iis, quæ vsu consumuntur, vt tamen earum nomine caueatur{f}. Vsus iisdem modis constituitur & finitur, quibus & vsusfructus{g}: minus iuris est in vsu quàm in vsufructu{h}: habitatio, neque vsus est neque vsusfructus, sed proprium aliquod ius{i}.
units.tr: Thus ownership in usufruct is acquired: we may use another's property with its substance preserved, but not forever. For it is extinguished by certain modes and reverts to the owner; it is established, however, in all things, even those which are consumed by use, provided that security is given in their name. Use is established and ended by the same modes as usufruct; there is less right in use than in usufruct; habitation is neither use nor usufruct, but a certain right of its own.

units.la: Hic dicendum erat de hereditatibus & obligationibus: sed tamen Tribonianus transit ad modos rerum acquirendarum iure ciuili{k}. Eo varie res acquirimus, puta vsucapione{l}, donatione{m}, & quodam speciali iure adcrescendi, testamento{n}, ab intestato iure ciuili vel Prætorio{o}, per adrogationem{p}, bonorum addictione{q}, & olim per bonorum possessionem, & ex Senatusconsulto Claudiano{r}, olim & hodie obligationibus{s}: de Vsucapionibus primo loco est videndum, de quibus hoc constitutum est: Res mobiles per triennium, res immobiles inter præsentes decennio, inter absentes viginti annis usucapi & nostras fieri, vbicunque sitæ sint{t}: qualescunque sint: libero homine, re sacra, religiosa, seruo fugitiuo{x} rebus fisci{y}, furtiuis, vi possessis, exceptis{z}: quæ neque à fure, neque ab alio, nisi ipso domino, idque quantum ad res furtiuas & vi possessas attinet{a}, quamuis bonæ fidei possessores vsucapi possunt: res tamen alienas mobiles, si bona fide eas nostras existimemus, alienare possumus{b}: Fiscus & Imperator in eadem causa sunt, quas res enim alienas ignorans vendit, vel donat, vel quocunque titulo transfert, statim facit accipientis: quo casu aduersus fiscum vel imperatorem intra quadriennium dominis ipsis vel hypothecariis competit actio{c}. Immobiles vacantes propter absentiam aut negligentiam domini, alio bona fide accipienti tradere possumus: etiam in præiudicium fisci (si modo sequatur vsucapio) vt eas longa possessione adquirere possit{d}. Nec enim earum, vt pote immobilium, furtum fit: cum furtum sine affectu furandi non committatur: idque vtilitas eorum, qui longa & indubitata possessione muniti sunt, exposcit {a}. Adhæc, ut res à bonæ fidei possesso-re vsucapi possit, res vitio carere debet {b}: qui vsu-capit, errore falsæ causæ carere {c}. Diutina bonæ fidei possessoris vel vsucapio, vel possessio, ad hæredem qualemcunque cōtinuatur {d}veluti emptorem {e}. Sequitur Donatio,secundum iure ciuili mortis causa, vel inter viuos {f}: illa, fere per omnia legatis connumeratur {g}: hæc, non item, perfectaque temere reuocari non potest: perficitur scripto, vel non scripto: nec requiritur traditio. quæ 50. solidos excedit insinuatione non indiget {h}: (quemadmodum & quæ fit vel pro redemptione captiuorum, vel à magistris militum ipsis militibus, vel à quouis iis quorum domus incendio vel ruina corruptæ sunt {i}.) Reuocari possunt donationes ob ingratitudinem donatarij & aliis ex causis {k}. Tertium quasdam donationis olim ante nuptias, hodie propter nuptias, vocatur, dotibus exæquatum. Potest n. ante vel post matrimonium fieri {l}. Tertius acquirendi modus olim iure ciuili fuit, scilicet accrescendi, de quo vide paragraphum vltimum {m}. Hic dicendum erat de testamentis: sed Triboniaus hic interseruit tractatum de persoois alienantibus & acquirentibus, quod ad priores attinet hoc definitur, Maritim res dotales, etiam consentiente vxore, alienare non potest quamuis sit earum dominus {n}; Creditorem pignus ex pactione alienare posse: quamuis non sit eius dominus {o}: pupillos nullam rem sine tutoris auctoritate alienare, mutuam dare, in solutum (nisi de iudicis mandato) accipere, aut soluere posse {p}. Quod ad alteras attinet: Acquiritur nobis per nosmetipsos {q}, per liberos nostros, vtriusque sexus, quos in potestate habemus. Totum, si ex re nostra: vsufructu tenus, si aliunde quæsierint {r}, adquirimus. per emancipatos dimidiam vsusfructus tantum nō dominij {s}.
units.tr: Here it was necessary to speak of inheritances and obligations, but Tribonian nevertheless passes on to the modes of acquiring things under the civil law. In various ways we acquire things: for instance, by usucaption, by gift, by a special right of accretion, by will, by intestacy under the civil or the praetorian law, by adrogation, by adjudication of goods, and formerly by possession of goods, and under the Claudian Senatus-consultum; formerly and today also by obligations. Concerning usucaptions we must look first at what has been laid down about them: movable things are usucaptured and become ours after three years, immovable things between present parties after ten years, and between absent parties after twenty years, wherever they are situated; whatever their kind, except things belonging to a free man, sacred things, religious things, a runaway slave, things of the fisc, things stolen, and things taken by force. These cannot be usucaptured either by a thief or by anyone else, except the owner himself, and this holds as far as stolen and forcibly possessed things are concerned, although possessors in good faith may usucapt them. Nevertheless, we may alienate movable things belonging to another, if we believe in good faith that they are ours. The fisc and the Emperor are in the same position: whatever thing of another's a person sells, gives, or transfers under any title while ignorant of its owner's rights, immediately becomes the property of the recipient; in this case, an action lies against the fisc or the Emperor within four years for the owners themselves or for the holders of a mortgage. Immovable things which are vacant through the absence or negligence of the owner, we may hand over to another who receives them in good faith, even to the prejudice of the fisc (provided usucaption follows), so that he may acquire them by long possession. For there is no theft of such things, being immovable, since theft is not committed without intent to steal; and the advantage of those who are protected by long and undisputed possession demands this. Moreover, for a thing to be usucaptured by a possessor in good faith, the thing must be free of defect; he who usucapts must be free of error about a false cause. The usucaption or possession of a good-faith possessor, if long continued, passes on to any heir whatever, just as to a purchaser. Next comes gift, which under the civil law is either mortis causa or inter vivos. The former is for almost all purposes counted among legacies; the latter is not, and once completed cannot rashly be revoked. It is completed in writing or without writing, and delivery is not required. A gift exceeding fifty solidi needs no insinuation (as also a gift made either for the ransom of captives, or by the masters of soldiers to the soldiers themselves, or by anyone to those whose houses have been ruined by fire or collapse). Gifts may be revoked on account of the donee's ingratitude and for other causes. The third kind of gift, formerly called ante nuptias and today propter nuptias, is equated with dowries; for it can be made before or after marriage. The third mode of acquiring under the civil law was formerly accretion, concerning which see the last paragraph. Here it was necessary to speak of wills, but Tribonian has interposed here a treatise on persons alienating and acquiring. As far as the former are concerned, this is laid down: a husband cannot alienate dotal property, even with his wife's consent, although he is its owner; a creditor may alienate a pledge by agreement even though he is not its owner; wards may alienate nothing without their guardian's authority, nor give a loan, nor accept or pay in settlement (unless by the judge's mandate). As for the latter: we acquire through ourselves, and through our children of either sex whom we have in our power. We acquire the whole if from our own property; only the usufruct if they have obtained it from elsewhere. Through emancipated children we acquire only half the usufruct, not ownership.

units.la: Per seruos quos in potestate habemus etiam ignorantes & inuiti (nisi forte hæredes instituti sint. tunc enim, nisi nostro iussu, hæreditatem adire non possunt) adquirimus dominia, possessiones, vsucapiones, præscriptiones: quodcumque denique, traditione, stipulatione, donatione, legato, testamento, vel ex alia causa ab iis acceptum fuerit {t}: per seruos vsufructuarios & bona fide possessos, quod ex re nostra vel operis suis adquisiuerint {u}. Per alienos seruos, & per liberos hominies (excepto tamen procuratore) nobis nil acquiritur {x}. Nunc dicendum est de quarto {a}adquirendi modo, iure ciuili: Tale est testamentum, quod hic definitur esse mentis testatio: huius olim diuersæ formæ ac genera (quæ nunc desueta sunt) fuerunt. Vnum pacis, quod calatis comitiis: alterum belli, quod procinctum. Terrium per æs & libram vocabatur: hodie in testamentis paganorum & nō militum scriptis, hæc quę sequuntur necessaria sunt.
units.tr: Through slaves whom we have in our power we acquire ownerships, possessions, usucaptions, and prescriptions, even when they are ignorant or unwilling (unless perhaps they have been instituted heirs, for then they cannot take up the inheritance without our order); and whatever is received from them by delivery, stipulation, gift, legacy, will, or any other cause, we acquire; through slaves in usufruct and possessed in good faith, whatever they acquire from our property or by their own work. Through another's slaves, and through free men (except, however, a procurator), we acquire nothing. Now we must speak of the fourth mode of acquiring under the civil law. Such is the will, which is defined here as the testimony of the mind. Formerly there were various forms and kinds of it (now fallen into disuse). One was of peace, made in the Calata comitia; another of war, made in the procinctus; a third was called per aes et libram. Today, in the wills of civilians and not of soldiers, the following are required.

units.la: Vno & eodem tempore ac contextu fieri debent, septem testibus adhibitis, subscribere testes oportet, eorum signacula testamento imponenda, per manus testatoris vel testium, nomen hæredis exprimendum est: possunt omnes testes vno etiam alieno anulo signare: testes in testamento esse non possunt mulier, impubes, seruus, furiosus, mutus, surdus, bonis interdictus, infamis, & is cum quo testamenti factio non est: seruus (nisi eo tempore quo testamentum signabatur, omnium consensu, liberi loco habebatur.) Pater, ac eius liberi (nisi in alieno negotio hæres defuncti, eiusdem hæredis pater liberi, & fratres, qui in eiusdem patris potestate sunt testes esse non possunt. Legatarij & fideicommissarij, & personæ illis coniunctæ testes esse possunt. Et hæc de testibus. Testamentum in quacunque materia fieri potest: & pluribus codicibus: & hæc de forma scripti testamenti dicta sint. In eo quod sine scripto fit, seu nuncupatiuo, sufficit septem testibus adhibitis nostram voluntatem coram eis nuncupare. Et hæc testandi forma hodie passim apud omnes gentes vsitata est. Supra dicta diligens obseruatio testium & solennitatum in ordinandis testamentis paganorum, in testamento militis (dum in expeditione occupatus est, quatenus militat & in castris degit, non post misionem: nisi, quod ad veteranos attiner, intra annum testati sint) non obseruatur. Testamentum fecisse dicitur, non si simpliciter dixit, Te hæredem facio, sed tunc demum cum id dixerit in præsentia testium ad id conuocatorum. E contrario testamentum militis censetur, cui ante expeditionem facto, posteaue constante militia resignato, aliquid detractum vel adiectum est. Singularia & hæc sunt, quod filiusfamilias miles testari posit, mutus & surdus, quod milite adrogato, vel emancipato testamentum eius irritum non fiat tanquam capitis minutione: Quod dictum est de militari testamento, ad eos qui quasi militant extenditur, ratione peculij quasi castrensis. Longè ab huiusmodi priuilegio absunt filij familias, quibus, {a}etiam permittente patre, testari non licet, (nisi, vt antea diximus, de castrensi vel quasi peculio{a}) vt & impuberibus & furiosis constante furore{b} sed & in-terdiêtis bonis, & prodigis{c}, surdis & mutis, (nisi beneficio principali{d}) coecis (nisi fecundum obser-uationem D. Iuftini{e}) captis ab hoste{f}. Est & haec obseruatio, praeter superiores, in testamentis obser-uanda, vt pater (aliud est in matre & auo mater-no{g}, aliud in militepatre quoad post humos{h}) libe-ros cuiuscumque sexus sint, natos & post humos de quibus v. paragr. 1. 2. 6.{i} tam suos, quam emanci-patos, haeredes instituat, vel nominatim exheredet. Alioquin, fi eos silentio praeterierit, inutiliter testatur: adeo quidem, vt fi viuo patre filius ita praeteritus mortuus fit, nemo haeres ex eo testamento possit existere: quia fc. ab initio non constitit testamentum{k}. De adoptiuis vide paragraphum quartu & quintum in fine{l}. De emancipatis paragraphum tertium, & quartum in verf. emancipati{m}. Porro de extraneis haeredibus instituendis, hoc tenendum est: nobis permissum esse instituere tam liberos homines quam seruos, & tam proprios quam alienos{n}, & vnu homine & plures vsque in infinitum{o}, quemadmodum eos quos nunquam vidimus{p}, & haereditatem diuidere in plures vncias quam duodecim{q}. quin vel in nullas, vel partim in quasdam, partim in nullas. Quod cum accidit, quid iuris fit vide paragraph. 6. 7.{r} Haeredem pure & sub conditione (non tamen impossibili, talis enim pro non scripta habetur{s}) quin & sub diuersis conditionibus (quae si communi omnibus: si separatim, similiter obtemperadum erit{t}) instituare possumus. Ex certo tempore, aut ad certum tempus non possumus: quo casu dies habetur pro superuacuo, & perinde est ac si pure haeres scriptus fuerit{u}. Possumus quoque in testamento plures gradus haeredum facere{x}, & plures in vnius, vel vnu in plurium, vel singulos in singulorum locum, vel inuicem substituere{y}. Possumus & ex disparibus partibus haeredes scriptos inuicem substituere, & nullam mentionem in substitutione partium facere, quo casu videmur eas in substitutione partes dedisse, quas in institutione expressimus{z}. Possumus quoque & institutio haeredi cohaeredem substitutum dare, & alium ei substituere: quo casu ad vtramque partem substitutus adiuvatur{a}. Item possumus haeredi sub hac conditione, Si hæres non erit, scripto, alium substituere, de quo quid iuris sit vide paragr. vlt. Possumus præterea liberis impuberibus & furiosis (quo casu ad exemplum pupillorum eis substituimus quos in potestate habemus, non solum ita, Si hæredes nobis non extiterint alius sit eis hæres, sed eo amplius, Si (instituti vel exhæredati liberi, etiam posthumi) hæredes nobis extiterint, & adhuc impuberes mortui fuerint, alius, (puta Seius,) sit eis hæres. Talis substitutio vocatur pupillaris: eaque & sibi & filio, pater testamentum facit, hocque illius est sequella: illud si non valet, hoc etiam non valebit: Possumus etiam singulis liberis, vel ei qui vltimus impubes morietur substituere, specialiter, i. nomine expresso, vel generaliter: masculo ad decimum quartum, fœminæ ad duodecimum annum. Extraneo vel puberi filio, ita non possumus substituere: eos tamen grauare per fideicommissum possumus, vt hæreditatem alii totum, vel pro parte restituant. Quomodo parens substitutione pupillari vitæ filij periculum creare non potsit, vide paragr. tertium. Valent ergo superioribus modis testamenta, quæ interdum accidit rumpi vel irrita fieri. Rumpitur ad gnatione sui hæredis, posteriore testamento. Prius testamentum non valide reuocatur, si simpliciter dixerimus nolle nos id valere. item, si posterius facere tantum coepimus: & ita quidem vt his duobus casibus princeps non capiat. fit irritum capitis minutione. Vtcunque autem tanta nobis testantibus competat potestas, non possumus tamen iniquè liberos vel parentes exhæredare aut iniquè præterire, sed nec fratres & sorores, turpibus personis ferri ptis hæredibus, postponere. alias huiusmodi personæ de inofficioso defuncti testamento agere possunt: vt sc. vel quarta eis detur, vel suppleatur. Quod si huiusmodi personæ quantam vel iure legati, vel fideicommissi, vel mortis causa, vel inter vivos, vel aliis modis habuerint, inofficiosi agere non possunt. Quartam ita intellige vt sive vnus fuerit, sive plures, quibus agere de inofficioso permittitur, vna quarta eis detur, quæ pro rata eis distribuatur. Et hic notandum est, nostrorum hæredum alios esse nobis necessarios (vt seruos) alios suos & necessarios (veluti filios) alios extraneos. Extraneis deliberandi de adeunda hæreditate, vel non adeunda: suis & necessariis, abstinendi potestas datur. Extraneus
units.tr: All of this must be done at one time and in one continuous act. With seven witnesses present, the witnesses must sign and place their seals on the testament, and the heir's name must be expressed by the hand of the testator or of the witnesses. All the witnesses may even seal with a single ring, even one that belongs to someone else. Women, minors below puberty, slaves, the insane, the mute, the deaf, those deprived of their goods, the infamous, and anyone without the capacity to make a will cannot be witnesses to a testament. A slave cannot be a witness unless, at the time the testament was sealed, he was by common consent regarded as free. A father and his children cannot be witnesses (except in another's business, when the heir of the deceased is involved), and neither can the father, children and brothers of the heir, who are under the same father's power. Legatees and fideicommissaries, and persons connected with them, can be witnesses. So much on witnesses. A testament may be made on any material and on several tablets, and so much may be said of the form of a written testament. In the unwritten form, which is called nuncupative, it is enough, with seven witnesses present, to declare our will orally before them. This manner of making a will is nowadays commonly used among all peoples. The careful observance of witnesses and formalities described above, in drawing up the wills of civilians, is not observed in the testament of a soldier, while he is busy on campaign, so long as he serves and lives in camp, but not after his discharge; except that, as far as veterans are concerned, they must have made their testaments within a year. A man is said to have made a testament not if he merely said "I make you heir", but only when he said it in the presence of witnesses summoned for that purpose. Conversely, a soldier's testament is judged to be one to which something has been removed or added, either before the expedition or afterwards during his service. These too are special rules: a son under power may make a soldier's will; a mute and a deaf man may do so; and when a soldier has been adrogated or emancipated, his testament is not made void, as it would be by loss of status. What has been said of the military testament extends to those who, as it were, serve in the army, by reason of the quasi-camp peculium. Sons under power are far from this privilege: they are not permitted to make a will even with their father's consent, except, as we said before, concerning the castrense or quasi-castrense peculium. Likewise minors below puberty, the insane while the madness lasts, those deprived of their goods, prodigals, the deaf and the mute (unless by imperial favour), the blind (unless according to the observance of the emperor Justinian), and those taken captive by the enemy, are not permitted. There is also this rule, to be observed in testaments besides the above: a father (the rule is different for a mother and a maternal grandfather, and different for a soldier-father as regards posthumous children) must institute as heirs, or disinherit by name, his children of either sex, whether born or posthumous, concerning whom see paragraphs 1, 2 and 6, both his own children and those emancipated. Otherwise, if he passes them over in silence, he makes his testament ineffectively. So much so that if a son so passed over dies while the father is still alive, no heir can arise from that testament, because the testament never had validity from the beginning. On adopted children see paragraphs 4 and 5 at the end. On emancipated children see paragraph 3, and paragraph 4 under the words "emancipati". Further, concerning the institution of outside heirs, this must be held: we are permitted to institute as heirs free men as well as slaves, both our own and others', and one man or several, even to infinity, and also those whom we have never seen; and to divide the inheritance into more than twelve parts (unciae). Indeed, we may divide it into none, or partly into some and partly into none. When this happens, see what the law is in paragraphs 6 and 7. We may institute an heir purely and under a condition (not, however, an impossible condition, for such a condition is held as not written), and even under different conditions (if the conditions are common to all, or if separate, they must be obeyed in the same way). We cannot institute an heir from a certain time or up to a certain time; in such a case the day is held superfluous, and it is just as if he had been written heir purely. We can also make several degrees of heirs in a testament, and several in place of one, or one in place of several, or each in the place of each, or substitute them reciprocally. We may also substitute reciprocally heirs written in unequal shares, and make no mention of shares in the substitution; in which case we are seen to have given, in the substitution, the shares which we expressed in the institution. We may also, in instituting an heir, give him a co-heir as substitute, and substitute another for him; in which case the substitute is helped on either side. Likewise we may, in writing, substitute another heir under this condition: "If he shall not be heir"; on this see the last paragraph. Moreover, we may substitute for our children who are minors or insane (in which case, on the model of wards, we substitute for those whom we have under our power), not only in this way, "If they shall not be heirs to us, let another be their heir", but further, "If the children, instituted or disinherited, even posthumous, become heirs to us, and have died while still under puberty, let another (say Seius) be their heir." Such a substitution is called pupillary, and a father makes a testament both for himself and for his son, and the one is a consequence of the other: if the first is not valid, the second will not be valid either. We may also substitute, for individual children, or for whichever of them dies last while still under puberty, either specifically, that is with the name expressed, or generally: for a male up to fourteen years, for a female up to twelve. We cannot so substitute for an outside son, or for a son who has reached puberty; yet we can burden them by fideicommissum to restore the inheritance wholly or in part to another. On how a parent cannot create danger to a son's life by pupillary substitution, see paragraph 3. Thus testaments stand valid by the above modes, though sometimes they happen to be broken or made void. A testament is broken by the begetting of a heir, by a later testament. A former testament is not validly revoked if we have merely said that we are unwilling for it to stand; likewise if we have only begun to make a later one; and indeed in these two cases the prince does not take. It is made void by loss of status. However great the power we have in making testaments, we cannot, however, unjustly disinherit or unjustly pass over our children or parents, nor place brothers and sisters after shameful persons as heirs. Otherwise persons of this kind can bring an action against the deceased's testament as inofficious, so that either a quarter is given to them or what is lacking is supplied. But if such persons have received as much as by right of legacy, or fideicommissum, or mortis causa, or inter vivos, or by other means, they cannot bring an inofficious action. Understand the quarter thus: whether there is one person or several to whom the action on an inofficious testament is permitted, one quarter is to be given to them, and it is distributed among them pro rata. And here it must be noted that some of our heirs are necessary to us (like slaves), others are our own and necessary (like sons), and others are outsiders. To outsiders is given the power of deliberating whether to enter upon the inheritance or not; to our own and necessary heirs, the power of abstaining.

units.la: [The remaining lines are not visible on this scan, the text runs on to the next page.] neus hæres hæreditatem adit vel nuda voluntate vel pro hærede gerendo. Pro hærede gerit,qui rebus hæreditariis tanquâ hæres vtitur. Vtitur,qui vendit, qui colit, qui locat{a}. Et hæc omnia non tantum possumus, sed etiam legâdi nobis potestas data est{b}. Legatū,est donatio à defuncto relicta, ab hærede præstanda{c}. Olim variis generibus legabatur,per vindicationem, damnationem, sinendi modum,& præceptionem. Sed hodie omnium istorum legatorum vna est natura,& quibusque verbis legare licet: actione personali, in rem, & hypothecaria legatariis data{d}. Olim etiam legata fideicommissis strictiora erant, hodie exæquata{e}. Videndum est de rebus quas legare possumus. Legare possumus res nostras, hæredis,rem alienâ (scilicet tamen,& in commercio posita quo vltimo casu cogitur hæres eam rē redimere, vel æstimatione dare{f} fidei. nisi legatarius ex causa nō onerosa, sed lucrativa,puta donationis,eā rē viuo testatore fuerit consecutus{g}) rē obligatā creditori{h}, quod futurū esse potest: rem nostrā quasi alienā{i}, rem nostram eamque postea alienare (totam,sc.vel in parte,ac pignori dare: quo casu non videmur legatum ademere, aliud erit si res legata sine facto hæredis periit. tūc enim res legatario decedit{k}) debitori nostro liberationē{l}. Creditori pure legare possumus quod in diem & sub condicione et debemus, (alias si nihil est plus in legato quàm in debito legatum erit inutile{m}) dotem vxori (plenius enim est legatum, quàm de dolo actio{n}) ancillas cum suis natis,ordinarium seruum cum vicariis, seruum cum peculio, fundum cum instrumento,sed eo casu mortua ancilla & ordinario,partus & vicarius debetur: mortuo seruo, fundo alienato, peculium & instrumentum non debetur{o}. Gregem quoque legare possumus,de quo quod superfuerit,etiam minimum, putavna ouis,à legatario vindicari poterit{p}. Aedibus legatis, quæque eis post testamentum testator adiecerit ædibus cedent{q}. Legare etiam possumus peculia seruorum{r}, res corporales & incorporales{s}, optionis facultate{t}. Rem legatarii ei legare non possumus{u}. & hæc de rebus. Illis solùm legare possumus cum quibus testamenti factio est{x}, incertis personis{y}, alieno posthumo (posthumus alienus dicitur, qui natus inter suos hæres testatori futurus non est{z}, qui & olim & hodie heres institui potest, nisi in vtero eius sit quæ iure nostro vxor esse non potest{a}. Non idem est in tutore,
units.tr: [The remaining lines are not visible on this scan; the text runs on to the next page.] An outside heir enters upon the inheritance either by mere will or by acting as heir. He acts as heir who uses the inheritance goods as heir does. He uses them who sells, who cultivates, who lets out. And all these things we can not only do, but also the power of bequeathing has been given to us. A legacy is a gift left by the deceased, to be delivered by the heir. Formerly legacies were given in various kinds: by vindication, by condemnation, by the mode of permission, and by preception. But today all these legacies have one nature, and a legacy may be made in any words; it is given to legatees with a personal action, a real action, and a hypothecary action. Formerly, too, legacies were stricter than fideicommissa; today they are made equal. We must consider what things we can bequeath. We can bequeath our own things, the heir's things, another's thing (provided it is however within commerce; in this last case the heir is compelled to buy that thing back or to give its value, unless the legatee obtained it during the testator's life from a gratuitous and not an onerous cause, such as a gift), a thing pledged to a creditor, which can happen; our own thing as if it were another's; our own thing, and afterwards to alienate it (wholly or in part, or to give it in pledge: in which case we are not seen to have revoked the legacy; it is otherwise if the bequeathed thing perished without any act of the heir, for then the thing is lost to the legatee); and to our debtor, a release. We can purely bequeath to a creditor what we owe him, whether at a day or under a condition (otherwise, if there is nothing more in the legacy than in the debt, the legacy will be void); a dowry to a wife (for the legacy is fuller than an action for fraud); handmaids with their offspring; an ordinary slave with his vicarii; a slave with his peculium; a farm with its equipment. But in that last case, if the handmaid or the ordinary slave has died, the offspring and the vicarius are still owed; if the slave has died, or the farm has been alienated, the peculium and the equipment are not owed. We can also bequeath a flock, and whatever remains of it, even the smallest part, such as a single sheep, can be vindicated by the legatee. When houses are bequeathed, whatever the testator added to the houses after the testament will go with them. We can also bequeath the peculia of slaves, corporeal and incorporeal things, with the faculty of option. We cannot bequeath to a legatee his own thing. And so much on things. We can bequeath only to those with whom we have testamentary capacity, to uncertain persons, and to a posthumous stranger (a posthumous stranger is one who, born among his own, will not be heir to the testator; such a person both formerly and today can be instituted heir, unless the womb carries one who cannot be a wife under our law). It is not the same for a guardian,

units.la: {a} §.vlt. {b} Tit.20. {c} §.1. {d} §.2. {e} §.3. {f} §.4. {g} §.6. {h} §.9. {i} §.5. {k} §.7. {l} §.11. {m} §.16. {n} §.13. {o} §.14. {p} §.15. {q} §.17. {r} §.18. {s} §.19. {t} §.20. {u} §.21. {x} §.22. {y} §.10. {z} §.24. {a} §.25. {b} §.26. {c} §.28. qui incertus dari non debet ) & hæc de persoris. Videndum est qua forma legare possumus. Possumus vero legare coniunctim vel disiunctim, & generaliter, puta seruū, vt eo casu electio sit legatarij: Possumus in nomine, cognomine, prænomine, agnomine legatarii errare, (sufficit si de persona eius constet) possumus eundem fallo demonstrare, eiusque falsa causa legare, sub condicione, seruo hæredis, ante hæredis institutionem, & inter medias hæreditas institutiones, post mortem hæredis aut legatarii, poenæ nomine. Possumus quoque adimere legata (siue eodem testamento, siue codicillis, sine contrariis verbis, siue aliis quibusque) & transferre ab alio ad alium. Possumus quoque vniuersa bona legatis errogare: sed tamen ea potestas primum per legem Furiam, dein per legem Voconiam, tandem per legem Falcidiam est restricta, qua cauetur ne plus legare liceat, quam dodrantem totorum bonorum, id est, vt siue vnus hæres institutus sit siue plures apud eum eosve pars quarta remaneat. Ea lex in singulis hæredibus locum habet, tam iis quorum pars legatis onerata est, quam illis quorum pars non est onerata. Quantitas patrimonij mortis tempore spectatur: ideoque, quæ mortuo testatore hereditati ante aditam hæreditatem adiunguntur vel adimuntur ad lucrum vel damnum hæredum pertinent. Falcidiæ ratio ponitur, ære alieno, funeris impensa, & pretiis seruorum manumissorum deductis. Nunc transeamus ad fideicommissa. Ea primum eo fini reperta fuerunt, vt quibus hereditas vel legatum relinqui non poterat, ij per alium vtrumque caperent. Ea diuus Augustus, iustis rationibus motus, confirmauit: confirmata paulatim in asiduam iurisdictione versa sunt, Prætore ad id peculiariter creato, qui fideicommissarius dicebatur. Est autem fideicommissum, quoties hæredem institutu rogamus vt hereditatem alii restituat: eaque restituta nihilominus est hæres, quanquam olim ei & in eum darentur omnes actiones, cui ita erat restituta hereditas. Postea permissum fuit, Senatusconsulto Pegasiano, hæredi perinde quartam retinere, atque ex lege Falcidia ex legatis retinere conceditur: quo subiecuto, ipse hæres onera hæreditaria pro rata parte sustinebat: alter, legatarij partiarij loco erat, id est, eius cui pars bonorum legata est: eaque species legati partitio vocabatur, quia cum hærede partiarius partic-batur. batur hæreditatem, atque ita in hæredem, iure ciuili: in eum qui recipiebat hereditatem, ex Sc. Trebelliano actiones pro rata parte dabantur. Hodie hæres in solidum vel pro parte, testamentarius vel legitimus vel honorarius, quin & is cui aliquid restitui mãdauimus, & à nobis rogatus vt id, aut totum, aut parte tenus, alij restituat, hæreditatem restituere debet, quartamque, vel quod quartæ deest, retinere & repetere poterit: pro rata portione actionibus, tam in eum, quam in fideicommissarios, competentibus: nisi huiusmodi personæ volentes scientes totam restituerint, vel noluerint adire. tunc enim soli fideicommissarij tenentur. Fideicommissi fa cora quinque testibus relinquere potuimus, quin coram solo hærede: quo casu fideicommissarius hæredi iusiurandum deferre potest, hæresque cogitur vel iurare se nihil tale à testatore audiuisse, aut, si recusat iurare, fideicomissum præstare. Nec tantum vniuersam hæreditatem per fideicommissum relinquere possumus, sed & res singulas, proprias, hæredis, legatarij, fideicommissarij, aut cuiuslibet alterius, liberatiis verbis potissimum, peto, rogo, volo, mãdo, siuei tuę committo, quæ perinde singula firma sunt, ac si in vnum congesta sint. Possumus quoque non tãtum per testamentum solenne, de quo antea diximus, sed & codicillis vno vel pluribus, (qui minorem solennitatem requirunt) relinquere fideicommissum vel quid aliud, non tamen hæreditatem directo, licet per obliquum. Per obliquum relinquimus quoties fideicommittimus. ante vel post testamentum fieri possût, adeo vt ex iis fideicomissum peti possit, si appareat restatorem à voluntate, quam in codicillis expresserat, non recessisse. Et hæc de testamentis.

And this is said about persons. We must consider in what form we may bequeath. We may bequeath jointly or severally, and in general terms, for example a slave, so that in that case the choice belongs to the legatee. We may make a mistake in the name, surname, forename or nickname of the legatee (it is enough if his identity is established). We may also describe the same person falsely and bequeath to him on a false ground; subject to a condition; to the slave of the heir; before the heir is instituted; between the institutions of heirs; after the death of the heir or of the legatee; by way of penalty. We may also revoke legacies (whether in the same testament, or in codicils, without contrary words, or in any other way), and transfer them from one person to another. We may also burden the whole estate with legacies. But this power was first restricted by the Furian law, then by the Voconian law, and finally by the Falcidian law, which provides that it is not lawful to bequeath more than three quarters of the whole estate; that is, whether one heir has been instituted or several, a quarter remains with him or with them. This law applies to each heir, both to those whose share is burdened with legacies and to those whose share is not burdened. The amount of the estate is judged at the time of death; therefore whatever is added to or taken away from the inheritance after the testator's death, but before the inheritance is accepted, pertains to the gain or loss of the heirs. In the calculation for the Falcidian quarter, debts, funeral expenses and the prices of manumitted slaves are deducted. Now let us pass to trusts (fideicommissa). These were first devised for this purpose: that those to whom an inheritance or a legacy could not be left might take it through another. The deified Augustus, moved by just reasons, confirmed them; once confirmed, they gradually became the subject of ordinary jurisdiction, a praetor being specially appointed for this purpose, who was called the trust praetor (fideicommissarius). A trust is whenever we request an instituted heir to restore the inheritance to another; and although the heir who has been so charged remains heir after restoring it, all actions were formerly given both to and against the person to whom the inheritance had been restored. Later, by the Pegasian senatus consultum, it was permitted that the heir should retain a fourth just as, under the Falcidian law, a fourth is allowed to be retained from legacies. Once this was done, the heir himself bore the inheritance debts in proportion to his share, and the other party took the place of a partiary legatee, that is, of one to whom a part of the estate was bequeathed; this kind of legacy was called a partition, because it was shared (partitio) with the heir, and the estate was divided (partiebatur) between them. Thus, under civil law, actions were given against the heir, and under the Trebellian senatus consultum, against the one who received the inheritance, in proportion to their shares. Today the heir, whether for the whole or for a part, whether testamentary, legitimate or honorary, and also the person to whom we have ordered something to be restored and whom we have charged to restore all or part of it to another, must restore the inheritance, and may retain and recover the fourth, or whatever is lacking of the fourth, with actions against him and against the trust beneficiaries competent in proportion to their shares; except where such persons, knowingly and willingly, have restored the whole, or have been unwilling to enter upon it. For then only the trust beneficiaries are liable. We could leave a trust before five witnesses, or even before the heir alone; in which case the trust beneficiary may defer an oath to the heir, and the heir is compelled either to swear that he has heard nothing of the kind from the testator, or, if he refuses to swear, to perform the trust. Nor can we leave only an entire inheritance by trust, but also individual things belonging to the heir, the legatee, the trust beneficiary or any other person, using especially the words of request, I ask, I beg, I wish, I command, or I commit to your good faith; and these individual items are as binding as if they had been gathered into one. We may leave a trust, or anything else, not only by the solemn testament mentioned above but also by one or more codicils (which require less solemnity), though not directly an inheritance, but indirectly. We leave indirectly whenever we entrust by trust. They may be made before or after the testament, so that a trust can be claimed under them, if it appears that the testator has not departed from the wish which he had expressed in the codicils. And this is enough about testaments.

units.la: Sequitur quintus acquirendi modus iure ciuili, nempe ab intestato. Intestatus decedit, qui aut omnino testamentum non fecit, aut non iure, cuius testamentum ruptum, irritumve, aut ex quo nemo hæres extitit. Intestati hæreditas primum ad suos hæredes pertinet. Sui hæredes sunt iure ciuili, liberi qui in potestate positi defuncti, cum moritur, (cum iis etiam succedunt filij emancipati iure Prætorio: mancipati, inquam, licet ab aliis sint adoptati, idque constitutione Iustiniani, explosio ea in parte veteri iure) siue legitimi, siue naturales, siue legitimati, siue adoptiui, siue nati, siue posthumi sint. Ij hæredes sunt, etiam ignorantes, & in eos, morte parentis, continuatur dominium ipso iure. Suorum numero continetur & is, qui ab hostibus reuertitur post mortem patris. Suus. est etiam cuius pater perduellionis damnatus, ac memoria damnata suus esse desiit, quia bona parentis ad fiscum deferuntur. Filij & filiæ æqualiter parentibus succedunt. Cum iis nepotes ex altero filio mortuo concurrentes succedunt, non in capita, sed in stirpes: nec eo casu qui gradu proximior est, posteriorem excludit. Nepotes vero & deinceps liberi ex filia concurrentes cum superius enumeratis personis, minus tertia parte accipiunt, quàm mater eorum vel auia acceptura fuerat. Concurrentes cum agnatis trâfuerfalibus eos excludunt. Vbi verò nulli sui sunt, vel quasi sui, hæreditas ab intestato ad proximum agnatum olim pertinebat: sed hodie agnatis cognati, quoad successiones, sunt exæquati. Agnati, sunt cognati per viriles personas coniuncti. Succedunt sibi inuicem agnati, etiam si gradu (de gradibus, vide Tit.6.) longissimo sint, puta decimo. Sed hodie, soror cum fratre fratri succedit, veteri iure explosa: hæreditate, non in stirpes, sed in capita diuidenda. Olim frater & soror defuncti, filios & filias alterius defuncti excludebant. sed hodie non sunt semoti, propter cócessum eis ius repræsentationis, eóque casu cum patruo suo succedunt in stirpes, non in capita. Olim cum fratribus defuncti mater non succedebat, sed cum solis sororibus: eo etiam casu pater defuncti matrem eius excludebat, sed hodie, etiá cum masculis fratribus, vtroque etiam parente coniunctis defuncti pater ac mater concurrit æqualiter, vt tantum percipiat, quantum vnusquisque fratrum defuncti. Cum iis etiam concurrunt filij fratris defuncti: fratris, inquam, qui defuncto fratri ex vtroque parente iungebatur nouella 127. c. 1. Vbi vero agitur de successione agnati, vel cognati, fine liberis, vel parentibus, vel fratribus, aut sororibus mortui: soli fratrum vel sororum liberi, ac deinceps cognati relicti, patruo suo ab intestato succedunt, non in stirpes, sed in capita. Hinc constat, magnum indicium adhibendum esse in legendo titulo secundo, tertio, quarto, quinto huius libri. De seruili cognatione, vide tit.7.: libertorum, titulum 8 & 9. Quod ad bonorum possessiones attinet, quæ iure Prætorio conceduntur, notandus est ordo qui sequitur, eas sc. dari vel ex testamento, vel ab intestato. Ex testamento duplicitér dupliciter,contra tabulas liberis præteritis: secundum tabulas,scriptis hæredibus. Ab intestato, hoc ordine,unde liberi,unde legitimi, unde cognati,unde vir & vxor, & ex legibus explosō[?] veteri ordine{a}. De sexto acquirendi modo iure ciuili per adrogationem vide titulum 11.{b} De septimo per bonorum addictionem vide titulum 12.{c} De aliis modis, qui fiebant per bonorum venditiones, & ex Sc. Claudiano, sublatis vide tit.13.{d} Qui nunc sequitur modus, utilissimus est: constat autem obligatione{e}. Ea nihil aliud est, quàm iuris vinculum, quo necessitate astringimur, alicuius rei soluendæ causa, secundū ciuitatis Romanæ iura{f}. Obligationum prima divisio ea est, qua aliæ ciuiles sunt, aliæ Prætoriæ, ceu honorariæ. Hæ ex Prætoris iurisdictione: illæ,aut legibus constitutæ,aut certo iure ciuili comprobatæ{g}. Altera diuisio in quattuor species diducitur. Aliæ enim sunt ex contractu vel quasi, Aliæ ex delicto vel quasi. Quę sunt ex contractu, aut re, aut verbis, aut literis, aut consensu contrahuntur{h}. Re,veluti mutui{i}, indebiti{k}, commodati{l}, depositi{m}, pignoris acceptione{n}. Harum obligationum nomine, compe-tit nobis condictio mutui, indebiti, commodati, de-positi pignoris{o}. Ii In mutuo semper dominium transfertur, in commodato, deposito, & pignore nunquam{p}, in indebito, interdum. In mutuo ab accipiente casus fortuiti praestantur: in commodato & pignore, exacta diligentia, ac consueta observari à bono patrefamilias{q}: in deposito, solus dolus praestatur{r}. Hinc colligere possis,quid iuris fit in indebito. Verbis contrahitur obligatio{s} interrogatione & responsione: quoties quid dari fieri ve (in huiusmodi stipulationibus,quę factum continent optimum est poenam subiicere, ne quantitas stipulationis in incerto sit: ac necesse sit actori probare quod eius interfit{t}) stipulamur: certum, unde condictio certi: vel incertum, unde ex stipulatu actio prouenit. Stipulatio à stipulo,id est firmo,vel à stipite dicitur{u}. Et hæc de definitione, effectu & etymo stipulationis. Olim solenia stipulationum verba hæc fuerūt Spádes[?]? promittis? fidepromittis? fidejubes? dabis? facies? respondes? Hodie quibuscunque verbis fit. Fit stipulatio omni lingua, sufficit congruéter ad interrogata respondere{w}. Fit etiam aut pure, aut in diem, aut sub conditione. Priori modo, consestim peti potest res promissa duobus postremis, postquam dies venerit, vel condicione impleta. Qui stipulatur annua quoad viuet, heredem suum non iuuat. Quoties sub condicione stipulamur, in casum ceu factum differtur obligatio: ex ea spes est, debitum iri, eaque ipsam spem: ad heredem transmittimus, si priusquam condicio extet, mors nobis contigerit. Si ita stipulamur, debis si non fecero[?], perinde est ac si stipulati essemus cum moriemur. Conditiones ad præsens, vel ad præteritum tempus relatæ, aut statim infirmant obligationem; (puta si falsæ sint) aut omnino non differunt, puta si verè sint. Nam quæ per rerum naturam certa sunt, non morantur obligationem, licet apud nos incerta sint. Loca interdum inseruntur stipulationibus, veluti Carthagini dabis, talis stipulatio, reipsa, ceu tacite, habet tempus adiectum, quo promissor Carthaginem ire poterit: ideoque qui Romæ ita stipulatur, hodie Carthagini dabis, nil agit. Est enim inutilis repromissio. Et hæc de forma stipulationis dicta sint. Stipulandi & promittendi duo plures sive fieri possunt, Rei simul quoties vel plures stipulantur, vel promittunt: utrouis modo solidum debetur, à quouis eorum solidum præstatur & accipitur. Eorum unus pure, alius in diem, vel sub condicione obligari potest. Nec impedimento erit dies aut condicio quominus ab eo, qui pure obligatus est, petatur. Quod liberi in potestate positi & serui, etiam hereditarij, quouis modo stipulantur domino acquirunt: nisi factum in stipulatione contineatur. Communis seruus, unicuique dominorum pro portione dominij acquirit, nisi aut uni nominatim, aut unus iussu stipulatus sit: aut alter dominus adquirendi capax non sit: tunc enim ei soli adquiritur. & hæc de personis. Stipulationum alię iudiciales, quæ à mero iudicis officio proficiscuntur: Prætoriæ & ædilitiæ, quæ à mero Prætoris officio promanant: Communes, id est, partim Prætoriæ, partim iudiciales: Conuentionales, quæ ex conuentione utriusque partis concipiuntur. Alię inutiles vel utiles, de quibus hoc primum tenendum est. Res omnes, mobiles, vel soli, dominio nostro subiectas, in stipulationem deduci posse. Contra, non possumus stipulari utiliter rem quæ in rerum natura non est, aut esse non potest, rem sacram, religiosam, publicam, liberum hominem, rem nostram, etiam eo casu quo nostra erit, factum turpe, vel ob turpem cau-sam. sam factum alienum, seu alium facturum vel datu- rum , alii,cui dari nostra non interest ( nisi pœnam ) stipulemur: quo casu ita factum non erit , vel citra stipulationem pœnalem, nisi ei cuius iuri subiecti sumus stipulemur, nisi in extraneam personam solutionem conferamus, nisi eis qui iuri nostro subiecti sunt stipulemur. hoc enim ultimo casu nobis acquirimus nisi pupillo vel procuratori: tunc enim no- stra interest eis dari ) vel ab eo qui nostro iuri subiectus est, vel ab eo cuius iuri subiecti sumus . Instrumentum tilis est etiam stipulatio, si ad interrogata non fuerit responsum . Exemplo erit is, qui de vna re inter- rogatus,de alia respondit . Mutus , furiosus neque stipulari neque promittere possunt. Pupillus, sine tutore stipulari potest: at non promittere . Pupil- lum intelligimus, qui proximus est infantiæ,non in- fantem . Sub codicione impossibili, (qualis ea est, cui natura impedimento est,quominus existat) si sti- pulati fuerimus, perinde est ac si pure stipulatio fa- sta esset: ideoque statim peti potest . Inter absen- tes concepta stipulatio inutilis est. Absens fuisse non intelligitur, quem præsentem fuisse scriptura seu in- strumentum testatur: (hoc enim casu scripturæ cre- ditur & præsumitur pro instrumento) sed tamen reus potest manifestissimis probationibus,vel per scriptu- ram,vel per testes idoneos probare,toto eo die, quo cosiciebatur instrumentum, se,vel aduersarium suum, in aliis locis fuisse . Post mortem,siue pridie quàm moriamur,dari,stipulari,vel promittere possumus ; sed & ita, cum moriar, vel ita, cum morieris : post mortem alterius , possumus etiam præpostere sti- pulationem concipere, putà hoc modo, si nauis ex Asia venerit, hodie dabis . Ité plures res vna stipu- latione comprehendere quo casu si ad omnes promis- sor responderit, ad omnes tenebitur . Præterea sub condicione,cuius spem ad hæredes nostros, & in hæ- redes promissoris transmittimus . Postremò , hoc anno,hoc mense: tunc, nisi omnibus anni vel mensis partibus præteritis, non rectè petitur . Si fundum dari stipuleris,vel hominem,non poteris continuò gere,nisi tantum spatium præterierit, quo traditio in fine. fieri possit . Stipulationum promissionibus solent sideiussores adiici , in omni cótrastu : ij hæredem relinquunt obligatum . Obligationem præcedere possunt & subsequi . Quouis idiomate obligari pos- sunt, Si plures sint, epistolæ D.Hadriani, ceu diuifionis beneficium habent, de qua vide §. 4. {a}Nota possunt obligari, ut plus debeant, quàm principalis ut minus debeant, possunt. Minus intelligimus rem, vel tempore {b}. Si quid rei principalis nomine soluerint, pro eo recuperando mandati habent iudicium {c}. Quem fideiussisse constat, eum solenniter & maturo consilio fideiussisse præsumimus{d}. Et hæc de obligatione, quæ verbis perficitur. Literis, siue scriptura quæ constat obligatio promissorem obligat: sed tamen intra biennium exceptionem pecuniæ non numerate obiicere possumus {e}. Et hæc de literarum obligationibus. Restant quæ fiunt consensu: in quibus neque scriptura, neque præsentia, neque rei traditione opus est. Sufficit ut qui contrahunt, consentiant, etiam absentes per epistolam vel nuncium. In quibus etiã alter alteri, ex æquo & bono, obligatur {f}. Eius generis est emptio & venditio, quæ, simul atque de precio conuentum est, contrahitur: quamuis nondū pretium numeratum sit: ac ne arra quidem data fuerit. Nam quod arræ nomine datur argumentum est emptionis contractæ, non ipsa emptio. Pretium igitur in venditione constitui oportet: nam sine pretio nulla emptio esse potest {g}. Certum pretium esse debet, (certum illud etiam existimamus, quod tertius æstimauerit {h}) & in numerata pecunia (quain re emptio à permutatione differt {i}.) Venditione ita contracta, periculum & commodum rei venditæ statim ad emptorem pertinet: tametsi res emptori tradita non sit {k}. Emptio sub conditione, & purè contrahi potest {l}. Res sacram, religiosam, publicam, frustra quis sciens emit: ignarus si emerit, habet actionem ex empto aduersus venditorem, ut consequatur quod sua interest, non fuisse deceptum{m}. Præter superius genus emptionis, aliud est quod scriptura perficitur: quod tunc demum perfectum intelligitur, cùm instrumenta venditionis fuerint cöscripta, vel manu propria contrahentium, vel ab alio scripta & à contrahëtibus subscripta, vel à tabellione compleþa & absoluta. Donec aliquid deest ex his, pœnitentiæ locus est. Potest alteruter contrahentium sine pœna recedere à contractu, nisi arra data sit. tunc n. pœnitens emptor, arram: venditor, duplum arræ restituere compellitur {n}. Et hæc de venditione & emptione, cui proxima est locatio & conductio. Utraque contracta intelligitur si merces constituta est {o}, etiam alieno arbitrio. Merces in pecunia esse debet. Nam si inuicem rem utendam accipimus, non ex locato & conducto, sed praescriptis verbis agimus{a}. Si aurum meum dedi aurifici, ut anulos conficeret, mera locatio: si is & aurum, & operas praestitit, auri ratione emptio & venditio: operarum vero locatio & conductio intelligitur{b}. Locare possumus alteri praedia perpetuo fruenda, ea lege ut quandiu pensio pro his praestabitur, conductor, cuiusve haeres, aut qui ab eo causam habet quocunque modo, expelli non possit: quod genus contractus Emphyteusim vocamus. Particularia huiusmodi predij damna, colonus patitur: vniuersalia, ipse praedij dominus{c}. Caeterum conductor legem conductionis seruare debet: eamque ex aequo & bono supplere, qui, accepta pecunia, rem custodire promisit. Custodiam diligentissimi patrisfamilias debet, de casu fortuito non tenetur{d}. Mortuo conductore, intra tempus conductionis, haeres eius eodem iure in successione succedit{e}. Locatori, locati: conductori, conducti actio datur{f}. Sequitur societas, quae aut totorum bonorum: aut vnius alicuius negotiationis est{g}. Partes lucri & damni expressae, seruandae sunt: si non expressae, aequales erunt{h}. Coire ita societatem potuimus, vt ego pecuniam conferam, tu non conferas, & tamen lucrum sit commune, (si modo opera tua pro pecunia valet) vt lucri partem feras, de damno non tenearis, si modo in alia re lucrum, in alia damnum illatum sit{i}. Sui in vna causa (puta lucro) pars expressa est, in altero (puta damno) omissa: in eo, quod omissum est, eadem pars seruabitur{k}. Soluitur societas dissensu legitimo, non fraudulento{l}. morte vnius socij, nisi in coeunda societate aliter conuenerit{m}, finito rei negotio{n}, publicatione omnium bonorum vnius socij{o}, vel cessione{p}. Socius culpae tenetur & diligentiae, (diligentiam intellige non exactissimam, sed qualem suis rebus adhibere solet){q}. Sequitur mandatum{r}, quod fit vel vt mea tatum, vel vt mea & tua, vel vt alterius, vel vt mea & socij, vel vt tua & alterius, vel vt tua tantum geras negotia: cuius generis mandatum, magis consilium est quam mandatum: &{s}. ob id non est obligatorium {*}. ut & illud quod contra bonos mores est omni modo {b}. Qui mandatū accepit non debet excedere fines mandati {c}. Manda-tum reuocari potest, re integra {d}. Intelligitur reuo-catum morte mandatis, fi modo mandatarius morte eius intellexit {e}. Mandatum non suscipere, liberum est:susceptum,confumadum est,aut renunciandum{f}. In diem differri & sub condicione fieri potest {g}: gra- tuitu esse debet {h}. Et hæc de obligationibus,quæ ex quasi cótractu fiunt,dicta sint.Sequitur ut videamus que ex quasi contractu nascuntur {i}. Inter negotiorum geftore & eius cuius negotia gesta sunt {k}, inter tu- torem & pupillum {l}, inter eos qui communem rem habent {m},inter hæredem & legatarios {n}, inter eum qui per errorem non debitum soluit ,accepit , ultro citróq. nascuntur obligationes ex quasi contractu {o}. Hic dicendum erat de obligationibus ex delicto vel quasi:sed quia Tribonianus inserit tractatu de per-sonis obligationem acquirentibus, & de contrariis obligationis, utrunque caput considerandum erit. Acquirimus obligationem per nos,per seruos,per fi-lios in potestate {p},per liberos homines,& per alienos seruos quos bona fide possidemus {q}, per feruū vsu-fructuarium & vsuarium {r}, & communem {s}. Tolli-tur vero obligatio solutione eius quod debetur {t} acceptilatione, cein imaginaria solutione {u}, novatio-ne sen interuentu nouæ personæ {x} ,contraria volun-tatey{y}. Sequuntur obligationes ex delicto, vel quasi: illæ , nascuntur ex re,id est,ex ipso maleficio, veluti furto,rapina,damno,iniuria {z}. Furtum,est cotrecta-tio fraudulosa rei alienæ lucri faciendi causa {a}. Di-citur à furuo,i.nigro (fit enim clam) vel à ferendo {b}. Manifestus fur est, qui in ipso furto deprehenditur, vel in eo loco quo furtum fit: quinque ibi furtiuam rem tenet. Non manifestus, est ei contrarius {c}. (de concepti, oblati, prohibiti furti actiquis [?] actionibus, v.§.4.{d}) manifestus,quadruplo: non manifestus,du-plo puniebatur {e}. qui pignore, aut deposito utitur, furtum committit: ut & commodatarius rem uten-dum acceptam in alium vsum transferens:{f} fi modo intelligit id fe inuito domino facere {g}, nisi domino volente id faciat. Si seruum meum,à te de furto mi-hi faciendo sollicitatum,permisi quasdam res mihi surripere,ut te in ipso delicto deprehenderem, furti ,& ferui corrupti nomine mihi teneris: utcunque,me volente, eo casu videaris rem meam centrectaffe {h}.
