Furtum comittit, qui liberum hominem surripit{a} qui creditori suo pignus datum subtrahit{b} sed & is, cuius ope & consilio furtum factum est, qualis is est qui tibi nummos excussit, ut alius eos raperet, qui tibi obstitit quominus furem adprehenderes, qui boues tuos fugauit ut alius eos acciperet, qui scalas fenestris supponit, aut sciens commodat, ferramenta ad effringendum, vel qui ostium effringit, ut alius furtum faciat. Qui tantum consilium dedit furti non tenetur{c} Serui dominis, liberi parentibus furti non tenetur{d} Furti actio competit ei cuius interest rem saluam esse{e} : ideoque & creditori, ob pignus subreptum{f} : & fulloni, ob vestimenta subrepta: & bonae fidei emptori{g} & certis casibus ei, qui rem commodatam accepit{h} non idem est in depositario{i} Impubes proximus pubertati furti teneri potest{k} Rem nobis subreptam a quouis possessore vindicare possumus: eam vero ipsi furi condicimus, & praeterea dupli, vel quadrupli poenam exigimus{l} & haec de furto. Rapina, furto deterior: cuius nomine intra annum, quadrupli: post annum, simpli actio nobis competit{m} aduersus eum qui non errore ductus, sed dolo malo rapuit. Sed tamen, qui rem suam ab eius possessore per vim rapit, eius dominio priuatur: qui suam existimans, alienam tamen rapit, eam cogitur restituere: praeterea eius aestimationem praestare: quod & in immobilium iuuasionibus locum habet{n} & haec de vi & rapina. Damni iniuriae actio constituitur per legem Aquiliam: cuius primo capite de seruo & quadrupede, (quae pecudum numero sit, quaeque gregatim pasci dicitur{o}.) alterius occisis agebatur{p} Non iniuria occidit qui insidiatorem{q}, qui casu occidit. Contra, hoc iniuria occidit, qui culpa{r}, vel imperitia{s}: Reus eo casu tenetur de occiso, quanti eo anno plurimi fuit{t}: & in id quod praeterea perempto illo corpore, damni illatum fuit{u}. Idem etiam tenere potest lege Cornelia{x}. Caput secundum legis Aquiliae non est in usu. Forte in eo agebatur de intercepta nobis utilitate per iniuriam ab alio{y}. Tertio capite agebatur de seruo & quadrupede vulneratis, de feris occisis, de damno dato rebus inanimatis: ut siquid in eis ultum, ruptum, fractu, corruptum, scissum, collisum, effusum, mixtum fuerit{z}. Reus tenebatur eo nomine, non quanti eo anno res plurimi fuisset: sed quanti in diebus triginta proximis{a}. Porro, ex lege Aquilia directa actio datur in eum, qui corpore suo damnū dedit: Vtilis, in eum qui non corpore, sed tamen in corpus aliquod, damnum dedit: veluti si hominem, vel pecus inclusit, vt fame necarentur: iumentum egit, vt praecipitaretur: seruo persuasit vt in arborem ascenderet, vel in puteum descenderet, vt laederetur. In factum, si neque corpore, neque in corpus damnum datum est ab aliquo: qualis is est qui, miseria ductus, alienū seruum compeditum soluit, vt fugeret 4. Et haec de damno. Iniuria generaliter dicitur, quod non in re fit: specialiter, ut cotumelia{b}. Iniuriā facit, pugno pulsat, fustibus cedit, aut q verberat. Conuicium q[?] facit, vel voce vel scripto{c} is q procurat iniuria sibi id{d}. Nihil in ereft nobis, an liberis, aut vxori fiat iniuria{e}. Si seruis nostris, in nostri contumeliam iniuria facta est, iniuriae actio nobis competit: non si eis simpliciter convicium factum, aut pugno sint percusi{f}. Seruum nostrum intellegimus, & quae cum alio habemus communem, cuius funus proprietarij{g}, qui bona fide nobis seruit, (si modo in nostri contumeliam ei iniuria facta sit{h}.) Qui iniuriam intulit, arbitrio iudicis punitur pro circumstantiis personarum, & rei, & facti atrocitate{i}. Ciuiliter, quanti iniuriam passus aestimauerit: vel minoris, prout iudici visum erit. Criminaliter, poena extraordinaria{k}. Haec actio dissimulatione aboletur{l}. & haec de obligationibus ex delicto. Quasi ex delicto obligatur iudex, cum litem suam facit{m}, is ex cuius coenaculo deiectum effusumve aliquid est, ita vt alicui noceretur{n}, exercitor nauis, aut cauponae, aut stabuli, de damno, aut furto, quod in naui, aut caupona, aut stabulo factum erit{o}. & haec de personis & rebus dicta sint. Sequuntur actiones, tertiu iuris obiectum. Actio nihil aliud, est quam ius persequendi in iudicio quod sibi debetur{p}. Actionum aliae in personam sunt (quae & condictiones) aliae in rem (quae vindicationes dicuntur) corporalem vel incorporalem, vt seruitutes{q}. Et hae quidem legitimae suntque & ciuiles. Praetorie vero in re & personam, sunt variae. In rem, veluti Publiciana: qua experitur is, cui ex iusta aliqua causa res tradita fuit, cuiusque possessione amisit, antequam eam vsucaperet. Perinde enim eam rem vindicat, ac si vsucepisset{r}. Rescisoria datur captiuo, aut absenti reipublicae causa, ad vsucapionem suorum bonorum rescindendam{s}. Pauliana qua creditores rescindunt in fui fraudem alienationem factam a suis debitoribus{t}. Seruiana domini aduersus colonum: Quasi Seruiana qua creditores pignora,& hypotheca persequúntur *Præiudiciales,per quas quæritur An ali- quis liber,An libertus,vel de partu agnoscendo b{b}. In personam,veluti de pecunia constituta{c}, (constituit, quicumque pro se vel pro alio citra stipulationem se soluturum promittit{d}.)De peculio aduersus patrem & dominum{e}. Ex iureiurando{f}. Poenales, in albi corruptorem & alios{g}. Secunda actionum diuisio.
units.tr: Next comes the fifth mode of acquiring by the civil law, namely by intestacy. A person dies intestate who either made no will at all, or made one that was not valid in law, or one that was broken or annulled, or one under which no heir came to exist. The inheritance of an intestate person belongs first to his own heirs (sui heredes). By the civil law the children who were under the power of the deceased at his death are his own heirs, and with them the emancipated sons also succeed by praetorian law. I say "mancipated" sons, even if they were adopted by others; this was settled by a constitution of Justinian, which removed that part of the old law. This applies whether the children are legitimate, natural, legitimated, adoptive, born, or posthumous. They are heirs even if they do not know it, and ownership passes to them by law at the parent's death. The son who returns from the enemy after his father's death is also counted among the own heirs. A son is likewise an own heir if his father was condemned for treason, and the condemned man's memory is damned, because the father's goods are then transferred to the treasury, and the son ceases to be an own heir. Sons and daughters succeed their parents equally. Grandchildren by a son who has died succeed together with the others, not per capita but per stirpes, and in that case the nearer degree does not exclude the more remote. Grandchildren and further descendants by a daughter, however, when they come in together with the persons listed above, take less than a third of what their mother or grandmother would have taken. Those who come in together with agnates of the transverse line exclude them. Where there are no own heirs, or quasi-own heirs, the intestate inheritance formerly went to the nearest agnate; but today agnates and cognates are made equal as regards succession. Agnates are cognates connected through male persons. Agnates succeed one another even if they are at the most remote degree (on degrees see title 6), for example the tenth. Today, however, a sister succeeds together with a brother to a brother, the old law having been abolished, and the inheritance is divided not per stirpes but per capita. Formerly the brother and sister of the deceased excluded the sons and daughters of another deceased person; but today they are not set aside, because the right of representation has been granted to them, and in that case they succeed with their uncle per stirpes, not per capita. Formerly the mother did not succeed together with the brothers of the deceased, but only with the sisters; in that case too the father of the deceased excluded her. Today, however, even with male brothers who are related to the deceased on both sides, the father and mother of the deceased come in equally, so that each takes as much as each of the brothers of the deceased. The children of a brother of the deceased also come in with them; I mean a brother who was joined to the deceased brother through both parents (Novella 127, c. 1). Where the question concerns the succession of an agnate or cognate, with no children, parents, brothers or sisters of the dead man surviving, then only the children of brothers or sisters, and the cognates left after them in further degrees, succeed their uncle intestate, not per stirpes but per capita. From this it is clear that great attention must be paid in reading the second, third, fourth and fifth titles of this book. On servile kinship see title 7; on freedmen, titles 8 and 9. As for the possessions of goods (bonorum possessiones) which are granted by praetorian law, the following order must be noted: they are given either from a will or intestate. From a will, in two ways: against the tablets, to children who were passed over; according to the tablets, to written heirs. Intestate, in this order: unde liberi, unde legitimi, unde cognati, unde vir et uxor, and, by the laws, the old order having been abolished. On the sixth mode of acquiring by the civil law, adrogation, see title 11. On the seventh, by addiction of goods, see title 12. On the other modes which took place through sales of goods, and those under the Senatus consultum Claudianum, which have been abolished, see title 13. The mode that now follows is most useful. It rests on obligation. This is nothing other than a bond of law by which we are bound by necessity to pay something, according to the laws of the Roman state. The first division of obligations is that some are civil and others praetorian, or honorary. The latter arise from the jurisdiction of the praetor; the former are either established by statutes or confirmed by the established civil law. There is another division into four kinds. Some obligations arise from contract, or quasi-contract; others from delict, or quasi-delict. Those which arise from contract are contracted either by a thing (re), by words, by writing (literis), or by consent. By a thing, as in loan for consumption (mutuum), undue payment (indebitum), loan for use (commodatum), deposit, and the receipt of a pledge. On account of these obligations we have the action (condictio) for a loan, for undue payment, for loan for use, for deposit, and for a pledge. In a loan the ownership always passes; in loan for use, deposit and pledge it never does; in undue payment it sometimes does. In a loan the borrower answers for chance events; in loan for use and in pledge, the exact diligence which a good paterfamilias customarily observes must be kept; in deposit, only fraud is answerable. From this you may gather what the law is in undue payment. An obligation is contracted by words through question and answer whenever we stipulate that something be given or done. (In such stipulations which concern a deed, it is best to add a penalty, so that the amount of the stipulation is not uncertain, and so that the plaintiff does not have to prove what his interest was.) If the thing is certain, the action that follows is the condictio certi; if it is uncertain, the action arising from the stipulation. The word stipulatio is derived from stipulum, that is firm, or from stipes (a stalk). Enough on the definition, effect and etymology of stipulation. Formerly the solemn words of stipulations were these: "Do you promise? Do you pledge yourself? Do you guarantee? Do you pledge surety? Will you give? Will you do? Do you answer?" Today it is done in any words whatever. A stipulation may be made in any language; it is enough to answer the questions fittingly. It may be made purely, or for a day, or under a condition. In the first way, the promised thing can be demanded at once; in the latter two, only after the day has come or the condition has been fulfilled. He who stipulates "yearly as long as he lives" does not benefit his heir. Whenever we stipulate under a condition, the obligation is deferred until the event, as it were, and from it there is a hope that a debt will arise; and we transmit this very hope to our heir, if death has come to us before the condition exists. If we stipulate, "You will owe if I do not do it," it is just as if we had stipulated when we are about to die. Conditions referring to the present or past time either at once invalidate the obligation (for example if they are false), or do not delay it at all, for example if they are true. For things that are certain by the nature of things do not delay an obligation, even if they are uncertain to us. Places are sometimes inserted into stipulations, as in "You will give at Carthage." Such a stipulation, in fact or tacitly, has a time added, within which the promisor will be able to go to Carthage; so whoever stipulates at Rome "You will give at Carthage today" achieves nothing, for the promise is useless. So much on the form of stipulation. Two or more persons may stipulate or promise together. Whenever several stipulate or promise together, jointly, the whole is owed in either way, and the whole is given and received from any one of them. One of them may be bound purely, another for a day or under a condition. The day or the condition will be no impediment to demanding it from the one who is bound purely. Children under power and slaves, even hereditary ones, acquire for their master by whatever kind of stipulation, unless the deed is contained in the stipulation. A common slave acquires for each of his masters in proportion to his share of ownership, unless he stipulated for one by name, or one of them by order, or unless the other master is not capable of acquiring; for then it is acquired for him alone. And so much on persons. Stipulations are of several kinds: judicial, which proceed from the mere office of a judge; praetorian and aedilician, which proceed from the mere office of the praetor; common, that is partly praetorian and partly judicial; and conventional, which are framed by the agreement of both parties. Some are useless, others useful; on these the following must first be held. All things, movable or immovable, subject to our ownership, can be brought into a stipulation. On the other hand, we cannot validly stipulate for a thing that does not exist in nature or cannot exist; a sacred thing, a religious thing, a public thing, a free man, our own thing (even in the case where it will be ours), a shameful deed, or a deed done for a shameful cause. Nor can we stipulate for another's deed, or for another's doing or giving, to another to whom it is not in our interest that it be given (except as a penalty); in that case the thing will not be done, or it will be done without a penal stipulation, unless we stipulate for someone under whose power we are, unless we make the payment to a stranger person, unless we stipulate for those who are under our power. In this last case we acquire for ourselves, except for a ward or a procurator; for then it is in our interest that it be given to them. Or it is stipulated from one who is under our power, or from one under whose power we are. A stipulation is also valid even if no answer was given to the questions; an example is the man who, asked about one thing, answers about another. A mute person and a madman can neither stipulate nor promise. A ward can stipulate without a guardian, but cannot promise. By a ward we understand one who is close to infancy, not an infant. If we stipulate under an impossible condition (such as one whose nature prevents it from existing), it is just as if the stipulation had been made purely, and so it can be demanded at once. A stipulation made between absent persons is invalid. A person is not understood to have been absent if a writing or instrument testifies that he was present (for in this case the writing is believed and presumed to be an instrument); yet the defendant may prove, by the clearest proofs, either by writing or by competent witnesses, that on the whole day on which the instrument was drawn up he, or his opponent, was in other places. We can give, stipulate or promise after death, either on the day before we die; and also in the form "when I die," or "when you die." Once another has died, we may even frame a stipulation in reverse order, for example in this way: "If the ship comes from Asia, you will give today." Also, several things may be comprehended in one stipulation; in that case, if the promisor answers to all of them, he will be bound for all. Moreover, one may stipulate under a condition, the hope of which we transmit to our heirs and to the heirs of the promisor. Lastly, a stipulation may be "this year" or "this month"; then it is not rightly demanded unless all the parts of the year or month have passed. If you stipulate for a farm or a slave to be given, you cannot immediately demand it, unless so much time has passed as would allow delivery to be made at the end. Sureties are commonly added to the promises of stipulations, in every contract; they leave the heir bound. Sureties may precede the obligation and may also follow it. Persons may be bound in any language. If there are several sureties, the letters of the deified Hadrian give them the benefit of division, of which see §4. Note that they may be bound so that they owe more than the principal debtor, or so that they owe less. We understand "less" as regards thing or time. If they have paid anything on account of the principal thing, they have an action on mandate to recover it. We presume that whoever is known to have stood surety did so solemnly and with mature deliberation. And so much on obligation which is made by words. An obligation made by writing, that is by a written document, binds the promisor; yet within two years we may object the exception that the money was not counted. And so much on obligations by writing. There remain those which arise from consent, in which neither writing, nor presence, nor delivery of the thing is needed. It is enough that those who contract agree, even when absent, by letter or messenger. In these, too, each is bound to the other by what is fair and good. Of this kind is buying and selling, which is contracted as soon as the price has been agreed, even if the price has not yet been counted out, and even if no earnest money has been given; for what is given as earnest is evidence of a contracted purchase, not the purchase itself. The price must therefore be fixed in a sale, for without a price there can be no purchase. The price must be certain (we also consider certain what a third party has appraised), and it must be in counted money (in which respect a purchase differs from barter). When a sale is contracted in this way, the risk and the benefit of the thing sold pass at once to the buyer, even if the thing has not been delivered to the buyer. A purchase may be contracted conditionally or purely. Anyone who knowingly buys a sacred, religious or public thing buys in vain; if he buys it in ignorance, he has an action on purchase against the seller to obtain what his interest was in not having been deceived. Besides the kind of purchase above, there is another which is completed by writing; this is understood to be completed only when the instruments of sale have been written out, either by the hand of the contracting parties, or written by another and subscribed by the contracting parties, or drawn up and finished by a notary. As long as any of these is lacking, there is room for repentance. Either of the contracting parties may withdraw from the contract without penalty, unless earnest money has been given; for then the buyer who repents is compelled to forfeit the earnest, and the seller to restore double the earnest. And so much on sale and purchase, to which letting and hiring is closest. Both are understood to be contracted if a price (merces) has been fixed, even if fixed by another's judgment. The price must be in money. For if we receive a thing to be used in exchange, we act not by letting and hiring but by an action with prescribed words. If I gave my gold to a goldsmith to make rings, it is a mere letting; if he supplied both the gold and the labour, it is a purchase and sale in respect of the gold, but a letting and hiring in respect of the labour. We may let farms to another to enjoy in perpetuity, on condition that, as long as the rent is paid for them, the lessee, or his heir, or whoever holds the right from him in any way, cannot be expelled. This kind of contract we call emphyteusis. The tenant bears the particular losses of such an estate; the owner of the estate bears the general ones. Moreover, the lessee must keep the terms of the lease, and supply them according to what is fair and good; he who has taken money and promised to keep the thing owes the care of the most diligent paterfamilias, but is not liable for chance events. If the lessee dies within the term of the lease, his heir succeeds in the lease by the same right. An action is given to the lessor for the thing let, and to the lessee for the thing hired. Next comes partnership, which is either of all goods or of one particular business. The shares of profit and loss that have been expressed must be kept; if they have not been expressed, they will be equal. We may form a partnership in such a way that I contribute money and you do not, and yet the profit is common (provided that your labour is worth as much as the money), so that you bear a share of the profit but are not liable for the loss, provided that in one matter there is profit and in another loss. If the share is expressed in one matter (say profit) and omitted in another (say loss), the omitted matter will be governed by the same share. A partnership is dissolved by lawful, not fraudulent, dissent; by the death of one partner, unless it was agreed otherwise when the partnership was formed; by the completion of the business; by the confiscation of all the goods of one partner; or by cession. A partner is liable for fault and for diligence (understood not in the strictest sense, but such as he is accustomed to apply to his own affairs). Next comes mandate, which is given either that you manage only my affairs, or my and yours, or another's, or mine and a partner's, or yours and another's, or yours alone. This kind of mandate is more a counsel than a mandate; and for that reason it is not binding. Nor is anything that is contrary to good morals binding in any way. He who has accepted a mandate must not exceed the limits of the mandate. A mandate may be revoked while the matter is still whole. It is understood to be revoked by the death of the mandator, if indeed the mandatary knew of his death. It is free to refuse a mandate; once accepted, it must be carried out or renounced. It may be deferred to a day and made under a condition; it must be gratuitous. And so much on obligations which arise from quasi-contract. Next let us see which arise from quasi-contract. Between a manager of affairs (negotiorum gestor) and the person whose affairs were managed; between a guardian and a ward; between those who hold a thing in common; between an heir and legatees; between one who by mistake pays what is not owed and the one who receives it, obligations arise on both sides from quasi-contract. Here it was necessary to discuss obligations from delict or quasi-delict; but since Tribonian has inserted into the treatise on persons the obligation that is acquired, and the opposite of obligation, both heads must be considered. We acquire an obligation through ourselves, through slaves, through children under power, through free persons, and through the slaves of others whom we possess in good faith; through a slave in which we have a usufruct or use, and through a common slave. An obligation is extinguished by payment of what is owed, by acceptilation, which is an imaginary payment, by novation, or by the intervention of a new person, and by contrary consent. Next come obligations from delict or quasi-delict. Those arise from a thing, that is from the wrongdoing itself, such as theft, robbery, damage, or injury. Theft is the fraudulent handling of another's thing for the sake of gain. It is named from furvus, that is black (since it is done in secret), or from ferre (to carry). A manifest thief is one who is caught in the act of theft, or in the place where the theft is done, and holds the stolen thing there; a non-manifest thief is the opposite. (On the actions for concealed, offered and forbidden theft, see §4.) The manifest thief was punished fourfold, the non-manifest twofold. He who uses a pledge or a deposit commits theft, and so does a borrower for use who transfers the thing received for use to another use, provided he understands that he does so against the owner's will, unless he does it with the owner's consent. If I have allowed a slave of mine, who was solicited by you to steal for me, to take certain things from me, so that I might catch you in the very act, you are liable to me on account of theft and of corrupting a slave, although in that case you seem to have handled my thing with my consent. He commits theft who steals a free man; who removes a pledge given to his creditor; and also he by whose aid and counsel a theft was committed, such as one who shook money out of you so that another might snatch it, who hindered you from seizing the thief, who drove off your oxen so that another might take them, who sets ladders to the windows, or who knowingly lends tools for breaking in, or who breaks open a door so that another may commit theft. One who gave only counsel for theft is not liable. Slaves are not liable for theft to their masters, nor children to their parents. The action for theft belongs to anyone whose interest is that the thing be safe; therefore also to a creditor, on account of a pledge taken away; to a fuller, on account of clothes stolen; to a buyer in good faith; and in certain cases to one who received a thing lent for use. This is not so in a depositary. A minor close to puberty may be held liable for theft. We may claim a thing taken from us from any possessor; we claim it from the thief himself by a condictio, and in addition we exact a penalty of double or fourfold. And so much on theft. Robbery is worse than theft; for it there is an action for fourfold within a year, and for simple damages after a year, against one who robbed by malicious intent, not under a mistake. But whoever takes his own thing by force from its possessor is deprived of ownership of it; whoever takes a thing he thinks is his own but is in fact another's is compelled to restore it, and besides to pay its value; this also applies to forcible seizures of immovable property. And so much on violence and robbery. The action for damage by wrong (damni iniuriae) is established by the Lex Aquilia. Under its first chapter, action was brought for the killing of another's slave or of a four-footed animal (one of the class of cattle, and of those said to graze in herds). He kills unlawfully who kills an ambusher, or one who kills by accident. On the other hand, he kills unlawfully who kills through fault or lack of skill. In that case the defendant is liable for the killed animal at the highest price it had in that year, and for any further loss that resulted from the destruction of that body. The same may also be claimed under the Lex Cornelia. The second chapter of the Lex Aquilia is not in use. Perhaps it dealt with a profit taken from us by another's wrong. The third chapter dealt with slaves and four-footed animals wounded, wild animals killed, and damage done to inanimate things, so that if anything was burned, broken, fractured, spoiled, torn, crushed, spilled, or mixed. The defendant was liable for that, not at the highest price the thing had in that year, but at its price within the thirty days before. Moreover, under the Lex Aquilia a direct action is given against one who caused damage with his own body; a useful action against one who caused damage not with his body but to some body, as for example if he shut in a man or a beast so that they died of hunger, drove a beast of burden so that it fell headlong, or persuaded a slave to climb a tree or go down a well so that he would be hurt. An action on the case (in factum) is given if damage was done by someone neither with his body nor to a body; such is the one who, moved by pity, unfettered another's slave so that he might flee. And so much on damage. Injury is said in general of whatever is done to a thing, and in particular of contumely. He does injury who strikes with his fist, beats with clubs, or lashes. He who makes an insult, by voice or in writing, or he who procures it, does injury to himself. It makes no difference to us whether an injury is done to our children or to our wife. If an injury is done to our slaves in order to insult us, an action for injury lies to us; but not if they were simply insulted, or struck with a fist. By our slave we understand also one whom we hold in common with another, and whose usufruct belongs to us, or one who serves us in good faith (provided an injury was done to him in order to insult us). He who has done an injury is punished at the judge's discretion, according to the circumstances of the persons, the thing, and the atrociousness of the deed. In civil cases, the injured party may assess the injury at what he thinks, or at less, as the judge sees fit. In criminal cases the penalty is extraordinary. This action is extinguished by dissimulation. And so much on obligations from delict. A judge is bound quasi from delict when he makes himself a party to the suit; so also is one from whose upper room something was thrown or poured out, so as to harm someone; a shipmaster, innkeeper or stable-keeper is bound for damage or theft done in his ship, inn or stable. And so much may be said of persons and things. Next come actions, the third object of law. An action is nothing other than the right of pursuing in court what is owed to us. Some actions are against a person (which are also called condictions), others against a thing (which are called vindications), whether the thing is corporeal or incorporeal, such as servitudes. These indeed are legitimate and civil. Praetorian actions, on the other hand, are various, both in rem and in personam. In rem, for example the Publician action, by which one who has received a thing for some just cause, and has lost its possession before he acquired it by usucaption, sues for it; for he vindicates it just as if he had acquired it by usucaption. The rescissory action is given to a captive, or to an absent man for the public good, to rescind the usucaption of his goods. The Paulian action, by which creditors rescind an alienation made by their debtors to their own fraud. The Servian action of a landlord against a tenant; the quasi-Servian action, by which creditors pursue pledges and hypothecs. Prejudicial actions, by which it is asked whether someone is free, or a freedman, or concerning the acknowledgment of a birth. In personam, for example the action on money promised (constitutum); a constitutum is anything by which one promises, without stipulation, that he will pay for himself or for another. The action concerning peculium against father and master. Action arising from an oath. Penal actions, against the corrupter of a white tablet (album) and others. The second division of actions.

units.la: Actionum alię sunt rei persequendæ{h} (vt omnes in rem, & fere omnes in persona{i}) aliæ poenæ per- sequedæ seu poenales (puta ex maleficiis{k}) aliæ mi- xtæ.Mixtæ sunt quibus vel rem & poenam persequi- mur{l}, vel quas in rem & personam dirigimus{m}.
units.tr: Some actions are for recovering a thing (as all actions in rem, and nearly all in personam), others for pursuing a penalty (penal actions, for example those arising from crimes), and others are mixed. Mixed actions are those by which we pursue both a thing and a penalty, or those which we direct against both a thing and a person.

units.la: Tertia diuisio. Actionum aliæ in simplum{n} (veluti ex stipulatione mutuo,empto, locato,& similibus{o}) in duplum{p}, in triplum{q}, in quadruplum sunt{r}.
units.tr: Third division. Some actions claim single damages (for example those from a stipulation, a loan, a purchase, a lease and similar contracts), others double, triple or quadruple damages.

units.la: Quarta diuisio. Actionum aliæ bonæ fidei sunt:quæ- dam stricti iuris{s}: quædam arbitrariæ{t}. Quinta di- uisio. Quibusdam actionibus solidum persequimur, quibusdam minus solidû{u}. De sexta diuisione{ƒ}. di- cemus tit.12. In actionibus danda est opera, ne plus quàm oportet,petatur. Plus petitur quatuor modis, re,tempore,loco & causa{x}. Non tantum actione vti- mur in eum qui ipsemet cotraxit,vel deliquit: quod ipse vel contraxerit,vel deliquerit:sed quia eius ser- uus filiusve nobis vel ex contractu, vel delicto obli- gatus est{y}. Ex contractu, puta si iussu patris vel do- mini cum filio vel seruo contraxero , pater & domi- nus tenetur etiâ directo in solidum *. Vterque ius- sisse intelligitur,si naui(hinc exercitoria)vel taberne (hinc institoria{b}) vel peculio seu peculiari merci (hinc tributoria{c}) personas sibi subiectas. quocun- que modo præposuerit{d}.Interdum etiam huiusmo- di personæ tenentur, licèt filios vel seruos non præ- posuerint: putà,si filij vel serui rem,quam nobiscum gesserunt,in vtilitatem patris vel domini necessario, vel vtiliter verterunt. tunc enim datur nobis de in rem verso actio{e}. Nunquam verò in patrem igno- rantem datur actio, ob mutuum filio eius datum, propter senatuscòsulti Macedoniani authoritatem{f}.
units.tr: Fourth division. Some actions are bonae fidei, some stricti iuris, and some arbitrariae. Fifth division: with some actions we pursue the whole amount, with others less than the whole. We will discuss the sixth division in title 12. In actions, care must be taken that no more is claimed than is owed. More is claimed in four ways: as to thing, time, place and cause. We do not use an action only against the person who himself contracted or committed the wrong, but also because his slave or son is bound to us either by contract or by delict. By contract: for example, if I contract with a son or slave by the order of his father or master, the father or master is held even directly for the whole. Each is understood to have ordered the contract if he placed the persons subject to him in charge of a ship (hence the exercitoria action), or of a shop (hence the institoria action), or of a peculium or peculiar merchandise (hence the tributoria action), in whatever way he set them over it. Sometimes such persons are bound even if their fathers or masters did not set them over the business: for instance, if sons or slaves turned the thing they dealt with us to the advantage of father or master, whether necessarily or usefully. For then we are given the actio de in rem verso. But an action is never given against a father who was ignorant, on account of a loan made to his son, because of the authority of the Senatus consultum Macedonianum.

units.la: Ex delicto vero serui datur in dominum actio noxa- lis, per quam ipse dominus seruum dedere tenetur, aut litis æstimationem sufferre{g}. Ex delicto libero- rum pater filium filiamve noxæ dedere non potest. Id enim naturalis amor & pudicitia filiarum non admittit. Conueniuntur ergo ipsimet liberi, si deliquerint{a}. Ex delicto seu pauperie animalium, ipsi domini etiam tenentur, si quid lasciuia, aut pauore, aut feritate damni dederint: sed tamen liberabitur dominus, si ea animalia noxae dediderit{b}, nisi canem, verrem, aprum, leonem, vrsum ibi habeat, qua vulgo iter fit. tunc enim tanti dominus condemnatur, quanti iudex arbitratus fuerit{c}. Et haec de dominis & parentibus. Postumus quoque per procuratorem, tutorem, curatorem legitimum agere, quia mortibus, aetas, & huiusmodi causae id requirunt{d}. Procurator dicitur, cui rem nostram agere permissus{e}. Rei praesentis onus est, (hic omittimus obseruationes iuris veteris) vt vel iuret, vel promittat, vel etiam fatisdet (si id qualitas eius personae exigat) quod in iudicio permanebit vsque ad terminum litis{f}. Absentis vero, fatisdare nomine sui procuratoris, iudicatum solui, & tempore recitandae sententiae sese in iudicium venturum{g}. Quod si absens est omnino, & nesciat litem sibi moueri, quiuis potest eius defensionem subire, satisdatione prius, iudicatu solui, prestita{h}. Et haec de reo. Procurator vero actoris, carens mandato domini, expresso, vel insinuato, cauere debet rem ratam dominus habiturum{i}. Sequitur sexta actionum diuisio superioribus adnectenda. Actionum aliae temporales, aliaeperpetuae ac in haeredes datur{k}. Et his quidem actionibus actores vtuntur. Exceptionibus vero rei{l}. Excipiunt autem de metu, dolo, errore{m}, de pacto conuento ne petatur{n}, de re iuramento decisa{o}, de re iudicata{p}, & similibus{q}. Earum exceptionum quaedam ex legibus, quaedam ex iis quae legis vicem obtinent, quaedam ex ipsius Praetoris iurisdictione, substantiam capiunt{r}. Aliae perpetuae, quae semper obstant agentibus{s}. Aliae temporales, quae ad tempus nocet: & teporis{t}, vel personae dilationem tribuut{u}. Exceptionibus opponuntur replicationes, quibus replicatur atque resoluitur ius exceptionis{x}. Ipsas replicationes elidit duplicatio{y}: duplicationem, triplicatio{z}: de quibus latius in Digestis tractatur{ä}. Quae debitoribus principalibus exceptiones prosunt, plerumque accommodari solent etiam fideiussoribus, quia quod ab iis petitur, id ab ipso debitore peti videtur, vt qui mandati iudicio redditurus est iis, quod ij pro eo soluerint{b}. Actiones, de quibus supra diximus, proprietatis causam definiunt. Interdicta vero proponuntur maxime, quoties de possessione, aut ne,aut quasi agitur {a}. Suntque prohibitoria, restitutoria, exhibitoria {b}, possessionis adipiscendae {c}, tinendę {d}, recuperandę {e}, simplicia (in quibus alter actor, alter reus) duplicia (in quibus vnusquisque tam rei quam actoris partes sustinet {f}.) Possidere dicimur, si ipsi pofsidenus[?], vel alij nostro nomine {g}. Interdicta hodie non sunt ita in magno vsu {h}. Actorum temeritas olim, vel pecuniaria poena, vel iurisiurandi religione, vel infamię metu coercebatur {i}. Siquidem actor iurare solebat se non calumniadi animo actione intedere: Reus, se bona instatia vti. Aduocati, etiam iurabant {k}. Ex quibusdam iudiciis damnati ignominiosi fiunt {l}. Omnium actionum instituendarum principium, ab in ius vocatione sumitur {m}. In iisdem omnibus, puta in noxalibus {n}, in rem {o}, in ad exhibendum {p}, in familiae erciscundae {q}, communi diuidundo {r}, finium regundorum {s}, iudiciis & actionibus, iudicis officium late patet {t}. Sequuntur publica iudicia {u}, ita dicta, quod cuiuis ex populo executio eorum plerunque datur {x}. Horum quedam mortem inferunt, quaedam infamiam cum damno pecuniario {y}. Publica iudicia sunt,crimen maiestatis {z}, adulterij {a}, homicidij {b}, parricidij {c}, falsi {d}: de vi publica, priuata, & de raptu {e}, peculatus (quo tenentur ij qui pecuniam publicam, vel sacram, vel religiosam, furati sunt {f}) plagij (in quod incidunt, qui liberos homines surripiunt {g}) ambitus, repetundarum, de annona, de residuis {h}. Et haec de iure in his Institutionibus comprehenso paucis dicta sint {i}.
units.tr: From the delict of a slave, a noxal action is given against the master, by which the master himself is bound either to surrender the slave or to pay the assessed damages. From the delicts of children, a father cannot surrender his son or daughter noxally; natural love and the modesty of daughters do not allow it. So the children themselves are sued if they have offended. From the delict or pauperies of animals, the owners themselves are also liable, if the animals have done any damage through playfulness, fright or ferocity; but the owner will be freed if he surrenders those animals noxally, unless he keeps there a dog, boar, wild boar, lion or bear where there is commonly a path. For then the owner is condemned for as much as the judge assesses. These things concern masters and parents. A posthumous person may also sue through a procurator, a guardian or a legitimate curator, because minority, age and such causes require it. A procurator is one permitted to pursue our affair. For a defendant who is present, there is the obligation (here we omit the observations of the old law) that he either swears, promises, or even gives surety (if the quality of his person requires it) that he will remain in the judgment until the end of the suit. For an absent defendant, a surety is to be given in the name of his procurator to pay what is adjudged, and that he will come into court at the time the sentence is read. But if the absent person is wholly absent and does not know that a suit is being brought against him, anyone may undertake his defence, after surety has first been given to pay what is adjudged. These things concern the defendant. But the procurator of the plaintiff, lacking an express or implied mandate from his master, must give security that the master will hold the matter ratified. Follows the sixth division of actions, to be attached to the above. Some actions are temporal, others perpetual, and these are given against heirs. Plaintiffs use these actions, but defendants use exceptions. They except on grounds of fear, fraud, error, of an agreement made not to be sued upon, of a matter settled by oath, of a matter already adjudged, and similar grounds. Some of these exceptions take their substance from laws, some from things that have the force of law, and some from the jurisdiction of the Praetor himself. Some exceptions are perpetual, always obstructing the plaintiffs; others are temporal, harming only for a time, and grant a delay of time or of the person. Replications are set against exceptions, by which the right of the exception is answered and dissolved. Replications are destroyed by duplication, and duplication by triplication; these are treated more fully in the Digest. Exceptions that benefit principal debtors are generally accustomed to be applied also to sureties, because what is sought from them seems to be sought from the debtor himself, since he will have to repay by the action of mandate what they paid on his behalf. The actions of which we spoke above determine the cause of ownership. Interdicts are chiefly put forward whenever the question concerns possession, or prohibition, or quasi-possession. They are prohibitory, restitutory, exhibitory; for acquiring possession, for keeping it, for recovering it; simple (in which one is plaintiff and the other defendant) and double (in which each bears both the part of defendant and of plaintiff). We are said to possess if we possess ourselves, or others in our name. Interdicts are not nowadays in great use. The rashness of litigants was formerly restrained either by a pecuniary penalty, or by the sanctity of an oath, or by fear of infamy. For the plaintiff used to swear that he brought the action not with a mind to calumny, and the defendant that he used a good cause. Advocates also swore. From some judgments the condemned become infamous. The starting point of all actions to be brought is the summons to court. In all these same matters, for instance in noxal actions, in rem actions, in the action ad exhibendum, in the action for family partition, for common division, for the fixing of boundaries, the office of the judge extends widely over judgments and actions. Next come public judgments, so called because the execution of them is generally given to anyone from the people. Of these, some inflict death, others infamy with pecuniary loss. Public judgments are: the crime of treason, adultery, homicide, parricide, forgery; concerning public violence, private violence, and rape; peculatus (by which are bound those who have stolen public, sacred or religious money), plagium (into which fall those who kidnap free men), ambitus, repetundae, concerning the grain supply, and concerning arrears. Let these things be said briefly about the law contained in these Institutes.
§ last.

units.la: ¶ Sequuntur Tituli DD. De verborum & rer. signif. & de reg. Iuris.
units.tr: ¶ Here follow the Titles of the Digest: On the meaning of words and things, and on the rules of law.
ON THE MEANING OF WORDS. TIT. XVI.
Paul, book one on the Edict.

units.la: VERBVM hoc si quis{e} tam masculos quam foeminas complectitur{d}. 2. Paulus libro primo ad Edictum. num recte? ut tandem eo redeat quaestio, An res aliquid significent, necne. Sic sentio, vocabula rerum notas esse, res ipsas vocabulis significari, res per se non significare, sed vel Dei iudicio tantum, vel hominum institutione. Dei, unde rerum futurarum, caelestium, ac invisibilium veritas certis rebus aspectabilibus adumbratur. Hominum, quoties inter se rebus citra verborum connexionem quasi loquuntur. hinc arrae, & annuli, nuptias, venditionem: claves, & instrumenta tradita, traditionem possessionis: alapae & circūductiones, manumissionem significant. Et apud AEgyptios hyeroglyphicae literae, & in re militari, tria sunt genera signorum, vocalia, ut puta, Deus nobiscum, triumphus: semiuocalia, quae per tubam, aut cornu, aut buccinam dantur: muta, ut sunt aquilae dracones, vexilla, flammulae rufae: sunt & alia in equis, & indumentis, & armis, & manuum motione v.3. Vegetium 5. c l.195.ƒ.eodem: l.3.ƒ.de negot. Indefinitae ƒ.l.3.§.1.ƒ.de homine libero l.16.ƒ.de iure fisci: alias in lege, statutis, testamento, vel cōtractu, si quid ita specialiter sit conceptum, puta si vir, si masculus, si frater, & avunculus: foeminae, sorores, materterae non comprehenduntur. aliud erit si in plurali quis fratrum (ex hoc exemplo iudicium sit de caeteris) mentionem fecerit (tunc enim sorores l.35.ƒ.de pactis: l.93.§.3.ƒ.de legat.3.) aut seruorum, tunc enim ancillae comprehenduntur l.82.ƒ.de legat.2.
units.tr: If someone includes this word both males and females, 2. Paul, book one on the Edict. Is that correct? So the question comes back at last to whether things signify anything or not. My view is this: words are the signs of things, and things are signified by words. Things do not signify by themselves, but only either by the judgment of God or by human institution. By God's judgment, the truth of future, heavenly and invisible things is foreshadowed by certain visible things. By human institution, people speak to one another through things without the linking of words: thus betrothal gifts and rings signify marriage, and the sale; keys and handed-over instruments signify the transfer of possession; slaps and turning around signify manumission. Among the Egyptians there were hieroglyphic letters, and in military affairs there are three kinds of signs: vocal ones, such as "God is with us" and "triumph"; semi-vocal ones, which are given by trumpet, horn or bugle; and silent ones, such as eagles, dragons, banners and red pennants. There are also others in horses, clothing, arms and the movement of hands v.3. Vegetius 5; l.195 ƒ. same; l.3 ƒ. de negot. Indefinitae; ƒ. l.3 §.1 ƒ. de homine libero; l.16 ƒ. de iure fisci. Otherwise, in a law, statute, will or contract, if something is so specially expressed, for example "if a man," "if a male," "if a brother" and "an uncle," then females, sisters and maternal aunts are not included. It will be different if someone makes mention in the plural of brothers (and judge the rest by this example), or of slaves; for then sisters are included, l.35 ƒ. de pactis; l.93 §.3 ƒ. de legat. 3; for then female slaves are included, l.82 ƒ. de legat. 2.

units.la: {d}Ideoque filiis institutis & filiae institutae videntur, l.1.§.3.ƒ.de-venire in possess. filiis dato tutore & filiabus datus intelligitur l.15.ƒ.de testam. tut. hinc constat, foeminas masculorum nomine compre-hendi[?], nisi consuetudo aut leges aliâ fuisse mente testatoris demonstrent. Ideoque si quis filiis tutelam, institutionem testamenti, seu
units.tr: Therefore sons instituted and daughters instituted seem to be included, l.1 §.3 ƒ. de venire in possessionem; a guardian given to sons is understood to be given to daughters as well, l.15 ƒ. de testam. tut. Hence it is established that females are comprehended under the name of males, unless custom or the laws show by the intention of the testator that it was otherwise. Therefore if someone leaves to sons the guardianship, the institution of an heir in a will, or

units.la: VRbis [?] appellatio muris: Romae autem cōtinentibus aedificiis finitur, quod latius patet.
units.tr: The name "city" (urbis) is bounded by the walls; but at Rome it is bounded by the continuous buildings, which extends more widely.

units.la: ¶ Cuiusque diei maior pars est horarum septem primarum diei, non supremarum .
units.tr: The greater part of each day is the first seven hours of the day, not the last.
3. Ulpian, book two on the Edict.

units.la: Itinerę faciendo viginti milliapassuum in dies singulos peragenda, sic sunt accipienda: ut, si post hanc dinumerationem minus quam viginti millia superiunt, integrum diem occupent. veluti viginti unum millia sunt passus: biduum eis attribuetur quę dinumeratio ita demum faciendae erit, si de die non conueniat. ¶Eius,qui apud hostes decessit,di-
units.tr: For the journey of twenty Roman miles to be made in each day, they are to be understood thus: if after this count fewer than twenty thousand paces remain, they fill up a whole day. For example, if there are twenty-one thousand paces, two days will be allotted to them. This counting is to be done only if there is no agreement about the day. Of one who died among the enemy, the di-

units.la: na,quae sunt Tiburi duntaxat debentur. aliud erit, si domus Tiburtina integro statu legata sit, tunc enim adiacetia, i.pecora, fructus, macipia, his verbis comprehenditur .
units.tr: goods (bona) which are at Tibur alone are owed. It will be otherwise if the house at Tibur was bequeathed with its whole condition; for then accessories, that is, flocks, fruits and slaves, are included under these words.

units.la: Hęc lex scitu utilis est in quaestionibus privilegiorum, immunitatis concessae, venditione, locatione, iurisdictione, exiliis, & similibus.
units.tr: This law is useful to know in questions about privileges, a granted immunity, sale, lease, jurisdiction, exile, and similar matters.

units.la: Nox totidem horis constat. diei pars media sex horae, pars maior septem horae. hinc constat, sextam diei naturalis horam esse ipsum meridiem l. 2. §. de annuis legatis. Diurnarum operarum debitor solis ante meridianis l. 3. inf. §. de operis libertorum, vel solis pomeridianis non liberabitur d.l. 2. dies vero civilis 24. horis constat, cuius principium est ipsa media nox l. 8. §. de feriis. Inde Calendis (demus ea die natum Titium) Titius festabitur, si pridie ipsas Calendas, post sextam horam noctis, id est, post mediam noctem fuerit testatus l. 5. §. qui testam. Item Calendis natus decimum quartum vel vicesimum annum aetatis inchoat pridie Calendas, post sextam horam noctis, quod in testamentis l. 5. §. qui testam. & manumissio- nibus observatur l. 1. §. de manumiss. Caeterum diei civilis horae sunt aequales, naturalis non sunt. longius enim spatium est Orientis solis ad Occasum astate, quam hyeme: hinc horologia astiua & hyberna v. Vitruuium 9. cap. 9. d & merito, quia recentes & integri homines libentius dant se ad laborem quam fessi iam. e quibus, etiam locatore inuito (longis praeferrim diebus) qui operas conduxerit adquiescere & meridiari licet argum. l. 26. §. de operis libert. Iisdem horis Romani litibus vacabant v. Cuiacium 2. de praescript. f In itinere vulg. Itineri. Hal. g l. 1. §. fi quis cautionibus l. 1. §. 2. §. 3. §. quis ordo. Id spatium, tempus iter faciendum ... praefitutum dicitur l. 8. l. 38. §. 1. §. ex quib. causf. maior: adde h 37. §. 2. §. de verb. obl. h veluti vulg. Hal. i Conuentiones enim contractibus formam dare solent, ci hereditas non {*}potest, qui seruus decessit.
units.tr: The night consists of as many hours (twelve). The middle part of the day is six hours, the greater part seven hours. Hence it is established that the sixth hour of the natural day is noon itself, l.2 §. de annuis legatis. A debtor of daily labourers is not freed by paying wages in the morning, l.3 inf. §. de operis libertorum, nor by paying in the afternoon, d.l.2. But the civil day consists of twenty-four hours, whose beginning is midnight itself, l.8 §. de feriis. Hence, if on the Calends (suppose Titius was born on that day), Titius will be of age if he made his will on the day before the Calends, after the sixth hour of the night, that is, after midnight, l.5 §. qui testam. Likewise, one born on the Calends begins his fourteenth or twentieth year of age on the day before the Calends, after the sixth hour of the night; this is observed in wills (l.5 §. qui testam.) and in manumissions (l.1 §. de manumiss.). Moreover, the hours of the civil day are equal, but those of the natural day are not. For the space from sunrise to sunset is longer in summer than in winter; hence there are summer and winter clocks, v. Vitruvius 9, cap. 9, and rightly so, because fresh and vigorous people give themselves more willingly to labour than those already tired. From these hours, even against the employer's will (especially on long days), the one who has hired the workers may let them rest and take a midday break, arg. l.26 §. de operis libert. At these same hours the Romans attended to lawsuits, v. Cujas 2 de praescript. The space is said to be set for making the journey, l.8; l.38 §.1; ex quibus causis maior; add 37 §.2 de verb. obl. For agreements usually give form to contracts, but a inheritance cannot ... who died as a slave.
4. Paulus, book 1 on the Edict.
Proculus says that by the naming of a thing (noun) the thing itself is signified.
5. The same, book 2 on the Edict.

units.la: Rei appellatio latior {d}est {e}, quàm pecuniæ {f}: quàm {g} etiam ea, quæ extra {h} computationem patrimonij nostri sunt, continet: cùm pecuniæ significatio ad ea referatur, quæ in patrimonio sunt. ¶ Opere locato {i}, conducto: his verbis Labeo significari ait id opus, quod Græci ἀποτέλεσμα vocant, [non ἔργον,] id est, ex opere facto corpus aliquod perfectum {k}.
units.tr: The term "thing" (res) is broader than "money" (pecunia), since it also includes those things that lie outside the reckoning of our estate, whereas the meaning of "money" refers only to what is in the estate. On "a work let out" and "a work taken on": Labeo says that by these words is meant the work that the Greeks call a finished product [ἀποτέλεσμα], not the labour [ἔργον], that is, a completed body made from a work done.
6. Ulpian, book 3 on the Edict.

units.la: NOminis {l} & rei appellatio ad omnem {m} contra-ctum & obligationem pertinet. 1 ¶ Verbum Ex legibus sic accipiendum est: tam ex legum sententia {n}, quàm ex verbis.
units.tr: The term "name" and the term "thing" apply to every contract and obligation. 1 ¶ A word in the laws must be understood in this way: according to the sense of the laws as much as according to their words.
7. Paulus, book 2 on the Edict.

units.la: Sponsio appellatur, non solum quæ per sponsus {o} interrogationem fit, sed {p} omnis stipulatio promissioque.
units.tr: A "sponsio" is called not only what is made by the question of a sponsio, but every stipulation and promise.
{f} On which see law 178, §. same title.
{g} Because also the Vulgate.

units.la: {h} Pecunia dicitur mea, quę est in patrimonio meo: res mea, quæ est etiam extra patrimonium: sic res mea dicitur quum vicini paries ardet Horatius. rei vocabulum est latius. Imperium, litem, venerem, cur una notat res? Aufonius: adde quæ notauit ad l.1. §.de rebus creditis.
units.tr: {h} Money is called "mine" when it is in my estate; a thing is "mine" even when it is outside my estate: thus a thing is called "mine" when my neighbour's wall burns (Horace). The word "thing" is broader. Why does one thing denote empire, a lawsuit, love (venus)? (Ausonius.) Add what was noted on law 1, §. on loans of things.
{i} "legato," Vulgate, Haloander.

units.la: {k} sensus est, Operis faciendi debitor, nisi perfectionem operi addiderit, nō liberatur, ut & partis præstatione. Est enim facti obligatio indiuidua l.139. in f. j. eod: l.80. §.1. §.ad legem Falcid: l.72. §.de verb.oblig. Interdum tamen operis vocabulo, coeptum necdum perfectum intelligitur l.19. §.11.§.de auro. l Ecl. ibid.c.6.v.l.4.§.eo.
units.tr: {k} The sense is: a debtor of a work to be done is not freed, unless he has added perfection to the work, nor by the performance of a part; for the obligation to do something is indivisible (law 139 in fine; also law 80, §1, on the Falcidian law; law 72, §. on the meaning of obligations). Sometimes, however, by the word "work" what has been begun but not yet finished is understood (law 19, §. 11, §. on gold). Eclogues on the same, chapter 6, verse 1, §. same title.
{m} See law 1, §. on loans of things.

units.la: {n} i.voluntate l.5.C. de legibus. hinc magna oriuntur in legibus dissidia, quoties mens, scripto opponitur Quint.3.Inst.6.& 7.c.7. vnde mens legis colligatur dicam ad d.l.5.
units.tr: {n} That is, by the will (law 5, C. on laws). Hence great disagreements arise in laws whenever the mind is set against the writing (Quintilian, Institutes 3, 6 and 7, chapter 7). From this the mind of the law is gathered, as I shall say at the said law 5.
{o} "sponsi," Vulgate, Haloander.

units.la: {p} Eclog.ibid.c.7. sensus est, spondere dicimur quibuscunque verbis promittamus, ut-cunque nemo à nobis stipuletur l.19.§.2.§.de adilitio: §.1. Instit.de verbor.obligat.
units.tr: {p} Eclogues, same place, chapter 7. The sense is: we are said to "spondere" (promise) in whatever words we promise, provided no one stipulates from us in the form of a question (law 19, §. 2, §. on the edilician action; §. 1, Institutes, on the meaning of obligations).
8. The same
2. The same, book 3 on the Edict.

units.la: VErbum {a}Oportebit tam praesens, quam futurum tempus significat. I {b}Actionis verbo non continetur exceptio.
units.tr: The word "oportebit" (it will be right) signifies both the present and the future tense. An exception is not contained in the word for an action.
9. Ulpian, book 5 on the Edict.

units.la: MArcellus apud Iulianum notat, verbo Perisse {c}& scissum & fractum contineri, & vi rapum.
units.tr: Marcellus, as reported by Julian, notes that under the word "perisse" (perished) are contained "scissum" (torn), "fractum" (broken), and "vi raptum" (seized by force).
10. The same, book 6 on the Edict.

units.la: CReditores accipiendos esse constat eos, quibus debetur ex quacumque {d}actione, vel persecutione {e}, vel iure simili sine ulla exceptionis perpetuae {f}remotione, vel honorario, vel exordinario {g}, siue purè, siue in diem, vel sub condicione {h}. Quod si natura debeatur, non sunt {i}loco creditorum. Sed si non fit mutua pecunia, sed {k}contractus; creditores accipiuntur.
units.tr: It is agreed that creditors are to be understood as those to whom something is owed by any action or suit, or by a similar right, without any perpetual exception being removed, whether by the honorary or by the extraordinary procedure, whether owed purely, or at a day, or under a condition. But if something is owed by natural law, they are not in the place of creditors. But if it is not a loan of money but a contract, then creditors are understood.

units.la: 11. Gaius libro primo ad Edictum Prouinciale.
units.tr: 11. Gaius, book 1 on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: CReditorum appellatione non hi tantùm accipiuntur, qui pecuniam crediderunt: sed omnes, quibus ex qualibet {l}causa debetur.
units.tr: By the term "creditors" are understood not only those who have lent money, but all to whom something is owed from any cause whatever.
12. Ulpian, book 6 on the Edict.

units.la: VTI si cui ex empto, vel ex locato, vel ex alio {m}vllo debetur. Sed etsi ex delicto debeatur, mihi videtur posse creditoris loco accipi. Quod si ex populari {n}causa, ante litis contestationem pererit.
units.tr: Namely, if something is owed to someone from a purchase, or from a hire, or from any other source. But even if something is owed from a delict, it seems to me that such a person can be taken in the place of a creditor. But if it is owed from a popular action, it perishes before litis contestation.

units.la: a Eccl. ibid. 8.demus ita formulâ conceptam, quod te dare oportebit sponsdes? l.76.§.1. l.89.§.de verborum obligat.
units.tr: a Ecloga, same place, chapter 8. Let us suppose the formula is framed thus: "Do you promise (spondes) what you will be bound to give?" (laws 76, §1; 89, on the meaning of obligations).

units.la: b Imo continetur l.1.§.de except. c Ecl.ib.cap.9: adde l.4.§.10.§.vi bonorum, rapuisse vulg. d Ex qualibet causa l.11.§.eod: ex quolibet contractu, vel delicto l.12.§.eod: Ecl.ibid. l.1.§.de rebus cred. qui ipsum habent actionis l.54.§.eodem: l.42.§.de oblig. qui exceptione perpetua submoueri non possunt l.55.§.eod.
units.tr: b Indeed it is contained (law 1, §. on exceptions). c Ecloga, same place, chapter 9; add law 4, §. 10, §. on the goods of the deceased; "rapuisse," Vulgate. d He who has the action, whether from any cause (law 11, §. same title), or from any contract or delict (law 12, §. same title; Ecloga, same place; law 1, §. on loans of things), who has the action itself (law 54, §. same title; law 42, §. on obligations), who cannot be removed by a perpetual exception (law 55, §. same title).

units.la: e vide l.28.§.de oblig. f l.55.§.eodem. ideoque debitor dicitur is à quo inuito exigi potest l.108.§.eod. g ordinario vulg. h l.54.§.eo. l.42.§.de oblig. i proprie scilicet, aliud si abusiue l.16.§.3.§.4.§.de fideiuss: l.94.§.3.§.de solutionibus. k ceu contractus. Alciatus hic: vide l.12.§.eod. l Ecloga ibidem cap.10. m v.l.10.§.eod: vel ex alio contractu Hal. vel ex alio vllo contractu vulgata. n ἀπὸ ὀρφανικὰς Eclog.ibid. id est pupillari, & male. sic Graeci e contrario legunt populi pro pupilli, in lege 48.§.de adquirend. rerum. Vide Cuiacium 11.obs.12. {d} qui habet actionem popularem, non dicitur esse locupletior, vel nihil non liberabitur ipsius debitoris praestatione, nisi praestet quoq. vsuras morae, nem recte dicetur creditoris loco non esse {e}, postea esse. 1 ¶ Minus soluit, qui tardius {b}soluit: nam & tempore {d}minus soluitur.
units.tr: e See law 28, §. on obligations. f Law 55, §. same title; therefore he is called a debtor from whom payment can be demanded against his will (law 108, §. same title). g "Ordinario," Vulgate. h Law 54, §. same title; law 42, §. on obligations. i Properly, of course; otherwise if used abusively (laws 16, §3, §4, on sureties; law 94, §3, on payments). k As a contract. Alciatus here: see law 12, §. same title. l Ecloga, same place, chapter 10. m See law 10, §. same title; "or from another contract," Haloander; "or from any other contract," Vulgate. n "From orphans" [ἀπὸ ὀρφανικὰς], Ecloga, same place, that is, pupillary, and wrongly; so the Greeks in turn read "populi" for "pupilli" in law 48, §. on acquiring things; see Cujas, Observations 11, chapter 12. {d} He who has a popular action is not said to be richer, nor is anything released except by the debtor's own performance, unless he also pays interest for delay; nor is it rightly said that he is not in the place of a creditor, but afterwards he is. 1 ¶ He pays less who pays late, for a thing is also paid less by time.
13. The same, book 7 on the Edict.

units.la: Mulieris appellatione etiam virgo viripotens continetur {f}. 1 ¶ Res abesse videntur (vt Sabinus ait, & Pedius probat) etiam hæ, quarum corpus manet, forma mutata est. & ideo si corruptæ redditæ sint, vel transfiguratæ, videri abesse: quoniam i plerumque plus est in manu, pretio, quàm in re. 2 ¶ Desinere autem abesse res tunc videtur, cum sic redit in potestatem, ne amittere {i}eius possessionem possimus. 3 ¶ Ob hoc, quod furto pridem subtracta est, abest & ea res quæ in rebus humanis {o}non est.
units.tr: The term "woman" also includes a virgin of marriageable age. 1 ¶ Things also seem to be absent (as Sabinus says, and Pedius approves) when their body remains but their form has been changed. So if they are returned spoiled or transformed, they seem to be absent, since their value lies more in the hold we have over them than in the thing itself. 2 ¶ A thing ceases to be absent when it comes back into our power in such a way that we can keep possession of it. 3 ¶ For this reason, a thing that was stolen long ago is also absent, even though it no longer exists among human affairs.
14. Paul, book 7 on the Edict.

units.la: Abeo & Sabinus existimant, si vestimentum scissum reddatur, vel res corrupta reddita sit, veluti scyphi collisi, aut tabula rasa pictura, videri rem abesse: quoniam earum rerum pretium non in substantia, sed in arte {p}sit positum. Item si dominus rem, quae furto sibi aberat, ignorans emerit: recte dicitur res abesse, etiam si postea id ita esse scierit: quia videtur res ei abesse, cui pretium {q}abest. 1 ¶ Rem amisisse videtur, qui aduersus nullum {r}vis. eius persequendæ actionem habet.
units.tr: Abeo and Sabinus hold that if a garment is returned torn, or a thing is returned spoiled, such as a dented cup or a painting with its surface scraped clean, the thing seems to be absent, since the value of such things lies not in their substance but in their workmanship. Likewise, if an owner who was unaware of it buys back a thing that had been stolen from him, the thing is rightly said to be absent, even if he later learns that this is so, because a thing seems absent to the person from whom its value is absent. 1 ¶ A person seems to have lost a thing when he has no action against anyone to pursue it.
15. Ulpian, book 10 on the Edict.

units.la: BOna ciuitatis abutiue{a} publica dicta sunt[?], bona sola enim, ea{b} publica sunt, quæ populi Romani sunt.
units.tr: The goods of a city are called public only in a loose sense, for only those things are truly public which belong to the Roman people.

units.la: 16. Gaius libro tertio ad Edictum Prouinciale.
units.tr: 16. Gaius, book 3 on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: EVm, qui vectigal populi Romani conductum habet, publicanum{c} appellamus. nam publica appellatio in pluribus causis ad populum Romanum respicit: ciuitates{d} enim priuatorum loco habentur{e}.
units.tr: We call a man who has leased the revenue of the Roman people a publican. For the term "public" in many cases refers to the Roman people, since cities are regarded as private persons.
17. Ulpian, book 10 on the Edict.

units.la: INter{f} publica habemus non sacra, nec religiosa, nec quæ publicis vsibus destinata sunt: sed quæ sunt ciuitatum (velut bona, seu peculia seruorum ciuitatium) proculdubiò publica habentur. {g}Publica vectigalia intelligere debemus, ex quibus portus{g}, vel venalium{h} rerum, item salinarum{i}, & metallorum{k}, & picatiarum{l}.
units.tr: Among public things we do not count sacred things, religious things, or things destined for public uses; but things belonging to cities (such as the goods or the slave property of cities) are undoubtedly regarded as public. We should understand public revenues to be those from which harbours, the sale of goods, likewise salt-works, metal mines and pitch-works are derived.
18. Paul, book 9 on the Edict.

units.la: MVnus tribus modis{m} dicitur. vno donum: & altero onus: inde munera dici, dari, mittiue.
units.tr: The word munus is used in three ways: as a gift, as a burden, and as a duty. Hence munera are said to be given, sent and so on.

units.la: {f} sensus est, Res religiosæ, sacræ, publicis vsibus destinatæ, bona ciuitatis, peculia seruorum ciuitatis, inter publica habentur.
units.tr: {f} The sense is: sacred and religious things, things destined for public uses, the goods of a city, and the slave property of a city are counted among public things.

units.la: {g} Vectigal portus à vectigali rerum venalium hic distinguitur. portorium exigebatur à venditore, ob venditionem l. 1. Cod. de veteranis: l. 4. Cod. de proximis sacrorum, scriniorum. vectigal mancipiorum venalium quintæ, & vicesimæ (nisi malis cum Cuiacio legere quinquagesimæ ex Dione 55.) fuisse scribit Tacitus lib.13. De vectigali vicesimæ quintæ, quadragesimæ, quinquagesimæ, centesimæ, ducentesimæ, vide eundem 6.obs.28. de decimalitium, vide eundem 7.obs.5. de publicis & vectigalibus, vide eundem 7.obs.4.
units.tr: {g} Here the revenue of a harbour is distinguished from the tax on saleable goods. The harbour dues were exacted from the seller on account of the sale (see law 1 Cod. de veteranis; law 4 Cod. de proximis sacrorum scriniorum). Tacitus, in book 13, writes that the tax on slaves for sale was a fifth and a twentieth (unless you prefer, with Cuiacius, to read fiftieth, from Dio 55). On the taxes of the twentieth, fortieth, fiftieth, hundredth and two-hundredth, see the same author, book 6, obs. 28, on the decimal tax; book 7, obs. 5, on public property and taxes; and book 7, obs. 4.

units.la: {h} vectigal rerum venalium non est octaua, vt vult Accursius ad legis 7. Cod. de vectigal. vide Cuiacium 6.obs.28. {i} v.l.13. §. de publicanis: & l.8. §.8.5. de pœnis, Cuiacium 3.obs.37. {k} d.l.13. vide l.16. §.7. ib. {l} piscariarum vulg. Hal. vt merito inter regalia numerentur piscationum reditus 2.feud. 56. picariæ sunt e quibus foditur pix: nam & picem fossilem inueniri Plinius scribit 16.cap.11. {m} munus tria significat, donum, onus, officium. Ecloga ibidem cap.18: adde l.12. l.14. §. de muneribus, hinc munus gladiatorium dictum est ab officio, quod mortuis facere gentiles exhibebant[?], defunctorum animas humano sanguine propitiari. quod cùm remittatur, vacationem militiae mune-risque praestat: inde immunitatem appellari. tertio officium: unde munera militaria, & quosdam mili-tes munificos {*} vocari. Igitur municipes dici, quod munera civilia capiant.
units.tr: {h} The tax on saleable goods is not the eighth, as Accursius holds on law 7 Cod. de vectigalibus; see Cuiacius, book 6, obs. 28. {i} Variant reading: law 13 §. de publicanis; and law 8 §8.5 de poenis; Cuiacius, book 3, obs. 37. {k} The same law 13; see law 16 §7 ibid. {l} The vulgar and Halo. edition read "piscariarum", so that the revenues from fishing are rightly counted among the regalia (2 feud. 56). Picariae are places where pitch is dug, for Pliny writes that mineral pitch is also found (book 16, ch. 11). {m} Munus has three meanings: gift, burden, and office. The same Ecloga, ch. 18; add law 12 and law 14 §. de muneribus. Hence the gladiatorial munus was so called from the duty which the heathen performed for the dead, namely to appease the souls of the dead with human blood. Since this was remitted, it conferred exemption from military service and from munera, and hence the name immunity. Third, office: whence military munera, and some soldiers are called munifici {*}. Hence municipes are so called because they take up civic munera.
19. Ulpian, book 11 on the Edict.

units.la: Labeo libro primo praetoris urbani definit, quod quaedam {b} agantur, quaedam gerantur, quaedam contrahantur. Et actum quidem generale verbum esse, sive verbis, sive re quid agatur: ut in stipulatio-ne, vel numeratione. Contractum autem ultro {c} citroque obligatione {d}, quod Graeci συναλλαγμα[?] {e} vocant, veluti emptionem, venditionem, locationem, conductionem, societatem. Gestum rem significare sine verbis factam.
units.tr: Labeo, in book 1 of the Urban Praetor, defines that some things are done (agantur), some are managed (gerantur), and some are contracted. He says that actum is a general word, meaning that something is done either by words or by deed, as in a stipulation or a payment. A contract, however, is an obligation running both ways, which the Greeks call [συναλλαγμα], such as buying, selling, letting, hiring and partnership. Gestum signifies a thing done without words.

units.la: {*} Haloand. (quae lectio placet Budaeo) ij sunt qui non vacant, sed munus principi, id est militi principali (de quo vide 2. Veget. 7.) faciebant. beneficarij, qui vacant muneris officio. Milites munifices Vegetio 2. capite septimo & 19. qui munia faciunt, munia inquam, & quidem vilia, puta lignum, foenum, aquam, stramen portando. Vegetio dicto cap.29. quod principalibus militibus obire ignominia erat non levis. qui principales milites essent, vide apud Vegetium 2.cap.7. munifex maxima, id est, latens[?]. Plinius 11.cap.40. munificum praedium 1.2.Cod.de praediis navicular. τὸ λειτουργοῦν, καὶ συντελεῖς, id est publicae functioni, & vectigalis collationi subditum. munificium lex 4.§.1.in fine 5.de publicanis: vide Budaeum hic: & Petrum Fabrum 1. semestr. 17.
units.tr: {*} Haloander (a reading that pleases Budaeus): these were men who were not exempt, but performed a munus for the prince, that is, for a principal soldier (on whom see Vegetius 2.7). The beneficiarii were those exempt from the duty of munus. Vegetius, 2.7 and 2.19, calls them milites munifices, who perform the munia, that is, menial tasks, such as carrying wood, hay, water and straw. In Vegetius, cited ch. 29, because it was no small disgrace for principal soldiers to undertake them. On who the principal soldiers were, see Vegetius 2.7. A munifex was the greatest, that is, hidden. Pliny 11.40. A munificum praedium, 1.2 Cod. de praediis navicular. [τὸ λειτουργοῦν, καὶ συντελεῖς], that is, subject to public service and to the collection of taxes. Munificium, law 4 §1, at the end, 5 de publicanis; see Budaeus here, and Petrus Faber, 1 semestr. 17.

units.la: {b} sensus est, Agimus re & verbis, contrahimus etiam consensu, gerimus etiam sine verbis, id est, citra animum contrahendi l. 88. §. eodem: l.7. §. de minoribus.
units.tr: {b} The sense is: we act by thing and by words; we also contract by consent; we also manage without words, that is, without the intention of contracting (law 88 §eodem; law 7 §de minoribus).

units.la: {c} sensus est, Contractus, est factum, (inde dicitur facti potiùs quàm iuris l.7. in fine, §. de curatore furioso) obligationem inter aliquos constituens. factum, quo obligamur, sed non ipsum vinculum iuris. Contractus, non est obligatio, cùm ea ex contractu oriatur, vide Hugonem Donellum ad leg. 1. numero 8.12. §. de rebus credit.
units.tr: {c} The sense is: a contract is a deed (hence it is called a matter of fact rather than of law; law 7 in fine, §. de curatore furioso) which establishes an obligation between certain persons. It is the deed by which we are bound, but not the bond of law itself. A contract is not an obligation, since the obligation arises from the contract; see Hugo Donellus on law 1, number 8, 12 §. de rebus credit.

units.la: {d} hinc colligit Alciatus, mutuum, stipulationem, & donationem proprie non esse contractus: & male. nam inter contractus stipulatio differtis verbis numeratur l.1. in fine §. de pactis: l.1. §.4. §.de verborum obligat: §. ultim. Inst.de obligat. quemadmodum & donatio vide l.7. Cod. de his quae metus causa. vide Bellonum 2. supput.2.
units.tr: {d} Hence Alciatus infers that a loan, a stipulation and a donation are not properly contracts, and he is wrong. For a stipulation is counted among contracts, being distinguished by its words (law 1 in fine §. de pactis; law 1 §4 §. de verborum obligat.; final §. Inst. de obligat.). So too a donation (see law 7 Cod. de his quae metus causa). See Bellonus, 2 supput. 2.

units.la: {e} l.7.§.2. §. de pactis. contrahere seu distrahere opponuntur, quemadmodum & apud Graecos συναλλάττειν καὶ διαλλάττειν. Aristotelei quinto Ethi-corum.
units.tr: {e} Law 7 §2 §. de pactis. To contract [contrahere] and to dissolve [distrahere] are opposed, just as among the Greeks [συναλλάττειν καὶ διαλλάττειν], in Aristotle's Ethics, book 5.
20. The same, book 12 on the Edict.

units.la: Verba Contraxerunt, gesserunt, non pertinent ad{a} testandi ins.
units.tr: The words contracted, managed do not pertain to the right of making a will.
21. Paul, book 11 on the Edict.

units.la: Princeps bona* concedendo videtur etiam obligationes{d} concedere.
units.tr: A prince, by granting goods, seems also to grant the obligations attached to them.
22. Gaius, book 4 on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: Plus est in restitutione{e} quàm in exhibitione, nam exhibere{f} est, praesentiam corporis praebere. restituere{g} est, etiam potestatem facere, fructúsque reddere, pleráque praeterea restitutionis verbo continentur.
units.tr: There is more in restoring than in exhibiting, for to exhibit is to offer the physical presence of a thing, whereas to restore also means to give power over it and to return its fruits; many other things are included under the word restoration.
23. Ulpian, book 14 on the Edict.
Under the word res (thing) both causes and rights are included.
24. Gaius, book 6 on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: Nihil est aliud hereditas, quàm successio{i} in universum ius, quod defunctus habuit.
units.tr: An inheritance is nothing other than succession to the whole right which the deceased held.
25. Paul, book 21 on the Edict.

units.la: Rede dicimus eum fundum totum nostrum esse, etiam cum{k} usufructus alienus est: quia usufructus non{l} dominij pars, sed seruitutis{m} sit: ut via, & iter. nec falsò dici, totum meum{n} esse, cuius non potest villa pars dici alterius esse. hoc & Iulianus. & est verius. ¶ Quintus Mucius ait, partis appellatione rem pro indiviso{o} significari. nam quod pro{p} diviso nostrum sit, id non partem, sed
units.tr: We rightly say that a whole estate is ours even when a usufruct over it belongs to another, because a usufruct is not a part of ownership but of servitude, like a right of way or of passage. Nor is it wrong to say that the whole is mine, when no part of it can be said to belong to another. Julian says this too, and it is more true. ¶ Quintus Mucius says that the term "part" signifies a thing undivided, for what is ours undivided is not a part, but

units.la: l.75. {h} v.l.1. s.de rebus creditis l.5. l.6. s.[illegible, ~6 letters] Ecloga ibidem
units.tr: l.75. {h} Variant reading: law 1 §. de rebus creditis; law 5; law 6 §. [illegible, about six letters]. Ecloga, same place.

units.la: cap.23. {i} v.l.9. §.12. s.de hered.instit: Eclog. s.id.[?] cap. 29. §. 2.
units.tr: ch. 23. {i} Variant reading: law 9 §12 §. de hered. instit.; Ecloga, same place, ch. 29 §2.

units.la: Inst. de rebus corporalib. de eo quod nostrum est, & quod meum, vide l. 49: l.52 in f: l.96 in fine: l.105. s. cod. l.49. s.de rei vindicat: l.12 §.3. s. ad exhib: l.42. l.52. s. de adquir.rerum: l.139. in f. l. 190. s. de regul.iur.
units.tr: Inst. de rebus corporalibus. On what is ours and what is mine, see l. 49; l. 52 in fine; l. 96 in fine; l. 105. §. cod.; l. 49. §. de rei vindicatione; l. 12 §. 3. §. ad exhibendum; l. 42; l. 52. §. de adquirendo rerum dominio; l. 139 in fine; l. 190. §. de regulis iuris.

units.la: {k} cuius vulgat. Haland. l.74. s.de legat.3.
units.tr: {k} Whose: Vulgate, Haloander; l. 74. §. de legatis 3.

units.la: {l} Imò usufructus dominij pars est l.4. s.de usufr. {m} seruitus Hal. {n} meum etiam dicitur, cuius nulla pars alterius est. {o} partis appellatione, pars indivisa intelligitur. {p} pars à suo toto divisa, totum quoddam constituit. totum esse. Seruius non inelegantèr {a}partis appella-tione vtrumque significari {4}[?].
units.tr: Indeed, usufruct is part of ownership (l. 4, s. de usufr.); a servitude too is called "mine," and no part of it belongs to another. By the term "part" an undivided part is understood.
