A part separated from its whole constitutes a certain whole, to be a whole. Servius not inelegantly said that both are signified by the term "part" [?].
26. Ulpian, book 16, on the Edict.

units.la: PArtum[?] {b}non esse partem rei furtiuæ, Scæuola li-bro vndecimo quæstionum scribit.
units.tr: Scaevola, in the eleventh book of his Questions, writes that the offspring is not part of a stolen thing.
27. The same author, in the seventeenth book on the Edict.

units.la: AGer {c}est locus, qui sine villa est.
units.tr: A field (ager) is a place that has no villa on it.

units.la: ¶ 1[?] Stipendium {d}à Hipe appellatum est, quòd per stipendes, id est modica æra, colligatur. Idem hoc etiam tributum appellari Pomponius ait. Et sanè appellatur ab intributione {e}tributum: vel ex eo, quod militibus tributur.
units.tr: ¶ 1[?] The stipendium is so called from small sums of money, because it is collected in small amounts. Pomponius says that this same thing is also called tributum. And indeed tributum is so called from the assessing of contributions, or because it is distributed to soldiers.
28. Paulus, book 21 on the Edict.

units.la: Alienationis verbum etiam vsucapione{g} continet. vix est enim, vt non videatur alienare, qui patitur vsucapi. Eum quoque alienare dicitur, qui non {h}vtendo amisit seruitutes. Qui occasione {i}ad-quirendi non vtitur, non intelligitur alienare: vel-uti qui hereditatem omittit, aut optionem {k}intra certum tempus datam non amplectitur.
units.tr: The word "alienation" also covers usucaption, for it is scarcely possible for a person who allows usucaption to occur not to appear to alienate. A person is also said to alienate who, by not using them, has lost his servitudes. One who does not make use of the opportunity to acquire is not understood to alienate, as for example one who lets an inheritance go, or does not accept an option given within a fixed time.

units.la: ¶ Oratio, quæ neque coniunctionem, neque disiunctionè haber,ex mente pronuntiantis, vel disiuncta{l} vel coniuncta accipitur.
units.tr: A sentence that has neither a conjunction nor a disjunction is taken as either disjunctive or conjunctive according to the intention of the speaker.
29. From the same author, book sixty-sixth, on the Edict.

units.la: Coniunctionem enim nonnunquàm {m}pro disiunctione accipi, Labeo ait: vt in illa stipulatione, Mihi heredique meo, te heredemque tuum.
units.tr: For Labeo says that a conjunction is sometimes taken for a disjunction, as in that stipulation: Mihi heredique meo, te heredemque tuum.
30. Gaius, book seven on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: Silua cædua {n}est,(vt quidam putant) quæ in hoc habetur {o}, vt cæderetur. Seruius eam esse, quæ
units.tr: A coppice wood is (as some think) that which is kept in order to be cut down. Servius says it is that which

units.la: {h} non vtendo seruitutes amittuntur l.3.§.1:l.4.§.qua in fraud.credit.
units.tr: {h} Servitudes are lost by non-use: l. 3. §. 1; l. 4. §. qua in fraud. credit.
{i} See l. 6. §. qua in fraudem.
{k} Add l. 8. §. de optione.

units.la: {l} Quae disiunctiua habet oratio,disiuncta est:quae coniunctiua,coniuncta:quae neutrum, qualis erit? v.l.142. §.co.
units.tr: {l} A sentence which has disjunctive words is disjunctive; one which has conjunctive words is conjunctive; one which has neither: what sort will it be? See l. 142. §. co.
{m} See l. 53. §. cod.; Ecl. ibid. c. 29.
{n} l. 10; l. 48. §. 1. §. de usufructu; l. 80. §. 2. §. de conservanda emptione; l. 7. §. 7. §. soluto.

units.la: {o} hic interim nota,Siluam non tantum de arboribus dici, sed & de herbis. Virgilius,subit aspera silua lappaeque,tribulique. Cuiac.ad obs.15. sumitur etiam pro viriditario l.17.§.1.§. si seruus vindicetur. succisa, rursus ex stirpibus aut radicibus renascitur.
units.tr: {o} Here meanwhile note that silva is said not only of trees but also of herbs: Virgil, "the rough thicket, and burdock and caltrop". Cujacius ad Obs. 15. It is also taken for a viridarium: l. 17. §. 1. §. si servus vindicetur. Once cut down, it springs up again from the stumps or roots.

units.la: 1 ¶ Stipula illecta est spicae in messe deleetae[?], nec dum lectae, quas rustici, cum vacauerint colligunt.
units.tr: 1 ¶ Stipula is the ear of grain left in the harvest, not yet gathered, which country folk collect when they have leisure.

units.la: 2 ¶ Noualis est terra praecisa, quae anno cessauit, quam Graeci [illegible, ~2 words] vocant.
units.tr: 2 ¶ Novalis is land broken up, which has rested for a year, which the Greeks call [illegible].

units.la: 3 ¶ Integra autem est, in quam nondum dominus pascendi gratia pecus immisit.
units.tr: 3 ¶ Integra is land into which the owner has not yet let animals in to graze.

units.la: 4 ¶ Glans cadu-ca est, quae ex arbore cecidit.
units.tr: 4 ¶ Glans caduca is that which has fallen from the tree.

units.la: 5 ¶ Pascua silua est, quae pastui pecudum destinata est.
units.tr: 5 A woodland pasture is a wood set aside for the grazing of livestock.
31. Ulpian, book eighteen on the Edict.

units.la: PRatum est, in quo ad fructum percipiendum falce duntaxat opus est, ex eo dictum, quod pa-cas[?], quae post messorum terga a tenuioribus legi solent, stipulas appellari. Terentius in Adelphis: praeter hęc, meridie ipso, faciam ut stipulam colligat: huc refer
units.tr: A meadow is land where only the scythe is needed to gather the crop. It is called a stipula (stubble) from this, because the stalks that the poorer people usually gather after the reapers' backs are called stipulae. Terence in the Adelphi: "Besides this, at noon itself, I will make her gather stubble." Refer here.

units.la: 19. Lucit. vers. 9. [?] 22: Ruth. 2. verficul. 3. & 7. [illegible, ~3 words] Eclog. ibid. c. 30. hinc illæ voces Nouelletum l. 39. 5. de hered. pet: nouellum l. 8.
units.tr: 19. Lucret. vers. 9. [?] 22; Ruth 2, verses 3 and 7. [illegible] Ecl. ibid. c. 30. Hence those words: novelletum, l. 39. §. 5. de hered. petit.; novellum, l. 8.

units.la: 5. de fundo dotali: noualis ager, Varro 4. de lingua: l. vlt. in f. 5. de termino. Nouale 18. Plin. 19: nouata terra Cicero de oratione.
units.tr: 5, on dotal land: fallow field (noualis ager); Varro, book 4, On the Latin Language; last law, in fine, 5, on boundaries. Novale: Pliny, book 18; "newly broken land" (nouata terra): Cicero, in his oration.

units.la: proscissa Hal. [illegible, ~1 word] Ecloga ibid. cap. 30.
units.tr: proscissa, Haloander. [illegible] Ecloga ibid. cap. 30.

units.la: Liber variorum auctorum de finitibus, nouialis ager dicitur, qui primum proscissus. & apud Seruium 1. Georgicon. Nouales, sunt arua primum proscissa. Idem refert Hieronimus & Innocentius iii. in c. nouale 1. & 2. extra de verbor. fignif. vbi tractant interpretes, num ex nouali-bus debeantur decimæ. Ea res facit vt hic legendum putem. Noualis est etiâ terra primum procisa, & quæ anno cessauit. vt huius vocis duæ sint significationes.
units.tr: In the book of various authors on boundaries, a novalis ager is said to be land first ploughed (proscissus). And in Servius on Georgics 1: "Novales are fields first ploughed." Jerome and Innocent III in c. novale 1 and 2, extra de verborum significatione, report the same, where the commentators discuss whether tithes are owed from novalia. That matter makes me think that here one should read: "Noualis is also land first ploughed, and that which has rested for a year," so that this word has two meanings.

units.la: Addatur tertia, vt nouale, fit ager, cuius vetus facies immutata fit in nouam, veteri non absimilem. Vt fi vetus aliuetum succidas, vt nouellum reponas l. 8. 5. de fundo dotali: ex silua nouale facias l. vlt. 5. de termino, quod nihil aliud esse puto, quâ nouelletum in fundo facere l. 32. 5. de heredit. petit. l. 6. 5. de impensis. scio tamen Seruium 1. Ecloga scribere nouaiia dici, vnde silua tollitur.
units.tr: A third may be added: that a novale becomes a field whose old appearance is changed into a new one, not unlike the old. For example, if you cut down an old grove and replace it with a novelletum: l. 8. §. 5. de fundo dotali; if you make a novale out of a wood: l. ult. §. 5. de termino, which I think is nothing other than making a novelletum on an estate: l. 32. §. 5. de hered. petit.; l. 6. §. 5. de impensis. I know, however, that Servius in the Eclogues writes that novalia are so called because the wood is removed from them.

units.la: quæ alternis annis cessauit nouandarum sibi virium causa. hinc illud Virgilij 1. Georgicon, Alternis idem tonsas cessaro nouales. Huiusmodi agro opponitur ager restibilis, qui quotannis feritur, qui & [illegible, ~2 words] & [illegible, ~2 words]. Igitur noualis ager hic est, ad nouam sementem restitus Festus, qui quatenus cessat opponitur segetibus, Virgilius 1. Eclog. versu 71. 72. Pecus gaudet nouali graminosoque solo. Columell. 6. in princ. v. Turneb. 18. aduerf. 12.
units.tr: which has rested in alternate years for the sake of renewing its strength. Hence Virgil's line in Georgics 1: "Alternately the same fields rest, cut and novel." The kind of field opposed to this is the restibilis ager, which is sown every year. Therefore the novalis ager here is that restored to new sowing. Festus, who, so far as it lies fallow, is opposed to the crops; Virgil, Eclogue 1, verses 71–72: "The flock delights in the fallow and grassy soil." Columella 6 in principio; see Turnebus, Adversaria 18, 12.

units.la: hinc illud Ciceronis in Topicis, Si compascuus ager est, ius est copascere. [?] de Pascuis 11. f. 60.
units.tr: Hence Cicero's words in the Topics: "If a field is common pasture, it is lawful to graze together." De pascuis, 11, f. 60.

units.la: Ecl. ib. e. 31. {a} quod protinus sit paratum, nec magnum labore desideret. Co-lumelli 2.cap. 17: Varro 1. de lingua 7. in fine. Alii dant primatu bonis pratis, ut ego quoque: a quo antiqui prata, parata appellant. apud eundem tamen Cato hos bonitatis agrorum gra-dus facit. Vineam, hortū irriguum,
units.tr: Ecl. ibid. c. 31. {a} that which is at once ready, and does not need great labour. Columella 2, cap. 17; Varro 1, de lingua, 7 in fine. Others give the first place to good meadows, as I also do, from which the ancients called meadows "parata" (prepared). In the same place, however, Cato makes these degrees of goodness of fields: vineyard, irrigated garden,

units.la: saliatum[?], olinetum, pratum, campum frumentarium, cædnam siluam, arbustu, glandariā siluam.
units.tr: salictum, olive grove, meadow, grain field, coppice wood, plantation, acorn wood.

units.la: ratum{d} sit ad fructum capie idum[?].
units.tr: It is settled that it is to be taken for the gathering of the fruit [ratum sit ad fructum capiendum]...
32. Paulus, book twenty-fourth on the Edict.

units.la: Minus{b} solutum intelligitur{c}, etiam si nihil est[?] solutum.
units.tr: Less is understood to have been paid, even if nothing has been paid.
33. Ulpian, book twenty-one on the Edict.
It is plain: before several people.
34. Paul, book twenty-four on the Edict.
Under the word "action" the reading out (perlectio) is also included:
35. The same, in book seventeen on the Edict.

units.la: Restituere autem is intelligitur, qui simul & cam sam[?] actori reddit, quam is habiturus esset, si statim iudicii accepti & tempore res ei reddita fuisset. id est & usucapionis causam{h} & fructuum{i}.
units.tr: Now, one is understood to restore who at the same time gives back to the plaintiff that which he would have had if the thing had been returned to him at once, from the time the suit was accepted; that is, both the cause of usucaption and the fruits.
36. Ulpian, in the twenty-third book on the Edict.

units.la: {b} minus etiam soluit, qu. nihil soluit l.82. l.150. ꝑ eo. Ecl. ibid. c.12: & qui tardius l.12. s. eod: & is in quem ampliores summæ copetit actio l.17. ꝑ eod: vel qui non integram summam soluit l.85. s. de solut: vide quæ notauit ad l.116. s. de verborum obligat.
units.tr: {b} "minus" also means "he pays less" (that is, one who pays nothing, see laws 82 and 150, §. eo, Ecl. ibid. c.12; and one who pays late, law 12, §. eod; and one against whom larger sums can be claimed by action, law 17, §. eod; or one who does not pay the full sum, law 85, §. de solut.); see what he noted on law 116, §. de verborum obligat.

units.la: {c} & ita comparatiuum, minus, sumitur interdum pro positiuo.
units.tr: {c} And so the comparative "less" is sometimes taken for the positive.

units.la: {e} l.8. §.1. s. eodem: l.178. §.2. ꝑ eodem.
units.tr: See l. 8 §1 s. eodem; l. 178 §2 ꝑ eodem.

units.la: {f} l.57. in fine ꝑ. eodem: ad de l.25. s. de obligat. in rem, in personam, extraordinaria l.178. §.2. ꝑ eod: l.28. s. de oblig: directa, vtilis, prætoria, interdicta, l.37. s. de obligat. exceptiones l.1. s. de exceptionib.
units.tr: l.57 at the end, same title; ad de l.25 s. de obligat.; in rem, in personam; extraordinary: l.178 §.2 same title; l.28 s. de oblig.; direct, useful, praetorian, interdicts: l.37 s. de obligat.; exceptions: l.1 s. de exceptionib.

units.la: {g} Restituere iussus, fructuum à tempore litis cōtestatæ perceptorum nomine tenetur l.20. s. de rei vind: l.9. §.5. s. ad exhib: l.31. s. de rebus creditis: 2. Ecloga 2.c.35: l.2. Cod. de petit. heredit.
units.tr: One ordered to restore is bound, in the name of the fruits received from the time of the joinder of issue (litis contestatio), see l. 20 s. de rei vind.; l. 9 §5 s. ad exhib.; l. 31 s. de rebus creditis; 2 Ecloga 2 c. 35; l. 2 Cod. de petit. heredit.

units.la: {h} Rem restituit, qui causam usucapiendi vt hic. possessionem l.22. s. eodem: fructus vt hic, & d.l.22. ꝑ l.73. ꝑ. eod. l.38. §.4. s. de usuris: l.173. §.1. ꝑ. de regulis iuris: l.2. Cod. de petit. heredit: partus l.20. s. de rei vindicat: l.9. §.7. s. ad exhib: vtilitates l.9. §. vlt. s. ad exhib. omnes vtilitates l.81. ꝑ. eod: corpus rei, omnem rem, conditionemque eius l.vlt. in f. ꝑ. eodem. omnem causam l.31. s. de reb. credi. & pristinum statum restituit l.2. §.43. s. ne quid in loco publico: 6. Harmenop. 3.
units.tr: He restores the thing who restores the cause of usucapion, as here (possession, see l. 22 s. eodem); fruits, as here, and the same d. l. 22 ꝑ l. 73 ꝑ eod.; l. 38 §4 s. de usuris; l. 173 §1 ꝑ de regulis iuris; l. 2 Cod. de petit. heredit.; offspring (partus), l. 20 s. de rei vindicat.; l. 9 §7 s. ad exhib.; advantages (utilitates), l. 9 §ult. s. ad exhib., all advantages, l. 81 ꝑ eod.; the body of the thing, every thing, and its condition, l. ult. in f. ꝑ eodem; every cause, l. 31 s. de reb. credi.; and restores the former state, l. 2 §43 s. ne quid in loco publico; 6 Harmenopulus 3.
See l. 73 ꝑ eod.

units.la: {4}Litis nomen {b}omnem actionem significat: sive in rem, sive in personam sit.
units.tr: The word lis signifies every action, whether it be in rem or in personam.
37. Paulus, book 26 on the Edict.

units.la: VErbum Oportere{c} non ad facultatem{d} iudicis pertinet, qui potest vel pluris{e}, vel minoris{f} condemnare: sed ad veritatem{g} refertur.
units.tr: The word oportere does not pertain to the discretion of the judge, who may condemn for more or for less, but is referred to the truth.
38. Ulpian, book 25 on the Edict.

units.la: OStentum{b} Labeo definit, omne contra naturam cuiusque rei genitum{i}, factumque duo genera sunt ostentorum: vnum, quotiens quid contra naturam nascitur: tribus manibus forte, aut pedibus{k}, aut qua alia parte corporis, quæ naturæ finium', ad lapides & arma discurrunt. cui loco cupio coniungi legem 13. §.3. §. de vsufructu. Quin etiam dici solet, communionem matrem esse discordiæ v. l. 26. §. de feruitut. vrban. præd.
units.tr: Labeo defines a portent (ostentum) as anything born or made contrary to the nature of each thing. There are two kinds of portents. The first: whenever something is born contrary to nature, for example with three hands, or feet, or some other part of the body, which run beyond the limits of nature, to stones and weapons. To this passage I wish to join law 13 §3 §de usufructu. Indeed it is also commonly said that joint ownership is the mother of discord, see l. 26 §de servitut. urban. praedior.

units.la: {b} lis idem est quod actio,& quod actione continetur. hinc illa, litem æstimare l.29.§.de negotiis: l.9.§. quod certo: l.15.§.7.§. quod vi: contestari v.l.1.Cod.de litis contestatione. in iudicium deducere l.3.§.2.§.de negotiis: l.2.Cod.de petit.hereditat. vel condemnationem l.3.§.vlt.§.de act.empt. addicere (quod nihil aliud est quam vel secundum præsentem iudicare, vel ei poreftatem facere actionis monendæ 16.Gell.2.) mori (quod euenit transfactis temporib* agendi l.3.§.1.§.quæ in fraudem: l.2.§.iudicat.) perire l.1.§.3.§. de calumniatoribus: l.18.§.4.§. de dolo: viuere l.vlt.in f.C.de fide instrum: lite cadere Festus. liti renunciare l.10.§. de iudicijs: in lite persequerare d.l.10. adde & alia quædam ex Quintino in c.tempus mota litis, Extr.de verb.signif.
units.tr: Lis is the same as actio, and what is contained in an action. Hence those phrases: to assess the suit (litem aestimare) l. 29 §de negotiis: l. 9 §quod certo: l. 15 §7 §quod vi:; to join issue (contestari) see l. 1 Cod. de litis contestatione.; to bring into court (in iudicium deducere) l. 3 §2 §de negotiis: l. 2 Cod. de petit. hereditat.; or condemnation (condemnationem) l. 3 §ult. §de act. empt.; to adjudge (addicere) (which is nothing else than either to judge according to the present facts, or to give him the power of bringing the action to be warned) 16 Gellius 2.; to die (mori) (which happens when the times for acting have lapsed) l. 3 §1 §quae in fraudem: l. 2 §iudicat.; to perish l. 1 §3 §de calumniatoribus: l. 18 §4 §de dolo:; to live l. ult. in f. C. de fide instrum.:; to fall in the suit (lite cadere) Festus.; to renounce the suit (liti renunciare) l. 10 §de iudiciis:; to pursue the suit (in lite persequi) d. l. 10. Add also certain other things from Quintinus in c. tempus mota litis, Extr. de verb. signif.

units.la: Porro lis semper in iudicio: lurgium extra iudicium esse potest. Litem à controuersia & causa distinguere difficile. lurgium inter fratres l.vlt.§.familiæ: inter virum & vxorem l.31.§. de iure dotium: l.27.§.de pactis dotalib. v.c.iurgium extr.de verb.signif. & ibid. Quintinum.{c} quo actor vel stipulator ita vti solet, aio te mihi dare oportere. Dare promittis quidquid te dare oportet l.76.in f.l. 88.§.de verborum obligat.{d} v. quæ notaui ad l. 21.§.de interrogationibus.{e} l.1.§. de in litem: Inst.de pœna temerè litigantis: l.3.Cod.de fructibus & litium.{f} v.l.16. §.de re iudicata.{g} debiti scilicet.
units.tr: Moreover, a lis always exists in a judicial proceeding; a quarrel (iurgium) can exist outside a court. It is difficult to distinguish lis from controversy and cause. A quarrel between brothers, l. ult. §familiae: between husband and wife, l. 31 §de iure dotium: l. 27 §de pactis dotalib.; see c. iurgium, Extr. de verb. signif. and ibid. Quintinus. The formula by which the plaintiff or stipulator is wont to use it: I say that you ought to give me. You promise to give whatever you ought to give, l. 76 in f.; l. 88 §de verborum obligat. See what I have noted on l. 21 §de interrogationibus. l. 1 §de in litem: Inst. de poena temere litigantis: l. 3 Cod. de fructibus et litium. See l. 16 §de re iudicata. namely of a debt.

units.la: Ostenta quæ ostendunt tantummodo monstra: Porteuta quæ quid porro tendant, indicant. Festus in Portentum. Cicero 2.de natura. Prædictiones & præsensiones rerum futurarum quid aliud declarant hominibus nisi ea quæ fiunt oftedi, nonstrari, portendi, prædici. ex quo illa ostenta, monstra, portenta, & prodigia dicuntur. Idem 1.de diuinatione, quia ostendunt, portendunt, monstrant, prædicant. ostenta, portenta, prodigia dicuntur,
units.tr: Ostenta are those which merely show monsters; portenta are those which indicate where they tend further. Festus on Portentum. Cicero, De natura deorum 2. What else do predictions and presentiments of future things declare to men, except that those things which are going to happen are shown, pointed out, portended, foretold? From this those ostenta, monstra, portenta and prodigia are so called. The same, De divinatione 1, because they show, portend, point out, foretell: ostenta, portenta, prodigia are called.

units.la: {h} [?]l.4.§.de statu. {i} vel digitis l.10.§.2.§. de ædilicio. contraria est, alterum, cum quid prodigiosum detur, quae Graeci φαντάσματα vocant, i. visiones, vocat.
units.tr: [?] l. 4 §de statu. Or with the fingers l. 10 §2 §de aedilicio. The opposite of this is the other, when something prodigious is given, which the Greeks call phantasmata [φαντάσματα], i.e. visions, he calls.
39. Paulus, book 53 on the Edict.

units.la: SUbsignatum dicitur, quod ab aliquo subscriptum est , nam veteres subsignationis verbo prosscriptione vti solebant. 1 Bona intelliguntur cuiusque, quae deducto aere alieno superfuint. 2 Detestari est, absenti denuntiare. 3 Inceu sigillo: sit certus possessor est, quem ignoramus.
units.tr: "Subsignatum" is said of what has been signed by someone, for the older writers used the word subsignatio in the sense of prescriptio. 1 The goods of anyone are understood to be what remains after the debts have been deducted. 2 To detest is to denounce to someone who is absent. 3 "Under an uncertain seal": the possessor is certain, but we do not know who he is.
40. Ulpian, book 56.

units.la: Detestatio est denuntiatio facta cum testatione. 1 Serui appellatio etiam ad ancillae refertur. 2 Familiae appellatione liberi quoque continentur. 3 Vnicus seruus familiae appellatione non continetur. Ne duo quidem familia faciunt.
units.tr: A detestation is a denunciation made with a witness. 1 The term "slave" (servus) also refers to the female slave. 2 Under the term "family" children are also included. 3 A single slave is not included under the term "family." Nor do even two make a family.

Against this, read "resignation" for "rescription" (f. flus.); e l. 72 §. de iure dotium; l. 2 §. 1 §. de collation; l. 6 in fine, Cod. de collationib.; l. 6 Cod. ad l. Falcidi.; l. vlt. §. 4 Cod. de bonis quae liberis; §. vlt. Inst. de legi Falcidia. Hence they are said to be "benefited" (beare dicuntur), l. 49 1. cod., which does not happen if they have more burden than benefit, l. 83 1. cod. They differ from an inheritance in this: when the usufruct of an estate is bequeathed, the bronze (aes) is deducted from all the goods, l. vlt. §. de usufr. legato; l. 69 §. ad l. Falcidiam. When an inheritance is bequeathed, nothing is deducted, l. 104 in f. §. de legat. 1; l. 8 in f.; l. 9 §. de legat. 2, because burdens can exist within an inheritance. And so goods and inheritance are distinguished in l. 83 §. de legat. 3; l. 16 §. 1 §. ad Treb. f. "to attest" (attestari) in the Vulgate and Hal.; and "although to attest" in Horace, §. l. 25 §. de rei vindicat. So too an uncertain person, an uncertain heir, whom someone places under his mind by an uncertain opinion, §. 25 Inst. de legatis; and Cod. de incertis personis. "Uncertain as to the truth of the matter," l. 7 in f. §. de cont. empt.; "uncertain opinion," l. 21 §. 3 §. de arbitris; an uncertain day, l. 1 §. 1 §. 2; l. 75 §. de conditi. & demonstr.; uncertain as to his own status, l. 14 §. qui testament.; an uncertain guardian, l. 10 §. de testament. tutela; uncertainty of condition, l. 1 Cod. de pactis; h l. 2 §. 1 §. eo. "Protesting" (Διαμαρτυρόμενοι), Ecl. 10 c. 39. See on this passage Alciatus, where he treats of testatio, detestatio, nunciatio, denuntiatio, obnunciatio, antestatio, contestatio, renunciatio, protestatio, and their effects. Add Cuiacius 7 obs. 16, where he treats of antestatio; i see the whole of l. 1 inf. 1 eo.; l. vl. 195 §. 1 §. 2 1. cod.; l. Ecl. ib. c. 40; and the slaves, l. 2 §. 14 §. de vi bonorum. m Ecl. ib. Indeed, Paulus says a family is made by two persons, 5 sent. 6 §. 3; or by one, l. 2 §. 6 §. vi bonorum; n or one represents the whole body, l. 7 in f. §. quod cuiusque; and yet two do not make a family, as here. Two make a quarrel, l. 4 §. 3 §. vi bonor.; three make a college, l. 85 1 eo.; ten or fifteen or more make a crowd, d. §. 2; ten make a flock, l. vlt. §. de abigeis; but also ten persons make a people, Bartolus, Epist. 41.
41. Gaius in book twenty-one on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: ARmorum appellatio non utique scuta, & Agladios[?], & galeas significat: sed & fustes, & lapides.
units.tr: The term "arms" does not necessarily mean shields, swords and helmets, but also clubs and stones.
42. Ulpian in book fifty-seven on the Edict.

units.la: Robrum & opprobrium, id est probra quædam natura turpia sunt, quædam similiter, & quasi more ciuitatis. utputa furtum, adulterium, natura turpe est. enimuero tutelæ dānari,hoc nō natura probrum est, sed more ciuitatis. nec enim natura probrum est, quod potest etiam in hominem idoneum incidere.
units.tr: Disgrace and infamy: some kinds of disgrace are naturally shameful, others are so by analogy and by the custom of the state. For instance, theft and adultery are shameful by nature. But to be condemned in a guardianship is not a disgrace by nature, but by the custom of the state. For a thing is not disgraceful by nature if it can even befall a worthy man.
43. Idem in book fifty-eight on the Edict.

units.la: Verbo Victus continentur, quæ esui, potuique, cultuique corporis, quæque ad viuendum ho-mini necessaria sunt. vestęm quoque victus habere vicem, Labeo ait.
units.tr: Under the word "food" (victus) are included those things which are needed for eating and drinking, for the care of the body, and for the necessities of living. Labeo says that clothing also has the force of food.
44. Gaius in book twenty-two on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: ET caetera, quibus tuendi, curandiue corporis nostri gratia utimur, ea appellatione signi-ficantur.
units.tr: And the other things which we use for the protection and care of our body are signified by that term.
And the other things we use for the sake of protecting and caring for our body are signified by that name.

is condemned by the law of nations. Add law 38 §2, de adulteriis.

units.tr: {g} Eclog. ibid. cap. 43; add l. 44 ꝗ eod.: the word "food" (vitus) extends more widely than the words for daily and dietary provisions, l. 21 §. de alimentis.

S. eo: l. 45. ꝗ eo: & d.l.234. adde l.21.S.de alimentis: recto, quod hæc lex innuit: & aperte probatur in lege l.21.S.de alimen. ar non ea quæ ad disciplinam pertinent, nisi aliud probetur d.l.21. An & pharmaca continentur? id hac lege innuitur & probatur àRebuffo in tractatu de sententijs prouisionalib. articulo 1. gloss. 5: in verbis, Et medicamenta: & gloss. 2. in verbis donnec en matiere dalimens, & articulo 2. vbi de priuilegijs alimentorum & medicamentorum disserit. hæc omnia, non diarij aut cibarij l.21.S. de alimentis. sed victus & educationis vocabulo continentur: nisi quis forte de victu transigat. tunc enim, suoris causa, nec de habitatione, nec de vestiario transegisse legarius intelligitur l.8.§.12.S.de transactionibus, adde Roll.à Valle 1.conf.22.
units.tr: {h} We maintain the life of the body by food and drink, l. 43 §. eod.; l. vltima §. de alimentis; l. 234 in f.; l. 5 §. 12 §. de agnosc. liber; by clothing, l. 43 §. eo.; l. 45 ꝗ eo.; and d. l. 234. Add l. 21 §. de alimentis. Correctly, this is what the law implies, and it is plainly proved in the law l. 21 §. de alimen., that those things which pertain to discipline are not included, unless the contrary is shown, d. l. 21. Are drugs (pharmaca) also included? This law implies it and proves it, as Rebuffus shows in his treatise on provisional sentences, article 1, gloss 5, on the words "and medicines," and gloss 2, on the words "as to the matter of maintenance," and article 2, where he discusses the privileges of maintenance and medicines. All these things are included under the term "food and upbringing" (victus and educatio), not under the terms of daily or dietary provision, l. 21 §. de alimentis, unless someone perhaps settles a matter concerning food. For then, in the sense of food, it is understood that he did not settle a matter concerning dwelling, nor concerning clothing, l. 8 §. 12 §. de transactionibus. Add Rolandus à Valle 1 conf. 22.

units.la: IN stratum{e} omne vestimentum contineri, quod iniiciatur, Labeo ait. neque{b} enim dubiū est, quin stragula{c} vestis sit{d} omne pallium [illegible, ~12 letters]{e}, ergo vestem accipiemus, non stragula{g}: in stratu{h} omnem stragulam vestem.
units.tr: Labeo says that every garment that is thrown over a couch (stratum) is included in the term "couch covering." For there is no doubt that any cloak is a covering-garment (stragula vestis); therefore we shall understand a garment, not a covering: in a couch, every covering garment. [illegible]
46. Idem in book fifty on the Edict.

units.la: PRonuntiatum & statutum idem potest, promiscuè enim & pronuntiasse & statuisse solemus dicere eos, qui ius habent cognoscendi.
units.tr: To announce (pronuntiatum) and to decree (statutum) can mean the same thing, for we usually say indiscriminately that those who have the right of judging both announced and decreed.

units.la: 1 ¶Matremfamilias{m} accipere debemus eam, quae non inhonestè vixit. matrem enim familias a caeteris foeminis mores{n} discernunt, atque separant.
units.tr: 1 We ought to understand as "matron of the household" (matrem familias) her who has lived not dishonourably. For manners distinguish and separate the matron of the household from other women.

Gell.8. huc refer c.statuo c.quod præcipitur. Extra de verb.signif.vbi v. Quintinum. l l.1.s.quod quisquè iuris.starnere διορίσασθαι pronunciare ψηφίσασθαι 2.Ecloga 2.cap. 46: v.d.cap.statuo. Iudex imperans,vetans,permittens,puniens, & ius reddens,dicitur statuere:sed & magistratus cum legem sancit: hinc statuta. m vide l.3.in fine s.de liberis exhib. n Ecloga ibidem cap. 46: & dignitas vide l.49.§.4.s.de legat.3.l.29.Cod.de adulteriis: honestas l. 4r.in fine s.de vitu (quàm Græci σεμνὴν. Ecloga ibidem) vestitus l.15.§.15.s.de insuriis,ceu stola. Festus.adde Cuiacium 3.obs. 18; Petrum Fabrum 1.se-mestr.15: non virginitas 7.cod. proinde nihil intererit, nupta sit, an {4}vidua, ingenua sit,an libertina. nam neque nuptiæ {b}neque nuptiæ tales faciunt matremfamilias:sed boni mores.
units.tr: It is included, and both coverings and cloaks and everything that we throw over, as the Ecloga says. Compare l. 12 §. 18 §. de instructio. Thus covering-garments, l. 23 §. de auro, adjectively derived from "to furnish." They are also called "instrata" by Cato, c. 10 de re rustica in fine, which the Greeks call peristromata [περιστρωμάτα], and also katastromata [καταστρωμάτα], epaulomata [ἐπαυλωμάτα]; see Cuiacius 10 obs. 18; peripilaia [περιπίλαια] (because they are hung over dining couches) and hypertitasmata [ὑπερτιτάσματα]; hangings (aulaea), from the courts of kings in which they are stretched; Attalic work, Babylonian work, tapestries, tapestry, coverlets; and, if they have animals woven into them, zōa [ζῶα], figured work. Plautus in the Pseudolus: "nor Alexandrian figured tapestries." Eudaeus here: amphitapa, psilotapa, concerning which see l. 23 §. 2 §. de auro. s In the Vulgate and Hal. "in the vide." g "stragulam" in Hal. and the Vulgate. h "Instratum" and "instratus" are said. i "idem dici" in the Vulgate and Hal. k Ecl. ib. c. 46; l. 35 §. 1 §. de auro; l. 59 §. 2; l. 60 §. de re iudicata. Hence: a freedman is pronounced (pronunciatur libertus), l. 8 §. 1 §. de in ius; a guardian is pronounced, l. 11 §. de administr. tut.; a free-born man (ingenuus), l. 29 in s. §. de liberali; unworthy (indignus), l. 8 §. de his quae ut indign.; free (liber), l. 8 Cod. de sententiis. Add l. 1 §. 19 §. ad Turpill. Sometimes "to pronounce" also means to promise something openly (as "to pronounce money," Suetonius in Julius c. 19; a feast, ib. c. 25; a gift; the same in Galba c. 16, "tesserae"; the same in Domitian c. 4, "prizes"; Livy 2); to express openly, l. 11 §. 18 §. de actu empt.; l. 1 §. 1 in f.; l. 31 §. 1 §. de aedilitio; l. 69 §. 1 in f. §. de cuist.; l. 15 §. 1 §. de statuliberis; to affirm or deny. Hence "pronounced" (pronunciatum) by Cicero is the same as Varro's "proloquuis"; in dialectic, dialektikos [διαλεκτικὸς]; Gellius 8 (16). Refer here to c. "statuo" in c. "quod praecipitur," Extra de verb. signif., where see Quintinus; l. 1 §. quod quisque iuris. "To establish" (statuere) is "to determine" (diorisasthai [διορίσασθαι]), "to pronounce" is "to vote" (psēphisasthai [ψηφίσασθαι]), Ecloga 2 cap. 46; see the said c. "statuo." A judge who commands, forbids, permits, punishes, and renders justice is said "to establish"; and so is a magistrate when he sanctions a law, hence "statutes." m see l. 3 in fine §. de liberis exhib. n Ecloga, ibid. cap. 46. Also "dignity": see l. 49 §. 4 §. de legat. 3; l. 29 Cod. de adulteriis; "honour," l. 41 in fine §. de vitu (which the Greeks call semnēn [σεμνὴν], Ecloga ibid.); "clothing," l. 15 §. 15 §. de iniuriis, as the stola. Festus. Add Cuiacius 3 obs. 18; Petrus Faber 1 semestr. 15. Not virginity, 7 cod. Therefore it makes no difference whether she is married or a widow, freeborn or freedwoman; for neither marriage nor such a marriage makes a matron of the household, but good morals do.

units.la: 47. Paulus libro 56.ad Edictum. Liberationis verbum eandem {c}vim habet, quam solutionis.
units.tr: 47. Paulus, book 56 on the Edict. The word "liberation" has the same force as "release."

units.la: 48. Gaius libro ad Edictum prætoris urbani titulo {d}Qui neque {d}sequuntur neque ducantur. Solutum non intelligimus eum, qui, licet vinculis sleuatus sit, manibus {e}tamen tenetur. ac ne eum quidem intelligimus solutum, qui in publico sine vinculis seruatur.
units.tr: 48. Gaius, book on the Edict of the urban praetor, under the title "Those who neither follow nor are led." We do not understand as "released" one who, although freed from chains, is still held by the hands. Nor do we understand as released one who is kept in public without chains.

units.la: 49. Vlpianus libro 59.ad Edictum. Bonorum {f}appellatio aut naturalis, aut civilis est: Naturaliter bona ex eo dicuntur, quòd beāt {g}, hoc est, beatos faciunt. beare est prodesse. In bonis {h}prodesse. Porrò ne quis in uestiis vocabulo decipiatur, eò significatur Impubes. Eorum qui in ius vocati sunt, alij sequuntur vltrò, nec deducuntur, veluti c domo sua vocati l.21.s.de in ius vocando. vel ex aylo,Nonell.17. vel satis offerentes s. in ius vocati.vt cant, vel satis dent (vnde constat non licere continuò manum iniicere ei,qui in ius vocatus est. Qui trahitur in ius,antestatur prius) vel intestati,id est non antestati, seu testato non conuenti. Alij ducuntur,vt cæteri fere omnes qui in ius vocari possunt. Alij neque ducuntur, neque sequuntur,vt qui in ius vocari non possunt,quales sunt vinculi neruo, aut compedibus, vel qui religione loci,quasi vincti tenentur l.2.s.de in ius vocando: v.Cui.cium 7.obs 16. e sensus est, Captus dicitur in quem manus iniecta est,qui vinculis tenetur,ad-de l.116: l.224.s.eo: l.22.s.quod metus causa. adde l.9.l.25. s.ex qui-bus causis maiores: l.7.s.depositi: l.2.s.de homine libero: l.8.§.9. s.de pœnis. f adde l.21.l.9.§.1.s.eo: l.83. l.208 s.eo:l.5.§.6.s.vt in possessi.l.8.s.de reb.author.iudicij: l.9.s.rem pupilli. g Inde beati, diuites dicuntur. Plautus in Pœnulo bonam ego quam beatam esse primo dici mauolo: & Seneca s.controuerf. insolens malum est beata vxor,&s. Epist. nunquàm vidi hominem beatum indecentiùs. sic, bona incommoda,non beant,l.8.s.eodem. h l.1.s.de rer.diuif.l.2. in f.s.fi ex noxali:l.9.§.6.s.quod metus:l.8.§.12.s.quib.mod.pign:l.52. s.de adquir.rer: l.vlt.§.4.s.qua in fraud.cred: l.2.§.22.s.vt bon.rapt. autem nostris computari sciendum est, non solum quæ dominij nostri sunt, sed & si bona fide à nobis possideantur, vel superficiaria sint. AEque bonis adnumerabitur, etiam si quid est in actionibus, petitionibus, persecutionibus. nam hæc omnia in bonis esse videntur.
units.tr: 49. Ulpian, book 59 on the Edict. The term "goods" is used either in a natural or in a civil sense. Naturally, goods are so called because they make (beant) people blessed, that is, they make them happy. To bless (beare) is to benefit. Goods benefit the owner. Moreover, so that no one is deceived by the word in wills, it signifies a minor. Of those who are summoned to court, some follow of their own accord and are not led, as those called from their own house (l.21 s. de in ius vocando), or who give bail (Nonell. 17), or who offer sufficient security (s. in ius vocati, as in the Cant.), or who give sufficient security (whence it is clear that one summoned to court may not be seized at once; one who is dragged to court is first called as a witness). Or those who are intestati, that is, not called as witnesses, or not summoned by a will. Others are led, as nearly all the rest who can be summoned to court. Others neither are led nor follow, such as those who cannot be summoned to court, as those bound with a neck-chain or fetters, or those who are held by the sanctity of a place, as if bound (l.2 s. de in ius vocando; see Cuiacius, 7 Obs. 16). The sense is this: he is said to be "captured" on whom a hand has been laid, who is held by chains. Add l.116, l.224 s. eo, l.22 s. quod metus causa. Add l.9, l.25 s. ex quibus causis maiores, l.7 s. depositi, l.2 s. de homine libero, l.8 §.9 s. de poenis. Add l.21, l.9 §.1 s. eo, l.83, l.208 s. eo, l.5 §.6 s. ut in possessionem, l.8 s. de reb. auctoritate iudicii, l.9 s. rem pupilli. From this the blessed and the rich are called "beati." Plautus, in the Poenulus: "I would rather the good woman be called blessed first"; and Seneca, in the Controversiae: "A blessed wife is an unbearable evil"; and in the Epistles: "I have never seen a man blessed more indecently." Thus "unprofitable goods" do not bless, l.8 s. eodem. Goods are "in our possession" (in bonis) l.1 s. de rerum divisione, l.2 in fine s. si ex noxali, l.9 §.6 s. quod metus, l.8 §.12 s. quibus modis pignus, l.52 s. de adquirendo rerum dominio, l.ult. §.4 s. qua in fraudem creditorum, l.2 §.22 s. ut bonorum raptorum. It must be known that what is counted among our goods is not only what is of our ownership, but also what is possessed by us in good faith, or what is held by superficies. Equally, whatever is in actions, petitions and prosecutions will be counted among goods, for all these seem to be in goods.
50. Idem, book 61 on the Edict.

units.la: NUrus appellatio etiam ad pronurum, & ultra porrigenda est.
units.tr: The term "daughter-in-law" is to be extended even to the daughter-in-law's daughter-in-law and beyond.

units.la: 51. Gaius libro vicesimo tertio ad Edictum provinciale.
units.tr: 51. Gaius, book 23 on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: APpellatione parentis non tantum pater, sed etiam avus, & proavus, & deinceps omnes superiores continentur: sed & mater, & avia, & proavia.
units.tr: Under the term "parent" are included not only the father but also the grandfather, the great-grandfather, and all the ancestors in turn; but also the mother, the grandmother and the great-grandmother.
52. Ulpian, book 61 on the Edict.
Under the term "patron" the patroness is also included.
53. Paulus, book 59 on the Edict.

units.la: SAEpè ita comparatum est, vt coniuncta pro disiunctis accipiantur, & disiuncta pro coniunctis, interdum soluta pro separatis. Nam cum dicitur apud veteres Adgnatorum gentiliumque pro separatione hoc quomodo fit verum, vide Vlt. Cod. si aduersus fiscum.
units.tr: It is often the case that conjoined things are taken for disjoined ones, and disjoined for conjoined, and sometimes loosed for separated. For when among the ancients it is said of agnates and gentiles in the sense of "separately," how this is true, see the last law of the Code, "If against the fisc."

units.la: {i} in quibus non est particula coniunctiua, vel disiunctiua.
units.tr: {i} in which there is no conjunctive or disjunctive particle.

units.la: {ix}verba legis duodecim tabularum ea fuerunt, Si paterfamilias intestatus moritur, familia pecuniaque eius agnatorum gentilium-que esto: & rursus, Si furiosus existit, agnatorum gentiliumque in eum, pecuniamque eius potestas esto. Auther ad Herennium. Porro gentiles sunt nati ex ingenuis, quorum maiores nullam seruitutem seruierunt. Cicero in Topicis. possunt quidem esse agnati inter se, non tamen gentiles, & in hac quoque lege agnati, & gentiles separantur. Interdum gentilis est, qui ex eodem cognomine, nec tamen agnatus est. {l}His verbis Budæus negat disiunctiua significari, aliud enim esse [?]διαξευτικὸν μόριον, i. particulam disiunctiuam, aliud separatiuam [?]ἀπογεγραμμένην. accipitur. At cùm dicitur, Super pecunia{a}tutelae suae {b}, tutor separatim sine pecunia dari non potest. Et cùm dicimus, Quod dedi aut {c}donavi: utraque {d}continemus. Cùm vero dicimus, Quod cùm dare oportet: quòdnis {e}eorum sufficit probare. Cùm vero dicit praetor, Si donum, munus, operas redemerit: si omnia imposita sunt, certum est, omnia redimenda esse. ex re ergo pro coniunctis habentur. si quaedam imposita sunt, caetera non desiderabuntur. 1 ¶ Item dubitatum, illa verba, Opeg, consilio, quem admodum accipienda sunt: sententiae coniungentium, aut separatium. sed verius est, quod & Labeo ait, separatim accipienda: quia aliud factū est eius, qui ope: aliud eius, qui consilio furtum fecit. sic enim alij {h}condici potest, alij {i}non potest. & sanè post veterum auctoritatem eò peruentum est, vt nemo ope videatur fecisse, si {k}& consilium malignum habuerit: nec consilium habuisse noceat, nisi {l}& factum secutum fuerit.
units.tr: The words of the Law of the Twelve Tables were these: "If a father of a family dies intestate, let his family and money be for his agnates and gentiles." And again: "If someone becomes insane, let the power over him and his money belong to his agnates and gentiles." Author on Herennius. Moreover, gentiles are those born of freeborn parents whose ancestors never served in slavery. Cicero in the Topics. Agnates can indeed be among themselves without being gentiles, and in this law too agnates and gentiles are separated. Sometimes a gentile is one who bears the same name but is not an agnate. Budaeus denies that these words signify disjunctives, for one thing is a disjunctive particle [διαξευτικὸν μόριον], that is, a disjunctive particle, and another is taken as a separative one [ἀπογεγραμμένην]. But when it is said concerning money of his guardianship, a guardian cannot be given separately without the money. And when we say what I have given or donated, we include both. But when we say what it is fitting to give, proof of either of them is sufficient. But when the praetor says if he has redeemed a gift, a service, or labour, if all have been imposed, it is certain that all must be redeemed. From the matter, therefore, they are taken as conjoined; if only some have been imposed, the rest will not be required. 1 Likewise it is doubted how the words by aid, by counsel are to be understood: as conjoining or separating clauses. But it is truer, as Labeo also says, that they are to be taken separately, because the act of one who helped is different from that of one who committed theft by counsel. For thus one may be sued by condiction, the other may not. And indeed, after the authority of the ancients, it has come to the point that no one is seen to have acted "by aid" if he also had a malicious intent; nor does having had counsel harm, unless the deed also followed.

units.la: 54. Vlpianus libro sexagesimo secundo ad Edictum.
units.tr: 54. Ulpian, in book sixty-second on the Edict.

units.la: {m}Condicionales creditores dicuntur & hi, quibus nondum competit actio, est autem competitura: vel qui spem {n}habent, vt competat.
units.tr: Conditional creditors are also those to whom an action does not yet belong but will belong, or who have the hope that it will belong to them.
55. Paul, in book sixteen of the Short Edict.

units.la: Creditor autem is est, qui exceptione {o}perpetua summoueri non potest. qui autem temporalem timet, similis est condicionali creditori.
units.tr: A creditor, however, is one who cannot be repelled by a perpetual exception. One who fears a temporary exception is similar to a conditional creditor.

units.la: 56. Vlpianus libro sexagesimo secundo ad Edictum.
units.tr: 56. Ulpian, in book sixty-second on the Edict.

units.la: Cognoscere {p}instrumenta, est relegere, & recognoscere. dispungere {q}est conferre accepta & primit, quasi diceret quod
units.tr: To know documents (instrumenta) is to read them through and review them. To dispunge is to compare receipts and payments, as if to say that I gave it on account of a gift.

units.la: ob causam donationis dedi. {d}aliud est enim dare, aliud donare. dari potest aliquid etiam citra titulum donandi. {e}id est alterutrum.
units.tr: For it is one thing to give, another to donate. Something can be given even without the title of donation. It is one or the other.

units.la: cognoscimus instrumenta cum ea legimus aut relegimus. dispungimus, cùm accepta & data diligentissimè inter se condata. ¶Liberorum{a} appellatione continentur non tantum qui sunt in potestate: sed omnes, qui sui iuris sunt: siue virilis, siue foeminini sexus sunt, exve{b} foeminini sexus descendentes.
units.tr: We know documents when we read or re-read them. We dispunge when receipts and payments have been most carefully compared with one another. Under the name of children are included not only those who are in power, but all who are sui iuris, whether of the male or female sex, and those descended through females.

units.la: 57. Paulus libro quinquagesimo nono ad Edictum.
units.tr: 57. Paul, in book fifty-ninth on the Edict.

units.la: CVi praecipua cura rerum incumbit, & qui magis quam caeteri diligentiam, & sollicitudinem requibus praesunt, debent: hi magistri{c} appellantur. Quinetiam ipsi magistratus per derivationem a magistris cognominantur{d}, unde etiam cuiusque discipline praeceptores, magistros{e} appellari a monendo, vel monstrando. ¶Persequi{f} videtur, & qui satis accepit.
units.tr: He to whom the chief care of affairs is entrusted, and who owes greater diligence and anxiety than others over those whom he governs, these are called magistri. Indeed the magistrates themselves are named after the masters by derivation; whence also the teachers of each discipline are called magistri from advising (monendo) or showing (monstrando). It seems that one who has received enough is also "pursued" (persequi).

units.la: 58. Gaius libro vicesimo quarto ad Edictum provinciale.
units.tr: 58. Gaius, in book twenty-fourth on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: LIcet inter gesta & facta videtur quaedam esse subtilis differentia: attamen [illegible, ~6 letters], id est, abusque, nihil inter factum & gestum interest.
units.tr: Although there seems to be some subtle difference between gesta and facta, nevertheless [illegible, about six letters], that is, abusque: there is no difference between factum and gestum.

units.la: ¶Paternos libertos recte videmur dicere nos-stros libertos. liberorum libertos non recte nonpollicitat.
units.tr: We rightly seem to say "our freedmen" of paternal freedmen. To say "freedmen of children" is not correct.

units.la: Imo, non comprehenduntur liberorum appellatione descendentes ex foeminis l.1.j.de iure immunit. sicut albatus ab albo Varro. Imo magistri a magistratib. Hinc magistri societatis v.l.14. j. de pactis, vniuersitati & venditioni bonorum praepositi vide quae dixi ad l.9.j.ratam rem.nauium, vide l.1.§.j.de exercitoria, equitum l.2.§.19.j.de origine iuris: l.1. j. de officio praefecti vrbi, memoriae, Epistolis,libellis, vide l.11. Cod.de iuris Emphiteutico,xris,l.vnica Cod.de annona,admissionum, l.vnica Cod.Theodosiano qui a prebitione, inter agetes§.2.j.de Iustinianeo Codice, scrinij, libellorum, sacrarum cognitionum, §.1.j.de nouo Codice faciendo, legum §.1.ibi voce magistra j. ad antecessores, scriniorum,l.vlt.§.1.in fine Cod.de appellat. pagorum, vide apud Sicculum Flaccum libro de condicionibus, agrorum, vicorum. Suetonius in Augusto cap.30.& vlt. conuiuij, Cicero in Catone, ludi literarii, l.1.§.6.j.de variis & extraord.condicionibus, ceremoniarum, populi curiae, de quibus vide Budaeum in Annotationibus in Pandectas.
units.tr: Indeed, descendants through women are not included under the name of children; see l. 1, j. de iure immunit. Just as albatus is from albus, says Varro. Indeed magistri are from magistrates. Hence the masters of a partnership, see l. 14, j. de pactis; those set over a corporation and the sale of goods, see what I said on l. 9, j. ratam rem; of ships, see l. 1, §. j. de exercitoria; of cavalry, l. 2, §. 19, j. de origine iuris; l. 1, j. de officio praefecti urbi; of memorials, of letters, of libels; see l. 11, Cod. de excusat. muner. officiorum; the title of the Code on the master of offices; of the census, l. last, Cod. de iuris emphyteutico; of the grain supply, l. unica, Cod. de annona; of admissions, l. unica, Cod. Theodosiano qui a prebitione; among the agents, §. 2, j. de Iustinianeo Codice; of the writing office, of libels, of sacred cognitions, §. 1, j. de nouo Codice faciendo; of laws, §. 1, where the word magistra is used, j. ad antecessores; of the writing offices, l. last, §. 1, in fine, Cod. de appellat.; of the villages, of the fields, of the streets; see Siculus Flaccus in his book on conditions. Suetonius in Augustus ch. 30, and last of the banquet; Cicero in Cato; of the schools of letters, l. 1, §. 6, j. de variis & extraord. condicionibus; of ceremonies, of the popular assemblies; on these see Budaeus in his Annotations on the Pandects.

units.la: {g} Hinc magistrare,id est moderari Festus magistreria potestas vide l.33.Cod.de appellat. magisterium militum vd 25.Cod de procurat.
units.tr: {g} Hence "magistrare," that is, to govern; Festus: "magistreria potestas" (the power of a magistrate). See l.33 Cod. de appellat. "magisterium militum" (the office of commander of soldiers), see 25 Cod. de procurat.

units.la: {h} ne dicas cum Accursio consequi. sensus est,Is nondum suum assecutus intelligitur,cui datus est fideiussor: nondum enim ei plenè satisfactum est. {i} v.l.19.j.eodem. {k} vide l.5.j.de alimentis. {l} vide l.19.j.eodem.
units.tr: {h} Do not say, with Accursius, "to follow". The sense is: he is understood not yet to have obtained his own, to whom a surety has been given; for it has not yet been fully satisfied to him. {i} See l. 19, j. eodem. {k} See l. 5, j. de alimentis. {l} See l. 19, j. eodem.

{b} l. last, j. de pollicitat. [?] we say "our freedmen".
59. Ulpian, in book sixty-eighth on the Edict.

units.la: Portus appellatus est conclusus locus, quò im-portantur mercès, & inde exportantur. eáque nihilo minus statio {b} est conclusa, atque munita. inde angiportum {c} dictum est.
units.tr: A port is called an enclosed place, into which merchandise is imported and from which it is exported. A station likewise is enclosed and fortified. From this a angiportum is so called.
60. The same, in book sixty-ninth on the Edict.

units.la: Locus {d} est non fundus,sed portio {e} aliqua fundi. fundus {f} autem integrum aliquid est. & plerumque lineꝝ villa {g} locum accipimus. Caeterum adeo s opinio nostra & constitutio locum à fundo separat, vt & modicus {h} locus possit fundus dici, si fundi animo eum habuimus. Non etiam magnitudo locum à fundo separat, sed nostra affectio. & quàlibet {i} portio fundi poterit fundus dici, si iam hoc constituerimus. necnon & fundus, locus constitui potest. nam, iuris: adde Es eum alij adiunxerimus {k} fundo, locus fundi elficietur, {l} ¶Loci appellationem non solùm ad rustica {m}, verùm ad vrbana quoque prædia pertinere, Labeo scribit. {n} ¶ Sed fundus quidem suos habet fines {o}: locus verò latere potest, quatenus determinetur, & definietur.
units.tr: A place (locus) is not a farm (fundus), but some portion of a farm. A farm, however, is something whole. And in common usage we take locus for a villa, or a country house. Moreover, our opinion and decision separate place from farm so much that even a small place can be called a farm, if we have held it with the intention of a farm. Nor does size separate place from farm, but our disposition does. And any portion of a farm can be called a farm, if we have so decided. Likewise a farm can be constituted as a place. For, by law, if we add it to a farm, as others have joined it, it becomes a place of the farm. Ulpian writes: ¶ Labeo writes that the name locus applies not only to rural estates but also to urban properties. ¶ But a farm indeed has its own boundaries; a place, however, can lie hidden, until it is determined and defined.
61. Paul, in book sixty-fifth on the Edict.

units.tr: (Varro, book 4 de lingua.) {b} A place is a portion of a farm; Eclogue 2, ch. 6. {f} Add l. 115, §. eo. {g} And without a building, if it is in the city, that open space is called a place; if outside the city, a field; l. 201, §. eo. {h} Hence that saying of Cicero: Varro calls a farm that which I could throw with a sling, "unless it has fallen where the sling's hollow lies open." Yet I see that Varro in book 4 de lingua says a farm is so called because it yields (fundat) much every year. Festus, however, says a farm is a flat field, like the bottom (fundus) of vessels. Isidore's etymology is more useful to the householder and the kitchen: Origines 15, 13: a farm is so called because the patrimony is founded and established in it. {i} l. 34, in fine, §. de legatis. {k} l. 6, §. 1, §. communia praediorum; l. 24, §. 2, §. de legat. {l} l. 211, §. eo; Eclogue cited ch. 6, 15; Isidore 13. {m} Hence the boundaries of a farm, l. 4, §. 8, §. finium regundorum; l. 54, §. de legat. 2. {n} Elsewhere it is opposed to a bare security, l. 45, §. de procuratoribus; l. 5, §. de hereditate petit.; l. 56, §. de cognitionibus; l. 2, in fine, §. quod legatorum; l. 1, §. 3, in fine, §. de stipul. praetor. {o} Bare, namely ὁ μὴ λεγίας [?], Eclogue 2, ch. 61; on which see l. 1, §. 5 and following, §. de stipulat. strictum. {p} A stipulation between the strict parties, to which a satisdation was owed.

units.la: 61. Gaius libro vicesimo sexto ad Edictum Prouinciale.
units.tr: 61. Gaius in book twenty-sixth on the Provincial Edict.

units.la: {Tigni}Tigni{a} appellatione in lege duodecim tabula-rum omnem genus materiae, ex qua aedificia con-stant, significatur.
units.tr: Under the name of tignum (beam) in the Law of the Twelve Tables is signified every kind of material of which buildings consist.
63. Ulpian [in book seventy-first on the Edict.]

units.la: Penes{b} te amplius est, quàm apud{c} te. nam apud te est, quod qualiter qualiter a te tenetur[?]{d}: pe-nes te est, quod quodammodo possidetur.
units.tr: Penes te means more than apud te. For apud te is what is held by you in some way; penes te is what is in some measure possessed by you.
64. Paul, in book sixty-seventh on the Edict.

units.la: Intestatus{e} est, non tantum qui testamentum non fecit, sed etiam cuius ex testamento hereditas adita non est.
units.tr: One is intestate not only who has made no will, but also one whose inheritance under a will has not been entered upon.
65. Ulpian, book 72 on the Edict.

units.la: Heredis appellatio non solum ad proximum heredem, sed & ad ulteriores{f} refertur. nam & heredis heres, & deinceps, heredis appellatione con-tinetur.
units.tr: The term "heir" refers not only to the nearest heir but also to later heirs. For the heir of an heir, and so on down the line, is included under the term "heir."
66. The same author, book 74 on the Edict.

units.la: Mercis appellatio ad res mobiles{g} tantùm per-tinet.
units.tr: The term "merchandise" applies only to movable goods.

units.la: men illa duo confunduntur.{e} Intestatus dicitur, qui vel testamentum non fecit, vel heredem testamentarium non habet, Ecloga ibid.cap.64. cuius bonorum possessio à nemine petita est l.1. §. quia ordo, qui iure testamentum non fecit, aut cuius testamentum irritum est, vel ruptum: Instit. de heredit. quae ab intestato in principio: sed & is qui testari non potest l.1. §. de suis, vt & in tutelis, qui tutorem non dedit l.6. §.de legit. tut. §.2. Instit. de legitima adgnatorum. An aliud intestatum mori, quàm sine testamento? Inmola ait in l.15. §. de vulgari, & Raphael Fulgosius in l.6. Cod. de Instit. Briffonius negat. Porrò intestatus etiam alio sensu sumitur, cùm opponitur antestato, id est ei, qui testato conuentus est, vide Cuiacium 7. observat.16. Mercis verò causa parata, quae [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: Yet those two things are confused. He is said to be intestate who either has not made a will or has no heir appointed by will: Ecloga, ibid., chap. 64. Whose possession of goods has been sought by no one: l.1 §. quia ordo; one who has not made a will by right, or whose will is void or broken: Instit. de heredit. quae ab intestato, in principio; but also one who cannot make a will: l.1 §. de suis; as also in guardianships, one who has not appointed a guardian: l.6 §. de legit. tut.; §.2 Instit. de legitima adgnatorum. Does dying intestate mean anything other than dying without a will? Inmola says yes in l.15 §. de vulgari; Raphael Fulgosius says so in l.6 Cod. de Instit.; Brisson denies it. Moreover, "intestate" is also taken in another sense, when it is set against "antestate," that is, one who has been sued as a witness to a will: see Cuiacius, Observations 7, chap. 16. But merchandise prepared for [illegible, about 20 letters]

units.tr: {f} l.170 §. eo; l.194 §. de regulis iuris; Ecloga, ibid., chap. 65. See l.70 §. eo.

units.la: {g} veluti vinum, oleum, & similia l.vltima, Cod. de conditione triticaria, non ad homines, qua de re vide legem 209.§.eo. vnde possis colligere, mobilium appellatione seruos non venire.
units.tr: {g} such as wine, oil, and the like: l. ultima Cod. de conditione triticaria. It does not apply to men, on which matter see law 209 §. eo. From this you may gather that servants are not included under the term "movables."

units.la: 67. Idem libro septuagesimo sexto ad Edictum.
units.tr: 67. The same author, book 76 on the Edict.

units.la: Alienatum{a} non proprie dicitur, quod adhuc in dominio venditoris manet. venditum tamen recte{b} dicetur. 1 ¶ Donationis verbum, simpliciter loquendo, omnem{c} donationem comprehendit: videtur{d}: siue mortis causa, siue non mortis causa fuerit.
units.tr: Something is not properly said to be alienated when it still remains in the seller's ownership, but it will rightly be said to be sold. 1 ¶ The word "donation," speaking simply, comprehends every gift; it is seen to be so whether it was made in view of death or not in view of death.

units.la: 68. Idem libro septuagesimo septimo ad Edictum.
units.tr: 68. The same author, book 77 on the Edict.

units.la: Illa verba arbitratu{e} Lucy Titii[?] fieri, ius{f} significat, & in seruum non cadunt.
units.tr: Those words, "to be done at the discretion of Lucius Titius," signify a right, and they do not fall upon a slave.

units.la: 69. Idem libro septuagesimo octavo ad Edictum.
units.tr: 69. The same author, book 78 on the Edict.

units.la: HAEc verba, Cui rei dolus malus absit[?], afuerit, generaliter comprehendant omnem{g} dolum, quicunque in hanc{h} rem admissus est, de qua stipulatio est interposita.
units.tr: These words, "provided that the fraud was not present" or "was absent," generally comprehend every fraud that has been committed in the matter about which the stipulation was made.

units.la: qui veniam: l.1. Cod. de fundo dotali: Improprie tamen alienasse dicitur, qui non dominium, sed ius aliquod rei transfulit l.28. §. eodem: puta possessionem l.4. §.2. §. de alienatione iudicii mutandi. quin alienatio latius patet, estque multiplex l.14. in fine §. qui & à quibus. qui vendit & tradit, alienat: alienat autem, nedum qui vendit, sed qui permutat, vel donat, Nouell.7. Qui mutuum mittit, quique hypothecae, pignori in vsufructum, vel emphyteusim dat l. ultima Cod. de rebus alien.
units.tr: Who grants permission: l.1 Cod. de fundo dotali. Yet someone is improperly said to have alienated who has transferred not ownership but some right in a thing: l.28 §. eodem; for example, possession: l.4 §.2 §. de alienatione iudicii mutandi. Indeed alienation extends more widely and takes many forms: l.14 in fine §. qui & à quibus. He who sells and hands over alienates; yet one alienates not only by selling but also by exchanging or giving: Novel. 7. He who lends a loan, and he who gives a pledge, a mortgage, a usufruct, or an emphyteusis: l. ultima Cod. de rebus alien.
{b} l.11 §.2 §.3 §. de adi. empti[?].

units.la: Sciendum est, heredem etiam per multas successiones accipi. nam paucis speciebus heredis appellatio proximum continet. Veluti in substitutione impuberis, quisquis mihi heres erit, idem filio heres esto: vbi heredis heres non continetur, quia incertus est. Item in lege Aelia Sentia lius heres proximus poterit libertum paternum vt ingratum accusare, non etiam heredi heres exhaeriterit. Idem dicitur in operarum exactione, vt filius heres exigere posset, non ex successione effectus. Verba haec, Is ad quem tales pertinet, nec intelligitur, vt, qui in vniuersum [?] dominio succedit, minimum vel iure ciuili vel iure praetorio succedit, continentur.
units.tr: It must be understood that an heir is also taken to mean one who succeeds through many successions. For in a few kinds of cases the term "heir" includes only the nearest heir. For example, in the substitution for a minor: whoever shall be my heir, let him be heir to my son; here the heir of the heir is not included, because he is uncertain. Likewise in the Lex Aelia Sentia, the nearest heir of a son may accuse a freedman of his father as ungrateful, but not the heir of an heir, who has inherited. The same is said in the exaction of services, so that a son could exact them as heir, though he had not become so by succession. The words "he to whom such things belong" are not understood to include one who succeeds to the whole ownership, but one who succeeds to a lesser right, either under civil law or under praetorian law.
7a. Ulpian, book 79 on the Edict.

units.la: vel vt ascendentes, vel vt collaterales: quin & fiscus heredis loco habetur. & generaliter ijsunt in ea causa quibus adquisita est hereditas ad Trebellianum de diuersis id est, tribus quae sequuntur & aliis eodem de quibus dicetur ad legem 194. §. de regulis iuris. prima exceptio regulae. l 227 in fine l.eo: l.8 in fine §.de vulgari: Edicto loco cap 70. nihil etiam ab eo legari poterit. Paulus §.fent.6 §.5. eaque erat olim causa, ob quam post mortem heredis legari non poterat. secunda exceptio regulae. l.pen. Cod. de liberis. & eorum liberis. Tertia exceptio regulae l.22 §.1 l.29 §.de operis libertorum: adde quartam exceptionem in vsufructu l.9 Cod. de vsufructu, adde quintam ex l.9 in fine §.de suis. vlteriore scilicet. in aedilium edicto, ita quoque accipitur is, ad quem res ea pertinet l.1 §.1 l.19 §.5: l.31 §.21 §.de aedilitio: adde l.1 §.de rebus eius: l.73 §.3 §.de legat.3: l.1 §.11 §.14 §.15 §. quod legatorum: l.53 §.de oblig. at in edicto de iureiurando etiam rei particularis successores intelliguntur l.7 l.8 §.de iureiurando. Idem in cautione de rato l.22 §.7 l.23 §.ratam rem. in adoptionis causa l.18 l.29 §.de adopt. & in lege Iulia de adulteriis l.27 §.de adult. eaque diuersitas sumitur pro subiecta materia, & aequitate, vt si aequum est etiam particulari successori succurri. Iisdem verbis intelligitur etiam curator bonis diffrahendis datus l.9 in principio, §.§. §.de rebus auth. spe successor l.1 §.10 §.12 §.de ventre in possessione, dominus l.33 §.tertio l.39 §.primo §.2, Sed praetoribus [?] Vlpianus.
units.tr: either as ascendants or as collaterals. Indeed the fiscus is also regarded as an heir. And generally those are in the same position to whom an inheritance has been acquired, with respect to the Trebellianic senatus-consultum, which is about the different things (that is, the three that follow and others) that will be discussed under the law 194, §. de regulis iuris. First exception to the rule: law 227 at the end, law eo; law 8 at the end, §. de vulgari; in the Edict, in the place cited at chapter 70. Nothing may even be bequeathed by him either. Paulus, Sent. 6, §5. This was formerly the reason why nothing could be bequeathed after the death of the heir. Second exception to the rule: law pen., Cod. de liberis et eorum liberis. Third exception to the rule: law 22 §1, law 29 §. de operis libertorum. Add a fourth exception in usufruct, law 9 Cod. de usufructu, and a fifth from law 9 at the end, §. de suis, namely in the wider sense. In the edict of the aediles, "the one to whom the thing pertains" is likewise understood in this way: law 1 §1, law 19 §5, law 31 §21, §. de aedilitio. Add law 1 §. de rebus eius; law 73 §3, §. de legatis 3; law 1 §§11, 14, 15, §. quod legatorum; law 53 §. de obligationibus. But in the edict on the oath, even successors to a particular thing are understood: law 7, law 8 §. de iureiurando. The same applies to the cautio de rato: law 22 §7, law 23 §. ratam rem. In the matter of adoption: law 18, law 29 §. de adoptionibus. And in the Julian law on adultery: law 27 §. de adulteriis. This difference is taken from the subject matter and from equity, so that if it is fair, relief is given even to a particular successor. In the same words is understood also a curator appointed to sell off goods: law 9 in principio, §§. §. de rebus auctoritate iudicis possidendis; a successor in hope: law 1 §§10, 12, §. de ventre in possessione; an owner: law 33 §tertio, law 39 §primo, §2. But Ulpian ... to the praetors.

units.la: Aliud est capere, aliud accipere. capere , cum esse[?]u accipitur. accipere est, si quis non accepit, vt habeat. ideoque non videtur quis capere, quod erit restituri. sicut peruenisse proprie illud illud dicitur, quod est remansurum . ¶Hæc verba, Hu[?] f rebus re[?]ctè præstari, hoc significant, ne quid periculum vel damnum g ex ea re stipulator sentiret.
units.tr: It is one thing to take (capere), another to receive (accipere). To take is used when a thing is had as one's own; to receive is when someone has not received so that he may have. And therefore a person is not thought to take what he will have to restore. Just as that is properly said to have arrived which is going to remain. The words "that the things be rightly delivered" mean this: that the stipulator should suffer no risk or loss from that thing.
72. Paulus, book 76 on the Edict.

units.la: HAEc verba in stipulatione posita, Eam rem re-stitui[?] fructus continent. Restitui enim verbum pro viri boni arbitrio est.
units.tr: These words, placed in a stipulation, "that the thing be restored," include its fruits. For "restore" is judged according to the discretion of a good man.

units.tr: {h} What is law generally stated of the whole is equally law of a part: law 7 ff. de pactis; law 76 ff. de rei vindicatione; law 2 §3 ff. de servitutibus rusticorum praediorum; law 25 ff. de usufructu; law 51 inf. ff. de administratione tutorum; law 82 inf. ff. de acquirenda hereditate; law 7 ff. de exceptione rei iudicatae; §vlt. Inst. quibus ex causis manumittuntur. An argument drawn from the whole will therefore hold for a part of an integral whole (such as a wall or a house; the usufruct of ownership; a table; a year: law 7 §6 ff. solutio), for a part of a quantity (a smaller number relative to a larger: law 10 ff. de regulis iuris; a particular statement relative to its universal: law 29 ff. de heredibus instituendis), for a part of a universal (such as a part of an inheritance relative to the inheritance itself: law 1 §1 ff. si pars hereditatis), and for a part in mode, or accidental, such as possession in good and bad faith: law 42, near the end, ff. de rebus creditis; law 40 ff. de rebus creditis; law 137 §1 ff. de verborum obligationibus. "To drive the olive press properly at the discretion of Lucius": Cato, On Farming, chapter 44. "That these things be properly given, and done with security": the same, chapter 146. "Do you promise that it is lawful to keep those sows properly?" Varro, On Farming, book 2, chapter 4. [Greek phrase, illegible in the scan], Ecloga book 2, chapter 73. Or "to be defended": law 63 ff. de iudiciis; law 10 ff. de administratione tutorum; law 5 §3 ff. quibus ex causis in possessionem. Restitution is not made properly without fruits: see law 35 ff. eodem; law 1 ff. usufructuarius quemadmodum cautionem; law 5 §3 ff. iudicatum solvi. Otherwise it means without fault, not by force, not secretly, not by permission: law 6 ff. de itinere actuque privato. Suitably, as it ought, usefully: law 20, at the end, ff. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum. In the order of law being observed: law 31 ff. de minoribus; law 2 ff. de inofficioso; law 2 §1 ff. ad senatusconsultum Velleianum; law 3 ff. de liberis et posthumis; law 6, at the end, ff. de iure patronatus; law 27 §1 ff. de liberali causa.

units.la: F{i}rugem pro reditu {i}appellari, non solum quod frumentis, aut {k}leguminibus: verum & quod ex vino siluis caeduis, cretifodinis, lapidicinis capitur. Iulianus scribit fruges omnes esse, quibus homo vescatur, falsum esse: non enim carnem {l}, aut aues fe-rasve, aut poma fruges dici. Frumentum {m}autem id esse, quod arista {c}se teneat, recte Gallum definisse. Lupinum vero & fabam fruges potius dici: quia non maiori natu liberorum anulum dari solitum a patre cum clauibus constat, ex lege 77. §.22. s.de legatis. Erant & alij, ornatus causa. 7.eodem. ad annulos fignatorios referri etiam potest l.30.s. de falsis. anulos etiam arrae nomine interdum dabant l.5.§.15.s.de institoria: l.11.§.6.s.de act.empt. Hic locus indicat fuisse & alios, a fignatoriis, anulos, ornatus causa: Paulus 3.sent.6.§.84:l.25.§.10.s.de auro: l.6.s.de bonis damnat. Aureis soli vtebantur ingenui, 19.Isid.32. vt & libertini si modo eos impetrassent v.s & Codice de iure aureorum anulorum. alias, libertini argenteo, serui ferreo vtebantur, & quidem vnico. pluribus enim vti olim infame erat. duobus virgines vti poterat, isque a sponso acceptis. horum qui Thyrius dicebatur, purus erat: samothracius, aureus quidem, sed capite ferreo: rngulus, genimatus v.Isidor.ib. v adde l.22.s.eo:l.81.l.vlt. 7.eo:l.28.§.4.s.de vsuru: l.137. §.1.s.de regulis iuris. d l.35.s.eo: Ecloga ib.cap.75: 6.Harmenop.3. in princ: l.28.s.de vei vindicat:l-31. s.de rebus credit. e adde l.53.s.eo. f l.25.s.de iure dotium:l.19. s.de liberali. g aut remisit l.10. s.de condiß.causa data: l.45.s.de condit.& demonstrat. h Ecloga ib.cap.77. i Sunt enim duo frugum genera: frumenta, vt triticum & ordeum: legumina, vt faba & cicer, Plin.18:v.Paulum 3.sent.6.§.78. k Fruges sunt quibus homo vescitur praeter carnem & poma. l Frumenti strictior appellatio, quam frugum. frumenti appellatione continetur hordeum, avena, triticum, siligo siue zea (Longobardi speltam vocant) secale siue tistha, milium, panicum, milium indicum (quod Accursio meleca, aliis surgum.) Triticum, per eminentiam, Galli blatum appellat a blateo colore, v.Cuia.ad l.96.s.de ver.obl. m in se Hal.vulg. arista ", sed siliqua continentur. quæ Servius apud Alfenum in frumento continere putat.
units.tr: "Crop" is called "return" not only in the sense of grain or pulse, but also what is taken from vineyards, from felled woods, from chalk pits and stone quarries. Julian writes that all the things on which a man feeds are crops; this is false, for meat or birds or wild beasts or fruit are not called crops. It is rightly defined that grain is that which holds itself upright on the ear, as Gallus defined it. Lupine and bean are rather called crops, because it is agreed that the father customarily gave the signet ring with keys to the eldest child, from law 77 §22 ff. de legatis. There were also others, for ornament. Law 7 eodem. The signet rings may also be referred to in law 30 ff. de falsis. Rings were also sometimes given in the name of earnest money: law 5 §15 ff. de institoria; law 11 §6 ff. de actionibus empti. This passage indicates that there were other rings, apart from signet rings, for ornament: Paulus, Sent. 3, 6, §84; law 25 §10 ff. de auro; law 6 ff. de bonis damnatorum. Only freeborn men used gold rings, Isidore, book 19, chapter 32; freedmen also, if they had obtained them, as in the Code, on the right of gold rings. Otherwise freedmen used silver rings and slaves iron, and only one. For to use several was once disgraceful; a virgin could use two, received from her betrothed. Of these, the one called Thyrian was plain; the Samothracian was gold, but with an iron bezel; the signet ring was ornamented. Isidore in the same place. Add law 22 §, eodem; law 81, last, ff. eodem; law 28 §4 ff. de usuris; law 137 §1 ff. de regulis iuris. {d} law 35 ff. eodem; Ecloga in the same place, chapter 75; Harmenopulus, book 3, in the beginning. Law 28 ff. de rei vindicatione; law 31 ff. de rebus creditis. {e} Add law 53 ff. eodem. {f} Law 25 ff. de iure dotium; law 19 ff. de liberali causa. {g} or remitted: law 10 ff. de condictione causa data; law 45 ff. de condicionibus et demonstrationibus. {h} Ecloga in the same place, chapter 77. {i} For there are two kinds of crops: grains, such as wheat and barley; pulses, such as bean and chickpea. Pliny, book 18. Paulus, Sent. 3, 6, §78. {k} Crops are those things on which man feeds, apart from meat and fruit. {l} The term grain is narrower than that of crops. Under the term grain are included barley, oats, wheat, spelt or emmer (the Lombards call it spelt), rye or tistha, millet, panic, Indian millet (which Accursius calls melica, others surgum). Wheat, by pre-eminence, the Gauls call blatum, from the colour blateum. See Cujas on law 96 ff. de verborum obligationibus. {m} In the Vulgate, "ear" is included, but not the husk; Servius, quoted by Alfenus, thinks that the husk is included in grain.
78. Paulus, Book 3 on Plautius.

units.la: INterdum {a} proprietatem [?] quoque verbum possef-sionis {b} significat {c}: sicut in eo, qui possessiones suas legasset, responsum est.
units.tr: Sometimes the word "possession" also signifies property, as in the response concerning a man who had bequeathed his possessions.

units.la: Impensæ {d} necessariæ {e} sunt, quæ si factæ non sint, res aut peritura aut deterior futura sit. 1 Vtiles impensas esse Fulcinius ait, quæ meliorem dotem faciant, non deteriorem esse, non sinant: ex quibus reditus mulieri adquiratur: sicuti arbusti pastinatione {f} vltrà quàm necesse fuerat: item domus atrinam {g} puerorum. quorum nomine onerari mulierem ignorantem {h} vel inuitam {i}, non oportet: ne {k} cogatur fundo, aut mancipiis carere. In his {l} iuris expositā.
units.tr: Necessary expenses are those which, if they were not made, would leave the thing either perished or worse. (1) Fulcinius says that useful expenses are those which make a dowry better and do not allow it to become worse, and from which income is gained for the wife: for example, the pruning of a vineyard beyond what was strictly necessary; likewise the atrium of a house, and the children's quarters. A wife who is ignorant of such expenses, or unwilling, should not be burdened with them in her name, lest she be forced to lose land or slaves. The law on these matters is set out here.

units.la: {a} nō semper. Est enim quiddam à proprietate seiunctum l. 115. §. 1. eo.
units.tr: {a} Not always. For there is something separated from ownership; see l. 115 §1 eo.

units.la: {b} Eccl. ib. c. 78. l. 41. §. 6. §. de legat. 3; l. 4. C. de contr. empt. l. vlt. Cod. de prædijs minor. ea significatione possessio significat agros late patentes.
