units.tr: {c} And conversely, ownership signifies possession; l. 15 Cod. de rei vindicat.

units.la: {d} Tres sunt impensarum species, necessariis, res non fit deterior: vtilibus, fit melior: voluptariis, speciosior.
units.tr: {d} There are three kinds of expenses: necessary, which do not make the thing worse; useful, which make it better; and voluptuary, which make it more splendid.

units.la: {e} Impensis necessariis non factis, res aut peritura, aut deterior futura est, vt hic. vt que necessitatem impendendi habeat l. 1. §. 1. l. 14. §. de impensis.
units.tr: {e} If necessary expenses are not made, the thing will either perish or become worse, as here; so one who has the duty to spend, see l. 1 §1, l. 14 §... de impensis.

units.la: {f} pastinum l. 7. in fine. §. fo-luto τε ἀλσκς φιλοκαλίᾳ Ecl. ib. c. 79: hinc, ager pastinandus l. 15. §. 1. §. quod vi: pastiones l. 8. in f. §. de instructio. Vt pastinum, ferramentum bifurcum quo femina panguntur: vnde etiam repastinatæ dictæ fuerunt vineæ. Columell. 18. vlt. Isidorus 14. Ager repastinatus, cuius natura immutatur fodiendo, v. 3. Columell. 13. 15. 16: Pallad. in Februario 2. c. 9. Pastinare Galli hortes. §. l. 27. in f. l. 28. §. de rei vindicat: l. 27. §. 2. §. de vsufructu: l. 25. §. de pignoratitia: l. 13. §. 12. §. de adl. empt: l. 6. §. de impensis: Seneca 9. controvers. 3: pete quantum vis pro disciplinis, imputa quantum vis pro alimentis. An sumptus studiorum causa facti à patre, in rationem portionis filij imputentur, v. l. 50. §. familiæ. An filiofamilias, studiorum causa, mutuum reddere dari possit v. l. 7. §. 13. §. de senatusc. Macedoniano. An seruus studiorum ac disciplinæ causa missus, desinat eius esse fundi in quo prius erat v. l. 78. §. de legat. 3: l. 20. §. 6. §. de instructio.
units.tr: {f} Pastinum: l. 7 in fine §... Greek: love of beauty [φιλοκαλίᾳ]; Ecl. ib. c. 79. Hence ager pastinandus, l. 15 §1 quod vi; pastiones, l. 8 in f. de instructo. A pastinum is a two-pronged digging tool with which the ground is dug; hence vineyards were also called repastinated. Columella 18 ult.; Isidore 14; a repastinated field is one whose nature is changed by digging; Columella 3, 13, 15, 16; Palladius in Februarius 2 c. 9. The French call pastinare "to dig". See also l. 27 in f.; l. 28 §... de rei vindicat.; l. 27 §2 de usufructu; l. 25 de pignoratitia; l. 13 §12 de adl. empt.; l. 6 de impensis. Seneca, Controversies 9.3: "Seek as much as you like for teaching, charge as much as you like for food." On whether expenses made by a father for his son's studies are charged against the son's share, see l. 50 familiae. On whether a son under power may be lent money for study, see l. 7 §13 de Senatusconsulto Macedoniano. On whether a slave sent for study or training ceases to belong to the estate where he was before, see l. 78 de legat. 3; l. 20 §6 de instructo.

units.la: {h} Nemo ignorans sumptibus est obnoxius l. 38. §. de rei vindicat: l. 25. in f. §. de pignoratitia: l. 8. §. de impensis: l. 3. §. de contraria tutela: l. 15. §. 34. in f. §. de damno: Harmenop. 3. titulo 9. in f.
units.tr: {h} No one who is ignorant is liable for expenses. See l. 38, §. de rei vindicatione; l. 25 in fine, §. de pignoratitia; l. 8, §. de impensis; l. 3, §. de contraria tutela; l. 15, §. 34 in fine, §. de damno; Harmenopulus, book 3, title 9, in fine.

units.la: {i} l. 27. inf. §. de rei vindic. {k} l. 8. §. de impensis. {l} d. l. §. de rei vindic. Imo non in his, sed in necessariis l. 1. §. 1. §. de impensis & pistrinum{a}, & horreum{b} infulx[?] dota-li adictum, plerumque dicemus. {c}¶Voluptarie sunt,quæ speciem duntaxat ornant,non etiam fructu augent: vt sunt viridia{c}, & aquæ salientes{d}, incrustationes{e}, loricationes{f}, pictura{g}.
units.tr: {i} l. 27 inf. de rei vindic. {k} l. 8 de impensis. {l} d. l. de rei vindic. Indeed we will say, for the most part, that these expenses are not among those, but among the necessary ones (l. 1 §1 de impensis), and the mill and granary attached to a dowry. {c} Voluptuary expenses are those which merely adorn the appearance and do not increase the yield: such as green gardens, splashing fountains, incrustations, plasterings, and paintings.
80. The same, Book 9 on Plautius.

units.la: IN{h} generali reperitione legatorum etiam datæ li-bertates continentur ex mente legis duodecim ta-bularum{i}.
units.tr: In the general reading of legacies, even liberties that were given are included, according to the intention of the law of the Twelve Tables.
81. The same, Book 10 on Plautius.

units.la: CVm prætor dicat, vt opus factum restituatur, etiam damnum datum actor consequi debet: nam verbo restitutionis{k} omnis vtilitas{l} actoris continetur.
units.tr: Since the praetor orders that the work done be restored, the plaintiff must also recover any damage caused; for the word "restitution" includes all the advantage of the plaintiff.
82. The same, Book 14 on Plautius.

units.la: VErbum Amplius{m} ad eum quoque pertinet,cui nihil{n} debetur. sicuti ex contrario minus{o} so-lutum videtur,etiam si nihil esset exactum.
units.tr: The word "more" (amplius) also applies to one to whom nothing is owed; conversely, "less" (minus) is taken to be paid even if nothing was collected.
83. Javolenus, Book 5, from Plautius.

units.la: PRoprie bona dici non possunt, quæ plus incom-modi{p},quam commodi habent.
units.tr: Things cannot properly be called goods if they have more inconvenience than advantage.

units.la: beis terra aggesta posita, quin supra ædes habebantur{d}. l. 12.{d} & in fenestris{q} 19.Plin.14. {d}ἀναβρυτὰ ὕδατα[?] Ecloga ib. quæ ex tubulis aut fistulis erumpunt: l.12. §.4. §.de instructo: v.l.11.§.de supelleƈtile: saliebant etiam vel cantharis vel rostris personarum: l. 43. §.11.§.de legatis 1: adde quæ notauit de salientibus adl. 15. l.17 §. 9.§.de actio. empti. {e}μαλαμάτων[?] Ecloga ib: hinc,incrustare parietem communem l.13.§.de ieruit. vrban: ollam sapa & farre, Varro 3.de re rustica 14. in sine: sincerum vas, Horat.1.Satyra 3.calicem Lucilius satyra 18,{f} est testacea struƈtura semifastigij, quæ mu-rum a stillicidio arcet [illegible, ~12 letters] hinc lorica testacea 2. Vitruvius: loricæ ex calce & arena inductæ 7. Vitruv. 1: alio sensu Varro loricare parietes. Varro 1. de re rustica 57: se loricare apud Plinium 8 cap.24: & lorica apud Vegetium, de quibus vide Philandrum in 7.Vitruuij 1. & Budæum hic.{g} l.38. §.de rei vindicat: l.13.in fine.§. de feruitut.vrban. [illegible, ~10 letters] Ecloga ib.de ratione pingendi in ædificijs, v.7.Vitruuij 5.{h} 2.Ecloga 2. cap.80: l.77.§.de legat.3.{i} de qua v.l.20.§.eo. l.{k} Ecloga ibidem cap.81. {l} v.l.75 §.eo. {m} de hoc verbo amplius,vide l.27.l.33.in fine,l.34.l.54.§.de legat. 3: l.77.§.de condic. & demonstr. l.1.§.11.§.si cui plus quam: l.4. §.1.§.de verborum obligat: l.14.l.15.l.23.§.ratam rem: l.24.l.31. Cod.de transactio. {n} l.108.§.§.§.de legat.1. {o} v.l.32.§.Verba. {p} v.l.49.§.eodem.
units.tr: A heap of earth thrown up... was considered to be above the houses; l. 12; and in windows, l. 19; Pliny 14. {d} Springing waters [ἀναβρυτὰ ὕδατα]: Ecloga ib.; these burst out of pipes or conduits; l. 12 §4 de instructo; see l. 11 §... de supellectile. They also used to spring from cups or from the mouths of masks; l. 43 §11 de legatis 1. Add what he noted about fountains on l. 15, l. 17 §9 de actio empti. {e} Plasterings [μαλαμάτων]: Ecloga ib. Hence to plaster a common wall, l. 13 §... de iure urbano; a pot of sapa and spelt, Varro 3 de re rustica 14 in fine; a clean vessel, Horace, Satires 1.3; a cup, Lucilius, Satire 18. A "testacea structura" is a half-gabled tiled structure which keeps the wall from the dripping of the eaves; hence "lorica testacea", Vitruvius 2; "loricae ex calce et arena inductae", Vitruvius 7 and 1; in another sense Varro speaks of "loricating" walls, Varro 1 de re rustica 57; "se loricare" in Pliny 8 cap. 24; and "lorica" in Vegetius, on which see Philander on Vitruvius 7.1 and Budaeus here. l. 38 de rei vindicat.; l. 13 in fine §... de servitutibus urbanorum. Ecloga ib. on the method of painting in buildings; see Vitruvius 7.5. {h} Ecloga 2, c. 80; l. 77 §... de legat. 3. {i} On which see l. 20 §... eo. {k} Ecloga ib. c. 81. {l} See l. 75 §... eo. {m} On the word "amplius", see l. 27, l. 33 in fine, l. 34, l. 54 §... de legat. 3; l. 77 §... de condic. et demonstr.; l. 1 §11 si cui plus quam; l. 4 §1 de verborum obligat.; l. 14, l. 15, l. 23 §... ratam rem; l. 24, l. 31 Cod. de transactionibus. {n} l. 108 de legat. 1. {o} See l. 32 §... Verba. {p} See l. 49 §... eodem.
84. Paulus, Book 2 on Vitellius.
By the word "sons" we understand all children.
85. Marcellus, Book 1 of the Digest.

units.la: Neratius Priscus tres facere existimat collegium, & hoc magis sequendum est.
units.tr: Neratius Priscus thinks that three persons make a college, and this view is to be followed more.
86. Celsus, Book 5 of the Digest.

units.la: Quid aliud sunt iura praediorum, quam praedia qualiter se habentia? ut bonitas, salubritas, amplitudo?
units.tr: What else are the rights of estates than estates in a certain condition, such as their goodness, healthfulness, and size?
87. Marcellus, Book 12 of the Digest.

units.la: Ut Alfenus ait, urbs est Roma, quae muro cinge-retur. Roma est etiam, qua continenti aedifi-cantis voluntate gantis voluntate l.41.§.5.ff. de leg.3: & in senatusconsulto Macedoniano, l.6.C.ad senatusc.Maced. & in eo senatusconsulto quo cavetur ne tutor pupillam filio suo elocet l.9.ff. de vitu. huiusmodi interpretatio usta est l.20.§.eo. nepos enim filij loco habendus est l.14.Cod.de inoff.testam. l.1.Cod.de natur.filiis. Vice versa, patris appellatione continetur avus l.20.& parentes pro parentibus accipiuntur l.20.§.de adulterijs. Cuiac.ad l.2.§.de excus.tutorum. hinc constat in omnibus prope, filij appellatione etiam nepotes contineri, in tutela nullo modo quamuis in eadem quaestione filiae comprehendantur l.16.ff. de testam.tutel. homines liberos. Quidam ita legunt apud Cuiacium d.loco. Monentur, quod servitijs cognatio nulla est l.1.§.1.ff.unde cognati: Ulp.12.§.3: Paul.4.sententi.10.§.2. Verum, in iis quae sunt naturae non parcimus his nominibus in ternis l.10.§.5.ff.de gradib. Imo pauciores, nam etsi in unum reciderit ius omnium, stat tamen universitatis nomen l.7.in f.§.quod cuiusque: adde l.4.o.in f.§.eo: Ecl.ib.c.4. ad vf.de collegiis. dem Titium restituere tenere praedia, cui suis iurib: adhaec, quaeri iuris nomine, quid intelligatur. [illegible, ~12 letters] c.8.5.An sunt servitutes? sic putat Fornerius 2. felcell.28. quod à Cuia cio 9. obser.37. non simpliciter probatur. monetur, quod ius emphiteuticor, sit ius praedij, non tamen servitus. iura tamen praediorum, quatenus definiuntur praedia [illegible, ~10 letters] (id est qualitatibus affecta, quarum nomine alienis praedijs subiiciuntur) servitutes dici posse, admittit. [illegible, ~8 letters] aequaliter vulg. Graeci ita explicant, iura praediorum sunt ipsa praedia [illegible, ~12 letters] &c. etiam intelligi de nova, seu Constantinopoli, quae iisdem privilegiis ac vetus, utitur, de qua vl.6.in f Cod.de sacr.Eccles. Utriusque etiam natalitia festiua sunt 7.Ecl.tit.17.cap.13. ut interim noremus idem aliis urbibus quantum ad patria attinet, dari: cum ex vico oritus, eam patriam habere intelligatur, cui Reipubl.vicus ille respondet l.3.§.ad municipalem. in continenti Hal.quantum continentia vulg. Romae igitur fieri intelligantur, quae in eius interclucia essent. nam Romam non muro tenus exstimari, ex consuetudine cottidiana diceremus Romam nos ire, etiam si extra urbem habitaremus.
units.tr: As Alfenus says, Rome is the city which is surrounded by a wall. Rome is also that which is continuous with the buildings, by the will of those building (l. 41 §5 ff. de legat. 3); and in the Senatusconsultum Macedonianum (l. 6 C. ad Senatusc. Maced.), and in that Senatusconsultum by which it is provided that a guardian may not marry his ward to his own son (l. 9 ff. de ritu nuptiarum). This interpretation has been used in l. 20 §... eo, for a grandson is to be counted in the place of a son (l. 14 Cod. de inoff. testam.; l. 1 Cod. de naturalibus filiis). Conversely, the word "father" includes the grandfather (l. 20), and "parents" are taken for parents (l. 20 §... de adulteriis; Cuiacius on l. 2 §... de excusationibus tutorum). Hence it is generally agreed that by the word "sons" grandsons are also included, though in guardianship not at all, although in the same question daughters are included (l. 16 ff. de testam. tutel.). "Free men": some read it thus in Cuiacius at the passage cited. It is warned that between slaves there is no kinship (l. 1 §1 ff. unde cognati; Ulpian 12 §3; Paulus, Sentences 4.10 §2). But in those things which belong to nature we do not spare these names in the third degree (l. 10 §5 ff. de gradibus). Indeed fewer: for although the right of all has come to one, the name of the body still stands (l. 7 in f. §... quod cuiusque; add l. 4 o. in f. §... eo; Ecloga ib. c. 4; ad ff. de collegiis). "To restore the estates to Titius, to whom they belong by their rights." Besides, one asks what is understood by the name of a right. [illegible] c. 8 §5: are they servitudes? Fornerius thinks so (2 Felcell. 28), which is not simply approved by Cuiacius (9 Observ. 37). It is warned that the emphyteutic right is a right of an estate, but not a servitude. Yet he admits that the rights of estates, insofar as estates are defined (that is, affected by qualities, for the sake of which they are made subject to other estates), can be called servitudes. [illegible] the common translation is the same; the Greeks explain it thus: the rights of estates are the estates themselves, [illegible] etc. It may also be understood of the new city, or of Constantinople, which uses the same privileges as the old, on which see l. 6 in f. Cod. de sacrosanctis Ecclesiis. Both birthdays are also festive: Ecloga 7, tit. 17, c. 13. So that meanwhile we may note that the same is given to other cities as far as one's native place goes: since one is understood to have that as native place from which one's village descends, to which the village of the state corresponds (l. 3 §... ad municipalem). "In the neighbourhood": Hal. "as far as neighbouring" in the common text. Therefore they are understood to be done in Rome which were in its boundaries; for we would say, from daily custom, that we go to Rome, even if we lived outside the city, since Rome is not reckoned up to the wall.
88. Celsus, book 18 of the Digests.

units.la: Antum relinquit, quantum ex bonis eius refici sic dicimus, centies , qui tantum in praediis, terisque similibus rebus habeat. Non fundo alieno , quanquam pecunia parari potest neque quisquam eum, qui pecuniam numeratam habet, habere dicit, quidquid ex ea parari potest.
units.tr: He leaves as much as we say can be made good out of his goods, a hundred times over, meaning one who has that much in estates, lands and similar things. Not in another's estate, although money can be got for it, nor does anyone say that a man who has money in cash has whatever can be got from that money.
89. Pomponius, book 6 on Sabinus.

units.la: BOues armentorum , quàm iumentorum generis appellantur. 1 nuptae erit, primae nuptiae significantur. 2 edere & reddi refecta pecunia, id est redacta
units.tr: Oxen are called part of the herds (armenta) rather than of the beasts of burden (iumenta). "Will be married" (nuptae erit) signifies a first marriage. "To give out and to return" money restored, that is, brought back in.

units.la: centum aureos ἑκατὸν ἑκατὸν χρυσᾶς ἑκατὸν, i. centum centenos habere summa decem millia aureorum nostrorum facit. Tantum quisque pecuniae relinquere intelligitur, quantum ex bonis eius refici potest, fundus alienus legatus, hereditaria pecunia parari potest. fuit igitur in pecunia defuncti fundus alienus. at non ita est, nec enim sequitur, ex pecunia hereditaria fundus Tuscula-nus emi potest, is igitur in hereditate fuit. An quia ad opus armorum (unde armenta Festus) bobus vel possumus? An quia armentum ab arando dicitur 12.Isid. 1. bos autem ad id natus videtur? quod magis est. ἀπολεγόμενα ἐκ ἔτι ἐκ τὰ δηλοῦνται Eclog. ib.c.89. Plus est enim reddere rationes, quàm edere, qui edere rationes iussus est, non reddit reliqua: sed qui reddere iussus est l.69 §.4.§.de cuiti: l.8.§.5: l.9.§.de liberationem: l.31.l.81.l.82.l.111.§.de condicionib.& demonstr.l.22.in f.§.de mammis. reliquam eo l.91.§.7.§. de fideicommiss.libert; l.26.§.de ftalib.l.31.§.de liberalit. l.4.C.de testamentis. qui edere iussus fit, reliquum reddere debet. nam & argentarius edere rationem videtur, etiamsi, quod reliquum fit apud eum,non soluat.
units.tr: A hundred aurei [ἑκατὸν ἑκατὸν χρυσᾶς ἑκατὸν], that is, a hundred hundreds, make a sum of ten thousand of our aurei. One is understood to leave as much money as can be made good out of his goods. A farm belonging to another, bequeathed, cannot be got from hereditary money. So a farm belonging to another was among the dead man's money. But that is not so, for it does not follow that the Tusculan farm can be bought with inherited money, and so it was among the inheritance. Or is it because oxen can be used for the work of arms (whence Festus derives armenta)? Or because armentum is named from ploughing (arare), and the ox seems born for that? The latter is more likely. The Greek words [ἀπολεγόμενα ἐκ ἔτι ἐκ τὰ δηλοῦνται] are in the Ecloga, book 1, chapter 89. For "to render an account" is more than "to show" an account: one ordered to show accounts does not hand over the balance, but one ordered to render is bound to pay it (Dig. 69 §4; 8 §5; 9; 31; 81; 82; 111; 22 in fine). One ordered to show is bound to pay the remainder (Dig. 91 §7; 26; 31; Cod. 4 on wills). A banker is also said to show an account even if he does not pay the balance owed by him.
90. Ulpian, book 27 on Sabinus.

units.la: Qui vti{a} optimæ maximæque sunt, ædes tradit: non hoc dicit, seruitutem illis deberi: sed{b} illud{c} solum,ipsas ædes liberas esse,hoc est,nulli seruire.
units.tr: Those who are of the best and greatest kind (the best and greatest estates) he hands over; he does not say that a servitude is owed to them, but only that the houses themselves are free, that is, serve no one.
91. Paulus, book 2 of the Fideicommissa.

units.la: Forum{e} & tuorum appellatione actiones quoque continueri[?], dicendum est.
units.tr: It must be said that under the name of "forum" and "tuorum" (of yours), actions are also included.
92. The same, book 7 of the Questions.

units.la: Proximus{d} est, cui{e} nemo antecedit, supremus est, quem nemo sequitur{f}.
units.tr: The nearest is the one whom no one precedes; the last is the one whom no one follows.
93. Celsus, book 19 of the Digests.

units.la: Quoetium[?]{g} & item mobilium appellatione idem significamus, si tamen apparet{h} defunctum a-
units.tr: Under the name of "quoetium" [unclear] and likewise of movables we mean the same thing, if however it appears that the deceased ...

units.la: §. 6. 5. unde cognati. f qui post aliquem,& post quem nemo d.l.34.supremus,aut solus l.162.1.eo.l.9 5.de reb.dub. sic supremæ tabulæ,post quas aliæ nullæ l.1.§ 1.1.in f.5.de bon. possess.contra tabulas.
units.tr: §6, 5: "whence cognates". "f" [marginal note]: one who comes after someone, and after whom no one comes (Dig. 34), or the last, or the only one (Dig. 162; 9 §5, de reb. dub.). So the "last tablets" are those after which there are no others (Dig. 1 §1 in fine, §5, de bon. poss., contra tabulas).
{g} I shall say elsewhere, in book 2, chapter 93, which things are considered movable and which immovable.

units.la: {h} Gilbertus Regius 2.Enantioph Florentinam interpretatur, nisi tamen apparet. sed Alciatus hic negatiuè ita legit,si non apparet,& ita exrat nō in mea vulgata editione,sed Hugonis à Porta. Alciati lectionem defendit Robertus 2.recept.30. Græci ita legunt [illegible, ~30 letters] &c.2.Ecl.2.c.93.i.nisi li probetur testatorem per mouentia,animalia intelligi. Reiectis superioribus lectionibus, Græca excepta, reperio res mouentes ab animalibus distingui l.2. §. de supellectile. Animales esse quæ se moueant vt hic,& ita coniun gi mobiles,vel se mouentes l.49.Cod.de Episcopis l.3.Cod.de seruitu tib:l.13.Cod familiæ: l.30.Cod.de iure dotium: l. unica §.7. Cod.de rei uxor: l.2.l.3.verfic.quæ omnia,Cod. de quadriennij præscripione: l.2. verfic.sed vbi quarta,Cod.quando & quibus quarta, mobilium appellatione intelligi animalia, excepto homine, seu seruo l.3.§.13.5.de acquir.possess.mouentes, quæ ab alio mouentur, putà supellectile l. 22.5.de supellectile,fructus l.vlt.§.2.5.de requirend.reu: adde l.32.in f.5.de usufructu legato. Has Græci [illegible, ~12 letters] illas [illegible, ~12 letters] Ecl. ib.appellant. Re ita constituta,demus testatori vtrasque fuisse,eique metem fuisse Titio supellectilis legandæ,quin & animalium, seu mobilium: demus his verbis legasse,Mouentia mea Titio do,lego. quæ-ro an animalia debeantur? non debebuntur (in quiunt Græci) nisi Probetur te-statorem per monentia intellexisse animalia. Recur-rendum est i-gitur ad mentem testatoris scripto de ficiente. At, inquies, mo-uentium ap-pellatione, mobilia non posse intelli-gi. Imo pos-sunt: in eo v-tique conueniunt, quòd moueantur, quamuis (sic enim interpretor vocem, quia 1.[?] cod.) mouentia ab alio, mobilia à seipsis moueatur. nouum autem non est, vt testator appellationes rebus, alias seu impropriasi tribuat l.9.ff.de vsufr. legat. Video quoque Iurisconsultum illa duo confudisse inter se in l.15. §.1. ff. de re iudicata, & quòd magis est, mobilium duas species fecisse, vnam animalium, alteram eorum, quæ anima carent l.1.§.1.ff.de rei vindicat.l.30.§.4. ff.de adqu.poss.ff. hinc videmus, pecuniam mobilium appellatione coprehendi l.79.§.1.ff.de leg.3. {a} nimalia[?] duntaxat, quia se ipsa mouerent, mouentia vocasse. quod verum est.
units.tr: {h} Gilbertus Regius, in Enantiophanes book 2, reads "Florentine": "unless however it appears." But Alciatus reads it here negatively, "if it does not appear," and so it is in Hugo à Porta's edition, not in my common edition. Robertus, in Receptae book 2 chapter 30, defends Alciatus's reading. The Greek reads in this way [illegible]. In book 2 of the Ecloga, chapter 93, that is, unless it is proved that the testator understood by "moving things" animals. Setting aside the earlier readings, apart from the Greek, I find that moving things (res mouentes) are distinguished from animals (Dig. 2 §de supellectile). Animals are those which move themselves, as here, and so movables are joined to self-movers (Cod. 49, de episcopis; Cod. 3, de servitutibus; Cod. 13, familiae; Cod. 30, de iure dotium; Cod. unica §7, de rei uxoriae; Cod. 2 and 3 verf. "quae omnia," de quadrienni praescriptione; Cod. 2 verf. "sed ubi quarta," quando et quibus quarta). Under the name of movables are understood animals, excluding man or slave (Dig. 3 §13, §5 de acquir. poss.). Things moved by another, such as furniture (Dig. 22 §5 de supellectile) and fruits (Dig. last §2 §5 de requirend. reu; add Dig. 32 in fine, §5 de usufructu legato), the Greeks call by different names [illegible], in the Ecloga book ... Things being so arranged, let us suppose the testator had both kinds, and that he left Titius his furniture, and also his animals or movables. Let us suppose he left in these words: "I give and bequeath to Titius my moving things." I ask whether the animals are owed? They would not be owed, say the Greeks, unless it is proved that the testator by "moving things" meant animals. We must therefore return to the mind of the testator, the written words being deficient. But, you will say, under the name of "moving things" movables cannot be understood. Indeed they can: they agree in this, that they are moved, although (for so I interpret the word, since it is in the ...) moving things are moved by another, movables by themselves. It is not new for a testator to give names to things in a different or improper sense (Dig. 9, de usufr. legato). I see also that the jurist confused those two things in Dig. 15 §1, de re iudicata, and, what is more, made two kinds of movables, one of animals, the other of those that lack a soul (Dig. 1 §1, de rei vindicatione; Dig. 30 §4, de adqu. poss.). Hence we see that money is included under the name of movables (Dig. 79 §1, de legatis 3). Only animals, because they move themselves, were called moving things. This is true.
94. The same, book 20 of the Digests.

units.la: VErbum reddendi quanquàm significatum habet retro {a} dandi, recipit {b} tamen & per se dandi significationem {c}.
units.tr: Although the word "reddere" (to render) has the meaning of giving back, it nonetheless also takes on the meaning of giving on its own.
95. Marcellus, book 14 of the Digests.
The term "reliquorum" (of the remainders) can also signify all of them.
96. Celsus, book 25 of the Digests.

units.la: Itus {e} est, quousque maximus {f} fluctus {g} à mari puenit {h}.idq; Marcū Tullii aiunt, cùm arbiter esset, primum constituisse. ¶ Praedia dicimus {i}
units.tr: Access (itus) extends as far as the greatest wave reaches from the sea. They say Marcus Tullius first laid this down when he was arbiter. We call estates (praedia) ...

units.la: {a} reddere proprie est retro dare. id est dare quod antea accepimus vt hic & l.39.§ 2.ff.de statulib.
units.tr: {a} "Reddere" properly means to give back, that is, to give what we received before, as here and in Dig. 39 §2, de statuliberis.

units.la: {b} non ex proprietate sermonis l.1.§.37. in f.s. depositi: sed ex interpretatione legis. ex legibus autem id esse dicitur, quod ex legis inter pretatione est l.6.in f.s.co l.21.in f.s.de legat.2: l.93.§.1.s.100 s.de legat.3: l.2.Ecl.2.c.94.
units.tr: {b} Not from the proper sense of the word (Dig. 1 §37 in fine, §5 depositi), but from the interpretation of the law. Something is said to be from the law when it is from the legal interpretation (Dig. 6 in fine; 21 in fine, de legatis 2; 93 §1, §100 §5 de legatis 3; Ecloga book 2 chapter 94).

units.la: {c} Ergo & reddere iussus, dare tenetur d.l.100. & redditio mutabit fideicommissum d.l.93.
units.tr: {c} Therefore one ordered to render is bound to give (Dig. 100). And a rendering will alter a fideicommissum (Dig. 93).
{d} See Dig. 160.
{e} See Dig. 112 in fine; Ecloga, same book, chapter 95.

units.la: {f} τὸ μέγιστον χῦμα Ecl.ib. hybernus §.3.Inst.de rer.diuif. μέχρις δὲ τὸ χειμέριον χῦμα ξέ- σι 2.Harm.1.c. [illegible, ~20 letters] vtrúque coiungit Theophilus, Inst.de rer.diuif. μέχρις δὲ τὸ χειμέριον χῦμα fluctus maximus decumanus dicitur: decimus enim talis est, vt inter omnia decimum maius censeatur Festus. sic decumana pyra 12.Columell.12. decumana porta in castris praecipua Caesar 3, de bello Gallico. decumanus accipenser Cicero 2. de finibus.
units.tr: {f} the greatest surge [τὸ μέγιστον χῦμα], Ecloga, same book; hibernal (Inst. 2 §3, de rerum divisione). as far as the winter surge reaches [μέχρις δὲ τὸ χειμέριον χῦμα ξέσι], Harmenopulus book 2 chapter 1 [illegible]. Theophilus joins both, Inst. de rerum divisione: as far as the winter surge [μέχρις δὲ τὸ χειμέριον χῦμα]. The greatest wave is called "decumanus," for the tenth is such that among all the tenth is thought the largest (Festus). So "decumana pear" (Columella 12); "decumana gate," the chief gate in a camp (Caesar, Gallic War 3); "decumanus sturgeon" (Cicero, De finibus 2).

units.la: {g} Quid littus? quà fluctus eludit Cic.in Topicis: adde Quint.5.Inst.vit.[?]
units.tr: {g} What is a shore? Where the waves break against it (Cicero, Topics; add Quintilian 5, Institutes).

units.la: {h} eludit Cic ib.vel,vt est apud Isidorum, c.8. alludit Quintil.ib. exaestuat & effluit l.112. ff.ea. excurrit §.3. Inst.de rer.diuif. ἐξαίρει[?] Ecl.ib.c.112 littus est, vel quòd fluctibus eluditur, vel quod aqua alluitur 14.Isidor.8.
units.tr: {h} "eludit" (plays against) in Cicero, same place; or, as in Isidore chapter 8, "alludit" (washes against) in Quintilian, same place; "exaestuat" (surges) and "effluit" (flows out) Dig. 112, ea; "excurrit" (runs out) Inst. 2 §3, de rerum divisione. The Greek [ἐξαίρει] Ecloga, same place, chapter 112. The shore is either because it is played upon by the waves, or because it is washed by water (Isidore, Etymologies 14, 8).

units.la: {i} rationem dubitan di fume[?] ex lege 25. ff.cod. §.1. ff.de diuif.rer.l.10.ff.de auro. aliquorum esse, non {a}vtique communiter habentiū ea, sed ‖vel‖ alio aliud habente.
units.tr: {i} The reason for doubt, from Dig. 25 of the same title, §1 of de divisione rerum; Dig. 10 de auro. Belonging to some, not necessarily to all who hold them in common, but either one holding one thing or another.
97. The same, book 32 of the Digests.

units.la: Cum stipulamur, Quanta {b}pecunia ex hereditate Titij ad te peruenerit: res {c}ipsas, quæ peruenerunt, non {d}pretia earum spectare videmur.
units.tr: When we stipulate, "how much money has come to you from the inheritance of Titius," we seem to look at the things themselves which came, not at their prices.
98. The same, book 39 of the Digests.

units.la: Cum bisextum Kalendis est: nihil refert, ‖vtrum‖ priore an posteriore die quis natus sit, & deinceps sextum Kalendas eius natalis dies est. nam id vi-duum pro {f}vno die habetur: sed posterior dies {g}intercalatur, non prior. ideo quo anno intercalatum non est, sexto Kalendas natus, cum bisextum Kalendis est, priorem diem natalem habet. {1} ¶Cato putat, mensem intercalarem {h}additicium esse, omnesque eius dies pro momento temporis obseruat, extremoque diei mensis Februarij adtribuit Quintus Mucius. {2} ¶Mensis autem intercalaris constat ex diebus viginti octo.
units.tr: When there is a bissextile year at the Kalends, it makes no difference whether a man was born on the earlier or the later of the two days; and thereafter his birthday falls on the sixth day before the Kalends. For that doubled day is regarded as one day, but the later day is the intercalated one, not the earlier. So in a year in which nothing was intercalated, one born on the sixth day before the Kalends, when there is a bissextile year at the Kalends, has the earlier day as birthday. (1) Cato thinks the intercalary month is an addition, and observes all its days as a moment of time; Quintus Mucius assigns it to the end of the day of the month of February. (2) The intercalary month consists of twenty-eight days.

units.la: 99. Vlpianus libro tertio de officio consulis.
units.tr: 99. Ulpian, book 3, On the Duties of the Consul.

units.la: Nomen {i}accipere possumus & cognitionem iurisdictionem. {1} ¶Continentes {k}prouincias accipere debemus eas, quæ Italiæ iunctæ sunt: vtputa Galliam. sed & prouinciam Siciliam magis inter continentes accipere nos oportet, quæ modico alio habet commune. sed tamen ius controuersum recte tur, Aliquorum etiam dici, non tantum ea quæ diuisa, sed quæ adhuc communia sunt & notum est illud, quod commune est, qua si meum est l.5 §.pro socio: l.46. §.de vitu: l.15.§.36. §.de iniur. {b} Eclog.ibi-dem. {c}97: adde l.29.§.2. §.de legat.3. {c} Pecuniæ verbo in hac stipulatione, res hereditarias, non earum precia stipulari intelligimur {d} aliud videbatur ex lege 178.§. eod. {e} bis sexto Calendas est, Hal. cum bissextum in calendis est vulgata cum bissextus Calendas est Hugo à Porta. Bissextus dicitur, q quarto quoq. anno dies vnus ad 6. Calendas Martias intercalatur. de bissexto v. quæ notaui ad l. 2.§.de diuers.&temporalibus. {f} l.3.§.3.6.Harm 3. {g} dies intercalaris ἐμβόλιμος, ipsa intercalatio ἐμβόλιμος, {h} eius inicium erat pridie Calendas Martias v.d.l.2. hic sublatus est à Iulio Cæsare, reste Suetonio: hodie annus constat diebus 365.v.l.134.§.cod. {i} 2.Ecl.2.c.99. {k} Cognitio, angustior est iurisdictione: vtraque angustior est notione l.5.§.de re iudicata, quid iurisdictio & cognitio, alibi dicam. {l} l.9.§.de iudicijs.
units.tr: We can take nomen to mean also cognitio and iurisdictio. {1} When we speak of continentes provinciae (provinces on the mainland), we should understand those joined to Italy, for instance Gaul. But the province of Sicily should also be counted among the mainland provinces, since it has little in common with the others. Yet the disputed law is rightly read: "of some" is said not only of things divided, but also of things still held in common. And the saying is well known, that what is common is as if it were mine: see l.5 §pro socio; l.46 §de vitu; l.15 §36 §de iniur. {b} Eclog. ibid. {c} 97: add l.29 §2 §de legat. 3. {c} By the word pecunia in this stipulation we understand the hereditary goods themselves, not their prices. The matter seemed otherwise under the law 178 §eod. {e} "bis sexto Calendas est" (Haloander); the Vulgate has "cum bissextus Calendas est" (Hugo à Porta). The leap year (bissextus) is so called because one day is intercalated every fourth year before the sixth day before the Calends of March. On the leap year, see what I have noted on l.2 §de diuers. & temporalibus. {f} l.3 §3, 6, Harm. 3. {g} The intercalary day is embolimos, and the intercalation itself is embolimos. {h} Its beginning was the day before the Calends of March (see the aforesaid l.2). This was abolished by Julius Caesar, as Suetonius reports. Today the year consists of 365 days: see l.134 §cod. {i} 2 Ecl. 2 c. 99. {k} Cognitio is narrower than iurisdictio; both are narrower than notio: see l.5 §de re iudicata. I shall say elsewhere what iurisdictio and cognitio are. {l} l.9 §de iudiciis.

units.la: ordo est inuersus, sic restituo, prædia dicimus aliquorum esse, non (hac particulam accipe pro nō solum) vti-que alio aliud habentes, sed communiter habentium, & ita perspicua est sententia. solent. n. enunciationes ab eo q perse ad id quod minus confessum est, assumere. Aliquo priuatum prædium habente, nemo dubitat, si cum prætor, prædium eius esse. dubitari potest, si cum controuersum recte tur, ita dirimitur, aliquorum etiam dici, non tantum ea quæ diuisa, sed quæ adhuc communia sunt, & notum est illud, quod commune est, qua si meum est.
units.tr: The order is inverted; I restore it thus: we say that estates belong to some people (take hac particula as "not only"), not indeed to those each having a different thing, but to those who hold in common. The meaning is thus clear. For they are accustomed to draw their statements from what is less agreed upon. If a private estate belongs to someone, no one doubts that it is his when the praetor says so. Doubt can arise when the matter is disputed. Thus it is resolved: "of some" is said not only of things divided, but also of things still held in common; and the saying is well known, that what is common is as if it were mine.

units.la: {a} Ordo est inuersus, sic restituo, prædia dicimus aliquorum esse, non vtique alio aliud habentes.
units.tr: {a} The order is inverted; I restore it thus: we say that estates belong to some, not indeed to those each having a different thing.

units.la: {b} Pecunia ex hereditate: res ipsas, quæ peruenerunt, non pretia earum spectare videmur. nam si ex Italia Romae petuntur in-strumeta, mi-nor dilatio dabitur, q; si ex continen-tibus prouin-ciis c dignosce-mus, si in præsentia per-sonæ &c. Haloand. d ob præsentiam personæ, quæ actum gessit dilationem petit, qui tempus prorogari postulat ob absentiâ eius qui gessit: e sensus est, Instrumenta, sunt etiam personæ, quæ ad litis instructionem facere possunt. & breuiter, instrumenta sunt, quæ causam instruunt v.l.1.s.de fide instrum. f alias seruo homini, testimonij dictio non est. g Seruus actor est præstantissimus §.7. Ins. de iniuriis: l.vlt. s.de officio præsidis: l.30.s.de legat.1: l.40.§.3 s.de statulib.l.5.§.3.s.de doli exceptt. h [illegible, ~20 letters] Ecl.ib.c.100: his verbis speciabiles inteiligit Alciatus, q; non placet. i Intersenatores sunt tria tantum dignitatum genera, clarissimi, spectabiles (hæc dignitas à Iustiniano Noue.7.media dicitur) & Illustres. qui supra illustres sunt aliquam ex his dignitatibus habent, vel dicuntur illustrissimi. extra senatum equestris, perfectissima, & est egregia Cuiac. ad tit. de dignitatib. de quibus alibi dicam pleniùs. s & ita fœminas, quæ maritorum dignitate illustrantur l.1. s.de senato-ribus. ℓ honor laticlaui, vel laticlauij, quibusdam, à principibus dabatur.de quo vide Petrum Fabrum 1.femest.2. m v.l.6.§.1.s.de adult.adde 2.Eclog.2.c.101:6.Harmenop.in prin. n Eclog. ibidem:6.Harmenop.3.vide s.de dinortijs, ideóque sponsa non rede-diuertisse dicitur l.191.s.cod. o vide l.1.§.7.s.de adilitio Eclog. ibid. & 19. tit. 10. cap.1. Græci morbum ; s vitium, [illegible, ~6 letters] appellant Eclog.ibid. temporalem corporis imbecillitatem: vitium verò perpetuum corporis impedimentum, veluti fi talú excussit nam & luscus itaq.vitiosus est. 3 Servis legatis etiam ancillas deberi, quidam putant: quasi commune nomen vtrumque sexum contineat.
units.tr: {b} By "money from the inheritance" we seem to mean the things themselves that have come in, not their prices. For if the documents are demanded at Rome from Italy, a shorter delay will be granted than if we learn of them from the mainland provinces, if in the presence of the person, etc. Haloander. {d} Because of the presence of the person who did the act, he seeks a delay; he who asks that the time be extended asks it because of the absence of the one who did the act. {e} The sense is: "instruments" also include persons who can help in preparing the lawsuit. In short, instruments are whatever establish the case: see l.1 §de fide instrum. {f} Otherwise, testimony is not given by a slave. {g} A slave is the most excellent witness: §7 Ins. de iniuriis; l.last §de officio praesidis; l.30 §de legat. 1; l.40 §3 §de statulib.; l.5 §3 §de doli exceptt. {h} [illegible] Ecl. ib. c. 100. Alciatus understands "speciabiles" in these words, which I do not approve. {i} Among senators there are only three kinds of dignity: clarissimi, spectabiles (this dignity is called "middle" by Justinian in Novel 7), and illustres. Those who are above the illustres hold some one of these dignities, or are called illustrissimi. Outside the senate is the equestrian order, the most perfect, and it is the outstanding one (Cujas on the title de dignitatibus). I shall speak of these more fully elsewhere. {k} And so women are also ennobled by their husbands' dignity: l.1 §de senatoribus. {l} The honour of the broad stripe (laticlavus), or of the broad stripe, was given to some by the emperors. On this see Pierre Faure (Faber) 1, femest. 2. {m} See l.6 §1 §de adult.; add 2 Eclog. 2 c. 101; 6 Harmenop. in prin. {n} Eclog. ibid.; 6 Harmenop. 3. See §de dinortijs, and therefore a betrothed woman is said not to have returned: l.191 §cod. {o} See l.1 §7 §de aedilicio edicto, Eclog. ibid., and title 10, chapter 1. The Greeks call a temporary weakness of the body nosos, but a permanent impediment of the body vitium, as when one has lost the knucklebones (talus) of the dice; for a one-eyed man is also therefore vitiosus. {3} Some think that when slaves are bequeathed, female slaves are also owed, as if the common word servi contained both sexes.
102. Ulpian, book 7 of the Regulae.

units.la: Derogatur legi, aut abrogatur. derogatur legi, cùm pars detrahitur, abrogatur legi, cùm prior sus tollitur.
units.tr: A law is derogated or abrogated. A law is derogated when a part of it is taken away; it is abrogated when the earlier law is wholly removed.
103. Ulpian, book 8 of the Regulae.

units.la: Icèt capitalis Latinè loquentibus omnis causa existimationis videatur: tamen appellatio capitalis, mortis, vel amissionis ciuitatis, intelligenda est.
units.tr: Although in Latin speech every cause affecting reputation may seem capital, the term "capital" must be understood as referring to death or the loss of citizenship.
104. Ulpian, book 2 of the Excusationes.

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] Atorum appellatio & ad nepotes extendi- ditur.
units.tr: [illegible] The appellation "of the grandchildren" (atorum) is also extended to nephews.
105. Ulpian, book 11 of the Responsa.

units.la: Modestinus respondit, his verbis, Libertis libertabusque meis, libertum libertæ testatoris non contineri.
units.tr: Modestinus replied in these words: "my freedmen and freedwomen": the freedman of a freedwoman of the testator is not included.

units.la: 106. Idem libro singulari de Præscri- ptionibus.
units.tr: 106. Ulpian, in his single book On Prescriptions.

units.la: Dimissoriæ litteræ dicuntur, quæ vulgò apostoli dicuntur. dimissoriæ autem dictæ, quòd causa ad eum, qui appellatus est, dimittitur.
units.tr: Letters of dismissal (dimissoriae litterae) are what are commonly called apostoli. They are called dimissoriae because the case is sent (dimittitur) to the one who has been appealed to.
107. Ulpian, book 3 of the Pandects.

units.la: Disignare libertum hoc est, testificari, cuius ex liberis libertum eum esse voluit.
units.tr: To designate a freedman means to testify whom he wished that freedman to be, among his children.

units.la: 3: Ecl.ib.c.101. c derogatur [illegible, ~10 letters] abrogatur [illegible, ~8 letters] Ecl.ibi.c.102. derogatur parti, totum abrogatur. Lactantius 6. c.8: legi diuinæ nec subrogari (sic enim legendum non propagari, nisi cum Pitheo 4. Notar. legamus abrogari) fas est, neque derogari ex hac aliquid licet, neque tota abrogari potest. Vlpianus in frag-mentis. lex rogatur, cùm fit: abrogatur, cùm prior tollitur: derogatur, cùm pars tollitur: subrogatur, cùm adiicitur: obrogatur, cùm mutatur aliquid. f sic Paulus 4. collat. primum caput legis Iuliæ de adulteriis prioribus legibus pluribus abrogat, & Liuius 9. vbi duæ leges sunt, semper antiquæ abrogat noua v. Pitheum 4. no-tar. §. v.l.28.5.de pœnis: 2. Ecl. 2. c. 103. b Ecl.ib.c.104: adde d.l. §6.5. eo: l. 2. §.7. in f. 5. de excusat. tut. i liberti appellatione, liberta quidem continetur l. 172. 7. eo. non libertus liberti Ecleg. ibid. c. 105. k v.l. vnicam 5. de libel-lis dimissoriis. l v.l 3. 5. de adsign. libert.
units.tr: 3 Ecl. ib. c. 101. {c} "derogatur" [illegible] "abrogatur" [illegible] Ecl. ibi. c. 102. Something is derogated from a part; the whole is abrogated. Lactantius, 6 c. 8: it is not lawful to rescind (subrogari; for thus we should read, not propagari, unless with Pithou, 4 Notar., we read abrogari) the divine law, nor may anything be derogated from it, nor can the whole be abrogated. Ulpian in the fragments: a law is "rogated" when it is made; it is "abrogated" when the earlier one is removed; it is "derogated" when a part is removed; it is "subrogated" when something is added; it is "obrogated" when something is changed. {f} So Paul, 4 Collatio, the first chapter of the Lex Julia on adultery, abrogates several earlier laws; and Livy, 9: where there are two laws, the new always abrogates the old: see Pithou 4 Notar. §; see l.28 §de poenis. 2 Ecl. 2 c. 103. {b} Ecl. ib. c. 104; add the aforesaid l. §6 §eo; l. 2 §7 in f. §de excusat. tut. {i} By the appellation "freedman" a freedwoman is indeed included: l.172 §eo. But a freedman is not included under "freedman of a freedman": Ecl. ibid. c. 105. {k} See the single law §de libellis dimissoriis. {l} See l.3 §de adsign. libert.

units.la: 108. Idem lib.4.Pandectarum. DEbitor {a}intelligatur {b}is, à quo inhito {c}exigi {d}pecunia potest.
units.tr: 108. Ulpian, book 4 of the Pandects. A debtor is understood to be one from whom money can be exacted even against his will.

units.la: 109. Idem lib.5.Pandectarum. BOnæ fidei emptor esse videtur, qui {e}ignorauit BEam rem alienam esse: aut putauit {f}eum, qui vendidit, ius vendendi habere, puta procuratorem, aut tutorem esse.
units.tr: 109. Ulpian, book 5 of the Pandects. A buyer in good faith is seen to be one who did not know that the thing was another's, or who thought that the seller had the right to sell, for instance a procurator or a guardian.

units.la: 110. Idem lib.6.Pandectarum. EQuester {g}dicitur, apud {h}quem plures eandem Srem, de qua controuersia est, deposuerunt: diftus ab eo, quod occurrenti, aut quasi sequenti eos, qui contendunt, committitur.
units.tr: 110. Ulpian, book 6 of the Pandects. A sequester is one with whom several people have deposited the same thing about which there is a dispute. He is so called from being placed in the way of (occurrenti) those who contend, or as one who follows (sequenti) them, and so is entrusted to them.

units.la: 111. Iauolenus lib.6.ex Cassio. CEnseri {i}est constituere, & præcipere. vnde etiam dicere solemus, Censeo, hoc facias: & semet {k}aliquid censuisse. Inde censoris {l}nomen videtur esse tractum.
units.tr: 111. Javolenus, book 6, from Cassius. To censure is to establish and to prescribe. Hence we also customarily say, "I censure that you do this," and that someone has censured something on his own account. From this the name of censor seems to have been derived.

units.la: 112. Idem lib.11.ex Cassio. ITus publicum est eatenus, quà maximè {m}fluctus exstituat {n}. Idemque iuris est in lacu {o}, nisi is totus privatus est.
units.tr: 112. Javolenus, book 11, from Cassius. A public shore extends as far as the waves reach. The same law holds for a lake, unless it is wholly private.

units.la: 113. Idem lib.14.ex Cassio. MOrbus sonticus {p}est, qui cuique rei nocet.
units.tr: 113. Javolenus, book 14, from Cassius. A sonticus disease is one that harms any affair.

units.la: 114. Idem lib.15: (ex Cassio.) Oluendo {q}esse nemo intelligitur, nisi qui solidum soluere.
units.tr: 114. Javolenus, book 15 (from Cassius). No one is understood to be able to pay unless he can pay the whole.

units.la: 115. Idem lib.4.Epistolarum. QVæstio est, fundus à {r}possessione vel agro
units.tr: 115. Javolenus, book 4 of the Epistles. The question is whether a farm is named from its possession or from its field

units.la: hinc sequestrare l.22.§.8.5.soluto: sequestratio C.de prohib.sequest.pecunia: sequestraria actio aduersus sequestrem l.9.§.3.5.de dolo: l.12.§.2,5.depositi: in sequestre deponere l.33.5.depositi.
units.tr: hence "to sequester" (sequestrare): l.22 §8 §soluto; sequestration (sequestratio): C. de prohib. sequest. pecunia; the sequestrary action against the sequester: l.9 §3 §de dolo; l.12 §2, §depositi; to deposit with a sequester: l.33 §depositi.

units.la: {h} hinc Tertullianus in libro de resurrectione carnis de domino loquens, hic sequester Dei atque hominum appellatus ex vtriusque partis deposito commisso filio.
units.tr: {h} Hence Tertullian, in his book on the resurrection of the flesh, speaking of the Lord, calls him "the sequester of God and men," committed to the Son from the deposit of both parties.

units.la: {i} Κτισει Ecl.ib.c.iii. censere Hal. vulg. {k} κατὰ ἑαυτὸν τί ποτε κεκρίκεναι [?] Ecl.ib. & senatum Hal. and. vulg.
units.tr: Ktisei [Κτισει], Ecl. lib. 3, cap. 3: "to judge" (censere), reading of Hal. and the Vulgate; "to have judged of himself whatever" [κατὰ ἑαυτὸν τί ποτε κεκρίκεναι], Ecl. lib. (same place); "and the senate", reading of Hal. and the other editions of the Vulgate.

units.la: {l} censoris nomen à censu l.2.§.17.5.de origine iuris. {m} qua maximus Ecolog.ibi.c.12. {n} dixi ad legem 96.5.eod. {o} de quo v.l.1. §.3.5.vt in flum.publ. {p} Ψυσος λεγεται Ecl.id.c.iij.v.l.4.§.5.legem vlt.5.de aedilitio addel.95.§.de reg.iur.
units.tr: The name of censor, from census. See l. 2 §17, 5, de origine iuris. "By which the greatest," Ecl. ib. cap. 12. I have said this on l. 96, 5, eod. Of which see l. 1 §3, 5, ut in flum. publ. "Is said" [Ψυσος λεγεται], Ecl. ib. cap. 3; see l. 4 §5, legem ult., 5, de aedilitio edicto; add l. 95, §de reg. iur.

units.la: {q} solidum non soluit, qui tardius l.12.inf.5.eo: qui nihil soluit,l.32.l.82.5.eod: qui non facit. {q} facere promisit l.176.§.eod. {r} puto id innui, vna & eadem res diuersas appellationes sortiri potest. sic terra, quatenus in eam quid agitur iure proprio ac nostro, ager: quatenus quotannis multa vel prædio quid distet. Fundus {a}est omne, quidquid solo tenetur. Ager est, [illegible, ~2 letters] species fundi ad vsum {b}hominis comparatur. Possessio ab agro {c}iuris proprietate distat. quidquid enim adprehendimus, cuius proprietas ad nos non pertinet, aut nec {d}potest pertinere: hoc possessionem appellamus. Possessio ergo vsus {e}. ager proprietas loci est. Prædium vtriusque suprascriptæ generale nomen est: nam & ager & possessio huius appellationis species sunt.
units.tr: He does not pay the whole who pays late (l. 12, inf., 5, eo); he who pays nothing (l. 32, l. 82, 5, eod.); he who does not do what he promised to do (l. 176, §eod.). I think this suggests that one and the same thing can have different names. Thus land, insofar as something is done on it by our own legal right, is called ager; insofar as it yields something each year, it is called prædium, or differs from a farm. Fundus is everything that is held by the ground. Ager is a kind of fundus that is set aside for human use. Possession differs from ager in legal ownership: for whatever we hold, whose ownership does not belong to us, or cannot belong to us, we call possession. Possession, therefore, is use; ager is the ownership of a place. Prædium is the general name for both of the above, for both ager and possession are kinds of this designation.
116. The same, book 7 of the Letters.

units.la: QVisquis mihi alius filij {f}filiusve heres sit, Labeo non videri filiam contineri : Proculus contra. mihi Labeo videtur verborum figuram sequi, Proculus contra. Proculus menerem restantis.respondit: Non dubito, quin Labeonis sententia vera non {g}sit.
units.tr: Whoever is heir to my son or daughter: Labeo does not think a daughter is included; Proculus disagrees. Labeo seems to me to follow the form of the words, Proculus the contrary. Proculus replied: I do not doubt that Labeo's opinion is not true.
117. The same, book 9 of the Letters.

units.la: NOn potest videri minus soluisse is, in quem amplioris {h}summæ actio non competit.
units.tr: He cannot be seen to have paid less, against whom an action for a larger sum does not lie.

units.la: 118. Pomponius libro secundo ad Quintum Mucium.
units.tr: 118. Pomponius, book 2 on Quintus Mucius.

units.la: HOstes {i}hi sunt, qui nobis aut quibus nos publice bellum decreuimus, ceteri latrones, aut prædones sunt.
units.tr: Enemies are those against whom we, or those by whom we, have publicly decreed war; the rest are brigands or pirates.
119. The same, book 3 on Quintus Mucius.

units.la: HEreditatis appellatio sine dubio continet etiam damnosam {k}hereditatem, iuris {l}enim non- vtique,si hereditatem proprie sumimus pro to-
units.tr: The word inheritance undoubtedly includes even a burdensome inheritance, since it is not always a matter of right, if we take inheritance strictly for the whole.

units.la: {a} quæ notaui ad l.178. in f.5.de verb.oblig: adde 2. Ecloga 2.cap.115.
units.tr: Which I have noted on l. 178, in f., 5, de verb. oblig.; add Ecl. 2, cap. 2, 115.

units.la: {b} Is esse potest sine villa l.27. 5.cod.
units.tr: He can be without any (property). See l. 27, 5, cod.

units.la: {c} Possessio est vsus rei a proprietate separatus.
units.tr: Possession is the use of a thing separated from ownership.

units.la: {d} Imò quis rem suam possidere potest l.1.§.2. 5.de acquiren.possess. vt e contrario, alienæ rei possessores esse possumus l.9. 5.de acq.possess. vnde bonæ & malæ fidei possessores distinguntur.
units.tr: Indeed, a man can possess his own thing (l. 1 §2, 5, de acquir. possess.), and conversely we can be possessors of another's thing (l. 9, 5, de acq. possess.); hence good-faith and bad-faith possessors are distinguished.

units.la: {e} & e contra, vsus est possessio, Horatius Quxdam,si credis consultis,mancipat vsus: & AElius Gallus,possessionem definit vsum.
units.tr: And conversely, use is possession. Horace: "Certain things, if you believe the learned, use takes by hand." And Aelius Gallus defines possession as use.
son or daughter as heir, reading of the Vulgate and Hal.

units.la: {g} Quid igitur hic statui oportet? nempe filij appellatione,filiam,non ex figura verborum,sed ex mente intelligi l.122.l.201.5.eo: l.16.5.de testam.tut.l.45.5.de leg.2:Ecl.ib.c.116.
units.tr: What then ought to be decided here? Surely that under the term son a daughter is understood, not from the form of the words but from the intention (l. 122, l. 201, 5, eo; l. 16, 5, de testam. tut.; l. 45, 5, de leg. 2; Ecl. lib. cap. 116).

units.la: {h} summæ ampliori,minor opponitur:qui amplioris, ab ea quæ est soluta,summæ non tenetur, minùs soluisse dici non potest adde l.32.5.eo.
units.tr: The greater sum is set against the smaller. He who is not bound for more than the sum paid cannot be said to have paid less; add l. 32, 5, eo.
l. 134, 5, eo; Ecl. ib. cap. 116. See l. 24, 5, de captiv.

units.la: {k} hereditas damnosa esse potest v.l.3.5.ad l.Falci bona non item v.l.39.§.1.5.cod.
units.tr: An inheritance can be burdensome; see l. 3, 5, ad l. Falcidiam. Goods are not likewise; see l. 39 §1, 5, cod.

units.la: {l} vel hinc constat,hereditatem iuris esse, quòd ea esse possit sine vllo corpore l.50.5.de har.pet.
units.tr: This too shows that an inheritance is a matter of right, since it can exist without any corporeal substance (l. 50, 5, de her. pet.).

units.la: Demus esse iuris, An ideo indiuidua? vtique,si hereditatem proprie sumimus pro tomen * est, sicuti bonorum possessio {b}.
units.tr: Let us grant that it is a matter of law. Is it therefore indivisible? Certainly, if we take "inheritance" strictly, but it is not so with bonorum possessio.

units.la: 120. Idem libro quinto ad Quintum Mucium.
units.tr: 120. The same, book five, on Quintus Mucius.

units.la: VErbis legis duodecim tabularum his, Uti {c} le-gafit sua rei, ita {d} ita esto, latissima potestas tributa videtur & heredis instituendi, & legata & liber-tates dandi, tutelas {f} quoque constituendi. Sed {g} id interpretatione coangustatum est vel legum, vel au-toritate iura constituentium.
units.tr: In the words of the law of the Twelve Tables, "As a man shall have legated concerning his property, so let it be law," the widest power seems to have been granted: to appoint an heir, to give legacies and freedoms, and to appoint guardians as well. But this has been narrowed by interpretation, either of the laws or of the authority of those who establish law.

units.la: 121. Idem libro sexto ad Quintum Mucium.
units.tr: 121. The same, book six, on Quintus Mucius.

units.la: VSura pecuniae {b}, qua percipimus, in fructu {i} non est: quia non ex ipso corpore, sed ex alia {k} causa est, id est, nova obligatione.
units.tr: Interest on money, which we receive, is not part of the fruit, because it does not arise from the principal itself but from another cause, namely a new obligation.

units.la: Qua iuris sunt, commoda, & incommoda continere possunt. Porro non sola hereditas, aut possessio in iure consistit, sed & alia, veluti usufructus, usus, obligationes §.2. Inst.de rebus corporalibus dos, peculium, seruitus, l.66 §.6. t.de legat.2. 4.15. §.2. t.de precario. l.vlt. in f.C.de praescript. longi temporis. Huius legis fragmentum extat in lege 53. t.eod. Integra vero ita legitur 1.ad Herennium. Paterfamilias vti super familia, pecuniaue sua legassit, ita ius esto. Adde l.1. t.ad l.Falci. Noueli. 22. c.2. Hinc Vlpianus, legata nobis adquiruntur ex lege XII. tabularum. Vlpian.12. §.17: adde l.47. inf.t.de peculio. Potestatis huius, testatori liberum est, tutorem subsituere priori lege pen. t.de testam.tut. Hugo à Porta. Id quod interest l.4. §.2. t.si seruitus vindicetur, & ipsi usurae improprie continentur l.34. t.de usuris. Nec tamen inde consequitur, usuras esse contrarias iuri naturali. Nam si ex obligatione causam habent ut hic & obligationes ad ius gentium, vel ciuile referuntur l. 5. inf.t.de iustitia & iure, dicendum erit ius utrumque naturæ repugnare, quod est absurdum. Si proximi mordendi (nam usuræ ab Hebræis Nesek. id est, a morsu dicuntur) libidinem ab usuris tuleris, perinde usuræ tolerari poterunt atque pensiones ædium conductarum, dimidium iusti non excedentes. Nihil enim interest fructum ex ædibus percipias, an ex nummis, sed de usuris alibi commodius.
units.tr: Things that belong to right can contain benefits and burdens. Moreover, not only inheritance or possession consists in law, but also other things, such as usufruct, use, obligations (§2, Inst. de rebus corporalibus), dowry, peculium, servitude (l. 66 §6, t. de legat. 2; l. 4, 15, §2, t. de precario; l. ult. in f., C. de praescript. longi temporis). A fragment of this law exists in law 53, t. eod. The whole, however, is read thus in the first book to Herennius: "If a father of a family has bequeathed the use of his family or money, let it be law." Add l. 1, t. ad l. Falcid.; Novel. 22, cap. 2. Hence Ulpian: legacies are acquired by us from the law of the Twelve Tables (Ulpian 12, §17); add l. 47, inf., t. de peculio. Of this power, it is free for the testator to appoint a guardian for a substitute, by the earlier law (pen., t. de testam. tut.). Hugo à Porta. That which is interesting (l. 4 §2, t. si seruitus vindicetur); and interest is improperly contained in the same sense (l. 34, t. de usuris). Nor does it follow from this that interest is contrary to natural law. For if they have their cause from an obligation, as here, and obligations are referred to the law of nations or to civil law (l. 5, inf., t. de iustitia et iure), it must be said that both laws are opposed to nature, which is absurd. If you remove from interest the lust for biting one's neighbour (for interest is called by the Hebrews Nesek, that is, from biting), then interest may be tolerated just as the rents of leased houses are tolerated, provided they do not exceed half of what is just. For it makes no difference whether you receive the fruit from houses or from money; but of interest, elsewhere more conveniently.

units.la: {c} Hæc facultas postea coangustata est, v.l.1. t.ad legem Falcidiam.
units.tr: This power was later narrowed. See l. 1, under the lex Falcidia.

units.la: 122. Idem libro octauo ad Quintum Mucium.
units.tr: 122. The same, book eight, on Quintus Mucius.

units.la: SEruius ait: si ita scriptum sit, Filio, filiusque meis hosce tutores do: masculis dumtaxat tutores datos: quoniam singulari casu hoc, filio, ad pluralem videtur transisse[?], continentem eundem sexum, quem singularis prior positus habuisset. sed hoc facti, non iuris habet quaestionem. potest enim fieri, vt singulari casu de filio senserit, deinde pleniùs omnibus liberis prospexisse in tutore dando voluerit. quod magis rationabile esse videtur.
units.tr: Servius says: if it is written thus, "To my son and sons, I give these guardians," guardians were given only for males, since in this singular case the word "filio" seems to have passed into the plural while keeping the same gender that the earlier singular had. But this is a question of fact, not of law. For it may be that he meant the singular case concerning a son, and then, in appointing a guardian, wished to provide more fully for all the children. This seems the more reasonable view.

units.la: 123. Idem libro vicesimo sexto ad Quintum Mucium.
units.tr: 123. The same, book twenty-six, on Quintus Mucius.

units.la: VErbum erit{b} interdum etiam praeteritum{c}, nec solùm futurum tempus demonstrat. quod est nobis necessarium scire, & cùm codicilli ita confirmati testamento fuerint, Quod in codicillis scriptum erit, vtrùmne futuri temporis demonstratio fiat, an etiam praeteriti, si ante scriptos codicillos quis relinquat. quod quidem ex voluntate scribentis interpretandum est. quemadmodum autem hoc verbum est non solùm praesens, sed & praeteritum tempus significat: ita & hoc verbum erit non solùm futurum, sed interdum etiam praeteritum tempus demonstrat. nam cùm dicimus, Lucius Titius solutus est [?]ab obligatione: & praeteritum & praesens significamus, sicut hoc, Lucius Titius alligatus est. & idem fit, cùm ita loquimur, Troia capta est. non enim ad praesentis facti demonstrationem refertur is sermo, sed ad praeteritum.
units.tr: A verb sometimes also refers to past time, and not only to the future. We need to know this when codicils confirmed by a will say What is written in the codicils shall be, whether it refers to future time only, or also to past time, if someone leaves codicils written before. This must indeed be interpreted from the will of the writer. Just as this verb is signifies not only the present but also the past tense, so the verb shall be sometimes signifies not only the future but also the past tense. For when we say Lucius Titius has been released from the obligation, we signify both past and present, as in Lucius Titius is bound. The same happens when we say Troy has been taken. For this speech refers not to the demonstration of a present act, but to a past one.
124. Proculus, book two of the Epistles.

units.la: HAEc{f} verba ille aut ille non solùm disiunctiuę, sed etiam subdisiunctiuae orationis sunt. Disiunctiuum est: veluti cùm dicimus, aut dies aut nox est. quorum posito altero, necesse est tolli alterum: ita sublato altero, poni alterum. ita simili figuratione verbum potest esse subdisiunctiuum. Subdisiunctiui proloquiis, & subdisiunctiuis inseruit. Caeterum disiunctiui proloquij, simul veri esse non possunt: subdisiunctiui, vel simul falsi vel simul veri esse possunt.{g} Gellius appellauit disiunctiuum, & disiunctiuū proloquium{h} ...
units.tr: These words ille aut ille belong not only to disjunctive but also to subdisjunctive speech. A disjunctive is, for example, when we say it is either day or night: if one of the two is posited, the other must be removed, and if one is removed, the other is posited. In a similar figure, a word may be subdisjunctive. Subdisjunctive premises are used in subdisjunctive inferences. Moreover, the premises of a disjunctive cannot both be true together, whereas those of a subdisjunctive can be both false or both true together. Gellius called it a disjunctive, and the disjunctive premise ...

units.la: {b} In proloquio disiunctiuo, necesse est alterum ex duobus quae disiunguntur, verum esse. §. Gell. 11. vel ita in disiunctione plus vno verum esse non potest. Cicero in Topicis.
units.tr: In a disjunctive premise, one of the two things disjoined must necessarily be true (Gell. 11). Or thus: in a disjunction, more than one cannot be true. Cicero in the Topics.

units.la: {i} subdisiunctiuū ὑποδιαζευκτικὸν [?] Eclog.ibid. autem genera sunt duo. Vnum, cùm ex propositis finibus ita non potest vterque esse, vt possit4 neuter esse, veluti cùm dicimus, aut sedet, aut ambulat. nam vt nemo potest virumque simul facere: ita aliquis potest neutrum, veluti is, qui accumbit. Alterius generis est, cùm ex propositis finibus ita non potest neuter esse, vt possit virumque esse, veluti cùm dicimus, omne animal aut facit, aut patitur. nullum est enim, quod nec faciat, nec patiatur: at potest simul & facere, & pati.
units.tr: The subdisjunctive (ὑποδιαζευκτικόν), from the Eclogae, has two kinds. In the first, of the stated alternatives both cannot be true, but neither need be true, as when we say: "he either sits or walks." For just as no one can do both at once, so someone can do neither, as one who reclines does. The second kind is when of the stated alternatives neither cannot be true, but both can be true, as when we say: "every animal either acts or is acted upon." For there is nothing that neither acts nor is acted upon, yet a thing can both act and be acted upon at once.
125. The same, Book 5 of the Letters.

units.la: NEpos Proculo suo salutem. Ab eo, qui ita dotem promisit, Cum {c}commodum erit, dotis filiae meae tibi erunt auuei centum, putásne protinus nuptiis factis dotem peti posse? quid, si ita promisisset, Cum potuero, doti erunt? quod si aliquam vim habeat posterior obligatio, possit verbum quomodo interpretaris? utrum aere alieno deducto, an extante? Proculus: Cum dotem quis [ita] promisit, Cum potuero, doti erunt centum: existimo ad id, quod actum est, interpretationem redigendam esse. nam qui ambiguè loquitur, id loquitur, quod ex his, quae significantur, sensisse existimem: {f}deducto aere alieno potero. potest etiam illa accipi significatio, cum salua {g}dignitate mea potero. quae interpretatio ea magis accipienda est, si ita promissum est, cum commodum erit. hoc {h}est, cum sine incommodo meo potero.
units.tr: Neratius to his Proculus, greeting. Suppose someone promised a dowry in these words: "When it is convenient, there will be a hundred aurei of my daughter's dowry for you." Do you think the dowry can be demanded straight after the wedding is made? What if he had promised: "When I am able, there will be a dowry"? And if a later obligation has any force, how do you interpret the word "able"? Is it with debt deducted, or as the estate now stands? Proculus: When someone promises a dowry in these words, "When I am able, there will be a hundred for the dowry," I think the interpretation must be governed by what was actually done. For a man who speaks ambiguously means what I judge he meant from among the things the words signify: that he can pay once his debts are deducted. The other meaning can also be taken: that he can pay with his dignity preserved. That interpretation is the more apt if the promise was "when it is convenient," that is, when he can pay without inconvenience to himself.

units.la: e Gellius ii. Noct. Attic. xi. Nullū, inquit, verbum est ambiguum (Chrysippus dicebat omne verbum esse ambiguū natura) nec quisquam ambiguū dicit aut sentit, nec aliud dici videri debet, quàm si dicere sentit, is qui dicit, at cùm ego aliud sentio, tu aliud accepisti, obscurè magis dictū quàm ambiguè videri potest. Ambigui verbi natura illa esse debuit, vt qui diceret duo vel plura diceret. Nemo a duo, vel plura dicit, qui se sentit vnū dicere.
units.tr: From Gellius, Attic Nights, Book 11: "No word is ambiguous," he says (Chrysippus used to say that every word is ambiguous by nature), "nor does anyone speak or understand an ambiguous thing, nor ought anything to seem said except what the speaker means to say. But when I mean one thing and you have understood another, what was said may seem obscure rather than ambiguous. The nature of an ambiguous word ought to be such that whoever uses it says two or more things. No one who knows that he means one thing says two or more."

units.la: {f} Posse facere promissor intelligitur aere alieno deducto, alias aere deducto posse facere, promissio est [illegible, ~8 letters]. nec enim posse videtur, q non potest nisi inhonestè, cum primùm incipit iste posse, primum incipit teneri: l.vltima, ff. de cond. Inst. l.29 ff. de aud. & dem. l.29 ff. quando dies legati. cùm res promissori in tuto esse incipiat. l.80 ff. de verb. oblig.
units.tr: The promisor is understood to be able to pay with debt deducted; otherwise the promise is to pay with debt deducted [illegible]. For a man does not seem able if he can act only dishonourably; as soon as he begins to be able, he begins to be bound: l. ultima ff. de cond. Inst.; l. 29 ff. de aud. & dem.; l. 29 ff. quando dies legati, when the matter begins to be safe for the promisor; l. 80 ff. de verb. oblig.

units.la: {g} tacita illa exceptio condicionib. inest l.35 ff. de neg. l.22 ff. de voxalib. l.vlt. ff. de act. empti v. l.137. §.4 ff. de verb. obl. l.105 ff. de solu.
units.tr: That tacit exception is implied in conditions: l. 35 ff. de neg.; l. 22 ff. de voxalib.; l. ult. ff. de act. empti; l. 137 §. 4 ff. de verb. obl.; l. 105 ff. de solu.
Note the definition from the removal of the contrary.
126. The same, Book 6 of the Letters.

units.la: SI,cum fundum tibi darem,legem ita dixi,Vti o-ptimus maximusque esset, & adieci, ius fundi dete-rius factum non esse per dominum{a} : praestitabitur{b}, amplius eo praestabitur nihil: etiam si prior pars, qua scriptum est,uti optimus maximusque sit, liberum{c} esse significat. eoque, si posterior pars adiecta non esset, liberum praestare deberem{d}. tamen inferiore parte satis me liberatum puto,quod ad iura attinet, ne quid aliud praestare debeam, quam ius fundi per dominum deterius factum non esse.
units.tr: If, when I gave you a field, I stated the condition thus, "that it be best and greatest," and added that its right had not been made worse by the owner, I shall be bound to warrant it, and nothing more will be owed beyond that, even though the first part, which says "that it be best and greatest," signifies that it is free. And so, if the added second part were not there, I ought to warrant it as free. Yet I think I am sufficiently released by the latter part, so far as rights are concerned, from warranting anything else than that the right of the field has not been made worse by the owner.
127. Callistratus, Book 4 on Cognitions.

units.la: VEstis appellatione tam virilis,quam muliebris{e}, & scaenica, etiam si tragica{f}, aut citharoedica sit,continetur.
units.tr: Under the term "clothing" (vestis) are included both men's and women's clothing, and theatrical clothing, even if it be tragic or citharoedic.

units.la: 128. Vlpianus [libro primo] ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 128. Ulpian [Book 1] on the Julian and Papian Law.

units.la: SPadonum{g} generalis appellatio est, quo nomine tam hi, qui natura{h} spadones sunt, Item thli-[?] eum fundum tradi emptori, cuius ius à domino. non esset factum deterius: venditor minime tenebitur ob seruitutes ei fundo ab aliis impositas, & ita generalis illa clausula vti optimus &c. restringitur per sequentem ius fundi &c.
units.tr: "Spadones" is a general term, under which name are included both those who are spadones by nature, and likewise ... that the field be handed over to the buyer, whose right from the owner had not been made worse: the seller will not be bound on account of servitudes imposed on that field by others, and so that general clause "as best and greatest, etc." is restricted by the following "the right of the field, etc."

units.la: {c} optimus ma ximus fundus.i.liber.non est liber,si ius eius à domino deterius factum est l.90.§.eo:l.169.§.eo: v. l.75. §.de cuiti:l.63.§.3.§.de legat.1.
units.tr: "Best and greatest field," that is, free. It is not free if its right has been made worse by the owner: l. 90 §. eo; l. 169 §. eo; v. l. 75 §. de cuiti; l. 63 §. 3 §. de legat. 1.
