units.la: {h} quales ij sunt qui ob meatum distortum coli,non ob infaecundum femen generare non possunt, quo vinculo abscisso generant Galenus 15. de vsu partium apud Prateium.generare possunt l.6.in f.§.de aedilitio spes est posse eos liberos procreare 19.Eclog.1.ex lib.60.sol.193. ideoque placeret ita scribi in lege 102.§.1.§.de adoptionib.& hi qui nondum generare possunt, vt eorum sterilitas (cuius sit mentio in lege 6.§.de liberis) temporaria sit, eòsque impediat inter morbosos censeri l.6.in f.§.de aedilitio, quod in castratis non est, à quibus sunt diuersi §.9. Inst.de adoptionib:l.6.l.7.§.de aedilitio:l.6.§.1.§.de liberis:l.14.in f.§.de manumiss.vindicta.Quod cum ita fit, non mirum spadonibus permitti matrimonium l.39.§.de iure dotium, & matrimonij causa ma-[?]ꝯmittere[?] l.14.in f.§.de manumiss.vindicta.adoptare.l.2.in f. l.47.in bie 4, thlasiæ b, sed & u quod aliud genus spadonum est,continentur.
units.tr: Such are those who cannot beget children because of a distorted passage, not because their seed is barren; when that obstruction is cut away they can beget. See Galen, On the Use of the Parts, Book 15, as cited in Prateius; they can beget, l. 6 in f. §. de aedilitio; there is hope that they can produce children (Eclogae 19, book 1, from Book 60, sol. 193). So it would please that it be written thus in law 102 §. 1 §. de adoptionibus; and those who cannot yet beget, so that their sterility (mentioned in law 6 §. de liberis) is temporary, and so that it prevents them from being counted among the sick (l. 6 in f. §. de aedilitio), which does not hold for eunuchs, from whom they differ (§. 9 Inst. de adoptionibus; l. 6, l. 7 §. de aedilitio; l. 6 §. 1 §. de liberis; l. 14 in f. §. de manumissione vindicta). Since this is so, it is not surprising that marriage is permitted to spadones (l. 39 §. de iure dotium), and that they may ... adopt (l. 2 in f.; l. 47 in ...), but also what other kind of spadones there is, are included.

units.la: 129. Paulus libro primo ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 129. Paulus, book one on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Qui mortui c nascuntur, neque nati, neque procreati videntur: quia numquam liberi appellari potuerunt.
units.tr: c Those who are born dead are seen neither as born nor as produced, because they could never be called children.

units.la: 130. Ulpianus libro secundo ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 130. Ulpian, book two on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Lege d obuenire hereditatem nō improprie, qui dixerit & eam, quæ ex testamento defertur e: quia lege duodecim tabularum testamentariæ hereditates confirmantur.
units.tr: d It is not improper to say that an inheritance comes e by law, including the one that is deferred by a will, because by the law of the Twelve Tables testamentary inheritances are confirmed.

units.la: 131. Idem libro tertio ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 131. The same, book three on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Aliud f fraus g est, aliud poena. fraus enim sine poena esse potest: poena sine fraude esse non potest. poena est noxae vindicta. fraus & ipsa noxa dicitur, & quasi poenae quaedam praeparatio. 1 Inter multam autem & poenam multum interest: cum h poena generale sit nomen, omnium delictorum multa specialis delicti.
units.tr: f Fraud is one thing, penalty another. Fraud can exist without penalty; penalty cannot exist without fraud. Penalty is the vengeance for a wrong. g Fraud itself is also called a wrong, and is in a way a preparation for penalty. h There is a great difference between a fine and a penalty: penalty is a general name for all offences, while a fine is the specific name for one particular offence.

units.la: c Qui mortuus nascitur, neque creatus videtur, neque filius appellatur 2.Eccl.2.c. 128. aborsus, vel abortus venter partum efficere non videtur Paulus 4.sent.9.§.6. nec rupit testamentum l.2.C.de postumis. Ab eo sunt diuersi, qui exacto ventre matris nascuntur l.6 in f.princ. s.de inoff.l. 12.s.de liberis, & ij qui nondum integrum animal, cum spiritu tamen, nascuntur d.l.12.in f. adde superioribus de muliere, quae semper mortuos parit l. 14. s. de ædilicio.
units.tr: c One who is born dead is seen neither as created nor as called a son. Paulus, Sentences 4, 9 §6, holds that an abortion, or a womb that does not bring forth a birth, does not count as a child, nor does it break a will (l.2 C. de postumis). Different from these are those who are born after the mother's womb has been opened (l.6 in f. princ. §. de inoff.; l.12 §. de liberis), and those who are born not yet a complete animal, though with breath (d.l.12 in f.). Add what was said above about a woman who always bears dead children (l.14 §. de aedilicio).

units.la: d lege obuenire intelligitur, quod ab ea veniat, quod legibus est confirmatum, adde l.1. s.de reædit.petit: adde l.6.inf. s.eod. deferre hereditatem leges dicuntur, quoties delatam confirmant.
units.tr: d "To come by law" is understood as coming from the law, which has confirmed it. Add l.1 §. de reaedit. petit; add l.6 in f. §. eod. Laws are said to "defer" an inheritance whenever they confirm it once it has been deferred.

units.la: e de verbo deferendi, & confirmandi adde l.6.s.de inofficiosi: adde l.36.in f.s. de donat.inter virum.
units.tr: e On the words "defer" and "confirm", add l.6 §. de inofficioso; add l.36 in f. §. de donat. inter virum.

units.la: f 2.Eccl.2.c.131. moyetur autem Iurisconsultus ad hac distinctionem afferendam, quod veteres fraudem pro poena ponere solebant l.23. §.2. s. ædilicio. hinc sine fraude capere.id est, sine poena legis l.1.s.ad legem Falci.non sine fraude in ius vocare.id est, non sine poena l.26. §.2. s. quibus ex causis maiores l.32. s.de iniuriis, l.8. s.de accusat. viro adulterium vxoris retinere horis diurnis non plusquam viginti, testandae eius rei causa, sine fraude licet l.25. s. de adulteriis.
units.tr: f The jurist was moved to draw this distinction because the ancients used to put fraud for penalty (l.23 §2 §. aedilicio). Hence "to take without fraud" means without penalty of the law (l.1 §. ad legem Falcidiam). "Not to summon into court without fraud" means not without penalty (l.26 §2 §. quibus ex causis maiores; l.32 §. de iniuriis; l.8 §. de accusationibus). For a husband to keep his wife's adultery for not more than twenty daylight hours, for the purpose of proving the matter, is allowed without fraud (l.25 §. de adulteriis).

units.la: g de fraude adde e l.79.s. de regulis. h Prima dicitur ferentia poenae & multae, poena generale nomen omnium delictorum, multa specialis delicti. exercitio:multa specialis peccati{*}, cuius animaduersio hodie pecuniaria est. poena autem non tantum pecuniaria, verum capitis & existimationis irroga-ri solet. & {b}multa quidem ex arbitrio eius venit, qui multam dicit: poena non irrogatur, nisi quae quaque lege, vel quo alio iure specialiter huic delicto imposita est. quinimmo multa ibi dicitur, vbi specialis poena non est imposita. Item {c}multam is dicere potest, cui iudicatio {d}data est: magistratus solos & praesides prouinciarum posse multam dicere, mandatis permissum est. poenam autem vnusquisque {e}in-rogare potest, cui huius criminis siue {f}delicti exse-cutio competit {g}.
units.tr: g On fraud, add e l.79 §. de regulis. h The first sense concerns the penalty and the fine: penalty is the general name for all offences, fine the specific name of a particular offence, whose punishment today is pecuniary. But a penalty is not only pecuniary; it is usually imposed on life and standing as well. A fine comes at the discretion of the one who imposes it; a penalty is not imposed unless a given law or other right specifically attaches it to this offence. Indeed a fine is spoken of where no specific penalty has been imposed. Likewise a fine may be imposed by one to whom judgment has been given. Only magistrates and provincial governors, by their mandates, are permitted to impose a fine; but anyone to whom the prosecution of this crime or offence belongs may impose a penalty.

units.la: 132. Paulus libro tertio ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 132. Paulus, book three on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: ANniculus {b}amittitur, qui extremo anni die moritur. & consuetudo loquendi id ita esse declarat, Ante diem decimum Kalendarum, post diem decimum Kalendarum. neque {f}vero enim sermone vnde-na lege, multa arbitrio iudicis definitur {a}. {c}Quarta differentia poenae & multae. Cui exsecutio criminis data est, poenam potest tantum irrogare, nisi specialiter hoc ei sit indultum {a}. ea authoritas tacite conceditur, vt vi magistratus, non tantum possit poenam irrogare, quemadmodum & priores, sed etiam multam dicere.
units.tr: A yearling is lost if he dies on the last day of the year. Common usage of speech declares this to be so: "before the tenth day of the Kalends, after the tenth day of the Kalends." For a fine is not defined by a fixed law in words, but by the judge's discretion. This is the fourth difference between penalty and fine: the one to whom the prosecution of a crime is given can impose only a penalty, unless this has been specially granted to him. This authority is tacitly conceded, so that by the power of the magistrate he can impose not only a penalty, as the earlier ones could, but also a fine.

units.la: {d} cui adiudicatio vulgat. Hal. id est, ei cui publicum iudicium est l.2. in f.5.de iudiciis.
units.tr: d "To whom adjudication is given": the Vulgate reads "to whom it is given", i.e. to him to whom the public judgment belongs (l.2 in f. §. de iudiciis).

units.la: {e} hinc colligit Cuiacius, etiam priuato dari publici iudicij executionem 15.obf.39.
units.tr: e From this Cuiacius concludes that even a private person may be given the execution of a public judgment (15 Obs. 39).

units.la: {f} Crimen a delicto vt distet v.in lege 17.§.18.5.de aedilitio.
units.tr: f On how crime differs from delict, see l.17 §18 §. de aedilicio.

units.la: {g} aliam differentiam poenae, & multae v.in lege 24.7.eo.
units.tr: g On another difference between penalty and fine, see l.24 §7 eo.
h l.134 §7 eo; 2 Eclog. 2 c.131.

units.la: {i} hanc negationem, quam etiam habent Graeci, vulgata non legit. legit.a, vtroque sermone. Autographum Florentinum neutro sermone vide Ant. Mercatorem 4.emendat.5.nx vtroque, quidam etiam ita legit.
units.tr: i This negation, which the Greeks also have, the Vulgate does not read. It reads it in either language. The Florentine autograph has it in neither language; see Antonius Mercator, Emend. 4, 5. Some also read it so.

units.la: Ideo magnus conflictus oritur. Budeus notat Paulum morari lectorem hoc gripho voluisse potius, quam docere. Paucis sic sentio, interea dum aliquis meliora. Anniculus moritur, qui extremo noni expirar, postdecendialis, qui extremo vndecimi. neutro sermone exacti dies (sic legendum puto arg.legis 34.7.eo. non vndecim dies, quam vocem Graeci verius deuorant, quam gustant) significantur, ac si diceret, qui moritur post extremum anni diem, non est anniculus, sed biennis: qui praestat aliquid postdecendio, vndecimo praestat, qui non praestat antecendio, praestat decimo. sic debitor, ante Kalendas, ante eas perfectas dare debet: aut si non ante, post certe dederit l.13. 5.de verb.oblig. Intra Kalendas iudicare iniussus, ante eas perfectas debet iudicare, autem ᵃ dies significantur. ¹ ¶Falsum est cam pe-perisse, cui mortuæ filius exsectus est.
units.tr: Hence a great conflict arises. Budaeus notes that Paulus wanted to hold the reader with this riddle rather than to teach. Briefly, I think, until someone offers something better: the yearling dies who expires at the end of the ninth; the "postdecendialis" dies at the end of the eleventh. The days are signified in neither language (I think it should be read so, by the argument of l.34 §7 eo). The Greeks swallow "eleven days" more truly than they taste it. It is as if he said: whoever dies after the last day of the year is not a yearling but a two-year-old. Whoever pays something after the tenth day pays on the eleventh; whoever does not pay before pays on the tenth. So a debtor must give before the Kalends, before they are complete; or, if not before, at least afterwards (l.13 §5 de verb. oblig.). To judge within the Kalends when not ordered to, one must judge before they are complete; but days are signified. It is false that a woman has given birth when a son has been cut out of her after she died.

units.la: 133. Ulpianus libro quarto ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 133. Ulpian, book four on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: SI quis sic dixerit, vt intra ᶜ diem mortis eius aliquid fiat: ipse ᵈ quoque dies, quo quis mortuus est numeratur.
units.tr: If someone should say that something is to be done within the day of his death, the day on which he died is also counted.

units.la: 134. Paulus libro secundo ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 134. Paulus, book two on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: ANniculus non statim vt natus est, sed trecensimo sexagetesimoquinto ᵉ die dicitur, incipiete plene, non ᶠ exacto die: quia annum ciuiliter, non ᵍ ad momenta temporum, sed ad dies numeramus.
units.tr: A yearling is reckoned not from the moment he is born, but from the 365th day, which is counted as begun in full, not as completed. For we count the year civilly, not by moments of time but by days.

units.la: 135. Ulpianus libro quarto ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 135. Ulpian, book four on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: QVaeret aliquis: si portentosum ʰ, vel monstrosum, vel debile Mulier ediderit, vel qualem visu vel vagitu nouum, non humanæ figuræ, sed al-terius magis animalis, quàm hominis partum: an, si non ... Ante diem duodecimum Kalendarum, post diem decimum Kalendarum: vtroque enim sermone vndecimus dies significatur. qua lectione, nulla apertior, dummodo particula enim, substuleris.
units.tr: Someone might ask: if a woman brings forth an monstrous, deformed or weak child, or one new in its look or cry, of no human shape but of another animal rather than a man, whether, if not... "Before the twelfth day of the Kalends, after the tenth day of the Kalends": for in either language the eleventh day is signified. Nothing is clearer than this reading, provided you remove the particle "enim".

units.la: a vndecima vulg.Hal.Ecl.ib. ne dicas nonam cum Budæo & Alciato. Ant.Augustinus, & Cuiacius in l.13.§.de verb.oblig.decimam esse volùt.Res ita habet,si de futuris Kalendis loquamur, dies ante decimum Kalendarum vicinior loquenti, est vndecimus dies, post decimum, est nonus: si de præteritis, dies vicinior loquenti ante diem decimum, est nonus: post diem decimum, est vndecimus. & ita neutro sermone dies vndecimus significatur, quod hæc lex innuit, haud nonus, vt vult Budeus, haud decimus, vt reliqui duo illi viri magni: à quibus tamen, propter eorum authoritatem, non facile discedi cupio.
units.tr: a The eleventh day: the Vulgate and Halander read it so, and do not say the ninth with Budaeus and Alciato. Antonius Augustinus and Cuiacius, on l.13 §. de verb. oblig., want it to be the tenth. The matter stands thus: if we speak of future Kalends, the day before the tenth of the Kalends nearest the speaker is the eleventh; the day after the tenth is the ninth. If we speak of past days, the day nearest the speaker before the tenth is the ninth; the day after the tenth is the eleventh. So in either language the eleventh day is signified, which this law implies: not the ninth, as Budaeus wishes, nor the tenth, as those two great men do. Yet I do not readily wish to depart from them, on account of their authority.

units.la: h l.38.§.eo:l.14.§.de statu hominum; l.35.in f. C.de posthumis heredibus [?]nia enixa est, praedesse ei debeat. & magis est, ut haec quoque parentibus prosint.nec enim est, quod eis in putetur, quae, qualiter potuerunt statutis obtemperauerunt: neque id, quod fataliter accessit, matri damnum iniungere debet.
units.tr: h l.38 §eo; l.14 §. de statu hominum; l.35 in f. C. de posthumis heredibus. ...should benefit her. And it is more right that these things also benefit the parents. For it is not right that they be charged to them, since they obeyed the statutes as far as they could; nor should what happened by fate impose a loss on the mother.

units.tr: 136. Idem, book 5 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Generi appellatione & neptis, & proneptis,tam ex filio,quàm ex filia editorum, ceterarúmque maritos contineri,manifestum est.
units.tr: It is clear that under the term "descendants" are included both the granddaughters and great-granddaughters, whether through a son or through a daughter, and their husbands.

units.la: 137. Paulus libro fecundo ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 137. Paulus, book 2 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Ter enixa videtur, etiam quae trigeminos pepererit.
units.tr: A woman is considered to have borne three times if she has given birth to triplets.
138. Idem, book 4 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Hereditatis appellatione bonorum quoque possessio continetur.
units.tr: Under the term "inheritance" the possession of goods is also included.

139. Ulpianus, book 7 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Aedificia Romae fieri etiam ea videntur, quae in continentibus aedificiis fiant. Perfecit aedificium is videtur, qui ita consummauit, ut iam in usu esse possit.
units.tr: At Rome, those things are also considered buildings which are made in buildings that adjoin one another. A building is considered complete when it has been finished to the point that it can already be in use.

units.la: 140. Paulus libro sexto ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 140. Paulus, book 6 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Epistolae quis intelligitur, quamuis alij adquisiit.
units.tr: A letter is understood to belong to the person who has acquired it, although others have acquired it too.
141. Ulpianus, book 8 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Etiam ea mulier, cùm moreretur, creditur filium habere, quae excíso vtero edere possit. nec non etiam alio casu mulier potest habere filium, quem mortis tempore non habuit: vtputà eum, qui ab hostibus remeauit.
units.tr: A woman is believed to have a son even when she dies, if the child could be taken out of her womb by cutting. Also, in another case, a woman can have a son whom she did not have at the time of her death: for example, one who has returned from the enemy.

units.tr: 142. Paulus, book 6 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: {m} l.66.s.haereditas inslit: l.85.s.de legatis 1: l.80: l,89.s.de Legat.3.v.Zas.1.Resp.18.19. enim re {*} per se coniunctio contingit, aut re {b} ad eandem rem & verbis, aut verbis {c} tantum. Nec dubium est, quin coniuncti sint, quos & nominum & rei complexus iungit. veluti, Titius & {d} Mœuius ex parte dimidia heredes sunto. vel [?]ita Titius Mœuiùsque heredes sunto. vel Titius cum Mœnio ex parte dimidia heredes sunto. Videamus autem: ne, etiam si hos articulos detrahas & {e}, quæ cum interdum{f} tamen coniunctos accipi oporteat veluti Lucius Titius, Publius Mœuius ex parte dimidia heredes sunto, vel ita Publius Mœuius, Lucius Titius heredes sunto. Sempronius ex parte dimidia heres esto. vt Titius & Mœuius veniant in partem dimidiam, & re & verbis coniuncti vi-deantur. Lucius Titius ex parte dimidia heres esto. Scius ex parte, qua {h} Lucium Titium heredem institui, heres esto. Sempronius ex parte dimidia heres esto. Iulianus dubitari {i} posse, tres semisses fiant, an Titius in eundem semissem cum Gaio Seio institutus sit. sed {k} eo quod Sempronius quoque ex parte dimidia scriptus est versimilius esse, in eundem semissem duos coactos, & coniunctim heredes scriptos esse.
units.tr: {m} l.66, s. haereditas institutio; l.85, s. de legatis 1; l.80; l.89, s. de legatis 3; see Zas. 1 Resp. 18, 19. By the thing alone a joining arises, or by the same thing and words together, or by words alone. Nor is there any doubt that those are joined whom the bond of both names and the thing unites: for example, "Titius and Maevius shall be heirs in half share"; or "Titius and Maevius shall be heirs"; or "Titius with Maevius shall be heirs in half share." Let us consider, however, whether, even if you remove these connecting words, they must still be taken as joined, which at times they are, as in: "Lucius Titius and Publius Maevius shall be heirs in half share"; or thus: "Publius Maevius and Lucius Titius shall be heirs"; "Sempronius shall be heir in half share," so that Titius and Maevius come into the half share and appear joined both in the thing and in the words. "Lucius Titius shall be heir in half share"; "Seius shall be heir in the part in which I have appointed Lucius Titius heir"; "Sempronius shall be heir in half share." Julian asks whether it can be doubted that the three halves would be made, or whether Titius was instituted in the same half with Gaius Seius. But because Sempronius too is written as heir in half share, it is more likely that two were compelled into the same half and were written as heirs jointly.
(see the second note above)

units.la: 143. Vlpianus libro nono ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 143. Ulpian, book 9 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: ID apud se quis habere {l} viderur, de quo habet actionem {m} habetur enim, quod peti potest.
units.tr: A person is considered to have that thing with himself about which he has an action; for that is considered to be had which can be claimed.

units.la: 144. Paulus libro decimo ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 144. Paul, book 10 on the Julian and Papian law.
Of the books of memorials.
{f} See l.28, §.s.5 eo.

units.la: {g} hæc oratio taxatiua est, quæ dimidiam Sempronio addicit. unde sequitur vt Mœuius & Titius comprehensi in superiore enunciatione ad alteram tantùm dimidiam admittantur.
units.tr: {g} This wording is restrictive, which assigns the half to Sempronius. Hence it follows that Maevius and Titius, included in the preceding clause, are admitted only to the other half.

units.la: {h} hic Titius & Seius re coniunguntur, re & verbis à Sepronio diuungun-tur.
units.tr: {h} Here Titius and Seius are joined in the thing, and are separated from Sempronius both in the thing and in the words.

units.la: {i} Ea fuit dubitandi ratio, Sempronio dimidia expressim datur, nulla Titio expressim: ad Seium igitur pertinet dimidia. at qui Titius ex ea parte heres institutus est, ex qua Seius: igitur ex dimidia & ex consequentia, tres semisses facient, & ita Iulianus argumetatus est.
units.tr: {i} This was the ground of doubt: a half is expressly given to Sempronius, none expressly to Titius; so the half pertains to Seius. But Titius is instituted heir in the same part as Seius; therefore, from the half and by consequence, they would make three halves, and so Julian argued.

units.la: {k} Ratio decidendi. Sempronius ex dimidia scriptus est nominatim, est igitur versimilius Titium & Seium ad alterum tantùm semissem vocatos: nam ex asse si dimidium sustuleris, q; remanebit, erit alteri dimidio æquale l. 15. §. de hæredibus Instit.
units.tr: {k} The ground of deciding: Sempronius is named as heir to a half; it is therefore more likely that Titius and Seius were called only to the other half. For if you take half from the whole as, what remains will be equal to the other half: l.15, §. de heredibus, Institutes.

units.la: {l} adde l.38.§.5.s.de verb.oblig. {m} l.52.§.de pblig.vsl.15.§.de reg. iur.2.Est.2.§.143. {n} memoralium vulg.
units.tr: {l} Add l.38, §.5, s. de verborum obligationibus. {m} l.52, §. de publicis usibus; l.15, §. de regulis iuris; 2 Est., §.143. {n} The Vulgate reads "memorialium."

units.la: MAssurius scribit pellicem{a} apud antiquos eam habitam, quæ cum vxor non esset, cum aliquo tamen viuebat: quam nunc vero nomine amicam, paulo honestiore concubinam appellari. Gransus Flaccus in libro de iure Papiriano scribit, pellicem nunc{b} vulgò vocari, quæ{c} cum eo, cui vxor sit, corpus misceat. quosdam eam, quæ vxoris loco sine nuptiis in domo sit, quam παλλακὰς Græci vocant.
units.tr: Massurius writes that among the ancients a pellex (mistress) was regarded as one who, not being a wife, nevertheless lived with a man; whom now, under the name "friend" (amica), or more respectably "concubine," they call. Granius Flaccus, in his book on the Papirian law, writes that now a pellex is commonly called one who has intercourse with a man who has a wife. Some call her who in the house takes the place of a wife without marriage, whom the Greeks call pallakas [παλλακὰς].

units.la: 145. Vlpianus libro decimo ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 145. Ulpian, book 10 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: VIrilis{d} appellatione interdum etiam totam{e} hereditatem contineri dicendum est.
units.tr: It must be said that under the term "virilis" sometimes even the whole inheritance is included.

units.la: 146. Terentius Clemens libro 2. ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 146. Terentius Clemens, book 2 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: Soceri, socrus appellatione auum{f} quoque & auiam vxoris vel mariti contineri, respondetur.
units.tr: It is answered that under the term "father-in-law" and "mother-in-law" the grandfather and grandmother of the wife or husband are also included.

units.la: 147. Idem libro 3. ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 147. Idem, book 3 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: QVi in continentibus{g} vrbis nati sunt, Romæ na-ti intelligantur.
units.tr: Those who were born in the buildings adjoining the city are understood to have been born at Rome.

units.la: 148. Gaius libro octauo ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 148. Gaius, book 8 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: NOn est sine liberis, cui vel vnus filius, vnaue filia est. hæc enim enuntiatio{h} habet liberos, habet liberos, semper pluratiuo numero profertur: sicut & pugillares, & codicilli.
units.tr: He is not without children who has only one son or only one daughter. For this statement, "has children," is always expressed in the plural number, just as "pugillares" and "codicilli" (writing tablets, codicils) are.

units.la: 149. Idem libro 10. ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 149. Idem, book 10 on the Julian and Papian law.

units.la: NAm{i} quem sine liberis esse, dicere non possumus: hunc necesse est dicamus liberos habere.
units.tr: For we cannot say that a man is without children; we must say that he has children.

units.la: Ecl. ib. c. 145. e adde l.2. C. de hereditibus instituend. f soceri appellatione prosocer continetur 2. Eclog.2.c.145: l.3.§.2. [?] de postliminio. g v.l. 87.§ eodem. h etiam naturalis l.17. §.4. supra ad Trebellian. nam & apud Latinos quædam etiam dictiones plurali numero conceptæ, rem vnam tantum interdum demonstrant vt Codicilli, pupillares: & è contrario singulari, pluures significantur l.158.§.7 eodem. i Qui non est sine liberis, liberos habet. Hinc colligit Vlpianus argumentum à contrariis semper concludere.
units.tr: Eclog., ib., c.145; add l.2, C. de hereditibus instituendis. {f} Under the term "father-in-law" the step-father-in-law is included; 2 Eclog., c.145; l.3, §.2, de postliminio. {g} See l.87, §. eodem. {h} Even natural; l.17, §.4, supra ad Trebellianum. For also among the Latins some expressions, though framed in the plural number, sometimes denote only one thing, as "codicilli" and "pupillares"; and conversely, things in the singular are sometimes meant in the plural: l.158, §.7, eodem. {i} "He who is not without children has children." From this Ulpian draws the argument that one always concludes from the contraries.

units.la: 150. Idem libro nono ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 150. The same, book nine on the Julian and Papian Law.

units.la: Si ita à te stipulatus fuero, Quanto {a}minus à Titio consecutus fuero, tantum dare spondes? non fo-let dubitari, quin si nihil à Titio fuero consecutus, totum debeas, quod Titius debuerit.
units.tr: If I stipulate from you thus: "Do you promise to give as much less as I obtain from Titius?", there is no doubt that if I obtain nothing from Titius, you owe the whole amount that Titius owes.

units.la: 151. Terentius Clemens libro quinto ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 151. Terentius Clemens, book five on the Julian and Papian Law.

units.la: Delata {b}hereditas intelligitur, quam quis possit adeundo consequi {c}.
units.tr: An inheritance is understood to be "offered" (delata) when a person can acquire it by entering upon it.

units.la: 152. Gaius libro decimo ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 152. Gaius, book ten on the Julian and Papian Law.

units.la: Hominis {d}appellatione tam feminam, quàm masculum contineri, non dubitatur.
units.tr: No one doubts that by the term "person" (homo) both a woman and a man are included.

units.la: 153. Terentius Clemens libro ii.ad legem Iuliam & Papiam.
units.tr: 153. Terentius Clemens, book two on the Julian and Papian Law.

units.la: Intelligendus est mortis {e}tempore fuisse, qui in utero relictus est.
units.tr: He who is left in the womb must be understood to have been alive at the time of death.
154. Macer, book one on the twentieth law.

units.la: Mille passus non à miliario {f}urbis, sed à conti-nentibus {g}ædificiis numerandi sunt.
units.tr: A thousand paces are to be counted not from the milestone of the city, but from the continuous line of buildings.

units.la: pax. dicitur etiam delata, etiamsi non possit adiri, id est, etiam si eius adeundæ non sit capax v.Bellenû 2.suppur.16.
units.tr: Something is also said to be "offered" even if it cannot be entered upon, that is, even if the person is not capable of entering upon it. See Bellenus, 2 Suppur. 16.
{d} Eclog. 2, c. 152: add l. 1, §1, de homine libero.

units.la: {e} 2.Eclog.2.c.153. Esse intelligitur, qui est in utero. Ideoque quandocunque eius pater moritur, mortis eius tempore fuisse intelligitur v.l.18. s. quando dies legatorum esse intelligitur, inquam, in rerum natura l.26.s.de statu: in rebus humanis l.7. s.de statu hominum. comparatur iam nato l.2.§.6. s.de excusat. tut. nec tamen adhuc censetur homo l.9.in f.s.ad leg. Falcid.
units.tr: {e} Eclog. 2, c. 153. He is understood to be alive who is in the womb. Therefore, whenever his father dies, he is understood to have been alive at the time of death. See l. 18, s. quando dies legatorum esse intelligitur; I say, in the natural world, l. 26, s. de statu; in human affairs, l. 7, s. de statu hominum. He is compared to one already born, l. 2, §6, s. de excusat. tut. Yet he is not yet considered a man, l. 9, in fine, s. ad leg. Falcid.

units.la: {f} non à muro urbis vulg. Hal. Miliarium erat columna quæ Romæ posita in foro ab Augusto à qua omnes viæ Italiæ initium & finem capiebant Dion.54. Pub.Victor. in libello de regionibus urbis Romæ. hæc columna à Dione vocatur χρυσοῦν μίλιον[?]: à Plutarcho in Galba χρυσᾶς κίων[?].adde Plin.3. Tacit.3. Alia significatione miliarium est vas v.l.120.s.de auro. & mensura viarum quas nos miliaria dicimus. Græci στάδια[?] appellant, Galli leucas, AEgypti σχοῖνον[?]. Schoeni, sic enim legendum est, non signes apud Herodot.2. Persæ parasangas 15. Ibid.16. adde Festum in dictione pa-rasangæ. Parasanga Persica efficit triginta stadia Herodot.26.
units.tr: {f} not "from the wall of the city", as in the common edition by Halm. The miliarium was a column set up in the Forum at Rome by Augustus, from which all the roads of Italy began and ended. Dion 54; Pub. Victor, in his booklet on the regions of the city of Rome. Dio calls this column the golden milestone [χρυσοῦν μίλιον]; Plutarch in Galba calls it a golden pillar [χρυσᾶς κίων]. Add Pliny 3; Tacitus 3. In another sense, miliarium is a vessel, see l. 120, s. de auro, and also a measure of roads, which we call miles. The Greeks call these stadia [στάδια], the Gauls leugae, the Egyptians schoeni [σχοῖνον]. For it must be read as schoenus, not signes, in Herodotus 2. The Persians have parasangs of fifteen (units). Ibid. 16; add Festus under the word parasanga. A Persian parasang makes thirty stadia, Herodotus 26.
{g} l. 2, l. 87, s. eodem.
155. Licinnius
155. Licinnius Rufinus, book seven of the Regulae.

units.la: PRoximi {a}appellatione etiam ille continetur, qui solus {b}est. bitandi ratio oriatur à voce pluralis numeri proximorum, ad singularem solus, proximus.
units.tr: The term "neighbour" (proximus) also includes the one who is alone. The ground of doubt arises from the plural word "proximi" compared with the singular "solus" and "proximus".
156. The same, book ten of the Regulae.

units.la: MAiore {c}parte anni possedisse quis intelligitur, etiam si duobus {d}mensibus possederit: si modo aduersarius eius aut paucioribus diebus, aut nullis possederit.
units.tr: A person is understood to have possessed for the greater part of the year even if he possessed for only two months, provided that his opponent possessed for fewer days or for none.

units.la: 157. AElius Gallus lib.1. de verborum, quæ ad ius pertinent, significatione.
units.tr: 157. Aelius Gallus, book one, on the meaning of words that pertain to law.
"Paries" is either a wall or a maceria (a rubble or dry-stone wall).

units.la: {b} Eclog. ibidem capite 155: l.9. s. de rebus dub: l.1. §.5. §.6. s.vnde cognati quem ante nemo: adde l.92. s.ea: & l.34. s.de vulgari hinc colligunt, stipulanti feudum, emphiteusim, aut quid tale sibi & primogenito, ciusinodi conuentionem etiam pertinere ad eum cuius fratres antea fuerint mortui, licet per rerum naturam non sit primogenitus.
units.tr: {b} Eclog., same chapter, 155: l. 9, s. de rebus dub.; l. 1, §5, §6, s. unde cognati; add l. 92, s. ea; and l. 34, s. de vulgari. Hence they conclude that a stipulation for a fief, an emphyteusis, or something of the kind, made to himself and his firstborn, also pertains to the one whose brothers have died before him, even though by the nature of things he is not the firstborn.

units.la: {c} hæc quæstio olim fuit vtilis in interdictis, vti possidetis, & vtrubi l.1. s.vtrubi §.4. circa finem: Inst.de interdictis v Paul.5.sent.6.§.1.
units.tr: {c} This question was once useful in the interdicts uti possidetis and utrubi. See l. 1, s. utrubi, §4, near the end; Inst. de interdictis; Paulus, Sent. 5, 6, §1.

units.la: {d} hoc penè videtur [illegible, ~6 letters] nec enim duo menses pars maior annifunt. Intelliguntur tamen pars maior in interdicto vtrubi d.l.1: d.§.4.
units.tr: {d} This seems almost [illegible]; for two months are not the greater part of a year. Yet the greater part is understood in the interdict utrubi, in the same law §4.

units.la: {e} Parietum alius proprius, alius communis l.14. s.si seruitus: l.39. s.de damno ventrem faciens, proie&tus l.17. s.si seruitus vindicetur: laterit ius, craticius v.l.52. §.1, §.3. s.prosocio adde 2. Vitruv. 8. & 7. c. rudis l.44. s.de vsufructu. integerrinus, Festus, siue confinis [illegible, ~8 letters] Plin.12. solidus, qui à solo continuo duƈtu ad fastigium exurgit: fornicatus, qui arcum habet: cæcus qui fenestras non habet adde quæ notaui ad l.40. s.de se ruitut. vrban. v.Cuiacius 3.obs.31. eodem sensu quo cubiculū coecum [?] Cuiac. 2.obs.40. s [illegible, ~5 letters] Eclog. ibid.c.157.
units.tr: {e} Walls are of two kinds, one private and one common. See l. 14, s. si servitus; l. 39, s. de damno; ventrem faciens; projectus; l. 17, s. si servitus vindicetur; laterit; ius craticium, see l. 52, §1, §3, s. pro socio. Add Vitruvius 2, 8, and 7; rudis; l. 44, s. de usufructu; integerrinus; Festus, or confinis; [illegible]; Pliny 12; solidus, which rises from the continuous solid ground up to the roof; fornicatus, which has an arch; caecus, which has no windows. Add what I noted on l. 40, s. de servitutibus urbanorum; see Cujas 3 Obs. 31, in the same sense as cubiculum caecum; Cujas 2 Obs. 40; s. [illegible]; Eclog., same chapter 157.

units.la: {f} [illegible, ~6 letters] Eclog. ibid. hinc, maceriam ducere l.17.s. communia prædiorum.
units.tr: {f} [illegible] Eclog., same place. Hence "to lead a maceria", l. 17, s. communia praediorum.
{g} [illegible] Eclog., same place.

units.la: Res tota ita haber, septorum quatuor genera, naturale fit virgultis, aut spinis: secundum, fit ex agresti ligno: tertium, ex fossa & terreno aggere: quartum, est fabrile, vt maceria. Maceria fit, vel ex lapide, vel lateribus cotilibus aut crudis, vel ex lapillis ex terra compositis inter formas v.Varronem 1.de re rustica 14. Isidorus, maceries sunt parietes longi quibus vineæ clauduntur 15. orig.9. alias, maceria est sine arenato, murus cum harena (quibus obest Cato de re rustica 15. nisi maceria ibi pro pariete accipitur.) hinc certe opponuntur murus, & maceria. Græci [illegible, ~9 letters]. vnde videtur murus esse qui ambit, maceria etiam si non ambiat. postis etiam referre muros ad vrbes, maceriam ad priuatorum domos.
units.tr: The matter stands thus: there are four kinds of enclosures. The natural kind is made of brambles or thorns; the second is made of rough wood; the third of a ditch and earthen bank; the fourth is made by craftsmen, such as a maceria. A maceria is made either of stone, of kiln-baked or unbaked bricks, or of small stones compounded with earth between frames. See Varro, 1 De re rustica 14. Isidore: maceriae are long walls by which vineyards are enclosed, Origines 15, 9. Otherwise, maceria is a wall without mortar, while murus is one with sand (which Cato, De re rustica 15, contradicts, unless maceria there is taken for a pariës). Hence murus and maceria are certainly opposed. The Greeks [illegible]. Whence it seems that murus is that which surrounds, while maceria may be used even if it does not surround. Posts also refer walls to cities and maceriae to the houses of private persons.

units.la: 1 ¶Item via {a}[?] est: siue semita, siue iter est.
units.tr: 1 Likewise, a via is either a footpath or a road.
158. Celsus, Digesta, book 25.

units.la: Vsu[?] iuris frequenter uti nos Cascellius ait singulari{b} appellatione, cum plura generis eiusdem significare vellemus. nam multum hominem venisse Romam. & piscem vilem esse dicimus. Item in stipulando satis habemus de herede cauere, Si ea res secu-dum me heredemve{c} meum iudicata crit. & rursus, Quod ob eam rem te heredemve tuum, nempe æque, si plures heredes sint, continentur stipulatione.
units.tr: Cascellius says that we often use a single word in law when we want to signify several things of the same kind. For we say that a man has come to Rome in large numbers ("multum hominem venisse Romam"), and that a fish is cheap. Likewise in drawing up a stipulation we are content to give security for the heir in the form: "if the matter is adjudged against me or my heir," and conversely: "because of this matter against you or your heir," which, of course, if there are several heirs, are covered by the stipulation equally.
159. Ulpian, On Sabinus, book 1.
We also call gold coins bronze ("aes").
160. The same, On Sabinus, book 2.

units.la: Eterorum{g} & reliquorum{h} appellatione etiam Omnes continentur{i}, vt Marcellus dixit circa eum cui optio{k}[?] ferui legata est, ceteri Sempronio: mentum duci potest l.13. §. de seruitutib. quà plaustrum potest du-ci l.7. §. de seruitutib. rustic. Via quà & iumerum[?] & vehiculum l.13. §. de seruitutib. rustic. §. de seruitutib. l.23. §. de seruitutib. rustic. & trahi lapis, ac lignum, & reda hasta ferri l.7. §. de seruitutib. rustic, hæc velim conferri cum principio tituli de seruitutibus Institut.
units.tr: By the term "the others" and "the rest" all are included, as Marcellus said about the case where the option of a slave was bequeathed to one person and the others to Sempronius. A path by which a cart can be driven (l. 13, §. de servitutibus; l. 7, §. de servitutibus rusticorum). A way by which both a beast of burden and a vehicle may pass (l. 13, §. de servitutibus rusticorum; §. de servitutibus; l. 23, §. de servitutibus rusticorum), and by which a stone or timber may be dragged, and a spear of iron carried (l. 7, §. de servitutibus rusticorum). I should like these to be compared with the opening title on servitudes in the Institutes.

units.la: {b} vox singularis interdum apud Latinos plures significat vt hic 2. Eclog. 2. c. 158, & contra pluralis, vnicam l.148. §. eodem.
units.tr: {b} In Latin a word in the singular sometimes signifies several things, as here (2 Eclog. 2, c. 158), and conversely a plural signifies a single thing (l. 148, §. eodem).
{c} By the term "heir" heirs are understood.

units.la: {d} quo tractauit de testamentis. Cuiacius inde colligit, hanc legem referendam ad formulam mancipationis familiæ, quæ fiebat per æs & libram, vel ad prodigos, quibus conceptis verbis æ re, commercioque interdicebatur 7. obs. 33. in sin.
units.tr: {d} Ulpian treats here of testaments. Cujas infers from this that the law should be referred to the form of the mancipation of a household, which was made by bronze and scales, or to prodigals, who by the formula were forbidden the use of bronze and commerce (7 Obs. 33, near the end).

units.la: {e} sensus est, Aureos etiam æs dicimus: hinc æs alienû, id est, nummi quos debemus: æs suum, id est, nummi qui debentur nobis adde l.113.§.1.§.eodem.
units.tr: {e} The sense is: we also call gold coins bronze. Hence "aes alienum," that is, the coins we owe, and "aes suum," that is, the coins owed to us (add l. 113, §. 1, §. eodem).

units.la: {f} aliter Graeci καὶ τὰ νομίσματα ὑ[?]μος λέγεται 2.Eclog.2.cap.159.
units.tr: {f} The Greeks put it otherwise: [καὶ τὰ νομίσματα ... λέγεται] (2 Eclog. 2, cap. 159).

units.la: {g} l.5. §.de rebus dubijs. Porrò notandū est, dici etiam in singulari cæteram partem l.2. §.de hiis quæ in testamento.
units.tr: {g} See l. 5, §. de rebus dubiis. Moreover, it should be noted that the other part is also spoken of in the singular (l. 2, §. de his quae in testamento).

units.la: {h} l.95. §.eodem: l.97. §. de legat. 3: l.17. §. de optione l.2. C. de hered. Instit.
units.tr: {h} l. 95, §. eodem; l. 97, §. de legatis 3; l. 17, §. de optione; l. 2, C. de heredibus instituendis.

units.la: {i} Caeterorum, hæc vox inclusionis nota est. interdum etiam exclusionis fa-citlex 39. §. de procuratoribus. nonnumquàm omnia significat l.5. §.7. in sin. §. de reb. cor. quisub tutela. De particula, & cætera, notariis familiari vide Bartolum ad l.19. §. idem credendum 2. in f. §. de liberis & posthumis.
units.tr: {i} "Caeterorum" is a word that marks inclusion. Sometimes, too, it marks exclusion (see l. 39, §. de procuratoribus). Sometimes it signifies all (l. 5, §. 7, near the end, §. de rebus corum qui sub tutela). On the particle "et cetera," familiar to notaries, see Bartolus on l. 19, §. idem credendum, 2, near the end, §. de liberis et posthumis.

units.la: {k} l.v.d.l.17. §.de opt. nam tentat,si non optet,omnes ad Sempronium pertinere.
units.tr: {k} See the law just cited, l. 17, §. de optione; for if he does not choose, all pass to Sempronius.
161. The same, On Sabinus, book 7.
He who is in the womb is not a ward (pupillus).
162. Pomponius, On Sabinus, book 2.

units.la: IN vulgari substitutione {b}, qua ei, qui supremus {c} morietur,heres substituitur,recte substitutus etiam unico {d} intelligitur:exemplo duodecim tabularum, ex quibus proximus {e} adgnatus & solus habetur.
units.tr: In a vulgar substitution, by which an heir is substituted to one who will die last ("supremus"), the one substituted is rightly understood even as the only one. The example is the Twelve Tables, by which the nearest agnate is held to be the only one.

units.la: 1 ¶Si quis ita in testamento scripserit, Si quid filio meo acciderit {f} Damas servus meus liber esto: mortuo filio, Damas liber erit. licet {g} enim accidant & vivis, sed {h} vulgi sermone etiam mors significatur.
units.tr: 1 ¶ If someone writes in his will: "If anything happens to my son, let my slave Damas be free," and the son dies, Damas will be free. For "happens" may refer also to a living person, but in common speech death is meant.
163. Paulus, On Sabinus, book 2.

units.la: Illa verba, Optimus {i}, maximusque, vel in eum cadere possunt, qui solus est. Sic & circa edictu praetoris supremæ tabulæ habentur & solæ, 1 ¶Pueri {m}appellatione etiam puella significatur, nam & feminas puerperas {n} appellant recentes ex partu, & Græcè παιδίον[?] communiter appellatur.
units.tr: The words "the best and greatest" ("optimus maximusque") may apply to one who is alone. So also, in the praetor's edict, the last tablets ("supremae tabulae") are held to be the only ones. 1 ¶ By the term "boys" ("pueri") girls are also signified, for they also call women recently delivered in childbirth "puerperae," and in Greek it is commonly called [παιδίον].
164. Ulpian, On Sabinus, book 15.

units.la: NOmen filiarum {o} & in postumam cadere, quæstionis non est. quamuis postumæ non cadere in eam, quæ {p} in rebus humanis sit, certum sit.
units.tr: That the name of daughters also extends to a posthumous child is not in question, although it is certain that a posthumous child does not fall under the name of one who is already among living men.

units.la: liabus posthumis,ventri,si postea edatur,dati quoq. intelligunter l. 5. l.6. l.16.§.de testam.tut.§.vlt.inst.qui testam. {b} v.l.34.§.de vulg. {c} supremus, id est vltimus est etiam dicitur qui solus est l.92.§.eod.; l.163.§.10. l.9.§.de reb.dub. {d} Ratio dubitandi in eo fuit,quod comparatio posterioris decedentis ex facto prioris mortui sumitur l. 9. §.de reb.dub. units.tr: Posthumous children are also understood as given, for those in the womb if they are afterwards brought forth (l. 5; l. 6; l. 16, §. de testamentaria tutela; §. ult., Institutes, qui testamenta). {b} See l. 34, §. de vulgari substitutione. {c} "Supremus," that is, last, is also said of one who is alone (l. 92, §. eod.; l. 163, §. 10; l. 9, §. de rebus dubiis). {d} The reason for doubt lay in this: the comparison of the one who dies later is taken from the fact of the earlier one's death (l. 9, §. de rebus dubiis). Therefore "supremus" will be used improperly of one before whom no one has died. {e} "Proximus," or the one who is alone, is held as such (see l. 92, §. eod.; Eclog. ib., c. 162). {f} See l. 26, §. depositi; l. 41, §. 12, §. de legatis 2; Institutes, de donationibus, near the end. {g} Hence the reason for doubt: the son of the deceased had been alive (Eclog. ibid.). {h} The reason for deciding is taken from common usage of speech. {i} See the same law, l. 126, §. eod. {k} From this we may infer that superlatives, such as "optimus," "maximus," "supremus," are taken for positives. {l} See l. 162, §. eod.; l. 1, §. 1, §. de bonorum possessione secundum tabulas. {m} See l. 204, §. cod. {n} Add l. 14, §. 2, §. de aedilitio edicto. {o} A daughter is also a posthumous child (see l. 5; l. 6, §. de testamentaria tutela; §. ult., Institutes, qui testamenta; on daughters add l. 116, §. eod.; l. 230, below, §. qu.; l. 17, §. de legatis 1). {p} l. 16, near the end, §. de testamentaria tutela.

units.la: 1 ¶ Partionis nomen non semperdimidium significat: sed prout est adiectum. potest enim iuberi aliquis & maximam partiri: posse & vicesimam, & tertiam, & prout libuerit. sed si non fuerit portio b adiecta, dimidia pars debetur. 2 ¶ Habere e, sicut peruenire d, cum effectu accipiendum est.
units.tr: 1 ¶ The word "portion" does not always mean a half, but according to what is added to it. For someone may be ordered to divide the greatest part, or the twentieth, or the third, or as he pleases. But if no portion has been added, a half is owed. 2 ¶ "To have" e, like "to come to" d, is to be taken in the sense of effect.
165. Pomponius, On Sabinus, book 5.

units.la: Venisse ad heredem nihil intelligitur, nisi deducto aere alieno.
units.tr: Nothing is understood to have come to the heir unless the debts have been deducted.
166. The same, On Sabinus, book 6.

units.la: Vrbana familia, & rustica non loco f, sed genere distinguitur. potest enim aliquis dispensator non esse seruorum vrbanorum numero: veluti is, qui rusticarum h rerum rationes dispenset, ibique habitet, non multum abest à vilico. insularius i aut vrbanorum numero est. videndum tamen est, ipse dominus, quorum loco quemque habuerit: quod ex numero k familiæ, & vicarii l apparebit.
units.tr: The city household and the country household are distinguished not by place but by kind. For someone may not be a steward within the number of the city slaves, for example one who manages the accounts of country property and lives there; he is not far from being a farm bailiff. A keeper of an apartment block ("insularius") belongs to the number of city slaves. We must consider, however, under what description the master himself has placed each one, which will appear from the number of the household and the substitutes l.

units.la: 1 ¶ Peruoctare extra m vrbem intelligendus est, qui nulla parte noctis in vrbe est. Per n enim totam noctem significat.
units.tr: 1 ¶ One is to be understood as staying overnight outside the city ("peroctare extra urbem") who is in the city during no part of the night. For "per" signifies the whole night.

units.la: {b} Qui portionem dicit, nec adiecit quotam, dimidiam significat 2. Eclog.2.
units.tr: {b} One who speaks of a portion and does not add its fraction means a half (2 Eclog. 2).

units.tr: custos insulae (the keeper of a block of flats), l.vlt. §. de off. praefid.; l.16. §. 1. §. de usu & habitat. An insula is a building set apart from others by its own enclosure.

units.la: {m} Pernoctare extra vrbem, est noćte integra vrbe abesse. Præsidi abnoćtare extra prouinciam non licet l.15. §. de off.præsid. Quę trinoćtio abnoćtasset vsurpabatur 3. Gell.2. in f. Flamen dialis non vltra binoćtium pernoćtare poterat Tacit.3.
units.tr: To spend the night outside the city is to be away with the whole night spent beyond the city. A governor is not allowed to spend the night outside his province, l.15. §. de off. praesid. What was called a "trinoctium" (three nights' absence) was used of a stay of three nights, Gellius 2, in fin. A flamen dialis could not stay away for more than two nights, Tacitus 3.

units.la: 167. Vlpianus libro vicesimo quinto ad Sabinum.
units.tr: 167. Ulpian, book 25 on Sabinus.

units.la: Carbonum appellatione materiam non contineri. Sed an lignorum? & fortassis quis dicet, nec lignorum: non enim lignorum gratia habuit. Sed & titiones, & alia ligna coda, ne fumum faciant, vtrum ligno, an carboni, an suo generi adnumerabimus? & magis est, vt propium genus habeatur. Sulpurata quoque de ligno aeque eandem habebunt definitionem. Ad faces quoque parata non erunt lignorum appellatione comprehensa, nisi haec fuit voluntas. Idem & de nucleis oliuarum, sed & de balanis est, vel si qui alij nuclei. De pinu autem integri strobili, ligni appellatione continebuntur.
units.tr: The word "charcoal" does not include timber material. But what about wood? Someone may perhaps say that it does not include wood either, since it was not kept for the sake of wood. But do we count firebrands and other wood, cut so that it will not smoke, under wood, under charcoal, or under its own kind? It is more likely that it should be regarded as a separate kind. Sulphured wood will likewise have the same definition. Torches prepared for lighting will not be included under the word "wood" unless that was the intention. The same applies to olive stones, and also to acorns, or any other kernels. But whole pine cones will be included under the word "wood".
168. Paul, book 4 on Sabinus.

units.la: Pali[?] & perr[?]ce in numerum materiae redigendi sunt & ideo lignorum appellatione non continentur.
units.tr: Stakes and poles are to be reckoned as material, and therefore are not included under the word "wood".
169. The same, book 5 on Sabinus.

units.la: Non tantum in traditionibus, sed & in emptionibus, & stipulationibus, & testamentis adiectio haec, vti optimus maximusque est, hoc significat, vt liberum praestetur praedium, non vt etiam seruitutes ei debeantur.
units.tr: This addition, "as good and greatest as it is", means not only in conveyances but also in purchases, stipulations and wills, that the estate is to be delivered free, and not that servitudes are also owed to it.

units.la: 170. Vlpianus libro trigesimo tertio ad Sabinum.
units.tr: 170. Ulpian, book 33 on Sabinus.

units.la: Heredis appellatione omnes significari successores credendum est, etsi verbis non sint expressi.
units.tr: It must be believed that under the word "heir" all successors are meant, even if they are not expressly named.
171. Pomponius, book 16 on Sabinus.

units.la: Peruenisse[?] ad te recte dicitur, quod per te ad alium peruenerit: vt in hereditate a liberto per patronum filium familias patri eius adoptiuo adquisita responsum est.
units.tr: It is rightly said that something has come to you when it has come to another through you. Thus it was answered in the case of an inheritance acquired from a freedman, through the patron, by a son under power, for his adoptive father.

units.la: 172. Vlpianus libro trigesimo octauo ad Sabinum.
units.tr: 172. Ulpian, book 38 on Sabinus.

units.la: Liberti appellatione etiam libertam contineri placuit.
units.tr: It has been agreed that under the word "freedman" a freedwoman is also included.

units.la: Collegarum appellatione hi continetur, qui sunt eiusdem potestatis. 1 ¶Qui extra continentia vrbis est, abest : ceterum vsque ad continentia, non abesse videbitur.
units.tr: Under the word "colleagues" are included those who are of the same power. 1 ¶ One who is beyond the bounds of the city is absent; but as far as the bounds, he will not be considered absent.
174. The same, book 42 on Sabinus.

units.la: Aliud est promittere furem non esse, aliud furto noxaque solutum. qui enim dicit furem non esse, de hominis proposito loquitur. qui furtis noxaque solutum, nemini elle furti obligatum promittit.
units.tr: It is one thing to promise that a person is not a thief, and another to promise that he is free from theft and noxal liability. For one who says that someone is not a thief speaks of the man's intention; but one who promises that he is free from theft and noxal liability promises that he is bound by no obligation of theft to anyone.
175. Pomponius, book 22 on Sabinus.

units.la: Faciendi verbo, reddendi etiam causa conti-netur.
units.tr: Under the word "to do" is included also the case of "to return".
176. Ulpian, book 45 on Sabinus.

units.la: Solutionis verbo, satisfactionem quoque omne accipiendam placet. soluere dicimus eum qui fecit, quod facere promisit.
units.tr: Under the word "payment" it is also agreed that satisfaction is to be understood. We say that he pays who does what he promised to do.

units.la: NAtura cauillationis {a}, quam Graeci σωρίτης {b}, (id est, acervalem syllogismum) appellauerunt, hæc est, vt ab euidenter veris {c} per breuissimas mutationes {d} disputatio ad ea, quæ euidenter falsa sunt, perducatur.
units.tr: The nature of the sophism that the Greeks called σωρίτης (that is, the heap argument) is this: a disputation moves from things that are plainly true, through very small changes, to things that are plainly false.
178. The same author, in book 49 to Sabinus.

units.la: PEcuniæ verbum, non solum numeratam pecuniam complectitur: verum omnem {e} omnino pecuniam, hoc est omnia corpora. nam corpora quoque pecuniæ appellatione continentur, nemo est, qui ambiget. 1 ¶ Hereditas iuris {f} nomen est, quod & accessionem {g} & deccessionem in se recipit, hereditas autem vel maxime fructibus augetur. 2 ¶ Actionis {h} verbum, & speciale est, & generale: nam omnis actio dicitur, siue {i} in personam, siue in rem sit petitio. sed plerumque actiones personales solemus dicere. petitionis autem verbo, in rem actiones significari videntur. persecutionis [?] verbo extraordinarias {k} persecutiones puto contineri: vtputa fideicommissorum, & si quæ aliæ sunt, quæ non habent iuris ordinarij executionem. 3 ¶ Hoc verbum debuit {m}, omnem omnino actionem comprehendere intelligitur, siue ciuilis, siue honoraria, siue fideicommissi fuit persecutio.
units.tr: The word "money" embraces not only coined money but all money whatsoever, that is, all goods of every kind. For no one doubts that goods too are included under the name of money. 1 ¶ "Inheritance" is a term of law which takes in both additions and losses, though an inheritance is chiefly increased by its fruits. 2 ¶ The word "action" is both specific and general, for every suit is called an action, whether the claim is in personam or in rem. But we usually speak of personal actions, while by the word "claim" actions in rem seem to be meant. By the word "prosecution" I think extraordinary prosecutions are included, for instance those for trust bequests and any others that do not have the ordinary procedure of law. 3 ¶ This word "owed" is understood to cover every action whatever, whether civil, praetorian, or a prosecution of a trust bequest.

units.la: INter hæc verba, Quanti ea res esse, vel, Quanti eam rem esse paret, nihil interest: in utraque enim clausula placet veram {n} rei æstimationem fieri. Res estne successor? utique. Quid legatarius? is quoque. Titius estne legatarius? certè. igitur Titius est hæres. At contra ex falsis verum sequi potest. Omne prædium in iure consistit, omnis seruitus est prædium, ergo omnis seruitus in iure consistit {v.Cuiac. d.loco.}. Interrogationum fc.est enim ea natura soritis. Ex veris falsum efficere conatur. Hæ-res estne
units.tr: Between these expressions, "as much as that thing is worth" and "as much as that thing is shown to be worth," there is no difference, for in both clauses the true value of the thing is meant to be fixed. Is the thing a successor? Certainly. What of a legatee? He too. Is Titius a legatee? Surely. Therefore Titius is an heir. But conversely, a true conclusion can follow from false premises. Every estate consists in law; every servitude is an estate; therefore every servitude consists in law. {v. Cujas, in that place.} For this is the nature of the sorites of questions: it tries to make a falsehood out of truths. Is he an heir?

units.tr: {d} of questions; for that is the nature of the sorites.

units.la: TUgurij appellatione omne aedificium,quod ni-sicæ magis custodiæ conuenit, quàm vrbanis ædibus, significatur. 1 ¶ Ofilins ait tigurium à tecto{b}, tanquam tegularium, esse dictum, vt toga, quod ea tegamur.
units.tr: Under the name "hut" (tugurium) is meant any building that is more suited to a watch-post than to a town house. 1 ¶ Ofilius says that a tugurium is so called from the roof (tectum), as if it were "tegularium," just as the toga is named because we are covered (tegamur) by it.

units.la: VErbum illud pertinere{c} latissimè patet. nam & eis rebus perendis aptum est, quae dominini nostri sint:& eis,quas iure aliquo posideamus, quamuis non sint nostri domini. pertinere ad nos etiam ea dicimus, quae in nulla eorum causa sint, sed esse possint.
units.tr: The word "to pertain" has a very broad scope. For it applies both to things that are the property of our master, and to those that we hold by some right, although they are not our masters' property. We also say that things pertain to us which are in no way of their cause but could be.

units.la: PAterfamilias{d} liber peculium non potest habere{e}, quemadmodum nec seruus bona{f}.
units.tr: A householder (paterfamilias) cannot have a private fund (peculium), just as a slave cannot have goods.

units.la: TAbernae{g} appellatio declarat omne vtile ad ha-bitandum{h} aedificium:non ex eo,quod tabulis{i} cluditur.
units.tr: The use of the word "shop" (taberna) shows that any building useful for living in is meant, not only one closed with boards.
Tabernacles and tent-mates (contubernales) are so named from this.

units.tr: A son under power can have property, as can a slave-son; a householder cannot, likewise. A free person can be under paternal right. A householder is one who is his own master (sui iuris). But "patrimony" is not used in the sense of "peculium," unless we abuse the word peculium, by which we may understand whatever we have: our wealth, our fortunes, our substance. Peculium is used very broadly. A slave has no goods. The Greeks call it σκυρά; 2 Eclog. c. 183. Of a shop: a shop for furnishing, hence a silversmith's shop; a butcher's shop; a forge; a cauponia (inn); a travelling shop; an instructed shop; a bakery; a purple-dyer's shop; hence a shopkeeper (tabernarius). Adde... {the rest of this note is too corrupt to restore}.

units.la: HAbere duobus d modis dicitur: altero, iure dominij: altero, obtinere e fine interpellatione id, quod quis emerit. 1 ¶ Cautum[?] f intelligitur: sine personis, sive rebus cautum sit.
units.tr: To have is said in two ways: one by the right of ownership, the other to obtain, without interpellation, what someone has bought. 1 ¶ "Cautum" is understood: whether the caution concerns persons or things.

units.la: FAcere g oportere & hanc significationem habet: Vt abstineat quis ab eo facto, quod contra conuentionem fieret: & curaret, ne fiat.
units.tr: "To act" (facere) also has this meaning: that one should abstain from that act which would be contrary to the agreement, and take care that it does not happen.

units.la: PRouinciales h eos accipere debemus, qui in provincia domicilium habent: non eos, qui ex provincia oriundi sunt.
units.tr: We ought to understand provincials as those who have their domicile in the province, not those who are native to the province.
191. Paulus, book 35 on the Edict.

units.la: INter diuortium i & repudium k, hoc interest: quod repudiari etiam futurum matrimonium poterit: nam recte autem sponsa diuortium dicitur. quod diuortium ex eo dictum est, quod in diuersas partes eunt, qui discedunt.
units.tr: Between divorce and repudiation there is this difference: a future marriage too can be repudiated, for a betrothed woman is also rightly said to be divorced. Divorce (divortium) is so called because those who separate go in different directions.

units.tr: This addition, "or more," does not cover an unlimited sum but a modest one, so that this valuation of "ten solidi or more" is reduced to a small amount.

units.la: Inter donum & munus {d}, hoc interest, quod inter genus & speciem. nam genus esse donum Labeo a donando dictum, munus speciem. nam munus esse donum cum causa, ut puta natalicium, {e}nuptalicium.
units.tr: Between donum (gift) and munus (present) there is this difference, that it is the difference between genus and species. For Labeo says donum is so called from donare (to give), and munus is a species, since a munus is a gift with a reason behind it, such as a birthday gift or a wedding gift.

units.la: Pronuntiatio sermonis in sexu masculino ad utrumq; sexum plerumque porrigitur. 1 ¶ {f}Familiae & appellatio qualiter accipiatur, videamus. & quidem varie accepta est. nam & in res, & in personas {g}deducitur. In res, ut puta in lege duodecim tabularum his verbis, adgnatus proximus familiam habeto. Ad personas autem refertur familiae significatio ita, cum de patrono & liberto loquitur lex: ex ea familia, inquit, in eam familiam. & hinc de singularibus personis legem loqui constat. 2 Familiae appellatio refertur & ad corporis cuiusdam significationem, quod aut iure proprio ipsorum, aut communi vniuersae cognationis continetur. Iure proprio familiam dicimus, plures personas, quae sunt sub vnius potestate, aut natura, aut iure subiectae, ut puta patremfamilias, matremfamilias, filiumfamilias, filiamfamilias, quinque deinceps vicem eorum sequuntur, ut puta nepotes, & neptes, & deinceps. Pater autem familias appellatur, qui in domo dominium habet. Recteque hoc nomine appellatur, quamuis filium non habeat. non enim solam personam eius, sed & ius {h}demonstramus. denique & pupillum patremfamilias appellamus. & cum paterfamilias moritur: quotquot capita ei subiecta fuerint, singulas familias incipiunt habere. singuli enim patrumfamiliarum nomen subeunt. idemque eueniet & in eo, qui emancipatus est: nam & hic sui iuris effectus , propriam familiam habet. Communi iure familiam dicimus omnium adgnatorum nam etsi patrefamilias mortuo singulas familias habent tamen omnes, qui sub vnius potestate fuerunt, recte eiusdem familiæ appellabuntur, qui ex eadem domo & gente proditi sunt.
units.tr: The use of a word in the masculine gender is generally extended to both sexes. 1 ¶ Let us see how the term familia (family) is understood. It is taken in various ways, for it applies both to things and to persons. It applies to things, as in the Law of the Twelve Tables in these words: let the nearest agnate hold the family. The meaning of familia applies to persons when the law speaks of a patron and a freedman: out of that family, it says, into that family. And it is agreed that the law here speaks of individual persons. 2 The term familia also refers to a certain body of persons, which is contained either by a right belonging to them individually or by a right common to the whole kindred. By right belonging to them we call a family the several persons who are subject, either by nature or by law, to the power of one man: for example, the father of the family, the mother of the family, the son of the family, the daughter of the family; and in turn, those who follow their place, such as grandsons, granddaughters, and so on. A man is called pater familias who holds dominion in the house, and he is rightly so called even if he has no son, for we are indicating not only his person but his right. Indeed we also call a ward a pater familias. And when a pater familias dies, all those placed under his authority begin to have each a separate family, for each one takes on the name of a pater familias. The same happens with one who has been emancipated, for he too, made sui iuris, has his own family. By common right we call a family all the agnates; for although, when the pater familias dies, they have separate families, all who were under the power of one man will rightly be called of the same family, those who have come forth from the same house and clan.

units.la: ¶ Seruitutium quoque solemus appellare familias, vt in edicto prætoris ostendimus sub titulo de furtis, vbi prætor loquitur de familia publicanorum. sed ibi non omnes serui, sed corpus quoddam seruorum demonstratur huius rei causa paratum, hoc est vectigalis causa: alia autem parte edicti omnes serui continentur, vt de hominibus coactis, & vi bonorum raptorum. item redhibitoria, si deterior res redditur emptoris opera, aut familiæ eius. & interdicto vnde vi familiæ appellatio omnes serui comprehendit. sed & filij continentur.
units.tr: ¶ We are also accustomed to call the slaves a family, as we show in the Praetor's edict under the title on theft, where the praetor speaks of the family of the publicani. But there it is not all the slaves that is meant, but a certain body of slaves prepared for this purpose, that is, for the sake of revenue. In another part of the edict, however, all slaves are included, as in the case of men forced together, and of goods seized by violence. Likewise in the redhibitory action, if the thing is made worse by the buyer's work or that of his family. And under the interdict unde vi the term familia includes all slaves. But children are included as well.

units.la: 4 ¶Item appellatur familia plurium personarum, quæ ab eiusdem vltimi genitoris sanguine proficiscuntur. sicuti dicimus familiam Iuliam, quasi a fonte quodam memoriæ.
units.tr: 4 ¶ Also a family is called a number of persons who descend from the blood of one and the same remote ancestor, as we speak of the Julian family, as if from a certain fountain of memory.

units.la: 5 ¶ Mulier autem familiæ suæ & caput, & finis est.
units.tr: 5 ¶ A woman is both the head and the end of her own family.

units.la: Familiæ appellatione & ipse princeps familiæ continetur. 1 ¶Feminarum liberos in familia earum non esse, palàm est: quia qui nascuntur, patris, non matris familiam sequuntur.
units.tr: Under the term familia the head of the family himself is also included. 1 ¶ It is plain that the children of women are not in their family, because those who are born follow the family of the father, not of the mother.
197. Ulpian, book 50 on the Edict.

units.la: Indicasse est detulisse, arguisse, accusasse, & conuicisse.
units.tr: To indicare is to report, to charge, to accuse, and to revile.

units.la: Vrbana prædia, omnia ædificia accipimus, non solùm ea, quæ sunt in oppidis, sed & si forte stativa sunt, vel alia meritoria in villis, & in vicis, vel si prætoria voluptati tantùm deserviēntia: quia vrbanum prædij non locus facit, sed materia.Proin
units.tr: We understand urban estates to be all buildings, not only those that are in towns but also, if perchance they are stationary or other lodgings in country houses and villages, or if they are merely pleasure-houses serving for amusement; for it is not the place that makes an estate urban, but its material. units.la: Absentem accipere debemus eum, qui non est eo loci, in quo loco petitur, non enim trans mare absentem desideramus. Si forte extra continentia urbis sit, abest, ceterum vsque ad continentia, non abesse videbitur, si non latitet. Abesse non videtur, qui ab hostibus captus est, sed a latronibus detinetur.
units.tr: We must understand an absent person as one who is not in the place where he is being sued, for we do not require someone who is across the sea to be present. If he happens to be outside the built-up area of the city, he is absent; but up to the built-up area he will not seem absent, provided he is not hiding. A man who has been captured by enemies is not considered absent, but one who is held by brigands is.
200. Julianus, book 2 of the Digest.

units.la: Hæc stipulatio <bl>Noxiæ</bl> solutum præstari non existimatur ad eas noxas pertinere, quæ publicam exercitionem, & coercitionem capitalem habent.
units.tr: This noxal stipulation is not thought to cover those noxae that carry public punishment and capital penalty.
201. The same, book eighty-one of the Digest.

units.la: Vsta interpretatione recipiendum est, vt appellatione filij, sicut filiasfamilias continere sæpe respondebimus, ita & nepos videatur comprehendi. & patris nomine auus quoque demonstrari intelligatur.
units.tr: By sound interpretation it must be accepted that, just as we have often answered that a daughter under power is included in the word "son," so a grandson also seems to be comprehended, and by the name "father" the grandfather is understood to be indicated as well.
202. Alfenus Varus, book 2 of the Digest.

units.la: Cum in testamento scriptum esset, vt heres in functione hanc appellationem non includimus. Cum in monumento dumtaxat aureos centum consumeret: non licet minus consumere, si amplius vellet, licet, neque ob eam rem contra testamentum facere videtur.
units.tr: Since it was written in a will that the heir should spend a sum on the funeral, we do not include this term in the funeral. If he was to spend only a hundred gold pieces on the monument, he may not spend less; if he wished to spend more, he is permitted to, and he does not seem to act against the will for that reason.
203. The same, book 7 of the Digest.

units.la: In lege censoria portus Siciliæ ira scriptum erat: Serui quos domo quis ducet ius suo, vsus, portoriū, hic portorium ne dato, quæreb atur, si quis à Sicilia seruos Romam mitteret.
units.tr: In the censorial law of the harbour of Sicily it was written thus: "Slaves whom anyone shall lead from home for his own use, let him not pay harbour dues on them." It was asked whether, if anyone sent slaves from Sicily to Rome, he should pay harbour dues on them.

units.la: {f} Filij appellatione filiasfamilias & nepos comprehenditur l.84. l.116.5.eod.120.§.1. 7.ee.Ecl.ib c.200. {g} Patris nomine auus comprehenditur Eelog.ibidem.c.201. {h} excipe l.44.§.1.§.2.5.de ritu. {i} quid si minus consumpserit reliqua summa hæredibus proficiet l.28.§.1.5.de leg.2. {k} non tamen in eo casu id quod plus expendit repetet l.31.§.4.5.denegotl.50 §.1.5.de hæreditate petit: l.5.5.mandati: adde l.5.§ 15.5.de donat. int. vir. {l} Ea dicta est non à censu, vt Accurius putat, sed à censoribus, quorum munus erat portoria & vectigalia locare. Liuius 4.de censura loquens, Sub ditione eius sunt vectigalia populi Romani. {m} l.5.C.de vectigal.commiss. mitteret fundi instruendi causa, vtrum pro his hominis portorium dare deberet, necne. respondit, duas esse in hac scriptura quaestiones: primam, quid esset domum ducere: alteram, quid esset suo vsu [?] ducere. Igitur quaeri soleret, vtrum vbi quisque habitaret, siue in provincia, siue in Italia, an domum aut[?] in sua cuiusque patria domus esse recte dicetur. sed de ea re constitutum esse, {a}eam domum vniuique no-strum debere existimari, vbi quisque sedes & tabulas haberet, suarumque rerum constitutionem fecisset. Quid autem esset vsu {c}suo, magnam habuisse dubitationem. & magis placet, quod victus cui causa paratum est, tamen contineri. Itemque de seruis eadem ratione quaeri, qui eorum vsus sui causa parati essent: vtrum dispensatores, iniularij, vilici, atrienses, textores, operarij quoque rustici, qui agrorum colendarum causa haberentur, ex quibus [agris] paterfamilias fructus caperet, quibus se toleraret [?]: omnes denique seruos, quos quisque emisset, vt ipse haberet, atque eis ad aliquam rem vterentur, neque ideo emisset, vt venderet. Et sibi videri eos demum vsus sui causa paterfamilias habere, qui ad eius corpus {e}tuendum, atque ipsius cultum praepositi, destinatique essent, quo in genere iunctores {f}, cubicularij, coci, ministratores, atque alij, qui ad eiusmodi vsum parati essent, numerarentur.
units.tr: {f} The word "son" includes a daughter under power and a grandson: law 84, law 116 §1 of the same title, law 120 §1; Ecloga, book 7, chapter 200. {g} By the name "father" the grandfather is included: Ecloga, same place, chapter 201. {h} Except law 44 §1 and §2 and §5 concerning ritual. {i} What if he has spent less? The remaining sum will benefit the heirs: law 28 §1 and §5 concerning legacies, book 2. {k} Yet in that case he will not recover what he has spent in excess: law 31 §4 and §5 on business; law 50 §1 and §5 on the petition for inheritance; law 5 §5 on mandate; add law 5 §15 on gifts between husband and wife. {l} It was called so not from the census, as Accursius thinks, but from the censors, whose duty was to let out harbour dues and tolls. Livy, speaking of the censorship in book 4: "Under their authority are the tolls of the Roman people." {m} Law 5 C. on the forfeiture of tolls. A person sent slaves to furnish a farm, and asked whether he ought to pay harbour dues on these men or not. He answered that there were two questions in this wording: first, what it meant to lead home; second, what it meant to lead for his own use. So it used to be asked whether wherever each man lived, whether in a province or in Italy, was rightly called his home, or whether a home was in each man's native place. But it had been settled about this matter that the home of each of us ought to be considered wherever a man had his seat and records and had established the arrangement of his property. But what "for his own use" meant had caused great doubt, and it is more acceptable that whatever is prepared for the support of the person is included. Likewise about slaves the same reasoning was asked: which of them were kept for their owner's own use, whether stewards, overseers, bailiffs, doorkeepers, weavers, and even rustic labourers who were kept to cultivate the fields from which the head of the household takes the produce, by which he supports himself; in short, all slaves whom anyone bought to keep for himself and use for some purpose, and not in order to sell them. And it seemed to him that the head of the household keeps slaves for his own use only those who are set over and appointed for the protection of his body and his personal care, a class in which masseurs, bedroom attendants, cooks, servers, and others who were prepared for such use are counted.
204. Paulus, book 2 of the Epitomes [of Alfenus].

units.la: PVeri appellatio tres significationes habet: vnam, cum omnes seruos {b}pueros appellaremus: de auro: adde l.43. §.codem.
units.tr: The word "boy" (puer) has three meanings: first, when we called all slaves "boys"; concerning gold: add law 43, same title.

units.tr: {e} We have as our own use those things that are prepared for protecting the body and its care: see law 166 and law 198 §, same title.
