Plautus in Trinummo, Ducitur familia tota, vestispici, vnctor, auri custos. Martial. XII, atque olei stillam donaret Opelicus vnctor. Antiqua inscriptio, Aurelius Eros vnctor. sed tamen in antiquis glossis, iunctor est [illegible, ~5 letters]: qui iungit mulas ad rhedam, qui & mulio vel leaticarius l.99.§.2. §.4.§. de leg.2. Hinc carruca cum iunctura apud Paulum §. feni. v. Cuiac. 14. obs. §Pueri appellatione, seruus: pueri masculi, aetas puerilis significatur.
units.tr: {f} Read "actores" or "vnctores" (for "iunctores"). Thus Arrian, among chattel slaves, counts those prepared for the head of the household's own use [illegible, about six letters]. Plautus in the Trinummus: "The whole household is led, the clothes-inspector, the anointer, the guardian of the gold." Martial, book 12: "and Opelicus the anointer gave a drop of oil." An ancient inscription: "Aurelius Eros, anointer." But in the ancient glosses, the iunctor is [illegible, about five letters]: one who yokes mules to a carriage, who is also called a muleteer or carter: law 99 §2 and §4 and §, on legacies, book 2. Hence the cart with its yoke, in Paulus, §. feni. Cuiacius, Observations, book 14. "By the word boy, a slave is meant; boys of the male sex, the age of boyhood is signified."

units.la: {b} Pueri pro seruis accipiuntur Varro apud Nonium. vix vulgus confuit non furiarum sed puerorum atque ancillarum. alteram, cum puerum contrario nomine puellæ {4} diceremus: tertiam, cum ætatem puerilem {6} demonstraremus.
units.tr: {b} Boys are taken for slaves: Varro in Nonius: "Scarcely has the common crowd fled, not of Furies but of boys and maidservants." The second meaning is when we called a boy by the opposite name, of a girl; the third, when we indicated the age of boyhood.
205. The same, in the fourth book of Alfenus's Epitomes.

units.la: QVi fundum vendidit, pomum {c} recepit: nuces {d}, & ficos {e}, & uvas dumtaxat duracinas {f}, & purpureas {g}, & quæ eius generis essent, quas non vini causa haberemus, quas Græci τρωξίμους {h} .i. comestibiles, appellarent, recepta videri.
units.tr: Whoever sold an estate kept the fruit. Nuts, figs, and only the hard grapes and purple grapes, and such kinds as we would not keep for making wine, which the Greeks call trōximous [τρωξίμους], that is, fit for eating, are held to have been kept back.

units.la: {c} Pomi appellatione continetur omnis fructus edendi causa paratus Macrobius 3. Saturnalium 19. malorum genera refert, aureum, cotoneum, citreum, coccymelium, conditiuum, [illegible, ~6 letters], musteum, mattianum, orbiculatum, ogranum, præcox, pannuceum, puuicum, Persicum quirianum, persicum rubrum, scandianum, syluestre, strutium, scantianū, tibur, verianum. Ibidem refert pyrorum genera. De nuce pinea illud notandum, lapidat[?] à populo Vatinius, cum gladiatorium munus ederet obtinuerat vt ædiles ediceret, ne quis in arenam nisi pomum mitisse veller. forte his diebus Cafellius consultus à quodam, an nux pinea pomum esset, respondit, Si in Vatinium missurus es, pomum est 2. Macrob. 6.
units.tr: Under the name of fruit is included every produce prepared for eating. Macrobius, Saturnalia 3.19, lists the kinds of apples: golden, quince, citron, coccymelium, preserved, [illegible], must-apple, Mattian, round, ogranum, early-ripening, pannuceum, pomegranate, Persian, Quirian, red Persian, Scandian, wild, strutium, Scantian, Tibur, Verian. In the same place he lists the kinds of pears. Concerning the pine nut it should be noted that Vatinius, when he was giving a gladiatorial show, had obtained an edict from the aediles that no one should throw anything into the arena except fruit. Then, by chance, when Cafellius was asked by someone whether a pine nut was fruit, he replied: "If you intend to throw it at Vatinius, it is fruit." Macrobius 2 and 6.

units.la: {d} Nux est, quod foris duro tegitur, & intus habet quod esui est: Malum vero quod foris habet quod est esui, durum intus. Macrob. 3. Saturnalium 19. vbi hæc genera nucium ab eodem recensentur, Nux iuglans, pontica, castanea, græca, molusca, tarentina, pinea.
units.tr: A nut is that which is covered on the outside by a hard shell and has inside what is fit to eat; whereas an apple has on the outside what is fit to eat and is hard inside. Macrobius, Saturnalia 3.19, where the same author lists these kinds of nuts: walnut, Pontic, chestnut, Greek, molusca, Tarentine, pine nut.

units.la: {e} ficus Hal. adde l. vlt. §.1. §.de vinico. Ficuum hæ species recensentur à Macrobio 3. Saturn. 20. Africa, albula, arundinea, asinaltra, atra, palusca, augusta, bifera, carica, caldica, alba, nigra, calphurniana, chia, cucurbitina, duricoria, herculanea, lauiana, ludia, leprolidia, marfica, numidica, pulla, pompeiana, precox, tellana.
units.tr: {e} fig. Haloander: add the last law, §1, de vino. Macrobius (Saturnalia 3.20) lists these kinds of figs: African, whitish, reedy, asinaltra, black, marsh, august, twice-bearing, Carian, warm, white, black, Calpurnian, Chian, gourd-shaped, hard-skinned, Herculanean, Lavian, Lydian, leprolidian, Marsian, Numidian, dark, Pompeian, early, Tellan.

units.la: {g} hinc vites purpureæ, Ouidius in metamorphosi 8. Et de purpureis collectæ vitibus vuæ.
units.tr: Hence the purple vines. Ovid, Metamorphoses 8: "and grapes gathered from the purple vines."

units.la: {h} vua τρωξίμως escaria. Plin. 14. capite 3. In pergulis feruntur vuæ escariæ, idem ibidem vua cibaria.
units.tr: Grape, trōximōs [τρωξίμως], eating grape. Pliny 14, ch. 3: "In the arbors are said to be the eating grapes (vuae escariae)." The same author, in the same place, calls them grapes for food (vua cibaria).
206. Julian, book 6, from Minicius.

units.la: {a}Vinaria vasa proprie vasa torcularia {b}esse placet. dolia autem & ferias {c}tamdiu in ea causa esse, quamdiu vinum haberent. cum sine vino esse deinerent, in eo numero non esse : quoniam ad alium vsum transferri possent. veluti si frumentum in his addatur. eandem causam amphorarum esse : vt cum vinum habeant, tum in vasis vinariis : cum inanes sint, tum extra numerum vinariorum sint: quia aliud in his addi possit.
units.tr: It is agreed that wine vessels are properly the vessels of the press. Vats and casks, however, remain in that category only as long as they hold wine; when they have been emptied of wine, they are not counted in that class, since they can be turned to another use, as when grain is put into them. The same reasoning applies to amphorae: when they hold wine they are wine vessels, but when they are empty they are not among the wine vessels, because something else can be put into them.
207. Africanus, book 3 of Questions.

units.la: {f}Mercis {g}appellatione homines {h}non {i}continentur, ut Mela air. & ob eam rem mangones {j}no mercatores, sed venaliciarios {k}appellari ait. & recte.
units.tr: By the term "merchandise" men are not included, as Mela says. For this reason, he says, mangones are called not merchants but dealers in slaves (venaliciarii), and rightly so.
208. The same, book 4, law 7, of Questions.

units.la: Bonorum appellatio, sicut hereditatis, vniuersitatem quandam ac ius successionis, & non singulares res demonstrat.
units.tr: The term "goods," like "inheritance," denotes a whole and a right of succession, not individual things.
209. Florentinus, book 10 of Institutes.

units.la: Coram m Titio aliquid facere iussus, non videtur praesente eo fecisse, nisi is intelligat. itaque si fuerit...
units.tr: One who is ordered to do something in the presence of Titius is not regarded as having done it if Titius is not present, unless he understands it. So if he is...

units.la: §.5.§.de furtu: lacum vini l.27.in f. §.ad l.Aquil: & ferias §.eod.ad-de & alia ex Catone de re rustica c.11.
units.tr: §5 de furtis; the wine vat, law 27 in fine; §ad l. Aquiliam; and the feriae, §eod. Also, from Cato, On Agriculture, ch. 11, and other passages.
b, that is, joined presses.

units.la: c 12. Columella 18, Dolia & ferias, caeteraque vasa ante quadragesimum diem vindemiae siccanda sunt. Alij feriam vas fictile arbitrantur Perf. satyr.2. Seriae tamen glossis vocabulum quo hodie Hetrusci vtuntur.
units.tr: c 12. Columella 18: "Casks and feriae, and the other vessels, must be dried before the fortieth day of the vintage." Others think a feria is an earthen vessel; Persius, Satire 2. Yet seriae is a word in the glossaries for what the Etruscans use today.

units.la: Nicetas dixit [illegible, ~20 letters] & interpretatur [illegible, ~12 letters] vnde dogae glossis dicuntur quasi [illegible, ~6 letters]. Vopiscus in Aureliano, fasta est ratio dogae, cuparum & nauium, dogae capacitati. Cupas [illegible, ~12 letters] exponunt veteres glossae, & a quibusdam gaulos vocari. Hinc Butte & buticellae vide Cuiac.9.obser.
units.tr: Nicetas said [illegible] and it is interpreted [illegible]; whence dogae are called in the glossaries, as if [illegible]. Vopiscus, in Aurelian: the reckoning of dogae, of casks and ships, the capacity of the dogae. The ancient glosses explain cupae [illegible], and by some they are called gauli. Hence butte and buticellae; see Cuiacius, Observations, book 9.

units.la: 26. d v.Cuiac.3.ad Afric.sol.30. e 2.Eclog.2.c.207. f seruos l.1.§.1.§.de tributoria: adde l.66.§.eod.44.§.de aedilitio. g mercis tamen loco haberi possunt l.73.§ 4.§.de leg.3. h [illegible, ~12 letters] Eclog.ibid. Seneca 4. de benef.11. Mercator, vrbibus prodest: medicus, aegrotis: mangones, venalibus. Idem, mangones (fi quod est quod displicet) aliquo lenocinio abscondunt. Sic Plinius 37. gemmarum politores, mangones vocat.
units.tr: 26. d, see Cuiacius, On Africanus, Solutions 30. e, Eclogae 2.2, ch. 207. f slaves, law 1 §1 §de tributoria; add law 66 §eod. 44 §de aedilitio. g nevertheless they may be held in the place of merchandise, law 73 §4 §de legatis 3. h [illegible] Eclogae, ibid. Seneca, On Benefits 4.11: "The merchant benefits cities, the physician the sick, the mangones those who are for sale." The same: "mangones (if there is anything that displeases) hide it with some sort of flattery." So Pliny, book 37, calls the polishers of gems mangones.

units.la: i l.1.§.1.§.de tributoria l.57. §.mandati:l.37.l.44.§.1.§.de aedilitio qui & venalicij l.vlt.in f.§.de aedilitio. Hinc venaliciarium vitam exercere l.73.§.4.§.de leg.3: qui ab his venduntur, venales l.1.§.de negotijs: venalitij l.5.in f.§.de iure deliberinde venalicia familia l.31.in f.§.de don.int.vir: venalitium, venditigal rerum venalium l.1.C.de veteran:l.4.C.de prox.sacri scrin. v.Cuiac.4.ad Afric.sol.61. v.l.66.l.119.§.eod: l.50. §.de haere.petit. m l.27.§.5.§.de arbitriis.De palam vide l.33.§. riosus, aut infans sit, aut dormiat: non videtur coram eo fecisse. Scire autem, non etiam velle is debet: nam & inuito eo recte fit, quod iussum est.
units.tr: i law 1 §1 §de tributoria; law 57 §mandati; laws 37 and 44 §1 §de aedilitio, which also concerns venalicii; last law in fine §de aedilitio. Hence to carry on the life of a dealer in slaves, law 73 §4 §de legatis 3; those who are sold by these are venales, law 1 §de negotiis; venalitii, law 5 in fine §de iure deliberandi; the venalicia family, law 31 in fine §de donationibus inter virum et uxorem; venalitium, the sale tax on saleable goods, law 1 C. de veteranis; law 4 C. de proximis sacri scrinii. See Cuiacius, On Africanus, Solutions 61. See law 66, law 119 §eod.; law 50 §de haeredis petitione. m law 27 §5 §de arbitriis. On "palam," see law 33 §... If he is mad, or an infant, or asleep, he is not regarded as having done it in his presence. But he must know, not merely will it; for it is rightly done even against his will, what he was ordered to do.
210. Marcianus, Institutes, book 7.

units.la: Is[?], qui natus est ex mancipiis vrbanis{a}, & missus est in villam nutriendus, in vrbanis seruis constituetur.
units.tr: He who was born of city slaves (mancipia urbana) and was sent to a farm to be raised shall be reckoned among the city slaves.
211. Florentinus, Institutes, book 8.

units.la: Fundi{b} appellatione omne aedificium, & omnis ager continetur. Sed in usu{c} urbana aedificia, aedes rustica, villæ dicuntur. Locus{d} vero sine aedificio, in urbe area, rure autem ager{e} appellatur. Idemque ager cum aedificio, fundus dicitur.
units.tr: The term "farm" (fundus) includes every building and every field. In common usage, however, city buildings are called houses (aedes), rural buildings farmhouses, and villas (villae). A site without a building is called an area (area) in the city, but a field (ager) in the country. And the same field together with a building is called a farm (fundus).
212. Ulpian, On Adulteries, book 1.

units.la: Præuaricatores{f} eos appellamus, qui causam aduersariis suis donant, & ex parte actoris in parte rei concedunt. A varicando enim præuaricatores di-cti sunt.
units.tr: We call prevaricators those who give their opponents the case, and who, on the side of the plaintiff, yield to the side of the defendant. For prevaricators (praevaricatores) are so named from straddling (varicare), that is, from walking with legs apart.
213. The same, Rules, book 1.

units.la: Cedere{g} diem significat incipere deberi pecuniam. Venire diem significat eum diem venisse, quo pecunia peti posit. Ubi pure quis stipulatus fuerit: & cessit{h}, & venit dies. Ubi in die cessit dies, sed nondum venit. Ubi sub condicione{i}: neque cessit, neque venit dies pendente adhuc condicione.
units.tr: "To fall due" (cedere diem) means that money begins to be owed. "To come due" (venire diem) means that the day has arrived on which the money can be demanded. Where someone has stipulated without condition, both the day has fallen due and it has come. Where the day has fallen due on a fixed day but has not yet come, ... Where the stipulation is under a condition, the day has neither fallen due nor come, since the condition is still pending.

units.la: 1 †Æs alienum{k} est, quod nos aliis debemus. Æs suum est, quod alij nobis debent. 2 †Lata{l} culpa est nimia negligentia: id est, non intelligere, quod omnes intelligunt.
units.tr: (1) A debt owed by others (aes alienum) is what we owe to others. Our own money (aes suum) is what others owe to us. (2) Gross fault (lata culpa) is excessive negligence, that is, failing to understand what everyone understands.
214. Marcianus, Public Judgments, book 1.

units.la: Munus{m} proprie est, quod necessarie{n} obimus, lege, more, imperioue eius, qui iubendi habet potestatem. Dona{o} autem proprie sunt, quæ nulla necessitate{p} iuris, officij, sed sponte præstantur. Quæ si non præstentur, nulla repræhensio est. & si præstentur, plerumque laus inest. Sed in summa in[?]
units.tr: A munus is properly what we undertake out of necessity, by law, by custom, or by the command of one who has the power to order it. Gifts (dona), properly speaking, are those rendered not from any necessity of law or duty, but of free will. If these are not rendered, there is no blame; and if they are rendered, there is usually praise. But in sum ...

units.la: non ex Vlpiani ingenio, sed ex Triboniani audacia potius emanasse.{i}
units.tr: ... not to have sprung from the talent of Ulpian, but rather from the audacity of Tribonian.
Add law 13, §5, De pignoribus.

units.la: quos debemus v.l.159. §.eod. vel Cuiac.7.obs.33. 2.Ecl.2.c.214. §.1. §.de mun.
units.tr: "quos debemus": see law 159, §. eod., or Cuiacius, Observations 7.33; 2 Eclogue, 2, c. 214, §1, De muneribus.
That is, coins.
See law 226, §. eod.
See law 194, §. eo.; 2 Eclogue, 2, c. 212; law 239, §3, §. co.
Title 14.

units.la: {o} hinc constat munus a dono separari, idq. confirmat lex 6. in f. §.de off. proconsul. l.8. §.de off. præf. l.37. l.47. §.de oper. liber. l.vlt. §.1. §.de liber. l.6. in f. §.ad l.Iul. repet.
units.tr: Hence it is established that munus is separated from donum, and this is confirmed by law 6, in fine, §. De officio proconsulis; law 8, §. De officio praefecti; law 37; law 47, §. De operis libertorum; law ult., §1, §. De libertis; law 6, in fine, §. ad legem Iuliam repetundarum.

units.la: {p} v.l.29. §.de do. hoc ventum est: vt {a}non quodcunque munus, id & donum accipiatur: at {b}quod donum fuerit, id munus recte dicatur.
units.tr: See law 29, §. De donationibus. Here it is said: "Not every munus is taken as a donum, but whatever is a donum may rightly be called a munus."

units.la: 215. Paulus libro singulari ad legem Fufiam Caninian.
units.tr: 215. Paul, single book on the Lex Furia Caninia.

units.la: Potestatis verbo plura {c}significantur. in persona magistratuum {d}, imperium. in persona liberorum, {e}patria potestas. in persona serui {f}, dominiū. At cum agimus de noxæ {g} deditione cum eo, qui seruum non defendit: præsentis corporis copiam facultatemque significamus. In lege Arinia {h} in potestatem domini rem furtiuam venisse videri, & si {i} eius vindicandæ potestatem habuerit, Sabinus & Cassius aiunt {k}.
units.tr: The word "power" (potestas) signifies several things: in the person of magistrates, imperium; in the person of children, paternal power (patria potestas); in the person of a slave, ownership (dominium). But when we speak of the surrender of a slave for noxal liability (noxae deditio) to one who does not defend the slave, we mean the present availability and opportunity of the body. In the Arinian law, a stolen thing is held to have come into the power of the owner, and if he has the power to claim it, Sabinus and Cassius say so.

units.la: 216. Vlpianus libro primo ad legem Aeliam Sentiam.
units.tr: 216. Ulpian, On the Lex Aelia Sentia, book 1.

units.la: VErum est, eum, qui in carcere clusus est, non videri neque {l}vinctum, neque in vinculis {m} esse, {n}nisi corpori eius vincula sint adhibita.
units.tr: It is true that a person shut up in prison is regarded neither as bound nor as in chains, unless shackles have been applied to his body.
217. Javolenus, from the Posterior Writings of Labeo, book 1.

units.la: INter illam condicione, {o}cum fari potuerit, & {p}post- quam fari potuerit, multum interest. nam posteriorem scripturam, vberiorem esse constat. at cum fari potuerit, atriorem: & id tantummodo tempus significari, quo primum fari possit. ɪ ¶ Item ita data condicione, Illud facito in diebus, si nihil præ-terea fuisset adiectum, in biduo {q}condicionem impleri oportet.
units.tr: There is a great difference between a condition "when he is able to speak" and "after he is able to speak." For it is agreed that the later wording is fuller, while "when he is able to speak" is narrower, and signifies only the time at which he can first speak. Likewise, if a condition is given thus, "Do that within days" (illud facito in diebus), and nothing further has been added, the condition must be fulfilled within two days.
218. Papinian, Questions, book 27.

units.la: VErbum Facere {r} omnem omnino faciendi causam complectitur: dandi, soluendi, numerandi, iudicandi, ambulandi.
units.tr: The verb "to do" (facere) embraces every cause of doing whatever: giving, paying, counting, judging, walking.
219. The same, Responses, book 2.

units.la: de noxalib. {h} Atilia §. 2. Institut. de vsucap. vbi vide Cuiac.
units.tr: On noxal actions, see the Atilian (law) and §2 of the Institutes, De usucapionibus, where see Cuiacius.

units.la: {i} vel si eius rei, velut suę possessionem ita nactus fit, vt iuste ei auelli nō possit l.4.§.12. s. de vsurp. {k} adde & illud de potestatis verbo, in persona pupilli tutorum auctoritatem l.1 s. de tutelis,
units.tr: Or if he has obtained possession of a thing as his own in such a way that it cannot justly be taken from him (law 4, §12, De usurpationibus). Add also, on the word potestas, that in the person of a ward it means the authority of guardians (law 1, §. De tutelis).

units.la: l 2. Eclog. 2. cap. 2. 6. {m} v l.224. j. co: l. 9. s. ex quib. causat. maior: l. 8. s. de pœnis. {n} Ecloga ibid. cap. 217. {o} adde l. 41. s. de manumiss. test. {p} v. l. 41. l. 109. in f. s. de verborum oblig: l. 12. s. de testib. {q} 2. Ecloga 2. cap. 218. l. 58. l. 175. s. cod: l. 60. s. de condit. demonstr.
units.tr: 2 Eclogue, 2, c. 2.6; see law 224, §. co.; law 9, §. Ex quibus causis maiores; law 8, §. De poenis. Eclogue, ibid., c. 217. Add law 41, §. De manumissis testamento. See law 41; law 109, in fine, §. De verborum obligationibus; law 12, §. De testibus. 2 Eclogue, 2, c. 218; law 58; law 175, §. cod.; law 60, §. De condicionibus demonstrandis.

units.la: IN conuentionibus contrahentium voluntatem potius, quàm verba, spectari placuit. Cum igitur ea lege fundum vectigalem municipes locauerint, vt ad heredem eius, qui iuscepit, pertineret: ius heredum ad legatarium quoque transferri potuit.
units.tr: In agreements between contracting parties, it has been held that the will rather than the words is to be regarded. Therefore, when the citizens of a municipality leased a tax-bearing farm on the terms that it should pass to the heir of him who took it on, the right of the heirs could also be transferred to the legatee.
220. Callistratus, book 2 of the Questions.

units.la: LIberorum appellatione nepotes, & pronepotes, cæterique, qui ex his descendunt, continentur. hos enim omnes suorum appellatione lex duodecim tabularum comprehendit: totiens enim legis necessarium ducunt in cognatione singulorum nominibus vel, veluti Filii, nepotes, pronepotes, cæterorumve, qui ex his descendunt: quoties non omnibus, qui post eos sunt, præstitum voluerint: sed solis his succurrent, quos nominatim enumerent. At vbi non personis certis, non quibusdam gradibus præsentia est, statur, sed omnibus, qui ex eodem genere orti sunt, liberorum appellatione comprehenduntur.
units.tr: Under the name of children are included grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and the others who descend from them. The Twelve Tables comprehend all of these under the name of "sui," for the lawgivers thought it necessary to name each degree of kinship whenever they wished to provide for some and not for all who come after them, and to favour only those they named one by one: sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, or others descending from them. But where a provision is made not for particular persons or certain degrees but for present persons, all who have sprung from the same stock are included under the name of children.

units.la: 1 Sed & Papirius Fronto libro tertio responsorum ait, prædio cum vilico & contubernali eius & filiis legato, nepotes quoque ex filiis contineri: nisi voluntas testatoris aliter habeat. filij enim appellatione sæpe & nepotes accipi, multifariam placere.
units.tr: 1. Papirius Fronto also says, in book 3 of his Responses, that when a farm is bequeathed with its steward, his fellow-slave, and his sons, the grandsons born of the sons are included as well, unless the testator's will provides otherwise. He holds that the name "sons" is often taken to include grandsons too, as is widely held.

units.la: 2 Di-uus quoque Marcus rescripsit, non videri sine liberis defunctum, qui nepotem suum heredem reliquit.
units.tr: 2. The deified Marcus also ruled by rescript that a man who left his grandson as heir is not to be regarded as having died without children.

units.la: 3 Præter hæc omnia natura nos quoque docet parentes pios, qui liberorum procreandorum animo & voto vxores ducunt: filiorum appellatione omnes, qui ex nobis descendunt, contineri. nec enim dubitare debemus, nepotes nostros, quam filij ciore nomine possumus nepotes nostros, quam filij.
units.tr: 3. Beyond all these points, nature herself also teaches us that devoted parents, who take wives with the intention and desire of having children, include under the name of sons all who descend from us. For we ought not to doubt that our grandchildren are as much our descendants as our sons are, and we may call them by the same name.

units.la: 4 Quàdo per sonis aut gradibus certum aliquid conceditur, liberorum appellatione descendentes in infinitum non intelliguntur. appellare, etenim idcirco filios filiasve concepimus, atque edimus,vt ex prole eorum earumve diuturnitatis nobis {a}memoriam in aeuum relinquamus.
units.tr: 4. When something is granted to certain persons or degrees, descendants without limit are not understood under the name of children. For we beget sons and daughters precisely so that through their offspring we may leave our memory to endure forever.
221. Paulus, book 10 of the Responses.

units.la: PAulus respondit,falsum {b}tutorem eum vere di-ci,qui tutor non est,siue habenti tutor datus est, siue non, sicut falsum testamentum, quod testamentum non est. & modius {c}iniquus,qui modius nō est.
units.tr: Paulus answered that a person is rightly called a false guardian when he is not a guardian, whether or not he has been given to one who already has a guardian, just as a false will is one that is not a will. And a dishonest measure is one that is not a measure.
222. Hermogenianus, book 2 of the Epitomes of Law.

units.la: PEcuniae {d}nomine non solum numerata pecunia: sed omnes res, tam soli, quàm mobiles, & tam {e}corpora,quàm iura {f},continentur.
units.tr: Under the name of money are included not only coined money but all goods, both land and movables, and both corporeal things and rights.
223. Paulus, book 2 of the Sentences.

units.la: IAtx[?]{g} culpae finis est,non intelligere id, quod omnes intelligunt. ¶Amicos {h}appellare debemus,non leui notitia coniunctos :sed quibus fue-rint iura cum patrefamilias, honestis familiaritatis quaesita rationibus.
units.tr: The limit of fault is not to understand what everyone understands. We ought to call friends not those joined by slight acquaintance, but those who have had dealings with the head of a household on honourable grounds of intimacy.

units.la: berorum procreandorum causa: & r. de nuptijs ad Valerium comitem, vt secundum matrimoniales tabulas, nonnisi liberorum procreandorum causa concumbant v. Cuia cium ad No uell. 22. Am-brosius super Lucam, Quinò causa procreandę sobolis,sed explen-dae libidinis sibi inuicem copulantur non tam coniungi, quam fornicari videntur, cap.pudor 32. quaest. 2. Idem refert Augustinus ferm.3.dominica post trinitatem. Alij sunt fines nuptiarum, liberorum educatio, constitutio familiarum, nominis, familiarum conseruatio l. 9. Cod. de quaestionib: generis humani conseruatio, vt sit veluti quaedam immortalitas l. 14. Cod. de legitim. heredibus: certitudo prolis l. 83. §. de condit. & demonstrat: vitatio fornicationis, humanitatis solatium 27. quaest. cap. nuptiarum: vicissitudo munerum inter virum & vxorem. Xenophon in Oeconomico, vitatio discordiarum quae sunt in concubinatu: Isocrates Cicero 4. de finibus: vt habeant parentes a quibus inuentur, Xenophon dicto loco: Hieronymus in Iouinianum: honor Dei. vide Antonium Gumbertum cap. 8. in commentario de matrimonio.
units.tr: Of the procreation of children: and in the Novel ... that, according to the marriage records, they lie together only for the sake of begetting children; see Cuiacius on Novel 22. Ambrose on Luke: those who join themselves to each other not for the sake of begetting offspring but to satisfy lust do not so much marry as seem to commit fornication, cap. Pudor, 32 quaest. 2. Augustine reports the same in sermon 3 for the Sunday after Trinity. Other ends of marriage are: the upbringing of children, the establishment of families, the preservation of name and family (L. 9 Cod. de quaestionibus); the preservation of the human race, so that it is a kind of immortality (L. 14 Cod. de legitimis heredibus); certainty of offspring (L. 83 §. de condit. et demonstr.); the avoidance of fornication; the solace of humanity (27 quaest. cap. nuptiarum); the reciprocal exchange of duties between husband and wife. Xenophon in the Oeconomicus; the avoidance of the discords found in concubinage. Isocrates; Cicero, de finibus book 4; that parents may have those by whom they are cared for. Xenophon, in the place cited; Jerome against Jovinian; the honour of God. See Antonius Gumbertus, ch. 8, in his commentary on marriage.
{a} L. 14 Cod. de legitimis heredibus; Novel 22.

units.la: {b} 2.Ecloga 2.cap.221, vt falsus emptor l.4.§.5.§.de in diem addictione.
units.tr: {b} Ecloga 2, cap. 221; as a false buyer, L. 4 §5 de in diem addictione.
{c} See L. 32 §1 de falsis.
{d} See L. 178 §, eo. Ecloga ib., cap. 232.
{e} Tam iura quam corpora: Petrus Faber, 1 semest. 23.
{f} And fruits: see L. 32 ad Trebellianum.
{g} L. 7 §2 de administratione tutorum; see Cuiacius, 7 obs. 8.

units.la: {h} de amicis tutoris v.l.vlt.§.vbi pupillus: pupilli v.l.44.§.de negotijs; l.2.§.quae petant tutor: heri l.43.§.1.§.de adilitio.
units.tr: {h} On the friends of a guardian, see L. ult. §, ubi pupillus; on wards, see L. 44 §, de negotiis; L. 2 §, quae petant tutor; on heirs, L. 43 §1 de adilitio.
224. Venuleius, book 7 of the Stipulations.

units.la: VInculorum {a} appellatione, vel priuata, vel publica vincula significant. custodiæ verò, tantum publicam custodiam.
units.tr: Under the name of chains, they signify either private or public chains; but custody signifies only public custody.
225. Tryphoninus, book 1 of the Disputations.

units.la: FVgitiuus {b} est, non is, qui solum consilium fugiendi à domino suscepit, licet id fe facturum ftanerit: sed qui ipso facto fugæ initium mente duxerit. nam & furem {c} adulterum, aleatorem, quàm aliquam significatione ex animi propositione cuiusque sola quis dicere posset: vt etiå is, qui nonnunquam alienam rem inuito domino subtraxerit, nūquam alienam ntatremfamilias[?] corruperit, fi modò eius mentis fit, vt occasione data id commissurus fit: tamen oportere eadem hæc crimina aslumpto[?] astu intelligi. & ideo fugitiuum {d} quoque, & erronè non fecùdum propositionem solam, sed cum aliquo actu intelligi constat.
units.tr: A fugitive is not one who has merely formed the plan of fleeing from his master, even if he has declared that he will do so, but one who by the very deed has begun the flight in his mind. For a thief, an adulterer, or a gambler can be described as such from the intention of the mind alone; likewise one who has sometimes taken another's property against the owner's will, or corrupted another's household, is not so described unless his disposition is such that he would commit the act when the occasion arose. Yet these same crimes must be understood as requiring that some act be undertaken. And so it is agreed that a fugitive and a wanderer is understood not from intention alone but only together with some act.
226. Paul, Manual books, book 1.

units.la: MAgna {e} negligentia, culpa est. magna {f} culpa, dolus est.
units.tr: Great negligence is a fault. A great fault is fraud (dolus).
227. The same, book 2 of the Manuals.

units.la: EX illa parte ediĉti, Tum & quem ei heredem esse o-portet, heredis heredibus bonorum possessio non defertur. Item in substitutione his verbis, {h} Quisquis mihi heres erit, proximus heres tantum significatur. imò non tantùm proximus heres, sed etiam scriptus.
units.tr: From that part of the edict, "and whom he ought to have as heir," the bonorum possessio is not granted to the heirs of an heir. Likewise, in a substitution, by the words "whoever shall be my heir," only the next heir is meant. Indeed, not only the next heir is meant, but also the one named in the will.
228. The same, in the single book On Cognitions.

units.la: MVnicipes {i} intelligendi sunt, & qui in eodem municipio nati sunt.
units.tr: Municipes are to be understood as those who were also born in the same municipium.

units.la: 229. Idem libro singulari de Tacitis fideicommissis.
units.tr: 229. The same, in the single book On Tacit Fideicommissa.

units.la: TRansacta {k} finitáve intelligere debemus, nõ solum quibus controuersia fuit, sed etiam quæ sine controuersia sint possessa.
units.tr: We ought to understand transacted or concluded matters not only as those in which there was a dispute, but also those which were possessed without any dispute.

units.la: 230. Idem libro singulari ad Senatusconsultum Orfitianum.
units.tr: 230. The same, in the single book on the Senatusconsultum Orfitianum.

units.la: VT sunt iudicio {l} terminata, transactione compo-sita, longioris temporis silentio finita.
units.tr: Such matters as are decided by judgment, settled by compromise, or ended by the silence of a long lapse of time.
(i) See l.1, §. ad municipalem.
(k) See l.1 in sin., §. ad Tertullianam.
(l) See d.l.1 in fine.
231. The same.

units.la: 231. Idem libro singulari ad Senatusconsultum Tertyllianum.
units.tr: 231. The same, in the single book on the Senatusconsultum Tertullianum.

units.la: Quod dicimus eum {a}, qui nasci sperātur, pro {b}superstite esse: tunc verum est, cum de ipsius iure quæritur. aliis autem non prodest, nisi natus.
units.tr: What we say of one who is expected to be born, that he counts as surviving: this is true when the question concerns his own right; but for others it helps only if he is born.

units.la: 232. Gaius libro primo de Verborum obligationibus.
units.tr: 232. Gaius, book 1 on Verbal Obligations.

units.la: Hæc enunciatio, Quæ sunt pluris {c}aureorum tri-ginta, simul & quantitatis & æstimationis significatiua est.
units.tr: This phrase, "which are of more than thirty gold pieces," signifies both quantity and value at once.

units.la: 233. Idem libro primo ad legem duodecim tabularum.
units.tr: 233. The same, book 1 on the Law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: Si caluitur {d} & {e} morcuty, & frustretur. Inde & calumniatores {f} appellati sunt, quia per fraudem & frustrationem alios vexarent litibus. Inde & cauillatio {g} dicta est. 1 Post {h} Kalendas Ianuarias die tertio pro salute principis vota suscipiuntur {i}.
units.tr: "If one calumniates and [...] and frustrates." From this the calumniators were so called, because by fraud and frustration they harassed others with lawsuits; and from this the word cavillatio is derived. 1. After the Kalends of January, on the third day, vows are undertaken for the safety of the prince.

units.la: 2 Telum {k} vulgò quidem id appellatur, quod ab arcu mittitur. sed nūc omne significatur, quod mittitur manu, <bl>ἀπὸ τοῦ τηλοῦ</bl> i. à iaciendo. Admonet nos <bl>ἐξ ἡφων</bl>, i. Pacuuius in Medo, lactans caluitur <bl>[?]</bl>.
units.tr: 2. The word telum is commonly applied to what is shot from a bow, but now everything that is sent by hand is meant, from [ἀπὸ τοῦ τηλοῦ], that is, from throwing. The Greek [ἐξ ἡφων] reminds us of this, that is, Pacuvius in the Medus, "caluitur" [...] .

units.la: Dictumque ab eo, quod in longinquum mittatur, Græca vocem figuratum <bl>ἀπὸ τὰ τηλὰ</bl>, i. ab eo, quod est longe. Et hanc significationem inuenire possumus & in Græco nomine: nam, quod nos telum appellamus, illi <bl>βέλος</bl> appellant. eóque nomine vulgò quidem id significatur, quod ab arcu mittitur: sed non minùs omne significatur, quod {cum} mittitur manu, <bl>[?] βάλλεσθαι</bl>. i. à iaciendo. Admonet nos <bl>[?]</bl>, i. tentiæ legis duodecim tabularum. Ea talis fuit, Sicaluitur pedemve struit, manum endo iacito. Festus {l}in voce struere. {m} ita legendum puto, caluitur, dictum est frustratur, vt apud Nonium.
units.tr: The word is said to be derived from what is sent far off, a Greek term used figuratively [ἀπὸ τὰ τηλὰ], that is, from that which is far away. We can find this same meaning in the Greek name as well: what we call telum, they call [βέλος]. By that name is commonly signified what is sent from a bow, but no less is signified whatever is thrown by hand [βάλλεσθαι], that is, from throwing. [...] that is, the sense of the law of the Twelve Tables. It ran thus: "If one calumniates or builds a footpath, let him throw by hand." See Festus under the word struere. I think it should be read thus: "caluitur" is said of one who frustrates, as in Nonius.

units.la: {f} l.1. §.de calumniatoribus. l.2. §.2. §. si mulier ventris nomine: l.1. §.1. §.ad Turpill. {g} l.177. §.eo: & callitas l.29. §. §.in f. §.mandati. {h} adde l.132. §. eo: nuncupantur vota ineunte anno pro salute principis vt hic, & l. vnica, Cod. de oblatione votor: & offerebatur libra auri in 72. solidis obrisiacis, siue obrisatis vide Cuiac. ibidem. {i} à sacerdotibus, scilicet, & consulibus. Erant & vota anniuersaria ob idem imperij, cum videlicet ad imperium princeps sumptus esset, vel cum natus esset l.7. in sin. Cod.de feriis: adde Plinium 10. Epist. 9: 44.45.60.61: v.Tertull.in Apologetico: erant & alia pro salute imperatoris & incolumitate 10.Plin. Epist.1:Tranquill.in Augusto. v.l.11.in f.§.ad legem Iul. de vi publ: l.54.§.2.§.de furtis.
units.tr: (f) See l.1, §. de calumniatoribus; l.2, §. 2, §. si mulier ventris nomine; l.1, §. 1, §. ad Turpill. (g) See l.177, §. eo; and callitas, l.29, §. in fine, §. mandati. (h) Add l.132, §. eo: vows are made at the beginning of the year for the safety of the prince, as here, and the single law in the Code, de oblatione votorum; and a pound of gold was offered at 72 solidi obrisiaci, or obrisati; see Cujas there. (i) By the priests, that is, and by the consuls. There were also anniversary vows for the same thing of empire, when the prince had been raised to power, or when he had been born, l.7, in sin., Cod. de feriis. Add Pliny, Epist. 10, 9; 44, 45, 60, 61; see Tertullian in the Apologeticus. There were also other vows for the safety of the emperor and his well-being; Pliny Epist. 10, 1; Suetonius in Augustus. See l.11, in fine, §. ad legem Iuliam de vi publica; l.54, §. 2, §. de furtis.

units.la: Græca voce <bl>ταλλέσθαι</bl> Bud. [?] Xenophon{a}: nam ita scribit: Καὶ τὰ ξύλα ὁμοίως ἐ[?]φέρετο λόγχαι, τοξεύματα, σφενδόναι, [?] δὲ καὶ λίθοι. i. Et tela simul ferebantur, hasta, sagitta, funda, plurimi item lapides. ‖ Et id, quod ab arcu mittitur, apud Græcos quidem proprio nomine τόξευ- μα (i.sagitta) vocatur: apud nos autem communi nomine telum appellatur.
units.tr: The Greek word [...] Budaeus; Xenophon, for thus he writes: "And the wood was carried in the same way: spears, arrows, slings, and also stones in quantity." That is: and missiles were carried together, the spear, the arrow, the sling, and likewise many stones. And what is sent from a bow is called among the Greeks by its own name, toxeuma (arrow), but among us it is called by the common name telum.

units.la: 234. Idem libro secundo ad legem duodecim tabularum.
units.tr: 234. The same, book 2 on the Law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: Quos nos hostes{b} appellamus, eos veteres perduelles appellabant, per eam adiectionem indicantes, cum quibus bellum esset. 1 ¶ Locu- ples{c} est, qui satis idonee habet pro magnitudine rei, quam actor restituendam esse petit. 2 ¶ Verbum Viuere{d} quidam putant ad cibum pertinere. sed Ofilius ad Atticum ait, his verbis & vestimenta & stramenta{e} continentur, sine his enim viuere nemini nem posse.
units.tr: Those whom we call enemies (hostes), the ancients called perduelles, by that addition indicating against whom there was war. 1. "Locuples" is one who has sufficient security in proportion to the value of the thing which the plaintiff seeks to have restored. 2. Some think the word "viuere" (to live) pertains to food; but Ofilius, writing to Atticus, says that by these words clothing and bedding are included, for without these no one can live.

units.la: 235. Idem libro tertio ad legem duodecim tabularum.
units.tr: 235. The same, in the third book on the Law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: {f}Ferri[?] proprie dicimus, quæ quis suo corpore ba- julat: portari ea, quæ quis iumento secum ducit. 1 ¶ Fabros ignarius{g} dicimus non eos duntaxat, qui digna{h} dolarent: sed omnes, qui ædificarent.
units.tr: We properly say "ferri" of things a person carries on his own body, and "portari" of things he leads along with a beast of burden. 1 ¶ We call fabri ignarii not only those who hewed timber (digna dolarent), but all who built.

units.la: 236. Idem libro quarto ad legem duodecim tabularum.
units.tr: 236. The same, in the fourth book on the Law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: Quì venenum{i} dicit, adiicere debet, vtrum ma- lum, an bonum. nam & medicamenta venena sunt: quia eo nomine omne continetur, quod adhibitum naturam eius, cui adhibitum esset, mutat. cùm id, quod nos venenum appellamus, Græci φάρμακον dicunt. apud illos quoque tam medicamenta, quàm quæ nocent, hoc nomine continentur. vnde adiectione alterius, nomine distinctio fit. ad-
units.tr: Whoever says "poison" must add whether it is harmful or beneficial, for medicines too are poisons, because the term covers everything that, when applied, changes the nature of the thing it is applied to. What we call poison, the Greeks call pharmakon [φάρμακον]. Among them the same word covers both medicines and things that do harm. Hence the distinction is made by an added qualifier. Ad-
d See Digest 43, §eo; see Relandus a Valle, Consilia 1, no. 22.
e See Digest 45, §ea.
f See Ecloga 2, b. 234.

units.la: {g} tignarios vulgat.Hal. τέκτονας ξύλων 2. Ecloga 2.cap.235. Fabros lignarios Cuiacius ad 3. Pauli 3.§.50. Cod. de excusat artificum.
units.tr: g The Vulgate reads tignarios. Hal. [τέκτονας ξύλων]. Ecloga 2, ch. 235. Cuiacius, on Pauli Sententiae 3, §50, reads fabros lignarios. Code, on the exemption of craftsmen.

units.la: {h} Tigna vulgata Hal. οἱ τὰ ξύλα Ecloga ibidem ligna, Cuiacius ibidem. hinc fabri lignarij 3.Paul.sent.6. §.5.
units.tr: h The Vulgate reads tigna. Hal. [οἱ τὰ ξύλα]. In the same place the Ecloga reads ligna; Cuiacius likewise. Hence fabri lignarii, Pauli Sententiae 3, 6, §5.

units.la: {i} l.35.§.2.§.de contrah.empt. appellatio veneni media[?] 2.Ecl.2.c.236; & 60. tit.39.c.
units.tr: i Digest 35, §2, §de contrahenda emptione; the meaning of veneni is intermediate, Ecloga 2, ch. 236; and tit. 39, ch. 60.

units.la: 4: Adde l.4.§.de sicariis. monet nos {4}summus apud eos poetarum Homerus, nam sic ait {6} Φάρμακα πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά.
units.tr: 4: Add Digest 4, §de sicariis. Homer, the chief of their poets, warns us of this, for he says [Φάρμακα πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά].

units.la: Venena multa quidem bona mixta, multa autem mala.
units.tr: Many drugs, indeed, good ones mixed in, and many baneful ones.

units.la: 1 ¶ Glandis {e}appellatione omnis fructus continetur, vt Iauolenus ait, exemplo Græci sermonis, apud quos omnes arborum {d}species ἀκρόδρυα (l.1. ex-tremitates arborum) appellantur.
units.tr: 1 ¶ By the term "acorn" (glans) every fruit is included, as Javolenus says, following the usage of Greek, in which all kinds of tree fruit are called akrodrya [ἀκρόδρυα] (Digest 1: the extremities of trees).

units.la: 237. Idem libro quinto ad legem duodecim tabularum.
units.tr: 237. The same, in the fifth book on the Law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: DVobus negatiuis {f}verbis quasi permittit lex, magis quàm prohibuit, idque etiam Seruius {g}animaduertit.
units.tr: By two negative words the law seems to permit rather than to forbid, and Servius also observed this.

units.la: 238. Idem libro sexto ad legem duodecim tabularum.
units.tr: 238. The same, in the sixth book on the Law of the Twelve Tables.
The plebs are the other citizens, apart from the senators.
1 ¶ Detestatum is what has been denounced by solemn testimony.

units.la: 2 ¶Pignus {l}appellatum à pugno: quia res, quæ pignori dantur, manu traduntur. vnde etiam videri potest verum esse: quidam putant, pignus proprie {m}
units.tr: 2 ¶ Pignus (pledge) is so called from pugnus (fist), because things given in pledge are handed over by hand. Whence it may also seem true, as some think, that pignus properly

units.la: e Græci ἀκρόδρυα nomen fructibus tribuunt. & ita D. Iohanne vicitafe ἀκρῶν δρυῶν Nicephorus ait, vt Diogene, AElianus ἀκρῶν φύλλων. Nicephoro adsentit Diaconus, qua de re vide Cuiacium in Paratitlis tit. de glande legenda.
units.tr: e The Greeks give the name akrodrya [ἀκρόδρυα] to fruits. So Nicephorus says [ἀκρῶν δρυῶν], as Diogenes does; Aelianus says [ἀκρῶν φύλλων]. The deacon agrees with Nicephorus; on this matter see Cuiacius, Paratitla, title de glande legenda.

units.la: f negantibus Hal. interdum tamen duo affirmatiua firmius negant & ponunt, εἰς ἀρνησιν μείζωσε vt Demetrius ait in Sophoclem. nemi-nem nihil facere l.24.§.de damno: nihil neminem habere. Lucilius, lapideo sunt corde multi, quos non miseret neminis Cato, v. Cuiacium 10.obs.26.
units.tr: f The Hebrews say the negatives; yet sometimes two affirmative words deny more firmly and assert, [εἰς ἄρνησιν μείζωσιν], as Demetrius says on Sophocles. Neminem nihil facere (Digest 24, §de damno); nihil neminem habere. Lucilius: "Many have hearts of stone, whom pity for no one moves." Cato; see Cuiacius, Observationes 10, ch. 26.

units.la: g Seruius ad illa verba legis duodecim tabularum, necnon mortuum inferunto, adnotauit duobus illis negatiuis verbis quasi permisisse legem magis, quàm prohibuisse. cui congruit quod Philosophus refert αἱ δύο ἀποφάσεις, ἡ ἐπηρείας μίαν καταφάσιν ἀποτελοῦσι. Caper. confessoria vox hic ex duplici abnutiua, vt non nolo, non nescio, nonnunquàm, necnon.
units.tr: g Servius, on the words of the Law of the Twelve Tables, "and let them carry the dead for burial" (necnon mortuum inferunto), noted that by these two negative words the law seems to have permitted rather than forbidden. With this agrees what the Philosopher reports: two negations make one strong affirmation [αἱ δύο ἀποφάσεις, ἡ ἐπηρείας μίαν καταφάσιν ἀποτελοῦσι]. Caper: a confirmatory expression here arises from a double negative, as in non nolo (I am not unwilling), non nescio (I do not not know), nonnunquam (not never), necnon (and also).

units.la: h §.4. Inst. de iure naturali l.2.§.24. in f.5. de orig. iur.
units.tr: h Institutes 1, tit. 2, §4, de iure naturali; Digest 2, §24, in fine; Digest 5, de origine iuris.

units.la: i χωρὶς τῶν ἀξιωματικῶν 2. Ecl.2.c.238. i. fine iis qui sunt positi in dignitate, sen patriciis & senatoribus d.§.4. Gellius ita definit. Plebs ea dicitur, in qua gentes ciuium patriciæ non insunt 10. Noct.c.10. Isidorus 9. orig.5. Plebs reliqui, vulgus sine senioribus ciuitatis.
units.tr: i Apart from those of worth [χωρὶς τῶν ἀξιωματικῶν], Ecloga 2, ch. 238; that is, apart from those placed in dignity, or patricians and senators (Institutes, §4 above). Gellius defines it thus: the plebs is that in which the patrician clans of citizens are not included, Attic Nights 10, ch. 10. Isidore, Origines 9, ch. 5: the plebs is the rest, the common people, without the elders of the state.
k Digest 40, §5, eodem.
l Digest 5, §1 and §5, de pignoribus.

units.la: m propriissimè, nam pignus proprie dicitur de re immobili '2. in f.5. de religiosis, sed & illud
units.tr: m Most properly, for pignus is properly said of an immovable thing (Digest 2, in fine; Digest 5, de religiosis), but also that

units.la: rei mobilis {a}constitui. 3 ¶ Noxiae {b}appellatio- ne omne delictum {c}continetur.

units.tr: A ward (pupillus) is one who, being below puberty, has ceased to be under his father's power, through the father's death or emancipation. 1 ¶ The name "slaves" (servi) arose from the fact that our emperors customarily sold captives, and thereby preserved them rather than killing them. 2 ¶ An incola (resident alien) is one who has transferred his domicile to some region. But the Greeks call paroikoi [παροίκους] (that is, "dwelling nearby") sometimes the same as those in noxia. Hence the phrases: noxam nocere (Digest 45, §1, de legatis); noxiam nocere (Digest 4, de noxalibus); noxam committere (Digest 32, de noxalibus); noxiam committere (Digest 1, si quadrupes); aestimatio noxiae (the same law, 1); noxam caput sequi (see Digest 1, end, de privatis delictis); hence the noxal action (Digest, de noxalibus); hence noxii servi, that is, slaves who cause harm (Digest 27, §11, ad legem Aquiliam; Digest 1, §1, de noxalibus; Institutes 4, §1, de noxalibus; Ecloga 2, ch. 238). Yet this does not mean that it contains public punishment (Digest 200, eodem). Sometimes it signifies a penalty: hence noxae dedere (to surrender for harm; Digest 19, de noxalibus); ad noxam dedere (the same, §a); in noxam (Digest 11); noxam dare (Digest 7, §1, quod vi); noxae deditio (Digest 10, de noxalibus); noxis solvi and solutum esse (Digest 200, eodem); noxam farcire and in noxam dare are distinguished (Digest 1, §11, de noxalibus). Hence pupillary age, which ends at fourteen (Digest 16, de iure fisci; Code 3, de praescriptione triginta annorum); pupillary tablets (Digest 32, in fine, de vulgari); a pupillary will (Digest 8, §5, de inofficioso; Digest 2, §2, de vulgari; Digest 34, §§9–10, de legatis 1); pupillary substitution, which is made for children below puberty in the case that they die before reaching the years of puberty (Digest 2, de vulgari); pupillary substitutes (Digest 10, §5, de vulgari). It ceases if he was previously in power. One who is in the womb is not such (Digest 262, eodem; Ecloga 2, b, ch. 239). 3 ¶ By these two means also the power of a patron ends (Institutes, quibus modis patria potestas). Do not infer that people become slaves only by capture, since they also become slaves in other ways (Digest 5, §1, de statu; Digest 4, in fine, de statu; Institutes, §2, de iure personarum; Ecloga 2, ch. 239). Hence it is established that it is not lawful, once an enemy has been captured by us, to kill him or to exact punishment from him. He has not acquired the rights of citizenship, for a person may be a resident of one city and a citizen of another (Digest 29, ad municipalem; add Digest 6, in fine, de muneribus). The Greek word is metoikos [μέτοικος]. Such was Abraham, who "sojourned in the land of promise" (Hebrews 5, verse 9 [as printed]). Hence the saying that we ought to be strangers and pilgrims in the flesh and the world (1 Peter 2, verse 11 [as printed]: [ἐνδημοῦντος παροικίας ὡς παροίκους καὶ παρεπιδήμους τῶν σαρκικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν]). On the contrary, for the faithful there is no sojourning, but their own city, hence the saying [ἀλλ᾽ ἐστὲ συμπολῖται τῶν ἁγίων καὶ οἰκεῖοι τοῦ θεοῦ] (Ephesians 2, verse 19).

units.tr: a Those who live in a town are not the only residents, but also those who hold land within the bounds of some town in such a way that they retreat to it as to a settled home. 3 ¶ A public office (munus publicum) is a duty of a leading man, from which advantage comes to individual citizens and to all citizens together, and to their property, by the command of the magistrate, as an extraordinary matter. 4 ¶ An advena (newcomer), whom the Greeks call epichoron [ἐπίχωρον], that is, one who has fled from home, is what they call an incoming settler. 5 ¶ Some say decurions were so named because at first, when colonies were led out, a tenth part of those led out was usually enrolled for the sake of the public council. 6 ¶ Urbs (city) is named from urbo (to plough round). Urbare is to mark out with the plough. Varro says that cities are named from the curve of the plough, which is usually used in founding a city. 7 ¶ Oppidum is said to come from ops (help), because walls are set up for that purpose. 8 ¶ Territorium is the whole of the fields within the boundaries of each city. Some say it is named from this, that the magistrate of that place has the right, within those boundaries, of terrifying [?], that is, of ... 9 ¶ The word suum is ambiguous, whether it means the whole or a part. And therefore, when you say that I think he is distinguished from the incola who has his domicile among foreigners, see Digest 2, §2, eodem. d I shall speak of decurions under the title of the Code on decurions and their sons, and on those who are considered decurions, etc. e Varro, de lingua 4, 15; Isidore 2; Plato [illegible]; Vruo, Hal. [illegible]; Ecloga 2, ch. 240. Vrbum is the plough; Varro, de lingua 4. f And exfunda, that is, to be overturned: Nonius; Horace, Odes 1, 16; Seneca, de Clementia 1, last. Hence Carthage is said to have suffered the plough, Digest 21, §quibus modis usufructus; and the temple of the Jerusalemites was ploughed by Titius Rufus, says Jerome. [illegible]. Lucian, in the dialogue Charon; P. Faber, Fenestra 1, ch. 8. g Varro, de lingua 4; Ecloga, ibid.; that is, for storing up or preserving goods, says Festus; but either by the placing of walls, or because they give mutual aid against enemies, Isidore 15, 1. h The city's territory: Digest 41, §5, §de legatis; of the town: Digest 3, §4, §de sepulchro; of the judge: last law, §de iurisdictione. k Not outside: last law, §de iurisdictione. l Territorium is a common space left near the town, so called because it is most worn down (teratur), says Varro, de lingua 4. Isidore, Origines 14, ch. 15, gives another etymology: territorium as if tauritorium, that is, trodden by oxen and the plough. Siculus Flaccus, in his book de condicionibus agrorum, derives it from terrifying the citizens; others from terrifying enemies. Frontinus, in his book de agrorum qualitate, derives it from terra; Cuiacius on Digest 53, §de decurionibus.

units.tr: Territory: a common place left near a town, so called because it is most worn down (teratur), Varro, book 4 On the Latin Language. Isidore, book 14 of the Origines, ch. 15, gives another etymology: territorium as if tauritorium, that is, worn by oxen and the plough. Siculus Flaccus, in his book On the Conditions of Fields, derives it from terrifying crows, and from terrifying enemies. Frontinus, in his book On the Qualities of Fields, derives it from terra. Cujas on Dig. 50.2.53 (on decurions). He swears that it is not his own, he must add that it is not common to him either.

units.la: CVm quærebatur, an verbum Soluto{b} matri-monio dotem reddai, non tantum diuortium{c}, sed & mortem contineret, hoc est, an de hoc quo-casu contrahentes sentient, & multi putabant hoc sensisse, & quibusdam aliis contrà videbatur: secundum hoc motus Imperator pronuntiauit, id actum eo pacto, vt nullo casu remaneret dos apud maritum.
units.tr: When it was asked whether the phrase on the dissolution of marriage the dowry is to be returned included not only divorce but also death, that is, whether contracting parties understood it to cover this case, many thought they had understood it so, while some others held the opposite view. Moved by this, the Emperor ruled that the agreement was made on the condition that the dowry should in no case remain with the husband.

units.la: {g}Malum nauis esse partem, artemonem {h}autem non esse, Labeo ait: quia plerumque naues sine malo inutiles essent, ideoque pars nauis habetur. artemo autem magis adiectamento {i}, quàm pars na-uis est. {k}Inter proiectum & immissum, hoc interesse ait Labeo: quod proiectum esset id, quod ita proueheretur, vt nusquam requiesceret, qualia Artemonis fit mentio,
units.tr: Labeo says that the mast is part of a ship, but the artemon is not: because ships would for the most part be useless without a mast, and so it is regarded as part of the ship. The artemon, however, is more an addition than a part of the ship. Labeo says the difference between proiectum and immissum is this: what is proiectum is that which projects so that it rests nowhere, such as the artemon is mentioned as being,

units.tr: On Dig. 27, verse 40; Ecl. 2 (?), p. 24, law 2, on urban servitudes: *maniana* and *suggrunda* b eaves, if they were there. *Immissum*, however, is that which is so placed that it rests at some point, like beams or rafters that are put in. 2 Lead which is placed on tiles d is part of the building, Labeo says. But what is placed for covering the open air (*hypaethrum*) is the opposite. 3 Labeo says that a woman is called a widow not only if she was once married e but also if she had been f without a husband g, for vidua was so named as if it were *vecors* h, that is, senseless, one without heart or sanity. Similarly, it is said that the widow is named from being without *duitas*. 4 A flooring i of some place made of boards, which are taken up in summer and put down in winter, is part of the house, Labeo says, since they are prepared for perpetual use. That they are taken up in the meantime is not relevant.

units.la: SCæuola respondit: Semper acceptum est, vt libertorum l appellatione etiàm hi contineri intelligantur, qui eodem testamento vel posteriore loco manumitterentur: nisi manifeste is, à quo peterentur, contra defuncti voluntatem doceret peti.
units.tr: Scævola replied: It has always been accepted that under the term "freedmen" l are understood also those who were manumitted by the same will or in a later clause, unless the party from whom they are claimed clearly shows that the claim is made against the wishes of the deceased.

Ad Turpillianum); an appeal can be made against a fine, perhaps wrongly understood by the judge from the business, or not fully proved, as said in the law 2 Code, quorum appellationes. And this sense is quite obvious. For as soon as someone is convicted of the offence for which a penalty has been established, the penalty is owed at once; but a fine is subject to appeal, and is not owed until either no appeal has been made or the appellant has lost, and then only if he has said what he is allowed to say. From this also the difference between these things can be seen: penalties are fixed for particular offences, whereas fines depend on the power of the judge, who assesses as much as he thinks fit, unless the law has set an amount.

units.tr: In Labeo's Pithana it is written as follows: He produces (exhibet) one who presents the person in question in person. For even one who brings him to court (sistit) presents the person in question, yet does not produce him. ¶ One who produces a mute, a madman or an infant cannot be thought to present his person, for no one of that class can fairly be called present. 1 ¶ He restores (restituit) not only one who gives back the body alone, but also one who supplies everything and the condition for the return. And the whole of restitution is an interpretation of law.

units.tr: For that rule is lacking: "the noxal penalty follows the head" (noxa caput sequitur). Compare the sentences and definitions. Rules of this kind are of great use in every branch of learning. Hence Vegetius (3.c.26) recounts certain general rules of warfare. The aphorisms of Hippocrates do the same service for physicians. To the same end Annianus chose for his Goths certain passages from the Sentences of Paul, which are today called the received Sentences of Paul. Do not say they are outdated: no rules of law that Justinian abolished are to be found here, but rules accepted by the older wisdom of the jurists, in agreement with the definitions of the jurisconsults (l.21 Cod. de furtis; l.vlt. Cod. Theodos. de diversis rescriptis). Hence the Catonian rule, and the one called "most certain" (§1 Inst. de perpetuis et temporalibus), and the old one (§5 Inst. de fidejussoribus; l.37 §de pactis). Cuiacius adds that laws 28, 62, 65 and 191 are quite foreign to this title. Κανὼν [canon] (Ecloga 2, 3, c.1) is a definition (l.202 §eodem); sententiae are κυρίαι δόξαι [kyriai doxai] (Ecloga 2, 3, c.1); maxims are ἀξιώματα [axiomata], things asked for or demanded, postulata. As for "the matter which is" (rei quae est), some understand by it the thing sought and the dispute. I see that the Greeks use πράγμα [pragma] in place of res (Ecloga ib.; Harmenop. ib.: ἄκαντα τὸ πράγματος). Gadenus, cited by Hotoman (2.obs.4), thinks thus: by these words "the matter which is" is meant the law, which must be followed in the matter in dispute, or the general cause by which the jurists were moved; for a rule does not answer to fact but to law, as I shall say in the same place. (g) Generally, and this from the law established and received in the various parts of law; Dynus on cap. 1 in Sexto, de eo; and from the agreement of several laws (Hotoman, ib.), so that nothing is superfluous and yet no obscurity is introduced. If this happens, brevity is to be praised (v. l.37 Cod. de donationibus), even if it is difficult to compose rules so that they are wholly complete and perfect (l.202 §e). It is therefore the property of a rule not that it always has a universal sign of affirmations or negations, or an indefinite one, as Dynus thinks; but that it briefly gives the principal counsels and the principal reason for deciding the disputed law. Hence the Greeks define it as "a brief narration of the matter and a connecting link" (τὸ πράγματος συντομος ἀφηγησις, καὶ συνδεσμος; Ecloga ibid.; Harmenop. ib.). So too among physicians, aphorisms set out the proper features of a matter in the briefest statements (Galen, cited by Hotoman, 2.obs.4). Various examples of this brevity occur in this title. (h) Not as in the Vulgate of Haloander. (i) Ecloga ibidem: the law is older than the rule, since the rule is born from it. The law is the very matter of equity; the rule is, as it were, its form and adaptation. Just as another building is made from another architect's plan, so the rule is not taken from the building, but the rule is made from the law which is (Sabinus says) by a kind of conjecture of the cause. This is grasped immediately as in a building, which, once it is spoiled in some part, loses its own shape; mediately it is grasped from the art itself. Thus

units.la: ei quoque potest ex regula ius fumi. id est regula, nisi ios aliquod præiacens habeat, regula esse non potest. Ius autem illud est, vel strictum, vel æquum ac bonum. Aequi obiecta sunt, honestum, natura, vtile. Vtile est fictione, repræsentatione{c} sic dolus possessionem, rem, condicionem, factum: culpa rem: factum seu persona, factum aliud, rem aliam, aliam personam representat) præsumptione, coniectura, seu interpretatione, non captiosa, sed ciuili. hinc interpretatio sumitur ex natura rerum ipsarum, puta genere, specie, toto, partibus, ab eo quod plus est, & minus, principali accessorio, priuatione, habitu, signis, verbis, & mente, id est obscuro, seu ambiguo, quo in genere præsumptio sumitur pro authore, pro eo quod verisimilius est, pro rei præsentis oportunitate, pro consuetudine, pro eo quod est benignius, vel fauorabilius: idque maximè quum agitur de libertate, dote, testamento, iudiciis, contractibus, poenis, lucro, onere, maiori parte, inter fiscum, & priuatos, de tacito, & expresso, vbi agitur de actus conseruatione, de coniunctis, & diuisionis, de odio, & fauore, de dusobus malis, de initio vtili, vel inutili, de iure novo. Hæc Iohanni Ramo, præceptori quondam meo, & apud Louanienses iuris antecessori doctissimo accepta refero. ne dicas negotij, sed (quia rei vocabulum latissimè patet, quemadmodum ostendi in lege 1.5 de verb. cred.) iuris. coniunctio vulgata, & male. Est enim metaphora sumpta ab oratoribus, qui vel in principio obiter summam totius causæ coniiciunt, vt attentiorem faciant auditorem: vel in fine, vt eum memoré dimittat Iohannes Ramus. Est igitur ea legis sententia, quod est causæ coniectio inter Rhetores, regula est inter Iurisconsultos. illa, iura omnia litigatorum in summa aliquam contrahit. hæc (vt sic loquar) succum elicit, & (vt Alchymistæ loquuntur) quintā essentiam exprimit. hæc Hotom. 2. obs. 3. Coniectio igitur, quia ex regula æquî cōiicitur, non aliter q ex dignis factum. puta, quia male & perperam est concepta, non quia exceptiones habet. nec enim exceptio vitiosum quid cōtinet, sed quid potius secretum, aut remotum a regula, quam declarat, & in ea declaranda officium suum facit Hotoman. ibid. vt in fabrica, si praua est regula prima, omnia mendose fieri, atque obstipa necesse est Lucretius Hotom. ib. [illegible, ~12 letters] Harmenop. 2.
units.tr: Likewise the law can be drawn from a rule. A rule cannot exist unless there is some law lying beneath it. That law is either strict or equitable and good. The objects of equity are honesty, nature and utility. Utility represents one thing by another by fiction, by representation (thus fraud represents possession, a thing, a condition, a deed; fault represents a thing; a deed or person represents another deed or another person), by presumption, by conjecture, or by interpretation that is not captious but civil. Hence interpretation is taken from the nature of things themselves, as from genus, species, whole, parts, from what is greater and less, principal and accessory, privation, habit, signs, words, and intention, that is, what is obscure or ambiguous. In this class presumption is taken for the author, for what is more probable, for the opportuneness of the present matter, for custom, for what is more kindly or more favourable; and this especially when the matter concerns liberty, dowry, a will, judgments, contracts, penalties, gain, burden, the greater part, the relations between the fisc and private persons, the tacit and the express, where there is question of the preservation of an act, of things joined and divided, of hatred and favour, of two evils, of a beginning useful or useless, of new law. I refer these things to Johannes Ramus, my former teacher and a most learned professor of law at Louvain. Do not say "of business" (negotii) but, since the word "matter" (rei) extends very widely, as I showed in law 1.5 de verb. cred., "of law." The phrase "conjunctio" is commonly used, but wrongly. For it is a metaphor taken from orators, who either at the beginning briefly sketch the sum of the whole cause, to make the hearer more attentive, or at the end, so that he may let him go mindful of it (Johannes Ramus). So the saying of the law is this: what is a conjecture of the cause among the Rhetoricians is a rule among the jurisconsults. The former gathers all the rights of the litigants into some summary; the latter, so to speak, draws out the juice, and (as the alchemists say) expresses the quintessence. Thus Hotoman (2.obs.3). Therefore a conjecture, since it is made from a rule of equity, is not otherwise than the deed is made from the worthy; for instance, because it is badly and wrongly conceived, not because it has exceptions. For an exception does not contain anything faulty, but rather something hidden, or remote from the rule, which it declares, and in declaring it performs its own office (Hotoman, ibid.). As in building: if the first rule is crooked, everything must be done faultily and askew (Lucretius; Hotoman, ib.). [illegible, about 12 letters] Harmenop. 2.

Harmenop. 2. quam lectionem defendit Cuiacius 6. obs. 39. & 15. obs. 23. reprehensus a Roberto 2. recept. 16. & 1. Animad. 30. defensus ab Antonio Mercatore 1. Notat. 30. Velle proprie dicitur, qui sciens l.1. §.4. §. de tribut. nec coactus l.4. §. eod. iubet, mandat & imperat, aut expressim approbat. nolle, qui scies nec coactus, expressim vel palam vetat, aut refragatur. Nō nolle is videtur, qui tacite approbat, qui sciens patitur, nec expressim fieri iubet, estque inter velle & nolle medium. Non est velle, quia palam non iubet: non est nolle, quia non refragatur, sed tamen probat. Non velle, non est expressim refragari, sed factum tacite reprobare. Non est velle, quia non iubet. Non est nolle, quia palam non vetat. Non nolle, non est iubere, sed approbando pati. Non velle, non est vetare, sed tamen reprobando pati. Velle igitur, & nolle, est iussio, & prohibitio expressa. non nolle, & non velle, tacita. Huc res redit, velle potes? potes nolle vt hic secundum Vulgatam, potes etiam non velle secundum Haloandrum, & Graecos, & non nolle secundum Florentinam. E contrario, non potes cum effectu velle? non videris nolle l.4. §. de acqu. hered: hunc adde l.37. §. eo. nolle non dicimur, quoties velle contrarium vtiliter non possumus, l.10. §. de condicionibus & demonstr. Nolle dicimur, cum contrarium possumus l.17. §.7. §. de aedilitia.
units.tr: is required (l.12 §2 de iudiciis; l.1 §1 ad Velleianum; l.13 de vacatione munerum; c.1 de honoribus et muneribus publicis; l.6 de capite minutis; l.78 de iudiciis), or personal, (l.3 §3 de muneribus), or bodily (l.18, "tenuo officium," de verborum significatione). It is different in mere dignities, for they receive nobility either from their father or from their husbands (l.8 de senatoribus). (d) Not because they lack judgment, but because of their sex itself (§3 and l.1 §5 de postulando). By Roman law, especially and by custom (l.12 §2 de iudiciis; l.1 §1 ad Velleianum), they are removed. (e) See l.12 §2 de iudiciis; l.18 §14 de muneribus. Today, by use and custom, by statute, or by the privilege of a prince, a woman can fill a hereditary jurisdiction (Decius here). On the contrary, there can be certain causes for which a man is at times excused from judging (l.13 de vacatione). (f) Add l.4 §2 de officio proconsulis. (g) l.1 §5 de postulando. (h) To act as surety (fideiubere): l.4 ad Velleianum. (i) See l.18 C. de procuratoribus. (k) "Eius est nolle" is the vulgate reading (Hugo a Porta). "Eius est non velle" is Haloander's reading, and μὴ θέλειν [me thelein] (Ecloga 2, c.3, 6; Harmenop. 2), a reading defended by Cuiacius (6 obs. 39 and 15 obs. 23), reproved by Robert (2 recept. 16 and 1 Animad. 30) and defended by Antonius Mercator (1 Notat. 30). To will is properly said of one who, knowingly and not under compulsion (l.1 §4 de tributis; l.4 §eod.), orders, commands, or expressly approves. To be unwilling is said of one who, knowingly and not under compulsion, expressly or openly forbids or opposes. Not to be unwilling seems to be the mark of one who tacitly approves, who knowingly permits and does not order the thing to be done expressly; and it lies between willing and being unwilling. It is not to will, because he does not openly order; it is not to be unwilling, because he does not oppose, yet he approves. Not to will is not to oppose expressly, but to disapprove tacitly while allowing the act. It is not to will, because he does not order. It is not to be unwilling, because he does not openly forbid. Not to be unwilling is not to order, but to allow by approving. Not to will is not to forbid, but still to allow while disapproving. Thus to will and to be unwilling are express command and prohibition; not to be unwilling and not to will are tacit. The matter comes to this: can you will? You can be unwilling, as here according to the Vulgate; you can also not will, according to Haloander and the Greeks; and not be unwilling, according to the Florentine. On the other hand, can you not will with effect? You do not seem to be unwilling (l.4 §de acquirenda hereditate; add l.37 §eo). We are not said to be unwilling whenever we cannot usefully will the contrary (l.10 §de condicionibus et demonstrationibus). We are said to be unwilling when we are able to will the contrary (l.17 §7 de aedilitio edicto).
i.e. functions.

units.la: VElle non creditur, qui obsequitur {b}imperio patris,vel domini.
units.tr: He is not thought to will a thing who obeys the command of his father or master.
5. Paulus, book 2 on Sabinus.

units.la: IN negotiis contrahendis alia causa habita est furio-forum,alia eorum,qui fari possunt,quamuis actum rei non intelligerent {c}. nam furiosus {d} nullū negotium contrahere poterat: pupillus {e} omnia tutore auctore agere poterat.
units.tr: In making contracts, one rule applied to madmen and another to those who can speak, even though the latter did not understand the nature of the act. For a madman could make no contract at all, but a ward could do everything with his guardian's authority.
6. Ulpian, book 7 on Sabinus.

units.la: NOn vult heres esse {f}, qui ad alium transferre voluit & hereditatem.
units.tr: He does not wish to be heir who has wished to transfer even the inheritance to another.
7. Pomponius, book 3 on Sabinus.

units.la: IVs nostrum non patitur {h} eundem in paganis {i} & testato {k} & intestato decedisse {l}. earumque rerum luntarius, & spontaneus sit dicendus: an, & quomodo voluntas coacta, voluntas dicatur, vide Decium hic. An iussus superioris excusat à delicto v.l.20.§. de oblig.An velle dicatur, qui cogitur v.Cuiacium 16.obs.vlt: adde l.142.§.eo.
units.tr: Our law does not allow the same person to die both testate and intestate as to non-military property. Whether and how a will that is coerced may be called a will, and whether the will should be called voluntary and spontaneous, see Decius here. Whether an order from a superior excuses from a crime, see law 20, §. de oblig. Whether one who is compelled is said to will, see Cuiacius, 16 obs. last; add law 142, §. eo.

units.tr: {c} He understands the Vulgate and Haloander. {d} See law 1, §12, de obligat. {e} See law 43, §. de obligat. {f} By will, or by intestacy. {g} That is, who has transferred, i.e. who has allowed himself actually to be transferred: law 88, in f., §. de hereditib. infl. For "to will" in many cases must be understood as having effect; see Decius here. {h} Indeed he does allow it: law 15, in f., §. de inofficioso. {i} Of pagan (civil) property, i.e. not military. {k} See law 6, in f., §. de testam. milit., and §5, Inst. de hereditib. infl. {l} We die partly intestate, since a universal heir can repudiate the inheritance in part: laws 1 and 2, §. de acq. hered. Likewise, if the portion of a repudiating heir does not accrue to the other named heirs, law 63, §. de heredib. infl. Therefore the right of accrual was introduced so that this does not happen. What if the testator omitted parts? The same law will apply, since he tacitly wills that they accrue to the named heirs.

units.la: Quid si vetuit scriptos heredes adcrescendi iure vti? non probo Dynum, & alios dicentes, nihilominus ius adcrescendi competere cum id testator vetuerit. Non probo Bartoli opinionem in l.9.§.si duo,§.de hered.infl.tota rem ad causam intestati reduci. non id probo quod Clarus ait 3.sent.§.testamentum,quest.74.testamentum cor-ruere,cuactui. i.testamento sit saucdum vt valeat. placet media sen-tentia,in partem non scriptam, heredes ab intestato ex præsumpta & collecta voluntate testatoris admitti, ne alioquin actus pereat l. 12.§.de reb.dub. nam qui vetat scriptos heredes adcrescendi iure vti,tali prohibitione,& testamentarios confirmat heredes,& ad alias partes vocates,heredes ab intestato satis expressè vocat, vt iam non ab intestato succeditur,sed ex testamento. Idem dicendum,si mandauit disertis & expressis verbis, vt partes non scriptorum heredū ad heredes ab intestato deferrentur. tunc enim successio non erit ab intestato, sed ex testamento:& ita intelligi volo, quod satis generaliter scripsi ad l.55.§.de legat.1. adde,statuto aliud cōstitui posse naturaliter inter se pugna est, {b}testatus, & intestatus.
units.tr: What if he forbade the named heirs to use the right of accrual? I do not approve of Dynus and others who say that the right of accrual nonetheless remains available even though the testator has forbidden it. Nor do I approve Bartolus' opinion on law 9, §. si duo, §. de hered. infl., that the whole matter is reduced to the case of intestacy. Nor do I approve what Clarus says in 3 Sent., §. testamentum, quest. 74: that the will would collapse unless it is saved so as to be valid. The middle opinion pleases me: that heirs on intestacy are admitted to the unwritten part on the presumed and gathered will of the testator, lest the act otherwise perish: law 12, §. de reb. dub. For he who forbids the named heirs to use the right of accrual, by that prohibition both confirms the testamentary heirs and calls others to the remaining shares, and he calls the heirs on intestacy quite expressly, so that they now succeed not on intestacy but under the will. The same is to be said if he commanded, in express and clear words, that the shares of the unwritten heirs be passed to the heirs on intestacy; for then the succession will not be intestate but under the will. I want this understood in the way I wrote fairly generally on law 55, §. de legat. 1. Add that something else may be established by statute is naturally contradictory: testate and intestate.
8. The same, book 4 on Sabinus.

units.la: Iura sanguinis {*}nullo iure ciuili dirimi possunt.
units.tr: The rights of blood cannot be dissolved by any civil law.
9. Ulpian, book fifteen on Sabinus.

units.la: Semper in obscuris {c}, quod minimum est, sequitur.
units.tr: Always in unclear matters, one follows what is the least.
10. Paul, book three on Sabinus.

units.la: Secundum naturam est, commoda {e}cuiusque rei sequi, quem sequentur incommoda.
units.tr: It is according to nature that the advantages of anything follow whoever bears its disadvantages.
11. Pomponius, book 5 on Sabinus.

units.la: Id, quod nostrum est, sine {f}facto nostro ad alium transferri non potest.
units.tr: What is ours cannot be transferred to another without our own act.
12. Paulus, book 3 on Sabinus.

units.la: In testamentis plenius & voluntates testantium interpretantur.
units.tr: In wills, the wishes of testators are interpreted more fully.
13. Ulpian, book 19 on Sabinus.

units.la: Non videtur cepisse, qui per exceptionem {b}petitione remouetur.
units.tr: He does not seem to have taken who is removed by an exception against a claim.
14. Pomponius, book 5 on Sabinus.
