units.la: DE NOVO{a} CODICE{b} faciendo ad Senatum urbis Constantinopolitanae.
units.tr: ON MAKING A NEW CODE, to the Senate of the city of Constantinople.

units.la: Imperator IUSTINIANUS Augustus ad Senatum urbis Constantinopolitanae.
units.tr: Emperor Justinian Augustus, to the Senate of the city of Constantinople.

units.la: AEC quæ necessario corrigenda esse multis retro principibus visa sunt, interea tamen nullus eorum ad effectum ducere ausus est: in præsenti rebus donare communibus auxilio Dei omnipotentis censuimus, & prolixitatem litium amputare: multitudine quidem constitutionum quæ tribus codicibus,Gregoriano, Hermogeniano, {*}atque Theodosiano, {‡}continebantur, illarum etiam quæ post eosdé codices à Theodosio diuinæ recordationis, aliisque post eum retro principibus & à nostra etiam clementia positæ sunt, refeccanda: vno autem codice sub felici nostri numinis vocabulo componendo, in quem colligi tam memoratorum trium codicum, quàm {*}nouellas post eos positas constitutiones o-portet. 1 ¶ Ideóque ad hoc maximum, & ad ipsius reipublicæ sustentationem respiciens opus efficiendum, elegimus tanto sastigio laborum, tantæque sollicitudini sufficientes, Ioannem virum excellentissimum exquæstore nostri palatij, consularem atque patricium: Leontium virum sublimissimum magistrum militum, exprefecto prætorio, consularem atque patricium. Phocam virum eminentissimum, magistrum militum, consularem atque patricium: Basilidem virum excellentissimum exprefecto prætorio Orientis, atque patricium: Thomam virum gloriosissimum quaestorem sacri nostri palatij, & exconsule: Tribonianū virum magnificum, magisteria dignitate inter agentes decoratum. Constantinum virum illustrem, comitem sacrarum largitionum inter agentes, & magistrum scrinij libellorum, sacrarumque cognitionū: Theophilum virum clarissimum, comitè sacri nostri consistorij, & iuris in hac alma urbe doctorem: Dioscorum & Præsentinum, difertissimos togatos fori amplissimi prætoriani. 2 ¶ Quibus specialiter permissimus (resecatis tam superuacuis quantū ad legū so-{?}liditatē pertinet præfationibus, quàm similibus, & contrariis, præterquam si iuris alia diuisione adiuuentur: illis etiam quæ in desuetudinem abierunt) certas & breui sermone conscriptas ex iisdem tribus codicibus & nouellis constitutionibus leges componere, & congruis titulis subdere: adiicientes quidem & detrahentes, immo & mutantes verba earum vbi hoc rei cōmoditas exigeret: colligentes vero in vnam sanctionem quæ variis constitutionibus dispersa sunt, & sensum earum clariorem effi-ietes: ita tamen, vt ordo temporum earum constitutionum non solùm ex adiectis diebus cōsulbusque, sed etiam ex ipsa compositione easum clarescat: primis quidem in primo loco, posterioribus vero in secundo ponen-dis.& si quae earum sine^die & consule in tribus ve-teribus codicibus,vel in quibus novellae constitutio-nes receptae sunt,inueniatur:ita his ponendis,nullá-que dubietate super generali earum robore ex hoc orinunda:sicut & illas vim generalis constitutionis obtinere palam est,quę ad certas personas rescriptę, vel per pragmaticam{b} sanctionem ab initio datę,eidem novo Codici propter utilitatem sanctionis ih-sertae fuerunt.
units.tr: Those matters which many earlier emperors judged must necessarily be corrected, yet none of them dared to bring to completion, we have now resolved, with the help of Almighty God, to bestow on the common good and to cut away the prolixity of lawsuits. We must, indeed, gather up the multitude of constitutions contained in the three codes, the Gregorian, the Hermogenian, and the Theodosian, and likewise those constitutions issued after these codes by Theodosius of divine memory, by other earlier emperors, and by our own clemency; and we must compose a single code under the fortunate name of our divinity, into which both the constitutions of the three said codes and the novels issued after them are to be collected. 1 ¶ For this great task, and for the maintenance of the commonwealth itself, we have chosen men sufficient for so great a height of labour and such anxious care: John, the most excellent man, former quaestor of our sacred palace, consular and patrician; Leontius, the most sublime man, master of soldiers, former praetorian prefect, consular and patrician; Phocas, the most eminent man, master of soldiers, consular and patrician; Basilides, the most excellent man, former praetorian prefect of the East, and patrician; Thomas, the most glorious man, quaestor of our sacred palace, and former consul; Tribonian, the magnificent man, adorned with the dignity of master among those in office; Constantine, the illustrious man, count of the sacred largesses among those in office, and master of the secretariat of petitions and of sacred cognitions; Theophilus, the most distinguished man, count of our sacred consistory and teacher of law in this kindly city; and Dioscorus and Presentinus, the most eloquent advocates of the most august praetorian forum. 2 ¶ To these we have specially granted the authority, after removing as superfluous, so far as concerns the strength of the laws, those prefaces, as well as similar and contrary constitutions (except where they help the division of the law), and also those which have fallen into desuetude, to compose laws that are certain and written in brief language, drawn from these same three codes and the novel constitutions, and to assign them to suitable titles; adding, removing, and even changing the words where the convenience of the matter requires it; and to gather into one enactment those provisions that are scattered among various constitutions and make their sense clearer. Yet the order of time of these constitutions is to be made plain not only by the added days and consuls but also by the arrangement itself, the earlier ones being placed first and the later ones second. And if any of them is found without day and consul in the three old codes, or in those into which the novel constitutions have been received, they are to be placed in the same way, and no doubt shall arise from this as to their general force; just as it is plain that those constitutions which were written to certain persons, or were issued at the outset by pragmatic sanction, have the force of a general constitution, and were inserted into this new Code for the usefulness of the sanction.

units.la: 3 ¶Haec igitur ad vestram notitiam ferre properavimus, ut sciatis quanta nos diuturna super rerum communi utilitate cura sollicitet, stn-dentes certas & indubitatas, & in unum codice col-lectas esse decretero constitutiones: ut ex eo tantum-modo sub felici nostro nomine nuncupando Codi-ce, recitatio constitutionum in omnibus ad citiorce litium decisiones fiat iudiciis. Dar. Idib. Febr. CP. DN. Instiniano PP. A. XI. COS. Anno Christi 528.
units.tr: 3 ¶ We have therefore hastened to bring these things to your notice, so that you may know how great a care for the common welfare of affairs has long troubled us, since we have decreed that the constitutions be certain and undoubted and collected in one code; so that, from that Code alone, which is to be named under our fortunate name, the reading of constitutions in all judicial decisions may be made for the speedier settling of lawsuits. Given on the Ides of February, at Constantinople, in the consulship of our lord Justinian, Augustus, for the eleventh time; in the year of Christ 528.

units.la: DE IUSTINIANEO Codice confirmando ad Mennam.
units.tr: ON CONFIRMING THE JUSTINIANIC CODE, to Menna.

units.la: Imp. IUSTINIANUS Pius, felix, inclytus, victor ac triumphator, semper Augustus, Menna praefecto[?] praetorio, ex praefecto huius almae urbis C P. ac Patricio.
units.tr: Emperor Justinian Pius, Fortunate, Illustrious, Victor and Triumphant, ever Augustus, to Menna, praetorian prefect, and former prefect of this kindly city of Constantinople, and patrician.

units.la: UMMA reipublicae [?]mirio de stirpe dua-rum rerum, armorum{d} scilicet, atque legum veniens, vimque sua exinde mu-nies, felix Romanorum genus omnibus anteponi nationibus omnibusque gen-tibus dominari tam praeteritis effecit temporibus, quam Deo propitio in aeternum efficiet. istorum e-tenim alterum alterius auxilio semper eguit: & tam militaris res legibus in tuto collocata est, quam ipse leges armorum praesidio seruatae sunt. Merito igitur ad primam communium rerum sustentationem, nostram sententiam & mentem laboresque nostros referentes, militaria{e} quidem agmina multiplicibus & omnem providentiam continentibus modis coreximus: & tam veteribus ad meliore statum breui tempore ductis, quam novis nō solum exquisitis, sed etiam recta dispositione nostri nominis sine novis expensis publicis constitutis,primo seruando posita, deinde nova ponendo, firmissima subiectis effeci-mus.
units.tr: The most high majesty of the Roman commonwealth, arising from the root of two things, namely arms and laws, and strengthening its power by these, has made the fortunate Roman nation set before all nations and rule over all peoples, as it did in past times, and as, by God's favour, it will do for ever. For each of these has always needed the help of the other: military affairs are secured by laws, just as the laws are preserved by the protection of arms. Rightly, therefore, referring our judgment, purpose, and labours first of all to the support of the common good, we have set in order the military companies in many ways, providing for every need; and by bringing the old things to a better state in a short time, and by establishing the new things, not only those sought out but also those set in right order without new public expense under our name, we have made them most firm for those subject to them, first preserving what was laid down and then laying down new things.

units.la: 1 ¶ Sed cùm sit necessarium multitudine con-stitutionum tā in {a}tribus veteribus Codicibus relatarum,quàm post earum cósectionem posterioribus temporibus adiectarum, ad breuitatem reducendo, caliginem earum rectis iudicum definitionibus insidiantem penitus extirpare: ad hoc commune praestandum beneficium Deo praesule prono animo nos dedidimus,& electis viris gloriosissimis, tàm doctrina legum,quàm experientia rerum, studioque reipublicae indefesso, & laudabili proposito pollentibus, sub certis finibus magnum laborem commisimus: per quem,tam trium veterum Gregoriani, Hermogeniani atque Theodosiani codicum constitutiones, quàm plurimas alias post eosdem codices à Theodosio dininæ[?] memoriæ, cæterisque post eũ retro principibus,à nostra etiam clementia positas, in vnũ codicem felici nostro vocabulo nũcupandum colligi præcepimus: Tolledis quidé tam præfationibus nullum suffragium sanctionibus conferentibus, {b}quàm contrariis constitutionibus,quæ posteriore promul-gatione vacuatæ sunt: similibus etiá præter eas quæ eadem pene sanciendo,diuisionem iuris aliquam facere noscuntur: ex qua diuidendo vetera novũ aliquid nasci videtur: multis insuper ad rectam huius Codicis compositionem pertinentibus, iisdem prudentissimis viris à nostro numine mãdatis: & nostro studio pro republica instituto, suum præsidiū Deus omnipotens annuit.
units.tr: 1 ¶ But since it is necessary to reduce to brevity the multitude of constitutions both recorded in the three old codes and added in later times after their collection, and to root out completely the obscurity that lies in wait for the correct decisions of judges, we have, for the carrying out of this common benefit, with God as our leader and with ready minds, committed a great labour, within certain limits, to men most glorious, who excel both in the learning of the laws and in experience of affairs, and in tireless zeal for the commonwealth and laudable purpose. Through them we have ordered that the constitutions of the three old codes, the Gregorian, Hermogenian, and Theodosian, as well as very many others issued after these codes by Theodosius of divine memory and by the other earlier emperors and by our own clemency, be collected into one code to be named by our fortunate name. Removed are the prefaces, which contribute nothing to the force of the enactments, as well as the contrary constitutions which were annulled by later promulgation; likewise similar ones, except those which, by enacting almost the same thing, are known to make some division of the law, from which dividing a new thing seems to arise from the old; and, besides, many matters pertaining to the correct composition of this Code have been entrusted by our authority to those same most prudent men, and God Almighty has granted his support to our zeal, established for the commonwealth.

units.la: 2 ¶Ad istum enim laborem,& tanti operis cõsummationem electi vir excellentis-simus exquæstore nostri palatij, consularis atque patricius Ioanes:&vir sublimissimus expræfecto prꝫtorio consularis atque patricius,Leontius:vir quoque eminentissimus magister militum,consularis atque patricius,Phocas: etiá vir excellentissimus expræfe-cto prætorio per Orientem,& patricius,& nunc præ-sectus prætorio per Illyricum,Basilides: & vir glo-riofissimus quæstor sacri nostri palatij,& exconsule Thomas:imo & vir magnificus magisteria {c}dignita-te inter agentes decoratus,Tribonianus: & vir illu-stris comes sacrarũ largitionũ inter agẽtes,& magi-ster {d}scrinij & libellorũ & sacrarũ cognitionũ,Cóstinus[?]:& vir illustris ex magistro,& iuris doctor in hac alma urbe Theophilus:viri etiam disertissimi togati amplisimi fori tuæ sublimitatis Diofcorus atque Præsentinus{4}: omnia quæ eis mandauimus, cū fedu& peruigili industria, moderataque digestione, cū Dei auxilio ad prosperum tulerūt terminum, & eunde nouū lustinianeum Codicē nobis obtulerūt ita compositum, vt & rebus profuturus esset comunibus,& nostro conuenisset imperio.
units.tr: 2 ¶ For to this labour and the completion of so great a work have been chosen: John, the most excellent man, former quaestor of our sacred palace, consular and patrician; Leontius, the most sublime man, former praetorian prefect, consular and patrician; Phocas, the most eminent man, master of soldiers, consular and patrician; Basilides, the most excellent man, former praetorian prefect of the East, and patrician, and now praetorian prefect of Illyricum; Thomas, the most glorious man, quaestor of our sacred palace, and former consul; and indeed Tribonian, the magnificent man, adorned with the dignity of master among those in office; and Constantine, the illustrious man, count of the sacred largesses among those in office, and master of the secretariat of petitions and of sacred cognitions; and Theophilus, the illustrious man, former master and teacher of law in this kindly city; also the most eloquent advocates of the most august forum of your sublimity, Dioscorus and Presentinus. All that we entrusted to them they have brought to a prosperous end with faithful and watchful industry and measured arrangement, with the help of God, and they have presented us with this new Justinianic Code, so composed that it would both benefit the common affairs and suit our empire.

units.la: 3 ¶Hunc igitur in æternū valituru iudicio tui culminis intimare perspeximus, vt sciant omnes tam litigatores quàm disertissimi aduocati, nullatenus cis licere decetero constitutiones ex veteribus tribus codicibus, quorum iam mentio facta est, vel ex iis quæ nouellæ constitutiones ad præsens tepus vocabatur, in cognitionalibus recitare certaminibus, sed solum eidem nostro Codici insertis constitutionibus necesse esse uti{b} falsi crimini subdedis his, qui cōtra hoc facere ausi fuerint: cum sufficiat earundem constitutionum nostri Codicis recitatio, adiectis etiam veterum iuris interpretatorum laboribus ad omnes dirimendas lites: nullaque dubitatione emergenda vel eo ꝗ sine die & consule quædam copositæ sunt, vel quod ad certas personas rescriptæ sunt: cum omnes generalium constitutionum vim obtinere procul dubio est, sed & si quę earum constitutionum detractis vel additis vel permutatis certis verbis (quod & ipsum præfatis excellentissimis viris specialiter permisim⁹) compositæ sunt: nullis cōcedimus ex libris veterum iuris interpretatorum aliter eas habentes recitare, sed solam iuris interpretationem sententiam commendare: vt tunc teneat, cum minime aduersetur euisdem nostri Codicis cōstitutionib. 4 ¶Si quæ vero pragmaticæ ꝺ sanctiones, quæ minime in eodē nostro Codice receptæ sunt, ciuitatibus forte, vel corporib. vel scholis, vel scriniis, vel officiis, vel alicui personæ impartitæ sunt: eas, siquidem aliquod priuilegium speciali beneficio indulgent, omni modo ratas manere: si vero pro certis capitulis factæ sunt, tūc tenere cum nulli nostri Codicis aduersantur constitutioni, præcipimus. Sed & si quæ regesta in tui culminis iudicio, vel in aliis iudiciis ciuilibus vel militaribus, vel apud principia numerorum, pro publicis expensis, vel quibuscunque titulis ad publicū pertinentibus posita sunt: ea etiam prout communis rei commoditas exigit, firma esse censemus. 5 ¶Illustris igitur & magnifica auctoritas tua pro
units.tr: 3 ¶ We have therefore seen fit to make this known to the judgment of your highness, so that it may stand for ever: that all, both litigants and the most eloquent advocates, may know that in no way is it permitted to them from now on to cite in judicial contests constitutions from the three old codes, already mentioned, or from those which are called novel constitutions up to the present time; but that it is necessary to use only the constitutions inserted into this our Code, under the charge of forgery against those who dare to act contrary to this. For the reading of the constitutions of our Code is sufficient, together with the labours of the old interpreters of the law, for settling all disputes; and no doubt should arise because some of them were composed without day and consul, or because some were written to certain persons. For it is beyond doubt that all have the force of general constitutions; and if any of these constitutions have been composed with certain words removed, added, or changed (which also we have specially permitted to the aforesaid most excellent men), we do not allow anyone to cite them from the books of the old interpreters as holding them otherwise, but only to commend the interpreters' opinion, so that it holds good when it is not opposed to the constitutions of this same Code. 4 ¶ If indeed there are any pragmatic sanctions, which have not been received in this same Code of ours, that have been granted perhaps to cities, bodies, schools, offices, bureaus, or to some person, we order that these, if they grant some privilege by special favour, remain valid in every way; but if they were made for certain chapters, we order that they hold good, provided they do not oppose any constitution of our Code. But also whatever has been registered in your highness's judgment, or in other civil or military courts, or before the commanders of numbered units, for public expenses, or under whatever titles pertain to the public, these also, as the convenience of the common matter requires, we judge to be firm. 5 ¶ Therefore your illustrious and magnificent authority shall...

Cod. de diuisis rescriptis. innato sibi circa rempublicā nostrasque dispositiones explendas studio ad omnium populorum notitiam eundem Codicem edictis ex more propositis peruenire faciat: ipso etiam textu Codicis in singulas prouincias nostro subiectas imperio, cum nostra diuina subnotatione mittendo, vt eo modo ad omnium notitiam eiusdem nostri Codicis constitutiones valeant peruenire: & vt extantibus sestis diebus, id est ex die sextodecimo Kalendarum Maij præsentis septimæ indictionis, consulatu Decij viri clarissimi recitationes constitutionū ex code nostro Codiant. Dat. vii. Id. April. C.P. Decio V.C. Cos.[?] 529.
units.tr: {d} l. vlt. §. vlt. Cod. de diuisis rescriptis. With the innate zeal we have for the commonwealth and for carrying out our arrangements, let him cause this same Code, by the customary posting of edicts, to come to the knowledge of all peoples. Let him also send the very text of the Code, with our divine subscription, to each province subject to our empire, so that by this means the constitutions of our Code may come to the knowledge of everyone. And let the recitations of the constitutions from our Code be made on the festival days now at hand, namely from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May of the present seventh indiction, in the consulship of Decius, most illustrious man. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Decius, most illustrious man, 529.
On the Compilation of the Digest, to Tribonian.

units.la: IMPERATOR CAESAR FLAVIUS, Iustinianus Pius, Felix, Inclytus ac triumphator, semper Augustus, Tribonia-no Quaestori suo, Salutem.
units.tr: THE EMPEROR CAESAR FLAVIUS Iustinianus, Pious, Fortunate, Renowned, Victor and Triumphant, ever Augustus, to Tribonian, his Quaestor: greeting.

units.la: EO CAVCTORE nostrum gubernante Imperium, quod nobis à coelesti maiestate traditū est, & bella felicē peragimus, & pacem decoramus, & statum reipublicæ sustentamus: & ita nostros animos ad Dei omnipotentis erigimus adiutorium: vt neque armis cōsidamus, neque nostris mi-litibus, neque bellorum ducibus, vel nostro ingenio: sed omnem spem ad solam referamus summæ proui-dentiam trinitatis, vnde & mundi totius elementa processerunt, & eorum dispositio in orbem terrarū produ-cta est. I. Cū itaque* nihil tam studiosum in omnibus rebus inueniatur, quàm legum auctoritas, quae & diuinas & humanas res bene disponit, & o-
units.tr: With God as the author, under whose guidance we govern the empire that has been handed down to us by heavenly majesty, we carry on our wars successfully, we adorn peace, and we sustain the condition of the commonwealth. We raise our minds in this way to the help of almighty God, so that we place no trust in arms, in our soldiers, in the generals of our wars, or in our own ability, but refer all our hope solely to the supreme providence of the Trinity, from which the elements of the whole world also proceeded, and from which their arrangement was brought forth into the orb of the lands. I. Since therefore nothing is found to be so deserving of care in all matters as the authority of the laws, which well ordain both divine and human affairs, and o-
c l.1.C. de veteri iure.
d Law expetendum.

units.la: f l.10.in ff.ff. de iustit. & iure. olim, legum interpretandarum scientia ad collegium Pontificum pertinebat l.2.§.6.in ff.ff.de origin.iur. ad quos de omnibus diuinis & humanis etiam referebatur. Cicer. 3. de Orat. mnem iniquitatem expellit: reperimus autem omnem legum tramitem, qui ab vrbe Roma condita & Romuleis descendit temporibus, ita esse confusum, vt in infinitum extendatur, & nullius humanae naturae capacitate concludatur: primum nobis fuit studium, a sacratissimis retro principibus initiu summere, & eorum constitutiones emendare, & vix dilucidae tradere: quatenus in vnum codicem eongrega tae, & omni superuacua similitudine, & iniquissima discordia absolutae, vniuersis hominibus promptum suae sinceritatis praebeant praefidiu. 2 ¶ Hocque opere consummato, in vno volumine nostro nomine praefulgente, coadunato: cum ex paucis & tenuioribus releuati ad summam & plenissimam iuris emendationem peruenire properaremus, & omnem Romanam sanctionem & colligere, & emendare, & tot auctorum diuersa volumina vno codice indita ostendere quod nemo neque spectare, neque optare ausus est: res quidem nobis difficillima, immo magis impossibilis videbatur. Sed manibus ad coelum erectis, aeterno auxilio inuocato, eam quoque curam nostris repositum animis, Deo freti, qui & res penitus desperatas donare, & consummare suae virtutis magnitudine poterit. 3 ¶ Et ad tuae sinceritatis opti mum respeximus ministerium: tibique primo & hoc opus commissimus, ingenij tui documentis ex nostri Codicis ordinatione acceptis: & iussimus, quos probaueris tam ex facundissimis antecessoribus, quam ex viris disertissimis togatis fori amplissimae sedis, ad sociandum laborem eligere. His itaque collectis, & in nostrum palatium introductis nobisque tuo te timonio placitis, totam rem faciendam permis mus: ita tamen: vt tui vigilantissimi animi gubernatione res omnis celebretur. 4 ¶ Iubemus igitur vobis antiquorum prudentium, quibus auctoritate conscribendarum interpretandarumque legum sapientissimi principes praebuerunt, libros ad ius Romanum pertinentes & legere, & elimare: vt ex his omnis materia colligatur, nulla, secundum quod possibile est, neque similitudine neque discordia derelicta: sed ex his hoc colligi, quod vnu pro omnibus sufficiat. Quia autem & alij libros ad ius pertinentes scripserunt: quorum scripturae nullis auctoribus receptae, nec vsitatae sunt: neque nos eorum volumina nostram inquietare dignamur sanctionem.
units.tr: f Law 10, in ff., ff. de iustitia et iure. Formerly the knowledge of interpreting the laws belonged to the college of the Pontiffs, Law 2, §6, in ff., ff. de origine iuris, to whom questions about all things divine and human were also referred. Cicero, De oratore 3. Our constitution expels all iniquity. Moreover, we have found that the whole track of the laws, which runs from the city of Rome founded and descends from the times of Romulus, has been so confused that it extends into infinity and cannot be enclosed within the capacity of any human nature. Our first concern was to take up the work from the most sacred emperors of former times, to amend their constitutions, and to hand them down scarcely clear, so that, gathered into one code and freed from all superfluous repetition and most unjust discord, they might offer to all people a ready protection of their purity. 2 ¶ When this work was completed and brought together in one volume bearing our name, we hastened from the few and slender remedies to the highest and most complete reform of the law. We aimed both to collect and to correct all Roman legislation, and to set forth in one code the diverse volumes of so many authors, something which no one had dared to look upon or to desire. The task seemed to us most difficult, indeed more nearly impossible. But with hands raised to heaven and eternal help invoked, we placed this care also in our minds, trusting in God, who can give gifts to things utterly despaired of and bring them to completion by the greatness of his power.

units.la: 5 ¶Cumque hæc materia summa nostri numinis liberalitate collecta fuerit, oportet eam pulcherrimo opere extruere, & quàm proprium & sanctissimum templum iustitiæ consecrare: & in libros quinquaginta, & cerros[?] titulos totum ius digerere, tam secundum nostri constitutionem Codicis, quàm edicti perpetui imitationem, prout hoc vobis commodius esse patuerit: ut nihil extra memoratam consummationem posit esse derelictum: sed his quinquaginta libris totum ius antiquum per millesimum & {*}quadringentesimum pene annum confusum, & a nobis purgatum, quasi quodam muro vallatum nihil extra se habeat omnibus auctoribus iuris æquâ{b} dignitate pollentibus, & nemini quadam prærogatiua seruanda: quia non omnes in omnia, sed certi per certa vel meliores, vel deteriores inueniuntur.
units.tr: 5 ¶ When this material has been collected by the great generosity of our divine power, it must be built up in a most beautiful work and consecrated as a proper and most holy temple of justice. The whole law is to be arranged into fifty books and two hundred titles, both according to the constitution of our Code and in imitation of the Perpetual Edict, as shall seem more convenient to you, so that nothing may be left outside this completed work. Rather, by these fifty books the whole ancient law, confused for nearly a thousand four hundred years and purified by us, is fenced in as by a wall and has nothing outside itself. All authors of law are to hold equal dignity, and no one is to keep any prerogative, because not all are found to be equal in all things, but certain ones are better or worse in certain things.

units.la: 6 ¶Sed Neque[?] ex[?] multitudine auctorum, quod melius & æquius est, indicatore: cū possitforsitā[?] & deterioris sententia & multas & maiores in aliqua parte superrare. Et ideo ea, quæ antea in notis AEmilij Papinia ni ex Vlpiano & Paulo, necnon Marciano adscripta sunt, quæ antea nullam vim obtinebant propter honorem splendidissimi Papiniani, non statim respuere: sed si quid ex his ad replctionem summi ingenij Papiniani laborum, vel interpretatione necessarium esse perspexeritis, & hoc ponere legis vicem obtinēs non moremini: ut omnes, qui relati fuerint in hunc codicem prudentissimi viri habeant auctoritatem, tamquàm si eorum studia ex principalibus constitutionibus profecta, & nostro diuino fuerant ore profusa: omnia enim merito nostra facimus, quia ex nobis omnis eis impertietur auctoritas. nam qui subtiliter factum emendat, laudabilior est eo, qui primus inuenit.
units.tr: 6 ¶ But neither is what is better and fairer to be judged by the number of authors, since the opinion of a lesser author may perhaps outweigh many and greater ones in some part. Therefore, those things which were formerly added in the notes of Aemilius Papinianus, from Ulpian and Paul, and also from Marcian, which previously held no force because of the honour of the most distinguished Papinian, you are not to reject at once. But if you perceive that anything from these is necessary for the completion of the labours of Papinian's great genius, or for its interpretation, and you do not hesitate to set it down in place of law, then all who have been cited in this code shall have the authority of the most prudent men, as if their studies had proceeded from our principal constitutions and had been poured forth from our divine mouth. For we rightly make all things our own, since all authority is imparted to them by us. For he who corrects a deed skilfully is more praiseworthy than he who first devised it.

units.la: 7 ¶Sed & hoc studiosum vobis esse volumus: ut si quid in veteribus non bene positum libris inueniatis, vel aliquod superfluum, vel minus perse-ctum[?]: superuacua longitudine semota, & quod imperfectum est, repleatis, & omne opus moderatum & quàm pulcherrimum ostendatis. Hoc etiam nihilo minus obseruando: ut, si aliquid in veteribus legibus vel constitutionibus, quas antiqui in suis libris imposuerunt, non recte scriptum inueniatis: & hoc reformetis, & ordini moderato tradatis, ut hoc videatur esse verum, & optimum, & quasi ab initio scriptum, quod à vobis elegtum, & ibi positum fuerit. Et nemo ex comparatione veteris voluminis quasi vi riosam[?] scripturam arguere audeat. cum enim lege antiqua,quae Regia {*}nuncupabatur,omne ius omnis que potestas populi Romani{b} in imperatoriam trāf lata sunt potestatem: nos vero sanctionem omnem non diuidimus in alias & alias conditorum partes, sed totam nostram esse volumus:quid polsit antiqui tas nostris legibus abrogare? Et in tantum volumus eadem omnia,cum reposita sunt,obtinere:vt,etsi{c} a-liter fuerant apud veteres conscripta, in contrariū autem in positione inueniantur:nullum crimen scri pturae imputetur, sed nostrae electioni hoc adscriba-tur. § Nulla vitaque in omnibus praedicti codicis membris antinomia (sic enim a vetustate Graeco vo cabulo nuncupatur) aliquem sibi videlicet locum, sed fit vna concordia, vna consequentia, adhuc arius remine constituto. § Sed & similitudinem,secun-dum quod dictum est, ab huiusmodi consummatio-ne volumus exulare. & ea,quae sacratissimis confti-tutionibus, quas in codicem nostrum redegimus, cauta sunt,iterum poni ex veteri iure non concedi-mus: cum Diualium constitutionum sanctio sufficit ad eorum auctoritatem : nisi forte vel propter diui fionem,vel propter repletionem, vel propter plenio-rem indaginem hoc contigerit.& hoc tamen perra-ro, ne ex continuatione huiusmodi lapsus oriatur aliquid in tali prato spinosum. Io § Sed & si quae leges in veteribus libris positae, iam in desuetudine abierunt: nullo modo vobis easdem ponere permit-timus.cum haec tatummodo obtinere volumus,quę vel iudiciorum frequetisimus ordo exercuit, vel longa consuetudo huius almae urbis comprobauit, secundum Saluij Iuliani scripturam, quae indicat {f}debere omnes ciuitates consuetudinem Romae se-qui,quae caput est orbis terrarum,nō ipsam alias ci uitates. Romam autem intelligendum est non solū veterem,sed etiam regiam{e} nostram,quae Deo pro-pitio cum melioribus codita est{g} auguriis. 12 Ideo iubemus, duobus istis codicibus omnia gubernari: Licio & legem 7.ff.de probationib.
units.tr: 7 ¶ But we also wish you to take care that, if you find in the old books anything not well put, or anything superfluous or less than perfect, you remove superfluous length and supply what is incomplete, and show every work in a moderate and most beautiful form. Also, observing this no less: if you find in the ancient laws or constitutions, which the ancients inserted in their books, anything not rightly written, you are to reform it and hand it down in a moderate order, so that what has been chosen by you and placed there appears to be true and best, and as if written from the beginning. And let no one dare to accuse the work of a violent writing by comparison with the old volume. For since the ancient law, called Regia, transferred all law and all power of the Roman people to the imperial power, why should antiquity be able to abrogate our laws? We wish all the same things to hold when they have been put back, so that, even if they were otherwise written among the ancients, and are found in a contrary position, no fault of writing be imputed, but this be ascribed to our choice. § Therefore let there be no antinomy [ἀντινομία] (for so antiquity calls it in Greek) in any of the members of the aforesaid code, which may claim some place for itself, but let there be one concord and one consequence, with a single law established. § We also wish, as has been said, that likeness of this kind be banished from such a completed work. Nor do we permit that those things which have been provided in the most sacred constitutions, which we have brought together into our code, be put again from the old law, since the sanction of the divine constitutions is sufficient for their authority, unless perhaps this happens because of a division, a repetition, or a fuller investigation; and this rarely, lest from such continuation some slip arise, something thorny in such a meadow. 10 § But also, if any laws placed in the old books have now fallen into disuse, we in no way permit you to put the same in. We wish only those things to hold which either the very frequent order of the courts has practised, or long custom of this nourishing city has approved, following the writing of Salvius Julianus, which indicates that all cities ought to follow the custom of Rome, which is the head of the world, and not the cities themselves. But by Rome it must be understood not only the old, but also our imperial city, which by the favour of God was founded with better auguries. 12 Therefore we command that everything be governed by these two codes: Lic. and law 7, ff. de probationibus.
{*} Add laws 34 and 35 and following, Digest, *de legibus*.

units.la: {e} Constantinopolim,quae alibi vrbs AEterna appellatur. l. 1.Cod.de diuer.prad.urb.
units.tr: {e} Constantinople, which elsewhere is called the Eternal City. Code, de diversis praediis urbanis, law 1.

units.la: {g} Remi necè subinnuit.quod si Zosimus credimus,Constantinus Romulo non erit probior ob vxoris & filii necem. vno constitutionum: altero iuris enucleati, & in futurum codicem compositi: vel si quid aliud à nobis fuerit promulgatum institutionum vicem obtines vt{4} a rudis animus studiosi simplicibus enutritus, facilius ad altioris prudentiæ redigatur scientiam.
units.tr: {g} He hints at the murder of Remus. If we believe Zosimus, Constantine will be no more upright than Romulus for the murder of his wife and son. One of the constitutions; the other, the law made clear and the code compiled for the future; or whatever else has been promulgated by us, takes the place of the Institutes, so that the untrained mind of the student, nurtured on simple things, may more easily be led on to the knowledge of higher prudence.

units.la: 22 ¶Nostram autem consummationem, quæ vobis Deo adnuente componetur, Digestorum vel Pandectarum nomen habere sancimus, nullis iuris peritis in posterum audentibus commentarios illi applicare, & verbositate sua supradicti codicis compendii confundere quemadmodum in antiquioribus factum est, cum per contrarias interpretantium sententias totum ius pene coturbatum est, sed sufficiat per indices{b} tantummodo & titulorum subtilitatem, quæ [illegible, ~8 letters] nuncupatur, quædam admonitoria eius facere, nullo ex interpretatione eorum vitio oriundo.
units.tr: 22 Our consummation, which will be composed by you with God's assent, we decree shall bear the name Digest or Pandects. No jurists in future shall presume to attach commentaries to it and confuse it with the verbosity of the aforementioned code's abridgement, as was done in earlier times, when almost the whole law was thrown into confusion by the conflicting opinions of interpreters. Instead, it is enough that by indexes alone, and the subtle arrangement of the titles, which is called (illegible word), it provides certain reminders, without any fault arising from their interpretation.

units.la: 13 ¶Ne autem per scripturam aliqua fiat in posterum dubitatio: iubemus non per simplorum{c} captiones & compendiosa ænigmata, quæ multas per se & per suum vitium{d} antinomias{e} induxerunt, eiusdem codicis textum conscribi etiam si numerus librorum significatur, aut aliud quicquam. nec enim per specialia sigla numerorum manifestari, sed per litterarum consequentiam explanari concedimus.
units.tr: 13 Moreover, lest any doubt arise in future from the writing: we order that the text of this same code not be written out through the captions of simple people and compendious enigmas, which have, through themselves and their defect, introduced many antinomies, even if the number of books is indicated or anything else. For we do not permit that things be made manifest by special numeral signs, but explained by the sequence of letters.

units.la: 14 ¶Hæc igitur omnia Deo placido facere tua prudentia vnà cùm aliis facundissimis viris studeat, & tà subtili,quàm celerrimo fini tradere:vt codex consummatus, & in quinquaginta libros digestus offeratur in maximā & æternā rei memoriam, Deiqe omnipotentis prudentiæ argumentum,nostriqe imperij vestrique ministerij gloriam. Data octauodecimo calendis Ianuariis,Lampadio & Oreste viris clarissimis consulibus,530.
units.tr: 14 Let your prudence therefore, together with other most eloquent men, take care to do all these things with God's favour, and to hand them over with the utmost subtlety and speed, so that the completed code, digested into fifty books, may be offered for the greatest and eternal memory of the matter, as a proof of the wisdom of almighty God and a glory of our empire and your ministry. Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, most illustrious men, 530.
FELICITER. (Happily.)

units.la: DE{a} CONFIRMATIO-ne Institutionum ad cupidam legum iuuentutem.
units.tr: On the Confirmation of the Institutes, to the Eager Youth of the Law.

units.la: IN NOMINE DOMINI NOSTRI IESU CHRISTI. IMPERATOR Cæsar Flauius Iustinianus, Alamanicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, Pius, Felix, inclytus, victor, ac triumphator, semper Augustus, cupida legum iuuentuti. [S.D.]
units.tr: IN THE NAME OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST. The Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, Pius, Felix, Inclytus, Victor, and Triumphator, ever Augustus, to the eager youth of the law. [S.D.]

units.la: IMPERATORIAM maiestatem nō solum {b}armis decoratam, sed etiam legibus oportet esse armatam, vt vt v-trumque tempus, & bellorum, & pacis, rectè posit gubernari: & princeps Romanus nō solum in hostilibus præliis victor existat, sed etiam, per legitimos {c}tramites, calumniantium iniquitates expellat & fiat tam iuris {d}religiosissimus, quàm victis hostibus triumphator || magnificus. ||
units.tr: The imperial majesty ought to be not only adorned with arms but also armed with laws, so that both kinds of time, of war and of peace, may be rightly governed. A Roman prince should not only be victorious in hostile battles, but should also, by lawful means, drive out the injustices of those who bring false accusations, and become as most scrupulous in law as he is glorious as a triumphator over defeated enemies.

units.la: 1 ¶ Quorum vtramque viam cum summis vigiliis, summaque prouidentia, annuente Deo, perfecimus. Et bellicos quidem sudores nostros Barbaricæ gentes sub iuga nostra redactæ cognoscunt, & tàm Africa, quàm aliæ innumeræ prouinciæ, post {e}tanta temporum spatia, nostris victoriis à coelesti numine præstitis, iterum ditioni Romanæ, nostróque additæ imperio, protestantur. Omnes verò populi legibus tàm à nobis promulgatis, quàm compositis, reguntur.
units.tr: 1 Both of these ways we have accomplished, with the greatest vigilance and the greatest foresight, with God granting it. Barbarian peoples brought under our yoke know our military labours, and Africa as well as countless other provinces, after so long a span of time, acknowledge through our victories, granted by the heavenly power, that they have been restored to the Roman dominion and added to our empire. Indeed, all peoples are governed by laws both promulgated and compiled by us.

units.la: 2 ¶ Et cum sacratissimas {f}constitutiones, antea confusas, in lucu-lentam ereximus consonantiam: tunc nostram extendimus curam ad immensa {g}veteris prudentiæ volumina: &opus desperatum, quasi per medium profundum euntes, cœlesti fauore iam adimpleuimus.
units.tr: 2 And when we had brought the most sacred constitutions, formerly confused, into a clear harmony, we then extended our care to the immense volumes of ancient wisdom, and, going as it were through the middle of a deep sea, we have now, by heavenly favour, completed a work that was thought hopeless.

units.la: 3 ¶ Cumque hoc, Deo propitio, peractum est: Triboniano viro magnifico, magistro, & exquæstore sacri palatij nostri, ||& exconsule||necnō Theophilo, &
units.tr: 3 When this had been accomplished, by the favour of God, we specially commanded Tribonian, a magnificent man, master and ex-quaestor of our sacred palace, and also ex-consul, together with Theophilus and

units.la: Dorotheo, viris illustribus, antecessoribus, quorum omnium solertiam, & legum scientiam, & circa eas iusiones fidem, iam ex multis rerum argumentis accepimus, conuocatis, mandauimus specialiter: vt ipsi nostra auctoritate, nostrisque suafionibus, Institutiones componerent, vt liceat vobis prima legū cunabula nō ab antiquis fabulis discere, sed ab imperiali splendore appetere: & tam aures, quam animi vestri, nihil inutile, nihilque perperam positum: sed quod in ipsis rerum obtinet argumentis, accipiant, & quod priore tempore vix post quadrienniū prioribus coringebat, vt tūc constitutiones imperatorias legeret: hoc vos à primordio ingrediamini, digni tanto honore, tantaque reperti felicitate, vt & initium vobis & finis legū eruditionis à voce principali procedat.
units.tr: Dorotheus, illustrious men and professors of law, whom we have summoned, and whose skill, knowledge of the laws, and faithfulness in these matters we have already learned from many proofs, that they should, by our authority and at our instruction, compose the Institutes, so that you may learn the first cradle of the laws not from ancient fables but may seek it from imperial splendour; and so that your ears and minds may receive nothing useless and nothing wrongly set down, but what holds good in the very substance of the matters. In an earlier age, students could scarcely, after four years, begin to read the imperial constitutions; but you, deemed worthy of so great an honour and found so fortunate, should enter upon them from the very beginning, so that both the beginning and the end of your legal learning may proceed from the voice of the prince.

units.la: 4 Igitur post libros quinquaginta Digestorum seu Pandectarum, (in quibus omne ius antiquum collectum est. quod per eundem virū excelsum, Triboniaunum: necnon cæteros viros illustres, & facundisimos confecimus) in quatuor libros easdem Institutiones parriri iussimus: vt sint totius legitimæ scientiæ prima elementa.
units.tr: 4 Therefore, after the fifty books of the Digest or Pandects (in which all the ancient law has been collected, which we have completed through the same lofty man, Tribonian, and the other illustrious and most eloquent men), we have ordered these Institutes to be divided into four books, so that they may be the first elements of the whole lawful science.

units.la: 5 In quibus breuiter expositum est: & quod antea obtinebat: & quod postea desuetudine inumbratū, imperiali remedio illuminatum est.
units.tr: 5 In them is set out briefly both what formerly held good and what, afterwards, obscured by disuse, has been illuminated by imperial remedy.

units.la: 6 Quas ex omnibus antiquorum Institutionibus, & præcipuè ex Commentariis Caij s nostri, tam institutionū, quàm rerū quotidianarum aliisque multis commentariis compositas, cūm tres viri prudentes præditi nobis obtulerunt: & legimus, & recognouimus, & plenissimum nostrarum constitutionum robur eis accommodauimus.
units.tr: 6 These Institutes, compiled from all the ancient institutes, and especially from the Commentaries of our Gaius, both on the Institutes and on the Everyday Matters, and from many other commentaries, were offered to us by three prudent men endowed with ability; and we have read them, reviewed them, and given them the full force of our constitutions.

units.la: 7 Summa itaque ope, & alacri studio has leges nostras accipite, & vofmetipsos sic eruditos ostendite: vt spes vos pulcherrima foueat, toto legitimo opere perfecto, posse etiam nostram rempubliciam in partibus eius vobis credendis gubernari. D.CP. xi. Kalend. Decemb. D. IVSTINIANO PP. A. III. CONS. 533.
units.tr: 7 Therefore, with the greatest diligence and an eager zeal, receive these our laws, and show yourselves thus instructed, so that the most beautiful hope may cherish you: that, once the whole lawful work is complete, you may also be able to govern our commonwealth in those parts of it entrusted to you. Given at Constantinople, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Justinian Perpetual Augustus, for the third time, 533.
{b} who in Greek [προχειροτάτοι?]

units.la: {c} i.7ιç χρήσεως ἐκέξηλωμένος, i. ab vsu reiectis. Teaph.
units.tr: {c} That is, [ἐκζηλωμένος], that is, rejected from use. Theophilus.

units.la: {d} Pandectae dicuntur ἐκ τὸ πᾶν τῆς ἐν ἀδοισθεὶν ὑποδέξασθαι.
units.tr: {d} The Pandects are so called from taking in everything [ἐκ τὸ πᾶν τῆς ἐν ἀδοισθεὶν ὑποδέξασθαι].
{e} Definition of the Institutes.

units.la: {f} qui vixit sub Adriano, quem sacratissimum Principem appellat. lex penal.ff. ad Tertull.
units.tr: {f} He who lived under Hadrian, whom he calls the most sacred Prince. Penal law, Digest, ad Tertull.

units.la: DE CONFIRMATIONE Digestorum ad Senatum & omnes populos.
units.tr: Concerning the Confirmation of the Digest, addressed to the Senate and all peoples.

units.la: IN NOMINE DOMINI DEI nostri Iesu Christi, Imperator Caesar Flavius Iustinianus, Alamanicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, Pius, Felix, Inclytus, Victor ac triumphator semper Augustus, ad Senatum & omnes populos.
units.tr: IN THE NAME OF OUR LORD GOD Jesus Christ, the Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, Pius, Felix, Inclytus, Victor and Triumphator, ever Augustus, to the Senate and all peoples.

units.la: TANTA{a} circa nos divinae humanitatis est providentia, ut semper aeternis liberalitatibus nos sustentare dignetur. Post bella enim Parthica aeterna pace sopita, postque Vandalicam gentem eruptam, & Carthaginem, immo magis omnem Lybiam Romano imperio iterum sociatam: & leges antiquas iam senio praegravatas, per nostram vigilantiam praebuit in novam pulchritudinem, & moderatum peruenire compendium. quod nemo ante nostrum imperium umquam speravit, neque humano ingenio possibile esse penitus existimavit. erat enim mirabile, Romanam sanctionem ab Urbe condita usque ad nostri imperii tempora, quae pene in mille{b} & quadringentos annos concurrunt, intestinis proeliis vacillantem, hocque & in Imperiales constitutiones extendentem, in unam reducere consonantiam: ut nihil neque contrarium neque idem neque simile in ea inveniatur, & ne geminae leges pro rebus singulis positae usquam appareat, namque hoc coelestis quidem providentiae peculiare fuit: humanae vero imbecillitati nullo modo possibile. Nos itaque more solito ad immortalitatis respeximus praesidium, & summo numine invocato, Deum auctorem & totius operis praesulem fieri optavimus: & omne studium Triboniano viro excelso, magistro officiorum, & exquaestore sacri nostri palatii & exconsule credi-
units.tr: Such is the providence of divine kindness towards us that it deigns always to sustain us with eternal bounties. For after the Parthian wars were laid to rest in eternal peace, and after the Vandal nation was driven out, and Carthage, or rather all Libya, was joined once more to the Roman empire, our vigilance has also restored the ancient laws, already weighed down by age, to a new beauty and to a moderate compendium. No one before our empire ever hoped for this, nor thought it could in any way be possible for human talent. For it was a wonder to bring back into one consistent whole the Roman legislation, which from the founding of the City down to our own times, a span of nearly fourteen hundred years, had wavered under internal conflicts, and which also extended to imperial constitutions, so that nothing contrary, nothing identical, nothing similar is found in it, and no twin laws laid down for the same cases appear anywhere. Indeed this was peculiar to heavenly providence; for human weakness it was in no way possible. Therefore, as is our custom, we turned to the protection of immortality, and, invoking the supreme divinity, we chose God as the author and overseer of the whole work. We entrusted the whole task to Tribonian, a man of high rank, master of offices, ex-quaestor of our sacred palace and ex-consul, and we imposed on him the entire charge of this sort of arrangement, so that he, together with other most illustrious and most prudent men, might fulfil our desire. Our majesty too, by searching and examining closely what these men were composing, corrected whatever was found doubtful and uncertain, raised it by this heavenly authority, and reduced it to a proper form.

units.la: {a} l. 2. C. de vet. iure. dimus,eique omne ministerium huiusce modi ordinationis impo-suimus,vt ipse vnà cū aliis {viris}[?] il-lustribus & prudentissimis viris noftrū desideriū adimpleret. nostra quoque maiestas semper inuesti-gando & perscrutando ea quæ ab his componebantur,quicquid dubiū & incertum inueniebatur,hoc nomine cœlesti erecta emendabat,& in competente formam redigebat.
units.tr: {a} l. 2. C. de vet. iure. We have entrusted it, and laid upon him the whole duty of this kind of arrangement, so that he, together with the other most illustrious and most prudent men, might carry out our desire.

units.la: 1 ¶Omnia igitur cōfecta sunt, Domino & Deo nostro Iesu Christo possibilitatem tam nobis quàm nostris in hoc satellitibus præstan-te.Et principales quidem constitutiones duodecim libris digestas, iam ante in Codice {*} nostro nomine præsulgentem contulimus.
units.tr: 1 Therefore all things have been completed, with our Lord and God Jesus Christ granting the possibility both to us and to our companions in this work. And indeed we previously brought together the principal constitutions, digested into twelve books, which already shone forth under our name in our Code.

units.la: Postea verò maximum opus adgredientes,ipsa vetustatis {♭}studiosissima opera iam pene confusa & dissoluta,eidem viro excelso permisimus tam colligere quàm certo moderamine tradere.
units.tr: Then, undertaking the greatest work, we entrusted to the same man of high rank the most diligent labour upon the ancient writings, now almost confused and dissolved by age, both to gather them and to hand them down under a sure guidance.

units.la: Sed cùm omnia percontabamur, à præfato viro excelso suggestum est duo pene millia librorū esse conscripta,& plus quàm {†}strecentiens decè millia versuum à veteribus effusa, quæ necesse esset omnia & legere & perscrutari, & ex his si quid optimū fuisset,eligere.
units.tr: But while we were examining everything, the aforesaid man of high rank reported to us that nearly two thousand books had been written, and more than three million verses had been poured out by the ancients, all of which it would be necessary both to read and to scrutinise, and from these to choose whatever was best.

units.la: Quod cœlesti fulgore & summæ trinitatis fauore confectū est secundum nostra mandata,quæ ab initio ad memorandum virum excelsum fecimus: & in quinquaginta libros omne quod vtilissimum erat,collectum est:& omnes ambiguitates decise.nullo sediuioso relicto. nomenque libris imposuimus Digestorum seu Pandectarum: qui omnes disputationes & decisiones in se habet legitimas,& quod vndique fuit collectum, hoc in sinus recepe-runt,in cētum quinquaginta pene millia {‡}versuum totum opus consummantes. & in septem partes eos digesimus non perperam,neque sine ratione:sed in numerorum naturam & artem respicientes, & consentaneam eis diuisionem partium conficientes.
units.tr: This was accomplished, by the heavenly splendour and the favour of the supreme Trinity, according to our commands, which from the beginning we gave to the aforesaid man of high rank. All that was most useful was collected into fifty books, and all ambiguities were resolved, with no dissension left behind. We named the books the Digests or Pandects. They contain all the lawful disputations and decisions, and they have taken into their bosom whatever was gathered from every quarter, completing the whole work in nearly one hundred and fifty thousand verses. We have divided them into seven parts, not carelessly nor without reason, but looking to the nature and art of numbers, and making a division of parts agreeing with them.

units.la: 2 ¶Igitur prima quidem pars totius contextus,quæ Græco vocabulo ἀρχὴ nuncupatur,in quatuor libros septem est. 3 ¶Secundus autem articulus {ε}septem libros habet,qui de iudiciis appellátur.
units.tr: 2 Therefore the first part of the whole contents, which is called by the Greek name archē, consists of seven books in four volumes. 3 The second division has seven books, and is called "on judgments."

units.la: 4 ¶In tertia verò congregatione omnia quæ de rebus minantur,contulimus,{s} octo libris eis deputatis.
units.tr: 4 In the third division we have brought together everything that concerns things which are threatened, assigning eight books to them.

units.la: 5 ¶Quartus autem locus,qui & totius compositionis quasi quoddam inuenitur vmbilicu, octo libros suscepit: in quibus omnia,quæ ad hypothecā {g} pertinent,reposita sunt, vt non pigno-raticia actione in
units.tr: 5 The fourth section, which is also found to be as it were the navel of the whole composition, has taken eight books. In these have been placed all things which pertain to hypothec,

units.la: {g} de qua.lib. 20. libris de rebus posita multùm distaret. Alio libro eodem inserto volumine, qui ædilicium edictum, & redhibitoriam actionem, & duplæ stipulatione, quæ de evictionibus propositá est, continet: quia hæc omnia titulis emptionum & venditionum consentanea sunt: & prædictæ actiones quasi pedisequæ illarum ab initio processerunt, in vetustioris quidem edicti ordinatione in loca devia & multo distantia deuagantes: per nostram autem prouidentiam his congregatæ: cùm oportuerat ea quæ de eodem pene loquutur, in confinio ponere. Alius itaque liber post duos primos nobis excogitatus est de vsuris, & traiecticiis pecuniis, & de instrumentis & testibus, & probationibus, necnon præsumptionibus. & memorati tres singulares libri iuxta compositionem de rebus positi sunt. Post hos si qua de spōsalibus vel nuptiis vel dotibus legibus dicta sunt, repositum est tribus librorum voluminibus ea concludentes. De tutelis autem & curationibus geminos libros conscripsimus. Et memoratam ordinationem octo librorum media totius operis reposuimus, omnia vndique tam veilissima quam pulcherrima iura continentem.
units.tr: {g} de qua lib. 20. libris de rebus posita, so that they would not differ greatly from the pignoratitious action. Another book, inserted into the same volume, contains the aedilician edict, the action for return of goods, and the double stipulation proposed concerning evictions. These are all consistent with the titles on purchase and sale, and the aforesaid actions, as it were attendants of those, had from the beginning proceeded, wandering in the arrangement of the older edict into remote and widely separated places. But through our providence they have been gathered together here, since it was fitting to place in a common boundary those things which speak of nearly the same matter. Another book, devised by us after the first two, deals with interest, sea-loans, documents, witnesses, proofs, and also presumptions. The three aforesaid single books have been placed according to the arrangement of "concerning things." After these, whatever has been said by the laws concerning betrothals, weddings or dowries has been placed, concluding them in three volumes of books. We have written two books on guardianships and curatorships. And we have placed the aforesaid arrangement of eight books in the middle of the whole work, containing laws on every side as useful as they are beautiful.

units.la: 6 ¶Quintus autem exoritur nobis Digestorum ariticulus, in quem de testamentis & codicillis tā priuatorum quàm militum, omne quidquid antiquis dictum inueniat quis depositum, qui de testamentis appellatur. De legatis autem & fideicommissis quin-que librorum numerus adgregatus est. Cùmque nihil tam peculiare fuerat, quàm ut[?] legatis quidē legis Falcidiæ narratio, fideicommissis autem Senatusconsulti Trebelliani singulis libris vtrique eorum applicatis tota pars quinta in nouem libros coadunata est. Solum autem Senatusconsultum Trebellianum ponendum esse existimauimus: captiosas etenim & ipsis veteribus odiosas Pegasiani Senatusconsulti ambages, & vtriusque Senatusconsulti ad se tam superuacuas quàm scrupulosas diuersitates re-spuentes, totum ius super his positum Trebelliano senatusconsulto adiudicauimus. Sed in his nihil de caducis à nobis memoratum est: ne causa, quæ in rebus non prosperè gestis, & tristis temporibus Roma-nis increbuit calamitatibus, bello coalescens ciuili, nostris maneat temporibus, quæ fauor cœlestis & pacis vigore firmauit, & super omnes gentes in bellicis victori periculis superposuit: ne luctuosum monu[?] mentum læta sæcula inumbrare concedatur.
units.tr: 6 Then the fifth part of the Digests arises for us, into which is gathered whatever ancient writers have set down concerning wills and codicils, both of private persons and of soldiers, which is called "on wills." Concerning legacies and trusts a number of five books has been added. And since nothing was more distinctive than the account of the Falcidian law for legacies, and of the Trebellian senatus-consultum for trusts, the whole fifth part has been combined into nine books, each of these being applied to its own. We have thought that only the Trebellian senatus-consultum should be set down, for we rejected the captious and even to the ancients hateful ambiguities of the Pegasian senatus-consultum, and the differences between the two senatus-consulta, as superfluous as they are scrupulous for those who use them, and we have adjudged all the law placed on these matters to the Trebellian senatus-consultum. But we have made no mention of caducary matters in these: lest the cause, which grew up in Roman times that were not prosperous and were sad with calamities, coalescing into civil war, should remain in our times, which heavenly favour and the strength of peace have confirmed, and which, in the victories over dangers of war, has set us above all nations. Nor should a mournful monument be allowed to overshadow happy ages.

units.la: 7 ¶ Sexta deinde pars Digestorum exoritur, in quibus omnes bonorum possessiones positæ sunt, quæ ad ingenuos, quæ ad libertinos respiciunt: vt & ius omne, quod de gradibus & adfinitatibus descendit, legitimæque hereditates. & omnis ab intestato successio, & Tertullianum, & Orphitianum Senatusconsultum, ex quibus mater & filij nuice sibi hæredes exiftút, in geminos {a}libros contulimus, bonorum possessionem. Multitudine in compendiosum & manifestissimum ordinem concludentes. Post hæc ea quæ de operis novi nuntiationibus, damnique infecti, & pro ædificiis dirutis, & eorum insidiis, & quæ de aqua pluuia arcenda veteribus auctoribus placita sunt: nec nō de publicanis, & donationibus tam inter vivos quàm mortis causa conficiendis cauta legibus inuenimus, in librum singularem deduximus. De manumisionibus autem & de liberali causa, alius {c}liber respondit: quemadmodum & de adquisitione tam dominij quàm possessionis, & titulis qui eam inducunt, multæ & variæ lectiones vni {d}sunt inserte volumini, alio {e}libro deputato his qui iudicati, vel in iure confesi sunt. & de bonorum detensionibus & venditionibus, & vt nequid in fraudem creditorum fiat. Postque hæc omnia interdicta glomerata {f}sunt: & deinceps exceptiones, & de temporum pro lixitatibus: & de obligationibus & actionibus liber {g}iterum singularis extenditur: vt præfata sexta pars totius Digestorum voluminis octo libris definiatur.
units.tr: 7 Then the sixth part of the Digests arises, in which all the possessions of goods are set out, those relating to freeborn persons and those relating to freedmen, so that all law which descends from degrees and affinities, legitimate inheritances, and every succession on intestacy, and the Tertullian and Orphitian senatus-consulta, by which mother and children become heirs to one another in turn, have been brought together in two books on possession of goods, gathered into a brief and very clear order. After these, we have drawn into a single book those matters concerning notices of new works, damage not yet done, and for buildings that have collapsed, and their snares, and what the ancient authors have decided concerning keeping off rainwater; and likewise concerning public matters, and concerning gifts, both between living persons and to be made in view of death, which we have found provided for by the laws. Another book has been devoted to manumissions and to free status; likewise concerning acquisition both of ownership and of possession, and the titles which induce them, many and varied readings have been inserted into one volume, and another book has been assigned to those who have been adjudged or have confessed in court, and to the seizure and sale of goods, and to ensuring that nothing is done to defraud creditors. After all these, the interdicts have been gathered together, and then the exceptions, and the time-limits of prescriptions; and once more a single book on obligations and actions is extended, so that the aforesaid sixth part of the whole volume of the Digests is completed in eight books.

units.la: 8 ¶ Septimus autem & nouissimus articulus Digestorum sex libris formatus est quos de stipulationibus seu verborum obligationibus, & fideiussoribus & mandatoribus, nec non nouationibus, & solutionibus, & acceptilationibus, & de prætoriis stipulationibus, omne quod ius inuenitur {h}gemino volumine inscriptum est, quod in libris antiquis nec numerari posibile fuit. Et post hoc duo {i}terribiles libri positi sunt pro deliclis priuatis, & extraordinariis necnō publicis criminibus, qui omnem continent seueritatem poenarum quæ arrocitatem. Quibus permixta sunt & ea quæ de audacibus hominibus cauta sunt, qui se celare conantur, & contumaces existunt: & de poenis quæ condemnatis infliguntur, vel concedunt: necnon de eorum iubstantiis. Liber autem {k}singularis pro appellationibus nobis excogitatus: est contra sententias tam civiles quàm criminales causas finiente. Cetera autem omnia quæ ad municipales, vel de decurionibus, & muneribus, vel publicis operibus, vel nundinis, & pollicitationibus & diversis cognitionibus, & censibus, vel significatione verborum veteribus innuenta sunt, quæque regulariter definita, in sese recepit {b} quinquagesimus totius summationis, pfectus.[?] 9 Quæ omnia cófecta sunt per e virum excelsum, necnon prudentissimum magi-strum, ex quaestore & ex consule Tribonianum, qui sin-gulariter eloquentiæ, & legitimæ scientiæ artibus deco-ratus, & in ipsis rerum experimentis emicuit, nihilque maius nec carius nostris unquam iussionibus duxit: necnon per alios viros magnificos & studio-sissimos perfecta sunt, id est Constantinum virum illustrem, Comitem sacrarum largitionum, & magi-strū scrinii libellorum sacrarumque cognitionum, qui semper nobis ex bona opinione & gloria sese commendavit: necnò Theophilum virum illustrem, magistrum iuris, isque peritum in hac splendidissima ci-vitate {d}laudabiliter optimam legum gubernationem extendentem: & Dorothæum virum, illustrem & facundissimum quaestorium, quem in Berutiensium splendidissima civitate leges discipulis {e}tradentem propter eius optimam opinionem & gloriam ad nos deduximus, participemque huius operis fecimus, sed & Anatolium virum illustrem magistrum, qui & ipse apud Berutienses iuris interpres constitutus ad hoc opus allectus est, vir ab antiqua stirpe legitima procedens, cum & pater eius Leontius & avus Eudoxius qui post Patricium inclytæ recordationis quaestorium & antecessorem, & Leontium virum gloriosissimum praefectorem, consularem, atque Patricium filium eius, optimam sui memoriam in legibus reliquerunt, necnon Cratinum virum illustrem, & comitem sacrarum largitionum, & optimum antecessorem huius almæ urbis constitutum, qui omnes ad praedictum opus electi sunt una cum Stephano Men-na, Profdocio, Eutolmio, Timotheo, Leonide, Leontio, Platone, Iacobo, Constantino, Iohanne, viris prudentissimis, qui patroni quidem sunt causarum apud maximam sedem praefecturæ quæ Orientalibus praetoriis praesidet. Omne autem suæ virtutis testimonium undique accipientes, & à nobis ad tanti operis consummationem electi sunt: & cum omnes in unum convenerunt gubernatione Triboniani viri excelsi, ut tantum opus nobis auctoribus posint có-ficere, Deo propitio in præsidistos[?] quinquaginta li-bros opus consummatum est.
units.tr: 8 The seventh and last part of the Digest is formed of six books, which deal with stipulations or verbal obligations, with sureties and mandataries, and likewise with novations, payments, acceptilations, and praetorian stipulations. All the law that is to be found is inscribed in a twofold volume, which could not be counted in the old books. After this, two dreadful books are set out for private delicts and for extraordinary and public crimes, which contain all the severity of the penalties that atrocity deserves. Mixed with these are the provisions concerning bold men who try to hide themselves and are contumacious, and concerning the penalties that are inflicted on or remitted to the condemned, and likewise concerning their property. A single book on appeals, devised by us, stands against the sentences that decide both civil and criminal cases. All the other matters, namely those concerning the municipalities, or decurions and offices, or public works, or markets, or promises, and various kinds of cognizance, and the census, or the meaning of words, found in the ancients, which are regularly defined, the fiftieth book, complete, takes into itself, of the whole summation. 9 All these things were completed by the most excellent man and most prudent master, Tribonian, formerly quaestor and consul, who, adorned singularly with the arts of eloquence and of lawful learning, and who shone in the actual experience of affairs, never held anything greater or dearer than our commands. They were also completed by other magnificent and most diligent men, namely Constantinus, illustrious man, count of the sacred largesses and master of the bureau of petitions and of sacred cognizances, who has always commended himself to us by good opinion and glory; and Theophilus, illustrious man, master of law, and skilled in this most splendid city, who expounds the best government of the laws with praise; and Dorotheus, illustrious and most eloquent quaestor, who, teaching the laws to students in the most splendid city of the Berytians, we brought to us on account of his excellent reputation and glory, and made a participant in this work. And also Anatolius, illustrious master, who himself was constituted an interpreter of law at Berytus and was chosen for this work, a man proceeding from an ancient and lawful stock, since his father Leontius and his grandfather Eudoxius, who after Patricius of illustrious memory, quaestor and teacher, and Leontius, most glorious prefect, consular, and Patricius his son, left an excellent memory of themselves in the laws. Also Cratinus, illustrious man and count of the sacred largesses, and an excellent teacher of this nourishing city. All of these were chosen for the aforesaid work, together with Stephanus Menna, Proclus, Eutolmius, Timotheus, Leonides, Leontius, Plato, Jacob, Constantinus, and John, most prudent men, who are indeed advocates of causes before the greatest seat of the prefecture, which presides over the Eastern praetorian prefecture. Receiving everywhere the testimony of their virtue, they were chosen by us for the completion of so great a work; and when all came together into one under the direction of Tribonian, the most excellent man, so that they might be able to complete so great a work under our authority, with God favouring, the work was finished in fifty books.

units.la: 10 ¶ Tanta autem à nebis antiquitati habita est reuerentia, ut a nomina prudentium taciturnitati{b} tradere nullo patiamur modo: sed vnusquisque eorum qui auctor legis fuit, nostris Digestis inscriptus est: hoc tantummodo à nobis effecto, ut si quid in legibus eorum vel superua-cuum vel perfectum vel minus idoneum uisum est: vel adiectionem, vel deminutionem necessariam ac-cipiat, & restissinus tradatur regulis, & in multis si-militibus vel contrariis quod restius habere appare-bat, hoc pro aliis omnibus positum est, unaque o-mnibus auctoritate indulta, ut quidquid ibi scriptū est, hoc nostrum appareat, & ex nostra voluntate co-positum: nemine audente comparare ea quæ anti-quitas habebat, & quæ nostra auctoritas introduxit: quia multa & maxima sunt, quæ propter utilitatem rerum transformata sunt, adeò ut etsi principalis co-stitutio fuerat in veteribus libris relata, neque ei pe-percimus: sed & hoc corrigendum esse putauimus, & in melius restaurandum: nominibus etenim veteri-bus relistis, quidquid legum veritati decorü & ne-cessarium fuerat, hoc nostris ementationibus serua-uimus. & propter hanc causam & si quid inter eos dubitabatur, hoc jam in tutissimam peruenit quic-tem, nullo titubáte relisto.
units.tr: 10 Such reverence has been shown by us for antiquity that we permit the names of the jurists in no way to be handed over to silence; rather, each one of those who was the author of a law has been inscribed in our Digest. This only has been done by us: if anything in their laws seemed superfluous, or imperfect, or less suitable, it should receive a necessary addition or reduction, and be handed down in the most correct form; and where in many similar or contrary passages the more correct opinion appeared, this was set forth in place of all the others, and one authority has been granted to all, so that whatever is written there appears to be ours and composed by our will. No one is to dare to compare what antiquity had with what our authority has introduced, because there are many and very great changes made on account of the usefulness of matters, so that, even if a principal constitution had been related in the old books, we have not spared it; rather we have thought that this too should be corrected and restored for the better. For, with the old names retained, whatever was seemly and necessary for the truth of the laws, this we have preserved in our emendations. And for this reason, if anything was doubted among them, this has now come to the most secure quiet, with no hesitation left.

units.la: 11 ¶Sed cùm prospexi-mus quod ad portandam tantæ sapientiæ molem nō sunt idonei homines rudes, & qui in primis legum vestibulis stantes intrare ad arcana eorum properát: & aliam{◆} mediocrem emendationem præparandam esse censuimus, ut sub ea colorati, & quasi primitiis omnium imbuti, possint ad penetralia eorum intra-re, & formam legum pulcherrimam non conniuen-tibus oculis accipere. Et ideo Triboniano viro ex-celso, qui ad totius operis gubernationem electus est, necnon Theophilo & Dorotheo viris illustribus & facundissimis antecessoribus accersitis, mandaui-mus quatenus libris quos veteres cōposuerunt, qui prima legum argumenta continebant, & Institutio-nes vocabantur, separatim colleCtis, quidquid ex his vtile & aptissimum & undique sit elimatum, & re-bus quæ in præsenti æuo in usu vertuntur, consenta-neum inuenitur, hoc & capere studeant, & quatuor libris reponere, & totius eruditionis prima funda-menta atque elementa ponere: quibus juvenes suf-
units.tr: 11 But when we perceived that rude men, who stand in the outer porches of the laws and hasten to enter its secrets, are not fit to bear so great a mass of wisdom, we judged that another modest emendation had to be prepared, so that, coloured by it and, as it were, first imbued with the rudiments of everything, they might be able to enter its inner sanctuaries and receive the most beautiful form of the laws without closed eyes. Therefore we summoned Tribonian, the most excellent man chosen to direct the whole work, and the distinguished and eloquent teachers Theophilus and Dorotheus, and we commanded them that from the books which the ancients composed, which contained the first elements of law and were called Institutes, they should separately gather whatever is useful, most apt, and refined from all sides, and whatever is found consonant with matters now in use, and that they should take care to receive these things, put them into four books, and lay down the first foundations and elements of all learning, by which young men, once instructed, may be able to sustain the weightier and more perfect enactments of the laws.

units.la: ◆ Instituiio-num defini-tio. sulti[?] posint grauiora & perfectiora legum scita su-stetare[?]. Admonuimus autem eos, ut memores etiam nostrarum fiant Constitutionum, quas pro emenda-tione iuris promulgauimus. & in confectione Institutionum etiam eadem emendatione ponere non morentur: ut sit manifestum & quid antea vacilla-bat, & quid postea in stabilitatem redactu est. Quod opus ab his perfectum, ut nobis oblatum & relectum est, & prono suscepimus animo & nostris sensibus nō indignum esse iudicauimus, & praedictos libros Constitutionum vicem habere usimus: quod & in oratione nostra, quam eisdem libris praeposuimus, aperius declaratur.
units.tr: Definition of the Institutes. We have also admonished them to become mindful of our Constitutions, which we promulgated for the emendation of the law, and not to delay in applying the same emendation in the composition of the Institutes, so that it may be plain both what was previously wavering and what has since been brought to stability. This work, perfected by them, was offered to us and read through; we received it with a ready mind, judged it not unworthy of our judgment, and decided that the aforesaid books should have the force of Constitutions. This is declared more openly in our address, which we have placed before the same books.

units.la: 12 ¶ Omni igitur Romani iuris dispositione composita, & in tribus voluminibus, id est Institutionum, & Digestorum seu Pandectarum, necnon Constitutionum, perfecta, & {4} in tribus annis consummata, quae ut primum separari coepit, neque in totum decennium compleri sperabatur: omnipotenti Deo & hanc operam ad hominum sustentatione piis obtulimus animis, ut vbere[?]que gratias maximae Deitati reddidimus, quae nobis praestitit ut bel[?]la feliciter agere, & honesta pace perpotiri, & non tantum nostro, sed etiam omni aeuo[?] tam instanti quam posteriori leges optimas ponere.
units.tr: 12 Therefore, when the whole arrangement of Roman law had been composed and completed in three volumes, namely the Institutes, the Digests or Pandects, and the Constitutions, and was finished in three years, although when it was first begun it was not hoped that it would be completed even in a whole decade, we with pious minds offered this labour to almighty God for the support of men. We gave abundant thanks to the greatest Deity, who granted us to conduct wars successfully, to enjoy an honourable peace, and to establish the best laws not only for our own time but for every age, both present and future.

units.la: 13 ¶ Omnibus itaque hominibus eandem Sanctione manifestam facere, necessarium esse perspeximus: ut sit eis cognitum, quanta confusione & infinitate absoluti, in quam moderationem & legitimam veritatem peruenerunt: legesque in posterum habeant tam directas quam compendio sas, omnibusque in promptu positas, & ad possidendi libros earum facilitatem idoneas, ut non mole diuitiarum expesa possint homines superuacuae legum multitudinis adipiscentur lumina,{b} sed vilissima pecunia facilis eorum comparatio pateat tam ditioribus quam tenuioribus, minimo pretio magna prudentia reparanda.
units.tr: 13 Therefore we have judged it necessary to make this sanction plain to all men, so that it may be known out of what confusion and infinite disorder they have come to such moderation and lawful truth. And so that in future they may have laws both as direct as they are brief, set ready before all, and suitable for the easy possession of the books, so that men need not be deprived of the light of law by the great expense of wealth, through the superfluous multitude of laws, but that its easy acquisition, at the lowest price, may be open to the richer and the poorer alike, and great wisdom be gained for a small sum.

units.la: 14 ¶ Si quid autem in tanta legum copositione quae ab im-menso librorum numero collecta est, simile forsitan raro inueniatur, nemo hoc vituperandum existimet: sed primum quidem imbecillitati humanae, quae naturaliter inest, hoc inscribat: quia * omnium habere memoriam, & penitus in nullo peccare, diuinitatis magis quàm mortalitatis est: quod & a maioribus dictum est: deinde sciat quod similitudo in quibusdam & his breuissimis adsumpta non inutilis est: & nec citra nostrum propositum hoc subsequutum est. Aut enim ita lex necessaria erat,vt diuersis titulis propter rerum co-gnationem applicari eam oporteat: aut cum fuerat {a}aliis [?]versis permixta,impossibile erat eam per partes detrahi ne totum confundatur & in his partibus in quibus perfectissimæ vitiones⁴ expositæ veterum fuerât,quod particulatim in eas fuerat sparsum,hoc diuidere ac separare, penitus erat inciuile:ne tam sensus quàm aures legentium ex hoc perturbentur.
units.tr: 14 If, however, in so great a composition of laws, which has been gathered from an immense number of books, something similar should perhaps be found rarely, let no one think it deserves blame.
