Rather, let him first ascribe this to human weakness, which is naturally present in us, because to have the memory of everything and to commit no fault at all belongs more to divinity than to mortality, as the ancients also said. Then let him know that a similitude taken up in some cases, and these very brief, is not without use, and that this has not followed without our purpose. For either the law was so necessary that it had to be applied under diverse titles on account of the kinship of matters, or, when it had been mixed with other things, it was impossible to draw it out part by part without confusing the whole; and in those parts where the most perfect definitions of the ancients had been set forth, to divide and separate what had been scattered through them piecemeal would have been wholly inept, lest both the understanding and the ears of readers be thrown into confusion by it.

units.la: Similique modo si quid principalibus constitutionibus cautum est,hoc in Digestorum volumine poni nullo concessimus modo:quasi Costitutionum reci-tatione sufficiente: nisi & hoc raro ex hisdem causis quibus similitudo adsumpta est.
units.tr: Likewise, if anything has been provided in the principal constitutions, we have decided that it should not be placed in the volume of the Digest in any way, as though the recitation of the Constitutions were enough, unless this happens rarely, for the same reasons for which the similarity was adopted.

units.la: 15 ¶Contrarium {b}autem aliquid in hoc codice positu nullu {c}sibi locū vindicabit, nec inuenitur. si quis subtili animo diuersitatis rationes excutiet,sed est aliquid nouum inuentum,{d}vel occulte positum, quod dissonantiæ querelam dissoluit, & aliam naturam inducit dis-cordiæ fines effugientem.
units.tr: 15 On the contrary, if anything contrary is placed in this code, it will claim no place for itself, nor is it found, if anyone with a subtle mind examines the grounds of difference. Rather, something new is discovered, or placed in hiding, which dissolves the complaint of inconsistency and introduces another nature that escapes the limits of discord.

units.la: 16 ¶Sed & si quid forsi-tan {e}præteremissum est,quod in tantis millibus quasi in profundo positum latitabat,& cum idoneum fue-rat poni,obscuritate inuolutum necessario dereliĉtū est:quis hoc adprehendere recto animo possit?primo quidem propter ingenij mortalis exiguitatem: de-inde proẽpter ipsius rei vitium, quod multis inutili-bus permixtum nullam sui ad eruendum præbuit copiam: dein quod multo vtilius est pauca idonea effugere,quàm multis inutilibus homines prægrauare.
units.tr: 16 But also, if something has perhaps been omitted, which lay hidden as if in the depths among so many thousands, and which was fit to be placed but has necessarily been left aside, wrapped in obscurity, who could grasp it with an upright mind? First, indeed, on account of the slenderness of mortal intellect; then on account of the very defect of the matter, which, mixed with many useless things, offered no means of drawing it out; and then because it is much more useful to avoid a few unsuitable things than to burden people with many useless ones.

units.la: 7. ¶Mirabile autem aliquid ex his libris emer-sit,quod multitudo antiqua præsente breuitate pau-cior inuenitur.homines enim qui antea lites age-bant,licet multæ leges fuerât positæ,tamen ex pau-ci lites perfecebant, vel propter inopiam librorum quos comparare eis impossibile erat, vel propter i-psam inscientiâ.& {f}volùtate iudicum magis quàm legitima auctoritate lites dirimebantur.In præsenti autem consummatione nostrorum Digestorum e tan-tis leges collectæ sunt voluminibus, quorum & no-mina antiquiores homines non dicimus nesciebant, sed nec vnquam audiebant,quæ omnia collecta sunt substantia amplissima congregata: vt egena quidem antiqua multitudo inueniatur, opulétifsima autem breuitas nostra efficiatur. Antiquæ autem sapientiæ librorum copiam maximè Tribonianus vir excellen-tissimus præbuit, in quibus multi fucrant & ipsis cruruditissimis hominibus incogniti:quibus omnibus perledtis, quidquid ex his pulcherrimum erat, hoc semotum in optimam nostram compositionem pertinet. Sed huius operis cōditores non solum ea volumina perlegerunt,ex quibus leges positæ sunt: sed etiam alia multa,quæ,nihil vel vtile vel nouum eis inueniēres, quod exceptum nostris Digestis applica ret,optimo animo respuerunt.
units.tr: 7 Something remarkable has emerged from these books: the ancient multitude, though brevity is now present, is found to be smaller. For men who formerly conducted lawsuits, although many laws had been laid down, nonetheless brought few suits to conclusion, either because of the scarcity of books, which it was impossible for them to acquire, or because of their own ignorance; and disputes were settled by the will of judges rather than by legitimate authority. But in the present completion of our Digests, laws have been gathered from so many volumes, whose names the men of old did not know, nor ever even heard, all of which have been collected into a very ample substance. So the ancient multitude is found to be needy, while our brevity is made very rich. Tribonian, a most excellent man, chiefly supplied the abundance of books of ancient wisdom, many of which were unknown even to the most learned men. Having read through all of them, whatever was most beautiful in them has been set apart and belongs to our excellent compilation. But the compilers of this work have not only read through those volumes from which the laws were drawn, but also many others, in which they found nothing useful or new that could be applied to our Digests, and these they rightly rejected with the best intention.

units.la: 18 ¶Sed quia diuinæ quidem res perfectissimæ sunt, humani vero iu-ris conditio semper in infinitū decurrit, & nihil est in ea quod stare perpetuò possit: multas etenim formas edere natura nouas deproperat,non desperamus quædam postea emergi negotia, quæ adhuc legum laqueis non sunt innouata. si quid igitur tale contigerit, augustum imploretur remedium: quia ideo Imperialem fortunam rebus humanis Deus præposuit, vt possit omnia quæ nouiter contingunt, & emendare,& componere, & modis & regulis compententibus tradere.&hoc non primum à nobis dictum est,sed ab antiqua descedit prosapia:cūm & ipse Iustinianus legum & edicti perpetui subtilissimus condi tor,in suis libris hoc renulit: vt si quid imperfectum inueniatur,ab Imperiali sanctione hoc repleatur, & non ipse solus,sed & Diuus Hadrianus in compositione edicti, & senatusconsulto quod eam secutum est,hoc apertissimè definiuit, vt si quid in edicto positum non inuenitur, hoc ad eius regulas eiusque coniecturas & imitationes possit noua instruere auctoritas.
units.tr: 18 But since divine things are indeed most perfect, while the condition of human law always runs on into infinity, and there is nothing in it that can stand forever (for nature hastens to produce many new forms), we do not despair that some matters may afterwards emerge which have not yet been brought within the snares of the laws. If anything of this kind should happen, let the august remedy be sought. For God has set the imperial fortune over human affairs, so that it may be able both to amend and arrange whatever newly arises, and to hand it down by fitting methods and rules. This is not first said by us, but descends from ancient lineage. For Justinian himself, the most subtle author of the laws and of the Perpetual Edict, declared this in his books: that if anything is found imperfect, it should be filled up by imperial sanction. And not he alone, but also the Deified Hadrian, in the composition of the Edict and in the senatus consultum that followed it, most clearly defined this: that if anything is not found in the Edict, the new authority may frame it by its rules, its conjectures and its imitations.

units.la: 19 ¶Hæc igitur omnia scientes patres conscripti,& omnes orbis terrarū homines,gratias quidem amplissimas agite summæ Diuinitati, quæ vetustis temporibus tam saluberrimum opus seruauit. quo enim antiquitas digna diuino non est visa iudicio, hoc vestris temporibus indultum est. Hasce itaque leges & adorare & obseruare omnibus anti qnioribus quiescentibus. nemóque vestrum audeat vel comparare eas prioribus, vel si quid dissonans in vtroque est,requirere: quia omne quod hic positum est , hoc vnicum & solum obseruari censemus. Nec in iudicio,nec in alio certamine , vbi leges necessariæ sunt,ex altis libris,nisi ab iisdem Institutionibus, nostrisque Digestis, & Constitutionibus à nobis compositis vel promulgatis,aliquid vel recitare vel ostendere conetur:nisi temerator velit falsitatis crimine subiectus , vnicum iudice qui eorum audientiam patiatur, pœnis granissimis laborare.
units.tr: 19 Therefore, knowing all these things, conscript fathers and all the men of the world, give the greatest thanks to the supreme Divinity, which in ancient times preserved so salutary a work. For what antiquity did not seem worthy of divine judgment has been granted to your times. Let all men of former times, now at rest, adore and observe these laws. Let none of you dare either to compare them with earlier ones, or, if anything in either is discordant, to seek it out. For we decree that everything set down here is to be observed as the one and only law. Let no one attempt, in a court or in any other contest where laws are needed, to recite or show anything from other books, except from these Institutes, our Digests, and the Constitutions composed or promulgated by us. The only exception is a reckless person who is willing to be subject to the charge of falsehood, and to suffer the most grievous penalties before the single judge who permits their hearing.

units.la: 22 ¶ Ne autem incognitum vobis fiat,ex {a}quibus veterum libris hæc collummatio ordinata est, iusti-nius & hoc in primordiis Digestorum nostrorum in scribi: vt manifestissimum fit,ex quibus legislatoribus, quibusque libris eorum, & quot milibus hoc iusticiæ Romanæ templum ædificatum est. Legislatores autem vel commentatores eos elegimus, qui digni tanto opere erant, & quos & anteriores piissimi principes admittere nō sunt indignati, omnibus vno dignitatis apice impertito,nec sibi cuidam aliquam {b}prærogatiuam vindicante.cùm enim cōstitutionum vicem & has leges obtinere censuimus,quasi ex nobis promulgatas:quid amplius,aut minus in quibusdam esse intelligatur,cùm vna dignitas, vna potestas omnibus est indulta?
units.tr: 22 So that it may not be unknown to you from which books of the ancients this collection has been ordered, Justinian has also ordered this to be written at the beginning of our Digests, so that it may be most manifest from which legislators, and from which of their books, and from how many thousands, this temple of Roman justice has been built. We have chosen as legislators or commentators those who were worthy of so great a work, and whom the earlier most pious princes did not disdain to admit, all being granted one summit of dignity, and none claiming any prerogative for himself. For since we have decided that these laws should hold the place of constitutions, as though promulgated by us, what more or less could be understood in some of them, since one dignity and one power has been granted to all?

units.la: 21 ¶ Hoc autē, quod & ab initio nobis visum est, cùm hoc opus fieri Deo adnuente mandabamus, tempestiuum nobis videtur & in præsenti sancire,vt nemo neque eorum qui in præsenti iuris peritiam habent,neque(qui)postea fiant,audeat commentarios {c}hisdē legibus adnectere: nisi tantum si velit eas in Græcam vocem,transformare sub eodem ordine,eáque consequentia,sub qua & voce Romana positæ sunt : hoc quod Græci {d}[illegible, ~4 letters] dicũt.& si qui forsitan per titulorum subtilitatem adnotare maluerint, & ea quæ paratitla nuncupantur,componere,alias autem legum interpretationes,immo magis peruersiones, eos iactare non concedimus:ne verbositas eorum aliquid legibus nostris adferat ex confusione dedecus.quod & in antiquis editi perpetui commentatoribus factum est, qui opus moderatè confectum huc atque illuc in diuersas sententias producentes, [contrahentes,] in infinitum detraxerunt, vt pene omnis Romana sanctio effet confusa. Quos si passi non sumus, quemadmodum posteritatis admittatur vana discordia? Siquid autem tale facere ausi fuerint, ipsi quidem falsitatis rei constituantur,volumina autem eorum omnimodo {e}corrumpentur,Si quid vero,vt supra dictum est, ambiguum fuerit visum: hoc ad Imperiale culmē per iudices referatur,&ex auctoritate Augusta manifestetur,cuius foli {g}concessum est leges & condere & interpretari.
units.tr: 21 But this, which also seemed right to us from the beginning, when we ordered this work to be done with God's assent, seems timely to us to enact now as well: that no one, neither of those who now have skill in law nor of those who shall arise afterwards, shall dare to attach commentaries to these same laws. The only exception is one who wishes to turn them into the Greek language under the same order and sequence in which they are set down in Latin, which the Greeks call [illegible in the scan]. And if anyone should prefer to annotate them by the subtlety of titles and to compose what are called paratitla, we do not permit them to boast of other interpretations of the laws, or rather perversions, lest their verbosity bring some disgrace to our laws through confusion. This also happened with the commentators on the old Perpetual Edict, who drew the moderately composed work this way and that into diverse opinions, [contracting it,] and dragged it out without end, so that almost all Roman sanction was confused. If we do not allow such things, how could vain discord be admitted to posterity? But if anyone has dared to do anything of this kind, let him himself be held guilty of falsehood, and let his volumes be destroyed in every way. If, however, as said above, anything has seemed ambiguous, let it be referred by the judges to the imperial summit and be made clear by Augustan authority, to which alone it is granted both to make and to interpret laws.

units.la: 22 ¶ Eandem autē poenam falsitatis constituimus & aduersus eos qui in posterum leges nostras per siglorum {h}obscuritates ausi fuerint conscribere.omnia enim,id est & nomina prudentium, & titulos,& librorum numeros,per conse-
units.tr: 22 We impose the same penalty of falsehood on those who in future shall dare to write out our laws with the obscurities of sigla. For all things, that is the names of the jurists, the titles, and the numbers of the books, through conse-

units.la: a Quibus ex libris Pandectarum exceptæ sunt.
units.tr: a From which books of the Pandects these were excerpted.
b Add the Constitution to Tribonian, §3.
c On commentaries on the laws, §21. See the next constitution.

units.la: d Iuxta pedes perinde ac si diceret, ea lege, vt iisdem vestigiis insistant & pedentim subsequantur hoc opus. vide Alciat. II. Parerg. 6.
units.tr: d Next to the feet, just as if he were saying: on the condition that they keep to the same footsteps and gradually follow this work. See Alciatus, Parerga II, 6.
e Add l.4 §2 ff. fam. ercisc.

units.la: f v. quæ notauimus ad l.1. C. de legibus.
units.tr: f See what we noted on l.1 C. de legibus.

units.la: g atque Senatus iusfacere potest. l.9.ff. de legib.
units.tr: g The Senate too can do what is just. l.9 ff. de legibus.

units.la: h leges, siglis non esse conscribendas. cosequentias literarum volumus,nō per {a}sigla manifestari: ita vt qui talem librum sibi parauerit, in quo sigla posita sunt in qualemcunque locum libri vel voluminis,sciat inutilis se esse codicis dominum:neque enim licentiam aperimus ex tali codice in iudicium aliquid recitare,qui in quacumque sua parte siglorum habet malitias. Ipse autem librarius qui eas inscribere ausus fuerit,non solum criminali {b}poena,secundum quod dictum est,plecetur:sed etiam libri aestimatione in duplum domino reddat, si & ipse dominus ignorans talem librum vel comparauerit, vel confici curauerit. quod & antea à nobis disposition est & in Latina constitutione & in Græca quá ad legũ profeffores dimisimus.
units.tr: h Laws should not be written with sigla. We wish the sequence of letters not to be made clear by sigla, so that whoever has acquired such a book, in which sigla are placed in any part of the book or volume, may know that he is the owner of a useless codex. For we do not open licence to recite anything in court from such a codex, which contains malicious sigla in any part of it. The scribe himself who dared to write them shall be punished not only with the criminal penalty, as has been said, but shall also repay the owner double the value of the book, if the owner, being ignorant, either bought such a book or had it made. This too was previously set down by us, both in the Latin constitution and in the Greek one which we sent to the professors of law.

units.la: ¶Leges autem nostras, quæ in his codicibus, id est Institutionum seu Elementorum,& Digestorum vel Pandectarum postimus, suum obtinere robur ex tertio nostro felicifimo sancimus consulatu præsentis duodecimæ indictionis,tertio calendas Ianuarias, in omne suum valituras, & vnà cum nostris constitutionibus pollentes, & suum vigorem in iudiciis ostendetes in omnibus causis, siue {c}quæ postea emerserint, siue quæ in iudiciis adhuc pendent,nec eas iudicialis vel amicalis forma cópefcuit:* quæ enim iam vel iudiciali sententia finita sunt, vel amicali pacto sopita,hæc {d}resuscitari nullo volumus modo. Bene autem properauimus in tertium nostrum consulatum & has leges edere:quia maximi Dei & Domini nostri Iesu Christi auxilium felicifimum eum nostræ reipublicæ donauit: cum in hunc & bella Parthica abolita sunt, & quieti perpetuæ tradita, & tertia pars mundi nobis adcreuit. Post Europam enim, & Asia & tota Libya nostro imperio adiunóta est,& tato opere legum caput impositum est: omnia œclestia dona nostro tertio consulatu indulta.
units.tr: Moreover, we decree that these laws of ours, which we have set down in these codes, namely the Institutes or Elements, and the Digest or Pandects, shall obtain their force from our third most fortunate consulship, in the present twelfth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of January, and shall remain in force for all time, and shall have effect together with our other constitutions, showing their power in judgments in all causes, whether those that arise hereafter or those that are still pending in the courts. Neither judicial nor amicable settlement shall restrain them: for matters already ended either by a judicial sentence or put to rest by an amicable agreement, we wish that they be revived in no way. We have hastened to publish these laws in our third consulship, because the greatest help of God and our Lord Jesus Christ has granted this most fortunate outcome to our commonwealth: in this consulship both the Parthian wars have been abolished and handed over to lasting peace, and a third part of the world has been added to us. For after Europe, Asia and all of Libya have been joined to our empire, and the crown of the laws has been placed upon so great a work; all heavenly gifts have been bestowed in our third consulship.

units.la: 24 ¶Omnes itaque iudices nostri pro sua iurifdi-ctione easdem leges suspiciat, & tam in suis iudiciis quàm in hac regia vrbe habeat, & proponat, & præ-cipuè vir excelsus huius almæ vrbis præsectus. curæ autem erit tribus excelsis præsectis prætoriis, tam Orientalibus quàm Illyricis necnon Lybicis, per suas auctoritates omnibus qui suæ iurisdictioni sup-positi sunt eas manifestare.Data septimodecimo Kalendis Ianuariis, Iustiniano domino nostro ter con-sule. 533.
units.tr: 24 Therefore let all our judges, each within his own jurisdiction, respect these same laws, and let them have and publish them both in their own courts and in this royal city, and especially the most exalted prefect of this nourishing city. It will be the care of the three most exalted praetorian prefects, the Eastern, the Illyrian, and likewise the Libyan, to make them known, through their own authority, to all who are subject to their jurisdiction. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of our lord Justinian for the third time. 533.
HAPPILY.

units.la: DE CONFIRMATIONE Digestorum ad magnum Senatum.
units.tr: ON THE CONFIRMATION OF THE DIGESTS, TO THE GREAT SENATE.

units.la: IN NOMINE DOMINI ET Dei nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: IN THE NAME OF THE LORD AND OF OUR GOD JESUS CHRIST.

units.la: Imperator Caesar Flav. IUSTINIANUS Alamanicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pius, felix, inclytus, victor, triumphator, semper colendus Augustus ad magnum Senatum & populum & omnes orbis nostri civitates.
units.tr: Imperator Caesar Flavius IUSTINIANUS, Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pious, fortunate, renowned, victor, triumphator, ever to be revered Augustus, to the great Senate and people and all the cities of our world.

units.la: D[?]EDIT nobis Deus post pacem cum b Persis initam, post Vandalica trophaea & totam Libyae adquisitionem, postque nominatissimam Karthaginem nostro iterum Imperio c sociatam, ut veterum legum renouationis opus ad optatum finem perduceremus. quod nemo principum ante nostrum Imperium aut in mentem induci posse, aut humano ingenio possibile esse existimavit. Erat enim mirabile, omnem Romanam sanctionem a condita vetere Roma usque ad nostri imperij tempora, quae d pene in mille & trecentos annos concurrunt, non solum secum in variis suis partib.sed in imperialibus quoque praesertim sanctionibus inter omne mutare consonantiam pariter ac discordiam: non tamen id solum, quod secum pugnabat, tollere: sed etiam quod idem aut simile reperiebatur, expellere, variamque ipsius pulchritudinis idea tribuere, ita ut pro singulis rebus singulae leges constitutae viderentur. Quod proculdubio superioris numinis & fluentis inde benignitatis fuit, non humanae cogitationis, aut inceptii, aut potestatis. Nos itaque, more solito manibus ad Deum erectis, eoque, ut nos completi dignare-tur, invocato, & rem aggresi sumus. & omnia tandem confecimus, Triboniano gloriosissimo magistro, & exquaestore sacri nostri palatij, & exconsule ad omne ministerium vi necnon aliis quibusdam illustribus, & prudentibus viris, inquirentes semper ea, quae ab eis coponebantur: & id, quod erat dubiu per-scruscrutátes,omnibus quoq. secúdum datá nobis à Domino Deo &salvatore nostro Iesu Chr:sto scientiam &intellectus vigorem imponentes copetentem formam. 1 ¶Et piissimas igitur constitutiones iam ante in duodecim libris comprehensas, Codicem no strae pietatis cognomine fulgentem compositmus. nunc vero omnium veterum iuris conditorum sententias ex multitudine, quae ad duo milia pene librorum, & trecentas myriadas versuum pertingebat, in moderatum & perspicuum collegimus compendium. Quinquaginta igitur libris omnia complexi nunc sumus coelesti fauore, colligentes omne id, quod erat utile, & omnes ambiguitates decidentes, nullo seditioso relicto. Quos libros Digesta seu Pandecta appellauimus ex eo,quod legum habeant diuisiones & decisiones, itemque ex eo, quod omne in unum congregatum receperint, hanc eis appellationem imponentes: nec vlra quindecim myriadum versuum numerũ eis dantes:& in septem eos disponentes tractatus: idque non perperam, neque sine ratione, sed ad numerorum naturam & har monia respicientes. 2 ¶Ea igitur, quae apud omnes πρῶτα, id est primordia, nuncupantur, in quattuor libros seposuimus. 3 ¶Deinceps f ea,quae de iudiciis tractant, in alios septem g libros. 4 ¶Item ea, quae de h rebus, non in plures quam i octo libros. 5 ¶Sequentem vero operis partem: quae quarta & media μέσον ἐστὶ τοῦ s totius operis, in aliis l octo libris deposuimus in quibus est quidem m hypothecaria, non longe admodum a pignoraticia actione distans. est & Aedilitium n edictum, & de euictionibus stipulatio: quae duo accessoria & consequentia constituta venditionum,o longe tamen admodum in veteri iuris ordinatione ab his deuagantia, congregauimus propiusque propter mutuam inter se cognationem, ne, quae de eo- dem pene loquuntur, longe a se distarent. Post hæc introduximus post duos illos libros ea, quae sunt scripta de vsuris tam terrestribus quam traiecticiis seu maritimis, & de probationibus, atque præsum- ptionibus in vnū librum. p his autem tribus monobiblis, singularibus libris post tractatū de rebus si- bi inuicem proximis depositis,& rursum ea, quae de sposalibus,& nuptiis,& dote legibus dicta sunt congregantes,his etiam q tria habere in hac ordinatione volumina concesimus.De tutoribus autem minoris ætatis geminos libros, eos, inquam, qui de tutelis apud omnes nominantur, & hic etiam in compendium concidimus, memoratam octo librorum ordinationem,& mediam (vt dictum est) hanc partem totius operis confecimus, pulcherrima & vtilissima iura in his describentes.
units.tr: After the peace made with the Persians, after the Vandal trophies and the whole conquest of Libya, and after the most famous Carthage was joined again to our Empire, God granted us that we should bring the work of renewing the ancient laws to its desired end. No prince before our rule thought that this could be conceived, or that it was possible for human ingenuity. For it was remarkable that every Roman enactment, from the founding of old Rome down to the times of our Empire, which span nearly thirteen hundred years, should not only conflict within its own parts, but especially in the imperial enactments should shift between agreement and discord throughout; and that it was not enough to remove what contradicted itself, but also to expel what was found to be the same or similar, and to give each part its own beauty, so that a separate law seemed to have been laid down for each single matter. This was undoubtedly the work of a higher power and of the benevolence flowing from it, not of human thought, undertaking, or power. Therefore we, having raised our hands to God in our usual manner and invoked Him so that He would deign to bring us to completion, set to work. At last we finished everything, with Tribonian, our most glorious master of offices, ex-quaestor of our sacred palace, and ex-consul, and with certain other illustrious and prudent men, always examining what they drafted, and settling what was doubtful, and giving to all, according to the knowledge and vigour of understanding granted us by the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, a suitable form. 1 Therefore, having already compiled the most pious constitutions in twelve books, we composed the Code, shining with the surname of our piety. Now we have gathered the opinions of all the ancient jurists, from a multitude that came to nearly two thousand books and three hundred thousand verses, into a moderate and clear compendium. Embracing them all in fifty books, we now gather everything that was useful, settle all ambiguities, and leave no seditious matter behind. We have called these books the Digests or Pandects, both because they contain the divisions and decisions of the laws, and because they have received everything gathered into one, and we have given them this name, not giving them more than fifteen myriads of verses; and we have arranged them in seven tractates, and this not carelessly or without reason, but with regard to the nature and harmony of numbers. 2 Those things which are called the first things [πρῶτα] among all, that is, the principles, we have set apart in four books. 3 Next, those which deal with trials, in seven other books. 4 Likewise, those on things, in not more than eight books. 5 The following part of the work, which is the fourth and middle part of the whole work (μέσον ἐστὶ τοῦ totius operis), we have placed in eight other books. In these is the hypothecary action, not far removed from the pledge action; there is also the Aedilician edict, and the stipulation concerning eviction. These two, accessory and consequential provisions of sales, though in the old arrangement of law they stray far from these, we have gathered together, and placed nearer, because of their mutual kinship, lest those that speak of much the same matter should be far apart. After these we have put, after those two books, what has been written about interest, both land-based and sea-borne, and about proofs and presumptions, in one book. After these three single books, following the tractate on things that are close to one another, and again gathering what has been said by the laws about betrothals, marriages, and dowry, we have also allowed three volumes in this arrangement. Concerning guardians of minors, we have also condensed the two books that are called by all "on guardianships" into a compendium here, and so we have completed the aforementioned arrangement of eight books, and this middle part (as has been said) of the whole work, describing in it the most beautiful and useful laws.

units.la: 6 ¶De testamentis autem,& legatis,& fideicommissis omnia congregauimus in nouem librorum numerum: quorum principatum obtinent ea, quae sunt de testamentis,& codicillis,cum omnium ,tum etiam militum, qui ea, vt volunt, faciunt duobus libris ordinata, & de testamentis inscripta. quinque autem sequentibus continentur ea, quae de legatis & fideicommissis & omni eorum ambiguitate disputata sunt. & quoniam Falcidiæ narratio continens & consentanea erat legatorum & fideicommis-forum proprio tractatui:propterea & ipsam cõtinuo legatorū supposuimus tractationi, libro integro ci applicato,cum breui quadam adiectione. & rursum quia ad Falcidiæ imitationem [introductum] erat Trebellianum Senatusconsultum in fideicommissis: & huic vltimum/huius ordinationis tribuimus locum totum ius super his positum, Trebelliano Senatusconsulto attribuentes, & superuacuum esse Pegasiani senatusconsulti positionem inuenientes, & absurdas horum Senatusconsultorum inter se differentias,& communiones:quas sane & veteres perosi, captiosas & damnosas appellarunt: simpliciore quadam narratione omne hoc schema congregantes,& ad vnius Senatusconsulti Trebelliani ordinationem applicantes,& hanc quintam partem totius ordinationis nouem his perfecimus libris. In quibus nouem libris nihil de quondam caducis dictum a nobis est: quia propter vsum quendam non prospe-rum cùm increbuissent in republica, & luctuosum monumentum bellorum ciuilium essent: non oportebat in his manere temporibus, in quibus & Deus dedit pacem nobis agere domi & foris, &, cum oportuit bellum gerere, facile cum ipsius fauore hostes superare & capere.
units.tr: 6 Concerning wills, legacies, and trust-bequests, we have gathered everything into a number of nine books. Of these, the first place is held by what concerns wills and codicils, for soldiers as well as for all others who make them as they wish, arranged in two books and entitled "On Wills." The five following contain what has been discussed about legacies, trust-bequests, and all their ambiguity. And since the account of the Falcidian law contains and is consistent with the proper tractate of legacies and trust-bequests, we have placed it immediately after the treatment of legacies, attached as a whole book with a short addition. Again, since the Trebellian senatusconsult was introduced in trust-bequests on the model of the Falcidian law, we have given it the last place in this arrangement, assigning the whole law laid down on these matters to the Trebellian senatusconsult. Finding the enactment of the Pegasian senatusconsult superfluous, and the absurd differences and common features of these senatusconsults, which the ancients too abhorred and called captious and harmful, we have gathered this whole scheme into a simpler account and applied it to the arrangement of the one Trebellian senatusconsult, and so have completed this fifth part of the whole arrangement with these nine books. In these nine books we have said nothing about the once-lapsed bequests, because, owing to a certain unfortunate practice that grew up in the commonwealth and became a mournful monument of civil wars, it was not fitting to dwell on them in these times, in which God has given us peace to act at home and abroad, and, when it was necessary to wage war, to overcome and capture the enemy easily with His favour.

units.la: 7 ¶Sequitur deinde & exoritur nobis & lexta pars totius compositionis,octo conclusa libris. Pulchre autem incipit ab his, quae possessiones nominantur,quas non similiter, vt cætera diligenter considerantes tam eas, quae ad ingenuos, quàm quae ad libertinos pertinent ex multa anteriorum temporum confusione & obscuritate in purū dedudeduximus cōpendium,geminorum {a}illis librorum numerum sufficere arbitrates. Adplicauimus autem {a}ipsis & omnes ab intestato appellatas successiones & ipsos generum ordines eorum gradibus etiam libro inscriptis, & circa omnium finem Tertullianum & Orficianum composuimus senatusconsultum,ex quibus matres & liberi iuuicem successores fiunt. Procedit autem post hæc alius liber {b}, qui de ædificiorum operibus,& de ea, quæ ob ruinosa & diruta ædificia [datur,] satisdatione, & his qui in his aliquid insidiarum aut fraudis admiserint, & de his qui ex aquarum impetu vicinos læserint, & de publicorum vectigalium coactoribus, atque insuper de donationibus tam indefinitis [seu simplicibus,]quæ in cogitationem mortis relatis leges ac iura ordinet. Rursum autem quicquid de quacunque manumissione extat, vel de his,quæ super ipsa agitantur, causis, & hoc vni {c}traditum est libro. Amplius autem & ea,quæ de possessione,& per ipsam adquisitione,& de causis eam introducetib.sunt,in {d}vnum seposuimus tractatum [seu librum.] Et quidquid etiam de iudiciariis extat sententiis, & his qui in his aliqua contra se ipsos confessi sunt, & de bonorum cessione, & creditorum detentione,& venditione, & de bonorum separatione & curatione,& ne quid patiantur creditores fraudis & id {e}vnum similiter collatum est libri. Sed & interdictorum modum non pluribus quàm {f}vni dedimus libro. Inde {g}autem & ad præscriptiones seu [exceptiones] & in his ordinata tempora venimus. Et obligationum quidem & actionum seposuimus modos,& coegimus omnem hanc partem, cui præsunt possessiones (vt dictum est) octo librorum numero descriptam, sextam hanc partem totius voluminis seponentes.
units.tr: 7 Then follows and arises for us the sixth part of the whole composition, concluded in eight books. It rightly begins with those matters that are called possessions, which, not in the same way as the others, we have carefully considered; and both those that pertain to freeborn persons and those that pertain to freedmen, out of the great confusion and obscurity of earlier times, we have drawn into a clear compendium, judging that two books would suffice for them. We have also applied to them all the successions called intestate, and the orders of kinship by their degrees, which are also entitled in a book; and at the end of all we have composed the senatusconsult of Tertullian and Orfician, by which mothers and children become successors to one another. After this comes another book, which lays down the laws and rights concerning the works of buildings, and concerning the security given for buildings that are ruinous or demolished, and for those who have committed any treachery or fraud in these matters, and concerning those who through the force of waters have injured their neighbours, and concerning the collectors of public revenues, and moreover concerning donations, both indefinite [or simple] and those made in view of death. Again, whatever exists concerning any manumission, or about the causes that are argued concerning these, has been assigned to this one book. Furthermore, we have set apart in one tractate [or book] those things that concern possession, and acquisition through it, and the causes that introduce it. And whatever also exists concerning judicial sentences, and concerning those who have confessed anything against themselves in these matters, and concerning cession of goods, and the detention and sale of creditors, and the separation and management of goods, and that creditors should suffer no fraud, this likewise has been gathered into one book. But we have not given the mode of interdicts to more than one book. From there we come to prescriptions [or exceptions], and to the times ordained for them. And the modes of obligations and actions we have set apart, and we have brought all this part, over which the possessions preside (as has been said), into the number of eight books, setting apart this sixth part of the whole volume.

units.la: 8 ¶Totius autem extrema pars, quæ & septima {h}est totius tractationis,sex librorum numero demandata est,incipiens quidem à stipulationibus, procedens verò ad ea quæ scripta sunt de fideiussione,& debitorum numeratione, solutione & liberatione ipsorum, & de introductis ex Prætorum iurisdictione stipulationibus: quæ omnia duobus à nobis contracta sunt libris: cum apud veteres nec dici posset,quot essent libri [ea de re.] Procedit & deinceps {k}ad delictorum narrationem: & omnia recensetquæ ad minora delicta pertinent, quæ vocant priuatas & item quæ ad ea, quæ necdum ordinaria appellant, sed ipsis extraordinariorum appellan-
units.tr: 8 The final part of the whole work, which is also the seventh part of the whole treatise, is assigned to six books. It begins with stipulations and proceeds to what is written about suretyship, the reckoning, payment and discharge of debts, and the stipulations introduced by the jurisdiction of the praetors. All of this we have compiled in two books, since among the ancients it could not even be said how many books there were on that subject. It goes on next to the narration of delicts, and surveys everything that pertains to the lesser delicts, which they call private, and likewise those matters which they do not yet call ordinary, but name extraordinary.

units.la: {a} 37.38. {b} 39. {c} 40. {d} 41. {e} 42. {f} 43. {g} 44. {h} Pars septi-ma. {k} lib.45.46. lib.47.48. tionem imponunt.descendit etiam & ad publica crimina, quæ atrocissima sunt, & magnam sibi aduo-canr[?] pœnam. Duo {*} autem & hic sunt libri, qui illa quidem, quæ ad delicta & crimina pertinent, complectuntur, quibus permixta sunt & ea, quæ de reis criminum, qui se celare tamen conantur, scripta sunt, & de eorum bonis, & de ea, quæ infligitur condemnatis, pœna vel indulgentia. Initium autem nobis alterius rursum {b}libri fit narratio de appellationibus, quæ communis est profecto ad restituendas tam pecuniarias [seu ciuiles] sententias, quàm criminales. {c}Quæcumque autem de ciuibus [seu municipibus,] & de decurionibus, & muneribus, & publicis operibus, & nundinis & redituum pollicitationibus, & variis cognitionibus [seu interrogationibus,] & publica descriptione, veteribus inuenta sunt, & quæcumque de verborum exstat significatione, & de his, quæ pro regulis apud veteres dicta sunt: hæc omnia in sese recipit vltimus liber. Huius igitur compositionis, cuius initiū est à stipulationibus, hic liber est sextus quidem, si ad proprium principium comparetur: sed est quinquagesimus, si conferatur ad totam consummationis perfectionem [seu harmoniam.]
units.tr: {a} 37.38. {b} 39. {c} 40. {d} 41. {e} 42. {f} 43. {g} 44. {h} The seventh part. {k} books 45-46. books 47-48. It also descends to public crimes, which are most atrocious and draw a great penalty upon themselves. Two books here also deal with those matters which pertain to delicts and crimes, and mixed in with them are the things written about the accused who nevertheless try to hide themselves, about their goods, and about the punishment or pardon inflicted on the condemned. The beginning of the next book is the narration about appeals, which is indeed common to the overturning of both pecuniary [or civil] sentences and criminal ones. Whatever the ancients devised about citizens [or townsmen], decurions, public offices, public works, markets, promises of revenues, various inquiries [or interrogations] and public registration, and whatever exists about the meaning of words, and about those things which the ancients stated as rules: the last book takes all of these into itself. Of this arrangement, which begins with stipulations, this book is the sixth if it is compared with its own starting point, but it is the fiftieth if it is compared with the whole completed harmony [or system].

units.la: 9 ¶Quæ omnia composita sunt & elaborata perpti-mè, & vt nostra iussione dignum fuit, per {d}Tribonianū {e}illustrissimū necnon prudentissimū magistrū, & exquaestore nostrorum palatiorū, & excosule, virū & in ipsis rerum experimentis, & in eloquentia, & in legibus scribendis satis spectatum, & qui nihil vnquam nostrarum iussionum contempsit: necnon per alios [viros,] qui sub ipso nobis hoc opus elaborarunt: id est, {f}Constantinum magnificentissimum comites sacrarum largitionum, & antigraphariū [seu magistrum] sacri scrinii, & sacrorum libellorum & cognitionum imperialium, qui nobis bonam de se opinionem in omnibus præbuit: necnon {g}Theophilum magnificentissimum magistrum, {h}& leges [seu iura] in regia hac vrbe laudabiliter, & cum summis vigiliis, & vt magisteria sedulitate dignum est, docentem: & {i}Dorotheum magnificentissimum quæstorem & Doctorem in legum ciuitate designatum: dicimus autem verendam & splendidam Berytiensium metropolin, quem de ipso optima opinio & gloria, & ad nos deduxit ipsum, & vt huius operis participem faceremus, hortata est: sed & {k}Anatolium magnificentissimū magistrum, qui & ipse apud Berytiensi[?]
units.tr: 9 All these things have been compiled and worked out most thoroughly, and as was fitting for our command, by Tribonian, most illustrious and most prudent master, quaestor of our sacred palaces, ex-consul, a man well tested in the actual experience of affairs, in eloquence and in the writing of laws, who has never despised any of our commands; and also by other men who worked on this task under him, namely Constantinus, most magnificent count of the sacred largesses and antigraphus [or master] of the sacred writing office, of sacred petitions and imperial cognitions, who has given us a good opinion of himself in all things; and Theophilus, most magnificent master, who teaches the laws [or rights] in this royal city praiseworthily and with the greatest vigilance, as the dignity of a master demands; and Dorotheus, most magnificent quaestor and teacher designated in the city of laws. We mean the venerable and splendid metropolis of the Berytians, which put forward the excellent opinion and glory of him, brought him to us, and urged that he be made a partner in this work. Also Anatolius, most magnificent master, who himself teaches at Berytus beautifully

units.la: {f} ea quę ex legibus[proficiscuntur,]pulchrę docet,vir ex tertia stirpe laudabili iuris apud Phœnices interpretum defcendetes(refert enim[genus]ad Leontiũ, & Eudoxium,hominesin legibus optimæ memoriæ post Patricium inclytæ recordationis, quæstorium & anticenforem,& Leontium gloriosissimum,expræ- secto, & exconfule, atque patrium eius filios sum- mæ admirationis viros) & Cratinum magnificentissimum atque prudentissimum comitem sacrarum largitionum:(Sæptimus quoque est is legum enarra- tor in regia hac vrbe) & præter hos etiam Stepha- num,Menam,Profdocium,Eutolmium,Timotheum, Leonidem,Leontium,Platonem,Iacobum,Conftan- tinum,Ioannem,viros prudentissimos, qui vniuersi Rhetores quidem sunt gloriosissimorum præfecto- rum sacrorum nostrorum Prætoriorum,gloriam autem laudem apud omnes prudentiæ iuste habet, & a nobis merito iudicati sunt digni, vt eligeren- tur tanti certaminis participes.Hæc igitur nobis cir ca Digestorum elaborata sunt conscriptionem per iam dictos gloriosissimos viros.
units.tr: {f} those things which proceed from the laws. He is a man of the third, praiseworthy line of legal interpreters in Phoenicia (for he traces his descent to Leontius and Eudoxius, men of most excellent memory in the laws, after Patricius of illustrious memory, quaestor and anticensor, and Leontius most glorious, ex-praefect and ex-consul, and the sons of his father, men of highest admiration); and Cratinus, most magnificent and most prudent count of the sacred largesses (he is also the seventh expounder of the laws in this royal city); and besides these, Stephanus, Menas, Prodocius, Eutolmius, Timotheus, Leonides, Leontius, Plato, Jacobus, Constantinus and John, most prudent men, who are all indeed rhetors of our most glorious sacred praetorian prefects, and who have glory and praise among all for their just prudence, and who have been rightly judged by us worthy to be chosen as participants in so great a contest. These things, then, concerning the writing of the Digest, have been worked out by us through the aforesaid most glorious men.

units.la: 10 ¶Tanta autem nobis reuerentia antiquitatis fuit,vt neque mutari nomina veterū Iurisconsulto- rū sustinuerimus,sed vniuscuiusq. illorū appellatio- nem legibus inscripsimus,mutantes quidem,si quid iam habere vitium est non rectè, partes vero illas nunc tollentes, has nunc addentes, ex multis denique optimum eligentes,& vnam atque parem omnibus præbentes potestatis vim, [seu robur: ita vt quicquid scriptum est in eo libro, id nostra sit sententia: nemine audente comparare ea,quæ nunc sunt his,quæ priùs erant: quia multa & numera- tu non facilia trăspofuimus in melius, etiam si quid imperiali aliqua antiquorum imperatorum consti- tutione in aliam distinctum fuerat formam. nam nomina quidem veterib. seruauimus, legum autem veritatem nostram fecimus. itaque si quid erat in illis seditiosum, (multa autem talia erant ibi reposita) hoc decisum est,& definitum, & in peꝛspicuum finem deducta est quæque lex.
units.tr: 10 Such was our reverence for antiquity that we did not allow the names of the ancient jurists to be changed. Instead we inscribed in the laws the name of each of them, changing whatever is faulty and not right, now removing certain parts, now adding others, and finally choosing the best out of many and giving one and the same equal force of authority to all [or strength]. So whatever is written in that book is our own opinion, and no one should dare to compare those things which are now with those which were before, since we have transposed many things, not easy to count, for the better, even where something had been put into another form by some constitution of an ancient emperor. For we have kept the names for the ancients, but made the truth of the laws our own. Thus if anything in them was seditious (and many such things were stored there), this has been decided and defined, and each law has been brought to a clear end.

units.la: 11 ¶Sed cum oportebat & aliquam mediocrem Ifagogen facere in eorum gratiam,qui receter leges attingunt,nec maiorem doctrinam portare possunt: argumenta,prima fundamenta atque elementa s.
units.tr: 11 But since it was also fitting to make some moderate Isagoge for the sake of those who approach the laws lightly and cannot bear greater learning: the arguments, first foundations and elements s.

units.la: mm §.11, neque hoc extra nostram prouidentiam reliquimus, scilicet Triboniano gloriosissimo, qui & ad totius operis legitimi gubernationem electus est, necnon Theophilo, & Dorotheo magnificentissimis & prudentissimis anticensorib. accersitis mundauimus: ut seligerent ex his, quae apud veteres erant ifagogarū modo composita, ea, quae essent aptissima, & in ipsis rerum argumentis obtinentia: utque colligerent, & nobis offerrent, & ut mentionem etiam facerent nostrarū Constitutionum, quas pro emendatione veteris iuris promulgauimus: & ita componerent libros quatuor futuros primae elementa totius ifagoges, quos vocari Instituta visum est. quā sane legitimi operis parte copositam nobis obtulerunt. & nos ea tota fiderata[?] à nobis, & perpessam, rectèque habere visum nostris sensibus non indigna esse iudicauimus, & {*}à nostris haberi Constitutionibus & nostrarū Constitutionum robur habere iussimus: quod & ex his, quae in procemiis erudisem voluminis disseruimus, omnibus manifestum fecimus.
units.tr: §. 11. Nor have we left this outside our foresight. Having summoned the most glorious Tribonian, who has also been chosen to govern the whole legitimate work, and the most magnificent and most prudent ex-censors Theophilus and Dorotheus, we commanded them to choose from among those things which the ancients had composed in the manner of Isagoges those which were most apt and which hold good in the very arguments of things; and to gather them and offer them to us, and also to make mention of our Constitutions, which we have promulgated for the emendation of the old law; and so to compose four books, which would be the first elements of the whole Isagoge, and which it was decided to call the Institutes. These they offered to us, composed as a part of the legitimate work. And we, having had the whole of it considered and examined by us, judged it right and fitting for our judgment, and not unworthy, and we ordered that it be held as our own Constitutions and have the force of our Constitutions. We have made this manifest to all from what we have set out in the prefaces of the erudite volume.

units.la: 12 ¶Sic itaq. omnI Romani iuris dispositione ordinata, & in tribus integris & voluminibus, & annis tanto opere perfecto: (quod nobis ab initio omnem spem excedere: circa finem autem, cūm iam penetrabilem esse rem docuimus, ne in decem quidem annis totum absolui posse videbatur:) tata[?] ergo trium {b}annorum celeritate cosum[?] mato opere, & hac opera Domino Deo oblata, quā[?] dedit & pacem agere, & bella feliciter dirigere, & leges ponere praeterito, praesenti, & futuro tempori iustum esse putauimus, omnibus hominibus facere manifestum nostrum in his rebus studium simul & prouidentiam: quomodo nempe priore soluti pertnr[?] ratione, & confusione, & nullum finem habente iuris positione, usuri sint posthac legibus rectis compendiosis & omnibus ad manum promptis & litium compendium adferentibus, & paratis, atque expositis omnibus [volentibus] ad facilem adquisitionem, nec amplius agentibus multis pecuniis, ut illorum inutilium librorum congerant multitudinem: sed utilissima pecunia tam ditioribus quàm ex tenuiore profestis patrimonio, copiā sui coparandi praebentibus.
units.tr: 12 Thus, therefore, with the whole Roman law arranged in order, in three complete volumes, and with the work so greatly completed (which at the beginning seemed to us to exceed all hope; and near the end, when we had shown the matter to be already passable, it did not seem able to be finished even in ten years), with the work finished in the swiftness of three years, and this work offered to the Lord God, who has given both to conduct peace and to direct wars successfully and to lay down laws, we thought it just to make manifest to all men, for past, present and future time, our zeal and foresight in these matters: namely, how, freed from the former disorder and confusion of the law, which had no end, they will henceforth use right and concise laws, all ready to hand, bringing relief to lawsuits, laid out and open to all who wish for easy acquisition; and no longer spending much money to heap up the multitude of those useless books, but a most useful sum, offering to the richer as well as to those of modest patrimony the opportunity of acquiring it.

units.la: 13 ¶Si quid autem ex multitudine ea, quae nunc congesta est, & ex tantis myriadibus collecta, videbitur esse simile [& geminatum{d}] (hoc autem putanius rarum esse) attamen humanae naturae [imbecillitatem] considerationibus, non exua iustam apologiam.
units.tr: 13 If anything in the multitude that has now been gathered together, and collected from so many myriads, should seem to be like [and doubled] (though we think this is rare), yet, by considering human weakness [frailty], we do not lack a just apology.
§13.5. Const. ad Senatum & omnes populos.

units.la: §. penult. Inst. [illegible, ~12 letters] iam ne hoc quidem videbitur esse. in nullo enim aberrare, [seu in omnibus irreprehensibilem seu inemendabilem esse,] divinae utique solius, non autem mortalis est constantiae [seu roboris,] quemadmodum & à maioribus dictum est. deinde est, ubi & similium adsumpsimus positionem: vel rebus subiectis id exigentibus, ut oporteret idem plurib. applicari titulis: vel quia cum extraneo loco esset commixtum id, quod simile superiori videbatur, impossibile fuit eam similitudine detrahi: vel etiam quia saepe custodienda fuit integra totius theoriae {a}[seu visionis] continentia, nec[separanda aut] diuellenda mens & intellectus[legentium] per eorum quae iam scripta fuerat, ademptionem. quin & hoc sicubi adsumptum est propter rei necessitatem: tamen id breve est, nec ullum fere sui sensum praebens.
units.tr: §. penult. Inst. [illegible] Now this too will not seem to be the case. For to err in nothing, or to be faultless or incapable of correction in all things, belongs to divine constancy alone and not to mortal constancy, as the ancients also said. Next, there is the case where we have also adopted the placing of similar matters: either because the subject matter required it, so that the same thing had to be applied under several titles; or because, when what seemed similar to what precedes had been mixed in an alien place, it was impossible to remove it from that similarity; or also because the unbroken coherence of the whole theory or vision often had to be preserved, and the mind and understanding of readers should not be separated or torn away by the removal of what has already been written. Indeed, wherever this has been adopted because of the necessity of the matter, it is nonetheless brief and offers almost no meaning of its own.

units.la: 14 ¶Hoc etiam ipsum & in Constitutionibus iam inter impe-riales Constitutiones relatis, & iure, quod ex his resultat, observavimus. nam quae in illis iam cauta e-rant, ea nec in hoc volumine poni concessimus, nisi ob aliquam interdum circunstantiam similitudinis aliqua causa relicta est.
units.tr: 14 We have observed this very thing also in the Constitutions already included among the imperial Constitutions, and in the law that results from them. For those things that had already been provided for in those, we have not allowed to be placed in this volume, unless sometimes, because of some circumstance of resemblance, a reason for it has been left.

units.la: 15 ¶Contrariam {b}autem aliis legibus legem ex his, quae in hoc volumine positae sunt, non facile quis reperit, si modo ad omnes contrarietatis fines animum intedere festiner. sed {c}inest aliquid diversum: quod adsumptum alterius generis forte hanc & il-lam legis positione apparere faciet.
units.tr: 15 It is not easy for anyone to find a law in this volume, drawn from the things placed in it, that is contrary to other laws, if only he hastens to examine all the limits of contrariety. But something different is present: when it is taken up as belonging to another kind, it will perhaps make this and that placement of the law appear.

units.la: 16 ¶Sed & si quid forte praetermissum {d}est eorum, quae poni debebant (forte enim & aliquid tale contigit) propter hu-manae imbecillitatem naturae, multo sane melius est nostris subditis multis inutilibus liberari[legibus,] dum privatur forte paucis quibusdam, quae videbantur idoneae
units.tr: 16 But even if something of those things that ought to have been placed has perhaps been omitted (for perhaps something of the sort has happened too), because of the weakness of human nature, it is certainly much better for our subjects to be freed from many useless laws, even though a few that seemed suitable may perhaps be lacking.

units.la: 17 ¶Hac enim ob causam tot libris {e}(quos antea scribi oportebat) destituti iudices, facilius ex pau-cissimis iuris auctoribus & libris ad finem litium perveniebant, & iudicia decidebant vel propter in-opiam librorum, vel quia non sufficiebant multis laboribus ad inveniendam multa utilia necessariis, & viribus erant impares. In praesenti autem confusione maximus legum obtinetium congestus est numerus ex libris raris, & qui vix inveniri potuerint, & quorum nec nomina nec eruditissimi quidem in legibus complures hominess noverant. Quorum sane copiam [ seu materiam ] nobis uberrimam dictus gloriosissimus Tribonianus præbuit, multorum librorum, & qui vix numerari possunt suppeditata multitudine, quibus omnibus perfecte lectis, congesta sunt hæc volumina, sed ex horum multis & variis hi, qui à nobis ad hoc congregati erant, cum nihil inuenissent idoneum aut nouum ab his, quæ iam congregata erunt, illationem ex his in hoc opere faciendam optimo animo respuerunt.
units.tr: 17 For this reason, judges, deprived of so many books (which earlier had to be written), used to reach the end of lawsuits more easily from very few authors and books of law, and they decided cases either because of the scarcity of books, or because they were not equal to the great labour of finding many useful things, and lacked the strength for it. But in the present confusion, a very great number of laws in force has been gathered from rare books, which could scarcely be found, and whose titles even many very learned men in the law did not know. The most glorious Tribonian, as is said, supplied us with a most abundant store of these, a multitude of many books which can scarcely be counted. When all of these had been read through completely, these volumes were compiled; but from many and varied sources, those whom we had gathered for this purpose, having found nothing suitable or new among those already collected, with the best intention rejected any inference to be drawn from them in this work.

units.la: 18 ¶ Si vero postea aliquid noui{4} controuertetur quod nō apparebit legibus his inscriptum : ({*}multa enim nouare nouit natura) sed Imperium Deus propter hoc imposuit hominibus ut emergentia & legis egentia lege definiat, & humanæ naturæ incertum repleat, & certis concludat legibus ac regulis. Neque hoc nostrum nunc dicimus: sed iam communium iuris conditorum, qui olim claruerunt, prudentissimus Iulianus hoc ipsum videtur dixisse, qui & ab imperiali auctoritate implorat fieri legum repletionem in emergentibus ambiguitatibus & quæstionibus. Sed & diuus Adrianus piæ memoriæ: quando ea, quæ à prætoribus quotannis edicta fuerant, breui complexus est libello, adsumpto ad id optimo Iuliano: in oratione quam in communi habuit in seniore Roma, hoc ipsum quoque ait: ut, si quid prætor id, quod iam ordinatum est, emerserit: conuenientes est, eos qui in magistratu sunt, illud conari decidere, & remedium imponere secundum eorum quæ iam ordinata sunt, consequentiam [imitatio-nem.]
units.tr: 18 But if afterwards something new should be disputed which does not appear to be covered by these laws (for nature knows how to bring forth many new things), yet God has placed the empire over men so that it may define by law what emerges and lacks law, fill up what is uncertain in human nature, and close it with fixed laws and rules. We do not say this as something of our own now, but the most prudent Julian seems to have said this very thing, among the common founders of law who were famous long ago; he also begs that the filling up of laws be done by imperial authority in emerging ambiguities and questions. And the divine Hadrian, of pious memory, when he gathered into a short book what the praetors had edicted each year, taking the excellent Julian as his helper, said this very thing too in the speech he delivered in the Senate at Rome: that if the praetor should bring forth something that is not yet ordained, it is fitting for those who hold magistracy to try to decide it and to impose a remedy in accordance with the consequence of what has already been ordained, by imitation.

units.la: 19 ¶ Hæc igitur omnes (dicimus autem vos, magni Senatus & omnes nostræ reipublicæ homi-nes) cognoscentes, gratiam quidem confitemini Deo, qui nostris temporibus tantum bonum serua-uit: utimini vero nostris legibus, nulli c earum, quæ veteribus libris inscriptæ sunt attendentes: neque ad ea quæ nunc posita sunt, illas comparantes, quia etsi videantur quædam inuicem non consonare, tamen prius {d}illud & vetustius nobis ut imperfectum displicuit, nūc autem hoc visum est debere obtinere. Nam prohibemus, illis in posterum uti. hæc autem [?]tem sola obseruari in republica, & obtinere concedimus, & sancimus. Ita ut qui conatus fuerit ex prioribus libris, & non ex his duobus foliis, & Constitutionum [libro] à nobis compositis, vel factis, uti qui-busdam legibus vel eas in iudiciis legere, vel si quis iudicauerit ex his apud se recitari eas passus: falsi reus {a}reus erit & publicorū criminū iudicatus, & pœnæ addictus : quod etsi non diceremus, vel ex hoc ipsis manifestum esset. 20 ¶ Sed & hoc optimum fore iudicauimus, præponere Digestorū volumine & veteres iuris conditores,& illorum volumina{b},& vnde collectio facta sit legum nunc à nobis congestarum. quod & fieri iussimus:& factum est: & simul ea,quæ de his rebus conscripta sunt, supponi huic diuinæ nostræ Constitutioni præcepimus, vt omnibus fiat manifestum & quid prioris inexperientiæ simul & incertitudinis esset, & quid à nobis sit adinuentum.
units.tr: 19 Therefore, knowing all these things (and we speak to you, great Senate, and to all the men of our commonwealth), give thanks indeed to God, who has preserved such a great good in our times; but use our laws, paying no attention to any of those that were inscribed in the old books, and not comparing those with what is now laid down. For although some things may seem not to agree with one another, nevertheless the former and older ones have displeased us as imperfect, and it has seemed that these now must prevail. For we forbid their use in future; these alone we allow and decree to be observed and to prevail in the commonwealth. So that whoever shall attempt to use any of the laws from the earlier books, and not from these two sheets and the Constitutions compiled or made by us, or to read them in judgments, or, if anyone has allowed them to be read before himself on the basis of these, shall be liable for falsehood and be adjudged guilty of public crimes and be assigned to punishment. And even if we did not say this, it would be plain from this very fact. 20 But we have also judged it best to place in front of the volume of the Digest both the ancient founders of law and their books, and the source from which the collection of the laws now gathered by us was made. This we have also ordered to be done, and it has been done; and at the same time we have commanded that the things written about these matters be placed under this our divine Constitution, so that it may be made plain to all both what was of earlier inexperience and uncertainty, and what has been devised by us.

units.la: Legislatores autem seu legum interpretes illos congesimus, qui apud omnes probati & recepti erant, & prioribus Imperatoribus placuerant,& qui ab his nominari meruerunt. Si enim aliquis nondum veteribus Legislatoribus cognitus est : nos & huic interdiximus huius voluminis communicationem. Omnibus sane his positis vnum ordinem & dignitatem parem dedimus: nulli cuipiam maiore, quam cæteris, data prærogatiua.Si enim his quæ ab illis scripta sunt omnibus imperialium Constitutionum{c} dedimus robur:quid est:quod in his amplius, quodque minus haberi debeat? 21 ¶ Illud autem: quod ßatim,cum hanc copositionem legü cögregati mandaremus, iussimus: iterum & nunc sancimus illud confirmando : omnibus similiter interdicimus, ne quis audeat hominum, qui sunt nunc,aut in posterum erunt,commentarios{d} scribere harum legū præterquàm si velit quis in Græcam linguam hæc transferre,quem etiam volumus sola secundum pedem seu cata{e} poda nuncupata vti legum interpretatione: & si quid secundùm nominarorum paratitlorum (vt conueniens est ) adscribere voluerint vsum : aliud autem nihil omnino ne tantillum quidem circa ea facere , nec rursum dare seditionis , & dubitationis , aut infinitæ multitudinis,legibus occasionem. id,{f}quod antea in antiqui editi ordinatione : ita vt illud breuissimum constitutum , ex differentium commentariorum differentia seu diuersitate in infinitam extenderetur multitudinem. Si quid enim forte ambiguum fuerit visum vel litium certatoribus, vel his, qui rebus iudicantibus præsunt hoc Imperator interpretabitur rectè. nam hæc facultas illi soli{g}à legibus permissa est.Itaque quisquis ausus fuerit ad hanc nostram legum compositionem commentarium aliquod adiicere, aliter atque nostræ huius iussionis forma præ-scribit:is sciat, quod & ipsi falsi reo legibus futuro, & quod composuerit, eripietur, & modis omnibus corrumpetur.
units.tr: We have gathered together those legislators or interpreters of the laws who were approved and accepted by all and had pleased the earlier emperors, and who deserved to be named by them. For if anyone is not yet known to the ancient legislators, we have also forbidden him the use of this volume. Having laid all this down, we have given them all one rank and equal dignity: no greater prerogative has been granted to any one of them than to the others. For if we have given the force of imperial Constitutions to all the things written by them, what is there in them that ought to be held more, or what less? 21 Moreover, that which we commanded at once, when we charged that this composition of laws be assembled, we now also decree again, confirming it: we likewise forbid anyone of the men who now are or will be in future to write commentaries on these laws, except that anyone who wishes may translate these into the Greek language, whom we also wish to use only the interpretation of the laws called word-for-word, that is, kata poda; and if they wish to add anything according to the names of the Paratitla, as is fitting, let them do so; but they must do nothing at all beyond this, not even the smallest thing, about these matters, nor again give occasion for sedition, doubt, or an endless multitude to the laws. This was done before, in the arrangement of the old edition, so that that very brief arrangement was extended, through the difference or diversity of the commentaries, into an endless multitude. For if anything should seem ambiguous to the contenders in lawsuits or to those who preside over judging cases, the Emperor alone, to whom this power has been granted by the laws, shall interpret it rightly. Therefore, whoever has dared to add any commentary to this our compilation of laws, otherwise than the form of this our command prescribes, let him know that he himself will be liable as a falsifier under the laws, and what he has composed will be taken away and destroyed in every way.

units.la: 22 ¶ Eadem pœna impossita & aduersus eos, qui notis{*} [seu signis] quibusdam in scriptura utentur, (quæ sigla singulas{b} vocant) & qui per ea conturbare scripturam tentauerint, nec per totam consequentiam literarum numeros, & nomina ve-terum prudentum & totam legum positionem scri-pserint. Sciant etiam librorum ita scriptorum com-paratores se inutilis fore libri domines. neque e-nim damus licentiam talibus libris in iudiciis uti, & aliquid agere: etiam si contingat librum in ea i-psa parte, quæ recitatur, nullum habere tale signum [aut notam] sed in alia quacunque sui parte quam-uis semel tantum id admissum sit. Itaque ipse quidem eum librum pro non scripto prorsus habebit. Is autem qui eum scripserit, & ignoranti emptori de-derit: duplum soluet eius æstimationis ei qui ita in quantitate damnum passus fuerit, nihilominus instigenda criminali{c} poena. Hoc etenim & in aliis constitutionibus ea de re positis scripsimus, tam his, quæ Latina processerunt voce, quam ea, quæ Græco-rum lingua: quam quidem ad legum professores re-scripsimus.
units.tr: 22 ¶ The same penalty is also imposed on those who use certain marks or signs in writing, which they call sigla (abbreviations), and who have tried by these to confuse the writing, and have written out, without any continuous sequence of letters, numbers and names of the ancient jurists, and the whole arrangement of the laws. Let those who buy books written in this way also know that such a book will be of no use to its owner. For we do not grant licence to use such books in courts or to act on them, even if it happens that the book has no such sign [or note] in the part that is read aloud, but the sign has been admitted, even only once, in some other part of it. Accordingly the buyer shall regard that book as wholly unwritten. The person who wrote it and handed it over to an ignorant buyer shall pay double the value of the book to the one who has suffered the loss in this way, and in addition a criminal penalty shall be inflicted. We have written this in the same way in other constitutions issued on this subject, both those issued in the Latin language and those in the Greek language; and we have sent these to the professors of law.

units.la: 23 ¶ Hæc igitur volumina (Institutorum, & Dige-storum dicimus) ex fine tertij nostri felicissimi con-sulatus suum robur obtinere sancimus, id est ex an-te tertium Kalendarum Ianuarium præsentis duo-decimæ indictionis, in omne ævuum valitura, & una cum imperialibus constitutionibus vigorem & lo-cum habitura tam in his, quæ postea{d} emerserint, quàm his quæ in iudiciis adhuc pendent, nec dum amicalibus tradita sunt transactionibus. *quodcun-que enim hactenus vel iudicatum, vel transactum est, retractari non sustinemus. Quem quidem consu-latum tertium nobis nominatissimum dedit Deus: quando & sub ipso pax{e} cum Persis confirmata est, & hoc tantùm legum volumen repositum est, quod à nemine maiorum unquam excogitatum fuit, at-que ad hæc tertia pars mundi (dicimus autem totam {f}Libyam) nostris adiuncta est sceptris: omnia hæc à summo Deo & servatore nostro IESU ΧΡΙΣΤΩ[?] dona tertio nostro consulatu indulta. 24 ¶ Omnes itaque laudatissimi nostræ reipubl. magistratus divinam hanc nostram suscipientes constitutionem, ut utanutantur prædictis nostris legibus, vnusquisque in suo pro curabit iudicio. Proponet autem eam in maxima & regia hac vrbe & eius gloriosissimus Præfectus. Curæ autem erit excellentiss. & laudatissimo nostro magistro, & gloriosiss. atque beatissimis præfectis sacrorum nostrorum Prætoriorum tam his quæ ad solem orientem, quàm his, quæ in Illyride: necnon his etiam, quæ in Libya sunt: per sua edicta his, qui sub ipsis ordinati sunt, ista facere manifesta, ad omnium nostrorum subditorum inexcusabilem notitiam. Data XVII. Kalendas Ianuarias, Domino nostro Iustiniano perpetuo Augusto III. Consule 533.
units.tr: 23 ¶ We therefore decree that these volumes (we mean the Institutes and the Digest) shall obtain their force from the end of our most fortunate third consulship, that is, from the day before the third Kalends of January of the present twelfth indiction, and shall remain valid for all time, and shall have force and standing together with the imperial constitutions, both in those matters which may arise hereafter and in those which are still pending in the courts and have not yet been settled by friendly agreement. For we do not allow whatever has so far been decided or settled to be reopened. This third consulship was given to us, most renowned, by God: under it peace was also confirmed with the Persians, this single volume of laws was compiled, which was never devised by any of our predecessors, and this third part of the world (we mean all of Libya) was added to our sceptre. All these gifts were granted in our third consulship by the highest God and our Saviour Jesus Christ [Χριστῷ]. 24 ¶ Therefore let all our most praiseworthy magistrates of the commonwealth, receiving this divine constitution of ours, each in his own court take care that they use our aforesaid laws. It shall be published in this greatest and imperial city by its most glorious Prefect. It shall be the care of our most excellent and most praiseworthy Master, and of the most glorious and most blessed Prefects of our Praetorian sacred offices, both those in the East, those in Illyricum, and also those in Libya, to make these things known by their edicts to those who are under their authority, so that all our subjects may have inexcusable knowledge of them. Given on the 17th day before the Kalends of January, in the year of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, third consulship, 533.

units.la: DE RATIONE ET methodo Iuris docendi ad Antecessores.
units.tr: On the Plan and Method of Teaching Law to the Antecessores.

units.la: IMPERATOR CÆSAR, Flavius, Iustinianus{*}, Alamanicus, Gothicus, Francicus, {b}Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pius, felix, inclytus, victor ac triumphator semper Augustus, Theophilo, Dorotheo, Theodoro, Isidoro, Anatolio, Thalleleo, & Cratino viris illustribus antecessoribus, {c}Item & Salaminio viro disertissimo antecessori Salutem.
units.tr: The Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pious, fortunate, renowned, victorious and triumphant, ever Augustus, to Theophilus, Dorotheus, Theodorus, Isidorus, Anatolius, Thalelaeus and Cratinus, illustrious men and antecessores; likewise to Salaminius, a most eloquent man and antecessor, greeting.

units.la: OMNEM reipublicæ nostræ sanctionem iam esse purgatam & compositam tam in quatuor libris Institutionum seu elementorum, quam in quinquaginta Digestorum seu Pandectarum, necnon in duodecim Imperialium constitutionum, quis am-plius quam vos cognoscit: Et omnia quidem quæ o-portuerat & ab initio mandare, & post omnium con-summationem, factum libenter admittentes, defini-re, iam per nostras orationes tam Græca lingua quaRomanorum, quas aeternas fieri optamus, explicita sunt. Sed cum vos & omnes postea profefsores legitimae scientiae constitutos etiam hoc oportuerat sci-re,quid & in quibus temporibus tradi necessarium studiosis credimus,ut ex hoc optimi atque eruditissimi efficiatur: ideo praesentem diuinam orationem ad vos praecipue facieadam existimamus, quatenus tàm prudentia vestra quàm ceteri antecessores qui eandem artem in omne xuum exercere maluerint, nostris regulis obseruatis, inclytam viam eruditionis legitimae posint ambulare. Itaque dubio procul quidem est,necesse esse Institutiones in omnibus studijs primum sibi vindicare locum,vtpote prima vestigia eius scientiae mediocriter tradentes. ex libris autem quinquaginta nostrorum Digestorum sex & triginta tantum modo sufficere tam ad vestram expositionem, quàm ad iuuentutis eruditionem iudicamus.sed ordinem eorum,& tramites per quos ambulandum est, manifestare, tempestiuum nobis esse videtur: & vos in memoriam quidem eorum quae antea tradebatis,redigere:ostendere autem Nouellae nostrae compositionis tam vtilitatem quàm temporis ra, vt nihil huiusmodi artis relinquatur incognitu.
units.tr: As you know better than anyone, every constitution of our commonwealth has now been cleansed and arranged, both in the four books of the Institutes or Elements, and in the fifty books of the Digest or Pandects, and also in the twelve books of Imperial constitutions. We have gladly admitted and set in order everything that it was fitting to commission from the beginning and to define once the whole work was complete, and it has now been explained in our orations, both in the Greek language and in the Latin, which we wish to be everlasting. But since you and all the professors of legitimate learning appointed after you ought also to know what, and in which periods, we believe must be taught to students, so that they may become excellent and most learned, we think this divine oration should be addressed chiefly to you. Thus both your prudence and the other antecessores who have chosen to practise this art for all time may, by observing our rules, be able to walk the illustrious path of legitimate learning. There is undoubtedly no question that the Institutes must claim first place in all studies, since they give the first footsteps of that science in a moderate way. Of the fifty books of our Digest, we judge that only thirty-six suffice both for your exposition and for the instruction of youth. But it seems timely to us to set out their order and the paths by which one must proceed, to recall to your memory what you taught before, and to show the usefulness and the arrangement of our newly composed Novels, so that nothing of this art remains unknown.

units.la: ¶ Et antea quidem, quemadmodū & vestra scit prudentia,ex tanta legū multitudine, quae in librorum quidem duo millia, versuum autè tricies cen-tena extendebatur: nihil aliud nisi sex tantummodo libros & ipsos confusos, & iura vtilia in se perraro habentes,à voce magistra studiosi accipiebant, certe quarū quae ris iam desuetis, iam omnibus inutiis. In his autem sex libris Gaij noftrie Institutiones,& libris singulares quatuor,primus de illa vetere re vxoria , secundus de tutelis , & tertius nec non quartus de testamentis & legatis connumerabantur: quos nec rot*s per sequentes accipiebant,sed multas partes corum quasi superuacuas praeteribant.Et primi anni hoc opus legeribus tradebatur non secundum editi per petui ordinationem,sed pasim, & quasi per faturà collectum , vtile cum inutilibus mixtum , maxima parte inutilibus deputata. In secundo autem anno praepostera ordinatione habita, prima pars legu eis tradebatur,quibusdam certis titulis ab ea exceptis, cum erat enorme post Institutiones aliquod legere, quàm quod in legibus & primum positum est,& istá nuncupatione meruerit. Post eorum verò lectionem,neque illam continuam,(sed particularem,&ex magna parte inutilem constitutam,tituli alij eis tra debantur tam ex illa parte legum quæ de iudiciis nuncupatur,& ipsis non continuam ,sed raram vti-lium recitationem præbentibus, quasi cetero toto volumine inutili constituto: quàm ex illa quæ de re bus appellatur,septem libris semotis, & in his nul-tis partibus legentibus inviis, utpote non idoneis, neque aptissimis ad eruditionem constituntis. In ter-tio autem anno quod ex utroque volumine,id est de rebus vel de iudiciis,in secundo anno non erat tra-ditum, accipiebant secundum vicissitudine utriusque voluminis: & ad sublimissimum[?] Papinianum, eiúsque responsa iter eis aperiebatur. Et ex prædicta responsorum consummatione, quæ decimo & nono libro concludebatur, octo tantummodo libros acci-piebant: nec eorum totum corpus eis tradebatur, sed pauca ex multis, ea brevissima ex amplissimis: ut ad-huc sirientes[?] ab eis recederent. His igitur solis à professoribus traditis, Pauliana responsa per semet-ipsos recitabant: neque hæc in solidum,sed per im-perfectum, & iam quodammodo male consuetum inconsequentiæ cursum. Et hinc erat in quartum annum omnis antiquæ prudentiæ finis {4}: ut (si) quis ea quæ recitabant, enumerare malit, computatione habita inveniat ex tam immensa legum multitudine vix versuum sexaginta[?] millia eos vacuæ notionis perlegere: omnibus aliis deviis & incognitis constitutis. tutis. & tunc tantummodo ex aliqua minima parte recitandis, quotiens vel iudiciorum usus hoc fieri coegerit vel ipsi magistri legem aliquid ex his perlegere festinabatis, ut sit vobis aliquid amplius di-scipulorum peritia. Et hæc quidem fuerant antiquæ eruditionis monumenta, secundum quod & vestro testimonio confirmatur.
units.tr: Formerly, as your prudence also knows, from such a great multitude of laws, which extended to two thousand books and three hundred thousand verses, students received from the living voice of the teacher nothing but six books, themselves confused and seldom containing useful law, some of them now obsolete and all of them useless. Among these six books were counted Gaius's Institutes and four single books: the first on the old dotal law, the second on guardianships, and the third and fourth on wills and legacies.
