Students did not receive these in order, but passed over many parts of them as if superfluous. In the first year this work was taught to learners not according to the published arrangement, but haphazardly, as if gathered into a medley, useful things mixed with useless, the greater part being reckoned useless. In the second year, however, in a preposterous order, the first part of the laws was taught to them, with certain titles excepted, since it was an absurd thing to read after the Institutes anything that stands first among the laws and deserves that name. After this reading, which was not continuous but partial and for the most part useless, other titles were given to them, both from that part of the laws called de iudiciis, which offered not a continuous but a rare recital of useful matter, as if the rest of the volume were useless, and from that part called de rebus, with seven books set apart, in which many passages were unreadable for readers, being unsuited and not very apt for learning. In the third year, what had not been given in the second year from either volume, that is de rebus or de iudiciis, they received in turn from each volume, and a way was opened to them to the most sublime Papinian and his responses. From the completion of those responses, which ended in the nineteenth book, they received only eight books; nor was the whole body of them handed over, but a few out of many, and those very brief out of very ample ones, so that they still went away thirsty. With these alone taught by the professors, they recited the Pauline responses on their own, and not in full but imperfectly, in a course now somewhat badly accustomed to incoherence. And hence in the fourth year came the end of all ancient wisdom: so that anyone who prefers to count what they recited will find, on reckoning, that out of so immense a multitude of laws they scarcely read through some sixty thousand verses of empty meaning, all else being neglected and unknown, and only some very small part being recited, whenever the practice of the courts forced it or the masters themselves hurried to read some law from these, so that you might have some greater skill among your students. These, indeed, were the monuments of ancient learning, as your testimony confirms.

units.la: 2 ¶Nos vero tantam penuriam legum inventes, & hoc niserrimum[?] iudicantes, legitimos thesauros volentibus aperimus, quibus per vestrâ prudentiâ quodâmodo erogatis, ditis-simi legum oratores efficiantur discipuli. Et{b} primo {c}quidé anno nostras hauriat Institutiones,ex omni pene veterum Institutionum corpore elimatas, & ab omnibus turbidis fontibus in unum liquidum slagnum[?] con-riuatas ra per Tribonianum viri magnificum magistrum & exquæstore sacri palatij nostri & excosule, quàm duos e[?] vobis,id est Theophilum & Dorotheum facundifimos antecessores. In reliquā vero anni parte se-cundum optimam cōsequentiam primā segum par-tem eis tradi sancimus, quæ Græco vocabulo πρῶτα [?] nuncupatur, qua nihil est anterius: quia quod pri-mū " est, aliud ante se habere non potest. & hæc eis exordium & fine eruditionis primi anni esse decerni mus. Cuius auditores non volumus vetere tā friuolo quàm ridiculo cognomine Dupondios{a}appellari, sed Iustinianos nouos nuncupari, & hoc in omne futurū æuum obtinere cesemus: vt hi qui rudes adhuc legi-timæ scientiæ adspirent, & scita prioris anni acci-pere maluerint, nostrum nomen mereant: quia illico tradendum eis est primum volumen, quod nobis e-manauit auctoribus: antea enim dignum antiqua cōfusione legum cognomen habebat. cū autē leges iam clarè & dilucidè animis eorum tradendæ erat, ne-cesse erat eos & cognomine mutato fulgere,
units.tr: 2 Now we, finding such a great scarcity of laws and judging it most wretched, open the legitimate treasuries to those who wish, which by your prudence are dispensed in a certain way, so that the students become the richest orators of the laws. In the first year indeed we decree that they draw from our Institutes, refined from almost the whole body of the ancient Institutes and channelled from all turbid springs into one clear pool, by Tribonian, the magnificent man, master of offices, quaestor of our sacred palace and ex-consul, and by two of you, namely Theophilus and Dorotheus, most eloquent antecessores. For the rest of the year, in the best sequence, we decree that the first part of the laws be taught to them, which is called in Greek [πρῶτα], than which nothing is earlier, since what is first can have nothing before it. We decree that this shall be the beginning and the end of the learning of the first year. We do not wish its hearers to be called by the old cognomen, as frivolous as it is ridiculous, Dupondii, but to be called new Justinians, and we order that this shall hold for all future time. Thus those who are still rude and aspire to legitimate learning, and who prefer to receive the knowledge of the earlier year, may earn our name. For the first volume, which has issued from us as its authors, must be taught to them at once; before, it bore a cognomen fitting the old confusion of the laws. But since the laws had now to be handed on to their minds clearly and lucidly, it was necessary that they also shine under a changed cognomen.

units.la: 3 ¶ In secundo {b}autè anno, per què ex edicto eis nomë antea positum, & à nobis probatur, vel de iudiciis {c}li-bros septè, vel de rebus octo[?] {d}accipere eos sancim, secundū quod téporis vicissitudo indulserit, quam intactā observari præcipimus, sed cofdé[?] libros de iu-diciis vel de rebus totos, & per suā cōsequentiā accipiant, nullo penitus ex his derelicto: quia omnia no-ua pulchritudine sunt decorata, nullo inutili, nullo desueto in his penitus inveniendo. Alterutri autem eorudê volumini, id est de iudiciis vel de reb̄[?] adiu-gi in secundi anni audietiā volumus quatuor libros singulares, quos ex omni cōpositione quattuorde-cim librorū excerpsimus. ex collectiōne quidē tripartiri voluminis, quod {e}dotibus cōpofuim̄.{f}vno libro excerpto: ex {f} duob. aut de tutelis & curationib. vno: vt ex gemino volumine de {g}testamentis, vno: & ex septem libris de legatis & fideicommissis, & quæ circa ea sunt, simili modo {h}vno tátúm libro. his igitur quatuor libros, qui in primordiis singularum memoratarū compositionum positi sunt, tantummodo à vobis eis tradi sancimus, ceteris decem oportuno tempore conseruandis: quia neque possibile est, neque anni secundi tépus sufficit ad istorū quatuor decim librorum magistra voce eis tradeudorū recitationem.
units.tr: 3 In the second year, however, according to the name previously given to it by edict and approved by us, we command that they receive either seven books de iudiciis or eight de rebus, as the vicissitude of time may allow, which we order to be kept intact. Let them receive those books de iudiciis or de rebus entire and in their sequence, with nothing left out, since all are adorned with new beauty, and no useless or obsolete matter is found in them at all. To either of those volumes, that is de iudiciis or de rebus, we wish four single books added to the hearing of the second year, which we have excerpted from the whole composition of fourteen books. From the collection of the three-part volume, which was composed on dowries, one book is excerpted; from the two books on guardianships and curations, one; likewise from the twofold volume on testaments, one; and from the seven books on legacies and fideicommissa and what is connected with them, similarly only one book. We therefore decree that these four books, which stand at the beginning of each of the aforesaid compositions, be taught to them by you alone, the other ten being reserved for a suitable time. For it is neither possible, nor does the time of the second year suffice, for all fourteen of these books to be recited to them by the living voice of the teacher.

units.la: 4 ¶ Tertij {i}insuper anni doctrina talē ordinem sortiatur, ut sive libros de iudiciis, sive de rebus secundum vices legere eis fors tulerit: concurrat eis tripartita legum singulariū dispositio: & in primis liber {k}singularis ad hypothecariā formulā, quem oportuno loco, in quo de hypothecis loqui-mur, posuimus: vt cùm ænula[?] sit pignoraticiis actionibus quæ in libris de rebus positæ sunt, non abhorreat eorum vicinitatem: cum circa eaidem res ambabus pene idem studium est. Et post eundem librum singulare alius liber similiter eis aperiatur, quem ad edictum ædilium, & de redhibitoria actione, & de evictionibus, necnon duplæ stipulatione co posuimus, cum enim quæ pro emptionibus & venditionibus legibus cauta sunt, in libris de rebus præfulgent: hæ autem omnes quas diximus definitiones in vltima parte prioris edicti fuerant positæ: necessario eas in anteriorem locum transtulimus, ne a venditionibus, quarum quasi ministræ sunt, vicinitate vlterius deuagentur. Et hos tres libros cum acutissimi Papiniani lectione tradendos posuimus, quorum volumina in tertio anno studiosi recitabant, non ex omni eorum corpore, sed sparsim pauca ex multis & in hac parte accipientes. Vobis autem pulcherrimus Papinianus non solum ex responsis quæ in decem & nouem libros compositæ fuerant, sed etiam ex libris septem & triginta quæstionum, & gemino volumine definitionum, nec nō de adulteriis, & pene omni eius expositione in omni nostrorum Digestorū ordinatione præfulgens propriis partibus præclarus fui recitationem præbebit. Ne autem tertij anni auditores, quos Papinianistas vocant, nomé & festiuitatem eius amittere videantur: ipse iterum in tertium annum per bellisimam machinationem in troductus est. librum enim hypothecariæ ex primor-diis plenum eiusdem maximi Papiniani fecimus lectione, vt & nomen ex eo habeant, & Papinianistæ vocentur, & eius reminiscentes, & lætificentur & fe-stum diem, quem cùm primum leges eius acceperunt, celebrare solebant, peragant: & maneat viti su-blimisimi præfectorij Papiniani & per hoc in æternum memoria, hócque termino tertij anni doctrina concludatur. § ¶ Sed quia solitum est anni quarti studiosos Græco & cófueto quodam vocabulo λύτας[?] appellari: habeant quidem si maluerint hoc cognomen: pro responsis autem prudentissimi Pauli, quæ antea ex libris viginti tribus vix in decem & octo recitabant, per iam expositam confusionem eos legentes: decem libros singulares qui ex quatuordecim, quos antea enumerauimus, supersunt, studeat lectitare: multo maioris & amplioris prudentiæ ex eis thesaurum consecuturi, quàm quem ex Paulianis habeant respondeant [?] Et ita omnis ordo librorum singularium à nobis compositus & in decem & septem libros partitus eorum animis imponetur: quem in duabus Digestorum partibus posuimus, id est, qui arta & quinta, secundum septem partium distributionem, & quod iam primis verbis orationis nostræ posuimus, verum inueniatur: vt ex triginta sex librorum recitatione fiat iuuenes perfecti, & ad omne opus legitimum instructi, & nostro tempore non indigni, duabus aliis partibus, id est sexta & septima nostrorum Digestorum, quæ in quatuordecim libros compositæ sunt, eisdem positis, vt possint postea eos & legere, & in iudiciis offendere. Quibus si bene se imbuerint, & in quinti anni, quo cupantur, metas, constitutione codicem tam legere quàm subtiliter intelligere studeant: nihil eis legitimæ scientiæ deerit, sed omnem ab initio vsque ad finem suis animis ampleciantur, & quod pene in alia nulla euenit arte, cum etsi vilissimæ sint, omnes tamen infinitæ sunt, hæc sola scientia habeat finem mirabilem, in præsenti tempore à nobis fortia.
units.tr: 4 ¶ Moreover, the teaching of the third year shall have this order: whether the students happen by lot to read the books on judgments or those on individual matters, they shall take up the threefold arrangement of the single laws together. First, the single book on the hypothecary formula, which we placed in the appropriate position where we speak of hypothecs, shall be read, so that, since it is a rival to the pledge actions set out in the books on things, its proximity to them is not out of place, for both concern nearly the same subject matter. After that same book, another single book shall similarly be opened to them, which we have put together on the aedile's edict, the action for rescission of sale, eviction, and the double stipulation. For since the laws' provisions on purchases and sales shine forth in the books on things, and all the definitions we have mentioned had been placed at the end of the earlier edict, we have of necessity transferred them to an earlier position, so that they do not wander too far from the sales to which they are, as it were, servants. We have decided that these three books are to be taught together with the reading of the most acute Papinian. The students of the third year used to recite their volumes, not from the whole body of his work, but taking a few passages here and there from many. For you, the most excellent Papinian, shining forth not only from the responsa composed in nineteen books, but also from the seven-and-thirty books of Questions, the twofold volume of Definitions, the books On Adulteries, and nearly his whole exposition, placed throughout the entire arrangement of our Digest, will provide a reading that is distinguished in its own parts. Lest the auditors of the third year, whom they call Papinianists, seem to lose both their name and their festivity, we have brought him back into the third year by a most beautiful contrivance. For we have made them read the book on hypothecs, which is full of the first principles of that greatest Papinian, so that they may have their name from it and be called Papinianists, and may remember him, rejoice, and keep the festive day which they used to celebrate when they first received his laws; and the memory of that most sublime prefect of the praetorian guard, Papinian, shall remain for ever. Here the teaching of the third year is brought to a close. § ¶ But since students of the fourth year are customarily called by a Greek and common term, [λύτας], let them have this surname if they wish. In place of the responsa of the most prudent Paul, which formerly they used to recite, hardly eighteen out of twenty-three books, and which, through the confusion already described, reading them was a burden, let them study the ten single books that remain out of the fourteen we listed before. They will thus obtain from them a treasure of much greater and wider prudence than they would have from the Paulinian writings. And so the whole order of the single books which we have composed and divided into seventeen books shall be imposed on their minds. We have placed it in the two parts of the Digest, namely the fourth and fifth, according to the division into seven parts; and what we have stated in the very first words of our address proves true. Thus, from the reading of thirty-six books, young men shall be made perfect, and instructed for every lawful task, and not unworthy of our age. The remaining two parts, namely the sixth and seventh of our Digest, which are composed in fourteen books, shall be set before them afterwards, so that they may both read them and encounter them in lawsuits. If they steep themselves well in these, and in the period of the fifth year, the term set for them, they strive to read the Code as well as to understand it thoroughly, nothing of lawful knowledge will be lacking to them; they will embrace it entire from beginning to end. And this one science, which in almost no other art occurs, though the lesser parts are of little worth, all of them are nevertheless endless, shall have a wondrous end, as we have now set forth.

units.la: 6 ¶ Disciputi igitur, omnibus e s legi i nis arcanis referatis, nihil habeant abscondtitum: sed omnibus perfectis, quæ nobis per Triboniani viri excelsi ministerium, cæterorumque compositæ sunt, & oratores maximi, & iustitiæ satellites inueniantur, & iudiciorum optimi tam athletæ quàm gubernatores in omni loco & quoque felices. 7 ¶ Hæc autem tria volumina à nobis compositi tradi eis tam in regiis vrbibus, quà in Berytienfium pulcherrima ciuitate, quam & f legum nutricem bene quis appellet, tamen modo volumus, quod iam & à retro principibus constitutum est, & non in aliis locis quæ à maiori bus tale non meruerint priuilegium, quia audiuimus etiam in Alexandrina plendidissima ciuitate, & in Cæsarientium, & in aliis, quosdam imperitos homines deuagare, & doctrinam disciplinis adulteri nam tradere. quos sub hac interminatione ab hoc conamine repellimus, vt si aliquid fuerint in posterum in hoc perpetrare, & extra vrbes regias, & Berytiensium metropolim hoc facere, denarum librarum auro [illegible, ~3 letters].
units.tr: 6 ¶ Therefore, students, let nothing remain hidden from you; reveal to yourselves all the secrets of the laws. When you have been made perfect in all the works composed by us, through the ministry of the most excellent Tribonian and the others, then may you be found both the greatest orators and the guardians of justice, and the best contenders and steersmen of judgments, prosperous in every place and at every time. 7 ¶ We wish these three volumes composed by us to be taught in the royal cities as well as in the most beautiful city of the Berytians, which one might well call the nurse of the laws. We wish this, as was already established by earlier emperors, and not in other places which, not being of such standing, did not earn this privilege. For we have heard that certain unskilled men in the most splendid city of Alexandria, in Caesarea, and elsewhere, wander about and corrupt the teaching of the disciplines by teaching it. We repel them from this attempt under this threat: if in future they dare to commit this offence, and to do it outside the royal cities and the metropolis of the Berytians, they shall pay a fine of ten pounds of gold [illegible, about three letters].

units.la: Pro omni experimento sufficit medico ad commendandum artis authoritatem, si Alexandriæ se dixerit eruditum. ri poena plectentur[?], & reiiciantur ab ea civitate, in qua non leges docent, sed in leges committunt.
units.tr: For a physician, a claim to have been trained in Alexandria is enough, as a proof of all his skill, to recommend the authority of his art. They shall be punished, and expelled from that city, in which they do not teach the laws but commit crimes against them.

units.la: 8 ¶Illud autem, quod jam tum[?] ab initio hoc opus mandantes in nostra oratione,& post completum in alia nostri numinis constitutione scripsimus, & nunc utiliter ponimus: ut nemo audeat eorum qui libros conscribunt,{4} sigla in his,ponere, & per compendiu ipsi legum interpretationi vel compositioni maximum adferre discrimen: sciturisomnibus librariis qui hoc in posterum commiserint,quod post crimi-nalem poenam no eius,si nescienti dederint,inferre compelleutur: cum & ipse qui talem librum comparauerit, nihilo eum habebit,nemine judice ex tali libro fieri recitationem concedente,sed pro non scripto eum haberi disponente.
units.tr: 8 ¶ As for the matter which we ordered from the beginning of this work in our address, and afterwards wrote in another constitution of our divinity once it was completed, and which we now usefully set down again: let no one of those who write books dare to place abbreviations (signs) in them, and so by shorthand bring the greatest danger to the interpretation or composition of the laws. Let all booksellers who commit this in future know that, after the criminal penalty, if they have sold such a book to someone unaware, they shall be compelled to pay its price. And the person who obtained such a book shall have nothing from it, since no judge may permit it to be read in court from such a book, and he shall order that it be regarded as unwritten.

units.la: 9 ¶Illud vero satis necessarium constitutum cum summa interminatione ed cimus, ut nemo audeat neque in hac splendidissima civitate, neque in Berytiensium pulcherrimo oppido ex his qui legitima perægunt studia, indignos & pessimos, immo magis serviles, & quorum effectus injuria est,ludos{b} exercere, & alia crimina vel in ipsos professores, vel in socios suos,& maxime in eos qui rudes ad recitationem legum peruenient, perpetrare.{c} quis enim c ludos appellet eos, ex quibus crimina oriuntur? hoc etenim fieri nullo patimur modo: sed optimo ordini in nostris temporibus & hanc partem tradimus, & toto postero transmittimus saeculo:cum oportet prius anima, & postea lingua sic eruditos. 10 ¶Et haec omnia in hac quidem florentissima civitate vir excelsus praefectus huius almae urbis tam observare quam vindicare, prout delicti tam juvenum quam scriptorum qualitas exegerit, curae habebit. In Berytiensium autem civitate tam vir clarissimus praeses Phoenicae maritimae, quam beatissimus ejusdem civitatis Episcopus, & legum professores.
units.tr: 9 ¶ We have also decreed, with the utmost threat, something very necessary: let no one dare, in this most splendid city or in the most beautiful town of the Berytians, among those who pursue the study of the laws legitimately, to practise unworthy and wicked games, or rather servile ones whose effect is injurious, nor to commit other crimes either against their own teachers or against their fellow students, and especially against those who arrive raw for the recitation of the laws. For who would call those things games which give rise to crimes? We do not allow this to happen in any way. We hand down this part too to the excellent order of our own times, and we pass it on to the whole succeeding age, since the soul ought first to be educated and only afterwards the tongue. 10 ¶ And all these things, in this most flourishing city, the most excellent prefect of this nourishing city will take care to observe and to punish, according to the nature of the offence, whether committed by the young men or by the scribes. In the city of the Berytians, the most illustrious governor of Phoenicia Maritima, as well as the most blessed bishop of the same city, and the teachers of the laws, shall have this care.

units.la: 11 ¶ Incipite igitur legum doctrinam eis Dei gubernatione tradere,& viam aperire quam nos invenimus: quatenus fiant optimi justitiae & reipublicae ministri, & vos m ximi decus in omne saeculum sequatur, quia vestris temporibus talis legum inventa est permutatio , qualem apud Homerum patrem {e} omnis virtutis Glaucus & Diomedes inter se faciunt dissimilia permutantes: {f} χρύσεα χαλκεῖα, [illegible, ~12 letters] h. e.
units.tr: 11 ¶ Begin therefore to teach the doctrine of the laws to them, under God's guidance, and open the way which we have discovered, so that they may become the best ministers of justice and the commonwealth, and so that honour may follow you for ever, since in your times such an exchange of the laws has been found as Glaucus and Diomedes made with each other in Homer, father of all virtue, exchanging unlike things: [χρύσεα χαλκεῖα], gold for bronze, that is [illegible, about twelve letters] h. e.
[illegible in the scan]

units.la: Quæ omnia obtinere sancimus in omne xuum ab omnibus tam professoribus quàm legū auditoribus, & librariis & ipsis & iudicibus obseruanda. Data xvij. Kalend. Januarias Constantinopoli,domino nostro Iustiniano perpetuo Augusto ter consule. 533.
units.tr: We decree that all these things shall hold good for ever and be observed by all, by teachers as well as by hearers of the laws, by booksellers, and by judges themselves. Given at Constantinople on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the third consulship of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus. 533.

units.la: DE EMENDATIONE codicis Domini Iustiniani & secunda {″} eius editione ad senatum urbis Constantinopolitanæ.
units.tr: On the Emendation of the Code of the Lord Justinian and its second edition, addressed to the Senate of the city of Constantinople.

units.la: Imperator Cæsar, Flauius, IVSTINIANVS, Alamanicus, Gothicus, Fracicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pius, felix, inclytus, victor ac triumphator, semper Augustus, Senatui urbis Constantinopolitanæ S.
units.tr: Justinian, Emperor, Caesar, Flavius, Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pious, fortunate, renowned, victor and triumphator, ever Augustus, to the Senate of the city of Constantinople, greetings.

units.la: ORDI nobis est, Patres conscripti, semper nostri animi curas rebus communibus auidissimè impedere, ut nihil à nobis inceptū, imperfectū relinquatur. Igitur in primordio nostri imperij sacratissimas constitutiones quæ in diuersa volumina fuerant dispersæ, & quàm plurima similitudine necnon diuersitate vacillabant, in unum corpus colligere, omníque vitio purgare proposuimus: & hoc iam per viros excelsos, & facundissimos perfectum est, & à nobis postea confirmatum: quod geminæ cōstitutiones nostræ, quæ ante positæ sunt, ostendunt.
units.tr: It is always our way, Conscript Fathers, that the cares of our mind most eagerly hinder us from public affairs, so that nothing begun by us is left unfinished. Therefore, at the start of our reign, we resolved to gather the most sacred constitutions, which had been scattered through various volumes and wavered between many likenesses and differences, into a single body, and to purge them of every fault. This has now been completed by men of distinction and eloquence and afterwards confirmed by us, as our two earlier constitutions, issued beforehand, show.

units.la: ¶ Postea verò cum vetus ius cōsiderandum recepimus, tam quinquaginta {a}decisiones fecimus, quàs alias ad commodum propositi operis pertinentes plurimas constitutiones promulgauimus: quibus maximus antiquarum legum articulus emendatus & coarctatus est, omnéq. ius antiquū superuacua prolixitate liberum atque enucleatum in nostris Institutionibus & Digestis reddidimus.
units.tr: Afterwards, when we took up the consideration of the old law, we also made fifty decisions and promulgated many constitutions pertinent to the purpose of our work. By these the greatest part of the ancient laws was emended and condensed, and we rendered all the ancient law free and clear of superfluous prolixity in our Institutes and Digests.

units.la: ¶Sed cùm nouellæ {b}nostræ tâ decisiones {c}quàm constitutiones quæ post nostri Codicis confectione latæ sunt, extra corpus eiusdem Codicis diuagabantur, & nostram prouidentiam nostrumque consilium exigere videbantur: quippe cùm earum quædam ex emersis postea factis aliquam meliore consilio permutationem vel emendationem desiderabant necessarium nobis visum est per Tribonianum virum ex celsum magistrum exquisitore & exconsule legitimum operis nostri ministrum, necnon virum magnificum quaestorem & Berutiensium legum doctorem Dorotheum, Mennam insuper & Constantinum & Ioannem viros eloquentissimos togatos fori amplissimae sedis, easdem constitutiones nostras decerpere, & in singulas discretas capitula, ad perfectarum constitutionum soliditatem competentibus supponere titulis, & prioribus constitutionibus eas adgregare.
units.tr: But since our novels, both the decisions and the constitutions enacted after the completion of our Code, were wandering outside the body of that Code and seemed to demand our providence and counsel, since some of them, owing to later events, needed change or emendation by better counsel, it seemed necessary to us to have Tribonian, the most exquisite magister and former consul, the legitimate minister of our work, and also the magnificent quaestor and teacher of the laws at Berytus, Dorotheus, together with Menna, Constantine and John, most eloquent men of the forum of the most distinguished seat, pick out these constitutions of ours, divide them into individual chapters, assign them under suitable titles for the soundness of the perfected constitutions, and add them to the earlier constitutions.

units.la: 3 Supradictis itaque magnificis & prudentissimis viris permisimus hæc omnia facere: & si qua emendatione opus foret, hanc facerent non ritubante animo, sed nostra auctoritate freti: constitutiones vero superfluas, vel ex posterioribus sanctionibus nostris iam vacuatas, vel si quæ similes vel contrariæ inuenirentur, circumducere, & à proprio Codicis congregatione separare: & tam imperfectas replere, quam nocte obscuritatis obductas[?], nova elimationis[?] luce detegere: ut undique non solum Institutionum & Digestorum via dilucida & aperta pateat, sed etiam constitutionum nostri Codicis plenum iubar omnibus clarum reat: nulla penitus nec simili, ne diuersa, nec inusitata relicta constitutione: cùm nemini venit in dubium, quod repetita prælectio probauit, hoc satis lidum[?], satisque esse formosum. In antiquis etenim libris non solum primas editiones, sed etiam secundas (quas repetitas {b} prælectiones veteres nominabant) subsecutas esse inuenimus: quod ex libris Vlpiani viri prudentissimi ad Sabinum scriptis promptum erat quærentibus reperire.
units.tr: 3 We therefore permitted the aforesaid magnificent and most prudent men to do all these things. If any emendation was needed, they were to make it not with a hesitant mind but relying on our authority; and to cut out superfluous constitutions, either already annulled by our later sanctions, or, if any similar or contrary ones were found, to remove them and separate them from the proper gathering of the Code; and to fill up the imperfect ones, and to bring to light with a new elucidation those covered by the night of obscurity. Thus not only the way through the Institutes and Digests would lie clear and open on every side, but also the full radiance of the constitutions of our Code would shine clear to all, no constitution being left at all, whether similar lest it be diverse, or unused. For no one doubts, as the repeated reading has proved, that this is sufficiently clear and sufficiently fair. In ancient books we find that not only the first editions but also the second (which the ancients called repeated readings) followed; this was readily found by those seeking it in the books of Ulpian, a most prudent man, written to Sabinus.

units.la: 4 His igitur omnibus ex nostra confectis sententia, commemoratus Iustinianeus Codex à prædictis gloriosissimis & facundissimis viris purgatus & candidus factus, omnibus ex nostra iussione & circumductis, & additis, & repletis, nec non transformatis, nobis oblatus est: & iussimus [?]secundo eum ex integro conscribi, non ex prio[?]re compositione, sed ex repetita prælectione: & eum nostri numinis auctoritate nitentem, in omnibus iudiciis solum quantum ad diuales constitutiones pertinet, frequentari ex die quarto Kalendarum Ianuarij,quarti nostri felicissimi consulatus & Paulini vi-ri clarissimi: nulla alia extra corpus eiusdē Codicis constitutione legenda: nisi postea varia rerū natura aliquid nouum creauerit, quod nostra sanctione indi geat. Hoc etenim nemini dubium est, quod si quid in posterum melius inueniatur, & ad constitutionem ne-cessario sit redigendum, hoc à nobis & constituatur, & in aliam congregationem referatur, quæ Nouell.-rum nomine constitutionū significetur. § Repeti-ta itaque iussione nemini in posterum concedimus vel ex decisionibus nostris, vel ex aliis constitutionibus, quas antea fecimus, vel ex prima Iustinianei Co-dicis editione aliquid rec tare: sed quod in præsenti purgato & renouato Codice nostro scriptum inuenitur, hoc tantum-modo in omnibus rebus & indiciis & obtineat, & recitetur, cuius scripturam ad similitudinem nostrarum Institutionū & Digestorum {4}sine vlla signorum dubietate cōscribi iussimus: vt omne quod à nobis compositum est, hoc & in scriptura, & in ipsa sanctione purum atque dilucidum clareat. li-cet ex hac causa in ampliorem numerum summa hu-ius Codicis redacta est.
units.tr: 4 Having made all these arrangements according to our judgment, the aforesaid Code of Justinian was purged and made bright by the said most glorious and eloquent men, and was presented to us with everything altered by our command, added to, filled up and transformed. We ordered it to be written out anew from the beginning, not from the earlier composition but from the repeated reading, and, relying on the authority of our divine power, to be used in all courts, so far as it concerns the divine constitutions, from the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth year of our most fortunate consulship and that of Paulinus, a most distinguished man. No other constitution outside the body of this Code is to be read, unless the varied nature of things later creates something new that needs our sanction. For no one doubts that if anything better is discovered in future, and must necessarily be brought into a constitution, it will be established by us and placed in another collection, which is designated by the name of Novels. Therefore, with this order repeated, we grant to no one in future to cite anything either from our decisions, or from other constitutions made by us before, or from the first edition of the Code of Justinian. Rather, whatever is found written in our present purged and renewed Code shall alone hold and be recited in all matters and courts. We have ordered its text to be written out, in the manner of our Institutes and Digests, without any doubtfulness of signs, so that everything composed by us may be clear and lucid both in the writing and in the sanction itself. Although for this reason the sum of this Code has been brought into a larger number.

units.la: {6} ¶ Vt igitur sanctissimi & florentissimi patres nostri labores vobis manifesti fiant, & per omne tempus obtineat, hanc præsentem legem ad frequentissimum ordinem vestrum duximus destinandam. Datum xxvii. Kalend. Decemb. Constantinopoli, Domino Iustiniano PP. A. IIII. & Theodoto Paulino Viris Clarif. Cos. 534.
units.tr: {6} So that the labours of our most holy and flourishing fathers may be made manifest to you and may hold good for all time, we have decided to send this present law to your most numerous order. Given at Constantinople, twenty-seven days before the Kalends of December, in the fourth consulship of our lord Justinian, Perpetual Augustus, and in the consulship of Theodotus Paulinus, distinguished men. 534.

units.la: DE ORIGINE IVRIS & omnium Magistratuum, & successione prudentium
units.tr: On the origin of law and of all magistrates, and the succession of the jurists

units.la: TIT. II, Gaius libro primo ad legem 12. tabularum.
units.tr: TIT. II, Gaius, book 1, on the law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: ACTVRVS legum vetustarum inter pretationem, necessario prius ab vrbis initiis repetendum exi-stimaui: non quia velim verbosos commentarios facere, sed * quod in omnibus rebus animadverto id perfectum esse, quod ex omnibus suis partibus constaret. Et certe cuiusque rei potissima pars principium est. Deinde si in foro causas dicetibus nefas, ut ita dixerim, videtur esse, nulla praefatione facta, iudici rem exponere: quanto magis interpretationem promittentibus inconueniens erit, omissis initiis, atque origine non repetita, atque illotis, ut ita dixerim, manibus, protinus materiam interpretationis tractare? namque, nisi fallor, istae praefationes & libentius nos ad lectionem propositae materiae producunt: & cum ibi venerimus, evidentiore praestant intellectum.
units.tr: I am about to interpret the ancient laws, and I think I must first go back to the beginnings of the city. I do not do this because I wish to write long-winded commentaries, but because I notice that in all things what is perfect is that which is made up of all its parts, and certainly the chief part of anything is its beginning. Moreover, if it seems improper for advocates pleading cases in the forum to lay the matter before the judge without any preface, how much more unsuitable is it for those who promise an interpretation to begin the subject at once, leaving out the beginnings and not going back to the origin, as it were with unwashed hands? For, unless I am mistaken, such prefaces both lead us more willingly into reading the matter proposed, and, once we have arrived there, give a clearer understanding of it.
2. Pomponius, in his single book, the Enchiridion.

units.la: Cap. I. De origine & progressu iuris Romani.
units.tr: Chap. I. On the origin and progress of Roman law.

units.la: Manus Regia. 1. leges Regiae 2: Ius incertum 3: Leges XII tabul. 4: Disputatio fori seu prudentium interpretatio 5. Legis actiones 6. Ius Flavianum 7. Plebiscita 8. Senatusconsulta 9. Edicta pretorum 10. Principum constitutiones 11. & 12.
units.tr: Regal power. 1. Royal laws. 2. Uncertain law. 3. The Twelve Tables. 4. The debate of the forum, or interpretation by the jurists. 5. The legis actiones. 6. The Flavian law. 7. Plebiscites. 8. Senatus consulta. 9. Edicts of the praetors. 10. Constitutions of the princes. 11. and 12.

units.la: NEcessarium itaque nobis videtur ipsius iuris originem, atque processum demonstrare, 2 quidem initio ciuitatis nostrae populus sine lege cer- ta,sine iure certo primum agere instituit:omniaque manu {*}à regibus gubernabantur.
units.tr: It seems necessary to us, therefore, to demonstrate the origin and development of law itself. At the beginning of our state, the people first began to act without any fixed law and without any certain right, and everything was governed by the kings by their own hand.

units.la: 2 ¶Postea,aucta ad aliquem modum ciuitate, ipsum Romulum tradi-tur populum in triginta {b}partes diuisisse:quas partes Curias appellauit: propterea quod tunc reipublicae {c}curam per sententias partium earum expediebat.Et ita leges quasdam & ipse curiatas {d}ad populum {e}tu-lit.tulerunt & sequetes reges. quae omnes cōscriptae exstant in libro Sexti Papirij:qui fuit illis temporibus,quibus Superbus Demarati Corinthij filius{f},ex principalibus viris. Is liber, vt diximus, appellatur ius ciuile Papirianum nō quia Papirius de suo quicquam ibi adiecit:sed quod leges sine ordine latas in vnum composuit.
units.tr: Afterwards, when the state had grown to some extent, it is related that Romulus himself divided the people into thirty parts, which he called curiae, because the care of the commonwealth was then carried out through the opinions of those parts. In this way he himself brought some laws, curiate, before the people, and the kings who followed also brought laws. All of these are extant in writing in the book of Sextus Papirius, who lived in the times when Superbus, son of Demaratus of Corinth, was among the leading men. This book, as we have said, is called the Papirian civil law, not because Papirius added anything of his own there, but because he gathered into one work laws that had been passed without order.

units.la: 3 ¶Exactis deinde regibus, lege & Tribunacia omnes leges hae exoleuerunt : iterumque coepit populus Roman{g} incerto magis iure, & consuetudine cli {h}, quàm per latam legem: idque prope viginti annis passus est.
units.tr: After the kings were expelled, all these laws fell into disuse through the Tribunician law, and the Roman people began again to live rather under an uncertain law and by custom, and not by a law that had been passed. It endured this for nearly twenty years.

units.la: 4 ¶Postea ne diutiùs hoc fieret:placuit publica auctoritate decē constitui viros,per quos peterentur leges à Graecis ciuitatibus,& ciuitas fundaretur legibus. quas in tabulas eboreas {k}perscriptas pro Rostris cōposuerint, vt possint leges apertius percipi. datumq. est eis ius eo anno in ciuitate summum:vti leges & corrigerer, si opus esset, & interpretarentur: neque prouocatio ab eis,sicut à reliquis magistratibus,sieret. Qui ipsi animaduerterunt aliquid deesse istis primis legibus: ideóque sequenti anno alias duas ad easdem tabulas adiecerunt.& ita ex accidentia {i}appellatae sunt leges duodecim tabularum. quarum ferendarum auctore fuisse decemuiris Hermodorum quèdam Ephesium, exulantem in Italia,quidam {m}retulerunt.
units.tr: Afterwards, so that this should not continue any longer, it was resolved by public authority to appoint ten men, through whom laws would be sought from the Greek states, and the state would be founded on laws. They drew up the laws they had written on ivory tablets, set up in front of the Rostra, so that the laws might be understood more openly. In that year they were given supreme authority in the city, to correct the laws if need be and to interpret them, and there was no appeal from them, as there was from the other magistrates. These men themselves noticed that something was lacking in those first laws, and so in the following year they added two more tables to the same set. And thus the laws were called the Twelve Tables from these additions. Some have reported that the author of the laws drawn up by the decemvirs was a certain Hermodorus of Ephesus, who was living in exile in Italy.

units.la: 5 ¶His legibus latis,coepit,vt {n}naturaliter euenire solet,vt interpretatio desideraret prudentium {o}auctoritate necessariam esse disputationem{p} fori. Haec disputatio,&hoc ius,quod sine scripto venit,compositum à &·ἀξονες vocabantur.
units.tr: Once these laws had been passed, as usually happens naturally, interpretation came to need a disputation of the forum, made necessary by the authority of the jurists. This disputation, and this law which came into being without writing, put together by the jurists, were called axones [ἄξονες].

units.la: &·ἀξονες vocabantur.Plut.in Solon.adde Naucl.9.c.15.in fine. ἐκ ἀ-reas.Halicar.10.Liuius 3: Diod:l.12.d.8.ff.ad Iul.peculat.34.Plini.9: ebore multis in rebus vsi veteres. Nam Quintilianus (ib.4.in Trium pho Caesaris Eborea oppida fuisse translata ait. {i} i. accidenti.
units.tr: axones [ἄξονες] were so called. Plutarch, in Solon; add Naucler., book 9, chap. 15, at the end. Halicarnassus, book 10; Livy, book 3; Diodorus, book 12; D., on the Lex Julia peculatus, 34; Pliny, book 9: the ancients used ivory in many things. For Quintilian (book 4) says, in his Triumph of Caesar, that the ivory towns were transferred. {i} i.e. accidental.

units.la: {m} Cicero Tusc:Plin.34: Strabo.14. {n} hinc colligescinatura pugnare statuta, quae interpretationes legum vetat. {o} non Grammaticorum tantum. {p} sic restituit Goueanus.1.var.24.coepit(v.n.e.f.v.i.desiderat p.auctoritatem) necessar.a esse disputatio fori. prudentibus,propria parte aliqua non appellatur,vt cæteræ partes iuris suis nominibus designantur, datis propriis nominibus cæteris partib9: sed comuni nomine appellatur ius ciuile.
units.tr: {m} Cicero, Tusculan Disputations; Pliny, 34; Strabo, 14. {n} Hence it is gathered that the nature of statutes is to fight against the interpretations of laws, which forbids them. {o} Not of grammarians only. {p} Goveanus restores it thus, Var. 1.24: the disputation of the forum was made necessary by authority. Prudentibus [of the jurists]; it is not called by any proper name, as the other parts of law are designated by their own names, the other parts being given their proper names, but it is called by the common name of civil law.

units.la: ¶ Deinde ex his legibus,eodem tempore fere,actiones copofitae sunt[?]: quibus inter se homines disceptarent. quas actiones ne populus, prout vellet, institueret: certas solemnesque esse voluerunt, & appellatur haec pars iuris, legis actiones,||id est legitimæ actiones.||Et ita eodem pene tempore tria haec iura nata sunt:leges{4} duodecim tabularum:ex his fluere cœpit ius ciuile: ex iisdem legis actiones compositæ sunt.Omnium tamen {b}haru & in terpretandi scientia,& actiones {c}, apud collegium Pontificum erant:ex quibus constituebatur, quis quoquo anno præesse priuatis {d} & fere populus annis prope centum hac consuetudine visus est.
units.tr: Then, from these laws, at about the same time, actions were framed by which men might contend with one another. So that the people should not set up these actions as they pleased, they wanted them to be fixed and solemn, and this part of the law is called legis actiones, that is, lawful actions. Thus at almost the same time three bodies of law were born: the laws of the Twelve Tables; from these civil law began to flow; and from the same source the legis actiones were composed. Yet knowledge both of interpreting all of these and of the actions lay with the college of pontiffs, and from them it was established who should preside over private suits each year; and for nearly a hundred years the people seem to have kept to this custom.

units.la: 7 ¶Postea cum Appius Claudi9 propositisset, & ad formam redegisset has actiones:Gnæus {e} Flauius,scriba eius,libertini filius subreptu libru populo tradidit.&adeo gratu fuit id munus populo, vt tribunus plebis fieret, & senator, & ædilis curulis. hic liber,qui actiones continet, appellatur ius ciuile Flauianum:sicut ille,ius ciuile Papirianum.nanec Gnæus Flauius de suo quicquam adiecit libro.Augescente ciuitate, quia deerant quædam genera agendi,nō post multum temporis spatium Sextus AElius alias actiones composuit:& libru populo dedit, qui appellatur ius AElianum.
units.tr: Afterwards, when Appius Claudius had made these actions public and reduced them to a form, Gnaeus Flavius, his scribe, the son of a freedman, stole the book and handed it over to the people. This gift was so welcome to the people that he became tribune of the plebs, senator, and curule aedile. This book, which contains the actions, is called the Flavian civil law, just as that other is called the Papirian civil law; for Gnaeus Flavius added nothing of his own to the book. As the state grew, and certain kinds of action were lacking, not long afterwards Sextus Aelius composed other actions and gave a book to the people; it is called the Aelian law.

units.la: 8 ¶Deinde cum esset in ciuitate lex duodecim tabularum, & ius ciuile:essent & legis actiones:euenit, vt plebs in discordia cum patribus peruenirer,& secederet, sibi que iura constitueret, quæ iura, plebiscita vocantur. Mox cum revocata est plebs: quia multæ discordiæ nascebantur de his plebis scitis, pro legibus placuit & ea obseruari, lege {f} Hortensia: & ita facta est , vt inter plebis scita, & lege species constituendi interessent: potestas [autem] eadem esset.
units.tr: Then, since in the state there were the law of the Twelve Tables and civil law, and there were also the legis actiones, it happened that the plebs fell into dispute with the patricians and seceded, and made laws for themselves; these are called plebiscites. Afterwards, when the plebs was recalled, because many quarrels arose over these plebiscites, it was decided by the Hortensian law that they too should be observed as laws. And so it came about that between plebiscites and laws there was a difference in the manner of enactment, but the power was the same.

units.la: 9 ¶Deinde quia difficile plebs conuenire cœpit,populo [certe] multo difficilius in tanta turba hominum:necessitas ipsa cura reipublicæ ad senatum deduxit. Ita cœpit senatus se interponere:& quid quid constituisset,ob-seruabatur.idque ius appellabatur Senatusconsultum.
units.tr: Then, because it began to be difficult for the plebs to assemble, and far more difficult for the people in such a crowd, necessity itself, and the care of the commonwealth, led matters to the senate. Thus the senate began to interpose itself, and whatever it decreed was observed. This law was called a senatus consultum.

units.la: 10 ¶Eode tempore & magistratus iura reddebant: &, vt scirent ciues,quod ius de quaque re quisq.di{a}éturus esset:fèque praemuniret: edicta pponebat,quae edicta praetorum,ius honorarium constituerunt.Honorarium dicitur, quod ab honore praetoris venerat. 11 ¶Nonisime,sicut ad pauciores iuris constitucdi via transfille,ipsis rebus d stantibus: videbatur: per partes eument, ut necesse esset reipublicae per vnū co- suli,nā senatus nō perinde omnes prouincias probe gerere poterant.Igitur constituto principe,datum est ei ius:vt,quod coltituisset,ratum esset. 12 ¶ Ita in ciuitate nostra,aut Iure,id est Lege constituitur:aut cst propriu Ius ciuile,q c fine scripto in sola prudentiā interpretatione consistiunt sunt Legis actiones,quę formam agendi cotinent: aut Plebiscitum,quod sine auctoritate patrum est constitutum:aut est magistra- tuum Edictum,vnde Ius Honorarium c nascitur:aut Senatusconsultum, q solum senatu constituente in- ducitur sine lege:aut est Principalis constitutio,id est, vt quod ipse princeps constituit, pro lege seruetur.
units.tr: At the same time the magistrates also gave judgments; and so that the citizens might know what law each man would apply in any matter, and might be forewarned, they published edicts. The edicts of the praetors established the honorary law. It is called honorary because it came from the honour of the praetor. 11. Lastly, since the way of making law passed to fewer people, with the matters themselves standing, it seemed that the work would proceed part by part, so that it became necessary for the commonwealth to be governed by one man. For the senate could not equally manage all the provinces well. Therefore, once a prince had been established, a right was given to him: that whatever he decreed should have the force of law. 12. Thus in our state, law is either established by statute, that is, by a law; or it is the proper civil law, which consists without writing in the sole interpretation of the jurists; or it is the legis actiones, which contain the form of acting; or it is a plebiscite, which was established without the authority of the patricians; or it is the edict of the magistrates, from which the honorary law arises; or it is a senatus consultum, which is brought into being by the senate's decision alone, without a law; or it is the princely constitution, that is, what the prince himself decrees is to be kept as law.
Chapter II. On the magistrates of the Romans.
