units.la: {f}13 ¶ Post originē iuris,& praecessum cognitū, cōfeenim ius in ciuitate esse,nisi sint,qui iura regere possint:Post hoc deinde auctorum successione dice m is,quod coftare no potest ius,nisi sit aliquis in- rispetitus,per puè possit cotidie in multis producî. 14 ¶Quod ad magistrat attinet,initio ciuitatis hu- ius constat reges omne potestate habuisse. 15 ¶lis- de temporib & tribunu celeru fuisse constat. is au- te erat,qui equitibus præerat,&veluti secundu locu a regibus obtinebat quo in numero fuit Iunius Brutus,qui auctor fuit regis,eiiciendi. 16 ¶Exactis de inde regibus,cósules constituti sunt duo: penes quos summum ius vti esset,lege rogatu est.dicti sut ab eo quod plurimum reipublicæ consuleret,qui tamen ne per omnia regia potestate sibi vindicarent, lege lata factum est,ut ab eis prouocatio esset,neque possent in caput cuius Romani animaduertere in iussu populi: solum relictu est illis,ut coercere possent,& in vincu la publica duci iuberent. 17 ¶Post deinde cum census iā maiori tepore agendus esset,& consules nō sufficerent huic quoq.officio, ceteres costituti sunt. 18 ¶Populo deinde auctoribus, cum crebra orirētur bel- ra,& quædā acriora a finitimis inferrentur: interdu re exigente, placuit maioris potestatis magistratum constitui, itaque dictatores prodit sunt, a quibus nec prouocadi ius fuit:& quibus ēria capitis animad- uersio data est.Hunc magistratum,quoniam summa potestatem habebat, non erat fas vltra sextum me- fem retinere. 19 ¶Et his dictatoribus magistri equitum iniungebantur sic, quo modo regibus tribu buni celerum, quod officium fere tale erat,quale bodie prefectorum pretorio,magistratus tamen habe bantur legitimi. 20 ¶Idem temporibus cum plebs a patribus seccessisset,anno fere septimodecimo post reges exactos,tribunos sibi in monte Sacro ære erat,qui equitibus [?] ...
units.tr: 13 Once the origin of law and the succession of its authors has been established, we should next consider that there can be no law in a state unless there are people who can administer the laws. After this, by tracing the succession of authorities, we say that law cannot exist unless there is always some person able to be consulted on it, which is in fact daily brought forward in many cases. 14 As for the magistrates, it is agreed that at the beginning of this state the kings held all power. 15 It is agreed also that in the time of the kings there was a tribune of the Celeres. He was the one who commanded the knights and held, as it were, the second place after the kings; Junius Brutus, who was the author of expelling the kings, was among their number. 16 After the kings were driven out, two consuls were appointed, in whose hands the supreme right was to rest, by a law passed on request. They were so called because they would take the greatest care of the commonwealth. Yet, so that they would not claim for themselves the whole of royal power, a law was passed making it possible to appeal from them, and they could not put a Roman citizen to death without the order of the people. It was left to them only to restrain offenders and order them to be led into public custody. 17 Afterwards, since the census had to be taken at a greater interval, and the consuls were not sufficient for this office too, censors were appointed. 18 Then, at the people's instigation, since wars broke out frequently and some fiercer attacks were made by neighbouring peoples, the need of the moment required that a magistrate of greater power be established. Accordingly dictators were appointed, from whom there was no right of appeal, and to whom the power of capital punishment was given. It was not lawful to keep this magistracy beyond six months, since he held supreme power. 19 Masters of the horse were assigned to these dictators in the same way as the tribunes of the Celeres had been to the kings. This office was much like that of the later praetorian prefects, yet they were regarded as lawful magistrates. 20 Likewise, at about the seventeenth year after the kings were expelled, when the plebs had seceded from the patricians on the Sacred Mount, they created tribunes for themselves, who ... [the passage breaks off here].

units.la: 1 recte hoc additum fuit: plebeior. n. fuit praefecti praetorio potestas. Molinaeus 1. feud. 20. numer. 20.
units.tr: 1 This was rightly added: for the power of the praetorian prefect was plebeian. Molinaeus, 1 feud. 20, number 20.

units.la: 2 Liuius 2: Halicarnass. 6; Augustus 2. de ciuitat. 18. Ouidius 3. Fast. diles appellati sunt. 22 ¶Deinde cum ærarium populi auctius esse coepisset: vt essent qui illi præ-essent, constituti sunt quæstores b, § qui pecuniæ præessent §: dicti ab eo, (quod) inquirendæ, & conferundæ pecuniæ causa creati erant. 23 ¶Et quia, vt diximus c, de capite ciuis Romani iniussu populi non erat lege permissum consulibus ius dicere: propterea quæstores constituebantur a populo, qui capitalibus rebus præessent. hi appellabantur quæstores parricidii: quorum etiam meminit lex duodecim tabularum. 24 ¶Et cum placuisset leges quoque ferri: latum est ad populum, vti omnes magistratus se abdicarent quo decerent viri d constituti vno anno, cum magistratum prorogarent sibi, & cum iniuriose tractarent, neque vellent deinceps sufficere magistratibus, vt ipsi & factio sua perpetuo rempublicam occupatam retinerent: nimia, atque aspera dominatione eo rem perduxerant, vt exercitus a republica secederet. Initium fuisse secessionis dicitur Verginius e quidam, qui cum animadvertisset, Appium Claudium (contra ius f quod ipse ex vetere iure in duodecim tabulas transtulerat) vindicias filiæ suæ g a se abdixisse h: & secundum eum, qui in ser viurem ab eo suppositus petierat, dixisse: captumque amore virginis, omne fas ac nefas miscuisse: ignarus, quod verustissima iuris obseruantia in persona filiæ suæ defecisset (vt pote cum Brutus, qui primus Romæ consul fuit, vindicias secundum libertatem dixisset in persona Vindicis i Vitelliorum servi, qui proditionis coniurationem indicio suo detexerat) & castitatem filiæ vitæ quoque eius præsendam putaret: arrepto cultro de taberna lanionis filiam interfecit: in hoc scilicet, vt morte virginis contumeliam stupri arcerer. ac protinus recens a cæde, madenteque adhuc filiæ cruore. ad commilitones confugit. qui vniuersi de Algido, vbi tunc belli gerendi causa legiones erant, relictis ducibus Ptistini, signa in Auentinum transtulerunt. omnisque plebs vrbana mox eodem se contulit. populusque consensu partim in carcere necati [?] ita tursus respublica suum statum recepit. 25 ¶Deinde cum post aliquot annos, quam duodecim tabulas decemuiris in carcere necatis, partim in exilium asti, tursus respublica statu suo recepit. addc l.1 §.2 ]de rei vin. fatæ sunt& plebs contenderet cum patribus, & vel-let ex suo quoque corpore consules creare,& patres recusarent: factum est, vt tribuni militum crearen-tur partim ex plebe, partim ex patribus, consulari potestate. hique constituti sunt vario numero: inter-dum enim viginti{4} fuerunt interdum plures, nonnū quam pauciores.
units.tr: 2 Livy 2; Halicarnassus 6; Augustine, On the City of God 18; Ovid, Fasti 3. They were called aediles. 22 Then, when the public treasury had begun to grow larger, quaestors were appointed to oversee it, b § who were in charge of the money §: they were so named from the fact that they were created for the purpose of inquiring into and collecting money. 23 And because, as we said c, the consuls were not permitted by law to pronounce judgment on the life of a Roman citizen without the order of the people, quaestors were therefore appointed by the people to preside over capital cases. These were called quaestors of murder, and the Law of the Twelve Tables also mentions them. 24 Then, when it was also decided that laws should be proposed, it was brought before the people that all magistrates should lay down their office, and that d ten men e be appointed for one year. They prolonged their magistracy for themselves, and, treating everyone unjustly, they would no longer consent to hand over office, so that they and their faction might keep the commonwealth occupied in perpetuity. By excessive and harsh domination they brought matters to such a point that the army seceded from the commonwealth. The beginning of the secession is said to have been a certain Verginius f, who, perceiving that Appius Claudius (contrary to the law g which he himself had transferred from ancient law into the Twelve Tables) had refused to hand over his daughter's claim h, and gave it to the man who had claimed her as a slave substituted by him, said that Appius, seized with love for the maiden, had confused all right and wrong. Verginius, not knowing that the most ancient observance of law had failed in the case of his own daughter (since Brutus, the first consul at Rome, had decided in favour of liberty in the case of Vindex i, the slave of the Vitellii, who had revealed the conspiracy of treason by his information), and thinking that his daughter's chastity was to be preferred even to her life, seized a knife from a butcher's shop and killed his daughter, plainly so that the insult of her defilement might be averted by her death. Straightway, fresh from the slaughter and with his daughter's blood still dripping, he fled to his fellow soldiers. All of them, from Algidus, where the legions were then waging war, left their leaders behind, and carried the standards over to the Aventine; and the whole urban plebs soon joined them there. The people, by common consent, ... and so the commonwealth recovered its former state. 25 Then, after some years, when the decemvirs had been killed in prison, some had been sent into exile, and the commonwealth had once more recovered its state, the plebs contended with the patricians and wanted to create consuls from their own body, but the patricians refused. It came about that military tribunes were created, some from the plebs and some from the patricians, with consular power. These were appointed in varying numbers: sometimes there were twenty, sometimes more, sometimes fewer. addc l.1 §.2 ]de rei vin.

units.la: 26 ¶ Deinde cum placuisset creari etiam ex plebe consules: coeperunt ex vtroque corpore constitui. Tunc, vt aliquo pluris patres haberet, placuit duos ex numero patrum constitui. ita facti sunt ædiles{b} curules.
units.tr: 26 Then, when it was decided that consuls should also be created from the plebs, they began to be appointed from both orders. Then, so that the patricians should have something more, it was decided that two should be chosen from the number of the patricians. Thus curule aediles were made.

units.la: 27 ¶ Cumque consules auocarentur bellis finitimis: neque esset, qui in civitate ius reddere posset: factum est, vt prætor quoque ædilitio & ii creareturq, qui urbanus appellatus est, quod in urbe ius redderet.
units.tr: 27 And since the consuls were called away by neighbouring wars, and there was no one who could administer justice in the city, it came about that a praetor was also created from among the aediles, who was called the urban praetor, because he administered justice in the city.

units.la: 28 ¶ Post aliquot deinde annos, non sufficiente[?] eo prætore, quod multa turba etiam peregrinorū in civitate veniret: creatus est & alius prætor, qui peregrinus appellatus est ab eo, quod plerumq. inter peregrinos ius dicebat.
units.tr: 28 Some years later, since that one praetor was not sufficient, because a great crowd of foreigners also came into the state, another praetor was created, who was called the peregrine praetor, because he mostly gave judgment among foreigners.

units.la: 29 ¶ Deinde cum esset necessarius magistratus, qui hastæ præesset: decemuiri{d} in{e} heibus[?] iudicandis sunt constituti.
units.tr: 29 Then, since a magistrate was needed to preside over the auction (spear sale), decemvirs were appointed for judging suits d... e.

units.la: 30 ¶ Eodem tempore & quatuor viri, qui curā vi-rum[?] gererent. & triumuiri monetales, aeris, argenti, auri flatores: & triumuiri capitales, qui carceris custodiam haberent: vt, cum animadverti oporteret, in rerutu[?] coră[?] ferret.
units.tr: 30 At the same time there were also four men, who had charge of the ... of men, and triumvirs of the mint, the makers of bronze, silver and gold coin, and triumvirs for capital cases, who were to keep custody of the prison, so that, when punishment had to be inflicted, they might carry it out.

units.la: 31 ¶ Et quia magistratibus{f}, vespertinis temporibus, in publicum esse inconueniens erat, quinqueuiri constituti sunt eis Tiberim, & vrbis Tiberim, qui pro magistratibus fungi.
units.tr: 31 And because it was unsuitable for magistrates to be in public in the evening hours, quinqueviri were appointed for them at the Tiber, and the city's Tiber, who would act in place of magistrates.

units.la: 32 ¶ Capta deinde Sardinia, mox Sicilia{g}, & Hispania, deinde Narbonensi prouincia: totidem praetores, pomp. & Va-rro, quot prouincie in dictione venerar, creati sunt: partim qui vrbanis rebus, partim qui prouincialibus praefe-rent. Deinde Cornelius Sylla quæstiones publicas constituit: veluti de falso, de parricidio, de sicariis{h}: & {f} hinc quinque praetores quatuor adiecit. Deinde Gaius Iulius Cesar duos praetores, & duos ædiles, qui[?] sententia no-minavit, & à Cerere Cerealis constituit. Ita duodecim praetores, sex ædiles sunt creati. Diuus deinde Augustus sedecim praetores constituit. Post deinde Diuus Claudius duos praetores adiecit, qui de fideicommissis dicere[?] rent. ex quibus vnum Diuus Titus detraxit & adiecit.
units.tr: 32 Then, after Sardinia was taken, soon Sicily, and Spain, and afterwards the province of Narbonese Gaul, as many praetors were created as there were provinces under their rule: some to deal with urban affairs, others to govern the provinces. Afterwards Cornelius Sulla established public courts, such as those on forgery, on parricide, and on assassins, and added four praetors to the five. Then Gaius Julius Caesar appointed two praetors and two aediles, who were named by his decision, and he appointed the Cerealis from Ceres. Thus twelve praetors and six aediles were created. The deified Augustus afterwards established sixteen praetors. Then the deified Claudius added two praetors, who were to deal with trust bequests; of these, the deified Titus removed one and added another.

units.la: Syllam quatuor Praetores adiecisse. ‡ §.1, sup. de fideicommiss.
units.tr: Sulla added four praetors. §.1, sup. de fideicommiss.

units.la: Diuus Nerua, qui inter fiscu & priuatos ius dicerét. Ita decem & octo prætores in ciuitate ius dicunt.
units.tr: The deified Nerva, who dispensed justice between the fisc and private persons. Thus eighteen praetors dispense justice in the city.

units.la: ¶ Et hæc omnia, quoties in republica sunt magistratus obseruantur, quotiens autem proficiscuntur: vnus relinquitur, qui ius dicat. is vocatur præfectus vrbi. qui præfectus olim constituebatur, postea ferè Latinarum feriarum a causa introductus est, & quotannis obseruatur. nam præfectus b annonæ, &c vigilum magistratu tantum non sunt magistratus, sed extra ordinem, vtilitatis causa, constituti sunt. & tamen hi, quos Ciftiberes d diximus e, postea ædiles senatusconsulto creabantur.
units.tr: And all these offices are kept whenever the magistrates are in the commonwealth, but whenever they go away, one is left behind to dispense justice. He is called the prefect of the city. This prefect was formerly appointed, but later was introduced, chiefly for the sake of the Latin festival, and is kept every year. For the prefect of the grain supply and the prefect of the watch are scarcely magistrates at all; they were appointed outside the ordinary order, for the sake of convenience. And yet those whom we called Ciftiberes were afterwards created aediles by senatus consultum.

units.la: ¶ Ergo ex his omnibus, decè tribuni plebis, consules duo, decem & octo prætores, sex ædiles, in ciuitate iura reddebant.
units.tr: Therefore, from all these together, ten tribunes of the plebs, two consuls, eighteen praetors and six aediles dispensed justice in the city.
Chapter III. On the Teachers and Jurists.

units.la: ¶ Iuris ciuilis scientiam plurimi & maximi viri professi sunt. sed qui eorum maximæ dignationis apud populum Romanum fuerunt, (earum, in præsentia mentio habenda est: vt appareat, à quibus, & qualibus hæc iura orta, & tradita sunt. Et quidem ex omnibus, qui scientiam nacti sunt, ante Tiberium Coruncanum publicè professum neminem traditur. ceteri autem ad hunc vel in latenti ius ciuile retinere cogitabant, solùm q. consultatoribus [?] vacarent: potiùs, quàm discere volentibus se præstabant.
units.tr: ¶ Many distinguished and eminent men professed the science of civil law. Those of them who held the greatest standing among the Roman people (I must mention them here, so that it is clear by whom and of what kind these laws arose and were handed down) are as follows. Of all who acquired this knowledge, no one is recorded as having taught it publicly before Tiberius Coruncanius. Before him, the others intended to keep the civil law hidden, and devoted themselves to giving opinions rather than to teaching those who wished to learn.

units.la: ¶ Fuit autem in primis peritus Publius Papirius, qui leges regias in vnum contulit. Ab hoc Appius Claudius, vnus ex decemuiris, cuius maximum consilium in duodecim tabulis scribendis fuit. Post hunc Appius Claudius eiusdem generis maximâ scientiam habuit. hic Centemanus g appellatus est, Appiam viam strauit, & aquâ Claudiam induxit, & de Pyrrho in vr be non recipiendo sententiâ tulit. hunc etiâ actiones scripsisse traditum est, primum de vsurpationibus, qui liber non extat. Idem h Appius Claudius, qui videtur ab hoc processisse, R literam inuenit: vt pro Valesij i Valerij essent, & pro Fusiis Furiis.
units.tr: ¶ The first skilled man was Publius Papirius, who collected the royal laws into one body. After him came Appius Claudius, one of the decemvirs, whose greatest counsel was in writing the Twelve Tables. After him, Appius Claudius of the same family had the greatest learning. He was called Centemanus g; he laid the Appian Way, brought water into the city by the Aqua Claudia, and gave an opinion against receiving Pyrrhus into the city. It is also recorded that he wrote actions, first on usucapions; this book is not extant. The same h Appius Claudius, who seems to have descended from this man, invented the letter R, so that instead of Valesii there should be Valerii, and instead of Fusii, Furii. i

units.la: ¶ Fuit post eos maximæ scientiæ Sempronius, quem k pulus Romanus sapientissimè appellauit: nec quisquam [illegible, ~6 letters] dicebant ma- iofibus, meliofibus, lafibus, fefis. Festus in R pro S. ad eundem pene modum Parisienses nostri loquuntur. k cum Attilio. de quo in
units.tr: ¶ After them came Sempronius, of the greatest learning, whom the Roman people called most wise. ... They used to say maiofibus, meliofibus, lafibus, fefis (for maiosibus, meliosibus, lasibus, sesis). Festus says that the R was put for S; our Parisians speak in nearly the same way. k with Attilius. de quo in

units.la: §.38.ʃ.cod. quam ante hunc, aut post hunc hoc nomine cognominatus est.Gaius Scipio Nasica,qui optimus{a}lena tu appellatus est,cui etiā publice domus in sacra via data est,quo facilius consuli posset. Deinde Quintus Mucius:qui {b}ad Carthaginenses missus legatus,cum esset duae tesserae, vna pacis,altera belli:arbitrio sibi dato, vtram vellet referret Romam?vtram-que fulit[?],& ait Carthaginienses petere debere, vtram mallent accipere.
units.tr: §.38. of this same title, than before or after him by this name. Gaius Scipio Nasica, who was called the best ..., to whom a house on the Sacred Way was also given at public expense, so that he could be consulted more easily. Then Quintus Mucius, who was sent as envoy to the Carthaginians. When he had two tablets, one of peace and the other of war, and was given the choice of which to bring back to Rome, he brought back both, and said that the Carthaginians ought to ask which they would rather receive.

units.la: 38 ¶Post hos fuit Tiberius Coruncanius,vt {c}dixi,qui primus profiteri coepit cuius tamen scriptum nullum exstat,sed responsa co-plura, & memorabilia eius fuerunt. Deinde Sextus Aelius,& frater eius Publius Aelius & Publius Atilius,maximam scientiam in profitendo habuerunt: vt duo Aelij etiam consules fuerint. Atilius autem primus à populo sapiens {d}appellatus est.Sextum Aelium {e}etiā Ennius laudauit.& exstat illius liber,qui inscribitur Tripertita qui liber veluti cunabula iuris continet. Tripertita autē dicitur:quoniam, lege duodecim tabularum prāpositā, iungitur interpretatio : dein subtexitur legis actio. Eiusdem esse tres alij libri referuntur,quos tamen quidam negat eiusdem esse.Hos sectatus ad aliquid est Cato. Deinde Marcus Cato {f}princeps Porcia familiae:cuius & libri exstant:sed plurimi filij eius,ex quib9 ceteri oriuntur.
units.tr: 38 ¶ After these came Tiberius Coruncanius, as I have said, who first began to profess the law publicly. No writing of his survives, but many of his responses and memorable opinions do. Then Sextus Aelius, and his brother Publius Aelius, and Publius Atilius had the greatest learning in teaching, so much so that the two Aelii were both consuls. Atilius was the first to be called "wise" by the people. Ennius also praised Sextus Aelius, and his book survives, entitled Tripertita, which contains, as it were, the cradle of the law. It is called Tripertita because, after the law of the Twelve Tables is set out, an interpretation is added, and then the form of action is appended. Three other books are cited as his, though some deny they are his. Cato followed these men to some extent. Then Marcus Cato, the founder of the Porcian family, whose books also survive; but his many sons, from whom the others descend, wrote as well.

units.la: 39 ¶Post hos fuerunt Publius Mucius, & Brutus,& Manilius: qui fundauerunt ius ciuile.ex his Publius Mucius etiam decem libellos reliquit:Brutus septē: Manilius tres. & exstant volumina scripta, Manilij monumenta. illi duo consulares fuerunt:Brutus prētorius:Publius autē {g}Mutius etiam pontifex maximus.
units.tr: 39 ¶ After these came Publius Mucius, Brutus, and Manilius, who laid the foundations of the civil law. Of these, Publius Mucius left ten little books, Brutus seven, and Manilius three; the volumes of Manilius, written works, still survive. The first two were consuls, Brutus was a praetor, and Publius Mucius was also chief pontiff.

units.la: 40 ¶Ab his profecti sunt Publius Rutilius Rufus,qui Romae consul,&Asiae proconsul fuit: Paulus Verginius : & Quintus Tubero ille {h}Stoicus, Pansæ auditor,qui & ipse consul. Etiam Sextus Pompeius Gnæi Pompeij patruus fuit eodem tempore:& Cœlius Antipater,qui historias conscripsit: sed plus eloquentiæ,quàm scientiæ iuris,operam dedit,etiam Lucius Crassus, frater Publij Mucij, qui Mucianus dictus est. hunc Cicero ait inrisconsultorum disertissimum.
units.tr: 40 ¶ From these came Publius Rutilius Rufus, who was consul at Rome and proconsul in Asia; Paulus Verginius; and Quintus Tubero, that Stoic, a pupil of Panaetius, who was himself also consul. Sextus Pompeius, the uncle of Gnaeus Pompeius, was also of the same time, and Caelius Antipater, who wrote histories but devoted himself more to eloquence than to the science of law. Also Lucius Crassus, the brother of Publius Mucius, who was called Mucianus. Cicero calls him the most eloquent of the jurists.

units.la: 41 ¶Post hos Quintus Mucium Publij filius pontifex {ℓ} maximus ius ciuile primus constituit, generatim in libros decem & octo redigendo.
units.tr: 41 ¶ After these, Quintus Mucius, the son of Publius, chief pontiff, first established the civil law, reducing it generally into eighteen books.

units.la: {ℓ} Cicer.2.de legib. & augur.& aedilis iussu Marij in Tyberim proiectus, Appian.1.bellicivil. Lucan.2.
units.tr: {ℓ} Cicero, De legibus 2, and De augurio; when aedile, he was thrown into the Tiber at the command of Marius. Appian, Civil Wars 1. Lucan 2.

units.la: 42 ¶ Mucij auditores fuerunt complures: sed præcipuæ auctoritatis Aquilii Galli, Balbi a Lucilius, Sexti Pa- pirius, Gaius Iuuentius, ex quibus Gallum maxime auctoritatis apud populum fuisse Seruius dicit. Omnes tamen hi à Seruio Sulpicio nominantur, alioquin per se eorum scripta non talia exstant, vt ea ad omnes adpetant. Denique nec versantur omnino scripta eorum inter manus hominum, sed Seruius libros suos complevit: pro cuius scriptura, ipsorum quoque memoria habetur.
units.tr: 42 ¶ There were many hearers of Mucius, but of special authority were Aquilius Gallus, Balbus, Lucilius, Sextus Papirius, and Gaius Iuventius. Of these, Servius says that Gallus had the greatest authority with the people. Yet all of them are named by Servius Sulpicius, since otherwise their writings do not survive in such a way as to reach everyone. Indeed, their writings are not at all in people's hands, but Servius filled his books, and their memory is held in regard for the sake of his writing.

units.la: 43 ¶ Seruius <bl>b</bl> cùm in caussis orandis primum locum, aut pro certo post Marcum Tullium obtineret, traditur ad consulendum Quintum Mucium de re amici sui peruenisse: cùmque cùm sibi responderet de iure, Seruius parùm intellexisset, iterum Quintum interrogasse, & à Quinto Mucio responsum esse, nec tamen percepisse: & ita obiurgatum esse à Quinto Mucio: nam que eum dixisse, turpe esse patricio, & nobili, & caussas oranti, ius, in quo versari tur, ignorare, ea velut contumelia Seruius tractatus, operam dedit iuri ciuili: & plurimum eos, de quibus locuti sumus, audiit: institutus à Balbo Lucilio, instructus autem maxime à Gallo Aquilio, qui fuit Cercinæ. Itaque libri complures eius esse Cercinæ confecti. Hic cùm in legatione periisset, statuam ei populus Romanus pro Rostris posuit: & hodieque exstat pro Rostris Augusti. Huius volumina copiùm exstant: reliquit autem prope centum & octoginta libros.
units.tr: 43 ¶ Servius, when he held the first place in pleading cases, or certainly the place after Marcus Tullius, is said to have come to Quintus Mucius to consult him about a matter concerning his friend. When Mucius gave him an answer on the law, Servius did not understand it well, and asked Quintus again, and received an answer from Quintus Mucius, but still did not grasp it. Quintus Mucius then rebuked him, saying that it was shameful for a patrician and nobleman who pleads cases not to know the law in which he works. Servius, stung by this rebuke, devoted himself to the civil law, and heard the men of whom we have spoken very often: he was taught by Balbus Lucilius, but was especially instructed by Gallus Aquilius, who was from Cercina. Hence many of his books were composed at Cercina. When he died on an embassy, the Roman people set up a statue of him before the Rostra, and it still stands before the Rostra of Augustus. His volumes survive in abundance; he left nearly one hundred and eighty books.

units.la: 44 ¶ Ab hoc plurimi profecerunt: ferè tamen hi libros conscripserunt: Alfenus Varus, Gaius, Aulus Ofilius, Titus Caesius, Aufidius Tucca, Aufidius Namusa, Flauius Priscus, Gaius Ateius Pacuuius, Labeo, Antistius Labeonis, Antistij pater, Cinna, Publicius, Gellius. Ex his decem libros octo conscripserunt. Quorum omnes qui fuerunt, libri digesti sunt ab Aufidio Namusa in centum quadraginta libros. Ex his auditoribus plurimum auctoritatis habuit Alfenus Varus, & Aulus Ofilius, ex quibus Varus & consul fuit: Ofilius in equestri ordine perseuerauit. Is fuit Caesari familiarissimus: & libri iure ciuili plurimos, & qui omnem partem operis fundarent, reliquit, nam de legibus Vicensimæ §. primus conscribit, de iurisdictione: idem edictum prætoris indicta & remissa à Nerone. Histor. ex Livij 7. Tacit. 15. Zafius tamen Vicesima intelligit hereditatis extraneo delatæ, fisco inferen- dæ ex Dione 55. & à Traiano sublatæ Plinius in Panegyrico. [?]tris primus diligenter composuit, nam ante eum Seruius duos libros ad Brutum per quàm breuissimos ad edictum subscriptos reliquit.
units.tr: 44 ¶ Many profited from him, but these few wrote books: Alfenus Varus, Gaius, Aulus Ofilius, Titus Caesius, Aufidius Tucca, Aufidius Namusa, Flavius Priscus, Gaius Ateius Pacuvius, Labeo, Antistius (the son of Labeo, and the father of Antistius), Cinna, Publicius, and Gellius. Of these, eight wrote ten books. All their books were digested by Aufidius Namusa into one hundred and forty books. Among these hearers, Alfenus Varus and Aulus Ofilius had the greatest authority; of them, Varus was also consul, while Ofilius remained in the equestrian order. He was very close to Caesar, and left many books on civil law, which laid the foundations of every part of the work. For he wrote the first book On the Twentieth (de vicensima), on the laws, and the first On Jurisdiction; he also composed the praetor's edict, which was ordered and abolished by Nero. Historical notes from Livy 7 and Tacitus 15. Zasius, however, understands the vicesima as the twentieth part of an inheritance left to a stranger and payable to the treasury, citing Dio 55, and abolished by Trajan, as Pliny says in the Panegyricus. ... he first composed the edict carefully. For before him Servius left two very brief books on the edict, addressed to Brutus.

units.la: 45 ¶ Fuit eodem tempore & Trebatius, qui idem Corneli Maximi auditor, fuit Aulus Cafcelius, Quintus Mucius Volusij auditor: denique in illius honorem testamento Publium Mucium nepotem eius reliquit heredem. fuit autem quaestorius: nec vltra procedere voluit, cùm illi etiam Augustus consulatum offerret, ex his Trebatius {4} peritior Cafcelio, Cafcelius Trebatio eloquentior fuisse dicitur, Ofilius vtrèque doctior. Cafcelij scripta non exstant, nisi vnus liber Benedictorum, Trebatij complures: sed minus frequentantur.
units.tr: 45 ¶ At the same time there was also Trebatius, who was likewise a pupil of Cornelius Maximus; Aulus Cascellius was another, and Quintus Mucius, a pupil of Volusius. Finally, in his honour, Trebatius left his grandson Publius Mucius as heir in his will. Trebatius held the rank of quaestor, but did not wish to go further, although Augustus offered him the consulship. Of these, Trebatius is said to have been more skilled than Cascellius, and Cascellius more eloquent than Trebatius; Ofilius was more learned than both. The writings of Cascellius do not survive, except one book of the Benedictorum; many of Trebatius survive, but they are less read.

units.la: 46 ¶ Post hoc quoque Tubero {b}fuit, qui Ofilio operam dedit: fuit autem patricius, & tradit à causis agendis ad ius ciuile, maximè postquam Quintum Ligarium accusauit, nec obtinuit apud Caium Caesarem. Is est Quintus Ligarius: qui, cùm Africæ oram teneret, infirmum Tuberone applicare non permisit, nec aquam haurire, quo nomine cum accusauit, & {c}Cicero defendit. extat eius oratio || satis || pulcherrima, quae inscribitur, pro Quinto Ligario. Tubero doctissimus quidem habitus est iuris publici & priuati: & complures vtriusque operi libros reliquit, sermone etiam antiquo vsus affectauit scribere: & ideo parum libri eius grati habentur.
units.tr: 46 ¶ After him, Tubero was also a figure, who devoted himself to Ofilius. He was a patrician, and turned from pleading cases to civil law, especially after he accused Quintus Ligarius and did not prevail before Gaius Caesar. This is that Quintus Ligarius who, when he held the coast of Africa, did not allow the sick Tubero to land or to draw water; for this reason Tubero accused him, and Cicero defended him. His speech, which is very fine, survives, entitled Pro Quinto Ligario. Tubero was thought most learned in public and private law, and left many books on both fields; he also affected to write in an archaic style, and therefore his books are little esteemed.

units.la: 47 ¶ Post hunc maximæ auctoritatis fuerunt Ateius Capito, qui Ofilium secutus est: & Antistius Labeo, qui omnes hos audiuit, institutus est autem à Trebatio. Ex his Ateius {d}consul fuit: Labeo {e}noluit, cùm offerretur ei ab Augusto consulatus, quo suffectus fieret, {&} honorem suscipere: sed plurimum studiis operam dedit: & totum annum ita diuiserat: vt Romæ sex mensibus cum studiosis esset, sex mensibus secederet, & conscribendis libris operam daret. Itaque reliquit quadraginta volumina: e quibus plurima inter manus versantur. Hi duo primum veluti diuersas sectas fecerunt. nam Ateius {f}Capito in his, quae ei tradita fuerant, perseuerabat. Labeo ingenij qualitate, & fiducia doctrinæ, qui & cæteris operis sapientiæ operam dederat, plurima innouare instituit, & ita Ateio Capitoni Massurius Sabinus successit, Labeoni Nerua, adhuc eas dissensiones auxerunt. ||Hic etiam|| Nerua Cæsari familiarissimus {g} fuit. Massurius Sabinus in equestri ordine fuit, & publicè primus scripsit, posteaque hoc cœpit. beneficium Idarij[?] à Tiberio Cæsare; hoc tamen illi[?] concessum erat. Et, ut obiter sciamus, ante tempora Augusti publicè respondendi ius non à principibus dabatur: sed qui fiduciam studiorum[?] suorum habebant, consulentibus respondebant, {a} neque responsa vtique signata dabant; sed plerumque iudicibus ipsi scribebant, aut testabantur, qui illos consulebant.
units.tr: 47 After him came the most authoritative men: Ateius Capito, who followed Ofilius, and Antistius Labeo, who heard all of these, though he was instructed by Trebatius. Of these, Ateius was consul; Labeo refused when Augustus offered him the consulship, by which he would have been appointed to fill a vacancy, and to accept the office; but he devoted himself chiefly to study. He had divided the year so that he spent six months in Rome with his students and six months in retirement, given over to writing books. Accordingly he left forty volumes, of which very many are in people's hands. These two first founded, as it were, different schools. For Ateius Capito kept to what had been handed down to him. Labeo, by the nature of his talent and his confidence in his learning, who had also devoted himself to the other branches of wisdom, set out to introduce many innovations. Thus Massurius Sabinus succeeded Ateius Capito, and Nerva succeeded Labeo, and these disagreements increased further. Nerva was also very close to Caesar. Massurius Sabinus was of the equestrian order, and he was the first to write publicly, and afterwards this began to be a benefit granted by Tiberius Caesar to Idarius[?]; yet this was granted to him only in this way. And, to know in passing, before the time of Augustus the right to give public responses was not granted by the princes; but those who had confidence in their studies gave answers to those consulting them, and they did not give the responses in sealed form, but for the most part they wrote for the judges themselves, or attested for those who consulted them.

units.la: Primus Diuus Augustus, ut maior iuris auctoritas haberetur constituit{b}, ut ex auctoritate eius responderent, & ex illo tempore peti hoc pro beneficio coe-Hicet[?], non cui pit[?], & ideo optimus princeps{*} Hadrianus, cum ab eo viri praetorij peterent, ut sibi liceret respondere, rescripsit eis, hoc non peti, sed praestari solere{c} & ideo si quis fiduciam sui haberet, delectari se: populo ad respondendum se praepararet. Ergo Sabino concessum est à Tiberio Cæsare, ut populo responderet, qui in equestri ordine iam grandis natu, & fere annorum quinquaginta receptus est, huic nec amplæ facultates fuerunt: sed plurimum à suis auditoribus sustentatus est. Huic successit Gaius Cassius{d} Longinus, natus ex filia Tuberonis, quæ fuit neptis Seruij Sulpitij: & ideo proauum suum Seruium Sulpitium appellat, hic consul fuit cum Quartino temporibus Tiberij, sed plurimum in ciuitate auctoritatis habuit eousque, donec eum Cæsar{e} ciuitate pelleret, expulsus ab eo in Sardiniam, reuocatus à Vespasiano, diem suum obiit. Neruae successit Proculus{f} fuit eodem tempore & Nerua filius, fuit & alius Longinus ex equestri ordine quidem, sed postea ad praeturam vsque peruenit, sed Proculi auctoritas maior fuit, nam etiam{g} plurimum potuit. appellatique sunt partim Cassiani, partim Proculeiani, quæ origo à Capitone & Labeone coeperat. Cassio Cælius Sabinus{h} successit, qui plurimum temporibus Vespasiani potuit. Proculo Pegasus{i} qui temporibus Vespasiani praefectus vrbi fuit. Caelio Sabino Priscus Iauolenus Pegaso Celsus{k}, patri Celso Celsus filius, & Priscus Neratius: qui utrisque consules fuerunt: Celsus quidem & iterum. Iauoleno{l} Prisco Aburnus{m} Valens, & Tuscianus, item Saluius Iulianus.{n} Pegasiani di-ci ex:stimatur.
units.tr: Divus Augustus was the first to establish that greater authority should attach to legal opinions, so that they would respond by his authority; and from that time it began to be sought as a favour, not as a right, and therefore the excellent prince Hadrian, when men of praetorian rank asked him that they might be allowed to respond, replied in writing that this was not sought but was customarily bestowed; and so, if anyone had confidence in himself, he should be pleased to prepare himself to respond to the people. Thus the right to respond to the people was granted to Sabinus by Tiberius Caesar; he was received into the equestrian order when already advanced in years, about fifty; he had no ample means, but he was chiefly supported by his pupils. Gaius Cassius Longinus succeeded him, born of the daughter of Tubero, who was a granddaughter of Servius Sulpicius; and therefore he calls Servius Sulpicius his great-grandfather. He was consul with Quartinus in the time of Tiberius, and he held great authority in the state until Caesar drove him from the city, banished him to Sardinia, and after being recalled by Vespasian he met his end. Proculus succeeded Nerva; he was of the same time as Nerva's son, and there was also another Longinus of the equestrian order, who afterwards rose as far as the praetorship; but the authority of Proculus was greater, for he also had very great influence. They were called partly Cassians and partly Proculeians, an appellation whose origin went back to Capito and Labeo. Caelius Sabinus succeeded Cassius; he had great influence in the time of Vespasian. Pegasus succeeded Proculus; in the time of Vespasian he was prefect of the city. After Caelius Sabinus came Priscus Javolenus; after Pegasus came Celsus, the father, and Celsus the son, and Priscus Neratius; these were consuls, both of them, Celsus even a second time. After Javolenus Priscus came Aburnus Valens, and Tuscianus, likewise Salvius Julianus. The Pegasians are thought to be so called.
He flourished under Trajan.

units.la: {l} Preceptor Iuliani l. 5. de manu. vind. {m} de quo l. 78. §. pen.
units.tr: Teacher of Julian, in book 5 on manumission by vindication; concerning whom, in law 78, last paragraph.

units.la: {n} fuit Praetor & Consul l. 5. j. de manumiss. vind.
units.tr: He was praetor and consul, in law 5 of the Digest on manumission by vindication.
FINIS
The Fragments of the Twelve Tables. Book One.
On divine worship.

units.la: AD DIVOS adeunto caste{a} pietatem adhibento. opes{b} a-moueto. Qui secus faxit, Deus{c} ipse vindex{d} erit.
units.tr: Let them approach the gods with chaste piety<sup>a</sup>, and let them keep away lavish expense<sup>b</sup>. Whoever does otherwise, God himself will be the avenger.
Who is to worship.

units.la: SEPARATIM nemo habessit{e} deos neve novos{f}: sed ne aduenas{g}, nisi publi-cè adscitos{h} priuatim colunto.
units.tr: Let no one have gods separately, nor new gods; but let them worship foreign gods privately only if they have been publicly adopted.
Where to worship.

units.la: CONSTRVCTA a patribus delu-[?]ra veterum legum, rerumque ipsarum vtilitas, vt eas lectori proponerem, non tam vt eas cognosceret, quàm ne ignorarét.
units.tr: Since the laws of our ancestors were established, and since the usefulness of the things themselves is clear, I have set them before the reader not so much that he should know them as that he should not be ignorant of them.
{a} in mind and body.
{b} that is, expense.

units.la: {c} nedum homo. & his quidem verbis, praesentis poenae metu reliqua confirmari videntur.
units.tr: {c} much less a man. And indeed by these words the rest seems to be confirmed through fear of present punishment.

units.la: {d} lege prima, Codice de rebus credit.
units.tr: {d} first law, Code, On Things Lent.
{e} that is, let him have.
{f} see Paul, Sentences 5, 21, §2.

units.la: {g} His verbis tollit confusionem religionum & ceremoniarum, Cicero. Diu certè hoc Romae seruatum non fuit. Testis erit dea Pessinuntia quae & mater deum, Phrygia aduecta non sine magnis miraculis, Herodianus 1: 18. Plin.3.
units.tr: {g} Cicero says this was meant to remove the confusion of religions and ceremonies. Certainly it was not kept at Rome for long. The Pessinuntian goddess, who is also called the mother of the gods, brought from Phrygia not without great miracles, is witness to this: Herodian 1:18; Pliny 3.

units.la: {h} Tertullianus 5 Apologet: Verus, inquit, erat decretum, ne quis Deus ab imperatore consecraretur, nisi à Senatu probaretur. & post, apud vos de humano arbitratu diuinitas pensitatur. Nisi homini Deus placuerit, Deus non erit. & post, Tiberi* nonne Christum detulerat ad senatum, cum praerogatiua suffragij sui? Senatus, quia ipse non probauerat, respuit: Eusebius 1[?]. hist.
units.tr: {h} Tertullian, Apology 5: "It was, he says, a true decree that no god should be consecrated by the emperor unless it had been approved by the Senate." And afterwards: "Among you divinity is weighed by human judgment. Unless God pleases man, God will not be." And afterwards: "Did not Tiberius bring Christ before the Senate, with the prerogative of his own vote? The Senate, because it had not itself approved him, rejected him." Eusebius 1[?] Hist.

units.la: 2. id ea de causa factum fuisse refert, quod salutaris praedicatio nulla opus habeat humana approbatione.
units.tr: 2. He reports that this was done for this reason: because the saving preaching has no need of human approval.

units.la: braa habento. lucos *in agris habento, & larumc sedes. ritusd familiaee, patrum-quef ieruanto.
units.tr: Let them keep altars; let them keep groves in the fields, and the seats of the Lares. Let them keep the rites of the family, and guard the fathers' rites.

units.la: Ponebat enim vel pileu vel scutum, vel alia susceptis votis. Isidorus 5.c.3. deluer a diluendo dici putat, eique esse templa fontes habentia, quibus ante ingressum diluebatur. Templum, aedificium Deo consecratum, Festus: in loco augurato, Fronto: singulorum diis attributorum locorum, Ajcontm: a contemplatione. Isidorus d.loco. seu tuendo, qua tuimur, i.Ipedamus Varro 6. de ling. Fanu a Fauno, Fronto: siue a fando, quod dum pontifex dedicat certa verba fatur, Festus: unde fata petuntur Asconius. Sacellum, parvulum aedificium diis consecratum, Fronto: Tesqua, seu Tesca, loca quidem angusta diis dicata; quod ibi mysteria fiant ac tueantur Varro 6. de lingua. b Locus est arborum spissitate tectus: vel locus flumine ictus, Fronto. c Lirum diuersae sententiae fuerunt. Vulgus lares vocabat, viarum atque itinerum deos, ex eo quod Graeci vicos cognominat lauras, Arnob. 3: alij, quasi aerios deos & heroas, Arnob. d.loco. Varro, Manes interpretatur: quorum mater, Arnob. d.loco, vel aula Mania fuerit: vel vt Lactantius 1. cap. 20. scribit, Muta seu Larunda & lara, Festus in voce Mania turpes: lauae. Manias ne-trices minitabatur pueris paruulis, Festus d.loco. Idem, in Vila. Lares, animas hominum redactas in numerum deorum interpretatur vt minus proprie is, Act. 12. vers. 15. ἄγγελος reddiderit, qui genio vertit, cum puntium a Petro fidelem potuerit intelligere. Eidem Festo in voce Pilae, Lares diu inferi: quibus tot pilae, quot capita: tot effigies, quot essent liberi, pro ebantur, vt viuis parcerent, & essent his pilis & simulachris contenti. Vt rem omnem finiam. Lares domuum custodes hic intellige vt s. non penates (i. Neptunum & Apollinem, qui urbem Ilium muro cinxerunt Arnob 3.) Lares idem qui genij. Genius seu lateranus, focorum (qui ex lateculis saepe fiunt) Deus. Arnob. 4. De lare sam li rivide Plautu in Aululavia. d Festus in voce vitus. Ritus, mos comprobatus in adu ii iflrandis sacrificiis. Varro 6. de lingua. ritu, i. iri tuto, vt cu Haruspex praecipit, vt suo quisque ritu sacrificium faciat: & nos dicimus XII. (alij legunt XV) viros Graeco ritu sacra, nō Romano facere, haec Varro. e ritus familiae, sacra gentilicia. f Vetus & antiquum fuit, patrum ceremonias cultodire. Tertull. c.5. aduersus gentes. Laudatus semper antiquitatem & nouae de die viuitis. & post. Videmini fidelissime tueri a patribus traditum studium deorum colendorum, de quo maxime errauit antiquitas. Est igitur iusta de causa a patru falsis opinionibus discedendum Ierem. 8:16. Ezech. 20: Nouell.15. Et recte Pythius, Atheniensis quaerentib quae more maiorum potissimum sequerctur ex variis, respondit: vt optimus sequeretur. vt sit id habendu antiquissimus & Deo proximus, qui sit optimus Cic.3.de legib.
units.tr: For he would set up either a cap or a shield, or other things, according to the vows undertaken. Isidore, 5 c.3, thinks deluere is derived from diluere, to wash away, and that there were temples with fountains, in which people were washed before entering. A temple (templum) is a building consecrated to God, Festus; a place marked out by augury, Fronto; the particular places assigned to individual gods, Asconius; from contemplation, Isidore in the same place; or from protecting (tuendo), by which we are protected, i.e. we are guarded, Varro 6 On the Latin Language. A shrine (fanum) takes its name from Faunus, Fronto; or from fari, to speak, because when the priest dedicates it he speaks certain words, Festus; whence fates (fata) are sought, Asconius. A chapel (sacellum) is a small building consecrated to the gods, Fronto. Tesqua or Tesca are indeed narrow places dedicated to the gods, because mysteries are performed and guarded there, Varro 6 On the Latin Language. b A place covered with a dense growth of trees, or a place struck by a river, Fronto. c Opinions about the Lares have been various. The common people called them lares, the gods of crossroads and roads, from the fact that the Greeks call villages lauras, Arnobius 3. Others called them, as it were, aerial gods and heroes, Arnobius in the same place. Varro explains Manes, whose mother, Arnobius in the same place, may have been Mania, or the hall of Mania; or, as Lactantius writes in 1 chap. 20, Muta or Larunda and Lara. Festus, under Mania: turpes, lauae. Mania threatened to be a nurse of little boys, Festus in the same place. The same, under Vila. Festus explains Lares as the souls of men reduced to the number of gods, less properly, just as in Acts 12:15 the word for angel [ἄγγελος] was rendered by genius, though it could have been understood as the messenger of Peter. The same Festus, under Pilae: the Lares of the underworld, to whom as many balls were offered as there were heads, and as many images as there were children, so that they would spare the living and be content with these balls and images. To finish the whole matter: here understand the Lares as guardians of the house, not the Penates (that is, Neptune and Apollo, who girded the city of Troy with walls, Arnobius 3). The Lares are the same as the genii. The genius, or lateranus, of hearths (which are often made of little bricks) is a god, Arnobius 4. On the lar, see Plautus in the Aulularia. d Festus, under vitus. Ritus is a custom approved in performing sacrifices, Varro 6 On the Latin Language. Ritu, that is, in the proper way, as the haruspex prescribes, that each should sacrifice in his own rite; and we say that twelve men (others read fifteen) perform sacred rites in the Greek rite, not the Roman; so Varro. e The family's rites, the sacred rites of the clan. f It was an old and ancient practice to observe the ceremonies of the fathers, Tertullian c.5 Against the Gentiles: "You seem most faithfully to guard the zeal for worshipping the gods handed down by the fathers, a matter in which antiquity above all went astray." Therefore it is for a just cause that one must depart from the false opinions of the fathers, Jer. 8:16; Ezek. 20; Novel. 15. And rightly Pythius of Athens, when asked which of the various customs of the ancestors one should especially follow, answered that the best should be followed. So that is to be held most ancient and nearest to God which is best, Cic. 3 On the Laws.
Who are to be worshipped.

units.la: Divos, & coe⁠lestes seper habi-ti,coluto,& ollos, quos in cœlū merita fiebat,vt Heroes, Liber, Aesculapius,&c. Merita in eorum muneribus & officiis perspicuntur, Arnob 4. Illud quod sequitur, quale est, quod deos vobis inducit fabros,alios medicos, alios lanarios, nautas, citharistas, aulædos,venatores,pastores, rusticos? Et ille Musicus Deus est, & hic alter diuinus est,obstetricis ille informatus artibus,medicorum alius est institutus disciplinis: hic in sermone sicudus est,bardi sunt alij. Hinc, Venus Libetina & Liburnus libidinis ardorem incitat.
units.tr: They always held as gods and heavenly beings those whom their merits raised to heaven, such as the heroes, Liber, Aesculapius, and so on. Their merits are plain from their offices and functions (Arnobius, book 4). What follows is of this kind: why do they make for you gods who are smiths, others who are physicians, others who are wool-workers, sailors, harpists, singers to the lyre, hunters, shepherds, and farmers? One is the god of music, another is divine in a different way: one is trained in the arts of midwifery, another is instructed in the disciplines of medicine; this one is skilled in speech, and there are other bards. Hence Venus Libitina, and Liburnus, who kindles the heat of lust.

units.la: Domiducus adest nuptæ, cùm in domum mariti deducitur: Virginensis, cùm virgini zona soluitur.(Arnobius 3. Cinxiam appellat.) Subigus & dea Prema,vt virgo subigatur & comprimatur, August. de ciuit.9. Persica voluptatem seu voluptatis præliium (vt Arnobius ait lib.5.) cum dulcedine procedere perficit. Pertunda(Augustinus Partundam appellat d.loco) scrobem virginalem defodientibus maritis ad st, Arnob.4. Viriplaca,cuius interuentu viri placabantur,2.Valer.1. Alcmona parrum alit in vtero. Partula,partu gubernat. Lucina,producit in lucem,Tertull.9.de anima.Postuerta & Prosam deprecabatur,vt recti ac non peruersus partus esset 16. Gell.16. Ossilago,ossium solidatrix Arnob.4: Cunina , quæ infantes in cunis tuetur 1.Lactant.20. Rumina, lactantes pueros tuetur. Est enim Ruma,mamma, vnde suf rumi agni. Virique,Cuniæ & Ruminæ lacte fiebat non vino. Nexius in Ruma. Nodutis,& Nodoturensis, nodus producit ad res saras & fruges. Limentinus à liminibus, Cardæa à cardinibus, Forculus à foribus, Tertull. lib.de Idolol. tr.Limus,obliquitatibus,Montinus,montibus: Nemestrinus, nemoribus: Puta,putationi arborum: Peta, petendis: Patela,patefaciendis: Patelata,patefactis rebus: Vibilia,erroribus viarù: Melonica,mellis dulcedini: Orbona (huius etiam meminit Plinius 2. c.7.) orbatis præest. Pecunia Arnob.ibid. Aesculanus & filius eius Argentinus æs & argentum largiuntur,August.4. de ciuit. 2r. Murcia segnium deus Arnob.4: August.4. de ciuit.6. s rè quia Murci belloram refugæ,dixi ad l.4.§.12.ff.de venilit. Educam & Potinam appellat Augustinus de ciuitate 9. Nonius vero in Edufa Edufam & Potinnam,cum priore,inquit, cibo & potione initiaret pueros,sacrificant,ab ednlibus Edufæ , & à potione,Potinnæ nutrices. Fessonia,fessis, Augustin.4 de ciuit.21. Omitto Præstanam,Pandam, Panticam, Pelloniam , Arnob.d.loco: pellendis hostibus,August.4. de ciuit.11: Arnob. 4: Fornacé deam, Cacam,Stercutium,qui itercorandi rationem primus induxit:Tervocauerunt, Herculem, Liberum, Æsculapium, Castorem, Pollucem, Quirinum, ast olla{a}, propter quæ datur homini adcensus in cœlum, Mentem{b}, Virtutem, Pietatem{c}, Fidem{d}, earumque laudū delubra sunto. Nec vlla vitiorū sacra solemnia obeuto{e}.
units.tr: Domiduca is present for the bride when she is led into her husband's house; Virginensis, when the girdle is loosed from the maiden (Arnobius, book 3, calls her Cinxia). Subigus, and the goddess Prema, so that the maiden may be subdued and pressed down (Augustine, City of God, book 9). Persica brings about pleasure, or the battle of pleasure (as Arnobius says, book 5), proceeding with sweetness. Pertunda (Augustine calls her Partunda, in the passage cited) is for husbands digging out the virginal pit (Arnobius, book 4). Viriplaca, through whose intercession husbands were appeased (Valerius, book 2, chapter 1). Alemona nourishes the child in the womb. Partula steers the birth. Lucina brings forth into the light (Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 9). Postverta and Prosa were also invoked, so that the birth might be correct and not breech (Gellius, book 16). Ossilago, the one who solidifies the bones (Arnobius, book 4). Cunina, who watches over infants in their cradles (Lactantius, book 1, chapter 20). Rumina watches over children at the breast; for Ruma means the teat, whence the suckling lamb is called "rumis". Cunina and Rumina were worshipped with milk, not wine (see Nexius on Ruma). Nodutus and Nodotensis: the knot brings about success in matters and crops. Limentinus is named from the thresholds, Cardea from the hinges, Forculus from the doors (Tertullian, On Idolatry, chapter 1). Limus from crooked paths; Montinus from mountains; Nemestrinus from groves; Puta from the pruning of trees; Peta from things to be sought; Patelena from the opening of things; Patelata from things opened; Vibilia from the wanderings of roads; Melonica from the sweetness of honey; Orbona (Pliny also mentions her, book 2, chapter 7) presides over the bereaved. Pecunia (Arnobius, same place). Aesculanus and his son Argentinus grant bronze and silver (Augustine, City of God, book 4, chapter 21). Murcia, god of the sluggish (Arnobius, book 4; Augustine, City of God, book 4, chapter 6). Since the Murci are the refuge of the lazy, I have said this on the Digest, book 4, §12, de venditione. Agenoria, Stimula, Strenua, Quies (Augustine, same place); add Augustine, City of God, book 4, chapters 20 and 21. Portunus, for those heading into port; Consus, for counsel; Flora presides over flowers; Juno aids in childbirth; Unctia, for anointings; Vitia, for sustenance; Potua, for drinking (Arnobius, book 3). Augustine calls her Edusa and Potina (City of God, book 9). Nonius, indeed, under "Edusa", says that Edusa and Potina, together with the former, initiate boys with food and drink; they are sacrificed to, Edusa from "edulia" (foods), and Potina from drink, as nurses. Fessonia, for the weary (Augustine, City of God, book 4, chapter 21). I omit Praestana, Panda, Pantica, Pellonia (Arnobius, same place), for driving away enemies (Augustine, City of God, book 4, chapter 11; Arnobius, book 4). Fornax, a goddess; Caca; Stercutius, who first introduced the method of manuring. They have invoked three: Hercules, Liber, Aesculapius, Castor, Pollux, Quirinus. But those things on account of which a path to heaven is open to man: Mind, Virtue, Piety, Faith. Let there be shrines to the praises of these. And let no solemn rites of vices be performed.

units.la: Rubigo (unde Robigalia) ne rubigo segetes occupet. Spiniensis, ne spinæ Augustin. 4. de ciuit. 21: Nocturninus noctí. Plaut. in Amphyt. Hieronym. aduersus Vigilantium: Martianus Capella de nuptijs: Vulcanus, igni: Pythius, diuinationibus: Æsculapius, morbis præest, Minerua dea memoriæ, quasi Meminerua. Neptunus, ita dictus quod terram nubat, i. cooperiat. Mercurius, quasi medicurius, & media currens via: Ceres, quod gerat frumenta: Nouendiles dii, i. nouem musæ: Penates, qui in intimis penetralibus cœli, qui & Consentes & Complices, quod simul oriantur & occidant. Trebiani, euersores vrbium. Summani, summi dij, Arnob. 3. minores qui & Semones, quasi hemi hemones, Varro apud Fulgent. Grundules lares, Lucrij, Aij, Locutij, Arnob. 1. Parcæ, nemini parcentes: Manes, i. immanes: Lamiæ, quasi Laniæ 8. Isidor. vlt. Patellarij, Medioxumi, ollares. Sed iam cohibeo me, plenius aliquando de his dicturus, Vide interim Augustini libros de ciuitate.
units.tr: Rust (whence the Robigalia), that rust may not seize the crops. Spiniensis, that thorns... Nocturnus for the night (Plautus, in Amphitryon). Jerome, against Vigilantius. Martianus Capella, On the Marriage of Philology. Vulcan, for fire; Pythius, for divinations; Aesculapius presides over diseases; Minerva, goddess of memory, as if "Meminerva". Neptune, so called because he covers (nubat) the earth, that is, covers it over. Mercury, as if "medicurius" and "running through the middle way". Ceres, because she bears grain. The Novensiles, that is, the nine Muses. The Penates, who are in the innermost recesses; also the Consentes and Complices, because they rise and set together. Trebiani, overthrowers of cities. Summani, the highest gods (Arnobius, book 3). The lesser ones, who are also called Semones, as if "half-men" (hemi-hemones) (Varro, cited by Fulgentius). The Grundules, the Lares; Lucrii, Ai, Locutii (Arnobius, book 1). The Parcae, who spare no one; Manes, that is, not gentle (immanes); Lamiae, as if "Laniae" (Isidore, book 8, last chapter). Patellarii, Medioxumi, Ollares. But now I restrain myself, intending to speak of these more fully at some other time. Meanwhile see Augustine's books on the City of God.

units.la: {a} Ex hoc loco satis constat, cultum diis tribui quos merita in cœlum vocarunt: delubra, his propter quæ datur adcensus in cœlum.
units.tr: From this passage it is sufficiently clear that worship was given to the gods whom merits called to heaven: shrines are given to those things on account of which a path to heaven is open.

units.la: {b} Lactantius 1. c. 2. Mentem inter deos collocauit senatus, quam profecto si habuisset, eiusmodi sacra nunquam suscepisset. Plin. 1. c. 7. Innumeros credidere, atque etiam ex virtutibus virtutibusque hominum, vt Pudicitiam, Concordiam, Mentem, Spem, Honorem, Clementiam, Fidem, Poenam & beneficium.
units.tr: Lactantius, book 1, chapter 2. The Senate placed Mind among the gods, which, if it had truly possessed it, it would never have undertaken such rites. Pliny, book 1, chapter 7: They believed in countless gods, even from the virtues and vices of men, such as Chastity, Concord, Mind, Hope, Honour, Clemency, Faith, Punishment and Kindness.

units.la: {c} Plinius d. loco: Lactantius d. loco. Si vitia consecranda non sunt, ne virtutes quidem. Nec enim per se sapiunt, aut sentiunt: neque inter parietes aut ædiculas luto factas, sed inter pedes collocandæ sunt & in terius comprehendendæ, ne sint falsæ, si extra hominem fuerint.
units.tr: Pliny, same place; Lactantius, same place. If vices are not to be consecrated, neither are virtues. For they do not perceive or feel anything of themselves; nor are they to be placed between walls or in little shrines made of mud, but among the feet, and grasped in the hand, lest they be false if they are outside the man.
Pliny, same place.

units.la: {e} Meretrices tamen coluerunt Romani, Acca Laurentiam (quæ & Lupa) & Faulam, Herculis scortum vt Verrio apud Lactantium 1. c. 20: & Lauernam, deam furum. v. Festum in voce Lauerniones: Plautus in Cornicularia, Mihi Lauerna in furtis celebrasiis manus. Horatius, Pulchra Lauerna, da mihi fallere. Ea diua, caput erat sine reliquo corpore. v. Ioseph. Scalig. apud Frisium d. loco: Bellona, discordias furias Arnob. 3. sic apud Athenienses Contumeliæ fanum fuit & Impudentiæ Cicero hic. Coluerunt etiam Gentiles interdum bruta, 2. Plin. 7: Arnob. 4. Tepla felibus, scarabeis & buc-nlis sublimiē sunt elata faltigiis. Quale autē illud fuit quod de Mutino legimus? Lactatius, Et Murinus, in cuius sinu pudēdo nubetes,
units.tr: Nevertheless the Romans worshipped prostitutes: Acca Laurentia (who is also called Lupa), and Faula, the mistress of Hercules, as Verrius says in Lactantius, book 1, chapter 20; and Laverna, goddess of thieves (see Festus, under "Laverniones"). Plautus, in the Cornicularia: "Laverna has been celebrated by my hand in thefts." Horace: "Beautiful Laverna, grant that I may deceive." She was a goddess whose head was all there was, without the rest of the body (see Joseph Scaliger, cited by Frisius, same place). Bellona, goddess of discord and madness (Arnobius, book 3). Thus among the Athenians there was a shrine to Reproach and to Impudence (Cicero, here). The Gentiles also sometimes worshipped beasts (Pliny, book 2, chapter 7; Arnobius, book 4): temples to cats, scarabs and... were raised high on pediments. But what was that which we read about Mutinus? Lactantius: "And Murinus, in whose lap brides, blushing, ..."
At what time they were to be worshipped

units.la: FERIIS iurgia amouento: eásque deus delibasse videatur 1.c.20: Arnob.4: Festus in voce Munuus, August. 4. de civit.11 & 6. de civit. 9: Febrim etiá coluerunt, Mala Fortuna [?] Plin.ibid.: Pavore & Pallore Tullus Hostilius figuravit & coluit. Cloacinæ simulachrum [?], in cloaca maxima repertum Tatius consecrauit: 1.Lactant. 20. Matrimonia inter deos etiá crediderunt: vt & alios canos, alios iuuenes, pueros, claudos, ouo editos, alternis diebus viuentes moriebantur [?] adulterium inter ipsos fingebat, iurgia, odia, furta Plin.d.loco. a Feria à feriedis.victimis appellata, Festus in voce Feria. Antiqui ferias festas dicebant, Idem ib. Harum aliae, Sementinæ, paganicæ, conceptiuæ: Varro 5.de lingua: Feriæ dies [?] Praecidaneæ 4.Gell.6.in f. publicæ, Latinæ l.2. §.33.ff.de orig.iuris: Varro 5.de lingua: denicales, quoties hominis mortui causa, familia purgabatur: vexu n. Græci mortuum appellat. Festus in Denicales, aftiuæ 9.Gell.15.in pv.l.7. C.de feriis: copitalicæ Festus in conceptiuæ: vindemiales 16.Gell.4.l.1.in pr. & fine.l. 4.ff.de feriis: imperiales l.4.C. de feriis statæ, quæ certo statutóq; tempore obseruari fiebant, Festus in voce Feria: quæ fiunt ex more & consuetudine l.7.ff. de off. proconsul: quæ & solennes l.26.§.7.ff.ex quib.causf.maior: l.3.C.de dilationibus: quibus opponi rei repetinæ d.l.3. extra ordine indicta d.§.7. Aliæ sunt sine Festo, vt Nundinæ: cum Festo vt Saturnalia, quibus adiungebantur epulationes ex prouerbio, fortuque pecorum F.ibid in voce Feria: aliæ sine proprio vocabulo, aliæ cum vocabulo, vt Nouendiales Varro 5.de lingua. Statiuæ, vniuersi populi communes. Conceptiuæ à magistratibus, vel sacerdotibus. Cocet ea vt Latinæ, Paganalia, Sementinæ, Capitalia. Imperatiuæ à consulibus, vel Prætoribus. (Hodie imperiales dicuntur, quod à principe indicentur l.4.C. de feriis) eorum arbitrio indictæ. Nundinæ, sunt pagorum & rusticorum. Proprie, familiarum: vt Claudiæ, Aemiliæ, Iuliæ Corneliæ. Singulorum, vt natalitii, fulguraque suscepiones: item funerum atque expiationum. Apud veteres etiam qui nominabant Salutè, Semoniam, Saiam, Segetiæ, Tutilinæ, ferias obseruabant, Flaminica quoties tonitru audierat, ferias agebat, donec deos placaret. In indictis & conceptis feriis nefas erat quidquam agi: idque per præconem edicebatur, qui id neglexisset, multabatur, & porco piaculo dabat. Non tamen polluebatur feriæ, si quis quid egisset ad deos pertinet aut sacrorum causa, aut ad vrgentem vitæ vtilitatem. Ideo non videbatur ferias polluisse, qui adhibitis operis bouë spec[u]liberasset, aut qui trabe tecta fractâ fulsisset, quive oue, scabiei causa, lauasset. Virg.Georg.1. & breuiter, Scæuola cofultus quid feriis agi liceret, respondit, quod prætermissum noceret Macrob.1.Satur.16. A feriis feriati dies l.6.ff. de feriis. Feriati gemini menses Cod.de feriis. b l.lites.Iurgare, iu-
units.tr: "On feast days they shall keep away quarrels," and the god is supposed to have taken his share of them. (Cited: Arnobius, book 4; Festus, s.v. Munuus; Augustine, City of God, books 4, 6 and 11.) They also worshipped Fever, and Bad Fortune [?]. Pliny, in the same place, says that Tullus Hostilius represented and worshipped Fear and Pallor. Tatius consecrated an image of Cloacina, found in the great sewer. (Lactantius, book 1, ch. 20.) They also believed that the gods married one another, and they invented adultery among them, along with quarrels, hatreds and thefts (Pliny, same place). The feriae are named from the feriae, the victims [?] (Festus, s.v. Feria). The ancients called festivals "feriae" (Festus, same word). Of these some were Sementinae, paganicae, conceptivae (Varro, book 5, On the Latin Language: feriae days [?]); praecidaneae (Gellius, book 4, ch. 6); publicae, Latinae (Digest 1.2.33, On the origin of law); denicales, whenever a household was purified because of a dead man (Varro, book 5; the Greeks call the dead man "vexu"; Festus, s.v. Denicales); astivae (Gellius, book 9, ch. 15; Code, On holidays, law 7); capitalicae (Festus, s.v. conceptivae); vindemiales (Gellius, book 16, ch. 4; Digest 1.4, beginning and end; Digest, On holidays, law 4); imperiales (Code, On holidays, law 4); stated feriae, which were kept at a fixed and appointed time (Festus, s.v. Feria); those which are held by custom and usage (Digest 1.7, On the duties of a proconsul); those which are also solemn (Digest 26.7, On the causes of greater restitution; Code, On delays, law 3); and those for which an unexpected matter may be brought forward (said law 3, and said section 7, declared outside the ordinary course). Others have no Festus, such as the Nundinae; others have a Festus, such as the Saturnalia, to which feasting was added, according to the proverb, "and the flocks rest" (Festus, same word); others have no proper name, others have a name, such as the Novendiales (Varro, book 5). The stated feriae were common to the whole people; the conceptivae were declared by the magistrates or priests, such as the Latinae, Paganalia, Sementinae and Capitalia; the imperativae were appointed by the consuls or praetors. (Today they are called imperial, because they are proclaimed by the prince; Code, On holidays, law 4.) They were fixed by their decision. The Nundinae belong to the villages and country folk. Properly they belong to families, such as the Claudian, Aemilian, Julian and Cornelian. Some belong to individuals, such as birthdays and the taking up of the toga; likewise those of funerals and purifications. Among the ancients, those who named the Salus, Semonia, Saia, Segetia and Tutilina also kept feriae; the Flaminica, whenever she heard thunder, kept a festival until she had appeased the gods. On declared and conceived feriae it was unlawful to do anything, and this was announced by a herald; whoever neglected it was fined and gave a pig as expiation. Yet the feriae were not violated if someone did something that pertained to the gods, either for the sake of the sacred rites or for the urgent need of life. So he was not thought to have broken the feriae who, with the help of work-oxen, drew out a ox [?], or who, when a beam was broken, propped up a roof, or who washed a sheep to cure mange. (Virgil, Georgics 1.) And briefly, when Scaevola was consulted what might lawfully be done on feriae, he answered: what, if left undone, would cause harm (Macrobius, book 1, Saturnalia, ch. 16). From feriae come "feriati" days (Digest 6, On holidays). "Feriati gemini menses" (Code, On holidays). "Lites" (law); "iurgare" [...]

units.la: a Festus in voce Feria. b Festus in voce Feria. in famulis, operibus patratis {a}, habento. Itaque, ut ita cadat in annuis amfracti-bus{b}, descriptum esto. Certásque fru-ges, certásque baccas sacerdotes publi-cè libanto : hoc certis factificiis, ac die-bus{c}. Itémque alios addes{d}, uberta-tem lactis, fœtúsque seruanto. Idque ne
units.tr: (a) Festus, s.v. Feria. (b) Festus, s.v. Feria. "...among the servants, once the work is done, let them keep [the feast]. So, that it may fall thus in the yearly turnings, let it be written down. And let the priests make a public offering of certain grains and certain berries, at certain sacrifices and days. And likewise you shall add others: let them preserve the fruitfulness of milk and of offspring. And let this not..."

units.la: {b} amfractum ab origine flexum. Lex duodecim tabularum, Vix latitudo, in amfractum sexdecim pedes. Varro sexto de lingua: lege 8. ff. de servitutibus rusticor[?]. Est igitur hic amfractus, temporis reuolutio. Annus enim flaris[?] temporibus in se redit & renoluitur.
units.tr: {b} amfractus: a bend, turned from its origin. Law of the Twelve Tables: "the width of a road at a turn, sixteen feet." Varro, book 6, On the Latin Language; Digest, On servitudes of rural estates, law 8. Here, therefore, amfractus is the turning back of time: for the year, by its seasons, returns into itself and is rolled round.

units.la: Plautus in Asinaria. si hoc patro. Saluftius in Catilin incepta patrauissent. Tacitus fecundo, si patrandae neci venenum imitteretur. Idem 4. Maluit patrari quam inceptafacinoris reus esse: adde 8. Quintilian. 5.
units.tr: Plautus, in the Asinaria: "if this is done." Sallust, in the Catiline: "had carried out the things begun." Tacitus, book 2: "if poison were sent in to carry out the killing." The same, book 4: "he preferred to have the deed carried out than to be the accused author of a begun crime." Add Quintilian, book 8, and book 5.

units.la: {c} De diebus aliquid dicendum videtur. Dierum alij, inquit Varro 5. de lingua, deorum: alij hominum causa instituti. Illi, vel statuti vel annales. Statuti, ut Carmentalia, Lupercalia, Quirinalia, Feralia (quod diis inferis ad sepulchra epulas deferrent) Terminalia (quod in extremis diebus anni, id est, Februarij, sacra fierent) Equirria[?], ab equorum cursu: Liberalia, in honorem Liberi patris: Megalensia (in honorem Magnae deae) Fordicidia, a fordeis bo[?]um: Carmentalia, Palilia, Cerealia, Vinalia (quae erant a Vinis) Vestalia (vide Festum in voce Penus[?]) Neptunalia, Furinalia, Portumnalia, Consualia, Volcanalia, Vortumnalia, Fortunalia, Opalia, Angeronalia (alij legunt Angeronalia) Accalia, seu Laurentalia, Opconsiua[?], a diis & deabus ita dicta sunt, Meditrinalia, quod eo die vinum vetus, & nouum degustarent medicamenti causa: Fontinalia, quod eo die putei coronarent, & in fontes coronas mitterent, Lupercalia, Varro quinto de lingua: Matralia, Varro quarto de lingua: Armilustrium, quod armati sacra facerent: Tubilustrium, quod tubae lustrarentur in foro Futorio: Nonae Caprotinae, dies Agonales, Quinquatrus, Sexatrus, Septimatrus, Quinquatrus minusculae, Fortis-Fortunae, Populi fugia. Et haec de statutis diebus quae in compitis per agebantur. Feriae in compitalia. Annales vero, ut Compitalia & Feriae. Hominum causa dies instituti, Kalendae, Nonae, Idus, dies fasti, Nefasti, Comitiales, quibus in comitio conueniebant. Fasti in Comitiis.
units.tr: {c} Something must be said about the days. Varro, book 5, On the Latin Language, says that some days were instituted for the sake of the gods, and others for the sake of men. Those were either fixed or annual. Fixed were the Carmentalia, Lupercalia, Quirinalia, Feralia (so called because they carried feasts to the dead at the tombs), Terminalia (because the rites were performed on the last days of the year, that is, of February), Equirria, from the running of horses; Liberalia, in honour of Father Liber; Megalensia (in honour of the Great Goddess); Fordicidia, from the sacrifice of pregnant cows; Carmentalia, Palilia, Cerealia, Vinalia (which were from the vines), Vestalia (see Festus, s.v. Penus), Neptunalia, Furinalia, Portunalia, Consualia, Volcanalia, Vertumnalia, Fortunalia, Opalia, Angeronalia (others read Angeronalia), Accalia, or Laurentalia, Opiconsivia, so called after gods and goddesses; Meditrinalia, because on that day they tasted old and new wine as a medicine; Fontinalia, because on that day they crowned the wells and threw garlands into the springs; Lupercalia (Varro, book 5, On the Latin Language); Matralia (Varro, book 4, On the Latin Language); Armilustrium, because those under arms performed sacred rites; Tubilustrium, because the trumpets were purified in the Forum Futorium; the Nonae Caprotinae; the Agonal days; Quinquatrus, Sexatrus, Septimatrus, the lesser Quinquatrus, Fors Fortuna, Populi fugia. And these are the fixed days, which were kept at the crossroads. Feriae at the Compitalia. The annual days, such as the Compitalia and Feriae. Days were instituted for the sake of men: the Kalends, Nones, Ides; fasti days, nefasti days, comitial days, on which they assembled in the comitium. Fasti: on the Comitia.

units.la: {d} ad dies. Legendum puto, illos ad dies: nisi mauis [illegible, ~8 letters] illos[?] ad dies. committi possit, ad eam rem, & rationem, cursus annuos sacerdotes finiunto.
units.tr: {d} "ad dies." I think we should read "illos ad dies"; unless you prefer [illegible] "illos ad dies," which could be applied to that matter and reasoning: let the priests fix the annual courses.
By what victims they are to be worshipped.

units.la: QVAE QVE quoque{a} diuo decorae, gratasque sint hostiae, pioui-dento.
units.tr: Let them provide whatever victims are fitting and pleasing to the god.
Concerning priests, pontiffs and flamens.

units.la: DIVISQVE alijs alij sacerdotes{b} omnibus pontifices{c} singulis flamines{d} iunto.
units.tr: And let them appoint other priests for the other gods, and pontiffs for all, and a flamen for each single god.

units.la: Rex sacrorum, ea sacra faciebat, quae facere reges fuerunt. Fest. in voce Sacrificulus. Diebus agonalibus arietem in regia immolabat: ferias edicebat. Varro 3. de lingua. Deinde Dialis id est, Iouis: post hunc Martialis: quarto Quirinalis: quinto Pontifex maximus: eoque ordine in conuiuiis adhibebant. Festus in voce ordo. Praeter eos erant Salij, dicti quod quotannis in comitio facere solebant. Luperci, quod in lupercali sacrificarent. Fratres aruales, quod sacra facerent, vt fruges ferrent: annua Varro 4. de lingua. erant numero XII, insigne spinea corona & albae infulae. 6. Gell. 7. Sodales Titij à Titiis auibus, quas in auguriis certis obseruare solebant. Varro 4. de lingua. Epulones, quod epulas Iouj indicendi potestatem haberet. Festus in voce epulones.
units.tr: The king of sacred rites performed those sacred rites which kings used to perform. Festus, s.v. Sacrificulus. On the agonal days he sacrificed a ram in the palace and proclaimed the holidays. Varro, De lingua Latina, bk 3. Next came the Dialis, that is, of Jupiter; after him the Martialis; fourth the Quirinalis; fifth the pontifex maximus; and in this order they were given places at banquets. Festus, s.v. ordo. Besides these there were the Salii, so called because they used to perform their rites every year in the Comitium. The Luperci, because they sacrificed in the Lupercal. The Fratres Arvales, because they performed sacred rites so that the fields might bear crops; Varro, bk 4 of De lingua, they were twelve in number, their badge a thorn-wreath and white fillets. Gellius, bk 6, ch. 7. The Sodales Titii, from the Tatian birds, which they used to observe in fixed augury. Varro, bk 4 of De lingua. The Epulones, because they had the power of appointing the feasts of Jupiter. Festus, s.v. epulones.

units.la: {c} Pontifices, à posse & facere, vel potius à ponte faciendo, nam ab his, sublicius factus est primum. Varro 4. de lingua.
units.tr: Pontiffs, from posse and facere, or rather from pontem facere, to make a bridge; for it was by these men that the first wooden bridge was made. Varro, bk 4 of De lingua.

units.la: Penes eos annis fere 100. mansit scientia interpretandi leges XII. tabularum l. 2. §. 6. ff. de origine iuris & confitendarum religionum Cicer. 2. de legib. vel vt abide legit Lipsius, cui fide tuendarum, in annales quoque referre, quoties annona cara, aut Lunae aut Solis defectiones arcidiffent. Gell. 28. in f.
units.tr: For about 100 years the knowledge of interpreting the laws of the Twelve Tables remained with them (Dig. 1.2.2.6, De origine iuris) and of prescribing the religious observances (Cicero, De legibus, bk 2); or, as Lipsius reads it, of guarding the faith; and they also recorded in the annals whenever the grain supply was dear, or eclipses of the moon or sun had occurred. Gellius, bk 28, at the end.

units.la: {d} Flamines, quasi filamines, quod caput eorum velatum esset & cinctum filo. Singuli cognomina habent ab eo deo cui sacra faciunt, sed partim sunt aperta, partim obscura. Aperta vt Martialis, Volcanalis Varro 4. de lingua: & lib. 6. Quirinalis, obscura, Volturnalis, Palatualis d. lib. 4. lib. 6. ei deo sacrificabat in cuius tutela palatium esset. Fest. in voce Palatualis, Furinalis d. lib. 4. lib. 5. lib. 6. Floralis, Falacer, Pomonalis, d. lib. 4. d. lib. 6. Dialis, Ionis Flamen, qui & Dionis, albo galero utebatur d. lib. 4. De Dialis ceremoniis, priuilegiis & authoritate, vide 10. Gell. 15. Inter cetera priuilegia, illud singulare, quod piaculum esset eo die verberari, qui ad verberandum ductus, ad pedes eius supplex procubuisset. Gell. ibid. Quod clerici & monachi secuto Iustiniani videntur vti vsurpare, imitari, & vsurpare te l. 6. C. de episcop. audientia.
units.tr: Flamens, as if filamines, because their heads were veiled and bound with a woollen thread. Each had a cognomen taken from the god to whom he performed sacred rites, but some of these are plain and some obscure. Plain ones: the Martialis, the Volcanalis (Varro, bk 4 and bk 6 of De lingua), the Quirinalis. Obscure ones: the Volturnalis, the Palatualis (ibid., bks 4 and 6), who sacrificed to the god in whose protection the palace was (Festus, s.v. Palatualis); the Furinalis (ibid., bks 4, 5 and 6); the Floralis, the Falacer, the Pomonalis (ibid., bks 4 and 6); the Dialis, the flamen of Jupiter, who was also called of Dis, used to wear a white cap (ibid., bk 4). On the ceremonies, privileges and authority of the Dialis, see Gellius, bk 10, ch. 15. Among his other privileges was this unique one: it was an offence against sacred law to beat on that day anyone who was being led off to be beaten and had fallen as a suppliant at his feet. Gellius, ibid. Clerics and monks seem, following Justinian, to use and imitate and usurp this privilege; see Cod. 1.6, De episcopali audientia.
Concerning the Vestals.

units.la: VIRGINES Vestales{a} in urbe custo-diunto{b} ignem{c} foci publici sempiternum quoque & priuatim,& publice modo{d},ri-tuque fiat, discunto ignari à publicis sa-cerdotibus.
units.tr: Let the Vestal virgins guard in the city the perpetual fire of the public hearth; and let them learn, from the public priests, the manner and rite by which it is to be kept up both privately and publicly, and let them learn it, not being ignorant.
Concerning the duties of the priests.
Let there be two kinds of them:

units.la: 12. Inter quæ illud notandum est,quòd Vestalis simul ac in atrium Vestæ deducebatur,ac pontificibus tradita erat,eo statim tempore sine emancipatione, & sine capitis minutione,à patria potestate exiret, & ius testamenti faciendi adipisceretur Plutarch.in Numa:qua de re dixi ad 10. Vlpian.§.vltim. Item, quòd neque hæres esset cuiquam intestato, neque intestatæ quisquam: sed bona eius in publicum redigebantur Gell. d. loco. Victu modico, aliisque priuilegiis honoratas fuisse, vt & ius ex testamento capiendi haberent, constat ex Symmacho in epistola pro suis paternis. Raro iurabant Vestales, nec vnquam, nisi per suam Vestam Senec.6.controuers.3.
units.tr: 12.
