Among these matters it is to be noted that a Vestal, as soon as she was led into the atrium of Vesta and handed over to the pontiffs, at that very moment, without emancipation and without loss of status, passed out of her father's power and acquired the right of making a will (Plutarch, Life of Numa; on this I spoke at Ulpian, 10, last section). Likewise, she could not be heir to anyone who died intestate, nor could anyone be heir to her if she died intestate; but her goods were carried over to the public treasury (Gellius, loc. cit.). That the Vestals were honoured with a modest allowance and other privileges, so that they also had the right of taking under a will, is established by Symmachus in a letter on behalf of his paternal estates. The Vestals rarely took an oath, and never except by their own Vesta (Seneca, Controversies, bk 6, contr. 3).

units.la: {b} ideoque dicitur ignis inextinguibilis à Tertulliano 2. ad uxorem. & si interstinctus esset, virgines verberibus afficiebantur à Pontifice, Festus in voce Ignis: Cuius rei extat exemplum apud Liuium 28. Cur ita ignem obseruarent, vide Plutarch. in Numa.
units.tr: Therefore the fire is called inextinguishable (Tertullian, To His Wife, bk 2); and if it went out, the virgins were beaten by the Pontiff with rods (Festus, s.v. Ignis). An example of this is found in Livy, bk 28. On why they kept the fire in this way, see Plutarch, Life of Numa.

units.la: {c} Vesta Græcis ἑστία. Cicero 2. de legib. Hamnia Ouid. 6. Fast. Nec tu aliud Vestam,quàm viuam intellige flammam Tertullian. 1. aduersus Marcion. Mos ille ignis asseruandi ab illo deducus Virgil. 2. Aeneid. vers. 295. 296. Ilienses forte hunc morem didicerant à Medis & Assyriis, apud quos ignis cultus fuit perenniter, Plutarch.de facie Lunæ: vt & apud Aegyptios Diodor. 1. cap. 2. & Persas Strabo 15: Herodot. 1. Athenienses, Pausanias in Attic. c. 1. Delphos Plutarch. in tract. περὶ τῆ εἰ.
units.tr: The Greeks call Vesta hestia [ἑστία]. Cicero, De legibus, bk 2. Hamnia: Ovid, Fasti, bk 6. "Do not understand Vesta as anything other than the living flame" (Tertullian, Against Marcion, bk 1). That custom of keeping the fire perpetually derives from that source (Virgil, Aeneid, bk 2, lines 295–296). The Trojans had perhaps learned this custom from the Medes and Assyrians, among whom fire was worshipped unceasingly (Plutarch, On the Face of the Moon); as also among the Egyptians (Diodorus, bk 1, ch. 2) and the Persians (Strabo, bk 15; Herodotus, bk 1), the Athenians (Pausanias, Attica, ch. 1), and at Delphi (Plutarch, in the treatise On E at Delphi).

units.la: {d} Mos is fuit, Tabulam felicis materiæ tandiu terebrabant, quousque exceptum ignem cribro æneo virgo in ædem ferret. Festus in voce Ignis Vesta. Simplicius 3. de cœlo [illegible, ~30 letters] Seneca 15. Quod de fumariolis ignis æterni citatur ex Tertulliano de pœnit. ntia. huc non pertinet, sed ad montem Vesuuum.
units.tr: There was a custom: they bored a tablet of lucky wood for a long time, until a virgin could carry the fire caught in a bronze sieve into the temple (Festus, s.v. Ignis, Vesta). Simplicius, On the Heavens, bk 3 [illegible] Seneca, bk 15. What is cited from Tertullian, On Repentance, about the eternal fire of the fumaroles does not belong here, but refers to Mount Vesuvius.

units.la: {e} Sacerdotum duo genera, Vnum, eorum qui ceremoniis præerant. Alte-rum, qui interpretarentur fatidica & vatum effata cere-moniis. id est, placandis diis. vnum 4, quod praesit caeremoniis{a}, & sacris: alterum, quod interpretetur fatidicorum{c}, & vatum{d} effata incognita, cum senatus populúsque adíciuerit.
units.tr: There are two kinds of priests: one, of those who presided over the ceremonies; the other, of those who interpret the prophetic utterances and obscure sayings of the seers, in matters pertaining to the ceremonies, that is, for appeasing the gods. The first is to preside over ceremonies and sacred rites; the second is to interpret the prophetic utterances and the obscure sayings of the seers, when the senate and people have so ordered.
On Augurs and Haruspices.

units.la: INTERPRETES autem Iouis optimi maximi, publici augures{e} signis, & auspiciis{f} poltea vidento, disciplinam tenento. Sacerdotes vinetas{g} virgetásque{h}, & salutem populi augurantò, quíque agét rem duelli{i}, quíque populare auspicum praemonento: ollíque obtemperanto: diuorúmque iras prouidento, iísque parento: cœlíque fulgura regionibus ratis{k} tē-peranto: vrbémque, & agros, & templa liberata & effata{m} habento: quæque augures publicè auspicabantur, Festus in voce Augur & Auguraculum.
units.tr: The interpreters of Jupiter Best and Greatest, the public augurs, shall keep the discipline of the signs and auspices, and afterwards shall observe the omens; the priests (vinetas and virgetasque) shall foretell the safety of the people, and whoever shall conduct a war, and whoever shall give warning of the popular auspices; they shall obey these, provide against the anger of the gods and obey them; and they shall hold the lightnings from the sky in their regions as fixed, and the city, the fields and the temples shall be held as consecrated and pronounced. And whatever the augurs publicly took auspices for: Festus, under the words Augur and Auguraculum.

units.la: {f} Auspicium ab aue ípiciénda. Veteres enim dicebant, Spicio non Aspicio. Festus in voce Auspicium.
units.tr: {f} Auspicium, from avis, a bird, to be looked at; for the ancients said spicio, not aspicio. Festus, under the word Auspicium.

units.la: {g} Vineta, ac vinex a vite multa. Varro 4. de lingua, scribens de oliuetis & vinetis: Idem 1. de re rustic. 18.
units.tr: {g} Vineta, and vinex from vitis, a vine, much. Varro, book 4 of On the Latin Language, writing about olive groves and vineyards (vinetis). The same, book 1 of On Agriculture, 18.

units.la: {h} Isidorus 17. cap.6. videtur appellare virectum: locum, vbi virgulæ, nouellæ & virentes. Forte apud Isidorum legi oportet virgectum: quod idem est ac virgetum. Veteres enim dumeta dicebant, quæ nos dumeta. Festus in voce Dumeta. Porrò virgetum ea forma dicitur, qua Pometum apud Sosipatrum, Myrthetum apud Serenium: Nucetum apud Tertullianum lib. adversus Valentin. Iuncetum apud Varronem 1. de re rust. 8. & alia infinita.
units.tr: {h} Isidore, book 17, chapter 6, seems to call it virectum: a place where there are small shoots, new growth and greenery. Perhaps in Isidore one ought to read virgectum, which is the same as virgetum. For the ancients called dumeta what we call thickets. Festus, under the word Dumeta. Moreover, virgetum is called by that form in which Pometum is used by Sosipater, Myrthetum by Serenius, Nucetum by Tertullian in his book against Valentinus, Iuncetum by Varro, On Agriculture, book 1, 8, and countless others.

units.la: {i} id est, belli. Festus in voce Duellum. Duellum enim duorum concursus. hinc Duellona Bellona. Perduellum etiam dicebant, unde perduelles, id est hostes, Varro 6. de lingua, vide l. 234. ff. de verborum significationibus.
units.tr: {i} That is, of war. Festus, under the word Duellum. For duellum is the meeting of two; hence Duellona, Bellona. They also said perduellum, whence perduelles, that is, enemies: Varro, book 6 of On the Latin Language; see law 234 of the Digest, On the meaning of words.

units.la: {k} id est, certis. Attius in Menalippe, nego ratum esse quod dicas, Festus in voce Ratus.
units.tr: {k} That is, with certainty. Attius in Menalippe: "I deny that what you say is valid." Festus, under the word Ratus.

units.la: {l} id est, effatu, elocuta, Festus in voce Liberata.
units.tr: {l} That is, by utterance, spoken. Festus, under the word Liberata.

units.la: {m} idem est quod liberata. Festus in voce Effata: Varro quinto de lingua. Effata dicuntur, quod augures sine auspicium extra vrbem agris sunt effati. hinc effari Templa dicuntur ab auguribus ad sacratus, qui in his fines sunt: fana, quod pontifices, in sacrando facuntur finem.
units.tr: {m} The same as liberata. Festus, under the word Effata: Varro, book 5 of On the Latin Language. They are called effata because the augurs, without the auspices, were pronounced (effati) outside the city in the fields. Hence the temples are said by the augurs to be "effata" when the consecrated ground is marked out by boundaries: the shrines, because the pontiffs, in consecrating, make the boundary.

units.la: [?]gur[?] iniusta, nefasta{a}, vitiosa, dira{b} defixerit{c}, irrita{d} infectaque{e} funto: quisque non paruerit, capitale esto{f}.
units.tr: If an augur has declared (defixerit) anything unjust, unlucky, faulty or ominous, let it be void and invalid; whoever does not obey, let it be a capital offence.
On the fetiales.

units.la: FOEDERVM{g}, pacis, belli, inducia- rum oratores, fetiales{h}, iudices sunto. belliquo eorum{i} la, disceptanto.
units.tr: Let the fetiales be the envoys and judges of treaties, of peace, of war and of truces, and let them settle disputes concerning these.
On the Etruscans and Haruspices.
Prodigies and portents (are to be referred) to the Etruscans.

units.la: {b} Dirum, ad Dei iram natum. Festus in Dirus. Diris deuouere, est deorum irae.
units.tr: {b} Dirum, from the anger of God. Festus, under Dirus. To curse with dire omens (diris deuouere) is the anger of the gods.
{c} That is, defined (definierit).
{d} Not rightly done.

units.la: {e} Quid si tali die Praetor imprudens verbum emisit, aut quem manumisit? Manumissus liber est, sed vitio: vt magistratus vitio creatus, nihilo secius magistratus. Imprudens qui dixisset, piacularî hostia piari poterat: quia prudens, vt impius non poterat, Varro 5. de lingua.
units.tr: {e} What if on such a day the praetor, without knowing it, spoke a word, or manumitted someone? The person manumitted is free, but defectively; just as a magistrate created with a defect is nonetheless a magistrate. One who spoke without knowing could be purified by an expiatory victim; because one who did so knowingly could not be purified, as an impious person could not. Varro, book 5 of On the Latin Language.

units.la: {f} hinc perspicitur satis, quaenam fuerit Augurum potestas. Cicero hic. Quid est magis quam posse comitia tollere, concilia vel instituta dimittere, vel habita rescindere? quid grauius quam rem susceptam dirimi, si vnus augur aliter dixerit, quid magnificentius, quam posse decernere, vt magistratu se abdicent consules. Quid religiosius, quam cum populo cum plebe agendi ius aut dare aut non dare? quid legem, si non recte rogata est, tollere? Nihil domi, nihil foris per magistratus gestum sine eorum authoritate potest quidquam probari?
units.tr: {f} From this it is clear enough what the power of the augurs was. Cicero here: "What is greater than being able to dissolve assemblies, to dismiss councils or institutions, or to annul what has been held? What is more weighty than for a matter undertaken to be broken off if a single augur has spoken otherwise? What is more splendid than being able to decree that consuls abdicate their magistracy? What is more sacred than being able to grant or refuse the right of acting with the people or the plebs? Or to annul a law if it was not properly proposed? Can anything be approved at home or abroad that is done by magistrates without their authority?"

units.la: {g} Fediales, oratores & iudices foederum, pacis, belli, & inducearum, a feriendo dicti: vt apud quos belli pacisque faciendae ius esset. Festus ibidem: vt qui fidei publicae inter populos praeessent, per quos etiam fieret, vt iustum concipere bellum. Varro ibidem. Porrò, quo ritu, quibusque verbis Fecialis populo Romano bellum indicerer, vide apud Gellium 16. cap. 4. De fecialibus adde Halicarnass. & Plutarchum in Numa.
units.tr: {g} Fetiales, envoys and judges of treaties, of peace, of war and of truces, so called from feriendo (striking), since they had the right to make war and peace. Festus in the same place: as those who presided over the public faith between peoples, through whom it also came about that a just war was undertaken. Varro in the same place. Moreover, for the rite and the words by which the fetialis declared war on the Roman people, see Gellius, book 16, chapter 4. On the fetiales add Halicarnassus and Plutarch in Numa.

units.la: {h} ita legitur apud Festum, in Fetiales: Feciales a Varrone dicuntur, de lingua.
units.tr: {h} So it is read in Festus, under Fetiales: "Feciales are called by Varro," On the Latin Language.

units.la: {i} Portenta, quae quid porro tendatur, indicant, Festus in Portentum: adde quae dixi ad leg. 38. ff. de verborum significatione.
units.tr: {i} Portenta, which indicate where something tends (quo porro tendatur); Festus under Portentum. Add what I have said on law 38 of the Digest, On the meaning of words.
{k} Some read it thus, Hetruria; Gellius, book 4.

units.la: {l} Etruria de coelo tacta scientissimè animaduertit, eademque interpretarur, quid quibusdam ostendatur, Cicero de divinatione. Nostrorum Etruscorum disciplinam res ita probauit Cicero libro 2. de natura. Auspicium autem primus Etrufcis tradidisse dicitur quidam strages 8. Iffior. 9.
units.tr: {l} Etruria most skilfully observed what was struck from the sky and interpreted what is shown to some people, Cicero, On Divination. Cicero, book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods, shows that the matter itself has confirmed the discipline of our Etruscans. It is said that a certain man first handed down augury to the Etruscans: Strages, book 8; Isidore, book 9.

units.la: & haruspices a si Senatus iusserit, deferun-to: Etruriaeque b principes disciplinam do-cento: quibus diuis creuerint, procuranto: iidemque fulgura atque obstita c pianto.
units.tr: And if the Senate has ordered it, let the haruspices be brought in; let the leaders of Etruria teach the discipline; let them take care of the gods by whom they were increased; and let them themselves expiate lightnings and obstructions.
On nocturnal rites.

units.la: NOCTVRNA d mulierum sacrifi-cia e ne sunto f, praeter olla, quae pro po-Quota enim quaeque res euenit praedicata ab his? aut si euenerit quidpiam, quis affirmare potest, cur no casu id euenerit? De perfidia aruspicum Arufpicina hodie damnata est Superiorum oblitus Cicero 2. de Natur.arufpicinaartem diuinam esse ait. & 2. de diuinat. commu-nis reipublicae causa, communisque religionis colendam censet.
units.tr: Let there be no NOCTURNAL sacrifices of women, except those which are offered for the people's welfare... For how seldom does an event turn out as these men predicted? Or if something does happen, who can say that it came about by chance and not otherwise? On the treachery of the haruspices: haruspicy is condemned today. Forgetting his predecessors, Cicero in book 2 of On the Nature of the Gods calls haruspicy a divine art, and in book 2 of On Divination he judges that it ought to be cultivated for the common good of the commonwealth and of religion.

units.la: b Cicero, Apud maiores inquit nostros Senatus decreuit, vt de principum filiis sex, singulis Etruriae populis in disciplinam tra-derentur, ne ars propter tenuitatem hominum a religionis antho-ritate abduceretur ad mercedem, atque quaestum. Cicero 1. de diui-nat. c alij legunt ostenta, ab Obstinet antiquo, i.ostendit, Fest. in voce Obstinet. Sed melius est in ea re sequi Cloatium & Aelii Stilonem, quibus obstitutum est idem quod violatum, attactumque de coelo Festus in Obstiinum. d Vide ea de re triste exemplum apud Liuium 39. Huc etiam facit Porrii Latronis declamatio contra Catilinam, de coetibus in vrbe noctu non agirandis. e Nocturna sacrificia Dionysius videtur appellare, [illegible, ~40 letters] f Concilium Eliberinum ea de causa vetuit nocturnas peruigilationes mulierum in coemeteriis, quod multae eo praetexu impudicitiae committerentur. Hinc enim apud Plautum in Aulul. v.ia, Lycomedes adolescens dicitur Enclionis filiam violasse in Cereris vigiliis. & Pentheus apud Euripidem in Bacchis, cum aud[?]rer Orgia noctu celebrari, exclamauit, [illegible, ~30 letters] & Eupolis in Baptis, ne mor is quidem piaculo adduci potuit, quominus damnaret nocturna sacrificia Athenien-sium quae Collytia dicebantur. Apud Myonem vrbem fuerunt etiam, [illegible, ~30 letters] nocturna quaedam sacrificia instituta, quae p[?] tea publicata a Constantino lege 5. Cod. Theodos. de paganis & sacrificijs. Illud quo-que legitur, Tertulliani etiam Christianos noctu conuenisse, sed cum aliis interdiu ac palam facile non possent, & tamen eis obiectum, quod in principis maleficium conuararent, quod infanticidia, quod Epulae Thyesteae, & ad incestum incestum, stupra, & illicitas coniunctiones apud eos fierent, Tertull. 9. Apolog. obiectum depulo rite fient. Neve initianto, nisi vt as-solet Cereri {a}, Græco {b} sacro.
units.tr: b Cicero: "Among our ancestors the Senate decreed that six sons of the leading men, from each of the peoples of Etruria, should be handed over for instruction in the discipline, so that the art, because of the poverty of men, should not be drawn away from the authority of religion to wages and profit." Cicero, On Divination 1. c Others read ostenta, from obstinet in the old sense of ostendit (Festus, under Obstinet). But in this matter it is better to follow Cloatius and Aelius Stilo, for whom obstitutum meant the same as violatum, touched by lightning from heaven (Festus, under Obstinum). d On this matter see the sad example in Livy, book 39. The declamation of Porcius Latro against Catiline, on not holding nocturnal gatherings in the city, also bears on this. e Dionysius seems to call them nocturnal sacrifices [illegible]. f The Council of Elvira for this reason forbade nocturnal vigils of women in cemeteries, because many acts of impurity were committed under that pretext. Hence in Plautus, in the Aulularia, the young man Lycomedes is said to have violated the daughter of Enclio during the vigils of Ceres. And Pentheus in Euripides' Bacchae*, when he heard that the orgies were celebrated at night, cried out [illegible]. And Eupolis in the Baptae [illegible]: not even a sacrilege could move him to condemn the nocturnal sacrifices of the Athenians which were called Collytia. Among the city of Myone too, some nocturnal sacrifices were instituted [illegible], which were afterwards made public by the law of Constantine, Cod. Theod. 5, On Pagans and Sacrifices. This too is recorded: Tertullian says that Christians also met at night; but since they could not easily do so by day and openly with others, they were charged with plotting against the emperor's life, with infanticides, with Thyestean feasts, and with incest, fornication and unlawful unions among themselves. Tertullian, Apology 9, refutes the charge. Nor let them be initiated, except as is customary for Ceres, in the Greek sacred rite.
On expiations

units.la: SACRUM {c}commissum,quod {d}neque {e}expiari {f}poterit, impie commissum est: quod expiari poterit,publici sacerdo-tes expianto.
units.tr: SACRED crime, which cannot be expiated, is committed impiously; a crime which can be expiated, let the public priests expiate.
On games.

units.la: Cereri (inquit) quam more Græco venerari instituerant, sacerdotem à Velleia petierant, ne Dea ve-rusti ritus deesset Antistes. Candida veste utebantur in sacris Cereris. Tertullianus de pallio, Cur istas non spectas? vel illos item habitus, qui novitate vestitus religionem mentiuntur, cum ob cultum omnia candidatum, & ob notam virtutis & privilegium galeri Cereri initiantur? Ouidius in Metamorphosi, Festa piæ Cereris celebrabant annua matris, illa quibus nivea velatur corpora veste.
units.tr: "They had sought out a priestess for Ceres from Velia," he says, "in the Greek manner, so that the goddess should not lack a priestess of the old rite." They wore white garments in the rites of Ceres. Tertullian, On the Cloak: "Why do you not look at those who, dressed in novelty, feign religion, when with all their white garments, and with the mark of virtue and the privilege of the cap, they are initiated into Ceres?" Ovid in the Metamorphoses: "They celebrated the yearly festival of the pious mother Ceres, in which their bodies were wrapped in snow-white robes."

units.la: {a} Eleusinia mysteria intelligit. Horum sacrorum meminit Cicero 1. de Natura: Plutarchus lib. de exilio: 3. Diodorus 5. & 5. cap. 2: Pausanias in Atticis: Arnobius 7: Lactantius 1. cap. 2: Augustinus 7, de civitate 20: Eleusine non procul ab Athenis 4. Plinius 7.
units.tr: {a} He means the Eleusinian mysteries. Cicero, On the Nature of the Gods 1, mentions these sacred rites; Plutarch, On Exile; Diodorus, books 3 and 5, chapter 2; Pausanias, Attica; Arnobius 7; Lactantius 1, chapter 2; Augustine, City of God 7 and 20; Eleusis, not far from Athens, Pliny book 4 and 7.

units.la: {b} Sacra enim Eleusinia a Græcis petita Diodorus dicto loco: vt & antea ab Aegyptiis Diodorus 3. cap. 5. Valerius 1. cap. 1. ibi, de Cerere placanda. Cereri (inquit) quam more Græco venerari instituerant sacerdotem à Velleia petierant, ne Dea ve-rusti ritus deesset Antistes.
units.tr: {b} For the Eleusinian rites were sought from the Greeks, as Diodorus says in the passage cited, and earlier from the Egyptians (Diodorus 3, chapter 5). Valerius 1, chapter 1, in the passage on appeasing Ceres: "They had sought out a priestess for Ceres from Velia in the Greek manner, so that the goddess should not lack a priestess of the old rite."

units.la: {c} Sacrum commissum, cuius causa homo sacer est: id est, dignus qui iudicetur ob maleficium vide Festum in voce Sacer.
units.tr: {c} A sacred crime, by reason of which a man is sacred, that is, a man worthy to be judged for a crime; see Festus, under Sacer.

units.la: {d} Cicero id ita interpretatur. Publicus, inquit, sacerdos impudentiam consilij expiatam metu liberet: audaciam in admittendis religionibus fœdis damnet, atque impiam iudicet. Vbi vereor ne sit legendum, impudentiam consilij. Idque ita vt emendem, adducor authoritate Varronis quinto de lingua: Prætor, inquit, qui tum fatus est, si imprudens fecit, piaculari hostia facta piatur: si prudens dixit, Quintus Mucius abnegabat cum expiari, & vt impium non posse dicebat. Exemplum denegatæ expiationis vide apud Zosimum 1.
units.tr: {d} Cicero interprets it thus: "The public priest," he says, "should free from fear the expiation of an impudent plan; he should condemn audacity in undertaking foul religious acts, and judge it impious." Here I fear the reading should be impudentiam consilij, and I am led to emend it so by the authority of Varro, book 5 On the Latin Language: "The praetor who spoke then, if he acted without thought, is expiated by a sacrificial victim; if he spoke knowingly, Quintus Mucius denied that he could be expiated and said that he could not be counted as impious." For an example of an expiation refused, see Zosimus 1.

units.la: {e} Nec, particula disiunctiua interdum apud veteres sumitur pro Non. Turpilius, Nec recte dici mihi, iamdudum audio. vide Festum in voce Nec.
units.tr: {e} Nec, a disjunctive particle, is sometimes used by the ancients for non. Turpilius: "I hear that it is not rightly said to me now." See Festus under Nec.

units.la: {f} Piare, vnde expiare, est propitium reddere, liberare incommodo atque metu. Hinc Piatrix porta ita dicta, quod quædam piacula ibi fieri solita. Piatrix sacerdos, expiare solita: Piamenta quibus vtimur in expiando Fest. in piatrix. L V D I S{*} publicis, quod {b}sine curri- culis fiebant in circo, Varro 4.de lingua. in honorē Neptuni, vt Cereales in honorē Cereris: Varro 5.de lingua, Tauri seu Tauricei, diis inferis cōsecrati: Varro 4.de lingua: Festus in Tauro. Capitolini, funebres, votiui, scænici, plebei, secula res qui cetesimo quoque anno Lofin. 2. Iuuenales, Latiares, Florales Tert. d. loco c. 2. Apud Græcos ludi nobiles, Pythia Apollini: Olympia Iouis: Nemæa Herculi Tertull. d. loco c. 9 Isthmia Neptuno. Minus nobiles, Panionia. Panathenaica in quibus virinsque sexus flos per mutua nexis manibus saltabant Pyrrhycā. Ludiones erāt nudi ( inde Gymnasia, ita certarunt Athletæ gymnici 1.4.ff. de his qui notantur:) aut vestiti aut armati, eorumque opera posita erat in iactu ( disci forte vel iaculi) saltu, cursu ( idque pedites vel equites vel curru vecti. Ad id genus exercitationis pertinebat populares 1.1.§.12.ff.de off.præsid. vrbi: iuuenes ...ueteres, 1.18.§.1.ff. de pœnis: factiones agitatorum, Veneta, Prasina, Albula, Russata, v. Tertull. 5. de spectaculis: quas Græci ... Nouell. 17: Latini etiam factionarios 1.1.Cod. Theodos. de equis: agitatores 1.2.1.4.Cod. de spectaculis. qui aquam equis spargebant, Xystici 1.4.ff. de his qui notant: vnde Xyftarches Tertull. lib. ad martyres) Lucia 1.7.§.4.ff.ad leg. Aquil: pugna seu pugillatu 1.7.§.4.ff.ad l. Aquil. Pugnis addebant interdum cestus, i. tora ceu cingula. Postremo plumbū affutum fuit tristissimo spectaculo. Pugillatui ... 1.7.§.4.ff.ad l.Aquil: 13.Gell.26: propior, vt qui etiā calcibus, genubus, dentibus abuteretur. Commissæ sunt paulò post inter se feras. vt & ipsis bestiis homines 1.1.§.6.ff.qui notant:1.3.§.5.ff de testib. &, quod tetrius est, homines hominibus. hinc munus gladiatorium, hinc spectacula Tertull. d.loco, c.10: Valer.2 c.1.ibi, mos ludorum, v.Lips. de gladiatorib. quod meritò sublatum est 1.1.Cod. de gladiatoribus penit. tell. Et his quidē ludis motu violento & neruis opus erat: in scenicis minus: vt qui voce, gestu, organis, sonis, &, vt ait Tertullianus d. loco c.7. litteris transigerentur. Hinc mimi, pantomimi 1.4.Cod.de spectaculis: archimimi 1.25.§.1.ff.de oper.libert: histriones 1.5. Cod.de spectaculis: γ-ἀστρολογοι Nouel. 107, c.1. gesticulatores, thymelici & thymelitæ. de quibus dixi ad 1.10.ff.de pollicitationib. His accommodata est Satyra, Comœdia, Tragœdia & similia poemata, de quibus Iul.Scaliger 1. Poëtices,
units.tr: {f} Piare, whence expiare, means to render propitious, to free from harm and fear. Hence the gate called Piatrix* was so named because certain expiations were customarily performed there. A piatrix was a priestess accustomed to expiate; piamenta are the things we use in expiating (Festus, under piatrix). PUBLIC GAMES, which were held without chariots in the circus, in honour of Neptune, as the Cerealia in honour of Ceres (Varro, book 4 On the Latin Language); the Tauri or Tauricei, consecrated to the gods below (Varro, book 4; Festus, under Taurus); the Capitoline, funeral, votive, scenic, plebeian, and secular games, which are celebrated every hundredth year (Lipsius 2); the Juvenalia, Latiaris, and Floralia (Tertullian, passage cited, chapter 2). Among the Greeks the famous games were: the Pythian for Apollo, the Olympic for Jupiter, the Nemean for Hercules, the Isthmian for Neptune (Tertullian, passage cited, chapter 9). Less famous were the Panionia and the Panathenaea*, in which men and women of both sexes danced the pyrrhica, holding hands. There were dancers who were naked (hence gymnasia, and so the athletes contended in the gymnastic games, Digest 1.4, On Those Who Are Marked by Infamy), or clothed, or armed; and their skill lay in throwing (of the discus or javelin), in leaping, and in running, whether on foot, on horseback, or in a chariot. To this kind of exercise belong the populares (Digest 1.1 §12, On the Duties of the Urban Prefect); the young men... the old (Digest 1.18 §1, On Punishments); the factions of the charioteers, Veneta, Prasina, Albula, Russata (Tertullian, On Spectacles 5); which the Greeks call... (Novel 17); the Latins also call them factionarii (Cod. Theod. 1.1, On Horses); the agitatores (Cod. 1.2 and 1.4, On Spectacles), who sprinkled water on the horses; the xystici (Digest 1.4, On Those Who Are Marked), whence the xystarches (Tertullian, book To the Martyrs); the lucta, wrestling (Digest 1.7 §4, On the Lex Aquilia); the pugna or boxing, also Digest 1.7 §4, On the Lex Aquilia. To their fists they sometimes added the cestus, that is, a thong or belt. Finally, lead was affixed to it, for a most grievous spectacle. The boxing... (Digest 1.7 §4; Gellius 13.26), where the contestant abused even with kicks, knees and teeth. Soon afterwards they were matched against each other with wild beasts, and men also against beasts (Digest 1.1 §6, On Those Who Are Marked; Digest 1.3 §5, On Witnesses); and, what is more foul, men against men. Hence the gladiatorial show, hence the spectacles (Tertullian, passage cited, chapter 10; Valerius 2, chapter 1, the custom of games; Lipsius, On Gladiators), which was rightly abolished (Cod. 1.1, On Gladiators, last section). These games needed violent motion and sinews; in the scenic games there was less of this, since they were carried on by voice, gesture, instruments, sounds, and, as Tertullian says in the passage cited, chapter 7, by letters. Hence mimes and pantomimes (Cod. 1.4, On Spectacles); archimimes (Digest 1.25 §1, On Services of Freedmen); actors (Cod. 1.5, On Spectacles); [astrologers] (Novel 107, chapter 1); gesticulators, and thymelic performers, male and female, of whom I spoke at Digest 1.10, On Promises. To these are suited satire, comedy, tragedy and similar poems, on which see Julius Scaliger, Poetics 1.

units.la: Poëtices, b obserua definitionem ludorum scoenicorum. culo, & sine certatione corporum fiat, populari laetitiam in cantu, & fidibus, & tibiis moderanto, eámque cum divûm honore iungunto.
units.tr: Poetics: observe the definition of scenic games: they are performed for the people, without the contest of bodies, and let them moderate the popular joy with song, lyres and flutes, and join it with honour to the gods.
On Rites.

units.la: EX PATRIIS ritibus{a} o-ptuma{b} colunto. praeter{c} Idaea{d} matris famulos {e},eósque iuítis[?] diebus, nequis sti-pem scogito.
units.tr: Let them observe the best of their ancestral rites, except for the servants of the Idaean Mother; and on forbidden days let no one collect alms.
On Sacrilege.
Let no one entrust a sacred thing, or a holy thing,

units.la: {c} Cybelei hæres posset institui[?]. Vlpianus 11. §. sexto.
units.tr: {c} that an heir could be appointed to the worship of Cybele. Ulpian, book 11, §6.

units.la: {d} quæ & Cybele, magna & deorum mater dicta est : & Pessinuntia, quòd eius simulachrum in agrum Phrygiæ, cui nomen Pessinunti, cœlitus delapsum crederetur, Ammianus 22: Herodianus x[?]: artifice & materia qua compositum esset ignoratis. Authoritas ex eo comparata, quòd responsum fuerat, auctum[?] iri imperium Romanum, & mansurum, si id Romam transferretur. Itaque, totius civitatis vir integerrimus, ut oraculo satisfieret, ad eam rem legatus quaesitus est Scipio, Cicero quinto de legibus: Livius 29: 8. Valerius 16: Ammianus 11. lege 11. §. trigesimo septimo, ff. de origine iuris. Cúmque simulachrum ad Tyberis fauces delatum, navigium ita substitit, ut nulla vi populi Romani certatim trahentis moveretur. Vestalis Claudia stupri accusata petiit à populo Romano, ut iudicium de se Pessinuntiæ Deæ committeretur, quo impetrato zonam recinxit, clarè precata, ut si se virginem esse dea sciret navim progredi iuberet. Hæc ubi dixisset, ducta navis, zonámque Vestalis sequi coepit, Herodianus i-bidem[?]: Tertullianus 21. Apologetic. in fine, quin, maior messis ea aestate, quàm antecedentibus annis decem fuisse traditur, Plinius 18.capite tertio. {e} euirati & castrati erant, & à Gallo fluvio Gallidicebantur Herod. 1. Iuvenal. Satyr. 6: Festus in voce Galli: Arnob. 7. dubius locis: 1. Lactant. 21. {f} de his loquitur ita Arnobius libr.
units.tr: {d} She is also called Cybele, the great Mother of the gods, and Pessinuntia, because her image was believed to have fallen from heaven into a field of Phrygia called Pessinus, the craftsman and the material of which it was made being unknown (Ammianus, book 22; Herodian). Her authority was established by an oracle which declared that the Roman empire would be enlarged and would endure if she were transferred to Rome. Therefore, to satisfy the oracle, the most upright man in the whole state was sought as envoy for this business: Scipio (Cicero, On the Laws, book 5; Livy 29.8; Valerius 16; Ammianus 11; law 11, §37, Digest, de origine iuris). When the image had been brought to the mouth of the Tiber, the ship carrying it stuck fast, and could not be moved by any force of the Roman people pulling eagerly on the rope. The Vestal Claudia, accused of unchastity, asked the Roman people that her case be committed to the judgment of the goddess of Pessinus. Having obtained this, she unfastened her girdle and prayed openly: if she knew herself to be a virgin, the goddess should command the ship to move forward. When she had said this, the ship was drawn along, and began to follow the Vestal's girdle (Herodian, ibid.; Tertullian, Apologeticus 21, at the end). Moreover, that summer's harvest is said to have been greater than in the ten preceding years (Pliny 18.3). {e} They were eunuchs and castrated men, and were called Galli from the river Gallus (Herodotus, book 1; Juvenal, Satire 6; Festus, s.v. Galli; Arnobius, book 7; Lactantius, book 1, ch. 21). {f} Arnobius speaks of these men in this way, in book 7:

units.la: 7. Mendicantes vicatim deos ducunt, Tertullianus 13: Apologetic. Circuit cauponas religio mendicans, exigens mercedem pro solo templi, pro aditu sacri, non licet deos nosse gratis, venales sunt: adde Clementem in Exhortatione. {g} de sacrilegio adde l.4.l.5.l. 6.l.9.l.10.ff.ad leg.Iul.peculat. {a}tum qui clepserit{b} rapseritque{e}, paricida{d} esto.
units.tr: Beggars go about the villages with the gods. Tertullian, Apologeticus 13: a begging religion goes round the taverns, demanding payment for the ground of the temple, for admission to the sacred place; it is not allowed to know the gods for nothing, they are sold for money. Add Clement, in the Exhortation. {g} On sacrilege, add laws 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10 of the Digest, ad legem Iuliam peculatus. {a} ...whoever steals and seizes, let him be a parricide.
On Perjury.
Divine punishment for perjury is destruction; human punishment is disgrace.
On Incest.
Incest, and the pontiffs with the supreme {h}

units.la: in Aulular.fabulas l.3 §.3.ff.de tabulis exhib. testamenta Plutarchus in Antonio; Tacitus l.Annalium,trâsactiones publicas Dion 48.Extat in lege 10.in fi.ff.ad leg.Iul.peculat.elegans exemplum eius,qui arculam in templo posuerat, eaque hominem incluserat,vt post clusum templum, de arca exiret reisque sacras templo subtraheret.
units.tr: Plutarch in Antony on wills in the Aulularia; Tacitus, Annals, public transactions; Dion 48. There is an elegant example in the law at the end of 10, ff. ad legem Iuliam peculatus, of a man who had put a chest in a temple and shut himself inside it, so that once the temple was closed he could come out of the chest and carry the sacred objects away from the temple.

units.la: {b} id est,sustulerit a Graeco [illegible, ~6 letters] vel ab antiquo clepere, vel clapere Varro 6. de lingua : videtur hoc verbum vsurpari in quadam antiqua Gallorum puerorum Nænia in qua Clope, furem denotat.
units.tr: {b} That is, he has taken away, from the Greek [illegible, about six letters], or from the old word clepere or clapere. Varro, book 6 on the Latin language. This word seems to have been used in an ancient Gallic children's lullaby, in which Clope denotes a thief.

units.la: {c} id est,rapuerit.Rapere,per vim. Clepere, clam auferre.
units.tr: {c} That is, has seized. To rapere is to take by force; clepere, to take away secretly.

units.la: {d} id est,capitale esto.Lex Numæ,si quis hominem liberum dolo sciens morti duit,parricida esto.Fest.in voce Paricida. De poena sacri-leg. vide Paul.5.sent.19.l.vnic.Cod.de crimin. sacri-leg.
units.tr: {d} That is, let it be a capital offence. The law of Numa: if anyone knowingly kills a free man by guile, let him be a parricide. Festus, under the word Paricida. On the penalty for sacrilege, see Paulus, Sentences 5.19, and the single law at the end of the Code, de criminibus sacrilegii.

units.la: {e} Iurisiurandi contempta religio satis Deum vltorem habet l.2.Cod.de reb.cred. vt negare non possis d. legem 2. ex hoc loco transcriptam. Macrobius 1.Saturnal.17.In ea,inquit,ferenda (Liciniani intelligit sumptuariam) quaesita est nomine legis authoritas, exolescente metu legis antiquioris. ita Hercules, vt de ipsis XII tabulis factum est: quas vbi contemni antiquitas coepit, eadem illa, quae illis legibus cauebantur,in alia latorum nomina transferunt.
units.tr: {e} Contempt for the religion of an oath has God as a sufficient avenger; Code, de rebus creditis, law 2. That you cannot deny, from the law 2 transcribed from this passage. Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.17: "In enacting it" (he means the sumptuary law of Licinius) "authority was sought in the name of law, as the fear of the older law faded away. So Hercules; as happened with the Twelve Tables themselves: when antiquity began to be despised, they transferred those same provisions that had been guarded in those laws to other names of proposers."

units.la: {f} de poena periu-rij dixi ad l.2.C.de reb.credit.adde l.2.in fi.Cod.de indicta viduitate.
units.tr: {f} I have spoken about the penalty for perjury at Code, de rebus creditis, law 2; add the end of law 2, Code, de indicta viduitate.

units.la: Graeci ἀνήκ[?]στορ, Fest.in voce Incestus. Cæterum , non hic agitur,meo iudicio,de quouis incestu, sed de incestu Vestalium, qui ad Pontificum audientiam curam pertinebat.
units.tr: Greek [ἀνήκ[?]στορ]; Festus, under the word Incestus. But in my judgment, the question here is not about incest of any kind, but about the incest of the Vestals, which fell under the care and hearing of the pontiffs.

units.la: {h} Stupri comperæ[?] Vestales, iuxta portam Collinam, viuæ in ædiculam subterraneam defodiebantur, in eaque lectus stratus & lucerna accensa ponebatur, eorum quoque,quæ ad victum sunt necessaria pauca, vt panis, aquæ in ampulla, lac, oleum. Damnatam lectica indebant ,atque undique obnubebant,vinciebantque, vt ne vocem quidem emittere, & à quoquam exaudiri posset. Posthac per forum deuehebant, procedebantque de via omnes taciti, sine voce, cum ingenti mœstitia. Vbi ad locum illum ventum esset, apparitores vincula damnatæ adimebat.vbi Pontifex quasdam preces arcanas tensis ad cœlum manibus peregisset,damnatam in ædiculam demittebant,quam mox iniecta humo cöplanabant Plutar. in Numa:cui adde Liuium lib.22[?].vbi de Opimio & Floronia.
units.tr: {h} Vestals convicted of debauchery were buried alive beside the Collline Gate, in a small underground chamber. In it a couch was spread and a lamp lit was placed, along with a few of the things necessary for sustenance, such as bread, water in a flask, milk and oil. The condemned woman was put in a litter, wrapped and bound on all sides, so that she could not even utter a voice or be heard by anyone. Afterwards they carried her through the forum, and all those on the road went silent, without a voice, in great mourning. When they had come to that place, the attendants removed the woman's bonds. When the pontiff had performed certain secret prayers with his hands stretched to heaven, they lowered the condemned woman into the little chamber, which they then covered over and levelled with earth thrown in. Plutarch in Numa; add to it Livy, book 22, where he speaks of Opimius and Floronia.
Let them be punished with the supreme penalty.
On Impiety towards God.

units.la: IMPIUS{b} ne{c} audeto placare donis iram deorum.
units.tr: Let no impious person dare to appease the anger of the gods with gifts.
On Vows.

units.la: SANCTE vota{d} reddunto. Pœna violati iuris esto. Quocirca ne quis agrum{e} consecrato. auri, argenti{f}, eboris{g} sacrandi modus esto.
units.tr: Let them fulfil vows solemnly. Let the penalty be that of violated law. Therefore let no one consecrate a field. Let there be a limit to what may be consecrated in gold, silver and ivory.
On private sacred rites.

units.la: SACRA privata{h} perpetua{i} manento.[?] ciperet ab impio, cum nemo vir bonus ab improbo se donari velit?
units.tr: Private sacred rites shall remain perpetual. Could they be taken from the impious, when no good man would wish to be given a gift by the wicked?
Plato, in Cicero, On the Laws 2.

units.la: {d} Votum, est ipsuillo[?], qua deo obligamur. Cic.hic de votis. v. quæ scripsi ad l.2. ff.de pollicitationib.
units.tr: {d} A vow is an undertaking by which we are bound to God. Cicero, here, on vows. See what I have written on law 2 of the Digest, de pollicitationibus.

units.la: {e} hanc rationem ex Platone adfert Cicero, Terra, inquit, domici-lium deorum est, igitur sacra. est autem absurdum iterum idem consecrari.
units.tr: {e} Cicero takes this argument from Plato: the earth, he says, is the dwelling of the gods, and so it is sacred. But it is absurd for the same thing to be consecrated again.

units.la: {f} Aurum enim & argentum in vrbibus & priuatis, inuidiosa res est. Plato apud Ciceronem 2. de legibus. Notum est illud Alexandri Seueri, qui in templis nunquam præter quatuor aut quinque argenti libras: auri, ne guttulam quidem aut bracteolam posuit, susurrans versum Persij 2. Satyr. Dicite Pontifices in sacro quid facit aurum?
units.tr: {f} Gold and silver in cities and in private houses are an invidious thing. Plato, in Cicero, On the Laws 2. It is well known that Alexander Severus, who never placed in the temples more than four or five pounds of silver, and not even a drop or a thin plate of gold, murmured the line of Persius, Satires 2: "Tell me, priests, what does gold do in a sacred place?"

units.la: {g} Nam ebur ex inari, (vel, vt Lambinus legit, immani) corpore extractum, haud satis castum donum deo. Plato d. loco. Item aes[?] atque ferrum, duelli instrumenta, non fani. Plato d. loco.
units.tr: {g} Ivory taken from the body of a wild (or, as Lambinus reads, a huge) animal is not a gift sufficiently pure for God. Plato, in the same place. Likewise bronze and iron, the instruments of war, are not for a shrine. Plato, in the same place.

units.la: {h} Publica sacra pro populo montibus, pagis, curiis, sacellis hebant publico sumptu. Priuata, pro singulis hominibus & familiis. Fest. in publica sacra. hinc gentilitia sacra. Liuius 5. feriæ propriæ familiarum 1. Macrob. 16.
units.tr: {h} Public sacred rites were performed at public expense on behalf of the people, in the mountains, villages, wards and shrines. Private ones were for individual men and families. Festus, under publica sacra. Hence the sacred rites of the clans (gentilitia sacra). Livy 5; the family's own festival days (feriae propriae familiarum), 1; Macrobius 16.

units.la: {i} In eadem familia scilicet, & gente. vxores enim in sacris maritorum: liberi, in sacris parentum erant. vide quæ scripsi ad l.2. C. de bon. quæ liber. Per emancipationem e sacris parentis dimittebantur. v.l.13. C. de legitim. hæredib. Quæ sacra ne interirent, receptum fuit: ea deferri certis gradibus ad eum qui maiore ex parte hæres, legatarius vel alio quoquo titulo honoratus foret vel creditor. Cic.hic.
units.tr: {i} That is, within the same family and clan. For wives shared in their husbands' rites, and children in their parents' rites. See what I have written on law 2 of the Code, de bonis quae liberis. By emancipation a child was released from the rites of his parent. See law 13 of the Code, de legitimis heredibus. So that these sacred rites should not perish, it was the accepted practice that they be transferred, by fixed degrees, to the one who was for the greater part heir, legatee, or honoured by some other title, or a creditor. Cicero, here.

units.la: {k} Interim eorum tamen horum sacrorum causa, iurisconsulti coemptiones, quæ à senib. fierent, excogitarunt. Cic. pro Murena. idque ita fiebat, Seniores orbi matrimonium per coemptionem contrahebant. qua ratione accidebat, vt eorum vxores sacrorum sociæ, suæ illis hæredes essent. mortuis senib. vxores alteri nubentes in aliena sacra hæreditatem deferebant, vt eo modo sacra prioris mariti interim eretur. Ea est Hotomani sententia. Alciat 9. pareg. 19. putat bona feni admodum vedi, nec ad vlterio res eius hæredes transmitti solita. Prior sententia aptior est & melior.
units.tr: {k} Meanwhile, for the sake of these sacred rites, the jurists devised the coemptions which were made by old men. Cicero, Pro Murena. And this was done thus: childless old men contracted marriage by coemption, by which means their wives became sharers in their rites and heirs to their property. When the old men died, the wives, marrying another man, carried the inheritance over into the rites of the other family, so that in this way the sacred rites of the former husband might be kept alive. This is Hotoman's opinion. Alciatus, Parerga 9, chapter 19, thinks that the goods of the old man were not at all sought, nor were his property usually passed on to a further heir. The former opinion is the more suitable and the better.
On the religious objects and the expenses of funerals.

units.la: DEORVM manium{a} iura{b}, sancta{c} funto. Hos{d} leto datos{e}, diuos habento. Sumptum in ollos{f}, luctumque{g} minunto.
units.tr: Let the rights of the spirits of the dead (Manes) be sacred. Let those given over to death be counted as gods. Let them reduce expenditure on them and mourning.

units.la: ita dicebantur à suppliciter eos venerantibus, propter metû mortis, quasi boni essent, Fest.in Manuos.{b}
units.tr: Festus, under Manuos. They were so called by those who worshipped them with supplication, out of fear of death, as if they were good spirits.

units.la: {b} circa defunctos sc. Dixi ad l.18 in f.ff.de stipulat. Iuruor. de ritu sepeliendi.
units.tr: {b} Concerning the dead, that is: I have spoken of this in the note on law 18 at the end of the Digest, de stipulationibus, and on the rite of burial.

units.la: Nunc de sacris mortuorum dicendum. Sacra seu sacrificia, quae diis manibus fiebant, Inferiae dicebantur Fest.in Inferiae. & Feralia dies flati in quibus ferebant tum epulas ad sepulchrum, quibus ibi ius erat parentare. Varro 5.de lingua. Sacrificia pro defunctis Graecis Xoes Plutarch. in Antonio: Tertullianus 10. Apologet. scribit, captiuos nonnunquam & seruos in exequiis immolatos: quoniam animas defunctorum sanguine humano propitiari credebant, quod quia crudele visum fuit, placuit ante sepulcrum quosdam dimicare, qui ob id bustuarij dicti Seruius in Aeneid. sed hoc rarius. Frequentius atras hostias, thura, salsas fruges, lac, oleum, sanguinem offerebant, Arnob.7.adueręus gentes. In eo etiam differebant sacra inferorum deorum, quod diis superis tantum libarent: inferis etiam vasa in ignem mitterent, Seruius 8. Aeneidos, ad illa verba fuso craterc oliuo. Videntur inter caetera ea formula vsi ad defunctos, Resurge tu, comede, & bibe & laetare. Epiphan. in Anchorato Hinc referendae sunt clausulae illae testamentariae, Quos liberos meos vbi corpus meum positum fuerit, ibi eos morari iubeo, vt per absentiam filiarum mearum ad sarcofagum meum memoriam meam quotannis celebrent lege 18.in fine ff.de alimentis legat: Titio relinquo, ita vt a monumento meo non recedat l.7.§.2.ff.de conditionibus & demonstrationibus. Eius fideicommitto vt det ex reditu caeraculi mei, & horrei post obitum, sacerdoti & hierophylaco & libertis qui in illo templo erunt, denaria decem die nundinarum quas ibi imposui lege 20.ff.de annuis. quo loco videtur intelligere denicales aut nouendiales ferias, seu Nouendial. de quo dixi ad Noct.115. capite quinto, ἐνάτῃ ἐπὶ τῇ ἐχῇ ὀγδόῃ ἡμέρᾳ, quibus diebus fiebant cenae funebres, epulasque Iulius Obsequens. Et alibi vt 1.44.ff.de manumiss.testament. Omnes sub hac conditione liberi funto, vt monumento meo alternis mensibus lucernam accendant, & solennia mortis peragant. e id est, intacta. d idest, manes, de quibus supra rodem. e legendum puto, Datis, vt sit sensus, Manes letho datos diuos esse, id est, mortuis, seu mortuorum deos esse. f mortuos sc. g de luctu mox dicetur.
units.tr: Now we must speak of the sacred rites of the dead. The sacred rites or sacrifices that were made to the spirits of the dead were called inferiae. Festus, under inferiae. The days of the festival of the dead, on which people then carried feasts to the tomb, at which it was lawful to make offerings to the dead (parentare), were called feralia. Varro, On the Latin Language 5. The sacrifices for the dead among the Greeks, the Choes [Χόες], Plutarch, in Antony. Tertullian, Apology 10, writes that captives and slaves were sometimes sacrificed at funerals, because they believed that the souls of the dead were appeased by human blood; and since this seemed cruel, it was agreed that some men should fight before the tomb, who for this reason were called bustuarii. Servius, on the Aeneid. But this was rarer. More often they offered black victims, incense, salted grain, milk, oil and blood. Arnobius, Against the Gentiles 7. In this too the sacred rites of the lower gods differed from those of the gods above, that to the gods above they poured only libations, while to the lower gods they also threw vessels into the fire. Servius, on Aeneid 8, at the words fuso craterae oliuo. Among other things, they seem to have used this formula for the dead: "Rise up, eat, drink, and rejoice." Epiphanius, Against the Anchoraté. From here should be derived those testamentary clauses: "I order that my children, wherever my body has been placed, shall remain there, so that by their presence at my sarcophagus they may keep my memory each year." Law 18, at the end of the Digest, de alimentis legatis. "I leave to Titius on condition that he does not withdraw from my monument." Law 7, §2, Digest, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. "I entrust to him that after my death he give, from the income of my candle-and-granary, ten denarii on the market days which I have fixed there, to the priest, the sacristan, and the freedmen who will be in that temple." Law 20, Digest, de annuis legatis. In this passage he seems to mean the funeral feasts of the ninth day (denicales or nouendiales), or the ninth-day festival, of which I have spoken in my note on Noctes 115, chapter 5, on the ninth day [ἐνάτῃ ἐπὶ τῇ ἐχῇ ὀγδόῃ ἡμέρᾳ], on which days funeral banquets and feasts were held. Julius Obsequens. And elsewhere, law 44, Digest, de manumissis testamento: "On this condition all my children shall be free: that they light a lamp at my monument in alternate months and perform the solemn rites of my death." e: that is, untouched. d: that is, the Manes, of whom above in the same place. e: I think we should read Datis, so that the sense is that the Manes given to death are gods, that is, the dead are gods of the dead. f: that is, the dead. g: concerning mourning it will be spoken of presently.

units.la: HOMINEM mortuum In vrbe ne sepelito, néve vrito.
units.tr: Do not bury or burn a dead man within the city.

units.la: HOC PLVS ne facito. Rogum quia non licet priuato sepulchrum facere in loco publico? non puto. Potest enim publicus locus esse ad eam rem destinatus. Sed & Vestæ virgines etiâ in ciuitate sepulchra habuerunt, & quod maius est, viux defossæ sunt intra pomerium. Mos etiam fuit antiquis in vrbe sepeliri. Seruius 5. Aeneidos. quid, quod quibusdam datum est virtutis causa post duodecim tabulas, vt in vrbe sepeliantur, vt Publicolæ, vt Lucretio? Cicero hic. Causa igitur fuit, ne vrbanum cœlum fœdo cadauerũ odore infectum, pe-stem ciuibus, qui spiritum ex eo ducerent, inferret: vel ne (vt illi putabant) sanctum ius municipiorum polluereatur. l.12.Cod.de religiosis. Contraria omnino consuetudo fuit apud Tarentinos, cum oraculo acceptum futuros beatiores, si cum pluribus habitarent, Polybius 8. Exemplo forte eodem veturum, ne quis in Apostolico vel Martyrio conderetur l.1.Cod. de sacrosanctis ecclef. eadem imitatione Synodus Valensis c.Præcipiendum 13. quaest.2. vetuit, Ne quis in Ecclesia sepeliretur, sed tantum in atrio vel porticu vel exhedris Ecclesiæ. de sepulchro illud Plinij notandum est 7.cap.54. Ipsum cremari, inquit, apud Romanos non fuit veteris institutionis, terra condebantur. At postquam longinquis bellis obrutos erui cognouere, tunc initium. Vetus certè institutum sepultura, Arnob. 8. quo apud Xenophontem Cyrus vtitur, & apud Romanos Numa & gens Cornelia, Cicero hic. vt merito compos mentis esse negetur, qui hæredem ita instituit, si reliquias eius in mare abiiceret, l.27.ff.de conditionib.instit. propter ignis periculum hoc adiectum est. Cicero, Quod ab eodem dicitur, Non qui vratur sepeliri, sed qui humatur, obscurius est, sic interpretor, Finem sepulturæ, vrionem non fuisse, sed humationem: Improprie sepelire qui vritur: proprie, qui terra conditur. Aliud est sepultura ab humatione. Sepultus dicitur quoquo modo, humatus terra tantum. vide quæ scripsi ad leg. 28. in fine, ff. de stipulatione seruorum. Ecquod illud? superius non dixit. Placet nonnullis decurtatam hanc esse sententiam, aut superioris alicuius appendicem. Possis tamen dicere, initium legis fuisse, ac si scriptum esset, Hoc plus ne facito. Plus, inquam, quam sequenti lege continebitur. Et ita loquitur Jurisconsultus in lege prima, ff. de pactis. Huius edicti æquitas naturalis est, quanquam edictum de quo loquitur l. septima, §. septimo, distii tituli continentur. id est, ligna, quæ ad rogum faciendum conferuntur. Rogus non est monumentum. Monumentum non exuritur, rogus exuritur. Cùm ascenderet in rogum ardentem, Cicero primo de diuinatione. incendo rogum Plautus in Menæchmis. quanquam etiam in monumen-ascia ascia ne polito. MVLIERES genas ne radunto neve lestum funeris ergo habento. tio (sumptuum lege 14.§.6.ff.de religiosis: lege 123. ff.de legatis l.lege ultima in fine,ff.de auro. Quod adiicit Cicero de tribus riciniis & vinculis purpurae & decem tibicinibus explicandum est. Ricinij, (Festus recinium scribit) nominem,vestem intelligit, cuius dimidia pars retrorsum iaci poterat, Varro quarto de lingua: Isidorus 19.cap. 25. vestes etiam non quasuis,sed quae in luctu sumebantur, Nonius in Ricinium. quibus interdum corpora defuncti conuoluebant, Lactantius 2.Iastit.4. quas, plus tribus, sepulchris condi Solon vetuit, Plutarchus in Solone. Quanto melius Iurisconsulti dissuadent vllas condi, cum sit hoc simpliciorum proprium lege 14. §.quinto, ff.de religiosis: Quod adiicit de vinculis purpurae, intelligefasciaspurpureas. hucque pertinet locus Liuij 34. Purpura viri vtemur: nec id vt viui habeant tantum insigne: sed etiam, vt cum eo cremantur mortui. De decem tibicinibus illud notandum,olim Siticines dictos fuisse, quod apud Sitos, hoc est, vita functos & sepultos canere soliti essent, tuba quadam differente a vetere Tuba proprietate. quos Sicinistas, vulgus: qui rectius loquuti, Sicinuistas dixere. Sicinnium enim genus veteris salrationis fuit. Siticinibus affines sunt Tubicines, qui tuba: Liticines, qui lituo, 2o.Gell.2. adde Ouidium 6. Fastorum, Videntur autem Iudaei didicisse quondam hoc genus Siticinij a Gentilibus, Matthaei 9.versiculo 23. a id est,dolabra. b ne alioquin & modum excedas, & videaris aedificium potius, quam rogum construere. Hoc igitur vetat,pyram ex aliis lignis, quam rudibus & impolitis confici. c ii. Plin. 37. adde sicubi captiui alicuius aut gladiatoris sanguis effundi non poterit, Seruius 12. Aeneidos. Moris enim fuit istiusmodi hominum sanguinem effundi ante sepulchra, vt supra dixi. Faciebant autem id mulieres, vt, sanguine ostenso, inferis satisfacerent. Caeterum, Radere hic, significat vanguibus genas dilaniare. Festus in verbo Radere. In declamationibus Quintiliani fit mentio mulieris, quae filium lugens sanguinales lacertos scissumque, laniatumque vultum & liuida vbera,ostendit. d id est, lugubrem eiulationem. Non vestis lunebris, vt Sextus Aelius & Lucius Acilius putabant, Cicero hic. [illegible, ~12 letters] Lex Solon. apud Plutarchum in Solone: adde Platonem duodecimo de legibus: Cicero secundo Tusculanorum. Eiulatus ne mulieri quidem concessus: & hic nimirum fletus est, quem duodecim tabulae in funeribus adhiberi vetuerunt. Iustinianus lessum veterum vertit in cantum praeficarum seu psaltriarum, Kouell.59. Hieronymus in Epistola Paulae testatur, Christianos in exequiis cecinisse, Alleluia. Quod ad luctum attinet, Paulus 1.
units.tr: Do not add more than this. Why is it not lawful to make a tomb for a private person in a public place? I do not think so. For a place can be public and set aside for that purpose. Moreover, the Vestal virgins had tombs even within the city, and, what is greater, they were buried alive inside the pomerium. It was also the custom of the ancients to be buried in the city. Servius on Aeneid 5. What of the fact that after the Twelve Tables some were granted, for the sake of their virtue, burial within the city, such as Publicola and Lucretius? Cicero here. The reason, then, was that the city air might not be tainted by the foul smell of corpses and bring pestilence to citizens who drew breath from it; or lest, as they thought, the sacred right of the municipalities be polluted. Cod. 12, on religious places. The custom among the Tarentines was entirely the opposite, since they had received an oracle that they would be happier if they lived together with many [dead], Polybius 8. Perhaps by the same example it was forbidden that anyone be buried in an apostolic or martyr's [church], Cod. 1, on sacrosanct churches. By the same imitation the Council of Valence Decretum, Praecipiendum 13, q. 2 forbade that anyone be buried in a church, but only in the forecourt, portico or exedrae of the church. Concerning burial, what Pliny says in book 7, chapter 54 should be noted: cremation, he says, was not among the Romans of older custom; they were buried in the earth. But after they learned that those crushed in distant wars were dug up, then cremation began. Burial was certainly the ancient custom, Arnobius 8, which Cyrus uses in Xenophon, and among the Romans Numa and the Cornelian gens. Cicero here. So that a man is rightly judged not of sound mind who appoints an heir on condition that he throw the man's remains into the sea. Dig. 27, on conditions and institutions. Because of the danger of fire this was added. Cicero, What is said by the same author, "not he who is burned is buried, but he who is laid in the ground," is rather obscure; I interpret it thus: the aim of burial was not burning but laying in the ground. It is improper to say that one is buried when he is burned; properly, one is buried when he is put into the earth. Burial is one thing, interment another. One is said to be buried in any manner, but interred only by earth. See what I wrote on law 28 at the end of the Digest, on stipulation of slaves. But what is that? He did not say it above. Some think this sentence is cut short, or is an appendix to some earlier provision. Yet one may say that it was the beginning of the law, as if it had been written: "Do not add more." More, I say, than is contained in the following law. And the jurist speaks thus in the first law, Dig., on pacts. The equity of this edict is natural, although the edict of which he speaks is contained in law seven, §7, of the title on the two tables. That is, the wood which is brought together to make the pyre. The pyre is not the tomb. The tomb is not burnt; the pyre is burnt. When he climbed onto the blazing pyre, Cicero, first book On Divination. "I set fire to the pyre," Plautus in the Menaechmi. although also in the tomb ... "Do not smooth with the axe." Women shall not scratch their cheeks nor hold a lament for the funeral. (On the costs: law 14 §6, Dig. on religious places; law 123, Dig. on legacies; the last law, end, Dig. on gold.) What Cicero adds about the three ricinia, the purple bands and the ten flute-players must be explained. A ricinium (Festus writes recinium) is a garment, half of which could be thrown backward; Varro in book 4 On the Latin Language; Isidore 19, chapter 25. Garments, too, not just any, but those worn in mourning, Nonius on ricinium, with which the bodies of the dead were sometimes wrapped, Lactantius 2 Institutes 4. Solon forbade that more than three of these be placed in tombs, Plutarch in Solon. How much better the jurists dissuade any from being placed there, since this is the mark of the common people, law 14 §5, Dig. on religious places. What he adds about the purple bands is to be understood as purple swathings. To this belongs the passage of Livy 34: "We use purple for men, not so that the living may merely have this mark, but also so that the dead may be burned with it." Concerning the ten flute-players it should be noted that formerly they were called Siticines, because they were accustomed to play at the funerals of the Sitoi, that is, those who had died and were buried, with a certain trumpet differing from the proper old trumpet; the common people call them Sicinistae, but those who spoke more correctly said Sicinuistae, for the sicinnium was a kind of ancient dance. Tubicines, who play the tuba, and Litucines, who play the lituus, are akin to the Siticines; Gellius 2.2. Add Ovid, Fasti 6. Moreover, the Jews seem once to have learned this kind of funeral music from the Gentiles, Matthew 9, verse 23.

units.la: HOMINI{a} mortuo ne ossa legito, quo{b} post funus faciat{c}: neve aurum adiro.
units.tr: Let no one gather the bones of a dead man, so that he may hold a funeral afterwards, nor touch gold.
Let the slave's anointing be removed, and every drinking-party around the tomb.

units.la: Λυ[?]πᾶσθε καθὼς καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα.
units.tr: "Do not grieve as the others do, who have no hope." [Λυπᾶσθε καθὼς καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα]

units.la: Et is quidem lugubris modo videtur ab Aegyptiis acceptus: apud quos lugentes mulieres nudatis mammillis: viri, pectus lanientes plateas ob-errabant.
units.tr: And this lamenting seems to have been received from the Egyptians, among whom the mourning women, with breasts bared, and the men, tearing their chests, wandered through the squares.
{a} of the dead man. Herodotus 2.

units.la: {b} Non simpliciter prohibet ossa legi, sed ita legi, ut post funus fiat, id est, sumptus in funus. ideoque crediderim pro funus,legendum sumptus, excepta tamen bellicae & peregrinae mortis causa translatione l.8.l.14.§.4. ff.de religiosis.
units.tr: {b} It does not simply forbid gathering the bones, but gathering them so that a funeral is held afterwards, that is, expense on the funeral. So I would believe that instead of funus one should read sumptus, except for the transfer of costs in the case of death in war or abroad, law 8, law 14 §4, Dig. on religious places.

units.la: {c} facias Hotomanus. nec male etiam possis legere fiat.
units.tr: {c} Hotomanus has facias. It would also not be bad to read fiat.

units.la: {d} Quid fit vnctura, audio. quid fit seruilis vnctura, nondum percepi, eti. mihi scio in rem domini versum intelligi, si odores & vnguenta seruus emerit, & ad funus erogauerit l.7.§.3. ff.de in rem verso. & inter funeris sumptus vnguenta referri l.37.ff.de religiosis: vt vnctuaram seruilem dicamus, eam quae fit seruandorum corporum causa, non video. Vix est enim vt talis vnctura prohibeari debeat.
units.tr: {d} What the anointing is, I hear. What a slave's anointing is, I have not yet grasped, although I know that it is understood to be turned to the owner's advantage if a slave buys perfumes and ointments and spends them on the funeral, law 7 §3, Dig. on what was turned to advantage. And ointments are counted among funeral expenses, law 37, Dig. on religious places. So I do not see what a slave's anointing would be, that is, the one made for the preservation of bodies. Indeed, such an anointing hardly ought to be forbidden.

units.la: {e} Vetus fuit consuetudo a Graecis etiam viurpata, vt mortuis ad monumenta cibum & potum deferrent. Tertullianus lib.de ieiun.animæ vocas securos mortuos, si quando extra portam cum tbfonis & matris, tibi potius parentans, ad busta cedis, aut à bustis dilutior redis. In Pandemiis diebus edulia quidem rota exurebant: vina vero libabant, quin mortuum provocabant his verbis. Resurge, comede & bibe, & laetare Epiphan.in Anchorato. Tertullianus de resurrectione in principio. Ego magis ridebo vulgus tunc quoque cum ipsos defunctos atrociter exurit, quo postmodum gulosissime nutrit. Genus farciminis quo vtebatur, Latini videntur appellasse silicernii (quibusdam tamen silicernii est [?]) Iuvenalis satyra 8. & Apuleius 4. Florid. coena fera le vocat, quia is cuius nomine infitiuebatur, iam silice cerneret Fest. in Silicernium. Gamaros etiam & oua parentalibus atque mortuali isti coenae apposuere Iuv. sat.8. vt & lenem & salem [?] Plutarch: in Crasso [?] Appian. in Parth. i. lente & libu, adde Xiphilinum id Domitiano. Vas autem quo potio funeraria continebatur, obba. Tertullianus 13. Apologet: quid omnino ad honorandos deos facitis, quod non etiam mortuis facitis? quo differt ab epulo Iouis silicernium, à simpulo obba, ab aruspice pollinctor? Nam & aruspex mortuis appareret. Inter hæc etiam pro mortuis orabant & requiem precabantur. Tertullianus de testimonio animae, ossibus & cineribus eius refrigerium comprecaris, & vt bene requiescat apud inferos cupis.
units.tr: {e} It was an ancient custom, adopted also by the Greeks, to carry food and drink to the tombs for the dead. Tertullian, in his book On Fasting: "You, you who call the dead secure, when you go outside the gate to the tombs, offering funeral rites to your father or mother, or return from the tombs more refreshed." On the Pandemia days they burned up the food, but poured out the wine, and even called the dead man back with these words: "Rise, eat and drink, and rejoice." Epiphanius in the Ancoratus. Tertullian, On the Resurrection, at the beginning: "I shall laugh more at the common people when they fiercely burn the dead themselves, whom afterwards they feed most greedily." The Latins seem to have called the kind of sausage they used silicernium (though for some it is ...). Juvenal, Satire 8; and Apuleius, Florida 4, calls it a funeral supper, because he whose name was invoked would now see by the light of the flint (silice cerneret), Festus on silicernium. They also set gammari and eggs before the parental and funeral suppers, Juvenal Satire 8, and ... Plutarch, Crassus; Appian, Parthica; lentils and ... add Xiphilinus on Domitian. The vessel in which the funeral drink was contained was an obba. Tertullian, Apology 13: "What do you do at all to honour the gods that you do not also do for the dead?" Thus the silicernium differs from the epulum Iovis, the obba from the simpulum, the pollinctor from the haruspex; for the haruspex also appeared for the dead. Among these practices they also prayed for the dead and asked for rest. Tertullian, On the Testimony of the Soul: you wish for refreshment for their bones and ashes, and that they rest well among the dead.

units.la: Ne sumptuosa asperlio Neve longae corona , ne acerrae praetereantur .
units.tr: Let there be no costly sprinkling, no long garland, and let censers not be passed over.

units.la: CORONAM virtute partam et ei qui peperisset, et eius parenti, sine fraude eis lex impositam iubet.
units.tr: The law orders that a garland won by virtue be placed, without fraud, on the one who earned it, and on his parent.

units.la: Vr vni plura funera ne fierent, neve lecti plures inferrentur. Neve au-
units.tr: That not several funerals be held for one person, nor several biers carried in. Nor au-

units.la: apud Ciceronem. mutilus tamen videtur. Festus in Murrata, refert X II. tabulis caueri, Ne mortuo murrata potio inderetur. Adiicit Plinius 14. cap. 12, Numae regis legem fuisse, Vino regum ne respergito, quae duo optime conueniunt huic loco. De murrata potione dixi ad l.6. §. 1. ff. de vitico. hoc tantum addidero, Videri mihi genus murratae potionis translatitium ab Aegyptiis, apud quos murrata potio ex myrrha et aliis quindecim compositæ, Cyphi dicebatur Plutarch. in Ifide. b An quae totum hominem a vertice ad pedes cingerent, quales fortasse deorum signis imponebant? An potius Lemniscatae, id est, ex quibus Falciolae pendarent, Festus in Lemnisci quales in ludis et certaminibus dabantur? Coronarum quae arhletis dabantur in iure nostro, fit mentio in lege 6. §. 13. ff. de excusat. tutor: lege 40. de re iudicata: lege 1. Cod. de athletis. De coronis adde Gellium 3. c. 6. Tertull. lib. de corona militis. De coronis mensarum v. l. 19. §. 14. ff. de auro. c Arnobius 8. nec mortuos coronamus. Ego vos in hoc magis miror, quod tribuatis exanimi facem, aut non sententi coronas. Tertullianus lib. de corona, Mortuorum est ita coronari. d Acerra, arca quae ante mortuum poni solebat: in quo odores condebantur, alij dicant arculam thurariam Fest. in Acerra. e quidam legunt adhibeantur. f Plinius 21. c. 3. Inde inquit, illa X II. tabularum lex, Qui coronam parit, ipse peccuniæ eius, viriuiu ego arguitur. Quam serui, equiue, merenissent, pecunia partam lege dici, nemo dubitauit. Quis ergo honos fuit? vt ipsi mortuo parentibusque eius dum intus positus esset, forisve ferretur, sine fraude esset imposita. Pro arguitur, quidam legunt diuiditor, legendum videtur duitor. g Exceptio superioris legis. Coronae longae mortuis non sunt praeferendae: nisi si quas virtute quondam parauerint. h nisi forte diuersis locis quis sepultus est: alibi corpus, alibi caput l. 44. ff. de religiosis. potest etiam sepulchrum vno loco fieri, alio monumentum l. 42. ff. de religiosis. i Apud veteres gloriosum erat pluribus lectis efferri. Sylla 6 coo lectorum habuisse diciitur. & Augustus ad honorem Marcelli, sororis suae Octauiae si lij, lectos intrare ciuitatem iussit. Lego, Constantinopoli in marum {a}addito{6}. Vt (legendum Ast) quoi auro dentes {c}iuncti (lege vinéti{d}) essent{e} (lege erunt) aftim (legendum Imf) cum illo sepeliretur (lege sepelire) & ne (lege vrerétve) fe fraude (lege fine {g}fraude esto. tum, eorumque vsum non gratuitum fuisse Noucll.59. cap.9.
units.tr: In Cicero, but it seems to be defective. Festus, under murrata, reports that the Twelve Tables provide that a murrata drink not be poured into the dead. Pliny adds, in book 14, chapter 12, that it was a law of King Numa: "Do not sprinkle wine on kings." These two fit this passage very well. I have discussed the murrata drink at l. 6, §1, ff. de vitico. I will add only this: the kind of murrata drink seems to have been borrowed from the Egyptians, among whom a murrata drink made of myrrh and fifteen other ingredients was called Cyphi, as Plutarch says in De Iside. Or were these garlands that wrapped the whole person from head to foot, such as were perhaps placed on statues of the gods? Or rather lemniscatae, that is, garlands from which little pendants hung, as Festus says of the lemnisci that were given at games and contests? Crowns given to athletes are mentioned in our law at l. 6, §13, ff. de excusationibus tutorum; l. 40 de re iudicata; l. 1 Cod. de athletis. On crowns, add Gellius 3, chapter 6, and Tertullian's book De corona militis. On crowns for tables, see l. 19, §14, ff. de auro. Arnobius, book 8: "Nor do we crown the dead. I am the more surprised at you, because you give torches to the lifeless, or garlands to the insensible." Tertullian, De corona: "It is the custom of the dead to be crowned thus." Acerra: a chest that used to be placed before the dead, in which perfumes were stored; others say it was a little incense box, Festus under Acerra. Some read adhibeantur (let them be used).

units.la: {a} Antiqui folebant vna cum mortuo in rogum vel sepulchrum res multas pretiosas conijccre, puta supellectilem, vide Plutarch. in tradat. Epicuri. Hinc illud legatum, Volo inferri mihi quodcumque sepulturae mea causa feram ex ornamentis, lineas duas ex margaritis & viriolas ex smaragdo. Quaeritur, an haeres, cogatur obtemperare conditioni? responsum est, non cogi l.vlt. in f. ff. de auro. quippe, iniustae voluntates defunctorum circa sepulturam (veluti si iubeant vestes aut quaedam alia superuacua in funus impendi) non valent l.113. in sin. ff.de legat.1. Lex etiam vetat ornamenta cum corporibus condi l.14. §.5. ff.de relig. ofs. Plinii 5 certe notat moris fuisse, vt morientibus annuli detrahcrentur 33.c.1: adde Suetonii in Tyberio.
units.tr: {a} The ancients used to throw many precious things into the pyre or tomb along with the dead, such as household goods; see Plutarch in his treatise on Epicurus. Hence that bequest: "I wish to be given to me, for my burial, whatever I bring of my ornaments: two necklaces of pearls and bracelets of emerald." It is asked whether the heir can be compelled to obey this condition. The answer is that he cannot be compelled, l. ult. in fine, ff. de auro. Indeed, unjust wishes of the dead concerning burial (for example, if they order that clothes or other superfluous things be spent on the funeral) are not valid, l. 113, in fine, ff. de legatis 1. The law also forbids ornaments to be buried with bodies, l. 14, §5, ff. de religiosis et sumptibus funerum. Pliny, book 5, certainly notes that it was the custom for rings to be taken off the dying; add Suetonius on Tiberius.

units.la: {b} funeri scilicet. Lambinus legit arduito, hoc est duito, idque [?] dato. Ar pro ad, vt tandem fiat verbum, addito.
units.tr: {b} That is, for the funeral. Lambinus reads arduito, that is, duito, and takes this as given. The ar stands for ad, so that the word finally becomes addito.

units.la: {c} Auro dentes eburneos non-nulli sibi deuinciebant: qualis fuit illa Aegle, de qua Martialis, Sic dentata sibi videtur Aegle, emptis ollibus Indicoque cornu.
units.tr: {c} Some people used to bind ivory teeth to themselves with gold, as did that Aegle of whom Martial writes: "Aegle seems to herself to be toothed, having bought ... of Indian horn."

units.la: Mos etiam fuit veteribus trientem in os defuncti, tanquam nauium imponere, quem apud inferos dari pro portorio opinio fuit. Apuleius 6. Sed non haftenus vacua debebis per illas tenebras incedere, sed offas polentae multa concreras ambabus gestare manibus, ac in ipso ore duas ferre stipes. Et pofi. Ergo & inter mortuos auaritia viuit? Iuuenal. Satyr.3. Iam seder in ripa, terricoque nouitius horret Porthmea, nec spirat gurgitis alueum Infer-nis, nec habet, quem porrigat ore trientem. adde Alexand. ab Alexandro 3. Gexial. 7.
units.tr: The ancients also had the custom of placing a triens in the mouth of the dead, as if for a ferry fare, which was believed to be given in the underworld as the toll. Apuleius, book 6: "But you must not go through those shadows empty-handed; you must carry many cakes of barley meal in both hands, and bring two coins in your very mouth." And afterwards: "So does greed live even among the dead?" Juvenal, Satire 3: "Now the newcomer sits on the bank and shudders at the ferryman of the dead, and has no coin to offer from his mouth." Add Alexander ab Alexandro, Genialium dierum 3, chapter 7.

units.la: {d} ita legunt: Horomanus, Balduinus & Lambinus e efcunt. Lambin. veteres enim dixerunt Efcit, seu Efit (quod magis probo, idque propter antiquum vsum literae S. pro R. Efit pro erit. Fest. in v. cit. meam sententiam confirmat Varro 4. de lingua Cafmenarum priscum vocabulum, ita narum atque scriptum est. Alibi, Carmenae, ab eadem origine sunt declinatae, vt in multis verbis, in quo antiqui dicebant S. postea dicunt R: vt in carmine Saliorum sunt haec Cofaui, Dolosi, Eso. & alibi Cufiatij, Mufes, Rufe, Melios, Fordefum, Plufma, Afena. Ianitos haec ille, quibus addi Cupio quaedam alia quae scripsi inirio huius libri.
units.tr: {d} They read it thus: Horomanus, Balduinus and Lambinus read escunt. Lambinus: the old writers said escit or esit (which I prefer, on account of the old use of S for R: esit for erit). Festus, cited above, confirms my view: Varro, book 4 On the Latin Language, writes that the ancient word was spelled with S, and later it was spelled with R, as in many words. In the Salian hymn, these forms occur, along with others; Varro, elsewhere, adds further forms of the same kind. The Ianitor said these things, and I would add certain other points that I wrote at the beginning of this book.

units.la: {f} id est, eum, idque [?] a nominatiuo I. Fest. in Is.
units.tr: {f} That is, eum, and this from the nominative is, Festus under Is.

units.la: {g} Ex particula Se-fecimus Sine, Feft. Se (ita legendum est non Scd) pro fine inueniuntur posuisse antiqui.
units.tr: {g} From the particle se, we made sine, Festus. The ancients are found to have used se (so it should be read, not scd) for sine.

units.la: UTI ne rogum{a} bustúmve{b} nouum propius{c} 60. pedes adiici aedes alienas in vito domino, neve forum{d} sepulchri, bustúmve{e} usucapi{f} liceret.
units.tr: That it be not lawful to acquire by usucapion a new pyre or tomb placed nearer than sixty feet to another's house against the owner's will, nor the forecourt of a tomb or a burial place.

units.la: FRAGMENTUM quod ex mori-bus P. Romani praeter superiora ex XII. tabulis descripsi ex Cicerone 2. de legibus.
units.tr: A fragment which I have set down, from the customs of the Roman people, besides the above, from the Twelve Tables, taken from Cicero, On the Laws, book 2.

units.la: FUNUS ut indicatur, si quid ludorum dominúsve funeris utatur accenso atque lictoribus.
units.tr: Funeral: as it is announced, if anyone uses something from the games, or the master of the funeral, with the attendant and the lictors.

units.la: HONORATORUM virorum laudes in concione memorantor, easque et-iam ad cantus tibiarum prosequuntor, cui nomen Nænix[?].
units.tr: The praises of honoured men are recited at the public assembly, and they are also accompanied by the sound of pipes, in a song called Naenia (?).

units.la: {a} feste[?] Acrone. vide Iosephum Scaligerum apud Festum in voce Bu-stum.
units.tr: {a} Feste(?) in Acron. See Joseph Scaliger, quoted in Festus under the word Bustum.

units.la: {b} quasi bene ustum. locus in quo mortuus ustus est. Festus. Cicero vertit τύμβον.
units.tr: {b} As if well burnt: the place in which the dead person was burnt, Festus. Cicero translates it as [τύμβον] (tymbon).

units.la: {c} Lex etiam vetat mortuum inferri propius aedes alienas, quam intra legitimum spatium l. 3. §. 1. ff. de mortuo inferendo: facit lex ultim. ff. sin. regundor.
units.tr: {c} The law also forbids a dead body to be carried nearer to other people's houses than the legal distance, l. 3, §1, ff. de mortuo inferendo. The last law, ff. finium regundorum, is relevant.

units.la: {d} id est, vestibulum sepulchri. Cicero: Festus in voce Forum: ut eo pacto haeres defuncti iter, aditum, abitum, iusque accedendi ad sepulchrum habeat l. 53. ff. de actionibus empti: l. 5. ff. de sepulchro: Cicero pro Rosc.
units.tr: {d} That is, the vestibule of the tomb. Cicero; Festus under Forum: so that the heir of the deceased has the way, the approach, the going out, and the right of going up to the tomb, l. 53, ff. de actionibus empti; l. 5, ff. de sepulchro; Cicero pro Roscio.

units.la: {e} Bustum etiam pro sepulchro usurpatur. quod si discrimen facere liber, Locus in quo mortuus est combustus, ustrina dicitur: in quo & combustus & sepultus, bustum: Fest. in bustum. obiter etiam hinc observabis, ustrinam aliquando fuisse separatam a sepulchro, interdum coniundam[?].
units.tr: {e} Bustum is also used for a tomb. If one wishes to make a distinction: the place where the dead person was burnt is called ustrina; the place where he was both burnt and buried is bustum, Festus under bustum. Incidentally, from this you will also note that the ustrina was sometimes separate from the tomb, and sometimes joined to it.

units.la: {f} Hac in re sepulchris lex prospexit. Quid vendi? vide l. 9. C. de religiosis.
units.tr: {f} In this matter the law made provision for tombs. What may not be sold? See l. 9, C. de religiosis.

units.la: EX LIBRO CICERONIS III. DE LEGIBVS.
units.tr: FROM CICERO'S BOOK III, ON THE LAWS.
On the greater magistrates in general.
