units.la: IUSTA imperia sunto, iisque cives mo-deste,ac sine recusatione parento{b}.Magistratus nec obedientem, & noxium civem multa{c}, vinculis{d}, verberibusque{e} coercento:ni par,maiorve potestas, populusq. prohibessit{f} : ad quos prouocatio esto. Cum magistratus iudicasset, inrogasitve: per{g} populum multae{h}, poenae certatio{i} esto.
units.tr: Let just commands be binding, and let citizens obey them modestly and without refusal. Magistrates shall restrain a citizen who disobeys and does harm with fines, chains and blows, unless an equal or greater power and the people forbid it; there shall be appeal from them. When a magistrate has judged or imposed a penalty, there shall be a contest before the people over the fine and the punishment.
Let all obey the pronouncement of judges.

units.la: {c} Omnibus magistratibus (non tamen duumuiris) concessum erat iurisdictionem suam defendere poenali iudicio : l.vn.ff.fi quis ius dicenti non obtemperauerit: adde l.131.§.1.l.244.in fi.ff.de verb.fignif. {d} l.9.ff.ex quib. caus.maior:l.8.§.9.ff.de poenis:adde l.216. l.224.ff.de verbor. fignific.
units.tr: {c} All magistrates (but not the duumvirs) were granted the right to defend their jurisdiction by a penal judgment: see the law "If anyone does not obey the one who declares the law" (l. un. ff.), and add l. 131 §1 and l. 244 in fine, ff. de verb. signif. {d} l. 9 ff. ex quib. caus. maior; l. 8 §9 ff. de poenis; add l. 216 and l. 224 ff. de verb. signif.

units.la: {e} ita tamen,vt nemo verberibus necetur,aut virgis interimatur, nec tormentis d.l.9.§.3.
units.tr: {e} Yet in such a way that no one is put to death by blows or killed with rods, nor by torture: d. l. 9 §3.

units.la: {f} Maior minorem prohibere potest,par, parem prohibere posse non videtur l.4. ff. de arbitris. & tamen hic habetur magis ratio prohibentis quàm iubentis.& merito,id n.prę ualet in re pari l.11.ff.de seruit.rust.[?] l.28.ff.comm.diuidundo.& in publicis iudiciis obtinet l.38 ff.de re iudicata.adde Fenestellä c.10.in fi.
units.tr: {f} A greater magistrate can forbid a lesser one; an equal does not seem able to forbid an equal (l. 4 ff. de arbitris). Yet here the reason of the one who forbids is held to count for more than that of the one who commands, and rightly, for this holds in an equal matter (l. 11 ff. de serv. rust. and l. 28 ff. comm. divid.), and it holds in public trials (l. 38 ff. de re iudicata). Add Fenestella c. 10 in fine.

units.la: {g} A magistratibus ad populum prouocabatur, vt cui poenae, multaeque remittendae ius esset: sic Flacco, Martiali flamini,populus Romanus multam remisit, quam Crassus Pontifex maximus ei,si à sacris discesserit,dixerat Cicer. XII. in Anton. Illud est etiam obseruandum,non tantum a magistratibus sed & a regibus ad populi prouocationem fuisse Cic.t. de repub.apud Senecam 19.epist.109. neque id mirum,cum iidem reges Quaestores non crearent, sed populus l.t. ff.de off.quaestor.[?] vt merito suspecta sit sententia legis Regis qua dicitur populus ei, & in eum ius omne suum transtulisse.
units.tr: {g} Appeal was made from the magistrates to the people, so that the people had the right to remit penalties and fines. Thus the Roman people remitted to Flaccus, the flamen of Mars, the fine which Crassus, the chief pontiff, had imposed on him if he withdrew from the sacred rites, as Cicero says in the twelfth Philippic against Antony. It must also be observed that appeal to the people was made not only from magistrates but also from kings, as Cicero says in his book On the Republic, cited by Seneca, epistle 109. Nor is this surprising, since the same kings did not appoint the quaestors; the people did (l. 1 ff. de off. quaestor.). So the opinion of the law of the king is rightly suspect, which says that the people transferred to him all its right, and into him.

units.la: {h} i.multae poenaeue. {i} Certatio, i.cognitio suprema.Liuius 25.Dū centum milia aeris multa Posthumi publicano dicta à Tribunisple-bis fuit,cuius certandae cum dies aduenisset conciliiumq. tam frequens adesset &c. additur hic in quibusdam Codicibus, lex quae sequitur. Quodcumque postremum populus iusserit, id ius ratumque esto. sed commodius visum est eam in librum sequentem reiicere.
units.tr: {h} That is, the fine or penalty. {i} Certatio, that is, the final hearing. Livy 25: "While the fine of a hundred thousand asses, which the tribunes of the plebs had imposed on Posthumius the publican, was being contested, and the day for the contest had come and the assembly was so crowded..." In some manuscripts the law that follows is added here: "Whatever the people last ordered, let that be valid and ratified." But it seemed more fitting to put it in the following book.
On military matters.

units.la: MILITIAE abeo, qui imperabit, prouocatio ne esto : quodque is, qui bellum gerat, imperassit, ius ratumque esto. Minores magistratus, periti iuris plures praelia sunto. Militiae quibus iussi erunt imperanto, eorumque tribuni sunto.
units.tr: Let there be no appeal from the one who commands in the field; and whatever the one who conducts the war has ordered shall be valid and ratified. Let the lesser magistrates, skilled in law, ... battles. Let them command the military as they have been ordered, and let them be tribunes of it.
On the magistrates and the quaestors.
At home let them keep guard over the public money.
On the capital triumvirs.
Let them guard the bonds of the springs.
On the quaestors of parricide.

units.la: visitatione[?], non tamen omnino legum imperitis, dicta lege 17. in ff. ne. quos ideo Romani in prouincias mittebant, & ad utrumque & pacis & belli tempus idoneos, Nouell. 24. Constat tamen ixe-pissimè indices Romae non ex doctrina, sed ex casu fieri solitos esse Plinius 14. capite primo. Minores tamen magistratus, de quibus hic agitur videtur, fuisse quasi adsessores maiorum: & adsessorum exemplo, peritiam iuris in iis requiri, lege prima ff. de off. adsess. l. 1. ff. quod quisque iur. lege prima Codice de adsessoribus. Nouell. 12. in principio. Pedaneos eodem modo peritos esse oportuit, it μὲν καὶ πειρᾶς Nouell. 82. cap. it.
units.tr: (A lengthy note on the examination of cases.) Not that the judges were not, in general, unskilled in the laws (see the law cited at ff. ne ...); which is why the Romans used to send them into the provinces, men fit for both the times of peace and of war (Nov. 24). Yet it is agreed that judges at Rome were very often chosen not for their learning but by chance, as Pliny says in book 14, chapter 1. The lesser magistrates of whom this passage speaks, however, seem to have been like assessors of the greater ones; and on the model of assessors, legal skill is required of them (law 1 ff. de off. adsess.; l. 1 ff. quod quisque iur.; the first law in the Code, de adsessoribus; Nov. 12 at the beginning). The pedanei had likewise to be skilled, as the Greek has it [μὲν καὶ πειρᾶς] (Nov. 82, cap. it.).

units.la: e in praelia, ita legitur in quibusdam exculsis. alij legunt in praelio.
units.tr: {e} "In battles": so it is read in certain excluded copies; others read "in battle."
{f} Perhaps it should be read "of the soldier."

units.la: g de munere & officio tribuni militaris, vide legem duodecimam ff. de re militari: Vegetius 2. capite duodecimo: vide epistolam Aureliani ad quendam eius vicarium, apud Vopiscum.
units.tr: {g} On the office and duty of the military tribune, see law 12 ff. de re militari; Vegetius 2, chapter 12; and see the letter of Aurelian to one of his vicars, in Vopiscus.

units.la: h Hoc caput refero ad quaestores, inquirendae & coercendae pecuniae causa creatos. Etsi scio apud Varronem 4. de lingua, nonnihil extare de tribunis aerarij & aere militari, quae huc non ita male cohaerent.
units.tr: {h} I refer this chapter to the quaestors, who were appointed to inquire into and restrain money matters. Although I know that in Varro, book 4 On the Latin Language, something is found about the tribunes of the treasury and the military money, which fit here not badly.

units.la: i Hoc etiam caput ad triumviros capitales refero: vt
units.tr: {i} I also refer this chapter to the capital triumvirs, so that
they may avenge capital crimes.
Let them stamp bronze, a silver, or gold by public authority.
On the triumvirs of the mint.
Let them stamp bronze b, silver c, or gold by public authority.
On the decemvirs of lawsuits.

units.la: Lites d cōtractas iudicanto: quod cunque senatus creuerit e, agunto.
units.tr: Let them judge the lawsuits d already begun; let them carry out whatever the senate has decreed e.
On the aediles.

units.la: Suntoque aediles f curatores vrbis g, annonae h, ludorum-que [?] [?] — Taciti 5. Annal. Tradunt temporis eius authores, quia triumviris capitalibus supplicio (ita emendo, pro triumvirali supplicio) affici virginem inauditum habebatur, à carnifice, laqueum iuxta, compressam [?] qua [?] nihil apertius. Necdum enim probatum animaduerti, Triumvirale [?] supplicium idem esse, quod poenam laquei potui [?] que error ex hac scriptura triumviral pro triumviris capitalibus, dimanare. a Hunc locum refero ad quaestores parricidii, de quibus l.2.§.23.ff.de orig.iur: vel similes magistratus. Nec enim Consulibus licuit de capite ciuis Romani ius dicere d.§.23. b & hoc etiam caput ad triumviros monetales, aeris (vt inquit Pomponius d.l.2 §.30) argenti & auri flatores, aut qui tempore XII tabularum hoc constituit non posse praesumprio est ea. c Legibus XII. tabularum hoc constituit non posse praesumptio est ea. Romani ante Seruium Tullium rudiare vrebantur Plin.33.e.3. Seruius, primus aes signauit Plin.d.loco.&18.c 3. Argentum non ante Pyrrhum signatum est: sed annis tantum quinque ante primum bellum Punicum, Plin.33.c.3. Aurum quo tempore signatum fuerit incertum est, Plin.d.loco. d Hac particula adducor, v credam hic tractari decemviris qui hastae praeessent, quique (vt Pomponius loquitur, l.2.§.19.) in litibus iudicandis olim constituti fuerunt. e decreuerit. f d.l.2.§.21.&26. Aediles curules intelligit. g idque aediles nonnunquam interuenerunt incendiis arcendis l.3. ff.de off.praef.vig. h Hinc aedilitiae actiones Cod.de aedilitys actionibus, ed. ita aedilitia sit de aedilit.edicto: vt hinc facile intelligas, ecquid Pomponius senserit, dum nobis retulit Praefectum annonae & vigilum non magistratus, (non perpetuo aut ex legibus duodecim tabularum) sed extraordinarie & vtilitatis causa fuisse constitutos l.2.§.33.ff.de orig.iur. Ob superiorem causam iidem aediles de mensuris ius dicebant, Iuvenal. S.14.7.10. Et de mensura ius dicere, vasa minora frangere, pannosus vacuis aedilis Vlubris. Qua de re que solemnium: ollisque vel honoris [?]am plioris gradum is primus {b} adscensus esto.
units.tr: Let there be aediles f, curators of the city g, of the grain supply h, and of the games... Tacitus, Annals 5: the writers of his time record that it was regarded as unheard of for a virgin to be put to death by the capital triumvirs (so, instead of "triumviral punishment", they say), by the executioner, with a noose beside her, and nothing could be more open than this. For it had not yet been proved that the triumviral punishment is the same as the penalty of the noose and the drink, and this error arises from the reading "triumviral" for "capital triumvirs." a I refer this passage to the quaestors of parricide, about whom see l. 2 §23 ff. de orig. iur., or to similar magistrates; for consuls were not permitted to pronounce judgment on the life of a Roman citizen (d. §23). b I also refer this chapter to the triumvirs of the mint, the moneyers of bronze, silver and gold (as Pomponius says, d. l. 2 §30). It is presumed that the Twelve Tables established that this was not allowed to be done. c The Romans, before Servius Tullius, used rough bronze, as Pliny says (33, c. 3). Servius was the first to stamp bronze (Pliny, loc. cit., and 18, c. 3). Silver was not stamped until after Pyrrhus, but only five years before the First Punic War (Pliny 33, c. 3). When gold was first stamped is uncertain (Pliny, loc. cit.). d I am led by this particle to believe that the decemvirs who presided over the auction are treated here, those who (as Pomponius puts it, l. 2 §19) were once appointed for judging lawsuits. e decreed. f Pomponius, d. l. 2 §§21 and 26, means the curule aediles. g The aediles sometimes also took part in preventing fires (l. 3 ff. de off. praef. vig.). h Hence the aedilician actions (Cod. de aedilitiis actionibus), and the aedilician edict. From this you may easily understand what Pomponius thought, when he told us that the prefect of the grain supply and of the night watch were appointed not as permanent magistrates, nor from the Twelve Tables, but extraordinarily and for reasons of utility (l. 2 §33 ff. de orig. iur.). For the same reason the aediles also pronounced judgment on measures, as Juvenal says (Sat. 14): "The ragged aedile of Ulubrae pronounces law about measures and breaks the smaller vessels." Concerning this matter, the solemn words... and for the holding of office, this shall be the first step of the higher rank.
On the Censors.

units.la: CENSORES {e}, populi ciuitates {d}, soboles {e}, familias {f}, pecuniásque {g} cen-sento: vrbis {h} templa, vias, aquas, aerarium, vectigalia {i} tuentor: populíque partes in tribus {k} distribuunto: exin pecuniam [?] iicit, muros, nauália, portus, aquæductus, & omnia quæ ad vsum reipublicæ pertinent, theatra, porticus, noua templa, impensas meliores ædilium censeri. {b} Ideóque notat Cicero 2. de officijs, præterminissionem ædilitatis Mamerco repulsam consulatus attulsse. Solebant enim ædiles auram popularem largitionibus variis demereri. Quod hîc dicitur de ædili, idem etiam tribuitur quæstori, in lege {t} in fine ff. de offic. quæstor. {c} l. 2. §. 17. ff. de origine iuris. Censores inde dicti, quòd tanti quisque res suas æstimaret, quantum illi censuissent. Festus in Censores. huic magistratui origo fuit, quòd populus diu incensus fuisset nec differri censu, neque consulibus, propter bella, id curæ esse poterat. {d} ætates l. 3. ff. de censibus. {e} liberos. {f} id est seruos l. 4. §. 5. ff. de c. nsibus. {g} agros dicta l. 4. {h} Liuius 4. units.tr: Let the censors take the census of the citizens of the state, of the offspring, the households, and the money, as follows. Let them guard the temples, roads, waters, and treasury of the city, and the public revenues. Let them distribute the people's parts into tribes, and then assess the money for walls, naval yards, harbours, aqueducts, and everything that pertains to the use of the commonwealth: theatres, colonnades, new temples, and the better expenditures of the aediles. {b} Hence Cicero, in the second book of On Duties, notes that the omission of the aedileship brought Mamercus a rebuff in his bid for the consulship, since the aediles were accustomed to win popular favour by various largesses. What is said here of the aedile is also attributed to the quaestor, in the law at the end of the Digest, de officio quaestoris. {c} See the second law, §17, Digest, de origine iuris. The censors were so named because each man valued his own property at whatever the censors had assessed it. Festus, under Censores. The office had its origin in this: since the people had long gone uncounted, and the census could not be deferred, nor could it be left to the consuls because of wars, it became a matter of care for this magistracy. {d} Ages: the third law, Digest, de censibus. {e} Children. {f} That is, slaves: the fourth law, §5, Digest, de censibus. {g} Fields, as the fourth law says. {h} Livy, book 4: the public rights and the first of the goods were under the nod and judgment of the censor. {i} Livy, book 24: they also let out public services for hire. {k} At the beginning there were three tribes (Livy calls them the centuries of the knights, book 1): the Tatienses, the Ramnes or Ramnenses, and the Luceres, according to Varro, On the Latin Language, book 4. Livy writes that they were named not from the tribute, nor from the parts of the people, but that at first there were four: the Suburana, Palatina, Collina, and Exquilina, so named from the regions of the city (Livy, book 18; Pliny). In Cicero's time there were thirty-five tribes, whose names, as Manutius followed them, I have thought it useful to share with readers. Aemilia: Cicero, Ad Atticum, book 11; Livy, book 8. Arniensis: Livy, book 10; Cicero, Ad Familiares, book 8. Arniensis: Livy, 6.39; Cicero, Against Rullus. Claudia: Livy, book 11; Dionysius of Halicarnassus. units.la: a Tres apud Romanos fuerunt ordines, Senatorius seu Patricius, Equestris & Plebeius. Senatorij ordinis tres etiam gradus postea fuere, clarissimi, spectabiles, & illustres, dixi ad Noncll.7.in fine. b Inter arrarios vnus relatus est ab iisdem Censoribus, qui cum vberrimus & habi-liffimus esset, rogatusque quam ob causam equum nimis strigo-sum haberet, respondert, se à seipso curari, equum à famulo. 4. Gellius 10: & 7. capite vltimo: Liuius 43. In equitibus, inquit, recensendis, tristis admodum & seuera fuit eorum censura, multis equos ademerunt. Idem libro 14: & Valerius 2. cap. 4. Censores citarunt eos qui post Cannensem pugnam Rempublicam deseruissent. his adde quaedam alia ex Valerio dicto loco. c Qui fine iusta missione discesserant a signis militum, Censores ita adigebant: Ex tua animi sententia, tu ex edicto C. Claudij Tiberij Sempronij censoris in prouinciam Macedonicam redibis, quod fine dolo malo facere poteris Liuius 43. d de coelibe quaedam dixi ad Vlpianum capite 13. & 14. & ad titulum Codicis de indicta viduitate: & de lege Iulia Miscella tollenda. & ad titulum Cod. de infirmandis poenis caelibatus. Hoc tantum addere visum est de Camillo & Posthumo censoribus, qui aera, poenae nomine, eos qui ad fene-ctutem caelibes permansissent, in aerarium deferre iusserunt: item-rum puniri dignos, si quo modo de tam iusta sententia quererentur 2. Valer.4. e quale illud fuit, Liuius libro 4. Censor, inquit, agebat de vxoribus solemne iusiurandum, quumque verbis conceptis aliquem Censor ita interrogasset, Et tu ex animi tui sententia vxorem habes? habeo equidem, inquit, sed non ex animi tui sententia. Tum Censor, quod intempestiue lasciuisser, in aeraros retulit. Alterum seueritatis Censoriae exemplum fuit in eo qui prope fuit (nisi vitio se ofcedinis teneri deieraffet) vt pleda-retur, quod apud Censorem clare nimis ac secure ofcitauiffet: tanquam illud vagi animi iudicium foret 4. Gell. 10. & 7. capite vltime. gregunto : probrum in senatu ne relin-quunto: bini sunto : magistratum quin-quennium habento : reliqui magistra-tus annui sunto: eaque potestas semper esto.
units.tr: a Among the Romans there were three orders: the senatorial or patrician, the equestrian, and the plebeian. Later the senatorial order also had three grades: clarissimi, spectabiles, and illustres. I have spoken of this at the end of my note on Nonius, book 7. b Among the cavalry, one was struck off by the same censors, who, though he was very wealthy and well-to-do, when asked why he kept a horse that was too thin, replied that he himself was looked after by himself, and the horse by his servant (Gellius, book 10, and book 7, last chapter; Livy, book 43). Livy writes: "In enrolling the knights, their censorship was very grim and severe; they took away the horses of many." The same in book 14, and Valerius, book 2, chapter 4. The censors summoned those who after the battle of Cannae had deserted the Republic. To these add some other matters from Valerius in the passage cited. c Those who had left the standards of the soldiers without lawful discharge, the censors bound with this oath: "By your own judgment, you shall return to the province of Macedonia by the edict of Gaius Claudius, Tiberius Sempronius, censors, which you can do without evil intent" (Livy, book 43). d I have said some things about the unmarried in my notes on Ulpian, chapters 13 and 14, and on the title of the Code de indicta viduitate, and on the Julian law, Miscella tollenda, and on the title of the Code de infirmandis poenis caelibatus. It seemed fit to add only this, concerning the censors Camillus and Postumius, who ordered that those who had remained unmarried into old age should be brought into the treasury under the name of a penalty for bronze; likewise they were to be punished if they complained in any way of so just a sentence (Valerius, book 4, book 2). e Such was that instance in Livy, book 4: "The censor," he says, "was conducting the solemn oath about wives, and when the censor had questioned someone in set words, 'And you, by your own judgment, have a wife?' 'I have one indeed,' he said, 'but not by your judgment.' Then the censor entered him in the treasury, because he had been wanton at an untimely moment." Another example of the censorial severity was in the case of a man who, nearly having been about to be acquitted (unless he had sworn he was held by the fault of yawning), had yawned too loudly and carelessly before the censor, as if that were a judgment of a wandering mind (Gellius, book 10, and book 7, last chapter). ...gregunto: let them not leave disgrace in the Senate. Let there be two of them; let them hold the magistracy for five years; the remaining magistrates shall be annual; and that power shall always be.
On the Office of the Praetor

units.la: IVRIS disceptator, qui priuata iudicet, iudicarīue iubeat, prætor esto. Iuris ciuilis custos esto. Huic potestati parento. Quotcumque senatus creauerit, populusque iusserit, tot sunto.
units.tr: Let him be the arbiter of law who judges private cases or orders them to be judged. Let him be the guardian of the civil law. Let them obey this power. Let there be as many as the senate appoints and the people commands.

units.la: natum securi percusserat, tempore supplicij ad arbitrium mulierculæ, cuius amore tenebatur, electo. & Rufinum, quòd decem pondo vasa argentea comparasset, perinde ac malo exemplo luxuriosum & Duronium, quod legem de coercendis conuiuiorum sumptibus latam abrogasset 2.Valer.4. Liuius lib.43. senatum censores legerunt, septem e senatu eiecti sunt. adde eundem lib.4.
units.tr: ...had struck his son with an axe, the time of the punishment being chosen at the whim of a little woman by whom he was held in love. Also Rufinus, because he had bought ten pounds' weight of silver vessels, as a bad example of luxury; and Duronius, because he had repealed a law passed to restrain the expenses of banquets (Valerius 2.4; Livy 43). When the censors chose the senate, seven men were expelled from it (add the same author, book 4).
Two censors.

units.la: c octodecim tantum mensium meminit Liuius lib.10. idque ex lege Aemylia quæ hanc abrogat.
units.tr: Livy, book 10, mentions only eighteen months, and that under the Aemilian law, which repeals this.
As with the consulship and the praetorship.

units.la: e id est, non sit extraordinaria vt Dictatura.
units.tr: That is, it is not extraordinary, as the dictatorship is.

units.la: f de criminibus ac delictis publicis non cognoscit. eius etiam authoritatis non erat, creare magistratus. sicuti nec penes eum belli ac pacis ius fuit. Interdicta tamen reddidit de rebus sacris, religiosis ac publicis l.1. in f.ff.de interdictis. hinc illa interdicta, Ne quid in loco sacro fiat. De locis & itineribus publicis: Ne quid in loco publico: De loco publico fruendo. De via publica. De fluminibus. Ne quid in flumine publico: Vt in flumine publico nauigare liceat. De ripa munienda.
units.tr: He did not take cognizance of crimes and public offences. Nor did he have the authority to create magistrates, just as the power of war and peace did not rest with him. He did, however, issue interdicts concerning sacred, religious and public matters (Digest, 'On Interdicts', law 1 at the end). Hence those interdicts: that nothing be done in a sacred place; concerning public places and roads: that nothing be done in a public place; concerning the enjoyment of a public place; concerning a public road; concerning rivers: that nothing be done in a public river; that it be lawful to sail on a public river; concerning the fortifying of a riverbank.

units.la: g v. titulum de Officio Prætoris.
units.tr: See the title "On the Office of the Praetor".

units.la: h Iuris etiam ciuilis admiuandi, emendandi, & supplendi potestas Prætoribus data l.7. in ff. ff.de iustitia & iure.
units.tr: The praetors were also given the power to administer, amend and supplement the civil law (Digest, 'On Justice and Law', law 7).

units.la: i Plures enim fuere, vrbanus l.2. §.27. de origine iuris: peregrinus d.l.2. §.28. Sardiniæ, Siciliæ, Hispaniæ, Galliæ Narbonensis, qui de falso, qui de parricidiis, qui de sicariis, qui de veneficiis, duo frumentarii & ita XII. aliquando fuere. Augustus XVI. Prætores constituit, quibus duos Claudius adiecit qui de fideicommisso iusdicerent, ex queis Nerua vnum detraxit alio subrogato, qui inter fiscum & priuatos ius diceret. Ad hunc mordum XVIII. Prætores fuere d.l.2. §.32. quinqueuiri Cistiberes & Vltiberes, i. cis & vls Tiberim constituti, quasi Prætorū vicarij d.l.2. §.31. & 33. in f. Et hæc quidem Romæ. Constantinopoli verò, tres Prætores fuerunt ab initio l.1. C. de episcopali audientia: l.vlt. C. de officio Prætorii. Flauialis, Constantinianus, Triumphalis. Succedaneis quidem tempo-ribus, interdum qua-tuor, interdū quinque, interdum o-do [?] fuere, Cō-stantinianus, Constantia-nus, Theodosius, Arcadius, Thriumphalis, Augustalis, Romanus, Laureatus
units.tr: For there were many: the urban praetor (Digest, 'On the Origin of Law', law 2, §27); the peregrine praetor (the same law, §28); praetors for Sardinia, Sicily, Spain and Narbonese Gaul; those concerned with forgery, with parricide, with assassins, with poisoning; two for the grain supply. Thus at times there were twelve. Augustus established sixteen praetors, to whom Claudius added two who would judge matters of trust-fideicommissa; of these Nerva removed one, another being substituted, who would adjudicate between the treasury and private persons. In this condition there were eighteen praetors (the same law, §32). The quinqueviri, the Cisiberes and Ultiberes, that is, appointed on this side of the Tiber and beyond it, were like the deputies of the praetors (the same law, §§31 and 33, at the end). And these were at Rome. At Constantinople, however, there were three praetors from the beginning (Code, 'On the Episcopal Audience', law 1; Code, 'On the Office of the Praetorian Prefect', last law): Flavialis, Constantinianus, Triumphalis. In later times there were sometimes four, sometimes five, sometimes eight: Constantinianus, Constantianus, Theodosius, Arcadius, Triumphalis, Augustalis, Romanus, Laureatus.
On the Office of the Consul

units.la: REGIO {b}imperio duo {c}funto : iisque praeeundo {d}, iudicando {e}, consulendo {f}, praetores {g}, iudices {h}, consules, appellan-tor : militiae summum {i} ius habento. Nemini parento. Talis populi [?] suprema lex esto. Eundem magistratum, ni-
units.tr: Let there be two with royal power; and in going before, judging and consulting, let them be called praetors, judges, consuls; let them hold the highest military right. Let them obey no one. Let this be the supreme law of the people. Let the same magistracy, if not...

units.la: {b} ut dixi ad d.l. ult. a v.ff. ad officio Conjuliu. b Consules regio fuerit imperio. in his tamen regium imperium paulo imminutum, quod duo, quod annui essent, quod statis tantum festis ac pompis & honoris Deorum gratia, sceptra, coronas aureas & purpuram vsurparent Halicarnass. 3. Fenestella 7. Regij imperij vestigiū fuit, sella eburnea in qua sedentes ius reddebat, quod quae praetexta candida vterentur, quod XII lictores, totidem lecures ante eos praeferrent.
units.tr: As I said above on the last law of the Digest, 'On the Office of the Consul'. The consuls had royal power, but in them this royal power was somewhat diminished, because there were two of them, because they were annual, and because they used the sceptres, golden crowns and purple only on fixed festivals and in processions, and for the sake of the honour of the gods (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, 3; Fenestella, 7). A trace of royal power was the ivory chair in which they sat to give judgment, that they wore the white-bordered toga, and that twelve lictors and as many attendants went before them.

units.la: {c} à Lacedaemoniis mos hic vsurpatus Halicarnass. 4. spectabant & aliud Romani, hoc scilicet, minus iniuriosos fore & molestos diuisa potestate. {d} inde Praetores etiam dicti. eod. {e} conflat Consules initio, ante consultos Praetores, ius in ciuitate reddidisse l.2.§.19. ff.de origine praeterquam in causis criminalibus d.l.2.§.23. Apud eosdem manumissiones expeditas fuisse conflat l.vnica ff.de officio Consul. {f} vel quod Reipublicae Fenestellae c.7. vel quod senatum, populumque consulerent Varro 4.de lingua vt inde lex fieret vel senatusconsultum.
units.tr: This custom was adopted by the Romans from the Lacedaemonians (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, 4, looks at this), and the other reason is evidently that a divided power would be less injurious and troublesome. Hence the praetors were also so named (same place). It is agreed that the consuls at first, before the praetors were appointed, gave judgment in the state, except in criminal cases (Digest, 'On the Origin of Law', law 2, §19 and §23). It is agreed that among them manumissions were carried out speedily (the single law in the Digest, 'On the Office of the Consul'). Either because they consulted for the commonwealth (Fenestella, c. 7), or because they consulted the senate and people (Varro, 4, 'On the Latin Language'), so that a law or senatus consultum might be made from this.

units.la: nisi illinc potius deriuemus vnde Actius ait apud eundem Varronem d.loco. Qui redeconsulat, cofulfiat. videtur etiam Cincius lib. de Consulis potestate, apud Festum in voce Praetor ad portam opinari Consules dictos, quod populos Latinos consulere solitti essent & imperium communi consilio administrare. {g} Festus in Praetoria porta. Initio Praetores erant, qui nunc Consules, iisque bella administrabant, quorum tabernaculum quoque dicebatur Praetorium. hinc Praetoria porta, qua exercitus in praelium educebatur. Festus ibid. Praetoria cohors, quae à Praetore non discedebat Festus in Praetoria cohors.
units.tr: Unless we rather derive it from where Accius says in the same Varro (the place cited): "He who takes counsel, consults." Cincius also, in his book 'On the Power of the Consul', as cited by Festus under the word "Praetor at the gate", seems to think that the consuls were so named because they were accustomed to consult the Latin peoples and to administer power by common counsel. (Festus, under "Praetorian gate".) At the beginning those who are now consuls were praetors, and they administered the wars; their tent too was called the praetorium. Hence the Praetorian Gate, through which the army was led out to battle. (Festus, same place.) The Praetorian cohort, which did not leave the praetor's side (Festus, under "Praetorian cohort").

units.la: {h} à iudicando vt s. cod. {i} ita vt eo tempore miles ab eorum sententia appellare non posset. capite de magistrat. l. nisi populo. {l} hoc innuit, Populi salutem omnibus rebus anteponi, à qua sententia nunquam boni principes abhorruere. Capitolinus in M.Antonino.fisco, inquit, in causis compendij, nunquam iudicans fauit adde Nouell. 149. inf. & 161. inf. {m} id est, vltima. Est enim suprenus post quem nullus, quem nemo sequitur l.34.ff.de vulgari; l.9. ff.de reb.dub.l.92.ff.de verb.significt. interfuerunt decem anni, ne quis capito. Æuitatem annali * lege seruanto.
units.tr: Because they judge (from judging, as in the section on this title). So that at that time a soldier could not appeal from their sentence (chapter 'On Magistrates', law 'Unless the people'). This hints that the safety of the people is placed before all things, a sentence from which good princes never shrank. Capitolinus, in the life of Marcus Antoninus: "He favoured the fisc in cases of gain, but never when judging." Add Novel 149 at the end, and 161 at the end. That is, the last: for it is the highest, after which there is none, and which no one follows (Digest, 'On Vulgar Substitution', law 34; Digest, 'On Doubtful Matters', law 9; Digest, 'On the Meaning of Words', law 92). Ten years intervened, lest anyone keep the ... Let them observe the annual law of the ... (sic).
On the Dictator and the Master of the Horse.

units.la: A s t quando duellum b grauius c, discordiæ d ciuium, estunto ne ampius lex e menses, si senatus creuerit, idem iuris, quod duo consules, tenento: isque aue f sinistra g fuerunt & aliæ leges annales quibus cauebatur, quo xratis suæ anno quisque magistratum posset adipisci. Gerebatur xdilitas curulis anno XXXVII [?]. biennio post, Prætura: Cicero epistola ad Furnium. Consulatus anno XLIII [?]. quibus tamen legibus nonnulli, virtutis causa, interdum soluebantur v.
units.tr: But when a graver war b, discords c among the citizens d, arise, let there be no law beyond six months e, if the senate has so decided, and let the two consuls have the same right. This was done f under an unfavourable omen g, and there were also other annual laws by which it was provided that each man could attain the magistracy in his own year. The curule aedileship was held in the thirty-seventh year [?]; two years later, the praetorship (Cicero, letter to Furnius). The consulship was held in the forty-third year [?]. Yet some men, for the sake of their virtue, were sometimes released from these laws v.

units.la: v. Pavlum Manvcium libro de legibus.
units.tr: v. See Paulus Manutius, On the Laws.

units.la: b id est, bellum. ita dicitur, quod ut quasi duorum se contendentium conflictus. inde Duellona Bellona. Varro 4. de lingua. Festus in Duellum duidens hostia, bidens. Festus in duidens. Duonum, bonum, idem in Duonum. Duellum etiam dicebatur perduellum. Varro 6. de lingua, vnde perduellis. Festus in Duellum. l.134. ff. de verb. signif.
units.tr: b That is, bellum (war). It is so called because it is, as it were, the clash of two parties contending against each other; hence Duellona for Bellona (Varro, book 4, On the Latin Language). Festus, under Duellum: duidens for bidens, a sacrificial victim. Festus, under duidens. Duonum for bonum; the same under Duonum. Duellum was also said as perduellum (Varro, book 6, On the Latin Language), whence perduellis. Festus, under Duellum. Digest 134, de verborum significatione.

units.la: c v.l.2. §.14. ff. de origine iuris.
units.tr: c See Digest 1.2 §14, de origine iuris.

units.la: d hinc legimus apud Liuium 7. Comitatione detecta XXX populorum vel vt Fenestella ait XL. Dictatoris primam mentionem ortam fuisse credi: nonnullis alierentibus, T. Largium primum dictatorem, Spurium Cassium Magistrum equitum creatos [?]. Fenestella [?]. Halicarnasseus [?]. l.134. ff. de verb. signif.
units.tr: d Hence we read in Livy, book 7, that when the conspiracy was discovered among thirty peoples (or, as Fenestella says, forty), the first mention of the dictator is believed to have arisen. Some others report that Titus Largius was the first dictator and Spurius Cassius the master of the horse. Fenestella. Halicarnassus. Digest 134, de verborum significatione.

units.la: e d. §.12. l. vnic. C. de officio Præfe-cti Prætorio. f id est, auspicato. Valer. 1. de quo mox etiam dicam. Illud addendum, moris etiam fuisse dictatorem nocte sub silentio dici, Liuius.
units.tr: e Ibid. §12; l. unic. C., de officio Praefecti Praetorio. f That is, auspicato (after taking the auspices). Valerius, book 1, of which I shall also speak shortly. It should be added that it was also the custom for the dictator to be named at night, in silence (Livy).

units.la: g Auis sinistra, non est mala, sinistra seu lævua auspicia, bona auspicia existimantur. lævuum omen, bonum omen. Varro 6. de lingua, sinistra enim in auspicando significare ait Atteius Capito, lævum & prosperum auspicium. Festus in Sinistrum.
units.tr: g Left-hand omens are not bad: the left (sinistra or laeva) auspices are considered good auspices, and a laevum omen is a good omen. Varro, book 6, On the Latin Language; for Atteius Capito says that sinistra, in taking auspices, signifies a left-hand and favourable auspice. Festus, under Sinistrum.

units.la: Causa vanitatis inde fuit, credidèrunt augures, quod homine in meridie (quæ deorum sedes ab iisdem existimabatur) spectante, ad sinistram eius partes mundi exorientes sint, ad dextram occidentes. Inde sinistra auspicia sausta dici, quod ea quæ oriantur, quæque ortus causam tribuunt, meliora sint iis quæ occidunt, quæue interitum rei demonstrant. vide Festum in sinistra auct.
units.tr: The reason for this error lay here: the augurs believed that when a man faces south at midday (which they held to be the seat of the gods), the parts of the world that rise are on his left and those that set are on his right. Hence left-hand auspices are called lucky, because things that rise, and that give the origin of a thing, are better than those that set or that signify the destruction of a thing. See Festus, under sinistra.

units.la: Partes exorientes ibi intelligi puto solem ipsum aut orientem, non ipsas stellas quæ nobis nunquam occidunt, & quæ ab Astrologis perpetuæ apparitionis dicuntur. Sed quam vana sit augurum & aruspicum opinio, sa. is ostendit contraria Aegyptiorum sententia, vt qui existimarent, Anticas mundi partes esse in Occidente, anticas in Oriente, dextras in Septentrione, sinistras in meridie v. Plutarchum in Iside: add Cælii Rhodigin. 1. Lect. 10, vbi explicat quæ sint in mundo Antica & Postica. {a}dictus populi magister{b} esto.
units.tr: I think the rising parts are to be understood here as the sun itself, or the east, not the stars themselves, which never set for us and which astrologers call of perpetual appearance. But how empty is the opinion of the augurs and haruspices, Sa. is shows by the contrary opinion of the Egyptians, who thought that the front parts of the world were in the west, the back parts in the east, the right parts in the north, and the left parts in the south v. See Plutarch, On Isis; add Caelius Rhodiginus, 1 Lect. 10, where he explains what the front and back parts of the world are. Let him be called master of the people.

units.la: AEQUITATEM{c} quicumque re-gat, habeto{d} pari{e} iure cum{f} eo, quicumque erit iuris discceptator{g}. Ast quando consulis{h} est, magistratúsve{i} populi, re-liqui magistratus ne sunto{k}.
units.tr: Whoever shall govern the cavalry, let him have equal right with him who shall be the judge of law. But when there is need of a consul or of a magistrate of the people, let the other magistrates not be.

units.la: le, inquam, vel ut Dionysius ait lib.4. à collega : ut alter Con-sulum alterum nominasse videatur Halicarnass. ibidem.
units.tr: Le, I say, or, as Dionysius says in book 4, by a colleague: so that one of the consuls seems to have named the other. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, ibid.

units.la: {b} Varro 5 de lingua Dictator, magister populi, quod is à consule debeat dici. Et paulo post, magister populi etiam dicitur. Dictatoris for-te appellatio, sumpta ab Albanis, apud quos magistratus annui dictatores vocabantur Halicarnass. 5. Fenest.8.
units.tr: b Varro, book 5, On the Latin Language: the dictator is the master of the people, because he ought to be named by a consul. And a little later, he is also called master of the people. The name dictator perhaps was taken over from the Albans, among whom annual magistrates were called dictators (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 5; Fenestella, 8).

units.la: {c} non improbarem, si quis ita legeret, Equites qui regat, habeto.
units.tr: c I would not object if someone read it thus: "Whoever governs the knights, let him have."

units.la: {d} creato. Nam magister equitum a dictatore creabatur Halicarnass. 5:
units.tr: d Read creato (let him create): for the master of the horse was appointed by the dictator (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 5).

units.la: {e} Imo plus iuris. A consulibus provocatio erat ad populum l. 2. §. 16. de origine iur: a dictatoribus non fuit d. l.2. §.18 : Consulibus nulla capitis animadversio d.§.16.&§.23. ibid. dictatoribus fuit d.§.18. his omissis puto id significari, inter caeteras dictatoris munera illud quoque adnumerari, ut magistrum equitum sibi crearet.
units.tr: e Rather, more right. From consuls there was an appeal to the people (Dig. 1.2 §16, de origine iuris); from dictators there was none (ibid. §18). Consuls had no power of capital punishment (ibid. §16 and §23); dictators did (ibid. §18). Leaving these aside, I think this means that among the other functions of the dictator this too is counted: that he should create a master of the horse for himself.

units.la: {f} id est,eodem tempore creatum. Alioquin,absurdum fuerit ius, de quo hic agitur, referre ad magistri equitum potestate, cum inaequalis fuerit potestas dictatoris & magistri equitum. Eodem tempore dixi. Nullus enim dictator fuit absque magistro equitum Halicarnass. 5. folebatque magister equitum dictatori adiungi: quo modo Regibus, Tribunus Celerum l.2.§.19. ff. de origine iuris: Fenest.9.& succedaneis temporibus praefecti praetorio, Imperatori l.vn.C.od.de off.praef.praetor. Possis etiam iuris vocabulo intelligere auspicia, nam magister equitum non sine auspiciis lectus fuit. Idque ex eo constat,quod soricis occentus auditus Fabio Maximo dictaturam, & Flaminio magisterium equitum deponendi causam praebuit 3. Valer. 1. usque adeo tributum a veteribus fuit soricis occentui Plutarch.in Marcell.8: Plin.57.
units.tr: f That is, created at the same time. Otherwise it would be absurd to refer the law discussed here to the power of the master of the horse, since the power of the dictator and of the master of the horse was not equal. I said "at the same time", for no dictator existed without a master of the horse (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 5), and the master of the horse was customarily attached to the dictator, just as to the kings was attached the Tribune of the Celeres (Dig. 1.2 §19, de origine iuris; Fenestella, 9), and in later times the praefects of the praetorium were attached to the emperor (l. unic. C. de off. praef. praet.). You could also understand the word ius as meaning auspices, for the master of the horse was not elected without auspices. This is clear from the fact that the squeaking of a mouse gave Fabius Maximus cause to lay down the dictatorship, and Flaminius the mastership of the horse (Valerius, 3. 1); so much was the squeak of a mouse held in regard by the ancients (Plutarch, Life of Marcellus; Pliny, 57).

units.la: {g} Iuris disceptator, Praetor 5.de off.praetor.quasi id innuat, Magistrum equitum dictatori, loco fuisse praetoris. & quoniam leginius, in omnes milites & accensos, ius (utamum militare magistris adtributum Fenestella 9.
units.tr: g Iuris disceptator: the praetor (Cicero, book 5, On Duties, on the office of the praetor), as if to suggest that the master of the horse stood in the place of the praetor for the dictator. And since we read that military law was assigned to all soldiers and to the accensi, see Fenestella, 9.

units.la: {h} consulatus est. quidam ita legunt, male ut opinor. De vera huius lociletione mox dicam.
units.tr: h Read consulatus est. Some read it so, wrongly, I think. I shall say shortly what the true reading of this passage is.

units.la: {i} magister populi. quidam etiam ita legunt, & male. Puto hunc locum corruptum esse & ita restitui posse, Ast quando consuli reipubl. opus est, magistratiue populi, &c. neque quidquam a veritate historiae alienum commi-niscor. Testatur enim Plutarchus moris fuisse, ut cum Dictator eligeretur, omnes magistratus deponerentur, excepto tribuno plebis Plutarch.in Fabio.
units.tr: i Magister populi. Some also read it so, and wrongly. I think this passage is corrupted and can be restored thus: "But when the consul or the magistrate of the people is needed for the republic," and so on. Nor do I invent anything foreign to the truth of history: for Plutarch testifies that it was the custom, when a dictator was elected, for all magistrates to be deposed, except the tribune of the plebs (Plutarch, Life of Fabius).
k Some read it thus: the auspices of the republic.
On the Auspices and the Authority of the Senate.

units.la: AVSPICIA patrum sunto: olli-{b}que ex {c}se produnto[?], qui comitiis creare consules rite possint.
units.tr: Let the auspices belong to the patricians, and let them be drawn from among themselves, those who are able to create consuls rightly at the comitia.

units.la: IMPERIA, potestates, legationes, cum Senatus creuerit, populúsve iusserit, ex vrbe exeunto.
units.tr: Commands, powers and embassies, once the Senate has decreed them or the people have ordered them, shall go out from the city.
On Military Affairs.

units.la: {d}DVELLA {e}iusta {f}iuste gerunto: {g}sociis parcunto: se,& seruos continento: populi sui gloria augento: domú cú {h}lau-
units.tr: Let war be waged justly and fairly: let them spare allies, restrain themselves and their slaves, increase the glory of their people, and bring them home with praise.

units.la: ff.de verb. signif. Sed cum ita suscipitur, vt nihil nisi pax quaesita videatur. Cicero l.officc. Iusta sunt etiam ea bella quae Deus iuber, in quibus ductor exercitus vel ipse populus, non tam auctor belli quam minister iudicandus. August lib.6. quaest.super Iohannem.
units.tr: Digest, de verborum significatione. But when a war is undertaken in such a way that nothing but peace appears to be sought. Cicero, De officiis. Those wars also are just which God commands, in which the leader of the army, or the people itself, is to be judged not so much the author of the war as its minister. Augustine, Quaestiones on John, book 6.

units.la: {f} non excludit dolum, qui aduersus hostem bonus esse dicitur l.1. §.3.ff.de dolo.
units.tr: It does not exclude deceit, which is said to be fair toward an enemy: Digest 1.3 §3, de dolo.

units.la: {g} hinc illud, Parcere subiectis & debellare superbos. Idem a praetoribus requirit Iuuenalis 8. miserere, inquit, inopum sociorum.
units.tr: Hence that line: "to spare the conquered and to subdue the proud." Juvenal, Satire 8, likewise asks this of praetors: "Have pity," he says, "on the helpless allies."

units.la: {h} hac occasione permoti imperatores, ob leuissima praelia triumphos sibi decerni postulabant: quibus vt occurreretur, lege cautum fuit, Ne quis triumpharet, nisi quinque millia hostium vna acie cecidissent. Iique legi rursus ne fraus fieret, altera lege cautum fuit, Ne quis hostium occisorum falsum numerum senatui referret, iussis imperatoribus, cum primum vrbem intrasset, apud quaestores vrbanos iurare de numero occisorum. Coronae in eum finem dabantur. Triumphales (inito laureae fuerunt, postremo vna littera dempta aureae) imperatoribus dabantur. idque vulgo dicitur aurum coronarium. Obsidionalis quae & graminea, quam dabat ij qui obsidione liberati erant et duci qui liberasset. Civica ex quercu vel ilice facta, ea appellabatur, quam ciuis ciui, a quo seruatus esset in praelio, teste mux, salutisque perceptae d.ret. Mu-ralem dabat imperator militi qui primus murum ascendisset: vt Castrensem, ei qui primus in castra hostium impetum fecisset: vt & Nauiale m, ei qui primus in hostium nauem vi armatus transilisset. Hae tres coronae fiebant ex auro. Quali (quae ex Myrto) vtebantur imperatores, qui ouantes vrbem introibant. Quandi causa erat, cum aut bella non rite indicta, neque cum iusto hoste, aut hostium nomen humile, aut deditio repente facta. Oleagina vtebantur qui in praelio non fuerant, qui tamen triumphu procurabant 5. Gell.6. de redeunto : rei suae ergò ne quis lega-tus cito[?].
units.tr: Commanders, emboldened by this opportunity, demanded triumphs be decreed to them for the slightest battles. To meet this, a law was passed that no one should triumph unless five thousand enemies had fallen in a single battle line. And lest fraud be practised against that law, a second law provided that no one should report a false number of enemy dead to the Senate; commanders were ordered, as soon as they entered the city, to swear before the urban quaestors to the number of the slain. Crowns were given for this purpose. Triumphal crowns, made of laurel (with one letter removed, they were gold), were given to commanders; this is commonly called the gold of the crown. The obsidional crown, also called grassy, was given to those who had been freed from a siege and to the leader who freed them. The civic crown, made of oak or holm oak, was the one a citizen gave to the citizen by whom he had been saved in battle, as Muxtor testifies, and that received the salvation. The mural crown the commander gave to the soldier who first climbed the wall; the castrensian crown to the one who first made an assault on the enemy camp; and the naval crown to the one who first leapt armed onto an enemy ship. These three crowns were made of gold. Crowns of myrtle were worn by commanders who entered the city in ovation. There was a reason for this: when wars were not duly declared, or were not against a lawful enemy, or the enemy's name was humble, or surrender had been made suddenly. Those who had not been in the battle but who had nonetheless managed the triumph wore olive crowns. Gellius, book 6, on returning; that no legate should hastily ...
On the Tribunes of the Plebs.

units.la: PLEBES 'quos pro se contra vim{d} auxilij ergo, decem creassit{e}, tribuni uni{f} eius sunto: quodque ij prohibessint{g}, quodque plebem rogassint, ratum esto: sanctique{h} sunto: neve plebem orbam tribunis relinquunto{i}.
units.tr: Let the tribunes whom the plebs have created for themselves, for the sake of aid against violence, be the tribunes of that people; and whatever they have forbidden, and whatever they have proposed to the plebs, let it be valid; let them be sacrosanct; and let them not leave the plebs bereft of tribunes.

units.la: {d} Plebs, exte ri ciues a fena toribus l.2§. ff.de verb. signific.
units.tr: Plebs: outside citizens from freedmen. Digest 2 §... de verborum significatione.

units.la: {e} Prima ccessione duo rantum fuere. Livius 2: alia secessione tres additi, mox quinque: & ita decem Festus, io, nonnunquam viginti l.2.§.25.ff.de origine iuris.quod vix eit vt credi possit.
units.tr: At the first secession there were only two. Livy, book 2: at another secession three were added, soon five, and so ten, as Festus says; sometimes twenty, Digest 1.2 §25, de origine iuris. This can hardly be believed.

units.la: {f} De tribunis plebis. {h} id est obtinuerunt, intercesserint. Gell.13.cap. 12. Tribuni plebis antiquitus creati videntur, non iuri dicundo, nec querelis de absentibus noscendis, sed intercessionibus faciendis, quibus praesentes fuissent. & Fenestella refert, patrum decreta prius rata non fuisse, quam si tribuni ea approbassent. Illud mirum est, tantae potestatis viros, praehendissent nam quidem habuisse vocationem in ius non habuisse, qua de re vide 13. Gell.12. i Livius 2.
units.tr: On the tribunes of the plebs. That is, they obtained, they interceded. Gellius, book 13, chapter 12. The tribunes of the plebs seem to have been created in early times not for administering justice, nor for hearing complaints about absent persons, but for making intercessions, by which they were present. Fenestella reports that the decrees of the fathers were not valid until the tribunes had approved them. It is remarkable that men of such power had the right of intercession but not the right of summoning to court; on this see Gellius, book 12, and Livy, book 2.

units.la: Agi de concordia cap tum,concellinque in condiriones, vt plebi sui magistratus esset lacrofanctii, quibus auxilij latio aduersus consules esset, neve cui patrum eum magistratum capere liceret. Eadem exiant apud Halicarnasseum 6. ix Hoc igitur innuit, Plebi Romanae vtiles fuisse tribunos plebis. In municipiis, tribunorum vicem fultinuerunt defensores civitatum de quibus vide Nouell.15. Quod ad tribunos plebis attinet, Cicero 3.de legibus, Tribunitia potestatem pestiferam vocat, vt quae in seditione & ad seditionem nata sit: idque euidenter etiam Tyberij Grachi tribunatu of endiffe: & Curi.tij hominis infimi,a quo D.Brutus & P. Scipio in vincula coniecti. Idem quoque perspectum in Caij Gracchi & Saturnini tribunatu. Syllam recte constituisse, vt tribunis plebis iniuriae faciendae potestas adimeretur,auxilii ferendi relinqueretur. l nisi di- moueretCiceronis in hunc locum interpretatio, putaret legendum esse Senatores,perinde ac si lex hoc velle videretur,Senatores authorisato eligi,iudicadi potestate penes eos esse,exque his senatu fieri.nec.n. ita proprie quis dixerit, Senatu ex praetoribus atque ex senatoribus fieri. & vt paucis dicam, Nemo non videt agi hoc capite de senatu atque senatoribus,non de praetoribus. l Non videntur magistratus electi,numine inconsulto. m i. potestatem iudicandi. esto: eius decreta, rata sunto. ast ni pote-stas par,maiorve{4} prohibessit.S.C.perscri-pta seruanto. Is ordo vitio{b} vacato: cæte-ris specimen{c} esto.
units.tr: A concord was made and conceded on conditions: that the plebs should have their own magistrates, sacrosanct, who would have the power of aid against the consuls, and that no patrician should be allowed to hold that magistracy. The same things are found in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 6. He thus implies that the tribunes of the plebs were useful to the Roman plebs. In the municipalities, the defenders of cities took on the role of the tribunes; on which see Novel 15. As for the tribunes of the plebs, Cicero, De legibus book 3, calls the tribunician power pestilential, since it was born in sedition and for sedition; and this was clearly seen also in the tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus, and of Curiatius, a man of the lowest rank, by whom D. Brutus and P. Scipio were thrown into chains. The same was also evident in the tribunates of Gaius Gracchus and Saturninus. Sulla rightly ordained that the power of doing injury be taken away from the tribunes of the plebs and that only the power of bringing aid be left to them. Cicero's commentary on this passage (unless I am mistaken) suggests reading "Senators," as if the law meant that senators were to be chosen by authority, with the power of judging in their hands, and the Senate made from these. For one would not properly say that the Senate is made from praetors and from senators; and, to say it briefly, everyone sees that this chapter concerns the Senate and senators, not praetors. "Magistrates chosen without consulting the divine will are not to be regarded as valid." Let the power of judging be theirs; let their decrees be valid. But if an equal or greater power forbids, let the decrees written down in the senatus consultum be observed. Let that order be free from fault; let it be a model for the others.
On Suffrages and the Creation of Magistrates.

units.la: CREATIO magistratuum, iudicia, populi iussa, vetita, cum suffragio consci-scentur{d}, optimatibus nota, plebi libera{e} sunto. di ne senatusconsultum fieret ius fuit iis solis, qui eadem potestate, qua ij qui senatusconsultum facere vellet, maiorei ve ellent. Hæc ille. Intercedere tamen proprium tribunorum fuit. Notandū est, quod superiore loco scribit idem Varro, Dictatores, Consules, Prætores, Tribunos plebis, Interregem, Præfectum vrbi, & extraordinario iure Tribunos militares, qui pro cosuli us fuissent, Decemuiros, quibus tum imperium consulare esset, item Triumuiros reipublicæ constituendæ causa creatos, iusconsulendi senatum eo ordine habuisse. Hinc illud s. capite de senatoribus. Probrum in senatu ne relinquito.
units.tr: The creation of magistrates, judicial decisions, and the orders and prohibitions of the people are settled by vote. Let them be open to the optimates and free to the commonalty. Whether a decree of the senate should be made, the right belonged only to those who held the same power as those wishing to make the decree, or greater. So he says. Intercession, however, was the peculiar right of the tribunes. It should be noted that in the passage above the same Varro writes that dictators, consuls, praetors, tribunes of the plebs, the interrex, the prefect of the city, and, by extraordinary right, the military tribunes who had stood in place of consuls, the decemvirs (who then held consular power), and likewise the triumvirs created for constituting the commonwealth, all had the right of consulting the senate in that order. Hence that passage in the chapter on senators: "Let no disgrace be left in the senate."

units.la: Quales enim summa ciuitatis viri fuerint, talis ciuitas erit. Claudianus, Nec sic inflectere sensus Humanos edicta valent, quam vita regentis.
units.tr: For what the leading men of a state are, such the state will be. Claudian: "Edicts cannot bend human minds as the life of the ruler does."

units.la: Suffragia ab initio palam & voce ferebantur a populo. Sed quoniam interesset populi (propter potentiores) voluntate in iudiciis tegere, latæ sunt quatuor leges tabellariæ. Gabinia, qua populo potestas facta est suffragia ferendi per tabellas, quoties ageretur de magistratu alicui demandando. Cassia, quoties ageretur de capite fortunisque ciuium, excepto perduellionis crimine. Papiria, quoties de iubendis ac vetandis legibus ageretur. Cœlia, in perduellionis etiam crimine tabellam populo dedit, quod lex Cassia exceperat. His de causis Cicero in Agraria 2 & lib.3. de legibus, tabellam appellat vindicem taciturnitatis libertatis: & in Oratione pro Cornelio, principium institutæ libertatis Cassiam legem appellat. Et tamen nostra lege suffragia populi, optimatibus nota esse iuber, Si nota, non igitur libera? Cicero hanc legem tabellariam ut non omnino probat, ita penitus non improbat. Improbat, quia bonorum interest, scire quid quisque sentiat, quam voluntatem tabella occultat. Ideoque magis grauiora iudicia de potentissimis hominib. extare voce, quàm tabella: minus multos tabella condemnatos, quâ voce. Probat vero, quoties ambitio locum habet, & ea tamen conditione, vt quisque optimo & grauissimo ciui tabellam offerat. Quod de lege Mariana adiicit, quæ fecit pontes angustos. Pontiū nomine intelligo men-
units.tr: At first the people gave their votes openly and by voice. But since it was in the people's interest (because of the more powerful men) to conceal their will in judgments, four tabellary laws were passed. The Gabinian law gave the people the power of voting by tablets whenever someone was to be entrusted with a magistracy. The Cassian law, whenever there was a matter of the life and property of citizens, except the charge of treason. The Papirian law, whenever laws were to be enacted or forbidden. The Coelian law gave the people a tablet also in cases of treason, which the Cassian law had excepted. For these reasons Cicero, in the Agrarian speech 2 and in book 3 of On Laws, calls the tablet the avenger of silence and of liberty; and in the speech for Cornelius he calls the Cassian law the beginning of established liberty. And yet our law orders that the people's votes be open to the optimates. If open, then not free? Cicero does not wholly approve this tabellary law, nor wholly disapprove it. He disapproves because it concerns good men to know what each person thinks, which the tablet hides. Therefore weightier judgments against the most powerful men stand by voice rather than by tablet, and fewer men are condemned by tablet than by voice. He does approve it, however, whenever ambition has a place, yet on the condition that each man offers his tablet to the best and most serious citizen. As for the Marian law, which he adds, that made the bridges narrow: by the name of bridges I understand the

units.la: {b} hinc illud s. capite de senatoribus. Probrum in senatu ne relinquito.
units.tr: Hence that passage in the chapter on senators: "Let no disgrace be left in the senate."

units.la: {c} Quales enim summa ciuitatis viri fuerint, talis ciuitas erit. Claudianus, Nec sic inflectere sensus Humanos edicta valent, quam vita regentis.
units.tr: For what the leading men of a state are, such the state will be. Claudian: "Edicts cannot bend human minds as the life of the ruler does."
That is, they are to be carried.
On the Quaestors.

units.la: A T si quid erit, quod extra magistratus cohærario sussissit, qui cohæret, populus creato, eique ius coercendi dato.
units.tr: But if there is anything which lies outside the magistracies and needs binding, let the people create someone to bind it, and give him the right of restraint.
On the Right of the People and the Senate.

units.la: CVM populo, patribusque agendi ius esto consuli, prætori, magistro populi, equitúmque, eíque, quem produnt, patres consulum rogandorum ergò: tribunisque, quos sibi plebs rogassit, ius esto cū patribus agendi: idem, ad plebem, quod census erit, ferunto. Quæ cum populo, quæ cum patribus agetur, modica iunto. Senatori, qui nec aderit, aut causa, aut culpa esto. Loco senator, & modo orato: causas populi teneтo. Vis in populo abitu in vrbe esto. Par, maiorve potestas plus valeto. temporibus, quia tunc ad principis cura magistratus creatio pertinebat: & Iuuenalis Satyr. 10. Iampridem ex quo suffragia nullï vendimus.
units.tr: With the people and the fathers, let the consul, the praetor, the master of the people and the master of the horse have the right of acting, and he whom they name for the purpose of asking the fathers' consent; and with the tribunes whom the plebs has asked for themselves, let there be the right of acting with the fathers. Likewise, to the plebs, let them carry whatever the census shall be. Let the business to be done before the people and that before the fathers be kept moderate. For a senator who does not attend, let there be either a reason or a fault. Let him speak in his place and in measured terms; let him keep to the affairs of the people. Let there be the power of withdrawal within the city in the presence of the people. Equal or greater power shall have more force.
a Law 2 §22 ff. de origine iuris; law 1 ff. de quaestoribus.

units.la: b Aerarij tribuni, ab aere dando diċti Fist.in Aerarij.
units.tr: b Tribunes of the treasury, so called from giving out money (aes). Festus under "Aerarii."
c See Gellius 14.7.

units.la: d Magister populi, dictator vt iuprà cap. de distatore.
units.tr: d Master of the people: dictator, as above in the chapter on the dictator.
e Same.

units.la: f censuerint: Ferunto Lambinus, quod oeius erit Lipsius 2. epistola 2: pro vsus. sic apud veteres Coerare pro curare, & coeratio pro Curatio.
units.tr: f "Censuerint": Lambinus reads "ferunto"; Lipsius (Epistle 2.2) reads "erit." Among the ancients "coerare" was used for "curare" and "coeratio" for "curatio."
g Modest.

units.la: h Multæ dicebatur senatori, qui cum in senatum venire deberet, non adesset, Varro apud Gellium 14.cap.7.
units.tr: h A fine was called for a senator who, when he ought to come into the senate, did not attend. Varro in Gellius 14.7.
i That is, asked (rogatus). Cicero.

units.la: k id est, ne lit infinitus. Nam breuitas non modo senatori, sed etiam oratori magna laus est, Cicero hic. Veritatis sermo simplex. Ambrianus 14. & alibi, Tunc laudanda breuitas, cum nihil detrahit cognitioni iustorum. hinc rescriptum est, Breuitate non minui fidem chirographi lege 13. Codice de donationibus.
units.tr: k That is, lest it become endless. For brevity is great praise not only in a senator but also in an orator, Cicero says here. Plain speech is the speech of truth. Ambrose (Ambrianus) 14 and elsewhere: "Brevity is to be praised when it takes nothing away from the knowledge of what is just." Hence the rescript: the faith of a document is not diminished by brevity, law 13, Code, on donations.

units.la: l Senatori, necessarium est, nosse rempublicam: puta, quid habeat militum, quid valeat aerario, quos socios habeat, quos amicos, quos stipendiarios, qua quisque sit lege, conditione, fœdere, tenore, consuetudinem decernendi, nolle exempla maiorum Cic.
units.tr: l A senator must know the commonwealth: what soldiers it has, what it holds in the treasury, what allies, friends and tributaries it has, under what law, condition, treaty and terms each is bound, and the custom of deciding; and he must not neglect the examples of the ancestors. Cicero.

units.la: m Nihil est enim tam exitiosum ciuitati, nihil tam contrarium iuri & legibus, nihil minus ciuile & humanum, quàm composita & constituta republica, quidquâ agi per vim.
units.tr: m For nothing is so ruinous to a state, nothing so contrary to right and to the laws, nothing less civil and humane, than that anything should be done by force in a commonwealth that is composed and established.

units.la: n Quod pars maior ciuium fecerit, omnes fecisse videntur. Ast qui turbassitur{a} in agendo, fraus auctoris esto. Intercessor vel malæ[?], salutaris{b} cuiue esto. Qui agent, auspicia seruanto: auguri publico parento: promulgata, propolita[?], in ærario cognita{c}, agunto: nec plus quàm de singulis rebus semel consuluto: rem populum docento: doceri à magistratibus, priuatisque patiuntor. Priuilegia{d} ne irroganto: de I capite ciuis, nisi per maximum{h} comitiatum, ollosque, quos censores in partibus populi locassint, ne Pu-niri etiam lex iubet, qui turbulentis se adclamationibus populi adcommodant l.28.§.1. ff. de pœnis: vt & auctores seditionis & tumultus l. 38. §. 2. ff. de pœnu.{e} Lex id innuit, intercessori deferendum, impediri enim bonam rem melius, quàm concedi malam{f}. Leges promulgatæ in ærario condebantur Suetonius in Iulio, vt & Senatus consulta.
units.tr: n What the greater part of the citizens has done, all are seen to have done. But whoever is disturbed in acting, let the fault be the author's. Let the intercessor, whether for evil or for good, be (?) ... Let those who act observe the auspices; let them obey the public augur. Let proposals, once promulgated, be brought forward and made known in the treasury, and let them act; let them not consult more than once on each single matter; let them teach the people the matter; let them be taught by the magistrates and by private persons. Let them not impose privileges. Concerning the life of a citizen, let nothing be decided except by the greatest assembly. The law also orders that those whom the censors have placed among the parts of the people be punished, who attach themselves to the people's noisy acclamations (law 28 §1 ff. de poenis), as well as the authors of sedition and tumult (law 38 §2 ff. de poenis). The law hints that the intercessor is to be yielded to, for it is better to hinder a good thing than to concede a bad one. Laws once promulgated were stored in the treasury, Suetonius in Julius, and so were senatorial decrees.

units.la: {b} lex id innuit, intercessori deferendum, impediri enim bonam rem melius, quàm concedi malam[?]. {c} Leges promulgatæ in ærario condebantur Suetonius in Iulio, vt & Senatus consulta.
units.tr: {b} The law hints that the intercessor is to be yielded to, for it is better to hinder a good thing than to concede a bad one. {c} Laws once promulgated were stored in the treasury: Suetonius in Julius, and likewise senatorial decrees.

units.la: {d} Hæc lex non tollit priuilegia certis personis aut corporibus data, sed negat legem de vna tantum persona concipi posse, in omnia tempora. Quintilianus declamat. 1[?]54. In præsens tempus ferri de singulis legesposunt, vt de Menandro l.7. in sin. ff. de capitis: de Hoftilio, Mancino l. ultim. ff. de legationibus: ad.
units.tr: {d} This law does not abolish privileges granted to certain persons or bodies; it denies only that a law can be framed concerning one person for all time. Quintilian, declamation 1[?]54: laws may be proposed concerning single persons for the present time, as about Menander (law 7 in fine ff. de capite), and about Hostilius and Mancinus (last law ff. de legationibus): ad ...

units.la: {e} Cicero pro domo. Vetant XII Leges priuatis hominibus irrogari. Cicero pro Sextio: XII tabulis sancitum, vt neque priuilegium irrogari liceret. Idem in Solonis legibus fuisse cautum Aeneas Gazæus scribit in Theophrasto his verbis: [Greek text, partly illegible] Idem institutum fuit apud Atheniensis, ne scilicet lex vlla ferretur, nisi in eas Atheniensis conuenissent non minus 6000. Demosth. contra Timocratem. Huc illud referri potest, Iura non in singulas personas, sed generaliter constituti l.8. ff. de legibus: a iudicibus generaliter constitutiones obseruari l. ult. Cod. si contra ius.
units.tr: {e} Cicero, pro domo: the Twelve Tables forbid laws to be imposed on private persons. Cicero, pro Sextio: it was sanctioned in the Twelve Tables that no privilege should be imposed. Aeneas of Gaza writes in Theophrastus that the same was provided for in the laws of Solon, in words which are partly illegible in the text, to the effect that no law was to be proposed unless the Athenians had assembled in no fewer than 6000. Demosthenes against Timocrates. To this may be referred: laws are established not for individual persons but generally, law 8 ff. de legibus; judges observe constitutions generally, last law, Code, "si contra ius."

units.la: {f} Cicero pro Sextio: XII. tabulis sancitum est, vt non liceret de capite, nisi comitiis centuriatis rogari & posit, de capite non modo ferri, sed ne iudicari quidem posse, nisi comitiis centuriatis. {g} & merito. Nam vniuersi populi grauius est iudicium, quàm partiti: descriptúsque populus censu ordinibus, ætatibus, plus adhibet ad suffragium consilij, quam fuit in tribus conuocatus. {h} Maximus comitiatus, centuriata comitia. {a} ferunto:donum {b}ne capiunto {c},néve dan-to {d},néue petenda, néue gerenda, néve gesta potestate. Quod quis earum rerum migrasiit {e},noxiæ pœna par esto. Censores fide legem custodiunto {f}. Priuata {g} adeos acta referunto: nec eo {h} magis lege liberi sunto.
units.tr: {f} Cicero, pro Sextio: it was sanctioned in the Twelve Tables that it was not lawful to propose a law concerning life except by the centuriate assembly, and that one could not even judge concerning life except in the centuriate assembly. {g} And rightly: the judgment of the whole people is weightier than that of its divided parts; and the people, divided by census, orders and ages, brings more counsel to the vote than when called together by tribes. {h} The greatest assembly is the centuriate assembly. ... shall be carried. Let them not take a gift, nor give one, nor seek, nor carry on, nor hold office once it is held. Whoever has transgressed in these matters shall suffer a penalty equal to the harm. Let the censors guard the law faithfully. Let them report private acts to the assembly; and let free men not be any freer by this law.

units.la: v.l.6.§.3.ff.de off.proconsf.l.18.ff.de off.præfid. Nouell. 3.c.1:& 17.c.1.1.2.Cod. de pœna iud: l.7. C.quando prouoc. non est ac eeffe:l.vlt. C.ad l. Iul.repetund. hinc venales sententiæ ipso iure nullæ {d} l.7.d.l.15.ff.de iudicijs Plato 2.de legibus.
units.tr: v.l.6.§.3.ff.de off.proconsf. l.18.ff.de off.præfid. Novell. 3. c.1: & 17. c.1.1.2. Cod. de pœna iud.: l.7. C. quando provoc. non est necesse: l.ult. C. ad l. Iul. repetund. Hence venal sentences are void by law itself: l.7. d. l.15. ff. de iudiciis; Plato 2. de legibus.

units.la: {b} per se vel per alios: quod tamen moderatum est. moderatio plausibilis videtur [illegible, ~40 letters] i.A nemine inhumanū:passim vilissimum:ab omnib.vero accipere auaritissimum est l.6. §.7.ff.de off.proconsf. Altera moderatio fuit,permitti præsidibus accipere executentū,potulentúque,quod intra dies paucos prodigeretur l.18.ff.de off.præsid. {c} l.1.in fi ff.ad l.Iul.de amb. {d} obseruanda sunt hæc tria tempora. {e} id est, quisquis has leges contempserit,aut neglexerit. {f} facit l.2.§ 13.ff.de origine: Nouell.26.§.1.Nomek. 133. c.4: Nouell. 161. Sic apud Græcos fuerunt [illegible, ~12 letters].
units.tr: "By himself or through others": yet this is moderated. A moderate course seems plausible: to accept from no one is inhuman, to accept from everyone indiscriminately is most base, but to accept from all is the most avaricious. l.6. §.7.ff.de off.proconsf. There was another moderation: governors were permitted to accept lodging and drink, provided it was consumed within a few days: l.18.ff.de off.præsid. l.1. in fin. ff.ad l.Iul.de amb. These three times are to be observed. That is, whoever has despised or neglected these laws. Compare l.2.§ 13.ff.de origine: Nouell.26.§.1. Nomek. 133. c.4: Nouell. 161. So among the Greeks there were [illegible, ~12 letters].

units.la: {g} priuati, sensus est,eos qui magistratu abierint, cogi apud censores edere & exprimere quid in magistratu gesserint v. quæ scripsi ad Nouel.8.c.6.
units.tr: "Private persons": the sense is that those who have left office are compelled before the censors to produce and set forth what they did in office. See what I have written on Nouell. 8, c. 6.
That is, not before.

units.la: FRAGMENTA LEGVM XII. TABVLARVM AD PANDECTARVM & Codicis seriem adcommodata. LIBER SECVNDVS.
units.tr: FRAGMENTS OF THE TWELVE TABLES, ADAPTED TO THE ORDER OF THE PANDECTS AND THE CODE. BOOK II.
On Laws. TITLE I.

units.la: Iura non in singulas personas sed generaliter constituì l.8.de legibus.
units.tr: Laws are laid down not for individual persons but in general. Law 8, On Laws.

units.la: PRIVILEGIA[?] ne irrogan-{e}to hæc Cicero 3. de legibus & pro Sestio. Cur, cùm XII. Tabulis sancitum esset, ut neque privile-gium irrogari liceret, nulla vox est audita Consulum.
units.tr: Privileges[?] That it should not be imposed. Cicero, On the Laws, book 3, and For Sestius. Why, when it had been enacted in the Twelve Tables that a privilege might not be imposed, was no voice of the consuls heard?
2. Earlier laws are carried over into later ones.

units.la: Interrex Fabius aiebat in XII. Tabulis legem esse, ut quodcunque postremum{b} populus iussisset id ius ratumque esset. hæc Livius 7. & 9: Cicero pro Balbo: & 2. de inventione.
units.tr: Interrex Fabius used to say that the Twelve Tables contained a law that whatever the people last ordered should be valid and ratified law. Thus Livy, books 7 and 9; Cicero, For Balbus; and On Invention, book 2.
On the Status of Men. TITLE II.
3. On birth in the tenth and eleventh months.

units.la: Decemuiri in X, mense gigni hominem non in undecimo{c}. hæc Gellius 3.c.6.
units.tr: The Decemvirs said that a human is born in the tenth month, not the eleventh. Thus Gellius, book 3, chapter 6.
2. On a deformed birth.

units.la: Deinde cùm esset citò legatus, tanquàm
units.tr: Then, since he was soon a legate, as if

units.la: {b} l.16.l.17.l.28.ff.de legib. ex XII Tabulis, insignis ad deformita-tem {a}puer, breui tempore nescio quo pa-cto creatus, multoque tetrior & fœdior na-tus est. Cicero 3.de legibus.
units.tr: Law 16, Law 17, Law 28, Digest, On Laws. From the Twelve Tables: a boy remarkable for his deformity, created in a short time by I know not what means, was born much uglier and more hideous. Cicero, On the Laws, book 3.
On Those Who Are Sui.
TITLE III.
1. That children are emancipated by a threefold sale.

units.la: ID enim lex XII. Tabularum iubet his verbis: Si pater filium ter{b} venūdarit{c}, filius a patre liber esto, hæc Vlpian. 10.§.1. Hanc legem ita restituit Iosephus, Scaliger apud Festum in addes[?]. Si pater filium ter venum-duit[?], filius a patre liber esto.
units.tr: For the Law of the Twelve Tables orders this in these words: "If a father sells his son three times, let the son be free from his father." So Ulpian, 10.§.1. Joseph Scaliger restores this law thus, in Festus, in the addenda: "If a father sells his son three times, let the son be free from his father."
Concerning Things.
TIT. IV.

units.la: 1. Quæ res sacræ fieri non possint.
units.tr: 1. Which things cannot be made sacred.

units.la: GAius libro sexto ad legem XII. Tabularum. Rem, inquit, de qua controuersia est, prohibemur in sacrum dedicare aliquid dupli poenam patimur. nec immerito, ne li-ceat eo modo duriorem aduersarij condi-cionem facere l.vlt.ff.de religiosis.
units.tr: Gaius, in the sixth book on the Law of the Twelve Tables: "Where a thing is in dispute, we are forbidden to dedicate it to sacred use; if we do, we suffer a double penalty." Nor is this without reason, lest it be permitted in this way to make the opponent's position harsher. See l. vlt. ff. de religiosis.
Concerning pacts.
TIT. V.

units.la: 1. Rem ubi pagunt, orato ni [quidam legunt oranto:alij orationi: lege oratione] pagunt [lege pagitho.] Author ad Heren. 1. Ioseph. Scaliger apud Festum in plorare hanc legem.
units.tr: 1. "When they plead a case, let him speak" (oratio, as some read it; others read "oranto" and "orationi"; the correct reading is "oratione"), "when they plead" (read "pagitho"). The author to Herennius, book 1. Joseph Scaliger on Festus, under "plorare", on this law.

units.la: verb.signific.quæ sumpta est ex Gaij libro V. ad legem XII. Tabularum. adde Cuiacium io.obs.26. gem ita restituit, Rem vbi pagunt, oranto-ni Pagunt, ante meridiem in foro aut in comi-tio causam conuiciunto,&c. quæ vide in titulo de Iudiciis .j. Cuiacius vero ad l. 6. ff. de pactis ita restituit, Vbi paguntor, ita ni pagunt,in comitio,&c.
units.tr: Cuiacius restores the text thus: When they plead a case, let them speak out; before noon in the forum or in the comitium let them argue the case, etc., which see under the title on judicial proceedings, book 1. Cuiacius, however, in his note on law 6 of the Digest, "de pactis", restores it thus: Where they plead, unless they plead in the comitium, etc.
2. Agreements are to be kept.

units.la: Cum nexum {a} faciet, mancipiumque {b} vti lingua nuncupassit,ita {c} ius esto. Festus in Nu-cupata.
units.tr: "When he makes a nexum and a mancipium, and has declared it with his tongue, so let it be law." Festus, under "Nuncupata".

units.la: Cum ex xII. tabulis satis esset cautum praestari quæ essent lingua nuncupata {d} quæ qui insiciatus esset,duplo {e} poenam subiret. Cicero 3.officiorum.
units.tr: Since the Twelve Tables had sufficiently provided that those things which had been declared by word of mouth were to be made good, and whoever denied them was to pay a penalty of double. Cicero, On Duties, book 3.

units.la: Vt totum illud vti lingua nuncupassit, non in xII. tabulis,sed in magistri carmine scriptum videretur Cic. 1.de oratore.
units.tr: That the whole phrase "as he has declared with his tongue" would seem written not in the Twelve Tables but in the verse of a teacher. Cicero, On the Orator, book 1.

units.la: 3. Pactis ipso iure {f} tolli actionem de membro rupto.
units.tr: 3. By agreement the action for a broken limb is removed by law itself.

units.la: Si membrum rupit, ni cum eo pacit {h} talio esto. Festus in Talionis.v.j.de damno.&tulum de iniuriis.
units.tr: "If he breaks a limb and does not come to terms with him, let there be retaliation." Festus, under "Talionis". See the law 1 on damage, and the title on injuries.
4. On oath.

units.la: Nullum vinculum ad astringendam fidem, iureiurando maiores arctiorem esse voluerunt, id indicant leges in xII. tabulis. Cicero 3. officiorum.
units.tr: The ancients wished that an oath should bind faith more tightly than any other bond; the laws of the Twelve Tables show this. Cicero, On Duties, book 3.
On received arbitrators.
TIT. VI.

units.la: tùm,soli domini ex iure Quiritum mancipio dare poterant,trade-re etiam non domini. {f} l.6 ff.de pactis
units.tr: Then only owners could transfer by mancipation under the law of the Quirites, but non-owners could also hand things over (tradere). {f} l.6 ff. de pactis
