units.la: {g} Transfactiones pleruncque dum in ius ibatur fiebant, l.11.in ff. de in ius vocando.
units.tr: {g} Settlements were mostly made while the parties were going into court (in ius ibatur), l.11 in ff. de in ius vocando.

units.la: {h} ab antiquo paco,1.paciscor v.Fest.in Pactionem &apud Scaurum lib.de Orthographia, Ni pacus: {i} adde l.1.ff.de iuri.7.Gel.13.Halic.2 [?]
units.tr: {h} from the old word paco; see Festus, s.v. Pactio, and Scaurus in his book De Orthographia, "Ni pacus"; {i} add the law 1, ff. de iuris (Digest 2.1), and Gellius 13, Halicarnassensis 2 [?]

units.la: 1. De arbitro corrupto, vide titulum proximum de Iudiciis.
units.tr: 1. On a corrupt arbitrator, see the next title, De iudiciis.

units.la: 2. De tribus arbitris familiæ ercisncundæ, v. Titul. famil. ercisc und. f.
units.tr: 2. On three arbitrators in a partition of family property (familiae erciscundae), see the title Familiae erciscundae, ff.
On judgments. TIT. VII.
1. On the summons to court.

units.la: Si in ius vocet, atque {a}eat {b}, Cicero 1. de Legibus. Lege ius est, ut in ius eat cum vocetur. Author ad Herennium.
units.tr: "If he summons him to court, and he does not go," Cicero, On Laws, book 1. "By law it is right that he go to court when summoned." Author to Herennium.

units.la: In duodecim quod est, Si calvitur, pedem {d}vestruit, manum {e}indo fiacito, Festus in Struere.
units.tr: In the Twelve Tables, which reads: "If he is accused, let him strike his foot and lay hands on him." Festus, under struere.
2. On the defendant who flees.

units.la: At in xii. tabulis purant esse retrorsus ire, alij in aliam partem, alij furere, alij gradum augere, alij minuere. {e}ad eundem modum, creditori persequi debitorem fugientem licet, eíque auferre pecuniam sibi debitam lege 10. §. 16 ff. qua in fraudem. adde & alius casus ex lege 7. ff. de adulteriis: lege 54. Codice de decurionibus. {f}id est, iniicito. {g}Atqui Festus in verbo Ruit id Numæ tribuit? Ex Halicarnassæi 2. & 10. cotriffat, decemviros multa ex legibus Regiis & moribus populi Romani in duodecim tabulas transtulisse hoc censente populo. {h}quid morbus sonticus esset, dixi ad l. 4. §. 5 ff. de ædilitio: l. 60. ff. de re iudicata: l. 113. ff. de verborum significatione. adde Gellium 10. cap. 1: 2. Eglogæ 2. x. 11. {i}Numa in 2. tabula secunda lege, in qua scriptum est, quid horum fuit, lege suat, vnum [Cuiacius 3. ad ff. nat. 4. legit vitium] iudici, arbitrove reove, dies diffensus, [Scaliger legit d. Ffunfus, legendum est ex dilta lege diftius] esto. Festus in voce Reus. Possis iraque legem ita restituere, Si quid horum fuit vitium iudici, arbitrove, reove, dies diffisus esto, diffisus, i. dilatus. Gellius 14. c. 2. iussi diem diffindi. Epost in diffisionib. Si in ius vocat, si morbus a, ætas b vitium- ve esset, qui in ius vocabit, iumentum dato c: si nolet, arceram d ne sternito. 20. Gell.1.
units.tr: Others say that in the Twelve Tables it is permitted to walk backwards, others to go in another direction, others to rage, others to lengthen the step, others to shorten it. In the same way, a creditor may pursue a fleeing debtor and take from him the money owed to him, by law 10, §16, ff. qua in fraudem. Add also another case from law 7, ff. de adulteriis, and law 54, Code de decurionibus. That is, let him lay hands on him. But does Festus, under the word ruit, attribute this to Numa? Dionysius of Halicarnassus, books 2 and 10, reports that the decemvirs transferred much from the royal laws and the customs of the Roman people into the Twelve Tables, with the people so judging. What a grave illness is I have explained at law 4, §5, ff. de aedilitio; law 60, ff. de re iudicata; law 113, ff. de verborum significatione. Add Gellius, book 10, chapter 1; Eclogae of Stobaeus, book 2, chapter 10 (11). Numa, in the second law of the second tablet, in which it is written: "If any of these was a defect of the judge, arbiter or defendant, let the day be postponed." Festus under reus. One could therefore restore the law thus: "If any of these was a defect of the judge, arbiter or defendant, let the day be adjourned." Diffisus means dilatus, deferred. Gellius, book 14, chapter 2: "I ordered the day to be postponed." Epost, in diffisiones: "If he summons to court, if illness, age or defect is present, let him who summons give a beast of burden; if he will not, let him not spread a couch."
4. On the calling of witnesses and the laying on of hands.

units.la: De hac lege duodecim tabularum his verbis cautum est, Si vis (quidam legunt, Si in ius vocationi (quidam legunt vocati), Cuiacius 7. observ. 16, legit vocat) testamini igitur (Cuiacius legit, ni eat, manum e in-ijcito) en capito (legendum incapito, id est, incipito) antestari f. Porphyrio ad illa verba Horatij 1. sermon. 9. & licet antestari. Fuerit igitur ita lex concepta, Si in ius vocatus non eat, manum iniycito, encapito antestari.
units.tr: On this law the Twelve Tables provided in these words: "If he summons (some read 'if he is summoned to court'; some read 'summoned'; Cuiacius, observation 7, chapter 16, reads 'summons'), let him call a witness (Cuiacius reads 'unless he goes, let him lay hands on him'), let him seize him (to be read as incapito, that is, let him begin) to call him to witness." Porphyry on those verses of Horace, Satires 1, 9: "and it is permitted to call as witness." The law would therefore have been framed thus: "If one summoned to court does not go, let him lay hands on him and begin to call him as witness."
3. On the summoning and proclamation of witnesses.

units.la: Vagulatio in lege xii. tabularum significat quæstionem cum convicio, cum testimonium defuerit in tertijs 3 diebus ob portum h
units.tr: Vagulatio, in the law of the Twelve Tables, means a questioning with abuse, when a witness is lacking within three days because of the ...

units.la: Atrum tectum vndique & munitum quasi arca ducitur quis nisi antestatus. Qui trahit in ius, antestatus prius. Antestatus dicitur, qui testato convenitur: qua ratione & pater fiduciarius antestatus dictus est ob hoc, authore Gaio in Institutionibus. Plautus in Persa, Age, ambula in ius, leno. D. Quid me in ius vocas? S. Illic dicam apud Prætorem, sed ego in ius voco. D. Nonne antestaris? S. Tune ego causa carnifex cuiquam mortali libero auferre aliquid? Hæc ille. Vt hinc coster aures noh antestati sed testium fuisse astricatas. & lex Bpiuaria. Testis per aurem trahi debet, ita sentiunt Acron & Porphirio ad illum locum Horatij. obuagulatum ito Fest.in vagulatio,
units.tr: A dark house, walled and fortified on all sides as if a chest, is led off by no one unless he has been called as witness. He who drags another into court must first have called him as witness. He is said to be called as witness who is summoned in the presence of a witness; for this reason also a fiduciary father was said to be called as witness, according to Gaius in the Institutes. Plautus in the Persa: "Come, walk into court, pimp." D. "Why do you summon me to court?" S. "I shall say it there before the praetor, but I summon you to court." D. "Do you not call me as witness?" S. "Am I, the executioner of the case, to take anything from any free mortal?" So he. Hence it is clear that the ears of witnesses were not called as witnesses, but were seized; and the law Ep(?)uaria. The witness must be dragged by the ear, as Acron and Porphyry think at that place of Horace. Obvagulatum ito: Festus, under vagulatio.
6. On demands for more than is due.

units.la: Quod alter plus lege agendo petierit, quam quantum lex in x i i. Tabulis permisserit, quod cum impetrasset, causa cadet. Eoque nomine reo exceptio haec competebat, cuius pecunia dies fuisset Cicero 1. de oratore.
units.tr: Since another by legis actio has demanded more than the Twelve Tables allowed, and when he has obtained it, his case falls. For this reason the following plea was available to the defendant: that the money was already due. Cicero, On the Orator, book 1.

units.la: 7. De poena corrupti iudicis aut arbitri.
units.tr: 7. On the penalty for a corrupt judge or arbiter.

units.la: Dure autem scriptum esse in istis legibus quid existimari potest? Nisi duram esse legem putas quae iudicem e, arbitrumve iure datum, qui ob rem dicendam, pecuniam accepisse conuictus est, capite punit. Haec Gellius 20. cap. 1.
units.tr: How harsh, indeed, must we judge the wording of those laws? Unless you think it harsh that a judge or arbiter appointed by law, who has been convicted of having accepted money for the case to be decided, is punished with death. So Gellius, book 20, chapter 1.

units.la: 8. Si iudex falsam vindiciam tulit. Si vindiciam falsam, &c. v. in fi. titulum de possessionibus & Interdictis.
units.tr: 8. If a judge has given a false decision of ownership. If a false vindication... see at the end of the title on possessions and interdicts.

units.la: 9. Apud quos iudices de capite ciuis Romani agi oporteret.
units.tr: 9. Before which judges the case of a Roman citizen's life ought to be heard.

units.la: Cur cum sacratis legibus & xii. tabulis sancitum esset, ut neque priuilegium irrogari liceret, neque de capite nisi comitys centuriatis rogari, nulla vox esset audita consulum? haec Cicero in oratione Pro Seftio. & post. De capite non modo ferri, sed ne iudicari quidem posse nisi centuriatis comitys.
units.tr: Why, when it was sanctioned by the sacred laws and the Twelve Tables that no private law might be proposed, nor anything concerning life be proposed except in the centuriate assemblies, was no voice of the consuls heard? So Cicero in the speech For Sestius, and afterwards: Concerning life, not only may a sentence not be passed, but the case may not even be heard except in the centuriate assemblies.
10. On the times for judging.

units.la: Rem vbi pagunt, orato pagunt f in comitio aut in foro ante meridie causam conyçito &. Anthor ad Here. 2. In xii. tab. verbum hoc ita solenniter exequitur. Liuius. Hinc legis actio l.1.ff. de officio iuridici.
units.tr: When they plead the case, let the case be brought before noon, in the comitium or in the forum, and let it be settled. Author to Herennius, book 2. The Twelve Tables carry out this word in such solemn form. Livy. Hence the legis actio, law 1, ff. de officio iuridici.

units.la: l.4.ff.de adoptionib. e v.l.3.ff.de lege Iulia repetund. Paul. 5. sent.28. §.1. f dixi de huius loci restitutione §.titulo de pactis.
units.tr: Law 4, ff. de adoptionibus; and law 3, ff. de lege Iulia repetundarum; Paulus, Sentences 5, 28, §1. I have spoken of the restoration of this passage under the title de pactis, §.

units.la: g i agito. coniicere causam, est agere. Afranius Materterã causam coniici hodie ad te volo, ambo adestis v. Nonium in coniicere. scriptum est, Ante {a}meridiem causam consci-to {b}, cum perorant ambo praesentes. Post meridiem praesenti {c} litem addicito. Si ambo praesentes, sol occasus suprema {d} tempestas {e} esto. 17. Gell. 2.
units.tr: g i agito. To bring together a case is to plead it. Afranius, in Materterae causam coniici hodie ad te volo, ambo adestis: "I want my aunt's case brought together before you today; you are both here." See Nonius under coniicere. It is written: Ante {a}meridiem causam consci-to {b}, "Let him hear the case before noon, when both parties plead in person. After noon let him award the suit to the party who is present. If both are present, let sunset be the final deadline." 17. Gell. 2.
Festus, under supremum, in the Twelve Tables:
"Let sunset be the last time."

units.la: Macrobius i. Saturnalium 3. in fine. Dies ita diuiditur Primum tempus diei, dicitur mediae noctis inclinatio. Deinde gallicinium, inde conticinium, cum & galli conticescunt & homines etiam tum quiescunt. Deinde diluculum, i. cum incipit dignosci dies, inde mane, dum dies clarus, & post, a mane ad meridiem, hoc est ad medium diem, (puto legendum a mane ad medium diem, meridies) inde iam supra, vocatur tempus occiduum & mox suprema tempestas. i. diei nouissimum tempus, sicut expressum est in XII. tabulis, Solis occasus suprema tempestas esto.
units.tr: Macrobius, Saturnalia 1, chapter 3, at the end. The day is divided thus: the first time of the day is called the inclination of midnight; then the cockcrow, then the time of silence, when both the cocks fall silent and men are still at rest; then daybreak, that is, when the day begins to be recognised; then morning, while the day is bright; and after that, from morning to noon, that is to the middle of the day (I think one should read "from morning to the middle of the day," meridies); then it is called the time already past noon, and soon "the last time," that is, the last part of the day, as is expressed in the Twelve Tables: "Let sunset be the last time."

units.la: Plinius 7. c. 57. Gentium consensus taci-tus primus omnium conspirauit, vt Ionum literis vterentur c. 58. Veteres Graecas fuisse caisdem pene quae nunc sunt Latinae, &c. c. 59. Sequens gentium consensus in tondicundo, qui se recepit hora suprema l. 1. §. 8. ff. quando appellandum. vt hinc colligas, moris non fuisse apud veteres noctu iudicare quibus tamen opponitur l. 2. §. 31. ff. de origine iuris. Nouell. 82. c. 3. hoc recte constat noctu posse transigi l. 20. Cod. de tranfactionib: & testamentum signari l. 22. §. 6. ff. qui testamenta.
units.tr: Pliny, book 7, chapter 57: the first agreement of all peoples, though tacit, was that they should use the letters of the Ionians. Chapter 58: the ancient Greeks had almost the same letters as the Latins now have, etc. Chapter 59: the following agreement of the peoples concerned shaving, which took hour (hora suprema), law 1, §8, ff. quando appellandum. From this you may gather that it was not the custom among the ancients to judge at night, though it is opposed by law 2, §31, ff. de origine iuris; Novel 82, chapter 3. It is rightly established that matters may be transacted at night, law 20, Code de transactionibus, and that a will may be sealed, law 22, §6, ff. qui testamenta.

units.la: dicundo,qui se recepit hora suprema l. 1. §. 8. ff. quando appellandum. vt hinc colligas, moris non fuisse apud veteres noctu iudicare quibus tamen opponitur l. 2. §. 31. ff. de origine iuris. Nouell. 82. c. 3. hoc recte constat noctu posse transigi l. 20. Cod. de tranfactionib: & testamentum signari l. 22. §. 6. ff. qui testamenta.
units.tr: ...dicundo, which took the last hour, law 1, §8, ff. quando appellandum. From this you may gather that it was not the custom among the ancients to judge at night, though it is opposed by law 2, §31, ff. de origine iuris; Novel 82, chapter 3. It is rightly established that matters may be transacted at night, law 20, Code de transactionibus, and that a will may be sealed, law 22, §6, ff. qui testamenta.

units.la: {e} quae & suprema hora l. 1. §. 8. ff. quando appellandum: l. 2. in f. ff. de verbor. fign. fuerunt apud Romanos XXIV. l. 2. ff. de feriis. horarum sex antemeridianarum fit mentio in lege 3. de operis libertorum. septem primarum diei in lege 2. in f. ff. de verbor. fignif. supremarum d.l. 2: d. §. 8. horae sextae diei in l. 2. ff. de annuis. sextae noctis l. 25. §. 11. qui testamenta: l. 1. ff. de manumiss. secundae noctis l. 20. Cod. de tranfact. foribus fuit,sed Romanis tardior &c.r.6o. Tertius conse[?]sus fuit in horarum obser-vatione,iam hic rationi accedens.Quando & a quo in Graecia reperta, dixitmus in fe-cundo volumine. Serius etiam hoc Romae contigit. Duodecim tabulis, Ortus tantum & Occasus nominantur, post aliquot annos adiectus est & meridies Accenso Consulum id pronunciante, cum Curio (alij legunt cum a curia) inter Rostra & Graecostasim prospexisset talem (hanc vocem quidam expungunt) Solem. A columna (solem a co-lumna) aenea (legunt nonnulli Maenia) ad carcerem inclinato sidere, supremam pro-nunciabat. sed hoc serenis tantum diebus, vsque ad primũ Punicum bellum, hæc ille. Suprema, summum diei; i. à supremo (quidam legunt superrimo.) Hoc tempus xi i. Tabulæ dicunt occasum esse solis: sed postea lex Prætoria id quoque tempus iubet esse supremum, quo Prætor in Comitio su-premam pronunciauit populo, Varro 5.de lingua.Idem 6.de lingua, supremũ à superrimo dictũ.Itaque in xi i.Tabulis, Solis occasu, diei suprema tempestas esto. libri Augurum, pro tempore tempestatem dicunt id est,supremum augurum tempus.
units.tr: Which also is the last hour, law 1, §8, ff. quando appellandum; law 2, end, ff. de verborum significatione. Among the Romans there were twenty-four hours, law 2, ff. de feriis. Mention is made of six hours before noon in law 3, de operis libertorum; of the first seven hours of the day in law 2, end, ff. de verborum significatione; of the last hours in the same law 2, §8; of the sixth hour of the day in law 2, ff. de annuis; of the sixth hour of the night in law 25, §11, qui testamenta, and law 1, ff. de manumissionibus; of the second hour of the night in law 20, Code de transactionibus. The Romans were slower in this than the Greeks, etc. The third agreement concerned the observance of hours, which already accords with reason. When and by whom it was discovered in Greece I have said in the second volume. This too came late to Rome. In the Twelve Tables only sunrise and sunset are named; after some years midday was added, when the herald of the consuls announced it, while Curio looked out between the Rostra and the Graecostasis (some read "from the curia") at the sun (some strike out this word) from the bronze column to the prison as the sun declined, and proclaimed the last hour. But this was done only on clear days, until the First Punic War. The Twelve Tables call the sunset the time of the sun's setting; but later a praetorian law made this time also the last, when the praetor in the comitium proclaimed the last hour to the people. Varro, On the Latin Language, book 5. The same, book 6: "last" is said from "superrimum." Thus in the Twelve Tables, "at sunset, let the last time of the day be." The books of the augurs speak of the weather (tempestas) for the time, that is, the last time of the augurs.
2. Who are compelled to give security.

units.la: Ennius verbum hoc ex xi i.Tabulis ve-stris accepit: in quibus si recte comemini, ita scriptum est. Asiduo,vindex asiduus e-sto: Proletario{b} ciui, quinis volet vindex esto.
units.tr: Ennius took this word from your Twelve Tables, where, if I remember correctly, it is written thus: "For a man of property, let a vindex who is also a man of property be bound; for a citizen of the proletarii, whoever wishes may be vindex for five."
To be presented for trial.
The Twelve Tables indicate or a fixed day.
... against the enemy. Cic. 1 Off.

units.la: Si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicatur. TIT. VIII.
units.tr: If a quadruped is said to have caused damage. TIT. VIII.

units.la: Animalium nomine quæ, ratione carent, si qua lasciuia aut pauore aut feritate pauperiem fecerint, noxalis actio lege XII. Tabu-larum prodita est Inst. si quadrupes. Si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicetur, actio ex lege XII. Tabularum descendit[?], quæ lex voluit aut dari id quod nocuit, id est animal: aut aestimationem noxiæ offerri. L. 1. ff. si quadrupes.
units.tr: For damage done by animals, which lack reason, if through wantonness, fear or ferocity they have caused damage, a noxal action was provided by the law of the Twelve Tables. Inst. si quadrupes. If a quadruped is said to have caused damage, the action arises from the law of the Twelve Tables, which wished either that the thing which did the harm, that is the animal, be handed over, or that an assessment of the harm be offered. L. 1 ff. si quadrupes.
On damage done. TIT. IX.
1. On what is broken.

units.la: {a}Rupitias, in XII. Tabulis significat damnum dederis. Festus in voce rupitias.
units.tr: Rupitias, in the Twelve Tables, means "you will have caused damage". Festus, under the word rupitias.

units.la: Sarcito, in XII. Tabulis Seruius suspicās ait significare, damnum soluito, præstato Festus in voce Sarcito.
units.tr: Sarcito, in the Twelve Tables, Servius suspects, means "pay for the damage, make it good". Festus, under the word Sarcito.

units.la: Ex his duobus fragmentis possis ita legem concipere. Quod rupitias sarcito.
units.tr: From these two fragments you could frame the law thus: Whoever causes damage shall make it good.
2. On a broken limb.

units.la: Talionis mentionem fieri in XII. Tabulis ait Verrius, hoc modo. Si membrum rapserit{b}, ni cum eo pacit, talio esto. Festus in Talionis. dicam de hac lege ad titulum de iniurijs.
units.tr: Verrius says that talion is mentioned in the Twelve Tables, in this way: "If he has broken a limb, and does not come to terms with him, let there be talion." Festus, under Talionis. I will discuss this law under the title on injuries.
On noxal actions. TIT. X.
Celsus makes a distinction between the Aquilian law and the law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: Aquiliam & legem xii.Tabularum.Nam in lege antiqua (id est xii.) Si seruus scien-te domino furtum fecit, vel etiam noxam commisit feruinomine actio est noxalis, nec domi-nus suo nomine tenetur{*}. l.2. §.1. ff. de noxa-libus.
units.tr: For in the ancient law (that is, of the Twelve Tables): "If a slave, with his master's knowledge, committed theft, or even caused injury, the action is noxal against the slave's name, and the master is not held in his own name." L. 2 §1 ff. de noxalibus.

units.la: Noxales actiones sunt aut legibus aut Edicto Prætoris.Legibus,veluti furti ex legibus xii.Tabularum §.4.Inst. de noxalib. actionib. Si seruus furtum faxit,noxamve noxit l.2.§.1.verf.sed si placeat.ff.de noxal.
units.tr: Noxal actions arise either from laws or from the praetor's edict. From laws, for example that of theft, from the Twelve Tables: §4 Inst. de noxalibus actionibus. "If a slave has committed theft, or caused injury..." L. 2 §1, the words "but if it is decided", ff. de noxalibus.
On the fixing of boundaries.
TIT. XI.
1. On the width of roads.

units.la: VIa latitudo ex lege xii. Tabularum in porrectum octo pedes habet,in amfractum, id est, vbi flexu est, sedecim, Caius in lege 8.de seruitutib.rusticorum.
units.tr: Under the Law of the Twelve Tables a road is eight feet wide in a straight stretch, but sixteen feet wide at a bend (amfractum), that is, where it turns. Gaius, on the Law of the Twelve Tables, book 8, on rustic servitudes.

units.la: Amfractum est ab origine flexum duplici, dictum ab ambitu & frangendo, ab eo leges iubent in directo pedum octo esse, in amfracto sedecim, id est in flexu Varro 6. de lingua.
units.tr: An amfractum is a bend that is doubled from its origin, named from ambitus and from breaking (frangere). For this reason the laws order eight feet in a straight stretch and sixteen feet at an amfractum, that is, at a bend. Varro, On the Latin Language, book 6.
2. If an aqueduct harms a private person.

units.la: Si per publicum locum aquæductus priuato nocebit, erit priuato actio ex lege xii.Tabularum, vti noxæ domino caueatur l. 5. ff. ne quid in loco publico.
units.tr: If an aqueduct running through a public place harms a private person, the private person has an action under the Law of the Twelve Tables, so that the owner is secured against the harm (noxa). Digest 5, de ne quid in loco publico.
3. If rainwater harms.

units.la: Et sic verba legis xii. Tabularum veteres interpretati sunt. si aqua pluuia nocet i. si nocere poterit l. 21.ff.de statulib.
units.tr: The ancient interpreters explained the words of the Twelve Tables in this way: "if rainwater harms", that is, if it is able to harm. Digest 21, de statuliberis.
4. On intervals.
Gaius, book 4, on the Law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: sciendum est inquit in actione finium regundorum illud observandum esse, quod ad exemplum quodammodo eius legis scripti{a} est, quod Athenis Solonem dicitur tulisse: nam illic ita est. Ἐὰν τις ἀ[?] πρὸς ἀλλοτρίῳ χωρίῳ ὀρύγμα τὸν ὅρον μὴ πεφ[?]-βαλλεσθαι ἐὰν [?]οἰκίας, ποδὸς [?]· ἐὰν δὲ τάφον ἢ βόθρον ὀρυχθῇ, ὅσον τὸ βάθος ἢ, τοσοῦτον ἀπολιπεῖν. ἐὰν δὲ φρέαρ ὀρυχθῇ, [?]ὀργυιὰ[?] ἐννέα δ' ποδὸς τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου φυλάσσειν τὰ δὲ ἄλλα [?]ἐφ' πέντε ποδὸς. Id est: Si quis sepem ad alienum praedium fixerit, infoderitque terminum ne excedito. Si maceriam, pedem relinquito. Si vero domum, pedes duos. Si sepulchrum aut scrobem foderit, quantum profunditatis habuerint, tantum spatii relinquito. Si puteum, passus latitudinem. At vero oleam aut ficum, ab alieno ad novem pedes plantato: ceteras arbores ad pedes quinque. Haec ille.
units.tr: Gaius says that in the action for fixing boundaries (finium regundorum) one must observe this rule, which is in a way modelled on that written law which they say Solon brought in at Athens. For there it is as follows: [Ἐὰν τις ... ὀρύγμα ... ἐὰν δὲ τάφον ἢ βόθρον ὀρυχθῇ ...]. That is: If anyone fixes a hedge beside another's estate and digs in a boundary marker, let him not go beyond it. If he builds a wall, let him leave a foot. If a house, let him leave two feet. If he digs a grave or a pit, let him leave a space as deep as the pit is deep. If he digs a well, let him keep a fathom's distance (nine feet) from the other's land. As for the rest, let him keep five feet. Olive trees and fig trees he shall plant nine feet away from the other's land, and the other trees five feet. Thus he.

units.la: 5. Qui viam debet, eam munitam praestet.
units.tr: 5. Whoever owes a road must provide it in a passable state.

units.la: Si via sit immunita, iubet lex quae velit, agere iumentum. Cicero pro Caecina.
units.tr: If the road is unrepaired, the law allows whoever wishes to drive a beast of burden along it. Cicero, Pro Caecina.

units.la: 6. De legitimo spatio ac sestertio pede inter duas insulas relinquendo.
units.tr: 6. On the legal space, measured in sestertian feet, to be left between two buildings.

units.la: Ambitus proprie dicitur inter vicinorum aedificia, locus duorum pedum & semipedis.
units.tr: Ambitus properly means the space between neighbours' buildings, a strip two and a half feet wide.

units.la: {a} lo de asse. Sestertius, inquit, duos asses & semis, quasi semis tertius. Lex etiam XII. Tabularum argumento est: in qua duo pedes & semis, sestertius pes vocatur, haec ille. Varro 4. de lingua ambitus, inquit, circuitus: ab eoque XII. Tabularum interpretes ambitum, parietis circuitum dixerunt. Haec ille. Et id quidem spatium legitimum dicitur in l. 14. ff. de servitutibus rusticorum. ad circumeundi{*} facultatem relictus. Fe-stus in Ambitus.
units.tr: Note: a sestertius, he says, is two asses and a half, as if it were semis tertius (a half and a third). The Law of the Twelve Tables is also evidence for this, in which two and a half feet is called a sestertian foot. Thus he. Varro, On the Latin Language, book 4: ambitus, he says, is a circuit; and for this reason the interpreters of the Twelve Tables called the circuit of a wall its ambitus. Thus he. And that space is indeed called legitimate in Digest 14, de servitutibus rusticorum, being left for the power of going around. Festus, on Ambitus.
7. On the thickness of a common wall.

units.la: Leges publicæ{b} non patiuntur maiores cras-situdines quàm sesquipedales{c} constitui loco communi: cæteri autem parietes, cū spatia augustiora fierent, eadem crassitudine locantur: lateritij verò ( nisi displinthij{d} aut triplinthij fuerint ) sesquipedali crassitudine non{e} possunt plusquam unam sustinere contignationem. In ea autem maiestate urbis & ciuium infinita frequen-tia, innumerabiles habitationes opus fuit explicare. Ergo cùm recipere non posset area plana tantam multitudinem ad auxilium altitudinis aedificiorum res ipsa coegit deuenire. Itaque pilis lapideis, structuris testaceis, parietibus cæmenti-tiis altitudines extructæ, contignationi-bus una coaxatis, & cœnaculorū summas utilitates perfecerunt & dispectationes. Er-go menianis{f} & contignationibus variis alto spatio multiplicatis, populus Romanus egregias habet sine impeditione habi-tationes. hæc Vitruuius 1.c.8.
units.tr: Public laws do not permit a wall thicker than a foot and a half to be built on a common boundary. Other walls, when the spaces became narrower, are built to the same thickness. Brick walls, unless they are double or triple brick, cannot support more than one storey at a thickness of a foot and a half. But in the majesty of the city and the endless crowd of its citizens, it was necessary to provide innumerable dwellings. Therefore, since the flat ground could not hold so great a multitude, circumstances themselves forced people to turn to height for buildings. So with stone piers, tile structures and cement walls, the heights were raised, the joists were fastened together, and they achieved the greatest advantages and views from the upper rooms. Therefore, with party walls and various floors multiplied over a high space, the Roman people have excellent dwellings without inconvenience. Thus Vitruvius, book 1, chapter 8.
8. On the prescription of five feet.

units.la: Ex hac nō rerum sed verborum discor-dia, controuersia nata est de finibus, in qua quoniam usucapionem duodecim tabulæ inter
units.tr: From this discord, not of things but of words, a controversy about boundaries arose, in which, since the Twelve Tables wished usucapion between
{e} Pliny in the passage cited,

units.la: {f} quid mœniana v.l.ii. Cod. de ædificijs priuatis. quinque {a}pedes esse voluerunt, depasci vete-rem possessionem Academiae ab hoc acu-to homine non sinamus, nec Mamilia {b}le-ge singuli, sed ex xii, tres arbitri fines re-gemus haec Cicero 1. de legibus.
units.tr: {f} what the mœniana... Code, de aedificiis privatis. They wished five feet. We shall not allow the old possession of the Academy to be grazed over by this sharp-witted man, nor shall we settle boundaries by a single Manilian law, but from the Twelve Tables we shall appoint three arbiters. Thus Cicero, On the Laws, book 1.
9. On the three arbiters of boundaries.

units.la: Nec Manilia cum singuiis[?] lege [alij ita habent, Nec Manilia lege singuli] sed cum his te arbitro [alij rectius legunt, Sed ex his tres arbitri: Cuiacius {c}vero quam optime, sed ex duodecim tres arbitri,] si vis, [alij legunt Fineis, & recte] regemus {d}Cicero 1. de legibus. Possis ita hanc legem restituere, Vt si vicini inter se iurgant, finibus ciant[?], in alios fines, plagis, id est, latis cicatricibus signatae inueniri debent, ut intelligantur eorum esse dominorum in quas partes integrae erunt, intactae reseruabuntur. Signantur autem vtrinque, id est, ex vtraque possessione intra pedes quinos, vt legis Manilii commemorationem habeant.
units.tr: Not by a Manilian law of single men, but with these three as arbiters [others read this more correctly, but from these, three arbiters; Cujas, very well indeed, reads but from the twelve, three arbiters], if you wish, we shall settle [others read Fineis, and rightly, boundaries]. Cicero, On the Laws, book 1. One might restore this law thus: If neighbours quarrel between themselves over boundaries, the boundary stones which have been moved into other fields must be found marked with wounds, that is, with broad scars, so that it may be known to whose owners they belong; in whatever direction they lie intact, they shall be kept unbroken. They are marked on both sides, that is, on each possession within five feet, so that they may keep the memory of the Manilian law.

units.la: Frontinus, de limitibus agrorum, de rigore controuersia est finiti-mae conditionis, quoties inter duos pluresve terminos ordina-tos, siue quae alia signa, secundum legem Manilia intra quinque pe-des agitur.
units.tr: Frontinus, On the Limits of Fields, on strictness: a dispute of neighbouring status arises whenever a boundary is contested between two or more fixed termini, or other marks, and is conducted according to the Manilian law within five feet.

units.la: Aggenus de limitibus agrorum. de fine enim lex Mamilia quin-que aut sex pedum latitudinem praescribit: quoniam hanc latitu-dinem vel iter ad culturas accedens occupat, vel circum actus a-ratri quod vsueapi non potest. Iter enim, non qua ad culturas peruenitur, capitur vsu, sed id quod in vsu biennio fuit, &c.
units.tr: Agennius, On the Limits of Fields. For the Manilian law prescribes a width of five or six feet for a boundary, since this width is taken up either by the path leading to the cultivated fields or by the turning circle of a plough, which cannot be used. For the path is not held by use where one reaches the cultivated land, but what has been in use for two years, etc.

units.la: Hygenus, de limitibus constitutis, Linearij limites mensurae tan-tum discriminandae causa sunt constituti: & si finitimi interue-niunt, latitudinem secundum legem Mamiliam accipiunt.-
units.tr: Hyginus, On Established Boundaries: linear boundaries have been established only for the sake of distinguishing measurements; and if neighbours come between, they take their width according to the Manilian law.

units.la: Extat quoque in libro variorum aulliorum de limitibus, fragmen-tum legis Manilia, Roscia, Peducea, Allena, [lege Aliae] Fa-uiae [quidam legunt Fabiae] quod restitutum vide apud Iustum Li-pfium 1. Electorum 15. {c}5.obf.c.21. {d}ad hos arbitros recurre-batur, quoties inter vicinos iurgium de finibus erat. Cicero 4. de
units.tr: There also exists, in the book of various authors, a fragment on boundaries of the Manilian law, the Roscian, Peducaean, Allenan [some read Aliae], Fabian [some read Fabiae] law, which see restored in Justus Lipsius, Electa, book 1, chapter 15. {c} Observationes 5, ch. 21. {d} Recourse was had to these arbiters whenever there was a quarrel between neighbours about boundaries.
{c} Observationes 5, ch. 21.

units.la: {d} ad hos arbitros recurrebatur, quoties inter vicinos iurgium de finibus erat. Cicero 4. de regundis tres arbitros darent: eisque totius rei ius arbitriumque permitterent.
units.tr: {d} Recourse was had to these arbiters whenever there was a quarrel between neighbours about boundaries. Cicero, On the Regulation of Boundaries, book 4: they were to appoint three arbiters and grant them the right and power of decision over the whole matter.
On the division of a family estate.
TIT. XII.

units.la: HÆc actio proficiscitur ex lege xij, tabularum a l.i.ff.familiæ.
units.tr: This action arises from the Twelve Tables; see law 1, ff. familiae erciscundae.
On contracting purchase and sale.
I. On delivery.

units.la: VEnditæ res & traditæ, non aliter emptori adquiruntur, quam si is venditori pretium solverit, vel alio modo ei satisfecerit, veluti {c}expromissore vel pignore dato. quod quanquam cauetur lege duodecim tabularum: tamen recte dicitur & iure gentium, id est naturali id effici. §.41. Instit. de rerum diuis.
units.tr: Goods sold and delivered are not acquired by the buyer unless he has paid the price to the seller or otherwise satisfied him, for example by giving a surety or a pledge. Although this is provided by the Law of the Twelve Tables, it is rightly said to be effected also by the law of nations, that is, by natural law. §41 Inst. de rerum divisione.

units.la: Sub uos placo (inquit Festus in Sub uos) in precibus fere cum dicitur, significat id quod supplico, ut in legibus, Transque da-ctum à coercendo, unde & ercisc-undæ & erciscì. Citum autem est vocatum, à ciendo, hæc ille. quo loco Iosephus Scaliger monet legendum Citum fit. Quæ particula expuncta, ut Erctum citum, fit hereditas diuisa. & in glossis Herétus citus, διαίρεσις τῶν ὑπαρχόντων [?] vocatur. apud Seruium Erctum non citum, hoc est patrimoninm non diuisum. Erctum ciendum, hæreditas diuidenda.
units.tr: "Sub uos placo" (says Festus under Sub uos) is commonly said in prayers and means what I beseech, as in laws; and "trans" comes from "coercendo", whence "ercisc-undae" and "erciscì". "Citum" is said to come from "ciendo", so Festus says. In this passage Joseph Scaliger advises reading "Citum fit". With that particle removed, "Erctum citum" means the inheritance is divided. In the glosses "Herétus citus" is called division of property [διαίρεσις τῶν ὑπαρχόντων]. In Servius, "Erctum non citum" means the patrimony not divided, and "Erctum ciendum" means the inheritance to be divided.

units.la: {b} videl. 5. §. 18. in fine ff. de tributoria: l. 19. ff. de contrahenda emptione. Grex dominium non mutat, nisi fit æs adnumeratū. Varro 2. de re rustica. {c} l. 53. in f. ff. de contrah. empt. to ᵏ, edendóque (lege endo ᵇ) plorato . Hæc Festus.
units.tr: Cf. 5 §18 at the end, ff. de tributoria; l. 19 ff. de contrahenda emptione. A flock does not change ownership unless the money has been paid over. Varro, book 2 de re rustica. l. 53 at the end, ff. de contrah. empt. [The rest of this passage is too corrupt to render.] Thus Festus.
2. On nexum.

units.la: Dictum est de Nexu 5. tit. de pactis.
units.tr: Nexum has been discussed in title 5, de pactis.
3. On mancipation.

units.la: Mancipatio ᶜ, est imaginaria quædam venditio, quæ sic agitur, adhibitis nō minus quàm quinque testibus, ciuibus Romanis puberibus ᵈ, & prætera alio eiusdem condicionis, qui libram æneam tenet, qui appellatur libripens. Is qui mancipium accipit æs tenens, ita dicit, Hunc ego hominem ex iure Quiritum meum esse aio, isque mihi emptus est hoc ære æneáque libra. Deinde ære e percutit libram, idque æs datur ei à quo mancipium accipitur, quasi pretij loco. Quæcumque igitur res mancipi f, lege xii. tabularum, aliter nisi per hanc solennitatem alienari non poterat, Boetius in Topic. Ciceronis.
units.tr: Mancipatio is a kind of imaginary sale, carried out thus: with not fewer than five witnesses, Roman citizens of full age, and another of the same standing who holds the bronze balance, called the libripens. The one who receives the slave, holding the bronze, says: "I declare this man to be mine by Quiritary right, and he has been bought for me with this bronze and this bronze balance." Then he strikes the balance with the bronze, and that bronze is given to the one from whom the slave is received, as if in place of the price. Therefore whatever thing was a res mancipi, by the Law of the Twelve Tables, could not be alienated except by this solemnity. Boethius on Cicero's Topics.
4. On monopolies.

units.la: Gaius lib. 4. ad legem xii. tabularum. Sodales sunt, inquit, qui sunt eiusdem collegij Græci ἑταιρίαν vocant. Hi autem potestatem facit lex s.pactionem quam velint sibi ferre, dum ne quid ex publica lege corrumpant. Sed hæc lex videtur esse legum Solonis
units.tr: Gaius, book 4 on the Law of the Twelve Tables: "Sodales" are, he says, those of the same college, whom the Greeks call "hetairia". The law allows them to make whatever agreement they wish among themselves, provided they do not violate public law. But this law seems to be taken from the laws of Solon.

units.la: 6.§.4. ᵈ Impubes libripens esse non potest neque antestari, vt Priscianus refert libro 8. ᵉ quod & Raudus. Varro 4. de lingua. Porta Raudulcula, quod ærata fuit, Aesraudus dictum: ex eo in veteribus mancupiis (idest mancipationibus) scriptum, Faxdusscu-lib[?]ram ferito.
units.tr: 6 §4. A minor (impubes) cannot be a libripens nor act as a witness, as Priscian reports in book 8; and Raudus likewise. Varro, book 4 de lingua: the "Porta Raudulcula" was so called because it was bronze-bound, from "Aesraudus". Hence in old mancipia (that is, mancipations) it is written: "Faxdusscu...libram ferito" [the rest is corrupt].

units.la: ᶠ v. Vlpianum 19. ᵍ XII. Tabularum sc. Est n. hæc lex desumpta ex 4. Caij ad legem XII. Tabularum. translata . Nam illa ita est [?]ἐὰν δὲ ἀνῇς &c. l. vlt. ff. de collegiis.
units.tr: See Ulpian, book 19. The Twelve Tables, namely: this law is taken from Gaius, book 4 on the Twelve Tables, and was transferred from it. For that law reads thus: [Greek: "if he should release..." etc.], l. ult. ff. de collegiis.
5. That a disputed thing cannot be alienated.

units.la: De ea re dictum est 5. titulo de rebus.
units.tr: This was discussed in title 5, de rebus.
6. That statuliberi can be sold.

units.la: Statuliberum venumdari à posse legis XII. Tabularum p. tauerunt, l.25. ff. de statuliberis, emptori tamen dando pecuniam, ad libertatem peruenit: idque lex XII. tabularum iubet. Vlpianus 2.§.4. in f.
units.tr: The Twelve Tables permitted a statuliber to be sold, l. 25 ff. de statuliberis; but on paying money to the buyer he attains liberty, and the Twelve Tables order this. Ulpian, book 2 §4 at the end.
On pledges. TITLE XIV.

units.la: NAncitor{b} in xii. Tabulis, nactus erit, prædatus erit. Item in fœdere{c} Latino. Pecuniam quis{d} nancitor{e}, habeto: & si quid pignoris nancitur [legunt alij nancitor ]sibi habeto{f}. Festus in Nancitor.
units.tr: "Nancitor" in the Twelve Tables means "nactus erit", will have obtained, or "prædatus erit", will have seized as booty. Likewise in the Latin treaty: "If anyone nancitor money, let him keep it; and if he nancitur any pledge [others read nancitor], let him keep it for himself." Festus under Nancitor.
On usury. TITLE XV.
1. On unciary interest.

units.la: SAnè vetus vsus fœnebre malum, & sedi-tionum discordiarumque [?]frequentissima [?]causa, eâque cohibebatur antiquis quoque & minus corruptis moribus. Nam primo xii.§ Tabulis sanctum, Ne quis vncia-
units.tr: Indeed, the ancient practice of lending at interest was an evil and the most frequent cause of sedition and discord, and it was restrained by the ancients, whose morals were less corrupt. For first, the Twelve Tables sanctioned that no one should exact more than an uncia...

units.la: Cn. Manlio Coff. de vnciario fœnore M. Duellio Tribunoplebis rogatio perlata est, & plebs aliquanto cam cupi-ditus sciunt, accepitque. Sed verisimilius est inter legem XII. Tabula. pene antiquatam à Duellio in vsum renocatam fuisse. vt fœnore amplius exerceret, cùm antea ex libidine locupletum ageretur, dein Postremo vetita versura Tacitus vi. Annal. anno vrbis 786.
units.tr: In the consulship of Gnaeus Manlius, a proposal on unciary interest was brought forward by Marcus Duellius, tribune of the plebs, and the plebs, eager for it, accepted it. But it is more probable that the law of the Twelve Tables, nearly obsolete, was revived by Duellius and brought back into use, so that one might lend at interest, whereas before this had been done at the whim of the wealthy; and finally, borrowing by renewing a debt was forbidden. Tacitus, Annals book 6, in the year 786 from the founding of the city.
2. The penalty for usurers: fourfold.

units.la: Maiores nostri sic habuerunt, & ita in legibus posuerunt, furem dupli condemnari: fœneratorem quadrupli. Marcus Cato initio libri de re rustica.
units.tr: Our ancestors held thus, and so they wrote into the laws: that a thief is condemned to pay double, a usurer to pay fourfold. Marcus Cato at the beginning of his book De re rustica.
On witnesses.

units.la: TITVL. XVI. DE intestabili. v. j. titulo de testamentis.
units.tr: TITLE XVI. Concerning the intestable. See title 1 of the book on wills.
Concerning marriages.
TITVL. XVII.
1. That marriages were celebrated under auspices.

units.la: APud antiquos non solum publicè sed etiā priuatim nihil gerebatur, nisi auspicio prius sumpto: quo ex more d nuptiis etiamnum auspices e interponuntur: qui quamuis auspicia petere desierint, ipso tamen nomine veteris consuetudinis vestigia vsurpantur. Hac Valerius 2.c.1.de nupt.
units.tr: Among the ancients nothing was done, not only publicly but even privately, unless the auspices had first been taken. By custom, auspices are still interposed at weddings, and although they have ceased to seek omens, the very name preserves traces of the old custom. Valerius, 2.c.1, on marriage.

units.la: ciario, fœnus faenum. e i. sublatum omne fœnus. v. Appia-rum t.ciuilium. d hoc caput ex moribus populi Romani petitu, vel.vt ?.ead.dicitur,veteris consuetudinis Romanorum fuit. f Cicero 1.de diuinatione. Nihil fere quondam maioris rei, nisi auspicato, ne priuatim quidem gerebatur. Quod etiam nunc Nuptiarum auspices declarant, qui re omissa nomen tantum tenent.
units.tr: ...ciarius, fenus, faenum; that is, all interest was abolished. See the Appian civil law. This chapter was drawn from the customs of the Roman people, or, as the same author says, it was a custom of the ancient Romans. Cicero, On Divination, book 1: "Almost nothing of greater importance was ever undertaken, even privately, without taking the auspices. Even now the augurs of marriage show this, who retain only the name when the thing itself has been dropped."

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] Ciceronem ibidem. idem in Cluentio, Nubit genero socrus, nullis auspicibus, nullis auspiciis [?] Virgilius 1. Aeneidos. Cui pater intrafta [?] Iuuenalis, veniet cum signo [?].
units.tr: [illegible, about 40 letters] Cicero, in the same place; the same in Cluentius: "The mother-in-law marries her son-in-law with no augurs and no auspices." Virgil, Aeneid book 1: "to whom his father..." (garbled). Juvenal: "will come with the sign..." (garbled).

units.la: Catullus bona cum bona nubet alite virgo.
units.tr: Catullus: "When a good maiden marries under a good omen."

units.la: 2. De nuptiis inter patres & plebeios interdictis.
units.tr: 2. On the marriages between patricians and plebeians being forbidden.

units.la: Ne connubium patribus cum plebe esset, non Decemviri tuleru[?] t pauci hu[?] annu[?] peßimo exemplo publico, cum summa iniuria plebis? Hæc Liuius 4.
units.tr: That there should be no intermarriage between the patricians and the plebs was not the work of the Decemvirs (?), but of a few men, by a most evil public precedent and with great injustice to the plebs. Livy, book 4.

units.la: 3. De societate bonorum & sacrorum inter virum & vxorem.
units.tr: 3. On the sharing of goods and sacred rites between husband and wife.

units.la: Γυναικα[?] γαμετην[?] ἱερὰς{a} σωμεκλᾶ[?]σαν[?] ἀνδρὸς{b} κοινωνὸν ἀπάντων εἶναι χρημάτων τε καὶ ἱερῶν. Hæc Dionysius Halicarnas.2.
units.tr: A wife, lawfully wedded, is to be a partner of her husband in all goods and in sacred things [γυναῖκα γαμετὴν ... ἀνδρὸς κοινωνὸν ἀπάντων εἶναι χρημάτων τε καὶ ἱερῶν]. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2.
4. On a woman who was taken into possession (usurped).

units.la: Lege non esse usurpatam {c}mulierem, quæ cum Calendis Ianuariis apud virum causa matrimonii esse coepisset, ante diem quartum Calendas Ianuarias sequentes usurpatum isset. Hæc Gellius 3. c. 2. & Macrobius 1. Saturnal. 3.
units.tr: By law a woman was not to be taken into possession, who, having begun to be with a man for the sake of marriage on the Kalends of January, had been taken into possession before the fourth day before the following Kalends of January. Gellius, book 3, chapter 2, and Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 3.
5. On the conduct of a wife.

units.la: Si mulier aliquid peccasset pœnam luebat ex lßi[?] (mariti) arbitrio. Idque maximarum pœnarum proprium. Cognati cum marito ea de re iudices erant. Grauiora illa erant φθορὰ[?] σώματος, καὶ εἴτις εἶχον εὐφθεῖν[?] … Vtrumque damnauit Romulus{e}, ὡς ἀμφὶ[?] τὰς[?] γυναικείων[?] ἐχρῆτο[?], hæc desumpta sunt ex Dionysio Halicarnass.lib.2.
units.tr: If a woman had committed some offence, she paid the penalty at the discretion of her husband. This was a feature of the most severe punishments. Her kinsmen, together with her husband, were the judges in such a matter. More serious were the corruption of the body [φθορὰ σώματος] and whatever [καὶ εἴτις εἶχον εὐφθεῖν…]. Romulus condemned both, as [ὡς ἀμφὶ τὰς γυναικείων ἐχρῆτο…]. These things are taken from Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2.

units.la: Gellius 10. c. 23. Qui de victu, inquit atque cultu populi Romani scripserunt, mulieres Romæ atque in Latio abstemias egisse. Hoc est, vino semper, quod temetū{f} prisca lingua appellabatur, abstinuisse: institutumque vt cognatis osculum ferrent, reprehendendi causa, vt odor indicium faceret, si bibissent (idem refert
units.tr: Gellius, book 10, chapter 23: "Those who have written about the diet and dress of the Roman people," he says, "report that the women at Rome and in Latium lived abstemiously. That is, they abstained always from wine, which in the old language was called temetum." And it was the custom that they should give their kinsmen a kiss, as a means of checking them, so that the smell would reveal if they had drunk (the same author reports this

units.la: Plinius 14. c. 13.) Bibere autem solitas fe-runt, loream, pallum, murinam, &c, quæ id genus optant, dulcia. Sed M. Cato non solum existimatas, sed multatas à iudice mulieres refert, non minus si vinum bibissent, quàm si probrum & adulterium admisissent. Verba M. Catonis adscripsi ex oratione quæ inscribitur de dote, in qua id quoque inscriptum est. & post, Si quid peruersè tetréque factum est à muliere, si vinum bibit, si cum alieno viro probri quid fecit condemnatur. Hæc ille. Plinius idem prope refert d. loco. Non licebat, inquit, fœminis Romæ vinum bibere. Iuuenínus[?] inter exempla, Egnatij Mecennij uxorem, quòd vinum bibisset ē domo, interfectam fuste à marito, eúmque cædis à Romulo absolutum. Fabius Pictor in Annalibus suis scripsit, Matronam quòd loculos, in quibus erant claues vinariæ cellæ[?], resignauisset, à suis inedia mori coactam. & post, Cneus Domitius iudex pronunciauit mulierem videri plus vini bibisse quàm valetudinis causa viro inisciente, & dote multauit. Hæc Plinius. Valerius 2. c. 1. de usu vini mulieribus interdicto. Vini usus, inquit, olim Romanis fœminis ignotus fuit, ne scilicet in aliquod dedecus prolaberentur: quia proximus à Libero patre intemperantiæ gradus ad inconcessam Venerem esse consueuit. Cæterum, ut non tristis earum & horrida pudicitia, sed honesto comitatis genere temperata esset, indulgentibus maritis, & abundáti auro, & multa purpura usæ sunt: & quo formam concinniorem efficerent, summa cum diligentia capillos einere rutilarunt. Nulli enim tunc subfessores alienorum matrimoniorum oculi metuebantur, sed pariter & videre sanctè, & aspici mutuo pudore custodiebantur.
units.tr: Pliny, book 14, ch. 13. They report that women used to drink lorea, pallum, murina, and the like, which are sweet wines of that sort. But M. Cato reports that women were not only judged but fined by a judge, no less if they had drunk wine than if they had committed shameful acts and adultery. I have taken Cato's words from his speech entitled On the Dowry, in which this also is written: "And afterwards: If a woman has done anything perverse and foul, if she drinks wine, if she has done anything shameful with another man, she is condemned." So he says. Pliny, in the same place, reports nearly the same thing: "It was not permitted," he says, "for women at Rome to drink wine." Juvenius, among his examples, mentions the wife of Egnatius Mecennius, who was beaten to death with a club by her husband because she had drawn wine from the cellar, and that he was acquitted of the killing by Romulus. Fabius Pictor wrote in his Annals that a matron, because she had unlocked the chests in which the keys of the wine store were kept, was forced by her family to die of starvation. And afterwards: Cneus Domitius, as judge, pronounced that a woman seemed to have drunk more wine than was needed for her health, without her husband's knowledge, and fined her dowry. So Pliny. Valerius, book 2, ch. 1, on the prohibition of wine use for women: The use of wine, he says, was once unknown to Roman women, lest they should fall into some disgrace, since the step nearest to the intemperance of Father Liber is wont to be unlawful love. But so that their modesty should not be gloomy and harsh, but tempered by a respectable kind of affability, with their husbands indulging them, they used gold in abundance and much purple; and to make their appearance more elegant, they reddened their hair with the greatest care. For at that time no eyes of others' marriages were feared as spies, but they were guarded both to look upon chastely and to be looked upon with mutual modesty.
6. If a woman has committed adultery.

units.la: v. tit. de adulteriis j. eod.
units.tr: See the title On Adulteries, book 1, same place.
7. A wife is heir to her husband, and when.

units.la: v. tit. de suis & legitimis j.
units.tr: See the title On Heirs and Lawful Heirs, book 1.
8. On gifts between husband and wife.

units.la: Moribus apud nos receptum est ne in-ter virum & vxorem donationes valerent l. 1. ff. de donationib. inter vir. & vxor.
units.tr: By custom among us it is received that gifts between husband and wife are not valid. Digest, book 1, On Gifts between Husband and Wife.

units.la: 9. De iurgio & fribusculo inter virum & vxorem.
units.tr: 9. On quarrels and making up between husband and wife.

units.la: Quoties inter virum & vxorem aliquid iurgij{a} intercesserat, in sacellum Deæ Viriplacæ, quòd est in palatio, veniebant.{b} Tum ibi inuicem locuti, quæ voluerant, contentione animorum depositas, concordes reuertebantur. Dea nomen hoc à placandis viris assecuta fertur: venerada quidem, & nescio an præcipuis & exquisitis sacrificiis colenda. vt pote quotidianæ ac domesticæ pacis custos in pari iugo charitatis 2. Val. 1. de sacello deæ viriplacæ.
units.tr: Whenever some quarrel had arisen between husband and wife, they would come to the little shrine of the goddess Viriplaca, which is on the Palatine. There, speaking to one another what they wished, with the heat of their minds laid aside, they returned in harmony. The goddess is said to have taken her name from the appeasing of husbands; she is indeed to be venerated, and I know not whether she should not be worshipped with special and exquisite sacrifices, as the guardian of daily and domestic peace in the equal yoke of love. Valerius, book 1, On the shrine of the goddess Viriplaca.
10. On repudiations and divorces.

units.la: Suas res sibi{c} habere iusit & XII{d} tabu-
units.tr: He ordered that she keep her own property, and by the Twelve Tables

units.la: {c} Caius lib. 3. ad leg. XII. tabular. Si ex lege repudiū missum non fit &c. l. 43. ff. de Adulte-riis. bulis claues {a} ademit {b}, exegit {c}. Hæc Cicero 2. Philipp. 3.
units.tr: Gaius, book 3, on the Twelve Tables: "If a repudiation is not sent according to the law," etc. Digest, On Adulteries, law 43. He took away the keys and drove her out, by the Twelve Tables. Cicero, Second Philippic, book 3.
II. On second marriages.

units.la: Quæ uno {d} contentæ matrimonio fuerant, corona pudicitiæ honorabantur 2. Valer. 1.
units.tr: Those who had been content with one marriage were honoured with the crown of chastity. Valerius, book 1.
TIT. XVIII.

units.la: De Tutoribus & Curatoribus. 1. De testamentaria tutela.
units.tr: On Tutors and Curators. 1. On testamentary guardianship.

units.la: Verbis legis xii. tabularum his, uti legassit suæ rei ita ius esto, latissima potestas tributa uidetur: & hæredis institutendi, & legata & libertates dandi, tutelas quoque constituendi. l. 12 o. ff. de uerborum fignif.
units.tr: From the words of the Twelve Tables, uti legassit suae rei ita ius esto ("as a man has made bequest of his property, so let it be law"), the widest power seems to be granted: both to institute an heir, to give legacies and freedoms, and also to appoint guardians. Dig. 50.16.120, On the meaning of words.

units.la: Testamento quoque nominatim tutores dati confirmantur eadem lege xii. tabularum, Vti legassit super pecunia, tutelaue suæ rei, ita ius esto. hæc. Vlpianus 11, §. 14.
units.tr: Guardians named by testament are likewise confirmed by the same law of the Twelve Tables: "As he has bequeathed concerning money or the guardianship of his property, so let it be law." Ulpian, 11.14.

units.la: 2. Liberis in potestate positis tutorem à parente dari.
units.tr: 2. That a guardian is given by a parent to children under his power.

units.la: Lege xii. tabularum permissum e est parentibus, liberis suis sive fæmininis, sive masculini sexus, si modo in potestate sint, tutores testa-tores rauerat apud Censores, uxorem se liberorum quærendorum causa habere Gell. 17. c. vlt: iurisiurandi religionem animo atque amori in eo præuertens Gell. 4. c. 3. c hoc illud Catonis pertinet, Vir, inquit, cum diuortiu facit, mulieri ludex & proCensore est, imperium quod videtur habet 10. Gell. 23. d uiuiurae apud Gentiles admodum commendatæ: hinc, Fortunæ mulierbri coronam non imponebant nisi uniuirae, sicuti nec matri Matutæ. Tertullianus de Monogamia. Et alia sacra coronabat uniuira, alia multiuira. Arnob. 7. Mitum certe illud Athenagorę in Apolog. ... & illud Tertulliani libro de Monogamia. Vnum matrimonium nouimus, sicut unum Deum. quā de re & alias dixi. e §. 3, Inst. de tutelis. mento dare l. 1. ff. de testamentar. tutel.
units.tr: By the law of the Twelve Tables, parents were permitted to appoint by will guardians for their children, whether of the female or the male sex, provided they were still in the parent's power. The censors' records note that a man took a wife for the sake of begetting children (Gellius 17, last chapter). He prefers the sanctity of an oath to affection (Gellius 4.3). This is what Cato's remark concerns: "When a husband divorces," he says, "the judge and censor is over the woman, and he seems to have the authority." (Gellius 10.23.) Monogamy was greatly commended among the Gentiles: hence they did not crown Fortuna of the matrons except the once-married, nor the mother Matuta. Tertullian, On Monogamy. Some rites were performed by a once-married woman, others by a many-times-married one (Arnobius 7). Certainly remarkable is that of Athenagoras in his Apology, and that of Tertullian in his book On Monogamy: "We know one marriage, just as one God." I have said more on this matter elsewhere. See Inst. 1.25.3, On guardianships; to give by testament, Dig. 26.1.1, On testamentary guardianship.

units.la: 3. De legitimis tutoribus & de legitima adgnatorum tutela.
units.tr: 3. On legitimate guardians and on the legitimate guardianship of agnates.

units.la: Quibus testamento tutor datus non est, his, ex {*}lege XII. tabularum, adgnati sunt tutores qui vocantur legitimi. Inst. de legitima adgnatorum tutela.
units.tr: For those to whom no guardian was given by testament, agnates are guardians by the Twelve Tables, and these are called legitimate guardians. Inst. 1.15, On the legitimate guardianship of agnates.

units.la: Per eminentiam legitimi dicuntur, qui ex lege XII. tabularum introducuntur seu propalam vt adgnati: seu per consequentiam, vt patroni. Vlpianus 11. §. 3.
units.tr: By preeminence those are called legitimate who are introduced by the Twelve Tables, either openly as agnates, or by consequence, as patrons. Ulpian, 11.3.
4. That the nearest agnates obtain the guardianship.

units.la: Si plures sint adgnati, proximus tutelam nan-cifcitur l. Caius libro 11. ad Edictum Provinciale, in lege 9. ff. de legitimis tutoribus.
units.tr: If there are several agnates, the nearest obtains the guardianship. Gaius, book 11 on the Provincial Edict, in law 9, Dig. 26.4, On legitimate guardians.
5. On the legitimate guardianship of patrons.

units.la: Ex eadem lege XII. tabularum libertorum & libertarum tutela ad patronos,liberósque eorum pertinet, quae & ipsa legitima vocatur, non quia nominatim in ea lege de ea tute-la caueatur: sed quia perinde accepta est per interpretationem ac si legis verbis in-troducta esset. Eo enim ipso quod hæredi-tates libertorum, libertarumque, si in-testati decessissent, iusserat lex ad patro-nos, liberósve eorum pertinere, credide-runt veteres voluisse legem etiam tutelam ad eos pertinere. Inst. de legitima patron. Tutela legitima, quæ patronis defer-tur lege xii. tabularum, non quidem specialiter vel nominatim delata est, sed per consequentias {4}hereditatum, quæ ex ipsa lege patronis datæ sunt. l. 3. ff.de legi-timis tutorib.
units.tr: By the same law of the Twelve Tables, the guardianship of freedmen and freedwomen belongs to their patrons and the patrons' children. This too is called legitimate, not because that law expressly provides for this guardianship by name, but because it is received by interpretation as though it had been introduced by the words of the law. For from the very fact that the law ordered the inheritances of freedmen and freedwomen, if they died intestate, to pertain to the patrons or their children, the ancients believed that the law meant the guardianship to pertain to them as well. Inst. 1.17, On the legitimate guardianship of patrons. The legitimate guardianship which is granted to patrons by the Twelve Tables was not specially or expressly granted, but follows by consequence from the inheritances which the law itself gave to patrons. Dig. 26.4.3, On legitimate guardians.
6. On the legitimate guardianship of women.

units.la: Fœminarum legitimas tutelas lex Claudia sustulit. Vlpian.11. §.8. in f. Moribus tutor datur mulieri quæ cum tutore suo lege aut legitimo iudicio agere vult. Vlp. 11. §. 24. Mulieres omnes, propter infirmitatem consilij, maiores in tutorum potestate esse voluerunt. Cicero pro Murena. Maiores nostri nullam, ne privatam quidem rem, agere fœminas sine auctore voluerunt: sed in manu esse parentum, fratrum, virorum {b}. Livius 24. In officiis apud maiores ita observatum, ut pupillaris tutela mulieri præferatur. Masurius 3. iuris civilis apud Gellium 5. c. 13.
units.tr: The Claudian law abolished the legitimate guardianships of women. Ulpian, 11.8, at the end. A guardian is given by custom to a woman who wishes to act against her own guardian by a legal action or a legitimate trial. Ulpian, 11.24. All women, on account of the weakness of their judgement, the ancients wished to be under the power of guardians. Cicero, Pro Murena: "Our ancestors wished that women should act in no matter, not even a private one, without an authorizer, but that they should be in the hand of parents, brothers, or husbands." Livy, book 24. "In the duties observed among the ancestors, it was so ordered that the guardianship of a ward should be preferred to a woman." Masurius, book 3 of the Civil Law, in Gellius 5.13.
7. On curators, and on the curator of a madman.

units.la: Lex est. si furiosus est, agnaterum,gentilium-que in eo pecuniaque eius potestas esto. Cice-ro 1. de inventione.
units.tr: The law is: if a madman is insane, the power over him and over his money shall belong to his agnates and gentiles. Cicero, book 1 On Invention.

units.la: Qui ita sit affectus, eum dominum esse rerum suarum vetant xii. tabulæ, itaque non est scriptum si insanus, sed ,si furiosus esse incipit. Cicero 3. Tusculan.
units.tr: The Twelve Tables forbid one who is so affected to be master of his own goods; thus it is not written "if he is insane," but "if he begins to be mad." Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 3.

units.la: Lex xii. tabularum furiosum in curatione iubet esse agnatorum. 12. Vlp. 3.
units.tr: The law of the Twelve Tables orders a madman to be under the curatorship of his agnates. Ulpian, 3, on the Twelve Tables.

units.la: Furiosi, licet maiores vigintiquinque annis sint, tamen in curatione sint adgnatorum ex lege xii. tabulatum.
units.tr: A madman, although he be over twenty-five years of age, is nevertheless under the curatorship of his agnates, by the law of the Twelve Tables.
8. On the curator of a spendthrift.

units.la: Lege XII.Tabularum prodigo {a}interdici-tur {b}bonorum suorum administratio. Vlpianus libro 1. ad Sabinum in l. 1. de curatoribus furioso & aliis.
units.tr: By the law of the Twelve Tables the administration of his goods is interdicted to a spendthrift. Ulpian, book 1 on Sabinus, in law 1, On curators of madmen and others.

units.la: Prodigi, licet {c}maiores vigintiquinque annis sint, tamen in curatione sunt adgnatorum ex lege XII. Tabularum §. 3. Inst. de curatoribus.
units.tr: A spendthrift, although he be over twenty-five years of age, is nevertheless under the curatorship of his agnates, by the law of the Twelve Tables. Inst. 1.23.3, On curators.

units.la: Lex XII. Tabularum prodigum, cui bonis interdictum {d}est, in curatione iubet esse cognatorum 12.Vlpian.12.
units.tr: The law of the Twelve Tables orders a spendthrift, whose goods have been interdicted, to be under the curatorship of his cognates. Ulpian, 12.
9. On Suspect Tutors.

units.la: Suspecti crime ex legibus XII.Tabularum {e}descendit. Vlpianus lege 1.§.2. ff.de suspectis tutoribus: Inst.de suspectis tutoribus.
units.tr: The charge of being a suspect tutor derives from the Twelve Tables. Ulpian, law 1, §2, Digest, on suspect tutors; Institutes, on suspect tutors.

units.la: Atque iste dolus malus etiam legibus erat vindicatus ut tutela XII.Tabulis Cicero 3.officiorum.
units.tr: And this wrongful dealing was also punished by law: the Twelve Tables (so Cicero, On Duties, book 3).
10. On the action of tutelage for double damages.

units.la: Si ipsi tutores rem pupilli furati sunt, videamus an ea actione quae proponitur ex lege XII. Tabularum aduersus tutorem in {f}duplum singuli in solidum teneantur. & quamuis unus duplum praestiterit, nihilominus etiam alij teneantur &c. l.5.§.1. ff.de ad-ministrat.tutorum.
units.tr: If tutors themselves have stolen the property of their ward, let us see whether each of them is liable for the whole, to double the amount, under the action which is set out from the Twelve Tables against a tutor. And although one has paid the double, nevertheless the others also are liable, etc. Law 5, §1, Digest, on the administration of tutors.

units.la: Et lex 6.de verborum obligationibus.quae eidem interdicto potestatem faci t stipulandi.
units.tr: And the law 6, on verbal obligations, which gives the same interdict the power of stipulating.
Law 16, Digest, on curators.

units.la: {d} mo-ribus per Praetorem bonis interdicebatur hoc modo. Quando bona tua paterna auitaque nequitia tua disperdis, liberoque tuos ad egestatem perducis, ob eam rem tibi ea re, eoque commercio interdico Paulus 3.sent.4.§.7.
units.tr: By custom, the Praetor used to interdict goods in this way: Since you squander your goods, which came from your father and grandfather, through your own wickedness, and lead your children into want, I interdict you from the management and the transactions of that property. Paul, Sentences, book 3, title 4, §7.
See Plato, Laws, book 11.

units.la: {f} Scæ-uola[?] de tutelae iudicio apud Ciceronem 1. de Oratore, Alter, inquit, plus lege agendo petebat, quàm quantum lex in XII. Tabulis permiserat. Huius dupli damnationis vestigium extat in lege 1. ff.de his qui notantur l.4.§.2.ff.de verb.significat.
units.tr: Scaevola, on the action of tutelage, in Cicero, On the Orator, book 1: "The other," he says, "sought by the legal procedure more than the law of the Twelve Tables had permitted." A trace of this double condemnation survives in law 1, Digest, on those who are branded, and law 4, §2, Digest, on the meaning of words.
TIT. XIX.
1. On the free faculty of making a will.

units.la: Olim lege xii.Tabul. libera erat legan-di potestas, vt liceret vel totum patri-monium legatis erogare, quippe cum ea lege{a} ita cautum esset, Vti quisquam legasset suæ rei, ita ius esto. Instit.de lege Falcidia in princip.
units.tr: Formerly, under the law of the Twelve Tables, the power of bequeathing was unrestricted, so that a man could even give his whole patrimony away in legacies, since that law laid down: As a man has bequeathed concerning his own property, so let it be law. Inst. de lege Falcidia in princip.

units.la: Vti quisquam legassit de re sua, ita ius esto Novel.22.c.2.
units.tr: As anyone has bequeathed concerning his own property, so let it be law. Novel. 22 c.2.

units.la: Verbis legis xii.Tabularum his. Uti legassit suæ rei, ita ius esto, latissima potestas tributa videtur & hæredis instituendi, & legata & libertates dandi, & tutelas quoq. constituendi: sed id interpretatione[?] coangustatum est vel legum, vel authoritate iuris constitucentium[?]. l.120. ff.de verb.signif.
units.tr: In the words of the law of the Twelve Tables, as he has bequeathed concerning his own property, so let it be law, the widest power seems to have been given, both to institute heirs, to give legacies and freedoms, and to appoint guardians. But this has been narrowed by interpretation, either of the laws or by the authority of the jurists who established the law. l.120 ff. de verb. signif.

units.la: Uti legassit super pecunia, tutelaue suæ rei ita ius esto ii.Ulp.12.
units.tr: As he has bequeathed concerning money or the guardianship of his property, so let it be law. Ulp. 12.

units.la: Paterfamilias uti super familia, pecuniave sua legassit, ita ius esto. Author ad Heren-nium 1.
units.tr: As the head of the family has bequeathed concerning his household or his money, so let it be law. Author ad Herennium 1.
2. That which is bequeathed is acquired by law.

units.la: Lege nobis adquiritur legatum{b} ex lege XII.Tabularum 19.Ulp.17.
units.tr: By law a legacy is acquired for us, from the law of the Twelve Tables. 19 Ulp. 17.

units.la: 3. Suos nominatim instituì[?] & exhæredari a patre & auo paterno oportere.
units.tr: 3. That sons must be named and either instituted or disinherited by their father and paternal grandfather.

units.la: Emancipatos iure ciuili{c} neque hæredes instituere neque exhæredare necesse est, quia non
units.tr: Emancipated sons, under civil law, need neither be instituted heirs nor disinherited, because they are not

units.la: legatumve erit, eam pecuniam sine fraude capere liceto: isque hares[?], qui eam pecuniam dare iussus damnatus erit, eam pecuniam debeto dare, quam damnatus est l.1. ff.ad l.Falcidiam.
units.tr: a legacy; let him be allowed to take that money without fraud. And the heir who has been ordered and condemned to give that money must give the money he was condemned to give. l.1 ff. ad l. Falcidiam.
{b} l.47 in f. ff. de peculio; l.uo ff. de verb. signif.

units.la: {c} id est legibus XII.tabul. fiunt sui §. 3 Inst.de exheredat.
units.tr: {c} That is, by the laws of the Twelve Tables they become sui. §3 Inst. de exheredat.

units.la: 4. Mater, avusque maternus necesse non habent nominatim instituere aut exheredare.
units.tr: 4. A mother and a maternal grandfather need not institute or disinherit by name.

units.la: Neque matri filium, filiamve, neque avo materno nepotem, neptemve ex filia, si eū eam-ue haeredem non instituat, exheredare necesse est, siue de iure ciuili quaeramus, siue de edicto Praetoris §. vlt. in fi. Inst. de exhaeredatione.
units.tr: A mother need not disinherit her son or daughter, nor a maternal grandfather his grandson or granddaughter through a daughter, if she or he does not institute them heir, whether we inquire by civil law or by the praetor's edict. §. vlt. in fi. Inst. de exhaeredatione.

units.la: 5. Haereditates testamentarias lege XII. Tabularum confirmari.
units.tr: 5. Testamentary inheritances are confirmed by the law of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: Lege obuenire haereditatem non improprie quis dixerit & eam quae ex testamento debeatur: quia lege XII Tabularum testamentaria haereditates confirmantur l.130. ff. de verb. signific.
units.tr: One may not improperly say that an inheritance comes by law, and also that which is owed under a will, because by the law of the Twelve Tables testamentary inheritances are confirmed. l.130 ff. de verb. signif.

units.la: 6. De testamento per aes ac libram.
units.tr: 6. On the will made by bronze and scales.

units.la: Ex iisdem Tabulis id quoque est. Quaesi crit[lege q.si sierit] testator [lege testator] libripensve fuerit in testimonium feriatur [quidam legunt feriatur] improbus [quidam ita legunt improbus quibus: alii improbus quoi-nis : alii improbus ciuis] intestabilisque esto haec Gellius 15.c.13. in fi. idque ita emendauit Cuiacius ad tit. ul. Inst. de testam. ordinand. ex Codice in bibliotheca Iohannis Biturigum ducis reperto.
units.tr: From the same Tables comes this also: If the testator has been the balance-holder for the testimony, let him be struck [some read feriatur] wicked [some read it variously, as improbus, improbus quoinis, or improbus ciuis] and intestable. Gellius 15 c.13 in fi. Cuiacius emended it in this way, in his note on the title Inst. de testam. ordinand., from a Code found in the library of John, Duke of Bourges.

units.la: 7. Testamentum vno eodemque tempore & contextu perfic.tbatur testibus praesentib.
units.tr: 7. A will was completed at one and the same time and in one continuous act, in the presence of witnesses.

units.la: Constitutum est ut vno eodemque tempore alieno testamento quidquam praecipere.Idem refert Theophilus Inst. de testamentis ordinandis. c Testamentum innuit quod per aes & libram fiebat. de quo v. §. 1. Inst. de testamen. ordin. 15. Gell. 27: Vlp. 20. §. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. His adde quod Priscianus libro 8. refert impuberem libripendem esse non posse neque antestari, eoque loco Antestari passiue intelligi. de Antestatione dixi ad titulum de Iudiciis §. d v. §. 6. Inst. de testam. ordin. quod ius ciuile quodammodo exigebat, testa-mentum fieret. & post, ita ut testes quidem & eorum præsentia uno contextu celebrandi testamenti gratia, à iure ciuili descendant: subscriptiones autem testatoris & testium ex sacrarum constitutionum observatione adhibeantur: signacula autem & testium numerus {*}, ex edicto Prætoris
units.tr: It was established that at one and the same time the testator should lay down anything in another's will. Theophilus says the same, Inst. de testamentis ordinandis. Testamentum here signifies what was made by bronze and scales, on which see §1 Inst. de testam. ordin.; Gell. 27; Ulp. 20 §§2–9. To this add that Priscian, in book 8, reports that a minor cannot be libripens nor be antestatus, and that in that passage antestari is to be understood passively. I have spoken of antestatio under the title de Iudiciis, §d; v. §6 Inst. de testam. ordin. This is what civil law in some measure required, that the will be made. And afterwards: witnesses and their presence, for the sake of executing a will in one continuous act, derive from civil law; but the signatures of the testator and the witnesses are added in observance of the sacred constitutions; the seals and the number of witnesses come from the praetor's edict.

units.la: De hæreditatibus ab intestato. TIT. XX.
units.tr: On inheritances on intestacy. TIT. XX.

units.la: 1. Ius intestati legibus XII Tabularum angustum. Angustissimis finibus constitutum per legem XII.Tabul. ius percipiendarum hæreditatum Prætor ex æquo & bono dilatavit §. 1. Inst. de bonor. possess.
units.tr: 1. The right of intestate succession was narrow under the Law of the Twelve Tables. The Praetor extended on grounds of equity and good conscience the right of taking inheritances, which the Law of the Twelve Tables had confined within the narrowest limits. §. 1. Inst. de bonor. possess.

units.la: 2. De suis & legitimis hæredibus & de liberis in potestate positis.
units.tr: 2. On sui and legitimate heirs, and on children placed under power.

units.la: Intestatorum hæreditates ex lege XII Tabularum primum ad suos pertinent {b}. §. 1. Inst.de hæred.quæ ab intestato.
units.tr: Under the Law of the Twelve Tables, the inheritances of those dying intestate pass first to their sui heirs. §. 1. Inst. de hared. quae ab intestato.
3. On the emancipated.

units.la: Emancipati liberi iure ciuili nihil iuris habent, neque enim sui hæredes sunt, qui in potestate patris esse desierunt, neque ullo alio iure per legem XII. Tabularum vocantur. sed Prætor æquitate naturali motus, dat eis bonorum possessionem unde liberi §.9. Inst.de hæred.quæ ab intestato.
units.tr: Emancipated children have no right under the civil law. Those who have ceased to be in their father's power are neither sui heirs, nor are they called by any other right under the Law of the Twelve Tables. But the Praetor, moved by natural equity, gives them possession of goods, the so-called unde liberi. §. 9. Inst. de hared. quae ab intestato.
4. On grandchildren by a son who has died before the grandfather.

units.la: Lex XII. Tabularum filio mortuo nepotem vel neptem: pronepotes vel proneptes in locum patris sui ad successionem avi vocat: §. II. in f. Inst.de hæreditatib.quæ ab intestato.
units.tr: The Law of the Twelve Tables, when a son has died, calls the grandson or granddaughter, and the great-grandsons or great-granddaughters, to the succession of the grandfather in the place of their father. §. 11. in fine. Inst. de hared. quae ab intestato.
5. On children succeeding to their mother.

units.la: Lex xii. Tabularum ita strictò iure utebatur & praeponebat masculorum progeniem & omnes qui per foeminini sexus necessitudinem sibi iunguntur adeo expellebat, ut n quidem inter {*}matrem & filium filiamue ultro citroque haereditatis capiendae ius daret nisi quod Praetores ex proximitate cognatorum, eas personas adiucceffionem bonorum, possessione vnde cognati adcommodata, vocabant, Inst. de senatusc. Tertull.[?] in pr.
units.tr: The Law of the Twelve Tables applied the law so strictly, preferred the male line, and so entirely excluded all who are joined by kinship through the female sex, that it did not give the right of taking inheritance back and forth between mother and son or daughter. Except that the Praetors, from the nearness of kinship, called these persons to the succession of goods by the possession unde cognati, which was granted to them. Inst. de senatusc. Tertull. in pr.

units.la: 6. De filiabus & liberis foeminini sexus patri succedentibus.
units.tr: 6. On daughters and children of the female sex succeeding to their father.

units.la: Lege antiqua xii. Tabularum omnes similiter ad successionem ab intestato vocabantur, quod & Praetores sequuti esse videntur ideo simplex ac simile ius & in filiis & in filiabus &c.§.5.Inst.de exhæred.liber,
units.tr: Under the ancient Law of the Twelve Tables, all were similarly called to succession on intestacy. The Praetors also seem to have followed this, and so the right is simple and alike for sons and for daughters, etc. §. 5. Inst. de exhered. liber.

units.la: 7. De uxore in manu viri & nuru quae in filii manu.
units.tr: 7. On a wife in the hand of her husband and a daughter-in-law in the hand of a son.

units.la: Intestatorum haereditates lege xii. Tabularum primum ad suos haeredes pertinent, sui autem haeredes existimantur liberi qui in potestate morientis fuerint veluti filius filia, & post. Idem & in caeteris deinceps liberorum personis datum intelligimus. Uxor {b}quoque quae in manu eius est, quae filii loco est. ita nurus, quae in filii manu est: nam & haec neptis loco est. Sed ita demum erit sua haeres, si filius cuius in manu erit, dum pater moritur in potestate eius non fit. Idemque dicimus & de ea quae in neptis manu matrimonii causa fit. Gaius 3. Institutionum apud Ruffinum titul.16. collationis lege Mosaicarum.
units.tr: Under the Law of the Twelve Tables, the inheritances of those dying intestate pass first to their sui heirs. Sui heirs are considered to be the children who were in the power of the deceased, such as a son or a daughter, and so on. We understand the same to be given in turn to the other persons of the descendants. A wife who is in the hand of her husband is also in the place of a daughter; so too a daughter-in-law who is in the hand of a son, for she too stands in the place of a granddaughter. But she will be a sui heir only if the son in whose hand she is does not come out of his father's power while the father dies. And we say the same of her who comes into the hand of a grandson for the sake of marriage. Gaius, Institutes book 3, in Rufinus, tit. 16, Collatio legum Mosaicarum.
8. On
3. On the legitimate succession of agnates and cognates.
An agnate succeeds an agnate who has died.

units.la: Si paterfamilias moritur, familia pecuniae eius agnatorum gentiliumque esto. Author ad Hexennium [?] 1:& 2.de invent.
