units.tr: If the head of a family dies, let his money belong to his agnates and gentiles. Author ad Herennium, 1 & 2, de invent.

units.la: 9. Agnatus agnato sine liberis mortuo succedit.
units.tr: 9. An agnate who dies without children succeeds to an agnate.

units.la: Si nullus sit suorum hæredum, tunc hæreditas pertinet ex eadem lege XII Tabularum ad agnatos. Gaius 3.Instit.apud Ruffinum lib.16.collationis legum Mosaic.
units.tr: If there is none of his sui heirs, then by the same Law of the Twelve Tables the inheritance passes to the agnates. Gaius, Institutes book 3, in Rufinus, lib. 16 of the Collatio legum Mosaicarum.

units.la: 10. Non quivis agnatus succedit, sed proximus.
units.tr: 10. Not every agnate succeeds, but the nearest.

units.la: Ast si intestatus moritur, cuius suus hæres nec extabit, proximus familiam habeto 26. Vlp.1. Hic cautum est lege XII Tabularum si intestatus moritur cuius hæres nec est, agnatus proximus familiam habeatur [legendum habeat] Vlpianus libro singulari sub titulo de legitimis hæreditatibus apud Ruffinum titul.16.collationis legum Mosaic.
units.tr: But if someone dies intestate, and no sui heir of his remains, let the nearest agnate hold the family. Ulpian, 26, 1. Here it is provided by the Law of the Twelve Tables: if someone dies intestate and has no heir, let the nearest agnate hold the family. Ulpian, in his single book under the title on legitimate inheritances, in Rufinus, tit. 16, Collatio legum Mosaicarum.

units.la: Si nemo suus hæres, vel eorum quos inter suos hæredes Prætor vel constitutiones vocant, existat, qui successionem quoquomodo amplectatur, tunc ex lege XII Tabularum ad agnatum proximum pertinet hæreditas. Instit. de legitima agnat.successi. in princ.
units.tr: If no sui heir exists, nor any of those whom the Praetor or the constitutions call sui heirs, who takes up the succession in any way, then by the Law of the Twelve Tables the inheritance passes to the nearest agnate. Inst. de legit. agnat. success. in princ.

units.la: Si plures sint gradus adgnatorum, lex XII Tabularum proximum vocat. §. 5. Instit. de legitima adgnat. successi.
units.tr: If there are several degrees of agnates, the Law of the Twelve Tables calls the nearest. §. 5. Inst. de legit. agnat. success.

units.la: dem varie accepta est. nam & in res & in persona deducitur. In res, vt puta in lege XII Tabularum his verbis Agnatus proximus familiam habeto. Hæc Vlpianus in l.195. §.1.ff.de verb.significat.
units.tr: ...is taken in various ways, for it is applied both to things and to persons. To things, as in the Law of the Twelve Tables in these words: "let the nearest agnate hold the family." Thus Ulpian in l. 195 §. 1 ff. de verb. significat.

units.la: 11. Adgnatus proximus dicitur etiam is qui solus est adgnatus.
units.tr: 11. The nearest agnate is also said to be the one who is the only agnate.

units.la: In vulgari substitutione qua ei qui supremus morietur, heres substituitur, recte substitutus etiam unicus intelligitur, exemplo legis XII. tabularum, ex quibus proximus adgnatus & solus habetur, l. 162. ff. de verborum significatione.
units.tr: In a vulgar substitution, by which an heir is substituted to whoever dies last, the one substituted as the only one is rightly understood as such, on the model of the Law of the Twelve Tables, under which the nearest agnate is also regarded as the only one, l. 162 ff. de verborum significatione.

units.la: 12. Vt quis proximus dicatur, mortis defuncti tempus spectatur.
units.tr: 12. For someone to be called the nearest, the time of the deceased's death is considered.

units.la: Non omnibus simul adgnatis dat lex XII. Tabularum hæreditatem, sed his qui tunc cum certum est aliquem intestato decessisse, proximo gradu sunt. Caius apud Ruffinum dicto loco.
units.tr: The Law of the Twelve Tables does not give the inheritance to all the agnates at once, but to those who, at the time when it is certain that someone has died intestate, are in the nearest degree. Gaius, in Rufinus, said place.
13. The sisters of the deceased exclude the more remote agnates.

units.la: Si sui heredes non sint, ad consanguineos, id est fratres & sorores ex eodem patre: si nec hi sunt, ad reliquos cognatos virilis sexus per mares descendentes eiusdem familiæ, intestati hereditas pertinet, his enim cautum est lege XII. Tabularum, &c. Vlpianus libro singulari sub titulo de legitimis hereditatibus apud Ruffinum, Tit. 16. Collation is legum Mosaic.
units.tr: If there are no sui heirs, the inheritance of one who died intestate passes to blood relations, that is, brothers and sisters from the same father; if there are none of these, to the remaining cognates of the male sex, descending through males of the same family. For this is provided by the Law of the Twelve Tables, etc. Ulpian, in his single book under the title on legitimate inheritances, in Rufinus, tit. 16, Collatio legum Mosaicarum.

units.la: Nostra hereditates ad fæminas ultra consanguineorum gradum non pertinent. Itaque soror fratri, sororive, legitima heres est. Amita vero & fratris filia, heres esse non potest. Gaius apud Ruffinum d. titul. 16.
units.tr: Our inheritances do not pass to women beyond the degree of blood relations. Thus a sister is a legitimate heir to her brother or sister. But a paternal aunt and a brother's daughter cannot be heirs. Gaius, in Rufinus, said tit. 16.

units.la: Soror iure consanguinitatis, tam ad fratris quam ad sororis hereditatem admittitur. Paulus 7. sententiarum[?], sub titulo De testamentorum torum successionibus, apud eundem Ruffinum dicto tit.16.
units.tr: A sister, by right of consanguinity, is admitted to the inheritance of her brother as well as of her sister. Paulus, Sentences book 7, under the title On the succession to wills, in the same Rufinus, said tit. 16.

units.la: 14. Post fratres & sorores defuncti succedunt adgnati.
units.tr: 14. After brothers and sisters of the deceased, the agnates succeed.

units.la: Si nec hi ( id est consanguinei ) ad reliquos cognatos viriiis sexus per mares descendentes eiusdem familiae, hereditas redit. hoc enim cautum est lege xij. Tabularum. Vlpianus sub Titulo de legitimis hereditatibus, apud eundem Ruffinum d.tit.16.
units.tr: If not even these (that is, blood relatives) exist, the inheritance passes to the remaining cognates of the female sex descended through males of the same family. For this is provided by the Law of the Twelve Tables. Ulpian, under the title On Legitimate Inheritances, in Ruffinus, the same title 16 cited above.
15. After the agnates, the gentiles succeed.

units.la: Si nullus agnatus sit, eadem lex xij. Tabularum gentiles ad hereditatem vocat. Gaius 3. Inst. apud Ruffinum dicto titulo 16.
units.tr: If there is no agnate, the same Law of the Twelve Tables calls the gentiles to the inheritance. Gaius, Institutes book 3, in Ruffinus, the title cited above, 16.

units.la: Si agnatus defuncti non sit, eadem lex xij. Tabularum gentiles ad hereditatem vocat, his verbis, Si gnatus [lege agnatus] nescit {*} [lege nec sit] gentiles familiam heres hanc. [familiam hercisc ant, Oiselius, familiam habeant, P.Pitheus.] nunc nec gentilitia iura in v-su{b}sunt. hæc Vlpianus libro singulari sub Titulo de legitimis hereditatibus apud eundem Ruffinum d.loco.
units.tr: If the deceased has no agnate, the same Law of the Twelve Tables calls the gentiles to the inheritance, in these words: "If there is no agnate [read agnatus] [read nec sit], let the gentiles have the family [familiam hercisc ant, Oiselius; familiam habeant, P. Pithoeus]." Now the gentile rights are no longer in force. Thus Ulpian in his single book, under the title On Legitimate Inheritances, in Ruffinus, the same passage cited above.

units.la: 6. De his qui sunt eiusdem gradus.
units.tr: 6. On those who are of the same degree.

units.la: Si plures eodem gradu consistunt, simul admittuntur. Paulus 7. sententiarum apud Ruffinum dicto loco.
units.tr: If several stand in the same degree, they are admitted together. Paulus, Sentences book 7, in Ruffinus, the passage cited above.

units.la: 17. Si cum fratribus defuncti fratres alterius filij vel nepotes concurrunt.
units.tr: 17. If the brothers of the deceased's brother's sons or grandsons share the inheritance with the brothers of the deceased.

units.la: Si plures sint gradus agnatorum, aperte lex xii. Tabularum proximum vocat. Itaque si sint defuncti frater & alterius fratris filius aut patruus: frater solus habetur. {b}§.5. Inst. de legitima agnatorum.
units.tr: If there are several degrees of agnates, the Law of the Twelve Tables clearly calls the nearest. Thus if the deceased leaves a brother and a brother's son or a paternal uncle, the brother alone is considered. §.5. Inst. de legitima agnatorum.

units.la: 18. Duorum fratrum filij succedunt in capita.
units.tr: 18. The sons of two brothers succeed per capita.

units.la: Si defuncti nullus frater exstet, sed sint liberi fratrum, ad omnes quidem hereditas pertinet. Sed quaesitum est, si dispari numero sint, forte nati ex uno unus vel duo: & ex altero tres aut quatuor, utrum in stirpes dividenda sit hereditas, sicut inter suos heredes iuris est, an potius in capita. Iamdudum autem placuit {c}in capita dividendam hereditatem. Itaque quotquot erunt ab utraque parte persona, in tot portiones succedent. Caius 3. Instit. apud Ruffinum dicto loco in fine.
units.tr: If the deceased has no brother surviving, but there are children of brothers, the inheritance belongs to all of them. But it has been asked whether, if the numbers are unequal, for instance one or two born of one brother and three or four of another, the inheritance should be divided per stirpes, as it is by law among the heirs in the household, or rather per capita. For a long time, however, it has been settled that the inheritance is to be divided per capita. Thus as many as there are persons on each side will succeed in as many shares. Gaius, Institutes book 3, in Ruffinus, the passage cited above, near the end.

units.la: Si duorum fratrum sint liberi, non in stirpes sed in capita hereditas dividitur, scilicet vt pro numero singulorum viritim distribuatur hereditas, Paulus apud eundem Ruffinum dicto loco.
units.tr: If the children are of two brothers, the inheritance is divided not per stirpes but per capita, that is, the inheritance is distributed man by man according to the number of individuals. Paulus, in Ruffinus, the passage cited above.

units.la: Omnes fratrum filij patruo suo ab intestato succedunt, non in stirpes, sed in capita. Caius 2. Instit. 8. §. penult.
units.tr: All the sons of brothers succeed their paternal uncle intestate, not per stirpes but per capita. Gaius, Institutes book 2, section 8, the penultimate paragraph.
19. On the tenth degree of agnation.

units.la: Adgnationis iure aliquem admitti ad hereditatem etiamsi decimo gradu sit, sive de lege xij. tabul. sive de edicto, & e §.5. Institut. de iure cognatorum.
units.tr: By right of agnation a person may be admitted to the inheritance even if he stands in the tenth degree, whether by the Law of the Twelve Tables or by the edict; and §.5. Inst. de iure cognatorum.
20. On agnates who have undergone capitis deminutio.

units.la: Adgnati capite diminuti d, quique ex his progeniti sunt, ex lege xij. Tabularum inter legitimos non habentur, sed a Praetore tertio ordine[?] vocantur §. 1. Institut. de successione cognatorum.
units.tr: Agnates who have undergone capitis deminutio, and those born of them, are not counted among the legitimate heirs under the Law of the Twelve Tables, but are called by the Praetor in the third order [?]. §.1. Inst. de successione cognatorum.
21. On women.

units.la: Lex xij. Tabularum nulla distinctione sexu[?] cognatos admittit. Paul. 4. sentent. 8. §. 3.
units.tr: The Law of the Twelve Tables admits cognates without any distinction of sex. Paulus, Sentences book 4, title 8, §.3.

units.la: Lex xij. Tabularum simplicitatem legibus amicam amplexa, simili modo, omnes adgnatos siue masculos, siue fœminas cuiuscunque gradus, ad similitudinem suorum inuicem ad successionem vocabat. §. 3. Inst. de legitima adgnatorum successione.
units.tr: The Law of the Twelve Tables, embracing a simplicity friendly to the laws, in the same way called all agnates to succession in the manner of their own kind, whether male or female, of whatever degree. §.3. Inst. de legitima agnatorum successione.
22. On agnates and cognates who have undergone capitis deminutio.

units.la: Legitimæ hereditatis ius quod ex lege xij. Tabularum descendit, capitis minutione amittitur. 27. Vlpian. 5.
units.tr: The right of legitimate inheritance that comes down from the Law of the Twelve Tables is lost by capitis deminutio. Ulpian, book 5, law 27.
23. On the succession of freedmen and the right of patronage.
On the patron and his children.

units.la: Si liberti intestati decesserint, nullo libertorum relicto, ius quod erat ex lege xij. Tabularum integrum reseruauit: §. 3. Inst. de successione libertorum.
units.tr: If freedmen die intestate, leaving no freedman, the right that existed under the Law of the Twelve Tables was kept whole. §.3. Inst. de successione libertorum.

units.la: Hæreditatem libertorum, si intestati decesent[?], iusserat lex ad patronos, liberóve eorum pertinere, Inst. de legitima patronorum tutela.
units.tr: The law had ordained that the inheritance of freedmen dying intestate should pass to their patrons or the patrons' children. Inst. de legitima patronorum tutela.
24. On the patroness.

units.la: Si libertinus est vel libertina, ad patronum eius legitima hereditas, patronáve lege xij. Tabularum refertur. Vlpianus d[?]. titulo 16. apud Ruffinum.
units.tr: If a freedman or freedwoman dies, the legitimate inheritance passes to the patron, or to the patroness, under the Law of the Twelve Tables. Ulpian, cited above in title 16, in Ruffinus.
25. On a freedman remancipated.

units.la: Si is qui decesit liber fuit, ex remancipatione manum sius[?], lex quidem xij. Tabularum manumissori legitimam hereditatem detulit. Sed Praetor æquitate motus decem personas co-gnatorū ei prætulit has, f. patrem, matrem, filium, filiam, auum, auiam, nepotem, neptem, fratres, sorores: ne quis occasione iuris sanguinis necessitudinem vinceret. Sed Imperator noster in hereditatibus quæ ab intestato deferuntur, eas solas personas vo-luit admitti, quibus decimæ immunitatem tribuit: Vlpianus dicto loco.
units.tr: If the man who died was free, then by remancipation from his power, the Law of the Twelve Tables indeed gave the legitimate inheritance to the manumittor. But the Praetor, moved by equity, preferred to him ten kinsfolk: namely the father, mother, son, daughter, grandfather, grandmother, grandson, granddaughter, brothers and sisters, so that no one should defeat the claim of blood kinship by reason of the law. But our Emperor wished that in inheritances which pass intestate only those persons should be admitted to whom he granted exemption from the tenth [share of the law]. Ulpian, in the passage cited above.
26. If a patron has accused his freedman of a capital crime.

units.la: Qui libertum capitis accusauit, ad legitimam hereditatem quæ ex lege xij. Tabularum de-fertur non admitt.tur, l.10. l.11. ff.de iure pa-tronatus.
units.tr: One who has accused his freedman of a capital crime is not admitted to the legitimate inheritance that is passed under the Law of the Twelve Tables. Laws 10 and 11, Digest, On the Right of Patronage.

units.la: 27. De successionibus quæ fiebant per bonorum venditionem.
units.tr: 27. On the successions that arose through the sale of goods (bonorum venditio).

units.la: Æris confessi{a}, rebusque iure iudicatis, tri-ginta{b} dies iusti{c} sunto. Post deinde{d} manus iniectio esto, in ius ducito, ni iudicatum facit, aut qui{e} pseudo eo in iure vim dicit{f} secum ducito, vincito aut neruo{g} aut compedibus quindecim pondo, ne{h} minore: aut si volet, maiore vincito. Si volet, suo viuito. Ni suo viuit, qui
units.tr: Let thirty days be granted for money acknowledged as owed and for matters adjudged by law. After that let a hand be laid on him, and let him be led before the magistrate. If he does not satisfy the judgment, or if someone speaks for him in court and claims him, let him be taken with him and bound with a thong or with fetters of fifteen pounds, not less; or if he wishes, let him be bound with heavier fetters. If he wishes, let him live at his own expense. If he does not live at his own expense, he who
quipsendo, etc.: "quips," in older usage, for quispiam (someone).

units.la: {f} vindicit, id est vindicauerit, eadem forma quo veteres lauit[?], sonit[?], vide Cuiacium 3. obseruat. 39.
units.tr: vindicit, that is, vindicauerit (has claimed), in the same form in which the ancients wrote lauit and sonit. See Cuiacius, Observations, book 3, ch. 39.

units.la: {g} Græci hunc nerunum vocabant κάλων[?] v. Iosepb.[?] Scaliger apud Festum in Ner-num.
units.tr: The Greeks called this thong a rope [κάλων]. See Josephus; Scaliger, in Festus under "nerum."

units.la: {h} ne maiore, aut si volet, minore. Cuiac.d.loco. cum vinctum habebit, libras a farris in {b}dies data. Erat autem ius interea paciscendi: ac nisi pacti eforent, habebantur in vinculis dies sexaginta d. Inter eos dies trinis nundinis continuus ad Praetorem in comitium producebantur, quanti pecunia iudicati essent, praedicabatur, tertiis nundinis capite poenas dabant, aut trans Tyberim peregrè venumibant. Verba legis XII: tabularum ea erant: Tertiis nundinis, partes secanto e: si plus minusve secuerunt, sine fraude esto. Haec Gellius 20.c.1.
units.tr: "...if he wishes, let him give more, or if he wishes, less." Cuiacius, loc. cit. When he has him in chains, let him give a pound of spelt for each day. Meanwhile there was a right to come to terms; and unless they had come to terms, they were held in chains for sixty days. During those days, on three successive market days, they were brought continuously before the praetor in the assembly, and the sum of money for which they had been adjudged was announced. On the third market days they paid the penalty with their lives, or were sold abroad as foreigners across the Tiber. The words of the Twelve Tables were these: "On the third market days let them cut the portions; if they have cut more or less, let it be without fraud." Thus Gellius, book 20, ch. 1.

units.la: Hanc legem ita restituit Iosephus Scaliger apud Festum in neruum. Aéris confessi rebusque iure iudicatis, triginta dies instei sunto. Postidea indu manus iacito, esto, in ious ducito, nei ioudicatum facit, aut quipsendo ioure vindicit, secum ducito, vincito aut neruo, aut compedibus, quindecim pondo ne minore: aut sei volet maiore vincito, sei volet suo viuito: Nei suo viuit, qui eum vinctum habebit, libras farris in dies dato. sei volet plus dato.
units.tr: Joseph Scaliger restored this law in the following way, in Festus under "in neruum": Of money acknowledged and of things adjudged by law, let thirty days be granted. Afterwards let a hand be laid on him, and let him be led into court, unless he satisfies the judgment, or unless someone who claims him by law speaks for him; let him be taken with him and bound with a thong, or with fetters, of fifteen pounds, not less; or if he wishes, let him be bound with heavier. If he wishes, let him live at his own expense. If he does not live at his own expense, let him who holds him bound give a pound of spelt for each day; if he wishes, let him give more.
On hereditary actions.
TIT. XXI.

units.la: 1. Mortuo debitore eius heredes conuen-niantur non legatarij.
units.tr: 1. The heirs of a deceased debtor, and not the legatees, are to be sued.

units.la: CRediτores hereditarios aduersus legata-rios non habere personalem actionem conue-nit, quippe cum euidentissimè lex XII. tabularum haeredes huic rei faciat obnoxios l. vlt. Cod. de hereditariis actionib.
units.tr: It is agreed that creditors of an inheritance have no personal action against legatees, since the Law of the Twelve Tables very clearly makes the heirs liable for this matter. l. ult. Cod. de hereditariis actionibus.

units.la: [?]dendatum ut diu ad l. 31. in f. ff. de re iudicata.
units.tr: [unclear] as noted long ago at l. 31 in fin., ff. de re iudicata.
2. Hereditary actions are divided among coheirs.

units.la: Defuncto creditore, multis relictis heredibus, actionem personalem inter eos ex lege XII. tabularum diuidi. l.1. Cod. si unus ex plurib. heredib. Obligatio diuiditur per legem XII. tabularum. l.25. §.13. ff. familiae.
units.tr: When a creditor dies, leaving several heirs, the personal action is divided among them by the Law of the Twelve Tables. l. 1. Cod. si unus ex pluribus heredibus. An obligation is divided by the Law of the Twelve Tables. l. 25 §. 13, ff. familiae.

units.la: 2. Actiones hereditarias diuidi inter coheredes pro portionibus hereditariis.
units.tr: 2. Hereditary actions are divided among coheirs in proportion to their hereditary shares.

units.la: Ea quae in nominibus sunt, non recipiunt diuisionem, cum ipso iure in portiones a hereditate ex lege XII. tabularum diuisae sint. l. 6.
units.tr: Those things which are owed as debts do not admit division, since by the Law of the Twelve Tables they have already been divided by the law itself into portions of the inheritance. l. 6.
Cod. familiae.
TITLE XXII.
1. On possessions and the interdict "whichever of the two possesses."

units.la: GEllius 10. c. 9. Ex iure manu confertum verba sunt ex antiquis actionibus: quae cum lege agitur & vindiciae contenduntur, dici nunc quoque apud Praetorem solent. & post, ex Ennio. Non ex iure manu confertum, sed mage ferro Rem repetunt, regnumque petunt, vadunt solida vi & post, Manum conferere, est de qua re disceptabatur in re praesenti, siue ager, siue quid aliud est, cum aduersarium simul manu prenderet, in ea re omnibus verbis vindicare: id est vindicia & correpta manu in re atque in loco praesenti, apud Praetorem ex XII. tabulis fiebat. In quibus ita scriptum est, Si qui in iure manum conferunt. Sed postquam praetores propagatis Italiae finibus, datis iurisdictionibus negotiis occupati, pacisci(lege proficisci) vindiciarum dicendarum
units.tr: Gellius, book 10, chapter 9: The words of the old actions, "by law, with hand joined" (ex iure manu confertum), are taken from the ancient actions: when a case is pleaded by law and the vindiciae are contested, they are still customarily spoken today before the praetor. And afterwards, from Ennius: "They do not seek back the thing with hand joined by law, but rather with iron; they make claim to the kingdom and advance with solid force." And afterwards: "to join hands" is said of a matter disputed in a present thing, whether land or something else, when a man at the same time takes hold of his adversary's hand and claims the thing by all the words. That is, the vindicia: by seizing the hand on the thing itself and in the present place, it was done before the praetor under the Twelve Tables. In these it is written, "If they join hands in law." But after the praetors had extended the borders of Italy and were occupied with granting jurisdictions and business, they began to find it burdensome to pursue the pleading of the vindiciae

units.la: {b} Festus in Superstites. Superstites praesentes significat, cuius rei testimonium est quod superstitibus praesentibus, ij inter quos controuersia est, vindicias sumere iubentur. dicendarum causa longinquas res {a}grauabantur, institutum est contra xii. tabu-las tacito consensu, vt litigantes non ex iure apud Prætorem manum consererent, sed ex iure manu confertum vocarent: id est alter alterum ex iure ad conserendam manum in rem, de qua ageretur, vocaret. Atque profecti simul in agrum de quo litigabatur, terræ aliquid ex eo, vti vnâ glebam, in ius in vrbem ad prætorem deterrent: & in ea gleba, tanquam in toto agro vindicarent. Idcirco Ennius significare volens bellum, non vt ad Prætorem solitum est, legitimis actionibus, neque ex iure manu confertum, sed bello ferróque, & vera vi atque solida: quod videtur dixisse con-ferens vim illam ciuilem & festucariam, quæ verbo diceretur, non quæ manu fieret cum vi bellica & cruenta. Hæc Gellius ad verbum.
units.tr: Festus, under "Superstites": Superstites means "present." The proof of this is that, when the living (superstites) are present, the parties between whom there is a dispute are ordered to take the vindiciae. Since bringing distant things to be pleaded was burdensome, it was established, by tacit consent and contrary to the Twelve Tables, that litigants should not join hands before the praetor by law, but should call one another "from law" to join hands. That is, one party would summon the other from law to join hands over the thing in question. Having set out together into the field about which they were litigating, they would carry some portion of the land, such as a single clod, into court in the city before the praetor, and claim the vindicia over that clod as though over the whole field. So Ennius, wishing to signify war, and not by the usual legitimate actions before the praetor, nor by hands joined by law, but "by war and iron, and by true and solid force," seems to have contrasted that civil and festuca-like force, which is done by words, with the force done by hand in bloody warfare. Thus Gellius, word for word.

units.la: 2. Si iudex falsam vindiciam in causa libertatis tulerit.
units.tr: 2. If a judge has given a false vindicia in a cause of liberty.

units.la: Vindiciæ appellantur res ea, de quibus controuersia est, quod potius dicitur ius, qui fit inter eos, qui contendunt. & post. De quo verbo Cincius sic ait, Vindiciæ olim dicebantur illæ, quæ ex fundo sumptæ: in ius adlatæ erant. At Ser. Sulpicius{*} iam[lege nomine etiam]singulariter formato vindiciam esse ait [lege rem] qua de re controuersia est ab eo quod vindicatur & in xii. Si vindiciam falsam tulit
units.tr: The things about which there is a dispute are called vindiciae, which is rather a right, arising between those who contend. And afterwards: Concerning this word Cincius says: "Vindiciae were formerly those things which were taken from the estate and brought into court." But Servius Sulpicius, also forming the word in the singular, says that vindicia is the thing about which there is controversy, from the word vindicare; and in the Twelve Tables: "If he has brought a false vindicia"

units.la: {*} [lege rei] si velit is [lege sine b litis] arbitros tres [quidam legunt, tot arbitros aeris] dato, eo-rum arbitrii fructus [quidam legunt fructi] duplione a damnum decidito. Hæc Festus in voce Vindicia.
units.tr: {*} [read: of the thing] if he is willing [read: without] let him give three arbiters [some read: as many arbiters of the bronze]; [some read: fruits] of their arbitration let him settle the damage by double. Thus Festus under the word Vindicia.

units.la: Initium fuisse secessionis dicitur Vergi-nius quidam, qui cum animaduertisset Appium Claudium contra ius, quod ipse ex vetere iure in xii. tabulas transtulerat, vindicias suas à se abdixisse, & secundum eum, qui in seruitutem ab eo suppositus petierat dixisse: captúmque amore virginis omne fas ac nefas miscuisse, indignatus, quòd vetustissima iuris obseruantia, in persona filiæ suæ defecisset,vt pote cum Brutus, qui primus Romæ consul fuerat, vindicias secundum libertatem dixisset, in persona Vindicis Vitelliorum serui, qui proditionis coniurationem indicio suo detexerat, & castitatem filiæ, vitæ quoque eius præferendam putaret: arrepto cultro de taberna lanionis, filiam interfecit. Hæc Pomponius in l. 2. §. 24. vers. initium ff. de origine iuris.
units.tr: Verginius is said to have been the origin of the secession. Noticing that Appius Claudius had repudiated his own vindicia contrary to law, which he himself had transferred from the old law into the Twelve Tables, and had said so in favour of the man who had been put forward as a slave by him and sought his servitude, and being captivated by love of a maiden, he confused all right and wrong. Indignant that the most ancient observance of the law had failed in the person of his daughter, since Brutus, who first had been consul at Rome, had given the vindicia in favour of liberty, in the person of Vindex, slave of the Vitellii, who had revealed the conspiracy of treason by his information, and thinking that her chastity ought to be preferred even to her life, he seized a knife from a butcher's shop and killed his daughter. Thus Pomponius in law 2, §24, at the beginning of the Digest on the origin of law.

units.la: Appius Claudius M. Claudio clienti negotium dedit, vt virginem in seruitutem assereret,neque cederet secundum libertatem possulantibus vindicias: quòd pater puellæ abesset, locum iniuriæ esse ratus, virgini venienti in forum minister manum iniecit,serua sua natam,suámque seruam appellans esse, sequíque se iubebat, cunctantem vi abstracturum. & post, fit concursus. & post, iam à vi tuta erat, cum assertor nihil opus esse multitudine concitata ait, se iure non vi grassari: vocat puellam in ius. ad tribunal Appij peruentum est. notam iudici fabulam petitor peragit. puellam domi suæ natam, furtóque inde in domum Virginij translatam, suppositámque ei esse, id se iudicio compertum afferre. Aduocati puellæ cum Virginium Reipublicæ causa dixissent abesse, biduo affuturum, si ei nuntiatum sit: iniquum esse absentem de liberis dimicare: postulant vt rem integram in patris aduentum differat: lege ab ipso lata Vindiciæ det secundum libertatem, neu patiatur Virginem adultam famæ prius, quàm libertatis periculum adire. Appius decreto prætfatur, quàm libertati fauerit, eam ipsam legem declarare, quam Virginij amici postulationi suę prętendant. Cæterum ita in ea firmum libertati fore prætfidium, si nec causis, nec personis variet.
units.tr: Appius Claudius gave M. Claudius, his client, the task of asserting that the maiden was a slave, and of not yielding the vindicia to those seeking them in favour of liberty. Because the girl's father was absent, he judged it an opportunity for wrong, and as the maiden came into the forum, his minister laid hands on her, calling her the born slave of his slave-woman, and ordering her to follow him, and threatening to drag her off by force if she hesitated. And afterwards, a crowd gathered. And afterwards, now she was safe from force, when the claimant, with the crowd stirred up, said there was no need for force; he was proceeding by law, not by violence, and summoned the girl to court. They came before Appius' tribunal. The claimant played out a tale well known to the judge: that the girl had been born in his house, and had been secretly carried from there into Verginius' house, and substituted, and that he brought this forward as something found out by inquiry. The advocates of the girl said that Verginius was absent on public business and would return within two days if he were informed; it was unfair to contend over free-born persons in the absence of one of them; they asked that the matter be left undecided until the father's arrival, and that, by a law proposed by himself, he give the vindicia in favour of liberty, and not allow the grown maiden to face danger to her reputation before the danger to her liberty. Appius, in his decree, declared before he showed favour to liberty that law itself, which the friends of Verginius put forward in their claim. Otherwise, he said, the protection of liberty would be firm only if it did not vary with the cases or the persons.

units.la: In {4}his enim quæ asseran-tur in libertatem, quia quiuis lege agere possit, id iuris esse: in ea quæ in patris manu sit, neminem esse alium, cui domi-nus possessione cedat. Placere itaque patrem accersiri: interea iuris sui iacturam assertorem non facere, quin ducat puellam, sistendámque in aduentum eius, qui pater dicatur promittat. & post, Id quod constat, nudum videtur proponendum, decresse vindicias secundum seruitutem. & post, I, lictor summoue turbam & da viam domino ad prætiendum mancipium. Cùm hæc intonuisset plenus iræ, tum Virginius, Quæso, inquit, Appi, primum ignoscere patrio dolori, si quid inclementius in te sum inuectus: deinde si-nas hic coram virgine nutricem percontari, quid hoc rei sit, vt si falsò patet dictus sum, æquiore hinc animo discedam. Data venia, seducit filiam ac nutricem pro-pè Cloacinæ ad tabernas, ibíque ab Ianio cultro arrepto, Hoc te vno quo possum, ait, modo filia in libertatem vindico, pectus deinde puellæ transfigit, respectánsque ad tribunal, Te, inquit, Appi, tuumque caput hoc sanguine consecro. Hæc Liuius 3.
units.tr: For in the matters asserted in favour of liberty, since anyone may bring suit by law, that is the right; but in what is in the father's hand, there is no one else to whom the owner might yield possession. It was therefore agreed that the father should be summoned; meanwhile the claimant should not lose his right by leading the girl away, but should promise to present her until the arrival of him who is called her father. And afterwards: "What is agreed seems to be stated bare: he has decided the vindicia in favour of servitude." And afterwards: "Go, lictor, remove the crowd and give the master way to take hold of the slave." When he had thundered these words, full of anger, Verginius said: "I beg you, Appius, first to pardon a father's grief if I have railed against you too harshly; then allow me to ask the nurse here, in the maiden's presence, what this matter is about, so that if I have been named falsely, I may leave with a more even mind." Permission given, he led his daughter and the nurse aside, near the Cloacina, to the shops, and there, seizing a knife from Janius, he said: "By this only way I can, I claim my daughter in liberty"; then he pierced the girl's breast, and turning to the tribunal said: "Appius, I consecrate you and your head with this blood." Thus Livy, book 3.
3. On cutting down trees.

units.la: Quod ait Prætor & lex XII. tabularum efficere voluit, vt quindecim pedes altius ra-mi circumciderentur. & hoc idcirco effectum est, ne vmbra arboris vicino prædio noceret. l.1.§.8.ff.de arboribus cædendis.
units.tr: What the Praetor and the Law of the Twelve Tables wanted to bring about was that branches growing higher than fifteen feet should be lopped off. This was done so that the shade of a tree should not harm a neighbouring estate. l.1.§.8.ff.de arboribus cædendis.
4. On gathering fallen acorns.

units.la: Cautum est lege XII. tabularū, vt glan-dem in alienum fundum procidentem liceret colligere. Hæc Plinius 16. c. 5.
units.tr: It is provided by a law of the Twelve Tables that it is lawful to gather acorns that fall onto another's land. So Pliny, book 16, chapter 5.
On Usucapions. TIT. XXIII.
1. Immovables by two years, movables by one year for usucaption.

units.la: LEx iubet vsum & authoritatem fundi, † esse biennium Cicero pro Cecinna: ca-terarum rerum annuus est vsus. Idè in Topicis. hic videtur.
units.tr: The law orders that the use and authority over land be two years, as Cicero says in the Pro Caecina; the use of other things is annual. On this see also the Topica; here it seems to be so.
Inst. de usucapionibus l.13. Cod. de servitutibus.
2. Title required in usucaption.

units.la: Iure ciuili constitutum fuerat ut qui bona fide ab eo qui dominus non erat, cum crederet eum dominum non esse rem emerat, vel ex donatione alicuius quamuis iusta causa acceperit usucaperet Inst. de usucapionib.
units.tr: By the civil law it had been established that whoever bought a thing in good faith from one who was not its owner, believing him not to be the owner, or received it by gift from someone, even with a just cause, should acquire it by usucaption. Inst. de usucapionibus.

units.la: 3. Quibus in locis annalis & biennalis usucapio locum habuerit.
units.tr: 3. In what places annual and biennial usucaption had effect.

units.la: Iure ciuili constitutum fuerat ut res mobiles, anno ubique uno:immobiles, biennio tantum in Italico † solo usucaperentur. Inst. de usucapio.
units.tr: By the civil law it had been established that movable things were acquired by usucaption everywhere in one year, but immovable things in two years only in Italian soil. Inst. de usucapionibus.

units.la: 4. Res furtiuae aut vi possessae non usucapiuntur.
units.tr: 4. Stolen things, or things possessed by force, are not acquired by usucaption.

units.la: Furtiuarum rerum lex XII Tabular. & lex Atilia {a} inhibent {b} usucapionem: vi possessorum, lex {c} Iulia & Plautia. {d} §.2.Inst.de usucapionib.
units.tr: The Twelve Tables law and the Atilian law forbid usucaption of stolen things; the Julian and Plautian laws forbid it for things possessed by violence. §2 Inst. de usucapionibus.

units.la: 5. Res ciuium Romanorum a peregrino non usucapi.
units.tr: 5. The property of Roman citizens is not acquired by usucaption from a foreigner.

units.la: Hostis apud maiores nostros is dicebatur quem nunc peregrinum dicimus. Indicant enim XII. Tabulae Aduersus hostem aeterna auctoritas esto. haec Cic. 1. officiorum.
units.tr: Among our ancestors, the one who is now called a foreigner (peregrinus) was called a enemy (hostis). For the Twelve Tables indicate this: "Let there be eternal authority against an enemy." So Cicero in the first book of De officiis.
6. On a woman taken by usucaption and by usurpation.

units.la: Quintus Mutius iuris consultus dicere solitum, lege non esse usurpatam f muliere, quae cum kalendis Ianuarijs apud virum causa matrimonij esse coepisset, ante diem quartum Calendas Ianuarias sequentes usurpatum isset[?].
units.tr: Quintus Mucius, the jurist, used to say that a woman who had begun to be with a man for the sake of marriage from the Kalends of January was not taken by usurpation by law, if she had been absent from the man for the purpose of usurpation before the fourth day before the following Kalends of January.

units.la: perius explicatum est. {f} de usurpatione v.l.2. de usucap. usurpationis verbum ex XII. Tabulis esse hinc constat. & quidem Appius Claudius proxime post XII I.Tabulas de usurpationib. scripsit l.2.§.3.ff.de origine iuris.de usurpationib.etiam aliquid ex Quinto Mucio hic affertur a Gellio & Macrobio. Non.n.impleri posse trinoctium,quod abesse à viro vsurpandi causa ex x 11. tabulis deberet, quoniam tertiæ noctis posteriores sex horæ alterius anni essent Gell.2.inf. 3. qui inciperet ex Calédis. Virgilius quoque id ipsum ostendit, Torquet ( inquit) medios nox humida cursus,Et me sæuus equis oriens asslauit anhelis. Macrob.1. Saturnal.3.
units.tr: This has been explained above. That the word "usurpation" comes from the Twelve Tables is clear from this; and indeed Appius Claudius wrote about usurpations shortly after the Twelve Tables (Digest, de origine iuris, 2.3). Something of Quintus Mucius is also cited here by Gellius and Macrobius. For the three nights which, according to the Twelve Tables, had to be spent away from the husband for the purpose of usurpation, could not be completed, since the last six hours of the third night belonged to the other year, beginning from the Kalends (Gellius 2). Virgil also shows this very thing: "The damp night turns my middle course, and the cruel east wind has blasted me with panting horses." Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.3.
7. On the forecourt of a tomb.

units.la: Quod forum,id est vestibulum sepulchri, bustumve vsucapi vetat, tuetur ius sepulchro-rum.Cicero 2.de legibus.
units.tr: That the forum, that is, the vestibule of a tomb or burial ground, forbids usucaption; the law of tombs protects it. Cicero, De legibus 2.

units.la: TIT. XXIIII. De priuatis delictis[?] & de furto.
units.tr: TIT. XXIIII. On private offences, and on theft.

units.la: 1. Nocturnum furtum quoquo modo posse occidi.
units.tr: 1. That a thief caught by night may be killed in any way.

units.la: NOn abs re puto hoc loco id quoq. ad-monere,quod Decemuiri in x 1 1.Tabulis inusitatissime. Nox pro {b}noctu di-xerut. verba hæc sunt: Si nox furtum factum sit, si im{c} aliquis occisit, iure casus esto{d}. Macrob.1.Saturn.4.
units.tr: I think it is not out of place to point out here also that the Decemvirs, in the Twelve Tables, used the very unusual form "nox" for "noctu" (by night). The words are: "If a theft is committed by night, and someone kills the thief, let the killing be lawful." Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.4.

units.la: Cicero pro Milone, xii. Tabulæ noctur-num furem quoquo modo interfici impune voluerunt.
units.tr: Cicero, Pro Milone 12: The Twelve Tables wanted a thief caught by night to be killed with impunity, in whatever way.

units.la: Caius in l.4.§.1.ff.ad l.Aquil.lex xii. Ta-bularum Furem noctu deprehensum occidere permittit.
units.tr: Gaius, in law 4 §1 ff. ad legem Aquiliam: The law of the Twelve Tables allows a thief caught by night to be killed.

units.la: Gellius 11.c.18.Deceuiri nostri post reges exactos leges quib.P.Romanus vteretur in xii.Tabulis scripserunt.Furem qui manifesto furto prehensus esset, tum demum occidi permiserunt. si aut cum faceret furtū nox esset,aut interdiu se telo, cū prehederetur, defenderet.
units.tr: Gellius 11.18: Our Decemvirs, after the kings were expelled, wrote the laws which the Roman people used, in the Twelve Tables. They allowed a thief caught in manifest theft to be killed only if it was night when he committed the theft, or if by day he defended himself with a weapon when he was seized.

units.la: 2. Interdiariū[?] furem se defendentem posse occidi.
units.tr: 2. That a thief who defends himself by day may be killed.

units.la: Furem interdiu {a}deprehensum non aliter occidere lex XII. Tabularum permisit, quàm si se telo {b}defendat. Caius in lege 54. §. 2. ff. de furtis.
units.tr: The law of the Twelve Tables allowed a thief caught by day to be killed only if he defended himself with a weapon. Gaius, in law 54 §2 ff. de furtis.

units.la: Interdiu deprehensum furem ita permittit lex occidere, si is se telo defendat, vt tamen æque cum clamore testificetur {c}l.4. in fi. ff. ad l. Aquil.
units.tr: The law permits a thief caught by day to be killed only if he defends himself with a weapon, provided that he also bears witness with a shout, just as much. Law 4 at the end, ff. ad legem Aquiliam.

units.la: Duodecim Tabulæ, furem diurnum, si se telo defenderit, interfici impunè {d}voluerunt Cicero pro Milone.
units.tr: The Twelve Tables wanted a thief caught by day, if he defended himself with a weapon, to be killed with impunity. Cicero, Pro Milone.

units.la: Decemuiri qui post reges exactos leges quibus P. Romanus vtere tur in XII. Tabulis scripserunt, furem tum demum occidi permiserunt si interdiu se cum telo, cùm deprehenderetur, defenderet ii. Gell. 18.
units.tr: The Decemvirs, who wrote the laws the Roman people used after the kings were expelled, in the Twelve Tables, allowed a thief to be killed only if, when he was caught by day, he defended himself with a weapon. Gellius 18.

units.la: Si quis furem occiderit, iniuria occiderit. Quamobrem? Quia ius nullum constitutum est. Quid si se telo defenderit? Non iniuria. Quid ita? Quia constitutum est. Oratio pro M. Tullio apud Quintilian. lib. 5.
units.tr: If someone kills a thief, he kills him unlawfully. Why? Because no law has been laid down. What if he defended himself with a weapon? Not unlawfully. Why so? Because it has been laid down. Speech for M. Tullius, in Quintilian, book 5.

units.la: Hoc & in legibus antiquis feculariribus inuenitur, impune occidi noctur num furem quo-quo modo: diurnum si se cum telo defenderit: iâ enim plus quàm fur est. August. ii. super Exod.
units.tr: This is also found in the ancient secular laws: a thief by night may be killed in any way with impunity; by day, if he defended himself with a weapon, for then he is more than a thief. Augustine, book 2 on Exodus.
3. On the punishment of a thief caught in manifest theft.

units.la: Decemuiri nostri qui post reges exactos leges quibus P. Romanus vteretur in XII. Tabulas retulerunt neque pari seueritate in puniendis omnium generum furibus, neque remissa nimis lenitate vsi sunt. Furem qui manifesto furto prehensus esset, tum demum occidi permiserunt si aut cum faceret furtum nox esset, aut interdiu se cum telo defenderet. Ex caeteris autem manifestis furibus, liberos verberari {a}, addicique iusserunt eicui furtum factum esset, si modo id luci fecif-sent,neque se telo defendissent. Seruos aute furti manifesti prehensos,verberibus affici & è {b}sa-xo præcipitari. pueros impuberes {c} Pratoris arbitratu verberari voluerunt, noxámque ab hus factam farciri hęc Gell.ii.c.18.
units.tr: Our Decemvirs, who after the kings were expelled brought the laws the Roman people used into the Twelve Tables, neither applied the same severity in punishing all kinds of thieves, nor used excessive leniency. They allowed a thief caught in manifest theft to be killed only if the theft was committed at night, or if by day he defended himself with a weapon. As for the other manifest thieves, they ordered freemen to be beaten and handed over to the person from whom the theft was made, if indeed they had committed it in daylight and had not defended themselves with a weapon. Slaves caught in manifest theft they wanted to be flogged and thrown from the Tarpeian rock; boys below puberty they wanted to be beaten at the praetor's discretion, and the harm done by them to be made good. Gellius 2.18 (sic) on these matters.
4. On the punishment of non-manifest theft.

units.la: Aliys furtis omnibus quae non manifesta appellantur poenam imposuerunt, dupli {d} hęc Gel-lius II.c.18.
units.tr: For all other thefts, which are called non-manifest, they imposed a penalty of double. Gellius 11.18 on these matters.
5. A compromise about theft is permitted.

units.la: Nec coniunctionem Grámatici fere di-cunt esse disiuctiuam, vt Nec legit,nec sen-tit: cùm si diligentius inspiciatur, vt fecit Sinnius Capito, intelligi possit eâ positam esse ab antiquis pro non, vt & in duode-cim s.Si adorat furto, quod nec manifestum erit. & apud Plautum in Phasmate. Nec recte si illi dixerim : & Turpillium in De-metrio. Nec recte dici mihi quod iamdu-dum audio.hęc Festus in voce Nec.
units.tr: Grammarians generally say that the conjunction "nec" is disjunctive, as in "nec legit, nec sentit" (he neither reads nor understands). But if it is examined more carefully, as Sinnius Capito did, it can be understood that the ancients used it in place of "non", as also in the Twelve Tables: "If he prays over a theft, which will not be manifest"; and in Plautus in the Phasma: "nec recte, si illi dixerim" (not rightly, if I said it to him); and Turpilius in Demetrius: "nec recte dici mihi quod iamdudum audio" (not rightly said to me, what I have been hearing for some time). Festus, under the word "Nec".

units.la: 6. De furto pet lancem & licium concepto.
units.tr: 6. On theft settled by the platter and the licium.

units.la: Decemuiri in XII Tabulis ea furta quae damnadum: foeneratorem quadrupli. {e} hoc ver-bum non accipio simpliciter pro agere, sed pro pacisci: nam inter caetera, adorare significat propitiare, Nonius in ador: & alloqui Apuleius 2. infusa aqua populum sic adorat & lib. X. ad istum mo-dum seniore adorante. Constatque de furto pacisci l.7 §.14. inf. ff.de pactis ac decidere licuisse l.7 ff. de condict. furtiua.
units.tr: The Decemvirs in the Twelve Tables ordered that those thefts which should be claimed: a thief for double, a usurer for quadruple. I do not take this verb simply as "to sue", but as "to come to terms", for among its other senses "adorare" means "to propitiate" (Nonius, under "ador"), and "to address" (Apuleius, book 2: "having poured water, he thus adores the people", and book 10: "the elder adoring in that manner"). And it is established that one may come to an agreement about theft (law 7 §14 inf. ff. de pactis), and that it was lawful to settle it (law 7 ff. de condictione furtiva).

units.la: {e} runt, fure dupli damnadum: foeneratorem quadrupli. e hoc verbum non accipio simpliciter pro agere, sed pro pacisci: nam inter caetera, adorare significat propitiare, Nonius in ador: & alloqui Apuleius 2. infusa aqua populum sic adorat & lib. X. ad istum modum seniore adorante. Constatque de furto pacisci l.7 §.14. inf. ff.de pactis ac decidere licuisse l.7 ff. de condict. furtiua. {a}per lancem & licium concepta essent, perinde ac si manifesta furent, vindicauerunt haec Gell II.c.18.
units.tr: ...they ordered that a thief be condemned to double, a usurer to quadruple. I do not take this verb simply as "to sue", but as "to come to terms": for among other senses "adorare" means "to propitiate" (Nonius, under "ador"), and "to address" (Apuleius, book 2: "having poured water, he thus adores the people", and book 10: "the elder adoring in that manner"). It is established that one may come to an agreement about theft (law 7 §14 inf. ff. de pactis), and that it was lawful to settle it (law 7 ff. de condictione furtiva). Those thefts that were settled by the platter and the licium they treated as if they were manifest. Gellius 11.18.

units.la: Furtorum quaestiones cum lance & licio euanuerunt {b}haec Gell.16.c.10.
units.tr: The courts for thefts vanished along with the platter and the licium. Gellius 16.10.
7. On the Beam Joined to a Building.

units.la: Tignum {c}non solum in aedificiis quo vtimur appellatur, sed etiam in vineis, vt est in xi i. Tignum{d} iunctum{e} aedibus vineaeque {f}& concaput{g} ne{h} soluito. haec Festus in Tignum.
units.tr: A beam (tignum) is called so not only in buildings, which we use, but also in vineyards, as in the Twelve Tables, xi. book: "A beam joined to a house or to a vineyard, let him not release (soluito)"; and "& concaput" (and the head...). Thus Festus, under Tignum.
8. Trees Felled Secretly.

units.la: Fuit & arborum cura legibus, cautumque est xii.Tabulis vt qui iniuria arboresᵏ alienas cecidisset, lueret in singulas aris x x v. hæc Plinius 17.c.1.
units.tr: There was also concern for trees under the laws, and it was provided in the Twelve Tables that whoever had wrongfully felled another's trees should pay twenty-five asses for each one. Thus Pliny, book 17, chapter 1.
9. On Grazing and Cutting of Crops.

units.la: Frugem aratro quaesitam furtim noctu pauisse aut secuisse puberi xii. Tabulis capitale erat : suspensumque Cereri necari iubebant grauius quàm in homicidio conuictum. Impuberem Praetoris arbitratu verberari, nexamque duplione decerni. hæc Plinius 18. cap.3.
units.tr: Under the Twelve Tables it was a capital offence for an adult to graze or cut crops secretly at night from a field that had been tilled by the plough; and they ordered that the offender be hanged up and put to death for Ceres, the penalty being heavier than for a convicted murderer. A minor was to be beaten at the discretion of the praetor, and a debtor (nexus) was to be condemned to pay double. Thus Pliny, book 18, chapter 3.
10. On the Grazing of Livestock.

units.la: Si glans ex arbore tua in meum fundū cadat,eámque ego immissō pecore depascam: Aristo scribit,non sibi occurrere legitimam actionem qua experiri possim. Nam neque ex lege xii. Tabularum de pastu pecoris, quia nec in tuo pascatur: neque de pauperie, neque damni iniuria agi posse. in factum itaque erit agendum l.14.in f.ff. de praescriptis verbis.
units.tr: If an acorn falls from your tree into my field, and I feed it off by letting in my livestock, Aristo writes that no proper action occurs to him by which I could be sued. For it cannot be pursued under the Twelve Tables' law on the grazing of livestock, since the acorn is not grazed on your land; nor by the action for damage done by a quadruped (de pauperie), nor by the action for wrongful damage (damni iniuria). Therefore an action on the facts (in factum) must be brought, D. 14 in fine, Digest, On Praescriptis Verbis.
11. On Arson.

units.la: Caius libro 4. ad legem xii. Tabularū, Qui ædes aceruumue frumenti iuxta domum positum combusserit, vinctus, verberatus ignī necari iubetur:l.9.ff.de incendio.
units.tr: Gaius, book 4 on the law of the Twelve Tables: whoever burns a building or a heap of grain placed beside a house is ordered to be bound, beaten, and put to death by fire. D. 9, Digest, On Arson.
On Injuries.
TIT. XXV.
1. The ordinary penalty for injury is twenty-five asses.

units.la: NOnne tibi videtur esse dilutum, quod de iniuria punienda scriptum est, Si iniuria [lege iniuriam] alteri faxit, viginti-quinque aeris poena sunto. Quis enim erit tā inops, quem ab iniuria facienda [Pitheus legit iniuriae faciendae libidine] vigintiquinque asses deterreant? & post, Lucius Neratius pro delectamento habebat, os hominis liberi manus suæ palma verberare. Eum seruus sequebatur crumenam assium plenam portans: & quemcunque depalmauerat, numerari statim, secundum xii. Tabul. 25. asses iubebat. Propterea Prætores hanc legem abolescere & relinqui censuerunt, iniuriisque æstimandis recuperatores se daturos,edixerunt: & post, non omnino omnes iniurias ære isto pau-co diluerunt, tametsi hæc ipsa paucitas as-sium,graue pondus æris fuit. Nam libra-riis assibus in ea tempestate populus usus est: sed iniurias atrociores ut de osse[?] fra-cto[?],non liberis modo, verum etiam seruis factas impensiore damno vindicaverunt. hæc Gellius 20.c.1.
units.tr: Does it not seem to you that what is written about punishing injury has been refuted? "If anyone does an injury to another, let there be a penalty of twenty-five bronze asses." For who would be so poor that the fine of twenty-five asses would deter him from inflicting an injury? And afterwards: Lucius Neratius used to amuse himself by slapping the face of a free man with the palm of his hand. A slave followed him carrying a purse full of asses, and whomever he had slapped, he at once ordered to be paid out twenty-five asses, according to the Twelve Tables. For this reason the praetors decided that this law should fall into disuse and be set aside, and they declared that they would appoint recuperators to assess injuries. And afterwards: they did not wholly remove all injuries by this small fine, although this very smallness of the asses was a heavy burden of bronze. For at that time the people used pound-weight asses; but more atrocious injuries, such as a broken bone, done not only to free men but also to slaves, they punished with a heavier penalty. Thus Gellius, book 20, chapter 1.

units.la: Paulus libro singulari,& titulo de iniuriis apud Ruffinum Titul. 2. Collationis legum Mosaicarum. Iniuriarum, inquit, astio[?] aut legitima est aut honoraria. Legiti-ma ex lege xii. Tabularum, Qui iniuriam alteri facit quinque & viginti sestertiorum poena subit. quæ lex generalis fuit libero trecen-tas: *seruos CL. poenam subito sextertiorum.{a}
units.tr: Paulus, in a single book, under the title on injuries, as preserved by Rufinus, title 2 of the Collatio of the Mosaic and Roman Laws: "An action for injury," he says, "is either legitimate or honorary. The legitimate one comes from the Twelve Tables: He who does an injury to another incurs a penalty of twenty-five sesterces. This was the general law: for a free man 300, and for slaves 150, the penalty of sesterces."

units.la: 2. De membro aut osse[?] fracto & Talione.
units.tr: 2. On a broken limb or bone, and on talion.

units.la: Phavorinus,Nonnulla autem in istis legibus nec consistere quidem (sicut dixi) visa sunt, Velut illa lex Talionis, cuius verba (nisi memoria me fallit) hæc sunt, Si membrum rupit [Festus legit rapserit in vocem Talionis] [illegible, ~10 letters] pacit*. Festus ita legit d.loco ] talio b effo. Hęc Gellius 20.c.1.purior est autem lectio Festi quam Gellij.
units.tr: Phavorinus: "Some things in those laws, however, do not seem even to hold together (as I said), such as that law of talion, whose words (unless my memory deceives me) are these: 'If he has broken a limb,' [Festus reads 'if he has torn' in the wording of talion] [illegible, about ten letters] ... ." Festus reads the passage in that place thus: talion ... effo. Thus Gellius. The reading of Festus is, however, purer than that of Gellius.

units.la: Poena iniuriarum ex lege xij. Tabularum propter membrum quidem ruptum talio erat: ptopter os vero fractum, nummaria poena erant constituta, quasi in magna veterum paupertate: & postea poena iniuriae, quae ex lege xii. Tabularum introducta est, in desuetudinem abiit. haec Iustinianus in §.7.Inst.de Iniuriis.
units.tr: Under the Twelve Tables, the penalty for injury was talion for a broken limb; but for a broken bone fixed monetary penalties were laid down, as if in the great poverty of the ancients. Afterwards the penalty for injury introduced by the Twelve Tables fell into disuse. Thus Justinian in §7 of the Institutes, On Injuries.
5. On insults and defamatory libels.

units.la: Nostrae xii. Tabulae, cum perpaucas res capite sanxissent,in his quoque hanc fan ciendam putauerunt. Si quis actitauisset[?] legunt nonnulli occentaffet ] fiue carmen condidisset,quod infamiam faceret,flagitiumue alteri: haec Cicero 4. de Republica apud Augustinum 2,de ciuitate dei 9.
units.tr: Our Twelve Tables, although they had sanctioned very few matters with capital punishment, thought this one should also be enacted: "If anyone has composed a song [some read 'has sung a charm'] or a poem that would bring infamy or disgrace upon another." Thus Cicero, book 4 On the Republic, quoted by Augustine, The City of God, 2, chapter 9.

units.la: Talionis poena & exemplis dixi multis locis. Nouell. 60.cap.1: Nouell.[?]15.cap.3.§.13: Nouell.123.cap.xv: Nouell. Leonis 60. Lex Talionis iusta sit necne, vide apud 20. Gell.1. c Legibus 12. Tabularum capitale fuit conuicium, carmenve in alterius iniuriam facere.
units.tr: I have discussed the penalty of talion and its examples in many places: Novel 60, chapter 1; Novel 15, chapter 3, §13; Novel 123, chapter 15; Novel of Leo 60. Whether the law of talion is just or not, see Gellius, book 20, chapter 1. Under the Twelve Tables, to compose a poem or song against another's injury was a capital offence.

units.la: Secuta est alia poena, fustuaria &c. Horatius epistola ad Augustum, Quin etiam lex, poenaque lata malo quae nollet carmine quenquam describi, vertere modum formidine fustis, Ad benedicendum delectandumque redacti. adde Cornutum in Persium. Tertia successit poena infamiae de qua vide l.5.§.9.§.10.ff.de iniuriis: hodie poena famosi libelli, capitalis l.vnica Cod.de famosis libellis. d occentassint antiqui dicebant quod nunc conuicium fecerint dicimus, &c. Festus in occentassit. & hoc quidem verbo maledictum & conuicium prohibetur Paul.5.sent.4.§.18. e Psalterii, canticum, Paul.5.sent.4.§.15. famosos libellos §.16:librum l.5.§.9.ff. de iniuriis: επιγραμματα d.l.5.§.10. Famosum carmen quod legibus 12. Tabularum vindicatu testatur Paulus 5.sent. 4.§.6: l.21.ff.de testibus: l.18.in fine ff.qui testamenta. Carmen malu,quo fama alterius coinquinatur & vita Arnob.4.contra gentes.Horat. 2.satyr.1.si mala codiderit in que quis carmina,ius est iudiciumque.Carmen ad alterius iniuriam conditum.Cicero 4.Tusculo.
units.tr: Another penalty followed, the cudgel, etc. Horace, in his epistle to Augustus: "Indeed a law was passed, with a penalty, that no one should be defamed by a poem that he did not wish; they changed the measure by fear of the rod, and the poets were reduced to blessing and delighting." Add Cornutus on Persius. A third penalty followed, that of infamy, on which see Digest 47.10.5 §9 and §10, On Injuries; today the penalty for a defamatory libel is capital, the single law in the Code, On Defamatory Libels. The ancients said occentassint where we now say conuicium fecerint, and so on: Festus, under occentassit. This word also forbids abuse and insult: Paulus, Sentences 5.4 §18. The psalm, the canticle; Paulus, Sentences 5.4 §15; defamatory libels §16; the book, Digest 47.10.5 §9; epigrams, the same law §10. The Twelve Tables' defamatory poem is attested as subject to vengeance by Paulus, Sentences 5.4 §6; Digest 22.5.21; Digest 28.1.18 at the end. An evil song by which another's reputation and life are defiled, Arnobius, book 4, Against the Gentiles. Horace, Satires 2.1: if someone has written evil songs against anyone, there is a right and a court. A song composed to the injury of another, Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 4.
On extraordinary crimes. TITLE XXVI.
1. On the moving of a boundary stone.

units.la: NUma{a} Pompilius statuit, eum qui ter-minum exarasset & ipsum & boues eius sacros esse, Festus in Termino.
units.tr: Numa Pompilius decreed that whoever ploughed up a boundary, he and his oxen were to be sacred, Festus under "Terminus."

units.la: Hanc legem ita restituit Josephus Scali-ger, Quei terminum exarasit, ipsus & boueus[?] sacrei sunto.
units.tr: Joseph Scaliger restored this law thus: Whoever has ploughed up a boundary, he and his oxen are to be sacred.
2. On the prevarication of a patron against a client.

units.la: Seruius ad illos versus Virgilij 6. Æneidos 609.610. Hic, quibus invisi fratres, dū vita manebat, pulsatúsve parens, & fraus innexa clienti. Ex lege,inquit, xii. Tabularum venit, in quibus scriptum est. Patronus si clienti{c} fraudem fecerit, sacer esto. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Servius, on those lines of Virgil's Aeneid 6 (609–610), "Here are those whom hated brothers, while life remained, or a struck parent, and the fraud woven against a client." "From the law of the Twelve Tables," he says, "in which it is written: If a patron has committed fraud against his client, let him be accursed." So far Servius.
3. On illegal associations.

units.la: maiores,inquit,fandius habuere defendi pupillos, quàm clientem non fallere, adversus cognatos pro cliente testatur. Testimonium adversus clientem nemo dicit. Patrem primum, postea patronum proximum nomen habere. Massurius autem Sabinus lib. antiquiorem locum tribuit hospiti, quàm clienti. Verba ex eo libro hæc sūt. In officiis apud maiores ita observatū est, primum tutelæ, deinde hospiti, deinde clienti, tum cognato, post-ea affini. De qua causa fœminæ viris potiores sunt habitæ, pupillarisque tutela muliebri prælata: etiam adversus quem assuerunt[?] eius filij tutores relicti, in eadem causa pupillo aderant. & post C.Cæsar in oratione quam pro Bithyniis dixit, Neque clientes,inquit, sine summa infamia deseri possunt, quibus etiam a propinquis nostris opem ferre instituimus. Idem Gellius 20.cap.1. Clientem in fidem acceptum chariorem habere, quàm propinquos, tuendumque contra cognatos censuit. Neque peius vllum facinus æstimatum est, quàm si quis probaretur clientem derisui habuisse,&c.
units.tr: "The men of old," he says, "thought it more right to defend orphans than not to deceive a client"; he testifies that, against relatives, one stands up for a client. No one gives testimony against a client. The father holds the first name, afterwards the patron the nearest. Massurius Sabinus, in his book, gives an earlier place to the host than to the client. His words from that book are these: "In the duties observed among our ancestors, first comes guardianship, then hospitality, then clientship, then kinship, afterwards affinity. For this reason women were regarded as more powerful than men, and a ward's guardianship was preferred to a woman's; even against the person whose sons had been left to them as guardians, in that same case they stood by the ward." Afterwards C. Caesar, in the speech he delivered for the Bithynians: "Clients cannot be abandoned without the greatest infamy, whom we have also established to bring aid even against our own kinsmen." The same Gellius, book 20, chapter 1: "He judged that a client received into protection should be held dearer than kinsmen, and defended against one's relatives. Nor has any worse crime been reckoned than if someone were shown to have made a client an object of ridicule," etc.

units.la: Duodecim Tabulis cautum esse cognoscimus, Ne quis in vrbe coetus noctu agitaret: deinde lege Gabinia promulgatum, qui conciones vllas in vrbe conflauisset, more maiorum, capitali supplicio multaretur. de te itaque Catilina sciscitor, tunc coetus istos commilitonum tuorum contra praecepta xii. Tabularum, contra leges nostras, contra senatus ac plebis authoritatem, noctu cogendos esse putauisti? haec Porcius Latro in declamatione aduersus Catilinam.
units.tr: We learn that the Twelve Tables provided that no one should hold a gathering in the city at night; then by the Gabinian law it was promulgated that whoever had called together any assemblies in the city should, according to the custom of our ancestors, be punished with capital punishment. So I ask you about yourself, Catiline: did you think those gatherings of your fellow soldiers should be held by night against the precepts of the Twelve Tables, against our laws, against the authority of the senate and the people? So Porcius Latro in his declamation against Catiline.
On public trials.
TIT. XXVII.
1. On accusations.

units.la: INterfici indemnatum{a} quemcunque hominem, etiam xij. Tabularum decreta vetuerunt. Hec Saluianus episcopus Massiliensis 8. de iudicio & prouidentia.
units.tr: Even the decrees of the Twelve Tables forbade that any man whatsoever be put to death unheard. So Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, book 8, On Judgment and Providence.
2. On the crime of treason.

units.la: Lex xij. Tabularum iubet eum, qui hostem concitauerit{c}, quiue ciuem hosti{b} tradiderit, capite puniri. Marcianus in lege 3. ff. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis.
units.tr: The Law of the Twelve Tables orders that whoever stirs up an enemy, or hands a citizen over to an enemy, be punished by death. Marcianus, in law 3, Digest, On the Julian Law of Treason.
3. On Adultery.

units.la: Matronas prostrata pudicitia, quibus accusator publicus deesset, vt propinqui maiorum more de communi{d} sententia coercerent, Tiberius author fuit. Suetonius in Tiberio capite 35.
units.tr: Tiberius was the author of the measure that, where matrons' chastity had been ruined and there was no public accuser, their relatives should punish them by common sentence, after the custom of the ancestors. Suetonius, Tiberius, chapter 35.

units.la: 4. In adulterio vxores deprehensas ius fuisse maritis necare. [?]
units.tr: 4. That in adultery husbands had the right to kill wives caught in the act. [?]

units.la: In adulterio vxorem tuam si deprehendisses, sine iudicio impune necares illa te(si adultera-res)digito non auderet contingere, neque tus est.
units.tr: If you had caught your wife in adultery, you could kill her without trial and with impunity; she would not dare to touch you even with a finger, nor is it right.

units.la: Cato in oratione de dote apud io. Gell.23. [?]
units.tr: Cato, in his speech On the Dowry, cited by Gellius, book 23. [?]
5. On the concubine.

units.la: Pellices nunc quidem appellantur alienis succumbentes non solum foeminis sed etiam mares. Antiqui eam proprie pellicem nominabant, quae vxore habenti nubebat: cui generi mulierum etiam poena constituta est a Numa Pompilio hac lege. Pellex aram Iunonis ne tangito: si tanget, Iunoni crinibus demissis agnum foeminam caedito. haec Festus in voce Pellices, & Gellius 4.c.3.init.
units.tr: Nowadays "pellices" are called those who give in to other people's partners, not only women but also men. The ancients properly used the name for a woman who married a man who already had a wife. Numa Pompilius also set a penalty for this class of women in this law: "Let a pellex not touch the altar of Juno; if she touches it, let her sacrifice a female lamb to Juno, with her hair loose." So Festus, under the word Pellices, and Gellius, 4.3 at the beginning.
6. On assassins.

units.la: Id autem fuisse indicat lex Numae Pompilij regis, his composita verbis. Si quis he-[?]minem liberum dolo sciens morti duit, parricida esto. Festus in Parricida. Sei imprudens se{c} dolo malo occisit, pro capite occisei, & natus eius in concione arietem subiicito{d}. Iosephus Scaliger apud Festum in Subici, hanc partem ita restituit ex schediis Seruianis.
units.tr: That this was so is shown by the law of King Numa Pompilius, composed in these words: "If anyone knowingly kills a free man by guile, let him be a parricide." Festus, under Parricida. "But if he killed without intent, yet with malice, let him, for the head of the one slain, and his son, put a ram before the assembly." Joseph Scaliger, citing Festus under Subici, restored this part in this way from the papers of Servius.
7. On parricide.

units.la: Plorare, flere, inclamare, idem significat & cum praepositione implorare, est inuocare. at apud antiquos plane inclamare. Regis Romuli & Latij (lege Tatij & Seruij Tullij) legibus, Si parentes puer verberit, ast olle(lege olce) plorassint(lege plorassint) parentes, puer dimittere parentum facere esto. Si nurus, sacra diuus parentum esto. haec Festus in plorare, apud quem tamen quae pars huius legis de nuru loquitur ordine praecedit anteriore. Preistat autem eam legem ita restituit fecu-[?]
units.tr: Plorare, flere, inclamare mean the same, and with the preposition, implorare, means to invoke; but among the ancients it was plainly inclamare. In the laws of Kings Romulus and Latius (read Tatius) and Servius Tullius: "If a boy strikes his parents, and the parents have cried out (read olce), let the boy be released from his parents' authority. If a daughter-in-law [...], let her be sacred to the parents' gods." So Festus, under plorare, though the part of this law that concerns the daughter-in-law comes earlier in his order. He restored that law in this way, as follows:
8. On poisonings.

units.la: Caius libro 4. ad legem xii.Tabularū, {a}Qui venenum, inquit dicit, adjicere debet utrum malum an bonum,&c. l.23. ff.de verborum significatione.
units.tr: Gaius, book 4 on the Law of the Twelve Tables: "He who adds poison, he says, ought to say whether it is bad or good," etc. Law 23, Digest, On the meaning of words.
9. On false witness.

units.la: An putas Phauorine, si non illa etiam ex xij. Tabulis, de testimoniis: si fis poena abolevisset, et si nunc quoque, tu antea qui si suum testimonium dixisse convictus esset, e saxo Tarpeio deiiceretur, mentiturosque fuisse pro testimonio tam multos, quam videmus? hæc Gellius 20.c.1. in fine.
units.tr: Do you think, Phavorinus, that if that penalty had not been abolished, which was also in the Twelve Tables concerning witnesses, namely that one convicted of giving false testimony should be thrown from the Tarpeian rock, so many men would lie as witnesses as we now see? So Gellius, 20.1, at the end.
10. On evil-doing.

units.la: Quid? nō & legum iplarū in xii. Tabulis verba sunt? si fruges excantasset, & alibi, qui malum carmen incantasset. hæc Plinius 28.c.2.
units.tr: What? Are not the words of the laws themselves in the Twelve Tables: "If he had charmed away the crops," and elsewhere, "who had sung an evil charm"? So Pliny, 28.2.

units.la: Hac pestifera sceleratáque doctrina, Fructus alieni in alias terras transferri perhibetur, nónne in xii. Tabulis, i. Romanorum, antiquissimis legibus Cicero commemorat esse conscriptum, & ei qui hoc fecerit supplicium constitutum? hæc Augustinus 8. de ciuitate dei 19.
units.tr: Through this pernicious and wicked doctrine, the fruits of another's field are said to be carried off into other lands. Does not Cicero record that this was written in the Twelve Tables, that is, in the most ancient laws of the Romans, and that a penalty was established for whoever did it? So Augustine, City of God, book 8, chapter 19.

units.la: Et apud nos in xii. Tabulis cauetur, ne quis alienos fructus excantasset. Rudis adhuc antiquitas credebat, & attrahi imbres <bl>cantibus</bl> & repelli: quorum nihil posse fieri, tam palam est, vt huius rei causa nullius Philosophi schola intranda sit, haec Seneca 4.Naturalium 7.in f.
units.tr: Among us too, the Twelve Tables provide that no one may charm away another's crops. Rude antiquity believed that rains could be drawn down by charms and driven off by them; and since none of this can happen, it is so plain that no philosopher's school need be entered for the matter. So Seneca, Natural Questions, book 4, chapter 7, at the end.

units.la: 11. De lege Iulia repetundarum, & corrupto iudice.
units.tr: 11. On the Julian law on extortion, and on a corrupt judge.

units.la: De Iudice qui ob rem dicendam pecuniam accepserit, dixi s.ad Titul.dei udiciis.
units.tr: I discussed above, under the title On Judgments, the judge who has taken money for pronouncing a sentence.
12. On false claims of ownership.

units.la: Dixi s.ad Titulum de Possessionibus & interdictis.
units.tr: I discussed above, under the title On Possessions and Interdicts.
On captives.
TIT. XXVIII.

units.la: Sanates dicti sunt, qui supra infraque Romam habitauerunt, quia cum defecissent a Romanis, breui post redierunt in amicitiam, quasi sanata mente. Itaque in xii. cautum est, Vt{*} idem{b} iuris esset sanatibus, quod fortibus [quidam legunt fortibus] id est bonis, & qui nunquam defecerunt a populo Romano, Festus in sanates.
units.tr: Those were called Sanates who lived above and below Rome, because after they had revolted from the Romans, they soon returned to friendship, as if their minds had been healed. Hence it was provided in the Twelve Tables that the Sanates should have the same right as the fortes [some read "fortibus"], that is, the good, and those who never revolted from the Roman people. Festus, under "sanates."
The end of the laws of the Twelve Tables.
Titles from the Body of Ulpian.

units.la: DE LEGIBVS{a} ET MO-ribus{6},& libertis. TIT. I.
units.tr: On Laws and Customs, and on Freedmen. Title I.

units.la: IMPERFECTA lex est veluti {c}Cincia, quae supra certum modum donari prohibet, exceptis quibusdam cognatis: & , si plus donatum sit, non {d}rescindit. Plautus eam muneralem appellat apud Festum.
units.tr: An imperfect law is, for example, the Cincian law, which forbids gifts beyond a certain amount, except to certain relatives; and if more than that has been given, it does not rescind the gift. Plautus calls it the "muneral" law, according to Festus.

units.la: 2 Minus quàm perfecta lex est, quae vetat aliquid fieri: &,si factum fit,non rescindit: sed poenam iniungit ei qui contra legem fecit,qualis est lex Furia {e}testamentaria,quae plus quàm mille assium legatum, mortiue causa prohibet capere: praeter exceptas personas: & adversus eum qui plus ceperit,quadrupli poenam constituit.
units.tr: A law less than perfect is one that forbids something to be done, and if it is done, does not annul it, but imposes a penalty on the one who acted against the law. Such is the Furian testamentary law, which forbids anyone to take, by reason of death, a legacy of more than a thousand asses, apart from the excepted persons, and which sets a fourfold penalty against the one who has taken more.

units.la: 3 Lex aut {f}rogatur,id est,fertur: aut abrogatur, id est,prior lex tollitur: aut derogatur,i.pars prima tollitur: aut subrogatur, i. adiicitur aliquid primae legi: aut abrogatur, id est, mutatur aliquid ex prima lege.
units.tr: A law is either proposed (rogatur), that is, brought forward; or abrogated, that is, an earlier law is removed altogether; or derogated, that is, the first part of a law is removed; or subrogated, that is, something is added to the first law; or obrogated, that is, something in the first law is changed.
Customs are the tacit consent of the people, grown old through long practice.
There are three kinds of freedmen: Roman citizens, Junian Latins, and those of the class of dediticii.

units.la: 6 Ciues Romani sunt liberti,qui vindicta {o},cen-su {p}, aut testamento {q}, nullo iure impediente ma-
units.tr: Roman citizens are the freedmen who, with no legal impediment, were manumitted by the rod, by the census, or by will, and were declared (not by vote, but by the facts and deeds themselves) free.

units.la: 39.40.ff. de legibus.sine scripto d.§.9: non suffragio, sed rebus ipsis & factis declaratus,d.l.33.v.tit.C.quae sit longa consuetudo. i d.l.35. inueterata d.l.33.§.1:diuturna d.l.34. k Caius 1.Instit.1. verf.libertorum. Libertorum status tripertitus §.3.Institut. de libertinis.
units.tr: On the Digest, de legibus (39.40); "without writing" (sine scripto), see §9 of the same; on what constitutes long custom, see the law 33 of the title; "grown old" (inueterata), law 35; "of long standing" (diuturna), law 34. Gaius, Institutes 1, on freedmen: the status of freedmen is threefold, Institutes §3 on freedmen.

units.la: l Ciues autem Romani fiunt tribus modis [?].eo.§.6. Caius 1.Inst.2. m §.10.[?].eo. n §.11.[?].eo. o v.§.7.[?]. p v.§.8.[?]. q v.§.9.[?] numissi sunt.
units.tr: Roman citizens are made in three ways (see the same title, §6; Gaius, Institutes 2). On the rest, see the same title, §§10 and 11; the rod (vindicta) is §7 and the census §8; the will is §9.

units.la: 7 Vindicta {a}manumittuntur apud magistratu, velut Prætorem {b},Consulem {c}, Proconsulem {d}.
units.tr: Those manumitted by the rod are freed before a magistrate, such as the praetor, the consul, or the proconsul.

units.la: 8 Censu manumittebantur olim, qui lustrali {e}censu Romæ, iussu dominorum, inter ciues Romanos censum {f}profitebantur.
units.tr: Formerly, those were manumitted by the census who, at the lustral census at Rome, declared themselves among the Roman citizens at the command of their masters. (The lustrum is a period of five years; on the form of the census see the title of the Digest on censuses.)

units.la: 9 Vt testameto {g}manumissi liberi sint, lex duodecim Tabularum facit, quæ confirmat, quod datu {h}legatum est:
units.tr: That slaves manumitted by will become free, the Law of the Twelve Tables provides, which confirms what has been bequeathed.

units.la: 10 Hodie autem ipso iure liberi sunt ex lege siquæ[?] hodie per tutorem verbáque solemnia, sicet non dicantur, vt dicta accipiuntur l.23.ff. d.tit. Porrò, Theophilus id genus manumissionis ex eo dictum putat, quod eo vindicatetur mancipium in naturalem libertatem (& male. Nam si ita esset, qui censu vel testamento manumittere-tur, vindicta quoque manumitti diceretur) vel à Vindice quoda[?], qui, cum seruus esset, eruptuam[?] aduersus Romanos coniurationem indicio suo patefecit, publiceque à Romanis manumissus est, & in honorem eius, quicunque apud magistratum manumittebatur, vindicta manumissi dicebatur, Theophil. §. καὶ τῆς μὲν Instit. de libert. Coniurationis à Vindice detectæ meminit quidem Liuius 2. Est etiam verisimile, vindicta manumissionem dici, quod lictor l.8. l. 23.ff. de manumiss. vindict: virgulam seruo manumittendo imponeret. Persius, Vindicta postquam meus à prætore recessi. & post, Non in festuca lictor quam gestat inani. Virgulam, inquam, quæ vindicta diceretur Boet. in Topic. Plutarchus de sera numinis vindicta κὲ ἀρρῶν λεῖ[?] appellat. hinc vindictam imponere l.14. in f. ff. de manumissionibus: l.12.§.2.ff. de liberali: l.19.§.4.ff. de castrensi peculio: l.2.Cod.si aduersus libertat. {b} l.1.l.8.ff. de manumiss. vindicta: l.4.Cod. de vindicta manumiss: l.1. Cod. de off. prætor: l.1.ff. de off. præt. {c} d.l.4: l.1.§.1.§.2.ff. de off. consul: l.20. in f.ff. de manumiss. vindict. {d} l.2 ff. de off. proconsul: l.17.ff. de manumiss. vindicta: & ita legendum est in lege 4. non prasules. An & apud alios? vtique apud magistratus ciuitatum, quibus huiusmodi ius est, v.d. l.4. in fine, apud magistratus municipales. hi habent legis actionem, Paul.2.sententt.25 §.4: apud Prætectum Aegypti l.21.ff. de manumiss. vindict: apud legatum proconsulis l.17.in f.ff. d.tit. quin apud ipsum imperatorem l.14.in f.ff. de manumissionibus. {e} Lustrum, spatium quinque annorum. de forma censendi vide titulum ff. de censibus. {f} id est, facultatem & libertatem suam, v.
