units.tr: {p} Pictures (picturis). See d.l.79 at the end, ff. [illegible]. Eclog. as cited. Cujas emends it; he bears witness in Obs. 6, c.37.

units.la: {q} v.d.l.79. in f. r v.14.ff.1: Paul.1.sentent.23.
units.tr: {q} See d.l.79 at the end; r; see l.14 ff.1; Paul. 1 Sent. 23.

units.la: {s} nota regulam. t ne mutuo amore spolientur v.l.1. in f.l.1.l.3 in pr. & §.10.ff.eo. u Exceptio regulae superioris. x id est, cu. mors insequetur l.9 §.2.l.1.§.1.ff.eo. Mortis causa donatio fit impendente metu mortis. Mors impendet quidem omnibus, eaque semper certa est, etiamsi incertum diem habeat l.68. in f.ff.de leg. 1: l.1. §.2.ff.de conditi. & demonst. Metum tamen hic, instantem inteligere l.6.ff.de mort.caus. Initat autem non tantum infirmo, sed peregrinaturo, navigaturo, militi Paul.1.sent.24.§.1: ifer facturo per insidiosa loca, feni l.3 l. 4 l.5 ff.de mort.causa. Id genus donationis morte donatoris conualescit Paul.d.loco §.vit. Morte donatatij,res redit uorrij caussa, seruï manumittendi gratia. Hoc ad eum qui donauit amplius principalibus constitutionibus concessum est mulieri, in hoc donare viro suo, vt is ab Imperatore, latoclauo, vel equo publico, similiue honorem.
units.tr: {s} Note the rule. t Let them not be despoiled by mutual love; see l.1 at the end, l.1, l.3 in pr. and §10 ff. eo. u An exception to the above rule. x That is, when death follows; l.9 §2, l.1 §1 ff. eo. A gift in contemplation of death is made when death is imminent. Death indeed threatens all men, and it is always certain, even if its day is uncertain; l.68 at the end, ff. de leg. 1; l.1 §2 ff. de condit. et demonst. Here, however, "fear" must be understood as imminent; l.6 ff. de mortis causa. It is made not only by the sick, but by one about to travel, to sail, or to go to war, or by one about to make a journey through dangerous places; Paul. 1 Sent. 24 §1; ff. de mortis causa, l.3, l.4, l.5. This kind of gift is confirmed if the donor survives. Paul, loc. cit., §Vit. A gift in contemplation of death is made, for example, of a thing that returns to the donor; for the sake of manumitting a slave. By imperial constitutions, this is granted to a woman, beyond the principal ones, that she may give to her husband so that he may obtain from the Emperor the broad stripe, a horse at public expense, or a similar honour.

units.la: Si maritus diuortij caussa res mouerit, retinebitur quoque amotarum actione tenebitur.
units.tr: If a husband has removed goods for the sake of divorce, he shall also be liable to the action for things removed.

units.la: Si maritus pro muliere se obligauerit, vel in rem eius impenderit, diuortio facto, eo nomine cauere sibi solet stipulatione tribunitia.
units.tr: If a husband has bound himself on behalf of his wife, or has expended money on her property, then, when a divorce has taken place, he is accustomed to secure himself on that account by a tribunician stipulation.

units.la: In potestate parentum sunt etiam ij liberi quorum causa probata est, per errorem contracto matrimonio inter dispares condignis personas. Nam seu ciuis Romanus Latinam, aut peregrinam, vel eam, quae Dediticiorum numero est, quae per ignorantiam vxorem duxerit: siue ciuis Romana per errorem peregrino, vel ei qui Dediticiorum numero est, aut etiam Latino ex lege Aelia Sentia nupta fuerit, causa probata, ciuitas redditur tam liberis quam parentibus, praeter eos qui Dediticiorum numero sunt, & ex eo fiunt in potestate parentum liberi.
units.tr: Those children also are in the power of their parents whose status has been proven, when a marriage has been contracted through error between persons who are unequal yet suitable to one another. For if a Roman citizen, through ignorance, has taken as wife a Latin, a foreigner, or a woman of the class of the Dediticii; or if a Roman woman, through error, has been married to a foreigner, to a man of the class of the Dediticii, or even to a Latin under the lex Aelia Sentia, and the cause is proven, citizenship is restored both to the children and to the parents, except for those who belong to the class of the Dediticii, and children born from such a union come into the power of their parents.
On Adoptions. Title 8.

units.la: Non tantum naturales liberi in potestate parentum sunt, sed etiam adoptiui.
units.tr: Not only natural children are under the power of their parents, but adopted children too.

units.la: Adoptio fit aut per populum, aut per principem.
units.tr: Adoption takes place either by the people or by the prince.

units.la: a Cur ita? Fa uore libertatis id receptum est, vel potius, quod nemo huiusmodi re donata fiat locupletior. Paul.d.loco §. 2: adde l.7. §. 3.§.vlt: l.8.l. 9.ff.eod. b Actio rerum amotarum datur etiam in maritum l.6.§.2.ff.rer.amotar. c i. constitutione Antonini l.41. & 42.ff.eod. d d.l. 42. e i.vt equestris conditionis fieret d.l.42. f Idem dicendum est de rebus donatis sepulturae causa l.5.§.8.9.10.11.ff.eodem: ad oblationem dei d.l.5.§.12: ad processus d. l.41. g d.l.41.42: l.45.ff.de negotiis: l.11.ff.de muneribus. h Actio rerum amotarum datur etiam in maritum l.6.§.2.ff.rer.amotar. i v.l.2.ff.de negotiis: l.28.ff.soluto. k l.7.in f. ff.soluto: & Titul.ff.de impensis. l l.25.in f.l.55.ff.soluto. m Stipulatio Tribunitia quae ex Iurisdictione Tribunorum venit: vt Praetoria, a Praetore: aedilitia ab aedilibus. n disparis condicionis Cuiacius. o dixi ad tit. 5.§.8.ʒ.eodem. p Ignoratia, errorem in nuptiis commissum excusat, facit l.57.§.1.ff.de vitu: lege 22.in fine ff.soluto: Novel.12. capite 1.in fine. q adde titul.3.§.3.§.eodem. r vide 1.ff.7. s vide leg.1. ff.eodem: 8.Cod.48: Institut.eodem, in principio: Caium 5. t vide §.3. §.eodem. per Praetorem {a}, vel Praesidem {b} prouinciae. Illa adoptio quae per populum fit, specialiter arrogatio dicitur {c}.
units.tr: Why so? This was adopted out of favour to liberty, or rather because no one is made richer by such a gift. Paul, d. loco §2; add l.7 §3, §last; l.8, l.9 ff. eod. b. The action for stolen goods is given also against the husband, l.6 §2 ff. rer. amotar. c. That is, by a constitution of Antoninus, l.41 and 42 ff. eod. d. d.l.42. e. That is, that he might become of equestrian rank, d.l.42. f. The same must be said of things given for the sake of burial, l.5 §§8, 9, 10, 11 ff. eod.; for an offering to God, d.l.5 §12; for legal proceedings, d.l.41. g. d.l.41, 42; l.45 ff. de negotiis; l.11 ff. de muneribus. h. The action for stolen goods is given also against the husband, l.6 §2 ff. rer. amotar. i. See l.2 ff. de negotiis, l.28 ff. soluto. k. l.7 in fine ff. soluto, and the title ff. de impensis. l. l.25 in fine, l.55 ff. soluto. m. A tribunician stipulation, which comes from the jurisdiction of the tribunes, as the praetorian comes from the praetor and the aedilician from the aediles. n. Of unequal condition, Cujas. o. I have said so at title 5, §8, and §3 of this title. p. Ignorance excuses an error committed in marriage; see l.57 §1 ff. de ritu nuptiarum, lex 22 in fine ff. soluto, Novel. 12, chapter 1 in fine. q. Add title 3, §3 and §3 of this title. r. See l.1 ff. eod.; 8 Cod. 48; Institutes of this title, at the beginning; Gaius 5. s. See §3 of this title. By the praetor {a}, or by the governor {b} of a province. That adoption which is made by the people is specially called arrogation {c}.

units.la: 3 Per populum {d}, qui sui {e} iuris sunt {f}. Per Praetorem autem, filij familiae {g} a parentibus dantur in adoptionem.
units.tr: 3. By the people, those who are sui iuris. By the praetor, however, children under paternal power are given in adoption by their parents.

units.la: 4 Arrogatio Romae {h} tantum fit: adoptio autem, etiam {i} in prouincia apud Praesidem.
units.tr: 4. Arrogation takes place only at Rome; adoption, however, also in a province before the governor.

units.la: 5 Per Praetorem vel Praesidem prouinciae adoptari tam masculi quam feminae, & tam puberes quam impuberes possunt. Per populum vero Romanum quidem non arrogantur {k}. Pupilli {l} antea quidem non {m} poterant arrogari: nunc autem possunt ex constitutione Diui Antonini.
units.tr: 5. By the praetor or the governor of a province, both males and females, and both pubescent and impubescent persons, may be adopted. By the Roman people, however, women are not arrogated. Pupils could formerly not be arrogated, but now they can, by a constitution of the divine Antoninus.

units.la: 6 Hi qui generare non possunt, velut spado {n}, utroque modo possunt adoptare. Idem iuris est in coelibe {o}.
units.tr: 6. Those who cannot beget children, such as a eunuch, may adopt in either way. The same law applies to an unmarried man.

units.la: 7 Item is {p} qui filium non habet, in locum nepotis adoptare potest.
units.tr: 7. Likewise, a man who has no son may adopt in place of a grandson.

units.la: 8 Si paterfamilias arrogandum sese dederit, liberi {q} quoque eius quasi nepotes, in potestate fiunt arrogatoris {r}.
units.tr: 8. If a head of household has given himself up to be arrogated, his children also, as grandchildren, come into the power of the arrogator.

units.la: 9 Feminae {s} vero neutro modo possunt {t} adoptare, quoniam {u} nec naturales liberos in potestate habent.
units.tr: 9. Women, however, can adopt in neither way, since they do not even have natural children in their power.

units.la: DE HIS QVI IN MANV SVNT. TIT. IX.
units.tr: On Those Who Are in Manus. Title 9.

units.la: qui non habebat, adrogabatur Caius 5.§.2. {h} quia fiebat apud populum. Nullibi autem populus Romanus extra Romam quaerendus erat. Fiebatque Romae curiatis comitiis 5. Gell.19. {i} quia in prouinciis erant praesides. {k} Nec arrogantur. ita legendum est ex 5.Gell.15. Causa illa erat, quod nulla cum feminis comitiorum communio esset. Fiebat autem adrogatio in comitiis. Gell.d. loco. & tamen principis rescripto adrogari possunt, l.21.ff.eod l l.17.l.18.l.20.§.1.ff.eod. {m} quia tutoribus in pupillos tantam esse authoritatem non erat, vt caput liberorum fidei suae commissum, alienae ditioni subiicerent 20. Gell.19. {n} l.2. §.1.l.40.in f.ff.eod: §.9.Inst.eo.1.Caius 5.§.4. {o} l.30.ff.eo.Coelebs est qui vxorem non habet. {p} l.37.ff.codem: §.7. Inst.eodem. {q} l.40.ff.codem. §.11.Inst.codem.1.Caius 5.§.vlt. {r} §.10.Inst.eod: l.5.Cod.eod. {s} Possunt tamen iussu principis adoptare l.29.§.3.ff.de inofficioso. {t} d.l.5.
units.tr: One who had no children was adrogated, Gaius 5 §2, because it was done before the people. Nowhere, however, was the Roman people to be sought outside Rome. It was done at Rome in the curiate assembly, Gellius 19, because in the provinces there were governors. Nor can women be adrogated; this is how the text should be read, from Gellius 15. The reason was that women had no share in the assemblies. Adrogation was done in the assembly, Gellius, loc. cit. Yet they can be adrogated by imperial rescript, l. 21 ff. eod.; l. 17; l. 18; l. 20 §1 ff. eod., because guardians did not have such authority over their wards that they could subject to another's power the head of children entrusted to their good faith, Gellius 20 and 19. l. 2 §1; l. 40 in fine ff. eod.; §9 Inst. eo.; Gaius 5 §4. l. 30 ff. eo. A bachelor is one who has no wife. l. 37 ff. codem; §7 Inst. eodem. l. 40 ff. codem; §11 Inst. codem; Gaius 5 §ult. §10 Inst. eod.; l. 5 Cod. eod. They can, however, adopt by the emperor's command, l. 29 §3 ff. de inofficioso. d. l. 5.

units.la: {h} l.5.Cod.eod. {i} Possunt tamen iussu principis adoptare l.29.§.3.ff.de inofficioso.
units.tr: l. 5 Cod. eod. They can, however, adopt by the emperor's command, l. 29 §3 ff. de inofficioso.

units.la: FARRE{a} conuenitur{b} in manu, certis verbis, & testibus X. præsenti-bus, & solenni{c} sacrificio facto, in quo panis{d} quoque farreus adhibe-tur.
units.tr: By confarreation (farre) one comes into manus, with set words, ten witnesses being present, and a solemn sacrifice having been performed, in which bread of spelt is also used.

units.la: QVI IN POTESTATE MANCIPIOVE SVNT, QVEM-admodum ex jure liberentur{e}.
units.tr: Those Who Are in Potestas or Mancipium, and How They Are Freed by Law.
TITLE X.

units.la: in manu pro quo Tribonianus dixit conuenire l.17.ff.rer.amot:couenire[?] in matrimonium l.13.ff.de ritu:l.12.§.1.ff.de verb.obl. quo genere loquendi usus est etiam Gellius 18.c.6. Conuentio in manum fiebat, etiam coemptione Cicero pro L. Flacco. In manum conuenerant: nunc audio, sed quæro utrum usu an coemptione? Farre(vn-de confarreatio, vel, vt Plinius 18.c.3. loquitur, confarratio: cui contraria dissarreatio, Fest. in voce Diffarreatio.) quo tantum genere Flamen Dialis Flaminiæ jungebatur Seru.4.Aeneid. ex eo matrimonio qui nascebantur patrimi & matrimi dicebantur Fest. in voce Flaminia: Seru.1.Georgic:1.Gell.12. Ex patrimis tres simul nominabantur, vt ex iis unus Flamen Dialis legeretur Tacit.4.Annal. Sed quia confarreandi adsuetudo omissa, aut inter paucos re-tenta propter incuriam virorum & fœminarum, & ipsius ceremo-niæ difficultatem: tum quòd qui ita conueniebant, de patria exibant potestate, placuit Tiberij tempore, vt Flaminica Dialis in potestate viri esset, cæteri promiscuè genere fœminarum agerent. Et hoc quidem genere nuptiarum postea non soli Flamines usi videntur, sed & alij: quòd hic innuitur, ibi, in quo panis quo-que farreus. Coemptione vero fiebat matrimonium Seru.1.Geor-gic: libra & ære adhibitis Seru.4.Aeneid. Eaque solennitate præeunte uxor quasi emebatur: eiusque coemptionis is erat ef-sectus, vt quæ ita in manum viri conuenisset, ea viro sua hæres esset Caius 3.Instit: apud Ruffinum, authore collationis legum Mosai-carum tit.16: adde Gel.18.c.6. in f[?]:adde quæ scripsi ad tit.C.de sponsalib. his adde Petr.Pithei 16.Notar.Mosaic.
units.tr: Into the hand [in manu], for which Tribonian said "to agree" (l.17.ff.rer.amot; couenire[?]) and "into marriage" (l.13.ff.de ritu; l.12.§.1.ff.de verb.obl.). Gellius also used this way of speaking (18.c.6). A conventio into the hand was made also by coemptio, as Cicero says in the speech for L. Flaccus: "They had come into the hand; now I hear it, but I ask whether by usus or by coemptio?" Confarreatio (so called from far, spelt; Plinius 18.c.3 calls it confarratio), whose opposite is dissarreatio (Fest. in voce Diffarreatio.), was the only kind by which the Flamen Dialis was joined in marriage to the Flaminica (Seru.4.Aeneid.). Children born of that marriage were called patrimi and matrimi (Fest. in voce Flaminia: Seru.1.Georgic:1.Gell.12.). Three of the patrimi were named together, so that one of them might be chosen as Flamen Dialis (Tacit.4.Annal.). But because the custom of confarreatio fell into disuse, or was kept up only by a few, through the carelessness of men and women and the difficulty of the ceremony, and because those who married in this way passed out of their father's power, it was decided in the reign of Tiberius that the Flaminica Dialis should be in her husband's power, while the other women should be dealt with in the common manner. Afterwards it seems that not only the Flamines used this kind of marriage but others too, as the passage there, where bread is also spelt, implies. Marriage by coemptio was made Seru.1.Georgic: with scales and bronze being used Seru.4.Aeneid.; with this solemnity going before, the wife was as it were bought, and the effect of this coemption was that a woman who had so come into the hand of her husband became his heir (Caius 3.Instit: apud Ruffinum, authore collationis legum Mosaicarum tit.16: adde Gel.18.c.6. in f[?]: adde what I have written on tit. C. de sponsalib.; add also Petr. Pithei 16.Notar.Mosaic.).

units.la: {c} Videtur innui ritus aquę & ignis, de quo Seru.4.Aeneid. Dotalesque tuæ Tyrios committere dextræ. Quid aliud dextræ committere, quam in manum conuenire? quæ conuentio eo ritu perficitur, vt aqua& igni adhibi-tis natura coniuncta habeat.
units.tr: {c} It seems that the rite of water and fire is implied, of which Servius speaks on the Aeneid 4: "and to entrust your dowry to Tyrian right hands." What is it to entrust to a right hand except to come into the hand? This agreement is completed by that rite, in which water and fire are applied, so that it has a natural union.

units.la: {d} Panis farreus, qui & farreum Festo & Plinio 18.c.3. genus libi ex farre compositum.
units.tr: {d} Farreus bread, which Festus and Pliny (18.c.3) also call farreum, a kind of cake made of spelt.
{e} Caius 1.tit.6. Nouel.81.1.Instit.12.8.Cod.49:2.Paul.sent.25.

units.la: LIBERI parentum potestate liberantur emancipatione{a}, id est, si postea quàm mancipati fuerint, manumissi sint. Sed filius quidem ter{b} mancipatus, {c}ter manumissus, sui iuris fit. Id enim lex duodecim Tabularum{d} iubet his verbis,Si pater filium ter venundarit{e}, filius à patre liber esto. Cæteri autem liberi præter filium{f} tam masculi quàm fœminæ, vna{g} mancipatione manumissioneque sui iuris fiunt.
units.tr: Children are freed from their parents' power by emancipation, that is, if after they have been mancipated they are manumitted. But a son who has been mancipated three times, and manumitted three times, becomes sui iuris. For the Law of the Twelve Tables orders this in these words: "If a father has sold his son three times, let the son be free of his father." The other children, besides the son, both male and female, become sui iuris by one mancipation and manumission.

units.la: 2 Morte{h} patris filius & filia sui iuris fiunt. Mortè autem aui nepotes ita{i} demum sui iuris fiunt, si post mortem aui in potestate patris futuri non sunt: veluti si moriente auo pater eorum aut iam decesserit, aut de potestate dimissus est. Nam si mortis aui tempore, pater eorum in potestate eius sit, mortuo auo, in patris sui potestate fiunt.
units.tr: 2. By the death of the father, son and daughter become sui iuris. By the death of the grandfather, grandchildren become sui iuris only if after the grandfather's death they are not going to be in their father's power; for example, if at the grandfather's death their father has either already died or been released from power. But if at the time of the grandfather's death their father is in the grandfather's power, then when the grandfather dies they pass into their father's power.

units.la: 3 Si patri vel filio aqua{k} & igni{l} interdictum fit, patria potestas tollitur: quia peregrinus fit is, cui aqua & igni interdictum est. Neque autem peregrinus{m} ciuem Romanum, neque ciuis Romanus peregrinum in potestate habere potest.
units.tr: 3. If water and fire are forbidden to a father or a son, paternal power is lost, because he to whom water and fire are forbidden becomes a foreigner. A foreigner cannot have a Roman citizen in his power, nor can a Roman citizen have a foreigner in his power.

units.la: 4 Si pater ab hostibus captus sit, quanuis seruus hostium fiat: tamen cum reuersus fuerit, omnia pristina iura recipit, iure postliminij. Sed quandiu apud hostes est, patria potestas in filio eius interim pendebit{n}: & cum reuersus fuerit ab hostibus, in potestate filium habebit. Si vero ibi decesserit, sui iuris filius erit. Filius quoque si captus fuerit ab hostibus, similiter propter ius postliminij, patria potestas interim pendebit.
units.tr: 4. If a father is taken by enemies, although he becomes a slave of the enemies, nevertheless when he returns he recovers all his former rights, by the law of postliminium. But as long as he is among the enemies, paternal power over his son remains in suspense in the meantime; and when he returns from the enemies, he will have the son in his power. If he dies there, the son will be sui iuris. If the son too is taken by enemies, in the same way, because of the right of postliminium, paternal power remains in suspense in the meantime.

units.la: deinceps,vnica l.8.in fi.ff.de iniusto:Caius 6.§.2.vcrf.fœmina vel nepotes. {n} d.l.4.in fi. {h} Institut.quib.mod.ius patriæ potest. in pr. l. 15. Cod.quando dies legat. quæ morte soluantur,dixi ad Nouell. 22. c.20. {i} Institut.cod.in pr.l.5.ff.de hu qui sunt sui. {k} His duobus elementis veteres vtebantur tanquam sacramento ad nuptias conciliandas Lactantius 2.Instit.10.ita,quem volebant perdiķum,priuabant vtroque elemento dixi ad l.6.ff.de donat.int.vir. {l} in huius pœnæ locum successit deportatio,eadem veteribus dicta exilium Caius 6.§.1.in cuius etiam vicem successit id genus exilij, quod hodie appellant Bannissement. {m} Peregrinus,ciuem;& contra,in sua potestate habere non potest Caius 6.§.1.Peregrini etiam non capiebant ex testamento l.1.C.de hæred.inst. Ex peregrino & ciue Romana natus,fiebat peregrinus lib.5.§.8.5.co. {n} §.5.Inst.qui.mod.ius.
units.tr: Then, the single law 8 at the end of ff. de iniusto; Caius 6.§.2, verb. woman or grandchildren. {n} d.l.4 at the end. {h} Institutes, de quib. mod. ius patriae potest. at the beginning; l.15 Cod. quando dies legat., which are dissolved by death; I have discussed this on Novella 22, c.20. {i} Institutes, same title, at the beginning; l.5.ff.de his qui sunt sui. {k} The ancients used these two elements as a kind of sacrament to bring about marriages; Lactantius 2 Instit. 10 says that whom they wished to be outlawed, they deprived of both elements; I have discussed this on l.6.ff.de donat.int.vir. {l} Deportation succeeded to the place of this punishment, which the ancients called exile; in its place succeeded also that kind of exile which people today call Bannissement (Caius 6.§.1). {m} A foreigner cannot have a citizen in his power, and conversely; Caius 6.§.1. Foreigners also could not take under a will (l.1.C.de hæred.inst.). A child born of a foreigner and a Roman citizen became a foreigner (lib.5.§.8.5.co.). {n} §.5 Inst. qui mod. ius.

units.la: 5 In potestate parentum esse desinunt {a} & bi qui Flamines {b} Diales {c} inaugurantur,& quæ virgines Vestæ {d} capiuntur.
units.tr: 5. Those who are inaugurated as Flamines Diales cease to be in their parents' power, and the maidens who are taken as Vestal virgins.
On Guardianships, Title 11

units.la: TVTORES constituuntur tam masculis {f}, quàm fœminis: sed masculis quidem impuberibus duntaxat, propter {g} ætatis infirmitatem: fœminis autem tam impuberibus, quàm puberibus, & propter sexus infirmitatem,& propter forensium rerum ignorantiam.
units.tr: Guardians are appointed for males as well as for females: for males only while they are under puberty, because of the weakness of their age; for females, both under and over puberty, because of the weakness of their sex and their ignorance of legal affairs.

units.la: 2 Tutores autem legitimi sunt, aut senatusconsultis constituti,aut moribus {h} introducti.
units.tr: 2 Guardians are either legitimate, or appointed by senatus-consulta, or introduced by custom.

units.la: 3 Legitimi tutores sunt,qui ex {i} lege aliqua descendunt. Per eminentiam autem legitimi dicuntur, qui ex lege duodecim Tabularum introducuntur, seu propalam,quales sunt agnati: seu per {k} consequentiam, quales sunt patroni.
units.tr: 3 Legitimate guardians are those who derive from some statute. Those are called legitimate in the strict sense who are introduced by the law of the Twelve Tables, either openly, such as agnates, or by consequence, such as patrons.

units.la: 4 Agnati sunt, à patre cognati virilis sexus, per virilem {l} sexum descendentes, eiusdem {m} familiæ veluti {n} patrui, fratres,filij fratris patruelis.
units.tr: 4 Agnates are kinsmen on the father's side of the male sex, descending through males of the same family, such as the paternal uncle, the brothers, and the sons of a paternal uncle's brother.

units.la: 5 Qui liberum caput mancipatum sibi vel à parente {o}, vel à coemptore {p}, manumisit: per {q} similitudinem statim tempore,sine emancipatione,ac sine capitis minutione, e patria potestate exibat.
units.tr: 5 A person who had manumitted a free person whom he had received by mancipation, either from a parent or from a coemptionator, by analogy left the father's power at once, without emancipation and without diminution of status.

units.la: {b} Qui flaminium Diale adipiscebatur iure patrio exibat Tacit. 4. Annal. an 776.
units.tr: (b) One who obtained the flaminate of Dialis went out of the power of his father by the law of the father. Tacitus, Annals 4, year 776.
(c) That is, of Jupiter.

units.la: {d} Gellius 1. c. Virgovesta lis, simul atq. capta in atrium Vestæ deducta, Pontificibusque tradita est,{e} o
units.tr: (d) Gellius, 1, c. The Vestal virgin, as soon as she was taken, was led into the atrium of Vesta and handed over to the Pontiffs.

units.la: {e} Caius 7: 1. Instit. 1,16. ff. 1. f l.1. §. 3. ff. cod. l.1. ff. de legitim. tut. g propter ætatem §.1. Instit. cod. l.1. ff. cod. [?] Theophil. ad. h l.1. ff. de curatore furioso. i l.5. de tutorib. k per consequentias hæreditatum l.2. ff. de legitim. tutorib: per interpretationem, ac si verbis legis introducti essent. Instit. de legitima patron. vt qui sperant successionem, idem bona consequerentur Instit. d. tit: l.1. ff. de legit. tut: v.l. 7. ff. de regul. iur. l per virilis sexus cognationem §.1. Instit. de legitima agnat. tut. per virilis sexus personas l.7. ff. de legitimis tut. per patrem cognati, ex eadem familia l.10. §.2 ff. de gradib. m d.§.2. communi n. iure familiam dicimus omnium adgnatorum l.195. §.2. verf. communi ff. de verb. sign. n veluti fratres, patrueles, filij fratris, patruelis Cuiac. obs. o fiduciario sc. de quo 7. p i. patre naturali v.7. q Patroni ad tutelam libertorum quos manumiserunt vocati sunt, lege XII. tabular. ex consequentia §.4. 5. co. Eadem igitur similitudine, patres vocari oportuit ad liberorum, quos emanciparunt, & manumiserunt tutelam. [?]nem patroni, tutor efficitur, qui fiduciarius tutor appellatur.
units.tr: (e) Gaius 1 Institutes 1.16; ff. 1 f l.1 §.3 ff. cod.; l.1 ff. de legitimis tutoribus; "propter aetatem", §.1 Instit. cod.; l.1 ff. cod.; [?] Theophilus on that passage; h l.1 ff. de curatore furioso; i l.5 de tutoribus; k "per consequentias hereditatum", l.2 ff. de legitimis tutoribus: "by interpretation, as if they had been introduced by the words of the law", Instit. de legitima patronorum tutela, since those who hope for the succession would obtain the goods in the same way; Instit. d. tit.; l.1 ff. de legit. tut.; l.7 ff. de regulis iuris; l "per virilis sexus cognationem", §.1 Instit. de legitima agnatorum tutela; "per virilis sexus personas", l.7 ff. de legitimis tutelis; "per patrem cognati, ex eadem familia", l.10 §.2 ff. de gradibus; m d.§.2, by common law we call the family all the agnates, l.195 §.2 verb. "communi" ff. de verborum significatione; n "veluti fratres, patrueles, filii fratris patruelis", Cuiacius, Observations; o "fiduciario", namely of whom 7; p i.e. the natural father, v.7; q patrons were called to the guardianship of the freedmen whom they had manumitted, by the Law of the Twelve Tables, by consequence, §.4 and 5. By the same analogy, fathers ought to have been called to the guardianship of the children whom they had emancipated and manumitted. [?] The patron becomes guardian by this means, and is called a fiduciary guardian.

units.la: 6 Legitimi tutores, alij tutela in iure cedere possunt.
units.tr: 6 Legitimate guardians can cede their guardianship in court to others.

units.la: 7 Is cui tutela in iure cessa est, Cesficus tutor appellatur: qui siue mortuus fuerit, siue capite minutus, siue alij tutela cesserit, redit ad legitimum tutorem tutela. Sed & si legitimus decesserit, aut capite minutus fuerit, cessitia quoque tutela extinguitur.
units.tr: 7 One to whom guardianship has been ceded in court is called a ceded guardian (cessicius tutor). If he dies, or suffers capitis deminutio, or cedes the guardianship to another, the guardianship returns to the legitimate guardian. But if the legitimate guardian dies or suffers capitis deminutio, the ceded guardianship is also extinguished.

units.la: 8 Quantum ad agnatos perr net hodie cessitia tutela non procedit: quoniam permissum erat in iure cedere tutelam fœminarum tantum, non etiam masculorum. fœminarum autem legitimas tutelas lex Claudia sustinet.
units.tr: 8 As regards agnates, today ceded guardianship does not take place, since it was permitted to cede guardianship in court only for women, not for men. The Claudian law, however, upholds the legitimate guardianships of women.

units.la: 9 Excepta tutela patronorum legitima tutela capitis diminutione amittitur.
units.tr: 9 Except for the legitimate guardianship of patrons, legitimate guardianship is lost by capitis deminutio.

units.la: 10 Capitis minutionis species sunt tres maxima, media, minima.
units.tr: 10 There are three kinds of capitis deminutio: the greatest, the middle, and the least.

units.la: 11 Maxima capitis diminutio est, per quam & civitas, & libertas amittitur, veluti cum incensus aliquis venerit: aut cum mulier alieno seruo se iunxerit, denuntiante domino, & ancilla facta fuerit, ex senatusconsulto Claudiano.†
units.tr: 11 The greatest capitis deminutio is that by which both citizenship and liberty are lost, as when someone is enrolled in the census (incensus), or when a woman joins herself to another's slave, after the master has given notice, and becomes a slave, under the Claudian senatus-consultum.†

units.la: Cuiacius hic ita restituit, exceptis his quæ I.A. P.P. his quæ in re agnationis proximis potissimum deferuntur. Hotomanus 3. obs. 9. legit, exceptis his quæ in nomine alieno positis personis deferuntur.
units.tr: Cuiacius here restores the text as follows: "except those things which are conferred on the persons nearest in agnation." Hotomanus, Observations 3.9, reads: "except those things which are conferred on persons placed in another's name."

units.la: g l.vlt ff. de capite minut. h Cicero pro Cecinna, in ƒ. Iam populus cum eum vendit, qui miles factus non est (i. quia ad dilectu non respondit, qua de re dixi ad l.20. ff. comm. præd. l.40. §.10. ff. de re militari) non adimit ei libertatem, sed indicat eum non esse liberum, qui cum liber esset, adire periculum noluit. Cum autem incensum (id est eum qui censum vitauit) hoc indicat: cum is, qui in seruitute iusta fuerint, censu liberetur, eum, qui, cum liber esset, ceseri noluerit, ipsum sibi libertatem abiudicasse. Quod si maxime hisce rebus adimi libertas aut amitti potest, &c. Halycarnassensis etiam lib. 4. refert Seruij Tullij iussu bona omnium ciuium censita, eis qui non censerent, poena proposita, vt bonis in fiscum redactis, cæsi virgis sub hasta venirent: eamque diu legem Romanis seruatam fuisse.
units.tr: (g) l.ult. ff. de capite minutione. (h) Cicero, Pro Caecina, in fine: "Since the people sell him who has not become a soldier (that is, because he did not answer the levy, about which I spoke at l.20 ff. comm. praed., l.40 §10 ff. de re militari), it does not take away his liberty, but shows that he is not free, who, being free, was unwilling to face danger. But when it shows him to be incensus (that is, one who avoided the census), since those who are in lawful servitude are freed by the census, it shows that he who, being free, was unwilling to be enrolled, had himself renounced his own liberty. If indeed liberty can be taken away or lost by these things, etc." Dionysius of Halicarnassus also reports, in book 4, that by the order of Servius Tullius the goods of all citizens were assessed, with a penalty set for those who did not register, so that, their goods having been confiscated to the treasury, they were beaten with rods and sold under the spear; and that this law was long kept among the Romans.

units.la: i l.27. ff. depositi. k d.l.27. ibi, nulla denunciatione a domino facta, vel, vt Hotomanus legit, §.obs.12. nulla denunciatione domino facta. Priori sententiæ optime cōuenit illud Tertulliani 2. ad uxorem, Nonne insuper censuerunt seruituti vindicadas, quæ cū alieno seruo post dominorum denuntiatione in cōsuetudine persŏueraret adde l.3. C. de muriley.
units.tr: (i) l.27 ff. depositi. (k) d.l.27: "no notice having been given by the master"; or, as Hotomanus reads, §. obs. 12: "no notice having been given to the master." That first opinion agrees very well with the words of Tertullian, To His Wife 2: "Did they not moreover decide that those were to be claimed as slaves who, after notice given by their masters, continued in custom with another's slave?" Add l.3 C. de ...

units.la: † Id hodie abrogatū est C. de Sc. Clandtollend: & Inst. de successionum sublat. quæ fiebat per bo. vend. &c.
units.tr: † This was abolished today: C. de Senatusconsulto Claudiano tollendo, and Instit. de successionum sublatione, which was done through the sale of goods, etc.

units.la: 12 {d}Media capitis diminutio dicitur, per quam sola ciuitate amissa, libertas retinetur:quod fit in eo cui aquæ & igni interdicitur.
units.tr: 12 The middle capitis deminutio is so called when, citizenship alone being lost, liberty is retained. This happens to one on whom water and fire are interdicted.

units.la: 13 {b}Minima capitis deminutio est per quam & ciuitate & libertate salua, status duntaxat hominis mutatur:quod fit adoptione,& in manu conuictione.
units.tr: 13 The least capitis deminutio is that by which, with citizenship and liberty safe, only the man's status is changed. This happens by adoption and by conventio in manum.

units.la: 14 Testamento quoque nominatim tutores dati confirmantur {c}eadem lege duodecim Tabularū his verbis: Vti {d}legassit juper pecunia tutelaue {e}suæ rei, ita ius esto:qui {f}tutores datiui appellantur.
units.tr: 14 Guardians named by name in a will are also confirmed by the same law of the Twelve Tables, in these words: As the head of the family shall have bequeathed concerning money or the guardianship of his property, so let it be law. These are called dative guardians.

units.la: 15 Dari testamento tutores possunt liberis qui {g}in potestate iunt.
units.tr: 15 Guardians can be given by will to children who are in power.

units.la: 16 Testamento tutores dari possunt hi, cum{h}qui- bus testamenti facien- di ius est, præter Latinum Iu- nianum. Nam Latinus {i}habet quidem testamenti fa- ctionem, sed tamen tutor dari non potest. id enim lex Iunia prohibet.
units.tr: 16 Those can be given as guardians by will who have the right of making a will, except the Junian Latin. For the Latin has indeed the capacity of making a will, but nevertheless cannot be given as guardian, since the Junian law forbids this.

units.la: 17 Si capite diminutus fuerit tutor testamento datus, non amittit tutelam: sed si abdicauerit {k}se tutela, definit esse tutor {l}. Abdicare autē est, dicere nolle se tutorem esse in iure. Cedere {m}autem tute- la testamento datus non potest. nam & legitimus in iure cedere potest, abdicare {n}se non potest.
units.tr: 17 If a guardian given by will suffers capitis deminutio, he does not lose the guardianship; but if he renounces the guardianship, he ceases to be guardian. To renounce is to say in court that one is unwilling to be guardian. A testamentary guardian cannot cede the guardianship, for although a legitimate guardian can cede in court, he cannot renounce.

units.la: 18 Lex Attilia {o}iubet mulieribus, pupillisve non habentibus tutores dari à Prætore & maiore {p}parte Tribunorum plebis: quos tutores Attilianos appellamus. Sed quia lex Attilia Romæ tantum locum habet, lege Iulia & Titia perfectum est, vt in prouincia quoque similiter à præsidibus earum {q}dentur tutores.
units.tr: 18 The Attilian law orders that guardians be given to women and to pupils who have none, by the praetor and the majority of the tribunes of the plebs; we call these Attilian guardians. But since the Attilian law has force only at Rome, it was provided by the Julian and Titian laws that in the provinces guardians should likewise be given by the governors.

units.la: {e} Paterfamilias vti super pecunia tutelaue sua legassit, ita iusefto. Author ad Herenium 1: super pecunia, tutelaue suæ rei l.53.ff.de verb.sig.vt eam pecuniā, eāsve res, quibusque dare legare volet ius poteftaisque esto l.1.ff.ad l.Falcid.& Vlpianus rit.1.§.9.§.eod. Lex XII. tabularum confi mat quod datum, legatum est. e melius quam in l.53.ff.de verbor.fignif. super pecunię, tutelăve suę. f verba quę sequuntur, esse quasi argumentum sententię sequentis videntur. alias improprie legitimi tutores datiui dicuntur l.5.ff.de legibus. quod tamen ex hoc §.sequitur.
units.tr: (e) "As the head of the family shall have bequeathed concerning money or the guardianship of his property, so let it be law." The author to Herennius, 1: "concerning money or the guardianship of his property"; l.53 ff. de verborum significatione: "that he may have the right and power to give and bequeath that money or those things to whomever he wishes"; l.1 ff. ad legem Falcidiam; and Ulpian, tit. 1 §.9 and the same §. The Law of the Twelve Tables confirms what has been given as a legacy. e better than in l.53 ff. de verborum significatione, "concerning money or the guardianship of his property." f The words that follow seem to be the argument of the sentence that follows; otherwise legitimate guardians are improperly called dative, l.5 ff. de legibus; which, however, follows from this §.

units.la: {k} lx id est se excusauerit l.11.§.2.ff.de testament. {l} eiusque loco non legitimus, sed datiuus constituetur d.§.2. {m} ad hanc cessionem in iure refer §.3.§.eod. {n} l.excusare. {o} v.Institut.de Attiliano tutore. {p} Institut.d.loco. {q} iisque qui sunt eius prouinciæ, vel ibidem domicilium habent l.1.ix f.ff.de tutoribus datis.
units.tr: {k} lx, that is, has excused himself: Dig. 11.§.2 de testamentis. {l} And in his place a non-legitimate but a dative tutor shall be appointed: ibid. §.2. {m} For this transfer, refer in law to §.3 of the same title. {n} Dig. excusare. {o} See Inst. de Attiliano tutore. {p} Inst. in the same place. {q} Those who belong to his province, or have their domicile there: Dig. 1.ix, de tutoribus datis.

units.la: 19 Lex Iunia tutorem fieri iubet Latino, vel Latinis impuberibus eum, qui etiam ante manumissionem ex iure Quiritium fuit.
units.tr: 19 The Lex Junia orders that a tutor be appointed for Latin or Latin minors who, even before manumission, was a citizen by Quiritary right.

units.la: 20 Ex lege Iulia de maritandis ordinibus, tutor datur a Praetore urbis ei mulieri virginive, quam ex hac causa lege nubere oportet, ad dotem dandam, dicendam, promittendamve, si legitimum tutorem pupilla non habeat. Sed postea Senatus censuit vt etiam in provincia quoque, similiter a praesidibus earum ex eadem causa tutores dentur.
units.tr: 20 By the Lex Julia de maritandis ordinibus, a tutor is given by the praetor of the city to a woman or virgin who ought to marry under this law, for the purpose of giving, declaring or promising a dowry, if the ward has no legitimate tutor. But afterwards the Senate decreed that tutors should likewise be given in the provinces, for the same cause, by their governors.

units.la: 21 Praeterea etiam in locum muti, furiosive tutoris, alterum dandum esse tutorem ad dotem f constituendam Senatus censuit.
units.tr: 21 Furthermore, the Senate decreed that another tutor should be given in place of a mute or insane tutor, for the constituting of a dowry.

units.la: 22 Item ex Senatusconsulto tutor datur mulieri ei, cuius tutor abest, praeterquam si patronus sit, qui abest. Nam in locum patroni absentis alter peti non potest, nisi ad hereditatem adeundam, & nuptias contrahendas. Idemque permisit in pupillo patroni filio.
units.tr: 22 Likewise, by a senatus consultum, a tutor is given to a woman whose tutor is absent, unless the absent man is her patron. For in place of an absent patron another cannot be sought, except for entering an inheritance and contracting marriage. The same was permitted for a ward who is the son of a patron.

units.la: 23 Hoc amplius Senatus censuit, vt si tutor pupilli pupillaeve suspectus a tutela submotus fuerit, vel etiam iusta de causa excusatus, in locum eius tutor alius detur.
units.tr: 23 Further, the Senate decreed that if the tutor of a male or female ward has been removed from the guardianship as suspect, or even excused for a just cause, another tutor be given in his place.

units.la: 24 Moribus tutor datur mulieri pupilloque, qui cum tutore suo lege aut legitimo iudicio agere vult, vt auctore eo agat (ipse enim tutor in rem suam auctor fieri non potest), qui Praetorianus tutor dicitur, quia a praetore urbis dari consueuit.
units.tr: 24 By custom a tutor is given to a woman or to a ward who wishes to sue his tutor by statute or by legal judgment, so that he may act with the tutor's authority (for the tutor himself cannot become the authorizer in his own affair). This is called the Praetorian tutor, because he is customarily given by the praetor of the city.

units.la: 25 Pupillorum pupillarumque tutores & negotia gerunt, & auctoritatem interponunt. Mulierum autem tutores auctoritatem duntaxat interponunt.
units.tr: 25 The tutors of male and female wards both conduct business and interpose authority. But the tutors of women only interpose authority.

units.la: 26 Si plures sunt tutores, omnes in omni re debent auctoritatem accommodare, praeter eos qui tunc dati sunt: nam ex his vel vnius auctoritas sufficit.
units.tr: 26 If there are several tutors, all must lend their authority in every matter, except those who were appointed at that time; for the authority of one of these alone is sufficient.

units.la: 27 Tutoris auctoritas necessaria est, mulieribus{u} tutelaribus datis.
units.tr: 27 The authority of a tutor is necessary for women who have been given tutelary tutors.

units.la: u tarib.datis l hanc particulam Cuiacius expunxit.
units.tr: u tarib.datis: Cuiacius deleted this particle.

units.la: ff.de tutelis:l 11.§.t.ff.de legit.tut. n d.l.11.§.r. o dixi ad leges XII.Tabularum lib.2.adde§.27.l.eo. p v.l.1.C.de iis lite dado. q pr torius §.vlt.Inst.de auth.tut. Hodie tutorem habenti tutor non datur sed curator. q l.1.ff.de administ.tut. r v.ff.C. Inst.de authorit.tutor.v.Cuiac.7.obs.11. t hodie id immutatum v.l.vlt.C. de authoritate praestanda. s qui testamento dati Cuiac. t d.l.vl. adde l.4.l.5.l.7.§1.ff.de auctor tut. u §.4.§.cod. quidem in his rebus, si lege aut legitimo iudicio agant, si se obligent, si ciuile negotium gerant, si li-bertæ suæ permittant in contubernio alieni serui morari, si mancipia alienent. Pupillis autem hoc amplius, etiam in rerum nec mancipi alienatione tutoris auctoritate opus est.
units.tr: Dig. de tutelis: Dig. 11.§.t, de legitimis tutoribus. n Ibid. 11.§.r. o I have said this on the Laws of the XII Tables, book 2; add §.27, l.eo. p See l.1 C. de iis qui lite dando. q Praetorian, §.vlt. Inst. de auctoritate tutoris. Today a tutor is not given to one who has a tutor, but a curator. q Dig. 1 de administratione tutorum. r See Dig., C., Inst. de auctoritate tutoris; see Cuiacius, Obs. 7.11. t Today this has been changed: see last law C. de auctoritate praestanda. s Those given by testament, Cuiacius. t Ibid. last law; add l.4, l.5, l.7 §1 Dig. de auctoritate tutoris. u §.4 of the same title: in these matters, indeed, if they sue by statute or legal judgment, if they bind themselves, if they conduct a civil business, if they permit their freedom to be spent living in cohabitation with another's slave, if they alienate slaves. But for wards, further, the authority of the tutor is needed even for the alienation of things not mancipable.

units.la: 28 Liberantur tutela, masculi quidem pubertate. Puberem autem Cassiani {b}quidem eum esse dicunt, qui habitu corporis pubes apparet, id est, qui generare potest: Proculeii {c}autem, eum qui quattuordecim annos explevit: verum Prisci {d}eum pubere esse, in quem utrumque concurrit, & habitus corporis, & numerus annorum. Feminæ autem tutela liberantur.
units.tr: 28 Males are released from guardianship by puberty. Cassianus indeed says that a pubescent person is one who appears pubescent by bodily condition, that is, who can beget; Proculeius, however, says one who has completed fourteen years; but Priscus holds that one is pubescent in whom both bodily condition and number of years concur. Women are released from guardianship by marriage.
DE CVRATORIBVS. TITVL. XII.

units.la: VRATORES aut legitimi sunt, id est, qui ex lege duodecim Tabularum dantur: aut honorarij {g}, id est, qui a Prætore constituuntur.
units.tr: Curators are either legitimate, that is, those given by the law of the Twelve Tables, or honorary, that is, those appointed by the Praetor.

units.la: 2 Lex {h}duodecim Tabularum furiosum, itemque prodigum cui bonis interdictum est, in curatione iubet esse agnatorum.
units.tr: 2 The law of the Twelve Tables orders that the agnates be the curators of a madman, and likewise of a spendthrift who has been interdicted from his goods.

units.la: 3 A Prætore constituitur curator, quem ipse Prætor voluerit, libertinis, prodigis, itemque ingenuis, qui ex testamento parentis heredes facti, male dissipant bona: his enim ex lege curator dari non potest: cum ingenuus quidem non ab intestato, sed ex testamento heres factus sit patri: libertinus autem nullo modo patri heres fieri potest, qui nec lege patre habuisse videtur, cum seruilis cognatio nulla sit.
units.tr: 3 A curator is appointed by the Praetor, whomever the Praetor himself wishes, for freedmen, for spendthrifts, and likewise for freeborn men who, having been made heirs by their parent's will, squander the goods badly. For by law no curator can be given to these: a freeborn man was made heir to his father by will, not on intestacy; and a freedman can never be made heir to his patron, who is not thought to have had a legal kinship with him at all, since there is no kinship of slaves.

units.la: 4 Præterea dat curatorem ei etiam, qui nuper pubes factus, idonee negotia sua tueri {m}non potest.
units.tr: 4 Moreover, the Praetor also gives a curator to one who, having lately reached puberty, cannot adequately manage his own affairs.

units.la: {g} dantur etiam testamento, postea confirmandi a prætore §.1. Inst. eo.
units.tr: {g} They are also given by will, to be confirmed afterwards by the Praetor: Inst. eod. §1.
{h} Dig. 1, de curatoribus, l.1.

units.la: {i} qui neque tempus, neque finem expensarum habent d.l.r.
units.tr: {i} who have neither time nor limit of expenses: the same law, d.l.r.

units.la: {k} vtitur Iurisconsultus argumento a priuatione: duo ... vt & alibi, Nemo cogitur reddere quod non habet l.22. §.3. ff. ad Trebell: Non repudiat, qui negat nuptam Nouell.74. c.5. Non latitat, qui sibi non est idoneus defensor l.5. ff. de reb. auctior: Seruus capite minui non potest, qui nullum caput habet l.3. in f. ff. de capit.minut. l Imò, aliqua Inst. de seruili cognat. {m} l.2. ff. eod.
units.tr: {k} The jurist uses an argument from privation: two things ... as also elsewhere, "No one is compelled to return what he does not have" (Dig. 36.1.22 §3, ad Trebellianum); "He does not renounce who denies that he is married" (Nov. 74, c.5); "He does not hide who is not a suitable defender for himself" (Dig. 26.8.5, de rebus auctoritate iudicis); "A slave cannot suffer loss of status, since he has no status" (Dig. 4.5.3 in fine, de capite minutis); and indeed, "in some" Inst. de servili cognatione. {m} Dig. 26.8.2, eodem.

units.la: TIT. XIII. {a}DE CŒLIBE{b}, ORBO{c} ET SOLITARIO patre.
units.tr: TIT. XIII. Concerning the unmarried, the childless, and the father of a single child.

units.la: PEGE Iulia e prohibentur uxores ducere, senatores † quidem liberique eorum, libertinas f, & quę ipsę, quatūmve pater matērve artem ludicram g fecerit: item corpore h quęstum faciente.
units.tr: By the Julian law, senators and their children are forbidden to marry freedwomen, and women who themselves, or whose father or mother, have practised the theatrical arts; likewise a woman who makes her living by her body.

units.la: Cæteri autem ingenui prohibentur ducere ie-nam i, à lenone, lenaue manumissam, & in adulterio deprehensam k, & iudicio publico damnatam l, & quę artem ludicram m fecerit: adiicit Mauricianus n, & à senatu o damnatam. tranei testamento capere: nisi intra centum dies nuptias contraxerit.
units.tr: Other freeborn men are forbidden to marry a prostitute, a woman freed from a pimp or procuress, a woman caught in adultery, a woman condemned in a public court, and a woman who has practised the theatrical arts. Mauricianus, who wrote on the Julian laws, adds: a woman condemned by the senate. Outsiders may take under a will only if they marry within a hundred days.

units.la: 17.§.1.1.eod: 1. Soxom. 9: l.35.ff.de mortis causa: l.12.ff.de vulgari:
units.tr: 17 §1.1 eod.; 1 Soxom. 9; l. 35 ff. de mortis causa; l. 12 ff. de vulgari.

units.la: Tertullianus libro de Monogamia. Aliud est si apud Christū, legibus Iuliis agi credunt & existimant cœlibes & orbes ex testamento Dei solidum capere non posse. Tacit. 3. Annal. Relatum de moderanda Papia Popœa, quā senior Augustus post Iulias rogatas incitandis cœlibū pœnis, & augendo ærario sanxerat &c. ad has pœnas respexit Plutarch 9 libro [Greek: περὶ φιλοσοφίας] [?] inquit, [Greek: γαμεῖσι καὶ γεννᾶσιν] [?] Author Panegyrici Maximo & Constantino dictati leges Iulias ita commendat.
units.tr: Tertullian, in his book on Monogamy: "It is otherwise if they believe, and suppose, that under Christ the unmarried and the childless are to be dealt with under the Julian laws, and that they cannot take the whole of an inheritance under God's will." Tacitus, Annals 3: "A proposal was made to moderate the Papian-Poppaean law, which the elder Augustus, after the Julian laws had been passed to increase the penalties on the unmarried and to enlarge the treasury, had enacted," etc. Plutarch, in the ninth book of [περὶ φιλοσοφίας] [?], alludes to these penalties when he says: "they marry and beget" [γαμεῖσι καὶ γεννᾶσιν] [?]. The author of the Panegyric delivered to Maximus and Constantine commends the Julian laws thus:

units.la: Leges, inquam, quæ multa cœlibes notarunt, parentes præmiis honorarunt, vere dicuntur esse fundamenta Reipublicæ, quia seminarium iuuentutis & quasi fontē humani corporis semper Romanis exercitibus ministrarunt.
units.tr: "Laws, I say, which marked out many unmarried men, honoured parents with rewards, are truly called the foundations of the Commonwealth, because they always supplied the Roman armies with a seedbed of youth and, as it were, a fountain of the human body."

units.la: {c} Orbus semisis capiēdi capax erat, nō solidi l. 6. ff. de vulgari: l. 42. ff. de leg. 1. 1: l. 16. §. 15. ff. ad Tuebl. 12. in f. ff. de iure fisci. hinc ille instituendi leges in tempus capiendæ hereditatis l. 61. ff. de hered. institut. ex parte quā quis per leges capere posset l. 78. in f. ff. de hered. instit. Et ita melior orbi quam cœlibes conditio, quia maritus orbus, salte dimidiū capit: cœlebs nihil.
units.tr: {c} The childless man (orbus) was capable of taking half, not the whole: l. 6 ff. de vulgari; l. 42 ff. de leg. 1; l. 1; l. 16 §15 ff. ad Trebell.; 12 in f. ff. de iure fisci. Hence the rule that an heir may be instituted for the time in which he can take the inheritance: l. 61 ff. de hered. institut.; for the part which a person can take under the laws: l. 78 in f. ff. de hered. instit. And so the condition of the childless man is better than that of the unmarried, because a childless husband takes at least half, while the unmarried takes nothing.

units.la: {d} Solitarius hīc dicitur, qui vnicū & solū filiū habet [Greek: μονοτέκνος], vt Aquila loquitur: quasi medius inter orbum & cœlibem, & multorum liberorum parentē. Priorum pœnas vt non patitur, ita posteriorum præmiis non fruitur.
units.tr: {d} Here "solitarius" is said of one who has a single and only son [μονοτέκνος], as Aquila puts it: as if he stood midway between the childless man and the unmarried, and the parent of several children. As he does not suffer the penalties of the former, so he does not enjoy the rewards of the latter.

units.la: {e} quæ & Papia l. 44. ff. de ritu: l. 28. Cod. de nupt. † l. 16. l. 31. l. 32. l. 34. in f. l. 44. ff. de ritu. Id hodie senatoribus remissum est Nouell. 78. c. 3. f l. 23. ff. de ritu: l. 28. C. de nupt. l. 7. C. de incest. g d. l. 7. l. 42. §. 1. ff. de ritu. h l. 41. l. 43. ff. de ritu: l. 7. in f. ff. de incest. i d. l. 43. §. 6. 7. 8. k d. l. 43. §. 12. 13. l d. l. 43. §. 10 §. 11. m d. l. 44. ff. de ritu. n qui ad leges Iuliias scripsit. o l. 16. l. 43. §. 10. ff. de ritu.
units.tr: Which also in Papia: l. 44 ff. de ritu; l. 28 Cod. de nupt.; † l. 16; l. 31; l. 32; l. 34 in f.; l. 44 ff. de ritu. This has today been remitted to senators: Nov. 78 c. 3; f l. 23 ff. de ritu; l. 28 C. de nupt.; l. 7 C. de incest.; g the said l. 7; l. 42 §. 1 ff. de ritu; h l. 41; l. 43 ff. de ritu; l. 7 in f. ff. de incest.; i the said l. 43 §. 6, 7, 8; k the said l. 43 §. 12, 13; l the said l. 43 §. 10, §. 11; m the said l. 44 ff. de ritu; n who wrote on the Julian laws; o l. 16; l. 43 §. 10 ff. de ritu.

units.la: DE POENA LEGIS IVLIAE TIT. XIIII.
units.tr: ON THE PENALTY OF THE JULIAN LAW. TITLE XIV.

units.la: FOEMINIS{b} lex Iulia à morte viri anni tribuit vacationem{c}: à diuortio, sex mensium: lex autem Papia à morte viri, biennij{d}: à repudio, anni & sex mensium.
units.tr: Under the Julian law, a woman is granted a period of exemption (from remarriage): one year from the death of her husband, and six months from divorce; but under the Papian law, two years from the death of her husband, and a year and six months from repudiation.
On Tenths. Title 15.

units.la: VIR & vxor inter se matrimonij nomine e decimam capere possunt{f}. Quod si ex alio matrimonio liberos superstites habeant, praeter decimam quam matrimonij nomine capiunt, totidem{g} decimas pro numero liberorum accipiunt. Item cō-munis filius, filiave, post nonū die amissus, amissave, vnam decimā adiicit. duo{h} autē post *nonū ⅓ diem rebat à lege lata. An à die diuortij vel mortis eius temporis esset vacatio, incertum forte, quoniam de foeminis Vlpianus hic tantum loquitur: in quas, leges quàm in viros maiores fuere semper{v}.
units.tr: A husband and wife may take a tenth from each other in the name of marriage. If they have surviving children from another marriage, then besides the tenth they take in the name of marriage, they receive as many tenths as they have children. Likewise a common son or daughter who dies after the ninth day adds one tenth; two who die after the ninth day add two tenths. Whether the period of exemption ran from the day of divorce or from the day of death is perhaps uncertain, since Ulpian speaks here only of women, against whom the laws were always harsher than against men.
Cuiacius, Observationes 6 and 7.

units.la: {c} hoc est, vt interim etiamsi cœlibe vitam agant, capere ex alterius testamento possint. Lex .n. Iulia verat cœlibes quidquam testamento extranei capere l. 11. ff.de vulgari: l.35.ff.de mort.cauf.
units.tr: That is, so that they may take by another's will even while they live as celibates in the meantime. For the Julian law forbade celibates to take anything by the will of a stranger: Dig. 11 de vulgari; Dig. 35 de mortis causa.

units.la: {d} triennij. ita legendum est. nam Augustus triennio constituit, teste Suetonio. {e} i.in honorem matrimonij. {f} l.13. ff. de auro: adde l. 6. ff. de vulgari: l. 42. ff. de legat. 2. respexit huc orator verus: Placet ergo, ô leges diligentissimæ pudoris custodes, decimas vxoribus,quartas meretricibus dari? Porro,decimaria ea lex sublata l. 2. Cod. de infirm. pœnis cœlib.
units.tr: Read "triennii," not "biennii," for Augustus fixed the period at three years, as Suetonius attests. (2) In honour of marriage. Dig. 13 de auro; add Dig. 6 de vulgari and Dig. 42 de legatis 2. The orator Verus had this in mind: "Is it then agreed, O most diligent guardians of modesty, laws, that tenths are given to wives and quarters to prostitutes?" Moreover, that law of tenths was repealed: Cod. 2 de infirmandis poenis caelibum.

units.la: {g} Alix decimæ erant, quæ nomine matrimonij, aliæ quæ propter singulos liberos percipiebantur. {h} tres. tit. prox. j. {i} Nam defuncti ante nominis susceptionem, pro non susceptis habentur. {k} tit. prox. l. Nominalia intelligit, quorum meminit Tertullianus in libro de idololatria, seu diem nonum ac lustricum, quo infantes lustrabant, eisque imponebant nomina. Macrob. 1. Saturnal. 16. Festus in voce lustrici dies, vbi vide Iosephum Scaligerum: Plutarch. in quæstionib: Suidas tamen refert nomen imponi solitum [illegible, ~12 letters]; deferebant autem infantulos [illegible, ~10 letters]. Ioseph. Scalig. d. loco. amissi, duas decimas adiiciunt. Præter decimam, etiam ulumfructum tertiæ partis bonorum[?] eius capere possunt: & quotcunque liberos habuerint, eiusdem partis proprietatem. Hoc amplius mulier potest legatam sibi tere præter decimam dotem potest legatam sibi.
units.tr: There were different tenths: some were given in the name of marriage, others were received on account of each individual child. (3) Three; see the next title, above. For those who die before a name is given are regarded as not having been received. Next title, below. He means the "nominalia," which Tertullian mentions in his book on idolatry, that is, the ninth day, the lustral day, on which infants were purified and given names. Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.16; Festus, under "lustrici dies," where see Joseph Scaliger; Plutarch, Quaestiones; Suidas, however, reports that the name was customarily given [illegible]; they carried the little infants [illegible]; Joseph Scaliger, in the passage cited. If they lose them, they add two tenths. Besides the tenth, they can also take the usufruct of a third part of his goods, and as many children as they have, the ownership of the same part. Moreover, a woman may be left a third, besides the tenth, as a legacy [illegible: dowry may be left to her as a legacy].

units.la: TIT. XVI. DE SOLIDI CAPACITATE INTER VIRUM & VXOREM.
units.tr: TIT. XVI. Concerning the capacity of husband and wife to take the whole estate from each other.

units.la: ALIQVANDO vir & vxor inter se solidum capere possunt: velut si uterque, vel alteruter eorum nondum eius ætatis sit, quæ quidem liberos exigit : id est, si vir minor annorum viginti quinque sit, aut vxor annorum viginti minor. Itè si utrique lege Papia finitos in matrimonio annos excesserint, id est, vir sexaginta ann. vxor quinquaginta. Itè si cognati inter se coierunt vsque ad sextum gradum: aut si vir absit, & donec abesset, intra annum postquam abesse desierit, libera inter eos testamenti factio est. Si ius liberorum a principe impetrauerint: aut si filiũ filiamve communem habeant: aut quatuordecim ann. filiũ, vel filiam duodecim amiserint: vel si duos trimos, vel si tres post nonum diem amiserint, vt intra annum tamen & sex menses. Etiam vnus cuiuscunque ætatis impubes amissus filii capiendi ius præstat. Item si post mortem viri intra decem menses vxor ex eo peperit, solidum ex bonis eius capit.
units.tr: Sometimes husband and wife can take the whole of each other's estate: for example, if both of them, or either of them, is not yet of the age that is required for bearing children, that is, if the husband is under twenty-five or the wife under twenty. Likewise, if both have passed the years of marriage fixed by the Lex Papia, that is, the husband sixty and the wife fifty. Likewise, if relatives have married each other up to the sixth degree; or if the husband is absent, then for as long as he is absent, and within a year after he has ceased to be absent, there is free capacity to make a will between them. If they have obtained the right of children from the emperor; or if they have a son or daughter in common; or if they have lost a son or a daughter aged fourteen, or twelve; or if they have lost two children aged three, or three children after the ninth day, provided that this happens within a year and six months. Even a single child of any age who dies before puberty confers the right to take the son's share. Likewise, if the wife has given birth by him within ten months after the husband's death, she takes the whole of his goods.

units.la: 2 Aliquando nihil inter se capiunt, id est, si contra legem Iuliam, Papiamque Popeam contraxerint matrimonium: verbi gratia, si famosam quis vxorem duxerit, aut libertinam senator.
units.tr: 2 Sometimes they take nothing from each other, that is, if they have contracted marriage against the Lex Julia and the Lex Papia Poppaea: for example, if a man has married a woman of infamous reputation, or a senator has married a freedwoman.

units.la: 3 Qui intra sexagesimum, vel quæ intra quin-
units.tr: 3 Those who are within the sixtieth year, or women within the fiftieth-

units.la: dof. de infirmand. his quæ sub Tyrannis, ibi, valeat impetratio iuris communium liberorum. quod ius hodie omnibus datum est Cod. de iure liberorum. Ius illud liberorum his negabatur, quorum anni simul dudi & computati centum transiisse dicerentur.
units.tr: (see the de infirmand. title, on the words his quae sub tyrannis, where the right of common children is said to stand). This right is today granted to all, Cod. de iure liberorum. That right of children was denied to those whose years, added together and counted, were said to have passed one hundred.
f Pliny, Epistles 2, and book 10. Dion 5.
g See tit. prax. 5, same title.

units.la: h Anni & sex menses, bis novem menses. Nouem menses, iustum tempus pariendi.
units.tr: h Years and six months; twice nine months. Nine months is the proper time for bearing a child.
i Law 29, Digest, de liberis.

units.la: † id abrogatum l. 1. l. 2. Cod. de infirmandis pœnis cælibatus. quag[?] fimum annum neutri {a} legi paruerit, licet ipsis legibus post hanc ætatem liberatus esset, perpetuis tamen pœnis tenebatur, ex senatusconsulto {b}Perniciano. Sed Claudiano senatusconsulto maior sexagenario {c}, si minorem quinquagenaria duxerit, perinde habetur, ac si minor sexaginta annorum duxisset uxorem. Quod si maior quinquagenaria minori sexagenario nupserit, impar {d} matrimonium appellatur: & senatusconsulto Caluitiano {e} iubetur non proficere ad capiendas hereditates, & legatas dotes. Itaque mortua muliere, dos caduca {f} erit.
units.tr: † This was abrogated by laws 1 and 2 of the Code, de infirmandis poenis caelibatus. If neither party had complied with the law by the fiftieth year, then although they were released from the laws' provisions after that age, they were still bound by perpetual penalties under the senatus consultum Pernicianum. But under the Claudian senatus consultum, a man over sixty who marries a woman under fifty is treated as if a man under sixty had married. If a woman over fifty marries a man under sixty, the marriage is called unequal, and by the Calvisian senatus consultum she is forbidden to benefit from taking inheritances and legacies of dowry. Therefore, when the woman dies, the dowry falls to the fisc.
On Caducous Bequests {g}.
TIT. XVII.

units.la: QVOD [?] quis sibi testamento relictum ita vt iure ciuili capere possit, aliqua ex causa non ceperit, caducum appellatur, veluti {h} cecidit ab eo: verbi gratia, si coelibi {i}, vel Latino {k} Iu-niano legatum fuerit, nec intra dies centum vel coelebs legi paruerit {l}, vel Latinus ius Quiri-tium consequutus sit: aut si ex parte scriptus {m}, vel nib. Lactantius 1. Quid ergo est quare apud Poetas falacisimus Iupiter desierit [?] liberos tollere? Vtrum sexagenarius factus esset & illi lex Papia fibulam imposuit? an impetrauit ius trium liberorum? & Apu-leio 2. Apologet. in iudicio obiectū, quod Pudentilla ei anno ætatis 60. ad libidinem nupsisset. Hodie maior sexagenario minorem quinquagenaria ducere potest. l. 27. Cod. de nupt. l. 11. Cod. de legitim. hæredib. Nam auctore Aristotele 5. περὶ ζῴων [?] ἱστορίας, vir vsque ad 70: fœmina vsque ad 50. gignit. l. 21. ff. de act. empti. quod & Senatusconsulto Claudiano comprehensum fuisse, hic constat. adde Suetonium in Claudio c.23. {d} impar matrimonium.
units.tr: What someone has been left in a will, in such a way that he could take it under the civil law, but for some reason has not taken, is called caducum, as it has fallen away from him. For example, if a legacy was given to a celibate person, or to a Latin under the Junian law, and the celibate did not comply with the law within a hundred days, or the Latin did not obtain Roman citizenship; or if he was instituted heir in part only, or [the legatee died before the will was opened, or became a foreigner]. Lactantius, book 1: "Why then is it that Jupiter, the most deceitful of the poets, ceased to beget children? Was it because he had become sixty and the Papian law had put a clasp on him? Or because he obtained the right of three children?" And Apuleius, Apology, book 2, where it was objected in court that Pudentilla had married him for lust at the age of sixty. Today a man over sixty may marry a woman under fifty (law 27, Code, on marriages; law 11, Code, on legitimate heirs). For, on the authority of Aristotle in the History of Animals, book 5, a man can beget children up to seventy and a woman up to fifty (law 21, Digest, on actions of purchase). That this was also covered by the Claudian senatus consultum is clear. Add Suetonius, Claudius, chapter 23. {d} unequal marriage.
{d} unequal marriage.
{e} Read Claudian (the law), as in 3.

units.la: {f} dos caduca l. 38. §.1. ff. de ritu.
units.tr: {f} dowry as caducum: law 38, §1, Digest, on the rite of marriage.

units.la: {h} Caduca sunt, quæ iure relicta capaci, aliqua ex causa post mortem testatoris ab eo cadunt in fiscum. Capaci dixi: nam quæ incapaci relinquuntur pro non scriptis habentur.
units.tr: {h} Caduca are those things that have been left to a person capable of taking them, but which for some reason fall away after the testator's death, passing into the fisc. I say "capable," for things left to an incapable person are held as not written.
{i} 1. Sozomen, book 9.
{k} Title 11, §16; Title 20, §18; Title 22, §3.
{l} the same law; {l} 1: if he has not married.

units.la: {m} recte id adiectum est. nam ex parte scriptus, etiam clausis tabulis testamenti, adire hæreditatem potest: quatenus lex Papia ius tantum adcrescendi aufert cohæredibus vel legatariis. legatarius ante apertas tabulas decesserit, vel perx-ger {a}factus sit.
units.tr: {m} This is rightly added. For a person instituted heir in part may take up the inheritance even when the tablets of the will are sealed, inasmuch as the Papian law removes only the right of accrual from co-heirs or legatees. [The legatee died before the tablets were opened, or became a foreigner.]

units.la: 2 Hodie {b}ex constitutione Imperatoris Antoni-ni, omnia caduca fisco vindicantur † sed seruato{c} iure antiquo liberis & parentibus.
units.tr: 2. Today, by a constitution of the Emperor Antoninus, all caducous property is claimed for the fisc, but the ancient right of children and parents is preserved.

units.la: 3 Caduca {d}cum suo onere fiunt: ideoque libertates & legata fideicommissa ab eo data, ex cuius persona haereditas caduca facta est, salua sunt: scili-cet {e}& legata, & fideicommissa cum suo onere fiunt caduca.
units.tr: 3. Caduca pass together with their burden. Therefore the freedoms and the fideicommissary legacies given by the person from whom the inheritance has become caducous remain valid; of course, legacies and fideicommissa also pass as caduca together with their burden.

units.la: QVI HABEANT IVS ANTIQVVM IN caducis. TIT. XVIII.
units.tr: Who have the ancient right in caduca. Title 18.

units.la: {f}Tem liberis f & parentibus & testatores vsque ad tertium gradum lex Papia ius antiquum dedit: vt heredibus illis ih-stitutis, quod quis ex eo testamento nō capit,ad hos pertineat,aut totum,aut ex parte,prout pertinere possit.
units.tr: The Papian law gave the ancient right to children and parents, and to testators up to the third degree, so that whatever a person cannot take under a will whose heirs have been instituted falls to these relatives, either wholly or in part, as far as it can pertain to them.

units.la: DE DOMINIIS ET ADQ̃VISITIONI-bus rerum. TIT. XIX.
units.tr: ON THE OWNERSHIP AND ACQUISITION OF THINGS. TIT. XIX.

units.la: Mnes res aut mancipi sunt †, aut nec mancipi. Mancipi {i}res sunt prædia in Italico solo, tam rustica, qualis est fun-dus: quàm vrbana, qualis domus. Item {g}iura prædiorum rusticorum: velut via, iter, actus, & aquæductus. Item serui & quadrupedes, quæ dorso collo ve domantur, velut boues, muli, equi, asini: cæteræ res nec mancipi sunt. Elephanti {h}& camelí, quanuis collo dorsòve domentur, nec mancipi sunt: quoniam bestiarum numero sunt.
units.tr: All things are either mancipi † or non-mancipi. Mancipi things are estates on Italian soil, both rural, such as a farm {f}, and urban, such as a house. Likewise the rights of rural estates, such as a way, a path, a driveway and an aqueduct. Likewise slaves and four-footed animals that are broken to the back or neck, such as oxen, mules, horses and asses. Other things are non-mancipi. Elephants and camels, although they are broken to the back or neck, are non-mancipi, since they belong to the class of wild beasts.

units.la: 2 Singularum rerum dominia nobis adquiruntur, mancipatione {l}, traditione {m}, vsucapione {n}, in iure cessione {o}, adiudicatione {p}, lege {q}: ri solet, vt homo, equus, ouis. Bestiæ mancipia sunt, cùm primùm domari incipiunt.
units.tr: 2 Ownership of single things is acquired by us through mancipation, traditio, usucapion, cession in law, adjudication, and by law {l}{m}{n}{o}{p}{q}: as is customary, such as a man, a horse, a sheep. Beasts become mancipi once they first begin to be tamed.

units.la: 3 Mancipatio propria species alienationis est a, & b rerum mancipi c: eáque fit certis d verbis,libri pende e,& quinque testibus praesentibus.
units.tr: 3 Mancipation is a proper kind of alienation a and b of mancipi things c. It is effected by set d words, with the bronze scale held e, and five witnesses present.

units.la: 4 Mancipatio locum habet inter cives Romanos,& Latinos Colonarios f, Latinoíque Iunianos, eósque peregrinos quibus g commercium datú est.
units.tr: 4 Mancipation takes place between Roman citizens and Latin colonists f, Junian Latins, and those foreigners to whom commercium g has been granted.

units.la: 5 Commercium est emendi h vendendique incuicem ius.
units.tr: 5 Commercium is the right of buying h and selling one another.

units.la: 6 Res mobiles non nisi praesentes mancipari possunt, & non plures quàm quae manu capi possunt. Immobiles autem, etiam plures simul,& quae diuersis locis sunt, mancipari possunt.
units.tr: 6 Movable things can be mancipated only when they are present, and only as many as can be grasped by hand. Immovable things, however, can be mancipated even several at once, and even those lying in different places.

units.la: 7 Traditio i, proprie est alienatio rerum l. Necmancipi rerum dominia, ipsa m traditione deprehendimus: scilicet, si ex iusta causa traditae sunt nobis.
units.tr: 7 Traditio is properly the alienation of things i. We find ownership of non-mancipi things l by traditio itself, namely if they have been delivered to us from a just cause m.

units.la: 8 Vsucapione n dominia adipiscimur, tam mancipi rerum, quàm necmancipi. Vsucapio o est autem dominij adeptio p, per continuationem possessionis anni, vel biennij: rerum mobilium anni, immobilium biennij.
units.tr: 8 We acquire ownership by usucapion n, of mancipi things as well as non-mancipi. Usucapion o is the acquisition of ownership p through continuous possession for a year or for two years: of movables for one year, of immovables for two years.

units.la: 6 In iure cessio quoque communis alienatio est, & mancipi, & nec mancipi, quae fit per tres q personas, in iure cedentes, vindicantes, addiquamcunque centes.
units.tr: 6 Cession in law is also a common form of alienation, both of mancipi and non-mancipi things, and it is effected through three q persons: the one ceding in law, the one claiming, and the one adjudicating.

units.la: tabularum, aliter quàm per hanc solennitatem non potuisse alienari, testatur: adde Contium r.dissputat.2. unde mancipatio intet actus legitimos refertur l.77.ff.de regulis iur. d Haec solennitas fuit verborum. Qui mancipium accipiebat, æs tenens ita dicebat, Hunc ego hominem ex iure Quiritum meum esse aio: isque mihi emptus est hoc æ ære æneáque libra. deinde æ re percutiebat libram idque ei dabat,à quo mancipium accipiebat. e Libripens libram æneam tenebat. f Latini libertini ad similitudinem antiquae latinitatis (quae in colonias missa est) videtur esse introducta: l.vn.Cod.de Latina libert. in pr. g Peregrinis datur ius commercij l.15.ff. de interdictis & releg. h Commercium, ius vendendi, emendi, permutandi l.5.ff.de iustitia. units.tr: tabularum; he testifies that otherwise than by this solemnity they could not be alienated. Add Contius r, disput. 2, whence mancipation is referred to among the legitimate acts, l. 77 ff. de regulis iuris. d This solemnity consisted of words. The one who received the mancipium, holding the bronze, spoke thus: "I declare this man to be mine by the law of the Quirites, and he has been bought for me with this bronze and balance." Then he struck the scale with the bronze and gave it to the one from whom he received the mancipium. e The libripens held the bronze scale. f The Latin freedmen seem to have been introduced in imitation of the ancient Latin status, which was sent out into the colonies: l. un. Cod. de Latina libertate, in pr. g The right of commercium is given to foreigners, l. 15 ff. de interdictis et relegatis. h Commercium is the right of selling, buying and exchanging, l. 5 ff. de iustitia. Yet this word is sometimes evident in a wider sense, l. 1 and the whole title Cod. de commerciis. i l. 20 Cod. de pactis. k proper, Cuiacius. l of non-mancipi things. "Of non-mancipi things," etc., Cuiacius here. m d.l. 20. n d.l. 20. o it is also called usucapio, as is pignoris capio, 7 Gell. xv. p Isidore reads it thus, 5 c. 25: adiectio; l. 3 ff. de usurpationibus. q Cession in law, or before the praetor, is done thus. The one to whom the thing is ceded, holding the thing, claims it thus: "I declare this man to be mine by the law of the Quirites."

units.la: Ab his,Prætor interrogat cedētem, An contra vindicet, vel A,F,A,
units.tr: Then the praetor asks the one ceding: "Does he claim against him, or A.F.A.?"
