units.la: 31 Legatorum a quae pure vel in diem certum relicta sunt, dies cedit an:iquo quidem iure, ex more tis restatoris tempore: per legem autem Papiam Poppeam, exap rtis b tabulis testamenti: eorum vero quae sub conditione relicta sunt, cum conditio existerit.
units.tr: 31 Of legacies: a Those left purely, or for a certain day, fall due: under the older law, at the time of the testator's death; but under the lex Papia Poppaea, when the tablets of the will are opened. Of those left under a condition, when the condition is fulfilled.

units.la: 32 Lex Falcidia iubet, non plus quam dodrante e totius patrimonij leg ri, vt omni modo quadrans d integer api d heredem remaneat.
units.tr: 32 The Falcidian law orders that no more than three-quarters (dodrans) of the whole estate may be left as legacies, so that in every case a full quarter (quadrans) remains with the heir.

units.la: 33 Legatorum perperam solutorum repetitio non e est.
units.tr: 33 A legacy paid in error cannot be reclaimed.
ON FIDEICOMMISSA. TITLE XXV.

units.la: Ideicommissi m est, quod non civilibus & verbis, sed precatiue relinquitur: nec ex rigore iuris civilis; [?]roficiscitur, sed ex voluntate datur relinquentis.
units.tr: A fideicommissum is what is left not by civil words but by request. It does not arise from the strictness of the civil law but is given by the will of the one who leaves it.

units.la: 2 Verba fideicommiss rum[?] in usu fere sunt haec b, Fideicommisso, feto, volo dari, & similia.
units.tr: The words commonly used for fideicommissa are these: b, I entrust, I request, I wish it to be given, and similar expressions.

units.la: 3 Etiam nutu relinquere fideicommissum in usu receptum est.
units.tr: It is also accepted in practice to leave a fideicommissum by a nod.

units.la: 4 Fideicommissum relinquere possunt, qui x testamentum facere possunt, licet non fecerint. Nam intestatus, quis moriturus, fideicommissum relinquere potest.
units.tr: Those who can make a will can leave a fideicommissum, even if they have not made one. For someone who is about to die intestate can still leave a fideicommissum.

units.la: 5 Res per fideicommissum relinqui possunt, quae m etiam per damnationem legari possunt.
units.tr: Things that can also be left by way of damnation can be left by fideicommissum.

units.la: 6 Fideicommissa dari possunt his, quibus legari potest.
units.tr: Fideicommissa can be given to those to whom a legacy can be given.

units.la: ratio abundat, aut hic agitur de legato damnationis obligat. quae ex qua si contraxit, aut certis personis soluto. Inst. t. de legat. f 6 Cod. 42: 2. Caius 7: & Paul. 4. sent. 1: adde 2. In-
units.tr: The reasoning is superfluous, or here it is treated of a legacy of damnation that binds, which, if he has contracted it, or paid it to certain persons. Inst. tit. de legatis. f 6. Cod. 42: 2. Caius 7; and Paul. 4. sent. 1; add 2. Inst.

units.la: [?]ut 2. de singulis reb. e l. 7 in pun ff. de vulgari. b adde Paul. 4. sent. 1. §. 6. & vlt. Instit. de singulis reb. i l. 21. ff. de legat. 3. 2.
units.tr: ... 2. de singulis rebus; and law 7 in pun. ff. de vulgari. b Add Paul. 4. sent. 1, §6 and last. Instit. de singulis rebus, law 21 ff. de legatis 3. 2.

units.la: Cod. de fideicommiss Nutu quae fieri possunt, dixi ad legem 52 in sin. de obligationib. k Qui testari potest fideicommittere potest, dixi d. § 10. Instit. Paulus 4. sent. §. 4.
units.tr: Cod. de fideicommissis. Things that can be done by a nod, I explained on law 52 at the end, de obligationibus. Whoever can make a testament can make a fideicommissum; I said so in d. §10 Instit. Paulus 4. sent. §4.

units.la: 6 Latini Iuniani fideicommissum capere possunt, licet legatum capere non possint.
units.tr: Latini Juniani can take a fideicommissum, although they cannot take a legacy.

units.la: 8 Fideicommissum & ante heredis institutionem, & post mortem heredis, & codicillis, etiam non confirmatis testamento, dari potest, licet legari non potest.
units.tr: A fideicommissum can be given both before the institution of an heir and after the death of the heir, and in codicils even if they are not confirmed by the will; a legacy cannot be given in these ways.

units.la: 9 Item Graece fideicommissum scriptum valet, licet legatum Graece scriptum non valeat.
units.tr: Likewise, a fideicommissum written in Greek is valid, although a legacy written in Greek is not valid.

units.la: 10 Filio qui in potestate est, seruoue heredibus institutis, seu si his legatum sit, patris vel domini fideicommitti potest, quamuis ab eo legari non possit.
units.tr: A fideicommissum can be entrusted by a father or master to a son who is in his power, or to a slave, who has been instituted heir, or to whom a legacy has been made, even though the father or master cannot leave them a legacy.

units.la: 11 Qui testamento heres institutus est, codicillis etiam non confirmatis, rogatus potest, vel vt heredi-tatem totam, vel ex parte alij restituat, quamuis ex directo heres institui ne quidem confirmatis codicillis possit.
units.tr: One who has been instituted heir in a will can be requested, even by unconfirmed codicils, to pass on the whole inheritance or part of it to another, although a person cannot be instituted heir directly even by confirmed codicils.

units.la: 12 Fideicommissa non per formulam petuntur, vt legata: sed cognitio est Romae quidem Consulis, fideicommissarius vocatur: in prouinciis vero, Praesidum prouinciarum.
units.tr: Fideicommissa are not sought by formula, as legacies are; but there is a hearing: at Rome before the Consul, and the one to whom the fideicommissum is due is called the fideicommissary; in the provinces, before the governors of the provinces.

units.la: 13 Poenae causa certae vel incertae personae quidem fideicommissa dari possunt.
units.tr: Fideicommissa can indeed be given as a penalty to a certain or an uncertain person.

units.la: 14 Is qui rogatus est alij restituere hereditatem, lege quidem Falcidia locum non habente, quoniam non plus (puta) quam dodrantem, restituere rogatus est, ex Trebelliano senatusconsulto restituit, vt ei & in eum dentur actiones, cui restituta est hereditas. Lege autem Falcidia interueniente, quoniam plus quam dodrantem, vel etiam totam hereditatem restituere rogatus sit, ex Pegasiano senatusconsulto restituit, vel deducta parte quarta, ipse qui scriptus est heres, hereditatem restituat, & in ipsum actiones conseruentur, is autem qui recipit hereditatem, legatarij loco habeatur.
units.tr: The one who has been asked to pass on an inheritance to another, when the Falcidian law does not apply, because he has been asked to restore no more than (say) three quarters, restores it under the Trebellian senatus consultum, so that actions are given both to him and against him to whom the inheritance is restored. But when the Falcidian law applies, because he has been asked to restore more than three quarters, or even the whole inheritance, he restores it under the Pegasian senatus consultum: either the heir who was named himself restores the inheritance after deducting a fourth, and actions are preserved against him; or the one who receives the inheritance is treated as a legatee.

units.la: 15 Ex Pegasiano senatusconsulto restituta hereditate, commoda & incommoda haereditatis commissario,
units.tr: When an inheritance has been restored under the Pegasian senatus consultum, the benefits and burdens of the inheritance pass to the fideicommissary.

units.la: a de quibus vide tit. 3. §. 5. eod.
units.tr: a On these matters see title 3, §5 of the same.

units.la: c quod olim non fuit in legatis tit. 24. §. 2. §. eod.

g Title 24, §24.

units.la: h Codicillis etiam confirmatis heres institui non potest: quamuis iisdem confirmatis restituendi iussio coprehendi viter possit.
units.tr: h An heir cannot be instituted even by confirmed codicils, although the command to restore can be included in confirmed codicils.

units.la: o vide Instit. de fideicommiss. hered. & ad Sc. Trebell.
units.tr: o See Instit. de fideicommissariis hereditatibus and on the Senatus consultum Trebellianum.

units.la: p legendum est, vt municantur. Inter heredem, & eum cui reliquae partes restitutae sunt interpositis stipulationibus ad exemplum partis & pro parte stipulationum. Partes autem & pro parte stipulationes proprie dicun-tur, quae de lucro & damno communicando solent interponi inter heredem & legatarium partiarium, i.cum quo partitus[?] est heres.
units.tr: p It should be read, "so that they may be shared." Between the heir and the one to whom the remaining parts have been restored, stipulations are interposed on the model of the partnership stipulation and the stipulation pro parte. Properly speaking, these are called partnership stipulations and stipulations pro parte, which are usually interposed concerning the sharing of gain and loss between the heir and a partner legatee, i.e. the one with whom the heir has shared.

units.la: 16 Si heres damnosam hereditatem dicat, cogetur a Prætore adire & restituere totam, ita ut ei & in eum qui recipit hereditatem actiones dentur, perinde atque si ex Trebelliano senatusconsulto restituta fuisset: idque ut ita fiat, Pegasiano senatusconsulto cautum est.
units.tr: 16 If the heir says the inheritance is damaging, he will be compelled by the Praetor to enter and restore the whole of it, so that actions are given both to him and against the one who receives the inheritance, just as if it had been restored under the Trebellian senatus consultum. The Pegasian senatus consultum provides that this is done.

units.la: 17 Si quis in fraudem taciam[?] fidem accommodauerit, ut non capienti fideicommissum restituat, nec quadrantem eum deducere Senatus censuit: nec caducum vindicare ex eo testamento, si liberos habeat.
units.tr: 17 If anyone, by fraud, lends his good faith so that he restores a fideicommissum to one who is not capable of taking it, the Senate has decided he may not deduct even a quarter, nor claim the caducum from that will if he has children.
18 Liberty can be given through a fideicommissum.
ON LEGITIMATE HEIRS. Title XXVI.

units.la: Ntestatorum ingenuorum hereditate pertinent, primum{l} ad suos heredes{»} id est, liberos qui in potestate sunt, ceterosque qui in liberorum loco sunt. Si sui heredes non sunt, ad consanguineos{»} id est, fratres & sorores ex eodem patre. Si nec hi sunt, ad reliquos adgnatos proximos, id est, cognatos virilis sexus, per mares descendentes, eiusdem familiae: id enim cautum est lege 12. Tabularum: Ac si intestatus{m} moritur, cui suus{n} extabit{o} heres, nec adgnatus proximus familiam{p} habeto.
units.tr: The inheritances of those who die intestate and are freeborn pass, first, to their own heirs (sui heredes), that is, the children who are under power and the others who stand in the place of children. If there are no sui heredes, they pass to the consanguines, that is, brothers and sisters from the same father. If there are none of these, they pass to the nearest remaining agnates, that is, the male kin descending through males of the same family. For the Twelve Tables provide this: "And if a man dies intestate, having a sui heres, let the nearest agnate hold the family" (Twelve Tables).

units.la: 2 Si defunctus{q} sit filius ex{r} altero filio mortuo, iam nepos unus, vel etiam plures, ad omnes hereditas pertinet: non ut in capita diuidatur, sed ut{s}
units.tr: 2 If the deceased left a son who was the son of a son who had died, then one grandson, or even several, inherit the whole estate. It is not divided per capita, but per stirpes
{l} On the laws of the Twelve Tables, book 2.
{»} Law 7, ff. de bonis damnatorum.
It ought to be read thus.
{q} It should be read "of the deceased" (defuncti).

units.la: vlt.in f.Inst.de hered.ab intest.dixi ad leges 12.tabul.lib.2.
units.tr: Last section in fine, Inst. de hered. ab intest. I have discussed this on the laws of the Twelve Tables, book 2.
{m} Law 9, §2, ff. de liberis et posthumis.
{o} "Nor shall the agnate heir appear," etc.
{p} Law 195, in fine, ff. de verborum significatione.
{r} "and from another," it ought to be read thus.

units.la: {s} §. in stirpes,id est, ut filius solus mediam partem habeat, & nepotes quotquot sunt alteram dimidiam, Aequum est enim nepotes patris sui loco succe-dere,& eam partem habere, quam pater eorum si vi-veret, habiturus esset.
units.tr: {s} §. "in stirpes," that is, the son alone takes one half, and the grandsons, however many there are, take the other half. For it is fair that grandsons succeed in their father's place and have the share which their father would have had if he were alive.

units.la: 3 Quandiu suus heres sperat ur heres fieri pos-se,tandiu locus agnatis non est: velut si vxor de-functi prægnans sit,aut filius apud hostes sit.
units.tr: 3 As long as a sui heres can be expected to become heir, there is no place for the agnates. This is so, for example, if the wife of the deceased is pregnant, or a son is among the enemy.

units.la: 4 Agnatorum hæreditates diuiduntur in capita, veluti si sit fratris filius, & alterius fratris duo pluresve liberi: quotquot sunt ab utraque parte personae, tot fiunt portiones, ut singuli singulas capiant.
units.tr: 4 Inheritances of agnates are divided per capita, as, for example, when there is a brother's son and two or more children of another brother. As many persons as there are on each side, so many shares are made, so that each takes one share.

units.la: 5 Si plures eodem gradu sunt agnati,& quidam eorum hereditatem ad se pertinere noluerint, vel antequam adierint decesserint: eorum pars adcre-scit his qui adierint. Quod si nemo eorum adie-rit, ad insequentem gradum ex lege hereditas non transmittitur: quoniam in legitimis hereditati-bus successio non {†}est.
units.tr: 5 If several agnates are of the same degree, and some of them refuse to accept the inheritance, or die before entering upon it, their share accrues to those who have entered. But if none of them enters, the inheritance is not passed by law to the next degree, since in legitimate inheritances there is no succession by representation (successio is not {†}).

units.la: 6 Ad fœminas ultra{g} consanguineorum gradu legitima hereditas non pertinet: itaque soror fra-tri sororiue legitima heres sit.
units.tr: 6 A legitimate inheritance does not pass to women beyond the degree of consanguinity; thus a sister is the legitimate heir of her brother or sister.

units.la: 7 Ad liberos matris intestatae hereditas ex lege XII{h} Tabularum non{i} pertinebat: quia fœmi-næ suos hæredes non habent. Sed postea Imperatorum Antonini{k} & Commodi oratione in Senatu recitata, id actum est, ut sine in manu{l} conuen-tione, matrum legitimae hereditates ad filios pertineant, exclusis consanguineis, & reliquis adgnatis.
units.tr: 7 By the Law of the Twelve Tables the inheritance of an intestate mother did not pass to her children, because women do not have sui heredes. But afterwards, when an address of the Emperors Antoninus and Commodus was read in the Senate, it was decided that, without a conventio in manum, the legitimate inheritances of mothers pass to their sons, excluding consanguines and the other agnates.

units.la: 8 Intestati filij hæreditas ad matrem ex lege duodecim{m} Tabularum non{n} pertinet: sed si ius liberorum habeat, ingenua trium, libertina qua-tuor, legitima heres sit ex Senatusconsulto Tertul-
units.tr: 8 By the Twelve Tables the inheritance of an intestate son does not pass to the mother; but if she has the ius liberorum, she becomes the legitimate heir, as a freeborn woman with three children, or a freedwoman with four, under the Senatusconsultum Tertullianum

units.la: {†} Iure Iustiniani hodie in suis successio est §.septimo,Instit.de legit. adgnatorum successione. nam & in legitimis tutoribus est successio l.3.§.9.ff.de legitimis tutorib.
units.tr: {†} By the law of Justinian today there is succession among the sui; §. seventh, Institutes, on succession of agnates by law. For there is also succession in legitimate tutelage: law 3, §9, ff. de legitimis tutoribus.

units.la: {g} idque iure ciuili & lege Voconia institutum Paulus 4.sent.8.§.tertio. De lege Voconia vide Cuiacium ad titul.Instit.de lege Falcid.
units.tr: {g} This was instituted by civil law and by the lex Voconia, as Paulus says, Sent. 4, 8, §3. On the lex Voconia see Cujas on the title of the Institutes de lege Falcidia.

units.la: {h} dixi in notis ad leges duodecim tabularum libro secundo.
units.tr: {h} I have said this in my notes on the laws of the Twelve Tables, book 2.

units.la: {i} Instit.de Senatusconsulto Tertull.& in prin.de Senatusconsulto Orphitiano.
units.tr: {i} Institutes, de Senatusconsulto Tertulliano, and at the beginning, de Senatusconsulto Orphitiano.
{k} Add law 9, ff. ad Tertullianum.
{l} See title 9, §. eod.
{m} I have said this on the laws of the Twelve Tables.

units.la: {n} Instit. de Senatusconsulto Tertull.in pr. liano {4}si {b}tamē ei filio neque suus heres sit,quive {c}inter suos heredes ad bonorum possessionem à Praetore vocatur: neque pater ad quem lege hereditas, bonorumve possessio cum re pertinet, neque frater consanguineus. Quòd si soror consanguinea sit, ad vtrasque {d}pertinere iubetur hereditas.
units.tr: {n} Institutes, de Senatusconsulto Tertulliano, at the beginning. Yet if that son has no sui heres, nor one who is called by the praetor to possession of goods among the sui heredes, then neither the father, to whom the inheritance or possession of goods pertains by law, nor the consanguine brother takes it. But if there is a consanguine sister, the inheritance is ordered to pass to both.

units.la: TITVL. XXVII. DE LIBERTORVM SVCCESSIONIBVS vel bonis.
units.tr: TITLE XXVII. CONCERNING THE SUCCESSIONS OF FREEDMEN, OR THEIR GOODS.

units.la: LIBERTORVM intestatorum heredi-tas primùm ad suos s heredes perti-net: deinde ad eos quorum liberti sunt, velut patronum, patronam, liberósve patroni.
units.tr: The inheritance of freedmen who die intestate first belongs to their own heirs; then to those whose freedmen they are, such as the patron, the patroness, or the children of the patron.

units.la: 2 Si vt patronus, & alterius patroni filius, ad solum patronum hereditas pertinet.
units.tr: 2 If the patron and the son of another patron are both in the position of patron, the inheritance belongs to the patron alone.
3 Likewise, the son of a patron stands in the way of the grandsons of a patron.

units.la: 4 Ad liberos patronorum, hereditas defuncti pertinet, vt in capita {h}, non in stirpes diuidatur.
units.tr: 4 The inheritance of the deceased passes to the children of the patrons, and is divided per capita, not per stirpes.

units.la: 5 Legitimae[?] hereditatis ius, quod ex lege duodecim Tabularum descendit, capitis minutione amittitur.
units.tr: 5 The right to a lawful inheritance, which descends from the law of the Twelve Tables, is lost by loss of civil status.
Title XXVIII. On Giving Possession of Goods

units.la: BONORVM possessio datur aut contra tabulas testamenti, aut aduersus {l}tabulas intestati.
units.tr: Possession of goods is given either against the tablets of a will, or against the tablets of intestacy.

units.la: 2 Contra {m}tabulas bonorum possessio datur liberis emancipatis, {n}testamento praeteritis {o}, licet legitima ad eos non pertineat hereditas.
units.tr: 2 Possession of goods against the tablets is given to emancipated children who were passed over in the will, although the legitimate inheritance does not belong to them.

units.la: 3 Bonorum possessio contra tabulas liberis tam {p}naturalibus, quàm adoptiuis datur. Sed naturalibus quidem emancipatis: non tamen & illis, qui in adoptiua familia sunt. Adoptiuis autem, his tantùm, qui in potestate manserunt.
units.tr: 3 Possession of goods against the tablets is given to natural children as well as to adopted ones. But to natural children only if they are emancipated, and not to those who are in an adoptive family. To adopted children, only to those who remained under power.

units.la: 4 Emancipatis liberis ex edicto datur bonorum possessio, si parati sunt cauere {a}a patribus {b}suis qui in potestate manierunt[?], bona, quae moriente patre habuerunt, se collaturos.
units.tr: 4 By the edict, possession of goods is given to emancipated children, if they are prepared to give security to their brothers who remained under power that they will bring into collation the goods which they had when their father died.

units.la: 5 Secundum {c}tabulas bonorum possessio datur scriptis heredibus, scilicet si eorum quibus contra tabulas competit, nemo sit, aut petere nolint.
units.tr: 5 Possession of goods according to the tablets is given to the instituted heirs, namely if there is no one to whom possession against the tablets is due, or if they are unwilling to seek it.

units.la: 6 Etiam si iure ciuili non valeat testamentum, forte quod familiae mancipatio vel cuncupatio defuit, si lignatum testamentum sit, non {d}minus quam tabulae.
units.tr: 6 Even if a will is not valid by civil law, perhaps because the mancipation or nuncupation of the family was lacking, if it is written on wood it counts no less than a written tablet.

units.la: 7 Intestati datur bonorum possessio per septem gradus. Primo gradu liberis: Secundo legitimis he-redibus: Tertio {e}proximis cognatis: Quarto fami-liae {f}: Quinto patrono, parentibus, liberisve patroni, patronave: Sexto viro, uxori: Septimo cognatis manumissoris, quibus per legem Furiam plus [?]ille aufes[?] capere licet. Si nemo sit ad quem bonorum possessio pertinere possit: aut si quidem, sed ius suum omiserit: populo bona deferuntur ex lege Iulia ca-ducaria {g}.
units.tr: 7 Possession of goods on intestacy is given through seven degrees. In the first degree, to children; in the second, to legitimate heirs; in the third, to the nearest cognates; in the fourth, to the family; in the fifth, to the patron, the parents or children of the patron, or the patroness; in the sixth, to husband and wife; in the seventh, to the cognates of the manumitter, to whom the Lex Furia permits taking a larger share. If there is no one to whom possession could pertain, or if there is someone but he has let his right lapse, the goods are passed to the people under the Lex Julia Caducaria.

units.la: 8 Liberi {b}bonorum possessio datur, tam his qui in potestate fuerunt usque in mortis tempus, quam emancipatis: item adoptivis, non tamen etiam in adoptionem datis.
units.tr: 8 Possession of goods is given to children both to those who were under power until the time of death, and to the emancipated; likewise to adopted children, but not to those who were given in adoption.

units.la: 9 Proximi cognati {i}bonorum possessionem accipiunt, non solum per foeminini sexus personam cogn: ti, sed etiam agnati capite deminuti. Nam licet legitimum ius agnationis capitis minutione amiserint, natura tamen cognati manent.
units.tr: 9 Nearest cognates receive possession, not only through persons of the female sex who are cognates, but also agnates who have suffered loss of status. For although they have lost the legitimate right of agnation by loss of status, they remain cognates by nature.

units.la: 10 Bonorum possessio datur parentibus & liberis intra {l}annum, ex quo petere potuerunt: caeteris intra centum dies.
units.tr: 10 Possession of goods is given to parents and children within a year from when they could seek it; to others within a hundred days.

units.la: 11 Qui omnes intra id tempus si {m}non petierint, ad bonorum possessionem sequens gradus admittitur: perinde acsi superiores non essent. idque per septem gradus fit.
units.tr: 11 If all of these do not seek it within that time, the next degree is admitted to possession, just as if the higher degrees did not exist. This happens through seven degrees.

units.la: 12 Hi quibus ex successorio edicto bonorum possessio datur, heredes quidem non sunt, sed he-
units.tr: 12 Those to whom possession of goods is given by the successory edict are not heirs, but they are placed in the position of heirs by the benefit of the Praetor.

units.la: {g} de qua in l. 96 §. 1. ff. de leg. 1: l. 4. §. 17. ff. de fideicommiss. libertatib.
units.tr: {g} On which see l. 96 §1 ff. de legatis 1; l. 4 §17 ff. de fideicommissariis libertatibus.
{b} See the title ff. unde liberi.
{i} See title 11, unde cognati.

units.la: {l} §. 4. Inftit. de bonor. poss: l. 1. §. 12. ff. de successor. edicto: l. 2. Cod. qui admitti ad bonor. l. 3. ff. unde cognati: l. 1. §. 11. ff. de successor. edicto.
units.tr: {l} §4 Institutes, de bonorum possessionibus; l. 1 §12 ff. de successorio edicto; l. 2 Cod. qui admitti ad bonorum possessionem; l. 3 ff. unde cognati; l. 1 §11 ff. de successorio edicto.

units.la: {m} §. 5. Inftit. de bonor. possess. rectis[?] loco constituuntur beneficio Praetoris. Ideoque seu ipsi agant, seu cum his agatur, fictitiis actionibus opus est: in quibus heredes esse finguntur.
units.tr: {m} §5 Institutes, de bonorum possessionibus. They are placed in the position of heirs by the benefit of the Praetor. Therefore, whether they sue themselves or are sued, fictitious actions are needed, in which they are feigned to be heirs.

units.la: 13 Bonorum possessio aut cum re datur, aut sine re. Cum re{a}, si is qui accepit, cum effectu bona re- tineat: sine re, quum alius iure civili evincere hereditatem possit: veluti si suus heres intestato sit{b}. Bonorum possessio sine re est, quum suus heres evincere hereditatem iure legitimo possit.
units.tr: 13 Possession of goods is given either with the thing or without the thing. With the thing, if the one who accepted keeps the goods with effect; without the thing, when another can evict the inheritance by civil law, as when a sui heres dies intestate. Possession is without the thing when a sui heres can evict the inheritance by legitimate right.
On the Goods of Freedmen. Title XXIX.

units.la: IVIS[?] Romani liberti hereditatem lex duodecim Tabularum patrono defert, si intestato fine suo herede liberti deceserit. Ideoque siue testamen-to facto decedat, licet suus heres ei non sit, seu intestato, & suus heres ei sit, quanuis non naturalis, sed uxor puta quae in manu fit, vel adoptiuus filius: lex patrono nihil praestat. Sed ex edicto Praetoris si testamento facto libertus moriatur, aut{e} vt nihil, aut minus quam partem dimidiam bonorum patrono relinquat: contra tabulas testamenti, partis dimidiae bonorum possessio illi datur, nisi libertus aliquem ex naturalibus liberis successorem sibi relinquat, siue intestato decedat, & uxorem forte in manum vel adoptiuum filium relinquat, aequae partis mediae bonorum possessio contra suos heredes patrono datur.
units.tr: Under the Roman law, the Twelve Tables grant a freedman's inheritance to the patron if the freedman dies intestate and without a heir of his own body. So whether he dies having made a will, although he has no suus heres, or dies intestate but has a suus heres who is not a natural one, such as a wife who comes into the husband's hand (in manu) or an adopted son, the law gives the patron nothing. But by the edict of the Praetor, if a freedman dies after making a will and leaves the patron either nothing or less than half of his goods, the possession of half the goods is granted to the patron against the tablets of the will, unless the freedman leaves a successor from among his natural children. If he dies intestate, and perhaps leaves a wife in manu or an adopted son, the possession of an equal half of the goods is granted to the patron against the sui heredes.

units.la: 2 In bonis libertae patrono nihil iuris ex edicto datur. Itaque si intestata moriatur liberta, semper ad eam hereditas pertinet.
units.tr: 2 Nothing of the patron's right in the goods of a freedwoman is given by the edict. So if a freedwoman dies intestate, the inheritance always passes to her.

units.la: 3 Licet{f} liberi sint libertae, quoniam non sunt sui heredes matri, obstat{g} patrono lex Papia Popea. Postea libertas quatuor liberorum iure tutela patronorum liberauit, & cum intulerit, iam posse eas sine auctoritate patronorum testari, prospexit vt pro numero liberorum libertae superstitum virilis pars patrono debetur.
units.tr: 3 Although children are born to a freedwoman, they are not sui heredes to their mother, and the Papian Poppaean law stands in the way of the patron. Later, the right of four children freed freedwomen from the guardianship of their patrons, and once this was established, that they could make a will without the patrons' authority, it provided that, in proportion to the number of children, the surviving freedwoman owes the patron a share equal to a man's share.

units.la: 4 Liberi patroni virilis sexus, eadem iura in bonis libertorum parentum suorum habent, quae & ipse patronus. Foeminae vero, ex lege quidem XII. Tabularum perinde ius habent, atque masculi patronorum liberi.
units.tr: 4 Sons of a patron of male sex have the same rights in the goods of their freedman parents as the patron himself. Daughters, indeed, under the law of the Twelve Tables, have the same right as the sons of patrons.

units.la: 5 Contra tabulas autem testamenti liberti, aut ab intestato contra suos heredes non naturalis {*} honorum possessio eis non competit. Sed si ius trium liberorum habuerunt, etiam haec iura ex lege Papia Popaea nanciscuntur.
units.tr: 5 But against the tablets of a freedman's will, or against the sui heredes in an intestate succession, the possession of goods that are not natural is not available to them. But if they have the right of three children, they also acquire these rights under the Papian Poppaean law.

units.la: 6 Patronae ex bonis libertorum illud ius tantum habent, quod lex XII Tabularum introduxit. Sed postea lex Papia patronae ingenuae duobus liberis honoratae {b} libertinae tribus, id iuris dedit quod patronus habet ex edicto.
units.tr: 6 Patronesses have from the goods of freedmen only that right which the Twelve Tables law introduced. But afterwards the Papian law gave to freeborn patronesses honored with two children, and to freedwomen honored with three, the right that the patron has under the edict.

units.la: 7 Item liberis ingenuae trium liberorum iure honoratae eadem lex id ius dedit, quod ipsi patrono {c} tribuit.
units.tr: 7 Likewise, the same law gave to the children of a freeborn woman who has the right of three children the right that it grants to the patron himself.
END
The Institutes of Gaius, Books II.

units.la: CUIACIUS in praefatione ad Codicē Theodosianum censet, Epitomen hanc Insti-tutionum esse Caij ab Aniano Alarici Cōsiliario confectam, quantum,quoque modo sui temporis usus exigere videbatur: nec verò omnem propterea Caio dignita-tem & elegantiam deperiisse: restare inter lateres Aniani male coctos adhuc lapillos quosdam, si quis non pigretur internosce-re, è quibus veluti è culmo fruges, & luculentiùs si reliquias eas adiunxerit, quae Pandectis insperlæ [?] sunt, quaeque Iustiniani Institutionibus leguntur, quanti momenti,ponderis artificij Caij Institutiones fuerint, æsti-mare posit.
units.tr: Cuiacius, in his preface to the Theodosian Code, holds that this epitome of the Institutes is the work of Gaius, made by Anianus, counsellor to Alaric, to the extent and in the manner that the practice of his own time seemed to require. Nor, he says, did Gaius lose all his dignity and elegance on that account. Among the badly baked bricks of Anianus there remain some little pebbles, if anyone is willing to take the trouble to pick them out, and from these, as grain from the straw, one can judge how great the weight and craftsmanship of the Institutes of Gaius were. This judgment will be clearer still if one adds the remaining fragments scattered through the Pandects and read in the Institutes of Justinian.
The First Book of the Institutes of Gaius.
ON THE LIBERTIES OF SLAVES. TIT. I.

units.la: AII[?] Institutionum liber primus dicit omnes homines aut liberos esse aut servos. Sed ex ipsis qui liberi sunt, alios esse ingenuos, alios libertinos. Ingenuos, qui ingenui nati sunt: Libertinos qui pro ju-sta servitute manumissi, liberi sunt. Ingenuorum omnium unus status est. Libertorum vero ideo non unus est, quia tria sunt genera libertorum: quia liberi aut cives Romani sunt, aut Latini, aut Dediticii. Tamen qui cives Romani fiunt, qui Latini, qui Dediticii, breviter explanandum est.
units.tr: The first book of the Institutes of Gaius says that all men are either free or slaves. But among those who are free, some are freeborn (ingenui) and some are freedmen (libertini). The freeborn are those born free; freedmen are those who, having been manumitted from lawful slavery, are free. All the freeborn have one status. Freedmen, however, do not have one status, because there are three kinds of freedmen: they are either Roman citizens, or Latins, or Dediticii. Yet how those who become Roman citizens, Latins, or Dediticii are made must be briefly explained.

units.la: 2 Cives Romani sunt, qui his tribus modis, id est, testamento, aut in Ecclesia, aut ante Consulem fuerint manumissi.
units.tr: 2 Those are Roman citizens who have been manumitted in one of three ways: by will, in the Church, or before the consul.

units.la: 3 Latini{i} sunt, qui aut per epistolam{k}, aut inter amicos{l}, aut convivij{m} adhibitione manumittuntur.
units.tr: 3 Those are Latins who are manumitted by letter, among friends, or by admission to a dinner table.

units.la: 4 Dediticii{n} vero sunt, qui post admissa crimina suppliciis subditi, & publicè pro criminibus cæsi sunt: aut in quorum facie{o} vel corpore quæcumque dicerer,apud prætorem, vel vindicta Ulp.d.loco §.7.
units.tr: 4 Dediticii are those who, after committing crimes, have been subjected to punishments and publicly beaten for their crimes; or those on whose face or body some mark has been placed, whatever it may be, before the praetor, or by the rod (vindicta). See Ulpian, the passage cited, §7.
{i} See C., on the Latin freedom.
{k} See l. un. §1, Cod., on Latin freedom.

units.la: {l} dixi ad Ulpianum. 1. §.10. adde l.un. §.2.C.de Latina libert.
units.tr: {l} I have spoken of this at Ulpian, 1 §10. Add l. un. §2, C., on Latin freedom.
{m} By the table: Theophilus, Institutes, on freedmen.
{n} See C., on the liberty of the Dediticii; Ulpian 1 §11.

units.la: {o} aut fronte Theophil.Institut.de libert. §. ὧν δὲ ἀπε-λευθε[?] {a}indicia aut igne. aut ferro {b}impressa sunt,& ita impressa sunt, ut deleri non possint. Si si manumissi fuerint, Dediticij appellantur.
units.tr: {o} or by the forehead: Theophilus, Institutes, on freedmen, §: [ὧν δὲ ἀπελευθε...] Some are marked by branding or by fire or iron, and so marked that the marks cannot be erased. If such persons are manumitted, they are called Dediticii.

units.la: 5 Sed inter hæc tria genera libertorum ideo ciues Romani meliorem statum habent: quia & testamenta facere, & ex testamento quibuscunque personis succedere possunt. Nam & Latini, & Dediticij nec testamenta condere{c}, nec sibi ex testamento aliquid dimissum possunt vllatenus vindicare. Tamen Latini certis{d}rebus priuilegiis ciuium Romanorum Libertorum consequi possunt: Dediticij vero nulla ratione possunt ad ciuium Romanorum Libertorum beneficium peruenire. Nam Latini patronorum beneficio, id est, si iterum{e}ab ipsis aut testamento, aut in Ecclesia, aut ante Consulem manumittantur, ciuium Romanorum priuilegia consequuntur.
units.tr: 5 But among these three kinds of freedmen, Roman citizens have the better status, because they can both make wills and succeed to inheritances under a will from any persons whatever. For Latins and Dediticii can neither make wills nor claim anything left to them under a will in any way. Yet Latins can obtain certain privileges of Roman citizens in certain matters; Dediticii, however, can by no means attain the benefit of the status of Roman freedmen. For Latins, by the favour of their patrons, that is, if they are manumitted again by them, either by will, in the Church, or before the consul, obtain the privileges of Roman citizens.

units.la: 6 Non tamen omnes domini seruos suos manumittere possunt. Nam si aliquis multa debita habeat, cuius substantia à creditoribus teneatur obnoxia{f}, si in fraudem creditoris seruos suos manumittere voluerit, collata manumissio non valet.
units.tr: 6 Yet not every master may manumit his slaves. For if someone has many debts, and his property is liable to his creditors, and he wishes to manumit his slaves in fraud of his creditor, the manumission so made is not valid.

units.la: 7 Aut si libertus ciuis Romanus filios liberos non habuerit, {g}& in fraudem patroni sui seruos suos manumittat, similiter data manumissio non valet.
units.tr: 7 Likewise, if a freedman who is a Roman citizen has no living children, and manumits his slaves in fraud of his patron, the manumission so given is similarly invalid.

units.la: 8 Præterea minor quicumque viginti annorum dominus,seruo suo libertate dare non potest,nisi forte tantum minor manumissor,cui pater Ivus & mater à patrono donati sunt,eosdem manumittat,aut certè paedagogum{h}, aut collaneum manumittat. Nam quilibet dominus.{i}quatuordecim annos egressus{k}, testamentum facere possit, & heredem instituere, & legata relinquere,libertatem tamen seruis non {†}po test in hac ætate[?] conferre.
units.tr: 8 Moreover, no master under twenty years of age can give liberty to his slave, unless perhaps a minor manumitter, to whom father and mother were given by the patron, manumits those same persons, or else manumits a tutor or a fellow-slave. For any master who has passed fourteen years of age may make a will, institute an heir, and leave legacies; yet at this age he cannot confer liberty on slaves.

units.la: DE NVMERO SER-VORVM TESTAMENTO manumittendorum. TIT. II.
units.tr: Concerning the number of slaves who may be manumitted by will. Title II.
{g} I have said this on Ulpian 1, §15.

units.la: {*}C[?]ONSTITVTVM est, quantum seruorum numerum testamento de quantum familiam[?] liceat manumitti, hoc ordine: vt si quis duos seruos habet, ambos manumittere; qui vero tres, duos tantum manumittat. Qui sex, tres. Qui quatuor, quinque. Qui decem, quinque, duodecim, tredecim, quatuordecim, quindecim, sedecim, deciem et septem similiter quinque, similiter quam et sex. Et ab hoc numero vsque ad triginta, tertiam partem manumittere liceat. Qui amplius quam triginta habuerit, vsque ad centum, quartam partem de numero seruorum manumittere potest. Qui vero plures quam centum habuerit, quintam partem manumittere potest. Sed & hoc statuendum est, vt de qualiber grandi familia nulli amplius quam
units.tr: It has been settled how many slaves, or what size of household, may be manumitted by will, in this order: if someone has two slaves, he may manumit both; if he has three, only two; if six, three; if four, five; if ten, five; if twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, similarly five, just as with six. And from this number up to thirty, it is lawful to manumit a third part. Whoever has more than thirty, up to a hundred, may manumit a quarter of his slaves. Whoever has more than a hundred may manumit a fifth part. But it must also be laid down that from any large household no more than

units.la: 2 Nam qui voluerit aut in Ecclesia, aut ante Consulem, aut inter amicos aut per epistolam manumittere, potest his manumissionibus omnem
units.tr: 2 For whoever wishes to manumit, whether in the Church, before the consul, among friends, or by letter, may extend all these manumissions to

units.tr: 3 For if anyone wishes to manumit by will more than the number stated above, the order must be observed, so that freedom holds good only for those... But if male or female slaves are not manumitted by name in the will, but the one making the will wishes to make all his slaves, male and female, free in a general way, then to none

units.la: 4 Nam si aliquis in ægri irridine constitutus, in fraudem b huius legis facere noluerit testamentum, sed epistolis s, aut quibuscunque aliis rebus serius volueris libertates, & sub tempore mortis hoc fecerit, ij quibus manumissi sunt, vsque ad nunc-zum.
units.tr: 4 For if someone, placed in the illness of sickness, does not wish to make a will in fraud of this law, but by letters or by whatever other means wishes to grant freedom to his slaves, and does so at the time of death, those whom he has manumitted shall be free, up to

units.la: {a} Lege Fufia Caninia. rum superius constitutum, liberi erunt. Qui verò post st.t tum [?] numerum manumissi fuerint, serui sine dubio permanebunt.
units.tr: {a} The Lex Fufia Caninia. ...of the number established above they will be free. But those manumitted beyond that number will undoubtedly remain slaves.

units.la: 5 Nam si incolumis quoscunque diuerso tempore manumisit: [?] inter eos qui per testamentum manumissi sunt, nullatenus computentur.
units.tr: 5 For if, while in health, he manumitted any at different times, they are not to be counted at all among those manumitted by will.
On the Law of Persons. Title II.

units.la: ALIQVAE personae sui {a}iuris sunt, aliquae alieno iuri subiectae sunt. Itaque cum {b}ostenditur quae personae alieno iuri subiectae sint, tunc euidenter agno-scitur, quae sui iuris sint.
units.tr: Some persons are sui iuris, while others are subject to the power of another. Therefore, when it has been shown which persons are subject to another's power, it is then clearly recognised which are sui iuris.

units.la: 2 In potestate itaque dominorum sunt serui, quam potestatem omnes gentes habere certum est: sed distringendi in seruos dominis pro sua potestate permittitur, occidendi tantum seruos suos domini licentiam non habebunt: nisi forte seruus dum pro culpa modo ceditur, casu forsitan moriatur. Nam si seruus dignum morte crimen admiserit, iis iudicibus, quibus publici officij potestas commissa est, tradendus est, ut pro suo crimine puniatur.
units.tr: (2) Slaves, then, are in the power of their masters, and it is certain that all peoples have this power. Masters are permitted to inflict punishment on their slaves within the bounds of their authority, but masters do not have the right to kill their own slaves; except that perhaps a slave who is merely beaten for a fault may by chance die. For if a slave has committed a crime deserving death, he is to be handed over to those judges to whom the power of public office has been entrusted, so that he may be punished for his crime.

units.la: 3 In {f}potestate etiam patrum sunt filij, ex legitimo matrimonio procreati.
units.tr: (3) Children born of a lawful marriage are also in the power of their fathers.
On Marriages. Title 4.

units.la: LEGITIMAE sunt nuptiae, si Roma-nus Romanam {g}nuptiis {h}interue-nientibus, vel consensu {i}ducat u-xorem.
units.tr: A marriage is lawful if a Roman takes a Roman woman as his wife, whether or not the nuptial rites intervene, provided there is consent.

units.la: 2 Sed non {k}omnes personas uxores ducere licet: quia nec {l}patri filiam, nec filio mat-rem, nec auo neptem, nec neposi [?] auiam. Quod non solum de personis, quae nobis propinquitate coniunctae sunt, sed etiam de adoptiuis, hoc est adsiliatis, iussum est. observari. Nam etsi{a} per emancipationem adoptio dissolvatur, nuptias tamen inter has personas lem-per constat illicitas.
units.tr: 2. But it is not permitted to marry just any persons: a father may not marry a daughter, nor a son a mother, nor a grandfather a granddaughter, nor a grandson a grandmother. This has been ordered to be observed not only of persons joined to us by blood kinship but also of adoptive ones, that is, those adopted as sons. For although adoption is dissolved by emancipation, it is always held that marriages between these persons are unlawful.

units.la: 3 Inter{b} fratrem quoque & sororem, sive eodem{c} patre ac matre nati fuerint, sive diversis matrib.aut patribus, matrimonia esse non possunt. Inter adoptivos e iam fratres illicita sunt coniugia, nisi{d} forte adoptio emancipatione fuerit dissoluta. nam si emancipatio interuenerit, nuptiæ inter huiusmodi fratres licito contrahuntur.
units.tr: 3. Marriages between brother and sister also cannot take place, whether they were born of the same father and mother, or of different mothers or fathers. Marriages between adoptive brothers are likewise unlawful, unless perhaps the adoption was dissolved by emancipation. For if emancipation has intervened, marriages between such brothers are lawfully contracted.

units.la: 4 Fratris quoque & sororis filiam{e} uxorem ducere non licet.
units.tr: 4. Nor is it permitted to take as wife the daughter of a brother or of a sister.

units.la: 5 Sororem quoque patris{f} ac matris{g} vxores accipere non licet.
units.tr: 5. Nor is it permitted to take as wives the sisters of a father or of a mother.

units.la: 6 Gencro[?] quoque socrum{h} suam[?]: nec socero nurum{i} vxorem accipere licet, neque vitrico priui-gnam{k}, neque privigno novercam{l}.
units.tr: 6. A son-in-law may not take his mother-in-law as wife, nor may a father-in-law take his daughter-in-law; nor may a stepfather take his stepdaughter, nor a stepson his stepmother.

units.la: 7 Fratres enim amitinos vel consobrinos in matrimonium jungi nulla ratione permittitur{m}.
units.tr: 7. Cousins, whether the children of a father's sister or of a mother's sister, are on no ground permitted to be joined in marriage.

units.la: 8 Sed nec uni viro duas{n} sorores uxores habere, nec uni mulieri duobus{o} fratribus jungi permittitur.
units.tr: 8. Nor may one man have two sisters as wives, nor may one woman be joined to two brothers.

units.la: 9 Quod si quis incestas vel nefarias, id est, quæ sunt superius comprehensæ, nuptias inierit, nec{p} uxorem habere videtur, nec filio{q}. Nam ij[?] qui ex huiusmodi conceptione nati fuerint, quamuis matrem videantur habere, patrem vero nullatenus habere censentur, & tanquam si de adulterio concepti fuerint, computantur: qui spurij{r} appellantur, hoc est, sine patre filij.
units.tr: 9. If anyone has entered into incestuous or unspeakable marriages, that is, those listed above, he is held to have neither a wife nor a son. For those born of such a union, although they seem to have a mother, are reckoned to have no father at all, and are counted as if they had been conceived in adultery; they are called bastards, that is, sons without a father.

units.la: 10 Regula juris hoc continet, ut qui legitimè concipiuntur[?], tempore conceptionis statum sumant: qui verò non{s} de legitimo matrimonio concipiuntur, statum sumant eo tempore quo nascuntur. Ac proinde legitima coniunctione conceptus, etiamsi mater eius statum mutet, id est, si ancilla fiat: ille qui legitimè conceptus est, ingenuus nascitur. Nam qui non legitimo matrimonio concipitur, si mater eius
units.tr: 10. The rule of law holds that those who are lawfully conceived take their status at the time of conception, but those not conceived in lawful marriage take their status at the time of birth. Accordingly, if one is conceived in lawful union, then even if the mother changes her status, that is, if she becomes a slave, the one lawfully conceived is born free. For one who is not conceived in lawful marriage, if his mother

units.la: {s} adde l.24.ff.de statu. ex ancilla dum praegnans est, libera facta fuerit, liber nascetur: si vero ex [illegible, ~6 letters] genua ancilla praegnans facta fuerit, seruus nascetur: quia non legitime, sed vul-go {a}conceptus est.
units.tr: {s} Add l.24 ff. de statu: if a female slave is made free while she is pregnant, the child will be born free; but if the pregnant slave was made a slave in some other way, the child will be born a slave, because he was conceived not in lawful marriage but by a casual union.
DE ADOPTIONIBVS
TIT. V.

units.la: ADOPTIO naturæ {c}similitudo est, vt aliquis filium habere possit, quem non generauerit.
units.tr: Adoption is an imitation of nature, so that a man may have a son whom he did not beget.

units.la: 2 ipsa adoptio duobus {d}modis fit. vna quæ adrogatio dicitur, alia, quæ adoptio. Adrogatio est, quando aliquis patrem non habens {e}adoptatur, & ipse se in potestatem adoptiui patris dat. Et ideo adrogatio dicitur {f}quia & ille qui adoptat interrogatur, vtrum illum quem adoptat filium habere velit: & ille qui adoptatur, interrogatur, vtrum id fieri velit. Illa vero alia adoptio {g}est, vbi quis patrem habens {h}adoptatur ab alio patre: & ita ille qui adoptatur, de certi patris potestate discedit, & in adoptiui patris incipit esse potestate.
units.tr: (2) Adoption itself takes place in two ways. One is called adrogation, the other adoption. Adrogation is when a man who has no father is adopted, and he himself gives himself into the power of the adopting father. It is called adrogation because the one who adopts is asked whether he wishes to have the man he adopts as a son, and the one who is adopted is asked whether he wishes this to happen. The other kind of adoption is when a man who has a father is adopted by another father; so the one who is adopted departs from the power of his certain father and begins to be under the power of the adopting father.

units.la: 3 Nam & fœminæ {i}adoptari possunt, vt loco fi-liorum adoptiuis patribus habeantur: fœminæ vero adoptare non possunt, quia nec filios ex se natos in potestate habent.
units.tr: (3) For women too can be adopted, so that they may be held by adopting fathers in the place of sons; but women cannot adopt, because they do not have in their power even the sons born from themselves.

units.la: 4 Spadones {k}[?]autem qui generare non possunt, adoptare possunt. Et licet filios generare non pos-sint, quos adoptauerunt filios habere possunt.
units.tr: (4) Eunuchs, however, who cannot beget, can adopt. And although they cannot beget sons, they can have as sons those whom they have adopted.

units.la: 5 Si quis vero filios habens se dederit adoptan-dum, non solùm ipse in patris adoptiui potestatem redigitur, sed {l}& filij eius, si tamen auum paternum non habuerint, in adoptiui patris transeunt potestatem, tanquam nepotes.
units.tr: (5) If anyone who has sons gives himself to be adopted, not only is he himself brought under the power of the adopting father, but his sons too, if they have not had a paternal grandfather, pass into the power of the adopting father, as grandsons.

units.la: {m}QVIBVS MODIS FI-LII EXEVNT DE PO-testate patris.
units.tr: How children go out from the power of their father.
TIT. VI.

units.la: ILII qui in potestate patris sunt, mor-tuo patre sui iuris fiunt. Sed si hic fi-lius, qui morte patris sui iuris effectus est, filios habeat, in eius post patris sui
units.tr: Children who are in the power of their father become sui iuris when the father dies. But if this son, who became sui iuris on his father's death, has children, they will be in his power after his death.

units.la: obitum erunt filij potestate. Nam fi pater moriatur, & auus {a}paternus viuat, nepos ex filio sui iuris esse non potest: quia in aui remanet potestate qui {b}auo mortuo fui iuris efficitur. Item fi moriatur pater, & relinquat filiu emancipatum,& ex eode emancipato nepotes,tunc {c}nepotes liberi & fui iuris erunt, & in patris emancipati potestatem non veniunt.
units.tr: For if the father dies while the paternal grandfather is alive, a grandson cannot become sui iuris through his own father, because the one who becomes sui iuris on the grandfather's death remains in the grandfather's power. Likewise, if the father dies and leaves an emancipated son, and grandsons by that emancipated son, then the grandsons are free and sui iuris, and do not come into the power of their emancipated father.

units.la: 2 Item de potestate patris exeunt filij, fi pater eorum in exiliu {d}missus fuerit: quia non potest filium ciuem Romanum in potestate habere homo peregrinae {e}conditionis effectus. Item filius fi viuo patre in exilium {f}missus fuerit, in potestate patris ciuis Romanus esse non potest, quia similiter peregrinae conditionis factus cognoscitur.
units.tr: 2. Children also go out of their father's power if he is sent into exile, because a man who has become a foreigner cannot have a Roman citizen son in his power. Likewise, if a son is sent into exile while his father is alive, he cannot remain a Roman citizen in his father's power, since he is recognised as having likewise become a foreigner.

units.la: 3 Item fi ab hostibus pater captus {g}fit: in potestate quandiu apud hostes fuerit, filios non habebit. Sed fi de captiuitate euaserit, iure postliminij omne, sicuti in aliis rebus, ita & in filios recipit potestatem. Si vero pater qui ab hostibus captus est, in captiuitate moriatur, ab eo tempore, quo ab hostibus captus est, filij fui iuris effecti intelliguntur.
units.tr: 3. Likewise, if the father is captured by enemies, he will not have his children in his power for as long as he is among the enemy. But if he escapes from captivity, by the right of postliminy he recovers power over his children, as over other things. If, however, the father who was captured by the enemy dies in captivity, the children are understood to have become sui iuris from the time he was captured.

units.la: 4 Item per emancipationem {h}filij fui iuris efficiuntur. Sed filius masculus tribus {i}emancipationib. de potestate patris exit, & sui iuris efficitur. Mancipatio autem, hoc est manus traditio quaedam similitudo venditionis est: quia & in {l}emancipationibus praeter illum, hoc est certum patrem, alius pater adhibetur, qui fiduciarius nominatur. Ergo
units.tr: 4. Children also become sui iuris by emancipation. A male son goes out of his father's power and becomes sui iuris by three emancipations. Now mancipation, that is, a certain handing over by hand, is a likeness of sale, since in emancipations, besides the one natural father, another father is employed, who is called the fiduciary father. Therefore

units.la: {e} Peregrinus ciuem in sua potestate non habet, vt hic: vt è contra, Ciuis in sua potestate peregrinū nō habet Vlp.10.§.3.
units.tr: A foreigner does not have a citizen in his power, as here; and conversely, a citizen does not have a foreigner in his power. Ulp. 10 §3.
See (?) there.

units.la: {g} Vlp.10 §.4:§.5. Inft.quid.mod.ius patria potest. h iit. Cod.de emancipationibus Paul.2.sent.25.§.2.3.4.5.
units.tr: {g} Ulpian, 10, §4–§5. Institutes, on how the power of the father is ended. {h} Cod., on emancipations. Paul, Sentences 2, 25, §2–§5.

units.la: {i} v.10.Vlp.10. Mancipatio, similitudo venditionis. Ter igitur mancipari, est ter vendi. Trina mancipatio, ttina [?] venditio.
units.tr: See 10. Ulp. 10. Mancipation is a likeness of sale. To be mancipated three times is therefore to be sold three times: a threefold mancipation, a threefold sale.

units.la: {l} Huiusmodi venditiones libertarum personarum figurate l.6.Cod.de emancip.liber: & imaginariae dicuntur §.6 Inflit.quib.mod. ius patria potest: vanae obseruationes d.l.6: & antiquae d.§.6. vt quae non sine iniuriis & alapis fierent Novell. 8i. Idque receptum erat ex lege XII. tabularum, si pater filium ter venundarit, filius a patre liber esto Vlp.10 §.1. quam itidem constat ex legibus Romuli mutuatam Dionysius Halicarn. 12. Olim parentibus licuit quoque filios interfecere dix: ad l.11.in f.ff.de liber:adde l.vlt.Cod.de patria potestate. Hodie veitum est, ne quis filios vendat, donet, vel pignoret l.1. l. 2. Cod.de patria potestate.
units.tr: Such sales of free persons are called figurative and imaginary: l. 6 Cod. de emancip. liber; and §6 Inst. quib. mod. ius patriae potest. They are called empty observances (d. l. 6) and ancient (d. §6), since they were not carried out without insults and slaps: Novell. 81. This was received from the Law of the Twelve Tables: if a father had sold his son three times, the son is to be free from his father. Ulp. 10 §1. It is agreed that this was likewise borrowed from the laws of Romulus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 12, says. Formerly parents were also permitted to kill their children, as said at l. 11 in fine ff. de liberis; add l. last Cod. de patria potestate. Today it has been forbidden that anyone sell, give or pledge his children: l. 1, l. 2 Cod. de patria potestate.

units.la: ih. qui filios distraxerunt. Veitum est etiam ne interficiat d. vlt. iste naturalis pater filium suum fiduciario {a}patri mancipat,hoc est manu tradit.a quo fiduciario patre naturalis pater vnum aut duos nummos,quasi in similitudinem pretij accipit ,& iterum eum acceptis nummis fiduciario patri tradit. Hoc secundo & tertio {b}fit, & sic de patris potestate exit. Quæ tamen mancipatio folebat ante Præsidem fieri , modo ante Curiam facienda est: vbi quinque testes ciues Romani in præsenti erunt, & pro illo qui Libripens {c}appellatur,id est stateram tenens,& qui Antestatus {d}appellatur,alij duo, vt septem testium numerus impleatur. Tamen cùm tertio mancipatus fuerit filius a patre naturali fiduciario patri,hoc agere debet naturalis pater;vt ei à fiduciario patre remancipetur {e}, & à naturali patre manumittatur : vt fi filius ille mortuus fuerit; ei in hereditate naturalis pater,non fiduciarius succedat. Fœminæ {f}, vel nepotes masculi ex filio,vna emàcipatione de patris vel aui exeunt potestate,& fui iuris efficiuntur . Et ij ipsi quamliber vna mancipatione de patris vel aui potestate exeant,nisi à patre remancipati fuerint,& à naturali patre manumissi, succedere eis naturalis pater non potest,nisi fiduciarius à quo manumissi sunt.nam fi remancipatum sibi naturalis pater vel auus manumiserit,ipse eis in hereditate succedit. Quod fi habeat quis filium,& ex eo nepotes, & voluerit filium emancipare, & nepotes in sua potestate retinere, in arbi rio eius est: aut fi voluerit nepotes emancipare , & filium in sua potestate retinere , & hoc ei pro iuris ordine licere manifestum est. Quod non solùm de nepotibus,sed & de pronepotibus similiter facere potest.
units.tr: Ibid., those who have sold their children. It is also forbidden to kill them: d. last. The natural father mancipates his son to a fiduciary father, that is, hands him over by hand. From this fiduciary father the natural father receives one or two coins, as if in the likeness of a price, and again, with the coins received, hands the son back to the fiduciary father. This is done a second and a third time, and so the son goes out of the father's power. Although this mancipation used to be made before the Praetor, it must now be made before the Curia, where five Roman citizen witnesses are present, and for the one called the libripens, that is, the holder of the scales, and the one called the antestatus, two others, so that the number of seven witnesses is complete. However, once the son has been mancipated a third time by the natural father to the fiduciary father, the natural father must arrange that he be remancipated to himself by the fiduciary father and manumitted by the natural father; so that if that son dies, the natural father, not the fiduciary father, succeeds to his inheritance. Women, or male grandchildren by a son, go out of the power of their father or grandfather by a single emancipation and become sui iuris. And even though these persons go out of their father's or grandfather's power by a single mancipation, unless they have been remancipated to the natural father and manumitted by him, the natural father cannot succeed to them, unless the fiduciary father from whom they were manumitted does. For if the natural father or grandfather has manumitted a child remancipated to himself, he succeeds him in the inheritance. But if someone has a son, and grandchildren by him, and wishes to emancipate the son while keeping the grandchildren in his power, it is in his discretion; or if he wishes to emancipate the grandchildren and keep the son in his power, and it is clear that this is permitted by the order of law. This he can do not only with grandchildren but likewise with great-grandchildren.
ON GUARDIANS. TITLE VII.

units.la: TVTORES aut legitimi sunt, aut testamentarij. Legitimi sunt, qui pupillo per virilem {h}lexum[?] {i}propinquitate coniunguntur: & qui proximior fuerit de agnatis,ad ipsum legitima tutela pertinet : quia {k}lx[?] is qui proximus fuerit ad tutelam, ipse proximus est ad hereditatem . Testamentarij {l}hæreditas
units.tr: Guardians are either legitimate or testamentary. Legitimate guardians are those related to the ward through the male line, and the nearest of the agnates has the legitimate guardianship, because whoever is nearest to the guardianship is also nearest to the inheritance. Testamentary guardians ... {l}
(a) The fiduciary father.

units.la: {b} ne id ita intelligas, quasi trinx illę vetiditiones fiet vno & eodem tempore:cùm singulis diebus,adhibitis testibus fieri possent, vel eodem die, vel intermisso, Paul. 2. sent. 25. §. 2. adeo vt filius ex prima,secundave mancipatione manumissus reuersus in patriam potestate, adgnascetur suus hæres Vlp. tit. 23. §. 3. j.
units.tr: (b) Do not take this to mean that those three sales happen on one and the same day. They could be made on separate days, with witnesses present, or on the same day, or with an interval between them. So a son who, after the first or second mancipation, has been manumitted and has returned to his father's power, will become a sui heres. Paul, Sent. 2.25 §2; Ulpian, tit. 23 §3, j.

ON CURATORS. TITLE VIII.

units.la: P[?]ERACTIS pupillaribus annis, quibus tutores absoluuntur, ad curatoris ratio minorum incipit pertinere. Sub curatore sunt minores aetate, maiores euersores, insani. Ij qui minores sunt, vsque ad viginti & quinque annos completos sub curatore sunt. Qui verò euersores, aut insani sunt, omni tempore vitae suae sub curatore esse iubentur: quia substantiam suam rationabiliter gubernare non possunt.
units.tr: When the years of pupillage have passed, at which guardians are released, the care of minors begins to belong to the curator. Under a curator are minors, adults who are prodigals, and the insane. Those who are minors remain under a curator until they have completed twenty-five years. Prodigals and the insane, however, are ordered to be under a curator for their whole lives, because they cannot manage their property reasonably.

units.la: AIVS superiori commentario de iure personarum aliqua disputauit. Nunc in hoc commentario de rebus iterum tractat.
units.tr: Gaius, in his earlier commentary, discussed some matters concerning the law of persons. Now, in this commentary, he treats again of things.

units.la: 2 Omnes itaque res aut nostri iuris sunt, aut di-uini, aut publici. Nostri iuris sunt, quæ in pro-prietate nostra esse noscuntur. Diuini iuris sunt ecclesiæ, id est, templa Dei, vel ea patrimonia, ac Res nostri substantiæ, quæ ad Ecclesiastica iura pertinent. Publici iuris sunt muri , fora, portæ , theatra , circus, aßena , quæ Antiqui fanda appellauerunt , dicitur in pro eo quod exinde tolli aliquid aut contingi non liceret. Sed hæc omnia in nullius bonis sunt, ideo publici iuris esse dicuntur. Sed & res hereditariæ antequam aliquis heres existat, id est, quando du-bitatur, vtrum scriptus, an legitimus heres succe-dere debeat, in nullius bonis esse videntur .
units.tr: 2. All things, therefore, are either of our law, or of divine law, or of public law. Those things are of our law which are known to be in our ownership. Those things are of divine law which belong to the Church, that is, the temples of God, or those patrimonies and property of substance which pertain to ecclesiastical law. Those things are of public law which are walls, fora, gates, theatres, circuses, and arenas, which the ancients called sacred (fanda), so named because it was not lawful to remove anything from them or to touch them. But all these things are in no one's goods, and therefore they are said to be of public law. Likewise, hereditary goods, before anyone becomes heir, that is, while it is doubtful whether the instituted heir or the heir at law ought to succeed, are seen to be in no one's goods.

units.la: 3 Præterea quædam res corporales sunt, quæ-dam incorporales .
units.tr: 3. Furthermore, some things are corporeal, and some incorporeal.

units.la: 4 Corporales sunt, quæ manu tangi possunt: ve-lut ager, mancipium, vestis, aurum, argentū, & iis si-milia. Incorporales sunt, quæ tangi non possunt: qualia sunt ea, quæ non in corpore, sed in iure cō-stiunt, sicut est hereditas , & obligationes diuersis contractibus scriptæ. Et licet hereditas, vel emptio, aut diuersi contractus res corporales in se habeant, ideoque ius tamen ipsius hereditatis vel emptionis, alio-rumque contractuum incorporale est.
units.tr: 4. Corporeal things are those that can be touched by hand, such as a field, a slave, a garment, gold, silver, and things like these. Incorporeal things are those that cannot be touched, such as those that consist not in a body but in law, like an inheritance and obligations arising from various contracts. And although an inheritance, or a purchase, or various contracts have corporeal things in themselves, nevertheless the right itself of the inheritance, or of the purchase, or of the other contracts, is incorporeal.

units.la: 5 Incorporalia etiā sunt iura prædiorū vrbano-rum vel rusticorū. Prædiorum vrbanorū iura sunt, stillicidia, fenestræ, cloacæ, altius erigedæ domus, aut nō erigendę & luminū: vt ita quis fabricet, vt vicinæ ea dicun-domui lumen nō tollat. Prædiorum verò rusticorū iura sunt, via vel iter, per quod pecus aut animalia debet ambulare, vel ad aquam duci, & aquæ ductus, quæ similiter incorporalia sunt. Hæc iura tamen rusticorum prædiorum seruitutes appellantur.
units.tr: 5. Rights over urban and rural estates are also incorporeal. The rights of urban estates are: eaves-drip, windows, drains, the right to build a house higher or not to build it higher, and rights of light, so that one builds in such a way that he does not take away the light from the neighbouring house. The rights of rural estates are: a way or path along which cattle or animals ought to walk, or be led to water, and a right of water-conduit, which are likewise incorporeal. These rights of rural estates, however, are called servitudes.

units.la: 6 Item regulariter constitutum est, vt fuperpo- sita inferioribus cedant: Vt fi quis in solo nostro fine nostro permissu domum aedificauerit ad eum cuius terra est, domus aedificata pertineat. Vel fi aliquis in agro nostro arbores, aut vineas, vel plantas quascunque posuerit, similiter superficies solo cedat . Vel fi messem in campo seminauerit , omnia haec quae in terram alienam iactantur, domino terrae adquiruntur. Quod & de chartis & pergamenis, fi in alienis scribat, licet aureis vel argenteis literis, similiter eius est scriptura, cuius charta aut pergamenum fuerit. Quod & de tabula, hoc est, fi aliquis in tabula mea pictura fecerit, obseruatur: quia statutum est, vt tabulae pictura cedat.
units.tr: 6. It is also a general rule that things superimposed yield to things below. So, if someone builds a house on our soil, with our permission, the built house belongs to the owner of the land. Or if someone plants trees, vines, or any plants in our field, likewise the surface yields to the soil. Or if he sows a crop in a field, all these things which are thrown into foreign ground are acquired by the owner of the land. The same applies to papers and parchments: if someone writes on them, even in gold or silver letters, the writing belongs to the owner of the paper or parchment. The same is observed for a panel, that is, if someone paints a picture on my panel, because it is established that the painting yields to the panel.

units.la: 7 Quod fi quis ex vuis meis vinum, aut spi- cis frumentum,aut ex oliuis oleum fecerit: eius vinum,triticum, vel oleum est,cuius spicae, aut vuae,aut oliuae fuerint. Si quis etiam ex tabulis alienis nauem aut armarium, aut quodcunque ad vsum pertinens, fecerit, simili ratione eius erunt quae facta fuerint,de cuius ligno facta probantur. Similiter etiam,fi ex lana vel lino vestimenta fecerit, eius erunt vestimenta,cuius lana vel linum fuif- fe probabitur.
units.tr: 7. But if someone makes wine from my grapes, or grain from my ears of corn, or oil from my olives, the wine, wheat, or oil belongs to the owner of the ears of corn, grapes, or olives. If someone also makes a ship, a cupboard, or anything for use from another's boards, by a similar reasoning those things that have been made belong to the one from whose wood they are proved to have been made. Likewise, if he makes garments from wool or linen, the garments will belong to the one whose wool or linen is proved to have been his.

units.la: 8 Sed in iis omnibus superius comprehensis, quicunque in terra aliena aliquid posuerit, aut aedificauerit,aut horum quae dicta sunt, aliquid fecerit, illis qui aliena praesumpserunt hoc competit, vt expensas vel impendia, quae in iis fecerint, a dominis qui rem factam vindicant, recipere possint.
units.tr: 8. But in all those cases mentioned above, whoever has placed something, or built something, on another's land, or has done any of the things that have been said, the one who presumed upon what was another's has this right: that he may recover from the owners who claim the thing made, the outlays or expenses which he has incurred on them.

units.la: 9 Acquiritur autem nobis non solum per nostros metipfos,sed & per eos qui in potestate nostra sunt, ficur filij vel ferui ; quia quicquid iis a quali- bet persona donatum,vel venditum fuerit,aut hereditas fuerint instituti, id patribus & dominis fine aliqua dubitatione conquiritur : praeter eos filios,
units.tr: 9. Moreover, we acquire not only through ourselves, but also through those who are in our power, such as sons or slaves; because whatever is given or sold to them by any person, or whatever they are instituted heirs to, is acquired for the fathers and masters without any doubt, except those sons

Nam si eis aut hereditas, aut legatum dimittatur, aut donationis aliquid conferatur, hoc proprietario domino, non usufructuario acquiritur.

Those to whom the laws have permitted a camp-peculium to be held. Those slaves, however, who are in our usufruct and in another's ownership, can acquire for the usufructuary only what they have made by their own work or hands, or have received from the wages of their labour. For if an inheritance or legacy is left to them, or some gift is conferred on them, this is acquired for the owner of the property, not for the usufructuary.
DE TESTAMENTIS
TIT. II.

units.la: Per universitatem{c} hoc est, omnia simul bona acquirimus hereditate{d}, eam ptione[?]{e}, ad optione, quia is quem adopraverimus[?], si sine patre est, cum{f} omnibus bonis suis ad nos transit.
units.tr: By universal succession, that is, we acquire all goods at once by inheritance, by adoption (or option), because the person whom we have adopted, if he is without a father, passes over to us together with all his goods.

units.la: 2 Id quo iue[?] statutum est, quod non{g} omnibus liceat facere testamentum. Sicut ij sunt, qui sui{h} iuris non sunt, & alieno iuri subiecti sunt, hoc est, filij{i} tam ex nobis nati, quam adoptiui.
units.tr: 2 It is also established that not everyone is permitted to make a will: such are those who are not their own masters (sui iuris) but are subject to another's authority, that is, sons, both those born of us and those adopted.

units.la: 3 Item testamenta facere non possunt impubere-res{k}, id est, minores quatuordecim{l} annorū, aut puellae x i r.
units.tr: 3 Likewise, those who are not of puberty, that is, minors under fourteen years of age, or girls under twelve, cannot make wills.

units.la: 4 Item & ij qui furiosi{m}, i. mente insani fuerint, non possunt facere testamenta.
units.tr: 4 Likewise, those who are mad, that is, insane in mind, cannot make wills.

units.la: 5 Sed ij qui insani sunt, si interualla{n} ipsius insaniæ habent, per interualla quibus sani sunt, possunt facere testamenta.
units.tr: 5 But those who are insane, if they have lucid intervals, may make wills during the intervals in which they are sane.
