units.la: Squi filium in potestate habet, curam agere debet, vt testamentum faciens, ma-sculum filium aut nominatim heredem instituat, aut nominatim exheredet. Nā si masculum filium in testamento præ-teriert, non valebit testamentum.
units.tr: Whoever has a son in his power ought to take care, when he makes a will, either to name the male son heir by name or to disinherit him by name. For if he passes over a male son in the will, the will will not be valid.

units.la: 2 Si vero filiam{a} praeterierit, non rumpit testamentum filia praetermissa, sed inter fratres suos, legitimo stante testamento, suam sicut alij fratres consequitur portionem. Si vero testamento extranei heredes scripti fuerint, stante testamento filia medietatem heredi catis[?] acquirit. Nam si facto testamento in quo filius masculus praetermissus est, euenerit, vt viuente adhuc patre filius qui praeteremissus est moriatur, sic quoque quamlibet filius ille mortuus fuerit, testamentum quod factum est non valebit.
units.tr: 2. If, however, he passes over a daughter{a}, the will is not broken by the omitted daughter. Instead, while the will stands, she receives her share among her brothers, as the other brothers do. If, however, outsiders have been written in the will as heirs, then while the will stands the daughter acquires half of the inheritance. For if, after a will has been made in which a male son was passed over, it happens that the omitted son dies while his father is still alive, then the will that was made will not be valid, however that son came to die.

units.la: 3 Posthumorum duo{b} genera sunt: quia Posthumi appellantur ij, qui post patris mortem de vxore nati fuerint: & illi qui post testamentum factum nascuntur. Et ideo nisi[?] is qui testamentum facit, in ipso testamento comprehenderit: Quicunque{c} si ius[?] aut filia mihi[?] natus natusve fuerit, heres mihi sit: aut certe{e} dicat, exheres sit, va[?] ere[?] eius non potest testamentum: quia sicut superius{d} jam dictum est, segitime[?] concepti pro natis habeantur. Nisi quod melior{f} conditio est posthumæ quàm natæ: quia nata, si præteriissa fuerit, non rumpit testamentum: posthuma vero, sicut masculus, testamentum rumpit.
units.tr: 3. There are two kinds of posthumous children. Those are called posthumous who are born of the wife after the father's death, and also those who are born after the will has been made. Therefore, unless the testator includes in the will itself a clause such as "whatever son or daughter is born to me, let him or her be my heir," or else expressly says that the child is to be disinherited, the will cannot be broken on that account, because, as has already been said above, lawfully conceived children are regarded as already born. There is, however, a difference in favour of the posthumous child over the daughter: a daughter, if passed over, does not break the will, but a posthumous child, like a son, does break it.

units.la: 4 Si quis post factum testamentum adoptauerit apud populum{g} illum qui sui iuris est, hoc{h} est, qui patrem non habet, aut apud Prætorem{i} illum adoptauerit qui in potestate patris est, quasi ei filius natus sit, ita eius rumpitur{k} testamentum.
units.tr: 4. If anyone, after making a will, adopts before the people someone who is sui iuris, that is, who has no father, or adopts before the praetor someone who is in the power of a father, as though he were born to him, then the will is broken.

units.la: 5 Posteriore{l} quoque testamento, quod iure factum est, id quod iure factum ante fuerat, rumpitur.
units.tr: 5. A will that was validly made earlier is also broken by a later will that is validly made.

units.la: {g} Hoc genus adoptandi mutatū est. Fit enim hodie adrogatio apud Principem l.2.ff.de his qui sunt sui, iure scilicet populi in principem translato.
units.tr: {g} This kind of adoption has been changed. For today adrogation takes place before the Prince, since the right of the people has been transferred to the Prince, l.2.ff.de his qui sunt sui.

units.la: {h} Sui iuris est, qui patre non habet.
units.tr: {h} A person is sui iuris who has no father.

units.la: {i} Est enim duplex adoptionis species l.1.in f.ff.de adoptionibus.
units.tr: {i} For there are two species of adoption, l.1.in f.ff.de adoptionibus.

units.la: {k} Adrogatione vel adoptione rumpitur testamentum §. 1. Instit.quib.mod.testam: l.8.ff.de iniusto: 23. Vlp.2.
units.tr: {k} The will is broken by adrogation or adoption, §. 1. Instit. quib. mod. testam.: l.8.ff.de iniusto: 23. Vlp. 2.

units.la: {l} §.2.Instit. quibus mod.testam: 23.Vlp.2; l.1.l.2.ff. de iniusto. Quod si facto posteriore testamento, heres scriptus, aut ante additionem hereditatis moriatur, aut viuo testatore defecerit, aut conditio possibilis, sub qua heres institutus est, impleta non fuerit: is qui testamentum fecit, intestatus mori videtur: quia testamentum quod prius fecerat, testamento posteriore rescissum est, & quod posterius factum est, iis rebus, quas diximus, infirmatur.
units.tr: {l} §.2. Instit. quibus mod. testam.: 23. Vlp. 2; l.1., l.2.ff. de iniusto. But if, after a later will is made, the heir named in it either dies before acceptance of the inheritance, or fails while the testator is alive, or the possible condition under which he was instituted heir is not fulfilled, then the one who made the will is considered to have died intestate. This is because the will he had made earlier was rescinded by the later will, and the later will is itself weakened by the things we have mentioned.

units.la: 6 Alio quoque modo testamenta iure facta in-firmantur, si aliquis post factum testamentum capite {a}minuatur: id est, aut ab hostibus capiatur, aut pro crimine in exilium deportetur. Similiter & si qui adoptatus fuerit, testamentum quod antequam adoptaretur fecerat, non valebit.
units.tr: 6. Wills validly made are also weakened in another way if someone, after making a will, suffers capitis deminutio, that is, if he is taken captive by enemies or is deported into exile for a crime. Likewise, if someone is adopted, a will he made before the adoption will not be valid.

units.la: 7 Heredes autem sui sunt, aut {b}necessarij, aut extranei. Sui {c}heredes appellantur filij aut nepotes ex filiis masculis, quos in potestate auus vel pater habet. Necessarij {d}sunt heredes servi qui cum libertate heredes instituuntur. Necessarij ideo, quia aut velint {e}aut nolint, necesse est eis heredes esse. Nam qui creditoribus tenentur obnoxij, & putant se non tantum in substantia, quantum in debitis relinquere, ipsi servos suos manumittunt, & heredes necessarios faciunt, ut quo magis heres quam dominus infamiam incurrat, cum res eius, id est, hereditas domini pro debitis venditur, & creditoribus datur. Extranei {g}sunt, qui nullo propinquitatis gratia du[?] testatori iunguntur, sed eos quicunque pro arbitrio suo scribit heredes.
units.tr: 7. Heirs are either sui heredes, necessarii, or extranei. Sui heredes are called the sons, or the grandsons through sons, whom the grandfather or father has in his power. Necessarii are slave heirs who are instituted heirs together with their freedom. They are called necessarii because, whether they wish it or not, they must be heirs. For those who are bound to creditors, and think they will leave behind not so much in substance as in debts, manumit their own slaves and make them necessary heirs, so that the infamy falls on the heir rather than on the master: the master's property, that is the inheritance, is sold for debts and handed over to the creditors. Extranei are those who are joined to the testator by no tie of kinship, but whom he writes as heirs at his own pleasure.

units.la: DE SUBSTITUTIONIBUS{h} ET DE FACIENDIS SECUNDIS TABULIS. TIT. IIII.[?]
units.tr: On Substitutions and on Making Second Wills. Title 4.

units.la: Vbstitutio est, quæ post institutionem à testatore fieri solet, id est, secundi {i}heredis appellatio. Et duæ sunt {k}, quarum vna vulgaris dicitur, alia pupillaris. tio. Substituitur etiam tertio gradu Paul.3.sent.4.§.17.22, Vlp.33. {k}duplex substitutio.
units.tr: A substitution is what is usually made after the institution by the testator, that is, the naming of a second heir. There are two kinds: one is called vulgar, the other pupillary. A substitution is also made in the third degree, Paul. 3 Sent. 4 §17, 22; Vlp. 33, a double substitution.

units.la: 2 Vulgaris {a}dicitur, Ille heres mihi esto : sive hoc filio sive extraneo, Quod si hereditatem meam adire noluerit, illum substituo ad quem hereditas mea de beat pertinere.
units.tr: A vulgar substitution is expressed thus: "Let N. be my heir, whether he is my son or a stranger. But if he is unwilling to take up my inheritance, I substitute in his place the person to whom my inheritance ought to pass."

units.la: 3 Pupillaris {b}substitutio filiis tantummodo im puberibus dari potest, quae ita fit : Ille filius meus, si {c}intra pubertatem decesserit, illum ei substituo. Sed pupillaris substitutio ita secreta {d}esse debet, ut ad notitiam substituti pervenire non possit, ne vitae pupilli aliquas substitutus insidias moliatur. Nam in extrema pagina {e}testamenti fieri debet, ut pars illa in qua substitutio pupillaris scripta est, quamdiu pupillus annos pubertatis egrediatur, obsignata permaneat, & prior pars testamenti, in qua heres scriptus est, referatur. Hoc etiam & {f}de donis fieri potest.
units.tr: A pupillary substitution can be given only to children who are under age, and it is made thus: "If my son N. dies before reaching puberty, I substitute M. in his place." But a pupillary substitution ought to be kept so secret that it cannot come to the knowledge of the substitute, lest the substitute plot some danger to the life of the ward. For it must be made on the last page of the will, so that that part of the will in which the pupillary substitution is written stays sealed for as long as the ward is under the age of puberty, and the earlier part of the will, in which the heir is named, is read out. This may also be done by means of gifts.

units.la: 4 Nam si extraneus {g}heres scriptus sit, etsi aliquem substituere non possumus {h}, ut si heres extiterit, & intra aliquod tempus mortuus fuerit, alius ei heres sit, potest tamen per fideicommissum obligari, ut alij, rogatus a testatore, hereditatem aut integram, aut pro parte restituat.
units.tr: For if a stranger has been named heir, then although we cannot substitute someone for him, as that another should be his heir if he becomes heir and dies within some period of time, he can nevertheless be bound by a trust (fideicommissum), so that, when asked by the testator, he hands over the inheritance to another, either whole or in part.
ON LEGACIES. Title V.

units.la: Legatorum genera sunt quatuor {k}, vindicationis {l}, damnationis {m}, sinendi modo {n}, & praeceptionis {o},
units.tr: There are four kinds of legacy: by vindication, by damnation, by permission (sinendi modo), and by preception.

units.la: 2 Vendicationis {p}legatum est, si testator sic {q}locutus fuerit : Illum servum tibi do, aut lego: Vel, Illam rem tibi praesume, habe, vel {r}dica. {r}Quod post mortem testatoris statim legatarius non expectato herede, sibi praesumit. Quam si praesumpserit, nec pro praesumpto legato ab herede potest calumniam sustinere, nec si aliena res fuerit, quae legata est, legatarius hoc poterit ab herede repetere. Si per vindicationem una res multis legata sit, & singuli hanc ipsam rem praesumere velint, quales singuli de re legata capiant portiones.
units.tr: 2. A legacy by vindication is made when the testator speaks thus: "I give or bequeath to you that slave," or "Let that thing be yours to take, to have, or to claim." After the testator's death the legatee takes this at once for himself, without waiting for the heir. Once he has taken it, he cannot be challenged by the heir over the legacy he has taken, and if the thing bequeathed belonged to another, the legatee cannot reclaim it from the heir. If one thing is bequeathed by vindication to several, and each wishes to take that same thing, they take it in shares.

units.la: 3 Per damnationem {s}isto ordine legatum dimittitur, ut testator in testamento scribat: Tu heres per vindicationem dictum. {s}vide 24.Vlp.3.
units.tr: 3. A legacy by damnation is left in this order: the testator writes in his will, "Let my heir give this to him," (see Ulp. 24.3).

units.la: {s} vide 24.Vlp.3. meum illi hoc da: aut, Illud illi ab herede meo dari iu- {a} In quo genere legati etiam alienæ{b} res per legatum dimitti possunt. Et necesse est heredi aut redimere eam rem, quæ iuris alieni est, & legatario tradere, aut si is cuius est res vendere noluerit, quanm tum res illa valebit, legatario in pretio compensa- re. Sed si testator rem alienam quasi suam credens, per hoc genus legatum reliquerit, legatarius hoc ab herede petere non potest: & inutile est legatum. Nam si sciens alienam esse, per legatum dederit, necesse est ab herede aut ipsam rem, aut æstimationem rei in pretio legatario dari.
units.tr: {s} See Ulp. 24.3. Or, "Let that be given to him by my heir." In this kind of legacy even another's property can be bequeathed. The heir must either buy the thing, which belongs to another, and hand it over to the legatee, or, if its owner is unwilling to sell, compensate the legatee with its value in money. But if the testator, believing the thing to be his own, leaves it to him by this kind of legacy, the legatee cannot demand it from the heir, and the legacy is void. For if he knew it was another's and gave it by legacy, the heir must give the legatee either the thing itself or its value in money.

units.la: 4 Cæterum inter damnationis legatum & vendicationis hoc interest, quòd per vendicationem res aliena relinqui non potest: per damnationem eo pacto, quo superius comprehensum est, potest. Ille etiam res, quæ in rerum natura non sunt, per damnationem legato dimitti possunt, velut si ita testator in testamento scribat: Fructus qui ex illo arvo nati fuerint: aut, id quod ex illa ancilla natum fuerit. quod in legato vendicationis fieri non potest; quia non potest hæc legatarius testatore mortuo continuo vendicare.
units.tr: 4. Otherwise, between a legacy by damnation and one by vindication there is this difference: by vindication another's thing cannot be left, but by damnation it can, in the manner stated above. Things that do not yet exist in nature can also be bequeathed by damnation, as when the testator writes in his will, "The fruits that shall be born from that field," or "that which shall be born from that maidservant." This cannot be done in a legacy by vindication, because the legatee cannot claim such things at once on the testator's death.

units.la: 5 Inter legatum vendicationis & damnationis ista similitudo est, quod legatum vendicationis, siue damnationis, si coniunctim, siue duobus aut pluribus una res in legato dimissa fuerit, in utroque legato simul ab omnib. præsumatur.
units.tr: 5. Between a legacy by vindication and one by damnation there is this similarity: if one thing is bequeathed jointly, whether to two or to several, then in either kind of legacy it is claimed by all together.

units.la: 6 Inter legatum vendicationis, & damnationis ista distantia est, ut si disiunctim, id est singulis quæcunque res per legatum damnationis relicta fuerit, singulis integra debeatur: id est, ut vnus rem ipsam accipiat, alij æstimationem rei ipsius in pretio ab hærede percipiant.
units.tr: 6. Between a legacy by vindication and one by damnation there is this difference: if the bequest is made disjunctively, that is, if whatever thing is left by damnation is left to each separately, each is owed the whole thing; that is, one receives the thing itself, while the others receive from the heir the value of that thing in money.

units.la: 7 Sinendi modo hæc legati verba sunt: Ille heres meus rem illam illam permitte præsumere & sibi habere. Nam & propriam rem testator & heredis sui, & alienam per sinendi legatū relinquere pòt.
units.tr: 7. The words of a legacy by permission are these: "Let my heir allow him to take that thing and have it for himself." For the testator can leave by a legacy of permission both his own thing, his heir's thing, and another's.

units.la: g 24. Vlp. 13. in fi. h Res pluribus legata per damnationem, non per vindicationem singulis legatariis debetur. vni res, alij æstimatio §. 8. in sin. s. eodem: adde Paul. 3. sent. 6. §. 3. in fi. i §. 2. Inst. eodem. k sunt & alia commodiora. quibus vide 24. Vlpian. §. l 24. Vlpian. 11. m hanc vocem superesse notat Cuiacius 24. ad Vlpianum. n possunt etiam iura relinqui sinendi modo Paul. 3. sent. 6. §. 11. In quo legato non quidem heres legatario rem quae relicta est iubetur tradere, sed vendicanti legatario non permittitur prohibere.
units.tr: g See Ulp. 24, at the end, ch. 13. h A thing left to several by damnation, not by vindication, is owed to each legatee separately: one thing to one, the value to another; see §8 at the end of this title. Add Paul, Sent. 3.6, §3 at the end. i §2 of the Institutes, this title. k There are also other, more convenient forms, which see in Ulp. 24, §. l Ulp. 24, 11. m Cujas, in his commentary on Ulpian book 24, notes this word superesse. n Rights can also be left by a legacy of permission; see Paul, Sent. 3.6, §11. In this kind of legacy the heir is not ordered to hand over the thing left to the legatee, but the legatee who claims it is not permitted to be prevented.

units.la: 8 Praeceptionis{a} vero legatum non nisi vni{b} ex heredibus dari potest, vt aliquid ei ex hereditate præ-cipuum relinquatur. & si aut coniunctim, id est, mutis, aut disiunctim singulis relinquatur, omnibus vnā res tantum quae nominata est debetur non vni res{c}, & alij æstimatio, sicut in legato damnationis est constitutum.
units.tr: 8. A legacy of preception can be given only to one of the heirs, so that something is left to him out of the inheritance as a preferred portion. If it is left either jointly, that is, to several, or disjunctively to each, only the one thing named is owed to all, not one thing to one and its value to another, as is laid down for a legacy by damnation.
TIT. VI.
ON THE FALCIDIAN LAW.

units.la: LEGE[?] Falcidia constitutum est: quicunque heres fuerit institutus, quartam{e} partem totius hereditatis habeat. Quod si testator hereditatem suam legatis exinanierit, hoc statutum est, vt Falcidiam sibi de imminutione legatorum heres retineat, con-stante nihilominus testamento. Hic de Pauli sententiis addendum.
units.tr: By the Falcidian law it was established that whoever is instituted heir shall have a fourth part of the whole inheritance. But if the testator has exhausted his inheritance by legacies, it has been provided that the heir may retain the Falcidian portion from the reduction of the legacies, the will nevertheless remaining valid. Here something should be added from the Sentences of Paulus.
TIT. VII.
CONCERNING TRUSTS (FIDEICOMMISSA)

units.la: POTEST[?] aliquis recto iure heredem instituere: & rogare eum, vt hereditatem suam, aut omnem, aut ex parte alij per fideicommissum reddat. Nam si heredem directo iure non instituerit, fidei-commissarius non poterit ad alium acceptam hereditatem transmittere. Sed in hac quoque re hoc ob-seruandum est, quod de Falcidia supra iam dictum est, vt heres in restituendo etiamsi omnem hereditatem alij restituere iussus sit, ita hereditatem alij restituat vt quartam{h} sibi ex ipsa hereditate retineat.
units.tr: Someone may institute an heir by direct right and ask him to hand over his inheritance, either the whole or a part, to another by way of trust. For if he has not instituted an heir by direct right, the trustee cannot pass on an inheritance received to another. In this matter, however, the same rule must be observed as was said above concerning the Falcidian portion: even if the heir is ordered to hand over the whole inheritance to another, he must hand it over in such a way that he keeps a quarter of that same inheritance for himself.
2. Individual things of any kind can be left by trust.

units.la: {i} Instit.de singulis reb.per fideicommiss. I[?], & legatum 24.Vlp.25. dimitti possunt, hoc est, fundus, aut domus, aut mancipium, aut argentum.
units.tr: See Inst. de singulis rebus per fideicommissum; and a legacy, 24 Vlp. 25. They can be left, that is, a farm, a house, a slave, or silver.

units.la: 3 Ab ips[?] fideicommissario alteri fideicommissum dimitti potest.
units.tr: 3. A trust can be left to another by the trustee himself.

units.la: 4 Et à legatario, licet legatum dimitti non possit, fideicommissum potest.
units.tr: 4. And although a legacy cannot be passed on by the legatee, a trust can.

units.la: 5 Et non solum propriæ res à testatore per fideicommissum dimitti possunt, sed etiam ipsius heredis, aut legatarij, aut cuiuslibet extranei.
units.tr: 5. Not only the testator's own property can be left by trust, but also that of the heir himself, of the legatee, or of any outsider.

units.la: 6 Ne legatarius cui per testamentum parum dimissum est, plus alij per fideicommissum quam id quod consequitur reddere iubeatur.
units.tr: 6. A legatee who has been left too little by the will cannot be ordered to hand over to another, by trust, more than what he receives.

units.la: 7 Cum autem aliena res per fideicommissum relinquitur, necesse est heredi, vel legatario, rem illam quæ per fideicommissum est relicta, aut redimere, & fideicommissario dare, aut pretium eiusdem rei, quantum æstimata fuerit, fideicommissario numerare, sicut in damnationis legato fieri diximus.
units.tr: 7. When another's property is left by trust, the heir or legatee must either buy that thing which has been left by trust and give it to the trustee, or pay the trustee the value at which it was assessed, just as we said is done with a legacy of condemnation.

units.la: 8 Libertas, etiam seruis per fideicommissum dari possunt, ut heres vel legatarius ea mancipia manumittant, quæ testator ab iis ut manumitterent, sp[?] rauit. Nec interest, utrum hoc testator de suis seruis, an de ipsius heredis vel legatarij, aut de alienis fieri iubeat. Quod si de alienis fecerit, similiter cogitur heres emere ipsum seruum & manumittere. Sed si illum dominus suus noluerit vendere, perit per fideicommissum data libertas: quia in hac re heres æstimationem in pretio dare non cogitur. Sed cum per fideicommissum libertas datur, is qui manumissus fuerit, non testatoris, sed heredis libertus est.
units.tr: 8. Freedom can also be given to slaves by trust, so that the heir or legatee manumits those slaves whom the testator has asked them to manumit. It makes no difference whether the testator orders this concerning his own slaves, or those of the heir or legatee, or those of others. If he orders it concerning others' slaves, the heir is likewise compelled to buy the slave himself and manumit him. But if the owner is unwilling to sell him, the freedom given by trust is lost, because in this case the heir is not compelled to pay an estimated price. But when freedom is given by trust, the one manumitted becomes the freedman not of the testator but of the heir.

units.la: 9 Præterea inter fideicommissa & legata sunt quædam distantiæ. Fideicommissum ad eum, cui aliquid commissum est, herede mortuo poterit pervenire, si talis fuerit conditio testamenti: nam legatum ita relinqui non potest. Item legatum per codicillum relictum, nisi codicilli testamento fuerint confirmati: fideicommissum vero etiam testamento codicilli non fuerint confirmati, nihilominus debetur. Item per legatarium legata alienâ legauerimus §. 8. ib.
units.tr: 9. Moreover, there are certain differences between trusts and legacies. A trust, if something has been entrusted to a person, can pass to him even after the heir has died, provided the terms of the will are such; but a legacy cannot be left in that way. Likewise, a legacy left by codicil does not take effect unless the codicils have been confirmed by the will; but a trust is owed even if the codicils have not been confirmed by the will. Likewise, if we have bequeathed another's property by legacy, see §8 there.

units.la: e dixi plenissime ad leg. 1. §. 17. in f. ff. ad Trebel. f Paul. 4. sent. 1. §. 7. g tit. 5. §. 4. 5. eod.
units.tr: e I have explained this very fully at l. 1 §17 in fin. ff. ad Trebell. f Paul. 4 sent. 1 §7. g tit. 5 §4, 5 eod.

units.tr: h 25 Vlp. 18 §2 Inst. de singulis rebus per fideicommissum; l. 12 §1 ff. de fideicommissariis hereditatibus. i Nowadays the differences between trust and legacy have been made equal, so that legacies are treated like trusts; see l. 1 ff. de legatis 1.

units.la: l Prima differentia. l Secunda differentia 25. Vlp. §. 8. in sin. m d. §. 8. Paul. 4. sent. 1. §. 10. n Tertia differentia. gatum alteri relinqui non potest, sed fideicommissum potest. Item per legatum seruo alieno directa libertas dari non potest, per fideicommissum potest. Item per codicillos nemo heres institui potest, quanuis testamento confirmati sint: sed is qui testamento heres fuerit institutus, potest per codicillum rogari, vt hereditatem, quæ ei data est, alij totam vel pro parte restituat. quod validum est, etiamsi codicilli testamento non fuerint confirmati. Item quanuis non possimus post mortem eius quem heredem instituimus, alium ei substituere, tamen per fideicommissum rogare eum possumus, vt cum moriatur, alij eam hereditatem vel totam, vel pro parte restituat. Et quia, sicut superius distum est, etiâ post mortem heredis fideicommissum ei cui relictum est, dari potest: quod hoc ordine fit, vt testator scribat: Illum heredem instituo, & volo, vt quum mortuus fuerit, ad illum hereditas mea pertineat. Præterea & in hoc alia fideicommissorum & legatorum conditio est, quia fideicommissa, si tardius quàm seriptum est soluta fuerint, vsuræ & fructus debentur: legatorum vero vsuræ non debentur, sed ex mora solutionis, si per damnationem relicta fuerint, duplicantur.
units.tr: l First difference. l Second difference: 25 Vlp. §8 at the end. m Ibid. §8; Paul. 4 sent. 1 §10. n Third difference: a legacy cannot be left to another, but a trust can. Likewise, by legacy a direct freedom cannot be given to another's slave, but by trust it can. Likewise, by codicils no one can be instituted heir, even if the codicils have been confirmed by the will; but one who has been instituted heir by the will can be asked by codicil to hand over the inheritance given to him, whole or in part, to another, and this is valid even if the codicils were not confirmed by the will. Likewise, although after the death of the one whom we have instituted heir we cannot substitute another for him, we can nevertheless ask him by trust that, when he dies, he hand the inheritance over to another, whole or in part. And because, as said above, a trust can be given to the one to whom it was left even after the death of the heir, this is done in this way: the testator writes, I institute him heir, and I wish that, when he has died, my inheritance should pass to him. Moreover, in this respect too there is another difference between trusts and legacies: trusts, if paid later than written, carry interest and fruits; but interest is not owed on legacies, though if they were left by condemnation they are doubled because of delay in payment.
On the Inheritances of Those Who Die Intestate. Title 8.

units.la: INTESTATORVM hereditates primùm ad suos heredes pertinent. Suiì autem heredes appellantur, filius filia, nepos neptis, pronepos proneptis ex ne-pote: quia omnes per virilem sexum de-scendentes, sui vocantur. Naturales sunt hæ personæ, ac adoptiuæ. Adoptiuorum enim comparatione legitimi naturales appellantur. Sed ita nepos vel neptis ex filio auo sui heredes sunt, si pater eorum de potestate patris, aut morte aut emancipatione di-scesserit: nam si eo tempore, quo aliquis moritur, filius in potestate habeat, & ex eo nepotes, illi viuo patre suo, & in potestate constituto, sui heredes auo esse non possunt .
units.tr: Inheritances of those who die intestate pass first to their own heirs (sui heredes). These are called own heirs: son, daughter, grandson, granddaughter, and great-grandson or great-granddaughter through a grandson, because all who descend through the male line are called sui. These persons are natural heirs, and also adoptive ones; compared with adoptive heirs, they are called natural legitimate heirs. But a grandson or granddaughter through a son is an own heir to the grandfather only if their father has left his father's power by death or emancipation. For if at the time of someone's death the son is still in power and has children by him, those children cannot be own heirs to the grandfather while their father is alive and under power.

units.la: ꝛ Similiter Posthumi , qui si viuo patre nati suis-sent, sunt, in potestate eius futuri erant, sui heredes sunt.
units.tr: Likewise posthumous children, who, had they been born while their father was alive, would have been in his power, are own heirs.

units.la: 3 Si quando aliquis moritur, & reliquerit filium, aut filiam, & ex alio filio mortuo nepotes, neptesve: filij vel nepotes ex filio defuncto, patri vel avo hac ratione succedunt, ut filius vel filia suas partes, & ne potes ex filio portionem, quàm pater eorum erat habiturus, accipiant. quia regulariter constitutum est, ut inter suos proximior longiore gradu positos non excludat: & non in capita, sed in stirpem dividatur hereditas. Itè si quis moriens filium non relinquat, sed ex duobus masculis filiis dimittat nepotes, hoc est, ex uno filio unum, vel duos nepotes, ex altero tres aut quatuor: similiter, sicut superius dictum est, in stirpe, non in capita hereditas dividatur, hoc modo ut illi duo nepotes ex uno filio medietatem percipiant, & illi quatuor ex alio filio aliam medietatem: hoc est, ut tales accipiant portiones, quales patres eorum si vixissent, habituri erant.
units.tr: 3. If someone dies leaving a son or daughter, and grandchildren or granddaughters from a son who has died, the children or grandchildren of the deceased son succeed to the father or grandfather in such a way that the son or daughter takes their own share, and the grandchildren through the son take the portion their father would have had. For it is a settled rule that the nearer heir, standing in a closer degree, does not exclude the more distant ones, and that the inheritance is divided by stirpes, not per capita. Likewise, if someone dies leaving no son but grandchildren from two male sons, one or two from one son and three or four from the other, then, as was said above, the inheritance is divided by stirpes, not per capita: the two grandchildren from one son take one half, and the four from the other take the other half. That is, they receive such portions as their fathers would have had, had they been alive.

units.la: 4 Si defuerint heredes sui, tunc hereditas defuncti pertinet ad agnatos. Agnati enim sunt per virilem sexum defuncto propinquitate coniuncti, id est, consanguinei fratres, hoc est, de vno patre nati. Nec disputari potest, si de diversis matribus nascantur qui vno patre geniti sunt. Item patruus , id est, frater patris, fratris sui filio agnatus est. Ipso modo sunt fratres patrueles , hoc est, qui de singulis germanis nati sunt. Hoc ordine agnoscitur qui sin agnati, sicut suprà diximus, per virilem sexum propinquitate coniuncti.
units.tr: 4. If there are no own heirs, the estate of the deceased passes to the agnates. Agnates are those joined to the deceased by kinship through the male line, that is, brothers related by blood, born of one father. Nor does it matter if those born of one father have different mothers. Likewise a paternal uncle (patruus), that is, the father's brother, is an agnate to his brother's son. In the same way, cousins on the father's side (patrueles fratres) are those born of two full brothers. In this order the agnates are recognised, as we said above: those joined by kinship through the male sex.

units.la: 5 Non tamen omnib. simul agnatis lex hereditatem propinqui intestati dat, sed iis qui defuncto mortis suæ tempore proximiores inveniuntur.
units.tr: 5. Yet the law does not give the inheritance of a relative who died intestate to all the agnates together, but to those who are found nearest at the moment of the deceased's death.

units.la: 6 In fœminis vero alia conditio est: quia inter fœminas sola tantùm soror consanguinea habetur agnata, ut germano suo defuncto, ab intestato ei agnata tionis iure succedat. Reliquæ fœminæ, hoc est, amitæ id est, patris soror, vel fratris filia, nec in capiendis hereditatibus propinquorum legitimæ sunt, nec masculis propinquis agnationis iure succeduntur. Ipsarum vero hereditates ad masculos propinquos agnationis conditione perveniunt.
units.tr: 6. With women the situation is different. Among women only a full sister is counted as an agnate, so that on the death of her brother she succeeds him intestate by right of agnation. The other women, that is, aunts (amitae, the father's sisters) and a brother's daughter, are neither lawful heirs in taking the inheritances of their relatives, nor do they succeed male relatives by right of agnation. But their own inheritances pass to male agnate relatives by the condition of agnation.

units.la: 7 Regulariter constitutum est, ut inter agnatos proximior posteriorem excludat, & inter eos nō in fe.
units.tr: 7. As a general rule, among agnates the nearer excludes the more remote, and among those of the same degree... (the text here is corrupt; the sense is that the brother is preferred to the more remote kin).

units.la: g Patruus, pa 26.Vlp.6:Paul. l.9; §.1.ff.ad. stirpem,sed in capita ab intestato diuidatur heredi-tas.Nam inter suos,sicut superiùs dixi-mus,alia ratio est,vt proximior posteriorem non {a}excludat,& semper hereditas in {b}stirpem non in capita diuiditur. Nam si quis moriens dimittat germanum,& ex altero filio germano[?] filios: germanus frater quia gradu proximior est, solus succedit, fratris filij non {†}sucedunt.Item si moriatur quis,& de duob. germanis fratrib. dimittat filios duntaxat masculos, ex vno fratre dimiserit duos,ex alio quatuor,similiter masculi omnes quidem fratrum filij patruo suo ab intestato succedunt,sed non in stirpes,sed {c}in capita: ita vt illi duo ex vna parte duas accipiant portiones,& illi quatuor ex alio quatuor portiones. Nam si sorores habuerint, in patrui hereditatem non veniunt,sicut nec sororis filij in auunculi hereditate sucedunt.
units.tr: g Paternal uncle (patruus)... 26. Ulpian 6; Paul, l. 9, §.1, ff. ad... on the stirps, but the inheritance is divided per capita on intestacy. For among own heirs, as I said above, the rule is different: the nearer does not exclude the more remote, and the inheritance is always divided by stirpes, not per capita. For if someone dies leaving a full brother and the sons of another full brother, the brother, being nearer in degree, succeeds alone; the brother's sons do not succeed. Likewise, if someone dies leaving only male sons of two full brothers, two from one brother and four from the other, all the sons of the brothers succeed their uncle intestate, but not by stirpes; they succeed per capita, so that the two from one side take two shares and the four from the other take four shares. For if there are sisters, they do not come into the inheritance of the paternal uncle, just as a sister's sons do not succeed in the inheritance of a maternal uncle.

units.la: § Nam & hoc regulare est, vt cognati tunc inte-statorum propinquorum hereditates capiant, quan-do {d}aut sui,aut agnati defuerint.
units.tr: It is also a general rule that cognates take the inheritances of relatives who died intestate when there are no own heirs or no agnates.
ON OBLIGATIONS. TIT. IX.

units.la: OBLIGATIO in duas species diuidi-tur. Nam omnes obligationes aut ex{f} contractu nascuntur,aut ex culpa. Quæ ex contractu nascuntur, quatuor{g} genere sunt, quæ singula hoc ordine distin-guuntur. Aut enim re{h} contrahitur obligatio, aut verbis{i},aut litteris{k},aut consensu{l}.
units.tr: An obligation is divided into two kinds. For all obligations arise either from contract or from fault. Those that arise from contract are of four kinds, which are distinguished one by one in this order. An obligation is contracted either by a thing (re), by words (verbis), by writing (litteris), or by consent (consensu).

units.la: 2 Re{m} contrahitur, quoties aliqua cuicunque mutuo{n} dantur, quæ in his rebus contingunt, quæ pondere{o},numero,mensura continentur: hoc est,si pecunia numeretur, vel frumentum detur, vinum, aut oleum,aut æs,ferrum,argentum,vel aurum.Quæ omnia numerando,aut pensando, aut metiendo , ad hoc damus vt eorum fiant qui ea accipiunt, & ad nos statuto tempore non ipsæ res,sed aliæ eius{p} na-
units.tr: 2 An obligation is contracted by a thing (re) whenever certain goods are lent to someone, goods that consist of weight, number or measure: that is, when money is counted out, or grain, wine or oil, or bronze, iron, silver or gold is handed over. We give all these things by counting, weighing or measuring, so that they become the property of those who receive them, and at an agreed time they are returned to us, not the very same things, but others of the same kind, in the same weight, number or measure as those given.
{o} l.2.§.1.ff.de verb.cred.

units.la: {p} l.2.§.1.ff.de verb.cred. turæ, quales datæ sunt, atque ipsius pòderis, numeri, vel mensuræ reddantur. Propter quod Mutuum appellatum est, quasi à me tibi itpdatū sit, vt ex meo tuum fieret.
units.tr: {p} l.2.§.1.ff.de verb.cred. of the same nature as those given, and of the same weight, number or measure. For this reason it was called a loan (mutuum), as if it had been given by me to you, so that what was mine might become yours.

units.la: 3 Verbis contrahitur obligatio ex interrogatione dantis, & respondentis accipientis. ita vt si ille qui dat, interroget, Hoc mihi dabis? [?] qui accipiet, respondeat, Dabo. Aut in obligatione debitoris, si aliquis fideiussor accedat, ille qui personam fideiussori tradit, interroget: Ipsum fide tua esse iubes? &'ille respondeat: Fide mea esse iubeo. hac conditione non solum ille qui debitor est, sed & is qui fideiussor existit, obligantur. Et non solum fideiussor ipse dum viuit, sed & heredes ipsius, si ille defecerit, tenentur obnoxij: Creditor autem, qui pecuniâ dedit, in potestate habet {†} ad reddendâ pecuniam quem velit tenere, vtrum ipsum debitorem, an fideiussorem. Sed si debitorem tenere elegerit, fideiussorem absoluit. Si vero fideiussorem tenuerit debitorem absoluit, quia vno electo, quem idoneum creditor iudicat, alterum liberat.
units.tr: 3. An obligation is contracted by words through the question of the one who gives and the answer of the one who receives: so that if the giver asks, "Will you give me this?" and the receiver answers, "I will give." Or in the obligation of a debtor, if some surety comes forward, the one who hands over the person to the surety asks, "Do you order that he be bound by your faith?" and the surety answers, "I order that he be bound by my faith." On this condition, not only the debtor but also the one who becomes surety is bound. And not only the surety himself, while he lives, but also his heirs, if he has died, are held liable. The creditor who has lent the money has it in his power, in demanding repayment, to hold whichever he wishes, either the debtor himself or the surety. But if he chooses to hold the debtor, he releases the surety. If on the other hand he holds the surety, he releases the debtor, because by choosing one, whom the creditor judges sufficient, he frees the other.

units.la: 4 Sunt & aliæ obligationes, quæ nulla præcedente interrogatione contrahi possunt, id est, vt si mulier siue sponso vxor futura siue iam marito dotè dicat: {f}Quod tam de mobilibus rebus, quàm de fundis fieri potest. Et non solum in hac obligatione ipsa mulier obligabitur, sed & pater eius, & debitor ipsius mulieris, si pecuniâ, quam ille debebat sponso creditricis, ipse debitor in dotem dxerit. Hæ tantum tres {g} personæ, nulla interrogatione præcedente possunt dictione dotis legitimè obligari. Aliæ vero personæ, si pro muliere dotem marito promiserint, communi iure obligari debent: id est, vt & interrogatæ respondeant, & stipulatæ promittant.
units.tr: 4. There are also other obligations which can be contracted without any preceding question: for example, when a woman says to her betrothed, who is to become her husband, or to a man who is already her husband, that she gives a dowry. This can be done as much with movable goods as with lands. And not only the woman herself will be bound by this obligation, but also her father, and her debtor, if the debtor gives as dowry the money which he owed to the creditress's fiancé. These three persons alone can be legitimately bound by the mere utterance of a dowry, with no preceding question. Other persons, however, if they have promised a dowry to a husband on behalf of a woman, must be bound by the common law: that is, they must both answer the question and promise in response to the stipulation.

units.la: 5 Item & alio casu, vno loquente, & sine interrogatione alio promittente, contrahitur obligatio. i. si libertus patrono aut donum, aut munus, aut operas se daturum esse iuraverit. Exponendum hîc quid sit donum, aut munus, vel operæ, in qua re supradicti liberti non tam verborum solemnitate, quàm iurisiurandi religione tenentur. Sed nulla altera persona hoc ordine obligari potest.
units.tr: 5. Likewise, in another case also, an obligation is contracted when one party speaks and the other promises without any question. That is, if a freedman has sworn to his patron that he will give a gift, a service or labour. What is meant here by a gift, a service or labour must be explained; in such matters the aforesaid freedmen are bound not so much by the solemnity of words as by the sanctity of an oath. But no other person can be bound in this way.

units.la: 6 Præterea inutilis est promissio, etiamsi stipulatione interveniente facta sit, si id aliquis daturum se promiserit, quod sui iuris non est: hoc est, si aut {h} ingenuum hominem quasi {i} seruum se daturum promittat. Aut si mortuum{4} aliquis, quem viuum credebat, promiserit. Aut locum sacrum,{b} aut sanctum,aut religiosum daturum se quicunque promiserit.
units.tr: 6. Furthermore, a promise is void, even if it is made with a stipulation, if someone promises to give what is not within his own right: that is, if he promises to give a free man as if he were a slave. Or if someone promises a dead man whom he believed to be alive. Or whoever promises to give a sacred, holy or religious place.

units.la: 7 Praeterea inutilis est promissio, si aliquis rem sub tali conditione promittat,quæ impleri pro[?] rei difficultate non possit.
units.tr: 7. Furthermore, a promise is void if someone promises a thing under such a condition that, because of the difficulty of the matter, it cannot be fulfilled.

units.la: 8 Praeterea inutilis est † interrogatio & promissio, si ita aliquis interroget debitorem, Post mortem meam vel tuam illud dari spondes? Quod propterea inutile visum est,quia à persona heredis obligatio incipere nō potest.Et ideo nec heredi creditoris sub hac sponsione obligatur debitor, nec debitoris heres creditori tenetur obnoxius.
units.tr: 8. Furthermore, the question and promise are void if someone asks the debtor, "Do you promise to give that after my death or yours?" Post mortem meam vel tuam illud dari spondes? This has been judged void for the reason that the obligation cannot begin from the person of an heir. And so the debtor is not bound by this promise to the creditor's heir, nor is the debtor's heir liable to the creditor.

units.la: 9 Item inutilis est † obligatio si dicat creditor, Pridie quàm moriar,dare spondes? Vel interroget debitorem, Pridie quàm moriaris? Similiter & hæc stipulatio inutilis iudicatur, quia non potest sciri, quando sit pridie quàm aliquis moriatur, nisi post quàm mortuus fuerit.
units.tr: 9. Likewise an obligation is void if the creditor says, "Do you promise to give on the day before I die?" or asks the debtor, "On the day before you die?" Pridie quàm moriar, dare spondes? Similarly this stipulation is also judged void, because it cannot be known when the day before someone dies is, except after he has died.

units.la: 10 Item si d pure interroget creditor, & debitor sub conditione promittat.
units.tr: 10. Likewise, if the creditor asks unconditionally and the debtor promises under a condition.

units.la: 11 Vel si creditor decem solidos debitorem interroget, & debitor quinque e promittat: hoc ordine integrum debitum vacillare cognoscitur.
units.tr: 11. Or if the creditor asks for ten shillings from the debtor and the debtor promises five: in this way the whole debt is recognised as uncertain.

units.la: 12 Si quis nobis pecuniam debeat, possumus debitorem nostrum compellere, vt pecuniam quā nobis rediturus erat,alteri f se caveat redditurum. Neque potest ei, cui pro nostro debito cauet, de cauto & non numerato, sicut fieri solet, aliquid disputatio nis afferre, cùm[?] id quod à nobis accepit, alteri cauerit reddiurum.
units.tr: 12. If someone owes us money, we can compel our debtor to give security to another person that he will repay the money which he was about to return to us. Nor can any dispute be raised, as is customary, by the one to whom he gives security for our debt, concerning the security given but not counted out, since he has given security to another that he will repay what he received from us.

units.la: 13 Literis g obligatio fit.aut à re in personā, aut à persona in personam.A re in personam, velut si id quod ex emptione aut conductione aut societate debes, alij reddas. A persona in personam, velut si id quod mihi alter debet,alteri personæ delegem[?], vt reddere debeat.
units.tr: 13. An obligation is made by writing (litteris), either from a thing to a person or from a person to a person. From a thing to a person, as when you pay to another what you owe from a purchase, a hiring or a partnership. From a person to a person, as when I transfer to another person what someone else owes me, so that he is obliged to pay it.

units.la: 14 Consensu h fiunt obligationes,ex emptionib. & venditionibus,locationibus,conductionibus,societatibus,& mandatis.quia in eiusmodi rebus consensus magis quàm scriptura i aut solemnitas quæritur. In quibus rebus etiam inter k absentes obligatio contrahi potest, quod in aliis rebus fieri non potest.
units.tr: 14. Obligations arise by consent in the case of purchases and sales, lettings, hirings, partnerships and commissions, because in such matters consent is sought rather than writing or formality. In these matters an obligation can also be contracted between absent parties, which cannot be done in other matters.

units.la: 15 Emptio igitur & venditio contrahitur,cùm de pretio inter emptorem & venditorem fuerit definitum, etiamsi pretium non fuerit numeratum, & nec pars pretij aut arrha data fuerit.
units.tr: 15. A purchase and sale is therefore contracted when the price has been agreed between buyer and seller, even if the price has not been counted out, and no part of the price or earnest money has been given.

units.la: 16 Locatio & conductio simili{a} ratione consti- stunt, vt consensu, etiam verbo definitio inter consentientes firma permaneat.
units.tr: 16. Letting and hiring are established on a similar principle, so that the agreement, even if made by word, remains firm between the consenting parties.

units.la: 17 Societatem{b} inire possumus, aut omnium bonorum aut vnius alicuius negotiationis. Et poterit i- ta{c} iniri societas, si tamen hoc inter socios conue- nit, vt vnus pecuniā det, alter operam suā pro pecunia donat. Et huius rei definitio etiā verbo inita va-let, ita vt quicquid societatis tempore quolibet modo fuerit adquisitum, sociis commune sit.
units.tr: 17. We may enter into a partnership either of all goods or of some single business. A partnership can be entered into in this way, provided that it has been agreed among the partners that one provides money and the other gives his labour in return for the money. And the agreement on this matter is valid even when made by word, so that whatever is acquired in any way during the partnership is common to the partners.

units.la: 18 Permanet{d} autem inita societas, quandiu in ipso consensu socij perseuerant: quia sicut consensu contrahitur, etiam dissensu soluitur. Dissoluitur ergo societas aut morte{e} vnius socij, aut contraria voluntate, aut capitis deminutione, id est si vnus ex sociis, sicut frequenter supra diximus, capite fuerit demi- nutus.
units.tr: 18. A partnership entered into remains in force for as long as the partners persist in the same consent, because just as it is contracted by consent, so it is dissolved by dissent. A partnership is therefore dissolved either by the death of one partner, or by a contrary will, or by loss of civil status (capitis deminutio), that is, if one of the partners has suffered a loss of status, as we have often said above.

units.la: 19 Similiter & mandati{f} verbo poterit. Et cum verbis mandatum fuerit, obligatio contrahitur. Possumus enim aut non nostra negocia, aut alterna cuicunque agenda mandare, dummodo honestum{g} aliquid agi mandemus. Nam si contra{h} mores bonos aliquid mandare voluerimus: hoc est, si cuicunque mandemus, vt alicui furtum faciat, aut homicidium{i} aut adulterium admittat, in his rebus mandati obligatio non contrahitur.
units.tr: 19. Likewise a commission can also be given by word. And when a commission has been given by word, an obligation is contracted. For we may commission someone either to conduct our own affairs or another's, provided that we commission something honest to be done. For if we wish to commission anything contrary to good morals, that is, if we commission someone to steal from another, or to commit murder or adultery, no obligation under the commission is contracted in such matters.

units.la: 20 Soluitur autem mandatum aut morte{k} eius, cui mandatum est, aut contraria{l} illius voluntate qui mandauit.
units.tr: 20. A commission is ended either by the death of the one to whom it was given, or by the contrary will of the one who gave it.

units.la: 21 Sed is cui mandatur, mandati formam egredi{m} non potest. Aut si egressus fuerit, & mandatori tenca{n} tur obnoxius, & quod extra mandatum egit, nō praejudicet mandatori.
units.tr: 21. But the one to whom a commission is given cannot go beyond the form of the commission. Or if he does go beyond it, he is bound to the one who commissioned him, and what he has done outside the commission does not prejudice the one who gave it.

units.la: QVIBVS MODIS OBLIGATIONIS TOLLATVR. TIT. X.
units.tr: BY WHAT MODES OBLIGATION IS REMOVED. TIT. X.

units.la: TOLLITVR[?] obligatio solutione{o}debiti. Praeterea aliquoties tollitur obligatio, etiam si aliud quàm cautum fuerat à debitore creditori reddatur. Nam si quicunque pro{p} pecunia quam creditori cauir.acquiescente {4}creditore,aurum,aut argentum, aut mancipia, vel alias quaslibet species, habita aestimatione consentiente creditore dederit, obligatio euidenter tollitur.
units.tr: Obligation is removed by payment of a debt. Moreover, an obligation is sometimes removed even when the debtor gives the creditor something other than what was agreed. For if anyone, in place of the money he promised the creditor, gives gold, silver, slaves, or any other goods, with a valuation agreed on and the creditor consenting and accepting them, the obligation is clearly removed.

units.la: 2 Quia de obligationibus quae ex contractu nascuntur,diximus, superest vt de his obligationibus quae ex delicto nascuntur, simpliciter disputemus. Ex{b} delicto nascuntur obligationes, si aliquis furtum{c} fecerit,vel bona aliena rapuerit{d}, vel damnum{e} alteri dederit,aut iniuriam{f} fecerit. Quarum omnium rerum vno genere ex delicto nascitur obligatio.
units.tr: 2 Since we have spoken of obligations that arise from contract, it remains that we discuss plainly those obligations that arise from delict. Obligations arise from delict when someone commits theft, or seizes another's goods, or causes loss to another, or does an injury. All of these give rise to an obligation from delict under one kind.

units.la: 3 Furtorum autem sunt genera quatuor{g}: manifesti,nec manifesti,concepti,& oblati.Manifestu{h} furtum dicitur,si quando fur cuiusc unque rem tollit, in ipso furto deprehenditur. Nec{i} manifestum furtum appellatur,quod qualibet dum fieret,inuenitum non est, tamen furtum factum fuisse probatur. Conceptum{k} furtum dicitur, cum apud aliquem alterum res furtiua inueniatur. Oblatum{l} furtum dicitur,cum res furtiua alicui ita a fure datur, vt apud ipsum furem inueniri non possit.
units.tr: 3 There are four kinds of theft: manifest, non-manifest, conceived, and offered. Theft is called manifest when the thief is caught in the act of stealing whatever thing it is. Theft is called non-manifest when it was not discovered while it was being committed, yet it is proved that the theft took place. Theft is called conceived when the stolen goods are found with some other person. Theft is called offered when the stolen goods are given by the thief to someone in such a way that they cannot be found with the thief himself.

units.la: 4 Praeterea, qui rem alienam inuito{m} aut sciente domino contingit,vel tollere,aut de loco moue nere praesumit,furtum facit.
units.tr: 4 Moreover, one who presumes to touch or to move from its place another's property, against the will or without the knowledge of the owner, commits theft.

units.la: 5 Et si quis rem vtendam{n} acceperit, aut commendatam{o} apud se habuerit,& aliter ea vsus fuerit quam acceperit,furti actione tenetur.
units.tr: 5 And if anyone has received a thing to be used, or has kept a thing entrusted to him, and has used it otherwise than he received it, he is liable to the action for theft.

units.la: 6 Praeterea,si quis iumentum{p} alterius ad hoc accepit,vt eum quinque millibus duceret, si id deposuit cem millibus, aut longius quam ab illo qui dedit fuerit constitutum duxerit,furti reus erit.
units.tr: 6 Furthermore, if anyone has received another's beast of burden on condition that he would carry it five miles, and if he has carried it ten miles, or further than was fixed by the one who gave it, he will be guilty of theft.

units.la: 7 Et multa praeterea quorumcunque similia sunt-secundum quae & ille furti tenetur, qui vt fer ret opem{q}, aut consilium,aut studium commodarit: velut si quis pecuniam, quam in manu aliquis tenebat,excusserit{r}, vt alij eam rapere possent.
units.tr: 7 And there are many other similar cases in which that person too is liable for theft who lends help, advice, or zeal so that the thing may be taken, as when someone shakes out money which another held in his hand so that others might snatch it away.
